papers.abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/
authors: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Jiayuan Yan, Bohan Fang, Wisdom Oluchi Ikezogwo, Ainaz Eftekhar, Max Argus, Jason Ren, Jiafei Duan, Ranjay Krishna

papers.abstract: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.
authors: Zehan Zheng, Yanyuan Chen, Deming Li, Yutao Tang, Jianwen Xie, Alan Yuille, Jieneng Chen, Cheng Peng
bullets: Evaluates VLMs in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting.

Finds outdoor environments are substantially more demanding than indoor settings, with poor performance from existing models.
Highlights multimodal interaction and long-term spatial reasoning as key directions for embodied intelligence.

papers.abstract: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.
authors: Feixiang Ruan, Guodong Lv, Kewei Zhang, Wenbo Huang, Yintianrun Zhang, Qiang Wang, Ruiyang Si, Shunyu Yang, Shulong Jiang, Weicheng Duan, Rui Ni, Jianxin Bi, Lekai Wang, Yuze Fan, Haobo Li, Zeliang Fu, Jiankun Zhang, Duomin Wang, Enze Xie, Daquan Zhou

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of PyRUA-Dex. All learning takes place in simulation. Stage 1 (exploration): eight agents (one is drawn) explore the task, each on a training layout of its own with state resets, and share a memory; their programs are evaluated without the agents and distilled into a task library and one program. Stage 2 (refinement): one agent finds the program’s bottleneck stage by a stage-wise failure analysis, refines it on randomized layouts and selects the version with the best held-out record. The resulting program runs frozen, without a language model. For the real world, the simulation is built from the real scene (real-to-sim), the frozen program is transferred (sim-to-real), and real-world feedback updates the simulation for the next round of refinement.

papers.abstract: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.
authors: Yueh-Cheng Liu, Snehal Jauhri, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner, Angela Dai
bullets: Covers household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces with detailed geometry, physically based materials, and curated layouts.
Provides object- and part-level semantic annotations for joint visual and embodied learning.
Supports inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation, improving state-of-the-art methods over alternative synthetic datasets.
Introduces a mobile manipulation benchmark for vision-language-action models, scoring both pick-and-place success and grasp location.
The dataset is intended for public release to support research in visual and embodied AI.

papers.abstract: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $\beta$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.
authors: Kshitiz, Zheyuan Hu, Robyn Wu, Yizhou Li, Yunchu Zhang, Vattanary Tevy, Kavya Tayal, Shawn Yin, Aykut Onol, Kushal Arora, Dhruv Shah, Abhishek Gupta, Zackory Erickson, Aviral Kumar
bullets: Standard human demonstrations emphasize competent behavior but underrepresent low-level behaviors needed for autonomous improvement.
The authors define “connected behavioral coverage” as behaviors linking challenging robot-environment states to states that enable further progress.
They introduce β-Data, collected through adversarial teleoperation with reversible perturbations and no resets, then relabel trajectory segments with local natural-language outcomes.
A pretrained policy is finetuned on these trajectories while conditioning on recent action history.

In simulation and across three real-robot platforms, the approach shows better zero-shot generalization, more favorable data scaling, and more effective online finetuning than standard demonstrations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Connected behavioral coverage (CBC) induced by training on 𝛽-Data in LEGO disassembly. From the same initial assembly and natural language goal, variations in grasps, orientations, and contacts produce diverse sequences of outcomes. The top and middle rollouts detach different red bricks, while the bottom rollout separates all bricks through a distinct strategy. The policy generates meaningful alternative interactions while sustaining progress toward task completion.

Figure 8: The policy trained on standard demonstrations is usually unable to make the final fold of either garment. The pants are folded twice: legs together, then in half. The T-shirt is folded three times: sleeves, in half, then in half again, which is the final fold. Yellow outlines mark the garment or the part that the final fold moves. Frames with a time range overlay several frames from that range. Top: pants. Both policies fold the legs together. The policy trained on standard demonstrations (first row) loses its grasp on the folded pants, and its repeated attempts do not fold them in half. The policy trained on 𝛽-Data (second row) folds the pants in half, and the fold holds. Bottom: T-shirt, from the same initial layout. Both policies fold the T-shirt in half. The policy trained on standard demonstrations (third row) then stops, and the T-shirt stays unchanged until the rollout ends. The policy trained on 𝛽-Data (fourth row) makes the final fold.

Figure 6: Recovery after a failed placement in simulated packing, from the same initial state. On an OOD task, both policies start from the same state and are instructed to pack the sugar box into the medium tray. The policy trained on standard demonstrations (top) packs the foam brick, then lifts the sugar box and holds it beside the tray until the rollout ends, packing one of five objects. The policy trained on 𝛽-Data (bottom) places the sugar box, and when the box slides over the tray rim, it regrasps the box, sets it flat in the tray, and packs all five objects.

Figure 7: Repeated grasp attempts and recovery in real-world packing. Both policies are instructed to pack a jar that lies on its side. The policy trained on standard demonstrations (top) repeats the same grasp below the lid, and the jar stays on the table. The policy trained on 𝛽-Data (bottom) lifts the jar, and when the jar falls, it grasps the jar across its body and packs it.

Figure 3:Measuring connected behavioral coverage for one object. Top: one annotated trajectory segment in 𝛽-Data transfers the cracker box from the large tray to the medium tray and contributes one directed edge between the two object-location states. Bottom: all directed edges of the cracker box in simulated packing. The number on an edge is the number of annotated trajectory segments that demonstrate it. Standard demonstrations and 𝛽- Data contain the same four states. Standard demonstrations connect them with three distinct directed edges, and 𝛽-Data connects them with seven.

Figure 9: Training data and test-time scaling of 𝛽-Data in simulation. Left: zero-shot success as a function of the amount of midtraining data across four matched data budgets. 𝛽-Data overtakes midtraining on standard demonstrations beyond the smallest budget and achieves comparable performance with roughly half as much data at the larger budgets. Right: success as a function of rollout time for policies trained at each data budget. From 1.3 hours onward, 𝛽-Data outperforms standard demonstrations at every rollout time limit and continues to gain from additional rollout time. Each point is evaluated over 600 trials (12 tasks × 50); error bars show pointwise 95% bootstrap intervals over tasks and trials.

Figure 11: On held-out long-horizon tasks, the policy trained on 𝛽-Data starts higher and improves more with online experience. On simulated grocery packing tasks, success rate averaged over the five tasks, against the number of admitted successful trajectories𝑀 (left) and against the total number of online rollouts, including failures (right). Dashed lines show the law fitted separately to each training dataset. At𝑀 = 50, the policy trained on standard demonstrations remains below the initial success rate of the policy trained on 𝛽-Data (dotted line).

Figure 12: [Spurious correlations analysis] In these rollouts, the policy trained on 𝛽-Data attends to the instructed item before and after online finetuning, while the baseline trained on standard demonstrations attends diffusely or elsewhere. Real-world bimanual xArm grocery packing rollouts. The first frame for each policy shows attention from the name of the item in the instruction to the wrist-camera image, computed on the same frame for both policies; the region receiving the most attention is circled and magnified. The remaining two frames show the rollout of that policy. Top: before online finetuning, both policies are instructed to pack the yak. The 𝛽-Data policy attends tightly to the yak and packs it; the attention of the baseline is diffuse, and it packs the chip bag into the large box. papers.abstract: Progress in embodied foundation models is largely measured by task success, while the physical safety of their decisions remains underexamined. Safety evaluations centered on rule following and binary judgments do not adequately assess whether embodied models understand environmental hazards and make safe decisions. We introduce EmbodiSafety, comprising 1,092 snapshot tasks and 540 trajectory tasks across 844 visual scenarios to assess safety over short and long horizons. Six response modes cover direct execution, refusal, clarification, constrained execution, autonomous recovery, and human escalation. Distinguishing recovery from human intervention makes the boundary of safe autonomy an explicit evaluation target. Our protocol assesses mode correctness, risk identification, and actionable handling, with complete decision accuracy requiring all applicable checks to pass. Claude-Opus-5.5 achieves the highest complete decision accuracy among reference models, reaching 56.1% on snapshots and 61.5% on trajectories. We further develop a data construction pipeline and curate 40k examples for safety alignment. Supervised training on this corpus raises the complete decision accuracy of Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B.

papers.abstract: Model-generated labels offer a scalable route to training lightweight vision models, but what makes a model a good teacher, and can we tell before training a student? We study this in gaze target estimation, where interactive robots need models that are both accurate and efficient. In a controlled comparison of eleven supervision conditions, we vary only the source of gaze-point labels, keeping the student, training protocol and 361k training samples fixed, across three video datasets, two student sizes and three seeds; every student is evaluated against human annotation. Three findings emerge. First, imperfect model-generated labels can replace human annotation: Gaze-LLE, never trained on the target datasets' gaze annotation, trains students that match annotation-trained ones on ViT-Tiny and are significantly more accurate on ViT-Small (average distance error 0.187 vs 0.196), and the ViT-Tiny student runs 32$\times$ faster than its teacher on a laptop CPU. Second, apparent competence can conceal unreliable supervision: given another person's face centre in the prompt, InternVL3 and Qwen3-VL return it on 93.4% and 81.1% of test samples, and a copy-the-coordinate baseline matches InternVL3's labels and students. Without that coordinate, both models fall far behind the specialist. Third, good teachers can be identified before training: validation label error ranks student test error (Spearman's $\rho = 0.91$), and ten annotated clips single out the two specialist teachers in 95% of draws. These findings give practical principles for assessing supervision, exposing shortcuts and selecting teachers for lightweight models.
bullets: Imperfect model-generated gaze labels can replace human annotations: Gaze-LLE matches annotation-trained students on ViT-Tiny and improves accuracy on ViT-Small.
The ViT-Tiny student runs 32× faster than its Gaze-LLE teacher on a laptop CPU.
Vision-language models may appear competent because they copy face-center coordinates; removing this shortcut causes their performance to fall substantially.
Teacher quality can be screened before student training: validation label error strongly predicts student test error (Spearman’s ρ = 0.91).
Just ten annotated clips identify the two specialist teachers in 95% of sampling trials.

papers.abstract: Scaling embodied simulation requires diverse objects with executable physical representations. We present RFW-W, a physical asset universe connecting rigid, articulated, and deformable asset sources to task-conditioned scene composition. Its reported inventories comprise 1,010,386 asset records: 524,611 rigid assets in 1,212 categories (RFW-R), 402,410 articulated assets in 531 categories (RFW-A), and 83,365 jointly verified deformables in 485 categories (RFW-S). These taxonomies contribute 2,228 dataset--category entries. RFW-R couples category-guided generation with collision geometry, composed physical properties, and interaction annotations; RFW-A uses reusable agent-authored procedural generators with explicit part and joint structure; RFW-S uses structure-aware simulation representations, calibration, and independent testing. A common interface preserves physical requirements specific to each asset type for retrieval and scene assembly. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that RFW-R provides broader asset coverage and stronger scene-fulfillment capabilities than existing datasets. Across five RoboTwin tasks, using 100 demonstrations per task for each asset source, policies trained on RFW-R achieve macro success rates of 71.2% in clean settings and 41.8% under randomization, exceeding the strongest baseline by 15.8 and 10.6 percentage points, respectively. RFW-W provides a scalable and unified asset foundation for generating physically grounded, task-conditioned embodied worlds.

papers.abstract: Physics-based soccer characters must perform diverse motor skills and transition smoothly between them, such as dribbling into a shot. However, skills that perform well in isolation may fail when executed sequentially, as preceding behaviors can leave the character and ball in unfamiliar states. We present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework that enables multiple soccer skill transitions through shared adaptation while preserving the original skill policy outside transitions. MESSI first trains eight task-competent experts using motion priors and task rewards, then distills them into a unified, skill-conditioned Transformer. Rather than retraining individual experts for different transitions, we train a shared, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student through online reinforcement learning. Activated upon skill switching, the adapter helps the target skill handle unfamiliar entry states, while a learned exit mechanism determines when to return control to the original student. By disabling the adapter during native skill execution, MESSI preserves the original student policy by construction. Experiments across individual skills, skill transitions, and continuous skill chains demonstrate substantial improvements over direct switching, including an increase in dribbling-to-shooting success from 19.8% to 61.8%.

papers.abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $\pi_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.
authors: Xuanchen Liu, Hejun Zhang, Boxuan Dong, Ying Wu, Heshuai Li, Wen Gao, Yonghong Tian, Weihao Yu
bullets: Introduces RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark comparing mirror-free tasks with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions.

Matched non-reflective panels show that collisions alone do not explain failures: 50–88% of mirror-specific failures involve no recorded robot–panel contact.
Analyses indicate phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real objects, with additional diagnostics for grasping, pushing, and occlusion.
Real-robot tests with π₀.₅ and FastWAM also show reduced success, motivating reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) used in robot task planning to derive assembly procedures from existing manuals may correctly interpret individual assembly actions yet confuse exact part identities, predict unsupported Part IDs, or produce inconsistent parts across assembly steps. Thus, we propose CAPER (Capacity-Aware Part-grounding and Evidence Refinement), a manual-guided robotic assembly framework that enables VLMs to generate assembly procedures with two modules--PartGround and PlanRefine. PartGround aligns step-level manual evidence with product-specific inventory and part-reference information to identify exact Part IDs and quantities, transforming free-form hardware prediction into evidence-guided assignments represented in a shared Assembly Intermediate Representation (Assembly IR). PlanRefine audits PartGround assignments against finite inventory by removing the lowest-confidence assignments. Uncertain identity cases remain marked for review in the Assembly IR. We evaluate CAPER on the IKEA Assembly in the Wild (IAW) dataset. Experiment results show that CAPER reaches a Finite-inventory Consistency Rate of 83.33% and produces zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences. At the plan level, PlanRefine removes all observed inventory-overuse pairs (9 -> 0) and excess units (51 -> 0). Overall, the results indicate that PartGround and PlanRefine improve part reliability, while also enhancing finite-inventory consistency and local prediction accuracy. Project page and video: https://xhzzzz123.github.io/CAPER/

papers.abstract: People can anticipate how an object moves and the effort an interaction may require by watching others. How can embodied agents acquire this understanding from video? Force measurements provide direct sensory supervision, but require specialized equipment and remain limited in quantity. We introduce VidForce, which estimates an interaction trajectory together with a force profile from a third-person RGB video; 2D contact clicks and textual object-action prompts are optional. Our approach makes limited instrumented measurements useful for interpreting human interactions through learned physical prototypes as a prior. The prototypes share learned force levels and temporal profiles across interactions of comparable effort, with visual and semantic cues determining their contribution to each observation. Geometric and vision-language features adapt this prior to the observed interaction, while a joint conditional flow refines an initial tracked trajectory together with the force profile. Paired human and instrumented-gripper recordings provide measured force references for supervising human video, and a separately trained torque model demonstrates that the formulation extends to other sensory quantities. We evaluate trajectory recovery and force estimation through baseline comparisons and controlled ablations on held-out interactions from the Hoi! dataset. On this evaluation subset, VidForce achieves 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE and RMSE of 4.81 N and 5.92 N, respectively, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N. On real-world videos, VidForce infers motion and force reliably and consistently despite the variability in human execution. We further deploy VidForce on a Spot robot, where trajectories and force profiles estimated from human demonstrations drive real-world articulated-object manipulation, and report success rates across repeated trials. Project page: https://rafaymhddn.github.io/vidforce
authors: Rafay Mohiuddin, Jiaqi Chen, Marc Pollefeys, Hermann Blum
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of force-measured interaction data for learning physical understanding from video.
Uses learned physical prototypes capturing shared force levels and temporal profiles across similarly effortful interactions.
Combines visual, semantic, geometric, and optional 2D contact cues, then jointly refines trajectories and force profiles with a conditional flow model.
Evaluated on held-out Hoi! interactions, achieving 6.6 cm trajectory ATE and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N, with peak-force MAE/RMSE of 4.81/5.92 N.
Demonstrates transfer to torque prediction and deploys video-derived trajectories and forces for Spot robot manipulation; performance is evaluated across repeated trials.

papers.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking enables humanoid robots to reproduce diverse skills from human demonstrations. Existing model-free reinforcement learning methods either distill motion specialists into a single policy at the cost of performance or train a generalist policy directly using cluster-scale computation. SuperMimic reduces this computational cost through a differentiable world model that implicitly learns the physics shared across motions by predicting the next state from the current state and action. However, this implicit formulation may not fully capture the underlying physical processes. Errors around changes of support can accumulate over imagined rollouts used to train the tracking policy. To address this challenge, we introduce DynaMimic, a differentiable world model that explicitly incorporates shared physics into state prediction. Specifically, its network predicts a contact wrench at each candidate support link and a residual generalized force. DynaMimic then uses these predictions to compute the next state through closed-form Lagrangian forward dynamics. Across 60 full LAFAN1 motions, DynaMimic reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 18.6% relative to SuperMimic. For terrain tracking, we give both methods the same local height maps. Relative to terrain-conditioned SuperMimic, DynaMimic reduces MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour (66.15 to 56.28~mm) and by 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips (141.88 to 126.57~mm). On a real A3 humanoid, the learned policies can perform diverse skills, such as floor recovery, cartwheel and a box vault.
authors: Chaoyue Xing, Linyi Huang, Yiting He, Yixuan Yin, Siqi Hou, Yi Zhang, Liyuan Pan, Miaomiao Liu, Daqi Liu
bullets: Addresses error accumulation near support transitions in imagined rollouts for whole-body motion tracking.
Predicts contact wrenches and residual generalized forces, then computes state updates using closed-form Lagrangian dynamics.
Reduces MPJPE by 18.6% across 60 LAFAN1 motions compared with SuperMimic.
With terrain conditioning, lowers MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour and 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips.
Demonstrated diverse skills—including floor recovery, cartwheel, and box vault—on a real A3 humanoid.

At each substep, the integrator maps each link’s mean wrench λ̄ (i) b,t to generalized forces, adds the residual, actuator, and passive forces, and advances the state. papers.abstract: Reasoning about human-object interaction from RGB cameras is important for gaming, VR environments, and robot learning. Yet 4D reconstruction from a monocular RGB camera is challenging, especially when articulated hands are involved. Prior full-body works neglect hands during reconstruction, causing them to penetrate into, or float from the object. We present HARI4D, a hand-articulation-aware method for reconstructing spatially and temporally consistent 4D human-object interaction from monocular RGB video. We introduce a history-aware object tracker that provides robust and stable tracking. Based on these tracks, we improve the interaction configuration through coarse-to-fine reasoning that follows the order of object manipulation: ReachNet first brings the full body and arms to the object during contact, and TouchNet then finalizes hand articulation according to temporal context and local object geometry. On ARCTIC, unseen in training, our method reduces the object error by 56% and improves hand contact F1 from 0.866 to 0.921 over prior art. Our method recovers accurate full body-object interaction with coherent hand articulations and applies to online videos. Our code and pretrained models will be released.
authors: Semin Kim, Xianghui Xie, Chuqiao Li, Jongyoo Kim, Gerard Pons-Moll
bullets: Targets hand penetration and floating artifacts in prior full-body reconstruction methods.
Uses a history-aware object tracker for robust, stable object motion estimation.
Applies coarse-to-fine interaction reasoning: ReachNet positions the body and arms, while TouchNet refines hand articulation using temporal context and object geometry.
On the unseen ARCTIC benchmark, reduces object error by 56% and raises hand-contact F1 from 0.866 to 0.921 over prior work.
Supports accurate full-body interaction reconstruction and online video processing.

papers.abstract: World models support embodied decision-making by predicting future environment states. In embodied visual tracking, uncertain target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes jointly affect visual observations, making future-state prediction challenging. We propose Motion-Conditioned World Modeling, which incorporates predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion into latent state transitions. A Geometry--Progress module jointly models geometric paths and single-step travel distances through shared motion modes and path-conditioned progress distributions. This formulation captures uncertainty in route selection and motion progress while preserving their dependence. Action-induced coordinate transformations express predicted paths in the next robot frame, providing geometrically grounded conditions for future visual-state prediction. Future visual feature reconstruction supervises the motion predictor through the conditioned transition branch, linking explicit motion representations to subsequent observations. The model is jointly optimized with motion likelihood, feature reconstruction, and expert-action supervision, enabling the tracking policy to combine visual context with predictive motion cues.Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks demonstrate improved tracking performance and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight $0.5$B backbone.
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Xuan Yao, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses uncertainty from target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes in embodied visual tracking.
Uses predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion in latent state transitions.
Geometry–Progress jointly models geometric paths and travel distance while preserving their dependence.
Action-induced coordinate transforms express predicted paths in the next robot frame; future feature reconstruction supervises motion prediction.
Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks show improved tracking and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight 0.5B backbone.

papers.abstract: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.
authors: Richmond Sin Jing Xuan, Peilin Feng, Wenbin Wang, Soujanya Poria
bullets: Agents often answer prematurely even when their beliefs still support multiple possibilities.
RLVB uses the simulator’s exact posterior to reward continued exploration under uncertainty and commitment once evidence is sufficient.
The reward requires no judge, critic, or reward model and does not inspect the agent’s written belief line.
Across three vision-language models and three benchmarks, RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average.
Agents trained with RLVB commit under insufficient evidence far less often than base models, indicating more evidence-grounded behavior.

papers.abstract: Recovering the continuous world-space motion of both hands from egocentric video is essential for applications such as human-to-robot policy transfer and augmented reality. Achieving this goes beyond reconstructing the hands from each individual frame, as the context that a frame needs is often spread over time, especially around occlusions or when a hand moves out of sight. Recent works have explored how to exploit temporal context, yet they mostly draw it from fixed-length windows. Such windows cannot guarantee that every frame has the context required to reconstruct the hands in world space with accurate poses and metric scale. To address this limitation, we introduce MemHand, a memory-enhanced framework for world-space hand motion reconstruction. MemHand maintains two complementary forms of memory. The Short-Term Event Memory keeps the context of the well-observed hand around each occlusion or out-of-sight event and supplies it to frames with weak or missing visual evidence. In addition, since the metric scale holds over the whole recording, the Long-Term Scale Memory retains the most reliable observations across the video as scale anchors within a bounded state. Across benchmarks featuring severe occlusions and frequent out-of-sight intervals, MemHand achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and generalizes well to unseen domains. Benefiting from the synergy of both memories, it cuts W-MPJPE by 57\% on ARCTIC and 70\% on HOT3D relative to StableHand, delivering continuous and metrically accurate world-space hand poses and trajectories. We will release our code and models at the project page: https://irmvlab.github.io/memhand.github.io
authors: Junyi Ma, Zhangshuo Qi, Erhang Zhang, Mingjie Li, Hesheng Wang
bullets: Targets failures caused by occlusions and hands moving out of view, where fixed temporal windows may lack sufficient context.
Uses Short-Term Event Memory to transfer well-observed hand context to frames with weak or missing visual evidence.
Uses Long-Term Scale Memory to preserve reliable metric-scale anchors throughout an entire recording.
Reports 57% and 70% W-MPJPE reductions versus StableHand on ARCTIC and HOT3D, respectively, with strong cross-domain generalization.
Code and models are planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.
authors: Maximilian Xiling Li, Nils Blank, Paul Mattes, Pankhuri Vanjani, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Discrete skill policies can fail because of their vocabulary, selector, or execution, but joint training makes these causes hard to separate.
MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with a nearest demonstrated motion, then boundedly corrects it toward the prediction without training new parameters.
Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped reference policy is statistically equivalent to the original.
On LIBERO-90, quantization has no measurable cost and skill choice costs at most 2 points; selector placement and correction explain nearly all remaining gaps, up to 12 points.
Offline reconstruction fails to predict these effects or reliably assess library size, design, and transfer across benchmark suites.

papers.title: What Does a Skill Vocabulary Cost? A Closed-Loop Decomposition over Demonstrated Motions
papers.tldr: MPQ turns a demonstrated-motion library into a parameter-free post-policy wrapper that isolates whether closed-loop failures come from skill choice or skill execution.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to translate task intent into physical interactions as the scene changes. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer semantic and spatial reasoning, while visuomotor policies provide fine-grained control. Yet ambiguous goals and dependencies between actions make their integration challenging. We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework that composes learned manipulation skills through grounded steering and execution feedback. A VLM estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver constructs a skill plan. An agentic harness steers each skill through language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies its outcome to guide phase transitions and replanning. A common phase-level interface supports specialized policies and generalist action models. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot show how Atomic Policy improves task following and supports recovery in complex, long-horizon manipulation. Project page: https://aaronzkd.github.io/atomic-policy/
authors: Kaidi Zhang, Pengyuan Guo, Zhengtong Xu, Caiyi Zhang, Huayi Gou, Guanlin Huang, Aaron Lim, Anas Rafei, Yu She
bullets: Targets the challenge of translating ambiguous task goals into changing physical interactions.
Uses a VLM for symbolic state and goal estimation, followed by PDDL-based skill planning.
Steers atomic manipulation skills with language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies outcomes for replanning.
Provides a common phase-level interface for specialized policies and generalist action models.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show improved task following and recovery in complex long-horizon tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Atomic Policy architecture, shown with point-steered skills for Tabletop Manipulation. The planner combines VLM state and goal estimation with PDDL planning. For the active pick blue cube phase, the grounder (MolmoPoint) supplies a 2D image point pk. The selected skill generates an action chunk At using a diffusion U-Net conditioned on images, proprioception qt, and pk. The VLM checker evaluates the outcome against a phase-specific checklist: done advances the plan, not_done continues the phase, and replan requests a new plan. Blue arrows indicate execution and phase transitions; the red arrow indicates replanning.

Figure 5. Real-robot trial outcomes. Top: in-distribution (ID); bottom: out-of-distribution (OOD). Boxes show the interquartile range (IQR), dark lines mark medians, and whiskers extend to the outermost observations within 1.5 IQR of the box edges. White diamonds mark means, and dots show individual trials (n = 10 per method, task, and condition). Tasks are arranged by increasing language-grounding and compositional demands, from Multi-drawer to Stacking to Crossword. The language-only end-to-end baselines show wide trial-to-trial variation on Stacking and poor performance on Crossword, suggesting limited steerability as language-conditioning demands increase. Atomic + MolmoBot improves over fine-tuned MolmoBot on OOD Stacking and Crossword, supporting the combined benefit of point guidance and atomic-phase execution. Atomic + π0.5 also improves on these tasks without point inputs, showing that high-level planning and checker-controlled execution can improve OOD performance through language-based phase guidance alone.

Figure 6. Completion time of successful real-robot trials. Top: ID; bottom: OOD. Only trials with a task score of 1 are included. Large dots show the mean completion time, vertical lines show ± one sample standard deviation, and faint dots show individual trials; n is the number of successful trials for each method. Fine-tuned MolmoBot completes no Crossword trial, and fine-tuned π0.5 completes a single ID Crossword trial. Completion time for Atomic Policy includes planning, verification, and replanning by the VLM, so successful Atomic Policy trials take longer than successful end-to-end trials; for example, Atomic + π0.5 averages 128.6 s on ID Stacking versus 61.6 s for fine-tuned π0.5. Means based on few successes, such as n ≤ 2, should be interpreted with caution.

Figure 3. Task instructions and phase execution. Each row pairs an instruction with selected observations from execution. Bold labels name atomic phases, and the text after each colon identifies the point target; n/a denotes a phase without point conditioning. Blue boxes mark replanning after a detected failure or uncertain task state, such as a fallen cube in Stacking. The checker uses phase-specific completion criteria to continue execution, advance the phase, or request a new plan. Ellipses omit repeated or previously illustrated phases.

Figure 7. Failure modes on Multi-drawer. Each panel traces the 20 trials of one method (10 ID and 10 OOD) from execution to outcome. Trials either proceed without a recorded failure or encounter an error that is recovered through replanning or remains unresolved. Outcomes are SUCCESS (task score 1), PARTIAL (0 < task score < 1), and FAIL (task score 0). Failure types are wrong object or order (incorrect object, sequence, word, target recognition, or plan), reach or stuck (target or receptacle not reached, drawer not opened, or robot motion stalls), grasp, and place. Recovery is counted only when explicitly recorded in the evaluation notes. No method produces a zero-score trial on Multi-drawer. The Atomic Policy variants fail mainly through grasp and place errors, with one planning error for Atomic + MolmoBot. For fine-tuned MolmoBot, 7 of its 11 unsuccessful trials involve failure to reach the OOD receptacle during placement: the policy fails to guide the grasped object to the white bowl, suggesting difficulty grounding the unfamiliar receptacle’s location.

Figure 4. Learning curves on MolmoSpaces PnP Next-To. MolmoBot and π0.5 are evaluated during task-specific fine-tuning. Solid curves show success averaged over the ten most recent checkpoint evaluations. For the first nine checkpoints, the average uses all checkpoints evaluated so far. Dashed horizontal lines indicate each model’s zero-shot success rate.

Figure 8. Failure modes on Stacking. Panels and failure types follow Fig. 7. All 17 unrecovered failures of Atomic + DP and 9 of 10 of Atomic + MolmoBot are grasp or place errors, while Atomic + π0.5 fails in only 3 of 20 trials. Atomic + DP struggles with the fine-grained alignment required for stacking, suggesting that its low-level visuomotor policy has not learned sufficient placement precision from the available demonstrations. High-level replanning can retry these actions but cannot ensure accurate execution. In contrast, wrong object or order accounts for 8 of 11 failed trials of fine-tuned MolmoBot and 3 of 4 of fine-tuned π0.5, which together produce 11 zero-score trials.

Figure 9. Failure modes on Crossword. Panels and failure types follow Fig. 7. Wrong object, order, or place accounts for 36 of 39 unsuccessful trials of the fine-tuned baselines, whose rollouts often follow the training word or misorder letters. In contrast, 25 of 31 unrecovered failures across the Atomic Policy variants are grasp or place errors, and four trials succeed after recovery. Together with Tab. 4, these results support the benefit of explicit guidance and closed-loop planning for both ID execution and OOD generalization: Atomic + MolmoBot raises task score from 30.0 to 82.5 on ID trials and from 0.0 to 72.5 on OOD trials. Atomic + DP achieves the highest task scores in both conditions (91.3 ID and 90.0 OOD), showing that a point-guided policy can perform well on a task with strong language-grounding and sequencing demands.

papers.title: Atomic Policy: Composing Atomic Manipulation Skills with Agentic Reasoning

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-robot manipulation have shown how robots can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. However, successful coordination does not reveal which robots are actually needed. The same task may require different teams as robot capabilities change, resources become unavailable, or objects replace robotic support. We argue that reliable multi-robot manipulation requires physical necessity reasoning: understanding what a task demands, which resources can fulfill those demands, and which are truly necessary. We introduce MRBench, a benchmark for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation. It comprises eight tasks with distinct concurrency and reach constraints, each evaluated under five configurations that change the required resources while preserving the task goal. Our evaluation reveals that existing coordination agents perform well with reference teams but struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support. To address this gap, we propose MRScissors, which separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities and identifies minimal feasible teams through constrained search. Across two model backbones, MRScissors achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points, respectively. Together, these findings expose a critical gap between coordinating robots and understanding their physical necessity.
authors: Yanzhe Chen, Zhijun Cao, Ruihe An, Chang Gong, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Existing coordination success with a reference team does not ensure agents understand which robots are necessary.
MRBench covers eight tasks with varying concurrency and reach constraints across five resource configurations.
Agents struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support.
MRScissors separates task requirements from measured capabilities and searches for minimal feasible teams.
It achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy across two backbones, outperforming baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MRBench and MRScissors for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation, addressing a critical gap in understanding robot team requirements.
papers.title: MRBench: Benchmarking Physical Necessity Reasoning in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Manipulation

papers.abstract: We present the Screw Attention Policy, a geometry-centric manipulation framework that supplies task geometry explicitly and learns only execution. The policy operates on object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes provided by perception and robot models. The policy requires only 30K learned parameters. Trained entirely in simulation on a single robot arm, the policy generalises to new scene layouts, transfers zero-shot across robot embodiments, and deploys directly on a real robot, without adaptation or fine-tuning. It achieves 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen robot arms, and 21 of 24 trials on a real robot. These results suggest that much of what manipulation policies learn at scale is geometric structure that can instead be supplied.
bullets: Uses object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes as explicit geometric inputs.
Learns execution rather than reconstructing task geometry from data.
Trained on a single simulated robot arm with no adaptation or fine-tuning for transfer.
Reports 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen arms, and 21/24 real-robot trials.
Scope: performance depends on accurate perception and robot-model geometry supplied to the policy.

papers.abstract: Most imitation policies that predict chunks of future actions use the dense action representation, in which the chunk holds one control target per step. In stage-structured manipulation, where a task can be divided into stages with definable endpoints, the keypose action representation instead sets each step of the chunk to the endpoint of the stage that step belongs to, and a speed-capped servo supplies the motion. We compare the two in several simulated manipulation tasks and on a real robot, with the same chunk length and matched demonstrations, observations, policy architectures and update budgets; in simulation, each one's execution rule is selected on tuning scenes. When the simulated demonstrations are slowed, paused and rerouted, dense success falls sharply while keypose stays roughly level, across three policy architectures and with endpoints extracted from the recorded demonstrations; keypose also leads under object-size and position shift. With clean demonstrations, keypose leads only when they are scarce and is otherwise close to or behind dense across the simulated tasks, provided that the demonstrations and execution rule suit its executor; when they do not, it falls far below dense. The same dependence on the executor appeared on a real robot learning to open a drawer from human demonstrations: dense succeeded more often, and keypose improved substantially only after its executor's rotation and forward speed were adjusted to the demonstrations. These results suggest that keypose trades sensitivity to such variation in the demonstrations for sensitivity to execution that departs from them.
authors: Haizhou Ge, Mengshuo Wang, Zhixing Chen, Lei Han, Chen Wang, Lu Shi, Guyue Zhou, Ruqi Huang
bullets: The study compares dense action chunks with stage-endpoint-based keypose chunks for stage-structured manipulation.
Experiments use matched policies, demonstrations, observations, chunk lengths, and update budgets in simulation and on a real robot.
With slowed, paused, or rerouted demonstrations, dense performance drops sharply while keypose remains roughly stable; keypose also handles object and position shifts better.
With clean demonstrations, keypose helps mainly when demonstrations are scarce and can perform much worse when its executor is mismatched.
In a real drawer-opening task, dense succeeds more often, while tuning keypose's executor substantially improves it.

Both are trained with the same demonstrations, policy architecture and update budget and execute the first eight of 50 slots before querying again; the keypose command toward a stage endpoint is capped at the 95th percentile of the demonstrations’ per-step motion. papers.title: Keypose or Dense? A Controlled Comparison of Action Representations for Stage-Structured Manipulation
papers.tldr: Keypose representations are more robust to timing and path variation in demonstrations, but their success depends strongly on a well-matched execution controller.

papers.abstract: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
authors: Tingting Liao, Mingjia Huo, Hao Li, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Represents the robot with a 3D model and potentially contacted objects as 3D points from the first frame and calibrated camera.
A parameter-free rule-based simulator applies actions, while a video model renders realistic video alongside the simulated state.
Across unseen DROID setups, robot motion follows the proxy more closely than end-to-end models, while rendering the robot alone is often sufficient.
Adding simulated objects reduces missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%; object-state adherence varies substantially by base video model.
Rigid-object lift behavior is more sensitive to freezing simulated objects for MiniMax-H3 than LTX-2.3, while rigidly modeling cloth and rope remains a limitation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Following the simulated state. Under the recorded actions (top), both base models lift the cup as the proxy does. With the gripper held open (middle) or the simulated objects frozen while the arm moves as recorded (bottom), the proxy leaves the cup in place; SimPWM-H3-C does too, whereas SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C still lifts it.

papers.selection_reason: Simulator-as-proxy video world model for robot manipulation, probing whether video follows simulated state.
papers.title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: SimPWM uses an explicit simulator as a proxy for robot video generation and shows that video models reliably follow simulated robot motion but only inconsistently follow simulated object states.

papers.abstract: In Minecraft, a common testbed for embodied agents, semantic tools such as mineBlock pick targets from the simulator's loaded world state without a visibility test, so a buried ore the agent has never seen is one call away, and scores cannot show whether the agent searched. We formalize the missing requirement as evidence closure: every decision of an agent system, including those inside its tools, may depend on the world only through facts for which the agent holds evidence. EviCraft is a runtime and benchmark that enforces closure below the agent and makes the admission rule an experimental variable: a perception-grounded regime (G) admits only what is in line of sight or returned by the agent's own actions, and a loaded-state regime (L) reproduces standard tool stacks, with agents, tools, and worlds held fixed. On Survival, the regime effect exceeds the strongest agent's lead: under G, three mid-sized agents reach the diamond in 32%-40% of runs, against 76%-94% under L, and the strongest agent under G scores below each of them under L. In two models, removing only the line-of-sight test closes 93%-96% of the score gap, and loading state only inside tools recovers 70%-98%, so safeguards on observations and queries leave most of the leak open. In open-ended acquisition, the gain from L concentrates in items that depend on buried resources or mobs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/AllenReder/EviCraft
authors: Wenyou Yi, Lantian Zhang, Guanlin Chen, Xingqiu Xu, Haiyang Sun, Minrui Huang, Tianle Liang, Hao Chen, Haorui Xu, Zhou Zhao
bullets: The paper formalizes evidence closure: agent decisions and tool calls may depend only on facts supported by the agent’s evidence.
EviCraft compares perception-grounded access (G) with standard loaded-state tools (L), holding agents, tools, and worlds fixed.
On Survival, three mid-sized agents reached diamond in 32%–40% of runs under G versus 76%–94% under L.
Removing only line-of-sight checks closed 93%–96% of the score gap in two models; tool-only state loading recovered 70%–98%.
Loaded-state advantages were concentrated on tasks involving buried resources or mobs.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing a scene for physics simulation requires recovering its spatial layout and the support relationships that govern its behavior. We present Support2Sim, a Real2Sim system that reconstructs simulation-ready scenes from a single RGB image. Our design objective is to maximize source fidelity, support realization, and stability within a practical time budget for scene generation. Support2Sim infers a support graph, which a contact-guided pose initializer uses to propose poses for objects with multiple supports. The initializer generates and ranks candidates by geometric fit and source-image agreement. A coarse-to-fine refiner allocates a fixed search budget across supported objects and evaluates pose updates with physics rollouts. After an accepted update, it searches from the new pose at a finer translation and rotation scale. We benchmark our method on 50 scenes spanning four datasets. Compared with the strongest baseline, Support2Sim improves source-mask IoU after 10 seconds by 21.4 pp, realizes 87.1% versus 73.2% of intended supports, and reduces mean object drift from 79.6 to 45.3 mm. See our project page at https://support2sim.github.io for more details.
authors: Samarth Chopra, Ankit Prabhu, Akshayan Nagarajah, Sumer Murthy, Pratik Chaudhari, Vijay Kumar
bullets: Targets visually faithful Real2Sim reconstruction with reliable object supports and practical generation time.
Infers a support graph and uses contact-guided pose initialization for objects with multiple supports.
Refines object poses through coarse-to-fine search, geometric/image agreement, and physics rollouts.
Across 50 scenes from four datasets, it improves 10-second source-mask IoU by 21.4 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
It realizes 87.1% of intended supports and reduces mean object drift from 79.6 to 45.3 mm.

papers.abstract: Recently developed World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, providing predictive context for control. However, existing WAMs typically learn implicit attention allocation with limited explicit action-relevant attention guidance, leading to limited performance. To unleash strong capabilities of WAMs, we introduce explicit attention guidance as a unifying principle and propose our Attention-Guided WAM (AG-WAM), an end-to-end framework with three plug-and-play attention guidance modules that directly reformulate internal attention paradigm in WAMs: the Content-Adaptive Predictive Attention module, the Guidance-Point Visual Attention module, and the State-Conditioned Text Attention module. Without any external plugin module adopted, our end-to-end framework with the unifying principle of explicit attention guidance boosts the accuracy and efficiency of WAMs. Without using any private embodied training data, our AG-WAM establishes new state-of-the-art performance on multiple public robotic manipulation benchmarks including LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, significantly outperforming other methods, even those using massive private embodied training data by a notable margin, meanwhile notably improving training and inference efficiency.
authors: Hongcheng Zhang, Lei Sun, Songxuan Liu, Tengteng Pan, Yuqiang Zhai, Xianglong Xu, Jianya Guo, Xiao Song
bullets: Existing WAMs rely on implicit attention, limiting action-relevant prediction and control.
AG-WAM introduces three plug-and-play modules: content-adaptive predictive, guidance-point visual, and state-conditioned text attention.
The framework is end-to-end and requires no external plugin modules or private embodied training data.
It reports state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, with improved training and inference efficiency.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
bullets: Quantising the transformer-based Depth Anything V2 directly causes severe information loss because many attention weights fall below int8 precision.
The proposed ResNet-34 U-Net student, distilled from Depth Anything V2-Large, runs at 27.1 FPS using 24.5M parameters.
Its int8 predictions closely match its float version (Pearson 0.99993) and achieve the best held-out simulated-yard accuracy among tested onboard models (AbsRel 0.269).
On 1,000 stereo-verified real-drive points, it performs comparably to the vendor’s Depth Anything V2-Small while running faster (27.1 vs. 21.6 FPS).
Integrated with mapping, planning, and SLAM, the system reaches goals without contact in most hardware-in-the-loop yard trials, though less often than with exact obstacle maps.

papers.selection_reason: Attention-free depth distillation enabling onboard robot navigation on low-power hardware; efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: An attention-free, distilled depth model enables real-time monocular obstacle ranging and navigation on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Hailo-8L hardware.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable simultaneous processing of egocentric video and textual target descriptions to produce action commands for embodied tracking platforms. However, these platforms rarely move exactly as commanded, in part due to unexpected environmental disturbances such as wind, unleveled terrain, and road bumps. Here we study how such models handle uncommanded egomotion. First, we explore performance across diverse disturbances by benchmarking three tracking VLAs on three datasets. We find that models differ in which environmental disturbances hurt them most, but all are sensitive to sudden target loss. Tracing egomotion from pixels to emitted actions, we identify two gaps. In representation, motion is reliably recovered through explicit relations between frames, but aggressive compression of past frames weakens small-motion readouts. In action, large rotations do reach the decision state, yet the decoded direction carries only a few percent of a mirrored rotation's effect on the turn. Targeting both gaps, we fine-tune one model, Uni-NaVid, on data amounting to just 1.7% of its original training set in a ladder of analysis-motivated variants. These gain 5-22 points after target-loss without degrading clean success; after a smooth loss, the best one improves success by 72% (relative), recovering 76% of its gap to clean. We also show that targeted fine-tuning improves recovery partly via a text-mediated action dependency, without new architecture, large-scale data collection or training from scratch.
authors: Dan Zlotnikov, Nadav Alali, Ohad Ben-Shahar
bullets: Benchmarks three tracking VLAs across three datasets and diverse disturbances.
All models are sensitive to sudden target loss, though disturbance susceptibility varies.
Explicit cross-frame relations recover motion, while aggressive frame compression weakens small-motion perception.
Large rotations reach the decision state, but their decoded turn direction has little effect relative to mirrored rotations.
Analysis-driven fine-tuning on 1.7% of original training data improves target-loss recovery while preserving clean performance; gains are strongest after smooth loss.

papers.title: Knocked Off Course: Tracing Uncommanded Motion from Perception to Action in Embodied VLAs
papers.tldr: Tracing uncommanded egomotion reveals perception and action bottlenecks in embodied VLAs, which targeted fine-tuning can substantially improve without architectural changes or large-scale retraining.

papers.abstract: Robot teams can split workloads or combine complementary bodies, but only if each robot leaves the shared world in a state its teammate can use. Existing multi-robot benchmarks emphasize task allocation and skill sequencing, rarely testing whether the resulting physical states are usable. To evaluate collective physical capability, we introduce DeCoNav-Act, a benchmark for language-guided multi-robot mobile manipulation in a shared physics simulation. Its 350 homogeneous and 150 heterogeneous tasks, each verified by joint reference execution, span two coordination mechanisms: parallel workloads in shared space and physical dependencies in which one robot establishes a condition for a teammate to use. Beyond team success, DeCoNav-Act measures path efficiency and handoff coverage and success, and adds a diagnostic from verified pre-handoff states. Evaluating sensor-grounded adaptations of ASPIRE and RAX and our agent CoMoMa, we find that with GPT-5.6-luna no method completes a task, at most 8.8% of dependencies are reached, and even from pre-handoff states no handoff is completed; with GPT-6.1-sol, CoMoMa establishes the condition in 26.5% of trials, but only 4.1% succeed.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong results in arm-centric manipulation, yet humanoid whole-body control (WBC) requires dynamic balance and tightly coupled full-body coordination. Existing hierarchical humanoid VLAs typically decouple motion generation from physical execution, leaving tracking and balance errors unable to directly optimize the VLA generator. We propose DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T N1.7 with SONIC, a pretrained whole-body behavior foundation model. To enable execution-aware differentiable training, we replace the non-differentiable simulator with a learned, action-conditioned world model, allowing multi-step body-execution losses to backpropagate through the frozen whole-body controller and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T improves average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2% to 71.7%), demonstrating that execution-aware gradients effectively align high-level motion generation with closed-loop whole-body dynamics.
authors: Sichen Wu, Qian Sun, Mengfan Liu, Weikai Qin, Bike Zhu, Hesheng Wang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between high-level motion generation and physical execution in humanoid whole-body control.
Couples GR00T N1.7 with the pretrained SONIC whole-body behavior model in an end-to-end differentiable framework.
Uses a learned action-conditioned world model instead of a non-differentiable simulator to backpropagate multi-step execution losses into the VLA action head.
On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, average success rises from 59.2% to 71.7%, a 12.5-point improvement over the supervised base VLA.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.
authors: Hongjia Liu, Dacheng Zhou, Minghao Fu, Chuanjun Guo, Tianze Wang, Qingtao Liu, He Wang, Li Yi
bullets: Uses robot demonstrations to jointly learn an actor, action-conditioned world model, and bootstrapped critic.
Predicts endpoint visual latents, proprioception, reward, and continuation for action chunks, avoiding intermediate video-frame generation.
Adapts the world model and critic on real rollouts, then improves the actor with imagined-rollout PPO or critic-guided best-of-N selection.
Outperforms large-scale VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and reaches 75% average success on two real-world tasks versus 45% for π₀.₅.
World-model accuracy and speed, plus ablations, support jointly learning dynamics and value for better policies.

papers.abstract: We were surprised to find that leading end-to-end driving models across major paradigms, despite scoring close to human drivers on NAVSIM, cannot reliably make a simple 90-degree turn in photorealistic closed-loop simulators. To investigate why, we build LaWanle, a benchmark of turns drawn from three such simulators. Driving each turn from several starts, we find that the same model passes it from one start and fails it from another, and that the two drives look alike until they enter the junction. Rotating the car by a few degrees at the junction entry can fail a turn it otherwise passes. Conversely, a slight heading correction to the plans can rescue about half of the failed turns we tested. Such errors arise when a model drives by itself, so we post-train an open-source lane-keeping model with closed-loop DAgger on its lateral path. Training 5% of its parameters is enough to raise its turn pass rate from 19% to 76%. The gain transfers to the two other benchmarks, where the policy also scores among the leading models. Further fine-tuning on recovery data repairs the deviations it is trained on but, against a control trained equally long, improves turns on none of the three benchmarks, and every variant stays far below a human driver.
authors: Chengzhi Gao, Junzhe Gao, Yongzhi Liu, Weichao Zhuang, Weilong Hu, Taonian Liang, Guodong Yin
bullets: Models that score near humans on NAVSIM often fail simple turns in photorealistic closed-loop simulators.

Closed-loop DAgger on lateral paths raises an open-source lane-keeping model’s turn pass rate from 19% to 76% after training 5% of its parameters.
Recovery-data fine-tuning does not improve benchmark turns beyond a matched control, and all variants remain well below human performance.

papers.title: LaWanle: Why Can't Leading Driving Models Make a Simple Turn?
