papers.abstract: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.
authors: Vinay Udit Mohan, Xuchuan Huang, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Addresses the high cost of action-labelled data and poor transferability of embodiment-specific world models.
Learns continuous latent actions from point-cloud observations using retargeted human demonstrations and a contrastive cross-embodiment objective.
Uses latent actions directly for model-predictive control with particle-based future prediction; executable commands are recovered from predicted geometric motion.
Reports 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, and 86% success across 50 real-world trials on five tasks with an unseen dexterous hand.
Demonstrates controllable, compositional, and transferable motion, including zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses latent-action world models for robotic manipulation with cross-embodiment transfer, fitting both robot learning and latent action model topics.
papers.title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: DexLatentWorld learns geometry-grounded latent actions from 3D demonstrations, enabling world-model planning and zero-shot manipulation across unseen robot embodiments without action labels or embodiment-specific decoders.

papers.abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
authors: Qinyue Li, Weijie Qiao, Qingyi Tao, Zerui Gong, Zhe Yang, Quanzhou Li, Taolin Zhang, Jinglin He, Zhonghua Wu, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Addresses learning actions from diverse videos that lack actions or share no common action space.
Uses one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both inverse- and forward-dynamics models, connected by learnable dynamics registers.
Trains on counterfactual video pairs differing only in motion to distill compact latent actions without video generation.
Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on LARY for action classification and control, and transfer motion across robots, scenes, and human-to-robot settings.
The PAWlicy pretraining paradigm achieves a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over pi_0.5 on both evaluated real-robot tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1 World models as native latent action models. (a) Existing LAMs learn an IDM and an FDM from scratch. (b) A pretrained video world model is already an FDM. (c) Native LAM runs one world model in two modes, reading a latent action â from video and regenerating the future from â. (d) Latent actions share one space and replay the same motion from edited first frames in new setups. (e) PAWlicy pretrains a VLA on â without reconstructing pixels.

A latent â is read once from a source clip (blue) in the IDM mode of Native LAM and replayed in its FDM mode from a different first frame (orange), which is generated with GPT image generation from the source first frame; dotted frames are generated. The generated videos carry out the source motion with another embodiment, in another scene, from human to robot, and from simulation to a photorealistic scene, although no transfer objective is used in training.

Figure 2 Training Native LAM. (a) Each video x is paired with a retimed copy x′ = x ◦ ϕ of the same footage that shares the first frame but not the motion. (b) In IDM mode, dynamics registers read the clean video through a read-only attention mask and are projected to the latent action â; on AgiBot World and DROID, a kinematic head grounds â in end-effector motion. (c) In FDM mode, the same DiT regenerates the future from v0 and â alone, with â inserted into the token sequence through the adapter MLPin, taking over the conditioning role of text, trained with its original flow-matching loss; both clips of a pair share the noise and diffusion time, so only â can explain their difference.

Figure 3 PAWlicy. A frozen Native LAM labels each video window with one past and three future latent groups; t−1, t, . . . , t+3 index temporal groups, each containing four video frames. Sharing attention with the VLM, the latent action DiT reconstructs the past and predicts the future, and the action DiT conditions on it to generate actions. Video without actions still trains the latent pathway.

Figure 5 Interpolating latents interpolates the motion. Latents read from a still clip and a full-action clip are blended and replayed from the same first frame. The top and bottom rows are the two source clips; the dotted frames between them are generated. Each intermediate latent yields one coherent motion that travels part of the way, further as β grows; blending pixels instead superimposes static and moving arms (red box).

Figure 7 Counterfactual pairs prevent posterior collapse. A latent action is read in IDM mode from a source clip in which the left arm grasps the tissue (top) or from its still counterfactual, which holds the first frame (bottom), and the FDM regenerates the clip from the same start frame with shared prompt, noise, and seed. Circles mark the end pose of the arm. Trained for 2k steps without counterfactual pairs, the FDM reaches for the cup in both cases. This is posterior collapse: the FDM ignores the latent and hallucinates a reach for the cup from the first frame alone. With counterfactual pairs, the same 2k steps already keep the still latent still, although the moving latent still reaches for the cup. At 13k steps the generated end frames match the source in both cases.

papers.abstract: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.
bullets: Existing benchmarks can be largely solved by timing alone: a video-blind timer surpasses published mistake-detection results on Ego-MC-Bench, while published per-step systems and tested zero-shot models remain within the timing-based frontier.
Evidence-Contrastive Training pairs examples from the same recording at the same elapsed time, preventing models from using time as a shortcut.
A 2B model trained with ECT crossed the video-blind frontier on both benchmarks across all four seeds, using 209 QICD videos and about 15 GPU-hours.
Without adaptation, the model confirmed 59% of mistake-free steps on Ego-MC-Bench, compared with 30% for a published comparable-backbone model.

Its decisions reflect video content: it distinguished finished from unfinished steps in 90–92% of equal-time pairs, while time-based instruction statistics reached 65%; performance degraded substantially when recordings were swapped.

papers.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
papers.tldr: Proactive task assistants should base step-completion and mistake alerts on visual evidence rather than elapsed time; Evidence-Contrastive Training helps them do so.

papers.abstract: Can foundation models pretrained for generic numerical prediction serve as in-context robot learners? We investigate this question through tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are pretrained to infer input-output relationships from labeled examples in context. We introduce TabAct, which casts visual imitation as numerical prediction: frozen visual features and robot proprioception form the inputs, future action chunks form the targets, and each demonstration time step provides one labeled example that conditions a frozen TFM for closed-loop control. The predictor receives no robot-specific training or target-task fine-tuning. With one target-task demonstration available to each method, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest average success among all evaluated methods on both LIBERO and Meta-World, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points, respectively. Additional demonstrations improve control without updating model weights: with five demonstrations, success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object. These results demonstrate that generic numerical pretraining can provide an effective foundation for in-context robot learning.
authors: Zhen Xu, Hao-Run Cai, Heng-Zhuang Li, Si-Yang Liu, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye
bullets: Recasts visual imitation as numerical prediction: visual features and proprioception predict future action chunks.
Conditions a frozen TFM on labeled examples from demonstration time steps for closed-loop control.
With one demonstration, TabICLv2 achieves the best average success on LIBERO and Meta-World among evaluated methods.
It exceeds the strongest baseline by 20.9 percentage points on LIBERO and 5.8 on Meta-World.
Using five demonstrations reaches 94.2% success on LIBERO-Object, while model weights remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Continuous-time multi-agent path finding on roadmaps (MAPF$_R$) offers a principled way to coordinate robot fleets with geometric collision avoidance, yet its deployment on industrial automated guided vehicle (AGV) infrastructures remains challenging, as highly connected and redundant roadmaps amplify both safe-interval reasoning and multi-agent interaction handling. To bridge this gap, we formalize AGV-MAPF$_R$-CTC, a configuration-space variant of MAPF$_R$ with precomputed continuous-time conflicts that enables the reuse of MAPF$_R$ solvers for AGV fleet coordination with minimal changes. We then revisit continuous-time priority-based search (CPBS), identifying the boundary conditions required by its safe interval path planning (SIPP) low-level planner under priority-induced constraints and enabling earlier solution detection. As a central contribution, we analyze the structure of the priority search space, clarifying which agents are affected by each priority refinement and when replanning can be avoided. Building on this analysis, we introduce a novel algorithm, Lazy-CPBS, which materializes high-level nodes lazily: a child's plans are computed only when it is expanded, so siblings that are never expanded cost no low-level search. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks and on industrial AGV roadmaps imported from a proprietary digital-twin simulator show that CPBS-based solvers remain effective well beyond the agent counts reachable by optimal MAPF$_R$ solvers, while Lazy-CPBS substantially reduces CPBS overhead and offers the most consistent robustness/runtime trade-off across industrial layouts.
authors: Federico Signorile, Raffaele Carli, Alessandro Bertogli, Roberto Olmi, Sven Koenig, Mariagrazia Dotoli
bullets: Introduces AGV-MAPF$_R$-CTC, a configuration-space formulation with precomputed continuous-time conflicts.
Analyzes CPBS priority refinements, including affected agents and conditions for avoiding replanning.
Improves SIPP handling under priority-induced constraints and supports earlier solution detection.
Lazy-CPBS computes child plans only when high-level nodes are expanded, reducing wasted CPBS overhead.
Experiments on standard benchmarks and industrial AGV roadmaps show strong scalability and a consistent runtime–robustness trade-off; specific numerical gains are not reported.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of the AGV-MAPFR-CTC formulation. (a) Excerpt of a directed configuration-space roadmap −→ R, where each vertex v ∈ V represents an admissible AGV stopping configuration and the outgoing edges Φ(v) ⊆ E encode the feasible motion primitives from that configuration. (b) Example of an AGV-MAPFR-CTC instance, with sample precomputed continuous-time conflict annotations. Geometrically coincident vertices may still represent different states if they correspond to different headings, as illustrated by v6 and v7. The annotation (v7, e14, ∞) ∈ CVEC means that, as long as an agent occupies v7, any other agent starting move(e14, ·) would cause a collision. (c) Interpretation of the relative-delay semantics of an edgeedge CTC annotation: if one agent executes move(e7, t), then t + τ is the earliest safe start time for another agent to execute move(e4, ·); in the illustrated case, any start time in the interval [t, t + τ) would lead to a collision.
Figure 3: Example of priority-induced safe intervals used by SIPP.
Figure 4: Parallel CPBS high-level exploration from independent frontier nodes.

Figure 5: Replan-list construction in Lazy-CPBS. A conflict between agents 1 and 5 generates two children with opposite precedence relations. Adding 1 ≺ 5 requires replanning only agent 5, whereas adding 5 ≺ 1 affects agent 1 and its descendants in the pDAG, producing N ′′.ReplanList = (1, 2, 3). Since Lazy-CPBS prioritizes the child with the smaller ReplanList, the branch induced by 1 ≺ 5 is expanded first.

papers.abstract: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. Where geometry permits, the distance readout uses range measurements alone, while the rest of the prediction draws on all available inputs. Paired tests across five datasets reveal helpful and harmful sensor additions. MakeSense reduces negative fusion on MM-Fi. With lightweight adapters and per-dataset training, the same design improves UAV localization on MMAUD, cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Real, few-shot pose transfer to RELI11D, and command prediction on Humanoid-Everyday, where a world model trained on the frozen core's outputs forecasts future fused states more accurately than a linear baseline at longer tested horizons. MakeSense supports embodied sensing across human activity, aerial systems, robotics, and autonomous driving.
authors: Cheng-Ru Chou, Shih-Yu Lai, Pei-Lin Chiang, Shou-Po Tsai, Jing-Zhe Huang, Fukuharu Tanaka, Hirozumi Yamaguchi, Bing-Yu Chen, Yu-Lun Liu, Hsun-Ping Hsieh
bullets: Negative fusion can make embodied vision predictions worse when extra sensors are added, especially under degraded sensing.
The framework separates private sensor streams from shared bottleneck tokens and trains on paired full- and subset-sensor views.
A geometry-aware distance readout relies on range measurements, while other predictions use all available inputs.
Paired evaluations across five datasets identify helpful and harmful sensor additions, with reduced negative fusion on MM-Fi.
With lightweight adapters and dataset-specific training, MakeSense improves tasks spanning UAV localization, 3D detection, pose transfer, and command prediction.

figures.caption: Figure 3: MakeSense overview. Each present sensor passes through its own adapter, while a missing sensor (faded) contributes no token. The fusion core first processes every sensor separately, then mixes them through shared bottleneck tokens. Dataset heads read the fused tokens, and range-measuring sensors set the distance. A world model on the frozen fused state forecasts its future from robot commands.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment.
authors: Qiwei Liang, Zhengtu Liang, Minghao Lai, Yikeng Chen, Yiming Wang, Boyang Cai, Yuetong Fang, Taowen Wang, Baiqiao Yin, Tianxing Chen, Yue Chen, Jiaming Liang, Guangyu Chen, Shaolong Zhu, Daolin Ma, Renjing Xu
bullets: Evaluates 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks using a shared flow-matching policy.
Preserving patch tokens is critical; pooling each view into one token substantially reduces success.
Adaptation improves all tested encoder-policy pairs, and one shared policy retains most of the performance of separate policies with fewer updates.
An inverse-dynamics readout is among the strongest pre-policy measurements of representation quality.
Recognition, depth, correspondence, and other statistics are not sufficiently reliable to replace rollout evaluation; fine-tuning can affect metrics inconsistently.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces HIVE-Bench to evaluate patch-level visual representations for egocentric robot manipulation, demonstrating the importance of dense token representations over pooled vectors for policy learning.
papers.title: HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: HIVE-Bench shows that dense patch tokens from egocentric vision encoders are important for bimanual robot manipulation, while standard representation metrics do not reliably predict policy success.

papers.abstract: Active 3D reconstruction aims to allocate a sparse view budget to recover complete geometry and high-fidelity renderings. However, existing methods degrade sharply in multi-room homes: myopic next-best-view scoring gives transit no credit for distant rooms and over-polishes irreducible nearby residuals, whereas dense mappers reach far rooms only by streaming thousands of frames. We propose ROAM-GS, a training-free active multi-room reconstruction framework that couples persistent goals with selective views: each decision selects a goal and a variable-horizon prefix toward it, capturing only at its endpoint. A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores poses by projecting post-update defects and viewing directions. Persistent goals credit transit with their remaining value and are released once arrivals stop measurably improving them. Without per-scene tuning, ROAM-GS achieves state-of-the-art multi-room reconstruction while preserving single-room Replica fidelity, raising mean coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and from 47% to 96% (+11.7 dB PSNR) on HM3D, and matching 90-minute dense mapping using $173\times$ fewer views.
authors: Jiawei Jiang, Haonan Zhou, Wendi Hu, Jiabei Hu, Yina Xiang, Kaiyue Zhou, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Addresses myopic view selection, which neglects distant rooms and over-focuses on nearby irreducible errors.
Uses a training-free planner that selects a goal and a variable-length transit path, capturing only at the endpoint.
A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores candidate poses using projected post-update defects and viewing directions.
Persistent goals assign value to transit and are released when further arrivals stop improving reconstruction.
Raises coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and 47% to 96% on HM3D, while matching dense mapping with 173× fewer views.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ROAM-GS. Each posed RGB-D capture updates the Gaussian map Gt, the occupancy grid Vt, and the Surface Reconstruction Memory Mt, whose cells store observed directions Ds and score query views by new-angle and defect gains without rendering. Persistent goals (top) keep a target region rg through search, travel, and observe until an arrival capture measurably improves it. Selective views (bottom) truncate the path to the goal view at variable horizons: only the prefix endpoint (orange) is captured, while query poses (hollow) are credited from memory. The joint score S = B + V selects the goal and prefix, and the agent captures once at qπ .

papers.title: Go Far, Look Less: Active Multi-Room Reconstruction with Persistent Goals and Selective Views

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies are often trained with static domain randomization for real-world deployment. However, real-world environments often exhibit unmodeled dynamic variations, such as payload changes or friction shifts, that lie outside the randomization distribution, leading to performance degradation upon deployment. We propose a framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by adapting a learned dynamics model to the deployed target conditions, with a concurrent teacher-student paradigm applied to both the policy and dynamics model. This framework integrates the dynamics model into an on-policy reinforcement learning pipeline, letting the performance of the policy align with the empirical target dynamics. Experimental validations on bipedal locomotion tasks demonstrate competitive adaptability under extreme physical variations, including a payload reaching 80% of self-weight and an oil-lubricated low-friction surface.
authors: Rui Dai, Shunpeng Yang, Zhen Fu, Maolin Lei, Jiaqi Song, Hua Chen, Nikos Tsagarakis
bullets: Static domain randomization can fail under unseen payload and friction changes.
The method adapts a learned dynamics model to deployed target conditions.
A concurrent teacher–student scheme updates both the policy and dynamics model.
The adapted dynamics model is integrated into on-policy reinforcement learning.
Bipedal experiments show adaptability under payloads up to 80% of self-weight and oil-lubricated low-friction surfaces.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the framework. The pipeline operates in four phases. (a) Simulator online pre-training, where a nominal policy is trained via a teacher-student architecture, while a dynamics model is learned concurrently using aggregated off-policy data. (b) Real world data collection with the pre-trained behavior policies. (c) The aggregated simulation and real data are used to fine-tune the dynamics model. (d) The dynamics model creates a high-fidelity surrogate to fine-tune the policy against physical variations.
Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed training architecture. The architecture consists of a concurrent teacher-student policy learning module (bottom) and dynamics modeling modules (top).

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects N in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on N. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all N objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget.
authors: Paul Mattes, Ayman Abdeldayem, Denis Shcherba, Wojciech Samek, Marc Toussaint
bullets: Addresses policy degradation and changing state dimensions as object counts exceed training ranges.
Uses a selection policy to choose the next object and a local-view warping policy to produce affine multipliers and offsets for skill inputs and actions.
Trains only the selection and warping policies with PPO, treating the pretrained skill as a black box.
Evaluated on cube arrangement with gantry and Franka Panda robots; training with at most nine cubes generalized to up to thirty on the gantry.
Compared approaches—including fine-tuning, local-view learning without warping, and an entity transformer—collapsed within their training counts under the same budget.

papers.selection_reason: Learned manipulation policy for object-count generalization via warping a frozen skill.
papers.title: Object Count Generalization Is an Interface Problem: Warping a Frozen Skill Instead of Retraining It
papers.tldr: WAVE extends a frozen single-object manipulation skill to many objects by warping its observations and actions, enabling zero-shot count generalization without retraining the skill.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved significant milestones, yet its reliance on the i.i.d. assumption renders it vulnerable to real-world distribution shifts. While Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm for on-the-fly enhancement, its application to driving is hindered by two barriers: (i) multi-task adaptation dependency, where updates to upstream perception also affect downstream planning, while perception confidence alone does not directly assess these downstream effects; and (ii) continuous adaptation instability, where recursive online updates over long horizons cause compounding parameter drift. To address these challenges, we propose P2-TTA, a plug-and-play TTA framework for the continual adaptation of end-to-end driving models. P2-TTA coordinates adaptation through a joint objective combining perception entropy minimization with a retrospective temporal planning consistency objective derived from observed ego motion. To stabilize online updates, we use an EMA teacher as a moving parameter reference and reject candidate updates that increase historical planning loss. Extensive experiments across multiple models demonstrate that, by updating an average of 0.11 per mille of parameters with an average adaptation time of 19.9 ms on different backbones, P2-TTA achieves average recovery rates of 36.4%, 30.0%, and 9.3% for L2, collision rate, and PDMS, respectively, under severe distribution shifts. Under a shared perception-planning objective, P2-TTA achieves the highest L2 and collision recovery among the compared TTA baselines on UniAD.

papers.abstract: We introduce EgoDepth-Bench, comprising 941,233 synchronized samples collected across 37 distinct physical environments. Each sample combines six calibrated RGB views with metric depth in the native fisheye view, reconstructed from five active-infrared stereo modules. A calibrated ball-bar confirms millimeter-level geometric accuracy, with a median error of 1.27 mm on a known sphere spacing. Environment-held-out splits enable evaluation of generalization to unseen environments. Across monocular, stereo, and multi-view models, the benchmark measures both depth accuracy and prediction coverage, including on hands and objects. Fine-tuning MapAnything on EgoDepth-Bench reduces metric AbsRel from 0.708 to 0.091 and scale-aligned AbsRel from 0.327 to 0.072 on unseen environments. These results demonstrate that EgoDepth-Bench provides effective supervision and enables rigorous evaluation of metric and relative depth estimation in egocentric manipulation. The project page provides the evaluation code and interactive RGB-depth sequences.
authors: Yuan Gao, Dongchen Wei, Xinyang Lin, Shuhua Cao, Xueliang Guo, Zhuohan Li, Yihao Wang

Evaluates depth on hands and objects, targeting egocentric manipulation scenarios.
Fine-tuning MapAnything substantially improves metric and scale-aligned AbsRel on unseen environments, from 0.708 to 0.091 and 0.327 to 0.072, respectively.

papers.abstract: General-purpose manipulation robots must acquire new skills over time without forgetting prior ones or retraining from scratch. We present a continual learning framework that represents each skill as a dedicated expert sub- network in a Progressive Neural Network (PNN). New tasks reuse prior knowledge through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on lateral connections controlled by learnable per-parent gates, enabling explicit attenuation of individual transfer paths while reducing the parameter cost of dense PNN laterals. For long-horizon deployment, a frozen local large language model decomposes natural-language instructions into sub-tasks, routes them to suitable experts, and requests a new expert only when the library is insufficient. Using a shared task-space action interface, we evaluate the framework on twelve MetaWorld tasks and in a Sawyer-to-Panda-to-UR5e cross-embodiment transfer experiment, showing improved task success relative to learning from scratch when demonstrations are limited. Real-robot manipulation experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework supports compositional execution and expert orchestration.
authors: Nilay Kushawaha, Abdalla Swikir, Fares Abu-Dakka
bullets: Represents each skill as a dedicated expert in a Progressive Neural Network, preserving previously learned skills.
Uses LoRA-based lateral connections with learnable gates to selectively transfer knowledge while reducing dense-lateral parameter costs.
A frozen local LLM decomposes natural-language instructions, routes subtasks to experts, and requests new experts when needed.
Evaluated on twelve MetaWorld tasks and cross-embodiment Sawyer, Panda, and UR5e transfer, with improved success over learning from scratch under limited demonstrations.
Real-robot experiments demonstrate compositional manipulation and expert orchestration.

papers.abstract: Robust visual servoing during robotic grasping remains challenging, as approach-phase occlusion frequently disrupts closed-loop control. To address this, we present an active observation framework in which one arm of an existing dual-arm platform carries an RGB-D camera as an active observer while the other executes grasping. The observer repositions to maintain or recover a shared target-gripper view within the feasible shared-view workspace. Occlusion during the final approach is particularly acute: fixed eye-to-hand lacks an active recovery mechanism once the target is hidden, while eye-in-hand can suffer from self-occlusion and sensitivity to hand-eye calibration. The observer first uses an active two-phase viewpoint strategy to align high-precision RGB-D axes with task-relevant error components. If visibility later degrades, an occlusion-triggered exploration module pauses the worker arm and scores candidate viewpoints by observation quality to recover a shared target-gripper view. Because both objects are detected in a single RGB-D image, the resulting Relative Servo Error avoids differencing two independently transformed target and gripper estimates. We evaluate the system on a dual 6-DoF Piper platform using an open-vocabulary detector with text prompts, without task-specific fine-tuning or demonstrations. Across 50 randomized trials per object, the system achieves 94% grasp success versus 76% for a reactive viewpoint baseline and 64% for a fixed camera. On triggered severe-occlusion trials, recovery takes $1.8 \pm 0.6$ s on average.
authors: Zhilun Hu, Yuqi Cheng, Yuxiang Tan, Wenpan Li, Weiming Shen
bullets: Occlusion during final grasp approach can disrupt closed-loop control, especially for fixed or eye-in-hand cameras.
A dual-arm setup uses one arm to reposition an RGB-D camera while the other performs the grasp.
A two-phase viewpoint strategy aligns observations with task-relevant errors, while occlusion-triggered exploration searches for recovery views.
A shared RGB-D image directly estimates relative servo error, avoiding differences between independently transformed detections.
In 50 randomized trials per object, grasp success reached 94%, compared with 76% for a reactive viewpoint baseline and 64% for a fixed camera; severe-occlusion recovery averaged 1.8 ± 0.6 seconds.

papers.abstract: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. authors: Hiroaki Honda, Koya Sakamoto, Shu Morikuni, Yusuke Iwasawa, Taiki Miyanishi
bullets: Benchmarks 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks across 16 skills and 13 speeds from 0.10–0.40 m/s, with matched static counterparts and randomized scenes.

Six models peak at intermediate speeds and often act for the average training speed rather than the observed belt speed.
Past frames improve success by 10–40 percentage points for three models; ground-truth or image-estimated speed improves all tested models.
Temporal context helps mainly when speed is more linearly decodable, including in models pretrained on multiple frames.

papers.abstract: Behavior-cloning policies show strong ability in sequential control by generating coherent multi-step action chunks, yet their purely imitative objective limits zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks. While offline reinforcement learning offers principled policy improvement, existing methods either require task-specific reward supervision or remain tied to a specific actor during critic training or policy deployment, inflating training cost and restricting cross-policy generalization. We observe that evaluating actions under the data-collecting behavior largely preserves their relative value ordering across target policies, offering a way around actor coupling. Combining this property with reward-free successor prediction, we propose Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations (ABI) to learn multi-horizon action-chunk representations from unlabeled trajectories without reward supervision or actor training. At test time, pairing the frozen representation with lightweight task readouts forms a chunk critic that guides target policies without parameter updates and transfers directly across distinct unseen policies. Our analysis establishes when the value ordering is preserved across policies and when selecting among proposed chunks improves closed-loop return. Across 65 locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks, ABI's chunk critic guides weak imitation policies to match or surpass zero-shot RL baselines with high sample efficiency, outperforms existing zero-shot critics on identical proposals, and improves externally trained RL actors without retraining. From raw pixels, ABI delivers substantial guidance gains and surpasses prior zero-shot RL baselines on visual manipulation, highlighting its potential for visuomotor control.
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Jianming Ma, Xing Gao, Chunhua Shen

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models excel at individual robotic skills, yet integrating heterogeneous skills into a single policy remains a key challenge for general-purpose robotic control, especially in whole-body tasks with differing manipulation and locomotion requirements. Common multi-skill integration strategies, such as joint fine-tuning and parameter merging, can induce unintended actions during closed-loop execution, severely degrading individual skills. Task-conditioned analysis of expert updates reveals response energy concentrated in a few dominant directions and opposing expert responses along high-energy directions within a shared, task-relevant response subspace. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, combining response-space regularization, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation. During independent expert fine-tuning, G-isometry constrains update-response gains within task-activation subspaces; the expert parameters are then statically merged into a student with preliminary multitask capabilities. Fine-tuned task experts serve as teachers, providing velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate action-flow states visited by the student to calibrate residual behavioral deviations. Experiments with two VLA backbones show strong, balanced humanoid skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, outperforming joint fine-tuning and multitask reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining robustness under perturbations.
authors: Le Yang, Haoyang Lyu, Honglei Jin, Wenshuo Chen, Jiawei Liang, Wenqiang Wang, Yutao Yue, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Multi-skill integration is difficult because joint fine-tuning and parameter merging can degrade individual skills during closed-loop control.
The method analyzes task-conditioned expert updates and identifies dominant, sometimes opposing directions in a shared response subspace.
GeoMerge-OPD combines response-space regularization via G-isometry, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation from independently fine-tuned task experts.
Experiments across two VLA backbones show balanced skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, including under perturbations.
The approach is evaluated on the reported benchmarks and focuses on mitigating behavioral interference during skill integration.

papers.abstract: Coordinating vessels through the shared waterways of busy ports grows more challenging as vessel traffic increases. Port authorities need realistic simulations to assess how arrival schedules, anchorage assignments, and routes affect vessel throughput and navigation safety. Existing AIS-based trajectory models predict a vessel's track from its past trajectory in an open-loop fashion. They do not simulate step-by-step responses to other ships or test whether a vessel collides or reaches its goal. To address this problem, we introduce JaxNaviSim, a data-driven simulator and learning benchmark coupling Automatic Identification System (AIS) data with fast, controllable traffic simulation, in which learned models steer vessels through recorded traffic. First, we release a dataset of ~141 million AIS records from over 30K vessels across eight high-density regions of the Singapore Strait, among the world's busiest waterways, with ~6.7 million vessel-hours. Unlike several existing AIS datasets which mostly cover open seas, ours captures close-quarters vessel traffic in the narrow strait. Second, we define a navigation task for each recorded vessel trajectory. A model steers that vessel every 10 s from its recorded state to its anchoring point or region exit, while surrounding ships follow their recorded tracks or are steered by the model. We implement a JAX simulator that runs these tasks in large batches on a GPU. We also incorporate multiple vessel dynamics models and sea surface currents. Finally, we benchmark imitation learning (IL), offline and online RL, and include Predictive Action Refinement (PAR) as a safety baseline that cuts collision rates to 1-3%. The comparison shows that low tracking error does not ensure arrival, and learned policies can reach most destinations yet collide in 20-45% of episodes.
authors: Quang Anh Pham, Janaka Chathuranga Brahmanage, Hue Tse Leong, Akshat Kumar, Tien Anh Mai, Siu Loon Hoe, Venky Shankararaman
bullets: Provides approximately 141 million AIS records from over 30,000 vessels across eight high-density Singapore Strait regions, covering close-quarters traffic.
Defines step-by-step navigation tasks in which vessels steer every 10 seconds toward anchorage points or region exits while interacting with surrounding traffic.
Implements large-batch GPU simulation in JAX with multiple vessel dynamics models and sea-surface currents.
Benchmarks imitation learning, offline and online reinforcement learning, and Predictive Action Refinement as a safety baseline.
Policies reach most destinations but collide in 20–45% of episodes; Predictive Action Refinement reduces collision rates to 1–3%.

Figure 12: The forward law of each dynamics model, as a vector sum. From the position pk, the commanded displacement is blue and the commanded turn green, while the drift δk contributed by the sea current is red. Their result, grey, is the step over ground the model produces, ending at the solid hull; the dashed ray is the bow f(ψk). Delta commands displacement on both axes and turns independently of it. Port-glide instead takes its heading from the AIS recording rather than choosing it, and can only push along that bow. Any sideways motion in the recording is therefore out of reach, so the vessel ends up somewhere other than the recorded pk+1, drawn as a dashed hull, indicated in pale red (Equation 27). The other three reproduce the recorded step ∆pk = pk+1 − pk exactly. Water-track turns first and defines the bow as the direction of travel through the water, and Nomoto does the same with a first-order lag, so that its commanded turn aψk (dotted) and the turn ∆ψk actually applied (grey) differ.

papers.abstract: Learning robot manipulation from egocentric human videos requires accurate metric 3D hand motion. Recent methods leverage pretrained video diffusion model (VDM) priors to recover occluded hands directly from full-frame videos, but their appearance-based depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, a geometry-driven framework that reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into fine-grained geometric constraint solving. Specifically, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting, which recover metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joints and the metric structure of MANO hands, while leveraging temporal observations across the clip. Since the lifting relies on these 2D joints, to improve robustness under occlusion and image truncation, we further develop Confidence-Gated Fusion to adaptively combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions according to localization confidence. Finally, we enhance the VDM backbone to better capture spatial-temporal representations and produce the per-frame 2D joint and MANO predictions that both steps rely on. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets demonstrate that ViDiHand2 consistently outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82x compared with the best baseline on each metric, while running at 57 FPS. The code is available at https://github.com/NTUYWANG103/ViDiHand.
authors: Yuxi Wang, Yufei Liu, Chengkai Jin, Qingyue Chen, Wenqi Ouyang, Tianyi Wei, Kerui Ren, Siyuan Huang, Zhiqi Shen, Hongsheng Li, Xingang Pan
bullets: Addresses poor cross-camera generalization of appearance-based hand depth regression in VDM-based methods.
Uses Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting to enforce consistency between 2D joints and metric MANO hand geometry across video clips.
Introduces Confidence-Gated Fusion to combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions under occlusion and truncation.
Enhances the video diffusion backbone to predict per-frame 2D joints and MANO parameters with improved spatial-temporal representations.
On seven public datasets, outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82×, while running at 57 FPS.

papers.abstract: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos. Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.

VeriIDM infers actions from verified videos using scene context, gripper details, and frame-to-frame motion.
Across five real-world tasks, synthetic data improved all four evaluated policies, with more trajectories yielding further gains.

papers.abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our \ours{} is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, \ours{} with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from \textbf{\color{blue}57.5\%} to \textbf{\color{blue}70.5\%} and preserves \textbf{\color{blue}90.4\%} of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy.
authors: Yihao Shen, Yuxuan Chen, Xuantong Liu, Jun Gao, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Addresses multi-skill task failures caused by wrong target selection and lost progress tracking.

On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, success increased from 57.5% to 70.5%, preserving 90.4% of standalone successes and rescuing 37 of 85 failures.
The same fixed supervision rules improved four other frozen policies by 8–10 percentage points on a shared 50-scene subset.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | How RoboHarness-Zero divides control between a frozen VLA and a supervising VLM. Execution loop: the VLA receives the full task instruction and controls the robot by default. VLM supervisor: at each checkpoint, the VLM checks progress on the current substage. If the substage advances, the policy continues. If it stalls, the VLM rewords the instruction and the policy keeps control. After two verified physical failures, the VLM can take over for a bounded number of steps before handing control back. Calibration: a profiling run of the policy alone sets how long the VLM waits and how long a takeover may last. Only the VLA, its adapter, and this calibration change with the policy.

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
authors: Hyeonjae Kim, Jeongsol Kim, Sunwoo Park, Chanyu Moon, Yoojin Oh, Youngjun Jun, Kyumin Choi, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Asynchronous action generation reduces latency but stale observations cause performance degradation, especially during failed policy rollouts.

With a 10-step delay, SmolVLA success rises from 70.2% with demonstration training to 78.7% with DelayOPSD, versus 70.4% for naive asynchronous execution.
DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among compared methods across LIBERO and Kinetix and improves real-robot success from 46% to 62%, without extra deployment modules.

papers.abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.

papers.abstract: This report presents a comprehensive pipeline for developing an end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving model for the Physical AI AV Track. The framework consists of data curation, HD map auto-labelling, data-driven imitation learning, and simulator-based reinforcement learning. To ensure safety in the closed-loop setting, we introduce a selection-based E2E planning approach that leverages object detection and BEV segmentation to filter out trajectory candidates likely to cause collisions or off-road driving. Trained on NVIDIA NuRec and the NVIDIA PAI-AV dataset, our method scores a fixed vocabulary of trajectory candidates for collision, drivable-area compliance, and progress learned from simulated rollouts, and selects the best candidate that passes the filter. This design highlights the effectiveness of combining E2E planning with perception-based trajectory filtering for safe and reliable closed-loop autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DexDuet. Inside πθ , two per-hand policies share one network, and each maps its own observation o and the partner observation z to an action a. (b) Two interaction rewards compare each robot hand with the human hand relative to the object. The hand graph reward compares the palm and finger directions and the fingertip gaps, and the hand-object contact reward compares the distance and the closest point of each hand region to the object. (c) A-RSI gives each segment b of the demonstration its own assistance level hb, which it lowers (green) or raises (red), never above a ceiling h̄(u) that decreases over the updates u. Episodes start from states that the policy has reached, and their start segment is drawn from p(b), which favors the segments with a high failure rate fb.

papers.abstract: Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) does not change the optimal policy, but how much it speeds up learning depends on the potential and on effects outside this guarantee. We analyse how PBRS changes the one-step reward while it preserves the discounted return: a per-step $(\gamma-1)\Phi$ term, the terminal-state rule, a constant shift of the potential, and positive cycles in a bonus that is not potential-based. We then measure these consequences in pre-registered experiments with a PPO agent. The agent has a limited egocentric view and is tested on two MiniGrid navigation tasks (160 runs, 10 seeds per condition). On LavaCrossing, a geodesic (BFS) potential learned faster than both the sparse baseline and a Euclidean potential with a 7x7 and a 5x5 view (AUC difference +0.27 to +0.39, Holm p between 0.007 and 0.0499). The Euclidean potential did not differ from the baseline. In 20 runs with a non-potential bonus, none of the agents learned the task. The Euclidean potential caused more than twice as many deaths in lava during early training. View size did not detectably change the benefit of shaping. With a 5x5 view on SimpleCrossing, some BFS runs got stuck in loops and never learned; shifting the potential did not remove this, so the per-step term alone does not explain it.
bullets: Analyzes per-step reward effects, terminal-state handling, constant potential shifts, and failures from non-potential bonuses.
In PPO navigation with limited egocentric views, a BFS/geodesic potential accelerated learning on LavaCrossing versus sparse and Euclidean shaping.
Euclidean shaping matched the sparse baseline and caused more than twice as many early lava deaths.
Non-potential bonuses failed completely in the tested runs, while view size did not detectably change shaping benefits.
On SimpleCrossing, some BFS agents became stuck in loops; shifting the potential did not resolve this.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.
authors: Puzhen Yuan, Yanjiang Guo, Yichen Liu, Xiang Zhu, Qingzhou Lu, Chenxin Liu, Tun Ban, Haodong Yan, Zhide Zhong, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Egocentric data transfer improves with greater diversity, trajectory alignment, and detailed language annotations.
Scaling primarily benefits end-effector translation prediction rather than fine-grained finger movement.
WAMs perform better with limited egocentric data, while VLAs gain more as egocentric data scale increases.
The study offers practical guidance for processing and co-training egocentric and robot data.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Which data processing and co-training designs improve transfer? Complete episodes, detailed captions, and the dataset diversity yield lower wrist translation error on both robot holdouts for both model families. This indicates that data diversity and alignment between trajectories and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Moreover, fixed-step sampling yields lower error for the VLA, and event-level sampling yields lower error for the WAM.

Figure 7. Which action components benefit most from scaling egocentric data? We measure mean squared error (MSE) separately for wrist translation, wrist rotation, and fingertip pose on high-quality, held-out robot trajectories. Across both robot domains and model families, wrist translation MSE generally decreases as egocentric data scale, while wrist rotation and fingertip pose errors show no consistent decline. We hypothesize that due to human–robot embodiment gap and errors in estimating actions limit transfer primarily to large-scale motions such as wrist translation, with less benefit for the finger movements and wrist rotations.

Figure 4. Does scaling egocentric data improve robot learning? We pretrain the VLA (left) and WAM (right) with 1%, 3%, 10%, 30%, and 100% of the egocentric human data while keeping robot training exposure and the optimization budget fixed. We evaluate wrist translation MSE on held-out trajectories from Bimanual XHand and RoboCasa-GR1. All four model–domain pairs show a consistent downward trend, indicating effective human-to-robot transfer in EgoStudy.

Figure 6. Do pretraining gains carry over to robot control? RoboCasa-GR1 task success increases after posttraining for both model families, consistent with the decrease in pretraining validation loss. Gray dashed lines mark the corresponding baselines without pretraining.

Figure 9. How does backbone choice affect scaling gains between VLA and WAM? The wrist translation error decreases to the same extent across different VLAs, indicating that the 4B backbone is already capable of effectively extracting features shared between the egocentric and robot data. When the backbone of WAM is changed to 5B, its human-to-robot capability declines indicating that WAM relies more heavily on a powerful video backbone to assimilate egocentric data.

Figure 8. How do VLA and WAM visual features change with scale? As egocentric data scale, relative separation R between human and robot features decreases in both robot domains for the VLA but shows no consistent decrease across the WAM layers examined. We hypothesize that human and robot features align more closely in our VLA because it only needs to output actions in a shared action space. Our WAM must also predict future video, which may encourage it to retain visual differences between human and robot hands.

Figure 3. Pretraining samples allocation. Egocentric datasets receive 75% of samples, with probabilities proportional to the square root of their filtered durations; VITRA aggregates three subsets. The sampling probabilities of Bimanual XHand (20%) and RoboCasa-GR1 (5%) are fixed across experiments.

papers.abstract: Coordinating locomotion and dexterous manipulation is fundamental to humanoid robots operating in human environments. A key challenge is learning motion priors from diverse data and using them effectively for coordinated robot control. We present CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive feature extraction. CHAMP pretrains a vision-language model to predict future body and hand motion from approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot data. A shared motion representation enables unified whole-body motion learning across embodiments from datasets with body annotations, hand annotations, or both. To ground these motion priors in robot control, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) and train it on replay data generated using the target controller. Through sparse routing, CAE adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from multiple layers of the pretrained model to jointly generate body and hand actions. In experiments, CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks with a Unitree G1, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings. In particular, CHAMP achieves 70.0% success on the long-horizon popcorn-serving task, compared with 40.0% for the best-performing baseline.

Achieves 84.8% success across seven simulated tasks and 91.4% across seven real-world tasks on a Unitree G1.
Reaches 70.0% success on a long-horizon popcorn-serving task, versus 40.0% for the best evaluated baseline.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models have made substantial progress, yet reliable closed-loop driving in complex traffic remains challenging. Beyond improving individual models, system-level orchestration offers a complementary approach by coordinating driving capabilities and computation. We introduce ROSE-Drive (Runtime Orchestration and System Evolution), a model-agnostic framework that jointly orchestrates driving execution and computation. It coordinates frozen driving models with driving skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers. A distilled vision-language model (VLM) proposes driving tasks and scene relations. Shared physical state and persistent tasks support capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling. The orchestrator combines model and skill outputs across control channels, maintains task responsibility through handover, and uses execution feedback to select controllers, reuse valid motion references, and schedule model inference. Offline revisions use execution records to refine skills and their coordination through a stable task interface. Successive system stages inherit these revisions while model, perception, and VLM weights remain fixed. Evaluations with four driving models on Bench2Drive v0.0.3, Bench2Drive v0.0.4, and Fail2Drive show accumulated capability and transfer before target-benchmark revision. On held-out Longest6, driving score (DS) rises from 25 to 52 for AutoMoT and from 22 to 47 for SimLingo across system stages, while both systems skip new model inference on over 71% of control steps.

Across multiple benchmarks and four driving models, held-out Longest6 driving scores improved substantially across system stages.
More than 71% of control steps skipped new model inference for both reported systems, reducing runtime computation demand.

papers.abstract: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. The relative-capability principle guides these choices by relating the benefit of additional computation or intervention to its cost. After open-loop initialization, dual-loop evolution trains the Router, agent, and self-scheduler from closed-loop experience while failure-driven updates refine skills and execution feedback. AgentMoT achieves state-of-the-art results on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4, with 94.48/92.33 driving score and 85.45/82.73% success rate, respectively. With skills disabled, learned routing improves over the strongest fixed pathway by 1.79 driving-score points and 4.09 percentage points of success rate on v0.0.3. Ablation studies further show gains from closed-loop agent learning, two-view queries, and event-triggered wake-up.
authors: Qihang Huang, Collister Chua, YuJie Yan, Shiyu Fang, Zhan Chen, Haoran Xu, Zirui Li, Chen Lv

Learns from closed-loop driving experience, with execution feedback triggering wake-up requests and failure-driven updates refining skills.
Achieves 94.48/92.33 driving scores and 85.45/82.73% success rates on Bench2Drive v0.0.3/v0.0.4.

papers.abstract: Efficient robotic manipulation requires temporally coordinated actions with low inference latency. Multi-step diffusion and flow policies progressively refine action trajectories but require costly iterative inference, whereas one-step policies eliminate iterative trajectory refinement to reduce inference cost. We introduce **SOAR**, a structure-guided one-step generative policy that improves action quality while preserving one-step efficiency. SOAR predicts an observation-conditioned discrete cosine transform (DCT) representation of future actions, capturing temporal variations across multiple frequency bands to provide explicit guidance from key temporal structural information. Unlike velocity-parameterized one-step flow policies that recover clean actions indirectly from a predicted velocity field, SOAR directly generates clean action trajectories in action space. This aligns the model output with the executable control target and provides a direct interface for structural calibration. The predicted structure further corrects the generated trajectory according to their spectral discrepancy, without requiring an additional evaluation of the generative backbone. During training, the corresponding MeanFlow velocity is derived from the calibrated clean action and used for consistency learning, while an endpoint objective aligns training with the pure-noise condition used for one-step inference. Across 53 Adroit and Meta-World tasks, SOAR achieves 83.9% overall success with only 8.7 ms inference latency. When applied to the VLA model, {\pi}0.5, SOAR further achieves 97.2% on LIBERO and 71.7% on RoboTwin 2.0. Real-world experiments and extensive ablations further validate its effectiveness and efficiency.
authors: Di Xin, Mingfei Han, Genming Cui, Yuanxiang Chen, Xiaolong Wu, Siyu Ning, Xiaojun Chang, Zhihui Li
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of iterative diffusion and flow policies while retaining temporal coordination.
Predicts observation-conditioned future actions in a discrete cosine transform (DCT) representation across multiple frequency bands.
Directly generates clean action trajectories in action space, rather than indirectly recovering them from velocity predictions.
Uses spectral discrepancy to calibrate trajectories without an additional generative-backbone evaluation, with consistency and endpoint objectives during training.
Reports 83.9% success across 53 Adroit and Meta-World tasks at 8.7 ms latency; with π0.5, it reaches 97.2% on LIBERO and 71.7% on RoboTwin 2.0.
