papers.abstract: Physics-based human-object interaction (HOI) has enabled multiple characters to cooperatively transport objects, but existing cooperative controllers largely assume homogeneous embodiments and predefined interaction tasks. We ask whether a single physics-based policy can enable cooperation across diverse embodiments, team compositions, and interaction skills. We present MorphHOI, a decentralised framework built on a key insight: effective heterogeneous cooperation requires a unified representation across embodiments while accounting for differences in their physical capabilities. To realise this insight, we introduce a canonical body interface that unifies observation and action spaces, together with an embodiment-conditioned transformer that adapts cooperative decisions to the physical capabilities of each agent and its teammates. To extend cooperation to new interaction skills, we reuse the learned cooperative policy through task-specific tokens and lightweight adaptation, preserving its original capabilities. Our framework achieves success rates of up to 96.7\% on seen embodiments, 95.6\% on unseen embodiments, and 91.4\% on novel payloads. Furthermore, the learned cooperation extends to diverse interaction skills with high success rates, including box carrying, transport on stairs, and waypoint following, while preserving previously acquired cooperative capabilities.
authors: Zhihao Cao, Tianxu An, Chenhao Li, Chenyangguang Zhang, Stelian Coros, Marco Hutter
bullets: Addresses the limitation of prior cooperative controllers that assume homogeneous agents and predefined tasks.
Uses a canonical body interface to unify observations and actions across different embodiments.
Applies an embodiment-conditioned transformer to account for each agent’s physical capabilities and teammates.
Extends the policy to new skills using task-specific tokens and lightweight adaptation while preserving prior abilities.
Reports success rates up to 96.7% on seen embodiments, 95.6% on unseen embodiments, and 91.4% on novel payloads, including box carrying, stairs, and waypoint following.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment? We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context. To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.
authors: Haihong Hao, Lei Chen, Mingfei Han, Chenglong Yan, Dong An, Yuqiang Yang, Changlin Li, Minghao Guo, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating robots without requiring shared policies or coordinated actions.
Aggregates partial egocentric observations into a shared environmental understanding for decentralized navigation.
Stores observations in shared memory, retrieves relevant spatio-temporal context, and encodes it with a predictive latent world model.
Injects the resulting shared representations as tokens into downstream navigation agents.
Improves navigation across specialized VLN and general vision-language agents while preserving single-agent capabilities.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.
authors: Yunhe Zhang, Long Gao, Yuedong Fu, Gang He, Li Xu, Chang Wu, Pengyu Li
bullets: Addresses incorrect cross-view associations and fragmented information about the same entity caused by 2D feature-based interactions.
Uses Cross-View Association Modeling to impose spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space.
Uses Entity Coherence Organization to combine local observations into coherent 3D entity evidence.
Uses Consistent Action Conditioning to guide actions with task-relevant, cross-view-consistent 3D evidence.
Evaluated on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks, where it is reported as effective and competitive.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically rely on vision-language model (VLM) features as the primary perceptual source for action prediction, showing strong generalization across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. Although VLM features can identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, precise manipulation also requires understanding where task-relevant entities are located within the spatial layout, how their geometric structure constrains physical interaction, and when spatial or geometric information should make a greater contribution to action prediction. To this end, we introduce {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA to organize VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. Specifically, {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA retains VLM-based semantic entity perception which and further introduces spatial distance perception where and geometric structure perception how with adaptive spatial-geometric guidance when to enrich the perceptual information available for action prediction. Experiments across real-world settings and simulation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA.
authors: Yunhe Zhang, Long Gao, Yuedong Fu, Gang He, Li Xu, Chang Wu, Songyuheng Gao
bullets: VLM features identify which entities matter, but may lack information about their location and physical structure.
The framework organizes perception around which, where, how, and when.
It adds spatial distance perception and geometric structure perception to semantic entity understanding.
An adaptive spatial-geometric guidance mechanism determines when these cues should influence action prediction.
Experiments in real-world and simulated settings demonstrate its effectiveness and superior performance.

papers.abstract: Adversarial object attacks pose a threat to BEV-based 3D object detectors in autonomous driving. Existing attacks typically target a single modality, coordinate camera and LiDAR observations at the current timestamp, or model temporal persistence mainly in camera streams. Without a unified construction of current and historical observations, attacks can leave part of the detector's accumulated evidence unsuppressed, limiting their effectiveness. In this paper, we propose AdvMTO, a 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) framework for suppressing detection of persistent adversarial objects. Its oriented surfels encode appearance, geometry, and opacity in one object state, from which camera images and scanline LiDAR returns are generated. AdvMTO then constructs current and historical inputs through detector-native processing, regenerating LiDAR returns in each native source sweep for fusion detectors. We optimize bounded appearance perturbations for each detector, propagating gradients through historical BEV memory for temporal camera detectors. For fusion detectors, bounded geometry refinement along local normals further perturbs both sensing modalities. Experiments on nuScenes demonstrate effective suppression of traffic-cone detection across three BEV detectors. Temporal ablations further highlight the importance of detector-native history modeling for both attack construction and optimization.
authors: Zhiyang Cui, Hao Tan, Ruonan Li, Shibin Wu, Junjian Zhang, Hong'an Lin, Zhaoquan Gu
bullets: Targets a gap in attacks that fail to jointly suppress current and historical camera–LiDAR evidence.
Represents objects with oriented surfels encoding appearance, geometry, and opacity, enabling camera and scanline LiDAR generation.
Builds detector-native current and historical inputs, including native-source LiDAR sweeps and temporal BEV memory.
Optimizes bounded appearance perturbations, with additional local-normal geometry refinement for fusion detectors.
Experiments on nuScenes show effective traffic-cone suppression across three BEV detectors; temporal ablations emphasize native history modeling.

papers.abstract: A UAV that flies without GNSS has to estimate its absolute position and heading without any external signal. Most existing methods for UAV-to-satellite cross-view geo-localization (U-S CVGL) treat the task as image retrieval: they compress the UAV image and each satellite tile into separate descriptors, rank the tiles by their similarity, and return the center of the best tile. The output can therefore only lie on a pre-defined grid, its accuracy is limited by the tile size, and no heading is produced. Regressing the pose in a single pass removes the grid, but it leaves no chance to correct the estimate afterwards. We observe that satellite tiles are not independent samples. They are laid on the map at a fixed spacing, scale and orientation, so neighboring tiles join into one continuous satellite block with a consistent metric, and a nadir UAV view of that block differs from it by a planar rigid transform only, i.e. a 2D translation plus an in-plane rotation. We therefore reformulate U-S CVGL as solving for this transform between two images of different sizes. Position and heading then become parts of one geometric quantity, and the accuracy is no longer limited by the tile grid. We propose RigidAnchor, which solves the transform iteratively. The network encodes the two images and builds a multi-level correlation pyramid between them. At each iteration, it indexes the pyramid with every aerial cell carried through the current estimate, pools the descriptors of all cells into one hidden state, and lets two decoupled heads predict a translation increment and a rotation increment, the latter being composed rather than added. On Bearing-UAV-90K, the cross-view mean errors are 78.6% lower in position and 69.7% lower in heading than Bearing-UAV, and HSR@15 increases by 19.06 points. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/RigidAnchor.
authors: Bo Wang, Dekang Zhu, Jian Li, Zhipeng Meng, Bo Wang, Dewen Hu
bullets: Addresses GNSS-denied UAV localization, where retrieval methods are grid-limited and typically do not estimate heading.
Models a nadir UAV view and a continuous satellite-image block as related by a 2D translation and in-plane rotation.
Uses a multi-level correlation pyramid and iterative updates, with separate translation and composed rotation prediction heads.
On Bearing-UAV-90K, reports 78.6% lower position error, 69.7% lower heading error, and a 19.06-point HSR@15 increase versus Bearing-UAV.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RigidAnchor. A UAV view Iu and the satellite block Ib that contains it are encoded by two independent branches and correlated into a four-level pyramid C1, . . . , C4, so that one volume serves every candidate pose. At each iteration the pyramid is indexed at the current estimate, the descriptors of all aerial cells are reduced by a motion encoder and a GRU to one hidden state hk, and two heads predict a single rigid increment. After K iterations the estimate is read out as localization and heading.

The footprint is a square of the same side length as the aerial coverage, drawn at the estimated offset and heading, so its displacement and tilt with respect to the ground truth are the errors of that iteration. Light yellow marks the starting pose (block center, nose pointing north), green the ground truth, and red darkens from iteration 1 through 2 and 3 to 12. The legend below each row gives the position and heading errors of the four iterations.

The Bearing-UAV row comes from a separate run of that baseline under the same protocol, so its mean errors differ slightly from the Bearing-UAV row of Table 1.

On the UAV-view split of Bearing-UAV-90K (9000 queries) the same weights are run with K swept from 1 to 32: (a) localization and (b) heading error on a logarithmic axis, with (blue) and without (red) renormalizing the rotation to unit length after each update, and (c) the recall of the normalized variant at 5 and 10 m. Both conditions share the first iteration, where the normalization is an identity, and they separate from the second on. Without it the error bottoms out at iteration 8 and then rises; with it the minimum (1.84 against 2.01 m) holds through 32. The dashed gray line marks the training setting K = 12.

It is concatenated with the context vector g and the current estimate (cos θk−1, sin θk−1, t̃k−1) to drive a GRU from the hidden state h0 given by the context encoder. Two separate heads read the resulting state hk: one predicts the translation increment ∆t̃k, and the other the rotation increment as the pair (cos∆θk, sin∆θk), which is composed with the previous rotation instead of being added to an angle.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes RigidAnchor for UAV cross-view geo-localization. This addresses autonomous navigation and pose estimation for UAVs, fitting Robot Navigation.
papers.title: RigidAnchor: Cross-View Geo-Localization for UAV via Iterative Planar Rigid Alignment
papers.tldr: RigidAnchor reformulates UAV-to-satellite geo-localization as iterative planar alignment, jointly refining position and heading beyond the satellite tile grid.

papers.abstract: Off-policy safe reinforcement learning (RL) faces a challenging trade-off between task optimality and constraint feasibility. In primal-dual methods, the coupled optimization of cumulative reward and constraint penalties through adaptive Lagrange multipliers may induce oscillatory policy updates near the safety boundary and amplify the effect of unreliable reward estimates outside the safe set. To address these issues, we formulate a new constrained optimization problem (COP) for safe RL by introducing a Safety-Guiding Policy (SGP) and a corresponding Safety-Guiding Policy Constraint (SGPC). The proposed COP augments the standard COP in safe RL with a conditional safety-guidance constraint. During actor updates, the current actor is evaluated using the learned cost critic. If it is predicted to be outside the safe set, SGP provides a nearby lower-cost training reference, and SGPC guides actor optimization toward this reference. Once the policy enters the safe set, the added constraint becomes inactive, and the formulation reduces to the original COP. This formulation leads to a plug-in actor-training constraint that can be integrated into off-policy safe RL algorithms. By applying primal-dual optimization to the auxiliary COP, we finally derive an SGPC-based off-policy safe RL algorithm and implement it in two representative off-policy algorithms, yielding SAC-SGPC and TD3-SGPC. Experiments on multiple Safety-Gymnasium benchmarks demonstrate that SGPC achieves a better optimality-safety trade-off by substantially reducing constraint violations and cost oscillations while maintaining competitive or better task returns.
authors: Yifan Liu, Nan Zhang, Yang Cong
bullets: Addresses instability near safety boundaries and unreliable reward estimates outside the safe set in primal-dual off-policy safe RL.
Introduces a conditional Safety-Guiding Policy Constraint that is active only when the current policy is predicted to violate safety constraints.
Uses a nearby lower-cost Safety-Guiding Policy as a training reference during actor updates.
Provides a plug-in formulation implemented as SAC-SGPC and TD3-SGPC.
On multiple Safety-Gymnasium benchmarks, reduces constraint violations and cost oscillations while maintaining competitive or better returns.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion policies have demonstrated strong effectiveness when integrated into hierarchical skill-based learning frameworks, leveraging offline data to capture multimodal and temporally abstracted behaviors. However, prior approaches have rarely considered the diffusion process as a learnable component, adopting fixed noise schedules applied uniformly across skills, regardless of their distinct behavioral contexts. Such a design fundamentally limits the achievable performance, particularly for contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks where different skills exhibit distinct couplings between action dimensions. In this paper, we present a skill-adaptive noise diffusion framework (SaND) which introduces a learnable, skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates the diffusion process per action dimension, adapting the noising dynamics to each skill. To prevent the learned noise schedule from collapsing into trivial solutions, we employ an auxiliary inverse objective that reconstructs the skill embedding from the Legendre coefficients of the derivative of the noise schedule, encouraging the schedules to remain skill-discriminative. This formulation naturally enables adaptive control over the denoising steps for each skill, where noise schedules are clustered in the Legendre coefficient space, and the appropriate number of denoising steps is determined at the point where reconstruction error abruptly increases. At inference, we identify each skill embedding's cluster from its noise schedule and apply the corresponding number of denoising steps, dedicating more compute to skills requiring fine-grained control and less to simpler ones. In simulation and on real robot hardware, SaND outperforms existing skill learning and planning baselines on contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, achieving higher success rates while requiring fewer denoising steps.
authors: Woo Kyung Kim, Gwangpyo Yoo, Eunyoung Park, Honguk Woo
bullets: Fixed noise schedules ignore behavioral differences between skills, limiting performance in contact-rich and dexterous manipulation.
SaND conditions a learnable noise schedule on the skill and adapts noising dynamics per action dimension.
An auxiliary inverse objective uses Legendre coefficients of schedule derivatives to keep schedules skill-discriminative.
Skills are clustered by schedule, with denoising steps selected based on reconstruction-error changes.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show higher success rates than existing baselines with fewer denoising steps.

figures.caption: Figure 2: SaND framework: In (i), skills are learned via a diffusion-based hierarchical structure with a skill-conditioned noise schedule and an inverse schedule. The skill-conditioned noise schedule assigns action dimension-wise noise rates for each skill, capturing mutual dependencies among action dimensions. In (ii), skills are clustered according to the Legendre coefficients of their noise schedule derivatives, and denoising budgets are assigned per cluster based on the smallest K that maintains reconstruction quality. This enables skill-adaptive inference with reduced computational cost.

Figure 1: Concept of SaND: The first two panels visualize per-step denoising residuals along each action dimension for two different skills (approaching and grasping), illustrating that SaND learns distinct per-dimension denoising priorities for each skill. Red arrows mark the convergence point of each action dimension, showing that dimensions are resolved at distinct stages of the denoising process. The rightmost panel compares success rates of SaND with those of SkillDiffuser, which uses a fixed noise schedule, on contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, showing consistent gains.

papers.abstract: In quantum pulse sequences, spacecraft attitude control and in-hand reorientation, actions act on a hidden physical state as non-commuting operators, so the outcome of a plan depends on the order of its actions. We let the value function carry this structure: each Q(s,a) is an N x N operator, and the Bellman backup applies the action's dual map to the continuation value, Q(s,a) = K_a^*(R(s,a) + gamma E V(s')). Unrolled along a plan, the recursion builds the ordered product of the actions' operators, and the value at any latent state is a linear trace readout. It is exact for policies that do not observe the latent, the backup contracts for unitary and orthogonal dynamics, and an asynchronous operator TD scheme learns it with almost-sure convergence. Classical values live in a lattice, so a maximum over actions exists; self-adjoint operators form an anti-lattice (Kadison) and have none. An operator log-sum-exp still gives one operator per state-action pair whose readout upper-bounds the value of every policy at every latent state. The sampled update converges to it for a finite horizon, and it reduces to soft Q-learning and the QMDP bound when actions commute. We prove that scalar values on observations that ignore action order must confuse swapped histories, that exact history tables grow exponentially for free action groups but polynomially for nilpotent ones, and give a Hankel-rank lower bound on the operator dimension. In experiments the learned policy matches 1000-simulation tree search on SO(3) pointing for horizons up to 20 at ~10^4 times lower decision cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen initial states, and acts exactly on its belief mean when the initial state is hidden, where plugging the mean into a DQN does not. A planner with the same model knowledge is more sample-efficient at short horizons, and a DQN given the operators matches or exceeds OpQ.
bullets: Scalar values cannot represent plans where swapping action order changes outcomes, while operator-valued Q-functions preserve ordered compositions.
The Bellman backup applies each action’s dual map to continuation operators; an asynchronous operator TD method converges under stated dynamics and finite-horizon soft backups.
An operator log-sum-exp provides a per-state-action upper bound on every policy’s latent-state value and recovers soft Q-learning and the QMDP bound when actions commute.

On SO(3) pointing, the learned policy matches 1000-simulation tree search through horizon 20 at roughly 10^4 lower decision cost, transfers to unseen initial states, and handles hidden initial states via belief-mean actions.
Scope includes theoretical dimension and history-complexity bounds; model-based planning is more sample-efficient at short horizons, while DQN with operator inputs matches or exceeds OpQ.

papers.abstract: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.
authors: Innata Team, Yu Bai, Ziyi Bai, Yuxuan Cai, Chenrui He, Wenhao Li, Zhe Lin, Heng Wang, Hai Yuan, Zhiwei Yu, Yuanhang Zhang, Luyou Chen, Tiezhu Gao, Zheng Geng, Jinbang Guo, Dongxu Han, Diqi He, B\"orje F. Karlsson, Jintao Li, Zhiyu Li, Xiongkun Linghu, Guang Liu, You Liu, Zhen Luo, Mengsi Lyu, Yufeng Lyu, Zheng Lyu, Quanyue Ma, Chunlei Men, Ziqiang Ni, Tengfei Pan, Yijun Shen, Liang Sun, Shaoxuan Xie, Xiang Yang, Guocai Yao, Hongjun Zhang, Yingli Zhao, Yonghua Lin, Zhongyuan Wang, Huan Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of executing long-horizon tasks under open-ended, partially observable conditions.
Introduces Innata-0-WAM, a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers model for understanding, prediction, and action generation.
Introduces Innata-0-Agent with memory, verification, and recovery for coordinated task execution.
Uses a co-design protocol to align model training with agent execution and reuse validated experiences for adaptation.
Evaluations report strong capabilities in embodied understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for spatial tasks such as navigation and manipulation, where they must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input in order to act correctly. Existing benchmarks usually test perception and reasoning in isolation, making it hard to tell whether failures come from visual understanding, downstream reasoning, or the bridge between them. We introduce VeriWorld, a benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with executable actions and deterministic verification. For task families where all three channels are well-defined, we evaluate matched visual, structured, and combined input conditions on the same instance, environment, and verifier; families without a clean visual/structured/combined split are reported separately. This design supports controlled comparisons of perception, reasoning, and their interaction. Using this setup, we uncover two diagnostic findings. First, models often perform much better when task-relevant information, such as object identity, current state, or target location, is given explicitly than when it must be read from the rendered scene, revealing a recurring visual-to-structure gap. Second, action-space and harness design can change outcomes even under the same task and information condition, showing that interaction protocol is itself a confounding variable. VeriWorld is open-sourced to support reproducible and fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.
authors: Yan Zheng, ShengYun Peng, Xuyao Liang, Xiaoyan Cong, Nuo Chen, Bangya Liu, Zihan Wang, Wenyan Cong, Zhiwen Fan, Zhangyang Wang
bullets: Targets failures in navigation and manipulation where models must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input.
Compares matched visual, structured, and combined inputs on identical instances, environments, and verifiers when possible.
Finds a recurring gap: models perform better when object identity, state, or target location is provided explicitly than when inferred from rendered scenes.
Shows that action-space and interaction-harness design can alter results, making protocol a confounding factor.
Open-sourced for reproducible, fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the 11 tasks in VERIWORLD, spanning four families. Interactive Control (closedloop, multi-round): MazeNavFPS (first-person grid maze navigation), Billiards (2D pool trajectory planning), TunnelNav3D (curved-tunnel flythrough), PlaceOnBottom (object stacking). Trial-and-Error Prediction (submit-and-check): BoxFold (predict the folded shape), MovingShooter (aim at a moving target), LightWar (aim and launch a projectile at a distant beacon across a large outdoor terrain). Photoreal Grounding (photorealistic 3D scenes): SceneGrounding (recover the camera pose of a given screenshot in two photoreal interior levels), ObjectGrounding (localize named kitchen objects with 3D markers in a photoreal apartment scene). Computational Physics (Slang/CUDA simulation): CurvyBilliards (ball dynamics on a parametric surface), DropToTarget (surface design for target landing). Family colours match the row banners in Table 2; Sec. 5 reports these tasks using separate core, specialized, and harness-diagnostic tracks.

Figure 1: Batch control improves performance under both evaluated information channels at an equal move budget. Same task (MazeNavFPS, 30 mazes), same model (Gemini-3.1-Pro), and the same budget of primitive moves for both protocols (125/170/210 moves for 3×3/4×4/5×5 grids): switching the action interface from Single (one move per call) to Batch (3–6 moves per call) lifts Pass@1 from 0.57 to 0.93 under VP (vision + position log) and from 0.57 to 0.97 under VRP (VP + raycast), while Batch uses fewer moves on average. Under an equal budget of 50 model calls, Batch also outperforms Single for every evaluated model (Sec. 5.3 and Table 10). This motivates VERIWORLD’s three-axis design — task, information channel, and action harness — in which the harness is treated as a first-class experimental variable rather than a fixed implementation detail.

Figure 2: VERIWORLD evaluation pipeline. A Python generator maps a seed to task parameters and instantiates the scene in Unreal Engine 5 (rendering + game-runtime bridge for in-process code execution). A VLM agent runs a closed step loop: screenshot + action log → thoughts / actions / updated knowledge → execute in UE5; the new screenshot and log feed back for up to T rounds. A deterministic Python verifier checks pass / fail at runtime for every task; some families additionally have a solvability certificate (Lean 4 or deterministic simulation, depending on the task; §3.3).

Figure 4: LightWar successful arc, V+Telemetry condition. A 2×3 stack of arc replay frames sampled at t = 0.51, 1.53, 2.54, 3.56, 4.58, 5.59 s after launch, taken from a Gemini 3.1 Pro Pass@1 episode on seed=0 (hit_forest_hilltop_beacon). The agent fires a glowing projectile from a low-elevation forest clearing (frame 1) and tracks the ballistic arc until it intersects a hilltop beacon (frame 6, bright impact flare). Each frame is the harness’s per-tick render passed back to the agent at the next round; together they form the visual evidence the agent uses to plan the next shot. Per-round screenshots like these are part of the V condition; V+Telemetry additionally reports the scalar miss distance of each shot. papers.title: VeriWorld: A Verifiable Visual SWE-Bench for Spatial Reasoning in 3D Environments

papers.abstract: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from training, the plan is often still right but is executed as if nothing had changed. Training on such variations in advance cannot handle unseen changes, while adapting once deployed either changes the plan, leaving the miscalibrated commands in place, or updates a robot model by gradient steps that do not know how reliable they are and can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. The key observation is that the robot's own motion reveals the change: after each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model of the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands it would have needed, yielding free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under them. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Zijian Jin, Shuaicheng Niu, Baian Chen, Weirui Ye, Jihun Hamm, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses hidden deployment shifts such as altered object weight, weakened joints, and controller lag.

Requires no reward, gradient updates, or data collected from the changed robot.
Across 11 physical shifts, improves average success from 27.8% to 62.9% and preserves performance when physics is unchanged.

papers.abstract: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.
authors: Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Ye Lu, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
bullets: Mean-instruction and task-conditioned velocities align strongly (cosine ≈0.94–0.95), so references are not pure harmful bias.
Averaging eight completed-state references leaves 98.3% of the individual mean norm, indicating a large shared transport component.
The proposed diagnostic and shrinkage analysis link correction strength to reference signal-to-noise.
Geometry-calibrated correction removes only the component orthogonal to task velocity and predicts a task-dependent scale.
In controlled RoboTwin experiments, centered orthogonal correction achieved 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one sweep; gains were non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) deliver fast visuomotor control, yet degrade sharply in challenging scenes and act blindly when about to fail; conversely, foundation-model-based agents generalize and recover reliably, but incur prohibitive latency and cost when queried at every step. To achieve both WAM (System 1)-level speed and agent (System 2)-level reliability--- we propose \textbf{\oursfull (\ours)}, a framework that calibrates WAMs' confidence--- adaptively triggering System~2 only when necessary, and distilling System~2's knowledge to form an evolving System~1. First, \ours equips a frozen WAM with \textbf{calibrated self-assessment}: a single lightweight judgment token reading internal video--action features is trained via our proposed \textbf{cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning} using only binary rollout success/failure signals. It can predict a \textbf{calibrated success probability} at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions. Second, this calibrated success probability schedules control chunk by chunk---invoking System~2 to resolve bottlenecks when confidence drops, and handing control back to the WAM once confidence recovers, preserving WAM-like speed while approaching System~2 reliability. Third, as System~2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, its takeover trajectories directly capture the WAM's capability gaps. JiL distills these takeovers into the WAM to repair those gaps so System~1 can operate standalone without System~2 at test time, while our mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating prevent degrading existing capabilities.
authors: Wenhao Li, Yu Han, Xiu Su, Dehao Wu, Keke Huang, Shan You, Fei Wang, Chang Xu
bullets: Addresses WAM failures in challenging scenes and the high latency and cost of invoking System 2 at every step.
Trains a lightweight judgment token with cross-fitted temporal-difference learning from binary rollout success/failure signals.
Uses calibrated success probabilities to switch between WAM control and System 2 assistance chunk by chunk.
Distills System 2 takeover trajectories into the WAM to repair capability gaps and support later standalone operation.
Mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating aim to preserve existing capabilities during self-evolution.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the Judgment-in-the-Loop (JiL) framework. (1) Non-Invasive Calibrated Self-Assessment (Sec. 3.2): A lightweight judgment token J attends to the frozen WAM’s internal video and action streams through a causal mask and token-gated adapters, predicting calibrated success probability qθ via our proposed cross-fitted TD learning without affecting action predictions. (2) Adaptive System 1 & 2 Takeover (Sec. 3.3): At each decision step, qθ schedules control chunk by chunk; the WAM hands control to a GPT-6-Astra-based agent when qθ < τ and reclaims execution once confidence recovers above τback. (3) Capability-Gap Consolidation (Sec. 3.4): Keeping πbase frozen, successful agent takeovers (Dhelp) are combined with mastered-skill anchor data—the WAM’s own confident successes (Down) and pre-training replay (Dreplay)—into Dmix to train a separate repaired action expert πrep, distilling System 2’s recovery skills into System 1. (4) Erosion-Free Confidence-Gated Deployment (Sec. 3.5): During standalone deployment, πbase dynamically switches to πrep when base confidence qbase drops below τ and reclaims control once confidence recovers, repairing hard states without degrading mastered skills or invoking System 2 (scores shown: Fast-WAM on RoboTwin 2.0, 1 round).

papers.tldr: A confidence-calibrated framework lets fast world action models invoke slower reasoning agents only when needed, then learn from those interventions to improve standalone reliability.

papers.abstract: Persistent object maps must incorporate new surfaces while retaining valid identities and correcting earlier associations. We present a map-revision module that separates historical identity changes from new-surface admission. Proposed merges are tested against shared and separate mask explanations across views; a merge is allowed only if its evidence margin remains positive after removing any one observed frame. New measured points are assigned through local identity competition, with a mask witness and a seed-frame stability check. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the fixed method increases mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 under a local evaluation protocol. Controlled output interventions attribute the gains to fragment consolidation, protection against harmful overwrites, and local assignment of new points. Four additional spatial holdouts increase mean AP from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision is slightly higher at 23.251. The extra seed-frame check yields no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment in either set. A 330-frame garage recording demonstrates offline integration with LiDAR--inertial--visual odometry. These results identify where observation-supported revision improves object maps and where conservative decisions still limit recovery.
authors: Haoxiang Jie, Yaoyuan Yan, Zhiyou Heng, Liang Li, Zhaosong Li, Lifeng Liu
bullets: Separates historical identity changes from admission of newly measured surfaces.
Allows object merges only when shared-mask evidence remains positive after removing any one frame.
Assigns new points through local identity competition with mask-witness and seed-frame checks.
Improves mean instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 on two KITTI-360 windows; spatial holdouts rise from 20.263 to 23.171.
Seed-frame stability adds no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment, highlighting limits of conservative revision.

papers.selection_reason: The paper presents a map-revision module for persistent object maps in SLAM, which is a core capability for embodied agents to maintain accurate world representations. papers.title: OmniSLAM: Evidence-Authorized Revision of Persistent Object Maps
papers.tldr: OmniSLAM revises persistent object maps conservatively by requiring observation-backed evidence for identity merges and new-surface assignments.

papers.abstract: Sustained lunar-base operations require robots that restore equipment and deliver cargo under conditions unforeseen before deployment. Flown space autonomy executes pre-validated procedures and enters a safe hold outside their scope, whereas foundation models synthesize plans on site that cannot be verified before execution. We formulate these operations as safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued physical evidence, and costly, deadline-constrained sensing. We propose asymmetric knowledge-level replanning (AKR), which treats the planner as an untrusted black box: reversible actions run on the planner's assumptions, and irreversible actions run only after a minimum-cost sensing cover verifies every precondition. Under sound measurements, no irreversible action executes on a false precondition for any planner or record, the sensing cost before an irreversible action is bounded below for every sound knowledge-based policy, and execution with a complete planner ends in a verified goal or a certified hold. AKR executed no hazardous action in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials with sound observations or in 58 full-stack runs; the FF-Replan acting rule executed one in 7% of those trials. The median AKR run took 1.10 times the fastest run on the same mission, against 1.50 under the K-replanner acting rule. AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model; the original PLEXIL and EUROPA$\rightarrow$PLEXIL procedures completed none.
authors: Bingqi Huang, Bingchuan Wei, Yingkai Cai, Zhaokui Wang
bullets: Addresses lunar operations where prevalidated procedures cannot handle unforeseen faults and foundation-model plans cannot be verified in advance.
Models safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued evidence, and costly deadline-limited sensing.
Treats the planner as untrusted: reversible actions follow assumptions, while irreversible actions require a minimum-cost sensing cover.
With sound observations, AKR executed no hazardous actions in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials and 58 full-stack runs; FF-Replan acted hazardously in 7% of comparable trials.
AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model, while baseline procedures completed none.

papers.abstract: Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths ($\le$ 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, $\pi_{0.5}$ still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit $\pi_{0.5}$ runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1$\times$ smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ
authors: Yanlong Chen, Thongthornpatch Chamadol, Yichen Guo, Yunfei Gao, Mohan Liu, Addison Lin Wang, Yawei Li
bullets: Standard PTQ fails at ≤2 bits because static calibration misses quantization-induced state drift and layer-wise reconstruction does not reflect action-generation needs.
LoopQ uses on-policy rollouts from the quantized policy for drift-aware calibration.
Readout-aligned fine-tuning updates lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors while keeping trellis codes fixed.
At 2-bit weights, LoopQ reaches 60.4% on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7 versus 61.8% full precision; 1-bit π₀.₅ completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks.
The 2-bit π₀.₅ model uses integer kernels on Jetson AGX Thor, reducing weight storage by 4.1× and memory by 44%, and remains close to full precision on three real-arm tasks.

(b) Layer-wise effect of closed-loop calibration relative to demonstration calibration. On-policy error decreases across the action head (top) and in 427 of 432 layers. Each 1% added on demonstrations removes 4.6% on on-policy states in the head (bottom). (c) Action-expert readout error on identical inputs from the pictured rollout, in the two leading directions of both models’ errors (top) and over policy calls (bottom). LoopQ halves the mean distance to full precision.

papers.selection_reason: Ultra-low-bit quantization of VLA models with on-policy calibration; directly relevant to embodied action models and efficient deployment.
papers.title: Quantizing in the Loop: Drift-Aware Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LoopQ enables ultra-low-bit VLA models to retain near-full-precision robot performance by calibrating on their own rollouts and aligning quantized representations with action readouts.

papers.abstract: Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM's network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1,605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism's signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.
authors: Shrikrishna Bhagirath Rajule, Srinath Neelamagam, Aniket Bera
bullets: Noise-only and real dark frame pairs produce nearly identical, high self-consistency, masking the absence of reliable scene structure.
On a dark sequence, the system processed 1,605 frames and produced 7 keyframes while rejecting no factor-graph edges; over 95% of accepted correspondences violated ground-truth epipolar geometry.
A single inflated statistic is interpreted in opposite ways by keyframing and relocalization, starving keyframes while accepting almost every relocalization candidate.
Reading the statistic at keyframe-pair baselines separates confident collapse from working runs on ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation, in-sample.
Low-light weights and threshold retuning increased tracking but did not recover accurate geometry; the failure signature also reproduced on the two darkest of four Jetson robot routes.

The keyframe rule fires when it falls below 0.333 and the relocalization rule accepts an anchor when it rises above 0.30. In good light it sits near 0.4 and both rules behave. Starved of structure, the network invents geometry that agrees with itself, the statistic rises to about 0.7, keyframing starves (7 keyframes in 1 605 frames) and relocalization accepts wrong anchors (497 of 543 on plant_dark). Labels never use g or m: an ETH3D dark run is working at ≥ 50 keyframes with a converging alignment, thrashing at ≥ 100 relocalization attempts, silent otherwise; a bright run is degenerate at ≥ 10 Cholesky failures; a raw run is lost if it relocalized at all. Middle and right: the saved reconstruction of each run, top-down, with its keyframe poses (square: start). Stock reported 14.6 FPS, no error, and no relocalization, and saved an empty reconstruction.

Fig. 5. Ablations. Nothing separates the arms until L3, where both fail loudly; the adapted arm’s keyframes span half the route, and the loud failure costs 2–4× the energy per frame.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes silent failure and confidence miscalibration in learned dense visual SLAM; relevant to embodied perception and 3D foundation model reliability.
papers.title: Confidently Lost: Silent Failure and Edge Deployment of Dense Visual SLAM under Photon Starvation
papers.tldr: Under photon starvation, dense learned visual SLAM can generate highly consistent but incorrect geometry, causing silent failure in real-time edge deployment.

papers.abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.
authors: Ruohao Guo, Jiatong Ye, Chenwei Dong, Jinxing Zhou, Dantong Niu, Guangyao Li, Zhenbo Li
bullets: Defines a task combining speech understanding, object retrieval, speaker localization, and delivery.
Provides a dataset with three query types, eight subtypes, and varied object-selection and delivery requirements.
Integrates motion-aware spatial audio into an audio-visual large language model to track spatial cues during movement.
Uses multitask instruction tuning for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding.
Reports baseline results in seen and unseen environments; code is planned for public release.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our baseline framework. Details of the Motion-Aware Spatial (MAS) Audio Encoder are shown in the left panel. The original audio encoder preserves speech understanding, while the parallel MAS Audio Encoder extracts binaural spatial cues and updates them according to the agent’s motion. A lightweight projector maps these features into the language model’s token space, where they are combined with speech, visual, and textual tokens to predict executable skills. The action executor interacts with the environment and returns execution feedback for closed-loop decision making.

Figure 1. Overview of Audio-Visual Rearrangement. Given a spoken request, an agent must (1) search for and pick up a suitable object and (2) navigate to the requesting speaker and hand it over. This requires understanding what to retrieve from speech, visually grounding the target object, and acoustically localizing the speaker among multiple people, as well as navigation and manipulation.

Figure 4. AVR trajectories in unseen environments. The top and bottom examples correspond to explicit and implicit requests. Each example shows a top-down scene view, an occupancy map, and egocentric observations during exploration (1), target acquisition (2), and approach to the speaker (3). Blue and orange paths indicate object search and sound-source search. Paths connect recorded decision locations along the navigation mesh. Selected views include a simulator-rendered snapshot for illustration.

Figure 3. Distributions of initial speaker azimuths and sourceagent Euclidean distances across AVR episodes. Left: Polar histogram showing the spatial distribution of initial speaker azimuths relative to the agent. Right: Histogram illustrating the distribution of source-agent distances, spanning from 2 to 12 meters.

Figure 5. Cumulative success across initial Geodesic distances. (a) Complete AVR task success. (b) Handover to the correct recipient. Blue and orange denote seen and unseen episodes. Distances are computed on the static-scene navigation mesh.

papers.abstract: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/
authors: Tianle Zeng, Hanjing Ye, Bingyi Xia, Yuchen Zhou, Zibo Zhang, Yufei Huang, Yonggen Ling, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling route execution with continuous follower- and scene-aware adaptation.
Uses a structured multimodal policy with an explicit Path, learned Pace for route progress, and Residual for local adaptation.
Introduces LeadInfra for closed-loop Unreal Engine data generation and LeadBench with 108 held-out episodes.
Trains on an approximately 4M-sample corpus and reaches 39.6% task success, the highest among evaluated policies on LeadBench.
Transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).
authors: Yiheng Du, Jingqi Tian, Xu Jiang, Jiexuan Zhang, Shuyu Wang, Zecheng Tang, Jian Zhang
bullets: Maintains task state and subgoals across visual updates so remembered object identities and progress guide current actions.
At each update, infers an event, revises the task state, grounds a subgoal in the current scene, and generates an action.
Jointly trains one VLA to reason and act without an external reasoning model.
Uses exact likelihoods of memory text tokens for GRPO refinement from rollout rewards while keeping action generation deterministic.
Reports 66.46% on RoboMME, 79.83% on its Reference category, and 90.08% on LIBERO-Mem; it doubles RoboMME success versus an otherwise identical non-recurrent model.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has progressed from simple control tasks to complex real-world challenges with large state spaces. While RL excels in these tasks, training time remains a limitation. Reward shaping is a popular solution, but existing methods often rely on value functions, which face scalability issues. This paper presents a novel safety-oriented reward-shaping framework inspired by barrier functions, offering simplicity and ease of implementation across various environments and tasks. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed reward formulations, we conduct simulation experiments on the Unitree Go1 quadruped robot in Isaacgym. The policy was better than the existing baselines and reduced safety violations from 27% to 0.1% without almost any compromise on the performance.
authors: Janani S K, Manan Tayal, Shishir N. Y Kolathaya
bullets: Targets slow RL training and safety violations in complex, large-state-space tasks.
Introduces simple, broadly applicable safety-oriented reward formulations inspired by barrier functions.
Evaluated in simulation on the Unitree Go1 quadruped using Isaac Gym.

papers.abstract: Robot policies act in real time but fail without knowing why, whereas a reasoning agent that watches the robot can often tell what went wrong. Existing systems either hand the agent control, which takes minutes per episode, or let it send instructions. Yet a policy follows a new instruction only from a fresh start, since a half-finished task leaves it in states outside its training data. Nor can an instruction fix how the robot moves. If a drift keeps pulling the hand to the left, "push right, slightly" is not a task the policy has learned. We propose RoboThink, in which the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent's guidance. An instruction channel tells the policy what to do. When the user says "the milk, not the butter" after the robot has started, the agent rewrites the instruction and the robot undoes its own motion, with no training. A feedback channel tells it how to move. It is taught from the agent alone with agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens and counterfactual feedback, and is read only by the policy's action module. On LIBERO, RoboThink with Claude Opus 5.5 raises success from 0.09 to 0.87 under an unknown constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one. It also completes misheard and changed requests in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. Acting alone, GPT-6 Astra needs 2.1 min per success and over a million tokens per episode, whereas RoboThink needs 55 s and 8k tokens. The same recipe works across policies, for both vision-language-action models and world action models, and across robots, from one arm to two arms and a mobile manipulator. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with two arms, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 under the constant drift and from 0.31 to 0.56 under the random one. Finally, the agent is a plug-in. A policy taught by one agent works with other agents, including open-weight ones, and grows stronger with a stronger agent, without retraining.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Zijian Jin, Janet Wang, Xingchen Zhao, Zhenyu Zhang, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses failures from unknown motion drift, mid-task instruction changes, and misheard requests that ordinary policy instructions cannot fix.
Uses separate instruction and feedback channels, agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens, and counterfactual feedback; only the policy’s action module reads the feedback.
On LIBERO, success improves from 0.09 to 0.87 under constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under random drift.
The system handles changed or misheard requests in 0.91–1.00 of episodes while using 55 seconds and 8k tokens per success, versus 2.1 minutes and over 1M tokens for an acting agent.
Transfers across policies, agents, robots, and multi-arm tasks; agent replacement or improvement requires no policy retraining.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation policies provide learned execution capabilities, while programming agents can reason about failures and construct recovery behaviors. Combining them effectively requires learning when intervention helps and when the policy can reliably resume. This challenge is inherently temporal: the physical world continues to evolve during reasoning, and a useful recovery may become infeasible before a decision takes effect. We introduce Agent on Guard (AoG), a hierarchical framework that improves collaboration between a frozen base policy and a programming agent through physical experience. An evolving outer planner allocates control as the physical state evolves, aligning decisions with the physical clock with attention to observation freshness, remaining recovery windows, and the time required for reasoning, recovery, and subsequent execution. Coupled inner loops jointly refine intervention timing, recovery skills, and handoff conditions. Rather than judging recovery by local correction alone, AoG uses downstream task progress, failure recurrence, final outcomes, and resource consumption to improve both recovery behaviors and scheduling. This turns temporary agent solutions into reusable collaboration capabilities that complement the frozen policy. On RoboDojo-Sim, AoG achieves a success rate of 50.57% and a task score of 57.26, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, respectively. It also reduces end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent.
authors: Gengming Cui, Mingfei Han, Jiawei Zhang, Mozheng Liao, Yunkai Guo, Minghao Jin, Tingwen Du, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang, Zhihui Li
bullets: Addresses the temporal challenge of deciding whether intervention remains useful as the physical state and recovery window evolve.
Uses a hierarchical outer planner to allocate control based on observation freshness, available recovery time, and reasoning, recovery, and execution costs.
Jointly improves intervention timing, recovery skills, and handoff conditions through physical experience.
Evaluates recovery using downstream progress, recurring failures, final outcomes, and resource consumption rather than local correction alone.
On RoboDojo-Sim, reports 50.57% success and 57.26 task score, with lower latency and token use than the GPT-6 Astra agent.

Three coupled inner loops refine intervention timing, recovery programs, and policy resumption. Across RSI rounds, the agent revises planner guidance and inner-loop rules and programs from complete trajectories; subsequent executions use the updated harness. (b) Online execution efficiency on RoboDojo-Sim, comparing AoG with agentic baselines in terms of token consumption and end-to-end latency per episode. Both metrics measure deployment costs, excluding RSI training costs. (c) Success rate and score across five task categories on RoboDojo-Sim, comparing AoG with policy-only and agentic baselines.

Figure 2. The planner coordinates agent observation and reasoning with ongoing frozen-policy execution on a shared physical clock. Temporal observations identify unmet object-level expectations and guide intervention at t0. Recovery programs check grasp retention and object support, while handover at t1 requires the physical prerequisites for the next policy subgoal. Subsequent policy execution reveals whether the recovered state supports continued task progress. Across RSI rounds, the agent uses this evidence within complete trajectories to jointly revise planner guidance, intervention rules, recovery programs, and handover conditions.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available. Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates. Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations. Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score. Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy. However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time. We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time. It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training. We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors). It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations. PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation. Its selection is also stable across seeds.
authors: Sunjae Jeong, Geunhyeok Yu, Dowoon Lee, Hyoseok Hwang
bullets: Few target-task demonstrations motivate reusing demonstrations from other tasks.
Retrieval-based curation ignores the policy, while performance-aware curation is effective but computationally slow.
PICKER uses forward passes of a pretrained policy to identify candidates whose errors align with target-demonstration errors.
It achieves success rates comparable to performance-aware curation, with runtime similar to retrieval-based curation.
Selection remains stable across random seeds.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of PICKER for the candidates of Figure 2. The pretrained policy processes every candidate sample and target sample with forward passes only. Its encoder returns the observation representation ϕ(s), and its action head returns the error e, which the figure labels as the residual. After centering, the affinity compares the representations of a candidate sample and a target sample, and the agreement compares the directions of their errors. Their product is the utility U , which is averaged into a score T (τ) for each candidate. PICKER selects the N candidates with the highest scores.

papers.abstract: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
authors: Zikang Wen, Yuning Zhang, Dong Yuan
bullets: Shared-GPU inference reduces the cost of deploying many task-specific VLA policies, especially with LoRA adapters sharing a frozen backbone.
MotionExec triggers observations using motion structure in predicted action chunks to overlap inference with buffered execution.
SlackBatch uses per-robot slack and estimated GPU workload to decide when to wait, batch requests, or dispatch them.
With up to 96 simulated robots, it reduces mean episode stall by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points across evaluated settings.
Backbone sharing reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave radar offers weather-resilient sensing for 3D occupancy prediction. Existing radar occupancy methods mainly model geometry, with limited joint modeling of semantics and motion. Cascaded imaging radar provides fine spatial detail but has a limited unambiguous velocity range, whereas single-chip radar offers a wider range but coarser spatial resolution. We propose RadarOSV, to our knowledge the first radar-only framework that jointly predicts occupancy, dynamic object semantics, and ground-relative velocity from raw radar data in unified voxels, by exploiting complementary measurements from both radars. Its Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry (PCG) backbone maps polar imaging-radar features into Cartesian voxels through fixed and deformable sampling, guiding cross-radar fusion for geometry and attribute prediction. Single-chip detection outputs provide class evidence, while raw Doppler spectra supply motion features and radial-velocity candidates. The velocity readout selects from these candidates using fused features to resolve aliasing, then combines the selected radial estimate with learned motion. Ego-motion compensation uses radar-estimated velocity, so inference requires no external odometry or other sensors. On K-Radar, single-frame PCG achieves 40.7% mIoU within 12.8 m, compared with RadarOcc's reported 34.3%. On the BRIDGE-Liv dataset, compared with a cascaded-radar baseline predicting the same outputs with external ego velocity, RadarOSV improves macro-averaged accuracy across four dynamic object classes within annotated object regions from 63.1% to 75.5% and reduces object radial-velocity MAE against manual Doppler annotations from 1.03 to 0.51 m/s, while maintaining geometric occupancy mIoU.
authors: Yuan Fang, Long Zhuang, Xijia Wei, Jingqi Jiang, Fangzhan Shi, Simon Julier, Kevin Chetty
bullets: Addresses the limited joint modeling of geometry, semantics, and motion in existing radar occupancy methods.
Uses a Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry backbone with fixed/deformable sampling to fuse radar features into unified voxels.
Combines single-chip class evidence with raw Doppler spectra and candidate selection to handle velocity aliasing.
Performs ego-motion compensation using radar-estimated velocity, without external odometry or other sensors.
Reports improved occupancy, dynamic-class accuracy, and radial-velocity error on K-Radar and BRIDGE-Liv.

papers.abstract: Humanoid box pushing is challenging when the physical properties of the task, such as the box mass and the ramp inclination, are unknown before the push begins. This paper presents PushMimic, a framework that learns adaptive humanoid box pushing from a single level-ground kinematic reference motion. The learned policy adapts its pushing posture to these properties without observing them. PushMimic augments the reference motion into a dynamically feasible motion dataset over these properties with sampling-based trajectory optimization, and distills the dataset into one motion tracking policy in one stage of training. Simulation results over box masses from 5 to 15 kg and ramp inclinations up to 15 degrees show that PushMimic raises the success rate from 57.8% to 88.8% compared with a baseline that tracks the original reference motion. It also reduces the cost of push of the arms by 22%. Hardware experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid show that the policy adapts its torso pitch during continuous pushing on an inclined treadmill, with box masses up to 19 kg and ramp inclinations up to 12.6 degrees. PushMimic therefore needs only one reference motion, instead of one for every box mass and ramp inclination.
authors: Yulun Zhuang, Hanyu Zhang, Jingyu Liu, Yanran Ding
bullets: Addresses adaptive pushing when physical task properties are unknown before execution.
Augments one level-ground kinematic motion into dynamically feasible trajectories across varying masses and inclinations using sampling-based trajectory optimization.
Distills the augmented motions into a single motion-tracking policy in one training stage.
In simulation, success improves from 57.8% to 88.8% over tracking the original reference, while arm pushing cost decreases by 22%.
Hardware tests on a Unitree G1 demonstrate torso-pitch adaptation while pushing boxes on an inclined treadmill.

Reference distilled motion tracking: an RL policy observes only the nominal reference motion and the states of the robot and the box, and is rewarded for tracking the augmented reference motion of its task parameter. Deployment: the policy adapts its posture to the box mass and the ramp inclination without observing them.

papers.abstract: Skill internalization offers a way for agents to learn useful behaviors from skills and use them without explicit guidance in context at inference time. A common approach is to generate demonstration trajectories with the skill in context and then fine-tune the same model on its own trajectories with the skill removed. However, this leads to the problem that the model may learn to reference the removed skill, which we named as context misalignment (CoMi). In this work, we first analyze agent behaviors related to CoMi under this common pipeline. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1, skill-removed fine-tuning consistently results in CoMi: 12.2-46.0% of test trajectories reference the removed skill. To address this problem, we develop Context-Grounded Skill Internalization (CGSI). CGSI uses a sentence detector to identify unsupported references and then masks or rewrites the selected sentences before fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGSI and reveal two key findings. (i) Compared with directly fine-tuning with the skill removed, CGSI reduces CoMi at test time by 72.5-94.6% while preserving task success. (ii) Compared with existing reinforcement learning-based skill-internalization baselines, CGSI achieves comparable performance with substantially less training time. CGSI also significantly reduces processing costs compared with large-scale trajectory auditing and correction.
authors: Jinlin Liu, Yumeng He, Qihan Huang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Han Peng
bullets: Skill-removed fine-tuning causes context misalignment (CoMi), with agents referencing removed skills across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1.
CGSI detects unsupported references in demonstration trajectories and masks or rewrites the affected sentences before fine-tuning.
CGSI reduces test-time CoMi by 72.5–94.6% while preserving task success.
It matches reinforcement-learning-based internalization baselines with substantially less training time and lowers processing costs versus large-scale trajectory auditing.
Scope: results are demonstrated on the three evaluated benchmarks and focus on sentence-level reference correction.
