papers.abstract: Autonomous exploration is widely used to map unknown environments, yet maintaining both path efficiency and low online computation remains difficult as environment scale increases. Hierarchical planners reduce global search through coarse regional representations but often rely on handcrafted local viewpoint-selection rules. Graph-based reinforcement learning can improve local decisions, but its inference cost grows with the exploration graph and global direction is usually represented only implicitly. To address these limitations, we present HERO, a hierarchical framework that assigns distinct responsibilities to global planning and learned local decision-making, enabling each level to focus on the function it is best suited to perform. To reduce the growing inference cost of graph-based policies, HERO restricts learned target selection to reachable candidates within the current region while using region-level planning to provide long-horizon guidance. To avoid informative targets causing excessive deviation from this global direction, the proposed Dual-Branch Graph Policy balances Frontier Utility with guidance toward the next region, improving both local exploration and global progress. Experiments on unseen 2D maps show the lowest overall mean path length and target-decision cost among the evaluated methods. MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites further demonstrate the framework's applicability with LiDAR-based mapping and chassis dynamics.
authors: Xulin Xiao, Shengyi Liang, Mingjie Zhang, Chengkai Wu, Chen Chen, Zhigang Li, Jinni Zhou, Jun Ma, Boyu Zhou
bullets: Targets the trade-off between path efficiency and online computation as exploration environments grow.
Uses hierarchical planning: global regions provide long-horizon direction, while learned decisions select reachable targets within the current region.
Introduces a Dual-Branch Graph Policy balancing frontier utility with progress toward the next planned region.
Achieves the lowest reported mean path length and target-decision cost among evaluated methods on unseen 2D maps.
MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites demonstrate applicability with LiDAR mapping and chassis dynamics.

Bottom: The Dual-Branch Graph Policy separately encodes Frontier Utility and the Guidance-Distance Feature, fuses the resulting representations through cross-attention, and selects a target from the feasible neighbors.

papers.abstract: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/
authors: Mingquan Liu, Peng Zhou, Shanming Yao, Shuai Wang, Simo Wu, Malu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large world-action models that repeatedly process dense video observations.

Introduces Body Frame Spike Coding, Grid Coincidence Attention, and Persistent Single Step Readout for precise, efficient planning.
Achieves competitive simulated-task success with substantially lower energy than ANN methods, surpasses compared methods on LIBERO-Plus, and works in real-robot experiments.

papers.abstract: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view's contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Residual world models forecast a driving scene through its temporal change, so feature components that stay constant over time vanish from the residual pathway. We ask whether evidence with weak temporal change, such as a waiting pedestrian or a stopped vehicle, can be used more effectively for planning, and introduce MOVER, a complementary event-routing mechanism. A training-time teacher measures how each spatially grounded event query responds when a past frame is removed from shared history and contrasts that sensitivity with the event's pooled temporal residual, prioritizing events that depend on history but receive weak residual evidence. A student predicts the resulting priorities from unperturbed history, so the teacher adds no inference cost. Under fixed total routing mass, one distribution scales a low-rank future bird's-eye-view update and biases trajectory-conditioned event reading. On nuScenes, MOVER reduces ResWorld's UniAD-style average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and its collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12% without direct planner ego status (0.50 m and 0.09% with it), adding 4.1 ms per frame. Matched controls show that the complementary teacher outperforms either signal alone and that the allocation acts mainly during training. Adapted to BridgeDrive-LEAD, MOVER reaches a 96.52 +/- 0.65 driving score over three seeds on the 220-route Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, exceeding matched controls in each paired seed by a margin within seed variation.

bullets: Residual world models may underrepresent static or slowly changing evidence, such as waiting pedestrians and stopped vehicles.

On nuScenes, MOVER reduces average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12%, with 4.1 ms/frame overhead.
On Bench2Drive, adapted MOVER achieves a 96.52 ± 0.65 driving score across three seeds and exceeds matched controls within paired-seed variation.

During training, a history-occlusion teacher produces complementary priorities from history sensitivity and residual evidence; a single-view student router distills these priorities. At inference, the learned allocation writes a low-rank update to the future BEV representation and provides a prior for trajectory-conditioned event reading. papers.abstract: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.
authors: Zehao Liu, Huashuo Lei, Xi Lin, Haoang Li, Yuliang Chen, Huarui Zhang, Yifan Wang
bullets: Problem: Embodied agents may be vulnerable to environment-only attacks even when models and instructions are unchanged.
Method: EnvTrap creates paired safe, trap, and benign null-trap scenarios to test action safety and consequence prediction.
Finding: Environment rearrangements produced hazardous actions at an average rate of 83.4% across five evaluated action policies.
Finding: Models performed near chance at predicting consequences, whereas human evaluators achieved high accuracy; similar vulnerabilities appeared in world models.

Defense and scope: A consequence-aware defense reduced trap triggers by 76.3 percentage points in simulation and 62.9 points across physical backends, while targeting a broader physical-reasoning deficit.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the EnvTrap attack pipeline. The diagnostic pipeline systematically constructs matched safe, null-trap, and trap embodied scenarios without modifying instructions or models. Through Semantic-Spatial Alignment, Spatial Constraint Sampling, and rigorous Plausibility Verification, it reveals how subtle physical layout changes cause consequence-blind embodied agents to execute hazardous actions in both simulation and real-world deployments.

Figure 3: The consequence-aware defense framework. A VLM is fine-tuned on the EnvTrap dataset to predict physical action outcomes. At inference, an asynchronous safety gate evaluates VLA actions in parallel, blocking hazardous actions and prompting replanning while allowing safe actions to proceed to the action buffer.

The shown executions fail to avoid consequences arising from (1) support loss, (2) motion-path collisions, (3) shallow-grasp drops, (4) speed-induced drops, (5) material hazards in microwaves, (6) thermal hazards in pans, and (7) path-blocking collisions.

papers.abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.
authors: Xiaoqian Hu, Ruihong Qiu, Yanran Tang, Sen Wang
bullets: Addresses the limits of supervised imitation and outcome-only rewards for embodied 3D reasoning.

Uses Group Coverage Sampling to maintain exploration across grounding tools.
On MSQA and Beacon3D, improves over SFT and answer/format-reward-only GRPO, particularly in spatial reasoning and grounding-answer coherence.

papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to interpret complex traffic interactions and support trajectory planning, but introduces additional computational demands. Determining when explicit reasoning can improve planning accuracy remains a key challenge, as its benefits vary across driving scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes Scene-Adaptive Gating of Explicit Reasoning for Driving (SAGE-Drive), a benefit-aware adaptive reasoning framework for autonomous driving planning. First, paired planning outcomes with and without explicit reasoning are analyzed to measure the reasoning benefit, i.e., the reduction in planning error achieved by explicit reasoning, which serves as the supervision label. SAGE-Drive then learns to predict these benefits using geometric features of the initial trajectory planned without reasoning and multimodal scene information, and invokes explicit reasoning only for the scenarios with the highest predicted benefits under a predefined reasoning budget. Experiments on 1,497 paired driving scenarios reveal that explicit reasoning improves planning accuracy in 53.5% of cases while degrading it in 46.5%, yielding a near-zero average benefit. On the test set, with a 20% reasoning budget, SAGE-Drive achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 1.5191 m, compared with 1.5252 m for random selection. At a 35% budget, it achieves an ADE of 1.5148 m, close to the 1.5141 m obtained when reasoning is applied to every scenario. These findings establish the predicted reasoning benefit as an effective criterion for reasoning selection, allowing explicit reasoning to be invoked where it improves planning accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost.

Explicit reasoning is allocated to the highest-benefit scenarios under a predefined reasoning budget.
With 20% and 35% reasoning budgets, SAGE-Drive approaches the accuracy of reasoning on every scenario while outperforming random selection at 20%.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. We train MoMa-NMP on these demonstrations through behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation, achieving 87.0% success on our simulation benchmark and 77.5% across 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes. See video results at https://adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.
authors: Adam Kan, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Jiahui Yang, Kenneth Shaw, Deepak Pathak

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.

papers.abstract: Underactuated grippers can form enveloping grasps through passive compliance, while the terminal pose and single width predicted by generic grasp generators do not fully capture the approach-closure process. Conventional collision filtering also struggles to distinguish harmful interference from acceptable contact. We present UnderGrasp, a post-hoc grasp refinement and evaluation framework for an underactuated gripper that reuses grasp candidates and quality priors from a frozen generator. The model jointly encodes the target, local environment, support surface, and approach-path geometry to propose diverse combinations of insertion depth, pre-grasp width, and target closing width for each candidate. These actions are ranked by combining separately predicted envelopment and interaction quality with upstream priors, balancing grasp feasibility, envelopment, and scene disturbance rather than rejecting all environmental contact. The back end is trained solely on configuration and interaction labels generated by gripper-specific simulations, without real-robot grasp labels. Real-robot experiments with an underactuated gripper show that UnderGrasp improves the overall success rate (SR) and the envelopment rate (ER) among successful grasps from 0.55/0.12 to 0.82/0.55 with AnyGrasp, and from 0.42/0.08 to 0.65/0.36 with GraspNet. In contrast, increasing the fixed insertion depth to 40 mm improves ER to 0.35 but reduces SR to 0.52, supporting the value of adaptive refinement. For trials involving target or environmental contact during approach, the conditional success rates increase from 0.36 to 0.89 and from 0.25 to 0.86, respectively, demonstrating more reliable execution under contact. papers.abstract: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

Evaluations cover long-horizon terminal control, short-horizon spatial and text-motion matching, and real-world interactive control on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: Particle filters flexibly represent complex, multimodal beliefs but expose them as weighted, unordered sets incompatible with conventional fixed-dimensional policies. We study particle-belief encodings as inputs to reinforcement-learning policies while holding belief estimation and policy optimization fixed. We compare statistical summaries, cumulant-generating-function (CGF) features, and permutation-invariant set encoders. Trainable encoders are learned end-to-end or pretrained through belief reconstruction or task-specific prediction. Across eight tasks, pooling-based set encoders and gradient CGF features are reliable end-to-end, while the Set Transformer achieves the highest performance with appropriate pretraining. Task-specific pretraining helps when its target captures decision-relevant belief structure, whereas reconstruction pretraining and latent alignment provide more selective benefits. For selecting and training particle-belief encoders in partially observable Markov decision processes, our results show that an encoding that reconstructs the belief well is not necessarily a good input for control.
authors: Himanshu Gupta, Brendan Crowe, Christoffer Heckman, Bradley Hayes, Zachary Sunberg
bullets: Particle filters produce flexible, multimodal beliefs, but their weighted, unordered particles are difficult for fixed-dimensional policies to use.
The study evaluates statistical summaries, cumulant-generating-function features, and permutation-invariant set encoders while keeping belief estimation and policy optimization fixed.
Pooling-based encoders and gradient CGF features perform reliably when trained end-to-end.
The Set Transformer performs best when given suitable pretraining; task-specific pretraining helps when it captures decision-relevant belief structure.
Scope: results span eight tasks and show that belief reconstruction quality is not a sufficient criterion for selecting control representations.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. We further provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model's role in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy, low-quality domains (-3.8% average and -14.3% worst-domain success rate), and that entropy regularization is needed to prevent weight collapse. Evaluated on 9500 real-world episodes from the Open-X Embodiment dataset, ProMix improves the average success rate over uniform mixing from 68.4% to 76.2%, matching Re-Mix within evaluation noise while reducing mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours - versus 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B for full-scale searches - with a +17.1% absolute gain on the worst-case domain.
authors: Qie Sima, Wei Xue, Yike Guo
bullets: Targets performance saturation caused by naively mixing heterogeneous robot, task, and environment data.
Uses a 15M-parameter proxy and frozen reference model to learn domain sampling weights via proxy-reference DRO.
Transfers learned weights without retuning to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters.
On 9,500 real-world Open-X Embodiment episodes, improves average success from 68.4% to 76.2% over uniform mixing and matches Re-Mix within evaluation noise.
Reference removal causes over-pessimistic weighting, while entropy regularization prevents weight collapse; optimization costs 11 GPU-hours and is backbone-independent.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The ProMix Framework Architecture. The pipeline consists of two stages: (Stage 1) a proxy-reference optimization loop that learns optimal domain weights p∗ by minimizing the worst-case excess loss of a 15M trainable proxy against a frozen reference model; (Stage 2) single-pass training of the final VLA model using the transferred weights p∗. The entire mixture search costs 11 GPU-hours,whereas a full-scale Re-Mix search costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B.

Fig. 2: Evolution of the domain weights during the proxy search. Each panel traces the seven domain weights pi from uniform initialization (top to bottom: full method, without the reference model, without entropy regularization); the shaded band marks the final 10k-step window averaged into p∗.

Fig. 3: Summary of the main empirical effects. (a) Mixture-search cost: a full-scale search costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B, whereas the ProMix search is fixed at 11 GPU-hours regardless of backbone. (b) Per-domain improvement over uniform mixing at the 50M scale. (c) Transfer of the 15M-learned mixture to final models at three scales without re-tuning (95% CIs over 5 seeds).

papers.abstract: Reproducing and modifying a meter-scale humanoid remains challenging for research and teaching groups with limited fabrication resources and engineering support. This paper presents Arcadian, an open-source humanoid ecosystem that offers accessible and customizable humanoid hardware and software with community support. Arcadian aims to strike a balance among cost-effectiveness, structural durability, and full customizability, lowering the barrier to entry for research and education. Specifically, this meter-scale humanoid adopts metal-embedded 3D printing to achieve a high strength-to-cost ratio, eliminating the need for computer numerical control (CNC) machining while retaining design flexibility. Extensive simulation and hardware tests validate the design: a reinforcement-learning (RL) locomotion policy trained in simulation transfers to the hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) teleoperation interface drives both arms for simple manipulation tasks. The robot is around one meter tall and costs approximately $6,800 to build. All computer-aided design (CAD) models, the bill of materials, assembly documentation, and training and deployment code are publicly released, distributed through Tnkr.ai and MakerWorld and supported by a Discord server and a project forum through which community feedback informs design updates. The ecosystem resources are available at https://anonymous-humanoid.gitbook.io/docs.
authors: Zelin Shen, Gabriel Ramos Salinas, Qiyu Zhang, Yue Qin, Chen Qian, Yanran Ding
bullets: Targets groups limited by fabrication resources and engineering support.
Uses metal-embedded 3D printing to balance strength, cost, and design flexibility without CNC machining.
Validated through simulation and hardware tests, including transferred RL locomotion and VR arm teleoperation for simple manipulation.
Costs approximately $6,800 to build, with CAD, bill of materials, assembly, and software resources publicly released.
Supported by community platforms that incorporate feedback into ongoing design updates.

papers.abstract: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.
authors: Ziyao Zeng, Xiatao Sun, Hao Wang, Ziyu Guo, Youheng Yao, Jingcheng Ni, Shenyuan Gao, Fengyu Yang, Renrui Zhang, Bangya Liu, Daniel Rakita
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting large-scale human wrist-camera data without disrupting natural hand movements.
Generates synchronized wrist views and three total views from egocentric video and task descriptions.
Introduces hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC) to evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth.
Across four datasets, reduces LPIPS by 28% versus fine-tuned WorldWander and receives human preference in 76% of responses.
HCC enables self-improvement on in-the-wild videos, with quality improving over three training rounds.

papers.abstract: Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost.
authors: Aditya Makineni, Amitesh Sahoo, Qing Tian
bullets: Addresses the loss of inference-time deliberation when VLA backbones are made lightweight.
Uses fast low-level and slow high-level latent states, updated from motor/proprioceptive and visual/instruction signals, respectively.
Performs nested reasoning cycles after one backbone pass, avoiding increases to backbone size.
A 22.5M-parameter head achieves 97.0% success on LIBERO and 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC→D.
Reports the lowest latency among compared methods and gains over a parameter-matched single-state head.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH). The VLM backbone extracts multimodal features from a deep layer (hviz, ha) and the embedding layer (hemb viz ). Inside the HR-AH, iterative latent reasoning is performed over S segments, each comprising KH hierarchical reasoning cycles. Within each cycle, the executor (fL) attends to concise action and proprioceptive context for frequent updates of the detailed motor commands, while the planner (fH ) processes the larger vision context and the instruction-informed compact zL at a slower rate to maintain an abstract task representation. The refinement module (fR) feeds the updated plan back into the action state, closing the bidirectional loop. All three modules share the same UBAttn block architecture (Sec. 3.3) with different context inputs. After each segment s, the action state is projected to a candidate action chunk Âs, and the reasoning halts once the relative change δs between consecutive predictions falls below a threshold τ (Sec. 3.5). The final prediction is executed as Â ∈ RNact×7.
Figure 4. Real-world rollout comparison between RD-VLA (top) and HR-AH (bottom) on the Put task. Both methods succeed in this example, isolating the difference in execution speed.

Figure 6. Success rate versus latency on LIBERO-Spatial. HRAH (star) achieves 98.0% at 49.63 ms, combining the highest accuracy with the lowest latency among compared methods. Circle: end-to-end, triangle: CoT reasoning, square: iterative refinement. Numbers in parentheses give the action-head size.

Figure 1. Attention maps over reasoning steps for RD-VLA (top row) and our HR-AH (bottom row). The dashed ellipse highlights the task-relevant region. HR-AH halts after only 3 steps with attention sharply focused on the target bowl and destination plate, whereas the single-state baseline requires 8 steps and attends more diffusely. Both rows visualize attention from the vision-grounded latent state. Only the third-person view is shown.

Figure 5. Architectural ablation on LIBERO-Spatial. Each point plots success rate against average reasoning segments (upper left is best). Solid arrows follow the additive build-up from a parametermatched single-state baseline to the full model, and the dashed arrow shows the effect of removing learned initialization. Hierarchical recurrence raises success from 85.2% to 94.6% while reducing average segments from 7.44 to 5.71. Modality-specific routing further raises success to 98.0% and reduces segments to 4.96. Removing learned initializations drops success to 96.8% and raises average segments to 7.27.
Figure 3. Real-world experimental setup using the Kinova Gen3 Lite robot arm.

Head size governs the memory footprint of the reasoning module on resource-constrained hardware. – indicates that a separately identifiable action head is not available. Bold: best; italics: second best. VLA-Adapter results are our reproduction of the released checkpoint.

papers.abstract: Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. We address it with three contributions that add just enough structure to guide exploration: Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) for whole-body manipulation, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) for sustained transport over long horizons, and a Hinted Object Path (HOP) that resolves collision and search complexity bottlenecks. Across all three, the policy remains free to discover its own manipulation strategy. The method generalises from rigid object to human transport. As a flagship demonstration, we show, to our knowledge, the first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution. In the domain of human transfer, we show that a single policy can adapt across substantial variations in body mass, size, and random force perturbations, all while training on a single GPU in under an hour. Our approach offers a pathway to fully RL-driven humanoid manipulation, enabling assistive robots that can help humans. Website: https://elle-miller.github.io/into_my_arms
authors: Elle Miller, Reem Almheiri, Takuma Tsukakoshi, Ben Sanati, Tamon Miyake, Yushi Wang, Namiko Saito, Shigeki Sugano, Tetsuya Ogata, Rika Antonova, Oisin Mac Aodha, Sethu Vijayakumar
bullets: Targets high-dimensional, contact-rich manipulation with long task horizons.
Introduces Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE), Interaction Gated Transport (IGT), and Hinted Object Path (HOP) to guide exploration while leaving strategies policy-discovered.
Generalises from rigid-object transport to human transport under variations in body mass, size, and external force perturbations.
Demonstrates autonomous bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin with no human intervention during execution.
The abstract reports training on a single GPU in under an hour for the human-transfer setting.

Fig. 3 Structured reinforcement learning for object transport. We propose three generalisable methods to guide learning in whole-body, contact-rich, and long-horizon manipulation: Sparse Interaction Edges, Interaction Gated Transport, and Hinted Object Path. These ideas can be integrated into the MDP’s observation and reward function without changes to the RL algorithm or training process.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
bullets: Targets cooperative transport in environments requiring obstacle detours and changing team configurations.
Models humanoids, shared objects, and obstacles as interacting entities in a relational latent world model.
Imagines outcomes of alternative waypoint commands using offline counterfactual simulator rollouts.
Selects guidance commands using predicted progress, failure, contact risk, and long-horizon value.

Evaluated on three obstacle-constrained transport tasks, with generalization from four-humanoid training to teams of two to ten and unseen configurations; experiments report improved success over evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved substantial progress across many domains, but training an agent \textit{tabula rasa} remains highly sample-inefficient. A common remedy is to initialize the agent using a neural network pretrained on demonstrations. However, collecting demonstrations is expensive, and the demonstrations themselves can be suboptimal. In this work, we use a large language model (LLM) to generate an advice policy that produces demonstration data with effectively no human cost. We use this data to warmstart a DQN agent, and use the advice policy itself to guide exploration during training. Because LLM-generated advice is often suboptimal, we further introduce a value warmstart method that initializes the agent to recognize promising states from the advice policy's behavior, without directly copying its actions. To characterize the robustness of this method, we systematically perturb individual sub-skills of an LLM-generated advice policy for a long-horizon, sparse-reward task. Degraded advice still meaningfully accelerates learning relative to unaided baselines. These results suggest that LLM-generated advice, though suboptimal, can be a cheap alternative to costly human demonstrations.
authors: Anurag Kadkol, Lawson L. S. Wong
bullets: Addresses the sample inefficiency and cost of collecting human demonstrations for RL.
Uses an LLM-generated advice policy to produce demonstrations and guide exploration during training.
Introduces value warmstart, which learns promising states without directly copying potentially suboptimal advice actions.
Systematic sub-skill perturbations show that degraded advice still accelerates learning versus unaided baselines.
Scope: evaluated on a long-horizon, sparse-reward task; the approach depends on the quality and coverage of LLM-generated advice.

papers.abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces \method, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, \method achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
authors: Siyuan Xie, Jinxi Xiao, Ran Ji, Yikai Liu, Mingxi Li, Xuebing Li, Ye Shi, Yuxiang Gao, Jiayuan Gu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning where objects are and how they move from action demonstrations without costly dense 4D supervision.
Attaches a query-based decoder to a pretrained policy and unifies tasks such as depth, point motion, correspondence, and hand–eye relations.
Learns rich spatiotemporal structure from a small number of sampled queries during training.
The decoder can be removed at inference, adding zero runtime overhead.
Achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance across simulated and real-world settings, with training up to 5× faster; probing shows the policy retains recoverable 4D structure.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SparQ4D (based on π0.5). Each query is embedded as one token, and a lightweight decoder cross-attends to the prefix tokens Zt to predict its 3D patch Ŷq. The decoder is removed after training, leaving the deployed policy unchanged.

papers.abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.
authors: Siyeon Kim, Mohanraj Devendran Shanthi, Joseph C. Liechty, Tucker Hermans
bullets: Contact variations and object geometry can produce distinct outcomes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating from similar states and actions.
The study models distributions over object pose changes from partial point clouds and actions using mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching with latent dynamics.
Explicitly multimodal models identify outcome modes more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines across diverse objects and skills.
Flow matching improves task success over the deterministic baseline for every skill and performs best on all evaluated multi-step sequences.
On a real robot, probabilistic models achieve roughly twice the pick success rate of the deterministic baseline.

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_0,\pi_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
authors: Jiyong Kwon, Yikun Bai, Amirhossein Mollaali, Guang Lin
bullets: Existing Flow-GRPO-style methods reweight stochastic denoising transitions by advantages but ignore distances between sampled actions.
JKO-GRPO treats actions sampled at each state as an empirical distribution and formulates policy improvement as a Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto step.
A soft discrete c-transform converts group-relative advantages into transport targets, trained via shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler.
The method combines these updates with clipped Flow-GRPO without KL regularization.
Random-time branching extends the approach to sequential VLA control by applying independent group-level JKO updates at selected action-chunk states.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of JKO-GRPO. (a) Along each trajectory of the old policy πold, we select M random chunk indices, restore the simulator state st at each, and form an independent group of G continuations; their returns give group-relative advantages. (b) The first action chunks of a group share the state st. Flow-GRPO reweights them by advantage. The added JKO step constructs soft c-transform targets yi that trade advantage against action distance. (c) On the first branch chunk, the masked transport loss fits the deterministic ODE sampler to stop-gradient targets, reusing each sample’s initial noise ϵi. The clipped Flow-GRPO objective acts on the post-branch segment. Both terms train the same velocity field, and the transport loss requires neither a critic nor a policy density.

papers.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
papers.tldr: JKO-GRPO enhances online RL for flow-matching vision-language-action models by combining advantage-based policy optimization with Wasserstein proximal updates over sampled actions.

papers.abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.
authors: Mohammadhossein Malmir, Mohammadali Rahmati, Mohammad Reza Kolani, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses the freezing-robot problem while supporting non-holonomic, continuous-velocity control.
Combines dual-selection attention for crowd encoding, time-to-collision anticipation, and a PPO policy.
Trained in high-fidelity simulated environments with randomized crowd sizes and social-force pedestrians.
Across 30,000 evaluation episodes, fewer than 0.5% timed out at every tested density.
Removing the time-to-collision feature reduced success by 4–7 percentage points; collisions reached 17.4% with ten pedestrians.

papers.abstract: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.
authors: Kunqi Xu, Xiaokang Sun, Xueyan Zou
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between diverse grasp strategies and robustness to disturbances.
Trains a simple MLP with PPO using a time-reversed curriculum and coordinated reset mechanism.
Learns multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while retaining closed-loop adaptation.
Demonstrates diverse and robust grasping behaviors in experiments.
Generalizes from approximately 400 training objects to more than 20,000 unseen objects.

papers.abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
authors: Taekyung Kim, Ege Yuceel, Steven Hong, Georgios Fainekos, Dimitra Panagou, Bardh Hoxha
bullets: Motivation: Image-based latent predictions alone do not guarantee that robot plans satisfy task-space safety constraints.
Method: A frozen action-conditioned JEPA predicts imagined rollouts, while downstream models estimate motion and unsafe geometry; split conformal prediction forms multi-horizon uncertainty tubes.
Safety mechanism: A backup-based shield checks candidate and final diffusion-inspired MPC trajectories against physical constraints.
Guarantee: Under exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, the returned plan satisfies constraints probabilistically at action-block boundaries without replanning.

Evaluation: On geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks in VParkBench, success rates were 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, with no observed constraint violations; shielding and calibration provided complementary benefits.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time. Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration. Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.
authors: Haoxiang Zhan, Haoqin Hong, Congcong Zhu, Jingrun Chen
bullets: Existing manipulation benchmarks only partially test time-sensitive everyday tasks.
AWAIT is a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion under explicit action windows.
Agents must identify when an intervention window opens and coordinate decisions with physical movements.
Results show difficulty detecting window onset and that repeated actions can exhaust the window, even when individual decisions are shorter than it.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces AWAIT, a benchmark for time-sensitive robotic manipulation. This addresses temporal constraints in manipulation, relevant to Robot Learning and Manipulation.
papers.title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
bullets: VLA policies can violate safety constraints despite strong benchmark performance, motivating safety filtering over sampled action chunks.
An exact-simulator lookahead filter improves safety rates by 11.5–25.7 points across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and selected RoboCasa tasks.
Learned critics detect dangerous states well (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates nearly at chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551–0.560).
Safety-selection gains degrade substantially when the world model’s state is perturbed; median position error can remove most of the benefit.
Evaluation should emphasize within-state ranking and state accuracy in tail cases and on handled objects, not just median error.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes what a world model must do to keep VLA policies safe via action-conditioned lookahead prediction, matching interactive world models and VLA safety.
papers.title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
papers.tldr: A safety world model for VLA policies must accurately rank candidate actions within each state—not merely detect dangerous states—and remain reliable under state-estimation errors.

papers.abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.
authors: Kevin Qiu, Zhao Yang, Marek Cygan
bullets: The study evaluates 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with PPO under Standard, Strict, and Reset-free torso-fall reset rules, using a shared evaluator.
Morphology rankings differ sharply: Strict versus Reset-free rankings correlate only 0.21, compared with about 0.89 expected from seed noise alone.
Removing fall resets hurts flat-ground-evolved bodies more (45% lower per-step reward) than variable-terrain bodies (16%).
The pattern is supported by permutation tests and also appears with SAC on a 24-body subset.
Selecting bodies by worst-case reward across protocols preserves at least 91% of each protocol’s best-body reward in-sample and over 80% across held-out seeds.

papers.abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.
authors: Anubhav Pandey, Harshit Nagpal, Aditya Agarwal, Tejasvi Alladi, Fei Richard Yu
bullets: Translates left/right human gestures into UAV navigation commands using RGB-D data, modified YOLOv11, and depth-weighted pose estimation.

Uses ROS2 DDS for scalable, maintainable communication, with reported end-to-end latency below 50 ms.
In simulation, RGB-D fusion improved cues over RGB alone by 46.7% on average in fog; depth retained 77% gesture accuracy at 10 m visibility versus 24% for RGB.
The open-source implementation supports migration from ROS1 and enables direct operator control without complex path planning.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.
authors: Rongze Tang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianjie Fang, Ziming Liu, Zhaolu Wang, Ziyou Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Wei Wu, Chen Gao, Yong Li, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses multi-robot manipulation requiring spatial-temporal coordination, role awareness, and embodiment awareness.
Expands a single-agent world action model across an agent dimension using shared weights and an agent-axis curriculum.
Uses joint self-attention, hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks to coordinate agent-specific behavior.
Introduces MA-Task Harness and MA-Bench, covering seven tasks with joint success, role, and collaboration metrics.
Achieves 82.7% mean joint success on MA-Bench and real-time closed-loop collaboration on a heterogeneous robot team.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.

papers.abstract: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or affordances. Unlike in image generation, where teachers for representation alignment (REPA) are assessed with encoder-intrinsic metrics, teachers for VLAs are still chosen largely by heuristics. We show that this practice is unreliable: across 14 teachers and 16 manipulation tasks, under matched training budgets, no off-the-shelf vision encoder improves the clean success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ by more than 1 point, and all of them reduce its success rate under perturbations by 10 to 39 points. Neither global semantics nor spatial structure, the criteria used in image generation, predicts which teachers help. We therefore propose the behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task. BSM correlates strongly with success rate under perturbations ($r=0.87$), and every off-the-shelf vision encoder scores below $\pi_{0.5}$ itself. Based on it, we introduce Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA), a general VLA alignment protocol that favors vision encoders whose BSM exceeds the student's and stops alignment early according to the student's BSM during training. On SmolVLA, BAVA matches continuous alignment with one third of the alignment budget, and improves the average success rate by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning. Our results suggest that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.
authors: Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Haoyuan Chen, Hexin Wang, Hanyu Zhou, Zhenglin Wan, Wangbo Zhao, Pengfei Zhou
bullets: Across 14 vision encoders and 16 manipulation tasks, off-the-shelf teachers provided little clean-task benefit and substantially reduced robustness to perturbations.
Common teacher-selection criteria such as global semantics and spatial structure did not predict VLA performance.
Behavioral Structure Metric (BSM) measures whether nearby teacher representations lead to similar expert actions and strongly correlates with perturbation success.
Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA) selects teachers with higher BSM than the student and ends alignment based on the student’s BSM.
On SmolVLA, BAVA matched continuous alignment using one-third of the alignment budget and improved average success by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and improves representation alignment for VLA models using behavioral structure metrics.
papers.title: Representation Alignment Is Only as Good as the Teacher's Behavioral Structure

papers.abstract: Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. The paper describes a lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that (1) uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; (2) is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and (3) automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles. Because TTT is a coarse visual cue, it is far simpler to use for robot navigation than current large visual depth foundation models. Our navigation model uses a 1.95M-parameter network that is two to three orders of magnitude smaller than well-known large vision foundation models, making it able to run in real time on edge hardware. Simulation and actual laboratory experiments validate the proposed approach in dynamic and spatially complex environments. Code, data, and video are available.
authors: Chiara Boretti, Philippe Bich, Manuel Morteo, Roberto Tron, John Baillieul
bullets: Uses the full camera field of view to produce rich visual time-to-transit estimates.
Is relatively robust to camera rotation and adapts to path geometry and obstacles.
Employs a 1.95M-parameter network, substantially smaller than large vision foundation models.
Enables simpler navigation from a coarse depth-related cue rather than full visual depth estimation.

papers.abstract: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing. Across three held-out retinal-injection evaluation blocks, our method achieves $94.27\pm0.64\%$ procedural completion and $64.40\pm2.43\%$ success within $35\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, with no hard violations. Applying the contract and decoder to the same frozen Correction network raises completion from $12.27\%$ to $90.47\%$. The trace exactly reconstructs 96,350 commands, and all 1,996 binding interventions follow their declared effects. These results show the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control.
authors: Jiaxi You, Yiwei Shi, Yanlin Li, Rihui Song, Weibing Li, Kai Huang, Weiru Liu

Across three held-out retinal-injection blocks, achieves 94.27±0.64% completion, 64.40±2.43% success within 35 μm, and no hard violations.
On the same frozen Correction network, contract-based decoding raises completion from 12.27% to 90.47%; all 1,996 binding interventions matched their declared effects.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically use flow-based generative modeling to learn a rich, often multimodal, distribution of robot actions. Generating samples from flow-based methods involves iteratively updating random noise, and distinct noise samples from the same state can result in distinct trajectories and task outcomes. Existing test-time scaling methods improve action chunk generation via selection, aggregation, or correction, but commonly require the generation of large ensembles of candidates or the training of an external corrector. We adapt Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement procedure for flow-based models originally used for mode-seeking in video generation, to the robotics domain. We find that applying P&P to VLA models requires modifications to the refinement process used in video generation due to differences in the underlying structure of the data. Across 400 episodes of LIBERO evaluated using SmolVLA, P&P improves upon the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points. Further, episode-level P\&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure (AUC 0.851).
authors: Jeff Duan, Arjun Sharma, Jennifer Cruden, Vansh Tibrewal
bullets: Flow-based VLA models can produce different action trajectories from different noise samples, leading to variable outcomes.
The work adapts Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement method originally developed for video generation, to robot action sampling.
P&P requires robotics-specific changes because action data differ structurally from video data.
On 400 LIBERO episodes with SmolVLA, P&P improves the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points.
Episode-level P&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure, with AUC 0.851.
