papers.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete $H$-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete $H$-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)
authors: Jiangtao Kong, Yuchen Wang, Yandong Luo, Rongchao Xu, Guang Wang, Yanbing Mao, Lu Gan, Tianyi Zhou, Huajie Shao

Introduces Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization, which uses MPPI evaluations and advantage estimates to improve policy targets while maintaining planner alignment.
Improves control performance and sample efficiency across 31 continuous-control tasks while reducing MPPI refinement iterations by 50%.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go2 for stable, high-frequency velocity-tracking locomotion.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.
authors: Tamoghno Das, Keyon Jazayeri, Yerin Cho, Nazmul Takbir, Arshia Aravinthan, Nikil Dutt
bullets: Addresses reliability failures when objects move during robot execution and policy switching causes stalls or stale observations.
Uses a learned trigger to selectively escalate from a lightweight policy to a higher-compute policy based on recovery potential and intervention risk.
Runs the incoming policy asynchronously alongside outgoing actions and aligns its context with the expected takeover state.
On LIBERO-Long, perturbed-task success rises from 69.5% to 77.1%, with 84.9% overall success—comparable to synchronous switching at 84.5%.
Reduces median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms and generalizes to unseen perturbations without retraining or recalibration.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of AsyncMixVLA. Trigger acceptance at Tpredict starts OFT preparation while committed Adapter actions execute. OFT is conditioned on the predicted context at bridge completion, Tswitch. Its first action is issued at Taction; fresh-observation replanning follows the initial prefetched takeover.

Fig. 3. Handoff context alignment. At trigger time, the current robot state and visual observation are aligned with the anticipated takeover state using the committed VLA-Adapter action bridge. State alignment predicts the robot state at handoff, while vision alignment projects the visual context into aligned visual tokens. The aligned state, visual tokens, and language instruction then form the takeover context for OpenVLA-OFT.

(b) Heterogeneous VLA policies exhibit complementary failures, motivating selective escalation. (c) Synchronous switching exposes incoming-policy inference latency to robot control. (d) AsyncMixVLA proactively launches OpenVLA-OFT, overlaps inference with committed VLA-Adapter actions, and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state.

papers.title: AsyncMixVLA: Runtime Asynchronous Robot Policy Switching for Adaptation to Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: AsyncMixVLA enables near-zero-latency switching among robot VLA policies, improving recovery from dynamic perturbations without retraining.

papers.abstract: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.
authors: Xuan Yao, Jiahao Zhang, Rongjunchen Zhang, Kaixuan Huang, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses underexplored cross-task world modeling for embodied agents whose actions and environments continually change future observations.
Uses inverse-forward dynamics to learn latent actions and a shared transition representation instead of relying on heterogeneous physical actions.
Combines shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation for downstream navigation and tracking decisions.
Evaluations across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks show consistent improvements over specialized baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of WORLDWEAVE. Task-specific adaptation then incorporates the predicted future states into each task’s decision process.

(b) Naive representation sharing creates cross-task trade-offs, which WORLDWEAVE mitigates through shared predictive dynamics and task-specific adaptation.
Figure 3. Real-world deployment for embodied navigation tasks.

papers.title: WorldWeave: Rethinking Embodied Navigation through Cross-Task World Modeling
papers.tldr: WorldWeave jointly learns transferable world dynamics from navigation and tracking tasks by inferring latent actions from observed state changes.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Weisong Shi
bullets: Addresses the gap between oracle-based evaluation and the risk of the single trajectory actually executed.
Uses the frozen VLA’s last prompt-prefill hidden token with each candidate trajectory to predict relative quality and collision/offroad risk.
Filters candidates dominated on both risk predictions, then selects the highest-scoring remaining trajectory.
On 525 AlpaSim scenes, improves selected regret and top-1 agreement over first-sample and uniform-random selection.
Reduces collision-at-fault or offroad rate to 4.93%, from 6.41% and 6.10%; adds 1.7M parameters and 0.75 ms per decision.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. AlpaSafe overview. (a) One forward pass of the frozen Alpamayo-1.5 generator yields the K=8 candidate trajectories and the prompt-prefill hidden states H; the selector reads only the last token h = H[−1]. (b) The selector head encodes each candidate, fuses it with h through one cross-attention block with a residual connection, and outputs a bounded relative score si and collision/offroad logits (ci, oi); the group-mean, future-trajectory, and progress heads supervise training only. (c) Candidates dominated on the two risk logits are removed, and the highest si among the survivors is executed. Camera frames, candidates, scores, and logits are recorded data from one decision group of the evaluation pool (LASTTOKEN).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a risk-aware trajectory selector for VLA models in autonomous driving that reuses internal VLA states to select safe trajectories without rollouts.
papers.title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: AlpaSafe selects safer trajectories from VLA-generated candidates using existing scene features, reducing collision/offroad risk without extra rollouts or VLA retraining.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces LoKiTO, a 3D local kinodynamic trajectory optimizer that combines a Chebyshev polynomial parameterization with an online neural Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) representation for aerial robotics. While current gradient-based planners often struggle with the high memory requirements of explicit volumetric maps or fail to strictly enforce dynamic limits, LoKiTO embeds kinodynamic constraints directly into a modular cost function and exploits the numerical conditioning properties of the Chebyshev basis. Collision awareness is provided by a continuous, memory-efficient neural ESDF updated online from LiDAR measurements, which drastically reduces map memory consumption to approximately 1.0 MB. Benchmarking in highly cluttered simulated environments against state-of-the-art baselines (Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner) demonstrates the superiority of our approach. Experimental results show that LoKiTO achieves over 99.4% dynamic feasibility compliance, significantly outperforming the baselines, and maintaining higher median clearance from obstacles. By coupling a well-conditioned continuous parameterization with explicit kinodynamic reasoning, LoKiTO provides a practical and extensible basis for local replanning in aerial robotics.
authors: Guillermo Gil-Garcia, J. A. Cobano, L. Merino, F. Caballero
bullets: Addresses the memory demands of volumetric maps and weak enforcement of dynamic limits in gradient-based local planners.
Uses Chebyshev polynomial trajectory parameterization with kinodynamic constraints embedded in a modular cost function.
Maintains an online neural ESDF from LiDAR for continuous collision awareness with approximately 1.0 MB of map memory.
In cluttered simulations, achieves over 99.4% dynamic-feasibility compliance and higher median obstacle clearance than Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner.
Provides a practical and extensible framework for local UAV replanning; results are reported in simulation.

papers.selection_reason: Local kinodynamic trajectory optimization using a learned neural ESDF, fitting learning-based local planning and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: LoKiTO: Local Kinodynamic Trajectory Optimization for UAVs based on Memory-Efficient Neural Distance Fields
papers.tldr: LoKiTO enables memory-efficient, collision-aware UAV trajectory optimization with explicit kinodynamic constraints and strong feasibility in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: Payload-carrying robots, such as delivery robots and autonomous trucks, must choose motions that keep them and their payload safe, so their planners predict the outcome of each candidate motion. Modern planners compare thousands of candidates per step on a GPU, using world models such as batched simulators or learned predictors. Most of them assume a rigid payload, but a liquid payload keeps moving after a maneuver, and its state is rarely measured. Near a safety limit, small prediction errors can make an unsafe plan look safe. Coupled fluid simulations are accurate but too costly for every candidate, while low-order slosh models are cheap but accurate only away from resonance. We study this trade-off on a ground vehicle with a partly filled tank near its rollover limit. First, we build PLiMB (Parallel Liquid-MultiBody), a GPU-parallel slosh simulator that, to our knowledge, couples FLIP liquid two-way with many multibody vehicles for the first time. It provides training data and a high-fidelity reference. Second, we propose a scalable physics-anchored world model that combines a modal-slosh and roll prior, an estimate of the hidden liquid state from the vehicle's own motion history (no sensor in the tank), and a learned correction. Without simulating the fluid, it scores thousands of candidate plans in one batched pass within a 20 Hz control tick on one GPU. We judge each world model by the plans it leads a planner to choose. Near the rollover limit, planners that treat the liquid as a rigid payload or use published low-order slosh models repeatedly pick unsafe plans when a safe one exists. Ours never does in our standard tank and makes about half as many in a wide tank whose sloshing mode lies in the maneuver band. There, the liquid state left by earlier driving can change the best plan, and reading it from the vehicle's history halves our model's near-limit prediction error.
authors: Yicheng Zhu, Linfeng Tian, Yang Chen, Tao Li, Zilin Bian
bullets: Liquid payloads can continue sloshing after maneuvers, making rigid-payload and simple slosh assumptions unsafe near rollover limits.
PLiMB is a GPU-parallel, high-fidelity simulator coupling FLIP fluid dynamics with many multibody vehicles to generate training data and references.
The proposed model combines modal slosh and roll physics, history-based hidden-state estimation, and a learned correction without requiring tank sensors.
It evaluates thousands of candidate plans in one GPU-batched pass within a 20 Hz control cycle.

Near rollover limits, it never selected an unsafe plan in the standard tank and made about half as many unsafe choices in a wide tank; history-based state estimation halved near-limit prediction error there.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The physics-anchored response model. papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world model for robotic planning with liquid payloads, fitting interactive world models and robot learning.
papers.title: Knowing What You Carry: Scalable Physics-Anchored World Models for Robotic Planning with Liquid Payloads
papers.tldr: A physics-anchored world model infers hidden liquid motion from driving history and enables fast, safer robotic planning with liquid payloads.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.
authors: Jiahao Wang, Ming F. Li, Han Xu
bullets: Transferable adversarial attacks can disrupt a VLA model’s perception of the robot itself across tasks.
The method compares the robot’s visually inferred location with a spatial reference derived from proprioceptive states.
Perception–proprioception discrepancies serve as an attack-detection signal and guide mitigation.
Experiments show effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance.
Real-robot evaluations demonstrate effectiveness on real-world robotic tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses security and robustness in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by leveraging proprioceptive consistency to detect transferable adversarial attacks.
papers.title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
papers.tldr: A proprioception-grounded defense detects and mitigates transferable attacks on vision-language-action robots by checking consistency between visual perception and trusted robot-state information.

papers.abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.
authors: Inkyu Sa, Gaurav Kuppa, Steve Van der Hoeven, Konstantin Stulov, Rajat Bhageria, Luis Rayas
bullets: Learns from 61,773 automatically labeled production picks using pre-pick heightmaps, actions, food, and utensil information.
Predicts post-pick heightmaps and picked mass with uncertainty; mass is evaluated on 12,294 held-out picks across nine foods.
Achieves 10.93 g RMSE, outperforming commanded-target/per-food-mean baselines and the controller’s internal estimate.
Rejecting the most uncertain picks yields 89.4% coverage with 10.28 g RMSE.
Performance is weakly sensitive to commanded volume/depth and can fail without warning on unseen target weights; broader food and utensil coverage is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Learns an action-conditioned food-picking world model from production data for robot planning and mass prediction.
papers.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
papers.tldr: A production-trained food-picking world model predicts both the next pan state and picked mass, enabling uncertainty-aware planning for assembly robots.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) are increasingly deployed on robots whose cameras and controllers differ from those used to collect their training data. Such deployment introduces two kinds of shifts. Visual shifts, such as a moved camera, change the observed images; actuation shifts, such as a retuned controller, latency or an added payload, change only how commanded actions translate into robot motion. Invisible to the policy, actuation shifts sharply degrade its success, even under domain randomization. In this work, we propose PEA, a test-time calibration method that identifies actuation shifts through active probing before task execution. Specifically, before each episode, the robot executes a short probe that moves one arm axis at a time with known commands, so that gain, delay and drift leave separable traces. A closed-form identifier estimates them from the response, and PEA compensates every subsequent command so that the robot executes the motion the policy intends. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts. Experiments on LIBERO with a WAM and a VLA show that, without any policy training, the identifier of PEA recovers most of the success lost to actuation shifts and generalizes to shifts unseen during training (e.g., from 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy).
authors: Jie Liu, Hui Xie, Qinfeng Feng, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Actuation changes such as controller retuning, latency, payload, or drift can severely reduce robot success without altering camera observations.
Before each episode, the robot performs short, axis-wise probes with known commands to reveal gain, delay, and drift.
A closed-form identifier estimates these effects, and PEA compensates subsequent commands without retraining the policy.
For combined visual and actuation shifts, a removable low-rank adapter adjusts the frozen policy to visible visual changes.
On LIBERO with a WAM and VLA, PEA recovered much of the lost performance and generalized to unseen actuation shifts, including 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PEA. Actuation shifts are invisible in images but revealed by motion, so PEA moves before it acts. (1) Probe: before each episode, the robot executes a 30-step probe that pushes one arm axis at a time with zero-sum commands, so that each gain, the delay and a constant drift leave separable traces. (2) Estimate: a closed-form identifier (orange), calibrated once offline and requiring no policy training, reads per-axis gain ĝ, delay d̂ and drift correction b̂ from the response (curves: logged x motion under gain 1.6 and a 1-step delay). (3) Act: every command of the frozen policy (gray) is rescaled and offset, and the arm holds for d̂ steps after each chunk; a lightweight LoRA adapter (blue) on the frozen weights, conditioned on the probe, handles visual shifts such as a moved camera.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.
authors: Tzu-Yuan Huang, Shao-Hsuan Chang, Dai-Jie Wu, Ralf R\"omer, Yung-Hui Li, Stefan Sosnowski, Angela P. Schoellig, Kenneth Marino, Sandra Hirche
bullets: Safety filters can prevent unsafe actions but may push robots into states poorly represented in training data, reducing task performance.
InteR-VLA broadens task-relevant state coverage with diverse demonstrations under the same data budget.
The framework aligns training data with safety-filtered deployment to mitigate intervention-induced distribution shift.
Real-world experiments cover in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings across two evaluated VLAs.
InteR-VLA maintains safety and raises Safe Success Rate up to 90%, compared with 0% for nominal policies.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real gaps caused by imperfect physics, perception errors, and unmodeled dynamics.
Uses conditional flow matching to infer physical parameters and residual fidelity domains in a latent space.
Samples realistic environments from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning.
Triggers adaptation only after detected anomalies, with sequential proposals and uncertainty-modulated exploration.
Across five robots, it achieves accurate posterior inference; on a damaged wheeled robot, rough-terrain success increases from 26% to 70% and orientation jerk decreases by 88%.

papers.abstract: A policy that transfers from simulation to a lab robot often fails in the field. Calibrating a simulator from real-world data typically targets only a few hand-picked parameters, and even calibrated simulators fail to capture unmodeled dynamics, while environments reconstructed via onboard perception inherit sensing noise and artifacts. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a framework based on conditional flow matching that infers online, directly from a robot's execution data, both simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity - the remaining dynamics discrepancy and the gap between perceived and true environment geometry. A simulation-trained anomaly detector determines when recalibration or fine-tuning is required using onboard sensory signals alone, while an exploration policy actively modulates posterior uncertainty using optimism in the face of uncertainty. Across five robot platforms with up to 39 calibrated parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain map, NFC achieves the most accurate posterior distributions compared to established simulation-based inference baselines. In physical outdoor experiments with a wheeled robot suffering an axle failure across snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC increases rough-terrain navigation success from 26% to 70% while reducing orientation jerk by 88%.
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real failures caused by incomplete dynamics models and noisy environment reconstruction.
Uses conditional flow matching to estimate physical parameters plus residual fidelity, including dynamics discrepancies and geometry errors.
A simulation-trained anomaly detector triggers recalibration, while uncertainty-driven exploration improves information gathering.
Across five robot platforms, NFC produced the most accurate posterior distributions among evaluated simulation-based inference baselines.
In outdoor tests with an axle failure, rough-terrain success rose from 26% to 70% and orientation jerk fell by 88%.

Only NFC singles out the front-left wheel with near-zero damping.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.
authors: Jintao Cheng, Yipu Zhang, Haozhe Wang, Lin Jiang, Jiang Xu, Wei Zhang
bullets: Targets high latency and memory use that hinder VLA deployment on edge devices.
Combines trajectory-aware token propagation, contiguous spatial token selection, and flow-conditioned action-block refresh.
Aligns computation with both scene motion and hardware locality to reduce wasted compute and KV-cache fragmentation.
Closed-loop LIBERO evaluations report a 2.13× end-to-end speedup over dense inference with 30% visual-token retention and essentially unchanged success rate.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.
authors: Mark Zhao, Pengcheng Wang, Rui Yang, Jiarui Yao, Xirui Jiang, Yuxi Chen, Bingxuan Li, Hanyang Chen, Ke Yang, Manling Li, Tong Zhang, Huan Zhang

With GPT-6.1 Sol, AutoPILOT achieves 68.6% real-time success versus 38.3% for VISTA and matches VISTA’s final success at one-fifth the API cost.
Results across models suggest that converting model outputs into temporally extended actions is a central part of agent design.

papers.abstract: In NAVSIMv1, the standard benchmark for end-to-end driving, $89.6\%$ of the test scenes lie within 4m of a training scene. We show that this geographic overlap inflates the reported scores. We propose a geographically disjoint split of NAVSIMv1 and an evaluation that compares models trained on either split on the same scenes, which neither has seen in training. All sensor-based models we test, DiffusionDrive, Latent TransFuser, and DrivoR, lose 3.4 to 6.1 PDMS points on these scenes, mainly by leaving the road and coming close to other objects, against 1.5 points for a baseline without sensors. The loss concentrates where a training drive of the original split passed the same place. At all other places, models trained on the original split are no better than those trained on the geographic split. Models trained on the original split predict road geometry that no camera can see. The gap persists when the auxiliary map loss is removed, so the models memorize locations even without being supervised to. On nuScenes, the geographic split cuts SparseDrive's mapping accuracy by $59\%$ and also degrades its planning. Driving scores on logged scenes thus partly measure how well a model remembers the test locations. We release the split to evaluate generalization to new places.
authors: Willi Poh, Kevin R\"osch, Christoph Stiller
bullets: 89.6% of NAVSIMv1 test scenes are within 4 m of a training scene.
A geographically disjoint split evaluates models only on places unseen during training.
Sensor-based models lose 3.4–6.1 PDMS points on disjoint scenes, mainly due to road departures and near-collisions.
The performance gap is concentrated where the original training data passed the same locations; elsewhere, the splits perform similarly.
Models infer unseen road geometry and retain location memorization even without auxiliary map supervision; similar degradation appears for SparseDrive on nuScenes.

papers.selection_reason: Exposes geographic overfitting in end-to-end driving benchmarks, directly relevant to learned navigation and planning.
papers.title: Don't Test Where You Trained: Geographic Overlap Inflates End-to-End Driving Scores

papers.abstract: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: Formalizes USR and five desiderata, relating it to representations including BEV features, occupancy, maps, neural fields, scene graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents.
Provides a sensor-to-decision taxonomy covering sensing platforms, cross-view matching, fusion, geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models.
Compiles 26 urban datasets and simulators spanning ego, V2X, aerial, trajectory, and language settings, alongside metrics, benchmark results, trends, and coverage gaps.
Introduces USR-5, a proposed five-test protocol and aggregate score for evaluating whether representations are genuinely shared across platforms and tasks.
Highlights open problems in cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance.

papers.selection_reason: Survey of urban state representations spanning multimodal perception, world-model latents, and vision-language-action models for autonomous mobility.
papers.title: Urban State Representation for Autonomous Mobility: A Survey of Multimodal Perception, Architectures, Datasets, and Benchmarks

papers.abstract: Anticipating the future behavior of surrounding objects is key for the safe and efficient navigation of autonomous vehicles. State-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models are typically trained and evaluated on large-scale, highly curated datasets obtained by filtering any object detection and tracking noise through extensive offline post-processing. However, in real-world deployments, the detected objects' state (position, heading, and speed) estimates are inherently affected by sensing and localization uncertainties. These uncertainties can be even higher for connected and automated vehicles receiving information from other road users through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this paper, we first investigate the sensitivity of five state-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models to realistic noisy object state estimates. Numerical results show that prediction accuracy degrades by up to a 6x factor as the noise level increases, highlighting the models' sensitivity to the mismatch between the noise conditions encountered during training and those experienced at deployment. We then show that retraining models on a more realistic noise-augmented dataset is a more effective strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy object state estimates on trajectory prediction accuracy than using denoising modules at the input. Retrained models limit the prediction accuracy degradation below a 1.5x factor. The noise-augmented dataset is openly released to support further research.
authors: Shahab Salehi, Luca Lusvarghi, Miguel Sepulcre, Javier Gozalvez
bullets: Evaluates five interaction-aware Transformer trajectory prediction models under noisy position, heading, and speed estimates.
Prediction accuracy can degrade by up to 6× as noise increases, exposing a deployment–training mismatch.
Retraining on realistic noise-augmented data is more effective than adding input denoising modules.
Noise-augmented retraining limits degradation to below 1.5×.
The augmented dataset is released openly for further research.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Egocentric Human Activity Recognition (Ego-HAR) leverages complementary cues from first-person vision (V) and inertial sensor data (S) to recognize daily activities, where video mainly captures appearance and object-related context while inertial signals capture motion cues that video may miss. However, existing pre-training methods typically supervise the fused representation with a single joint objective, which may underemphasize the complementarity between the two modalities and limit the model's ability to learn from distinct modality-oriented signals. To address this issue, we propose Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction (MDR2), a teacher-guided pre-training framework in which frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers each provide dense, modality-specific targets to a multimodal student trained on temporally sparse inputs. On the EvIs-Kitchen dataset, MDR2 improves noun/verb F1-macro over the supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at K=4 video key frames and by 1.21/1.82 points at K=32. These results show that MDR2 consistently achieves higher mean recognition performance across the evaluated video-observation settings under the unified backbone setting, with more pronounced gains under sparse inputs.
authors: Yuzhe Hao, Ikuro Sato, Rei Kawakami, Koichi Shinoda
bullets: Targets the limitation of single-objective pre-training, which can underuse differences between video and inertial modalities.
Uses frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers to provide dense modality-specific targets.
Trains a multimodal student from temporally sparse inputs through dual representation reconstruction.
On EvIs-Kitchen, improves noun/verb F1-macro over supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at 4 frames and 1.21/1.82 points at 32 frames.
Reports larger gains under sparse video observation settings within the evaluated unified-backbone setup.

papers.abstract: Simulation-based evaluation of embodied models requires calibrated interactions, diverse tasks, and explicit execution constraints. We present RoboColiseum, a platform combining system identification, composable physics and rendering, and multidimensional benchmarking. Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.
bullets: Uses recorded-command replay for system identification and combines rigid/deformable physics with shared rendering interfaces.
Provides eight evaluation tracks covering instruction following, reasoning, manipulation, robustness, coordination, precision, and cross-embodiment execution.
Across 22 paired real–simulation robot–task configurations, simulated task scores show a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686 with real-world scores.
Uses budget-aware scoring based on task progress, resource use, and completion rewards, and reports results for Season I and II policies.
Results show substantial variation across evaluation tracks, highlighting the need for capability-oriented assessment.

papers.abstract: Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $ρ\approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($ρ\approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.
bullets: Image-editing leaderboard performance does not predict the usefulness of generated control targets.
Manipulation adherence—choosing the correct object and final state—strongly correlates with policy success, while photorealism and aesthetics do not.
SGE-Goal predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before synthesizing the goal image.
On CALVIN and SIMPLER-Bridge, SGE-Goal makes smaller open models highly effective goal generators and improves robustness to chained tasks.
The work releases code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Automated data-extraction pipeline. Each robot video is processed by a chain of vision foundation models to produce spatially-grounded training tuples (Io, Ie,Mi,Mf , T ) without manual annotation.

Figure 1. Goal images are control targets, not artworks. General-purpose editors try optimizing for editing quality in general, but for robotic manipulation a goal image must primarily (i) manipulate the correct object to the correct final state and (ii) avoid spurious changes that mislead the policy. SGE-Goal achieves this through explicit spatial grounding, while strong general editors introduce unmentioned changes, miss the instruction, or hallucinate objects.

Figure 7. Qualitative goal-image comparison. For each instruction, the goal image produced by SGE-Goal (Ours, FLUX.1 Kontext) and five baselines. SGE-Goal moves the correct object to the correct final state while preserving the rest of the scene, whereas proprietary editors (Gemini 3 Pro Image, GPT Image 1.5) render more photorealistic frames but often miss the target object or alter unrelated content. As we show next, this photorealism does not translate into downstream success, while adherence does (Tab. 7).

Figure 5. Automatically extracted training data is high quality. Human quality ratings (1–5) for the four components of each extracted tuple: original image Io, edited image Ie, initial mask Mi, final mask Mf , across the three datasets (50 annotators, 500 tuples/dataset). Figure 4. SGE-Goal synthesizes the goal image in three steps with explicit 2D spatial grounding via the initial mask Mi and final mask Mf .

SGE-Goal goal images (green) yield the best success rates at every chain length and retain performance as chain length increases, while the strongest general editors collapse: at chain length 5, SGE-Goal (FLUX.1 Kontext [Dev]) reaches 30.9% vs. Gemini 3 Pro’s 4.4% under GRMG. Long-horizon manipulation is where goal-image utility matters most. Values are previewed here and tabulated in full in Tab. 2; base=untuned editor.

Figure 6. Chained multi-step prediction by SGE-Goal. The generated goal at each step becomes the input for the next. Scene structure is preserved across all five steps and only the instructed objects move, limiting the drift that destroys long-horizon performance for entangled editors.

papers.title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: For robotic manipulation, goal images should be optimized for spatially correct actions—not visual editing quality—and SGE-Goal improves long-horizon control by grounding edits in predicted regions.

papers.abstract: Dexterous hand design demands repeated expert work across geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training. We present Task2Hand, a Skill: a specification package that turns a functional manipulation brief into a parameterized hand model and routes every candidate through cost-ordered contact, dynamics, and learning gates. Each gate returns a status and an evidence record; on failure, the Skill records the earliest blocker, revises one bounded parameter group, and reruns the cheaper gates. The agent generates, validates, and trains autonomously within declared bounds, and escalates trade-offs, plateaus, and conflicting evidence to a human who sets the next design direction. An evidence-driven design trajectory for bidirectional in-hand manipulation yielded SAGE Hand (Skill-Aware Generative Embodiment): four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb. Under a matched training protocol, SAGE Hand reaches 45.6% task success on a hexagonal prism against 37.3% for the LEAP hand, and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder against 51.6%. Dense simulated tactile input more than halves the cylinder drop rate. In a controlled iteration study, the Skill path preserves capture at 164/165 trials while the path without the Skill degrades to 14/165, confirming that the gates act as a regression guard during refinement. Accepted candidates pack with URDF/MJCF, metrics, checkpoints, and a provenance manifest.
authors: Haoyang Wang, Weibo Gao, Zhengxiong Li, Lingfeng Tao
bullets: Addresses the repetitive, expert-heavy workflow spanning geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training.
Each candidate passes cost-ordered gates with status and evidence records; failures trigger bounded parameter revisions and cheaper reruns, while unresolved trade-offs escalate to a human.
The resulting SAGE Hand has four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb.
Under matched training, SAGE Hand achieves 45.6% success on a hexagonal prism and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder; tactile input more than halves cylinder drop rate.
The Skill preserves capture in 164/165 controlled iterations versus 14/165 without it, supporting its role as a regression guard.

Fig. 2: The Task2Hand Skill. (1) The user writes a functional brief and exposes the parameter set θ the agent may change; the contract, evaluator, and success rules are frozen before any comparison. One group is revised, and every cheaper gate is rerun. Where the evidence poses a choice it cannot settle, the Skill escalates with at most three costed options; the decision returns to the ledger and the search resumes inside the approved scope. papers.abstract: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next. We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner. A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route. We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction. We compare four interfaces. The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes. The third is an outcome model that predicts the feasibility and travel time of each route. The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the chance of success and the travel time of the robot on each terrain and composes them along a route. All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard. Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard. At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7-8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35-36% on H1 compared with the plain policy. Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target. Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.
bullets: Robot damage changes which routes are feasible and how much risk is acceptable per mission.
The study compares decision policies, fixed-penalty policies, generic outcome models, and capability contracts that compose terrain-level success and travel-time predictions.
Capability contracts rank hazardous terrains using two low-risk probes, avoiding the need for four new trials per hazard.
At a calibrated 5% infeasibility limit, outcome models reduce declined missions from about 32% to 7–8% on Go2 and 57% to 35–36% on H1.
Fixed penalties help but require retuning as the target risk changes; scope is simulated damaged quadruped and humanoid robots.

papers.abstract: Autonomous racing requires an accurate vehicle dynamics model near the limits of handling, yet a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics inevitably remains. To reduce this mismatch, existing methods learn from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions, by adapting the physical parameters of the nominal model or by learning a residual that captures the remaining mismatch. However, these on-track learning methods typically handle either the physical parameters or the residual separately, which restricts their ability to resolve the mismatch. To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective. Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other's latest update. Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines. Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.
authors: Jungbin Kim, Youngim Nam, Cheolhyeon Kwon
bullets: Addresses mismatch between nominal and actual vehicle dynamics during on-track racing.
Jointly learns physical parameters and residuals under one shared prediction-error objective.
Recursively alternates updates, accepting only changes that do not increase the objective.
The objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion.
Simulations and hardware experiments show large reductions in lateral-velocity and yaw-rate one-step prediction errors versus the nominal model.

papers.abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.
authors: Huaze Tang, Runqing Miao, Tianren Peng, Lam Nguyen, Chao Wang, Jairong Li, Wenbo Ding
bullets: Frames representation learning around which action–future-state dependencies matter for policy improvement and what is lost through compression.
Builds an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix and applies SVD to obtain paired Spectral Universal Advantage Features.
Leading singular modes provide optimal rank-constrained approximations under average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria.
An action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation learns SUAF from reward-free data.
Finite-state analyses and evaluations on discrete and continuous-control tasks demonstrate utility across reward functions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

bullets: Existing VLMs struggle with metric 3D inference because uncalibrated views leave geometry ambiguous.
StereoVLM learns from binocular observations through correspondence, disparity, calibration-conditioned depth, and semantic spatial reasoning.

Interventions show performance relies on cross-view geometry, while hierarchical supervision improves broader spatial and manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to ground instructions in changing observations, coordinate heterogeneous tools, and recover from failures that can propagate through downstream operations. Although existing LLM-based agents retain experience and refine reusable skills, successful local repairs do not by themselves establish complete-task gains over the current shared procedure library. We present EvoTER, an experience-driven framework that enables embodied agents to self-evolve tool-use skills without updating model parameters. EvoTER operates through a three-role evolution loop: Explorer records tool-use trajectories; Diagnoser distills successful and failed executions into skills for tool selection, parameter computation, postcondition checks, and recovery; and Validator retains candidate revisions only when they improve complete-task success in fresh sessions. In simulation, EvoTER improves overall task success from a pre-evolution baseline of 53.60% to 80.40%. In real-world experiments, simulation initialization reduces the attempts required to acquire short-horizon skills, while continued real-world evolution improves long-horizon success from 20% to 80%-100% across tasks and enables the evolving skill library to incorporate new tool functionality introduced after simulation development. Project page: https://evoter-project.github.io/
authors: Yingting Zhou, Yuyin Zhou, Yongliang Wang, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao

papers.abstract: Linear manufacturing typically operates in highly structured settings with standardized objects, allowing robots to execute pre-programmed motions based on precise models. In contrast, circular manufacturing involves dynamic and less controlled environments, where product components can vary due to appearance and physical changes across different product generations. In this context, uncertainty arises from both the unknown or partially observed states of components (e.g., damaged surfaces, altered shapes) and the unstructured disassembly environment, often characterized by heavy clutter, occlusions, and limited sensing viewpoints. This demands a flexible and adaptable robotic grasping system that can cope with unexpected object changes. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an autonomous grasp learning framework designed for highly uncertain and variable conditions. The framework explicitly distinguishes between uncertainty due to noisy or incomplete sensory observations (aleatoric uncertainty) and uncertainty due to limited knowledge and distribution shift (epistemic uncertainty). Moreover, the framework employs an active perception strategy to reduce visual ambiguity: semantic and spatial scene understanding is achieved using vision language models (VLMs), while view planning enables the robot to adjust its viewpoint to improve observability. In addition, the approach leverages large-scale human demonstration data to learn interaction patterns, which are then transferred to robotic end-effectors, enabling robust manipulation in these variable settings. Quantitative validation, including the utility of active vision on disassembled components in practice, is expected to form an important part of future work.
authors: Yitian Shi, Rosa Wolf, Rania Rayyes

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed CIRCA-Grasp framework. In the digital asset pipeline, existing CAD models are used to generate analytic antipodal grasps and simulation-based training environments, which support pretraining of the probabilistic grasp learner vMF-Contact [4]. In the physical asset pipeline, large-scale human demonstrations are transferred through HOGraspFlow [10] to provide hand-object interaction priors, while real-world robot executions continuously generate grasp experiences for deployment and adaptation. During inference, VISO-Grasp [5] integrates the uncertainty-aware grasp model with active view planning to search for and grasp partially visible or occluded objects in clutter. All simulated and real interactions are stored in a grasp learning database, enabling continual improvement of the grasp policy across perception, planning, and execution.

The high variance and unknown states of recycled materials require advanced, uncertainty-aware manipulation strategies to reliably grasp “out-of-distribution” (OOD) objects in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
authors: Zhenxuan Fan, Zhuoya Wang, Yuqian Yuan, Wenqiao Zhang, Juncheng Li, Jun Xiao, Siliang Tang, Yueting Zhuang

papers.abstract: Training a humanoid motion tracker by backpropagating imagined returns through a learned world model is fast, because the model gives a first-order policy gradient. We ask how much of that gradient holds in the simulator. On a tracker for the Unitree G1, the $0.5\%$ of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm, yet neither a second rollout from the same state nor the simulator confirms them. When the actions are moved along the model's gradient, the simulator returns 94% of the predicted change in return where the gradient norm is below the batch median, 48% between 3 and 10 times the median, and 1% above 30 times; the part of a gradient that either check confirms stops growing at a few times the median. We therefore cap each rollout's action-gradient norm at 10 times the batch median, draw imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient norm so that the cap removes less, and reset episodes where the world model and critic predict the lowest return. Trained on 223 hours of motion and tested on 353 motions that no actor performed in training, the method raises the normalized return of SuperMimic, the baseline it builds on, from 0.953 to 0.967 and the lowest $1\%$ of test clips from 0.65 to 0.76, halves the test clips that fall persistently, from 15--18 to 7--10, and reaches the baseline's final return in 40% of the baseline's iterations and half its training time. On LAFAN1, trained and evaluated on the same clips as prior work, it reaches 0.935 against 0.906.
bullets: Very large imagined gradients are poorly validated: simulator-confirmed return changes fall from 94% at low norms to 1% above 30× the batch median.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.
authors: Nan Tang, Han-Tao Zhang, Jing-Cheng Pang, Hao-Nan Wang, Hao-Xiang Ren, Yi-Fei Sheng, Jun-Yin Ye, Tian Xu, Fan-Ming Luo, Hao-Xin Lin, Yang Yu
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of image/video-based VLA model-based reinforcement learning.
Uses Hierarchical Forcing to mitigate compounding errors in recursive latent predictions.
Introduces Latent Subchunk Rollouts to connect latent imagination with frozen VLA action-chunk execution.
Applies a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum for learning from short imagined rollouts.
Reports strong task performance and training efficiency across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot.

papers.abstract: Driving models that reason may describe a hazard correctly while choosing their path for other reasons. We study where scene reasoning can enter an end-to-end planner so its influence can be checked. We freeze Drive-JEPA and use a fine-tuned vision-language model to state scene facts. Although fine-tuning improves fact accuracy, the two learned components we test show no detectable benefit from reading them. A rule-based fact check instead rejects or shortens paths that contradict the facts, linking each intervention to a stated fact. On the frozen planner alone, it gains 2.4 EPDMS points on navhard. Its 2.0-point margin over a control that changes the same frames without consulting facts remains statistically uncertain. A diagnostic using exact facts from maps and annotations yields a 3.6-point margin over its corresponding control, with a 95% confidence interval above zero. Separately, a path scorer and plan memory that read no stated facts raise navhard from 41.2 to 51.8. Bounding travel distance using the reasoner's facts adds 0.3 there and reduces navtest by 2.0. The fact check makes each intervention auditable, while the driving value of the reasoner's facts remains unresolved.
authors: Gautam Kumar Jain, Atharva Mahindrakar, Shubham Phoolari, Ignacio Alvarez, Carsten Markgraf, Constanze Hungar, Christoph Lauer, Julian Staehler
bullets: Learned scene facts did not measurably improve two tested planner components, despite better fact accuracy after fine-tuning.
A rule-based checker rejects or shortens paths that contradict stated facts, directly linking interventions to those facts.
On navhard, the checker gained 2.4 EPDMS points over the frozen planner; its advantage over a same-frame control was statistically uncertain.
Using exact map and annotation facts produced a statistically supported 3.6-point margin over its control.
A fact-independent path scorer and plan memory improved navhard from 41.2 to 51.8; fact-based distance bounding added 0.3 there but reduced navtest by 2.0.

papers.abstract: Type disciplines make programs safe by construction: components checked against each other's types compose into programs that cannot go wrong in the ways the types exclude. Types suit reinforcement learning: a type constrains what an agent may choose, not how it chooses, so the guarantee holds for every policy a learner produces. We introduce epistemic typestates, a type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning. An agent's type is a protocol whose states record its beliefs, the worlds it cannot rule out from its own observations and actions, and permits only actions that are safe in every world of the belief, whatever the others do within their public types. Agents learn inside their types, which are built and checked one agent at a time and run without communication. We prove type soundness and team safety, give a synthesis that is sound and complete, build types from guards when worlds are infinite, and show that shields are a special case. All proofs are mechanised in Rocq. On nine benchmarks, no typed learner causes a safety violation, and task performance does not differ significantly from that of two recent multi-agent shielding methods. Where a contract-based method fails at five and ten agents, types for ten agents are built in under a second. In the two continuous benchmarks, Lagrangian learners cause thousands of violations in every training run.
authors: Lorenzo Bacchiani, Mario Bravetti, Giovanni Pau, Roberto Girau
bullets: Agents’ types track observation-based beliefs and allow only actions safe in every possible world and under all teammates’ permitted behaviors.
Types are constructed and checked one agent at a time, letting agents learn within safety-preserving protocols without communication.
The work proves type soundness and team safety, provides sound-and-complete synthesis, supports infinite worlds via guards, and subsumes shields as a special case.
All proofs are mechanised in Rocq; across nine benchmarks, typed learners caused no safety violations and matched two shielding methods in task performance.
Types scaled to ten agents in under a second where a contract-based method failed; Lagrangian learners produced thousands of violations in each continuous-benchmark training run.
