papers.abstract: When interacting with objects of unknown physical properties, humans sometimes probe, over-exert, stagger, and adjust through iterative adaptation instead of succeeding immediately. We argue that this process is an expressive but largely overlooked aspect of human-object interaction in motion synthesis. Both kinematic data-driven methods and physics-based controllers tend to produce flawlessly executed motions: the former lack sufficient data for learning fine-grained adaptation, while the latter use reinforcement learning (RL) and privileged object dynamics to learn robust, deterministic behaviors. We propose ExpHOI (Expressive Human-Object Interaction), a test-time latent adaptation framework built on an RL-trained physics-based control policy. During policy training, we encode diverse object dynamics contexts into a structured latent space. At test time, Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) iteratively optimizes the latent code for an object with unknown physical properties. Temporary mismatches between this code and the true object dynamics produce an expressive progression from tentative, error-prone trials to proficient interaction. Adaptation behaviors inevitably come with occasional failures, so a high-level planner is introduced to handle failed cases to maintain full, consistent animations. We demonstrate our framework's effectiveness on a large-object transportation task, where such adaptation is especially pronounced. To train our framework, we introduce a mass-diverse object dataset with rich physical-property annotations. Across carrying and push-pull, our method pairs over 90% success with markedly higher posture diversity, and is rated the most lifelike in our user study on animation liveliness.
authors: Zijing Wu, Yiping Li, ZhiPeng Yu, Yuzhou Zheng, Ziyazhuo Wang, Binghui Zuo, Yangang Wang
bullets: Targets the overlooked expressiveness of probing, over-exertion, staggering, and adjustment when object dynamics are unknown.
Builds on an RL-trained physics controller with object dynamics encoded in a structured latent space.
Uses Advantage-Weighted Regression to iteratively adapt the latent code during interaction.
Adds a high-level planner to recover from adaptation failures and preserve consistent animations.
On carrying and push-pull tasks, achieves over 90% success, greater posture diversity, and the highest perceived liveliness in a user study.

The object interaction controller operates in two phases. During training, a context encoder (ctxEncoder) produces a latent estimate z of the object’s physical properties. During inference, the ctxEncoder is replaced by test-time latent tuning (AWR). With z∗ fixed, the intermediate trials themselves yield the expressive exertion we extract.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn language model agents often receive only a single binary reward at the end of a long interaction trajectory, making it difficult to separate decisive decisions from routine steps or estimate accurate intermediate values. Prefix-tree methods improve sample efficiency by merging trajectories that share action histories, yet two structural flaws remain: naive pooling mixes stale off-policy outcomes into critic targets with fixed weights, and uniform or entropy-driven branching wastes continuations on dead-end states whose outcome is already settled. We introduce WEIR (Watershed Exploration and Intrinsic-Drift Shrinkage), an actor-critic reinforcement learning framework grounded in a Doob turn-variance conservation identity. WEIR maintains a cross-iteration canonical action-prefix tree with exponentially discounted visit counts and trains a prefix-conditioned critic toward a minimax drift-aware shrinkage target that adapts from single-trajectory returns at rare nodes to pooled empirical means at dense nodes. Using the same pre-update critic, WEIR allocates rollout budgets across tasks via Neyman stratification $B_q \propto \sqrt{\hat{p}_q(1-\hat{p}_q)}$ and directs within-task branches to watershed forks where high survival-headroom uncertainty coincides with steep value cliffs. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, ALFWorld, and WebShop on Qwen2.5-3B/7B-Instruct, WEIR achieves $32.18\%$ and $37.85\%$ average QA exact match and $84.83\%$ and $87.81\%$ ALFWorld success rates, outperforming CAPO by $1.50$--$3.74$ points while generating $28$--$29\%$ fewer rollout tokens than chain sampling.
authors: Pixel Nomand, Elena Voss, Marcus Hale, Sofia Reyes
bullets: Addresses sparse end-of-trajectory rewards and inefficient exploration in long agent interactions.
Builds a cross-iteration canonical action-prefix tree with discounted visits and a prefix-conditioned critic.
Uses adaptive shrinkage targets that interpolate between individual returns at rare prefixes and pooled means at dense prefixes.
Allocates budgets by task uncertainty and explores watershed forks with high survival uncertainty and sharp value changes.
Across QA, ALFWorld, and WebShop, reports improved performance over CAPO while using 28–29% fewer rollout tokens.

papers.abstract: General-purpose whole-body trackers can execute diverse humanoid motions, but they require dense reference trajectories. However, tasks usually specify only where, in which posture, and when the robot should arrive, leaving the motion in between to a separate planner. Inspired by human motor coordination, our key idea is that a low-level controller can organize the intervening motion and its pace by itself from sparse goals with arrival times. In this paper, we propose S-BFM, a novel behavioral foundation model superior in its autonomy: it generates whole-body transitions from target postures, poses, and arrival times alone. Specifically, we first introduce Spatial Grounding, which adds world-frame position and heading to a forward-backward behavior representation through spatial reconstruction. Then, Time-Conditioned Distillation is designed to learn transitions and pace from real motion through closed-loop imitation of a dense-reference teacher. Lastly, Generative Fine-Tuning is introduced to broaden the covered distances and arrival times with a distilled motion generator. In simulation, S-BFM lowers global joint-position error by over 32% relative to the best baseline under fixed and mixed horizons, and raises fixed-goal reach from 43.5% to 74.6% while cutting terminal position error from 1.67 to 0.26 m. We further deploy S-BFM on the full-size AGIBOT A3 humanoid. Sparse spatiotemporal goals thus suffice for natural, well-timed whole-body motion.
authors: Kun Yang, Xuanyu Chen, Jing Tan, Yanjing Liu, Yubo Zhao, Renjing Xu, Addison Lin Wang
bullets: Addresses the need for autonomous motion generation when tasks provide only sparse spatial and temporal goals.
Uses Spatial Grounding to incorporate world-frame position and heading into behavior representations.
Applies Time-Conditioned Distillation to learn transitions and motion pacing from a dense-reference teacher.
Uses Generative Fine-Tuning to extend the range of achievable distances and arrival times.

In simulation, reduces global joint-position error by over 32%, improves fixed-goal reach from 43.5% to 74.6%, and lowers terminal position error from 1.67 to 0.26 m; it is also deployed on the full-size AGIBOT A3.

papers.abstract: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.
authors: Jan Miko{\l}ajczyk, Igor Rostkowski, Bartosz Og\'orkiewicz, Szymon Skierski, Sylwia Opat, Wojciech Rybak, Miko{\l}aj Sczogiel, Rados{\l}aw Pa{\l}ys, Jan Gogulski, Bartosz Ko\'scio{\l}ek, Andrzej Pijanowski, Szymon Kowalski, Marcin Misiewicz
bullets: TDMA communication delay grows with swarm size and causes collisions through stale neighbor estimates at the safety filter.
Without delay, up to 100-agent swarms remain collision-free; delays beyond roughly 125–175 ms, or 75–100 ms with held measurement noise at 100 agents, can break safety.
At the mean-field layer, delay mainly increases density noise and reduces throughput by at most about one tenth, without biasing local density.
Lightweight neighbor-position predictors restore safety and extend tolerated communication periods by about 1.4–2.3×, depending on predictor and noise conditions.
Prediction should be enabled only beyond the uncompensated safety limit, because its estimation errors can otherwise introduce collisions; widening safety margins performs worse in bottlenecks.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses learned delay compensation and safety filters for robot swarms, fitting robot navigation with learned components.
papers.title: Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter
papers.tldr: In delayed-communication drone swarms, delay compensation is most valuable—and should be activated—in the control-barrier safety filter rather than the mean-field routing layer.

papers.abstract: Human driving logs record only one trajectory per scene, leaving other feasible driving choices without explicit trajectory targets or quality labels. This limits supervision for end-to-end planners that generate and refine multiple candidate trajectories. Meanwhile, conditioning refinement on a large vision-language model adds substantial online inference cost. We propose DriveSTA, which extends autoregressive proposal generation and proposal-conditioned residual flow refinement with scored trajectory alternatives. For each training scene, we generate alternatives offline through smooth deformations of the recorded trajectory and evaluate their simulated execution against logged traffic. Diverse, high-quality alternatives supervise distinct proposals and define residual targets for quality-guided denoising, while candidates spanning the full score range train a scorer to assess driving quality. A shared joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), adapted through masked video-feature prediction, encodes observed frames once and provides temporal context for both refinement and scoring. On NAVSIM v1 Navtest, DriveSTA ranks first among the compared planners trained on NAVSIM data alone. With expanded training data, DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, while reducing mean planner forward-pass latency by 73% relative to ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.
authors: Xinyao Rao, Zecheng Tang, Liuxuan Sun, Zheyuan Lai, Minjun Yu, Xun Cao, Wei Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of quality-labeled alternative trajectories in single-trajectory human driving logs.
Generates alternatives by smoothly deforming logged trajectories and scoring their simulated execution against traffic.
Uses scored alternatives to supervise proposal generation, residual-flow refinement, and trajectory-quality scoring.
A shared JEPA-based video encoder provides temporal context for refinement and scoring without costly online vision-language-model conditioning.

Ranks first among compared NAVSIM-only planners; DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art compared results on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, with 73% lower mean forward-pass latency than ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.

papers.abstract: We present Ego4Gen (Egocentric 4D Future Generation), a world model for 4D future generation in robotic manipu lation. Given a single egocentric image and a text prompt, Ego4Gen jointly generates temporally aligned RGB frames, dense point maps, and dense scene flow, explicitly pre dicting the evolution of scene appearance, spatial struc ture, and motion. Built on Cosmos3-Nano, Ego4Gen ex tends the pretrained generative backbone through modality routed LoRA and asymmetric attention, using geometric pseudo-labels from MotionCrafter to learn to predict future geometry and motion latents. These latents can either be decoded into explicit 3D structure and motion or mapped to robot actions. To this end, we also introduce FlowIn verse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network trained in two stages to translate predicted 4D latents into robot ac tions. Experiments show that these geometry and motion latents outperform the evaluated latent-action and video latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings. Closed loop policy evaluations further demonstrate their utility for translating predicted 4D futures into robot control. To gether, these results support geometry-grounded motion to kens as a world-action interface, connecting 4D future gen eration with robotic manipulation and suggesting a path to ward reduced reliance on action-labeled data.
authors: Yang Liu, Chao Ye, Jiahao Zhang, Zeyuan Hou, Ruijie Fang, Xiyin Ni, Xinyang Ren, Weiyang Lin
bullets: Targets 4D future generation for robotic manipulation while modeling scene appearance, structure, and motion jointly.
Extends Cosmos3-Nano with modality-routed LoRA, asymmetric attention, and MotionCrafter-derived geometric pseudo-labels.
Introduces FlowInverse, a lightweight two-stage inverse-dynamics network that maps predicted 4D latents to robot actions.
Geometry and motion latents outperform evaluated latent-action and video-latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings.
Closed-loop policy evaluations demonstrate that the predicted futures can support robot control and reduce reliance on action-labeled data.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM-environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability.
authors: Guangzhao Dai, Guoxin Lian, Shuo Wang, Shengbin Yue, Qianru Sun, Xiangbo Shu, Bin Zhu
bullets: Addresses the dependence of VLN performance on manually designed tools, memory, and agent roles.
Collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, then uses a designer agent to revise and retain effective harnesses across iterations.
Uses privileged simulator diagnostics only for harness design, while the navigating LLM operates with a single RGB camera and primitive actions.
Reports consistent gains across LLMs from four vendors, including an 85.64% success rate on R2R-CE val-unseen with GPT-6-Astra.
Shows generalization to RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.
authors: Caoyuan Ma, Wendi Liu, Zhimin Zhang, Muyao Niu, Yujie Lu, Zengxi Zhang, Ji Zhao, Shuai Dong, Wenpu Liu, Ziyue Wang, Wenzheng Chang, Taiqiang Wu, Weichu Xie, Yuqi Xu, Haiyuan Wan, Xuehui Wang, Jiaqi Wang, Wenqi Shao, Yinqiang Zheng
bullets: Links a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop with shared goals and evaluators.
Agents observe only workstation camera views and use either a single-arm probe or dual-arm dexterous hands.
Across five models and 40 tasks, desktop performance exceeded physical performance; hands generally outperformed the probe.
Trajectory analysis shows strategic adaptation toward keyboard input, but execution fails from missed presses, wrong targets, and unintended contacts.
The benchmark quantifies the gap between digital task competence and physical execution.

papers.abstract: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.
authors: Chuhan Jiao, John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Guy Rosman, Andreas Bulling
bullets: Addresses visual perspective taking beyond state estimation, reconstruction, and discrete question answering.
Uses backbone-agnostic geometric modules with scene coordinate maps, 3D ray-space token alignment, and visual-memory-based view completion.
Handles extreme viewpoint changes, dynamic occlusions, and sparse overlap between collaborators’ views.
Across three video diffusion backbones on CoMind, improves visual quality, scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion over prior cross-view generation methods.
Enables applications in human–robot collaboration and synchronized multi-perspective video generation for robot learning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Ego2Ego. Given the ego person’s egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and both camera trajectories, Ego2Ego generates the collaborator’s egocentric video with a pretrained video diffusion transformer equipped with three geometry-grounded modules. All conditions are encoded by the frozen VAE and form a single token sequence with the noisy collaborator latent. (1) Since the same surface appears entirely different from the two viewpoints and hands occlude the scene, dense geometric rendering rasterises the point cloud into every view, colouring each pixel by its 3D coordinate in a shared frame, so that the same scene point carries the same colour across views and provides a shared spatial reference. (2) To relate tokens across substantially different viewpoints, relative geometric attention aligns the geometric components of keys and values to each query token’s ray-aligned frame. (3) To recover regions the ego person does not currently observe, the ego person’s visual memory supplies past ego-person frames together with their renderings.

papers.abstract: Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving 1.7-3.4x speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe.
authors: Zian Deng, Tianyi Zhang, Zilong Zheng, Ziyu Liu, Tao Zhang, Yao Lyu, Shengbo Eben Li
bullets: Motivation: Future visual prediction is often retained during training even though it is unnecessary at inference, adding cost and complexity.
Method: Fine-tunes an image-generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action-regression adapter while reusing the native generative objective for perception co-training.
Architecture: A shared image-editing interface supports current-scene perception, future prediction, and combinations without task-specific perception heads.
Results: Achieves 99.10% success on LIBERO, 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus, and strong robustness on real-world manipulation tasks.
Efficiency: Uses one backbone forward pass and reaches 20.9 ms per action chunk on an H100, with reported 1.7–3.4× speedups over VLA and WAM baselines.

papers.abstract: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.
authors: GiHyun Kim, JinMo Yang, Hyung-Sin Kim
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between light collection and motion blur in robot-camera depth sensing.
Uses a frozen depth model and a learned predictor of reference-relative disagreement to score candidate camera settings without ground truth at deployment.
A contextual Gaussian-process controller selects subsequent exposure and gain using recent scores plus motion, camera, and illumination context.
Evaluated across nine scene-illumination conditions, it reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned Abs_rel by 14.6% versus built-in auto-exposure and 10.0% versus the best evaluated prior controller.
Demonstrates online control on a mobile robot with the affine-invariant Depth Anything v2 variant.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.
authors: Kangyi Wu, Pengna Li, Yucheng Wang, Yance Fang, Xihan Ma, Zhizhong Su, Yang Wu, Ye Deng, Jinjun Wang, Jianyi Liu
bullets: VLN agents must plan beyond their current visual observation while following language instructions.
The paper argues that future representation should include goal-directed spatial states and route structure, inspired by predictive-map views of navigation.
FS-Nav predicts short-horizon waypoints and mid-horizon corridors from spatial memory and language instructions.
These future states are communicated to a vision-language navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces.
Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, though the abstract provides no further experimental details.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) exhibit strong manipulation capabilities yet often fail to follow test-time language instructions. Prior work shows that non-following (NF) WAMs encode information about the instructed target, but this information does not control their behavior. By comparing NF WAM with its instruction-following (IF) counterpart, we find that target information is substantially more linearly decodable in IF WAMs, despite being encoded in both. Motivated by this observation, we introduce linear decodability supervision (LDS), a simple yet effective auxiliary training objective that promotes the linear decodability of the instructed target information. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0-$\Delta$ with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6% and a grounding rate of 89.2%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. The effectiveness of LDS challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, we propose a prior-instruction competition mechanism, which explains NF and IF behavior as arising from the dominance of prior and instruction signals, respectively. We provide causal evidence for this mechanism by evaluating two training-free interventions derived from it. We reinterpret LDS through this mechanism, showing that it acts as a form of instruction signal enhancement. Finally, more comprehensive evaluations across diverse manipulation tasks and visual domains demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of LDS.
authors: Bokai Ji, Jiapeng Chen, Yi Zhang, Zeyuan Ding, Yong Dai, Xiaozhu Ju, Jian Tang, Lemao Liu, Dejing Dou, Yong Li
bullets: Non-following models encode target information, but it is less linearly decodable than in instruction-following models.
The proposed LDS auxiliary objective promotes linear decodability of the instructed target during training.
On LIBERO-CF, LDS improves InternW0-$\Delta$ to 74.6% success and 89.2% grounding, gains of 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
A prior-instruction competition mechanism explains failures as prior signals dominating instruction signals.
Training-free interventions and broader evaluations support the mechanism and show LDS transfers across manipulation tasks and visual domains.

(c) Why LDS works. Counterfactual grounding supervision amplifies the existing instruction signal I while largely preserving its direction.

papers.abstract: Parametric body models expose incompatible pose and shape controls, tying humanoid policies to particular input formats. AnyBodyCodec learns a shared representation through native conversion, then reuses it for new body models and control with its core frozen. Encoders map MHR, SMPL-X, and SOMA to aligned slots; native decoders recover target controls. The 1.090M-parameter converter covers nine routes and reaches 16.801 mm input-reference MPJPE across six cross routes: the 2.887M Transformer bank reaches 16.390 mm and its parameter-matched version 18.866 mm. Three measured routes take 7.43-7.67 ms on an RTX 4090. Adding ANNY shows that comparable conversion accuracy can accompany different action consistency under one frozen controller. Under a matched PPO budget, aligned slots support 60.78% full-action success across three formats. Separate 160-hour training reaches 66.10% source-weighted validation success, and the controller is deployed qualitatively on a physical G1 through three visual front ends. Together, these results establish reuse through both native geometric fidelity and downstream policy compatibility.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have recently attracted increasing attention in motion planning due to their ability to model high-dimensional and multi-modal trajectory distributions. However, existing diffusion-based planners still struggle to reliably satisfy geometric feasibility in unseen cluttered environments with complex obstacle layouts. To address this challenge, we propose GeoSDF-Diff, a geometry-aware diffusion planner that incorporates multi-scale SDF conditioning into trajectory denoising. The key idea is to provide the denoiser with both route-level geometric context and fine local clearance evidence, enabling generated trajectories to better adapt to unseen complex obstacle layouts. Specifically, a Geometric Encoder extracts multi-scale SDF features and injects them into a DiT-X denoiser through cross-attention. We further introduce a trajectory-level training objective that combines SDF clearance, violation emphasis, smoothness, and path-length regularization, so that local infeasibilities are penalized during training rather than corrected only at inference time. Experiments on held-out cluttered environments show that, without post-hoc trajectory repair or sampling-time guidance, GeoSDF-Diff achieves a 65.2% average success rate across diverse test scenarios, outperforming strong diffusion baselines by 25.4% to 28.5%.
authors: Yueming Li, Zhanjiang Yang, Yang Shen, Meng Li, Lijun Sun
bullets: Addresses unreliable collision-free planning in complex, unseen obstacle layouts.
Encodes route-level and local geometric information using multi-scale signed distance fields (SDFs).
Injects SDF features into a DiT-X denoiser through cross-attention.
Uses a trajectory-level objective combining clearance, violation, smoothness, and path-length terms.
Achieves a 65.2% average success rate without post-hoc repair or sampling-time guidance, outperforming diffusion baselines by 25.4–28.5%.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of GeoSDF-Diff, a geometry-aware diffusion planner with multiscale SDF conditioning. Fig. 3. Ablation of the SDF-conditioned DiT-X denoiser, multi-scale SDF conditioning, and trajectory-level violation objective.

papers.abstract: Bayesian state estimators, such as Kalman filters, estimate states from noisy observations based on dynamical models. However, obtaining accurate models can be challenging when the system involves effects that are difficult to model faithfully, such as friction, impacts, and deformation in contact-rich manipulation. Uncertainty in system parameters, inputs, and disturbances, together with simplified noise models, can further introduce simulation-to-reality mismatch and degrade estimation accuracy. These limitations motivate learning a distribution over state trajectories conditioned on observations and controls without explicitly specifying the underlying physical models. We introduce NormFlowSDE, an amortized Bayesian state estimator that learns a distribution over state trajectories by combining neural stochastic differential equations with conditional normalizing flows. Its key design choice is to utilize the capability of normalizing flows to learn stochastic behavior of variables, while leveraging the continuous-time dynamics of SDEs to model the evolution of states over time. Once trained, the model draws state paths for new measurement sequences without per-sequence optimization. In addition, we connect NormFlowSDE to stochastic continuous-time dynamics by proving weak convergence of a mean-centered, drift-corrected inference scheme to an It\^o diffusion under stated assumptions. Finally, we benchmark NormFlowSDE against direct estimators and learned particle filters based on normalizing flows on partially observed dynamical systems, including simulated systems and real-world robot datasets. The results show that NormFlowSDE attains the lowest estimation error with calibrated uncertainty intervals on both robot datasets and filters four times faster than the fastest particle filter on every dataset.
bullets: Addresses state-estimation errors caused by difficult-to-model dynamics, parameter uncertainty, disturbances, and simplified noise assumptions.
Combines neural stochastic differential equations with conditional normalizing flows to represent continuous-time stochastic state evolution.
Amortizes inference: after training, it samples state paths for new measurement sequences without per-sequence optimization.
Provides a theoretical weak-convergence result linking its drift-corrected inference scheme to an Itô diffusion under stated assumptions.
Achieves the lowest estimation error with calibrated uncertainty on robot datasets and filters four times faster than the fastest learned particle filter across evaluated datasets.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.
authors: Yongkang He, Xiaofen Xing, Xiangmin Xu
bullets: Existing models can preserve global appearance while missing local interaction details, causing implausible contact effects and robot-object behavior.
MoReWorld uses a shared motion region to guide local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning.
The motion region is inferred at test time from visual history and robot actions, without future observations or ground-truth motion labels.
On WorldSimProbe, it achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with strongest results in local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics.

(d) A shared Wan denoising transformer jointly processes RGB and VGGT latents and predicts the RGB velocity, clean future VGGT features, and an auxiliary flow velocity, supervised with the motion-region weighted loss.

papers.abstract: Given a pretrained general latent-conditioned whole-body humanoid controller, say a behavioral foundation model (BFM), how can we elicit complex and contact-rich out-of-distribution behaviors? Raw joint-action exploration enables direct, task-specific adjustments but can disrupt coordination learned by the pretrained controller, whereas latent exploration retains that coordination but is difficult to steer toward desired physical effects. To combine the complementary strengths of these exploration spaces, we propose Latent Jacobian Steer (LJS), which couples sampling in direct joint-action space with the semantics of the learned frozen controller's input latent space. For a task specified through desired physical effects, we sample task-relevant joint-action perturbations and map them through a damped local inverse of the policy Jacobian to obtain candidate latent ($z$) commands. These commands are executed through the frozen pretrained policy, while exploration is directed toward the physical outcomes required by the new task. Candidate outcomes are evaluated in simulation and composed into latent-command sequences that accomplish the task. Ablations show that neither action-space nor latent-space exploration alone provides the same capability as their coupling. Across diverse out-of-distribution tasks, simulation-based searching using this method produces contact-rich behaviors, including hurdling, manipulating articulated objects, and opening doors through non-prehensile contact. Over ten seeds, LJS completes more of each humanoid task than when searching in either space alone. Beyond humanoids, it also steers a goal-conditioned dexterous hand policy through four assembly tasks better than searching in goal space directly.
authors: S K Swaminathan, Shivam Sood, Shreyansh Kansal, Chengyang He, Guillaume Adrien Sartoretti
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of steering latent-conditioned humanoid controllers toward physical effects without disrupting learned coordination.
Maps task-relevant joint-action perturbations through a damped local inverse policy Jacobian to generate latent commands.
Executes candidates with the frozen pretrained policy, evaluates outcomes in simulation, and composes successful latent-command sequences.
Produces behaviors such as hurdling, articulated-object manipulation, and non-prehensile door opening across diverse out-of-distribution tasks.
Also improves steering of a goal-conditioned dexterous hand policy on four assembly tasks compared with direct goal-space search.

papers.abstract: A planner deciding whether to turn left or continue straight needs to inspect different parts of the scene for each maneuver. Yet many end-to-end driving planners evaluate every candidate trajectory against the same compressed scene representation. We let each candidate select the visual evidence used to refine and score it. A global glance first produces trajectory hypotheses from shared scene features. We then project a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and use the resulting mask to attend to patch features at the backbone's native resolution. After refinement, the scorer projects each final proposal again and ranks it using evidence along its own path. This geometric selection requires only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration. On three planners with different scene representations (learned registers, a perception-supervised bird's-eye-view grid, and a coarse image-token grid), adding this gaze improves planning scores. In ablations, path-aligned patches outperform both a matched number of randomly selected patches and attention over all patches. Using the gaze for ranking yields larger gains than using it for refinement alone. With a ViT-S backbone and no perception labels, GGDriver achieves a rater feedback score of 8.110 on the WOD-E2E test set, 94.2 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1, 48.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM-v2, and a closed-loop Driving Score of 72.18 on Bench2Drive.
authors: Jiawei Sun, Maosen Li, Jiamin Shi, Xiaoxu Zheng, Jiun Tian Hoe, Yechao Bai, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of scoring all trajectories from the same compressed scene representation.
Generates trajectory hypotheses from shared features, then uses trajectory-aligned camera corridors to select native-resolution patch features.
Refines and ranks each proposal using visual evidence specific to its path, requiring only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration.
Across three planner representations, path-aligned gaze improves planning scores and outperforms random or all-patch attention.
Ranking with gaze provides larger gains than refinement alone; the method operates without perception labels and reports results on WOD-E2E, NAVSIM, and Bench2Drive.

papers.abstract: Real-time human-robot social interaction requires continuous coordination between speech and physical behavior. Existing systems often separate interaction agents from motion generation, complicating coordination as conversational states change. We propose \textbf{Embodied Interaction Policy (EIP)}, a unified streaming framework that couples an Audio-Interaction expert with a motion expert through layer-wise joint attention. This allows motion generation to directly access the evolving interaction context. A chunk-wise causal mask prevents access to future context, while a vocal token encodes speaking state and the semantic emotion of the response. We construct \textbf{Embodied Interaction Dataset (EI-Data)} from co-speech and dyadic interaction data and train our model in two stages to learn state-adaptive and emotion-conditioned behavior. Combined with the frozen interaction expert, EIP supports continuous robot motion during proactive responses and interruption-aware turn-taking. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate improved motion quality over representative gesture-generation baselines. Compared with a representative cascaded system, EIP achieves higher interaction success and reduces warm-start latency by 64\%. Physical deployment and user studies further demonstrate improved motion naturalness and interaction comfort.
authors: Youqiang Gui, Yunfei Liu, Lijian Lin, Ye Zhu, Jianan Wang, Cheng Peng, Yu Li
bullets: Addresses coordination challenges caused by separating conversational agents from motion generators.
Couples an Audio-Interaction expert with a motion expert using layer-wise joint attention and causal chunk-wise masking.
Uses vocal tokens to represent speaking state and response emotion, trained on the EI-Data dataset in two stages.
Supports continuous motion during proactive responses and interruption-aware turn-taking.
Evaluations report better motion quality, higher interaction success, 64% lower warm-start latency, and improved naturalness and comfort in deployment studies.

figures.caption: Figure 3 - Overview of the EIP framework. EIP consists of a pretrained interaction expert that processes streaming audio and models the evolving interaction context, together with a motion expert that generates continuous and synchronized robot motions.

papers.tldr: EIP unifies speech interaction and robot motion generation to enable responsive, natural, and interruption-aware human–robot interaction.

papers.abstract: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $\gamma$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.
authors: Xiaotao Zhang, Lin Qian, Hao Zhang, Xuanrui Cui, Yuehao Huang, Yunzi Wu, Yucheng Deng, Jiankun Dong, Hujun Yin, Xinhai Li, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
bullets: Supports complete mobile-manipulation tasks in a persistent physical world, where agents compose motion tools and learned skills.
BenchForge links structured objectives to physical task instances, reference programs, instructions, and goal evaluators while allowing multiple valid solutions.
Collects contact-rich demonstrations and aligned observation–action records through autonomous, assisted, and human-guided execution.
Enables program refinement and policy learning from tool traces, with shared task-goal criteria for evaluation.
Benchmarks representative agents and demonstrates contact-data collection and trace-informed program revision; the abstract does not report quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Completing a manipulation task does not establish that a robot follows the requested goal rather than a familiar routine. ManipScope is an evaluation-only diagnostic benchmark for robotic instruction following under changed task requirements. Built on RoboTwin 2.0's simulation resources, it specifies 48 held-out scenes across six task families with explicit source-task links; policies are trained on unmodified RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrations, and no demonstrations of the scenes are provided, so success requires reusing skills under a changed request rather than fitting supplied examples. Beyond task success, ManipScope provides a chain of diagnostics in which each step tests one explanation of a failure. For twelve policy checkpoints, 84.6% of failures in 13,200 episodes on eleven selection scenes displace a distractor, and gripper records show that failed episodes usually grasp a non-target. When the target is reassigned among the candidates on identical initial states, ten checkpoints follow every instruction on 3.9% of 1,000 states, below the 16% of an instruction-blind chooser, while a GPT-6 agent run as positive control reaches 88%. The failure recurs on unmodified training tasks and is not explained by missing manipulation skills, so success in these scenes largely reflects instruction-independent preferences; two checkpoints trained on the same data nevertheless follow color instructions. In a feasibility test, letting an agent select the target and the policy execute partly restores instruction following. Case studies with future-video and internal-intervention probes further show that forecasts and execution can agree on the wrong target and that action changes need not transfer the goal. Success, consistency, and sensitivity must each be checked against the requested goal.
authors: Jiacheng Li, Yaping Li, Congsheng Xu, Qingchen Liu, Haonan Wang, Zhijie Deng, Jiahu Qin
bullets: Evaluation-only benchmark with 48 held-out scenes across six task families, using changed requirements and no demonstrations of test scenes.
A diagnostic chain separates task failure explanations, including distractor displacement, target selection, execution, and internal decision processes.
Across 13,200 episodes, 84.6% of failures displaced a distractor; target reassignment showed only 3.9% instruction-following across 1,000 states for the tested checkpoints.
The issue persists on unmodified training tasks and is not simply missing manipulation skill; some checkpoints trained on the same data do follow color instructions.
Results indicate that success, consistency, and sensitivity should each be evaluated against the specified goal; target selection before policy execution partly improves following.

papers.abstract: Manual assembly remains difficult to monitor because operator actions, components, and task progress must be interpreted together. This paper presents a modular framework based on a single overhead red-green-blue (RGB) camera, combining object detection, hand-motion tracking, region-aware interaction detection, finite-state verification, task-specific pose classification, and configurable visual guidance. The system was evaluated during pneumatic-piston assembly and disassembly with eight participants under three assistance conditions: full, mid, and no guidance. Mixed-effects analysis identified an association between assistance condition and a composite measure of motion quality, with lower estimated scores under mid and no guidance relative to full guidance. However, the condition-by-trial interaction was not statistically significant, and the estimated differences in learning trajectories remain descriptive. No condition differences were detected in completion time or failed-stage counts. The study demonstrates the integration of visual perception, procedural verification, and configurable operator feedback in a single-camera workflow. Selecting assistance according to operator expertise remains a design objective for future investigation.
authors: Naveen Joseph Delphin, Leonardo Venturoso, Isabella Soraruf, Marco Todescato
bullets: Targets the challenge of interpreting operator actions, components, and task progress together.
Integrates object detection, hand tracking, region-aware interaction detection, finite-state verification, pose classification, and configurable visual guidance.
Evaluated on pneumatic-piston assembly and disassembly with eight participants under full, mid, and no guidance.
Assistance condition was associated with motion quality, but not completion time or failed-stage counts; learning-trajectory differences were only descriptive.
Future work should tailor assistance to operator expertise.

papers.abstract: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.
authors: Ziyi Ding, Yiwei Wang, Zhongxing Wei, Xianxin Lai, Yechi Liu, Xiaodi Huang, Jinghua Hou, Xiaoquan Sun, Haijier Chen, Zhe Liu, Yinan Chen, Junqiao Zhao, Xiao-Ping Zhang, Jiayu Chen
bullets: Problem: Egocentric frame changes mix hand manipulation with camera motion, making action targets ambiguous.
Method: Supervises latent action codes with measured wrist translation and rotation while providing camera motion separately to the forward model.
Design: Pools object representations around each hand and decodes wrist motion in a shared reference frame; inference uses only two RGB frames.
Evaluation: Tests hand-motion retention and robustness to synthetic viewpoint and lighting changes, alongside LARYBench tasks.
Results: Achieves the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight models and 79.38% mean LIBERO success, outperforming behavior cloning and other latent-action models on average.

papers.abstract: While existing methods for reconstructing deformable object manipulation have made impressive progress, they typically represent a thin object with a single particle set that must serve two purposes at once: modeling bending, and resolving contact with the robot. To bridge this gap, we present HermiteTwin, a framework that reconstructs a physical digital twin of a thin deformable object from multiview video of a robot manipulating it. Our key idea is to represent deformation and contact separately, each at its own resolution. The object is simulated as a bicubic Hermite shell, a coarse grid of $C^1$ elements whose nodal positions and derivatives define a smooth surface with Kirchhoff--Love bending, while the gripper acts through dense samples in material space that are captured, clamped, and released, and whose attachment forces reach the shell through the Hermite basis. This decoupling keeps the physical state compact while contact stays fine-grained. We identify effective material and contact parameters with CMA-ES followed by adjoint-based refinement, and drive a reconstructed Gaussian appearance model with the simulated shell. In experiments on real cloth and foam manipulation, HermiteTwin outperforms the state-of-the-art spring--mass twin across reconstruction, resimulation, and future prediction.
authors: Kangrui Zhang, Mu Huang, Xing Shen, Tiantian Liu, Bo Ren
bullets: Addresses the conflict between representing bending and resolving robot contact with a single particle set.
Uses a coarse $C^1$ bicubic Hermite shell with Kirchhoff–Love bending for compact, smooth physical state modeling.
Represents gripper interaction through dense material-space samples whose forces are transferred to the shell via Hermite basis functions.
Estimates material and contact parameters with CMA-ES followed by adjoint-based refinement, and drives a Gaussian appearance model from the simulated shell.
Outperforms a spring–mass digital twin in reconstruction, resimulation, and future prediction on real cloth and foam manipulation.

The gripper captures dense samples in material space (red); each attached sample ri lies in one element, and its attachment residual reaches the 16 nodal vectors of that element through the Hermite weights J⊤ i (inset). The effective parameters θ are identified by minimizing a full-rollout observation loss with CMA-ES followed by adjoint-based Adam. The identified twin resimulates the recorded motion, predicts held-out frames, and drives the Gaussian appearance in synthesized scenes.

papers.abstract: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.
bullets: Addresses optimal control under parametric uncertainty, where surrogate errors can mislead gradient-based optimization.
Uses a physics-informed DeepONet to predict trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation and reuse the operator across targets and horizons.
Applies one parallel Newton correction to the dynamics, yielding second-order state-error control based on the residual alone.
On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, matches batched Adam and Ipopt accuracy at equal sample size while running 8× faster than Adam on GPU and 15× faster than Ipopt on CPU.

papers.abstract: Cloud--edge deployment enables asynchronous dual-system VLN on resource-constrained robots, but inference and communication delays cause latent mismatch and navigation errors. Existing adaptation methods reuse historical guidance but cannot provide updated navigation information when it becomes inadequate. We propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and edge-side compensation. Our analysis reveals that action-relevant mismatch is concentrated in a compact Critical Subspace and can be tracked through fast-system feature drift. Critical Feature Drift Entropy reflects navigation sensitivity and guides adaptive refresh, while Critical Drift Continuity indicates when recent latent updates can support compensation during latency spikes. AceVLN integrates subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh scheduling, and continuity-guided compensation. Experiments show that \textit{AceVLN} improves success rates by 1.7--2.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines, while reducing amortized computation time by 2.7--10.0\% and FLOPs by 18.4--22.3\%.
authors: Zihao Zheng, Hangyu Cao, Yulong Han, Xichang Wu, Zhihao Mao, Maoliang Li, Jiayu Chen, Hailong Zou, Donggang Cao, Xuanzhe Liu, Hong Mei, Xiang Chen
bullets: Addresses latent mismatch and navigation errors caused by asynchronous inference and communication delays on resource-constrained robots.
Identifies a compact Critical Subspace where action-relevant mismatch is concentrated and tracks it via fast-system feature drift.
Uses Critical Feature Drift Entropy for adaptive latent-refresh scheduling and Critical Drift Continuity for edge-side compensation during latency spikes.
Combines subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh, and continuity-guided compensation.
Reports 1.7–2.4 percentage-point success-rate gains, 2.7–10.0% lower amortized computation time, and 18.4–22.3% fewer FLOPs than the strongest baselines.

papers.abstract: Driving world-action models generate planned trajectories through iterative action denoising, with each update depending on the preceding state. This sequential dependency incurs substantial inference latency, limiting timely planning. Speculative inference offers an opportunity to reduce this latency by predicting future denoising states for parallel target evaluation, but requires efficient proposal generation and suitable verification for continuous actions. We present Trailblazer-F, a speculative action-flow inference framework in which a lightweight drafter acts as a trailblazer, charting a candidate denoising path through the compact, structured waypoint space so that the target model can verify multiple steps in parallel and advance with fewer sequential updates. Our method maintains planning quality while keeping the pretrained target model frozen.Across all 12,146 NAVSIM v1 navtest scenes, Trailblazer-F maintains near-baseline planning performance, with PDMS changes of +0.04 and -0.08 points for SimWAM and DriveWAM, respectively. Paired inference measurements on an NVIDIA L20 GPU yield 2.31x and 1.55x speedups. Real-vehicle experiments on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin further demonstrate 1.96x and 1.37x speedups, together with close qualitative trajectory agreement with native sampling. our code is here https://github.com/DanileHaibo/Trailblazer-F
authors: Haibo Hu, Lianming Huang, Qiao Li, Nan Guan, Chun Jason Xue
bullets: Addresses latency from sequential action-denoising updates in driving world-action models.
Uses a lightweight drafter to predict candidate paths in compact waypoint space while keeping the pretrained target model frozen.
Enables the target model to verify multiple denoising steps in parallel.
Across 12,146 NAVSIM v1 navtest scenes, PDMS changed by only +0.04 for SimWAM and −0.08 for DriveWAM.
Achieves 2.31×/1.55× speedups on an NVIDIA L20 and 1.96×/1.37× on Jetson AGX Orin, with close qualitative trajectory agreement.

papers.abstract: Existing legged-locomotion systems commonly rely on depth images or online elevation maps. However, depth-based policies suffer from perceptual sim-to-real discrepancies due to imperfect depth sensor modeling, while map-based approaches are vulnerable to drift and misalignment. LiDAR offers direct measurements of the surrounding geometry, but raw LiDAR scans lack a compact, structured representation for high-frequency control. We propose a LiDAR perception pipeline that maintains perceptual consistency across simulation and reality through sensing- and representation-level alignment. At the sensor level, we recover frame-wise angular sampling patterns from the physical LiDAR and replay them in simulation with GPU ray casting. At the representation level, simulated and real returns undergo the same spherical range image encoding, yielding a fixed-size policy observation for end-to-end training and direct deployment without teacher--student distillation, online elevation mapping, or adaptation. Experiments show that our range-image policies achieve stronger sim-to-real transfer than depth- and elevation-map-based baselines, while ablations confirm the importance of the proposed sensing components. More visualizations and real-world videos are available at the \href{https://lidar-img.github.io/}
authors: Nian Liu, Xinyi Tong, Ming Ren, Long Ye, Zhaofeng He
bullets: Addresses depth-sensor sim-to-real gaps and drift-prone elevation maps.
Recovers real LiDAR angular sampling and reproduces it in simulation via GPU ray casting.
Encodes simulated and real returns identically as fixed-size spherical range images.
Enables end-to-end policy training and direct deployment without distillation, mapping, or adaptation.
Experiments report stronger transfer than depth- and elevation-map baselines; ablations support the sensing design.

papers.abstract: A visual agent acts on what it sees: it taps and types on a screen, or points on a camera image to show a robot where to act. One wrong step can fail its task, yet the right action is often among its own samples, passed over by its greedy decode. Choosing it is a visual judgment, since an action is best judged where it acts, not by its text or coordinates alone: as text, a tap is two numbers; drawn on the screen, it is the Post button of an empty draft. We find that this is decisive: given the screenshot and a tap's coordinates, a decision model chooses among GUI-R1-3B's samples significantly worse on average than when the tap is drawn where it lands. Bel turns this finding into a method that trains nothing and needs only a frozen policy's samples and an image on which each action can be drawn. It marks each candidate on its own copy of the image it acts on, asks a decision model for the probability that executing it is the right decision, so that every kind of action shares one scale, and acts on another candidate only when greedy scores below a threshold and trails it by a margin. On recorded GUI steps, for each of three policies, Bel significantly beats greedy decoding on mobile, web and desktop screens alike and, on the same candidates, gives each a significantly higher mean step success than voting, CATTS, the trained GUI-Critic-R1 and two prompted Qwen3-VL judges shown the same marks; it also significantly improves the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B on every step-level test set. With GUI-R1-3B's thresholds unchanged, Bel significantly raises live AndroidWorld and MiniWoB++ task success for two other policies and robot-pointing success for three policies on each of two groups of benchmarks. Judging each action where it acts thus gives step-level policy improvement of visual agents without training, with significant gains for GUI agents and robot pointing.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Ziwen Wang, Zhaoyu Zhu, Changyi Yang, Neil He, Chaoran Cheng, Ge Liu
bullets: A single wrong action can fail a task, while the best action may be present among a policy’s sampled candidates but missed by greedy decoding.

Across recorded GUI steps, Bel outperforms greedy decoding, voting, CATTS, GUI-Critic-R1, and prompted visual judges.
It also improves live GUI task success and robot-pointing success across multiple policies and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Single-modality action-expert pretraining controls competition from visual shortcuts before vision--language--action (VLA) adaptation. Yet single-modality pretraining can impair the vision--language interactions needed for subsequent joint prediction. We construct a diagnostic model in which VA or LA pretraining can disable an initially active pathway for joint vision--language modeling. In this model, subsequent training with complete visual and language inputs cannot restore the pathway, even with unlimited adaptation. We therefore introduce Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining (SCAP), a new action-expert pretraining stage that precedes full-input training. During this stage, visual and text tokens are randomly masked before entering the VLM. In this unified diagnostic model, SCAP can preserve the joint vision--language modeling pathway during pretraining and subsequent full-input training. Compared with direct full-input training, it can also reduce reliance on visual shortcuts and increase reliance on language instructions. SCAP consistently improves performance across four different VLA architectures. In real-robot experiments, it achieves 76.67% average success across three instruction-conditioned manipulation tasks, outperforming full-input pretraining by 25 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.
authors: Sunli Chen, Yun Zong, Qinhong Zhou, Xiaowen Qiu, Jiaben Chen, Zeyuan Yang, Chuang Gan
bullets: Addresses the blind interval in turn-based agent harnesses, where humans can disrupt robot actions before the agent can reassess.

Evaluated with three VLAs and one WAM on 168 RoboCasa365 disturbance scenes in RoboHD, plus real-robot manipulation tasks.
With the strongest policy, TRIP improved safety from 61.3% to 81.3% and task success from 31.0% to 38.7% versus the same turn-based harness.
Real-robot tests showed successful completion of two manipulation tasks under human interference, where baseline approaches largely failed.

papers.abstract: As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.

papers.abstract: Vision-model-based robotic navigation has gained increasing popularity, yet existing approaches still struggle to deliver effective and efficient navigation performance, \textit{e.g.}, diffusion-based policies that require costly iterative denoising. In this work, we propose three improvements to bridge these gaps. First, we adopt a rectified flow framework to reduce the required inference steps to one while achieving comparable or even superior performance. Second, we leverage a bidirectional Mamba-based visual encoder that employs selective state-space modeling to more effectively capture bidirectional temporal dependencies across observation frames, even with longer input sequences. Most importantly, we find that na\"{i}vely combining these two components to balance accuracy with inference speed yields no further performance gains or even produces inferior results. Upon extensive analysis, we realized that the root cause lies in the fact that the Hydra-derived temporal context is shared unchanged across all flow timesteps, and timestep information is introduced only within the velocity network. This weak coupling limits the model's ability to adaptively exploit temporal visual features at different flow states. To address this, we propose a feature-wise timestep conditioning design that explicitly conditions the visual embedding on the flow timestep, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation, thereby restoring a meaningful gradient pathway and enabling coherent interaction between the rectified flow and the temporal encoder. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms both baseline and competitive methods.
authors: Xiaogang Wang, Debasish Mishra, Jia Hao Toh, Wangsheng Liu, Yash Shah
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of diffusion-based robotic navigation policies that require iterative denoising.
Uses rectified flow to reduce inference to one step and a bidirectional Mamba-based encoder to capture temporal dependencies across observations.
Finds that simply combining these components can hurt performance because temporal features are shared unchanged across flow timesteps.
Introduces feature-wise timestep conditioning of visual embeddings, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation and stronger interaction between the encoder and flow model.
Experiments across multiple datasets show consistent gains over baseline and competing methods, though specific metrics are not reported.
