papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
authors: Zhikang Shi, Yuk Tung Samuel Fang, Hongyu Ding, Zixuan Chen, Yujin Wang, Junhui Guo, You Wu, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
bullets: Organizes 2,071 episodes into 710 sessions across 34 scenes, with later instructions referring to earlier objects or routes.
Evaluates three capabilities: historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization with route reproduction.
The latter two levels require agents to align historical memory with current episode frames without cross-episode frame transformations.
Introduces MemBridge, combining semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval.
Experiments show MemBridge benefits existing VLN agents, while memory-dependent navigation remains challenging.

papers.abstract: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0x/1.25x speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return -- not blind IMU drift suppression - and uncover a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.
bullets: Position-dependent dark zones require active probing, unlike timed outages where hovering is effective; the two appear identical when vision is first lost.

The module interfaces with an unchanged host controller and combines loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height correction, and an optional prior-map branch.
On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark with 1,920 flights, the full configuration achieved 88.5% worst-condition completion and outperformed the reported baselines.
Attached to SimpleFlight without retraining, it improved worst-condition completion to 86.5% and achieved 90% completion across tested speed conditions with no hard failures.
Diagnostics indicate that recovery depends primarily on asymmetric visual-inertial re-acquisition at vision return, with a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on held-out EuRoC windows.

papers.title: Portable Active Recovery under Timed and Position-Dependent Visual Outages
papers.tldr: A portable, zero-retraining recovery module enables visual-inertial quadrotors to actively recover from both timed and position-dependent camera outages, achieving strong worst-case completion across diverse tests.

papers.abstract: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon's hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io
authors: Ankit Pal, Guillaume Kugener, Sofia Volpi, Joshua Schwartz, Alex Idarraga, Pranav Rajpurkar, Gabriel A. Brat
bullets: Provides 41,909 training hand instances and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows from 68 procedure recordings, covering 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees.
Includes multi-sensor imagery metadata, hand landmarks and confidence, timestamps, eye gaze, and SLAM extrinsics when available.
Uses procedure-disjoint and leave-one-wearer-out evaluation with sensor-fused, human-reviewed, surgeon-adjudicated, and multi-view reference labels.
Across eight zero-shot methods, JointTransformer performed best at 14.95 mm PA-MPJPE; ego-pretrained methods transferred better to held-out wearers.
MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1% of evaluation rows, and a substantial surgical domain gap remains; the dataset and benchmark code are released publicly.

figures.caption: Figure 6: JRN architecture. The frozen backbone f (any of the eight evaluated methods) maps the input image I to a 21-joint prediction x ∈ R21×3 in camera frame. JRN is a 58,306-parameter two-headed MLP residual corrector. The pose head (blue, 32,831 params) consumes the root-relative pose x− x0 ∈ R63 and emits a 21× 3 root-relative residual δp. The translation head (orange, 25,475 params) consumes the root-relative pose concatenated with the raw wrist xyz, [x− x0, x0 ] ∈ R66, and emits a 3-D wrist correction δt broadcast to all 21 joints via 121. The corrected output is x̂ = x+ δp + δt · 121. Both heads are zero-initialized, so JRN equals the identity at t=0. The training loss panel reproduces the formal definition; targets are computed from the training partition only. Pose head and translation head are orthogonal on four of the five reported metrics (Appx. A.4): the pose head drives PA-MPJPE / MPJPE-RR / PA-P2D (translation-invariant under Procrustes), while the translation head drives Root err. MPJPE-abs depends on both heads; the full JRN trains them jointly.

Figure 4: Benchmark: zero-shot error with 95% PR-bootstrap CIs, and the effect of JRN. Ego-pretrained backbones (green) have the lowest zero-shot error among single-hand methods, 40% (JointTransformer) and 18% (WildHands) below the non-egocentric reference HaMeR. Left: PA-MPJPE (mm, vs Aria MPS). Right: PA-P2D (px); protocol as in Tab. 2. Circles: zero-shot, colored by model family, with CI bars; diamonds: +JRN. The green band spans the two ego-pretrained +JRN results, which reach the label resolution scale (§6.2) and are not ranked. †MediaPipe on the 24.1% of rows where it detects a hand.

Figure 2: EgoSurgHands data pipeline. (1) Capture: four wearers in three experience tiers perform 13 tasks in three glove colors with smart glasses. (2) MPS: each .vrs session is processed by Meta Machine Perception Services for SLAM trajectory, 3D hand landmarks, calibration, confidence, and eye gaze; audio is not released. (3) Pseudo-GT: landmarks are projected into the RGB frames, time-aligned, confidence-gated at ≥0.97, and inspected. (4) Validation: training rows use gated MPS labels (41,909 rows / 55 PRs); evaluation rows are further validated by multi-rater review, examiner review, and surgeon adjudication (9,476 rows / 13 held-out PRs).

Figure 3: JRN architecture. A frozen backbone predicts 21 camera-frame joints x; the pose head (blue) corrects the root-relative pose and the translation head (orange) the wrist position. Both are zero-initialized (identity at start); details in Appx. B.

Figure 5: Per-stratum PA-MPJPE-MPS for WildHands and JointTransformer (ZS vs +JRN). JRN lowers error in every stratum; P4 (all brown-glove hand instances, n=661) is the hardest for both backbones. Glove color, experience tier, and wearer are confounded in the evaluation split, so stratum differences are not attributed to any single factor.

Figure 7: Annotation tool, bundle picker. Each evaluation pool is split into fixed-size bundles (1,000 frames each); annotators select a bundle to work on and resume across sessions. Per-bundle progress is persisted server-side. The “open access” flag enables multiple raters to independently tag the same bundle, which is the substrate for the multi-rater review and inter-annotator-agreement audit described in §3.4.

Figure 8: Annotation tool, frame canvas. Each frame is rendered with all available skeleton overlays (HaMeR-left/right, MPS-left/right) toggleable individually from the Settings panel (left). Reviewers translate skeletons by direct drag (wholeskeleton or per-point modes; only the whole-skeleton translation is stored), rotate the canvas in 90° increments, and zoom from 0.5× to 3×. The Status panel (right) holds the three-state labeling buttons (Good / Drag-and-save / Reject) plus Skip, an optional free-text note, prev/next navigation, and a keyboard-shortcut reference. The example frame shows a right-hand suturing pose with the MPS-right overlay (orange) about to be drag-corrected by the rater.

Figure 9: Per-task hand-pose fingerprints. For each surgical training task we show (left) the canonical neutral MANO mesh colored by per-vertex displacement from neutral, computed as the rigid-aligned distance between the per-task median MANO surface and the neutral T-pose, and (right) a representative raw ego frame. Red = high-displacement regions; blue = parts that stay near neutral. Colormap is shared globally so panels are directly comparable. Surgical tasks produce visually distinct surface fingerprints recovered from a single median pose.

papers.abstract: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.
authors: Weikang Qiu, Zheng Huang, Tinglin Huang, Yujun Yan, Rex Ying
bullets: Addresses the limited transferability of EEG motor representations learned from cue-based trials, coarse labels, or movement-agnostic objectives.
Learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations by treating current EEG as a latent action that predicts future visual representations.
Introduces a Lateralization-Aware Transformer to model shared bilateral and side-specific hemispheric features.
Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% over task-family baselines.
The world model has lower prediction error than an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline and benefits more from matched real actions, including on held-out subjects.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Existing approaches (top) versus MWM (bottom) on the three challenges of motor EEG representation learning. (1) Cue-based trials are costly to scale, and categorical labels give one class to movements that unfold differently (Tangermann et al., 2012; Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018). (2) General-purpose EEG foundation models (FMs) pretrain with EEG-only objectives (Kostas et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). MWM answers both with one mechanism: it treats the EEG recorded up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model that predicts the next visual state. It therefore learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations, and its target is the visual consequence of behavior rather than the EEG itself. (3) Existing methods do not explicitly separate bilateral from lateral activity (Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025a); MWM does, and pairs each horizontal video mirror with an exchange of only the lateral component Hlat.

Figure 2: The Mind World Model. (a) A frozen encoder g maps the current frame to patch features that a residual predictor advances; the same frozen g builds the target from the next frame. (b) The mind model encodes the EEG window, which ends on the current frame; its LAT encoder is detailed in Figure 3. The EEG reaches the predictor only as AdaLN modulation, never as an input token: it occupies the slot a recorded action would.

Figure 3: The Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT) for EEG encoding. (a) Patch embedding, applied within each channel, (b) the learned gate G ∈ [0, 1]C×N×De and the electrode permutation Π ∈ {0, 1}C×C , which act on the embedded tokens before any Transformer block; the mirror acts on the decomposed pair and is an involution, (c) a criss-cross block, (d) a shared Transformer with invariant and equivariant readout heads; under the mirror, Hbi is unchanged and Hlat flips sign after aligning homologous channels, and (e) the paired EEG–video mirror. Only the learned lateral component is exchanged across hemispheres; the raw signal is never permuted.

Figure 4: Lateralization analysis. (a,b) Hand-motion correlations with 95% confidence intervals estimated by bootstrap resampling, using participants as the resampling unit. (c–e) Participantaveraged motor-imagery feature-energy contrasts, normalized by channel-wise mean energy; left– right contrasts share a color scale. Control features h(1) and h(2) are equal-sized halves of h.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly important for robot learning, yet most generate each camera view separately or tile all views in a fixed layout. Robot demonstrations, however, are captured by synchronized cameras whose number, placement, and order vary across embodiments. We present ViewDreamer, a single world model that handles variable sets of cameras by disentangling per-view generation from cross-view interaction. Each view follows the generation path of a pretrained single-view model, and views interact only through shared slot tokens. We stabilize multi-view training with a curriculum that gradually increases the number of views. Cross-View Slot Agreement uses visual foundation models to group geometrically and semantically similar regions across views into shared slots. On RoboView-Bench, which covers one to four cameras, ViewDreamer achieves the best generation quality among the models evaluated and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. These gains carry over to our world-action model (WAM) and action-conditioned world model (AC-WM). Our WAM outperforms the FastWAM-Joint baseline on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboDojo, and on a real Franka robot. Both variants improve out-of-domain generalization to various camera settings and scenes.
authors: Ye Mao, Jinhui Xiong, Egor Larionov, Shiyang Lu, Krystian Mikolajczyk, Wei Ye
bullets: Addresses the limitation of models tied to fixed camera counts, placements, or layouts.
Disentangles per-view generation from cross-view interaction using shared slot tokens.
Uses curriculum training and Cross-View Slot Agreement to align geometrically and semantically similar regions.
Achieves the best evaluated generation quality on RoboView-Bench and improves cross-view consistency over independent view generation.
Transfers gains to world-action models, robot benchmarks, and a real Franka robot, including better generalization across camera settings and scenes.

papers.abstract: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. Project page: https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/
authors: Zhiyuan Li, Charles Eret, Dingsheng Liu, Xuan Zhao, Joshua Choi, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Amir Rasouli
bullets: Covers 80 bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished environments, with 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K language instructions.

Evaluates visual, linguistic, and object-level perturbations through per-factor analysis.
Experiments show clutter reduces success and increases non-target collisions, while perturbation type and training-data composition affect performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.

bullets: VLAs support generalizable robot control but can leave serving hardware under-utilized.
Multi-client serving may improve hardware utilization by processing requests concurrently.
The study evaluates batching and co-execution across latency, throughput, power, and utilization.
Results highlight trade-offs and challenges for designing future multi-VLA serving systems.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video is the most scalable source of manipulation data for robot learning, but its difficulty lies in producing high-quality supervision. Existing large corpora lack metric 3D labels or rely on heterogeneous devices, motion-capture labs, or a headset's built-in real-time tracker, whose accuracy is not reported for the released data. We introduce RoboCap-10k: 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation recorded during workers' paid shifts in 11 countries, spanning 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks. Every hour is captured on one device, the RoboCap, a 250 g hat with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs. Online calibration brings every device below 1 px of epipolar error, visual-inertial SLAM yields gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories, and a multi-view hand tracker yields metric cm-precise hand poses. Each episode is annotated with task and sub-task language captions. Project page: https://robocap10k.com
authors: Kheri Hughes, Qasim Ali, Nikash Bhardwaj, Owen Akhibi, Niresh Dravin, Vivek Sharma, Sam Cho, Ethan Lee, Paul Luo, Sunny Yu, Jonathan Victor, Amanda Young, Michael Cho, Ademi Adeniji, Vincent Liu
bullets: Contains 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation across 11 countries, 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks.
Uses a lightweight 250 g hat equipped with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs.
Provides gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories and centimeter-precise metric hand poses.
Includes task- and sub-task-level language captions for each episode.
Scope: recordings are collected during workers’ paid shifts using a single device per hour.

papers.selection_reason: Large-scale egocentric manipulation video dataset with metric labels and language captions directly supports learning robot skills from human video.
papers.title: RoboCap-10k: A Metrically Accurate Egocentric Dataset for Robot Learning
papers.tldr: RoboCap-10k is a large-scale egocentric manipulation dataset with calibrated multi-camera recordings and metric 3D hand and head-motion supervision.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of judging self-improvement using only task progress, QA accuracy, or episodic memory.
Evaluates agents in Outer Wilds, where each 22-minute episode resets the world but preserves the agent’s knowledge.
Measures reached locations, revealed rumor facts, correctness on 164 world-knowledge questions, and whether answers are supported by cited frames and positions.
In eight-episode baselines, the three measures did not consistently improve together; GPT-6.1 Sol’s correct answers rose from 14.6% to 26.8%, but only 59–68% were evidence-supported by episode 8.
After episode 3, GPT-6.1 Sol revealed no new rumor facts while exploration and memory continued growing; over half of later newly correct answers cited earlier-episode evidence.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Types of evidence an agent can ground knowledge in: observation (by eye or through an instrument), testimony (dialogue or writing, shown as on-screen text), and interaction, the result of the agent’s own action (Gopnik et al., 2004; Harris and Koenig, 2006). Screenshots from Outer Wilds, © Mobius Digital.
Figure 2: GPT-6.1 Sol with the knowledge base, GPT6.1 Sol judge. Left: correct and grounded answers. Right: newly correct answers per loop (bars) and cumulative rumor facts (line).
Figure 3: Places reached and rumor facts revealed, cumulative over eight loops.

Table 1: Challenging scenarios in the world of AstronautBench, with the knowledge types of Table 2. Each property makes evidence harder to collect or progress harder to make: a time window or an irreversible choice limits when the agent can act, a knowledge-gated route stays closed until the agent learns how to pass it, the world changing on its own makes one visit insufficient, similar-looking things and hidden hazards make a single observation misleading, and the environment can make an action differ from the intended one.
Table 5: Entity Knowledge QA per loop under the GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon judges. Correct and grounded are shares of all 164 questions. The score runs from −100 to 100.

Table 2: Questions by knowledge type, with the corresponding categories of OpenEQA (Majumdar et al., 2024) and NExT-QA (Xiao et al., 2021) and dimensions of Ilievski et al. (2021), and the GPT-6.1 Sol run’s correct and grounded answers at loop 8 (GPT-6.1 Sol judge).

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for embodied agent self-improvement across episodes measuring knowledge, evidence, and progress; fits test-time learning, embodied memory, and embodied AI.
papers.title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
papers.tldr: AstronautBench evaluates agent self-improvement across episodes by jointly measuring knowledge, evidence grounding, and world progress, showing these dimensions can diverge substantially.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.
authors: Qiang Zhou, Jianing Deng, Siyan Dong, Jingxian Chen, Han-Yi Lin, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of re-encoding long video histories when escalating from a continuously running small VLM to a large VLM.
Distills a label-free, per-layer linear map from the large model’s answers, using only the current frame to transform the small model’s KV cache.
The useful transfer is concentrated in one direction across the middle third of the large model’s layers; faithfully reproducing the large model’s cache does not improve performance.
On RoboMME, Baton outperforms the small model alone, pruned or shortened re-watching, and text memory, while matching re-watching with 28–47% less compute.
The approach transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA and scales with the large model’s capability across eight model pairs from four families.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Two ways to train the same handoff map, and what they give (2B→8B, RoboMME choice). (a) The small model’s KV memory is mapped into a memory the large model reads while it encodes the present itself. Translation fits it to the large model’s own cache; BATON distills the large model’s answer through the deployed path. (b) The translation maps are eleven times closer to the large model’s cache than BATON and gain nothing; BATON carries the gain in each of four runs (dots; bars: mean, 95% interval).

Figure 2. Perceive once, escalate on demand. (a) A small VLM runs continuously over the agent’s visual history and keeps its KV cache. When it is unsure, the decision is escalated: instead of re-encoding the whole history, the large VLM reads the small model’s memory through BATON, a per-layer linear map, and encodes only the current view itself. (b) Reader compute per escalation on 16-frame histories. (c) At a 25% escalation budget the memory cascade is within 0.7 points of re-watching for both readers.

Figure 5. The handoff gain tracks the reader’s headroom. Grey: gain of the large model over the small one by re-watching; colour: by reading the small model’s memory (whiskers: 95% intervals, Bonferroni-corrected). On choice the gain follows the headroom closely (r = 0.91, seven pairs; inset: Gemma 3, pointing).

Figure 6. What distillation adds is one direction, and it sits where the map departs least (RoboMME choice). (a) The step D that takes BATON to the translation map costs the gain (small markers: partial steps) and the opposite step far more; random steps of identical size (open markers) cost nothing. (b) Top: read-out error per layer of the 8B: BATON departs from the reader’s own cache everywhere, but least in the middle third. Bottom: layers taken from the translation map, four (first row) or twelve at a time, lose the gain only in the middle third; its three windows sum to 2.7, less than the 4.7 of the twelve together: the layers act jointly.

Figure 1. Escalation without re-watching. (b) With 25% of decisions escalated, BATON keeps nearly all the accuracy that re-watching adds (Sec. 6.4).

Figure 4. Accuracy vs. compute of the two escalation channels (RoboMME choice; budgets of 10–40%, same router and thresholds). At every budget the memory cascade is within 0.7 points of the re-watch cascade, at 21–46% less compute for the 8B reader (mean of three seeds) and 36–52% less for the 32B reader.

Table 2. Alternatives to the memory handoff (2B→8B, RoboMME test, 16-frame histories; TFLOP per escalation). Every other way of seeing the history costs more and loses on choice or point; text memory loses on both, even with a trained reader.

Last row: the pre-registered primary comparisons with 95% intervals (adapted map on HM3D, zero-shot map on ScanNet). BATON is best or statistically tied in every column.

papers.selection_reason: Hands off visual KV memory between VLMs for embodied agents; fits KV-cache efficiency and embodied memory.
papers.title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
papers.tldr: Baton lets a large VLM reuse a small VLM’s visual KV memory during escalation, preserving re-watching quality while substantially reducing compute.

papers.abstract: Learning robotic ultrasound policies requires interactive environments for scalable data generation and repeatable evaluation, while exploration on real patients is limited by acquisition costs and safety constraints. Generative world models offer an alternative, but image history and probe actions alone do not ensure anatomical consistency across wide-range scans and changing acoustic windows. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an ultrasound world model built on anatomy as state. A persistent 3D anatomical asset extracted from computed tomography (CT) anchors each scan to a specific anatomy. Probe actions determine anatomical and acoustic visibility conditions for a causal ultrasound generator trained on clinical videos. Our three-stage pipeline combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion and long-rollout alignment. Inference optimizations achieve pose-to-ultrasound throughput of 81.2 FPS. To evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity, we introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI), which measures normalized reconstruction gain over a static-prefix baseline. On 40 held-out 3D volumes, SonoAtlasWorld achieves liver and macro-organ AFI of 0.428 and 0.262, compared with at most 0.117 and 0.038 for the tested action- and geometry-conditioned methods. Long-rollout alignment reduces brightness drift by 3.46x at the end of 40 repeated scan cycles. SonoAtlasWorld also generates offline policy-training demonstrations and supports anatomically grounded closed-loop evaluation. Scaling the generated training data improves key-plane acquisition success from 48.2% to 81.2% on unseen anatomies in simulation, demonstrating its utility for robotic ultrasound policy learning.
authors: Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Mailhe, Hang Yu, Yikang Liu, Xiao Chen, Ankush Mukherjee, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, safe interactive environments for robotic ultrasound learning.
Conditions a causal ultrasound generator on CT-derived anatomy and probe-controlled anatomical and acoustic visibility.
Combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion, and long-rollout alignment; inference reaches 81.2 FPS.
Introduces the Action-Following Index to evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity.
On 40 held-out volumes, it improves liver and macro-organ AFI, reduces long-rollout brightness drift, and raises simulated key-plane success from 48.2% to 81.2%.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SonoAtlasWorld. (a) Five rendered poses illustrate interaction with one persistent scene. The final pose, anatomical rendering and generated observation share the same saved time step. The current pose provides anatomy and visibility conditions; generated history provides temporal context for causal ultrasound generation. Persistent anatomy supports consistent modeling under challenging bone-induced occlusion. (b) Training proceeds from anatomy-conditioned pretraining to causal few-step distillation and long-rollout alignment. The final stage applies DMD to a teacher-length window after a no-gradient generated prefix.

Figure 4. Long-rollout alignment mitigates accumulated drift. Compared with the short-rollout model (S), the aligned model (L) better preserves ultrasound appearance and anatomy over 40 repeated scan cycles, reducing cycle-40 brightness drift by 3.46×. Top: drift and anatomical agreement across cycles; shaded bands denote 95% confidence intervals. Bottom: generated frames at the same return pose for two cases. Early appearances are similar, but S progressively darkens and loses visible structures, while L maintains clearer boundaries.

Figure 3. Anatomical consistency across controlled scans. For each of two initial observations, slide, fan and wide-scan trajectories produce distinct ultrasound sequences. Right: liver reconstructions from generated frames along the executed poses, overlaid on the reference 3D anatomy. The shared anatomical state grounds each scan in the same spatial reference.

Figure 5. World-model data scaling improves downstream policy learning. (a) More training volumes and generated trajectories improve closed-loop key-plane acquisition on unseen volumes. (b) Lower offline action-prediction error is associated with higher closed-loop success across the displayed checkpoints.

Given anatomical inputs, SonoAtlasWorld’s benefits extend beyond gross liver structure to finer anatomical recovery and temporal continuity. Real/sim: real/generated training data. †Adapted re-implementations; real action/geometry baselines use EM tracking.
Table 3. Inference speed improvements. Static KV buffers, CUDA graphs and TAEHV decoding accelerate the causal world model by 2.26×. GPU anatomy sampling enables pose-to-US generation at 81.2 FPS.

papers.selection_reason: Anatomy-grounded interactive ultrasound world model for scalable robotic policy learning and evaluation.
papers.title: SonoAtlasWorld: Anatomy-Grounded Ultrasound World Models for Wide-Range Scanning
papers.tldr: SonoAtlasWorld uses persistent 3D anatomy to generate fast, anatomically consistent ultrasound scans for robotic policy training and evaluation.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for surgical robots is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. Meanwhile, many robot-assisted procedures are recorded as stereo video, yet policies cannot learn from them directly; clinical video carries no action labels. We present FlowScope, which pretrains a surgical policy network on unlabeled clinical video by forecasting scene flow, the metric 3D motion of scene points, with labels computed by off-the-shelf stereo depth and optical flow models. We pretrain the trunk of an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) on a dataset of 1,149 clinical procedures (1.35M clips) and discard the flow head afterward, so the deployed policy is a standard ACT with no added inference cost. On a real surgical robotic system, FlowScope raises needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and first-handover success on needle regrasp from 4% to 52% (full task: 2% to 14%) over training from scratch (n=50 trials each), and retains its gains with a generative flow-matching action head. Ablations indicate that metric 3D motion is the strongest pretraining signal among those tested; kinematics, 2D tracks, depth alone, and scale-free 3D flow, each paired with kinematics, yield smaller or no gains. Representation analyses suggest that scene-flow pretraining encodes metric needle depth more accurately, that kinematics pretraining increases reliance on the robot state, and that needle-depth probes follow the ordering of real-robot success where offline validation error does not.
authors: John J. Han, Adam Schmidt, Jingpei Lu, Zooey He, Muhammad Abdullah Jamal, Jie Ying Wu, Omid Mohareri
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of labeled robot demonstrations by learning from action-free stereo surgical video.
Pretrains an Action Chunking Transformer trunk to forecast metric 3D scene motion, using pseudo-labels from stereo depth and optical flow.
Uses 1,149 procedures and 1.35M clips; the auxiliary flow head is discarded before deployment.
Improves needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and full needle-regrasp success from 2% to 14% in 50-trial evaluations.
Metric 3D motion outperforms the other tested pretraining signals; analyses link gains to more accurate needle-depth representations.

figures.caption: Figure 1. FlowScope. Each image is encoded by a frozen DINOv2 pretrained on surgical images. Pretraining (top): point queries read the image features at their pixels, and the flow head predicts each point’s metric 3D position and future trajectory, supervised with an L1 loss on scene flow pseudo-labeled by off-the-shelf stereo and optical-flow models. The robot state is set to zero. Fine-tuning (bottom): the point queries and flow head are discarded, and the pretrained trunk is trained on robot demonstrations to predict action chunks with either the ACT or a flow-matching (FM) action head, giving a standard ACT policy. The CVAE (encoder not shown) is used only during training; z = 0 at test, similar to standard ACT rollout.

Figure 2. Scene-flow pseudo-labels on clinical video. Each track shows where a point on the anchor frame moves over the next 10 keyframes (1.7 s), computed from stereo depth and optical flow and kept only where both pass consistency checks. More visualizations can be seen in Figure S2.

Figure 3. Data efficiency. Real-robot performance with 50% and 100% of the demonstrations (ACT head, 50 trials per point). With half the demonstrations, FlowScope matches the pickup success of a policy trained from scratch on all of them and far exceeds it on regrasp, while kinematics pretraining is no better than training from scratch.

Table 3. What the policy trunk encodes. Linear probes on 80 held-out demonstrations. Bold: best trunk in each block. Over 2,000 bootstrap resamples of the validation demonstrations, flowonly pretraining gives the lowest needle and instrument depth error among pretrained trunks.

Table 2. Pretraining targets. Needle pickup success within three attempts and on the first attempt, after fine-tuning each pretrained trunk with the ACT head. n = 20 trials per target (10 needle configurations × the 40k and 60k checkpoints). All targets are computed from the same anchors and points. “Flow-matching flow head”: the pretraining flow head is generative instead of L1 (Sec. 3.3); the fine-tuned policy is unchanged. Different session from Tab. 1.

Table 1. Real-robot success (%). Pickup: success on the first attempt and within three attempts. Regrasp: subtasks completed (S1 pickup, S2 first handover, S3 second handover/full task) and the mean number of stages completed (max 3). n = 50 trials per policy (10 needle configurations × 5 checkpoints). ACT: the standard action-chunking transformer with its CVAE and L1 action loss. FM: the flow-matching action head (Sec. 3.4). 95% Wilson intervals for pickup (≤3): scratch [40, 67], kinematics [46, 72], FlowScope [79, 96] with the ACT head.

papers.selection_reason: Scene-flow pretraining on unlabeled clinical video improves surgical robot imitation learning policies.
papers.title: FlowScope: 3D Scene Flow Pretraining Improves Surgical Robot Policies
papers.tldr: FlowScope pretrains surgical robot policies on unlabeled clinical video via 3D scene-flow forecasting, substantially improving real-world manipulation success without adding deployment-time cost.

papers.abstract: Language models may enable general autonomy in robot planning, but onboard their reasoning can run for most of a minute while the robot and nearby pedestrians keep moving. The robot must then decide how long to follow a plan that the pending answer may overturn. Here we present staleness deadlines, which hand that decision to the robot's clock. Calibrated prediction regions for pedestrians and deviation tubes for the robot set the deadline. When the language model answers, a graph planner rebuilds the route, which the robot adopts only after it passes the same clearance check against walls and predicted pedestrians. Exact binomial tests determine which prespecified budget-selection policies keep close calls, wrong decisions and late arrivals below their targets at each inference profile. Candidate policies either fix one budget or set each query's budget from how long the robot can continue its plan before it must brake. We study corridor signs that close routes and delivery requests whose destination the language model must infer. In 81,000 simulated missions with recorded Qwen3-4B answers, full reasoning cuts wrong decisions about twentyfold, and tracking until the deadline cuts late arrivals by up to 64%. The robot never collides while it moves, although pedestrians who never yield still walk into the stopped robot in 23% of offline and 32% of live missions. On a Jetson AGX Orin under perception load, short budgets fail the wrong-decision target, and full reasoning the lateness target. Between these extremes, a fixed-budget policy passes for corridor signs and per-query policies pass for deliveries. Live Orin runs match offline replay on all three losses in 24 of the 32 missions where either run records a loss. The deadline turns slower reasoning into measurable mission outcomes, which let designers test how much reasoning each inference profile can support.
bullets: The problem is that onboard language-model inference can take nearly a minute while the robot and pedestrians continue moving.
Calibrated pedestrian prediction regions and robot deviation tubes define when the current plan becomes unsafe to keep following.
After the model responds, a graph planner rebuilds the route and accepts it only after checking clearance from walls and predicted pedestrians.
Across 81,000 simulated missions, full reasoning reduced wrong decisions about twentyfold, while deadline-based tracking reduced late arrivals by up to 64%.
Fixed budgets worked for corridor-sign tasks, whereas per-query budgets worked for delivery tasks; stopped robots were still entered by non-yielding pedestrians in some missions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a,b) A corridor sign and a delivery request. (c) The latest checked switch Tsafe from tracking to braking. (d) The robot tracks its current plan during reasoning, brakes at the deadline, and adopts a revised plan after a timed clearance check.
Figure 2: Budget screening over 1500 missions per policy. “Pass” meets all targets, and “follow” with † marks an exploratory fixed-budget follow-up.
Table 1: Live / replay counts on the Orin, 150 missions per row. Loss agreement is computed only on missions where either run records a loss, and κ is Cohen’s kappa for stopped contacts.

papers.selection_reason: Language-model-informed robot motion planning with staleness deadlines directly addresses onboard navigation and planning under uncertainty.
papers.title: Staleness Deadlines for Motion Plans during Onboard Reasoning
papers.tldr: Staleness deadlines let robots decide how long to trust a plan during slow language-model reasoning, balancing wrong decisions, close calls, and late arrivals without moving into collisions.

papers.abstract: Flow matching policies underpin the state-of-the-art in robot learning, with impressive results ranging from long-horizon planning to dexterous manipulation. However, they provide no measure of whether their predicted commands can be trusted, particularly in novel situations outside their training set. Epistemic uncertainty reflects uncertainty about the model's weights and quantifies this ignorance, but calculating it at inference time from a flow matching policy is not trivial. Actions are produced by an ODE solver, requiring uncertainty to be propagated through the entire integration process. BayesDiff addresses this problem for diffusion models by propagating the mean and variance of the state through the denoising chain under a last-layer Laplace posterior approximation, but it severely underestimates the epistemic uncertainty. In this paper we: i) prove that, for flow matching and diffusion ODEs, BayesDiff's total variance decays at rate $O(1/T)$ as the number of Euler steps $T$ used by the solver increases; ii) introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), two recursions inspired by the extended and unscented Kalman filters that fix this problem by carrying the cross-covariance between state and weights; and iii) widen the last-layer posterior with observation embeddings the policy already computes, improving uncertainty estimates without retraining for CoMP and several test-time estimators alike. We demonstrate these benefits on three manipulation benchmarks with applications in failure detection and demonstration selection for fine-tuning, where CoMP corrects BayesDiff's variance collapse while matching or outperforming several uncertainty estimators.
authors: Miguel Saavedra-Ruiz, Anqi Li, Claudia D'Arpino, Alperen Degirmenci, Tucker Hermans, Fabio Ramos
bullets: Targets unreliable confidence estimates for pre-trained policies in novel situations.
Proves BayesDiff’s propagated variance decays as O(1/T) with more Euler solver steps.
Introduces two extended/unscented-Kalman-inspired recursions that propagate state–weight cross-covariance.
Improves last-layer uncertainty estimates using observation embeddings already computed by the policy, without retraining.
On three manipulation benchmarks, supports failure detection and demonstration selection while matching or outperforming several estimators.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Variance collapse in moment propagation. State covariance PT at the end of integration of a flow matching model on a two-mode mixture under a last-layer Laplace posterior for one sample x0 at T = 100 Euler steps. (a) The reference is the empirical covariance of 4000 trajectories, one per posterior draw θ(m) ∼ N (θMAP,Σθ). (b) BayesDiff returns 1/46 of it, consistent with Theorem 1. (c) Our estimators CoMP-EKF and CoMP-UKF carry the cross-covariance between the state and the weights and recover the reference to within 1%. (d) The total variance trPT at the same seed for every estimator re-run on each grid from T = 10 to 400 Euler steps. BayesDiff halves with every doubling of T , while our methods track the reference regardless of the number of Euler steps.

Figure 4: Runtime failure detection on robomimic and LIBERO-90. Timestep-wise accuracy (TWA), accuracy and normalized detection time (DT), averaged over tasks, with mean and standard deviation over five random seeds. CoMP uses our augmented head; post-hoc baselines use the plain head. The ensembles (hatched, two trained members) are a reference only. CoMP-UKF is comparable to or better than the baselines in both suites; Table 4 reports comparisons with both heads.

Figure 3: Language instruction shift on RoboLab. Success rate (grey bars) and first-decision uncertainty (lines, scaled to [0, 1]) averaged over the ten tasks by wording. On the plain head (left) estimators are mostly flat with the wording; on the augmented head (right) every estimator but DECU rises as language ambiguity increases.

Figure 7: Ordering of the most and least uncertain observation windows on robomimic. Each estimator scores the ten observations per task ranked most uncertain (red) and the ten ranked least uncertain (blue) by a 6000-draw ensemble reference at T = 400 (i.e., 30 observations per group over the three tasks). The shaded bands mark the estimator’s own most and least uncertain observations, so a correctly ranked observation falls inside its band (filled) and an incorrectly ranked one outside it (hollow); percentages are the share of each group ranked correctly. BayesDiff mixes the two groups and reorders them across T , while CoMP keeps them apart and stable at every T .

Figure 8: The ten RoboLab tasks of §4.2. Initial scene of each task from the front camera view, with its default instruction; the study runs every task under three wordings (specific, default and vague) from the same scenes.
Figure 13: The ten LIBERO-10 tasks of §4.4. Initial scene and instruction of each task from the simulator’s front camera.

Figure 15: Data selection on LIBERO-10, per estimator. Success rate after fine-tuning on the ten LIBERO-10 tasks against the number of selected demonstrationsX , for every estimator on the plain head (dashed) and on the augmented head (solid), with random selection and the two-member VFD as references; mean and standard deviation over five pre-trained policies. On the plain Laplace head every estimator tracks random selection; our augmented head brings most estimators above random selection, with several also surpassing the two-member VFD.
Figure 12: The nine LIBERO-90 tasks of §4.3. Initial scene and instruction of each task from the simulator’s front camera.

Figure 9: RoboLab instruction shift, per task. Success rate (grey) and first-decision uncertainty (lines, min-max scaled to [0, 1] per estimator and Laplace fit across tasks and wordings) for the ten tasks and three wordings, under the plain (top) and augmented (bottom) Laplace heads. With the augmented head, every estimator except DECU generally reports higher uncertainty as language instructions become more ambiguous, while the plain head remains mostly flat, highlighting the benefits of our augmented Laplace posterior.

Figure 11: Perturbations on robomimic. The nominal initial state of each task from the front camera (solid), with perturbed resets overlaid as ghosts: the target object displaced in the table plane (translucent) and the end effector displaced from its reset pose (blue). Walls and floor are removed for clarity. The object displacements on PickPlaceCan are shown for illustration only, as its sweep perturbs the end effector alone.

Figure 14: Effect of augmented Laplace head on data selection. Demonstrations needed to reach 90% of random selection’s mean success at X = 250 (left; lower is better) and mean gain over random across budgets (right; higher is better), on all ten LIBERO-10 tasks. Paired bars compare plain and augmented heads for every estimator, with mean and standard deviation over five pre-trained policies. Horizontal lines mark random selection and two-member VFD. papers.abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.
bullets: Uses newly observed frames for label-free test-time training while preserving a short input history.
Accumulates updates within an episode and resets them between episodes, retaining information beyond the observation window.
Improves task success across four simulation benchmarks and two world-action models.
On RoboCasa GR-1, 2.4 seconds of history matches a 9.6-second model; 4.8 seconds exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points.
Adaptation improves predicted future frames and increasingly influences actions as episodes progress.

papers.abstract: Egocentric videos offer a scalable source of human demonstrations for robot learning. However, recovering metric object geometry and motion from monocular video is hindered by scale-depth ambiguity and hand-induced occlusion, while image-derived contact and shape priors alone cannot uniquely determine metric scale. We introduce TacHOI, a training-free framework that integrates tactile contact with monocular vision for joint hand-object reconstruction and tracking, without requiring object templates or depth sensors. Starting from pretrained visual estimates, TacHOI uses tactile contact to constrain object depth relative to the estimated hand, while spatially separated contacts on a metrically calibrated hand provide a physical ruler for object extent. It incorporates these constraints into a joint optimization of hand poses, object trajectories, and anisotropic object scale alongside visual alignment. Across 100 ARCTIC and HO3D sequences with synthesized tactile observations, TacHOI achieves the lowest median ADD-S* among the evaluated baselines, reducing error from 15.6 to 3.6 cm on ARCTIC and achieving 2.8 cm on HO3D. Additional experiments on OpenTouch demonstrate its applicability to measured tactile observations.
authors: Jackson Codd, Haoyu Li, Xianyi Cheng
bullets: Addresses scale–depth ambiguity and hand occlusion in egocentric monocular videos.
Uses tactile contacts to constrain object depth and a calibrated hand as a physical ruler for object extent.
Jointly optimizes hand poses, object trajectories, anisotropic scale, and visual alignment.
On 100 ARCTIC and HO3D sequences with synthesized tactile observations, reports median ADD-S* errors of 3.6 cm and 2.8 cm, respectively.
OpenTouch experiments show applicability to measured tactile observations; scope includes tactile sensing and relies on pretrained visual estimates.

papers.abstract: Kinodynamic motion planning in large-scale, cluttered environments remains challenging, as dynamically feasible, collision-free trajectories must be computed efficiently over long horizons. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) can strategically explore long-horizon alternatives but faces large branching factors in continuous control spaces and often relies on random default-policy rollouts, whereas Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) efficiently optimizes local trajectories yet remains susceptible to obstacle-induced local minima. To overcome these challenges, we propose Search-Informed MPPI (SI-MPPI), a unified framework that embeds MPPI trajectory optimization within MCTS-based tree search. The core concept is to fuse the expansion and default-policy simulation stages of MCTS into a single MPPI expansion stage guided by structured intermediate targets, termed baits. During each expansion, an adaptive bait-handling rule retains geometrically valid baits as local targets for GPU-batched MPPI optimizations that generate dynamically feasible candidate motion segments. Feasibility gating then checks these candidates for collision safety and sufficient progress, and top-$k$ selection admits the lowest-cost accepted candidates as tree edges, yielding sparse, directed tree growth; thereafter, effective sample size (ESS)-guided adaptation warm-starts subsequent expansions, while cost-based backpropagation updates tree statistics. Extensive simulations across four large-scale, cluttered 2D occupancy-grid maps demonstrate that SI-MPPI consistently produces the smallest search trees and smoothest angular control profiles compared with three kinodynamic baselines, while maintaining competitive planning times and path lengths. Ablation results further highlight the importance of GPU batching, adaptive bait handling, and retaining multiple expansion candidates for planning efficiency and robustness.
bullets: Addresses MCTS’s continuous-control branching and random rollouts alongside MPPI’s vulnerability to obstacle-induced local minima.
Uses structured intermediate targets (“baits”) to guide GPU-batched MPPI expansions within an MCTS tree.
Applies feasibility gating and top-k selection to create sparse, directed tree growth, with ESS-guided warm starts and cost-based backpropagation.
Across four large 2D occupancy-grid maps, it produced smaller trees and smoother angular controls than three kinodynamic baselines while maintaining competitive planning times and path lengths.
Ablations identified GPU batching, adaptive bait handling, and multiple retained candidates as important for efficiency and robustness.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.
authors: Guangyu Zhao, Yongchang Zhang, Ruizhang Jiang, Zhihong Yu, Yuhao Zhang, Tao Wu, Qimin Zhou, Kunsong Shi, Haoran Wen, Zeyu Zhang, Yin Li, Kun Zhan, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Introduces VMBench, a benchmark for manipulation tasks requiring memory of locations, appearances, and their associations.
Uses a hierarchical design: a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes, while an executor predicts actions from selected memories.
Achieves 49.9% average success on VMBench, 31.7 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.
Transfers zero-shot to unseen appearances and reaches 43.7% success on an unseen task with a few memory annotations, near 44.3% with full supervision.
Also reports competitive RMBench results and improvements in real-robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present FORTH, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. FORTH incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, FORTH's closed-loop gate peaks at 29 times lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, FORTH matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12 times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence.
authors: Junde Li, Wei-Han Yu, Xiangyi Chu, Yaoxin Li, Jiawei Xu, Ka-Fai Un, Pui-In Mak
bullets: Addresses three grounding failures: lost contact geometry, misaligned token-level gradients, and optimization collapse from discrete indicators.
Uses a forward-only tactile encoder, token-parallel zeroth-order activation updates, and SlipGuard for continuous incipient-slip verification.
On an elasto-plastic shell, its closed-loop gate reached 29× lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp and avoided permanent deformation.
Achieved 97.6% average success across three evaluated LIBERO suites while reducing peak activation memory 7.12× versus a backpropagated step.

papers.abstract: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by $29$ and $50$, sampling-based planners by $35$ and MPPI by $7$ percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4\% of MPPI.
authors: Hrishikesh Viswanath, Anindita Ghosh, Uttaran Bhattacharya, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of long-horizon planning, where sampling methods struggle and gradient methods can get trapped in local minima.
Uses Sequential Monte Carlo to evolve action-sequence populations through intermediate target distributions with importance weighting and resampling.
Combines SMC population updates with gradient-based plan optimization in learned latent world models.
Introduces a PDE-derived cost-to-go to guide sampling using latent-state-space structure.
On visual and proprioceptive navigation/manipulation tasks, improves average success rates over gradient-based, sampling-based, and MPPI planners, with competitive iteration counts.

papers.abstract: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology-state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision-language-action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch where identical joint values yield different spatial configurations across robot embodiments.
Uses a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that reconstructs both joint angles and link poses.
Generates scalable kinematic supervision with MorphGen and pretrains on 40 million morphology-state pairs.
Evaluated with a frozen tokenizer in a vision-language-action policy on RoboTwin 2.0 and the ten-task EmbodiBench benchmark.
Link-pose supervision is important: removing it lowers EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting to hidden, changing physical conditions that make identical robot states respond differently to the same action.
Re-infers a latent context from recent interactions and uses it to condition a fixed network modeling inertia and potential energy.
Requires neither retraining nor a hand-specified robot model to adapt to new conditions.
In Isaac Sim experiments with a Franka Panda arm, it predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing unseen-payload error by 1.6–3.8× over baselines.
The learned context captures payload properties and changes, supports counterfactual torque queries, and produces physically valid gravity and inertia components.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). The four methods are applied to the same AV decision-making problem at an unsignalized intersection and are compared in terms of optimality, safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. Observations suggest that RCPI provides the closest estimation to the exact solution and has the most stable training curve; however, it is data-intensive and requires the largest volume of data. D-DDPG is the most data-efficient one, but at the price of the training stability. Based on the observations, we provide suggestions for the algorithm selection for AV decision making.
bullets: Evaluates FVI, RCPI, DQN, and discrete-action D-DDPG on the same AV decision-making problem.
Compares optimality, safety, training stability, and training and decision costs.
RCPI most closely matches the exact solution and shows the most stable training.
D-DDPG is the most data-efficient but has less stable training.
The findings inform algorithm selection for AV decision-making.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/ε)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/ε)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.
bullets: Studies offline Q-learning in tabular, finite-horizon MDPs with KL regularization.
Introduces KLQ, a simple KL-regularized variant of classical Q-learning.
Proves KLQ achieves a fast sample complexity of \(\widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon)\) without explicit pessimism, but with exponential parameter and horizon dependence.
Introduces KLPQ, adding pessimism to retain the fast rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence.
Claims the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.
papers.selection_reason: Fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning with KL regularization, relevant to RL-based robot learning.
papers.title: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization
papers.tldr: KL-regularized Q-learning achieves fast O(1/) offline sample complexity, with pessimism removing its exponential dependence on regularization and horizon.

papers.abstract: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.
bullets: Behavioral diversity can support role specialization, but the ideal level depends on the task and is difficult to tune.
ADiCo uses fast-timescale Diversity Control to track a target diversity level and a slower Extremum Seeking Controller to adjust that target from mean episodic returns alone.
Across six configurations and two cooperative MARL tasks, it maintained low diversity when homogeneous behavior helped and higher diversity when heterogeneous behavior was needed.
ADiCo matched or exceeded DiCo with the best grid-searched target and unconstrained DiCo.
The method provides a model-free, gradient-free alternative to manually selecting diversity targets.

Colors denote task configurations; the left panel shows DiCo’s manually tuned SND target for each. (a) System Neural Diversity. (b) Mean episode reward. (c) Episode length.
