papers.abstract: Humanoid agents in everyday environments are expected to react to diverse cues as humans do, with semantically appropriate and physically executable behaviors. Existing cue-driven reaction generation methods support only a narrow range of cue modalities and are limited to purely kinematic generation, leaving the resulting reactions susceptible to physical artifacts. To this end, we present MixReact, the first unified framework for physics-based reactive humanoid control from text, audio, and video cues, integrating a Discrete--Continuous Mixture of Transformers (DisCo-MoT) for state prediction with a History-aware Action Transformer (HAT) for physical execution. DisCo-MoT couples a discrete masked-modeling branch with a continuous autoregressive diffusion branch via one-way mixture attention within a MoT architecture. Guidance from discrete context mitigates collapse into averaged behaviors in one-to-many reaction generation, while direct prediction in continuous state space bypasses the decoding bottleneck of discrete representations. HAT then maps the predicted next state and observed execution history to executable actions, enabling robust closed-loop control in physics-based simulation. Experiments across all three modalities demonstrate consistent improvements over the baselines in fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency, while ablations validate the complementary contributions of the components. Our code will be released to facilitate future research. Project page: https://binlee26.github.io/MixReact_Page/
authors: Bin Li, Xing Zhu, Jingya Wang
bullets: Addresses limited cue modalities and physically implausible artifacts in existing reactive humanoid generation methods.

Experiments across text, audio, and video show improved fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency over baselines.
Ablations support the complementary roles of the framework’s components.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can act as closed-loop robot-use agents (RUAs) by writing and executing control code through tool interfaces. However, turning an open-weight VLM into a high-performing embodied agent requires a complete post-training stack: out-of-the-box open VLMs fail completely at interactive tool contracts, strong frontier teachers are accessible only as black-box endpoints without exposed weights or token probabilities, and supervised imitation alone plateaus under rollout distribution shift. We present EmbodyAgent, an end-to-end post-training framework with three tightly coupled pipelines: (1) a black-box data synthesis pipeline that queries a strong teacher under a forced think-then-code contract and filters trajectories by task success; (2) an SFT pipeline that distills the explanation-and-program targets into an open-weight 9B VLM with both vision and language encoders trainable; and (3) an online RL pipeline that optimizes student-generated episodes via group-relative advantage with a runtime-error-penalized outcome reward. All three pipelines share one primitive-free Python execution tool exposing only raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control, with no action decoder and no interface shift across stages. Under a strictly separated evaluation protocol on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks (disjoint state splits, greedy test-time decoding, training-only safeguards), held-out success on 100 test states rises from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after RL), while training rollout success climbs from 8.4% to 87.7% and median model calls per episode drop from 36 to 11. We further identify a self-reinforcing runtime-error mode induced by outcome-based RL on executable code, and establish a failure-category monitoring and sampling-side curation protocol that stabilizes training.
authors: Wei Dai, Jinkun Liu, Jiayi Chen, Han Liu, Wenbo Ding, Shaolun Huang
bullets: Addresses failures in tool-contract following, limited access to frontier teacher internals, and imitation degradation under rollout distribution shift.
Synthesizes and filters teacher trajectories, distills explanation-and-code targets into a trainable 9B VLM, then optimizes student rollouts with runtime-error-penalized rewards.
Uses the same primitive-free Python tool throughout, exposing only visual observations and seven-dimensional end-effector control.
On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks, held-out success improves from 0/100 for the base model to 14/100 after SFT and 84/100 after RL; median calls per episode fall from 36 to 11.
Finds and mitigates a self-reinforcing runtime-error failure mode through failure monitoring and sampling-side curation.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to acquire visual evidence and integrate partial observations into coherent three-dimensional representations. We introduce SpatialScout-V2, which extends SpatialScout's active mapping task from simulation to real residential scenes through three advances: real visual observations, preservation of original scene content, and interactive exploration of recorded views. Built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, the benchmark covers 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. Given a fixed target inventory, agents autonomously select recorded viewpoints and viewing directions, integrate calibrated RGB observations, and iteratively estimate and revise object centers within a fixed interaction budget. We evaluate the localization accuracy and completeness of object-center maps using mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage. Evaluating seven frontier vision-language models (VLMs), we find that six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20\%. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches only 22.52\%, with just 18.36\% of targets exceeding an IoU of 0.5. Further analysis shows that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy, while target omissions further reduce overall scores. These results highlight substantial challenges in constructing accurate and complete object-center maps through active exploration of real scenes.
authors: Zhaoxi Zhang, Hao Liang, Linxuan Wu, Yiming Xu, Yifu Yuan, Kun Liang, Chenming Tang, Meiyi Qiang, Wentao Zhang, Weikang Li, Yunfang Wu

Across seven frontier VLMs, six score below 20% all-target mean IoU; the best model reaches 22.52% mean IoU, with 18.36% of targets above IoU 0.5.
High submission coverage can coexist with poor localization, while omitted targets further reduce map quality.

papers.abstract: Tight-space navigation requires a robot to clear obstacles and stop inside its goal despite uncertainty. We present GeoDiff, a motion-program planner coupling original-goal stopped-set inclusion, witness-guided terminal repair, and factored proof compilation. An exact feasible-translation characterization guides repair; request-local reuse reduces repeated geometric work. We establish conditions for compiler equivalence and reach-and-stop soundness. Across 11,440 floorplan-derived jobs, GeoDiff certifies 61/139 tasks at 5-cm tolerance within 15 s, versus 44/139 for the stop-set baseline. The strongest observed external certificate adapter certifies 13/139 tasks from 119/139 native routes, separating route availability from certification. On tasks derived from public BARN maps, GeoDiff certifies 202/270 at 5-cm tolerance for a Jackal-shaped body, versus 3/270 for the portal baseline. Development analyses distinguish emitter savings from solver coverage, and 1,420 route-tracking episodes characterize the execution interface. These results show how terminal reasoning and proof reuse increase finite-budget certification coverage while preserving the original physical task and goal.
authors: Runtian Zheng, Congpeng Zhang, Ying Liu
bullets: Addresses navigation under uncertainty where a robot must both clear obstacles and stop within its goal.

papers.abstract: Multi-view vision-language-action (VLA) models still face challenges in spatial generalization, particularly under changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. We propose One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), which learns to predict actions in each view's camera frame, allowing the same physical motion to provide diverse, observation-aligned supervision across views. OVOA-VLA jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific action experts, whose robot-state inputs and action targets are expressed in their respective camera frames. Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs' base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference. Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1% and 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from $\pi_{0.5}$'s 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.
authors: Jinxi Liu, Ruifeng Zhai, Hao Liu, Guangrun Wang
bullets: Addresses viewpoint and robot-initialization shifts in multi-view vision-language-action models.
Predicts actions in each camera frame, providing observation-aligned supervision for the same physical motion.

Uses Cross Graph Consistency to align the graphs’ base-frame predictions.
Achieves 88.1% full-inference and 85.7% base-only success on LIBERO-Plus; real-world base-only success reaches 58.3% under spatial shifts.

CGC encourages consistency between the two base-frame predictions. (c) Full Inference uses R → B; Base-only Inference uses B → R, omitting view-specific experts while retaining all input views. papers.abstract: Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) requires trajectories that avoid environmental obstacles and collisions between robots in a shared workspace. Diffusion-based planners often address obstacle avoidance through sampling-time guidance, while some conditioned approaches aggregate map geometry into a global representation. We present Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion (SCTD), a map-conditioned trajectory generator for multi-robot planning. SCTD retains multiple position-aware occupancy tokens accessed through cross-attention throughout a temporal U-Net, with hard endpoint inpainting enforcing start and goal states. One model trained on single-robot demonstrations across procedural environments generates obstacle-aware trajectories without sampling-time obstacle-cost guidance. High-level Conflict-Based Search (CBS) coordinates these trajectories through constrained replanning, retaining inter-agent guidance during sampling and reusing the model across workspace layouts and team sizes. Experiments assess single-robot success and trajectory quality, generalization to unfamiliar layouts with added obstacles, and coordinated multi-robot planning. On 15,000 held-out tasks, SCTD achieves higher success than the evaluated guided diffusion baseline, with the largest gains on hard-detour tasks, while trajectory-quality comparisons show smoother trajectories. Conditioning ablations show higher success with spatial tokens than with a global map embedding, and map-replacement tests demonstrate dependence on the supplied geometry. The resulting multi-robot system achieves higher team success than the compared diffusion baselines, with experiments covering teams of up to 15 robots.
authors: Yefim Nudelman, Dor Atzmon, Tom Tirer
bullets: Targets multi-robot motion planning with obstacle avoidance and collision-free coordination.
Uses position-aware occupancy tokens throughout a temporal U-Net and hard inpainting for start and goal states.
Trains on single-robot demonstrations and reuses one model across layouts and team sizes; CBS handles inter-robot conflicts.
Outperforms the evaluated guided diffusion baseline in held-out success, especially on hard-detour tasks, while producing smoother trajectories.
Ablations support spatial conditioning and map dependence; experiments cover teams of up to 15 robots.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Training and inference of the map-conditioned trajectory diffuser. During training, the temporal U-Net predicts noise added to normalized expert trajectories, conditioned on spatial occupancy-map tokens and the diffusion timestep. Endpoints are fixed by inpainting and excluded from the loss. During single-agent inference, map tokens depend only on the map and are therefore identical at every reverse step; endpoints are restored after every update. The raw trajectory is converted back to world coordinates without static-obstacle-cost guidance or a separate smoother; this describes the single-agent pipeline, not the multi-agent system. Start/goal markers on the maps are illustrative only.

These tokens condition the denoiser through cross-attention and retain spatial structure instead of compressing the map into a single global vector. In Stage 1 (bottom), the convolutional stem is pretrained to predict clipped analytic signed distances at sampled workspace points using an auxiliary head and an L1 loss. The head is then discarded, and the stem is finetuned jointly with the denoiser in Stage 2 (top). Analytic SDF supplies supervision only; occupancy is the planner’s only learned environmental input. papers.abstract: Active urban sensing orchestrates a mobile sensor fleet to proactively inspect a dynamic road network and gather critical information for system management. This problem simultaneously requires understanding the complex spatio-temporal evolution and making decisions with partial observations. In this work, we focus on active sensing in a large-scale urban road network with utilities grounded in dynamic traffic states, while prior work has rarely considered these factors jointly. We propose \emph{SenseAlign}, a Reinforcement Learning-based (RL) framework that learns decision-aligned predictive representations for coordinating an urban sensing drone fleet. SenseAlign first trains a privileged teacher agent that exploits future ground-truth traffic for optimal sensing choices. The student agent has an auxiliary branch that learns to predict future traffic with partial observations, in addition to the RL-trained actor and critic branches. During student learning, our framework matches the action distributions of the teacher under ground-truth and student-predicted future traffic, while keeping the teacher's observations unchanged. Such a design shapes the latent space for decision-making instead of prediction alone. At inference time, the student agent has no overhead as all this learning is done in training. We conduct comprehensive experiments with the real road network of central Barcelona containing 1570 road segments, and demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the baselines on multiple utility formulations. The codebase will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.
bullets: Addresses active sensing in dynamic, large-scale urban road networks where decisions must be made from partial observations.
Uses a privileged RL teacher with future traffic information and a student with prediction, actor, and critic branches.
Aligns the student’s action distribution with the teacher’s decisions to shape representations for control, not prediction alone.
At inference, the student incurs no additional prediction overhead.
Experiments on central Barcelona’s 1,570-road-segment network show consistent gains over baselines across multiple utility formulations.

papers.abstract: Predicting future scene or object states does not necessarily reveal how robot-object interactions will advance or hinder a task. This challenge is particularly pronounced in dynamic robotic manipulation, where objects continue moving during perception and execution. Effective action generation therefore requires not only modeling object dynamics but also anticipating how future interactions will shape task progress. To this end, we propose \textbf{PhysVAM}, a Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model that represents anticipated interactions through their effects on future task progress. This value-based formulation provides task-directed foresight without reconstructing future visual states. Conditioned on current observations and historical object and robot motion, PhysVAM jointly learns action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction. The value branch learns horizon-specific latent representations through future task-value prediction from successful and failed trajectories. These future-value representations are integrated into the action policy through gated cross-attention, guiding action generation toward interactions that facilitate task success. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate superior task success, with absolute success-rate improvements of 27.0 and 27.5 percentage points over the strongest baselines in simulation and real-world tasks, respectively. Project page: https://metarobo.github.io/physvam.github.io/.
authors: Yuxiang Yang, Jingbo Zhang, Jiaru Zhong, Junliang Chen, Yirui Zhou, Guangming Wang, Haitao Lin, Huaiyuan Xu, Yi Wang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Addresses the challenge of planning interactions with objects that continue moving during perception and execution.
Uses current observations plus historical robot and object motion to jointly learn action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction.
Learns horizon-specific value representations from successful and failed trajectories.
Integrates future-value features into the policy through gated cross-attention to favor task-progressing interactions.
Reports absolute success-rate gains of 27.0 percentage points in simulation and 27.5 points in real-world tasks over the strongest baselines.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.
authors: Zhengtu Liang, Qiwei Liang, Tao Lin, Shihang Weng, Boyang Cai, Xiangyu Chen, Yikeng Chen, Jiaming Liang, Bohan Tan, Yu Yan, Renjing Xu

It improves success and efficiency in simulated and real-world manipulation; on RoboTwin, one StarVLA run reaches 61.36% success versus 59.96% for the best single-target baseline using 16 runs.
With LiLa-WAM, two UniVEP runs outperform the best 16-step single-target baseline while reducing inference latency by 77.1%.

papers.abstract: Role allocation strategies in human-robot collaboration typically assign tasks to both the human and the robot, limiting the user's ability to take initiative. Furthermore, allocation decisions may conflict with the user's intentions, and the rationale behind such allocations may remain unclear, potentially reducing both acceptance and collaboration fluency. The novelty of the proposed framework is that the human is left free to contribute to the task, while the robot is dynamically allocated activities through a cost-driven Behavior Tree architecture according to user-expressed preferences and behavior. Explicit preferences are extracted from natural language instructions using a large language model, whereas human activity is monitored online through a Shannon entropy-based analysis of hand-object interactions. Furthermore, the framework can recognize anomalies in human execution and autonomously trigger corrective robot actions. The approach was validated through a pilot study and a multi-subject experiment involving 14 participants. Results demonstrate the potential of such an allocation strategy for enabling intuitive and engaging collaboration without increasing the perceived workload.

bullets: Addresses rigid human-robot role allocation, conflicts with user intentions, and unclear allocation rationale.

papers.abstract: Artificial Spiking Neural Networks have gained remarkable attention in the last few years due to their proven ability in simulating biological neural cultures and producing similar activity and trends. Nevertheless, whether they can be trained for humanoid locomotion while retaining biological plausibility and robust performance at once remains an open question. We study this problem by proposing a biologically inspired spiking network, trained by different learning schemes and tested on the H1-2 Unitree Humanoid. These schemes differ in how recurrent weights are trained. Ordered from most to least biologically faithful, they are: a fixed reservoir mimicking an in-vitro neural culture, where recurrent weights are kept frozen and only a linear readout is trained, the same network but with its synapses trained by reward-modulated spike timing dependent plasticity and eligibility propagation, and finally backpropagation through time as a non biological baseline for comparison. All schemes relied on distillation of a reinforcement learning expert policy with dataset aggregation. We show that e-prop reached 100% survival rate matching backpropagation through time, whereas both the fixed reservoir and the reward-modulated STDP, though the closest to biological cultures, plateaued at a much lower performance (~43.7% and ~11% survival). We explore in further detail which trends a real culture could and could not produce until now. Finally we demonstrate brief bipedal stepping on a full size humanoid H1-2.
authors: Fatima Atwi (LAAS-GEPETTO, Nantes Univ - ECN), Constant Roux (LAAS-GEPETTO), Christian Bergaud (LAAS-MEMS), Olivier Stasse (LAAS-GEPETTO)
bullets: The study asks whether biologically plausible spiking networks can be trained for robust humanoid locomotion.
It compares a fixed recurrent reservoir, reward-modulated STDP, eligibility propagation (e-prop), and backpropagation through time.
All approaches use reinforcement-learning expert-policy distillation with dataset aggregation.
E-prop achieved 100% survival, matching backpropagation through time; the fixed reservoir and reward-modulated STDP reached about 43.7% and 11%.
The experiments include brief bipedal stepping on a full-size Unitree H1-2 and examine which biological-culture trends can be reproduced.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion research has advanced rapidly on walking and running, but \emph {object-mediated} locomotion, in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive external object, remains difficult. One challenging task is skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve forward motion. Current methods for tackling skateboarding with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations or utilise analytic steering models that require system identification. In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid to learn to skateboard using model-free learning. The method combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations. We introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion. Their changing prevalence during training produces an implicit progression from stance control towards sustained robot--board locomotion.
authors: Ganeshvar Soenessardien, Michael Przystupa, Kevin Sebastian Luck
bullets: Addresses object-mediated locomotion requiring coordination with both the ground and a passive skateboard.
Combines task rewards with exploit-blocking termination conditions during training.
Constrains behaviors including losing the planted foot, placing both feet on the board, excessive twisting, board separation, and unstable board motion.
The changing prevalence of terminations implicitly progresses learning from stance control to sustained robot–board locomotion.
Demonstrated on a K1 humanoid, with no specific quantitative results reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing interactive physical twins from video requires accurately capturing how objects deform while maintaining efficient simulation. We observe that reproducing motion in a video does not guarantee correct responses to new forces when the physical representation restricts how an object can deform. In spring-based twins, coupling between volume and shape responses creates such a limitation. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes to capture and independently control these responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation. To support interpretable material editing and transfer, we use offline calibration to map shared relative response changes to stiffness updates on each reconstructed graph. Under identical inverse settings on synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces the mean absolute error of Poisson's ratio by 75.8% and the mean relative error of Young's modulus by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin. We introduce an egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark covering interactions with objects of varying stiffness. Real-world experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error than PhysTwin at interactive speeds.
authors: Haoqin Hong, Ding Fan, Fubin Dou, Tianyu Huang, Yuzhuo Chen, Zhemeng Zhang, Hanxiao Jiang, Congcong Zhu, Gerhard Petrus Hancke, Jingrun Chen, Rynson WH Lau
bullets: Addresses the limitation that matching observed video motion may not yield correct responses to new forces, especially in spring-based models coupling volume and shape changes.
Enriches local deformation modes while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation.
Uses offline calibration to translate shared relative response edits into stiffness updates for interpretable material editing and transfer.
On synthetic scenes, reduces Poisson’s-ratio error by 75.8% and Young’s-modulus relative error by 22.1% versus PhysTwin.
A new egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark and real-world tests show improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error at interactive speeds.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MorphTwin, a method for reconstructing interactive physical twins from video by enriching local deformation modes, which is relevant to simulation-based manipulation and 3D reconstruction.
papers.title: MorphTwin: Enriching Deformable Material Responses from Videos for Morphable and Interactive Physical Twins
papers.tldr: MorphTwin reconstructs deformable physical twins from video with independently controllable deformation responses, improving material accuracy and future-motion prediction over PhysTwin.

papers.abstract: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.
authors: Dong An, Tianyu Liu, Haoran Ding, Wen Yang, Anqing Duan, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Problem: Video world models often follow robot actions but predict inconsistent or collapsed object motion because scene dynamics and appearance are inferred together.
Method: Lift the initial frame into 3D points, predict their response to robot motion with a learned dynamics model, then render the simulated points into pixel-aligned videos for a video model.
Results: Object-motion error decreases by 8.6% and 6.2% with two DROID video renderers, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot, without reducing image quality.
The rendered video tracks the simulated dynamics: better point predictions produce better object motion, while editing points can steer the generated video.
Scope: Results are demonstrated in controlled DROID experiments and on a real bimanual robot.

papers.selection_reason: Separates dynamics prediction from visual rendering in robotic world models by using 3D point dynamics as a proxy, significantly improving object motion accuracy in simulation and real-world manipulation.
papers.title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: A 3D point-dynamics proxy separates robot interaction modeling from video rendering, improving manipulated-object motion while preserving visual quality.

papers.abstract: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}.
authors: Xiaoxin Mi, Zhen Cao, Chong Liu, Yuhao Li, Zhen Dong, Bisheng Yang, Yang Jia, Shengwu Xiong
bullets: Addresses gaps in existing datasets, including limited semantic richness, modality diversity, and scenario complexity.
Covers approximately 100 km of Chinese highways and urban streets.
Combines MLS point clouds, panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance labels.
Annotates 15 road-element categories, including boundaries, crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, and 10 direction-symbol types.
Supports research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction, road mapping, topology reasoning, map updating, and street-scene generation.

papers.abstract: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.
authors: Junyoung Hong, Minsu Kim, Jaehyun Kim, Jeonghwan Cho, Jiwoo Lee, Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Studies proactive spatial reasoning: answering whether and when a queried spatial condition becomes true as video unfolds.
Introduces ProSpace-Bench with nine object-, camera-, and scene-level reasoning tasks, plus ProSpace-Train for supervised learning.
Injects causal geometric encodings into intermediate VLM layers, uses the KV cache as spatial memory, and selects spatial tokens for efficient streaming.
Experiments show a substantial VLM–human gap, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines.
Analyzes how the model retains previously observed spatial information across viewpoint changes.

papers.abstract: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.
authors: Zhengru Fang, Zehao Liu, Mingyu Tsoi, Yaoyu Zhu, Junlong Li, Fengmao Lv, Sijie Cheng, Yuanliang Sun, Fang Yang, Jun Zhang
bullets: Benchmarks recalling where and when specific objects were last seen, who saw them, and room-visit relationships.

Direct VLMs achieve limited performance, with none exceeding 35% on identifying who last saw an object.
EgoClue retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial-temporal relations using five tools.
Two-stage SFT and GRPO training raises a 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65%; evidence traces reach 80.56% in unseen environments.

papers.abstract: Industrial bin picking requires pose estimates that are accurate under clutter, partial occlusion, and the reflective, texture-less nature of manufactured parts. Most recent approaches to 6D pose estimation follow multi-stage pipelines. These achieve high accuracy, but incur memory and runtime footprints that do not cope with the operational constraints of many real-world industrial deployments. Holistic pipelines estimate poses in a single pass, with cost controlled through indiscriminate subsampling or lowered resolution. Continuing this line, we present SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D estimator. We reconstruct the 3D space at millimeter precision, prune background via a staged heatmap mechanism, and predict class, translation offset and rotation at highest resolution for an arbitrary number of objects simultaneously. Rotation is formulated as canonical coordinate voting. Points vote for their canonical object coordinates with an associated confidence, enabling closed-form pose recovery with a symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve. Along an in-cluster point recovery induced by offset votes, this removes time-consuming post-processing stages. We reuse the task-supervised attention priors from the heatmap formulation for a novel attention-gated distillation objective that reweights teacher-student feature alignment. On the IPD test split we report competitive 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene, significantly faster than the leading entries. On MV-YCB our approach reaches 96.1 ADD-S, and remains competitive even on the densely packed bins of ROBI.
authors: Nico Leuze, Samed Dogan, Maximilian Hoh, Henry Schaub, Alfred Sch\"ottl
bullets: Reconstructs millimeter-precision 3D space and uses staged heatmaps to remove background points.
Predicts object classes, translation offsets, and rotations at high resolution for multiple objects in one pass.
Uses canonical-coordinate voting with confidence-weighted, symmetry-aware Procrustes pose recovery, avoiding costly post-processing.
Introduces attention-gated knowledge distillation guided by task-supervised heatmap priors.
Reports 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene on IPD, 96.1 ADD-S on MV-YCB, and competitive performance on densely packed ROBI bins.

papers.abstract: We present FAB (Fast and Accurate Body estimation), a human body estimator that jointly improves inference efficiency and body-recovery fidelity. Rather than predicting only parametric mesh-model parameters, FAB directly predicts human skeleton joints and dense surface points. In images, it predicts dense 2D and 3D body points alongside a parametric Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, then fits SMPL in one learned pass followed by two Gauss-Newton steps. Its ViT-L student, FAB-L, distilled from a fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, runs in real time for one person on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, from detection to a fitted body, at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch body-only path, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks. The same network predicts heel, toe, hand, and knee contacts, which connect the body to the scene. FAB also estimates world-space motion, fuses static-scene depth around the visible person, and aligns body and scene using predicted contacts. For human-to-humanoid real-to-sim transfer, an in-model G1 head and FAB-Retarget, a motion-level retargeter that reads dense points or the fitted mesh, map motion to a Unitree G1. FAB-Retarget produces references that follow the person more closely than specialized retargeters including SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget, and substantially more closely than Fast SAM 3D Body retargeted with our sequence IK. Project page: https://www.jinkuncao.com/FAB.
bullets: Predicts dense 2D/3D body points and an MHR representation, then fits SMPL with one learned pass and two Gauss–Newton steps.
FAB-L runs from detection to fitted body 4.6× faster than SAM 3D Body’s eager-PyTorch body-only path on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks.
Estimates foot, hand, and knee contacts to align the body with static scene geometry and support world-space motion recovery.
FAB-Retarget transfers motion to a Unitree G1 using dense points or fitted meshes, producing closer-following references than several specialized retargeters and an IK-based SAM 3D Body pipeline.

papers.abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10{\deg} off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.
authors: Wai Ka Sun, Waiyiu Pong, Bowen Wang
bullets: A collision-free route can still fail when the robot approaches a stair or ledge with the wrong position or heading.
A 27-minute teaching session records one successful crossing for each terrain transition as reusable route events.
Before each transition, an entry gate triggers turning or backing up when the robot is more than 10 cm or 10° from the taught approach.
Under localization noise, compliant crossings increased from 24.1% to 88.6%; simulation and real-robot tests also showed improved recovery and reliable completion.
The method was demonstrated over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain, with six autonomous successful runs in competition.

papers.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.
authors: Yajie Qi, Wei Wei, Lin Li, Lijun Zhang, Jianye Hao
bullets: Addresses sparse rewards, long horizons, and inconsistent goals from prompt-only language-model guidance.
Introduces CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset built from Craftax-Classic interaction trajectories.
Uses offline KLTDPO fine-tuning to align the VLM with goal preferences, followed by online goal-guided RL.
The method collects diamonds earlier and achieves the highest score and reward in experiments.
It attains the highest success rates on most achievements; results are scoped to Craftax-Classic.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.
authors: Yukun Dai, Tianshi Wang, Fengling Li, Jingjing Li, Xin Li, Lei Zhu
bullets: Targets world action models with one shared ℓ∞-bounded (4/255) perturbation across frames, tasks, and camera views.
Across eight models on LIBERO and RoboTwin, the attack drives task success near zero and shifts actions toward the chosen target; control attacks cause little target-direction shift.
Restoring future tokens removes 61–94% of the targeted effect in five models, while constrained attacks can make current-frame tokens more important.
Restoring only 0.36% of FFN neurons in layers 10–29 removes 72–96% of the effect in six models.
Low-energy residual directions can still be critical: removing directions 2–16 cancels most of the targeted effect despite containing only 11–18% of shift energy.

papers.tldr: SteerTrace shows that tiny universal perturbations can reliably steer world action models toward attacker-chosen actions and identifies the internal tokens, neurons, and residual directions responsible.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.
authors: Jun Xia, Shangwen Wang, Jun Ma, Ruichao Ren, Zhouyang Jia, Xin Zhao, Huijun Liu, Jie Yu
bullets: Targets the vulnerability of VLA policies that continuously depend on visual feedback during manipulation.
Searches a frozen text-conditioned diffusion model’s latent space for task-disruptive, natural-looking object textures.
Uses a gradient-free gray-box attack with an eight-expert latent proposal network refined through rollout feedback.
Evaluated on pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites, achieving 57.9% cASR versus 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures.
Produces higher scene similarity and a lower detector flag rate than optimized patch baselines, motivating defenses that assess appearance and task behavior jointly.

In Phase II, a frozen diffusion model decodes the selected latent into a candidate texture; appearance-screened candidates are evaluated by a frozen VLA in closed-loop rollouts, and paired behavioral signals update the proposal, critic, and exploration policy. The diffusion model, renderer, and VLA remain frozen.

papers.title: DMT-Attack: Diffusion-Prior Texture Search for Closed-Loop Vision-Language-Action Policies

papers.abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.
authors: Xudi Ge, Yepeng Liu, Haifeng Liu, Enze Shi, Liangqi Zhang, Yongchao Xu
bullets: Addresses action drift caused by illumination changes despite unchanged physical states.
VASE estimates visual action reliability from a frozen policy’s sensitivity to illumination perturbations.
TACE compares predicted and measured touch during execution to detect discrepancies.

Trained only in normal lighting, it achieves 87.5% success under normal and 73.8% under challenging unseen lighting across four real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.
authors: Kai Shi, Shiqi Zhao, Zimo Li, Hairong Qu, Hongyu Ma, Yongsong Yang, Jiahao Ai, Ziran Yin, Peng Yin
bullets: Addresses the gap between local latent reachability and persistent, task-level execution.
Uses a frozen LeWorldModel with a proposer for intermediate targets and CompassFlow to search trajectory-prior actions under limited evaluation budgets.
Adds patch-token spatial feedback and observation-based memory for phase transitions and bounded recovery.
State-indexed targets enable cross-episode context-goal composition.
Achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach on 1,000 TEST Cube trials; predictive ranking improves matched PushT success from 4.7% to 44.9% and TwoRoom from 33.8% to 77.7%.

papers.abstract: Early interactions can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show. These properties can still gov- ern the effects of future actions. Inspired by the distinction between retention and selective readout in working mem- ory and cognitive science, we introduce LATER, an action- conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA. LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories that remain fixed during candidate rollouts. A response bridge queries these memories using the current state and candidate action, while multi-cut auxiliary supervision trains the memory writ- ers. On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA. In a separate comparison across six models and two scratch- training seeds, LATER achieves the lowest mean physical readout error in both clean and distracted views, reducing along-push mean absolute error (MAE) under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA. Controlled history interventions show that later predictions depend on earlier physical evi- dence even when query observations and actions are fixed, with larger effects during pushing than waiting.
authors: Zihan Zhou, Wenxi Xu, Qilin Wang, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses the problem of physical properties becoming unobservable in later frames while still affecting future actions.
Stores completed transitions in fixed, partitioned memories and uses a response bridge to retrieve evidence based on the current state and candidate action.
Trains memory writers with multi-cut auxiliary supervision within a CF-JEPA-based world model.
On distracted Two-Stage PushT, improves terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA.
Achieves the lowest mean physical readout error across six models and two seeds, reducing distractor-induced along-push MAE by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.
authors: Xu Pan, Chubin Zhang, Xingrui Yu, Runmin Lan, Zihao Wang, Wenkai Guo, Bofang Jia, Bo An, Ziwei Wang
bullets: Addresses stale visual memory and disconnected action chunks caused by overlapping perception and execution.
Uses a Causal Latent World Model to predict current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history.
Applies action-sensitive distillation to preserve the frozen expert’s control behavior.
Uses Predictive Flow Warm-Starting for single-step correction of the remaining action horizon without additional training.
On LIBERO-10, achieves 93.8% success with 5.04× inference throughput, alongside improved robustness and motion smoothness.

papers.abstract: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Chenyuan Zhou, Chaoyi Huang, Zibo Wang, Zhiyuan Li, Yong-Lu Li
bullets: Addresses cross-tool manipulation by identifying geometric features shared across tools with similar functions.
Uses an embodied agent to reconstruct demonstrations in simulation, form and test affordance hypotheses, and refine extraction skills.
Encodes discovered functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone for training and inference.
Builds a reusable affordance-extraction skill library for unseen tools.
Achieves 86.1% simulated cross-tool trajectory-retargeting success and improves real-robot task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$ across three tasks.

papers.abstract: Federated reinforcement learning enables a fleet of robots to jointly learn a shared navigation policy without exchanging raw experience. In practice, however, the robots rarely operate in the same conditions: an open aisle is far easier to navigate than a cluttered room, and takes less learning to master. Standard federated aggregation rules ignore this. Uniform averaging weights every client equally, whether or not it is still learning, and weighting by episode return is worse, since easy environments permit high returns by construction. Both failures stem from what we call the \emph{plateau problem}: once a client masters its environment, its updates carry little new information even though its reported return remains high. We propose \emph{FedDIA}, which scores each client by how much its local training improves the global model it received, amplified by the difficulty of its environment. Difficulty is inferred from the model's own performance, without requiring any description of the environment. Both signals are measured against the global model, so they are comparable across clients. On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA reaches a mean success rate of $75.5\%$ across training and held-out environments, against $68.7\%$ for the strongest federated baseline. Its advantage holds when the models are transferred to hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts, or when one of the clients is defective.
authors: Ye Lin Tun, Chu Myaet Thwal, Eui-Nam Huh, Choong Seon Hong
bullets: Standard uniform or return-based aggregation suffers from the “plateau problem”: mastered, easy environments can receive undue influence despite providing little new information.
FedDIA estimates environment difficulty from the model’s own performance, requiring no environment descriptions.
It scores client updates by improvement over the received global model and amplifies contributions from more difficult environments.
On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA achieved a 75.5% mean success rate versus 68.7% for the strongest federated baseline.
The advantage persisted on hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts and with a defective client.

Each client evaluates it before local training and its updated model after, obtaining returns 𝑟pre𝑖 and 𝑟post𝑖 . Both are sent to the server with updated parameters 𝜃𝑘𝑖 . From these, the server derives an improvement signal 𝑐𝐼𝑖 and a difficulty signal 𝑐𝐷𝑖 , combines them into a per-client score, and computes aggregation weights by softmax. Across the two example clients, a plateaued easy client receives low weight, while a still-improving hard client receives high weight.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD)}, a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by $3.5$ points on NavTest and $5.0$ points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.
authors: Chengkai Xu, Yicheng Guo, Jiaqi Liu, Yiming Cui, Shiyu Fang, Peng Hang, Hao Zhang, Jian Sun
bullets: Addresses the problem that more demonstrations may be redundant or harmful, and that data value differs across planners.
Combines scene-level calibration feedback, projected policy gradients, and a regularized local-training-geometry approximation to estimate policy-specific influence values.
Controlled group-removal experiments support the directional fidelity of PAD’s valuations.
Candidate rankings vary substantially across planner families, highlighting the need for policy-aware curation.
Policy-specific curation improves EPDMS and consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across multiple planner types while reducing scene-level regressions.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.
authors: Anh Dao, Xinxin Liu, Hang Yu, Jeffrey A Chan Santiago, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: WAMs are costly because they combine video generation with action prediction using large transformers.
A shared six-block core is recurrently applied to execute 30 layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert; video and action experts use different depths.
Elastic self-distillation trains one checkpoint to support varied action-depth and sampling-step budgets.
The 0.58B-parameter model reports 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, with 7.4× lower peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched measurements.
On real hardware, it achieved 71.3% success over 80 trials; performance degrades when action depth is aggressively reduced without budget-aware training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. (a) Each expert stores a prelude, a shared core, and a coda, and loops the core Kv times in the video expert and Ka times in the action expert (shown for Kv=4, Ka=2). The video expert encodes the current frame once per query and caches its keys and values. At every sampling step, the action expert reads them in a joint attention; late alignment lets action loop r attend to video loop σ(r), so even a single action loop sees the deepest visual features. Both experts also cross-attend to frozen text embeddings of the instruction, and future frames are predicted only during training. (b) One student learns every setting (Ka, N) in S. The target of each macro step is the frozen teacher’s fine Euler map started from the student’s own state (Llocal), and the final chunk is matched to the teacher’s chunk from the same noise (Lend).

papers.abstract: Robotic planning from visual observations and signal temporal logic (STL) requires grounding task requirements in scene evidence while adapting plans to execution feedback. We present GraF-VTA, a graph-based framework that extends Vision-TL-Action with structured task representations, causal observation history, and closed-loop trajectory generation. Bidirectional cross-attention fuses STL syntax tokens with visual features, while an optional frozen automaton embedding supplies complementary untimed task structure. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations and compresses older frames to provide recent execution context. Conditioned on these features and robot state, a flow-matching model generates plans whose action prefixes are executed before replanning from refreshed observations. Across five simulation environments, the single-graph configuration achieves higher open-loop Success@$K$ than TeLoGraF and Vision-TL-Action on four environments at the reported budgets $K\geq16$. On Panda, matched-update ablations increase Success@256 from 53.91\% without observation history to 62.50\% with pyramid memory. In closed-loop Dubins evaluation, it reaches 64.06\% Success@1024, compared with 12.50\% for adapted S-MSP and 27.34\% for adapted Logic-VLA. These results support combining structured visual conditioning with observation history and replanning to improve coverage of STL-satisfying trajectories.
authors: Zezhi Liu, Zhiwei Zheng, Hanqian Luo, Deyun Qin, Shizhen Wu, Yongchun Fang
bullets: Represents task requirements with STL syntax, optional automaton embeddings, and graph-based visual–logical fusion.
Uses bidirectional cross-attention, temporal-pyramid memory, and robot state to condition a flow-matching trajectory generator.
Executes action prefixes, refreshes observations, and replans to adapt trajectories during execution.
Across five simulated environments, the single-graph model outperforms TeLoGraF and Vision-TL-Action on four environments at reported budgets of K≥16.
Observation history improves Panda Success@256 from 53.91% to 62.50%; closed-loop Dubins Success@1024 reaches 64.06%.

Logic tokens from the syntax tree and visual tokens from multi-view observations are fused through bidirectional cross-attention. The fused features, DFA embedding, and current state condition a Temporal U-Net to generate the planned trajectory via an ODE solver.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy's stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.
authors: Weile Gong, Zijian Lu, Jiahao Zheng, Bo Xu, Yiping Zuo, Jiajia Guo, Xin He, Weijun Wang, Weibei Fan
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of frequent inference in multimodal embodied navigation.
Uses a frozen navigation policy and retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback to set an adaptive cognitive horizon.
At stop requests, local visitation history enables a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls.
Cuts model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with corresponding success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points.
In physical tasks, achieves 18 versus 14 successes, while reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.
authors: Yuseon Choi, Sanghyeon Park, Eunjong Lee, Hanseo Lee, Sangjin Kim
bullets: Retrieving successful experiences to warm-start DiT denoising helps embodied agents adapt to OOD environments while reducing inference cost.
FlashX combines high-bandwidth parallel pSLC key search, interleaved Compute-in-Flash engines, and dense TLC latent storage.
Proprioception-aware clustering reduces search overhead and supports incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering.
Across VLA and WAM workloads, FlashX improves task success by up to 12.24 percentage points and search throughput by 2.57× over prior NAND search.
Compared with SSD-based retrieval, it provides 1.29–3.95× end-to-end speedup and 1.12–2.34× energy-efficiency improvement.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models are increasingly adapted into task specialists to expand their embodied capabilities. Yet these capabilities remain fragmented across separate policies, and existing model-merging methods do not reliably preserve them during closed-loop execution: parameter-space alignment provides only an indirect proxy for behavior, while regression may fail to preserve behavior at states not covered by its calibration inputs. We present Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), an execution-aware, gradient-free framework that consolidates robot specialists into a single policy. Across two complementary timescales, TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts spanning different stages of task execution and from intermediate states within iterative action generation. To account for representation shifts introduced by merging, TCR recomputes each block's input through the already merged blocks. It then uses each expert's computation within the block to form module inputs and fits merged weights to match the experts' linear outputs. A two-pass calibration procedure further refines the merged policy using separate rollout caches while retaining the frozen specialists as teachers. The resulting model preserves the original inference graph and requires neither expert routing nor additional gradient training. On LIBERO, TCR merges four $\pi_{0.5}$ specialists and achieves 77.83% success across 1,200 evaluation episodes, outperforming FeatCal, RegMean, and direct weight averaging by 9.50, 24.17, and 33.00 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Wenshuo Chen, Honglei Jin, Le Yang, Jianfei Song, Shaofeng Liang, Lei Wang, Junze Zhu, Kailong Wang, Zhengxi Jin, Haozhe Jia, Honglin Chu, Songning Lai, Xiucheng Wang, Yutao Yue

papers.abstract: Aerial sensing must combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement and image processing. AeroBelief uses the next executable action as the unit of verification against reference scores. It groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model (WM). Calibrated group bounds support strict commitment; a six-query controller connects selective prediction with belief updates, acceptance checks and scheduled sensing. Across four layout families, 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, the AeroBelief controller completes 75.42% of tasks, compared with 73.33% for exhaustive WM scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring. In fixed-reference replay with a six-query cap, proposer-scaled anchored bounds raised first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduced mean queries per state by 13.54% relative to unit-scale anchored bounds. A complete ground-hosted pipeline processes 2,685 self-collected 20-megapixel unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes. Context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight independently supported target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less accumulated active processing service than uncapped all-frame processing; feedback saves another 5.17% of images relative to static context. The studies connect budgeted action selection with evidence-driven processing of recorded flight imagery.
