papers.abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.
authors: Amit Feldman, Ilan Shimshoni, Rotem Dror
bullets: Addresses the need to identify and assess procedural mistakes before recovery is no longer possible.
Uses observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions to recognize completed steps, localize them temporally, and classify execution errors.
Compares separate modular components with a joint model that predicts step identity, timing, and correctness together.
The joint model improves binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 from 80.7% to 84.1%, with the largest gain for slips.
The dataset split is revised to include erroneous videos across all splits; omitted steps are identified only after the video ends.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents can now build interactive 3D worlds and games, yet these worlds, like those built by people, often contain glitches such as floating objects, walls that can be walked through, or objects that change when no one is looking. An automatic auditor could check such worlds at scale and provide rewards for agents that build them, but only if it is both accurate and cheap. Auditing requires three abilities, namely navigating to the objects that may contain a glitch, triggering glitches that appear only after a specific behavior, and recognizing what is wrong. Current auditors are either accurate but slow and expensive or cheap but unreliable. We study how much of the audit small models can take on. A 4B vision language model fine-tuned end to end on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers together match a frontier model on both, but recognition stays far behind. We therefore build an auditor in which a swarm of small explorers navigates and triggers, and a frontier model reviews what they record and report. On WorldAuditBench, our auditor succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest auditor reported, at less than a quarter of its cost. It matches the frontier reviewer exploring on its own at 4.6 times lower cost and about half the latency. Without further training, it also answers embodied questions about real-world scans, matching the frontier reviewer exploring on its own and surpassing four other frontier models by 6.4 to 16.6 points.
authors: Jingbo Yang, Ziyan Jiang, Li An, Jiabao Ji, Yujian Liu, Tommi Jaakkola, Yang Zhang, Shiyu Chang
bullets: Targets three auditing challenges: navigating to suspicious objects, triggering behavior-dependent glitches, and recognizing faults.
A fine-tuned 4B vision-language model learns navigation and glitch triggering from teacher-guided verified trajectories; six explorers match a frontier model on these abilities.
Recognition remains weaker in small models, so a frontier model reviews explorers’ recordings and reports.
On 213 WorldAuditBench tasks, the system succeeds on 55.9%, improving 13.6 points over the strongest reported auditor at under one-quarter the cost.
It also answers embodied questions about real-world scans without further training, matching the frontier reviewer and outperforming four other frontier models.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses the failure of robot policies to compose reliable atomic skills over long-horizon tasks.
A VLM observes camera images and provides the next step in the policy’s instruction format; successful rollouts are relabeled and used for fine-tuning.
On stalled states, next-step coaching increases subgoal completion by 4.6× over the original task instruction.
Unassisted success on unseen long-horizon scenes improves from 47.4% to 59.3%, outperforming human-demonstration and self-collected-success fine-tuning at equal data budgets.
The action backbone remains frozen; the approach is scoped to leveraging existing skills through language guidance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CoachSI. (a) Coached collection. At every action chunk, a frozen VLM coach reads the camera views and selects the policy’s instruction ℓt from the next-step candidates of the task, or keeps the task instruction g. The policy weights are fixed and every action is the policy’s own. (b) Hindsight relabeling and fine-tuning. Successful rollouts keep their observations and actions, and ℓt is replaced by g. Fine-tuning mixes them with human demonstrations and updates only the video backbone. (c) Deployment. The fine-tuned policy receives observations and g alone, with no coach. Each square is one action chunk, colored by the instruction the policy receives; ticks mark completed subgoals. The example is one long-horizon task: alone, the pretrained policy completes the first subgoal and stalls; with the coach, it completes the task; after fine-tuning, it completes the task in an unseen scene without the coach.

papers.tldr: CoachSI uses a frozen vision-language model to tell a robot policy the next atomic step, improving long-horizon task success without generating actions.

papers.abstract: Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSEPose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerancedilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.
authors: Junghoon Seo, Hakjin Lee, Jaehoon Sim
bullets: Addresses mesh-dependent reconstruction targets for unseen object instances from partial RGB-D observations.
Maps observed 3D points into normalized object coordinates and selects support within a tolerance-dilated pose-and-size envelope.
Combines the envelope target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context.
On REAL275 and HouseCat6D, closely matches surface-based supervision and remains stable across boundary perturbations and viewpoints.
Supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across both benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Deficits in reactive balance can increase fall risk among older adults and individuals with neuromuscular impairments, motivating the need for interventions that improve balance recovery. Wearable robotic exoskeletons offer a promising approach to addressing this need by augmenting balance control. However, developing controllers that deliver appropriately timed and scaled assistance remains challenging, as evaluating each candidate strategy requires repeated exposure to destabilizing perturbations. We propose a simulation-to-real framework that combines motion imitation and reinforcement learning to develop balance-assistive ankle exoskeleton control. A muscle-driven neuromusculoskeletal model was trained using a small set of motion-capture data from a single subject to reproduce kinematic and kinetic responses to backward-translation perturbations. This model served as a virtual human for training a reinforcement-learning exoskeleton controller. The resulting controller generated bilateral ankle assistance using only inertial sensor measurements, without explicit perturbation detection. We implemented the controller on-board a bilateral ankle exoskeleton and evaluated it in five healthy subjects whose data were not used for training. Assistance increased the perturbation magnitude that subjects could withstand without stepping by 11.8% and reduced peak center-of-mass displacement and velocity by 13.5% and 28.2%, respectively. Individual benefits varied with baseline recovery strategy and body mass. These results indicate that a single virtual human can yield transferable balance assistance, and that more diverse virtual humans could further improve its effectiveness.
bullets: Targets fall risk caused by impaired reactive balance and the challenge of tuning assistance without repeated physical perturbations.
Combines motion imitation with reinforcement learning in a muscle-driven neuromusculoskeletal simulation.
Uses only inertial sensors and requires no explicit perturbation detection to generate bilateral ankle assistance.
In five untrained healthy subjects, assistance increased no-step perturbation tolerance by 11.8% and reduced peak center-of-mass displacement and velocity by 13.5% and 28.2%.
Benefits varied with individuals’ baseline recovery strategies and body mass; broader virtual-human diversity may improve effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.
authors: Qiman Wu, Hanlin Chen, Yuhua Wei, Mingyuan Wang, Shaman Tang, Minghao Li, Rui Xin, Xingye Liu, Zhichao Yang, Yiqi Yu, Hongyan Pei, Xiaowen Tian, YingYing Liu, Shiwen Liu, Jiahui Hu, Yizhao Wang, Yuheng Zhang, Anhua Liu, Yue He, Shuang Su, Da Zhu, Hua Zhou, Pengfei Diao, Haojie Yang, Weichao Huang, Hang Zhang, Honggou Yang, Xianming Liu
bullets: Targets Physical AI systems that must understand spatial and temporal environments and convert observations into actions onboard.
Uses TuringPAI-VL, a 0.65B model combining HybridViT-MLQ visual processing, multi-scale latent queries, and geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision.
Provides a shared initialization for TuringPAI-Drive and TuringPAI-Embodied, supporting driving and manipulation applications.
TuringPAI-Drive stays within 1.2% of a full-token baseline on evaluated ADE/FDE metrics and runs at 12 Hz on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC.
TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill.
authors: Madeleine Nouri, Gelareh Mohammadi, Francisco Cruz

Reuses frozen Pick and Lift skills for stacking by adding a Place skill.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.
authors: Linfeng Dong, Jianwei Niu, Jiuyi Zhao, Ruibing Feng, Xinghao Wu, Wu Yang, Shuai Tao, Wulong Liu, Mu Li
bullets: Addresses memory-augmented VLA models that either retrieve past observations without reasoning or let long histories interfere with current perception.
Uses a vision-language backbone to infer the current subtask from timestamped history and preserve this reasoning as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought.
A flow-matching action expert uses the latent memory while Perception Attention directly grounds actions in the current view.
Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions to reduce inference cost for long histories.
Achieves strong simulated and real-world performance, including 68.8% average success on real-world memory tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ActMem. (a) A pretrained vision-language backbone (Qwen3-VL) encodes the instruction, the timestamped historical frames, and the current perception, and performs latent memory reasoning inside the backbone to produce the subtask together with its Latent Memory CoT states Ct, which condition a flow-matching action expert; Perception Attention additionally routes the current visual features to the action expert. (b) Inside the backbone, the subtask tokens that form Memory CoT follow the history and the current view in the sequence, so under the causal mask they read both, and their hidden states become Ct; the action expert receives only Ct, not the history tokens. (c) Efficient Memory CoT Inference. Consecutive decisions usually share the same subtask, so the previous subtask is reused as a draft and verified against the updated context in a single parallel pass. If it is accepted, its hidden states are recomputed to give the new Ct, with no token-by-token decoding.

papers.abstract: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and fragmented, model-specific training stacks of embodied models.
Uses a common abstraction layer to share infrastructure without restricting model architectures or execution requirements.
Combines reusable and hardware-aware optimizations spanning computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8 communication for DDP/FSDP.
Also provides unified data infrastructure, egocentric-to-robot data synthesis, and concurrent simulator evaluation.
Reports 1.47×–4.38× higher training throughput and 4.1×–23.2× faster evaluation than corresponding open-source baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LoongForge-Embodied system architecture. The framework unifies heterogeneous VLA and WAM models under a single native-PyTorch training stack, combining an integrated data pipeline (Ego2Robot, unified data loaders, and composable transforms), an acceleration toolkit of shared optimizations with model-specific execution paths, distributed training with FP8 communication, and an integrated evaluation orchestrator. The right-hand panels preview representative results on training speedup, trainingloss consistency, and benchmark success rates (Section 8).

Figure 3: Training-aligned evaluation architecture. A unified entry point launches a benchmark client process and a model inference server process, which exchange only model inputs and predicted actions over WebSocket RPC. Numbered markers denote the four pipeline stages: observation adaptation (1), payload construction (2), and action decoding (4) run in the client, whereas action prediction through the shared training-side predict_action interface (3) runs in the server, which also hosts the model registry/factory and the action-chunk cache. The client loop returns from each environment step to observation adaptation until the episode terminates.

Figure 2: Unified data architecture of LoongForge-Embodied. Heterogeneous embodied datasets are integrated through a format abstraction layer that exposes a common sample contract. Model-specific data processing is supported through extensible registries for transformations, preprocessing, collation, and sampling, enabling diverse VLA and WAM models to share the same data infrastructure.

papers.abstract: Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects. Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors. Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution. To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth. Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU. Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints. Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.
authors: Xinzhe Fu, Qi Shao, Yuanfei Xie, Taoyu Wu, Zhihao Cao, Long Hu, Hong Liang, Xianzhi Li, Anh Nguyen, Baoru Huang, Rongsheng Li
bullets: Addresses missing and corrupted depth caused by specular reflection and refraction in transparent-object RGB-D images.
Builds coordinate-aware global and local multi-range inverse-depth hypotheses around a prior-guided prediction.
Uses recurrent refinement with out-of-bounds masking and validity-aware fusion, followed by spatially gated residual correction.
Reportedly achieves lower error than several prior methods across five datasets.
Real-robot evaluations show improved surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of MIR-Depth. A frozen Depth Anything V2 model provides the relative-depth prior. Transformer and CNN encoders extract RGB-mask, relative-depth, and raw-depth features, which are summed at each scale. The summed features provide multi-scale context, while a decoder and depth head predict initial depth D0. Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses construct one shared global inverse-depth volume aggregated by a 3D hourglass alongside medium and fine pixel-wise local volumes filtered by depth-axis convolutions. Selective Recurrent Refinement queries these volumes, encodes lookup features together with per-offset validity indicators, and fuses active ranges to update inverse depth through a multi-scale ConvGRU. Spatially Gated Correction weights the full-resolution residual relative to D0 to produce completed depth for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.

Fig. 5. Real-world depth completion and 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Comparison across an upright bottle, a hollow container, and multi-object clutter captured on the platform in Fig. 4, where black pixels in Raw denote missing sensor returns.

Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison on TransCG. Examples span D435 and L515 test scenes, where yellow boxes mark zoomed regions and bottom error maps visualize pixel-wise absolute error in millimeters on valid transparent-object pixels alongside full-frame ROI MAE and RMSE.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle. Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself. We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks. In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress. The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles. We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode's prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan. With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts. A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Dongheon Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: At least 96% of observed failures are stalls: the object remains stationary while the model predicts progress.
Stalls arise both with and without distribution shift, challenging the attribution of failures solely to model error.
Unstick combines on-policy fine-tuning with a fixed-weight loop breaker: prediction-error memory or random re-initialization at each replan.
Residual memory recovers most adaptation gains on pushing tasks; re-initialization works well for shape shifts but less for visual shifts.
The findings identify planning-loop fixed points as a major limitation of warm-started gradient-descent planners.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor
authors: Zexun Lin, Yuan Feng, Xike Xie
bullets: WAMs incur high latency from multi-step denoising during robotic control.
The method addresses dual nonuniformity: velocity residuals vary sharply across denoising stages, and integration step sizes unevenly amplify state errors.
It derives a trajectory error tolerance bound linking velocity residuals and integration steps to final action-distribution error.
WAMotor selects reliable anchor velocities, delays speculation when needed, and uses integration-step-aware verification thresholds.
Evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show 2.86×–4.28× speedups with maintained success rates.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.
authors: Chengyang Dong, Ze Chen, Kai Ye, Chutian Wang, Heng Xu, Wei Mo, Maomao Li, Jiayan Xu, Jiayuan Wu, Yihao Xiao, Linhua Ye, Zhonghua Peng, Ruize Han, Jialong Sun
bullets: Targets VLA adaptation under deployment distribution shifts without source-domain retraining.
Addresses zeroth-order estimation noise, which can cause long-horizon adaptation to stall or degrade.
Uses a lightweight online historical error predictor fused with instantaneous zeroth-order estimates, without backpropagation or extra forward passes.
Theory links estimation variance to convergence limits in high-dimensional, small-population settings.
Experiments on LIBERO and real robots report higher success rates, improved closed-loop stability, and better post-disturbance recovery under low memory.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies from demonstrations typically samples trajectory segments uniformly or relies on static offline data curation before training. However, we find that demonstration data vary sharply in supervision value across temporal windows, and that each window's value to the policy evolves substantially during training rather than being fixed or captured by raw loss alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that periodically scores temporal windows from the evolving policy using five policy-native signals and dynamically adjusts their sampling weights during training. RefreshGrad focuses optimization on informative, learnable windows without altering the policy architecture, training objective, or inference cost. Across ten LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks, RefreshGrad boosts average success from 60.7% (Uniform) and 68.2% (FAKTUAL) to 76.1% under visual perturbations, and from 57.4% and 73.3% to 81.3% in clean scenes.

bullets: Demonstration windows differ in supervision value, and that value changes during training.

Scope: evaluated on LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks and focused on adaptive data sampling.

papers.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.
authors: Xuwei Ding, Skylar Zhai, Linxin Song, Jiarui Feng, Dongqi Fu, Huajun Xi, Junnan Li, Jingcheng Liang, Jieyu Zhao, Yinglong Xia, Hong Li, Jian Kang
bullets: Introduces 125 procedurally generated interactive CAPTCHAs covering five spatial abilities, solved via clicks and drags.

The benchmark and training gym are designed to scale spatial-action learning and support transfer to real-world scenes.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a lightweight policy model to mitigate the difficulty of handling higher-dimensional action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL), alongside an algorithm to effectively train it. To address this, we focus on drifting models, which can implicitly represent complex distributions and infer actions in a single forward pass. However, while drifting models can be straightforwardly trained via backpropagation of the Q-gradient, this alone cannot be expected to appropriately capture the desired action coordination. Therefore, this paper constructs a three-step learning algorithm to encourage the action coordination. First, the source distribution of the drifting model is co-optimized as a diagonal policy model. This conditions the drifting model to attach the coordination, which cannot be expressed by a diagonal distribution, as residuals. Second, a discriminator model before and after drifting is introduced with adversarial training for a regularization term. This actively promotes the extraction of the coordination that fundamentally separates the two distributions. Third, best-of-N sampling is applied for action selection during rollouts in order to give directionality toward/beyond the regions where the coordination is insufficiently extracted/sufficiently discovered. The proposed method consistently improves the sample efficiency and the final control performance over the conventional diagonal distribution modeling across three locomotion tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that this improvement is achieved by reducing variance in certain action dimensions, effectively coupling them with other actions as action coordination.
bullets: High-dimensional actions are difficult to coordinate when modeled with conventional diagonal distributions.
The method uses a drifting model that represents complex action distributions and generates actions in one forward pass.
Training combines co-optimization of a diagonal source policy, adversarial discrimination before and after drifting, and best-of-N rollout sampling.
Across three high-dimensional locomotion tasks, it consistently improves sample efficiency and final control performance over diagonal modeling.
Analysis attributes the gains to reduced variance in some action dimensions and stronger coupling among actions.

papers.abstract: Underwater vehicle-manipulator systems distribute actuation across thrusters and joint motors. Whole-body model predictive control (MPC), rather than separate vehicle and arm controllers, can coordinate both to extend the workspace and exploit the system's full kinematic capability. Doing so, however, requires a hydrodynamic model and derivatives throughout the prediction horizon. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) captures geometry-dependent forces and moments for such a model, but is too expensive to evaluate online. We present a differentiable analytical hydrodynamic model combining smooth spherical-harmonic force and moment fields with a coupled added-inertia matrix identified from CFD. It compactly represents velocity and acceleration-dependent loads and provides their derivatives in closed form. These derivatives are propagated through free-floating vehicle--manipulator dynamics for whole-body trajectory optimization and receding-horizon control, jointly optimizing thruster forces and joint torques for reaching and continuous tracking. Held-out CFD tests validate the principal translational-force and rotational-moment fields and the added-inertia response. The analytical Jacobians evaluate faster and avoid the step-size sensitivity of central finite differences. Closed-loop Stonefish experiments demonstrate whole-body MPC in an independent marine simulator. By making geometry-dependent hydrodynamics directly available to gradient-based control, the model incorporates water forces and their sensitivities into motion allocation between the vehicle and arm, rather than treating them only as disturbances.
authors: Hefan Wang, Yvan Petillot, Carlos Mastalli
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of using CFD hydrodynamics online for underwater vehicle–manipulator control.
Combines smooth spherical-harmonic force and moment fields with a CFD-identified coupled added-inertia matrix.
Provides closed-form hydrodynamic derivatives propagated through free-floating vehicle–manipulator dynamics.
Held-out CFD tests validate key force, moment, and added-inertia responses; analytical Jacobians are faster and avoid finite-difference step-size sensitivity.
Closed-loop Stonefish experiments demonstrate coordinated whole-body MPC for reaching and continuous tracking.

papers.abstract: The success of manipulation policies is closely tied to the spatial relationship between the robot and the target object, as well as the task being performed, making the ability to adjust the robot's pose critical for successful execution. When the robot starts away from the task, such adjustments require coordinating navigation with local manipulation. Jointly training these capabilities incurs substantial computational and data costs, while navigating toward a predefined goal pose limits the flexibility needed to adapt to task-specific manipulation requirements. To address these challenges, we propose Learning to Move from and for Manipulation Policies (M4M), a framework that learns manipulation-aware mobility directly from pretrained manipulation policies. By leveraging the hidden representations of the policy's action-generating network as dense supervision, together with a limited number of manipulation execution outcomes, we learn a spatially conditioned embedding that captures task-dependent manipulation success across candidate robot poses. From the robot's current stereo observations, this representation estimates manipulation success at unvisited poses without rolling out the manipulation policy at each location. It is further integrated into navigation policy training, while a learned handoff policy decides when to transition from navigation to manipulation, enabling the robot to move and manipulate in a unified, task-aware manner. Across eight articulated-object tasks in unseen RoboCasa kitchens, M4M achieves 47.0% mean task success, compared with 26.5% for the strongest baseline and 19.2% for direct manipulation execution, and refrigerator-closing experiments show consistent improvements across four frozen manipulation policies.
authors: Siyuan Zheng, Zhong Cao, Henry X. Liu
bullets: Addresses the need to coordinate navigation and manipulation when the robot starts away from the task, while reducing the cost of jointly training both capabilities.
Uses hidden action-policy representations and limited manipulation outcomes to learn a spatially conditioned embedding of manipulation success across robot poses.
Predicts success at unvisited poses from stereo observations without executing the manipulation policy at every location.
Integrates the learned representation into navigation and uses a handoff policy to decide when to switch to manipulation.

Achieves 47.0% mean success across eight unseen RoboCasa kitchen tasks, versus 26.5% for the strongest baseline and 19.2% for direct manipulation; refrigerator-closing tests improve across four frozen policies.

papers.abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at https://alwaysleepy.github.io/MoRE-WM-site/.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Shaowei Liu, Albert J. Zhai, Henry Che, Wei-Chiu Ma, Shenlong Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling heterogeneous physical interactions in robotics.
Assigns distinct motion experts to rigid, deformable, and prehensile physical regimes.
Trains on mixed simulation and real-world data and integrates with Model Predictive Control.
Improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes and strengthens real-world MPC performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MoRE. Given the current and historical object states and actions, represented as point clouds, we first encode the scene and actor inputs into point tokens using two encoders. An explicit gating network then selects among specialized motion experts, each tailored to a distinct physical regime, to predict the next object state in 3D. P = prehensile, NP = non-prehensile.

Figure 4: Model Predictive Control (MPC) performance. (a) Box pushing and (b) toy manipulation results. Each section details the prediction error across planning steps (left) and success rate vs. error threshold (right). MoRE achieves lower error and higher success than the baselines.

Figure 3: Qualitative results on DROID evaluation. We compare model predictions with ground truth on challenging DROID scenes with clutter, diverse objects, and partial observations. Even for small, low-resolution manipulated objects, our model produces accurate dynamics, demonstrating robustness to occlusion and noise.

The Vanilla model struggles to treat the box as rigid and the toy sloth as soft. In contrast, our model correctly handles the different cases.

Figure 6: Benchmark tasks visualization: Simulation and real-world benchmarks covering rigid and soft objects under non-prehensile and prehensile interactions, designed to evaluate generalization across diverse physical regimes.

Table 2: Dynamic model comparison across interaction types and physics. We report geometric accuracy (MSE, CD) and material structural metrics (rigidity or Laplacian). Privileged experts (gray) are domain-specific and assume known interaction types at test time, while our Mixture-of-Experts model handles diverse interactions in a unified framework with consistently strong performance.
Table 4: Comparison with Point-World on the DROID dataset. Our method performs better across all three cases, showing strong generalization to real-world object dynamics.

Table 5: Gating Network Accuracy. Expert selection accuracy (%) evaluated over 50 random interactions per task category. The gating network maintains consistently high accuracy across diverse regimes, indicating reliable expert routing for different physical dynamics.

papers.abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.
authors: Clinton Enwerem, Saleh Kemal, John S. Baras, Calin Belta
bullets: Residual reinforcement learning adapts an imitation policy under a limited environment-interaction budget.
The method separates a phase’s failure frequency from its impact on full-task completion by estimating completion gain from paired episodes.
Positive gain estimates select which action components to correct and how to distribute training episodes across phases.
In docking and bimanual assembly simulations, gain-based allocation targeted phases that were not always the most failure-prone and improved completion.
A release-phase residual policy improved held-out completion from release-start states by 16.9% in one assembly configuration.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.
authors: Qianzhong Chen, Muyuan Lin, Yuyin Sun, Mac Schwager, Cheng-Hao Kuo, Roberto Mart\'in-Mart\'in
bullets: Addresses unsafe real-world exploration and simulator exploitation of residual sim-to-real gaps.
Uses simulated play data to improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction in an action-conditioned video world model.
Aligns the world model with deployment observations using 20 autonomous real-robot rollouts per task, without teleoperation.
Forms a closed-loop RL environment from the VLA, whole-body controller, and video world model with dense progress rewards.
Across three real-robot tasks, video-world-model RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, versus 48.3% for real-robot RL.

papers.abstract: Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making. A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost. The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and resilience in agentic C-UAS systems.
bullets: Addresses security-relevant failures caused by degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations in autonomous C-UAS pipelines.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3\% task success, compared with 61.7\% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3\% for the VLM alone, and 46.7\% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30$\times$ fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.
bullets: Addresses the lack of grounded scene-change reasoning in VLM-generated multi-step manipulation plans and the inefficiency and drift of pixel-level world models.
Imagines candidate plans in DINOv2 feature space using a flow-matching world model with action cross-attention and causal temporal history.
A dual-head critic evaluates imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before robot execution.
On six language-conditioned tasks, it achieved 83.3% success, outperforming the reported latent-world-model, VLM-only, and pixel-diffusion baselines.

All executed plans were verified successfully; remaining failures came from low-level grasp or placement slips, while simulation results showed strong CALVIN and cluttered nut-assembly performance with 30× fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Verify2Act overview. Stage 1: a VLM proposes candidate multi-step plans from the camera observation and the language instruction. Stage 2: V2A-WM rolls out each candidate in the frozen DINOv2 latent space (St → St+k), conditioned on CLIP action tokens. Stage 3: a goal head scores the terminal latent state against the goal, and a temporal consistency head checks consecutive imagined states; the best verified plan is executed.

Fig. 4. Results on the robot. (a) Task success per task and averaged over tasks. (b) Outcome of the episodes of each method: success, execution failure (the plan was correct but a skill failed), or planning failure (the executed plan could not satisfy the goal).

Fig. 2. V2A-WM training and inference. Training: the delta encoder gives the target latent zgt = fenc(∆St); we interpolate zτ = τzgt + (1− τ)z0 and the flow-matching transformer, conditioned on past frames and CLIP action tokens through cross-attention, predicts the velocity v̂. Inference: a single Euler step integrates from noise z0 to z1 = z0 + v̂, and the delta decoder reconstructs Ŝt+1 = St + fdec(z1).
Fig. 5. CALVIN. Left: SR5 against reflective VLM calls (log scale). Right: success SRk over the chain length.

papers.abstract: Ferrofluids are liquids containing magnetic nanoparticles, enabling shape control through external magnetic fields. This deformability supports their use as soft robotic bodies that can navigate confined spaces and manipulate objects. Their nonlinear continuum dynamics, however, make reliable control challenging. Existing work shows how spatial magnetic fields from electromagnet arrays can establish and maintain desired ferrofluid configurations. A complementary objective is to exploit the fluid's dynamics under limited actuation to reach prescribed shapes that may not be sustainable at equilibrium. Here, we use deep model-based reinforcement learning to control these transient shapes. Learning directly through physical interaction, our policies select current commands for a single fixed electromagnet based on visual observations, guiding the moving ferrofluid toward prescribed geometries. The learned policies repeatedly attain a variety of shapes spanning polygons, asterisks and pentominoes. These results demonstrate that learning directly from physical interaction enables reliable fluid shaping, opening new possibilities for controlling ferrofluid-based soft robots.
authors: Anthony Czubarow, Antonio Terpin, Raffaello D'Andrea
bullets: Ferrofluids are promising soft-robot bodies but are difficult to control because of nonlinear continuum dynamics.
The approach learns current commands directly from physical interaction using visual observations.
It targets prescribed shapes that may not be sustainable at equilibrium, rather than only stable configurations.
Policies repeatedly formed polygons, asterisks, and pentominoes.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.
authors: Takahiro Miki, Robin Schmid, Manthan Patel, Turcan Tuna, Julia Richter, Julian Nubert, Joonho Lee, Matthias M\"uller, Marco Hutter
bullets: Targets robust autonomous navigation in diverse, unstructured real-world terrain.

These labels are converted into semantic images using open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, which operates at a higher frequency than the VLM analysis. The semantic images are then fused with elevation maps to create an environmental representation that reinforcement learning (RL) policies utilize for fast and robust robot control.

papers.abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
authors: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh
bullets: Addresses OOD failures caused by scarce, multimodal robotics data and policy overfitting to small distribution shifts.
Combines LVM/VLM semantic reasoning with object-relational distance pairs along meaningful geometric axes to form task-specific guidance.
Transfers motion patterns from successful in-distribution rollouts without retraining the policy.
Works in simulation for pose and task-goal shifts and on a real robot for cable placement and unseen-object steering.
In reported experiments, it more than doubled success one grid step outside training positions and nearly eliminated object confusion when steering toward unseen objects.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our visual-geometric policy steering framework. Offline analysis (at task initialization, once per episode): (1) we retrieve the most relevant successful in-distribution rollout τ∗ by weighted image (DINOv2) and text (CLIP) similarity; (2) a VLM selects the task-relevant object-relational distance pairs per motion phase (e.g., gripper–cube distance d1, cube–table distance d2, gripper orientation θ), evaluated per timestep into the reference trends Φ; (3) a VLM with SAM2 matches the demonstration objects to the live OOD scene (e.g., the cylinder takes the cube’s role), re-targeting each pair. Online steering (every action chunk): (4) perception projects the live scene into the same distance space and aligns each pair to Φ within a window, giving the reference d∗. At every denoising step, a differentiable dynamics model F forecasts the features d(A) of a candidate chunk A, and a line-searched gradient step on the trajectory loss corrects the frozen policy’s velocity field, yielding the steered chunk A′.

Fig. 5. Positional generalization. Every rollout is plotted at the Mahalanobis distance of its measured cable position (dots near 100 are successes, near 0 failures), with per-zone success rates and 95% Wilson intervals (squares) and a per-method logistic fit, crossing 50% at 2.8σ (base) and 3.4σ (VG-Steer).

Fig. 9. Visual-geometric guidance via VLM-selected distance pairs. Offline (a–c): the demonstration is segmented (Gemini 3 Flash + SAM2) and split into sub-trajectory phases (STRAP); the VLM selects each phase’s entity pairs, projections, and sub-goal constraints. Online (d–e): the live scene is matched to the demonstration, and the guidance steers the frozen policy so the selected projected distances track the reference.

Fig. 2. Differentiable guidance injection. At each denoising step, the candidate chunk is rolled out by forward kinematics, and the guidance loss (position, orientation, gripper) is differentiated; a golden-section line search sets the step size, and the correction is applied to the policy’s velocity field, steering the trajectory without modifying weights.
Fig. 8. Real-world outcome breakdown (share of rollouts, counts on bars). Residual failures concentrate in grasp and transport, which the guidance does not address.

Fig. 3. Per-action-chunk inference overhead on π0.5 (mean over the four suites, CUDA-synchronized). With VG-Steer a chunk takes ∼73 ms in total (1.2× the base’s ∼61 ms), comparable to gradient-only VLS (∼70 ms total); full VLS costs ∼20× more, scaling with its particle count (20 here).

papers.abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.

papers.abstract: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.
authors: Zirui Song, Jiadong Zhang, Zheng Lu, Xiaosong Ma, Xiaojun Chang, Xiuying Chen
bullets: The pipeline compares task instructions with checker code to predict possible disagreements.

The study recommends testing both incomplete executions and valid task completions that differ from expert demonstrations.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models learn to plan from data, and hand-written planners are widely treated as a thing of the past. We test whether this is justified: we implement sixteen textbook planners, each combining a path source (reference line, A*, hybrid A*, RRT*) with a trajectory method (Frenet lattice, nonlinear optimization, $s$--$t$ search, dynamic window), and evaluate them on three benchmarks: open loop on nuScenes, closed loop on nuPlan with ground-truth perception, and photorealistic closed loop on HUGSIM. On HUGSIM, they replace only the planner of the end-to-end model UniAD and read its frozen perception, without an HD map or other privileged information. On nuScenes and nuPlan, the best textbook planners are competitive (L2 error of 0.735\,m against 0.947\,m for UniAD's planner; a nuPlan score of 79.3 against 76.1 for the rule-based PDM-Closed on Test14-hard with reactive agents). On HUGSIM, nine of the sixteen score above UniAD's learned planner on the same perception,. The best, a hybrid A* path followed by nonlinear trajectory optimization, raises HUGSIM's driving score (HD-Score) from 32.0 to 41.8. The gain is largest with standing and oncoming cars; against cars that steer at the ego, there is none. In 31 of the 182 runs in which UniAD's planner hits a car, the best textbook planner completes the route on the same perception: these crashes are due to the planner, not the perception.
bullets: The study evaluates 16 planners combining four path sources with four trajectory-generation methods across nuScenes, nuPlan, and HUGSIM.
On nuScenes and nuPlan, the strongest textbook planners are competitive with learned or rule-based baselines.
Replacing UniAD’s planner with a hybrid A* plus nonlinear optimization planner improves HUGSIM HD-Score from 32.0 to 41.8.
Nine of 16 textbook planners outperform UniAD’s planner on HUGSIM under identical perception.
Planner failures explain some UniAD crashes: the best textbook planner completes 31 routes that UniAD fails, though it provides no gain against cars steering directly toward the ego vehicle.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.
authors: Yangchen Zhao, Ali Payani, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Long-horizon planning suffers from compounding prediction errors and weak guidance from distant goal similarity.
GEMS generates structured intermediate subgoals and selects relevant states from Latent Experience Memory (LEM).
A distance gate chooses whether to evaluate predicted outcomes against the generated subgoal or a retrieved memory state.
Across manipulation, navigation, and reaching tasks, GEMS achieves success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World.
The method outperforms evaluated world-model planning baselines, while relying on a frozen world model.

papers.abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

Achieves 67.8% mean success across three real-robot tasks and 90.3% across eight simulated tasks with up to four arms.
Ablations show cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision are important for coordination.

papers.abstract: Gas Source Localization (GSL) with mobile robots is challenging because wind and gas measurements are spatially sparse, noisy, and potentially affected by robot motion. Indoor airflow can vary substantially across space, while detailed environmental layouts, boundary conditions, or precomputed airflow fields are often unavailable. Moreover, hazardous sources must be localized as quickly as possible, making exhaustive exploration impractical. This paper presents a lightweight physics-informed probabilistic framework for efficient GSL under spatially varying indoor airflow. As the robot navigates, it continuously collects wind and gas measurements and reconstructs the spatially varying airflow field online. The estimated wind field drives a forward dispersion model that predicts the gas pattern for each candidate source location. These predictions are compared with the measured gas pattern to update a probabilistic belief over the source location. As the wind field is reconstructed incrementally, the framework also accounts for the spatially non-uniform reliability of wind field estimation and its influence on the source estimation. The resulting belief map is then used for informative path planning to guide the robot toward informative regions. High-fidelity simulations provide a comprehensive evaluation of the individual components and their integrations within the complete system, while physical indoor experiments assess the system performance under realistic sensing, motion, and airflow conditions. The results demonstrate that incorporating lightweight physical knowledge significantly improves localization robustness under spatially complex airflow and enables more efficient exploration.
authors: Wanting Jin, Thomas Wiedemann, Han Fan, Achim Lilienthal, Alcherio Martinoli
bullets: Addresses sparse, noisy gas and wind measurements in spatially varying indoor airflow without requiring precomputed airflow maps.

A probabilistic belief over source locations accounts for the spatially varying reliability of wind-field estimates.
Informative path planning guides the robot toward regions expected to improve localization.
High-fidelity simulations and physical indoor experiments show improved robustness and more efficient exploration under complex airflow.

papers.abstract: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.
authors: Yao Zhang, Zhuchenyang Liu, Yu Xiao
bullets: Targets multi-step household interactions involving movable objects, such as picking up and throwing a toy into a basket.

Achieves task completion rates of 98.7%, 93.3%, and 82.7% with three evaluated language models.
Ablations show spatial control is essential for task completion, while quantitative feedback improves motion precision.
