papers.abstract: Once deployed on vehicles, end-to-end driving models continuously encounter challenging scenarios, generating valuable human takeover data that capture both model outputs and human behaviors. However, human interventions are often imperfect, as drivers may intervene too late or unnecessarily. Consequently, direct imitation can reinforce late responses or discourage otherwise appropriate maneuvers. To address this challenge, we propose an offline post-training framework that transforms imperfect takeover data into proactive supervision. We first construct diverse trajectory candidates by augmenting the plans of the deployed model and shifting recorded human corrective maneuvers earlier in time. We then train a scene-conditioned trajectory scorer to rank these candidates using expert demonstrations and unpaired preference signals from takeover logs. Using this scorer, we selectively replace pre-takeover training targets with higher-scoring candidates while retaining the original targets in normal driving scenarios. Finally, we distill the resulting targets into the driving model without changing its inference architecture. In closed-loop evaluations using real-world scenarios reconstructed with 4D Gaussian splatting, our method achieves the highest overall success rate, outperforming the deployed model, direct imitation learning and trajectory post-optimization. These results highlight a practical path toward efficient updates of deployed driving models using existing fleet logs.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation. Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities. Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion. Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks. Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.
authors: Keke Tang, Guolin Qiu, Tianyu Hao, Daizong Liu, Yikai Zhang, Peican Zhu, Zhihong Tian
bullets: Targets the gap between VLA-predicted task-space commands and their downstream physical execution.

Real-robot experiments validate execution degradation on physical platforms.

papers.abstract: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.
authors: Johannes Mootz, Mani Amani, Reza Akhavian
bullets: Latent safety filters may reject many safe actions even when calibrated to accept unsafe actions only rarely.
The proposed overlap groups similar latents and actions into cells and measures the share of safe transitions in cells containing both safe and unsafe outcomes.
The overlap is proven to be the minimum fraction of safe transitions any cell-level filter must reject to accept no unsafe transitions in the data.
The framework applies to arbitrary latents and compares safety prediction via a classifier, the world model, or a separate encoder.
In visual navigation, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, rejects the fewest safe actions at the same conformal level, and enables the planner to reach the most goals.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $\pi_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
authors: Artur Kuramshin, Charlotte Cloutier, Michael Przystupa, Kirsty Ellis, Mohammad S. Akhter, Glen Berseth
bullets: Dexterous manipulation is difficult because most VLA training data targets parallel-jaw grippers, while multi-finger teleoperation data is scarce.
The study combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL) for adapting VLAs to a LEAP hand.
Across five fine-tuning recipes and two simulation tasks, SFT rollout success poorly predicts post-DSRL performance.
Freezing the VLM and tuning only the action expert yields the most steerable policy, including for out-of-distribution placements.
LoRA is reported as the least steerable adaptation approach.

papers.abstract: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models. A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.
authors: Wei Liu, Abrar Anwar, Huihua Zhao, Soha Pouya, Yan Chang
bullets: World-action policies are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise useful for steering.
LoRN uses a small actor to choose directions in a fixed low-rank projection of high-dimensional noise.
A norm-controlled construction keeps steered noise near the typical scale of Gaussian samples.
Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy.
Simulation-trained steering transfers to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks without additional real-world training.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LoRN enables low-rank noise steering of large generative robot policies. Existing noise steering methods improve frozen policies by steering the initial noise used to generate an action chunk. However, extending noise steering to the much higher-dimensional outputs of vision-language-action models and world-action models is challenging. Left: LoRN learns a small set of coefficients that selects a noise direction within a fixed low-rank subspace, keeping the actor’s output dimension small regardless of the full noise dimension. Middle: This formulation allows LoRN to steer either action noise or video noise in world-action models. We find that steering the video noise is surprisingly expressive for denoising actions, thus LoRN enables a new way to steer a world-action model’s actions. Right: Mean final success per policy family, averaged over its tasks, for the base policy, DSRL action-noise steering, and LoRN. Video-noise steering produces large gains on the evaluated world-action models; on action policies, LoRN achieves comparable final success to DSRL while generally improving early-training success (Table 11). The DSRL bars use the same variants as Figure 6, with its full-dimensional form on Cosmos3-Edge.

Figure 7: Action-noise steering across robot policies. Learning curves of LoRN (green), DSRL (gray dashed), and LP-DS (dark gray dash-dotted) on twelve tasks: the mean over five seeds with a band of one standard deviation across seeds. Dotted horizontal lines mark base-policy success. The 𝜋0 tasks use LIBERO and ALOHA, 𝜋0.5 uses YAM, and Diffusion Policy uses Robomimic. Horizontal axes show gradient updates for 𝜋0 and environment steps for the other policies, in millions; several panels end before the full training budgets of Table 4 to show the phase in which the methods separate, so training budgets should be compared within each task. The 𝜋0 and 𝜋0.5 curves are five-evaluation running means of 10- and 16-episode evaluations; the Robomimic curves are raw 200-episode evaluations. Diffusion Policy uses full-rank LoRN (𝑟 = 𝑁 = 28).

Figure 9: LoRN enables stronger steering while maintaining the noise norm. Steering-rule comparisons on Cosmos3-Edge using a rank-32 video projection. Bars show mean success with standard errors over three training seeds; dotted lines mark base-policy success. Increasing the steering strength 𝛼 improves LoRN’s performance, whereas additive steering increases the noise norm and loses task success. The LP-DS adaptation [24] and the PSS-related control [17] retain approximately the original noise norm but yield limited gains. Here, 𝛼 caps the steering strength while 𝛽 sets the LP-DS correction’s target norm limit √ 𝛽𝑁 . The relative noise norms are measured in units of √ 𝑁 . Both use our adaptations of the published steering rules within the shared setup, rather than reproductions of the complete methods.

Figure 6: Video-noise steering improves success across world-action models. Base-policy success, DSRL action-noise steering, and LoRN action- or video-noise steering on RoboLab and LIBERO. DSRL steers all 256 action-noise entries on Cosmos3-Edge, the stronger of its two forms there (Table 7); on DreamZero-14B it tiles a 32-dimensional latent over the chunk, and on DreamZero-5B it replaces the action noise with its latent. Bars show means; error bars show standard errors over three training seeds. Base-policy references have no training-seed error bars. Labels round means to whole percentages. Video steering achieves the highest mean on nine of ten model–task pairs; DSRL performs best on DreamZero-5B Moka pot. Evaluation protocols and retained training budgets differ across models and some configurations; see the appendix.

Figure 3: LoRN steers frozen generative robot policies through a low-dimensional noise subspace. (a) High-dimensional Gaussian noise concentrates near a thin shell. We find that moving far from its typical norm can degrade the policy’s actions. (b) A fixed random orthonormal projection 𝑃 maps 𝑟 actor coefficients into the full 𝑁 -dimensional noise space, with 𝑟 ≪ 𝑁 . The plane and its intersection with the sphere illustrate the low-rank subspace. (c) Given observation 𝑜, the actor learns coefficients 𝑢 through reinforcement learning to produce noise inputs that improve the policy’s actions. The projected output 𝑃𝑢 is normalized to √ 𝑁 and mixed with an independent Gaussian sample 𝜀 at strength 𝑠, using weights that preserve the expected squared noise norm. The colors illustrate advantage relative to the base policy, implying that our low-rank subspace captures high-advantage regions for policy improvement. The projection 𝑃 and pretrained model remain fixed while the steering actor is trained. (d) This construction enables LoRN to steer video or action noise in a world-action model. Algorithm 1 provides more details about LoRN.

Success (%) on four RoboLab tasks: MustardInLeftBin (Mustard), MarkerInMug (Marker), ButterAboveRaisin (Butter), and StackYellowOnRed (Stack). The LP-DS adaptation constrains an additive offset, with 𝛽 setting its target mean squared coefficient magnitude. papers.selection_reason: Noise steering for generative robot policies; improves policy learning and transfer.
papers.title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
papers.tldr: LoRN enables scalable reinforcement-learning-based noise steering for generative robot policies, substantially improving simulated and real-world task success without changing policy weights.

papers.abstract: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.
authors: Nidhi Parayil, Benjamin Greenland, Thierry Peynot, Chris Lehnert
bullets: Addresses contact-rich agricultural tasks where foliage blocks vision and contact observations are intermittent.
Uses a tactile-conditioned diffusion policy with tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback.

papers.abstract: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.
bullets: Frozen DINO and V-JEPA feature distances poorly reflect object-to-goal distance, with rank correlation at most 0.11 versus 0.87 for object-mask centroids.
The learned representation reduces interference from background and robot-arm patches by separating object identity, spatial displacement, and dynamics.
DOCK uses forward kinematics from joint angles as annotation-free supervision for grasped-object motion.
In 21 simulated kitchen tasks, DOCK places the object in 15 tasks, matching an oracle using true object position and outperforming mask geometry (10) and frozen features (9).
Its task ranking transfers to unseen layouts, object instances, and categories, including scenes where an unseen robot arm is visible.

papers.abstract: Low-cost tactile arrays have made touch a practical input for robot learning, but piezoresistive designs sense only pressure, while camera-based sensors that also resolve shear are too bulky to tile over a gripper. To solve this problem, we present LuxTac, a flexible, scalable optical taxel array, about 3.5 mm thick and built from off-the-shelf parts. Each taxel is a digital RGBC light-to-digital converter under a translucent white silicone layer capped by an opaque black film, so the back-scattered LED light falls monotonically with local indentation depth. The same board accepts two interchangeable gel cartridges: a plain one for normal sensing, and one with colored walls that encodes the local shear in the color of the returned light, with no camera, magnets, or bump overlay, making LuxTac, to our knowledge, the first optical taxel array to resolve shear at individual taxels. Characterized with an automated CNC indenter and a six-axis force/torque sensor, the normal cartridge responds linearly to force ($R^2$ = 0.999) from 104 mN to at least 5.8 N, with 2.0% repeatability, 5.9% hysteresis, and a taxel-to-taxel variation of 6-10% after normalization. With the shear cartridge, per-taxel models estimate the three-axis force at every taxel; across three indenter shapes and nine held-out sessions, the summed estimates reach $R^2$ = 0.96/0.96/0.92 in x/y/z, each taxel's estimate 0.92/0.93/0.94, and the median shear-direction error is 4.8 degrees. Adding LuxTac pressure readings to an Action Chunking Transformer policy substantially improves peg-in-hole success over a vision-only baseline. Design files, code, and videos are available at https://luxtac.github.io.
authors: Md Rakibul Islam Prince, John Pelan, Zhiyuan Zhang, Adyaa Khera, Katherine Pesetski, Adeesh Desai, Akimizu Sugiyama, Minwoo Ki, Benjamin Alan Capelle, Temitope Ibrahim Amosa, Zijie Xu, Yihan Huang, Taehun Chung, Long Wang, Wei Li, Shaoting Lin, Yu She
bullets: Uses digital RGBC light sensors beneath interchangeable silicone gel cartridges to infer indentation and shear without cameras, magnets, or bump overlays.
The approximately 3.5-mm-thick array is flexible, scalable, and built from off-the-shelf components.
Normal-force sensing is highly linear, while per-taxel models estimate three-axis forces and shear direction across held-out sessions.
Adding LuxTac pressure sensing substantially improves peg-in-hole success for an Action Chunking Transformer over vision alone.
Design files, code, and videos are publicly available; results are demonstrated within the tested force range, cartridges, and robot-learning task.

papers.abstract: Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their applicability to lightweight, compliant objects and slow motions. Inspired by recent advances in learning physically structured dynamics with coupled oscillator networks (CONs), we propose $\Phi$-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics. The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO's shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism $\Phi$ between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates. Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy. We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence. We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup. In simulation, $\Phi$-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with $97.2\%$ and $90.2\%$ fewer parameters, respectively. Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by $97.5$-$99.7\%$ in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of $27.9\%$ across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.
authors: Iv\'an L\'opez-Broce\~no, Maximilian St\"olzle, Daniel Feliu-Talegon, Daniela Rus, Cosimo Della Santina
bullets: Targets the limitation of deformation models that ignore dynamic and mechanical effects, especially for stiff, heavy, or fast-moving objects.
Combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network with a learned affine mapping from observed DLO positions to latent coordinates.
Its Lagrangian structure provides explicit energy expressions and supports a model-based PD controller with closed-loop stability and convergence guarantees.
Across simulated and real bimanual experiments, the approach improves prediction efficiency and substantially reduces endpoint regulation error versus model-free PD control.
The evaluation covers four simulated DLOs and one real robotic setup; broader conditions beyond these experiments are not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $\pi_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.
bullets: LIBERO-trained VLA policies often fail on LIBERO-PRO when objects move or instructions change.
The method augments demonstrations by relocating and rotating objects, transferring tasks across environments and surfaces, and paraphrasing instructions.
A perception module using frozen DINOv3 features provides object positions and gripper-state information alongside TinyCLIP image and instruction embeddings.
A from-scratch flow-matching diffusion transformer predicts actions from this decoupled representation.
RageVLA achieves 0.72 on LIBERO-PRO, compared with 0.53 for the best published model; performance remains strong under object displacement tests.

papers.abstract: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum's reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board's tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum's balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem's dynamics on the other's learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy's success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.
authors: Bao Trung Truong, Dat Thanh Nguyen, Thinh T. Doan
bullets: Studies learning and control when two dynamical subsystems disturb each other.
Combines an actively tilted, steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum.
Uses model-based reinforcement learning for the maze and model-free reinforcement learning for the pendulum.
Adding the pendulum sharply reduces maze success initially, but online adaptation restores pre-coupling performance within a few episodes.
Both independently trained policies successfully control their respective systems despite the coupling.

The two subsystems are physically coupled through the shared board, with the pendulum acting as a disturbance on the maze policy.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.
authors: Xuanwei Liu, Guipu Cao, Zhongyi Luo, Jiafei Duan
bullets: Existing tokenizers concatenate both arms’ actions, leaving shared motions and cross-arm dependencies for the policy to learn implicitly.
BiCAT uses a shared motion representation, symmetric cross-arm attention, and a joint decoder to condition each arm on its partner.
It predicts each arm’s tokens in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it.
Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among compared tokenizers.
It improves simulated mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with 40.5 ms per action chunk; gains are largest for tightly coordinated tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. We propose GRID, which combines both: (1) it lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV's frame for both cameras, and (2) during training only, it aligns its visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model, at no inference cost. GRID adding explicit lifting to implicit alignment significantly increases how often the policy reaches the target ($61.5\% \rightarrow 69.5\%$, $p<0.001$), and adding implicit alignment to explicit lifting significantly increases how often it completes the task once there ($57.7\% \rightarrow 61.4\%$, $p<0.05$). On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects) and 25.4% (unseen map).
authors: Anas Anwarul Haq Khan, Amrin Kareem, Muhammad Umer Sheikh, Biplab Banerjee, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Problem: 2D visual encoders and unreliable monocular depth struggle with long-range distances, altitude selection, and coordinating forward/downward views.
Method: Lift depth from both cameras into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV frame, while aligning visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model during training.
The two components address complementary failure modes: explicit 3D lifting reduces collisions, while implicit geometry alignment improves target completion.
GRID raises target-reaching from 61.5% to 69.5% and task completion after reaching the target from 57.7% to 61.4%, with reported statistical significance.
On TravelUAV, GRID achieves the best success rate across all splits, with relative gains of 9.5%–25.4% over the prior state of the art.

papers.abstract: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.
authors: Nikhil X. Bhattasali, Jaron Cui, Lerrel Pinto, Grace W. Lindsay
bullets: Introduces Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical rat body for embodied simulation.
Develops Rat NCAP, a mammalian spinal-circuit-inspired architecture with cell-type-specific connectivity and a flexor–extensor neuromechanical interface.
Uses GPU-accelerated simulation and training to optimize circuit parameters without imitation learning.
The model learns multiple locomotion speeds and gait transitions, with behavior, kinematics, and neural activity consistent with experiments.
Cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict responses to graded perturbations; interface design strongly affects trainability and gait quality.

papers.abstract: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.
bullets: Taylor reachability is limited by complex-plane singularities, especially in rational terms and sigmoid-like controller gates.
The proposed Chebyshev abstraction uses the full reachable set and avoids Taylor’s degree-dependent width cap, improving geometrically with polynomial degree.
The work derives closed-form rigorous remainders, including the first polynomial softmax-transformer abstraction.
In closed-loop systems and MNIST classifiers, Chebyshev certificates remain valid in cases where Taylor certificates diverge or become unknown.
Measured width limits agree with theory to 89–94%, and certified claims passed Monte Carlo checks with zero observed violations.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.
bullets: Pixel-level future generation contains many visually plausible but planning-irrelevant details.
The model represents each surrounding agent with discrete tokens encoding identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context.
Agent tokens are learned through geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning.
Open- and closed-loop experiments across diverse driving scenarios show stronger planning, better use of visual and dynamic information, and interpretable world states.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AgentWorld. Given multi-view observations, ego-status, navigation goals, and language prompts, AgentWorld constructs an agent-centric world state by grounding discrete agent tokens with 4D geometry and 2D visual features through multimodal routed anchoring. The grounded agent tokens are then used by the policy model for reasoning, action, and planning through grounding, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning stages.
Figure 4: The pipeline of the multimodal routed anchoring. Agent queries are routed to geometry and vision branches, and fused through cross-attention to produce grounded agent tokens.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison between VLA-World [30] and AgentWorld. For each scene, the left panels visualize the future ego trajectories of VLA-World (top) and AgentWorld (bottom), with AgentWorld additionally showing the traffic participants aligned with the special tokens ⟨agent_i⟩. The right panels present the corresponding perception, reasoning, and planning results.

Figure 1: (a) VLA models output actions from observations and prompts, lacking explicit spatiotemporal modeling and interaction awareness. (b) World models learn predictive latent futures, yet their imagined states fail to align with causal reasoning. (c) VLA World models integrate imagination and language reasoning, but reason over generated frames rather than interactive agents for driving decisions. (d) By contrast, AgentWorld models futures via discrete latent agent states, enabling VLA reasoning over physically grounded 3D geometry, motion dynamics and agent interactions.
Figure 2: Visual grounding results (UniAD metric) and token efficiency of VLA models.
Figure 8: Prompt design for reasoning with agent data generation.

Figure 11: Visualization of trajectories across VLA-World and our AgentWorld on the nuScenes validation dataset. The predicted and ground-truth trajectories are depicted in red and green, respectively.

Figure 7: Example of the Stage-1 agent grounding QA template. Given multi-view driving observations and a grounding instruction, AgentWorld outputs a fixed set of <agent_i> tokens inside the <perception> field. These tokens act as latent agent slots: active slots are supervised to align with physical traffic participants through 3D box and future trajectory targets, while unused slots are trained as no-object.

Figure 9: Example of the Stage-2 reasoning-oriented SFT template. Given multi-view driving observations, ego-state instructions, and the fixed <agent_i> slots in the <perception> field, AgentWorld learns to generate a structured response consisting of concise agent-grounded reasoning in <think>, a high-level driving command in <action>, and future ego waypoints in <answer>. The rationale explicitly references decision-relevant agent tokens, encouraging the policy to plan based on surrounding-agent interactions rather than shortcut cues.

papers.abstract: Ensuring the safety of complex neural network systems requires mathematically rigorous verification. While backward reachability analysis is a critical tool for identifying safe initial states, computing tight, formal bounds remains notoriously difficult to scale. Recent advancements have demonstrated that DeepBern-Nets neural networks utilizing Bernstein polynomial activation functions possess advantageous mathematical properties that enable exceptionally fast and tight forward reachability analysis. Building upon this efficiency, this paper introduces BernBRS, a highly accurate and scalable framework for the backward reachability analysis of DeepBern-Nets. BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS). Rather than relying on single convex bounding, our method intelligently refines a cover of the input space by analyzing activation patterns, splitting the input domain precisely where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the most significant reduction in error. This targeted refinement enables high levels of scalability to highly complex and massive architectures that remain intractable for existing certified methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on high-dimensional models, including a linearized closed-loop approximation of the Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block and we empirically study how these model-level guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier, respectively.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of formally identifying safe initial states through scalable backward reachability analysis.
Refines an input-space cover by analyzing activation patterns and splitting where the relaxation gap is predicted to be largest.
Produces certified inner and outer approximations rather than relying on a single convex bound.
Evaluated on high-dimensional models, including a linearized Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein Transformer block.
Also examines how model-level reachability guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT systems.

papers.abstract: Quadratic programs (QPs) are fundamental building blocks of many robotic tasks such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control. Extending these methods to large-scale robot learning and control requires solving many QPs concurrently and, for end-to-end learning, differentiating through their solutions. Efficient batched optimization is therefore essential to bringing established model-based methods into GPU-based robotics pipelines. We present \textsc{cuPIQP}, a batched and differentiable QP solver on GPUs based on a proximal interior-point method, with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage problems. The solver exploits parallelism across independent QPs and their internal structure while preserving per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions. Benchmarks with up to 16384 QPs per batch demonstrate solve-time speedups of up to $18.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau} and $4.26\times$ over eight-core \textsc{PIQP}. In an end-to-end learning task, \textsc{cuPIQP} accelerates training by $4.6\times$ over \textsc{QPAX} and $7.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau}. By reducing the computational cost, \textsc{cuPIQP} provides efficient, reusable infrastructure for integrating model-based optimization into large-scale robot learning and control.
bullets: Targets the need to solve and differentiate through many QPs concurrently in robotics applications such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control.
Uses a proximal interior-point method with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage QPs.
Exploits GPU parallelism across QPs and within their internal structure while retaining per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions.
In benchmarks with batches of up to 16,384 QPs, it achieves solve-time speedups of up to 18.8× over Moreau and 4.26× over eight-core PIQP.
Accelerates end-to-end learning by 4.6× over QPAX and 7.8× over Moreau.

papers.abstract: While velocity-commanded RL policies are effective for controlling quadrupeds, they are a limited interface for humanoids that need to perform complex whole-body motions. Furthermore, RL tracking policies for whole-body motions typically have limited information about the desired future motion, preventing them from performing controlled deviations to achieve long-term task success; such information is particularly relevant when a controller must prepare for transitions between behaviors. We address these challenges using concise motion representations that can be generated by a high-level controller, given a behavior label or text command. These representations can be fed directly into a tracking policy to provide a detailed motion reference. Our method exhibits a high degree of flexibility in performing real-world robot motions such as dancing, fighting, or walking based on conditional information. At matched capacity, our adopted stochastic motion tokenizer reconstructs motions from the Unitree G1 at a level that exceeds state-of-the-art approaches such as finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and the vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-VAE). The resulting discrete interface conditions whole-body tracking policies that execute generated dance, fight, and walk motions lasting 16.8 s each and a 35 s fight-to-dance sequence on a physical Unitree G1.
bullets: Velocity commands and short-horizon tracking references are insufficient for complex humanoid motions and behavior transitions.
The method tokenizes whole-body motion into concise discrete representations generated from behavior labels or text commands.
These tokens condition a tracking policy with detailed future motion information.
On a physical Unitree G1, the system executed 16.8-second dance, fight, and walk motions, plus a 35-second fight-to-dance sequence.
At matched capacity, motion reconstruction exceeded FSQ and VQ-VAE baselines.

papers.abstract: WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) enables fine-grained sensing of spatial relationships between wireless devices. The WiFi Sensor for Robotics (WSR) toolbox demonstrated that WiFi-CSI measurements collected during robot motion, combined with odometry, can be used to synthesize virtual antenna arrays, enabling motion-induced bearing estimation in multi-robot experiments. However, deploying the WSR approach has remained challenging due to its limited integration with standard robotics tools and reliance on deprecated WiFi-CSI acquisition hardware. This work presents an open-source simulation framework that integrates the WSR sensing pipeline within the robotic simulator Gazebo. The framework generates synthetic WiFi-CSI measurements with realistic physical signal properties and leverages realistic robot motion required for motion-induced sensing and downstream localization. It further supports processing both simulated and real WiFi-CSI data for direct comparison and validation. Our aim is to make WSR-style sensing accessible as a modular sensing modality for robotic research. We validate our framework by comparing simulated and real-world experiments using TurtleBot3 robots, and demonstrate its use for bearing estimation and robot localization. This work lowers the barrier to entry for WiFi-CSI-based sensing in multi-robot systems and provides a foundation for integrating WiFi-CSI sensing with multi-modal perception for localization and coordination. All code and experimental details are publicly available at https://github.com/baharhaghighat/DARS_2026_Dijkstra_et_al
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of using WSR sensing due to limited robotics-tool integration and deprecated CSI hardware.
Integrates the WSR pipeline into Gazebo with synthetic CSI based on realistic signal properties and robot motion.
Processes both simulated and real WiFi-CSI data to support direct comparison and validation.
Validated with TurtleBot3 experiments for bearing estimation and robot localization.
Provides a modular foundation for WiFi-CSI-based multi-robot perception, localization, and coordination.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking policies predict future controls but execute only a prefix before replanning. How should a fixed action-token budget be organized to support execution? We propose LeapBot-JAC, which allocates sparse future-control references and dense execution targets within one shared action expert. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and jointly denoised at aligned physical-time positions. Directed attention allows execution tokens to read reference tokens subject to the host's visibility constraints. JAC adds neither action tokens nor parameters and retains the host's world-modeling process; both chains participate in inference, while only the execution chain drives the robot. On LIBERO, JAC reaches 98.3% success with FastWAM and LeapBot-WA, up from 97.0% and 97.3%. On zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, their success rates improve from 53.5% to 70.4% and from 73.1% to 77.3%, respectively. RoboTwin and two real-world tasks provide additional deployment evaluations. Single-training-seed comparisons and FastWAM ablations support action-role organization as a practical design choice under a fixed action-token budget.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between predicting long action chunks and executing only a prefix before replanning.
Uses one shared action expert to jointly denoise sparse future-control references and dense execution targets at aligned physical times.
Directed attention lets execution tokens use reference tokens while respecting visibility constraints.
Adds no action tokens or parameters and preserves the host world-modeling process; only the execution chain controls the robot.
Improves LIBERO success to 98.3% and zero-shot LIBERO-Plus success to 70.4% for FastWAM, with additional RoboTwin and real-world evaluations.

papers.abstract: Stereo vision is increasingly used for robotic manipulation, with a growing body of work incorporating it into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, the scarcity of large-scale, real-world stereo datasets remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling such policies. Recent generative monocular-to-stereo methods target settings such as VR content and autonomous driving. No prior work produces realistic synthetic stereo data for robotic manipulation, where stereo supervision has come predominantly from simulation. We propose StereoEngine, which introduces two complementary methods to synthesize stereo data for robotic manipulation. In the first, we warp a monocular (left) video into the right view using estimated depth and inpaint the disoccluded regions with a video diffusion model, lifting monocular demonstrations into stereo pairs without training on real stereo. In the second, we render a stereo pair in simulation and jointly generate both photorealistic views, producing consistent left-right data without any real video as input. StereoEngine outperforms existing baselines in generated stereo quality, and using its synthetic data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves downstream bimanual manipulation. Project website: https://stereoengine.github.io
bullets: Addresses the shortage of large-scale real-world stereo datasets for vision-language-action manipulation models.
Warps monocular left-view video into a right view using estimated depth and video-diffusion inpainting for disocclusions.
Alternatively, jointly renders photorealistic, left-right-consistent stereo views from simulation.
Produces higher-quality synthetic stereo data than existing baselines, according to the abstract.
Using the generated data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves bimanual manipulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Method Overview. StereoEngine-L applies when a ground-truth left video is available. The warping module (1) moves every left pixel to its position in the right view, giving a warped right video and a mask marking the pixels no left pixel could reach. A video diffusion model (2) fills the masked region from these and a language prompt ℓ, giving a right video (3) that pairs with the original left. StereoEngine-S applies when no real video exists. We render (1) the episode in simulation from two cameras, convert both renders to Canny edges, and (2) pass the edge videos to the model with two reference images and the instruction ℓ. The edge map defines the scene geometry, while the reference images supply the appearance of the real workspace such as background, lighting, and surface texture. Then (3) a video generation model generates the synthetic video. In both methods, the resulting stereo pairs can be used to train a downstream bimanual stereo-conditioned policy.

Fig. 4: Real-world rollouts. Each row shows a successful policy rollout by ExStereo [24] trained on StereoEngine data, from top to bottom: Stack Two Bowls, Lift Transparent Bottles, Close Door, Lift Two Bottles, and Container Plate. Both StereoEngine methods test Stack Two Bowls, while the other four tasks are tested on one of our methods. Columns show the progression of time (left to right).

Fig. 3: Warping Module. (1) the ground truth left view is abstracted into a grid of pixels, where A to N label the background and O1 to O4 label the object, and each pixel is given the disparity it must move by, d = 4 for the object and d = 1 for the background. (2) every pixel moves left by its own disparity, since the camera translates right. The object moves further and covers C,D,E, and the nearer pixel is kept, so only B survives. (3) the background G,H, I was hidden behind the object and never observed, so nothing can fill the gap it leaves and those columns become the mask. (4) the rest of the background shifts left by one, leaving the right border without any source. (5) the grid is mapped back to pixels to give the warped right view, correct where a pixel arrived and empty where the left camera never saw the surface.

Fig. 5: Synthetic episode generation. The top three rows show synthetic episodes generated by StereoEngine-S, one per task, from top to bottom: Stack Two Bowls, Lift Two Bottles, and Container Plate. Below the dashed line, the last row (Fold Clothes) shows a largescale data generation example from StereoEngine-L, where a real monocular demonstration is lifted into stereo. papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors provide rich contact information, but processing high-resolution images can be costly for resource-constrained platforms such as space robots. This work investigates whether a compact representation of tactile motion can classify object rotation across different gravity conditions. Dense optical flow from a simulated GelSight Mini is aggregated over a 7x9 grid into 126 features and used to classify the direction of load-induced rotation under Earth, Mars, Moon, and orbital gravity. Gravity causes a small but significant shift in these features, accounting for 1.6% of their variance (R2 = 0.016). Despite its small magnitude, this shift affects models trained only on Earth data: XGBoost accuracy decreases from 94.4% on Earth to 75.9% in orbit. In contrast, a single model trained across all four gravity domains achieves 96.3% overall accuracy and 95.1%-97.0% across individual domains, without using gravity as an input. The representation can also be reduced to 40 features while retaining 95.7% accuracy, with XGBoost requiring only 0.14 ms per inference. These findings show that Earth-gravity performance alone is insufficient to establish the transferability of tactile perception for space robotic manipulation, highlighting the need to account for gravity-induced domain shifts during training and validation.
bullets: Dense optical flow from a simulated GelSight Mini is aggregated into a 7×9 grid, producing 126 features.
Gravity shifts the representation slightly (1.6% of variance), yet Earth-only training drops orbital accuracy from 94.4% to 75.9%.
Training one model across all four gravity domains achieves 96.3% overall accuracy, with 95.1%–97.0% accuracy per domain.
The representation can be reduced to 40 features while retaining 95.7% accuracy; XGBoost inference takes 0.14 ms.
Earth-gravity performance alone does not establish reliable transfer to space; gravity-induced domain shifts must be included in training and validation.

papers.title: A Minimal Optical-Flow Representation for Vision-Based Tactile Rotation Classification in Robotic Manipulation Across Gravity Domains

papers.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.
authors: Pranav Gupta, Deepan Muthirayan, Ravi Banavar
bullets: Addresses prediction errors in DDPC caused by nonlinear manipulator dynamics.
Uses a mechanical model to map virtual accelerations to torques, with recorded data capturing residual dynamics.
Robustly optimises prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball around the fitted trajectory subspace.
In planar 2R simulations, it tracks better than double-integrator MPC but requires greater torque effort.
Performance compared with direct regularised DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.

papers.abstract: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.
bullets: Studies trajectory prediction from V2X-like histories sampled at 10, 5, 2, and 1 Hz.
Uses an LSTM RNN with only focal-agent history, without maps or neighboring agents, and compares it with CV and CA models.
The frequency-specific RNN’s error increased as sampling dropped, by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz.
Its advantage over the better kinematic model remained 24–30% for straight motion and turns at every frequency; for pedestrians, CV was more accurate.
A 10 Hz-trained model with interpolation nearly matched frequency-specific training down to 2 Hz but was 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz; hypotheses were only partly supported.

papers.abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of symbolic recognizers and methods requiring hard-to-transfer dynamics models.
Learns a trajectory prior and runs a warm-started denoising process for each candidate goal.
Steers samples toward observed motion using a closed-form likelihood gradient, then applies Bayes’ rule to estimate goal posteriors.
Evaluated on simulated robots, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories with four metrics covering distinct failure modes.
Preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs during ambiguous trajectory prefixes, unlike filter- and classifier-based observers that may collapse or become overconfident.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Four metric trade-offs across the five evaluation domains. Each panel scatters one point per (method, domain) for the six methods over the five domains. Colour identifies the method; marker shape identifies the domain (legend below). WORD points carry a thicker outline. The desirable corner is bottom-right in every panel; panel (d) reverses the x-axis so lower Brier still points right.

Figure 2: WORD online inference on a 2-goal synthetic scenario. An agent (green) starts at the bottom of a 10× 10 world and must reach one of two goals separated by a circular obstacle; WORD maintains one denoising chain per candidate goal and updates a posterior as observations arrive. (a) Prior. Before any observation, the score network ϵθ shapes Gaussian noise into two obstacle-aware trajectory clusters, one towards each waypoint, and the goal prior is uniform. (b) Ambiguity. The agent has skirted the lower edge of the obstacle but its heading is still consistent with both goals; both clusters survive and the posterior remains nearly balanced. A filtering baseline would already have collapsed onto one mode here. (c) Observation guidance. Once the agent commits left of the obstacle, the score-guidance term ∇τ log p(Z | τ ) (orange) pins each chain to the observed path; the right cluster must arc awkwardly over the obstacle to remain reachable, and posterior mass shifts toward w1. (d) Commitment. As the agent approaches w1, the surviving chain dominates and the posterior collapses. Pseudocode is in algorithm 1.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.
authors: Haosong Peng, Xiangyang Liu, Zhengshen Zhang, Yunfeng Fan, Tianyu Qi, Xin Xia, Yufeng Zhan, Wenchao Xu
bullets: Recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3), gripper states, scene geometry, and camera parameters from RGB videos with initial 2D TCP queries.
Uses a shared 4D scene representation for both tracking observed motion and generating future TCP trajectories conditioned on robot observations and language.
Introduces cross-embodiment augmentation by retargeting recovered motions and synthesizing observations without source-robot state recordings.
Reports 7.60 mm and 16.07 mm absolute trajectory errors on DROID and RoboLab, respectively, and 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin.
Joint training with source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

papers.abstract: Model-based quadruped controllers usually step on a cyclic gait, which lifts the legs in a fixed order on a fixed period, wherever the safe footholds are. We present CADENCE, a learned step planner with a small action space. Every 40 ms, it picks one of at most 65 discrete choices: no step, or one leg's step to a safe foothold. It also predicts a swing time. We train CADENCE by reinforcement learning on top of a convex model predictive controller (MPC). Nothing prescribes a gait: there is no gait schedule, and the reward has no gait term, only a cost per step. The one structural constraint is that at most two legs may swing at once. The policy we analyzed developed an acyclic gait, with no fixed period or stepping order, yet it still paired diagonal legs. An inverse footstep model (IFM), fitted on a controller's logged steps, turns each foothold into a command. With only the IFM refitted, on fewer than 20,000 steps, CADENCE ran frozen on OCS2's nonlinear MPC. In simulated trials on a range of terrains (26% to 49% voids) and speeds (0.1 m/s and 0.2 m/s), it succeeded in 85.1% (mean of five seeds), against 67.8% for OCS2-Trot, 65.5% for OCS2-Single, and 39.6% in a static walk ablation of CADENCE. At 49% voids, it succeeded in 72.9%, against 43.0% for OCS2-Trot.
authors: Owen Sullivan, Sourav Selvaraj, Mahdi Agheli
bullets: Replaces fixed-period cyclic gaits with per-step decisions over at most 65 actions, including no step or stepping one leg to a safe foothold.
Uses reinforcement learning on top of a convex MPC, predicting both the selected foothold and swing time.

Across simulated terrains and speeds, CADENCE achieved 85.1% mean success, including 72.9% on terrains with 49% voids.

papers.abstract: Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success. In this work, we take a more principled perspective by studying when and how transferring knowledge between MDPs (a source and a target) can be provably beneficial. Specifically, we consider the case where there exists an undo map such that applying this map to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. We propose an algorithm that learns this map by matching state feature statistics gathered from both MDPs, and then uses it to transfer the source policy to the target. We theoretically justify the algorithm by analyzing the setting when the undo map is linear and the source is linearly-$Q^\star$ realizable, where our approach has strictly better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL in the target MDP. Empirically, we demonstrate that these benefits extend beyond this regime: on challenging continuous control tasks and Atari games, our method achieves significantly better sample efficiency. Overall, our results highlight how shared structure between tasks can be leveraged for efficient transfer of policies across environments.
authors: Mridul Mahajan, Aldo Pacchiano, Xuezhou Zhang
bullets: Studies when transfer between source and target MDPs is provably beneficial under an exact state-space undo map.

papers.abstract: Household robots often need to operate appliances, and smart appliances offer both control panels and device APIs. Existing embodied AI simulation environments, however, model appliances solely as physical objects. We introduce PAIR, a smart-home simulation environment grounded in the Matter protocol~\footnote{https://csa-iot.org/all-solutions/matter/}, the industry standard for smart-home devices. PAIR provides 84 smart-device assets whose functional control panels and APIs act on a shared device state, with ambient conditions that evolve in response to both. From a survey of 1,443 requests, we construct a benchmark of 40 tasks that all require object manipulation yet remain solvable without API access, with 340 human demonstrations for policy training. Whether run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner, two fine-tuned VLA policies complete none of the 120 evaluation episodes. Robots rarely get far enough to use the API: even with oracle plans and API access, over 90\% of failed rollouts stall at navigating, grasping, or operating a door. With a perfect oracle in place of the robot's body, the best planner still gets through only 57.3\% of its plan. When choosing between pressing a button and calling an API, several planners go by whether they can read the panel, not by API latency.\footnote{We will release our code and data upon publication.}
authors: Junseong Pyo, Hyeongjin Kim, Jongwook Han, Seungwon Kook, Sungjib Lim, Yohan Jo

papers.abstract: Large-scale robotic simulation requires diverse deformable objects with executable physical properties and realistic interaction behaviors. However, existing 3D asset collections primarily emphasize visual diversity, while scalable physical construction and verification remain challenging. We introduce RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified assets spanning 485 everyday categories across five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of independent verification and characterize deformable responses under different physical configurations. We further evaluate robotic grasping in terms of both task success and object integrity, and demonstrate the physical realism of our simulated objects through sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation. RFW-S provides a scalable foundation for physically grounded simulation and embodied robotic learning.
authors: Jiarui Guo, Saining Zhang, Jiaying Wan, Jiawei Weng, Junhao Chen, Rui Zhang, Yuanbo Lyu, Zhiheng Lee, Peishuo Li, Jingrun Du, Weiqing Xiao, Weiyi Lin, Zenan Meng, Hu Wei, Lin Qu, Zongzheng Zhang, Hao Zhao, Chaojian Li
bullets: Contains 83,365 assets across 485 categories and five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags.
Combines reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration.
Uses independent simulation verification with interaction conditions distinct from calibration to assess physical reliability.
Evaluates deformable responses, robotic grasping with object integrity, and sim-to-real replay for fragile-object manipulation.
Provides a scalable foundation for embodied robotic learning with physically realistic deformable objects.

papers.abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.
authors: Hoang Pham Cong, Long D. Nguyen, Ho Viet Duc Luong, Nguyen Tran Minh Nhat, Binh P. Nguyen
bullets: Targets decision-relevant missed objects rather than relying only on image cues or uniformly increasing resolution.
Builds a decision-sensitivity field by testing how hypothetical objects at different locations would affect the planner’s draft action.
Repeatedly verifies the sensitivity field and the detections supporting the current action until the action stabilizes.
For two planner classes, it is theoretically equivalent to whole-frame high-resolution perception when crop detections and coverage conditions hold.

Across three driving datasets, it matches the full-resolution action on about 98% of frames using about one-quarter of the pixels, while reducing false braking and recovering more relevant missed objects.
