papers.abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.
authors: Rapha\"el S\'egas, Bal\'azs Opra, L\'eo Ghafari, Thomas Stewart
bullets: A 13-node lumped RC thermal model predicts all 12 motor temperatures across robots, gaits, payloads, and speeds with mean RMSE below 1°C.
The policy minimizes predicted long-term motor-temperature asymptotes based on gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds.
This bypasses slow thermal dynamics: asymptotes respond within one gait cycle, enabling reinforcement-learning credit assignment without temperature input.
On a Unitree Go2 carrying 5 kg at 1 m/s, runtime increased from 19 to 174 minutes, while distance increased from 1.1 to 10.0 km.
On an unloaded circuit with stairs and ramps, the policy completed 47 laps versus 25 for the baseline, retaining 22°C of thermal margin.

papers.abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.
authors: Daehee Lee, Dongsu Lee, Sanghyun Ahn, Minjong Yoo, Honguk Woo

papers.abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.
authors: Guochen Zhou, Yijun Yang, Qiqi Duan, Qing Su, Weiming Ou, Li Shen, Shihao Ji, Yuhui Shi, Zhisong Zhang
bullets: Offline-to-online distribution shifts make it difficult to choose a fixed optimism–pessimism balance.
Optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, while pessimistic policies perform better on familiar online tasks.
The method formulates the trade-off as a bi-objective problem and constructs a Pareto policy pool with MOSAIC.
A hierarchical contextual bandit selects the most suitable policy during online fine-tuning.
HiP3 achieves the strongest aggregate performance across same and novel tasks, including under stronger distribution shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3). In the offline stage (gray box), our MOSAIC algorithm generates a diverse pool of Pareto policies exhibiting varying optimism-pessimism trade-offs via multi-objective optimization with reference vectors and neighborhood search. In the online stage (blue box), a contextual bandit (LinUCB [33]) selects a candidate policy conditioned on the current state from the top-K subset; the selected policy is then fine-tuned via a Dyna-style method [15].

Figure 1: (a) Pareto policy pool discovered by HiP3, containing policies with different optimism-pessimism trade-offs. P1 maximizes model-predicted return (most optimistic), P4 minimizes uncertainty (most pessimistic), while P2 and P3 represent balanced trade-offs. (b) On the novel online task (details in Appendix C.1), optimistic P1 achieves the highest return. (c) On the same online task, pessimistic P4 achieves the highest return. Together, these results motivate preserving multiple trade-off policies offline and deferring the choice among them to online adaptation, rather than committing to a single trade-off in advance.

papers.abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.
authors: Zhekai Wang, Luqing Luo, Wenhao Yao, Junjie Lu, Huanan Zhu, Feifei Gao, Yuhua Jiang
bullets: Targets border misses, occlusion errors, and temporal jitter in egocentric 3D hand pose estimation.
Alternates coding-agent refinement of an executable inference harness with selective distillation into the video estimator.
Accepts refinements only when they improve all ten benchmark metrics without significant regression.
Reduces MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC, while roughly halving jitter.
Provides Lite, Medium, and Heavy accuracy-speed variants; code, evaluators, harnesses, and weights are public.

papers.abstract: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.
authors: Kailin Wang, Haoxiang Jie, Yaoyuan Yan, Zhiyou Heng, Zhaosong Li
bullets: EgoHandWAM predicts future wrist/fingertip trajectories and visual features from current images and recent hand states.
On held-out EgoDex sessions, action-only forecasting improves two-second wrist endpoint error over a stationary baseline, but underestimates long reaches.
Future-feature supervision leaves trajectory accuracy nearly unchanged.
Recorded hand history improves visual-feature prediction; shuffling histories removes the gain, indicating session-specific temporal information.
Observed future displacements and tracking-validity masks help in a four-task probe, while predicted trajectories and human examples do not consistently improve RoboTwin success.

papers.abstract: HandUMI captures robot-free bimanual demonstrations with a hand-worn parallel-jaw interface. Swappable fingertips match the robot's installed gripper; Quest/PICO controllers track hands and encoders measure aperture. Robot-agnostic recordings are retargeted by inverse kinematics to seven simulated bimanual arms (median position error $\leq 1.2$ mm; $\leq 4.7$% of episodes rejected). On bimanual towel folding, 562 robot-free demonstrations train policies on real PiPER arms: ACT succeeds in 12/20 attempts and fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ in 7/20; ACT on the first 101 and base $\pi_{0.5}$ each succeed in 0/20. Hardware and software are open source (Apache-2.0), and a pair costs USD 557 with Quest 3S, excluding the optional ZED Mini and host computer. Project website: https://murobotics.ai/research/handumi.

From 562 towel-folding demonstrations, ACT succeeded in 12/20 real-robot attempts and fine-tuned π₀.₅ in 7/20.
A pair costs USD 557 with Quest 3S; hardware and software are open source under Apache-2.0.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.
authors: Changxuan Fan, Zhongwei Xie, Boyi Zhang, Shaoli Hu, Chang Xu, Xiyu Ren, Yufei Li, Qiao Xiao, Huihao Jing, Kawai Chung, Wenbin Hu, Hongyu Luo, Lingyun Xie, Yisen Gao, Chunyang Li, Haoyu Huang, Wuganjing Song, Yuxuan Liu, Chiu Yeung Tang, Fangneng Zhan, Xi Yang
bullets: Introduces 36 simulated tasks requiring teams of robot arms to coordinate on extended jobs, such as passing timbers and assembling cube pictures.
Agents must act from camera images alone while the environment continues running, without ground-truth object positions.
The adaptive system completes 28 tasks with gpt-6.1-sol and 27 with opus-5.5; four other models complete at most 3.
Adaptive, single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized systems achieve similar task counts but trade off speed and token use.
No evaluated model or control system is simultaneously fast, inexpensive, and reliable; retries are common and tasks can take hours.

papers.abstract: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.
authors: Joel Sadler, Daniel Graham, Melanie Worley
bullets: Addresses the need for accessible, automated monitoring of fruit-fly lifecycle transitions that are often recorded manually.
Uses a single-board Linux computer, day/night camera, deterministic image capture every ten minutes, and a cloud-based coding agent operating through the device.
The agent helps configure capture, repair software errors, monitor experiments, and notify researchers when recording stops.
A 26-day pilot produced about 3,580 frames; capture continued during 11 days of agent logout, while a 51-hour outage informed the layered system design.
Pupariation curves were generated through a researcher-in-the-loop workflow; accuracy validation and real-time computer vision remain future work.

figures.caption: Figure 2: System composition. The solid path (camera, capture service, storage) is conventional software and needs neither the agent, the network, nor the cloud. The dashed elements are the agent. The harness runs on the board, the model runs in the cloud, and the agent’s job is to write, maintain, and check the software around the capture path.

Figure 1: Pupavision in three steps. (1a) Build the instrument: a single-board Linux computer with a day/night camera. The agent harness runs on the board. (1b) Place it on a shelf in a temperature-controlled incubator, facing the vials. (2) Capture: the vials are imaged every ten minutes, and the pupae the researcher selects are tracked in the browser interface. (3) After eclosion, the adult flies that emerge can be imaged and analyzed with computer vision for assisted phenotyping, shown here with a segmentation model measuring a wing.

It wakes on a daily health check or a message from the researcher, looks, and either repairs something or reports. Loop C receives check-ins from loop A and alerts the researcher when they stop, because neither A nor B can announce its own failure.

papers.title: Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions

papers.abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).
authors: Hang Zhang, Qijian Tian, Yuan Xie, Xuhong Wang, Xin Tan
bullets: Motivation: LEGO generation must ensure physical support and prevent bricks from being blocked during construction.
Method: A versioned construction SDK compiles decisions from semantic subparts to individual bricks into canonical building operations.
Verification: A Meta-Reviewer replays the generated model and construction process, diagnoses failures, and routes bounded repairs.
Contribution: The system produces models and instructions suitable for both human builders and robot assembly.
Results: Experiments report better performance than recent agentic systems and demonstrate downstream robot-manipulation utility.

papers.abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.
authors: Lihao Zheng, Ying Wu, Chen Jiang, Randy Freeman
bullets: Addresses the limitation of binary safety constraints in safety-critical navigation.
Estimates kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal risks for objects and people.
Combines risk factors into continuous object-level risk scores.
Uses a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as an online safety filter.
Demonstrated in a simulated restaurant scene; broader real-world performance is not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.
authors: R. Gnana Praveen, Ali Rouzbayani, Zhiying Jiang, Bidhan Roy

At deployment, removes the auxiliary latent-action and world-model branches so the VLM directly predicts robot actions.
Achieves 97.9% on LIBERO, 70.0% on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations, and ranks second on both LARY metrics among compared methods.

papers.abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.
bullets: Addresses adapting automatic tractor guidance when the machine or steering actuator changes, without gradient descent or an optimiser.

The generated controllers were sparse and classically cascaded, and all operated the real tractor without intervention with errors comparable in order to pure pursuit.

papers.abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.
authors: Javad Amirian, Armin Kiani, Lo\"ic Schaeffer, Tim Sprecher, Mohamed Taha, Karthik Yadati
bullets: Addresses the limited environmental and object diversity of imitation-learning data and the scarcity of skilled work in existing egocentric video.

Provides 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0.
Measures dataset diversity and discusses collection, curation, privacy, data formats, and properties linked to policy performance; benchmarks are deferred to later releases.

papers.abstract: We use neural networks to optimize trajectories by modeling the position as a function of time and minimizing the thrust with respect to the network parameters. This corresponds to an unsupervised training procedure in which physical laws are incorporated directly into the optimization objective. In standard physics-informed neural networks, initial and terminal states are enforced through additional weighted loss terms, resulting in a multi-objective optimization problem that is highly sensitive to the choice of loss weights and can lead to poor convergence and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we construct a simple transformation, exploiting the mathematical structure of trajectory optimization problems, to enforce boundary conditions exactly a-priori. This transformation can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the solution space that embeds the boundary conditions directly into the function. This converts the original constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over admissible trajectories. I.e. the transformation eliminates the boundary condition penalty terms and reduces the problem to a single-objective optimization. Crucially, trajectory optimization comes with a low-dimensional boundary, which allows particularly simple and stable constructions of distance functions compared to general domains in partial differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach meaningfully improves convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
authors: Samuel Sch\"onherr, G\"unther Waxenegger-Wilfing, Sascha Ranftl
bullets: Standard PINNs enforce initial and terminal states with weighted penalties, making training sensitive to loss-weight choices.
The method embeds boundary conditions directly into the trajectory representation through a simple transformation.
This converts constrained, multi-objective training into unconstrained single-objective thrust minimization over admissible trajectories.
Numerical experiments show improved convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
The approach leverages the low-dimensional boundary structure of trajectory optimization problems.

papers.abstract: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, can reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system. In online linear quadratic control, certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret when the optimal controller is identifiable from data collected under optimal feedback. With a positive definite input penalty, however, this condition is restrictive, since for an invertible state matrix it requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback. We show that singular input penalties relax this requirement, expanding the class of problems in which certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret. Specifically, we prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves $O(\log^2 T)$ expected regret over $T$ interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. We complement this guarantee with an $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ minimax lower bound for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails. For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker requirement than knowing the full input matrix, as assumed in prior work with positive definite input penalties. This condition also covers underactuated systems, as we illustrate with a cart-pole example.
authors: Luca Vignola, Melanie Zeilinger, Bruce D. Lee
bullets: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system.

papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.
authors: Katharina Winter, William Engel, Zain A. Alishammat, Fabian B. Flohr

papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/
authors: John Hua Yao. Qi Wu, Yihuai Gao, Chelsea Finn, Zipeng Fu
bullets: Collects natural, near-human-speed demonstrations through kinesthetic teaching on a backdrivable bimanual platform.
Uses test-time action smoothing for smoother high-speed policy execution.
Applies masking to align visual data during demonstration collection and deployment.
With 50 demonstrations per task, achieves over 80% success on tasks including ball catching, clothing folding, battery insertion, and table bussing.
Demonstrates performance close to human speed across these bimanual tasks.

papers.abstract: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, including pouring, sweeping into a dustpan, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning, assessing both simulation-based robot data generation and downstream visuomotor policy learning.
authors: Yanghong Liu, Yang Chen, Kailang Xu, Bang Du, Feiyang Yang, Jiawei Xia, Zhengtao Yao, Yubiao Zhang, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Ruihai Wu, Wei Zhan
bullets: Addresses costly robot demonstration collection and the embodiment gap between humans and bimanual dexterous robots.
Uses human-object interactions to select task-relevant robot grasps from geometry-based candidates.
Combines object trajectories with relative bimanual wrist trajectories to preserve task structure and coordinated motion.
Adaptively weights object- versus wrist-level guidance according to confidence in video-derived object motion, then refines behavior under robot constraints in simulation.
Evaluates simulation data generation and downstream vision-based diffusion-policy learning on pouring, sweeping, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate-cleaning tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of PriDex. Given a human manipulation video, PriDex reconstructs object motion, relative bimanual wrist motion, interaction regions, and time-varying object-motion confidence, and uses the recovered contact cues to initialize robot-specific grasps. The PPO policy then refines these priors in simulation: reliable object motion provides task-level guidance, while lower-confidence segments allow greater residual adaptation and increased wristmotion guidance. Successful full-episode rollouts under perturbed initial conditions are retained as robot demonstrations and distilled into a vision-based Diffusion Policy for real-robot deployment.

papers.abstract: This paper presents FlowRRT, a kinodynamic planner for agile monoped hopping on discrete terrain. Steering for kinodynamic RRT on complex dynamical systems currently relies on motion primitives or closed-loop policies, limiting the diversity of motions or the planning speed. Distilling a trajectory optimizer avoids both, but existing methods regress a single solution per query, which fails on monoped hopping, where the feasible action set is narrow and disconnected. Our key insight is to treat steering as set-valued and predict the distribution of feasible actions instead. A multi-start MPPI expert collects the entire feasible set of each query offline, and conditional flow matching distills it into a generative sampler. With this sampler, FlowRRT coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and finds non-greedy maneuvers that are hard for reactive policies to discover. Benchmarks across different terrains show higher success rates and substantially shorter planning times than sampling-based baselines. On terrains with inclined platforms, FlowRRT reaches $80\%$ success within $1$~s, versus $24$~s for RL-RRT and $77$~s for SST. Sim-to-sim tracking in MuJoCo confirms accurate execution under full-order dynamics.
authors: Yue Qin, Denglin Cheng, Jingyu Liu, Yanran Ding
bullets: Addresses kinodynamic planning challenges caused by narrow, disconnected feasible action sets in monoped hopping.
Uses multi-start MPPI to collect feasible action sets offline, then applies conditional flow matching to learn a generative steering sampler.
Coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and discovers non-greedy maneuvers beyond reactive policies.
Outperforms sampling-based baselines in terrain benchmarks, including 80% success within 1 s on inclined platforms versus 24 s for RL-RRT and 77 s for SST.
MuJoCo sim-to-sim tracking confirms execution under full-order dynamics.

papers.abstract: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Instead of relying on human preference or synthetic rewards, the system uses environmental outcomes as the primary training signal, enabling policy learning grounded in ecological impact. We propose a multi-instance reinforcement learning simulation in which agents navigate a 2D grid representation of India integrated with a precomputed AQI matrix and geographic state boundaries. The framework combines bird call metadata from the Xeno-canto dataset, spatial discretization, and real environmental data to learn adaptive navigation strategies under pollution constraints. To ensure scalability and efficiency, repeated real-time API queries are replaced by a structured AQI mapping that enables fast lookup during training and execution. Multiple baselines, including Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration, are evaluated for comparison. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.

bullets: Models bird movement as pollution-aware reinforcement learning grounded in environmental outcomes rather than human or synthetic preferences.

Uses structured AQI lookup instead of repeated real-time API queries to improve training and execution efficiency.
Compares DQN with Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration; the abstract reports stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance for DQN.
Scope is a simulation-based framework for ecological decision modeling, not a direct account of real bird trajectories.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.
authors: Baiting Luo, Shatadal Mishra, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar
bullets: Addresses the cost of repeated history encoding and iterative video generation in driving-oriented video foundation models.
Uses causal autoregressive temporal modeling to incrementally update visual context from a single front camera.
Computes future features in one forward pass to condition trajectory generation, avoiding iterative video generation.
Applies reinforcement learning to optimize driving rewards and improve the policy.
Achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1; it also performs well in continuous dynamic driving while retaining visual history.

papers.abstract: Autonomy development for marine autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) remains challenging because field testing is costly and difficult to reproduce. Existing marine simulation tools provide mature capabilities in vessel dynamics, robotics integration, and visual rendering, but these strengths are emphasized differently across platforms. This paper presents ASTRA, an ASV simulation framework built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim that combines marine vehicle dynamics, photorealistic perception, and Robot Operating System (ROS 2) autonomy interfaces within a common environment. ASTRA incorporates a Fossen-style marine dynamics model together with geometry-based buoyancy and programmable spectral wave disturbances, enabling non-planar hydrostatic and wave-induced motion. The simulator reproduces the sensor configuration of a physical BlueBoat testbed, including GPS, IMU, LiDAR, and RGB-D sensing exposed through ROS 2. This allows localization, perception, planning, and control software to be developed against interfaces consistent with the physical platform. The BlueBoat's existing ROS 2 localization and perception modules were ported directly into ASTRA, while targeted zero-propulsion experiments were used to verify the implemented wave-body coupling. The simulated roll response was consistent with the expected non-oscillatory hydrostatic behavior, and heave remained highly coherent with the generated wave field, with approximately unity gain at the dominant wave frequency in the tested sea states. ASTRA is intended as an open-source testbed for marine autonomy development, simulation-based benchmarking, and sim-to-real experimentation.

Targets autonomy development, simulation benchmarking, and sim-to-real experimentation.

papers.abstract: Monitoring oil spills with fleets of Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) requires mapping a heterogeneous pollutant field from sparse, noisy measurements under tight time and energy budgets. Informative Path Planning (IPP) addresses this problem by coupling a reconstruction model, which infers the field and its uncertainty, with a planner that decides where to sample next. Prior work has focused on planning strategies and has largely relied on Gaussian Processes (GPs), leaving the calibration of the model's uncertainty underexplored. We study how uncertainty calibration conditions multi-vehicle IPP with a fleet of ASVs that coordinates online through a shared uncertainty map. We introduce Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) as an uncertainty-calibrated information model. We benchmark EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles against a GP in closed loop with five planners on physics-based oil spill simulations. Across 60 maps, the choice of model dominates the outcome, explaining 80\% of the variance of the final reconstruction error, against 1\% for the planner among the deep models. EDL achieves the lowest error and the highest IoU under every planner, is the best calibrated model and runs at 3.9 ms per step. With 50 cells per vehicle it reconstructs the spill better than MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles with 150. Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error grows, whereas EDL is unaffected. Robustness of the information model to the data its own planner collects is therefore a requirement of uncertainty-aware IPP.
authors: Alejandro Casado-P\'erez, Marija Popovi\'c, Daniel Guti\'errez-Reina, Sergio L. Toral., Samuel Yanes
bullets: Multi-ASV monitoring must reconstruct heterogeneous oil-spill fields from sparse, noisy measurements under time and energy constraints.
The study evaluates Evidential Deep Learning, Monte Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and Gaussian Processes within closed-loop IPP using five planners.
Across 60 physics-based maps, the information model explains 80% of final reconstruction-error variance, compared with 1% for the planner among deep models.
EDL achieves the lowest error and highest IoU under every planner, is best calibrated, and runs in 3.9 ms per step.
Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error increases, highlighting the need for uncertainty models robust to planner-collected data.

papers.abstract: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.
authors: Renhe Sun, Yueying Feng, Bohan Yu, Tong Niu, Yunqi Liu, Zitong Wang, Haolin He, Kexin Shi, Hualei Wang, Qiuqiang Kong, Chang Yao, Yuge Huang, Weiqiang Wang, Jingyuan Chen, Jian Liu
bullets: Covers social reasoning in first-person video and interactive service tasks involving dialogue, tools, and closed-loop execution.
Evaluates emotional and social cues, grounded reference resolution, request interpretation, and state-changing actions.
Track 1 uses a multi-stage pipeline for MCQ, chain-of-thought, quality grading, and video filtering.
Combines answer accuracy with process- and outcome-based measures; top reported results were 0.9263 Track 1 accuracy and 0.844 joint success/0.916 micro accuracy in Track 2.
Participant solutions emphasize explicit evidence verification, robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction.

papers.abstract: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.
bullets: Fixed-gain PD control cannot simultaneously optimize motion and contact-force tracking across swing and contact phases.
A reinforcement-learning policy predicts per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements during training.
The policy uses inertia-scaled impedance priors, enabling control across subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric inputs.
Across 129 participants and six activities, it improves kinematic and force fidelity over fixed-gain PD, torque-based, muscle-actuated, and existing imitation controllers.
The learned impedance representation transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot, and generalizes to withheld activities.

papers.abstract: The goal of Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning (QD-RL) is to find a population of high-performing policies that solve a decision-making problem in diverse ways. Despite recent progress, QD-RL methods predominantly rely on evolutionary operators--including black-box optimizers, mutations, and crossovers--to facilitate exploration and induce diversity. Scaling these methods becomes increasingly costly as policies and behavior spaces grow larger. Building on the Soft QD view of quality-diversity optimization, we introduce \textbf{Re}pulsive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (\textbf{RePPO}), which adapts PPO to jointly optimize a compact population of diverse, high-quality policies using a population-dependent, dynamically shaped reward. On standard continuous-control tasks, RePPO achieves a strong quality-diversity tradeoff compared with state-of-the-art QD-RL methods. Ablations further characterize this tradeoff by examining how each component affects individual quality and collective diversity. To assess RePPO's scalability, we extend our evaluation to learning from pixels and fine-tuning large language models. In pixel-based tasks, where large policies make most traditional QD-RL methods infeasible, RePPO maintains quality on par with standard PPO while achieving substantially higher diversity. Its successful application to language model fine-tuning further demonstrates, for the first time, that QD-RL methods can scale to this domain. Together, these results show that directly optimizing compact populations with RePPO provides a scalable approach to QD-RL across increasingly complex domains.
bullets: Targets the scalability and exploration costs of evolutionary Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning.
Adapts PPO with a dynamically shaped, population-dependent reward inspired by the Soft QD framework.
Jointly optimizes a compact policy population for both individual performance and collective behavioral diversity.
Matches standard PPO quality while achieving substantially higher diversity in pixel-based tasks.
Also scales QD-RL to large-language-model fine-tuning, extending evaluation beyond conventional control settings.

papers.abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.
authors: Ruixi Yu, Dairu Liu, Xuchuan Chen, Zekun Qi, Zekai Li, Zhuo Cao, Luyang Niu, Yingsheng Zhang, Sikai Liang, Ke Fan, He Wang, Li Yi

papers.tldr: ScaleVLA shows that connecting a 552B frontier VLM to an action diffusion transformer substantially improves robot policy sample efficiency, generalization, and precise manipulation while maintaining 216 ms median action latency.

papers.abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.
authors: Minjae Kwon, Amir Moeini, Shangtong Zhang, Lu Feng
bullets: Safe ICRL requires fixed-parameter policies to learn unseen constrained tasks from interaction histories while respecting a cost budget.
The revised Safe AD teacher explores according to remaining budget, then switches to an expert policy after observing reward or cost.
Training with dynamic budgets increases the diversity of return-and-budget histories and improves return while reducing cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah.
A-Lag reweights actions using predicted cost and an adaptive Lagrange multiplier updated from observed costs.
Across all five environments, A-Lag lowers mean episode cost but also lowers mean final return in four.

papers.title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Safe Algorithm Distillation improves safe in-context RL by training on budget-aware teachers and adjusting actions online to control cost, reducing costs across five environments.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.
authors: Itamar Mishani, Mukund Krishnakumar, Oren Salzman, Maxim Likhachev
bullets: Targets the costly search over skill sequences and parameters in multi-skill manipulation tasks.
Uses a fast learned world model to predict skill feasibility and resulting world states.
Repairs only affected search regions when predictions are invalidated, while simulating every skill in the final plan.
Evaluated on increasingly difficult cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks and demonstrated on a physical robot.
Plans faster with fewer simulator queries while matching or exceeding baseline success rates across settings.

papers.title: Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models
papers.tldr: Lazy-MOSAIC speeds up long-horizon robot manipulation planning by using learned skill-effect predictions to limit expensive simulation to promising candidates.

papers.abstract: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between ring-free, front-facing hybrid solid-state LiDAR and methods designed for spinning 360° LiDAR.
Traces each scan curve and detects two geometric cues: height steps and range fold-backs.
Introduces HySoLiD-Drive, a benchmark with 100 labeled and 7,000 unlabeled real-driving frames from two vehicles.
Reports 0.907 road IoU and 0.896 ground IoU, with over 0.96 precision and roughly 22 ms per frame on one CPU core.

papers.abstract: Formation maneuver control enables a multiagent system to cooperatively navigate through constrained environments in collective motion. While various formation controllers exist, they rely heavily on high-quality and dynamically feasible reference trajectories provided a priori, making formation motion planning (FMP) essential. To address the computational challenges for high-dimensional joint trajectories faced by conventional constrained optimization-based solutions, this paper introduces a hybrid optimization-generative framework with a focus on affine formations, which provide the necessary spatial flexibility. By formulating the planning task as a constrained Maximum-a-Posteriori estimation, we decouple multiagent objectives to leverage pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors for dynamic feasibility, obstacle avoidance, and smoothness. We then interleave the generative process with projected gradient descent (PGD) to strictly enforce affine geometric constraints with safety guarantees. Simulations demonstrate that our framework generates highly smooth, collision-free plans that are readily trackable by common distributed controllers and outperforms state-of-the-art planners in various metrics.
authors: Zhonggang Li, Hongyu Zhou, Raj Thilak Rajan
bullets: Targets the computational difficulty of planning high-dimensional joint trajectories for formation motion.
Formulates planning as constrained maximum-a-posteriori estimation using pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors.
Interleaves diffusion sampling with projected gradient descent to enforce affine formation constraints and safety.
Simulations show smooth, collision-free, controller-trackable plans with strong performance across multiple metrics.
Scope: focuses on affine formations and simulation-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk may fail to reflect the changes that the proposed actions would induce in visual representations, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.
authors: Haoyun Tang, Baqiao Deng, Enjin Zhou, Songwen Tian, Keyao Xu, Bowen Jing, Kun Wang, Ke Ma, Zhandong Mei, Huibin Li
bullets: Addresses the limitation of future predictions that ignore how proposed actions alter visual representations.
Uses a proposal–rethink–refine loop with latent multi-horizon predictions and residual corrections.
Adds affordance-guided observation–action memory plus near-fine, far-coarse prediction granularity.
Reports strong results across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa24, and three real-world OOD conditions.
Diagnostics and ablations support complementary benefits from rethinking and affordance guidance, with two-pass latency reported across platforms.

papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.
bullets: Cloud assistants face challenges involving data governance, continuous availability, and reliable physical actions in homes.
The home local server is used to organize nine recurring architectural responsibilities across whole-home systems.
Generative models handle perception, intent understanding, and planning, while deterministic checks, knowledge graphs, and authorization leases constrain actions.
Home control, companionship, and guarding share state and memory but differ in latency, error trade-offs, proactivity, and permissions.
Current benchmarks rely mainly on virtual environments; local deployment is not automatically safer, and social or medical effects remain insufficiently established.

papers.title: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications
papers.tldr: A design-oriented review proposes a local-first architecture and evaluation framework for generative-AI-powered whole-home services, emphasizing inspectable action control, privacy, safety, and real-world validation.

papers.abstract: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.
authors: Lucas Schulze, Sucheth Shenoy, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Addresses uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics while limiting sensitivity to measurement disturbances.
Uses a gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network with stable linear filtering to encode context across frequencies.
Provides guarantees for exponential forgetting and finite-horizon, frequency-weighted context perturbation bounds.
In simulated and real manipulation tasks, it reduces high-frequency sensitivity and residual torque error, produces smoother motion, and degrades less under injected disturbances.
Evaluation includes model predictive control and real-robot frequency-sensitivity analysis; results are scoped to the tested low-pass realization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Frequency sensitivity of the context z and predicted torque τ for the LSTM and REN, estimated over 12 real-robot runs. A sinusoidal disturbance with amplitude Asj and frequencies ranging from 0.2 to 24 Hz is applied to one joint torque input j at a time, where A = 0.5 and sj denotes the standard deviation of the input. Dashed curves indicate REN reference curves (γ = 0.5), computed using the gain |W (f)| of the second-order low-pass input filter at fb = 2 Hz. The references on τ additionally account for Lz, the maximum norm of ∂τ/∂z over the real-robot data.

papers.abstract: Cooperative mobile manipulation requires robots to coordinate their motions while ensuring whole-body collision avoidance and preserving task-relevant behaviors. We propose CALDS (Cooperative Adaptation of Learned Dynamical Systems), a framework that enables mobile manipulators to adapt learned single-agent behaviors for coordinated execution. Building on individual dynamical systems (DSs) learned from demonstrations, CALDS enables cooperative adaptation through two key components: Cooperative Policy Selection, which identifies compatible combinations of learned policies, and Temporal Adaptation, which ensures collision-free cooperation while preserving the spatial structure and convergence properties of the original behaviors. We evaluate CALDS across three diverse scenarios: assistive dressing, restaurant cleaning and serving, and drawer opening and object placement. Quantitative results demonstrate its effectiveness in improving task success and enabling safe, coordinated simultaneous execution while maintaining fidelity to demonstrated behaviors.
authors: Saray Bakker, Wendelin B\"ohmer, Javier Alonso-Mora
bullets: Addresses coordination, whole-body collision avoidance, and behavior preservation in cooperative mobile manipulation.

Reports improved task success and safe simultaneous execution while maintaining fidelity to demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding benchmarks usually do not consider the contextual uncertainty of real-world scenarios. In this study, we construct a novel benchmark, the Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D) dataset. It consists of human-robot conversational multimodal interactions covering different types of ambiguity, arising from visual and linguistic categories. We evaluate the capabilities of different state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) for ambiguity recognition and resolution. We compare dialogue context grounding performance for visual and linguistic ambiguity resolution. Our experiments show that VLMs can substantially improve the resolution of linguistic ambiguity, especially Japanese zero anaphora, by using dialogue context. We further conduct a comparative analysis to understand whether grounding improvements arise from the semantic content of the dialogue or from its conversational structure.
authors: Edoardo Cecchinato, Shun Inadumi, Angel Garc\'ia Contreras, Giuseppe Riccardi, Koichiro Yoshino
bullets: Existing visual grounding benchmarks often overlook ambiguity in real-world interactions.
JAG-D contains Japanese human–robot multimodal dialogues spanning visual and linguistic ambiguity.
The benchmark evaluates VLMs on ambiguity recognition and resolution using dialogue context.
Dialogue context substantially improves linguistic ambiguity resolution, particularly for Japanese zero anaphora.
The study examines whether gains come from dialogue semantics or conversational structure.
