papers.abstract: Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity. However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging. Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed. We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric-temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual-inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction; (2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data-model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation; and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo-inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets. Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS. On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual-inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error. We achieve 7.6 and 3.6 times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm-hand teleoperation. Project website: https://fruitrabbit.github.io/WinDEX/.
authors: Hongyu Ma, Hairong Qu, Shiqi Zhao, Yongsong Yang, Kai Shi, Jiahao Ai, Xin You, Peng Yin

Achieves 43.61 FPS offline and 171 FPS streaming; reports 14.5-pixel reprojection error and 37.29 mm world-frame joint error on held-out evaluations.
Motion references improve reinforcement-learning task success by 7.6× over WiLoR and 3.6× over HaWoR, with demonstrated real-time arm-hand teleoperation.

papers.abstract: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes.
authors: Yoonseok Kang, Dayeon Jung, Seunghoon Jeon, Wonjib Kim, Dongchul Park
bullets: Addresses how robots can repurpose past observations for requests that were unknown when the observations were recorded.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.
authors: Ke Sun, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yike Zhang, Yanzhe Chen, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fast-evolving contact forces and slow API-only model decisions.
Uses calibrated force sensing or joint torques with self-terminating force primitives that return on contact events.
Converts force traces into physical quantities with uncertainty for model reasoning instead of exposing raw force streams.
Introduces HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables.
Reports large gains in real and simulated zero-shot success, with performance matching expert controllers on HiddenPhys.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.
authors: Jing Yi, Cehao Yang, Hualei Zhang, Haitao Li
bullets: Addresses token-to-action misalignment and conflicting teacher policies in autoregressive VLM distillation.
Uses complete-action alignment to calibrate command likelihoods over each game's legal actions.
Selectively retains on-policy data and probes visual specialists using uncertainty margins.
Cross-evaluates specialists across source games to upweight compatible teachers and suppress conflicting corrections.
With Qwen3.5-4B, achieves 86.7% and 80.0% Task-1 success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of CAMOPD. (1) Complete-action alignment scores complete semantic actions to form a calibrated policy with reliable margins, initializing the shared student and frozen per-game specialists. (2) Selective on-policy retention rolls out the student with rule teachers (τ1, . . . , τM ) to retain high-confidence teacher corrections on student-error or low-margin states in a replay bank. (3) Conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates specialists without target data (C̄g ↓ ⇒ γg ↑) to reweight asymmetric recovery gradients under L = Laction + λLanchor. (4) Zero-shot deployment runs the consolidated pixel-only student on unseen games.

papers.abstract: Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency. Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) explores alternatives through interaction, but coordinated learning and safe execution remain challenging. Their integration nevertheless faces challenges in exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and execution reliability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation framework. A potential-game (PG) formulation provides a fixed-path longitudinal reference, around which a residual MARL policy learns longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path corrections. A hard-case curriculum concentrates experience on interactions that PG leaves unresolved or substantially delayed. A comparative rollout selector evaluates the joint consequences of learned corrections against PG before choosing the executed action. Experiments in merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios compare CoopDistill with six baselines at four connected automated vehicle penetration levels. Relative to PG, success improves by 2.1--27.1 percentage points and delay decreases by 7.3--27.3\%, with no observed collisions. Code is available at https://github.com/FanGShiYuu/CoopDistill
authors: Shiyu Fang, Sheng Zhao, Jiarui Zhang, Chengkai Xu, Xiaocong Zhao, Peng Hang, Jian Sun

Across merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios, it improves success and reduces delay versus the potential-game baseline, with no observed collisions.

papers.abstract: Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present \textsc{LightAct}, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, \textsc{LightAct} improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

papers.abstract: Egocentric hand motion provides physical motion supervision for dexterous manipulation and vision-language-action pretraining. Reliable use of this supervision requires accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. Existing methods typically lift framewise estimates produced under weak perspective into world coordinates. By ignoring joint-dependent depth variation at close range, this approximation couples errors in translation, orientation, and articulation that persist after world lifting and worsen under occlusion. We present MetricHand, a geometry-aware flow matching framework for 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. MetricHand encodes depth priors from hand-object interaction regions into joint-associated representations that preserve local spatial structure and metric scale. Fused with visual features, this geometry guides coarse metric estimation and conditions every step of temporal generation. The model jointly recovers world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and shape, while structural priors and temporal context support estimation under partial occlusion. MetricHand reduces camera-space MPJPE by 49.3% and 52.9%, absolute world-space MPJPE by 28.7% and 21.7%, and wrist localization error by 48.5% and 37.9% relative to HaWoR, respectively. World-space acceleration error decreases by 44.2% and 64.3%, demonstrating improved temporal fidelity alongside more accurate absolute localization.

Fuses geometric and visual features for coarse metric estimation and conditions each step of temporal generation.
Jointly predicts world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and hand shape.
Reports substantial reductions in camera-space and world-space MPJPE, wrist error, and acceleration error relative to HaWoR.

papers.abstract: Dynamical-system-based motion policies provide a framework for learning reactive robot motions with stability and convergence properties. Many manipulation tasks, however, admit several distinct goals or a continuous set of acceptable outcomes, requiring motion primitives that preserve these alternatives. Accommodating both goal structures within a unified framework with continuous, autonomous dynamics remains an open challenge. We propose a CONDOR-based framework, multi-CONDOR, for learning motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour. The approach combines imitation learning with losses that encourage agreement between the learned task dynamics and latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure. We provide a Lyapunov-based analysis of the convergence properties of the learned motion dynamics. We evaluate the framework on simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, qualitative examples with continuous goal contours, and robotic grasping experiments. In simulation, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared with separately learned single-goal motion primitives selected by a state machine. For tasks with two and three goals, respectively, it reduces the fraction of evaluated initial states ending outside the goal tolerance from StableNODE's 0.31% and 7.29% to 0% in both settings. Experiments with a Franka Emika robot arm demonstrate successful grasping of a container by either of its two handles using motions learned from demonstrations. Together, these results show multi-CONDOR combines motion reproduction with the flexibility to converge to alternative valid outcomes.

papers.abstract: Similar tactile contacts can call for different corrections depending on the configuration of the hand, object and target. Rather than supplying touch and wrist vision separately, fusing them before policy injection better grounds tactile features in visual context, yielding more accurate contact representations. We introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that learns such representations before action generation. Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data, WiTac deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views into a comprehensive contact representation. Conditioning downstream VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$) on WiTac substantially improves task success over vision-only base policies across four contact-rich manipulation tasks (+28.8% and +15.0% on average), and further outperforms a wrist-free tactile encoder by 18.8% and 7.5%, respectively. Offline analyses further show that incorporating wrist vision yields more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task-contact discrimination, greater feature stability under tactile noise, and clearer action-direction readout from similar contacts.Project page: https://wrist-informed-tactile-representations.github.io/.
authors: Haotian He, Yiyang Chen, Congsheng Xu, Wenchao Yue, Mingze Ye, Shuai Chen, Yi Yang, Yaping Li, Haonan Wang, Weinan E, Wenzhao Lian, Zhijie Deng

papers.abstract: Autonomous monitoring and intervention in semi-structured agricultural environments, such as orchards and vineyards, require mobile robots to navigate to locations across diverse field configurations. This entails performing navigation behaviors including in-row driving, row turning and skipping, and inter-row traversal. Recent learning-based approaches have enabled robust in-row navigation from onboard perception, but navigation across rows typically requires a priori knowledge of field geometry to specify and tune row-transition maneuvers, preventing arbitrary transitions between rows. We address this challenge by framing navigation in these environments as a goal-directed navigation task, where a long-horizon goal is expressed relative to the robot and a planner generates local paths based on the goal and the robot's perceptual observations. We present FlowRow, a flow-matching-based local planner which models the distribution of diverse agricultural navigation behaviors as $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ paths using the long-horizon goal and depth perception. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce RowNavBench, a navigation benchmark for semi-structured agricultural environments developed in Isaac Sim, comprising 900 episodes across grape vineyards, lemon orchards, and apple orchards with varying row lengths, row and plant spacings, plant positions, and weed growth. FlowRow achieves 87% success, compared to 44% for the strongest generative behavior cloning baseline retrained on the same demonstrations. We will release our benchmark, data, and code upon acceptance.
authors: Utkarsh Bajpai, C\'{e}dric Pradalier, St\'{e}phanie Aravecchia

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, but attention-based scores do not directly measure a token's effect on the predicted action. We define action sensitivity as the magnitude of the first-order action change when a token is replaced by its camera's mean token and estimate it for all tokens with a single backward pass. Computing it online is costly: scoring on the full (unpruned) graph needs an extra forward pass at every control step. Scoring on the pruned forward pass is cheaper but causes scoring-graph lock-in: removed tokens lose their direct paths through later layers and tend to receive lower scores, making those locations less likely to return. On replayed observations, even with a random conditioning mask, pruned-graph scoring re-selects 59% of the mask's tokens, versus 6% expected by chance; attention histories show a similar bias. POKE (Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently) computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with under 0.3M parameters. At inference, the student scores the current observation without backpropagation or previous masks, and score-guided diversity selection retains the tokens. Keeping 32 of 512 visual tokens on LIBERO, POKE achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on $\pi_{0.5}$ at $1.85\times$ and $1.26\times$ speedups, outperforming attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners, with larger margins on LIBERO-Plus.
authors: Jaehyuk Lee, Yeajin Lee, Suhyun Bae, Donghun Lee
bullets: Attention scores poorly reflect how visual tokens affect predicted actions, while online action-sensitivity scoring is computationally expensive and biased by prior pruning.
POKE computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with fewer than 0.3M parameters.
At inference, the student scores observations without backpropagation or previous masks, and diversity selection retains informative tokens.
Keeping 32 of 512 tokens achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on π0.5, with 1.85× and 1.26× speedups on LIBERO.
The method reports larger gains on LIBERO-Plus than competing attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners.

papers.abstract: Furniture assembly planning requires inferring subassembly hierarchies from individual parts and a target illustration. Existing raster-based methods do not explicitly exploit the geometric and structural information in SVG drawings. We introduce VASR, a framework that fuses features from a dedicated SVG encoder with visual representations from a pretrained vision-language model to predict assembly hierarchies. To avoid penalizing valid alternatives to a reference assembly tree, we propose Repair-Aware Hierarchical Policy Optimization (RHPO) with hierarchy-preserving equivalence rewards. RHPO further uses repair-cost feedback to favor decisions with lower downstream correction costs among candidates with comparable equivalence-aware rewards. VASR achieves the highest Equivalent-Hard F1 among the evaluated methods, outperforming GPT6-Astra by 17.69 percentage points on the IKEA-derived test set while maintaining strong performance on an independent furniture dataset.
authors: Ruizhe Wang, Rui Liu, Hongliang Chen, Junyi Guo, Fangyu Wu, Yaran Chen
bullets: Targets assembly hierarchy inference from individual parts and target illustrations.
Fuses a dedicated SVG encoder with representations from a pretrained vision-language model.
Uses RHPO to reward hierarchy-preserving equivalent solutions rather than only matching one reference tree.
Adds repair-cost feedback to prefer decisions requiring fewer downstream corrections.
Achieves the best Equivalent-Hard F1 among evaluated methods, including a 17.69-point gain over GPT6-Astra on an IKEA-derived test set, with strong independent-dataset performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Assembly architecture and RHPO training (a–c) The indexed parts and target drawing illustrate four assembly steps. Each resulting subassembly maps to an internal node of the reference tree, also shown in nested JSON. (d) For a fixed goal or action, unassisted rollouts estimate full success (Q) and tree quality (V). Separate repair rollouts estimate the mean number of subsequent repairs (C). At the first certified downstream error, the verifier rolls back, replaces the erroneous merge using the annotated graph and reference tree, and resumes the frozen policy. GRPO uses Q and V at both decision levels and favors lower repair cost among eligible candidates with near-best quality and a certified paired cost gap. Action-only distillation transfers probability mass from verified invalid actions to verified valid actions while preserving the mass on unknown actions.
Figure 3. Ablation study of VASR. VASR-S is trained only through the supervised stages (T2–T4).

IKEA-SingleStep and IKEA-GeoCluster are the two IKEA-Manual planning baselines [1]; Manual2Skill is from Tie et al. [4]. Simple and Hard denote Equivalent-Simple and Equivalent-Hard F1. For GPT6.0-Astra and the VASR variants, Δ is the Hard F1 difference from full VASR on the same dataset (method minus VASR), in percentage points (pp). VASR-S is supervised only; + denotes further reinforcement learning.

papers.title: VASR: Vector-Aware Assembly Planning with Equivalent Structures and Repair-Cost Feedback
papers.tldr: VASR improves furniture assembly planning by combining SVG geometry with visual-language features and optimizing for valid, low-repair-cost assembly hierarchies.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video representations provide rich temporal information for robotic manipulation, yet effectively integrating them into existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies remains challenging. We present Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework for flow-aware visual conditioning of frozen VLA policies. FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state through linear Test-Time Training (TTT) and retrieves action-conditioned visual features throughout flow-based action generation. By exploiting the affine structure of the frozen action head, we explicitly characterize how injected visual features influence predicted action velocities and formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem. We develop a FISTA-based solver for joint gate optimization and derive an efficient closed-form approximation through diagonalization and rescaling. With only 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps, FAVR improves pretrained VLA policies across benchmarks. On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions. A controlled ablation on five RoboTwin tasks further shows that flow-aware gating increases average success from 72.0% with a gate shared across flow steps to 82.0%, demonstrating the benefit of adapting visual conditioning throughout action generation.
authors: Qixuan Wu (School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Xiaole Yang (School of Software, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Yuguang Yang (School of Electronic and Information Engineering, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Canyu Chen (National College for Excellent Engineers, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Linlin Yang (Communication University of China, Beijing, China), Haixia Pan (School of Software, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Guodong Guo (Lane Department of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering, West Virginia University, Morgantown, USA), Baochang Zhang (School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of integrating pretrained temporal video representations into existing VLA policies.
Uses linear test-time training to maintain a compact temporal visual state and retrieves action-conditioned features during flow-based generation.
Formulates flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem, solved with FISTA and approximated efficiently through diagonalization and rescaling.
Uses only 1.74–2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps.
Improves LingBot-VLA on RoboTwin 2.0 from 87.12% to 90.04% in clean settings and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomization; flow-step gating raises ablation success from 72.0% to 82.0%.

papers.abstract: Optical tactile sensors record tactile videos that capture local deformation and its temporal evolution during contact, supporting robot manipulation, force estimation, and tactile representation learning. Differences in imaging geometry, background appearance, illumination, resolution, and deformation response lead to sensor-dependent observations of the same contact across GelSight, DIGIT, GelSlim, TacTip, and other optical tactile sensors. This variability limits representation transfer and the joint use of multi-sensor data. We introduce TacBridge, a framework for learning unified representations from multi-sensor tactile videos through cross-sensor correspondence. Specifically, multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training learns spatiotemporal representations across sensors. We then train the same masked model jointly on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction, using paired source and target videos of matched contact events. Experiments on cross-sensor translation and downstream perception demonstrate the cross-sensor generalization and task transferability of the learned tactile representations.
authors: Yongji Fu, Yijiong Lin, Yi Zhou, Yi Qi, Guanqun Cao
bullets: Addresses sensor-dependent differences that hinder transferring representations and combining multi-sensor tactile data.
Uses multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training to learn shared spatiotemporal features.
Jointly trains on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction using paired videos from matched contact events.
Experiments show cross-sensor translation and transferability to downstream perception tasks.
Scope: applies to optical tactile videos and relies on paired cross-sensor observations of corresponding contacts.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of TacBridge. Multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training and event-paired cross-sensor learning yield a shared spatiotemporal tactile representation. The learned representation supports controllable tactile video generation conditioned on source-video features and target-sensor information. We further evaluate the learned representation on downstream tactile perception tasks and new real-world tactile data.

Fig. 3: Tactile attribute classification on a real robot. A robot arm presses a GelSight sensor on two fabrics and records one tactile reading per fabric. The frozen TacBridge encoder turns each reading into multi-layer patch tokens, and a linear probe trained on our real-robot fabric recordings maps them to 24 sigmoid attribute scores. Attributes reported as present are shown in blue and attributes reported as absent are struck through. The chips illustrate the output format with the annotated attributes of these two fabrics; the measured accuracy is reported in Table III. The encoder is not updated at any point.

Fig. 2: Target-conditioned tactile translation. Each row fixes one sourcecontact video, recorded by the sensor named in the row label: GelSight Mini, GelSlim, DIGIT, and a second GelSight Mini contact. Each column requests one target sensor: GelSight Mini, GelSlim, DIGIT, and GelSight. The cell outlined in orange is the recorded source frame and always lies in the column of that row’s own sensor, so it falls on the diagonal for the first three rows and returns to the GelSight Mini column for the fourth. Every other cell in a row is a decoding of the same latent under the target-sensor condition of its column. Switching that condition changes imaging colour, marker layout, and texture, while the contact location and deformation of the source are largely retained.

Bold marks the best result per column.

papers.abstract: Tool-handover interaction calls for preparation before a response is warranted. The model waits until interaction cues appear, then prepares while assessing whether the accumulating evidence supports a response or calls for cancellation. We introduce EviBridge, a framework that integrates predictive visual representations into a vision-language interaction model for joint state and tool prediction. A trainable evidence interface maps features from a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into the language decoder alongside native visual inputs, preserving their temporal context and using only observations available at each decision time. The framework has two instantiations. EviBridge-E distinguishes recent from historical evidence and encodes the timing and spatial location of each observation. EviBridge-I preserves the temporal order of pooled V-JEPA 2 features and interaction turns and generates dedicated interaction tokens. We evaluate on FuGIBench, a streaming-video benchmark for preparation, response, and cancellation in tool-handover assistance. The best-performing variants of EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I achieve Overall scores of 0.6448 and 0.5892, compared with 0.2178 and 0.5327 for their respective task-adapted native baselines. These gains span target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests, demonstrating the value of predictive visual evidence for interaction decisions.
authors: Zhichao Huang, Changheng Cai, Song Ren, Zhichen Zhao, Hongsen Liu, Chaoyang Zheng, Wenxi Wu, Yichen Long, Yuan Fang, Luya Wang, Gufeng Liu, Yuchen Wang
bullets: Addresses the need to prepare for handovers before an explicit response cue, while deciding whether to respond or cancel.
Maps frozen V-JEPA 2 features into a language decoder alongside native visual inputs, using only evidence available at each decision time.
EviBridge-E separates recent and historical evidence with timing and spatial information; EviBridge-I preserves temporal order and adds interaction tokens.
On FuGIBench, the best EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I variants score 0.6448 and 0.5892, versus 0.2178 and 0.5327 for their respective native baselines.
Benefits extend across target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests.

Bottom: frozen native and V-JEPA 2 encoders provide visual features to the interaction model. The evidence interface encodes type, age, and position in EVIBRIDGE-E, or preserves slot order and turn order in EVIBRIDGE-I. The shared decoder, adapted with LoRA, generates interaction states and tool fields.

Figure 2: Evidence interfaces in EVIBRIDGE, shown for (a) E-RecentHist and (b) I-MLP. The explicit interface adds type, age, and position encodings to recent and historical V-JEPA 2 features. The implicit interface retains ordered V-JEPA 2 slots and earlier interaction turns in the decoder context. Both generate JSON with a state field and state-dependent fields. W, P, and R denote WAIT, PREPARE, and RESPONSE, respectively.

Off-the-shelf baselines are evaluated without task-specific training. Shading highlights the best Overall model in each E/I series. Bold marks the best value in each column.

papers.abstract: Training and verifying neural network-based control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) can be computationally demanding. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that jointly learns a CLF and a stabilizing controller using structured neural networks and a projection-based parameterization. Specifically, we employ Polyak-Lojasiewicz networks (PLNets), which parameterize nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates, and construct a stable-by-design surrogate of the closed-loop dynamics that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by construction. The controller combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction term resembling Sontag's universal formula and is trained to align the resulting closed-loop dynamics with the stable-by-design surrogate. Unlike classical approaches based on Sontag's formula, our framework does not require a known CLF; instead, it learns the CLF and controller simultaneously. We establish local and global stability guarantees for the learned controller and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through numerical examples.
bullets: Addresses the computational difficulty of training and verifying neural control Lyapunov functions (CLFs).
Uses Polyak–Lojasiewicz networks to represent nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates.
Constructs a surrogate closed-loop system that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by design.
Combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction inspired by Sontag’s universal formula.
Provides local and global stability guarantees and demonstrates effectiveness through numerical examples.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Closed-loop responses (seed 0). (a) Academic example: LQR diverges from 8 of 12 initial conditions, whereas the learned controller converges from all. (b) Van der Pol oscillator: states and control input from x(0) = (9.8, 0). The input uses the signed logarithmic scale sign(u) log10(1 + |u|); dense bands indicate rapid input oscillations.

papers.selection_reason: Joint learning of control Lyapunov functions and stabilizing controllers; transferable to learning-based robot control.
papers.title: Joint Learning of Control Lyapunov Functions and Controllers via Stable-by-Design Surrogates
papers.tldr: A framework jointly learns a neural control Lyapunov function and stabilizing controller by matching the system to a stable-by-design surrogate.

papers.abstract: Achieving human-like behavior on humanoid robots has advanced rapidly by leveraging motion-capture demonstrations rather than hand-crafted cost functions. Adversarial imitation supplies a style signal that lets a policy fulfill a task while adhering to a desired style, but is difficult to transfer to hardware. Whole-body tracking through reinforcement learning instead deploys reliably and imitates demonstrations faithfully, but the resulting policies are conditioned on the future reference, so they require a reference trajectory at runtime and can fail when the motion differs from the training data. We train a humanoid policy directly with whole-body tracking rewards while restricting its actor to compact locomotion commands and robot observations. Reference motion supervises the reward and privileged critic, without supplying reference joint trajectories to the actor or requiring teacher distillation. The demonstrated style is thereby encoded in the policy through the tracking reward, so the robot reproduces the whole-body style under commanded velocities. Trained on a single random-walk motion and commanded with velocity profiles from held-out motions, our policy reaches at least 98\% success in simulation and completes every trial on the Unitree G1. On held-out slow walking, whole-body tracking drops to 2\% success and command-conditioned distillation to 56\%, and both fail on the real robot. On the trained motions, the joint position error of our policy stays within 8\% of whole-body tracking, and it has a higher style coverage than adversarial motion priors (AMP), which fell on the real robot without a safety crane.
authors: Murad Dawood, Oezge Drama Berkenkamp, Antonio Gonzales Marin, Nutan Chen
bullets: Addresses the need for reference trajectories at runtime and poor transferability in conventional whole-body imitation.
Trains with whole-body tracking rewards and a privileged critic, while withholding reference joint trajectories from the actor and avoiding teacher distillation.
Encodes demonstrated style directly into a velocity-conditioned policy from a single random-walk motion.
Achieves at least 98% simulated success and completes every Unitree G1 trial under held-out velocity profiles.
Scope: performance degrades substantially on held-out slow walking, where competing tracking and distillation methods also fail on hardware.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Distribution of the velocity command in the training data (random walk, gray) and in each held-out motion (blue). The small forward velocities of slow and side walking, on which our policy succeeds, are covered by the random walk. Fig. 1: Our policy learns the jogging style from a motion-capture clip (top) and reproduces it on the Unitree G1 (bottom). Only the base velocity of the clip (orange) is given to the policy as a command. The reference joints and body poses are used only during training.

Fig. 2: Share of held-out frames that lie inside the support of the random-walk training data, for the input of our policy (velocity command) and of the Teacher (reference joint positions and velocities). The numbers under each motion are the simulation success of ours / Teacher. The velocity command of our policy keeps 87 to 100% of the held-out frames inside the training support, which matches its success on all of them.

Fig. 3: Share of held-out frames inside the support of the training data, with the Teacher input split into reference joint positions and reference joint velocities. The reference joint positions, which our policy does not observe, are where the Teacher input leaves the training support on slow walking.

papers.abstract: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.

bullets: Addresses the problem that retained, transported, or subsurface heat can affect later contact outcomes.

Provides a paired six-task benchmark with 4,448 trajectories and integrations for MuJoCo and Isaac Sim.
Reported studies show improved contact-site selection with visible thermal history and higher transfer completion when training uses dynamic histories.

papers.abstract: Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs. QTOP outperforms on and off-policy RL baselines both in simulation and real-world tracking scenarios on multiple datasets by up to 10\%. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law for QTOP and find that, aside from scaling predictably, dataset size has minimal impact on performance for moderately sized GPU hour regimes.
authors: Markus Peschl, Dana Kianfar, Daniel Dijkman
bullets: High-fidelity generalization to unseen motions is compute-intensive due to interference across diverse motion tasks.
Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP) introduces a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state–reference pairs.
It outperforms on-policy and off-policy RL baselines in simulation and real-world tracking across multiple datasets, by up to 10%.
The work establishes a QTOP scaling law and reports limited dataset-size impact in moderately sized GPU-hour regimes.

papers.abstract: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.
authors: Tao Tao, Anke Tang, Enneng Yang, Zhi Hou, Xiaogang Wang, Dacheng Tao
bullets: Targets storage growth from separately deploying specialists and interference from dense weight merging.
Retains each specialist’s feed-forward block as a routable expert and compresses experts with a shared floating-point anchor plus binary, row-scaled deviations.
Uses closed-form alternating factorization from source weights alone, then adapts token-level routing by updating fewer than 0.6M parameters.
Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, it uses 20.3 GB—1.16× one dense specialist and 59.6% less than the uncompressed MoE.
Across 22 benchmarks and R2R, factorization is nearly lossless on 21/22 benchmarks; VSI-Bench is the main exception, likely due to weaker cross-frame evidence use.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.
bullets: Temporal inconsistency between modalities can corrupt fused representations and cause driving-policy failures.
STA jointly optimizes when to delay observations and which modality to attack, using historical states instead of modality-specific noise.
The method uses clean policy actions to identify sensitive decision patterns and includes theoretical analysis of distribution shift and modality selection.
In CARLA, STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest PPO baseline with 17.8% fewer attack attempts and also generalizes to a VLM-based policy.
The results emphasize temporal consistency and robustness as important for safe autonomous driving.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed Split Temporal Adversary (STA). At each time step, the adversary observes the current state and driving policy information, then decides whether to attack based on the attack budget and policy awareness. If activated, it selects which modality to manipulate (visual or numerical) and replaces the selected modality with a delayed observation from the history buffer. This creates cross-modal temporal misalignment that leads to erroneous control decisions by the driving policy.

papers.abstract: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.
authors: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Shangchen Zhou, Wenzheng Zeng, Yanzhe Chen, Zechen Bai, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Organizes 114 robotic reward-model methods into five families: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid.
Identifies a gap in common evaluations: demonstration-order agreement and policy gains may not measure task fulfillment.
Introduces RRM-Bench-1K, containing 1,117 real-robot videos with task-state and camera-evidence labels plus four contrast suites.
Across 27 evaluators, final scores rank whole executions effectively, while dense credit more often tracks temporal progression than task state.
Releases RRM-Hub, supporting 14 existing reward models and standardized capability testing; needed fidelity depends on the downstream decision.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Place Recognition (PR) can improve robustness, but most systems rigidly read and process every sensor for every query, even when the primary sensor is sufficient, with implications for energy consumption, second sensor update rate, and domain-specific considerations such as passive stealth. We introduce selective, controllable sensor acquisition, where a user specifies a desired second sensor usage rate and the system acquires the additional sensor only when the primary sensor's estimated performance is sufficiently poor. An online threshold adjustment achieves the requested usage rate by adapting to recent primary sensor performance, directing additional sensing towards queries where fusion is most likely to help without calibration specific to sensor modality, PR method, or environment. The approach requires only a PR method that produces a match score and applies to both single-frame and sequence-based PR. Our system, across multiple datasets, PR descriptors, and sensor combinations, recovers 55% of the available PR performance gain while using the second sensor on only 25% of queries, and 81% while using it on 50%. We further analyse alternative acquisition decision mechanisms and usage-rate control methods, and examine performance when the second sensor is stronger than, comparable to, or weaker than the primary sensor.
authors: Margaux Edwards, Tobias Fischer, Michael Milford
bullets: Targets unnecessary processing and sensing when the primary sensor is already sufficient, improving efficiency and supporting application constraints such as passive stealth.
Uses the primary sensor’s match score to estimate when performance is poor and selectively acquire the second sensor.
An online threshold adapts to a user-specified second-sensor usage rate without modality-, PR-method-, or environment-specific calibration.
Works with both single-frame and sequence-based place recognition across multiple datasets, descriptors, and sensor combinations.
Recovers 55% of the available gain at 25% second-sensor usage and 81% at 50%.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone pi_0-ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency.
authors: Haixiang Wu, Zhihao Guan, Yang Yang
bullets: Equal fusion can overwhelm proprioception despite its rich dynamic information; inter-joint coupling is identified as the key action-determining structure.
Inverted State Encoding forms a proprioceptive prior with per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention.
State-Visual Grounding allows joint tokens to query visual evidence for goal and calibration information.
Inverted Action Chunking independently decodes per-joint trajectories.
ACiT improves success on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, especially those requiring dynamics and coordination; the design also improves pi_0 execution efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ACiT architecture, organized by its three modules. (b) State-Visual Grounding: the joint tokens query the visual tokens of the multi-view observations and produce grounded tokens Gt . (c) Inverted Action Chunking: Gt is the memory of a transformer decoder whose learnable joint queries output one T -step trajectory per joint.

(b) Biological inspiration: proprioception forms a body-centered prior in S1, vision reaches PPC via V1 only to remap and calibrate the goal, and M1 issues the command. The two modalities are not symmetric, and their order is fixed. (c) Conditioning interface: ACT concatenates a single-frame state with vision into one condition shared by all joints; ACiT keeps the per-joint prior as the primary condition, retrieves visual evidence per joint, and decodes one trajectory per joint.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich manipulation, yet heterogeneous sensing mechanisms and observation formats hinder cross-hardware transfer. Since physical contact is governed by Newtonian mechanics, we ground tactile representations in six-dimensional wrenches, establishing a common physical reference across sensing mechanisms. Specifically, we pair tactile observations from all sensors with wrench measurements, enabling shared physical supervision without requiring direct tactile-to-tactile pairing between sensors. To support learning at scale, we develop a dedicated acquisition platform and collect over 100 million paired tactile observations and wrench measurements from 24 sensors spanning four families of sensing principles. Building on this dataset, our framework combines sensor-specific input adaptation with a shared tactile encoder. By learning to reconstruct wrenches, the encoder maps observations from different sensors into a shared, continuous feature space grounded in contact physics. To leverage these representations for manipulation, we introduce TaF-Policy, which integrates tactile features with visual observations and robot states to generate action chunks. We evaluate the learned representations through wrench estimation, cross-sensor retrieval, few-shot adaptation to unseen sensors, and robotic manipulation. On the core benchmark, our method reduces single-frame force RMSE by 17.1% and improves cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baseline. In manipulation experiments, TaF-Policy achieves average success rates of 51.33% across three simulated tasks and 46.25% across four real-world tasks, compared with 47.33% and 23.75%, respectively, for the strongest baselines evaluated on the same task sets. Project page: https://mrjiangjm.github.io/TaF-Foundation/.
authors: Jiaming Jiang, Yuzhe Huang, Baokun Yang, Hao Liang, Li Gao, Haoran Guo, Pei Lin, Shengcheng Luo, Chenxi Xiao, Wanlin Li, Ziyuan Jiao
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of transferring tactile models across sensors with different mechanisms and observation formats.
Pairs observations from 24 sensors across four sensing families with wrench measurements, avoiding direct tactile-to-tactile pairing.
Uses sensor-specific input adaptation and a shared encoder trained to reconstruct wrenches, producing a common physical feature space.
Improves single-frame force RMSE by 17.1% and cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baselines.
TaF-Policy combines tactile features with vision and robot states, achieving higher average success on the reported simulated and real-world task sets.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of our methodology for wrench-grounded tactile representation learning and downstream evaluation. (a) Sensorspecific input adapters and family-specific projections map heterogeneous tactile observations into tokens for a shared Transformer. A learnable physical query aggregates the encoded tokens into a 768-dimensional continuous tactile representation. (b) Six-dimensional wrench reconstruction and alignment with EMA wrench embeddings provide shared physical supervision. The learned representations are evaluated on single-frame wrench estimation, temporal wrench estimation with historical wrench inputs, cross-sensor retrieval, and robotic manipulation using TaF-Policy in simulation and the real world.

papers.abstract: Many everyday objects, such as storage boxes, baskets, and chairs, are too large or heavy for a gripper to grasp, yet a single arm can still pick them up by wrapping around and supporting them. Such grasps are hard to learn: wrapping motions are difficult to teleoperate, and existing datasets contain little whole-arm pickup data. We introduce WAG (Whole-Arm Grasp Dataset), the first large-scale dataset for single-arm pickup of large objects, with 1.7~million joint configurations across 793 objects. We sample configurations directly in joint space, execute each through squeeze and lift primitives in simulation, and stress-test survivors under active shaking and external forces. To demonstrate the utility of WAG and accomplish the whole-arm pickup task, we develop ARMFUL, a whole-arm pickup pipeline that pairs a diffusion model trained on WAG, generating whole-arm grasps from the object's point cloud, with a motion planner that reaches them collision-free before the same squeeze-and-lift execution. In simulation, ARMFUL reaches 85.4\% lift success on training and 69.9\% on held-out objects, and it lifts the object in 70 of 100 trials on a physical Franka arm across 10 IKEA objects.
authors: Xinyi Yu, Yunshuang Li, Daniel Seita, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
bullets: Addresses the lack of whole-arm grasp data and the difficulty of teleoperating wrapping motions for large-object pickup.
Introduces WAG, a dataset with 1.7 million joint configurations spanning 793 objects, filtered through squeeze-and-lift simulation and robustness tests.
Uses a diffusion model to generate whole-arm grasps from object point clouds, combined with collision-free motion planning and squeeze-and-lift execution.
Achieves 85.4% lift success on training objects and 69.9% on held-out objects in simulation.
On a physical Franka arm, successfully lifts objects in 70 of 100 trials across 10 IKEA objects.

(b) Motion planning. The arm follows an RRT-Connect path to the selected arm grasp configuration, and the same squeeze-and-lift execution completes the pickup.

Fig. 2. Construction of WAG. We sample candidate whole-arm grasp configurations, discard penetrating candidates, and test the rest directly in a GPU-parallelized simulator. The arm is teleported to the candidate grasp configuration and executes the squeeze and lift primitives. Configurations that hold the object throughout the lift and maintain the grasp with base-joint shaking and external force applied to the object are added to WAG.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to track instruction progress and recover from local errors before they propagate across subtasks. However, executors trained on expert trajectories encounter policy-induced state shifts during deployment, and their stop signals do not reliably indicate subtask completion. We introduce Learning and Verifying Progress for VLN (LeaP-VLN), an agentic VLN system that couples progress-aware execution with independent progress verification through plan--execute--verify--recover cycles. LeaP-VLN leverages progress both explicitly, through a progress verifier that verifies subtask completion before the agent advances and triggers dual-phase recovery upon route deviation, and implicitly, by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction to enhance the executor's progress awareness and corrective control. To adapt the executor to this closed-loop interface, we propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum: behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, followed by joint training on demonstrations, expert action corrections, and progress-reasoning supervision. Policy-generated trajectories expose the executor to both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, aligning training with the deviations encountered during closed-loop execution. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation.
authors: Kangjie Zhou, Sukai Wang, Yuhan Xiao, Qinghang Liu, Zhejia Wen, ChunXuan Jiao, Wei Shan, Guanghui Ren, Maoqing Yao, Chang Liu
bullets: Addresses executor drift and unreliable stopping decisions that can cause errors to propagate across subtasks.
Uses plan–execute–verify–recover cycles with a progress verifier that confirms subtask completion and triggers dual-phase recovery after route deviations.
Co-trains the executor on action prediction and progress reasoning to improve progress awareness and corrective control.
Adapts training through a two-stage curriculum using expert demonstrations, corrections, progress supervision, and policy-generated trajectories.
Achieves state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods without additional navigation datasets on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with further validation in real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed closed-loop agentic framework with test-time verification and recovery. Two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum learning, which clones expert actions and then co-trains intra- and inter-subtask on-policy action corrections with progress-reasoning supervision, produces the low-level VLN executor, while the high-level multimodal agent maintains landmark memory and accepted anchors and orchestrates subtask planning, progress verification, and dual-phase failure recovery.

Fig. 1. Comparison of long-horizon VLN execution paradigms. End-toend policies map the complete route instruction and visual observations directly to actions, with route progress implicitly inferred within the action policy. Hierarchical planner–executor pipelines without outcome verification dispatch local subtasks and advance based on executor termination. Our LeaP-VLN couples progress-aware execution with progress verification and dual-phase recovery to ground subtask transitions in observed outcomes and limit error propagation.

Fig. 5. Qualitative visualization of long-horizon instruction following. The complete navigation instruction is shown at the top of each example. For every subtask, the egocentric observation is paired with the corresponding top-down map, where the colored trajectory indicates the agent’s stage-wise navigation progress. In the top example, the agent sequentially executes all subtasks and successfully reaches the target location. In the bottom example, the verifier detects a mid-route deviation and triggers a subtask retry, enabling successful completion.

Fig. 7. Real-world long-horizon navigation on the AgiBot Genie 02 robot. LeaP-VLN decomposes the route instruction into three local subtasks: approaching the divider, passing the sink, and stopping before the toilet. For each subtask, the top image shows the robot’s third-person start state and the bottom row shows the corresponding egocentric image.

Fig. 3. Low-level VLN executor training. (a) Boundary-aligned localinstruction data generation cleans and merges segment annotations, aligns frame–action targets, and adds explicit STOP supervision at subtask boundaries. (b) The two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum first initializes the executor by behavior cloning, then collects intra- and inter-subtask on-policy rollouts for expert action correction and progress reasoning, and finally jointly trains on all supervision.

Fig. 6. Qualitative effects of progress co-training on action prediction. Without co-training, the executor either continues after task completion (top) or stops prematurely (bottom). papers.abstract: Self-evolving language agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for continuously improving agent behavior through experience. However, most existing approaches evolve textual artifacts, which can influence action preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete and often irreversible actions. We propose MetaAct, which shifts self-evolution from textual guidance to executable action constraints by synthesizing GEAR (Grounded Executable Action Rules) from execution feedback. Each rule is represented as a typed specification, compiled into a deterministic guard, and validated offline through trajectory replay without additional model calls or environment interactions. Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; on ScienceWorld and WebShop, violations drop from 70% to 0% and 40% to 1%, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0. Our code is available at https://github.com/BaiCubed/MetaAct.
authors: Jiaxing Zhao, Hanwen Wang, Di Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Jing-Ran Su, Yanheng Li, Qian Zha, Jiaxi Li, Hongbin Xie, Haoran Zhang, Xuan Song, Haoxuan Che
bullets: Addresses the limits of textual self-evolution, which cannot reliably enforce action admissibility for discrete or irreversible actions.
Synthesizes Grounded Executable Action Rules (GEAR) from execution feedback.
Represents rules as typed specifications, compiles them into deterministic guards, and validates them offline via trajectory replay.
Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; violations fall from 70% to 0% on ScienceWorld and 40% to 1% on WebShop.
Reported score gains are +10.1 on ScienceWorld and +8.0 on WebShop.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a unified approach to perception, reasoning, and control for autonomous driving, but accurate action prediction alone does not establish compliance with traffic regulations. This paper presents a rule-guided VLA framework that incorporates symbolic traffic-rule feedback into policy optimisation. The framework combines supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations with reinforcement learning (RL) refinement using a reward that encourages encoded-rule compliance while penalising deviations from expert actions. Selected provisions of the United Kingdom Highway Code are formalised as executable first-order logic rules using PyReason, covering speed adaptation, following distance, and road-user priority. A frozen vision-language model extracts scene predicates, which are combined with vehicle-state information to assess the projected consequences of candidate control actions. Offline evaluation on held-out data collected in the CARLA simulator compares three group-based RL methods. The results show improvements in both action prediction accuracy and encoded-rule compliance over the supervised baseline. The best-performing variant increases the overall rule pass rate from 92.9% to 97.6%, with zero observed violations of the encoded road-user-priority check in the evaluated samples. These findings support symbolic rule feedback as a means of improving VLA policy alignment with explicit traffic-rule criteria.

papers.abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) requires planning that accounts for environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles. This paper presents JEPTERA, a navigation architecture that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), Model Predictive Control (MPC), PID control, and a safety layer. JEPA predicts the UAV's motion response to candidate commands for MPC action selection, while the safety layer checks trajectories against occupied space and predicted obstacle motion. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations separate the planning core from simulator interfaces. An ablation study evaluated six configurations across three gym scenarios, totaling 180 runs. The complete architecture achieved the highest aggregate success rate, completing 28 of 30 runs. Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces.

papers.abstract: Existing autonomous driving datasets and benchmarks provide extensive resources for routine driving, yet real-world data covering safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions remain limited. To address this gap, we present ExtremeDrive, a real-world dataset and benchmark covering emergency maneuvers, complex traffic interactions, and adverse conditions such as slippery or snow-covered roads, alongside routine driving. The dataset comprises 589 driving scenes curated from a larger pool of real-world driving recordings, with calibrated and aligned multisensor data and reviewed annotations of road structure and traffic participants. We further establish a benchmark to evaluate planned trajectories through simulated vehicle execution, measuring safety-related metrics and driving performance. Experiments at equal training set sizes show that incorporating critical driving data reduces trajectory prediction errors and improves mean critical-success rates in critical scenarios. ExtremeDrive provides a unified resource for learning and evaluating autonomous driving in safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions.

papers.abstract: Language-guided navigation enables mobile robots to interpret natural language commands and navigate toward user-specified targets in unstructured environments. However, integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics pipelines for mapping and navigation remains a challenging problem. In this work, we present a complete ROS2-based system that combines frontier-based exploration, open-vocabulary object detection using Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, and semantic mapping to enable end-to-end vision-language grounded navigation in simulation. The system accepts natural language commands such as ``go to the yellow box,'' detects candidate objects from RGB images using text prompts, estimates their positions in the world frame, and generates navigation goals executed by the Nav2 stack. In a Gazebo-based indoor environment with a TurtleBot3 robot, the system autonomously explored the room, detected three of the five target objects, and successfully executed both natural language navigation commands tested, without task-specific training. The results indicate that open-vocabulary grounding models can be integrated into classical navigation pipelines, though performance is limited by detection uncertainty, depth-based localization error, and incomplete exploration coverage. These findings highlight both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying vision-language grounded navigation systems using lightweight, CPU-only architectures.

papers.abstract: Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6 times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: https://asymeef.vercel.app/.

papers.abstract: Proposal-conditioned scene predictions can lack a common object-level reference across candidate trajectories. Aggregate planning scores also leave the objects and times associated with violations implicit. We present WTR-Drive (World-Task-Risk Driving), a Drive-JEPA-based planner that separates shared scene estimation from proposal-conditioned reasoning. A proposal-independent World Memory estimates object states, map structure, and future motion by re-reading the original visual features at each refinement round. Proposal feedback updates a residual Task branch without writing back to World Memory. This branch guides refinement through candidate-specific retrieval and gated visual feedback. A final Task readout supplies candidate-conditioned features for scoring. We derive structured risk targets from existing candidate-scoring rollouts without additional simulator calls. For at-fault collision and time-to-collision violations, the targets encode event existence, association with shared object slots, and the first violation time bin. On the NAVSIM navtest split, WTR-Drive achieves 94.66 PDMS on v1 and 88.24 EPDMS on v2 (expert-frame sequential evaluation). These scores are 0.96 and 0.44 points above the published Drive-JEPA values, respectively. Candidate-level analysis shows that higher best-candidate scores can coexist with lower selected-trajectory scores, revealing a gap between candidate quality and selection effectiveness.
