papers.abstract: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.
authors: Chenhao Ding, Jizhou Han, Lixin Xiu, Muyao Wang, Songlin Dong, Hideki Nakayama
bullets: Addresses the underuse of feedback from previous navigation episodes in online VLN.
Success-Failure Memory retrieves task-relevant successful and failed experiences using incoming instructions.
Prior-Anchored Adaptation reinforces successful trajectories, suppresses failed ones, and limits drift from a frozen pretrained policy.
Evaluated on REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE with five navigation backbones, showing consistent gains.
On REVERIE unseen validation, DUET’s SR rises from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of R2A. (a) The agent navigates using the adapted policy and obtains queried feedback or a self-predicted outcome. (b) Success–Failure Memory: Before navigation, the incoming instruction triggers the retrieval of the most similar experience from the entire memory based on instruction similarity, together with a randomly sampled experience. (c) Prior-Anchored Adaptation: The preceding episode and recalled experiences jointly update the policy through reference-relative outcome learning and pretrained-policy regularization.

(b) Success memory: recalling a successful experience guides the agent toward the target phone. In both cases, Task-Cued Recall reaches the intended destination, while uniform replay fails.

Figure 1. Learning from past successes and failures for navigation. (a) People recall successful experiences and mistakes to guide navigation. (b) Similar visual cues may cause an agent to confuse a kitchen with a laundry room; replaying a past failure helps correct this mistake. Inspired by episodic memory, R2A reuses successful and failed experiences with outcome feedback for adaptation.

papers.tldr: R2A improves online vision-and-language navigation by retrieving past successful and failed episodes and adapting the policy without source data or expert supervision.

papers.abstract: Most robot navigation stacks implicitly bind mapping, localization, planning, and control to specific representations and data flows, yielding architectures hard to extend, compare experimentally, or reason about end-to-end timing. This is critical in heterogeneous scenarios, where multiple spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames coexist and evolve at different rates. This paper presents a navigation architecture centered on an explicit, shared navigation state that serves as the sole interaction interface between modular components. Constraining mapping, localization, planning, and control to operate over this shared state enables interchangeable, representation-agnostic pipelines under explicit compatibility and timing contracts. We realize this architecture as EasyNav, an open source ROS 2 framework, and validate it through real-robot experiments, including indoor navigation with laser sensing and large-scale indoor-outdoor navigation with GPS and 3D LiDAR across multi-level routes. Compared with Nav2 under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency from 377 to 33 ms indoors and from 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while also using less CPU and memory.
authors: Francisco Mart\'in Rico, Francisco Miguel Moreno, Juan Sebasti\'an Cely Guti\'errez, Esther Aguado, Miguel \'Angel De Miguel Para\'iso, Jos\'e Miguel Guerrero
bullets: Existing navigation stacks tightly couple mapping, localization, planning, and control, making them difficult to extend, compare, and analyze for timing.
EasyNav uses an explicit shared navigation state as the sole interface between components, with compatibility and timing contracts.
The architecture supports interchangeable pipelines across spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames.
Real-robot experiments cover indoor laser navigation and large-scale indoor-outdoor GPS/3D LiDAR navigation across multi-level routes.
Under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency versus Nav2 from 377 to 33 ms indoors and 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while using less CPU and memory.

papers.abstract: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.
authors: Zhanjiang Yang, Lijun Sun, Yueming Li, Meng Li, Yijun Yang
bullets: Addresses the limited generalization of existing MORL methods beyond task- or objective-specific policies.
Uses a multimodal diffusion transformer with likelihood-free flow matching to model diverse trade-off trajectories.
Trains in three stages: large-scale pre-training, curated-data mid-training, and few-shot post-training on new tasks and trade-offs.
Outperforms prior methods on most D4MORL tasks, including zero-shot interpolation/extrapolation and few-shot adaptation in continuous control.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Network architecture of Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for MORL. FP2 is a rectified flow-based model with a multi-modal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) backbone that denoises state-action chunks and is guided by multimodal conditions including numerical and textual preferences and multi-objective returns. FP2 is trained offline and deployed as an online policy.

Figure 2: Three-stage training pipeline of Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2). In Stage 1, FP2 is pre-trained to learn diverse long-horizon trade-off behaviors based on large-scale trajectories Dpre. In Stage 2, FP2 is continuously mid-trained to align policy behavior with the target preference using curated high-quality Pareto non-dominated trajectories Dmid. In Stage 3, FP2 can be further post-trained to efficiently adapt to unseen preference configurations or new tasks with the remaining trajectories Ddrop or a very small amount of new task data Dtask. (See Sec. 4.3 for more details.)

Figure 1: Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for MORL. FP2 is a rectified flow-based policy conditioned on numerical and textual user preferences. Through principled pre- and mid-training on diverse datasets (yellow region), FP2 learns a reusable multi-objective trade-off prior that generalizes to out-of-distribution preferences and can be efficiently adapted to new locomotion tasks (blue region) via few-shot post-training.
Figure 6: Cross-task performance comparison.

papers.abstract: In 2025, there was a total of 358 weather-related disasters worldwide affecting millions of people. For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to autonomously aid these people, they need to be able to navigate around complex obstacles and reach their destinations to deliver supplies or quickly locate survivors in disaster-stricken areas. Our research addresses this need by providing a method to compute minimum-time trajectories in real time while providing guarantees of obstacle avoidance along the trajectory. Previous approaches treat the problem of computing time-optimal trajectories without considering obstacle avoidance. Our work not only includes obstacle avoidance constraints, but also improves overall mission time for navigation. We define mission time as the sum of planning time and traversal time. In time-sensitive emergencies, rapid trajectory planning is essential to ensure the prompt delivery of critical medical aid. As such, we consider the combined planning and traversal time as the key metric for how quickly the vehicle can reach a survivor. We show a sample mission in Fig. 1 where the quadrotor navigates through multiple canyon-like obstacles to deliver aid; during most of this trajectory, it is applying the near-maximum thrust.
authors: Pranav Nedunghat, Jeffrey Mao, Praveen Merumugumala
bullets: Targets autonomous drone navigation through complex obstacles to deliver supplies and locate survivors.
Optimizes mission time, defined as planning time plus trajectory traversal time.
Incorporates obstacle-avoidance constraints into time-optimal trajectory computation.
Demonstrates a sample quadrotor mission through multiple canyon-like obstacles, often using near-maximum thrust.
The abstract does not report quantitative evaluation results or specific limitations.

papers.abstract: We introduce a unified formulation of imitation learning from demonstrations as a conditional sampling problem solved by triangular transport: a policy is the second block of a triangular map that transports a reference distribution to the conditional distribution of the action chunk given the observation history. Unlike in Diffusion Policy, where it is a fixed Gaussian, the reference becomes a design variable; we take it to be the empirical distribution of the demonstrated action chunks and introduce three instances of the formulation: an optimal transport policy (OTP), a flow matching policy (FMP), and a stochastic interpolant policy (SIP). On the Push-T and robomimic Square tasks, the three policies are competitive in task performance with Diffusion Policy and Consistency Policy while using considerably smaller networks and shorter training, and the informative reference accounts for a substantial part of their performance when few network evaluations are used. The three instances offer different trade-offs rather than a single best method: OTP generates an action chunk with a single evaluation of the smallest network (0.23 million parameters on Push-T) and is suitable for settings in which inference time and model size matter, whereas SIP attains the highest scores among the proposed policies at a higher cost.
authors: Mohammad Al-Jarrah, Yuhang Mei, Karen Leung, Bamdad Hosseini, Amirhossein Taghvaei
bullets: Frames imitation learning as conditional sampling of action chunks given observation histories.
Introduces three variants: optimal transport policy (OTP), flow matching policy (FMP), and stochastic interpolant policy (SIP).
Unlike Diffusion Policy, uses the empirical demonstration distribution rather than a fixed Gaussian reference.
On Push-T and robomimic Square, the methods are competitive with Diffusion and Consistency Policies while requiring smaller networks and shorter training.
OTP minimizes inference cost with one evaluation; SIP achieves the strongest scores among the proposed methods at higher cost.

papers.abstract: Experiments near vehicle handling limits must keep three questions apart: what a maneuver requests, what the closed-loop system executes, and whether the task is completed. We present DynLimit, a simulation platform that organizes this process end to end. Scenarios are composed from road, friction, obstacle, and reference objects; planners and controllers attach through a shared observation and control interface; a vehicle adapter runs either a license-free four-wheel model or an external dynamics solver; and synchronized records feed task evaluation, replay, and response inspection. The platform carries a task-oriented evaluation method that pairs a prescribed reference demand with a sampled passing set and event-aligned diagnosis. Across eight task families, three friction environments, and three reference-assisted baseline chains we executed 450 runs: 360 nominal, 18 locally refined, and 72 with prescribed initial offsets. Method differences depend on the task family, equal aggregate pass counts arise from different passing cells, and local refinement narrows two sampled transitions without locating a continuous boundary. Two case comparisons show why sideslip or tire-utilization peaks cannot replace task constraints. The three views therefore stay distinct in every reported run: an outcome can be traced from the prescribed demand, through the executed response, to the task rule that decided it. Code is available at https://github.com/Yang2581/dynlimit
authors: Yang Xiao, Yongzhi Liu, Sunan Zhang, Kang Wang, Guodong Yin, Weichao Zhuang
bullets: Supports composable scenarios with road, friction, obstacle, and reference objects.
Connects planners and controllers through a shared interface to either a four-wheel vehicle model or an external dynamics solver.
Uses task-oriented evaluation with prescribed reference demands, sampled passing sets, and event-aligned diagnosis.
Across eight task families and three friction environments, it found that methods with equal aggregate pass counts can differ in which task conditions they pass.
Shows that sideslip and tire-utilization peaks alone cannot substitute for task-specific success criteria.

papers.abstract: Safety-critical high-speed legged locomotion requires motion planners to balance safety foresight with online computational efficiency. Although short prediction horizons reduce rollout costs, they provide limited safety foresight, and strict safety constraints severely restrict the feasible trajectory space. We propose a recovery-guided model-based diffusion (MBD) framework for safety-critical legged locomotion. It incorporates a learned terminal recovery critic into short-horizon trajectory optimization. Specifically, the critic approximates the worst-case future clearance margin along rollouts of a designated recovery policy. We introduce a feasibility-guided refinement strategy that combines within-horizon constraints and terminal recoverability at each sampling stage, while retaining feasible elites to mitigate sampling-support loss. Across 50 paired randomized Unitree Go2 obstacle-avoidance trials, our approach achieves zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success, while requiring substantially less computation than long-horizon MBD baselines. A project page is available at https://zack4417.github.io/rg-mbd/.
authors: Lei Zheng, Shivam Sood, Mithun Vanniasinghe, Guillaume Sartoretti, Armin Lederer
bullets: Short prediction horizons reduce computation but offer limited foresight, while strict safety constraints shrink feasible trajectories.
The method adds a learned terminal recovery critic that estimates worst-case future clearance under a recovery policy.
Feasibility-guided refinement enforces current-horizon constraints, terminal recoverability, and preserves feasible elite samples.
In 50 paired randomized Unitree Go2 obstacle-avoidance trials, it achieved zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success.
The approach required substantially less computation than long-horizon model-based diffusion baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations, robot states, and natural-language instructions to robotic actions, but their multimodal interfaces introduce new security risks. Existing VLA backdoor attacks primarily study trigger-based activation and stealthy action manipulation, leaving conditional suppression of malicious behavior underexplored. We investigate suppression-aware backdoors, which combine conjunctive trigger activation with instruction-conditioned suppression. We instantiate this design through three variants: Cross-Modal Trigger, combining robot-state and spatially separated visual triggers; Self-Suppressing Trigger, requiring a state trigger and a [DISRUPT] instruction token for activation, with [RESTORE] token suppressing the attack; and Multi-Trigger, additionally requiring a visual trigger while retaining suppression even when physical triggers persist. We evaluate these attacks using SmolVLA on two SO-100 manipulation datasets against four baselines: State Backdoor, BadVLA, TabVLA, and SilentDrift. Self-Suppressing and Multi-Trigger reduce Isolation Forest detection from 96--98% to 1--18% and action-space l divergence by 10--14X, achieving 63--71% attack success rates with perfect clean-task performance. Experiments with OpenVLA on LIBERO further show that the attacks transfer to a 7B-parameter policy, evading STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection. Our findings establish conditional suppression as an important dimension for evaluating backdoor threats in VLA policies.
bullets: Targets security gaps in vision-language-action models, especially conditional suppression of backdoor behavior.
Proposes three designs: Cross-Modal Trigger, Self-Suppressing Trigger, and Multi-Trigger.
Evaluations on SmolVLA and OpenVLA show reduced detectability, 63–71% attack success, and preserved clean-task performance.
The attacks also evade STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection, highlighting suppression as a key threat dimension.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.

Policies trained only in a digital twin transfer zero-shot to a real arm with gripper and dexterous hand.

papers.abstract: Water--land cross-domain robots require continuous localization across land, transition and underwater phases, where sensor characteristics and availability change abruptly. Existing datasets and conventional metrics are not designed to capture transition-induced degradation and failures. We present \textbf{M-CROSS}, to the best of our knowledge, the first multisensor simulation dataset and benchmark for SLAM across continuous water--land transitions. It provides synchronized LiDAR, sonar, stereo camera, IMU, DVL, and depth measurements; 6DoF pose ground truth; sensor-wise medium-state annotations; and medium-dependent sensor degradation models. We establish a transition-aware protocol comprising the Trajectory Completion Rate (TCR), Piecewise Absolute Pose Error (PW-APE), Transition End Error (TEE), and Transition Survival Period (TSP), which measure trajectory completion, single-domain accuracy, transition-induced error, and localization survival under prolonged partial immersion, respectively. Experiments with 6 representative SLAM systems show that existing methods fail to maintain both localization accuracy and trajectory continuity across the full set of water--land transitions, exhibiting transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures. M-CROSS is publicly available https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MCross-Dataset
authors: Yan Dong, Tianyi Wu, Junyu Yang, Shaoqiang Qiu, Zefeng Yan, Tao Zhang, Bin Han
bullets: Addresses localization degradation and failures caused by abrupt changes in sensor characteristics and availability during water–land transitions.
Provides synchronized LiDAR, sonar, stereo camera, IMU, DVL, and depth data, along with 6DoF pose ground truth and medium-state annotations.
Introduces medium-dependent sensor degradation models and four metrics: TCR, PW-APE, TEE, and TSP.
Evaluation of six representative SLAM systems reveals transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures.
Dataset and benchmark are publicly available.

papers.abstract: A distributed multi-robot object transportation strategy is proposed for objects of unknown shape, size, geometry, mass and mass distribution without any prior knowledge about the object or number of robots involved in the transportation process. Robots follow the boundary of the object and dynamically determine viable pushing points. A novel object-model-free heading-error-driven pushing effort regulation method is proposed to promote goal-directed object motion; robots regulate their pushing effort using individual and collective heading errors. Robots dynamically relocate around the object boundary if a pushing point is lost or the required pushing effort exceeds its capability to correct its heading. The proposed method is validated using simple and complex shapes with convex and non-convex boundary regions and dynamically changing weight distribution of objects. Detailed analysis on the effects of robot distribution and initial object pose on the transportation performance in terms of required time and path efficiency is also presented. Scalability analysis revealed that object transportation time is dependent on the number of pushing surfaces available which in turn depends on the object size, shape, and set inter-robot safety distance. The proposed system yielded highly efficient object paths with consistent elapsed transport times over several trials robust to external disturbances such as non-uniform friction between contacting surfaces and robot wheel slip.

bullets: Robots track an object’s boundary and dynamically identify viable pushing locations without a prior object model.

Validation covers convex and non-convex shapes, complex geometries, changing weight distributions, friction variation, and wheel slip.
Transport paths were highly efficient with consistent elapsed times across trials; scalability depends on available pushing surfaces, object properties, and inter-robot safety distance.

papers.abstract: Progress in autonomous navigation in off-road environments requires not only advances in algorithms, but also robust and capable physical platforms suited to both development and deployment. Today, off-road autonomy is typically developed and tested at one of two extremes of vehicle scale, each with different drawbacks. Full-size vehicles are capable but expensive, require large logistic infrastructure for deployment and maintenance, and expensive when pushed beyond their limits. RC-scale vehicles are small and inexpensive, but limited in the terrain they can traverse and the payload that they can carry, which includes their sensors and compute. We present the AlphaTruck platform, which leverages recent advances in compact sensing and compute to integrate multimodal sensing, embedded CPU-GPU compute, and an onboard autonomy stack for high-speed, off-road navigation, all integrated into a large-scale, 1/5th RC vehicle chassis. AlphaTruck is designed as both a research testbed and a field-deployable platform for commercial and defense missions such as survey, search and rescue, and agriculture, with the capacity to carry task-specific payloads. At 1/5 scale, the autonomy stack, sensors, and batteries all compete for the same mass, power, and cooling budget, so the platform must balance five needs: mobility over rough terrain, rich sensing, onboard computation, payload capacity to carry the autonomy stack while leaving room for task-specific equipment, and practical operation and repair. Thus, AlphaTruck navigates off-road environments autonomously at 6-10 m/s using only onboard sensing and compute.
authors: Rwik Rana, Adam J. Thorpe, Jesse Quattrociocchi, William Ward, Goktug Poyrazoglu, Adam Uccello, Christian Ellis, Rahul Moorthy Mahesh, Yukang Cao, Nathan Tsoi, Garrett Warnell, Volkan Isler, Ufuk Topcu, Joydeep Biswas

Supports research and field missions such as surveying, search and rescue, and agriculture.

papers.abstract: Although object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) approaches are usually evaluated in simulation, which offers scale and repeatable environments, real-world deployments are rarely examined beyond feasibility demonstrations. This paper presents the deployment of Room-Mediated Co-occurrence, an ObjectNav policy that reasons over Room Probability Vectors (RPVs), on two robotic platforms (Boston Dynamics Spot and Clearpath Robotics TurtleBot 4) through a robot-agnostic ROS 2 bridge. We study how these semantic priors generalise to physical environments and describe the adaptations required to transfer RPV from simulation to hardware, covering sensing, localisation, and the action interface. Across 66 trials on Spot, searching for 11 object categories from two starting positions in a university postgraduate research facility, RPV achieves a raw Success Rate (SR) of 0.455. Our analysis identifies undetected glass walls, entry into off-limits areas, limited usable depth range, target size, and mismatch between the room lexicon and physical layout as plausible contributors to the 8.4 percentage-point gap between the real-world SR and the reported simulated SR of 0.539. Code is available at https://github.com/Matthew-K-Chua/rpv-ros2-bridge.
authors: Matthew Chua, Adam Scicluna, Gavin Paul

papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal. Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed. Under PyTorch's default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms. This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14--40 points. These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings. We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.
bullets: The study compares computation reuse across replanning calls with simply reducing denoising steps on LIBERO-Goal.

Caching offers limited speedups when fresh steps and image/video processing remain necessary; estimated savings were at most 11–14% in one setup.

papers.abstract: Accurate and timely air pollution monitoring and tracking are critical for protecting public health and supporting effective environmental management. This paper presents an adaptive Density-Driven Control (D$^2$C) framework for coordinating multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to track and map dynamically evolving pollutant distributions. The proposed framework extends the D$^2$C strategy to guide UAV trajectories based on predictive pollutant propagation and dynamically updated reference densities. A sensor-driven surrogate plume update mechanism is employed, in which reference samples are propagated using locally sensed concentration gradients and wind estimates through gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, enabling UAVs to maintain an accurate spatio-temporal representation of the pollution field. The framework utilizes a coordinated structure where individual UAVs share their local measurements with a central coordinator to maintain a unified set of reference samples, facilitating systematic target allocation and trajectory planning. Simulation results under both mild and strong wind conditions demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of Sinkhorn distance. Specifically, in scenarios where the plume drifts beyond a fixed monitoring domain under high-velocity, time-varying wind fields, the tested baseline methods fail to maintain tracking, whereas the proposed D$^2$C framework successfully adapts to the evolving distribution. These findings highlight D$^2$C as an efficient and resilient solution for atmospheric monitoring in dynamic environments.
authors: Julian Martinez, Ruchika Singh, Mohammad Afrazi, Kooktae Lee
bullets: Addresses real-time monitoring of dynamically evolving air-pollution distributions, including plumes leaving a fixed monitoring area.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation missions must satisfy timed and conditional requirements that can be expressed in signal temporal logic (STL). While a practical means of monitoring these requirements is from camera images, this is challenging because STL robustness depends on physical margins, such as distances and clearances, that are not directly observed. Rather than learning a separate visual monitor for each formula, we learn a shared latent representation from multi-view images and decode physically meaningful margins for individual predicates. Co-training the encoder with predicate decoders increases the certification rate from 58.7% to 96.3% compared with a frozen encoder, despite nearly unchanged predicate sign accuracy. STL semantics then compose these margins into robustness estimates for any bounded formula over the trained predicates, without retraining. We further calibrate the decoding errors of selected STL clauses using conformal prediction, yielding two-sided intervals that certify both satisfaction and violation and propagate through interval STL to any formula composed from the clauses. In simulated kitchen missions (LIBERO), our monitor correctly predicts satisfaction or violation in 98.9% of 4662 evaluations across 18 unseen formulas. For missions lasting up to 17 min, calibrated bounds establish satisfaction or violation for 96.9% of missions without incorrect conclusions. A single calibration also provides simultaneous 91.0% coverage across all 255 conjunctions of eight clauses, allowing new formulas without recalibration.
authors: Xinpei Ni, Glen Chou, Samuel Coogan
bullets: Targets timed and conditional robotic manipulation requirements that are difficult to monitor from images because STL robustness depends on unobserved physical margins.
Learns a shared multi-view latent representation with predicate-specific decoders, then composes decoded margins using STL semantics without retraining per formula.
Conformal calibration produces two-sided robustness intervals and propagates guarantees through interval STL to certify both satisfaction and violation.
In simulated LIBERO kitchen missions, it achieved 98.9% correct decisions over 4,662 evaluations across 18 unseen formulas.
Scope: results are demonstrated in simulation and for trained predicates; calibration is needed for selected STL clauses, though one calibration supports new formula conjunctions.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based driving planners can generate multiple trajectories for the same scene, but these candidates vary in quality. Can their internal states reveal which candidate will be better before denoising is complete? We systematically study this question in three pretrained planners: Alpamayo, ReCogDrive-IL, and HDP, using linear probes to predict final trajectory quality from intermediate states and evaluating candidate ranking and selection on held-out scenes. Across all three planners, we observe that states from the first denoiser evaluation already support informative selection, while further denoising does not consistently improve selection quality. Further analyses show that readout depends on the representation and reader, and that selection can coexist with limited overall ranking accuracy. These findings motivate an early-selection method that selects after the first denoiser evaluation and completes only the chosen candidate. This reduces computation relative to fully denoising every candidate and improves open-loop trajectory quality over random selection across all three planners. In particular, it reduces Alpamayo's average displacement error by 17.8% and 13.4% in one- and four-camera configurations, respectively. Closed-loop evaluations also show higher mean driving scores and progress.
authors: Xiang Zhang, Ziyang Leng, Yuxin Bao, Zhihao Zhao, Bolei Zhou, Xugui Zhou
bullets: Across Alpamayo, ReCogDrive-IL, and HDP, first-step states already support informative candidate selection.
Further denoising does not consistently improve selection quality.
Linear-probe readout varies by representation and reader, and selection can work despite limited overall ranking accuracy.
Selecting one candidate early and fully denoising only it reduces computation versus denoising every candidate.

The method improves open-loop quality over random selection across all planners; Alpamayo’s average displacement error drops 17.8% and 13.4% for one- and four-camera setups, with higher closed-loop driving scores and progress.

papers.abstract: Physics-based control is central to robot learning, but differentiating through implicit physics steps typically requires Hessian or Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) linear solves; we ask whether gradient steps suffice. Each simulation step minimizes an energy under many contact and collision constraints. Without constraints, we view control over $K$ steps as $K$-level optimization with strongly convex lower levels, recast as one min--max problem. Our Penalized Single-loop $K$-level method (PSK) uses only gradients and a projection, updates all levels in parallel, and reaches an $\epsilon$-stationary control in $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ iterations, with a $K$-independent exponent but a $K$-dependent constant. Contact-rich constraints, however, typically violate a constraint qualification (CQ). We replace each constraint by a smooth wall that acts on a band of constant width. Under mild assumptions that need no CQ, every exact solution of the banded lower levels is then feasible and banded Fritz--John, and PSK keeps the $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ complexity. Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, however, a shrinking band loses the $K$-independent exponent: with width $\epsilon$ and fixed $K\geq2$, deterministic zero-respecting methods need $\Omega(\epsilon^{-(K+3)/4})$ calls on a hard instance whose control dimension grows with $1/\epsilon$. We prove our assumptions for smoothed kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles. In navigation experiments, PSK, tuned per case, reaches every goal with sixteen levels and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10.
bullets: Recasts unconstrained K-step control as a single min–max problem with strongly convex lower levels.
Uses only gradients and projection, updating all levels in parallel without Hessian or KKT solves.
Achieves an $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ iteration bound, with an exponent independent of the number of levels $K$.
Smooths contact constraints using fixed-width bands to avoid requiring constraint qualifications; shrinking bands can worsen complexity.
In navigation experiments, PSK reached all goals with 16 levels and had lower equal-time loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation was better in 10.

papers.abstract: Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task. Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify. We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination. Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor. Surface material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect. The magnitude of a global image statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change. We found that a model based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance. Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.
authors: Aarav Srivastava, Vishwas Sathish, Rajesh P. N. Rao
bullets: Evaluates visual generalization by changing one or more factors while keeping ProcTHOR layouts, objects, goals, and starts fixed.
Surface material changes cause most of the average success degradation; clutter and lighting have comparatively little effect.
Global image-statistics shifts do not reliably predict navigation performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially hurt end-to-end agents.
A model-based agent planning over frozen DINOv2 features achieves the highest reported full-shift success (0.83), but remains sensitive to surface appearance.
Results span model-free RL, model-based RL, and frozen-visual-representation agents, highlighting the need for appearance-invariant planning representations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to acquire complex skills, but standard RL formulations do not guarantee that learned policies satisfy safety constraints, which limits their use in safety-critical settings. Existing safe RL methods with provable guarantees typically support only restricted classes of constraints and require unbiased estimators of the objective and constraint functions, which prevents their direct integration with state-of-the-art algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO). In this paper, we extend the recently introduced robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework to overcome these limitations. Our formulation accommodates a general class of trajectory-level safety constraints, including chance constraints such as collision avoidance with a prescribed probability, and our analysis allows for biased value and gradient estimators. We show that, with high probability, the constraint violation throughout training is bounded by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as the number of rollouts grows, and decays to this level if the initial policy is unsafe. We also establish the convergence properties of the iterates to approximate KKT points of the original safe RL problem. Finally, we show that RSGF-RL implemented with PPO-style estimates enables zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body control policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.
authors: Pol Mestres, Varun Gabbita, Jason H. K. Siu, Sergio A. Esteban, Hampus Serneke, Joel W. Burdick, Aaron D. Ames
bullets: Handles general trajectory-level constraints, including chance constraints such as collision avoidance with a prescribed probability.
Permits biased value and gradient estimators, enabling integration with PPO-style methods.
Bounds constraint violations with high probability by estimator bias plus a term that vanishes with more rollouts.
Proves convergence toward approximate KKT points and decay of violations from unsafe initial policies.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real whole-body control on a Unitree G1 and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over $\pi_{0.5}$) at 92.7 ms latency.
authors: Chongyu Fan, Gaowen Liu, Ramana Rao Kompella, Jason Corso, Sijia Liu
bullets: Existing world-action models waste capacity reconstructing mostly static backgrounds instead of modeling robot and object motion.
The method learns residual feature changes between current and future frames in frozen DINOv3 space, emphasizing manipulated regions.
A lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT jointly models actions and visual residuals using conditional flow matching.
Without robot pretraining, ResWAM reports strong results across LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, and real-robot tasks, with 92.7 ms latency.
Scope: results target action-conditioned visual prediction and manipulation; the abstract does not establish broader settings beyond these evaluations.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a depth-aware path planning and collision avoidance framework for the safe navigation of robotic nursing assistants in cluttered environments with low-height obstacles. Conventional LiDAR-based navigation systems, while accurate for mapping and localization, fail to detect transparent or low-height obstacles, whereas vision-based systems are prone to noise and occlusion. The proposed framework integrates RGB-D depth sensing, rule-based obstacle avoidance, and the NavfnROS global path planner to drive the robot from an initial point to a goal point. The proposed approach is implemented on the Husky A200 robot, equipped with a Kinova Gen3 arm, to form a complete setup for a robotic nursing assistant. This system features a multi-layer architecture for global planning, perception fusion, and real-time control in the ROS-Gazebo environment. Experimental evaluations in a simulated cluttered environment demonstrate up to 40\% higher success rate and 35\% improvement in minimum clearance compared with single-sensor baselines. Furthermore, real-world experimental results validate the proposed approach as a computationally efficient and safety-aware navigation solution for autonomous healthcare robots.
authors: Peeyush Thakur, Dharmendra Sharma, Archit Sharma, Sandeep Gupta, Anuj Nandanwar, Laxmidhar Behera
bullets: Addresses LiDAR blind spots and vision noise or occlusion during healthcare-robot navigation.

Simulated evaluations report up to 40% higher success and 35% better minimum clearance than single-sensor baselines.
Real-world tests support the framework’s computational efficiency and safety-aware navigation, though the abstract emphasizes simulated cluttered environments for quantitative evaluation.

papers.abstract: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.
bullets: Addresses safety constraints that sampling-based planners handle only by scoring or rejecting action sequences.
Uses a successive convex program in latent space, initialized from a sampled plan, with a learned discrete-time control barrier function enforced across the horizon.
Builds smooth, spectrally normalised networks and bounds linearisation error using Lipschitz bounds and smoothing width.
On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks, it had fewer violations than MPPI and CEM under the reported equal-time comparison, with higher return at longer horizons.
Planning converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models and reports whether a feasible first-order KKT point was found nearby.

papers.abstract: Modern autonomous driving and driver assistance systems rely predominantly on cameras, radars and LiDARs for environmental perception. However, these modalities face different environmental limitations, including poor illumination for cameras and adverse weather for LiDAR. Acoustic sensing, particularly using microphone arrays, could provide complementary perception capabilities for autonomous driving, but has remained largely underexplored. In this work, we design a horizontally arranged microphone array that functions as the "ears" of a vehicle, enabling localization of nearby moving vehicles in a bird's-eye view (BEV) representation that captures both their relative direction and distance. Using this array, we collect a real-world driving dataset, AcousticScenes, which contains 2,117 static and 2,863 dynamic samples with synchronized spatial acoustic signals, LiDAR point clouds and 3D bounding box annotations. Building on this dataset, we propose AcousticBEV, a learning-based method for acoustic BEV object localization, which estimates the center locations of moving traffic participants in BEV from the microphone-array signals, conditioned on the ego vehicle's own speed. Experimental results demonstrate that AcousticBEV outperforms both classical signal-processing baselines and other learning-based methods, achieving F1 scores of $47.7 \pm 1.2$% on "Easy" scenarios and $45.1 \pm 1.4$% on "Difficult" cases. Our findings demonstrate that acoustic signals from a low-cost, vehicle-mounted microphone array can localize nearby moving vehicles in both azimuth and distance.
authors: Ziang Liu, Shiming Wang, Joseph Adeola, Julian F. P. Kooij
bullets: Addresses limitations of camera, LiDAR, and other conventional sensors under poor illumination or adverse weather.
Introduces a horizontally arranged microphone array and the AcousticScenes real-world driving dataset with synchronized acoustic signals, LiDAR point clouds, and 3D annotations.
Proposes AcousticBEV, which predicts moving traffic participants’ BEV center locations conditioned on the ego vehicle’s speed.
Reports F1 scores of 47.7 ± 1.2% on Easy scenarios and 45.1 ± 1.4% on Difficult scenarios, outperforming classical and learning-based baselines.
Demonstrates low-cost acoustic sensing for nearby moving-vehicle localization in azimuth and distance.

papers.abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.
authors: Yinghao Li, WeiHsien Lee, Zeyu Zhang, Canyang Zhao, Ke Fang, Xing Li, Bing Liu
bullets: Addresses whether brain activity can provide task-level intent without symbolic commands or hand-designed skills.
Uses a hierarchical framework: neural activity is read once as intent, then a learned visuomotor policy closes the control loop.
In counterfactual grasping, changing the neural intent changed which object the robot grasped, even when vision alone could not determine the target.
Representing the full neural population latent improved grasp completion from 69% to 81% across 132 held-out scenes; direction-only decoding did not help.
Intent effectiveness depended on neural location and timing: preparatory PMd signals supported grasping, with PMd outperforming M1 in one dual-array session.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The NI-ACT framework. (A) Control division. Conventional BCIs decode continuous velocity commands at every time step and keep the user inside the fast control loop. In NI-ACT, cortical activity supplies a task-level intent token once per task, sent at task start, and an embodied policy closes the fast perception–action loop with the robot and its environment. (B) Network architecture. A temporal convolutional network (TCN) maps binned PMd and M1 spikes to a 128-D population latent, a 2-D goal direction, and 7-class direction logits; an intent interface (Hard-7, Soft-2D, or Full-Latent) passes one of these to an action-chunking transformer (ACT) that also observes two cameras and the joint state, and the policy predicts 32 future joint targets. Fig. 3a gives how each interface enters the policy.

Figure 3: Architecture and data protocol of NI-ACT. (a) The frozen temporal convolutional encoder maps a window of binned spikes to a 128-D population latent z, from which a direction head reads a unit goal direction v̂ and a class head reads 7-way logits ℓ. The interface G selects one output: Hard-7 (one-hot of arg max ℓ) and Soft-2D (v̂) are appended to the 9-D joint state, giving 16-D and 11-D state inputs; Full-Latent (z) is kept separate from the joint state, projected from 128 to 512 dimensions, and enters the transformer encoder as its own intent token. The interfaces therefore differ in content, dimensionality, and injection pathway. Both camera images pass through one shared ImageNet-initialized ResNet-18, giving 7 × 7 feature maps (49 tokens per camera). With the VAE disabled, the latent token is constant. The encoder (4 layers) attends over all tokens; the decoder (1 layer, 32 learned queries) and a linear head predict 32 future 9-D joint targets. (b) Neural trials are split into training and held-out sets before any pairing. Each of the 207 counterfactual demonstrations is paired with a training trial of the same target direction, and the resulting intent is held constant over every frame; ACT is trained by behavior cloning, one policy per interface and neural source. At deployment, each of the 132 held-out scenes receives a held-out trial of its target direction; the intent is read once and held fixed while the policy replans every 32 steps. No neural trial is shared between training and evaluation. Trial counts refer to the monkey-J recording.

papers.title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation

papers.abstract: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.
authors: Akhil S. Anand, Xun Shen, Marc Peter Deisenroth, Sebastien Gros
bullets: Co-design couples system design with the policy operating it, since each affects the other.
The design gradient separates direct design effects from indirect effects through the design-dependent optimal policy.
Policy sensitivity is computed with the implicit function theorem applied to the policy-gradient stationarity condition.
A proof-of-concept algorithm combines this sensitivity with stochastic value gradient policy optimization.

On a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional designs, it consistently outperforms Bayesian optimization and evolution strategies; convergence to an approximately stationary design is proved.

papers.selection_reason: Gradient-based co-design of systems and RL policies is transferable to robot morphology and control co-optimization.
papers.title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
papers.tldr: A differentiable-simulator method jointly optimizes system designs and RL policies by computing how the converged policy changes with the design, avoiding costly black-box design search.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.
authors: Zequan Zeng, Junqin Yang, Kai Wang
bullets: Targets critical stages such as grasping, alignment, and insertion, where generalist VLA control may be imprecise or unstable.
Trains specialized atomic-skill policies with a shared RL Token state representation and the VLA policy’s reference action.
Uses a Mamba-based router with temporal history and semantic attention to select skills based on evolving task state.
Achieves 90.47% average Macro-F1 across four LIBERO task suites, 7.08 percentage points above an MLP router.
Raises Tube Transport full-task success from 20.04% to 85.67% in simulation.

The dynamic router then combines historical state information and skill semantics to coordinate policy selection and switching during multi-stage manipulation.

papers.abstract: We address tracking a moving object on a conveyor with a Franka Emika Panda robot arm, despite an imprecise digital twin, measurement errors, and noise. Our novel approach augments a loop-shaped inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a residual policy learned via Soft Actor-Critic in the digital twin. A delay-compensated Kalman filter fuses out-of-sequence camera measurements to provide latency-aware moving target position estimates. We compare the achieved performance to a performance bound for a class of model-based controllers derived from a frequency-domain sensitivity analysis, quantifying the minimum achievable error imposed by uncertain kinematic model mismatch. Simulation and hardware experiments indicate that our residual policy drives tracking error below the bound. Across conveyor speeds (27.9-41.8 mm/s), our method reduces mean tracking errors from 1.1-1.4 mm (baseline inverse-Jacobian PI) to 0.3-0.7 mm. These results show that learning residual corrections in a limited-fidelity simulator, combined with delay compensation, can substantially improve model-based control under modeling and measurement uncertainties while maintaining reliable sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Mahdi Nobar, Alisa Rupenyan, John Lygeros, J\"urg Keller
bullets: Targets conveyor-borne object tracking despite model mismatch, camera delays, measurement errors, and noise.
Combines an inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a Soft Actor-Critic residual policy trained in a digital twin.
Uses a delay-compensated Kalman filter to fuse out-of-sequence camera measurements and estimate target position.
Simulation and hardware tests show mean tracking error decreasing from 1.1–1.4 mm to 0.3–0.7 mm across the tested conveyor speeds.
The approach achieves errors below a frequency-domain performance bound for the evaluated controller class.

papers.abstract: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.
authors: Ruizhe Xie, Honghua Chen, Binglin Wang, Tong Guo, Xu Tang, Puti Yan, Shaoxiong Cai
bullets: Addresses the latency of autoregressive action-by-action decoding in robot navigation.
Training-free decoder evaluates the complete short-horizon action-prefix tree in one forward pass while preserving conditional action distributions.
Uses score margins to adaptively choose how many actions to execute before observing again.
Achieves nearly 3× faster action decoding and improves success/SPL, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points on reported benchmarks.
On a Unitree GO2, improves navigation success and reduces mean inter-action wait by about 160 ms, excluding network transmission time.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of parallel action decoding. The instruction and observation history are formatted as the model query x, followed by candidate action tokens. An attention mask restricts each candidate action token to attending only to the query, its branch ancestors, and itself. The VLN backbone processes the resulting sequence in a single forward pass. The hidden state of the last query token and those of all candidate tokens are then decoded into action distributions through the shared LM head. The last query token predicts the first action, so K = 3 uses two candidate levels. Scoring K = 4 adds a third level with 27 candidate tokens.

Figure 5. Real-world deployment trajectories on a Unitree GO2. The left and right scenes show a corridor and a classroom, respectively. In each scene, both methods start from the same position and receive the same instruction shown above. Baseline and Ours correspond to the autoregressive and parallel decoding variants of StreamVLN, respectively. Across the decision steps shown in these two scenes, our method reduces the average wait by 172 ms.

Figure 2. Comparison between autoregressive and parallel decoding. Autoregressive decoding (left) requires three sequential forward passes to predict a1, a2, and a3, whereas parallel decoding (right) computes all candidate action distributions in a single forward pass. For each action prediction, the visible tokens (highlighted) are identical along the corresponding branch in both methods, yielding equivalent conditional action distributions in exact arithmetic.

Figure 3. Adaptive execution via joint path scoring. Nodes are labeled with conditional action probabilities, while L(path) denotes cumulative joint log-probabilities. The greedy path can be outscored by the selected path in joint probability. The scan compares the fixed greedy prefix with its strongest alternative at each depth. When their score margin falls below δ, the highestscoring branch at that depth is executed and deeper actions are skipped. Here, m1 = 0.58 > δ continues the scan, whereas m2 = −0.18 < δ at δ = 0.2 selects a left turn followed by a forward step (L → F ).
Figure 4. Success rates on the GO2 over 20 trials per environment, using the same StreamVLN policy, instructions, and start poses. Bar labels show success rates and successful-trial counts.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.
authors: Gaytri Jena, Kapil Wanaskar, Aman Chadha, Vasu Sharma, Vinija Jain, Amitava Das
bullets: Benchmarks 10 hospital chores in Isaac Sim, each with five scored sub-tasks linked by persistent state.
Tracks chain-break locations, post-failure behavior, and drift between estimated and true position.
Uses a scripted robot as a solvability check and evaluates agents through image-based, skill-level tools.
In 15 preliminary runs, 2 completed all five sub-tasks; only three chores had scripted-robot proofs.
Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by another call and 111 by a non-failing call; results are not yet a full benchmark.

papers.abstract: In simulation, Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs pick-and-place in robot cells with gripper or base-frame changes without robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. It uses pre-trained vision-language and language models for interpretation, measures the command map and camera geometry from its own motion and fingertips, estimates lens distortion, and plans grasps from measured object depth. A controlled study of eight public LIBERO-fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs) varies robot hardware, camera geometry, appearance, and base frame. Gripper and frame changes dominate their losses in the tested fractional design. Across 18 cells with these changes, frozen VAA achieves 230/360 successes (64%), the refined VAA 268/360 (74%), and the strongest released VLA on this subset 76/360 (21%). Paired ablations support the self-calibration bundle, lens estimation under compounded changes, and the measured-depth pipeline. On a two-step LIBERO-Goal chain with object state carried between instructions, VAA completes 54/60 chains in changed cells, while four evaluated VLAs complete none.
authors: Jae Hun Hwang, Yechan Seo, Hong-In Won
bullets: Targets deployment failures caused by changes in grippers, base frames, cameras, and appearance.
Uses pretrained vision-language and language models with self-measured command maps, camera geometry, lens distortion, and object depth for grasp planning.
Across 18 changed cells, frozen VAA succeeds in 64% of trials and refined VAA in 74%, versus 21% for the strongest evaluated VLA.
A two-step task chain succeeds in 54/60 changed-cell chains, while the four evaluated VLAs complete none.
Results and ablations support the combined self-calibration, lens-estimation, and measured-depth components.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for visuomotor policies typically relies on teleoperated robot demonstrations, which are costly because every episode requires a trained operator controlling a physical robot in real time through teleoperation interfaces and wearable body-tracking hardware. Egocentric glasses capture human demonstrations without a robot or handheld grippers, yet they track only the head and in-view human hands, and directly copying human motion to a robot with different stature, arm reach and hand morphology fails to produce feasible contacts. \method{} converts egocentric glasses recordings into physically verified robot training trajectories. An agentic real-to-sim stage reconstructs collision and textured visual assets from the recorded RGB-D and head streams, completes unseen surfaces when needed, and predicts target contact bands on the manipulated objects. During motion adaptation, a grasp planner turns each contact band into a feasible robot wrist pose and finger closure, bilevel stance optimization plans collision-free standing postures that keep hand targets reachable, and a whole-body motion generator synthesizes lower-body locomotion and out-of-view arm motion. Two-stage motion correction then blends visibility transitions kinematically and trains a reinforcement-learning tracking policy in physics simulation under agent-designed semantic rewards, completing manipulation phases even when the object leaves the camera view. Rendering the reconstructed scene through the robot's onboard camera along the optimized rollout yields synchronized robot-view images, proprioception and verified action labels. Fine-tuned exclusively on this converted dataset, without real-robot demonstrations, GR00T N1.7 performed loco-manipulation tasks autonomously on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://robonana.github.io/ego2sim2humanoid/
bullets: Addresses the cost and impracticality of collecting teleoperated robot demonstrations.
Reconstructs scenes and predicts object contact regions from egocentric RGB-D and head-motion recordings.
Adapts human actions to a humanoid using grasp planning, stance optimization, whole-body motion generation, and physics-based RL correction.
Produces synchronized robot-view observations, proprioception, and verified action labels for policy training.
A GR00T N1.7 policy trained exclusively on the converted data autonomously performed loco-manipulation tasks on a Unitree G1.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Architecture of E2S2H, illustrated on a bottle-lift recording. From egocentric video and tracked hand landmarks, agentic real-to-sim masks objects and builds a textured visual scene with simplified collision geometry. Each object pairs a visual mesh with a collision model marked by target contact regions. Along the human (orange) and adapted robot (green) camera paths, the robot poses trace adaptation and correction. During the approach with hands out of view (cyan), the whole-body motion generator drives locomotion and unseen arm motion, then begins blending arm targets prior to visibility. Once hands enter the camera view (blue), tracked human landmarks take over arm guidance. Placing the robot directly on the projected human head path (red) does not guarantee a collision-free stance. Stance adaptation is therefore required to keep clear of the table while holding targets within reach in a comfortable posture. Directly copying the human palm onto the robot hand likewise fails, causing finger penetration or missed contact in the grasp comparison above. The final pose (grey) combines bilevel stance adjustment with contact-band Dex3 grasp planning. Kinematic optimization and reinforcement learning in physics simulation refine this plan into a dynamically feasible rollout. E2S2H then renders the robot camera view from the reconstructed scene along the rollout path to produce synchronized training data.

Fig. 4. Views of the bottle-lift scene. From left: a frame from the glasses; the simulated robot view, rendered from the reconstruction at the robot camera as used for training; the real robot view from the G1 head camera during a real-robot trial. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can teach robot teams to navigate shared spaces, but trial and error causes collisions that real robots cannot afford. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters prevent these collisions by correcting unsafe actions, yet in a team the filter becomes a centralized optimization whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. We propose an approach that builds the filter's safety into the RL policy and examine how such a system behaves during filter-free deployment. However, the filter that keeps training safe also hides what the policy must learn: it masks the cost of unsafe actions, which actor-critic methods then overvalue, and it keeps near-collision states out of the training data. Our approach therefore learns only from executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning and distills the filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states. We prove that filter distillation loss bounds the policy's constraint violation and hence how far agents can cross their safety margin, so errors never accumulate. When distillation states cover deployed states, the loss also bounds the collision probability at every step. Without a filter and acting only on local observations, our policies have no collisions in 1,800 test episodes with multiple agents. A policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to teams of twenty at constant per-agent computation and stays collision-free with up to eight agents. We test our policies on Crazyflie quadrotors with up to five flying at the same time.
authors: Srikar Babu Gadipudi, Somayeh Sojoudi, Claire J. Tomlin
bullets: CBF safety filters make training safer but scale poorly because team constraints grow quadratically with team size.
The method learns only from executed safe actions using implicit Q-learning and distills filter behavior at synthetic near-collision states.
Theory bounds policy constraint violations—and, with sufficient state coverage, per-step collision probability—through distillation loss.
Filter-free policies had no collisions in 1,800 multi-agent test episodes and transferred from three-agent training to teams of up to twenty with constant per-agent computation.
The approach was also tested on Crazyflie quadrotors, with up to five flying simultaneously.
