papers.abstract: JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA.
authors: Tao An, Weihang Liang, Tianqi Wang, Chuqing Cao, Wenming Tan, Kai Zhang, Haibo Lei, Tao Xie, Lijun Zhao, Ruifeng Li
bullets: Addresses the high online cost of repeatedly evaluating candidate action sequences in JEPA-based world models.
Generates an action proposal, predicts future scenes and proprioceptive states, then iteratively refines the same plan using the task goal.
Combines goal-discrepancy residual feedback with future-scene context feedback for chunk-wise action refinement.
Learns the action generation and predictive feedback process from offline demonstrations.
Evaluated on short-horizon reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution, achieving competitive performance with a compact model and low online computation.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.
authors: Jieyuan Pei, Xin Yan, Mingwei Xu, Haiyi Zhang, Siyu Zou, Zhangyi Hu, Zhuoxuan Li, Yuguang Yang, Rongjunchen Zhang, Cheng Chi, Hui Xiong, Yan Wang
bullets: Uses the VLM’s pre-decoding hidden state to drive and answer scene questions without autoregressive generation.
A linear head scores 5,273 fixed candidate trajectories, enabling offline reward weighting and exact expected-reward reinforcement learning.
Maintains visual capabilities with multiple-choice training and limits drift with KL regularization.
Plans in 84 ms—six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0—while matching or exceeding it on reported driving benchmarks.
Performance remains comparable under delays up to 300 ms but degrades beyond that; at 1.2 s, it falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its native latency.

papers.selection_reason: Uses VLM hidden state as a fast one-pass driving policy; relevant to VLA and inference efficiency.
papers.title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
papers.tldr: SuperGlance converts a decoder-only vision-language model into a fast, one-pass driving policy while preserving its visual question-answering ability.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable embodied artificial intelligence (AI) by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Emerging use cases in physical AI are expected to drive the need for efficient inference and communication, as the computational demands of the VLA models pose challenges for real-time control with limited onboard resources. Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). A Lagrangian-constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) approach, namely trust region policy optimization Lagrangian (TRPO-Lag), learns to balance task performance and resource consumption under varying wireless conditions and task requirements. We evaluate the framework using LIBERO manipulation tasks, profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced wireless channels. Experimental results demonstrate that TRPO-Lag achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success rate compared to benchmark CDRL methods.
bullets: Targets efficient real-time VLA inference for physically embodied AI with limited onboard resources.
Jointly adapts where inference runs and when latent reasoning should stop based on wireless conditions and task needs.
Models the decision process as a constrained Markov decision process and solves it with TRPO-Lag.
Evaluated on LIBERO manipulation tasks using profiled VLA costs and ray-traced wireless channels.
Achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success than benchmark constrained deep-RL methods.

Fig. 3: Training Performance and Normalized Constraint Costs

Fig. 6: TRPO-Lag action distribution by task suite the offline characteristics in Fig. 2. TRPO-Lag predominantly selects τ = 10−3 for Goal and Object, preserving high task success while requiring fewer recurrent iterations than stricter thresholds. For LIBERO-10, which comprises longer-horizon tasks, it selects τ = 5 × 10−4 in approximately 82% of requests, consistent with the substantial success degradation observed at larger thresholds. Location selection complements these decisions: Spatial and LIBERO-10 are offloaded in 63.0% and 67.9% of requests, whereas Goal and Object are primarily executed locally. These results indicate that TRPOLag also learns suite-dependent operating points that preserve task success while reducing inference latency and managing shared edge resources.

papers.title: Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models in Physical AI

papers.abstract: Cyber-physical-human systems close a loop around people by sensing human behavior, predict it and act on it. Human teams are a natural target, because collaboration breaks down in ways that a timely prompt could prevent. Collaborative mixed reality makes this loop practical, since each headset senses who speaks, where its wearer looks and who stands together, and it can deliver a light prompt. In this loop, the headsets are sensors, the prompts are actuators and the team is the plant. Closing the loop needs a plant model that is small enough to learn from few teams, safe to iterate and readable by a designer. We propose ANCHOR, which models a team as a ball in an energy bowl. The bottom of the bowl is where the team rests, and it is set by the team's recent behavior, its own history and other teams. Formally, ANCHOR is a switched port-Hamiltonian system with 52 parameters, and each part stands for a testable claim from team psychology. Because of this structure, for any fitted parameters, a forecast moves away from rest only when task progress or a prompt pushes it, and prompts of bounded size that are spaced in time move it a bounded distance. On \nGroups{} four-person teams held out from training, a team that drifts from its usual behavior returns most of the way within half a minute. After 32 s, about 24% of the deviation remains, and ANCHOR predicted 30%. Forecasts are clearly better when the resting point blends its three sources than when it uses one. ANCHOR matches the accuracy of a black-box baseline with about 40,000 parameters. It anticipates conversation collapse with an AUROC of 0.85. In simulation under assumed prompt effects, it removes 2.2 times as much breakdown time per prompt as periodic prompting.
bullets: Models teams as a ball settling in an energy bowl whose resting point reflects recent behavior, team history, and other teams.
Uses 52 psychologically motivated parameters, designed for learning from few teams and supporting safe, interpretable prompting.
On held-out four-person teams, it predicted recovery from behavioral drift and retained 30% of the deviation after 32 seconds, versus about 24% observed.
Matched a roughly 40,000-parameter black-box baseline and detected conversation collapse with AUROC 0.85.
In simulation with assumed prompt effects, it removed 2.2× more breakdown time per prompt than periodic prompting.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ANCHOR, a Port-Hamiltonian model for forecasting human team dynamics in mixed reality loops, directly relevant to embodied AI agents and world models for environment prediction.
papers.title: ANCHOR: A Port-Hamiltonian Model for Forecasting Team Dynamics in Human-in-the-Loop Systems
papers.tldr: ANCHOR is an interpretable, compact port-Hamiltonian model that forecasts and helps prevent breakdowns in human team dynamics.

papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the maximal safe set and a safety filter for a given obstacle configuration, but it must be re-solved whenever the obstacles change, which a deployed robot cannot afford. Learning a single value function conditioned on the obstacle set removes the re-solve, yet it sharpens the central weakness of learned reachability: one network must now cover a whole family of safety problems, and its approximation error carries no preferred sign, so rare obstacle configurations silently produce false-safe states. To address these challenges, we present a conditioned reachability model designed so that the remaining error falls on the conservative side. Specifically, our method caps the obstacle margin, which makes the value function provably local, in the sense that obstacles farther than a known threshold cannot affect it, so the model reads only a body-frame window, trains on small scenes, and transfers to scenes of any size with millisecond per-scene preparation. Moreover, the output structure builds the value bound into the model. By training with counterexample mining over the finite-dimensional window configuration space, we maximize the claimed safe volume subject to the HJ inequality, so the learned set grows toward the true safe set from the conservative side. Across all tested obstacle settings, ours is the only method that combines recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach training with near-zero rollout collisions. We also extend the method to a 10D quadrotor, again with markedly lower collision rates than the baselines.
bullets: Targets the cost of re-solving HJ reachability whenever obstacles change and the false-safe errors of a single conditioned network.
Caps the obstacle margin to make the value function provably local, enabling body-frame window inputs, small-scene training, and scene-size transfer.
Uses an output structure that enforces conservative value bounds and counterexample mining to expand the learned safe set under the HJ inequality.

papers.abstract: Integrating MLLM-based agents with robotic foundation models has attracted increasing attention as a means of enhancing robotic capabilities. However, the improvement of such integrated systems remains largely decoupled across their agent and model components, with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other, substantially limiting the capabilities of the combined system. As both MLLMs and robotic foundation models become increasingly capable, fully realizing their combined potential calls for co-evolution, an iterative process in which improvements in agents and robotic foundation models reinforce one another. We propose RoboCoEvo, a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of the agent's explicit and reusable executable knowledge with parameter learning in robotic foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models. Through a code-as-policy formulation, the agent develops and refines executable failure-detection and recovery programs, generating targeted corrective experience. Post-training consolidates the resulting corrective behaviors into the robotic model's end-to-end policy, improving autonomous task execution. Changes in the updated policy's failure distribution, in turn, guide subsequent revisions to the agent's programs. Experiments on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin demonstrate sustained improvements in autonomous VLA task performance across successive co-evolution rounds.
authors: Ran Qi, Yixin Xiao, Dawei Wang, Zhiyuan Li, Jinbang Huang, Xuan Zhao, Yintao Ma, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited gains from improving robot agents and models independently.
Uses code-as-policy so agents create reusable programs for failure detection and recovery.
Converts corrective experiences into end-to-end policy updates for vision-language-action models.
Uses the updated model’s changing failure distribution to guide further agent-program refinement.
Experiments across BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin show sustained performance gains over successive rounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RoboCoEvo. The co-evolution framework of agent and policy improving each other over successive rounds. (a) Policy-Guided Agent Evolution: the agent locates failures in the policy’s failed rollouts and groups recurring failures into failure modes (FMs), shown at the top for each round. For each FM, it writes a detector that identifies the failure state in a rollout (red) and a recovery program that completes the failed subtask from this state in simulation (green). As the policy improves, its rollouts expose FMs that did not occur in earlier rounds. In each subsequent round, the agent writes detectors and recovery programs for the newly identified FMs and refines those of persisting FMs to improve detection accuracy and recovery success. (b) Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion: the policy is fine-tuned on the corrective experience together with the original demonstrations, which enables the policy itself to avoid or recover from the targeted failures. The rollouts of the updated policy initiate the next round, and its task success increases over successive rounds. The scores compare the base policy with the policy after RoboCoEvo.

Figure 2: The RoboCoEvo pipeline. Each round proceeds clockwise, starting with rollouts of the current policy πi. Policy-Guided Agent Evolution (right): the agent identifies failure modes (FMs) from K sampled failures and writes a detector dm for each FM. The detectors localize failure states in all failed rollouts, from which the agent writes a recovery program ρm for each FM. Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion (left): failure-conditioned augmentation perturbs each localized state s into J states s̃j of the same FM, and ρm completes the failed subtask from both the original and the perturbed states, which yields the corrective experience Ri. The policy is then post-trained on D0 and the accumulated corrective experience to obtain πi+1, whose rollouts start the next round. Steps marked with circular arrows are updated in every round.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of the base policy and RoboCoEvo on targeted failure modes. Each row shows one failure mode on one benchmark. Left: the base policy π0 enters the failure mode and fails to recover. Right: after RoboCoEvo, π1 enters the same failure mode and recovers without the agent. Frames are aligned by stage.

Figure 3: Failure-conditioned augmentation on two BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. From an observed failure state s (left), the agent edits the robot and object states in the simulator to obtain perturbed states s̃1, s̃2, . . . (right) that preserve the same FM. Each perturbed state serves as an additional initial state for the recovery program, so a single observed failure yields multiple recovery runs.

Figure 5: Per-FM failure rates on RoboTwin, first round. Base vs. first-round policy, first-round detectors. Each spoke is a targeted FM, and shaded sectors group the FMs by task. Bars give the fraction of the task’s test episodes that fail with the FM never recovered from, before (yellow) and after (blue) the round; gray marks their overlap.
Figure 6: Per-FM failure rates on RoboTwin, second round. First-round vs. second-round policy, detectors after the second round of co-evolution. Same format as Figure 5.
Figure 7: Per-FM failure rates on RoboCasa (XR-1). Same format as Figure 5. Round 1 uses the first-round detectors and Round 2 the detectors after the second round.
Figure 8: Per-FM failure rates on BEHAVIOR-1K, tasks 0 to 5. Same format as Figure 5. Round 1 uses the first-round detectors and Round 2 the detectors after the second round.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: https://clmoro.github.io/cast.
bullets: Addresses deployment-time constraints not present in demonstrations without retraining the policy.
Samples several action chunks, certifies them with a barrier condition, then selects the highest-valued certified chunk.
Certification guarantees safety independently of the critic and bounds deviation from the policy conditioned on feasibility.
CAST-V estimates policy-conditioned viability to preserve future safe control authority; CAST-VL learns it from controller logs.
Across manipulation, quadrotor, humanoid, and unicycle tasks, CAST generally improves joint task-and-constraint success over output filtering.

(a) A safety filter keeps the robot in the safe set h ≥ 0 (shading: the barrier), but its rollouts on the blocked route stall at the zone: the policy never learned to continue from there (40 rollouts, with counts). (b) Viability v of the policy’s certified chunks, by simulation: the probability that it keeps sampling certified chunks over the next 8 decisions. Certified chunks exist in the red region too, but lead to a dead end; of the N = 8 drawn at one decision four head into it, and CAST-V executes a viable one. (d) Joint success on 500 unseen zones per policy; CAST, CAST-V and CASTVL use the task critic, MPPI the model, map and goal.

Figure 10: Two diagnostics. (a) Viability or success as the learning target? Both networks are trained on the same logged episodes of the critic-free controller, with the same features, architecture and recipe; only the label differs (viability of the executed chunk, or the episode’s joint success). Unicycle, unseen zones, three policies × 500 scored scenarios; bands: 95 % intervals, and at 100 episodes the range of three disjoint subsets, in each of which viability is ahead. Theorem 1 covers the second group; none of its episodes violated.

papers.selection_reason: Runtime safety certification and viability-aware action selection for frozen diffusion robot policies; directly relevant to embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
papers.tldr: CAST safely steers frozen diffusion policies at runtime by certifying sampled action chunks, ranking viable options, and avoiding future dead ends.

papers.abstract: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.
bullets: Studies deployment-time compute allocation for a frozen chunked robot policy: more denoising per call versus more frequent replanning.
Evaluates both nominal compute rate and total compute per completed attempt, using discovery and held-out task comparisons.

In synchronous LIBERO simulation with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint and chunk length K=50, d=2 with h=2 achieved 139/160 successes versus 122/160 for d=5, while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step.

papers.abstract: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.
authors: Yiting Chen, Kelin Yu, Sarthak Kaingade, Bryan Trinh, Kaiyu Hang, Roberto Martin-martin, Nima Fazeli, X. Alice Wu
bullets: Addresses forceful multi-finger manipulation under uncertain contact and interaction dynamics, beyond geometry-based interaction.
Uses tactile-observable interaction representations with cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contacts.
Adapts motor behavior from tactile history while coordinating an upper-body manipulation policy with a pretrained locomotion controller.
Trained entirely in simulation and transferred zero-shot to a Unitree G1 with multi-fingered hands.
Substantially outperforms standard RMA and reactive tactile-policy baselines across four real-world commercial round doorknobs.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation. (a) The upper-body manipulation policy commands the right arm and hand, while a pretrained locomotion controller commands the leg and waist joints to maintain whole-body balance under interaction-induced disturbances. The two policies share whole-body proprioceptive feedback, coupling manipulation and balance within an integrated control system. (b) Each fingertip contact force is parameterized in cone coordinates by the normal load n, force cone angle α , and circularly encoded shear direction (sinφ ,cosφ). This formulation separates the uncertainty source while preserving the contact mechanics. (c) The policy learning proceeds in two stages. First, the privileged encoder and tactile-centric policy are optimized jointly end-to-end under the task objective, forming an oracle policy and yielding a task-relevant interaction latent. Both modules are then frozen, and the adaptation encoder is trained through latent regression to estimate the interaction latent from a 2s history of deployable observations. (d) During real-world deployment, the adaptation encoder updates the interaction latent online from tactile interaction history and conditions the frozen tactile-centric policy to generate manipulation motor commands.

papers.abstract: Robots in homes, warehouses and farms must pick up objects they have never seen, usually without a 3D model or a category label. A grasping policy that works directly on the point cloud from a depth sensor needs only the geometry the robot observes, so it applies to any new object. Offline grasp generators such as Contact-GraspNet work this way, but they rank grasps by learned plausibility rather than by whether the grasp actually lifts the object. Reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize for that directly and make a point-cloud grasping policy much better on average, yet it leaves specific grasps persistently unsolved. We present a human-in-the-loop failure loop that targets those grasps: situations an RL policy keeps failing are mined automatically, sent to a virtual-reality application where a person picks the object up with their own hands, and returned to training as two grasp points. The person contributes only where to grasp; the robot chooses its own approach. In simulation, RL raises success on unseen objects from 55% with Contact-GraspNet to 83%. Adding 58 human demonstrations nearly doubles success on the hard cases RL kept failing, from 24% to 45%, and recovers performance that RL alone loses on similar cases that were never demonstrated, without reducing success on unseen objects.
authors: Achyuthan Unni Krishnan, Karthik Rengarajan, Bharath Narasimhan, Chris von Csefalvay
bullets: Targets objects and grasps that an RL policy repeatedly fails to lift, without requiring object models or category labels.
Humans demonstrate only where to grasp in VR; the robot independently selects its approach.
In simulation, RL improves unseen-object success from 55% with Contact-GraspNet to 83%.
Adding 58 demonstrations raises success on persistent hard cases from 24% to 45%.
The method also recovers performance on similar undemonstrated cases without reducing unseen-object success.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.
authors: Mohamed Salim Aissi, Olivier Sigaud, Laure Soulier, Nicolas Thome
bullets: VLA fine-tuning on robot demonstrations can cause catastrophic forgetting of the original VLM’s language and visual grounding.
The method decomposes the VLA–VLM task vector with SVD and learns per-component mixing coefficients.
Coefficients are optimized to balance action prediction with vision-language capabilities.
Experiments show strong performance on both capabilities and consistent gains over established merging baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our VLM–VLA merging method. (a) The task vector ∆(l) is extracted by subtracting the VLM weights from the VLA weights for each layer l. (b) ∆(l) is decomposed via Singular Value Decomposition, revealing the orthogonal directions of adaptation introduced during VLA fine-tuning. (c) A scalar mixing coefficient α (l) k is assigned to each singular component, controlling how much of each direction is retained in the merged model. The coefficients α are optimised by minimising a composite objective that jointly penalises degradation of language generation quality and action prediction accuracy with respect to both source models.

Figure 1: (Left) Given the same visual scene, a VLM responds accurately to descriptive language prompts but produces no action output. Fine-tuning into a VLA enables action prediction from a task goal, but at the cost of language grounding — the VLA generates incoherent text when prompted with the same descriptive query. Our merged model recovers both capabilities, producing coherent language responses while retaining the ability to predict actions. (Right) The VLM achieves strong language performance but cannot act, while VLAs excel at manipulation but lose language capability. Our merged models are the only ones that achieve the best of both worlds, reaching the upper-right region of the trade-off space.

Figure 6: Per-layer similarity to source models. (Top) Oursπ0Fast . (Bottom) Oursπ0.5 . For each of the 602 weight matrices, we compute the cosine similarity between the VLM and VLA weights (blue), between the merged model and the VLM (orange), and between the merged model and the VLA (green). In both cases, the merged model is consistently closer to the VLA than to the VLM across all layers, while remaining well above the VLM–VLA baseline throughout.

Figure 8: Qualitative captioning examples. Given the same visual observation, the VLM produces coherent scene descriptions, the VLA (π0.5) generates fragmented or incomplete text due to catastrophic forgetting, and Oursπ0.5 merged model recovers meaningful captions while retaining action capabilities.

Figure 5: Effect of SVD rank. (Left) Training losses for varying rank r ∈ {4, 16, 64, 256, 1024, full}: Ltext is largely insensitive to rank, while Lact improves markedly with higher rank, indicating that the VLA adaptation is diffuse across many singular components. (Right) Downstream evaluation confirms this asymmetry: ROUGE-L saturates from r = 16, while LIBERO success rate requires r ≥ 1024 to exceed 90% — language recovery needs far fewer singular directions than action preservation.

Figure 7: Mean α vs. rank index. (Top) Oursπ0.5 . (Bottom) Oursπ0Fast . For each rank index k, we average α (l) k across all 602 layers. Both VLA variants show the same overall pattern: mean α is near 0 for the most dominant directions and rises monotonically toward the tail of the spectrum, confirming that this asymmetry is not specific to a single action decoding strategy.

Figure 3: Qualitative captioning examples. Given the same visual observation, the VLM produces coherent scene descriptions, the VLA (π0.5) generates fragmented or incomplete text due to catastrophic forgetting, and Oursπ0.5 merged model recovers meaningful captions while retaining action capabilities.

Figure 4: Granularity of mixing coefficients. We compare two levels of granularity for α — per-layer and per-component (ours) — and report the evolution of Ltext, Lact, DKL(πα∥πVLM) and DKL(πα∥πVLA) over training. Per-component α converges to substantially lower values on every metric, confirming that fine-grained SVD-based control is essential to simultaneously preserve language and action capabilities.

Table 1: Vision-language, embodied reasoning, and robot manipulation performance of all methods. The pure VLM cannot act, and both VLAs lose language and reasoning ability despite strong action performance. Existing merging baselines largely collapse on manipulation, while our merged models recover strong performance on all three axes simultaneously, without retraining either source model.
Table 4: Task success rate (%) on three RoboCasa kitchen tasks. All fixed-coefficient merging baselines collapse to zero, while our merged models retain meaningful performance on both VLA variants.
Table 3: Hyperparameters used to optimise α for each VLA variant. λ1, λ2 weight Ltext and Lact respectively; λ3, λ4 weight the KL regularisation terms toward the VLM and VLA respectively.

Table 2: Contribution of each loss component. We ablate each term of the training objective and evaluate using ROUGE-L for language quality and Success Rate SR for action predictions. Best results in bold.

papers.abstract: This report presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' 1:10 scale autonomous vehicle, developed at Shahid Beheshti University's Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory. The platform integrates a custom mechanical chassis, a distributed embedded system based on ESP32 microcontrollers, and a Jetson Orin NX module for high-level perception and control. The embedded layer manages sensor interfacing, real-time data acquisition, and actuator control, while the Jetson handles environment perception through deep-learning--based lane, sign, and traffic light detection, as well as decision-making and trajectory control. System communication is achieved via structured UART links, ensuring synchronized operation between perception and control subsystems. The vehicle's software stack incorporates ROS, modular firmware design, and multiple control algorithms---Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit---to achieve stable autonomous navigation in structured driving scenarios. The overall system demonstrates robust performance and reliability in urban-like environments, serving as a modular research platform for future autonomous driving studies.
authors: Marya Sabouri Dodaran, Ali Taheri Garakani, Mandana Shabanzadeh Nasrollah-Abadi, Yousef Ashrafi, Mohammad Mahdi Azimi, Erfan Nekouei Ghahfarokhi, Amirhossein Kheiri Holighi, Seyyed Sobhan Hosseini Hajibakandeh, Matin Jamshidi, Amirhossein Gholizadeh Behbahani, Mohammad Hossein Moaiyeri
bullets: Integrates a custom chassis, ESP32 microcontrollers, and a Jetson Orin NX.
Uses deep-learning perception for lane, traffic-sign, and traffic-light detection.
Employs ROS, modular firmware, and UART communication between embedded and high-level systems.
Supports Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit controllers for trajectory control and navigation.
Demonstrates robust and reliable operation in urban-like, structured driving scenarios.

papers.abstract: Single-pass primitive decoders such as LocateAnything and VFlash predict all quantized coordinate tokens of a geometric primitive in one forward pass, enabling fast, System-1 visual planning. We study what matters when such a decoder serves as a System-1 world model: a fast action-conditioned predictor that ranks candidate pushes by their predicted outcome. On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (512 held-out test families, 8,192 rollouts) and on human demonstrations from lerobot/pusht (2,384 test windows), we compare decoders, training losses, rigid-body projections and coordinate frames, using matched checkpoints, hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm correction. Two factors of similar size dominate. First, expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object's initial pose lowers decision regret by 1.9-2.2x for each of five decoders, and the object-frame model trained on 128 families matches the world-frame model trained on 512. Second, single-pass decoding outperforms iterative decoding: in the object frame, single-pass heads reach 0.020-0.021 regret at 1.6-1.8 ms per decision, against 0.046 for 10-step DDIM diffusion and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression at 10.3 and 12.9 ms. The choice among single-pass heads has no measurable effect on regret, and our registered hypothesis that the frame effect exceeds the decoder spread is not supported. Soft-token expectation with an end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection gives the lowest trajectory error (11.35 px on ManiSkill3, 3.78 px on lerobot/pusht), exact rigid-body consistency, and lower regret than diffusion at every budget from 4 to 50 DDIM steps, at 3-29x lower latency.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.
authors: Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, Chao Zhang

Introduces video-SALMONN-VEX, an audio-visual computer-use agent, and AGGO to optimize video-derived guidance for action prediction.
Augments AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with more than 24K real-world tutorial videos.
Reports a 22% relative OSWorld success increase over the Qwen3.5 backbone; generated guidance also improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong capabilities as generalist agents that perceive, reason, and act in interactive environments. Yet real-time environments such as video games demand both deliberate control for exploration and split-second reactions to fast-moving hazards. Existing agents struggle to handle both: relying solely on direct VLM actions is too slow for sudden events, whereas delegating execution to fixed scripts leaves the agent blind at the moment of action, leading to frequent misfires whenever the scene shifts. Humans overcome this by pairing normal conscious control with conditioned reflexes-while the mind handles deliberate actions and shapes reflex rules, the reflex itself still relies on live vision to make the final instant decision. Emulating this mechanism, we propose ViCoR (Visual Conditioned Reflex). Alongside normal gameplay actions, the main VLM defines and updates lightweight situational guidance for recurring events, while a fast visual reflex branch (invoking the VLM in no-thinking mode) inspects live local views with motion cues to make the final sub-second action decisions. By offloading 67.8% of high-frequency reactions to the reflex branch (680 ms per check), ViCoR reduces average per-action decision latency by 2.6x (from 14.0 s to 5.4 s) and cuts token consumption by 36.9%. Across 17 diverse 2D and 3D games in the GameWorld benchmark, ViCoR achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving task success rate by +11.8% (from 52.9% to 64.7%) and average normalized progress by +13.9% (from 66.5% to 80.4%) over the strongest deliberative VLM and script baselines. In fast-paced real-time games, ViCoR refines its reflexes across episodes to boost progress by 1.67x, and even with a low-effort main planner, surpasses high-effort deliberative baselines by +8.1% at one-third of the token cost.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between slow deliberative VLM actions and brittle fixed scripts in fast-changing environments.
Uses a main VLM to guide recurring situations and a fast visual reflex branch to make final, sub-second decisions from live views and motion cues.
Offloads 67.8% of high-frequency reactions, reducing average decision latency 2.6× and token use by 36.9%.
Across 17 GameWorld games, improves task success from 52.9% to 64.7% and normalized progress from 66.5% to 80.4%.

papers.abstract: Training generalist GUI agents requires large volumes of interaction trajectories comprising screenshot sequences paired with grounded UI actions, yet collecting such data through human demonstration is expensive and difficult to scale. Although public software tutorial videos contain rich operational demonstrations, their continuous pixel streams lack discrete action boundaries, semantic intents, and precise spatial coordinates, making them difficult to use directly for model training. To address this, we present T2T (Tutorial-to-Trajectory), a fully automated pipeline for synthesizing GUI agent trajectories at scale. T2T spans desktop, web, and mobile platforms to convert unannotated video tutorials into structured, executable interaction trajectories. To guarantee trajectory quality, T2T combines active segment filtering, keyframe identification via localized UI change, shortcut-free observation frame selection, presence-aware grounding, and two-stage action-space normalization. These refined trajectories are then converted into multi-task training views spanning navigation, planning, forward dynamics, and grounding. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B on a subset of the more than one million human-annotation-free training samples generated by this pipeline. Evaluations show that the model achieves consistent gains across multiple benchmarks covering desktop, web, and mobile environments, including OSWorld-G, ScreenSpot-Pro, AndroidControl, and AgentNetBench, indicating improved core capabilities in grounding, step-level instruction execution, and trajectory-level decision-making. Notably, all gains are achieved without any in-distribution training data from target domains. Learning exclusively from trajectories extracted from public videos via the T2T pipeline, the model exhibits cross-application and cross-task generalization capabilities.
authors: Qingsong Xie, Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, Jiacheng Tang, Madalina Ciobanu, Navan Preet Singh, Qingqing Mao, Ritankar Das

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are vulnerable to adversarial visual perturbations, while defenses often require task-specific adversarial fine-tuning. We investigate whether robustness learned on source manipulation tasks can protect independently specialized target policies without target-side adversarial training. We first show that even a single source defense update improves robustness on held-out tasks, establishing cross-task defense reuse independently of multi-source aggregation. To combine source updates, we introduce Source-Norm Transferable Robustness Vector (SN-TRV), which retains the direction of their mean while calibrating its magnitude using source-update norms. The resulting update is applied to the target visual encoder without target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or additional inference modules. Evaluations across three VLA backbones, fixed and adaptive attacks, and different source defense recipes show improved robustness over naive averaging and identify limits in attack coverage. Physical PiPER trials increase average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.
authors: Jinquan Zhang, Run Yang, Dongfu Yin, Qiang Lai, Yufeng Yan, Pengshuai Yin, F. Richard Yu
bullets: A single source-task defense update already improves robustness on held-out target tasks.
SN-TRV combines source defense updates by preserving their mean direction while calibrating update magnitude from source norms.
The transferred update modifies only the target visual encoder and requires no target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or inference modules.
Across three VLA backbones and fixed/adaptive attacks, SN-TRV outperforms naive averaging, though attack coverage remains a limitation.
Physical PiPER trials raise average success against printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.

papers.abstract: Efficient aerial visual-language navigation (VLN) requires reducing model storage and inference costs while maintaining instruction-conditioned action prediction. We present ARC-VLN, a token-type-aware recursive computation framework built on a language backbone with shared parameters. ARC-VLN retains full-depth computation for text and action tokens while adaptively selecting exit depths for visual tokens. Representations of early-exiting visual tokens are retained, and active-token compaction shortens the sequences processed by subsequent recursive blocks. To mitigate routing collapse to a single exit depth, we design a dedicated learning strategy that encourages the model to distribute visual tokens across multiple exit depths.On OpenFly's Test-Seen and Test-Unseen subsets, ARC-VLN achieves the lowest navigation error and the highest success rate and success weighted by path length among all compared methods. Meanwhile, it reduces the average number of decision steps per trajectory, total floating-point operations, mean model inference time per trajectory, and average GPU memory usage during inference, indicating its great potential as a VLN backbone for lightweight applications.
authors: Xiang Zhang, Xiangyu Dong, Yang Lu, Xiaoguang Ma
bullets: Targets lower storage, computation, latency, and memory costs in instruction-conditioned aerial VLN.
Uses shared-parameter recursive computation with token-type-aware routing: text and action tokens run to full depth, while visual tokens exit adaptively.
Retains early-exited visual representations and compacts active tokens to shorten later processing.
Introduces a learning strategy that distributes visual tokens across multiple exit depths and avoids routing collapse.
On OpenFly Test-Seen and Test-Unseen, reports the best navigation error, success rate, and success weighted by path length among compared methods, while also reducing inference costs.

papers.abstract: Agentic ecosystems are emerging as a new platform layer in which agents maintain persistent memory, retrieve from shared knowledge bases, execute through tool interfaces, and coordinate through shared states. These capabilities create a security problem that per-turn defenses miss: compromise can accumulate across sessions, agents, and system layers before visible failure. We define this threat as Agentic Sleeper, a system-level adversary that first behaves legitimately, gains routing trust, and later activates across memory, agent logic, and infrastructure. We formulate defense as inference under partial observability and propose Swarm Shepherd, a system-level defense framework centered on an inference filter for early warning, paired with a backward trace-back module for entry attribution. Our analysis yields a two-scale deployment rule that balances longer event histories against broader agent coverage. Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper drift begins 2.7--8.9$\times$ faster than natural baselines, propagates across agents on most topologies, and evades per-turn and stateful defenses above 80\%. Swarm Shepherd warns at least three sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions when failure is scored by the benchmark's own task grader), while trace-back reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 over 24 variants. The two-scale deployment rule is empirically confirmed, and in live end-to-end runs on LangGraph and AutoGen the posterior-guided defense stack drives cross-agent propagation below the self-sustaining regime, which removing only the visibly compromised agent does not achieve.
bullets: Targets “Agentic Sleeper” attacks that appear legitimate initially, accumulate across sessions and agents, then activate across memory, logic, and infrastructure.
Frames defense as partially observed inference, combining an early-warning inference filter with backward trace-back for entry attribution.
Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, sleeper drift is 2.7–8.9× faster than natural baselines and often evades existing defenses.
Warns at least three sessions before visible degradation and achieves 0.69 top-1 trace-back accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 across 24 variants.
Live LangGraph and AutoGen evaluations show posterior-guided defense reduces propagation below the self-sustaining regime; removing only visibly compromised agents does not.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses security in multi-agent ecosystems (Swarm Shepherd), focusing on memory, shared states, and agent coordination, which are core components of embodied AI and agent systems.
papers.title: Swarm Shepherd: Securing Multi-Agent Ecosystems Against Persistent Latent Compromise
papers.tldr: Swarm Shepherd detects and traces persistent, cross-agent compromises early enough to suppress self-sustaining propagation in multi-agent ecosystems.

papers.abstract: Depth-aware augmented reality on phones needs dense geometry of the surrounding room. iPhones and iPads without LiDAR expose only sparse feature points and detected planes, and ARKit often takes tens of seconds to report the first wall. We describe a scan-free pipeline for these devices. A point-map network (MoGe-2) predicts metric geometry from each camera frame, the remaining depth shift is recovered from the camera intrinsics, and each frame's scale is aligned to views already in the map. A persistent voxel map with visibility-based expiry answers occlusion and collision queries. Co-located devices share one coordinate frame by solving yaw and floor-plane translation from sightings of each other. We evaluate the deployed system on 309 device-sessions from 19 device models without LiDAR, with 179 device-sessions from LiDAR phones in the same deployment as a reference population. A first dense depth map was recorded within 10 s in 80% of sessions, while ARKit had reported a wall plane by then in 25%. The median session scale was 0.98 against ARKit's wall planes and 1.00 against its camera translation. Scale changed by a median of 9% between nearby frames, against 0.4% with LiDAR, and depth points spread three times as widely around walls. In multi-device sessions, 69% of devices without LiDAR reached a converged shared frame, against 84% of LiDAR phones. The main remaining error is scale that changes from frame to frame.
bullets: Addresses slow and sparse room geometry reconstruction on non-LiDAR iPhones and iPads.
Uses MoGe-2 to predict metric geometry, recovers depth shift from camera intrinsics, and aligns frame scales to an existing map.
Maintains a persistent voxel map for occlusion and collision queries, while co-locating devices via shared sightings, yaw, and floor-plane translation.
Across 309 non-LiDAR device-sessions, dense depth appeared within 10 seconds in 80% of sessions, versus wall-plane detection by ARKit in 25%.
Shared-frame convergence reached 69% for non-LiDAR devices, compared with 84% for LiDAR phones; scale variability and wall-spread depth errors remained higher.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon reinforcement learning under sparse and delayed feedback remains an open challenge. Existing return-decomposition methods redistribute episodic rewards to ease credit assignment, but they operate on raw state--action transitions and disregard the subgoal structure that governs meaningful progress in complex tasks. We propose Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework in which a vision--language model identifies the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model generates a matching latent reward formulation through a two-stage prompting process. By conditioning reward signals on the currently active subgoal, Skill-LR produces stage-specific credit that evolves with the hierarchical plan, reducing temporal variance and improving sample efficiency. On multi-stage MiniGrid and BabyAI benchmarks, including DoorKey and Unlock-to-Unlock, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse environmental rewards and strong credit-assignment baselines such as RUDDER and LaRe, demonstrating that subgoal-aligned latent rewards offer a principled path toward stable, interpretable credit assignment in long-horizon tasks.
bullets: Targets sparse, delayed feedback and the limitations of transition-level return decomposition.
A vision-language model identifies the active subgoal at each timestep.
A two-stage LLM prompting process generates a matching latent reward formulation.
Subgoal-conditioned rewards reduce temporal variance and improve sample efficiency.
On MiniGrid and BabyAI tasks, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse rewards, RUDDER, and LaRe.

This suggests that subgoal-conditioned latent reward decomposition yields a more stable and learnable return-modeling objective in more challenging hierarchical tasks.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision. Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction. We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.
bullets: Addresses robot learning from human videos without action supervision.
Builds on a pretrained VLM with a mixture-of-training architecture for shared action and representation prediction.
Uses future visual-state prediction as an independent, complementary signal to action prediction.
Egocentric-video representations improve downstream performance, with larger gains as video data scales.
Studies objective design and data curation for scalable use of action-free video.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architecture Overview of SPAR. Starting from a common VLA [8, 9], SPAR extends it with a generation expert that mirrors the action expert design, and predicts the representation of the future visual state simultaneously. Robot data supervises both experts, while the egocentric videos supervise only the generation expert. The VLM backbone can therefore be optimized with heterogeneous data composition. The generation expert is removed at inference.

papers.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
authors: Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Junxian Guo, Fangzhou Zhao, Yilong Zhao, Zekai Li, Xingyang Li, Yuyang Zhao, Song Bian, Zhijian Liu, Song Han

papers.abstract: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
bullets: Addresses the heuristic assumptions and sensitive hyperparameters used by existing self-supervised movement-representation methods.
Predicts in latent space rather than reconstructing precise joint configurations, aligning with semantic anticipation of actions.
Uses forward and backward autoregressive prediction to exploit temporal ordering and combine past and future context at inference.
Separates prediction targets into global sequence semantics and local context-independent movement to prevent representation collapse.
Performs strongly on motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most reported metrics.

papers.abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
authors: Tony H. Zhang, Connor Mattson, Daniel S. Brown
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting demonstrations for multiple agents simultaneously.
Uses Round-Robin Behavior Cloning to train initial per-agent imitation policies.
At each step, centralized critics choose among imitation- and RL-proposed actions for each agent.
A gated, Q-filtered cloning penalty regularizes RL toward imitation only when imitation actions are judged better.

Across four cooperative benchmarks, IBMARL improves beyond imitation faster than demonstration-based baselines and can exceed demonstrator performance; it also outpaces imitation learning with real human demonstrations.

(5)–(6)). Right: the critics bootstrap through the same arbiter (Eq. (7)), and the actor loss adds the gated imitation term (Eqs. (8)–(9))

(2) Act: each robot’s IL and RL policies propose an action, and the centralized critic ensembles choose, per robot, which one the team executes. (3) Learn: the experience trains the critics, and each RL policy is pulled toward its IL action only where the critics prefer it. At deployment, each robot runs its RL policy alone.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robots are widely used for persistent monitoring of spatiotemporal environments, where quantities of interest (QoI) change across space and time and require repeated measurements. In practice, robot motion can be affected by external disturbances that vary across the environment. When such external disturbances are not considered in trajectory optimization, it can lead to inaccurate predictions of robot motion and, consequently, the information acquired about the QoI during execution. However, estimating disturbances throughout the environment can be inefficient, as disturbances in regions with little overlap with monitoring trajectories have limited impact on monitoring performance. We therefore propose a two-stage informative planning framework for unknown, spatially varying but time-invariant disturbances, combining informed disturbance sampling with disturbance-aware trajectory optimization. First, we identify where QoI measurements are needed and generate alternative paths to these locations using the environment geometry. We then prioritize disturbance measurements based on their expected reduction of disturbance uncertainty along these paths. Second, rather than optimizing information acquisition based on nominal robot motion, we incorporate the learned disturbance belief into trajectory optimization to account for its effects on robot motion and information acquisition. Across four simulation scenarios, the proposed method reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0--52.3 percent compared with environment-wide estimation and identifies paths that appear costly under nominal dynamics but become preferable when disturbances are considered.
authors: Kaleb Ben Naveed, Haejoon Lee, Anouck Girard, Dimitra Panagou
bullets: Targets persistent monitoring when spatially varying disturbances can make nominal motion and information predictions inaccurate.
First identifies needed QoI measurements, generates candidate paths, and prioritizes disturbance sampling by expected uncertainty reduction along those paths.
Then incorporates the learned disturbance belief into disturbance-aware trajectory optimization.
Across four simulation scenarios, it reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0–52.3% versus estimating disturbances across the entire environment.
The approach can favor paths that seem costly under nominal dynamics but are preferable once disturbances are accounted for.

papers.abstract: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.
authors: Mohammad Khoshnazar, Mike Degany, Deyuan Qu, Qing Yang, Matyas Szanto
bullets: Self-play handover succeeds with the trained partner but fails with unfamiliar scripted partners.
The learned giver always offers immediately, causing the receiver to rely on one fixed rendezvous timing.
A one-second delay sharply reduces success, confirming timing overfitting as the main failure mode.
Hidden start-delay randomisation improves unseen-partner success to 80% in both seeds, versus 35–41% for a matched control.
The improvement generalises to new scenarios and held-out partners, reduces high-force contact, and requires no partner retraining.

papers.abstract: AR-Classroom uses physical models and virtual overlays to help learners explore spatial transformations. To align these overlays on a standalone headset, we developed a markerless six-degree-of-freedom(6DoF) tracker for a LEGO airplane on the Meta Quest 3. A compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders predicts 20 keypoints from dynamic RGB crops resized to 128 by 128 pixels. A perspective-n-point solver estimates the airplane's pose from these predictions and the corresponding 3D landmarks. In a paired evaluation on 1,000 synthetic validation images, cropping guided by ground-truth boxes increased the detection rate on annotated images from 32.5 to 46.2 percent. Mean keypoint F1 increased from 42.9 to 44.6 percent, with lower keypoint precision in the cropped view. In preliminary headset tests, 2 Hz was the highest tested tracking target at which the application maintained approximately 72 frames per second. A headset demonstration illustrates virtual overlay alignment with the physical airplane before and after a manual rotation. Quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage will be measured in future work.
authors: Guangxi Feng, Philip Yasskin, Wei Yan
bullets: Motivation: AR-Classroom requires robust alignment between virtual overlays and a physical manipulative during spatial-learning activities.
Method: A compact YOLO model predicts 20 airplane keypoints from 128×128 RGB crops, and a perspective-n-point solver estimates 6DoF pose from corresponding 3D landmarks.
Synthetic evaluation: Ground-truth-guided cropping improved detection on annotated images from 32.5% to 46.2% and mean keypoint F1 from 42.9% to 44.6%, while reducing keypoint precision.
On-device demonstration: The application sustained approximately 72 FPS with a tested tracking target of 2 Hz and showed overlay alignment before and after manual rotation.
Scope/limitation: Results are preliminary; quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage remains future work.

papers.abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
authors: Run Luo, Kuan Zhang, Qi Deng, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yufei Zhang, Renrong Hu, Yi Zhang, Guiyu Ma, Tianyu Fan, Longze Chen, Hao Sun, Jiaming Li, Jiaming Yang, Xiaohao Liu, Tao Tan, Minzheng Wang, Hangtian Jia, Shuai Yuan, Lvdi Wang, Xiao Liu, Chao Ma, Yuting Zou, Yinhe Zheng, Xiaobo Xia, Dawei Jiang, Shaoqing Ren
bullets: Targets complex, long-horizon tasks in both conventional graphical interfaces and 3D simulated worlds.
Continues pre-training on tens of thousands of hours of keyboard-and-mouse interaction trajectories from games and embodied environments.
Uses sparse-thinking instruction tuning and multi-turn reinforcement learning to reduce redundant computation and address finite context, rollout errors, and sparse rewards.
Employs a cloud-edge inference engine for concurrent environment interaction, unbounded-context execution, and low online latency.
Shows solid generalization and operational efficiency across challenging 3D open-world games, with competitive performance on 2D game benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of Gamer. A generalist game agent framework operates across a broad range of visually and mechanically diverse games. At each step, the agent uses the current screen, task context, recent interaction history, long-term memory, and reasoning to generate native keyboard and mouse actions in real time. The agent interacts continuously through this loop. Cross-game training, multi-level supervision, and persistent memory support transferable control and sustained task execution.

Figure 6 Streaming-vLLM for persistent multi-environment inference. Each game client maintains separate short-term history, long-term memory, and logical KV-cache state. Paged allocation and memory-aware KV-cache reuse avoid repeated context processing, while incremental rotary position embedding (RoPE) refresh corrects retained keys after compaction. The runtime combines architecture-aware execution, BF16-verified FSM speculation, and early action dispatch to serve concurrent real-time interactions.

Figure 5 Memory-linked long-horizon optimization with TA-GRPO. A long interaction may exceed the model’s context budget (top). Memory compaction divides online rollouts into finite segments whose task states remain connected by generated summaries (bottom). Segments at corresponding stages are compared using environmentverifiable outcomes, and temporal credit assignment distributes their group-relative advantage across decisions. The figure is schematic, and model execution uses the real-time serving backend in Sec. 5.

Figure 4 Sparse reasoning and cross-context memory in supervised fine-tuning. The shared autoregressive policy integrates visual observations, task memory, optional reasoning, and executable keyboard-mouse actions. Context memory compaction preserves task progress across long interactions, while adaptive reasoning allows the policy to act directly at routine steps and generate explicit reasoning when needed.

Figure 2 CPT for unified keyboard-mouse control. Synchronized gameplay observations and device events are mapped to a shared action representation. Random key remapping reduces reliance on key identity, while repeat-aware loss decay reweights temporally persistent actions. The resulting control prior is used by the subsequent task-conditioned training stages.

Figure 7 Bottom-up construction of multi-level task supervision. The diagram illustrates the organization of aligned gameplay segments into local operations, intermediate subgoals, and extended task stages. Separate GPT-5.6-Luna passes produce sparse Think annotations, segment-level instructions and scene descriptions, and memory updates as detailed in Secs. 6.2-6.3. The diagram focuses on hierarchy assembly rather than depicting every annotation call.

Trajectories with aligned action annotations are further used to construct SFT examples at three levels: short-horizon operations, medium-horizon subgoals, and long-horizon tasks. For RL, online policy interaction provides trajectories and environment-verifiable outcomes.
