papers.abstract: We present contraction-certified sampling-based model predictive control (CS-MPC) for tracking and safety of nonlinear robotic systems under parametric uncertainty, disturbances, and safety constraints that are revealed online. CS-MPC uses a contraction-certified tracking feedback inside every sampled rollout, which concentrates the rollouts around the reference, and an execution layer that verifies the applied input using a quantile-tightened discrete-time control barrier function condition. We derive a verification procedure for nonlinear contraction of the feedback-closed dynamics, and we prove a finite-sample stochastic stability bound and a mission-level probabilistic safety guarantee. We validate CS-MPC in simulation on a rover, a quadrotor, and an asteroid landing. When compared with standard model predictive path integral (MPPI) control, CS-MPC attains the same tracking error with 7 to 20 times fewer rollouts for the rover, and a 2 to 4 times lower tracking error for the quadrotor, with no safety violations in 200 Monte Carlo missions.
bullets: Targets tracking and safety for nonlinear robotic systems with uncertainty, disturbances, and online-revealed constraints.
Uses contraction-certified tracking feedback within each sampled rollout to concentrate trajectories near the reference.
Applies a quantile-tightened discrete-time control barrier condition to verify executed inputs.
Provides finite-sample stochastic stability and mission-level probabilistic safety guarantees.
In simulations, matches MPPI tracking with 7–20× fewer rover rollouts, reduces quadrotor error by 2–4×, and reports no violations across 200 missions.

The system is affected by a mission parameter ϑ drawn once per run, process noise, actuator quantization, and constraints revealed during the mission.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($\pi_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.
authors: Suvarna Kadam (Witsense AI), Soran Parsa (University of Huddersfield)
bullets: Reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, focusing mainly on robotic manipulation and navigation, with coverage of humanoid control, world-action models, and evaluation.
Organizes VLA development into seven axes spanning inputs and memory, architecture, action outputs, intermediate predictions, pretraining data, post-training, and real-time execution.
Analyzes 22 models, including their training data, parameter scale, inference speed, and hardware requirements.
Identifies trends toward broader training data, a split between 3–7B-parameter models and sub-billion consumer-GPU models, and generalists handling both manipulation and navigation.
Notes that strong benchmark performance may not translate to robustness under slight object or camera movement.

Several models span more than one body: π0 trains on single-arm, dual-arm and mobile manipulators [17]; Gemini Robotics 1.5 transfers skills between ALOHA, a bi-arm Franka and the Apollo humanoid [55]; NavFoM covers quadrupeds, drones, wheeled robots and cars [62]; and Qwen-VLA unifies manipulation and navigation [61].

Figure 5: Executing action chunks. (a) A synchronous policy stops the robot while the model computes the next chunk, so the robot pauses at every chunk boundary. (b) Asynchronous execution computes the next chunk while the current one runs, as in SmolVLA’s inference stack [47] and the remote-VLA and edge-adapter split of AsyncVLA (navigation) [53]; but if the new chunk plans a different motion, the robot jumps when it switches, causing jerky movement. (c) Real-time chunking [82] prevents this. The robot carries on executing chunk 1 while the model computes chunk 2; those actions cannot be changed, so the model keeps them fixed (hatched) and predicts the rest of chunk 2 (inpainted), guided by the remainder of chunk 1, so that it continues smoothly.

Figure 2: Three architectural patterns. (a) One network maps observations to actions (RT-2, OpenVLA, π0). (b) A slow VLM reasoner passes latent features to a fast action module trained jointly with it (GR00T N1, CogACT). (c) The high-level model emits an interpretable intermediate that a separately trained low-level policy executes (Hi Robot, HAMSTER, MemER, Mobility VLA, NaVILA).

papers.selection_reason: Comprehensive survey of the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) field, covering design, training, and deployment of VLA models for manipulation, navigation, and humanoid control.
papers.title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
papers.tldr: A life-cycle survey of vision-language-action models maps how they are designed, trained, and deployed, highlighting growing data diversity, smaller deployable models, and emerging general-purpose capabilities alongside robustness gaps.

papers.abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that \ac{RL} in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels. This work demonstrates that \ac{RL} and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors. Videos: https://sites.google.com/leggedrobotics.com/heavy-metal-acrobatics This is the author's version of the work. It is posted here by permission of the AAAS for personal use, not for redistribution. The definitive version was published in Science Robotics on 11 November 2026, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.aef0894
authors: Pierre-Jean Lorentz, Pascal Egli, Edo Jelavic, Cliff Li, Ramitha Sundar, Harikrishnan Suresh, Paul Montgomery, Lee Redden, Matthias M\"uller, Ozan Sener, Vladlen Koltun, Marco Hutter
bullets: Heavy machinery is difficult to automate because of complex hydraulic dynamics, nonlinear delays, and the risks of physical experimentation.
The approach trains reinforcement-learning policies in simulation and transfers them to a John Deere 332G skid-steer loader.
The loader autonomously performs two-wheel balancing, rough-terrain driving, trajectory tracing, spinning, bucket swinging, and safe four-wheel landings.
The work demonstrates sim-to-real reinforcement learning for dynamic control of heavy construction equipment.
The demonstrated scope focuses on specific high-dynamic acrobatic maneuvers and does not establish general-purpose autonomy.

papers.abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.
authors: Grid Robotics, :, Qingfeng Lan, Duo Li, Siyao Li, Yiheng Lyu, Shijian Lu, Zhenghao Qi, Shizun Wang, Xinchao Wang, Ming Yang, Zhiqin Yang, Zuhao Yang, Tao Yu
bullets: Frames agentic robots as open-world systems that observe, interpret intent, reason, use skills and tools, verify outcomes, and adapt.
Defines “Embodied System 2” as a foundation model plus an embodied harness for physical decision-making.
Highlights the challenge of converting general reasoning into safe actions under time, mechanical, environmental, and irreversibility constraints.
Proposes evaluating both foundation-model capabilities and end-to-end closed-loop robotic performance.
Outlines a roadmap from executing individual primitives toward safely fulfilling sustained roles with broader responsibility.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | A reference framework for agentic robotics. An Embodied S2 consists of a foundation model and an embodied harness, whose five core parts manage context, tools, planning, memory, and verification. S2 runs on demand or in response to events, whereas S1 and S0 execute at their own rates. A real-time event monitor outside the three systems watches the user, the robot body, and the physical world at a high rate. It interrupts S2 when an event may change the task and, under predefined safety rules, triggers an immediate reaction in S0 without waiting for S2. S2 may call S0 directly through the tool interface; S0 keeps its own real-time loop.

Figure 2 | Two paradigms. (a) An action policy maps the task instruction and observation to action targets. It might include reasoning, subtask prediction, or in-context adaptation. (b) S2 combines a foundation model with an embodied harness. Together, they interpret intent, orchestrate skills and tools, verify outcomes, and adapt subsequent decisions. S1 provides callable skills and tools. S0 performs body control. The S1 path is illustrative; S2 may also call S0 or external tools.

Figure 4 | Three typical execution paths. One system may use all three paths within a single task. For simplicity, the robot body is omitted. (a) Layered orchestration: S2 invokes S1 skills and tools, which produce control targets that S0 executes. (b) Direct control: S2 controls S0 directly through an action interface; S0 still runs its own real-time control loop. (c) Code as policy: S2 writes code that a runtime interpreter executes in the role of S1.

Figure 6 | Core abilities of Embodied S2. These abilities are necessary for Embodied S2 to perform successfully and reliably in the physical world; some reside in the foundation model, while others emerge from its integration with the embodied harness.

Figure 8 | How long each layer takes per decision or control update. All values are given as times, with the equivalent rate in parentheses (time = 1/rate). The S0 and S1 bands are indicative ranges. The S1 band covers control skills only, since the perception and planning modules of S1 are invoked on demand and have no fixed rate. S2 is event-driven rather than periodic, so we plot time per decision; the S2 band is a target for dynamic manipulation, not a requirement for every task. Helix’s “System 2” is a vendor label: its output is a latent representation, so our criterion does not classify it as S2 (Section 3.1); we include it as the fastest upper-level module plotted. The Astra measurements come from different tasks and settings and are not directly comparable with one another.

Figure 11 | What physical agents must rebuild. Foundations replace the four enabling conditions of Figure 10; runtime constraints, which follow from time, irreversibility, and a changing body, govern how the system operates; and evaluation in the running world validates its claims.

Figure 5 | The agentic loop. Top: one cycle comprises six steps. S2 interprets intent, reasons about goals and constraints to decide how to proceed, and invokes an S1 skill, an S0 interface, or an external tool as needed. The invoked capability executes under its contract. S2 then observes and verifies the outcome by answering four questions (whether the request was accepted, whether execution terminated, whether the physical effect holds, and whether the user’s intent is satisfied). Based on the verification, it continues, recovers, asks, or reports. The real-time event monitor, which watches the user, the body, and the scene, can interrupt S2 at any point. Bottom: the same steps on a schematic time axis, labeled with their step numbers and colors. S2 deliberates on demand, S1 runs while a tool executes, and S0 runs continuously; after an interruption, S2 cancels the running tool call and replans while S0 keeps the body stable; the hatched segment marks the canceled execution.

Figure 1 | A vision for agentic robotics: from executing tasks to fulfilling roles. A home breakfast scenario illustrates progressively broader responsibility entrusted to robots: from executing a primitive (L1), completing a task (L2), coordinating a workflow (L3), to fulfilling a standing role (L4).

A decision that arrives after the deadline is usually too late, even if it is correct: the situation has already changed, so acting on it could fail the task or create a hazard. Note that the curves are schematic: they illustrate the qualitative relationship, not measured data.

papers.abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.

papers.abstract: Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments. However, the reliability of such systems heavily depends on visual observations, which are inherently susceptible to occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination variations, often resulting in catastrophic locomotion failures under degraded perception conditions. In this paper, we present PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion), a perceptive locomotion framework that enables robust locomotion under severe visual disturbances. Our method adopts a two-stage teacher-student learning paradigm that explicitly models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven and proprioceptive fallback behaviors, while the student predicts exteroceptive features with uncertainty and suppresses them under out-of-distribution inputs. We evaluate our method on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a RealSense D435 depth camera in real-world settings. Under normal visual conditions, our method enables the robot to successfully perform high-dynamic parkour maneuvers, including traversing large gaps, elevated platforms, and narrow beam terrains. Under severe visual degradation, such as heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes, the robot continues to maintain stable and robust locomotion performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong semantic and spatial reasoning capabilities in 3D environments. Recently, connecting VLMs with model-predictive controllers (MPC) has emerged as a paradigm for combining strong semantic reasoning with physics-based planning. However, connecting these two for contact-rich robotic manipulation requires a task representation that bridges the two and captures how physical interactions can be reasoned by VLMs. In this work, we introduce Objectives as Policies (OaP), a framework that connects a pretrained VLM to a shared sampling-based MPC through an editable objective program. Each program specifies a sequence of stages for completing a task, combining running and terminal costs from a cost library with stage completion conditions. Given a natural-language task instruction and scene observation, we build a simulation-based digital twin through real-to-sim, and the VLM generates an objective program that is executed by the MPC in the simulation. The program is iteratively updated by the VLM based on MPC rollouts, before being deployed in the real world. We evaluate our framework in both simulation and the real world on four tabletop manipulation tasks, and show that it outperforms strong baselines. Additional videos and examples are available on the project website: https://zihaolu001.github.io/oap-project/
authors: Zihao Lu, Trong Gia Hung Nguyen, Fuquan Wang, Yifan Zhu

Scope is demonstrated on tabletop manipulation tasks and relies on simulation-based planning with iterative VLM updates.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Method Overview. Given the task specification in the form of a scene observation and a language description, we generate a digital twin through real-to-sim. VLM then generates objective programs given the task specification, the digital twin, and a predefined cost library. The objective program describes the running and terminal objective terms for the MPC, on a potentially multi-stage task, along with completion conditions for every stage. The VLM iteratively improves the objective programs based on the rollouts in the digital twin, with an MPC that optimizes controls based on the objective program. A stage verifier decides when to advance to the next stage when all completion conditions are met. Finally, the object program is deployed in the real world with the same MPC while the digital twin is synced to the real world execution.

papers.abstract: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.

bullets: Addresses coordination failures where VLA actions diverge from LLM intent or undo recovery progress.
Uses LLM subtask decisions as semantic supervision and corrections plus continuations as action-level supervision.
Treats the modular LLM–VLA agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly redeploying improved components together.
On ten RoboDojo tasks, reports a mean Score of 62.03 and 49.41% mean success without task-specific control code.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ESI architecture and round-level updates. The agent combines a fixed LLM with decision guidance 𝑃𝑟 , a shared skill catalog 𝑆𝑟 , and a VLA policy 𝜃𝑟 . Interaction across tasks produces records for three update paths: reviewing difficulties to refine guidance, consolidating recurring custom operations into reusable skills, and constructing policy supervision from locally effective execution. Prompt and skill review uses the interaction records, while VLA training uses the retained effective actions. Training windows preserve continuity across teacher–student handoffs and retain useful behavior from unsuccessful episodes. Updated components form the next-round agent.

Figure 1: The ESI collect–learn flywheel. Within each episode, the LLM plans and reviews, the VLA proposes actions, and teacher corrections create states from which the VLA continues. The shared experience record links local intent, control source, and local execution outcomes. After each collection round, experience informs prompt and skill refinement, while retained effective actions provide VLA training data. The three updated components are deployed together in the next round; LLM weights remain fixed.

papers.title: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents

papers.abstract: Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries is a multi-objective control problem that requires reducing charging time and sustaining high energy throughput while suppressing accelerated degradation and safety-critical electrochemical reactions. Conventional protocols are easy to implement but have limited ability to adapt to variations in battery chemistry, operating conditions, and aging state. Model-based optimization and conventional data-driven control often require accurate models, costly iterative search, or task-specific policies. We develop a large language model (LLM)-empowered intelligent agent for adaptive battery fast-charging control. In this closed-loop framework, the agent interprets structured battery states, generates executable charging actions, observes the resulting battery response, and continuously adjusts subsequent decisions. We construct a large-scale simulation corpus with PyBaMM across five battery chemistries and 11 parameter sets and convert the resulting state-action-response trajectories into structured process data for agent training. Our two-stage strategy combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). SFT establishes battery-control semantics and feasible decision priors from simulation-derived demonstrations. GRPO aligns the agent with a multi-objective control objective covering energy throughput, degradation mitigation, and operational constraints. Closed-loop simulations show that, under matched energy-throughput requirements, the agent achieves longer cycling life than conventional charging baselines and optimization-based strategies across heterogeneous battery configurations. This study provides a simulation-grounded proof of concept for using LLM agents as sequential decision makers in battery management and takes a step toward language-model-enabled control of physical energy systems.
authors: Joey Chan, Haoyu Pan, Zhen Chen, ErShun Pan
bullets: Addresses the limited adaptability of conventional, model-based, and task-specific charging controllers.
The agent interprets battery states, executes charging actions, observes responses, and updates subsequent decisions.
Training uses PyBaMM simulations spanning five battery chemistries and 11 parameter sets, with supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO.
The multi-objective policy targets energy throughput, degradation mitigation, and operational constraints.
Simulations show longer cycling life than conventional and optimization-based baselines at matched energy throughput across heterogeneous configurations.

papers.abstract: Semantic exploration methods for object-goal navigation use large language models (LLMs) to score how strongly a target object is associated with a room type or with a nearby object. This paper considers obtaining from the LLM a spatial prior instead: a distribution over the position of the target in a room. We evaluate whether two open-weight LLMs, Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, can provide such a prior. Using real room layouts from CubiCasa5K and ScanNet, we measure the likelihood the models assign to real and perturbed layouts, and the layouts they generate. The object frequencies and room sizes of the generated rooms follow the room type, but the proximity of the objects to the walls does not follow the differences between room types found in real rooms. The likelihood distinguishes real layouts from perturbed ones partly through their geometry and partly through the agreement between the coordinates and a field that states the wall each object touches; for the movable furniture of ScanNet, it is higher for layouts with all objects piled near the room center than for the real layouts in most rooms. When an object is given in the prompt, the models place a related object relative to it. When the wall of each object is given, they place most objects against that wall, but do not keep all objects inside a given room rectangle. As a prior for object search, the generated placements reduce the searched area relative to a uniform prior, but by less than a third of the reduction obtained with a prior built from real layouts, and by less than two thirds when both priors are spatially smoothed. These results support the use of LLMs for object-room associations and for writing coordinates under constraints determined by another component, followed by a geometric check, but not as a source of placement priors where real layouts are available.
bullets: The study evaluates Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it as spatial-prior generators for object-goal navigation.
Using CubiCasa5K and ScanNet layouts, it tests likelihoods on real and perturbed rooms and examines generated layouts.
Generated rooms capture room-type object frequencies and sizes, but not room-specific wall proximity or reliable room containment.
Models use provided object and wall information to place related objects, though generated placements often need geometric validation.
Generated priors reduce search area versus uniform search, but substantially less than priors learned from real layouts, especially after smoothing.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the evaluation. (a) The likelihood that an LLM assigns to a real layout, written as text, is compared with that of a perturbed copy (here, two objects exchanged); the pairwise accuracy is the fraction of rooms in which the real layout scores higher. (b) Layouts generated for a room type are compared with real rooms of that type. (c) A prior over the target’s position built from the generated layouts is evaluated by the area searched before the target is found. The real layout is a ScanNet bedroom; the generated layout and the prior (target: bed) are Qwen’s under condition A. In the prior, the door is on the south wall (green) and brighter cells are more probable.

Figure 4: The perturbations applied to one real CubiCasa kitchen. Objects whose position or size the perturbation changes are outlined in red. The bottom-right panel marks the two single-object moves of Sec. 4.1.2, along the nearest wall and away from it; the arrows are not to scale (the moves are 0.10 m).

Figure 6: Left: wall-proximity excess by room type, ordered by the real data. The real excess varies with the room type; Qwen’s is nearly constant; Gemma’s varies, but not in the order of the real data. Right: the slope of the model’s excess regressed on the real excess. Full agreement would be 1.00; no interval reaches it. Bars are 95% bootstrap intervals over rooms.

Figure 3: Examples of layouts under the three generation conditions. Top left: a real ScanNet living room. Others: one layout generated by Qwen for the living room under each condition. Each panel is the layout of its set closest to the median object count and then to the median area. Below each panel are the room size and the wall-proximity excess (Sec. 3.2) of all layouts of the set; the panels are examples, and the numbers are not.

Figure A12: Priors of the most frequent target categories in living rooms: real rooms (R) and condition A generations (M-A), in the oriented and normalized frame of Fig. 12. Each row shows two categories, each with R and with M-A for Qwen and Gemma. Empty panels are categories the model did not generate.

Figure A11: Priors of the most frequent target categories in offices: real rooms (R) and condition A generations (M-A), in the oriented and normalized frame of Fig. 12. Each row shows two categories, each with R and with M-A for Qwen and Gemma. Empty panels are categories the model did not generate.

Figure 5: Pairwise accuracy of the real layout against each perturbation, with 95% intervals over rooms. Top: CubiCasa; bottom: ScanNet; left: Qwen; right: Gemma. Below the dashed line the perturbed layout is preferred. Detach moves objects away from their walls but leaves their wall contact field unchanged, so the field contradicts the coordinates; its accuracy combines this contradiction with the geometric change (Sec. 4.1.3). Tables A1, A2, A3 and A4 give the values.

Figure 12: Priors over the position of a chair in a bedroom (top) and a toilet in a bathroom (bottom): the histogram of real rooms (R), of the generated rooms of the same type (M-A), and of the generated rooms of all four types (M-A/room). Rooms are oriented with the door (green) on the south wall, left of center, and normalized to the unit square; brighter cells are more probable. Appendix A.15 shows the priors of every target category.

Figure 7: Generation with an observed object (Gemma; Qwen behaves alike, Table 6). Top: one bedroom each. The listed object is drawn at its position under O-anchor (orange) and O-move (blue); dots are the generated target in the five samples of each prompt, the solid arrow joins the means of the target, and the dashed arrow the two positions of the listed object. The chair moves in the same direction as the desk (left) and in the opposite direction to the bed (right). Bottom: every room; the displacement of the generated target along the direction in which the listed object was moved, against that object’s displacement. The dashed line is full following.

Figure 9: Distance between each object’s face and the wall it declares (A, A′) or is given (A′′), over the four ScanNet room types. The shaded band is the 0.15 m within which an object counts as touching the wall. Emitting the wall first moves part of the mass into the band; supplying the wall moves most of it there.
Figure 2: Canonical coordinates.

Figure 8: The four versions of one generated kitchen used in the wall-snapping control (Qwen, condition A). Snapping moves each object that declares a wall perpendicularly onto that wall; the random version moves each object by the same distance in a random direction; the other-wall version snaps to a different wall and rewrites the declaration.

Figure 10: Layouts generated by Qwen under condition A′′-i, which gives the room, the objects and their footprints and asks only that every object lie inside the room. Objects that extend beyond the room are shown in red. One example per room type.

Figure 11: Search curves: the probability of having found the target against the fraction of the room opened, averaged over rooms (Qwen’s priors; the dotted line is Gemma’s M-A). In every room type, the curve of R lies above all others, the curve of W below that of U, and the curve of M-A slightly above that of U (Table 10).

Table 1: Pairwise accuracy when one object is moved by 0.10 m in three directions (CubiCasa, both models, symmetrized, ties excluded). The tangential and the normal move rewrite the same coordinate pair; only the geometric consequence differs. “Isolated objects” restricts to rooms whose moved object has no neighbor within 0.30 m (n = 1268 kitchens, 1069 bathrooms). The last row moves one object by 0.01 m and was scored with Qwen only. Intervals, sample sizes and the distance sweep for Qwen are in Table A5.

Table 4: Three properties of conditioning, all measured on the same ScanNet set of real rooms and the same closed vocabulary, condition A. The ratio of standard deviations is model over real for the room dimensions, so that a value above 1 means that the model varies more than the real data, and real over model for the placement, so that a value above 1 means that the model varies less than the real data.

Table 2: Pairwise accuracy of the three versions of the detach comparison (CubiCasa, symmetrized, no ties). Keep: detach with the wall contact field unchanged. Claim only: one character of the field changed, no object moved. Drop field: the field removed from both layouts. Intervals are in Table A6.

Table 7: Wall-snapping control on the models’ own generations (Qwen and Gemma, condition A, CubiCasa, 200 layouts per room type and model, symmetrized; each model scores its own generations). Each row compares two versions of the same layout: pairwise accuracy is the fraction of layouts in which the first-named version scores higher, and ∆ its mean margin in nats. The random version moves each object by the same distance as snapping, in a random direction; the other-wall version snaps to a wall other than the declared one and rewrites the declaration (Appendix A.11). Intervals and tie rates are in Table A22.

Table 6: Following slope κ in ScanNet bedrooms: how far the generated target moves when the listed anchor is moved to another wall, as a fraction of the anchor’s displacement (1 = moves with it, negative = moves away). The difference rows subtract the negative control, with rooms present in both pairs resampled together. “Other objects” are the generated objects of neither the anchor’s nor the target’s category, in the runs of the pair named. The reversed pair lists the night stand and measures the bed. Room counts and intervals are in Table A21.

Table A11: Quality checks of the pair perturbations (room means; the strings are the same for both models). Distinct integer parts and distinct first decimals are counted over all coordinates of the layout, spread is the standard deviation of the coordinates, overlap is the summed pairwise footprint overlap in m2, outside the summed protrusion beyond the room in m, and declared-wall agreement is the share of wall contact declarations consistent with the geometry at 0.15 m. The no-neighbor subset is the rooms in which all three versions exist; d is the mean displacement of the target there. Versions: the real layout and the None, Wrong and Same versions of Table A10. Token counts are preserved by construction.

Table A22: Wall-snapping control on the models’ own generations (condition A, CubiCasa, 200 layouts per room type and model, symmetrized). Each row is a pairwise comparison of two versions of the same layout; pairwise accuracy is the fraction of layouts in which the first-named version scores higher, ∆ its mean margin in nats. Appendix A.11 defines the versions.

Table A24: Likelihood gap between the model’s own generations and real rooms, matched on object count (condition A, CubiCasa). Gap is the object-count-weighted mean over bins of (mean log-likelihood of generated minus mean log-likelihood of real), in nats, after quantizing both sets of layouts to the grid in the second column; the per-bin columns give the gap with the number of real and generated layouts in the bin in parentheses. Appendix A.12 gives the matching rule.

Table A38: Orientation profile per category (ScanNet, condition A, categories with at least 60 real objects). For each category, the JSD (nats) between the model’s wall distribution for that category and (i) the real distribution for the same category, (ii) the real distribution pooled over all categories; “Closer” says which of the two is nearer. The third column is the JSD between the category’s own real profile and the pooled real profile, which bounds what there is to track. Summary: the model is closer to its own category for 3 of 16 categories (Qwen) and 4 of 15 (Gemma). Appendix A.16 gives the procedure.

Table A36: Variation of the search cost across the four room types. SD is the sample standard deviation of the four room-type means of the per-room mean cost; its interval resamples rooms within each room type (10 000 draws). The ratio column is the real-data prior’s SD over this prior’s, with its bootstrap interval. p is the permutation test of Appendix A.10 applied to the per-room mean costs, with the variance of the four group means as the statistic. U is omitted: with random tie-breaking its cost is 0.502 in every room. W and R do not depend on the model; they are repeated because the bootstrap seeds differ between the two runs. M-A/room carries no room-type information by construction, yet its cost varies across room types, because the same prior meets differently placed targets.

Table 10: Search cost (expected fraction of the room opened before the target is found; lower is better) by prior and room type (ScanNet, rooms oriented with the door on the south wall). The uniform prior gives 0.502 in every room type. W and the R rows do not depend on the model. Intervals and episode counts are in Tables A33 and A34, paired differences in Table A35.

Table 5: What the prompt changes, condition A against the two route conditions (ScanNet). The first four columns are the wall-proximity excess by room type; the real data runs from + in bathrooms to − in living rooms. Slope intervals are in Table A15; the full excess table, with the permutation tests, is Table A17, and the validity rates per room type are in Table A18.

Table A32: Paired differences in search cost after spatial smoothing (ScanNet), with 95% intervals that resample rooms. “Smoothed − unsmoothed” compares a prior with itself at σ = 0; “M-A − R” and “M-A/room − M-A” compare two priors at the same σ; “Gemma’s change − Qwen’s change” is the difference between the two models in the change of M-A from σ = 0. Table 13: Summary of the results along the two axes of the evaluation, by level of description. Numbers are for ScanNet, four room types, and condition A unless noted (Qwen /Gemma).

Table A23: Diagnostics for the wall-snapping control. For each version: the number of coordinate and footprint values (x, y, w, d over all objects), the number of distinct values among them after rounding to two decimals, the share on the 0.05 m lattice, and the median token count of the serialized layout. The last two rows per room give the snapping displacement over the objects that moved, and the number of objects whose target had to be clamped inside the room.

Table A33: Search cost by room type and prior, Qwen generations (ScanNet; Sec. 7.2). Cost is the expected fraction of the room opened before the target’s cell, with tied cells opened in uniformly random order; lower is better and an uninformative prior gives 0.502. Objects is the number of search episodes; a model prior has fewer when its heat map for a category is empty. M-A/cat and R/cat ignore the category, M-A/room and R/room the room type. Top-1 dist. is the median distance from the center of the most probable cell to the target; S@10% the probability of having found the target after opening 10% of the room.

Table A34: Search cost by room type and prior, Gemma generations (ScanNet; Sec. 7.2). Cost is the expected fraction of the room opened before the target’s cell, with tied cells opened in uniformly random order; lower is better and an uninformative prior gives 0.502. Objects is the number of search episodes; a model prior has fewer when its heat map for a category is empty. M-A/cat and R/cat ignore the category, M-A/room and R/room the room type. Top-1 dist. is the median distance from the center of the most probable cell to the target; S@10% the probability of having found the target after opening 10% of the room.

Table A13: Object identity, condition A: p(o | c), the fraction of rooms containing each category, for the real data (R), Qwen (Q) and Gemma (G). These are the columns the Spearman ρ of Sec. 5.1 is computed from, one correlation per room type over the 18 vocabulary words; the mean of the four is the figure quoted in the main text. Generated categories are mapped to NYU40 before counting. The real n counts every room of that type in the set of real rooms; the placement statistics of Sec. 5.1 use the subset for which an excess can be computed (173–273 per room type), so their n differs.

Table A37: Band-width sweep for the wall rule (Sec. 7.4). c is the fraction of floor area the band covers, p the fraction of object centers inside it, both averaged over rooms; the prediction is (c−p)/2 from Equation (6), which holds exactly per room because tied cells are opened in random order.

Table 12: Search cost of the real-layout prior R and of M-A after spatial smoothing with a Gaussian kernel of standard deviation σ cells (ScanNet; σ = 0 is the unsmoothed prior of Table 10). Lower is better; U costs 0.502. Paired differences and intervals are in Table A32.

Table 14: Effects of properties of the text on likelihood comparisons, compared with geometric perturbations (Qwen, CubiCasa kitchens). Pairwise accuracy is the fraction of rooms in which the first layout has the higher likelihood (chance 0.5); ∆ is the mean log-likelihood difference, first minus second, in nats. Mirroring is not symmetrized here, because it is the transformation that the symmetrization removes.
Table A26: Consistency between the declared or supplied wall and the emitted coordinates (ScanNet). Chance is computed from each condition’s own distribution over walls (Equation (16)).

Table A39: Wall-proximity excess of ScanNet living rooms by subset (Sec. 9). The subsets split the 221 living rooms by sofa count, chair count and floor area (median 26.9 m2); “domestic” is their intersection. The last two rows give the regression slope of Appendix A.9 when the living-room point is taken from the full set and from the domestic subset.

Table A25: Coordinate values of the real and the generated layouts (CubiCasa, condition A): number of x and y values, number of distinct values after rounding to two decimals, and the share that are multiples of 0.05 m.

Table A35: Paired differences in search cost (Sec. 7.2). Each difference is taken room by room over the episodes for which both priors are defined, then averaged over rooms; intervals resample rooms (2 000 draws), shown on the line below each difference. Negative means the first prior is better.

Table 3: Pair perturbations scored by likelihood: pairwise accuracy of the real layout against each version (symmetrized, ties excluded). The columns None, Wrong and Same are the no-neighbor, wrong-neighbor and same-neighbor versions. Wrong-neighbor and same-neighbor exist in every room; no-neighbor exists only where an empty stretch of wall is available, and the number of those rooms is given in parentheses. The neighbor effect is wrong-neighbor minus same-neighbor over all rooms, the effect of the target’s neighbor with the displacement held fixed; the proximity effect is no-neighbor minus wrong-neighbor over the rooms in which no-neighbor exists, so it is not the difference between the no-neighbor and wrong-neighbor columns, which cover different rooms. Intervals resample rooms. The breakdown by room type, the quality checks of the three versions and the pairs used are in Appendix A.5.
Table A19: Orientation distribution q(wall | c), all objects (ScanNet, canonicalized rooms only).
Table A18: Geometric validity of the generated layouts (ScanNet): the fraction of objects extending outside the room rectangle, and the fraction of object pairs that overlap.

Table 8: Consistency between the wall an object is said to touch and the wall its coordinates place it against, within 0.15 m. ScanNet, four room types. Under A and A′ the wall is the model’s own declaration; under A′′ and A′′-i it is the wall of the real object, given to the model under A′′ and withheld under A′′-i. Chance is computed from each condition’s own distribution over walls, not as 1/4 (Appendix A.13). Sample sizes and the remaining conditions are in Table A26.

Table A14: Room dimensions, condition A: floor area in m2 by room type — sample size, median and interquartile range. The SD ratio quoted in Sec. 5.1 is the standard deviation of the four medians in a column, divided by that of the real column (real 8.23, Qwen 12.37, Gemma 8.95). The quartiles are not used by any statistic in the main text; they are here to show the spread the medians come from. Each model generated 200 rooms per room type. The real n counts every room of that type in the set of real rooms; the placement statistics of Sec. 5.1 use the subset for which an excess can be computed (173–273 per room type), so their n differs.
Table A15: Agreement with the real room-type differences. Slope is the regression of the model’s excess on the real excess over the four room types (Appendix A.9); the SD ratio is real over model.

Table A31: Condition A′′, auxiliary quantities (ScanNet). Natural / unnatural: consistency with the supplied wall for objects of categories that are usually against a wall in the real data and for those that rarely are, with the number of objects in each group. None: objects supplied with “none” and the fraction of them that nonetheless end up within 0.15 m of a wall; Uniform is the same fraction expected if each of these objects were placed uniformly in its room (Equation (2)), while the real objects are by construction all farther than 0.15 m from every wall. Appendix A.13 gives the definitions.

Table 11: Spread of the M-A priors and of the real-layout prior R (ScanNet, condition A; medians over the 26 priors in which every set contains at least five objects of the target category). Cells: number of the 256 cells with non-zero probability, with all objects and with an equal number of objects drawn from each set. Distinct positions: number of distinct positions, normalized by the room dimensions and rounded to 0.01, divided by the number of objects. Most frequent position: share of the objects at the most frequent normalized position.

Table A16: Agreement with the real differences for two placement statistics (ScanNet, four room types), condition A. Full agreement would be 1.00 in every row. Orientation shares sum to one, so the four orientation rows are not independent.

Table A27: Selection of the input rooms of condition A′′ and its variants (ScanNet). Each column applies one more rule: rooms with at least one floor-standing object in the closed vocabulary; rooms whose rectangle and door can be recovered (Appendix A.1); rooms with 2 to 14 such objects. At most 200 eligible rooms per room type are drawn after a seeded shuffle; only bedrooms exceed the limit. The last two columns count the objects supplied and, among them, those supplied with no wall (“none”) because the real object is farther than 0.15 m from every wall. Inputs are identical for both models and all variants.

Table A21: Generation with an observed object (Sec. 5.3; ScanNet bedrooms, O-anchor against O-move, five samples per room and condition). Rooms is the number of bedrooms that contain both categories; dropped are those in which the anchor could not be moved to another wall without overlap; used are those in which the target was generated under both prompts. κ is the following slope of Equation (12) with a room-resampled interval; |∆a| is the median displacement of the anchor. Other objects is the same slope for the generated objects of neither category, given for the two related pairs (intervals in Table 6).

Table A12: Same-category neighbors at the wrong-neighbor destination. The layouts carry categories but no instance identity, so a target re-attached next to a second instance of its anchor’s category (a chair moved to another desk) has not had its pairing broken at the category level. The construction already rejects destinations whose only neighbor is such an instance; the rows count the triples in which the destination is adjacent to both an object of another category and a second instance of the anchor’s category. The last column is the number of rooms with at least two instances of the anchor’s category.
Table A17: Wall-proximity excess by room type (ScanNet), the standard deviation across the four room types, and the permutation test of equality across room types.

Table A28: Declared wall against nearest wall, per object (ScanNet, all room types pooled, objects that declare a wall). “Declared” is the distribution of wall contact values; “Nearest” is the distribution of the wall nearest to each of the same objects by its coordinates; JSD is the Jensen– Shannon divergence between the two distributions in nats; Agreement is the fraction of objects whose declared wall is their nearest wall, and Chance the agreement expected if declarations were independent of the coordinates, ∑ ω q(ω) p(ω) over the two distributions (Appendix A.14).

Table 9: Objects placed partly outside the room, on identical inputs (ScanNet, four room types). Differences are paired by room against A′′ with a bootstrap over rooms (Table A30). The instruction added to A′′ is given for each condition (Appendix B).

Table A29: The conditioning measurement of Sec. 5.1 repeated on the layouts generated with the field order reversed (condition A′), alongside condition A. Columns as in Tables A17 and A15; the A rows repeat those tables.

papers.abstract: Reaching a goal state in a complex environment often requires a robot to overcome challenging terrain and obstacles. Which routes are accessible depends on the robot's physical design, the control policy it uses, and how it modifies its surroundings. We present a kinodynamic rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) planner that uses physics simulation to exploit skills encoded in the control policy, which allows it to find a path in the scene with respect to the robot's capabilities. The planner samples states from a reduced state space in 3D around the scene and expands the RRT toward each sample using policy rollouts. We guide sampling with a preplanned path for a simple mass-point model to focus exploration on promising regions leading toward the goal state, reducing planning time by up to 63%. Simulation experiments with quadrupeds, humanoids, and wheeled robots demonstrate that our approach supports drop-in integration of various robots and control policies, exploiting their physical and policy capabilities without modifying the underlying planning algorithm. Predefined environmental modifications, such as placing a plank across a gap to build a bridge, will automatically be picked up by the planner as the robot's reachable space expands.
authors: Yael Fassbind, Valentin N. Hartmann, Huang Su, Yijiang Huang, Stelian Coros
bullets: Plans routes according to each robot’s physical design, control policy, and ability to modify its surroundings.
Samples a reduced 3D state space and expands the tree using simulated policy rollouts.
Uses a simple mass-point path to guide exploration toward promising regions, reducing planning time by up to 63%.
Demonstrated in simulation with quadruped, humanoid, and wheeled robots using drop-in robot and policy integration.
Automatically accounts for predefined environmental changes, such as placing a plank to create a bridge.

papers.abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.
authors: Xianxu Wu, Shang-Ching Liu, Zhaocong Liang, Hengxiang Chen, Yujian Ma, Shenwen Deng, Qiang Li, Jianwei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that tabletop manipulation safety constraints are scene-dependent and often absent from instructions.
Stores reusable textual safety rules in an explicit Constraint Space rather than relying only on semantic retrieval.
Uses a lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model to select applicable constraints from the task and environment context.
Employs a multimodal Safety Inspector to detect incorrect selections and unseen hazards, then provide corrective planning feedback.
Uses validated feedback for test-time adaptation and adds newly identified constraints to the knowledge base.

papers.abstract: V2X collaborative perception improves single-vehicle perception by aggregating multi-view features from collaborative agents. However, existing methods typically rely on simple spatial warping to align the collaborative features, which can cause semantic misalignment during fusion. Meanwhile, these deterministic warping-based methods are highly sensitive to the positional noises. In this paper, we propose a plug-in module called Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner (RSSA), which performs semantic and probabilistic spatial transformations for robust feature alignment. Specifically, a Semantic Transformation (SemT) block modulates feature channels based on the observed relative pose to correct semantic inconsistencies. Subsequently, a Probabilistic Spatial Transformation (P-SpaT) block performs probabilistic warping by sampling from the Gaussian-modeled relative pose space. A Relative Transformation Augmentation (RT-Aug) strategy is further introduced to augment the relative poses and facilitate the training of the RSSA. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that RSSA improves the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin under the configuration of both clean and noisy positions.
authors: Zhihao Yang, Zhiyu Xiang, Peng Xu, Tianyu Pu, Kai Wang, Eryun Liu, Dongping Zhang, Yong Ding
bullets: Addresses semantic misalignment and sensitivity to positional noise in spatial-warping-based collaboration.
Uses a Semantic Transformation block to modulate feature channels from the observed relative pose.
Uses probabilistic spatial warping by sampling relative poses modeled as Gaussian distributions.
Introduces Relative Transformation Augmentation to support RSSA training.
Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show large gains over existing methods under clean and noisy positions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust humanoid locomotion, yet training recipes (rewards, architectures, hyperparameters) remain hard to reuse across robots with different native joint coordinates, since policies output native joint angles while action scales, bounds, gains, and penalties are defined in those robot-specific coordinates. Existing transmission models convert native targets into actuator commands but do not standardize the coordinate interface exposed to the policy. We introduce a body-aligned virtual joint space upstream of this mapping: policy actions and observations follow a common anatomical convention, and a deterministic kinematic layer maps virtual targets to native ones, leaving the existing transmission and low-level control stack unchanged. Under a single unmodified recipe on three humanoids with different leg-axis layouts, it is the only interface that tracks accurately, keeps the feet aligned with the travel direction, and trains stably on all three, and on Unitree G1 hardware it reduces heading drift by nearly a factor of six.
authors: Sol Choi, Mingon Kim, Seokin Seo, Jongeun Choi, Donghyeon Kim, Yisoo Lee
bullets: Native joint coordinates make rewards, action bounds, gains, and penalties robot-specific, hindering recipe reuse.
The method exposes policy actions and observations in a common anatomical space.
A deterministic kinematic mapping converts virtual joint targets to each robot’s native coordinates while preserving the existing control stack.
Across three humanoids, it tracked accurately, maintained foot alignment, and trained stably with one unmodified recipe.
On Unitree G1 hardware, it reduced heading drift by nearly sixfold.

papers.abstract: Multi-view visual augmentation often seeks consistency across cameras, but it is unclear which forms of consistency matter for downstream control. We use simulation-state replay to manipulate cross-view coupling while preserving the per-camera perturbation distributions, physical trajectories, and action labels. Across seven LIBERO manipulation tasks, marginal-matched changes in global appearance, ghost injection, and target color have small average costs for a late-fusion Diffusion Policy: point estimates are near zero or negative, and the largest upper endpoint of the 90% posterior credible intervals is 2.55 percentage points. In contrast, geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations (90% CrI [0.64, 6.28]), with displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and the number of affected views matched. Camera interventions reveal substantial dependence on wrist-view geometry, while feature analysis shows appearance sensitivity patterns associated with the factors randomized during training. ACT shows a higher target-color cost estimate than DP, with uncertainty that includes zero and sensitivity to task composition. Within the tested tasks and policy configurations, these findings motivate selective consistency constraints: appearance coupling can sometimes be relaxed, whereas task-relevant geometry and cross-view spatial correspondence warrant protection.
bullets: The study isolates cross-view coupling effects while preserving per-camera perturbation distributions, trajectories, and action labels.

papers.abstract: Depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry from RGB images, allowing zero-shot object navigation without a depth sensor. However, when predicted depth is mapped as if it came from a sensor, view-dependent errors accumulate in the map, remove exploration goals, and end the search before the agent can observe and correct them. We propose ERA, a training-free object navigation system that replaces the depth sensor with depth predicted from RGB images and poses. ERA follows a paradigm we call Move with Error: movement provides new views that correct map errors, and the corrected map enables further movement. It realizes this paradigm with revisable occupancy and with exploration from reachable viewpoints, which continues the search when no frontier remains, and verifies the target across views before stopping. On three benchmarks, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors. Its map and exploration components also raise VLFM's success from 10.8% to 61.7% under the same predicted depth. We further deploy ERA on a real robot.
authors: Shunyang Huang, Shuo Wang, Wenyuan Xie, Mingyu Lin, Yue Ding, Hongtao Lu
bullets: Addresses accumulated errors when RGB-predicted depth is treated like sensor depth, which can prematurely end exploration.
Introduces the “Move with Error” paradigm: movement provides views that correct the map and support continued navigation.
Uses revisable occupancy, reachable-viewpoint exploration, and multi-view target verification.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free, sensor-free methods on three benchmarks.
Improves VLFM success from 10.8% to 61.7% under the same predicted depth and is deployed on a real robot.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving is predominantly evaluated through ego-vehicle safety and task completion. Its deployment in urban traffic, however, creates sustained interactions among vehicles whose collective effects remain insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Ego2Flow, a closed-loop benchmark for assessing the traffic-system impact of autonomous driving on maps distilled from real-world cities. To construct realistic 3D urban environments for sustained closed-loop traffic simulation, we develop an agent-guided map distillation framework that integrates real-world maps and observations with complementary geographic information. Through an iterative feedback mechanism and a traffic information graph that jointly guide scene generation, the framework preserves lane topology, critical road geometry and decision-relevant visual conditions while simplifying nonessential details and completing unobserved regions. Using our proposed framework, we generate and publicly release six CARLA maps from the Argoverse 2 dataset, covering the corresponding real-world regions and enabling paired comparisons of driving behavior under real and simulated observations. On these maps, Ego2Flow evaluates how autonomous driving policies affect traffic efficiency, safety, stability and energy consumption across diverse road structures. Compared with existing construction methods, our framework achieves the lowest average displacement error between planning outputs from paired real and simulated observations. We further benchmark representative driving policies to characterize their system-level impact on urban traffic. Project Page: https://github.com/Fisher-007/Ego2Flow.
authors: Yu Dong, Weiying Shen, Hangyu Li, Shu Han, Hong Li, Xiangbo Gao, Keshu Wu, Zhengzhong Tu, Soyoung Ahn, Zhiyuan Liu, Xiaopeng Li
bullets: Introduces a closed-loop benchmark measuring traffic efficiency, safety, stability, and energy consumption across diverse urban roads.
Builds realistic 3D environments by distilling real-world maps and observations, completing unseen regions while preserving key road geometry and visual conditions.
Uses iterative feedback and a traffic information graph to guide scene generation and simplify nonessential details.
Releases six CARLA maps derived from Argoverse 2, enabling paired comparisons between real and simulated observations.

The proposed map construction achieves the lowest average displacement error among compared methods for paired planning outputs; representative policies are evaluated for system-level traffic effects.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.
bullets: Policies weight noisy object observations by α = V/(V + s²), where V is the learned proprioceptive anchor’s error variance.
A single measurement of V predicted 10 held-out sensitivities far better than classical errors-in-variables regression (MAE 0.025 vs. 0.37).
In deployment, persistent observation offsets produced closed-loop sensitivities greater than α in all 15 tested policies; full offset following occurred in 8.
Lower α was associated with lower success, especially for diffusion policies; a prospective test predicted success within 0.03.
All results used simulated manipulation, synthetic Gaussian noise, and preregistered evaluations; some findings were post hoc.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how imitation policies discount perception noise via a proprioceptive anchor, relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
papers.tldr: Imitation policies learn to combine proprioception with noisy object readings in a predictable way, but this noise discounting does not reliably transfer to closed-loop deployment.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor imitation learning has become a predominant paradigm for real-world robotic manipulation, yet it remains data-inefficient and brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by distilling priors from internet-scale data, but the ``right'' representation for robotics remains unresolved: existing studies span broad but sparse task distributions and reach conclusions that vary and even conflict, pointing to strong task and setting dependence. We examine this question by bringing a magnifying glass to a common contact-rich manipulation task: insertion. We compare representations from widely used vision foundation models against an explicit contact-centric representation on two closely related insertion tasks, perturb each along controlled axes of occlusion and physical tolerance, and test whether conclusions transfer to the real world. Task dependence proves to be more subtle than previous, broadly scoped evaluations revealed: the best representation differs even between our near-identical tasks, and small changes shift trends in unpredictable ways. Despite this variability, results across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the distinct value of spatially-grounded, and in particular, contact-centric information for contact-rich policy learning, while underscoring how difficult it is to estimate such cues reliably under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise. We hope these findings motivate further study of representations in contact-rich manipulation, along with advances in contact perception and its integration into visuomotor policy learning.
authors: Leon Kim, Dinesh Jayaraman, Michael Posa
bullets: Evaluates vision foundation-model representations against an explicit contact-centric representation for two closely related insertion tasks.
Tests controlled changes in occlusion and physical tolerance in simulation, then examines transfer to real-world settings.
Finds that small task or condition changes can unpredictably alter which representation performs best.
Across experiments, contact-centric and spatially grounded cues provide distinct benefits for contact-rich manipulation.
Reliable contact estimation remains difficult under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are becoming the main source of data for dexterous manipulation, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines multiply each demonstration in simulation. These pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers how the hand moves. Which fingers touch, when, and how hard remain unobserved, because a hand pose shows where each finger stops on the surface rather than how far it is driven to close. This gap is a force gap: on held-out recordings, a hand policy that imitates the observed pose grips with 0.31x the recorded force, and a policy trained on physics replays of vision-tracked poses grips with 1.55x. TouchTwin closes the gap with measured human touch. Each selected TouchScale recording, captured with head and wrist RGB-D cameras and an 880-taxel glove, is rebuilt in MuJoCo. Coding agents write the objects as physics-tested programs, and a per-subject tactile hand replays the interaction with the recorded touch setting the contact and the closing force of each finger. In simulation, a policy trained on touch-grounded replays grips at 0.99x the recorded force and succeeds in 20/20 trials on held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations; a contact predictor trained on them misses 13% of real contact frames, against 32% for vision-based replays. Each replay also seeds perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered as realistic video in new views and scenes.
authors: Huiwen Han, Nuo Chen, Ziyao Zeng, Dayou Li, Hao Wang, Amir Hossein Rahmati, Xiaoning Qian, Bangya Liu, Zhiwen Fan
bullets: Vision-based replays miss finger contact timing and force, creating a force gap in simulated demonstrations.
The system combines RGB-D views with an 880-taxel glove and reconstructs interactions in MuJoCo using subject-specific tactile hands.
Recorded touch determines finger contact and closing force during physics-based replay, while coding agents create physics-tested object programs.
Touch-grounded policies reproduced 0.99× recorded force, succeeded on 20/20 held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations, and reduced contact-frame misses to 13% versus 32% for vision replays.
Replays can seed perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered in new views and scenes.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.
authors: Jiaxin Huang, Chengxing Lin, Xiaoyu Luo, Sirui Chen, Jingyu Guo, Aolin Li, Kairui Chen, Rui Zhen, Cheng Wen, Kerui Gu, Shunyao Wang, Zhihui Peng, Shaoli Huang
bullets: Addresses autonomous navigation across rooms, doors, roads, and changing destinations for humanoid robots.
Uses MELIOR, an RGB-only navigation model with action-prediction and goal-prediction variants.
X-Navarch decomposes brief instructions into subtasks and coordinates navigation with explicit target and obstacle avoidance.
Demonstrated on a Lingxi X2 over roughly 100 metres from an office lobby to a neighbouring-building store, including door traversal and static/dynamic obstacle avoidance.
Digital-twin adaptation improved closed-loop success in simulation before deployment; MELIOR also achieved competitive R2R-CE and RxR-CE results.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a full system for language-instructed indoor-to-outdoor navigation on a humanoid robot, directly relevant to vision-language navigation.
papers.title: X-Nav Technical Report: Real-World Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor Navigation on a Humanoid Robot
papers.tldr: X-Nav enables a humanoid robot to execute language-directed, long-horizon indoor-to-outdoor navigation using camera-based visual navigation, task decomposition, and obstacle avoidance.

papers.abstract: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io
authors: Mariana Sosa Guzm\'an, Yide Song, Amin Abyaneh, Gregory Dudek, Hsiu-Chin Lin
bullets: Uses RGB-D observations and natural-language task instructions to reason about semantic, object-to-object safety hazards.
Rejects tasks likely to cause non-recoverable harm; otherwise identifies preventable object-pair hazards and unsafe spatial relations.
Grounds hazards in 3D using open-vocabulary segmentation and depth, producing continuous risk fields.
