papers.abstract: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: https://github.com/flyingView/AstroMemBench-v1.
authors: You Wu, Guhong Zhang, Hongwei Li, Xinyue Hong, Yuan Jia
bullets: Benchmarks 16 memory subchallenges across 9 spacecraft-operation tasks, using 140 templates and 2,240 instances.
Uses deterministic scoring for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use.
Tests six configurations and nine ablation conditions to assess memory recovery, use, and design differences.
Memory systems and RAG improve same-session performance over native Pi Agent, while no memory system clearly beats RAG overall.
After session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points; gains are stronger for instruction retention and result reuse than for state tracking or energy reservation.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $\pi_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{https://stvla.github.io/}{https://stvla.github.io/}
authors: Zhuo Han, Yeqiang Wang, Xinran Wang, Hongwei Han, Yi Xiong, Zunian Wan, Jianbo Mao, Huan Peng, Yongcheng Liu, Wei Shan, Maoqing Yao
bullets: Addresses VLA policies that overlook spatial structure and task history when making action decisions.
Adds features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model to temporal memory alongside visual representations.
Uses a principled scoring rule to select history that is relevant to the current observation and complementary to existing memory.
Achieves the highest average success rate among compared methods across LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge.
Improves real-world success over π₀.₅ by 58.33, 30.00, and 35.00 percentage points on block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, respectively.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable future prediction in latent space without pixel reconstruction. However, latent predictive consistency alone does not establish the relative driving quality of candidate plans. We present ActWorld-JEPA, a joint-embedding formulation for candidate-based driving. Where Plan-Conditioned JEPA (PC-JEPA) uses global and step-wise trajectory intentions to guide recurrent latent prediction, then combines the predicted future with the current scene through gated cross-attention; Relational Residual Reranking ($R^3$) models agreement and discrepancy between plan and future representations under planning supervision, yielding bounded, gated residual corrections to the base planning scores. This formulation connects latent prediction to candidate selection using only observed context and proposed trajectories at inference. Benchmark-specific implementations report 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, with the final selector calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback, and 91.6 and 42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard, respectively. The nuScenes evaluation reports a mean $L_2$ error of 1.20 m and a predicted collision rate of 0.76% over 1--6 s. This work provides an effective path from JEPA's predictive representations to driving decisions informed by anticipated consequences.
authors: Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Caiyan Jia, Lei Yang, Lin Liu, Yuchen Liu, Ziyang Liu, Zirui Li, Gang Wang, Peiliang Wu, Li Wang, Yadan Luo, Chen Lv

Reports 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 91.6/42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest/navhard, and 1.20 m mean L2 error with 0.76% predicted collision rate on nuScenes.
Inference uses only observed context and proposed trajectories; the reported selector is calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback.

papers.abstract: Choosing robot model capacity and demonstration budgets also requires decisions about data composition, representation, optimization, and deployment. We connect these decisions through a common conditional-distribution target. Nested learning oracles give exact risk accounting; local information geometry, conditional mutual information, and empirical convergence provide conditional training prescriptions. Known-target numerical checks expose capacity-data coupling, representation-induced mixture mismatch, and an example where deployment KL increases while negative log-likelihood decreases. An analysis of 206 public PushT trajectories evaluates fixed-feature information-design criteria without fitting a policy. Under asymmetric evaluation targets, the selected allocations reduce this criterion by 4.5-6.2% relative to target matching; balanced targets show no benefit. These results clarify which quantities can support training recommendations and when an apparently favorable predictive metric has a different interpretation.

papers.abstract: Learning whole-body mobile manipulation requires demonstrations that coordinate bimanual actions with locomotion across extended workspaces. However, existing interfaces trade off direct robot control, perception and action alignment, and natural operator mobility, making such demonstrations difficult to collect. We introduce HALO, a human-aligned data collection system for whole-body mobile manipulation. The system aligns the operator's perception and action space with the robot while preserving direct physical feedback and natural locomotion. Operators guide the robot end-effectors through kinesthetic teaching and move a low-resistance platform without the deployed mobile base while performing bimanual manipulation. This interface enables more natural whole-body demonstrations, but the close human-robot coupling introduces discrepancies between the demonstration and deployment settings. We address these discrepancies with deployment-aligned demonstration processing, which calibrates and temporally aligns platform motion with the deployed base response and masks and inpaints demonstrator hands in recorded observations. Compared with Mobile ALOHA and VR teleoperation, HALO enables up to 2.9x faster demonstration collection while maintaining comparable or higher success rates. Policies trained with HALO perform precise manipulation tasks, including zip-tie fastening, and achieve a 73.3% success rate on a six-stage long-horizon mobile manipulation task involving repeated coordinated base and arm motion. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/Lingbot-ALOHA/
authors: Shuai Yang, Fangyi Xu, Yishu Shen, Kecheng Zheng, Yinghao Xu

papers.abstract: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.

papers.abstract: Vision-based dexterous in-hand manipulation requires knowing not only where an object is, but also how it moves. However, most robotic manipulation systems rely on off-the-shelf visual perception models whose outputs are limited to static object masks, geometry, or 6D poses, leaving downstream controllers to infer object dynamics implicitly from noisy visual observations. We present VOKE, a kinematics-aware perception framework that augments existing object and hand-object pose estimators to recover a complete object kinematic state comprising pose, linear and angular velocity, and linear and angular acceleration. VOKE contains two core perception modules and a downstream application study. First, a Pluggable Kinematics Module (PKM) attaches to the output of a standard pose estimator and predicts the object's linear and angular velocity and acceleration from temporal visual features. Second, a Kinematics-guided Pose Refinement Module (KPRM) converts this motion vector into a second-order, motion-prior reference pose and refines the per-frame pose estimates. We evaluate VOKE on DexYCB and OakInk, where it consistently improves object pose estimation across three different backbones and substantially reduces velocity and acceleration estimation error compared with pose differencing. As a downstream application, we use Kinematics-Augmented Reinforcement Learning (KARL) to compare a kinematics-augmented policy with a pose-history baseline. After training the policies in simulation, we transfer the kinematics-augmented policy to the physical robot without policy fine-tuning, demonstrating the complete perception-to-control pathway in the target domain.
authors: Shengjia Zhu, Wenqiang Xu, Lin Shao
bullets: Addresses the lack of dynamic object-state information in vision-based manipulation systems.
Uses a Pluggable Kinematics Module to estimate linear and angular velocity and acceleration from temporal visual features.
Uses a Kinematics-guided Pose Refinement Module to refine per-frame poses with motion-based priors.
Improves pose estimation across three backbones on DexYCB and OakInk, while reducing motion-estimation error versus pose differencing.
A kinematics-augmented policy transfers from simulation to a physical robot without policy fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of VOKE. Given a sequence of RGB(D) frames, a base pose estimator shares its image encoder with the Pluggable Kinematics Module (PKM) and produces per-frame pose estimates. PKM aggregates the last k frame features and decodes the motion vector Vt = (vt, ωt, at, βt). The Kinematics-guided Pose Refinement Module (KPRM) constructs a motion-prior reference pose from Pt−1,net and Vt, then refines the per-frame pose using Vt and the pose history Pt−k+1:t,net. The refined pose and motion vector form the complete kinematic state Kt = (Pt,fin, Vt) consumed by the KinematicsAugmented Reinforcement Learning (KARL) policy together with robot proprioception.

papers.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking lets a humanoid robot follow reference motions, but training a tracking policy for a library of motions has usually taken hours of GPU time. SuperMimic showed that the policy can instead be trained by backpropagating through a world model learned from parallel simulation, and InstantTrack added Muon updates, a residual policy around the reference and an averaged deployed policy. We build on both and present BlinkMimic, a recipe that makes this training faster. On a simulated Unitree G1, BlinkMimic trains one policy for all 40 LAFAN1 clips in 3.4 minutes on a single RTX 4090, measured until three consecutive checkpoints reach a normalized return of at least 0.82 with no failed clip (mean of three seeds). We split training time into the cost of an iteration, the iterations needed to fit the motions, and the iterations needed to remove the last failures, and assign each component, inherited or new, to one of these terms. The new components are a step size that decreases once training has progressed, resets directed by failures of the deployed policy under deployment conditions, and GPU graph capture of the whole iteration. A leave-one-out ablation with three seeds per component shows which term each component affects, and further measurements of the gradient, the update rule and the failure cases explain these effects. Code and per-seed results are available at https://github.com/fuyichen0725/blinkmimic.

papers.title: BlinkMimic: Training a Humanoid Motion Tracker in Minutes on a Single GPU

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.
authors: Xiangyi Jia, Kaixian Qu, Shengzhi Wang, Chenyu Yang, Robert Katzschmann, Marco Hutter
bullets: Frames operator intent prediction hierarchically as atomic action plus overarching mission from short visual histories.
Introduces VI AMO, containing 6,600 episodes, 13,653 action annotations, and 9,702 mission annotations from eleven robot sources.
The resulting Vision-Intention Model substantially improves intent similarity over GPT-4o and GPT-5.6 Luna, including on many labels unseen during training.
In a downstream real-world takeover task, predicted missions reduce human teleoperation time and intent-prediction latency relative to the proprietary baselines.
Scope: the approach is evaluated on teleoperation histories and a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: We present VBot Exo2Ego Policy, a video generation model that turns third-person videos into first-person observations of a selected actor, offering a practical way to expand first-person operation data from abundant real-world footage. To support this goal, we introduce a lightweight data collection pipeline and mobile app that support first-person recording, third-person recording, and synchronized capture of both views. This setup combines accessible single-view collection with paired RGB and camera geometry for learning cross-view correspondence. Building on a pretrained video diffusion transformer, our model incorporates geometric guidance and auxiliary supervision from semantic masks and hand keypoints to facilitate optimization and improve the fidelity of hand-object interactions. Camera geometry is injected stochastically during training and gradually removed, allowing inference without target-camera calibration. To accommodate the diversity of Internet videos, we combine source-video perception and reasoning, optional actor references, and multi-shot adaptation to identify the intended actor and follow an operation across camera cuts. The collection system and generation model provide a foundation for expanding first-person operation data across tasks, scenes, and participants.
authors: Tong Rao, Zhihao Zhang, Yuntian Wang, Siyu Zhou, Hailong Qin, Yinan Yu
bullets: Introduces a lightweight app and pipeline for first-person, third-person, and synchronized multi-view recording.

Handles diverse Internet videos through actor identification, optional references, and multi-shot operation tracking.
Targets improved fidelity for hand–object interactions and broader first-person data collection across tasks and scenes.

papers.abstract: In long-horizon manipulation, a robot may need to take different actions under identical observations, depending on task progress and the outcomes of earlier attempts. We refer to this ambiguity as decision aliasing. Resolving it requires the policy to maintain memory of its execution history. To reduce the cost of processing full observation histories, recent methods build compact event memories using perceptual, semantic, or kinematic cues. However, these criteria may miss events that matter for task success. We instead propose an outcome-grounded principle: remember events that substantially change the predicted probability of eventual success. Following this principle, we introduce CGEM, a critic-gated event memory that uses a critic to select events with large estimated changes in success probability. Positive and negative changes are encoded as progress and failure records, respectively. Failure records are discarded once the corresponding subtask is completed. In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment with exactly computed success probabilities, CGEM achieves 88.0% success, compared with 0.0% for both a 36-step observation window and a kinematic event memory. Removing failure records reduces success to 1.7%.
authors: Xuanzhuo Liu, Chuankang Li, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Addresses decision aliasing, where identical observations require different actions based on task history.
Uses a critic to gate event memory by estimated changes in success probability.
Stores positive changes as progress records and negative changes as failure records, deleting failures after the related subtask is completed.
In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment, CGEM reaches 88.0% success versus 0.0% for a 36-step observation window and kinematic event memory.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robotic manipulation have enabled increasingly complex and dexterous behaviors, yet existing benchmarks still focus on simple pick-and-place tasks and lack a systematic framework for measuring progress in robot learning along the axis of task difficulty. We present ManiLadder, a large-scale and organized simulation benchmark for robotic manipulation. ManiLadder contains 112 carefully designed tasks stratified into 4 difficulty levels, with 8 categories in each level, spanning rigid-body and deformable-object manipulation, single-arm and dual-arm settings, and gripper and dexterous-hand end-effectors. To calibrate difficulty, we fix the data amount the same for every task and use a unified flow- matching imitation learning policy under the same training and evaluation protocols, then use its evaluation success rate as an operational empirical difficulty signal. All tasks are iteratively refined until they fall into target difficulty ranges, which are then verified across different random seeds, policies, and agentic learning systems. We further analyze the task properties, compare different policy performances and training settings, analyze task transfer and data scaling behaviors, and conduct real-world experiments showing that the designed tasks preserve their difficulty ordering beyond simulation. ManiLad- der provides a calibrated ladder for measuring, comparing, and advancing robotic manipulation capabilities. More results are available at https://maniladder-benchmark.github.io/.

Validates task difficulty ordering across random seeds, policies, agentic learning systems, and real-world experiments.
Supports analysis of policy performance, training settings, task transfer, and data scaling.

papers.abstract: Reusing a demonstrated gait can reduce the work of specifying the same motion for each biped. A video captures the timing of a step, but each robot must execute it with its own limbs and actuators. MotionSkill recovers a timed reference once from monocular video and adapts it to each target in simulation. It aligns root motion and body landmarks in a common frame and records which landmarks are available at each instant. At each source timestamp, the mapper preserves limb directions, uses the target segment lengths, and solves inverse kinematics under joint limits and closure constraints. In MuJoCo, we train a separate residual policy for each of ten bipeds on its mapped reference from one four-second walking clip. Each policy uses the measured robot state to correct joint commands during contact. From initial states held out during training, MotionSkill completed 98% of trials on the original video and 26% with the upper body occluded for one second.

papers.abstract: At disaster sites and on unstable slopes, robot contact can collapse uninspected terrain, requiring retreat upon support loss. Massively parallel reinforcement learning of collapse-reactive retreat requires independent state--action experiences. However, on shared rigid-body collapsible terrain, one robot's collapse alters others' contacts without direct interaction. We call this indirect interference. Duplicating terrain objects prevents this but is memory-intensive, limiting parallel sampling. Our key insight is that policy learning does not necessarily require rigid-body collapse modeling, which is feasible but computationally expensive; collapse-induced contact responses can suffice. We therefore propose a memory-efficient parallel policy-learning framework for collapse-reactive retreat via hybrid terrain modeling. Hybrid terrain modeling combines rigid-body simulation of non-collapsible terrain with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions. A State-Multiplexed Contact Model shares terrain geometry and a contact-response law while maintaining environment-specific collapse states, enabling independent experiences without terrain objects for collapsible regions. The framework trains a proprioceptive policy for both normal locomotion and collapse-reactive retreat. It supports over 100 times as many parallel environments as fine-resolution rigid-block terrain within the same GPU memory limit. This scalability and improved sample efficiency enable over 50 times faster policy convergence with comparable retreat performance. Sim-to-sim and real-robot experiments demonstrate retreat under multiple collapse conditions. A supplementary video is available at: https://youtu.be/_RrhwjzEPE0
authors: Yuki Kadokawa, Ritsuki Matsunaga, Yuqi Yang, Edgar Anarossi, Takamitsu Matsubara
bullets: Addresses indirect interference in parallel reinforcement learning caused by shared collapsible terrain altering other robots’ contacts.
Replaces rigid-body collapse simulation with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions while retaining rigid-body modeling for stable terrain.
Uses a State-Multiplexed Contact Model to share terrain geometry and contact laws while keeping collapse states environment-specific.
Supports over 100× more parallel environments and over 50× faster policy convergence than fine-resolution rigid-block terrain under the same GPU memory limit.
Sim-to-sim and real-robot experiments demonstrate retreat across multiple collapse conditions.

The objective is to learn a policy that enables the robot to retreat to non-collapsible terrain without falling. (Bottom) Comparison of terrain modeling approaches for parallel policy learning. With rigid collapse, shared rigid terrain enables efficient simulation but causes indirect interference, as collapse induced by one robot affects others. Individual rigid terrain prevents interference but increases simulation cost and training time. With virtual collapse on shared rigid terrain, our hybrid approach combines rigid-body simulation for non-collapsible terrain with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions, enabling memory-efficient parallel learning without indirect interference.

papers.abstract: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU. We also report how throughput grows with the number of worlds, depth-camera throughput, agreement with closed-form references, and a reliability test over a thousand worlds.

papers.abstract: This paper presents an overview of the integrated technologies developed for the Open Platform League at RoboCup@Home 2026 in Incheon. A vision system integrated with learning-based, training-free models enables robust object recognition for both known and unknown objects. We introduce a RoomPlan-based method that semi-automatically registers furniture geometry and labels to generate semantic maps. Additionally, a large language model-based planner interprets the instructions recognized by Whisper and generates primitive skill sequences for execution. A reservoir-computing framework serves as a lightweight temporal-processing model for action recognition. Its field-programmable gate array-based implementation enables low-power, real-time operation. This is key to removing operational time constraints for service robots. Open-source releases, including task environments, dataset tools, and navigation frameworks, enhance reproducibility, reuse, and continuous progress within the RoboCup@Home community.

papers.abstract: We study robot navigation in indoor environments from fixed exocentric cameras (infrastructure-mounted, external to the robot). We show that standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which succeeds with onboard cameras, fails to learn this navigation end-to-end in our setup. This failure results from the perspective mismatch between exocentric observations and egocentric action and goal formulations, which is too complex to resolve from the reward signal alone. To address this, we propose Viewpoint-Invariant Navigation from Exocentric Cameras (VINE). VINE uses an obstacle map estimation network, trained with supervised learning, that takes exocentric images, camera pose, robot pose, and room dimensions as input and produces a viewpoint-invariant obstacle map. This map can be used either by a PPO policy or by a planner such as A*. VINE's map estimation performs better than perspective mapping approaches, handles cameras placed across a wide range of positions and orientations without view-specific tuning, requires only approximate camera pose estimates (noise with a standard deviation of 30cm per axis in x, y, and z and about 20{\deg} of rotation error on average), is robust to intrinsic variation, and extends to two-camera setups with partial coverage. Despite operating from cameras randomized in position during evaluation, VINE surpasses the navigation success rate of PPO with an onboard camera in simulated environments.
authors: Raul Steinmetz, Jair Augusto Bottega, Ayanori Yorozu, Akihisa Ohya
bullets: Standard PPO fails end-to-end because exocentric observations mismatch egocentric actions and goals.
VINE estimates obstacle maps from images, camera and robot poses, and room dimensions using supervised learning.
The maps support either PPO policies or classical planners such as A*.
It works across varied camera positions and orientations, tolerates approximate poses and intrinsic variation, and supports partially covering two-camera setups.
In simulation, VINE outperforms PPO using an onboard camera despite randomized camera placement at evaluation.

papers.abstract: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.
authors: Jinze Tao, Yuxiao Han, Kangkang Dong, Yancong Wei, Xiaojun Zhu, Bokui Chen, Houde Liu
bullets: Motivation: Calling an LLM planner at every episode adds cost and delay.
Method: Convert planner-driven motions, sub-instructions, detours, and resulting poses into VLA training data under the original task instruction.
Training: Mask losses for goal-averse steps, label states within 1 m of the goal as stops, and update the VLA with low-rank adaptation.
Result: The VLA learns to stop at goals and reach goals the base model misses, across all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of H2E. (a) On training scenes, a frontier LLM planner with a place graph and its own tools calls the base VLA. We keep the sessions that reach the goal. They leave the loss but stay in the history. ③ Visited states within 1 m of the goal are labelled as stops. (c) The VLA keeps its vision encoder and LLM frozen. It trains LoRA adapters and the waypoint head with the masked L1 loss and runs alone at test time.

papers.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present \ourmethod{}, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. \ourmethod{} extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate \ourmethod{} on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.
authors: Sahit Chintalapudi, Xiaoyan Wang, Aryan Zoroufi, Aditya Agarwal, Nancy Kanwisher, Tom\'as Lozano-P\'erez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
bullets: Addresses long-horizon manipulation with occlusion and uncertainty.
Interleaves sensing actions into task-and-motion plan skeletons designed for full observability.
Uses persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map.
Evaluated on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks with heavy occlusion and partial visibility.
Outperforms baselines lacking active perception or persistent memory.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of VA-TAMP. RGB-D observations update an object-based memory (OBM), which maintains observed occupancy Vt and object mesh hypothesesMt. Given a goal G, a fully observed TAMP solver computes a plan p overMt. JUSTIFY uses Mt and Vt to derive a set of visibility preconditions Φ and insert look actions to produce a justified plan p̂. These preconditions are checked against Vt to select the next action at or trigger replanning. The plan also guides OBM refinement, prioritizing mesh hypotheses that are relevant to the plan and inconsistent with accumulated observations.

The finger contacts Fa (pink) must read full, and the swept volume of the gripper along the grasp trajectory Ea must read empty. The blue cells are known to be empty, the orange cells are unknown. (b) After the look, the required cells are observed and ϕa holds.

papers.title: Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning with Task-Centric Perception
papers.tldr: An algorithm extends deterministic task-and-motion planning to partially observable rearrangement by actively sensing and maintaining persistent object memory.

papers.abstract: Motion imitation enables humanoid robots to acquire whole-body skills such as walking and dancing. However, fine-tuning an entire policy for a new skill can affect existing behaviors, while training a separate policy for each skill increases training and maintenance costs. We present PERA, a method for learning new skills by reusing existing motion capabilities. PERA freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an additional task expert and its routing score using task rewards or teacher-action supervision. In Unitree G1 simulation, each added task module contains approximately 1.03% of the parameters of the base actor. Built on our pretrained policy, PERA successfully completes all ten new tasks. Disabling the expert restores the original computation path of the base policy, which still fully executes all 126 original motions. Enabling the expert also improves the execution of some dance motions not used to train that expert, indicating that its benefits extend beyond its training motions. Experiments with HoloMotion further demonstrate the applicability of PERA to different base policies.
authors: Shangchao Hu, Yadan Sun, Xibo Yu, Wei Huang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between catastrophic interference from fine-tuning and the cost of maintaining separate policies.
Freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an added task expert with its routing score using rewards or teacher actions.
Each task module is about 1.03% the size of the base actor in Unitree G1 simulation.
Successfully completes all ten added tasks while retaining all 126 original motions when the expert is disabled.
Also improves some unseen dance motions and transfers across base policies in HoloMotion experiments.

(b) The eight existing routed experts and one enabled new expert jointly participate in Top-2 selection; the shared FFN is combined separately. Disabling the new expert restores the original routing.

papers.abstract: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.
authors: Fabian Deuser, Peter Mortimer, Robin-Nico Kampa, Anna B\"o{\ss}end\"orfer, Mirko M\"ahlisch, Martin Werner, Norbert Oswald
bullets: Targets ground-to-aerial localization when GNSS is unreliable, especially in forests, fields, and rural tracks.
Provides 9,356 georeferenced scenes near Munich across four seasons, pairing aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB and 3D LiDAR.
Includes paved/unpaved terrain labels and seasonal variation to study terrain structure and appearance gaps.
Fine-tuned state-of-the-art baselines degrade substantially off-road, while the proposed RGB–LiDAR baseline improves localization performance.
Data and baselines are publicly released for future research.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured off-road terrain, providing a valuable resource for evaluating navigation and perception methods in challenging environments.
papers.title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain
papers.tldr: GOOSELoc introduces a multimodal benchmark showing that cross-view localization methods struggle in seasonal, unstructured off-road environments and benefit from combining RGB imagery with LiDAR.

papers.abstract: Potholes impose billions of dollars in annual vehicle damage, yet detectors report only where potholes are, not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from a single RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded vision-language model (VLM) assessments tend to be over-conservative. We present a five-stage modular framework for the offline assessment of already-detected potholes that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning: perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. We evaluate it on 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes against independent references. Severity agreement with a prediction-free three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.139$, 95% CI [0.00, 0.28]; $n = 101$) and far below the annotators' agreement with one another ($\kappa = 0.605$); against physically measured depth on an independent RGB-D dataset, it is also weak ($\kappa = 0.098$), although the predicted classes preserve the order of measured depths. The severity classes are therefore perceived visual categories, not depth measurements. Geometric grounding does change the warnings: relative to an image-only baseline, it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109% (Stuart-Maxwell $p < 10^{-15}$), and in a blind study, three raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. A six-arm prompt ablation attributes the hybrid prompt's rule adherence to the per-pothole measurements rather than to the rubric or worked examples. At USD 0.105 per scene, it suits large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; its maneuver suggestions are advisory research outputs, not validated vehicle guidance.
authors: Abdalmalek Aburaddaha, Zaid A. El Shair, Ali Al-Bustami, Samir A. Rawashdeh
bullets: Pothole detectors locate defects but generally do not assess severity or recommend actions; single-image severity estimation is inherently ambiguous.

The five-stage offline pipeline applies perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro classification with composite risk scoring, and warning generation.

Geometric grounding substantially changes warnings: it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier, increases critical-tier assignments by 109%, and is preferred 3.5:1 over image-only warnings in a blind study.

Severity agreement is weak with both human references and measured depth, although predictions preserve the ordering of measured depths; the categories should be interpreted as visual perceptions, not depth estimates.
The system costs USD 0.105 per scene and is intended for large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; maneuver suggestions are advisory and not validated vehicle guidance.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the five-stage modular pothole hazard assessment framework. Stage 1 applies perspective transformation to raw dashcam imagery. Stage 2 performs zero-shot pothole segmentation using SAM. Stage 3 extracts deterministic geometric features from segmentation masks. Stage 4 performs VLM-based severity classification grounded in geometric context and computes composite risk scores. Stage 5 generates natural language warnings with maneuver recommendations. Structured outputs are passed sequentially between stages.

Fig. 5. Warning urgency distribution across all 1,119 scenes for the imageonly and hybrid methods. The hybrid pipeline shifts a substantial portion of high-urgency assignments to medium while increasing critical-tier assignments.

The hybrid output localizes hazards to wheel paths, recommends a specific steering offset, and reports a composite risk score.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the problem of pothole severity assessment by integrating geometric measurements with VLM reasoning, providing a modular framework for infrastructure assessment that leverages spatial understanding.
papers.title: Pothole Risk Assessment with Geometrically Grounded Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: A geometry-grounded VLM framework produces more useful pothole severity warnings than image-only assessment, but its severity classes are not reliable measurements of physical depth.

papers.abstract: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding. Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.
authors: Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji, Filip Rybansky, Quoc Vuong, Frank Guerin, Andrew Gilbert
bullets: Introduces sub-action detection, requiring explicit recognition of hand roles and manipulated objects during high-level actions.
Adds FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention module that emphasizes action-relevant visual cues without changing the underlying vision or language encoders.
Uses MetaLoss, a masked object-weighted loss that prioritizes visually grounded terms.
Introduces BiScopeCap-100K, a densely captioned egocentric video dataset with hand-role, object, action, and spatial metadata.
Improves action, hand-role, and object recognition across evaluated Video-LLM backbones, with the strongest aggregate performance among tested configurations on BiScopeCap.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a framework for pothole risk assessment that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning, demonstrating the utility of geometrically grounded vision-language models for driving safety and spatial understanding.
papers.title: Sub-actions in Action: Text-Guided Hand-Role Alignment for Sub-Action Recognition
papers.tldr: BiScopeNet improves egocentric video models’ ability to identify left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within ongoing actions using text-guided feature alignment and targeted supervision.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning (IL) typically relies on large-scale offline demonstrations collected from multiple human or algorithmic demonstrators. However, most existing approaches assume these demonstrators are homogeneous or near-optimal experts, a convenient but unrealistic assumption in real-world applications. In practice, demonstrations are often collected from heterogeneous demonstrators with unknown and varying levels of expertise, resulting in highly mixed-quality data. In this work, we study a challenging yet practical setting of imitation learning from such heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators. We propose Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning (LEOS-IL), a principled framework that jointly learns (i) a state-action optimality scoring model and (ii) latent expertise levels for each demonstrator from unlabeled suboptimal offline demonstrations. The learned scoring model is then integrated into an online policy optimization procedure, where the agent is trained to maximize estimated optimality scores while its online rollouts are iteratively leveraged to refine the scoring model, thereby mitigating distributional shift during online adaptation. We further provide theoretical guarantees for optimality score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines across highly heterogeneous and low-quality demonstration regimes.
authors: Cheng Pan, Nan Lu, Kai Arulkumaran, Josie Hughes
bullets: Addresses imitation learning when offline demonstrations come from heterogeneous, imperfect, and unknown-quality demonstrators.
Jointly learns state-action optimality scores and latent expertise levels from unlabeled suboptimal demonstrations.
Uses the learned scores for online policy optimization and incorporates new rollouts to reduce distributional shift.
Provides theoretical guarantees for score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery.
Experiments on continuous-control benchmarks show consistent gains over existing baselines in highly heterogeneous, low-quality regimes.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.
authors: Leonardo Vanni, Stefano Gasperini, Federico Tombari, Chiara Plizzari
bullets: Addresses failures of existing 4DGS methods on splitting, merging, opening, and closing interactions.
Introduces TopoEgo, a benchmark covering fission, fusion, opening, and closing in egocentric video.
Assigns independent rigid motion to interacting parts and activates or deactivates Gaussians as surfaces change.
Outperforms existing 4DGS approaches across topological changes, particularly in post-event frames.
Code and data are planned for public release.

papers.abstract: GPT-6 Astra can drive a robot arm directly through a fixed harness, and scores of such robot-use agents on RoboDojo have risen quickly since. Reported systems differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is hard to tell which choices produce the gains. We take these designs apart and test them in one framework, along the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model. A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way. Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free lunch, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone. JustRUA starts from the official L3 harness and keeps only what matters most. Even with no learned policy, self-improvement loop or task-specific tuning, this simple harness raises the score on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark substantially, from 29.7 to 50.3.
authors: Zefan Wang, Yufan Dang, Xuanwei Shi, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yin, SikYuen Tam, Hanyu Liu, Yasheng Wang, Yaxi Lu, Songyang Zhang, Xin Cong, Yuan Yao
bullets: Provides a controlled comparison of harness design, action interface, experience reuse, and scene geometry.
Finds that retaining full episode history and terminating motions early are especially effective design choices.
Experience reuse changes behavior but does not provide universally free improvements.
Scene geometry is highly beneficial, including when depth is predicted from RGB alone.
Raises RoboDojo performance from 29.7 to 50.3 without a learned policy, self-improvement loop, or task-specific tuning.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require separating adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained targets. We study this setting as removal manipulation, where progress depends on evolving contact states that are only partially observable from vision and kinematics. We introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. To make multi-finger force observations easier to fuse, we express fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, giving force components consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time. Using an Action Chunking Transformer backbone, policies fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force observations to predict closed-loop action chunks from demonstrations. Evaluation uses six core benchmark tasks for controlled fingertip-input and force-frame ablations, plus three extension scenarios for additional held-out coverage. Across these evaluations, the learned policies achieve consistent removal performance, and ablations show that wrist-frame forces, especially with fingertip pose, improve stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs and no-force baselines. Project website: https://dexremo.github.io
authors: Liman Wang, Hanyang Zhong, Sun Zhaole, Wenting Cao, Babar Jamil, Andy Tyrrell, Shan Luo, Jihong Zhu
bullets: Targets removal tasks involving adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained objects with partially observable contact states.
Provides a high-force robotic hand with modular fingertips, three-axis fingertip force sensing, and nine real-robot scenarios.
Represents fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame to align force meaning across fingers and time.
Uses an Action Chunking Transformer to fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force data for closed-loop control.
Experiments report consistent removal performance, with wrist-frame forces—especially combined with fingertip pose—improving stability and generalization over local-frame and no-force inputs.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of removal manipulation and the proposed framework. (a) DexRemo Hand removes strongly adhered 3D-printed barnacles from a curved turtle mockup, demonstrating variable and partially observable attachments. (b) Representative human removal behaviors reveal task-intrinsic interaction principles. (c) Fingertip forces are transformed from local sensor frames RSi to a shared wrist frame, then fused with vision, fingertip poses, and proprioception. An ACT-based policy generates observation-conditioned action chunks for progressive, edge-initiated debonding.

Fig. 7. Physical objects used in each manipulation task (A1–C2). Each object is photographed alongside a standard ruler to indicate real-world scale. Objects are labeled as seen or unseen according to whether they appear in policy training. Detailed dimensions and preparation parameters are summarized in Table VI and Appendix E.

Fig. 11. Blu-Tack removal (A3): force feedback enables observation-driven switching in an ACT-based policy. (a) P+W (fingertip pose + wrist-frame forces) and (b) P (fingertip pose only). Left: fingertip trajectories for right/middle/left fingers. Right: wrist-frame force components over time (color indicates finger; line style indicates Fx, Fy , and Fz). Vertical dashed lines mark the timestamps of snapshots t1–t4. With P+W, changes in force patterns during side-finger boundary interaction provide an observable cue for switching to a distinct action chunk dominated by the middle finger, which ramps up force and achieves detachment. With P only, the policy exhibits prolonged oscillatory contact and fails to satisfy the success criterion within the time limit.

Fig. 10. Task-specific efficiency–force/contact trade-off across input configurations. Columns correspond to the three core task groups: adhesive removal (A1–A4), buried retrieval (C1), and surface cleaning (B1). Each point summarizes one input configuration over the same three training seeds and matched rollout budgets used in Fig. 8, with rollouts pooled across seeds before the class-level scores are computed; the point markers therefore carry no seed-level dispersion. The top row relates completion efficiency, Eq. (23), to the class-specific force/contact score; the bottom row relates success rate to the same score. The vertical axis is the task-specific score Qc,m of Eq. (27): for A- and C-class tasks Qc,m = 1− Īc,m, so a higher score indicates lower cumulative contact effort, whereas for B-class cleaning Qc,m = Īc,m, so a higher score indicates stronger sustained contact. Vertical scores should therefore be compared only within a task class. The full (P +W ) policy shows the most favorable class-specific trade-offs.

Fig. 12. Failure-mode distribution across tasks and input configurations. Stacked bars show the number of failed rollouts assigned to each dominant failure mode for the six core ablation tasks A1–A4, B1, and C1. Counts are pooled over the three training seeds for each task–input configuration and are not normalized by total rollouts. As each input configuration uses the same evaluation budget within a task, lower total bar height indicates fewer failures.

Fig. 13. Teleoperation interface used during demonstration collection. The demonstrator observes synchronized camera views together with a real-time visualization of the follower hand configuration and fingertip force vectors, which provides augmented visual feedback about contact direction and magnitude.

Fig. 9. Completion and termination time across input configurations over all core tasks. (a) Termination time over all rollouts, where failed trials are assigned the 120 s timeout. The success rate of each input configuration is reported below the x-axis. (b) Completion time over successful rollouts only. Boxes show the interquartile range, horizontal lines denote medians, whiskers show the non-outlier range, and dots denote individual real-robot rollouts. The full P + W configuration achieves the highest overall success rate and substantially reduces timeout-dominated failures, while maintaining competitive successful-rollout completion time.

(c) Calibration with suspended masses applying known Cartesian forces. (d) Calibration for mid/left/right sensors: corrected outputs vs. ground-truth forces along x, y, z (dashed: ideal).

papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation requires precise alignment and controlled handling of rigid, deformable, and flexible components. Yet, the benefits of pretrained visuomotor policies remain underexplored in settings where limited access to specialized hardware, components, and fixtures constrains demonstration collection and evaluation. Understanding task-specific data requirements is important for assessing their scalability across diverse processes on the factory floor. We investigate whether video pretraining can support reliable industrial manipulation with limited action data. We propose FLUX-mimic, a video-action model, motivated by the potential of video pretraining to capture motion and interaction patterns that enable sample-efficient training. FLUX-mimic is built on a backbone pretrained on large-scale web and industrial task data, and an action expert to generate robot trajectories. We train our policy by joint video-action training. Across four automotive manufacturing benchmark tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, FLUX-mimic outperforms all considered baselines on the dexterous robot platform and matches pi_{0.5}'s average success rate on the gripper-based robot platform. On a deformable part kitting task, FLUX-mimic reaches 77.5% success with as little as two hours of task-specific action-labeled demonstrations.

Combines a backbone pretrained on web and industrial task video with an action expert that generates robot trajectories.
Uses joint video-action training to learn motion and interaction patterns for sample-efficient policy training.
Evaluated on four automotive manufacturing tasks across two bimanual robot platforms.

Outperforms considered baselines on a dexterous platform, matches pi_{0.5}'s average success on a gripper-based platform, and achieves 77.5% success on deformable-part kitting with two hours of demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Deep networks that estimate ground reaction forces and centers of pressure from motion-capture markers are validated within one laboratory, in a seldom-stated coordinate frame, and sometimes with trial-level splits that put the same person in the training and the test set. We measured what each practice costs, and whether such models transfer between laboratories. Three sequence models (convolutional, convolutional-recurrent, and convolutional-transformer) were evaluated on two independent datasets, locomotion (6 subjects) and occupational patient handling (10 subjects), under one pipeline, one tuning procedure, three seeds, and four protocols: trial-level split, leave-one-subject-out, pooled two-laboratory training with matched held-out subjects, and cross-laboratory transfer. At a fixed configuration, trial-level splits overstated the subject-held-out coefficient of determination by +0.040 to +0.194; on occupational data the overstatement exceeded every difference between architectures. With subjects held out, the three models reached values between 0.583 and 0.804; the leader differed between datasets, and gaps lay within subject-to-subject variability. Pooling the laboratories changed neither dataset on matched subjects. Transfer between laboratories was below chance in both directions, including the vertical force, which no in-plane rotation can affect. Leaving force targets in the plate frame while inputs were heading-aligned cost 0.57 of locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance, enough to make that force look hardest; a Newton's-law correlation detected the mismatch before training. Split protocol and target frame changed reported accuracy more than architecture did. Learned force estimators should be validated with subjects held out, checked for frame consistency before training, and tested across laboratories before deployment claims are made.
authors: Hernan David Santos, Yinong Chen, Yu Ding, Xudong Zhang, Jian Tao
bullets: Trial-level splits overstated subject-held-out performance by 0.040–0.194.
With subjects held out, model performance ranged from 0.583 to 0.804, and no architecture consistently led across datasets.
Pooling laboratories did not improve matched-subject performance, while cross-laboratory transfer was below chance in both directions.
A mismatched target frame reduced locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance by 0.57; a Newton’s-law check detected the mismatch before training.
The findings support subject-held-out validation, frame-consistency checks, and cross-laboratory testing before deployment claims.

papers.title: Subject-Held-Out Evaluation of Deep Ground Reaction Force Estimators Across Two Laboratories: Leakage and Cross-Laboratory Transfer

papers.abstract: This work addresses the problem of finding a concealed object in an environment by unifying formalisms for partially observable environments with multi-modal priors drawn from a mix of ontologies, semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs. We propose a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP (CA-MOMDP), a Bayes-adaptive setting where uncertainty is over both object locations and which nodes can conceal them, held as a hypothesis with a bounded ontology prior and resolved only by interaction. We define a hierarchical transition system (HTS) to abstract the environment into room and object nodes that can be planned over via our CA-MOMDP. We further propose a COMBS-score: a multi-modal fusion of a human informed semantic network, LLM, and VLM, to initialize the belief over object locations, which grounds our abstractions and reduces reliance on a single model. Belief is maintained via Bayes' rule, which never lets a look rule out a closed container. We prove a present target is found in a bounded number of searches under exact perception and that its location is never ruled out given missed detection under noisy perception. We ablate each component to demonstrate their significance. Across five simulator configurations, from a gridworld to Matterport3D with a real detector, COMBS finds 92-100% of in-distribution and 92-100% of out-of-distribution targets, matches or beats the baselines in processing speed, significantly outperforms a per-step LLM policy at lower cost on the larger scenes, recovers more out-of-distribution placements than a TidyBot ranking, and matches an LLM-only prior at a fraction of its per-decision latency. COMBS is the only standalone method that can declare a target absent at a stated error level, and the per-step LLM policy offered a termination action abandons 12-22% of targets that were present, against 1.6-3.2% for COMBS on the same episodes.
bullets: Models uncertainty over both object locations and which environmental nodes may conceal them using a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP.
Plans over room and object nodes through a hierarchical transition system.
Fuses human-informed semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs to initialize location beliefs, then updates them with Bayes’ rule.
Across five simulated settings, finds 92–100% of in- and out-of-distribution targets and generally matches or outperforms comparison methods.
Can declare a target absent at a stated error level; it abandons fewer present targets than a per-step LLM policy.

The policy selects the search with the highest expected detection per unit cost, and each observation that does not reveal the target updates the belief until the target is found or the absence test fires.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes COMBS, a multi-modal Bayesian search method that unifies ontologies, LLMs, and VLMs to locate concealed objects in partially observable environments.
papers.title: COMBS: Concealed Object Multi-modal Bayesian Search
papers.tldr: COMBS combines Bayesian search, hierarchical environment abstractions, and multimodal priors to efficiently find concealed objects while avoiding false conclusions that objects are absent.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in robotic manipulation, yet most rely primarily on 2D visual observations and language instructions, leaving scene geometry and obstacle relationships to be inferred implicitly. This limitation is particularly problematic in cluttered environments, where small spatial errors can lead to unintended contacts or collisions. We propose MOSAIC, a modular spatial- and obstacle-aware framework that can be integrated with pretrained VLA policies to improve object-level scene understanding and action generation. Our method augments the VLA backbone with an auxiliary semantic grounding task that predicts role-specific masks for the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles. We further combine the target and destination masks with depth estimated from 3D scene reconstruction to construct role-specific geometric tokens that are injected directly into the action expert. In addition, we propose obstacle-aware attention supervision that emphasizes obstacles near the robot body during task execution. The resulting attention features are subsequently injected into later action-expert layers to further guide action generation. Together, these components provide explicit semantic, geometric, and obstacle-aware cues while preserving the underlying pretrained VLA architecture. We evaluate our framework on pretrained VLA model using the RoboPRO benchmark, including visual perturbation tests, and further validate it on real-world manipulation tasks. MOSAIC improves the success rate by 5.1% in cluttered scenes, and by 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains of up to 25.0% in the most challenging environment. We will release our code and dataset upon acceptance at the following Github page: https://mmahdavian.github.io/MOSAIC/
authors: Richard Shi, Mohammad Mahdavian, Mehrdad Momeni Zadeh, Mohammed Elmahgiubi, Amir Rasouli
bullets: Addresses the weakness of primarily 2D VLA models in reasoning about geometry and obstacle relationships.
Uses auxiliary semantic grounding to predict masks for the target, destination, and surrounding obstacles.
Builds role-specific geometric tokens from masks and reconstructed depth, injecting them into the action expert.
Adds obstacle-aware attention supervision focused on obstacles near the robot during execution.
Improves success by 5.1% in cluttered scenes and 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains up to 25.0% in the hardest environment; also validates real-world manipulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: MOSAIC Model Structure. (a) A vision–language backbone encodes observations, instructions, and robot state, with role tokens supporting semantic mask prediction. (b) The action expert attends to the shared prefix and produces learned attention maps. (c) Object-level depth is extracted using the VGGT-Ω combined with the predicted masks. The depth tokens are generated and injected into the action expert final layers. (d) Contact-relevant expert targets supervise attention through forward KL divergence during training. (e) Predicted attention maps are averaged, detached, and injected through residual cross-attention into late action layers. (f) Flow matching generates actions for robot execution.
Fig. 1: MOSAIC overview. A pretrained VLA is augmented with role-specific masks, object-level depth tokens, and obstacle-focused attention guidance.

Fig. 5: Average attention maps from the first three action-expert layers for the RoboPRO-finetuned base π0.5 model (top) and our final model (bottom) across two manipulation actions. Blue regions indicate higher attention. Our model consistently focuses on potential collision regions, while the base π0.5 exhibits less obstacle-aware attention.

Fig. 3: The pipeline for groundtruth attention map generation. (a) The original RGB countertop camera view. (b) Per-object contact disk generation. The closest point of each object’s bounding box is projected onto pixel space. Disks are centered at these points to highlight potential contact zones. (c) Proximity weight map β. Higher weight for objects closer to the robot body, less weight for farther objects, zero weight for very distant objects. (d) Obstacle contact mask. Using the proximity weight map β to filter out irrelevant objects. (e) Groundtruth attention heatmap H. Obstacle contact mask convolved with a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation σ to represent the spatial distribution of visual attention. (f) Patch-wise distributed groundtruth attention map. Matches the granularity of the action expert’s attention modules.

Fig. 4: Task-conditioned visual annotations for (a) Simulation and (b) Real-world data. In (a), rows show RGB images, mask overlays, and binary target (T), destination (D), and obstacle (O) masks. Simulation overlays use red/green/blue for T/D/O. In (b), examples (b-1) to (b-4) show four real-world tasks with one to four added distractors.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MOSAIC, a framework that augments VLA policies with geometric tokens and obstacle-aware attention to improve manipulation success in cluttered scenes.
papers.title: MOSAIC: Modular Obstacle and Spatial-Aware Framework for Manipulation In Cluttered Scenes
papers.tldr: MOSAIC enhances pretrained vision-language-action policies with explicit object, destination, depth, and obstacle cues to improve manipulation in cluttered and visually perturbed scenes.

papers.abstract: Full-size humanoid robots are being considered for hazardous industrial work such as disassembling electric-vehicle batteries. We describe the safety mechanisms of an open-source autonomy stack for the Unitree H1-2 humanoid and what deploying them taught us. All joint commands pass through a safety layer that runs separately from the control software. It enforces joint position, velocity, and torque limits, and it stops the robot when a state estimate becomes stale or when the hard-wired emergency stop (e-stop) is pressed or disconnected. We pushed the standing robot until it lost balance. With a model-predictive lower-body controller it never recovered, and the operator had to press the e-stop in every trial. Pressing it removes balance control, and the robot falls. The safety layer's own limits trigger the same stop, and limits chosen for manipulation were exceeded during normal walking. Near an operator or a battery pack, the fall can be more dangerous than the cause of the stop. Joint limits bound how much force a robot can apply, but not when applying it is appropriate. Drawing on research on responsibility and on child and adolescent development, we therefore make a case for granting robots force authority in stages, with a person or organization explicitly responsible for its use.
authors: Max Conway, Yutong Zhang, Allen Devaraj, William Xie, Alessandro Roncone, Nikolaus Correll
bullets: An open-source safety layer independently enforces joint position, velocity, and torque limits.
It stops the robot when state estimates become stale or the hard-wired e-stop is pressed or disconnected.
In balance-loss trials, neither the controller nor safety limits recovered the robot; stopping led to a fall.
Limits selected for manipulation could be exceeded during ordinary walking, especially near people or battery packs.
The authors propose gradually increasing robot force authority under explicit human or organizational responsibility.

papers.abstract: Generated touch could extend robot learning beyond recorded contacts. A tactile generator needs a latent space, and we choose one by testing whether a material classifier trained on real GelSight presses still works on encode-decode reconstructions from pretrained image models. On ObjectFolder Real, the classifier loses 6.5 to 9.7 points on reconstructions from three 16x discrete tokenizers and 0.3 points on those from the Stable Diffusion VAE (SD-VAE). The 16x tokenizers again lose far more on Touch and Go and on DIGIT object recognition (YCB-Slide). Retraining the classifier on reconstructions, with no new labels, narrows the discrete gap. SD-VAE reconstructions also keep object identity, with 76.7% object-matching accuracy against 78.9% for real touch and 67.0% for MAGVIT-v2. We therefore select SD-VAE latents and show a photo-to-touch generator trained in them. Code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Wanghao Ye, Aarosh Das, Sihan Chen, Yiting Wang, Bowei Tian, Guoheng Sun, Shwai He, Zheyu Shen, Ziyao Wang, Yexiao He, Zhaoyi Liu, Meng Liu, Yuning Zhang, Meng Feng, Ziyi Wang, Yilong Dai, Yifei Dong, Siyuan Peng, Zhenle Duan, Joshua Liu, Lang Xiong, Daeun Jung, Aditya Sarkar, Parastoo Pilevar, Xiaochuan Gong, Yancheng Zhu, Yingying Fan, Qiong Wang, Ang Li

The discrete tokenizers also perform substantially worse on Touch and Go and DIGIT object-recognition tests.
Retraining classifiers on reconstructions narrows the discrete-tokenizer gap without requiring new labels.
SD-VAE preserves object identity well and is used for a demonstrated photo-to-touch generator.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require carefully controlled contact forces for successful execution, yet large-scale, force-aware datasets remain scarce. Handheld interfaces can help by transmitting interaction forces directly through the operator's arm, but most existing designs are tailored to simple linear grippers and do not match the nonlinear mechanics of widely used robotic grippers. We present RUMI, a handheld universal manipulation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 with exchangeable fingertip sensors that preserves the target gripper geometry while enabling natural input before contact and force measurement after contact. By integrating the tracking system into a virtual reality headset, our method provides real-time augmented reality feedback about the kinematic feasibility of motion on the target robot platform. We further introduce a haptic feedback mechanism that supports force-aware teleoperation for simulated and real robots. A user study shows fewer episodes containing joint-limit violations with live robot visualization and pose initialization (3/50) than without augmented reality (16/50). We additionally train imitation policies from demonstrations, collected using two different fingertip modalities enabled by the gripper-matched hardware, and assess the haptic interface's capability for collecting force-aware teleoperation datasets in simulation.
authors: Kevin Avdiu, Seongjin Bien, Yannik Blei, Philine Meister, Johannes Hechtl, Philipp Schmitt, Kai Wurm, Georg von Wichert, Wolfram Burgard
bullets: Addresses scarce force-aware manipulation data and the mismatch between existing interfaces and nonlinear robotic grippers.
Preserves target-gripper geometry while supporting natural pre-contact input and post-contact force measurement through exchangeable fingertip sensors.
Provides real-time AR feedback on motion feasibility and haptic feedback for force-aware teleoperation in simulation and on real robots.
A user study reports fewer episodes with joint-limit violations using live robot visualization and pose initialization than without AR (3/50 vs. 16/50).
Demonstrates imitation-policy training with two fingertip modalities and evaluates force-aware dataset collection in simulation.
