papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation of mobile robots in crowded environments, while preserving pedestrians' psychological comfort, requires distinguishing pedestrians from other obstacles, predicting their future motion, and accounting for uncertainty in the predicted trajectories of both pedestrians and the robot. This work extends a previous MPC framework by integrating obstacle and pedestrian detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online prediction-error estimation directly within the collision-avoidance mechanism. To reduce collision-avoidance complexity in crowded scenarios, nearby obstacles are aggregated, thereby reducing the number of collision-avoidance constraints. Simulation studies evaluate the prediction-error margins and the computational benefits of semantics-aware aggregation. In a paired 300-seed closed-loop comparison with a moving generic obstacle, Markov residual tightening reduces the fraction of runs with physical contact from $10.0\%$ to $1.33\%$, at a mean travel-time cost of $0.68$ s. In a separate crowd-navigation semantic ablation, the offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap occupies $2.11\%$ of observed time with pedestrian-aware handling versus $22.84\%$ with generic-obstacle handling.

papers.abstract: Parameterized-action MDPs (PAMDPs) ask an agent to choose a discrete action together with continuous parameters whose meaning depends on that choice. Model-free PAMDP methods act fast but need many interactions; model-based methods are sample-efficient but plan at every decision, which makes them slow to act. We introduce HyLI (Hybrid Latent Imagination), a model-based agent that learns a hybrid policy entirely in the latent imagination of a world model and acts with a single forward pass. To address learning problems that the PAMDP structure creates, HyLI adds counterfactual mode evaluation, which gives every discrete action a learning signal at every imagined state, and success-window replay, which keeps rare successes in training. On seven standard PAMDP benchmarks, HyLI is within one published standard deviation of, or above, the published score of the strongest model-free baseline in our comparison on all 7 tasks, reaches 90% of that score with 2.4x fewer environment steps than that baseline (5.0x when its reward-free pre-training is counted), and decides 67x faster than the model-based planner DLPA at its published planner settings. It is the only method in our comparison that is both more sample-efficient than that baseline and fast enough for real-time control.

Reaches 90% of that baseline’s score with 2.4× fewer environment steps and decides 67× faster than the DLPA planner under its published settings.

papers.abstract: Robot mechanics can bias kinematic measures of recovery and limit comparisons across rehabilitation devices. We developed a closed-loop human-robot simulation calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics. Paired runs held motor-control parameters and movement plans fixed to quantify bias in seven metrics relative to a low-impedance reference, normalized using external repeatability benchmarks. Within a subset informed by published device specifications, median log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) bias was 0.93 and 1.79 benchmark units for stroke and healthy profiles, respectively. Sobol analysis identified Coulomb friction and apparent mass as leading contributors; LDLJ bias persisted across 11 robustness variants. LDLJ bias increased as simulated movements became less fragmented. If recovery similarly reduces fragmentation, this effect could partly mask improvement in measured smoothness. Correction combining identified robot dynamics and observed metrics with gradient-boosted trees reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.77 to 0.10 for LDLJ and from 0.24 to 0.08 for spectral arc length (SPARC) in the device-informed subset of a random 20% hold-out. Median smoothness residuals remained at or below 0.15 benchmark units across four separately held-out parameter regions. Under an alternative controller, LDLJ error decreased from 1.60 to 0.17 without retraining, although transfer varied across metrics. These simulation results support mechanical characterization and movement-dependent correction toward more comparable robotic assessments, motivating validation in patients.

bullets: A calibrated closed-loop human–robot simulation quantified bias in seven kinematic metrics against a low-impedance reference.

Correction generalized to an alternative controller for LDLJ, though transfer varied across metrics.
Findings are simulation-based and require validation in patients.

papers.abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.
bullets: Imperfect detections make both search-location and stopping decisions uncertain.
The method models target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors in a Bayesian active-search framework.
Ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses evaluate these representations and their update mechanisms across detector configurations.
Target belief and its updates are critical, especially as false detections and missed detections become more prevalent.
The work informs world-model design for embodied agents operating under uncertain observations.

papers.abstract: This paper focuses on improving the behavioral diversity and effectiveness of language-conditioned manipulation policies trained through imitation learning. Recently, continuous-action policies have become mainstream in robotic manipulation, but the lack of diverse demonstrations tends to restrict their behavioral diversity. For grasping, a fundamental subtask of manipulation, 6-DoF grasp detection provides diverse grasp hypotheses, but open-loop execution constrains responsiveness in dynamic environments. This motivates us to combine the diversity of grasp hypotheses with the adaptability of continuous-action policies. To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight and effective spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as geometric priors. In particular, we employ spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics, and integrate them with grasp hypotheses through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction. On LIBERO, GraSLA achieves an average success rate of 99.30%.

bullets: Addresses limited behavioral diversity in imitation-learned, language-conditioned manipulation policies.
Uses spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics.
Integrates grasp hypotheses as geometric priors through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction.

Targets more responsive behavior than open-loop grasp execution in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Embedded perception-to-control systems must combine visual targeting with reliable contact handling under tight computational constraints. We present a shared architecture on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin controlling a Franka Research 3 through Cartesian impedance control. RealSense D435i observations, YOLO11-seg segmentation, depth back-projection, and hand--eye calibration provide metric robot-frame targets. We compare two strategies: compact proximal policy optimization (PPO) policies transferred from simulation for object- and hole-region reaching, and force-guided Cartesian placement using approximately 2 N normal contact and spiral search. The PPO policies achieved 87.2% and 83.1% success over 1000 simulation episodes each. Across 50 real-robot trials per strategy, the learned hybrid and force-guided analytical pipelines achieved 70.0% and 74.0% completion, respectively. Mean perception latency with TensorRT was 34.55 ms. These results support an embedded architecture combining learned free-space reaching with explicit contact correction.
authors: Dezhi Sun, Duy Khang Banh, Kenan Niu
bullets: Integrates RealSense perception, YOLO11-seg, depth back-projection, hand–eye calibration, and Cartesian impedance control on a Franka Research 3.
Compares simulation-transferred PPO policies for reaching with analytical force-guided placement using approximately 2 N contact and spiral search.
PPO reaching achieved 87.2% and 83.1% success in simulation across 1,000 episodes per task.
In 50 real-robot trials per strategy, the learned hybrid and force-guided pipelines achieved 70.0% and 74.0% completion.
TensorRT reduced mean perception latency to 34.55 ms, supporting embedded operation.

papers.selection_reason: Presents an embedded sim-to-real architecture combining PPO policies for reaching and force-guided placement, demonstrating practical deployment on Jetson hardware.
papers.title: Embedded Sim-to-Real Visual Servoing: Learned Reaching and Force-Guided Placement
papers.tldr: An embedded Jetson-based system combines learned visual reaching with force-guided contact correction for robot placement, achieving 70–74% completion in real-robot trials.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.
authors: Miao Pan, Kaixiang Yao, Xiaohe Zhou, Xu Wang, Qinfeng Li, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Targets three missing abilities: causal failure localization, capability-aware adaptation, and experience-driven decision revision.
Builds recovery data by perturbing successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and retaining observable, recoverable failures.
Uses Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision with evaluation-first SFT to structure failure diagnosis before recovery planning.
Applies OPD to reduce errors from self-generated planning prefixes without adding a deployment-time branch.
Improves composite task success by 6.1 points with a frozen VLA and manipulation/navigation success by 13.9 points with fixed GPT-5.5 execution.

papers.abstract: Persistent deformation complicates elasto-plastic manipulation by coupling physical interaction with spatially distributed shape changes. We investigate the force--deformation relationship using a standard robot, a single eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, and intrinsic force estimates. A 7-DoF Franka Emika FR3 performs normal indentations while an Intel RealSense L515 captures pre- and post-contact surfaces. Point-cloud processing localizes deformation and estimates displaced volume. Force--volume characterization includes 27 measurements over nine force levels. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP), trained on 52 force--volume pairs at four levels, achieves a held-out RMSE of 1.857 N and $R^2=0.440$. A separate comparison shows lower error for a quadratic model at 16 N and for the MLP at 19 and 23.5 N. An eight-step experiment at 4 N per interaction demonstrates cumulative deformation localization from the second indentation onward. These results establish a practical measurement basis for deformation-aware manipulation using intrinsic force estimates and single-view geometry.
authors: Dezhi Sun, Marijn van Hilten, Kenan Niu
bullets: Addresses persistent, spatially distributed deformation during elasto-plastic robotic manipulation.
Uses intrinsic robot force estimates, pre/post-contact RGB-D surfaces, and point-cloud processing to estimate displaced volume.
Characterizes force–volume behavior from normal indentations across multiple force levels.
An MLP achieves a held-out RMSE of 1.857 N and R² of 0.440; quadratic modeling performs better at 16 N, while the MLP performs better at 19 and 23.5 N.
An eight-step 4 N experiment localizes cumulative deformation from the second indentation onward.

papers.abstract: Compositional diffusion planners extend short-horizon trajectory models to long-horizon goal-conditioned planning by generating and stitching multiple local trajectory chunks. However, in multimodal environments, local plausibility is not sufficient for global consistency: independently initialized chunks may denoise toward incompatible overlap modes, producing plans that are individually feasible but incoherent after stitching. Existing remedies typically add search, guidance, pruning, or graph-based structure at inference time, increasing computational cost or relying on task-specific machinery. We instead investigate graph-structured dependence among chunk-wise initial diffusion noises as a lightweight coordination mechanism for compositional trajectory planning. We propose \textbf{M}arginal-Preserving \textbf{C}oupled \textbf{D}iffusion \textbf{C}omposition (MCDC), a training-free inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners. Instead of sampling chunk noises independently, MCDC constructs coupled Gaussian initializations whose per-chunk marginals remain exactly standard Gaussian, as required by the pretrained denoiser, while neighboring chunks receive positively correlated noise components. This preserves the standard-Gaussian initialization marginal of each chunk while biasing adjacent chunks toward compatible overlap-mode choices. We prove exact marginal preservation and show, under a simple multimodal overlap model, that positive coupling increases the probability of compatible mode selection. On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently improves over independent compositional diffusion sampling while retaining nearly the same inference time, and achieves a favorable success--cost trade-off compared with search-based composition methods.
authors: Hengrui Zhang, Qiyu Wang, Yuhu Cheng, Brooks Paige, Xuesong Wang
bullets: Problem: Independently sampled chunks can select incompatible overlap modes, making globally stitched plans incoherent in multimodal environments.
Method: Couple neighboring chunks’ initial Gaussian noises with positive correlations while preserving each chunk’s exact standard-Gaussian marginal.

Contribution: A training-free, lightweight inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners, with proofs of marginal preservation and improved compatibility under a multimodal overlap model.

Results: On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently outperforms independent sampling, with nearly unchanged inference time and a favorable success–cost trade-off versus search-based methods.

(e) Coupled noise shifts joint mode mass from incompatible off-diagonal pairs to compatible diagonal pairs. papers.abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) is a foundational primitive in robotics, mapping the task-space objectives expressed by higher-level planners to robot configurations that realize them. Traditional IK methods generally treat each query as an isolated pose-to-configuration problem, but planners often need a distribution over valid realizations that accounts for future reachability and preferences such as collision avoidance and stability. We introduce GenGenIK, a generative modeling approach that supports mobile bases, multiple end-effectors and targets, scene awareness, and preferences over robot behavior within a common interface. Experiments show that GenGenIK outperforms existing methods in both solve rate and runtime across tasks such as bimanual lift and flip-up, while allowing flexible control over the sampled distribution and remaining effective under partial scene observations. Website: https://icra-2027-gengenik.github.io/.
authors: Kaitlyn Zhang, Tom\'as Lozano-P\'erez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
bullets: Addresses the need for distributions of valid IK solutions rather than isolated pose-to-configuration answers.
Supports mobile bases, multiple end-effectors and targets, scene awareness, and behavioral preferences such as collision avoidance and stability.
Allows flexible control over the sampled solution distribution and remains effective with partial scene observations.
Outperforms existing methods in solve rate and runtime on tasks including bimanual lift and flip-up.

papers.abstract: Tabletop games offer a compelling scenario to study the interaction between artificial and human agents, combining social interaction with game state tracking and physical manipulation. To assess the game state, a robot needs to precisely detect closely related game objects, such as different card designs, requiring dedicated training data that is costly to annotate in the real world. Instead, we develop a fully automated synthetic data collection pipeline, using re-projection of known 3D coordinates to generate labels automatically and domain randomization to bridge the reality gap. This approach is used to collect a dataset of 25413 samples to finetune an object detection and a segmentation model, which are combined to assign detected cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state. When evaluated on a real NICO humanoid robot, our pipeline achieves an F1-score of 0.906 for card-to-zone assignment, thus providing the perceptual foundation for a robot that can autonomously play Chef's Hat against human players.
authors: Connor G\"ade, Matthias Kerzel, Hauke B\"unning, Jan-Gerrit Habekost, Mariana Barros, Stefan Wermter
bullets: Addresses the costly real-world annotation needed to distinguish similar card designs.
Uses 3D-coordinate re-projection for automatic labels and domain randomization to reduce the sim-to-real gap.
Trains object detection and segmentation models on 25,413 synthetic samples.
Combines detections to assign cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state.
Evaluated on a real NICO humanoid robot as a foundation for autonomous play against humans.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.
authors: Zhuoyue Li, Zhendong Han, Pankhuri Vanjani, Wenting Li, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Dynamic objects can make predicted action chunks stale before execution.
The study varies prediction/execution horizons, inference synchronization, action delivery, motion cues, and latent-space reinforcement learning.
A prediction horizon of about one second performs best, while the optimal execution horizon depends on the model checkpoint.
Shorter horizons benefit asynchronous execution, and trajectory-continuity methods outperform latency-only approaches.
Policy adaptation repairs targeted failures, but changing the execution horizon can provide comparable gains on some tasks.

papers.abstract: Most action tokenizers for autoregressive vision language action (VLA) models compress motion into chunks that must be decoded in full before their actions become executable. We introduce ActionCodec2, a non-neural streaming tokenizer that releases actions incrementally while keeping trajectory reconstruction error within a prescribed tolerance. Its encoder quantizes each step relative to the decoder's reconstructed state, so the selected motion primitive corrects residual error rather than allowing errors from independently quantized increments to accumulate. Finding the smallest such primitive set is a geometric covering problem; we derive the exact minimum for translation and constant-factor-tight bounds for rotation. Set-BPE then losslessly merges co-occurring primitive symbols across coordinates and neighboring steps, without a fixed coordinate ordering. A universal version fitted on 20k hours of data from 24 embodiments averages 8.8 tokens per second for 15 Hz end-effector motion on this corpus. With the same VLA backbone, ActionCodec2 outperforms the compared tokenizers on three simulation benchmarks and in zero-shot real-robot evaluation. Its streaming representation allows policies to incorporate state feedback within an action chunk, substantially improving performance over open-loop execution under randomized dynamics, external disturbances, and moving objects. The same tokens also can serve as a direct control interface for VLM agents, which compose successful action sequences into reusable macros. These agent-built macros reduce control decisions and thinking-token usage across attempts and transfer to a held-out task. More results are available at https://zibindong.github.io/actioncodec2-page/
authors: Zibin Dong, Yicheng Liu, Shiduo Zhang, Tianyuan Yuan, Baijun Ye, Jinqiu Wang, Hang Zhao
bullets: Releases actions incrementally instead of requiring full chunk decoding.
Quantizes relative to the reconstructed state to correct residual errors and maintain a target reconstruction tolerance.
Uses geometric primitive sets and Set-BPE to losslessly compress co-occurring symbols without fixed coordinate ordering.
A universal version averages 8.8 tokens/s for 15 Hz end-effector motion across 20k hours and 24 embodiments.
Improves compared-tokenizer performance in simulation and zero-shot real-robot settings, especially under feedback-demanding disturbances and moving objects.

papers.abstract: Existing methods for predicting surrounding vehicles' forward occupancy may under-approximate the ground-truth occupancy, exposing the ego vehicle to collision risk, or produce overly conservative regions that unnecessarily restrict feasible space and cause planning failures. To address these issues, we propose FloCOS, a conditional flow-matching framework that predicts compact forward occupancy sets with high occupancy coverage. FloCOS represents the forward occupancy set as a time-varying union of half-space convex polygons parameterized by temporal basis coefficients. Conditional flow matching captures the conditional distribution of these coefficients to govern the temporal evolution of the convex components, trained under coverage and union-area losses that penalize missed occupancy and excess area. For downstream trajectory optimization, the predicted nonconvex union is directly incorporated into hyperplane-based collision-avoidance constraints. Evaluations on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset show that FloCOS generates compact forward occupancy sets with high coverage and achieves a higher interaction completion rate than evaluated baselines. Real-world vehicle experiments further confirm its ability to support collision-free planning in interactive scenarios.

papers.abstract: The RoboCup Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition (SPARC) is a new competition under development of the RoboCup Rescue Robot League that uses the Unitree A2-W as a common robot platform. SPARC aims to make research on artificial intelligence for autonomous rescue robots accessible to a broader research community, including groups without expertise in developing and maintaining custom robot hardware. By providing a capable standard platform and established benchmark environments, researchers can focus on autonomous navigation, perception, manipulation, and embodied AI for challenging disaster-response scenarios. This paper introduces the SPARC competition, its benchmark environment, and the Unitree A2-W standard platform. Furthermore, we present the first open SPARC datasets collected during the IEEE ICRA 2026 Legged Robot Challenges and RoboCup Rescue 2026, release an open-source software stack for autonomous navigation, and provide initial simulation assets representing RoboCup Rescue test environments. Together, these resources aim to lower the barrier to entry for autonomous rescue robotics and facilitate reproducible research and collaborative development on a common hardware platform.

papers.abstract: Titan is a compelling target for future deep space exploration, while its extreme Earth-Titan distance and complex environment make continuous ground-in-the-loop planning impractical. Existing planning methods, primarily developed for Earth-observation scenarios, have limited generalizability to uncertain deep space conditions and adaptability to time-varying mission states. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a physics-constrained maskable proximal policy optimization (PCM-PPO) method for Titan autonomous mission planning. A Titan-specific discrete-time Markov decision process is established to characterize mission feasibility and resource constraints. A system dynamics and geometric model is incorporated to enhance physical representation, including central gravity, J2 perturbation, third-body attraction, and downlink occultation. To accommodate opportunity targets under a bounded action dimension, PCM-PPO organizes predefined and opportunity targets through a fixed-capacity target pool and represents the mission state with a target-wise state matrix and a global state vector. A physics-constrained action mask constructs an admissible decision domain from current mission states, guiding policy learning toward physically executable decisions and avoiding infeasible exploration. An integrated training strategy facilitates policy optimization under coupled constraints. Comparative, ablation, and uncertainty experiments validate the effectiveness of PCM-PPO. PCM-PPO provides a feasible and interpretable scheme for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising capabilities for robot manipulation, but their performance on accessible mobile bimanual platforms remains underexplored. We present a low-cost and reproducible mobile bimanual platform integrating two LeRobot SO-101 manipulators with a TurtleBot 4 and a LeRobot-ROS 2 software stack. Using long-horizon toilet cleaning as a case study, we collect 250 real-world demonstrations and evaluate $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, and GR00T under the same embodiment and task conditions. We further evaluate variants using SARM-derived task-progress signals and short-term MEM observation history. Among the evaluated models, $\pi_0$ performs best, achieving 60% strict and 70% relaxed autonomous success, increasing to 90% with limited human intervention. In contrast, the evaluated progress- and memory-augmented variants do not improve their corresponding baselines. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of long-horizon mobile bimanual manipulation on accessible hardware while highlighting remaining challenges in reliable VLA deployment. papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bring multimodal understanding and world knowledge to end-to-end autonomous driving. To further improve the quality of predicted trajectories, existing studies introduce candidate refinement, residual denoising, and token correction. However, these methods typically focus on unified refinement of the entire trajectory, paying limited attention to the distinct physical quantities and their interactions. We further investigate physical specialization and coordination in trajectory refinement, centering on position and heading for simpler and more intuitive correction modeling. To this end, we propose CARE-Drive (Coupled Alternating Refinement for Ego-trajectories), which decomposes trajectory refinement into waypoint residual correction and position-conditioned heading generation. Through imitation learning and a future-token auxiliary task, the backbone provides predictive representations and a base trajectory. The position expert predicts bounded metric waypoint residuals, while the heading expert reconstructs vehicle orientation from adjacent angular increments conditioned on the corrected path. With the backbone frozen, the two experts are optimized alternately through supervised initialization and reinforcement fine-tuning. This design simplifies refinement through clear physical specialization while preserving conditional coupling during prediction and optimization. On NAVSIM v1, CARE-Drive achieves 88.8 PDMS, improving by 2.4 points over the unrefined base trajectories generated by the same backbone. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of specialized experts and staged training.

papers.abstract: Granular materials exhibit complex and highly variable interaction dynamics, making their reliable manipulation challenging without knowledge of their physical properties. We present an interactive perception framework that infers granular material properties directly from force-torque measurements acquired during scooping. The proposed Latent Filter++ combines a bio-inspired frequency-temporal filter-bank representation with a causal latent dynamical model, allowing the representation to evolve as interaction observations become available while avoiding hand-crafted signal preprocessing. The learned latent representation captures physically meaningful variation in granular materials and supports estimation of properties including grain size and bulk density. Evaluated on 26 diverse granular materials, the approach generalizes to materials excluded from training and enables few-shot adaptation of property-specific mappings using a small number of additional interaction samples. Finally, we demonstrate the relevance of the inferred properties to downstream manipulation by examining their correlation with the maximum acceleration the materials can withstand without spilling from the spoon during transport.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robotic manipulation is versatile, yet its central challenge lies not only in executing dexterous motion with each hand, but also in coordinating the two arms for long-horizon manipulation under coupled spatial and temporal constraints. Prior work has largely focused on endowing robots with human-level manipulation skills, paying less attention to the structure of bimanual behaviour itself: many practical tasks are a coordinated composition of reusable unimanual skills and a small set of synchronous bimanual skills. This makes high-level spatio-temporal coordination, rather than skill acquisition alone, a key bottleneck for efficient bimanual execution. We propose BiPOP, a framework that couples Large Language Models (LLMs) with Temporal Partial-Order Planning for long-horizon bimanual manipulation. At its core is an explicit spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and captures inter-arm dependencies, arm assignment, synchronization requirements, and opportunities for safe concurrent execution. Building on this model, an LLM translates natural-language instructions into a formal PDDL specification, while a temporal planner enforces the constraints and schedules actions, yielding plans that are logically consistent at the symbolic level and efficient through parallel execution. On simulated long-horizon tasks of varying complexity, BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with strong reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency, and the full pipeline runs end to end on the real bimanual robot NICOL. A failure analysis further shows that LLM-only planners mainly violate spatial and temporal coordination constraints, which motivates delegating these constraints to a symbolic planner. papers.abstract: Vision-based high-speed navigation requires a trajectory planner that can reactively generate smooth, collision-free trajectories from onboard visual observations. Deep reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to vision-based trajectory planning, as it enables the optimization of sequential decision-making policies in complex environments. However, model-free policy gradient methods rely on sample-based policy gradient estimation, which yields noisy gradient estimates and inefficient training. To this end, we propose a framework for learning trajectory planning policies using the analytic policy gradient (APG) method and use it to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed framework leverages differential flatness to analytically reconstruct vehicle states from planned trajectories, thereby enabling differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without requiring an explicit low-level dynamics model. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct a differentiable episode rollout and analytically compute policy gradients from episode-level losses, improving both training efficiency and policy performance. After approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU, APG-Planner demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing baseline methods in simulation and achieves speeds of up to 11\,m/s in real-world flight experiments. We further validate the proposed framework on a skid-steer ground robot, demonstrating its applicability to differentially flat robotic systems beyond quadrotors.

papers.abstract: Navigating off-road trails on a mountain bike requires diverse locomotion skills, including aerial maneuvers, cornering, and slip recovery, paired with sophisticated perception for scene understanding. Translating these capabilities to autonomous, two-wheeled robots remains a formidable challenge. We show that autonomous, high-speed trail navigation can be achieved through a single idea: encoding the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain. In simulation, this layer embeds the navigation task into the training environment; during deployment, it is reconstructed onboard from camera and LiDAR data. First, we introduce a unified learning framework that treats local navigation and locomotion as a joint optimization problem, bypassing the twist or pose command interface of classical control hierarchies. With fixed reward weights, the same framework produces both trail racing and agile parkour, shaped only through terrain semantics and episode length. Second, our perception pipeline combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight dual-head decoder that predicts per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores, which are fused with LiDAR range measurements into an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz onboard an NVIDIA AGX Orin. We validate our framework on the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a bicycle robot that autonomously raced across all sections of a kilometer-long, unstructured mountain bike trail at speeds exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s. In simulation, our policy fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.
authors: Fabian Jenelten, Deepana Ishtaweera, Pablo Garcia, Liana Margolese, Igor Bogoslavskyi, Luca Buonocore, Jan Migliazza, Aleksandrs Ecins, Annika Wollschlaeger, Dario Bellicoso, Gabriel Nelson, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter
bullets: Encodes trails as semantic terrain layers used for both training and onboard deployment.
Jointly optimizes local navigation and locomotion without traditional twist or pose command interfaces.
Combines a frozen vision foundation model, lightweight semantic/confidence decoding, and LiDAR into a semantic elevation map running at 30 Hz.
Autonomously traversed all sections of a kilometer-long unstructured mountain-bike trail, exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s.
In simulation, failed up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Approach overview. (A) Deployment: The policy, parametrized as Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with three hidden layers, observes proprioceptive states, an operator-triggered stand command, and a semantic height scan. Joint action targets are computed at 50Hz to control the rear wheel velocity, the fork angle, and the two DOFs of the torso. (B) Training: Our learning framework utilizes synthetic trails or high-fidelity digital twins and applies to both trail racing and parkour. (C) Semantic pipeline: An incoming RGB image passes through a frozen DINOv3 model and a frozen upsampler to produce high-resolution per-patch features. A lightweight trainable decoder maps these features to a per-pixel segmentation mask. A parallel reconstruction head, scored by cosine similarity to the original features, yields a per-pixel confidence score. A coefficient assignment operation converts the segmentation mask into a traversability image. Finally, an elevation mapping pipeline fuses traversability and confidence scores with odometry and point clouds at 30Hz.

Finally, semantic information is embedded into the vertex colors. (B) Each trail segment may contain one or more skill element(s) of a unique type, such as stairs, pump-track waves, jumps, drops, rocks, curves, skinnies, roots, and ramps. papers.abstract: We present DroneDiffusion, a perception-aware diffusion planner for local 3-D UAV trajectory generation that explicitly models and avoids failure zones caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces. A vision-language perceptual safety estimator produces a pixel-aligned reliability map that highlights regions of degraded sensing. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) is conditioned on this map together with the onboard RGB image, goal point, and initial velocity to generate egocentric 3-D trajectories. To enforce obstacle avoidance at inference time without retraining, we apply training-free CHOMP guidance over a 3-D Euclidean signed distance field. The model is trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot on a real drone. Reliability conditioning raises the mean perceptual reliability along generated trajectories to 0.71, compared with 0.63 for a geometric baseline, while guidance halves the collision rate of the learned prior from 14.7% to 7.8%. Perceptual safety conditioning and geometric guidance are therefore complementary: treating sensor reliability as a first-class signal reduces incursions into unreliable regions while maintaining competitive navigation performance.
authors: Ivan Valuev, Iana Zhura, Valerii Serpiva, Miguel Altamirano Cabrera, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Targets navigation failures caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces.
Conditions a DDPM on an RGB image, goal point, initial velocity, and pixel-aligned perceptual reliability map.
Uses training-free CHOMP guidance over a 3-D signed distance field to enforce obstacle avoidance at inference time.
Trained only in simulation but deployed zero-shot on a real drone.
Reliability conditioning increased mean trajectory reliability from 0.63 to 0.71, while guidance reduced collision rate from 14.7% to 7.8%.

Right: scene and reliability tokens enter the U-Net bottleneck through two sequential cross-attention blocks, which keeps appearance and perceptual-reliability reasoning separate.

papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.
authors: Shunming Liu, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu
bullets: Addresses domain gaps when transferring discrete diffusion generation to autonomous driving.
Optimizes planning representations during supervised fine-tuning to reduce hallucinations.
Uses metric-guided diversity filtering during reinforcement learning to improve exploration.
Introduces Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding, which adapts decoding to scene complexity.
Reports a 29.7% improvement over the unoptimized model and stronger performance than same-architecture autoregressive baselines across closed- and open-loop benchmarks.

Reinforcement Learning: Checkpoints of varying maturity levels are screened based on diversity and accuracy metrics, after which they are fed into the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training process. Inference: dVLM exhibits distinct confidence trends across different driving scenarios. DAD mechanism transforms these trends into specialized inference sequences to optimize output quality.

papers.abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.
authors: Haoyi Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yunfan Ren, Yi Bin, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets world-model failures when robot dynamics change unexpectedly, such as after grasping an unknown payload.

Evaluated on five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, achieving lower multi-step mean error than ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task.

papers.abstract: Quadrupedal mobile manipulators can extend their manipulation workspace by coordinating the mounted arm with the mobile base. At the task level, short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories provide an interface for specifying the desired manipulation motion without prescribing how it should be realized by the arm and base. However, executing such trajectories remains challenging because the controller must determine when and how the base should move, and this decision depends on the mounted-arm morphology. We therefore present PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical controller that takes an EE trajectory as the sole task-level motion command and generates coordinated arm--base motions across four families of 6-DoF mounted arms, with extended-reach trajectories beyond the initial fixed-base reach. Within PolyMorphWBC, a trajectory-conditioned coordinator determines the base motion from previewed EE targets, while arm-specific Inverse Kinematics (IK) tracks the current target, and a frozen locomotion backend executes the resulting motion. Cross-arm reuse is enabled by a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF)-derived morphology conditioning, together with online residual-wrench feedback. We train PolyMorphWBC on procedurally generated arms and structured trajectories within and beyond fixed-base reach. In IsaacLab, it achieves 93.95% completion with 2.30cm position error and 4.81{\deg} orientation error on held-out trajectories and arm morphologies. In MuJoCo evaluation against UMI-on-Legs, PolyMorphWBC reduces EE position error by 69--72% and orientation error by 91--97% across four within- and extended-reach trajectories. On a physical Go2--ARX5 system, we demonstrate language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place using EE trajectories from pi_0 without vision-language-action (VLA)-generated base commands.

Achieves 93.95% completion in IsaacLab with 2.30 cm position and 4.81° orientation error on held-out arms and trajectories.

papers.abstract: When robots interact with elastic surfaces such as mattresses and trampolines, changes in loading cause the surfaces to deform and rebound, altering subsequent contact locations and forces. We present Elastra, a simulation framework for modeling this interaction and supporting the training and evaluation of robot control policies. Elastra represents each surface using elements that move only vertically, with elastic connections and damping to model deformation and recovery. Contact forces drive surface motion, and the updated surface geometry is used to compute subsequent contact forces. We systematically validate our simulations against an independent implementation and a real mattress load curve. We further use Elastra to train the Unitree G1 humanoid to stand up on mattresses and trampolines. Using the pretrained HoST policy and ProtoMotions motion tracker as original controllers, we train residual policies through reinforcement learning to add corrections to their joint targets. Adding these residual policies increases the success rate with HoST from 44.1\% to 72.5\%, and from 55\% to 89\% on the trampoline. With ProtoMotions, the success rate increases from 19.0\% to 45.0\% for initial poses not encountered during training. The code and video are available on https://github.com/yichg/elastra.
authors: Youran Sun, Chugang Yi, Xingyu Ren, Haizhao Yang
bullets: Models surfaces as vertically moving elastic-damped elements whose deformation updates future contact forces.
Validates the simulation against an independent implementation and a real mattress load curve.
Uses reinforcement-learned residual policies to correct pretrained HoST and ProtoMotions controllers.
Improves reported standing success for HoST from 44.1% to 72.5% on mattresses and from 55% to 89% on trampolines.
Also improves ProtoMotions success from 19.0% to 45.0% on initial poses not seen during training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The two surface models of Elastra. Top: a steel ball resting on the simulated mattress (left) and trampoline (right); the dashed lines mark the sections A–A and B–B drawn below. papers.abstract: Generating whole-body gestures that are simultaneously rhythmically synchronized with speech audio and semantically aligned with text descriptions is a fundamental challenge in embodied AI and social robotics. We tackle this Audio-Text-to-Motion (AT2M) problem by composing two independently-trained diffusion models at inference time and refine bias in joint inference by modeling the copula score $s_I$. A rigorous theoretical analysis reveals that naive epsilon blending corresponds to a Product-of-Experts formulation that omits the copula score $s_I$: the cross-modal interaction between audio and text that neither marginal model can capture. We propose CFGComposer: a jointly-trained AT2M diffusion model that estimates $s_I$ via a CFG analogy and injects it as an $\epsilon$-space correction. Experiments on BEAT demonstrate best-in-class semantic fidelity (SRGR $0.9916$, FID $27.18$) with GT-level beat alignment (BA $0.1826$ vs. GT $0.1743$), and 76-83% win rate in blind pairwise human evaluation against all prior methods. Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid confirms direct sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Pengyang Shi, Jinlu Zhang, Chunze Lin, Yizhou Wang, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses Audio-Text-to-Motion generation for whole-body gestures in embodied AI and social robotics.
Shows that naive epsilon blending acts as a Product-of-Experts and misses cross-modal audio–text interactions.
Estimates the missing copula score using a jointly trained diffusion model and injects it as an epsilon-space correction.
On BEAT, reports SRGR 0.9916, FID 27.18, and near-ground-truth beat alignment (BA 0.1826 vs. 0.1743).
Human evaluations favored CFGComposer in 76–83% of pairwise comparisons; deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrated sim-to-real transfer.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: CFGComposer method overview. Pre-trained A2M and T2M experts compose at inference time via the exact PoE score decomposition (Eq. 9). CFGComposer trains a jointly-conditioned AT2M model and applies its CFG guidance direction as an ϵ-space copula correction within the gesture window.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison on BEAT. Each row shows a selected utterance with a semantic gesture annotation. Columns correspond to Diffsheg, SemTalk, Semantic Gesticulator, RoboGesture, and CFGComposer (ours). CFGComposer reproduces the iconic gesture shape while maintaining smooth human-like movement. It should be noted that in the third row, the audio input is listing festivals while the text caption is “gesture for giving examples”, CFGComposer is the only method to generate correct semantic gesture.
Fig. 5: Physical deployment on Unitree G1 + BrainCo hand. CFGComposer generates semantically accurate gestures synchronized to live speech. Generated results show agile finger movements.

papers.title: CFGComposer: Compositional Audio-Text-to-Motion Generation via Copula Score Correction

papers.abstract: Open-world navigation requires a robot to locate a user-specified target in an indoor scene under open-vocabulary queries. Realistic indoor environments are semi-static: walls and furniture largely persist while smaller objects move, relocate, or vanish between visits. Prior-map systems answer queries from object poses recorded at reconstruction time, which expire as soon as objects move, whereas online methods re-derive where to look from current observations every few steps, often through expensive calls to a vision--language model. Assuming that walls and large furniture do not move, we keep their map to plan paths, but use a target--furniture co-occurrence prior to decide where to search. We present PreNav, an ObjectNav framework on semi-static environments. Rather than invoking a vision-language model at each step, PreNav generates a single global search reference before the robot moves: an LLM converts target--furniture co-occurrence into a spatial prior, a conditional diffusion model turns that prior and the persistent structure into an ordered centerline with a band around it, and the robot approaches the target once it is detected online. Experiments on a Gibson ObjectNav benchmark show that PreNav outperforms a strong online baseline under matched structural priors, using a generator trained only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes and applied to floor-level Gibson without fine-tuning. Real-world experiments under object relocation and open-vocabulary queries further validate the approach.
authors: Yuxuan Feng, Fujing Xie, S\"oren Schwertfeger, Hermann Blum
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between stale object maps and costly step-by-step vision–language-model planning when objects move.
Keeps persistent walls and large furniture for navigation while using target–furniture co-occurrence to predict where to search.
An LLM creates a spatial prior, and a conditional diffusion model converts it into an ordered centerline with a search band before movement begins.
Experiments on Gibson show improved performance over a matched online baseline, despite training only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes without fine-tuning.
Real-world tests with relocated objects and open-vocabulary queries support the method’s practical validity.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of PreNav. (a) For a query q, an LLM scores how useful each furniture category c is for finding the target; the scores rc(q) are computed once and cached. (b) The normalized weights αc(q), projected onto the mapped furniture, form the spatial prior Dq , which is stacked with the wall raster W and the start map S(s0). (c) Conditioned on these three channels, a diffusion model denoises random points into the search reference. (d) The reference on the real lab map: a centerline that fixes the visiting order, and a band (teal) that widens over high-scoring furniture (outlined). (e) Real-robot execution: viewpoints are sampled near the centerline to cover where the band overlaps furniture whose weight αc(q) clears a threshold—the regions most worth searching, shown in violet. The robot visits them in order, detects the target with an open-vocabulary detector, and approaches it. Steps (a)–(d) run once, before the robot moves.

Fig. 3. Real-world test scene, a laboratory of over 200 m2. (a) The Fetch robot that used for real-world experiments, photographed in the test scene. (b) The room’s osmAG map [9] with the 21 annotated furniture boxes, the only semantic input, colored by category. (c) A 3D scan of the same room with the osmAG walls overlaid.

(c) The top-down GT semantic map used to judge success marks the cup (grid) but has no bottle anywhere in the scene; 3DSG objects are projected onto it for comparison, and the wedge marks the camera’s field of view.
Fig. 5. Target recognition and navigation outcomes across 600 episodes. Node labels give counts and percentages; ribbon widths represent episode counts.

Fig. 4. Search references of diffusion and its TSP teacher on the 600 six-category episodes. (a,b) Search references of diffusion and TSP for one episode in the Gibson validation scene DARDEN, with the query potted plant. The native band is the region swept by each generator’s own halfwidths wj along its centerline; the purple GT targets are the potted plants in the scene, overlaid for evaluation only. (c) Planning: share of episodes whose band, swept along the reference, contains the target, against reference length; each curve ends with that generator’s longest reference. (d) Execution: share of episodes that succeed within a distance traveled, under Mask R-CNN.

papers.abstract: Real-world robot imitation learning is often limited by the cost of collecting physical demonstrations, which typically yield only one action label per visited state. We present CrowdMAPS, a web-based crowdsourcing paradigm for augmenting real-robot datasets with Multiple Actions per State (MAPS). After or during standard robot data collection, CrowdMAPS distributes visited robot states to remote annotators through a web-based 3D interface, where they specify alternative valid actions without requiring access to physical robot hardware. This expands robot datasets along a complementary "width" dimension--by increasing the number of actions per visited state--rather than only by collecting more trajectories. We evaluate CrowdMAPS using keyframe-centric goal-pose annotations supplied by non-expert annotators and train imitation policies on the resulting MAPS data. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, increasing MAPS width from one to ten actions per state improves sample efficiency and increases average success rates by 35.6 percentage points for keypose policies and 33.0 percentage points for trajectory policies. These results show that software-mediated human annotations can augment physical robot data to afford denser supervision, establishing CrowdMAPS as a scalable digital layer for real-robot data collection.
authors: Yilong Song, Harshvardhan Chandirasekar, Karthik Desingh, Chen Zhu-Tian
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited action diversity of physical robot demonstrations.
Remote annotators provide alternative actions for visited robot states without using robot hardware.
Expands datasets in “width” by adding actions per state rather than collecting more trajectories.
Across five real-world manipulation tasks, increasing actions per state from 1 to 10 improved average success by 35.6 percentage points for keypose policies and 33.0 points for trajectory policies.
Uses non-expert, keyframe-centric goal-pose annotations to provide denser supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 3: CrowdMAPS web annotation pipeline. Recorded real-robot keyframes (a) contain RGB-D and proprioceptive data. Using task-specific CAD models and object text descriptions, LangSAM segments the relevant objects, Any6D estimates their 6-DoF poses, and the corresponding meshes are placed in Isaac Lab to reconstruct the scene. The reconstructed scene is displayed alongside raw sensor views in the annotation interface (b), where annotators manipulate the rendered robot to specify an alternative goal-pose action, submitted as an unexecuted label g ∈ A¬exec

Bottom: scaling trends for crowdsourced MAPS widths on Insertion, Pouring, Sorting, and Switches−. Each entry is evaluated over 25 real-world rollouts with randomized initializations; best results are in bold.

Purple markers denote predictions; the white cross denotes the current gripper position. (a) Insertion: increasing K reduces both the offset and dispersion of the predictions. (b) Sorting: increasing K results in sharper, more clearly separated valid action modes.

CrowdMAPS preserves the executed trajectory but augments selected keyframes t ∈ K with additional valid, unexecuted goal-pose labels A¬exec

Figure 6: Annotation User Interface. Our annotation user interface contains a text description for the next keypose, six views, controls (a red cross that can be dragged to translate the end-effector, red, blue, and green wheels for rotating the end-effector), and other functionalities.

Figure 8: Crowdsourced annotation statistics across all five tasks (rows, alphabetical). Left: Distribution of submission times with median lines. Center: Median interaction time vs. per-user submission number with IQR shading. Right: Approval rate vs. per-user submission number. Drawer only shows quality (submission times were not recorded). Distances measure the maximum displacement of fixed reference points on the gripper body between two goal poses, so both translation and orientation differences contribute in millimetres.

Figure 7: Crowdsourced Labels for Selected Keyframes. We show executed and crowd-submitted end-effector goal poses projected to the corresponding image observation for five keyframes, one from each task, from our crowdsourced datasets. papers.abstract: Mechanistic localization does not by itself yield usable control: causal sensitivity may occupy little activation energy, an accurate local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable numeral target may be wrong. We introduce AROMA (Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation), a frozen-VLM control framework separating where to intervene, which geometry and gain to use, how to reach a target, which target to pursue, and when to act. In Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, four dimensions of a causally validated cross-attention head explain 89.82% of cardinality sensitivity but only 9.52% of median activation energy; magnitude-normalized causal subspace actuation converts this mismatch into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy on untouched procedural data by +8.00 pp. Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation (MEA) reaches 81.25% of oracle targets versus 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched step budgets. With target and gate frozen before evaluation, targeted MEA improves the previous frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% on a new natural Stage-2 cohort (N=630; paired p=4.63e-7) and yields 65.741% versus 65.153% over all 7,992 examples while editing only 63 inputs. Prospective routing, replication across heads and models, and comparisons with attribution-steering baselines further characterize each stage, separating localization, actuation, reachability, target quality, and selective deployment as distinct control problems.
bullets: Addresses why identifying causally sensitive components alone may not enable reliable finite-scale control.
Uses a frozen VLM framework that separates localization, actuation geometry and gain, target reachability, target selection, and gating.
Magnitude-normalized actuation converts a low-energy causal subspace into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy by 8.00 percentage points on untouched procedural data.
Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation reaches 81.25% of oracle targets, compared with 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched budgets.
On a new natural cohort, targeted actuation improves the frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% while editing only 63 inputs; gains are modest overall.

figures.caption: Figure 7. From low-rank sensitivity to independently confirmed control. (a) Same-α rank-4 CSA severely underactuates; magnitude normalization restores and slightly exceeds whole-head accuracy on the v3 development intervention subset. (b) The learned Top-4 subspace exceeds every one of 20 frozen random rank-4 controls; random mean is 27.18% and random maximum is 30.78%, versus 52.53% for Top-4. (c) After the CSA method is closed, a newly generated v4 confirmation set yields 50.25% baseline, 57.25% whole-head, and 58.25% MN-CSA. (d) MN-CSA obtains 174 repairs and 14 breaks versus 150 repairs and 10 breaks for whole-head, producing 20 additional net repairs.

Figure 8. Utility-aware routing confirms adaptive control within the frozen low-rank candidate family. (a) The router improves over the fold-selected global comparator in grouped OOF development and the frozen global comparator in external validation and the untouched final population; only the last stage is the primary confirmatory test. (b) On the final N = 294, the advantage combines six additional repairs with eleven fewer breaks, yielding 17 router-only versus 0 global-only paired wins. (c–d) The learned policy does not collapse to a single method or gain: it selects identity, MN, and SA and uses every nonzero gain in the frozen grid. Final primary effect: +5.782 pp, 95% CI [+3.401, +8.503] pp, exact McNemar p = 1.53 × 10−5.

Figure 1. AROMA at a glance. Mechanism (top): a frozen VLM exposes a causally validated cross-attention head; its Top-4 sensitivity subspace supports magnitude-normalized MN/SA edits, while WHOLE is an alternative full-head intervention geometry on the same actuator. Policy (bottom): a ground-truth-free gate decides when to act; on gated examples, either a target rule selects which target to pursue and MEA determines how to reach it, or a candidate router selects geometry and gain without an explicit target.

Figure 3. Local projected geometry is quantitatively valid at small scale, but global target control requires iterative re-linearization. (a) Pearson agreement between first-order predicted and realized numeral movement is near-perfect at β = .05 and declines as intervention scale grows. (b) Oracle MEA accumulates reachability as it recomputes the current target–competitor margin and projected gradient. (c) Matched-budget controls under the same realized per-step norms: iterative MEA, a frozen initial target-gradient direction, and activation-aligned control.

Figure 4. Target quality converts controllability into prospectively confirmed deployment utility. (a) Accuracy on the prespecified N = 630 Stage-2 population (+4.286 pp over old Unified; 29:2 paired discordance; exact McNemar p = 4.63×10−7). (b) Repairs and breaks relative to identity. (c) Correct predictions on the 63 frozen APPLY cases under the same gate; the GrAInS minimal port, the counting-adapted GrAInS-inspired comparator, and the constant-zero rule are post-confirmation controls.

Figure 11. Cross-model replication and held-out gain calibration in IDEFICS-9B-Instruct. (a) Independently screened B2H28 shows held-out bidirectional actuator behavior. (b) Sensitivity trace rises monotonically with rank (point labels), but finite causal steering peaks at rank 4 and deteriorates at ranks 8 and 16. (c) On the development-only screen set, larger gain substantially increases balanced low-rank steering; only the top two configurations are carried forward. (d) Independent dev validation selects r = 4, β = 2 before the final cohort is touched. On the untouched final set, the fixed low-rank intervention reaches 79.67% directional consistency in both directions and recovers about 81% of same-run whole-head mean shift. Because β = 2, this is a gain-calibrated, not equal-norm, comparison.

Figure 2. Sensitivity is not activation energy. (a) The top four dimensions explain 89.82% of the uncentered cardinalitysensitivity second moment and 86.78% after centering; both are far above the rank-matched null distribution. (b) The same Top-4 subspace contains little of the pooled activation norm: median ρ = 0.309, corresponding to only 9.52% median projected activation energy. This mismatch predicts why same-α low-rank scaling under-actuates and motivates magnitude normalization.

Figure 15. Natural hierarchical UGR converts complementary action-space capacity into an untouched gain. On the prespecified N = 631 Stage-2 population from a new 8,000-example TallyQA cohort, frozen Unified routing improves over frozen Whole-only routing by +1.902 pp (95% CI [+0.792, +3.170] pp; exact McNemar p = 0.00418; 14:2 paired discordance). The unified candidate oracle adds +6.181 pp over the Whole oracle. The realized policy is sparse (52/631 interventions), increases repairs while reducing breaks, and does not collapse to WHOLE: 48.1% of its non-identity selections use MN or SA.

Figure 12. Transfer separates geometry from deployment policy. (a) Frozen Llama rank-4 geometry retains positive natural-domain utility, though below whole-head control. (b) The synthetic router fails zero-shot on a separate TallyQA set even while the same actuator/action family retains large oracle headroom. (c) Relearning only the lightweight utility map is sample-efficient; K = 500 is frozen as an efficiency elbow before a new confirmation set. (d) HoloCount preserves large oracle headroom while the transferred policy is essentially neutral, exposing a stronger routing/readout boundary.

Figure 6. Frozen procedural confirmation. The synthetic router is frozen before evaluation on the untouched 2,000-example Proc-Count-Causal v3 set. (a) Accuracy increases from 999/2000 = 49.95% to 1161/2000 = 58.05% (+8.10 pp; paired 95% CI [+6.85, +9.40] pp). There are 173 repairs, 11 breaks, and +162 net repairs, with interventions on 32.65% of examples. (b) All prespecified visual conditions improve: dense, +10.25 pp; distractors, +7.25 pp; grid, +12.00 pp; random_sparse, +7.00 pp; and row, +4.00 pp. These gains support generalization beyond v2 within the procedural benchmark family.

Figure 9. Prospective unified geometry routing improves the strongest development-selected restricted policy. (a) Development OOF and untouched-final exact accuracy for the prospectively selected full-head restricted comparator and UGR; triangles show candidate-oracle upper bounds. The paired final gain is +2.212 pp (95% CI [+0.316, +4.265] pp; exact McNemar p = 0.0385), with 27 unified-only versus 13 restricted-only correct examples. (b) Selection shares show that the unified router uses the prespecified intervention families non-degenerately. These shares are descriptive rather than an attribution of the paired improvement; the primary claim is the frozen comparison in (a).

Figure 14. Lightweight natural-domain calibration restores routing utility. (a) With the actuator and routing model family fixed, mean development gain rises from +0.33 pp at K = 50 to +2.12 pp at K = 500 and then largely saturates. The selected K = 500 is a sample-efficiency elbow, not the maximum-gain point; error bars denote across-run standard deviations. (b) Frozen evaluation on a new 4,000-example image-disjoint TallyQA set improves accuracy from 64.925% to 67.050% (+2.125 pp; paired 95% CI [+1.50, +2.775] pp), with 130 repairs, 45 breaks, and +85 net repairs (exact McNemar p = 9.176 × 10−11). (c) Both prespecified subsets improve: Simple by +1.10 pp and Complex by +3.15 pp. (d) The policy retains identity (α = 1) for 80.0% of examples and applies non-identity actions to 20.0%.

Figure 5. Bidirectional cardinality steering. (a) In the 300-sample characterization, α = 0.5 shifts the normalized expected numeral downward on 91.33% of samples, and α = 1.5 shifts it upward on 90.67%. Strict ordering µ0.5 < µ1 < µ1.5 holds on 88.67%; downward and upward response magnitudes are strongly coupled (Spearman ρ = 0.9514, p = 1.59 × 10−154). (b) On Proc-Count-Causal v2, gains α ∈ {0, 1, 1.5, 2, 4} produce monotonic mean expected-numeral shifts, from −0.151 at α = 0 to +0.439 at α = 4; α = 1 exactly reproduces baseline. These results support a bidirectional, dose-responsive cardinality actuator.

Figure 10. Bidirectional actuator behavior generalizes across the frozen historical candidate pool. (a) Attenuation (α = 0.5) and amplification (α = 1.5) directional consistency for all seven candidates on the same fresh N = 300 cohort; the dashed line marks 0.5. Six heads pass both one-sided exact directional tests after Holm correction across the 14 head-by-direction tests. (b) The stricter per-example ordering µ0.5 < µ1 < µ1.5 varies substantially across heads and is not itself the replication criterion. L8H30 provides a useful negative case: historical causal candidacy does not automatically imply stable finite controllability.

Figure 16. Finite-step response geometry explains selective repair and failure. (a) AROMA intervenes selectively rather than globally. (b) Larger expected-numeral movement creates both repair opportunity and break risk. (c) Repairs are strongly concentrated in target-aligned movement directions. Target alignment is a post-hoc diagnostic using ground truth and is not available at inference time.

Figure 13. Diagnosing limited zero-shot policy transfer. (a) The frozen synthetic router improves procedural v3 accuracy by +8.10 pp but changes zero-shot TallyQA accuracy by −2.975 pp. The post hoc natural action oracle reaches 71.575% (+6.725 pp over the 64.85% baseline), indicating retained actuator headroom. (b) Baseline errors shift from 93.76% undercounts and 6.24% overcounts on synthetic v2 to 21.12% undercounts and 78.88% overcounts on natural TallyQA. (c) Selected-score/realized-utility Spearman correlation is positive on v2 and v3 (ρ ≈ 0.409 and 0.411) but near zero and slightly negative on natural data (ρ ≈ −0.0667). (d) Without fitting or tuning parameters, SPUC-v1 clips standardized features to empirical v2 training support. Clipping affects 39.825% of samples; accuracy remains 61.875%, while intervention rate changes from 65.275% to 63.275%. Support violation contributes to extreme extrapolation but does not explain the accuracy decrease, indicating a conditional-utility shift.

papers.abstract: Safe trajectory tracking (STT) aims to enable autonomous vehicles to follow a reference trajectory accurately while avoiding collisions. This problem is particularly challenging for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) in highly dynamic environments. Existing non-learning-based STT methods often use simplified vehicle and interaction models to meet real-time requirements, which may result in suboptimal tracking accuracy. Although Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) can help address this limitation, widely used Lagrangian DRL methods often suffer from unstable training because increasing Lagrange multipliers amplify policy-gradient magnitudes. To address these issues, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for STT, called STT Control Epigraph Form RL (STTC-EFRL). In this framework, the STT problem is formulated as an epigraph-form min-max optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we develop a learning mechanism that uses a decreasing scalar related to the epigraph to adjust the policy gradient descent direction without increasing the gradient magnitude, thereby improving training stability. We also develop a computationally efficient ray-casting method to compute a polyhedron scaling factor for safety quantification. Experimental results, including Vehicle-in-the-Loop tests, show that STTC-EFRL achieves higher tracking accuracy than the considered non-learning-based baseline and more stable training than widely used Lagrangian DRL methods, while satisfying safety requirements in connected environments.

papers.abstract: Embodied continual learning requires controllers to infer changing situations, retain prior behavior and reuse motor skills without task labels or known boundaries. The challenge is deciding when to recover earlier behavior and which skills can support new learning. We introduce Situation-guided Primitive Integration for Recurrent Embodiment (SPIRE), a recurrent-spiking system that infers latent contexts from action-outcome evidence and learns context-specific motor actors online. Mature actors become protected sources that combine with a target-context residual to drive recurrent-spiking motor populations. Across coordinate, three-joint and hidden-force control, SPIRE maintained control, autonomously inferred situations, retained prior behavior and accelerated acquisition of an unseen source composition, reducing mean interactions to criterion by approximately 40% relative to matched fresh controllers. Rewinding compatible source actors impaired early acquisition in every matched intervention, demonstrating causal reuse. Against seven recurrent continual-learning and modular-control comparators, SPIRE achieved 2.4 times the mean prior-learning advantage of the strongest eligible task-free alternative selected for each paired stream. These results demonstrate autonomous recovery and causal reuse of motor skills for new learning in continuous embodied control.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3\% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6\%.
