papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from formal specifications often separates task definition, reward shaping, curriculum design, and policy diagnostics into different mathematical objects. This fragmentation requires additional conversion steps and discards structure already present in the specification, such as subtask boundaries, ordering constraints, and quantitative measures. We introduce TBTCL (Temporal Behavior Tree Centric Learning), a framework that uses Temporal Behavior Trees (TBTs) as a unified interface for specification-guided reinforcement learning. A single TBT specifies the task, induces dense robustness-based rewards, defines a curriculum, and supports better understanding of learned policies. By adapting TBT syntax and semantics for specification-guided reinforcement learning, we provide a formalism that is more expressive than popular specification languages such as LTL and inherently hierarchical. We present algorithms to automatically extract a curriculum DAG and derive dense, robustness-based rewards directly from TBT semantics. Furthermore, we utilize TBT trace segmentation to build understandable competence profiles and automatically adapt the reward toward bottlenecks. We evaluate TBTCL on six specifications across discrete and continuous domains and show that Temporal Behavior Trees can serve as a specification, a reward, a curriculum, and a diagnostic.

Segments execution traces to produce competence profiles and adapt rewards toward learning bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: In recent years, humanoid loco-manipulation has progressed to whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport. A basic requirement underlying these tasks is carrying the object to its destination, which depends on the locomotion controller accurately executing velocity commands from the navigation policy. However, carrying an object in one hand introduces a persistent asymmetric upper-body load that can degrade velocity tracking. Persistent tracking biases can accumulate into position and heading deviations, increasing the risk of collisions and navigation failure. To address this problem, we present ReACT, a framework for accurate velocity tracking under asymmetric upper-body loads. Reflection-consistent disturbance modulation uses the estimated wrench to modulate actor features for load compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations. Cross-load tracking consistency training compares loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands to promote consistent velocity tracking across loading conditions. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved velocity tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads. Real-world experiments demonstrate collision-free goal reaching in all 40 tested navigation trials under unilateral hand loads with a fixed mapless navigation policy.
authors: Xianghui Wang, Aoran Fu, Liyou Luo, Shanze Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Dan Zhang, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses persistent velocity-tracking and directional biases caused by carrying an object in one hand.
Uses estimated-wrench modulation of actor features to compensate for asymmetric loads while preserving reflected-action correspondence.
Trains consistency between loaded and unloaded conditions under identical velocity commands.
Simulation results show improved tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads.
Real-world tests achieved collision-free goal reaching in all 40 navigation trials with unilateral hand loads and a fixed mapless policy.

papers.abstract: Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose \emph{Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest)}, a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for \emph{nonlinear} stochastic systems with \emph{unknown} initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system's state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete. Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.
authors: Eduardo Figueiredo, Adrien Banse, Qi Heng Ho, Raphael Jungers, Morteza Lahijanian, Luca Laurenti
bullets: Targets high-probability goal reaching and unsafe-state avoidance under nonlinear dynamics and distributional uncertainty.
Uses optimal transport to learn high-confidence ambiguity sets containing the true system distributions.
Efficiently propagates and safety-checks these sets while growing a sampling-based forest of search trees.
Proves correctness with prescribed confidence and probabilistic completeness under feasibility and distributional assumptions.
Demonstrates strong performance on several robotic benchmarks while retaining formal guarantees.

papers.abstract: Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model. Coverage-preserving anchor selection constructs one-second targets, and an attention mask prevents teacher-forced future actions from entering foresight queries. The selected corpus contains 394 recordings across 20 games, with 223.36 hours of recorded timestamp span and 2,072,084 training anchors. After 12,400 game-pretraining updates, we compare the resulting initialization with the public base under the same suite-specific robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success increases from 1,718/2,000 (85.90%) to 1,811/2,000 (90.55%), a gain of 4.65 percentage points. Suite gains are 9.2, 6.8, 0.2, and 2.4 points on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. The 40-task breakdown shows 24 improvements, 10 declines, and six ties. These results support the practical value of the complete game-pretraining stage in this evaluated setting, while revealing heterogeneous task outcomes. The comparison includes additional optimization and does not isolate the effects of game data, the two objectives, or training variability.
authors: Lianlei Shan, Han Jin, Yaunchao Ma, Xinpeng Chen, Linhao Zhou, Xin Bin
bullets: Uses human gameplay recordings that pair observations, actions, and visual consequences for robot-policy pretraining.
Combines keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual foresight from a frozen video model.
Coverage-preserving anchor selection and attention masking create one-second targets while preventing teacher-forced future actions from affecting foresight queries.
On four LIBERO suites, success rises from 85.90% to 90.55% after the complete pretraining and fine-tuning pipeline.
Results are heterogeneous: 24 of 40 tasks improve, 10 decline, and 6 tie; the study does not isolate individual training components or variability.

papers.abstract: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.

Avoids recursive self-improvement, agentic harnesses, and closed-source models while sustaining over 2 FPS per evaluation port on limited hardware.
Achieves a 0.615 mean Q-score and 41.2% full-task success on the official private test set.

papers.abstract: Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated. Four imitation-learning policies (ACT, SmolVLA, Diffusion Policy and pi0.5) were trained on the same 50 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. Each was run for ten rollouts at about 520 lux and again at about 45 lux, an 11.5x reduction. Success was 20/40 in normal light and 19/40 in low light: a change of -2.5 percentage points (95% CI -23 to +19), with no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity (interaction p = 0.86). The recorded video shows why: mean image brightness was only 3% lower in low light on the front camera and 19% lower on the wrist camera. Both cameras were set to automatic exposure and white balance, which most likely absorbed the difference; exposure was not locked in this experiment. An accidental repeat of one 10-rollout block reproduced its success count (7/10) but matched the first block at only 6 of 10 placements, consistent with chance. We conclude that lux alone does not describe what a policy sees. Camera settings, and image statistics compared with the training recordings, are the quantities to report and control. Data and code are public.
bullets: Four imitation-learning policies were evaluated on the same 50-demonstration pick-and-place task using an SO-101 arm.
Across 40 rollouts per lighting condition, success was 20/40 at ~520 lux and 19/40 at ~45 lux.
There was no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity to the lighting change.
Image brightness fell only 3% on the front camera and 19% on the wrist camera, likely due to automatic camera adjustments.
The study argues that camera settings and image statistics—not room lux alone—should be reported and controlled; exposure was not locked.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.
authors: Yu Zhao, Hongyi Duan, Ming Yin, Hongyuan Zhang, Fan Yang, Hongzhi Wang, Xiubo Liang
bullets: Addresses delayed failures, tail risk, and unstable candidate rankings in end-to-end autonomous driving.
Uses candidate-conditioned latent future rollouts to estimate distributions of long-horizon outcomes.
Ranks candidates with a tail-risk-aware, perturbation-robust decision criterion rather than deterministic point scores.
Evaluated on NAVSIM-v1, NAVSIM-v2, and closed-loop HUGSIM, where it reports state-of-the-art performance and more robust candidate selection.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the RiSE-Drive pipeline. Multi-view observations are encoded, and the proposal generator produces 𝐾 ego-trajectory candidates. A future-condition generator predicts 𝐿 branch-specific condition codes that parameterize plausible downstream evolutions. For each candidate–condition pair, RiSE-Drive initializes a latent consequence state, propagates it along the trajectory, and decodes one branch-level long-horizon outcome sample. The resulting branchwise consequence traces are pooled over time and across branches and mapped to ordered outcome quantiles by a distribution head. The final ranking score combines the mean estimate, lower-tail CVaR, and cross-condition instability, thereby favoring candidates that remain reliable under plausible future deviations rather than merely optimal under a single nominal forecast.

Figure 3: Qualitative results of RiSE-Drive on representative NavSafe safety-critical scenarios. From left to right, columns (a)–(d) correspond to UNPL (unprotected left turn), EXR (exit ramp), YLD (yielding), and RDBT (roundabout). Each column shows two temporal snapshots of one representative case. Magenta denotes the RiSE-Drive plan, green the human future trajectory, orange dashed the ego history, and blue the future trajectories of surrounding vehicles. Across all four cases, RiSE-Drive produces smooth, route-consistent, and interaction-aware behaviors while remaining close to safe human driving in conflict-prone regions.

papers.title: RiSE-Drive: Risk-Sensitive Long-Horizon Candidate Evaluation for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: RiSE-Drive evaluates driving trajectory candidates by modeling long-horizon outcome distributions and selecting options that remain reliable under uncertainty and safety-critical deviations.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth foundation models make it tempting to replace depth sensors on mobile robots with a single RGB camera. We show that, used off the shelf, this is unsafe: in a simulated indoor navigation benchmark, a standard Nav2 stack driven by Depth Anything V2 (metric) collides in 63\% of 120 episodes, because the model systematically over-estimates the distance to nearby obstacles. We propose a lightweight plug-in module that turns predicted depth into \emph{safe depth}. A 0.58\,M-parameter head on top of the \emph{frozen} depth model predicts, per pixel, a log-depth correction $\mu$ and an uncertainty $\sigma$, trained with a $\beta$-weighted Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The navigation stack consumes the one-sided bound $\hat d_{\text{safe}}=d\,e^{\mu-k\sigma}$, where $k$ is set by conformal calibration on a held-out world, and uncertainty also decides which pixels may be treated as floor. The correction halves the depth error (AbsRel $0.262\rightarrow0.134$) and reduces near-range over-estimation from 59.8\% to 12.0\%. In navigation, safe depth raises the success rate from 37\% to 70\% and lowers collisions from 63\% to 3\%, close to the 2\% of ground-truth depth. A constant safety margin calibrated to the same pixel coverage reaches only 30\% success because it freezes the robot; uncertainty-aware safety wins 52 of 56 discordant paired episodes against it. Gains hold on glass, texture-less walls and dark regions.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $\pi_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of CIALLO. (A) During pretraining, three encoders map an action chunk with proprioception, a pair of current and future frames, and an instruction grounded in the current frame into a shared intent space. (B) To learn a policy, Qwen-CIALLO predicts intent from observations and instructions, using the frozen action encoder as a teacher and the demonstrated actions to supervise the decoder output. The decoded action is the softmax expectation over the bin centers.

The text codec compresses the instruction into a task-level intent, grounds it using features reused from the current frame to form the same K ×D intent interface, and reconstructs masked instruction tokens from the task-level intent.

papers.abstract: Reliable state feedback of excavator front-end mechanisms is essential for autonomous excavation, yet retrofitting existing machines with dedicated joint sensors, external cameras, or visual markers can increase deployment and maintenance burdens. This paper proposes a closed-loop autonomous excavation framework for continuous inference of excavator joint states using onboard visual observations and control-related temporal information. The framework encodes structural cues from the current cab-view image, models short-term motion trends from historical joystick commands, and introduces a rolling state buffer for the bucket joint to preserve temporal continuity under severe occlusion. Mechanical joint-range constraints are incorporated into the learning objective to suppress infeasible estimates. The current cab-view image and inferred states are supplied to an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)-based control policy for online action generation. Experiments in an AGX Dynamics for Unity simulation environment under diverse operating conditions evaluate joint-state inference and end-to-end task execution. Across 20 autonomous excavation trials, the framework achieved a 95% task-completion rate, with an average joint-state-inference-and-control latency of 10.11 ms per step. The bucket-joint inference achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.965 degrees. These results demonstrate a sensor-light and computationally efficient joint-state-inference approach that can support closed-loop autonomous excavation with reduced dependence on additional sensing infrastructure.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about people's plans and goals based on their actions is fundamental to human social interaction and essential for cooperative, embodied artificial intelligence. Formalizing this capacity in naturalistic, embodied settings has been a longstanding challenge. Here, we present GenEA, a novel agent representation capable of reasoning over multi-step, long-horizon embodied plans. At the heart of GenEA lies a multilevel state-space that couples the coarse biomechanics of an articulated body and its interactions with nearby objects by extending the task-and-motion planning framework from robotics with simulation-based intuitive physics. By embedding this state-space in a generative model, GenEA yields a joint probability distribution over goals and embodied plans. Across several experiments spanning the qualitatively distinct domains of object manipulation and navigation, featuring diverse tasks and multiple behavioral measures, we show that GenEA, through simple transformations of this joint distribution, recapitulates how humans reason about embodied plans. Crucially, GenEA consistently outperforms strong alternative models, including plausible heuristics, standard task-and-motion planning, and a state-of-the-art vision-language model. GenEA thereby offers a new perspective on the architecture of human reasoning and social cognition, suggesting that embodied artificial intelligence systems seeking to seamlessly interact with humans should adopt GenEA-like generative models of action planning.
authors: Aalap D. Shah, Basil Saeed, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Tobias Gerstenberg, Hyowon Gweon, Ilker Yildirim

papers.abstract: The complex interactive dependencies between human behavior and 3D scenes make accurately predicting human intent a major challenge for human motion prediction (HMP). While recent studies use human gaze to infer intent, gaze signals suffer from ambiguity, drift, and a reliance on eye-tracking hardware. Research in cognitive science indicates that egocentric views inherently encode potential interactions, while head motion serves as a crucial precursor in motion planning. Motivated by this, we propose EgoHMP, a novel framework that uses egocentric views and head motions as robust carriers of interaction intent. By translating this intent into an envisioning of future interactions, EgoHMP achieves precise HMP in 3D scenes. EgoHMP first employs a vision-motion alignment encoder to align the visual and motion feature spaces. Based on these aligned features, an egocentric intent predictor with a modality-aware modulation mechanism adaptively suppresses invalid interaction cues to predict an accurate interaction probability map. Furthermore, to enhance the stability and realism of the generated motions, we propose a contact-aware motion decoder. Specifically, inspired by the human cognitive process of planning trajectories prior to action execution, we first predict a global trajectory to serve as a self-prompt, effectively mitigating the optimization conflict in diffusion models. Subsequently, we introduce a multi-stage denoiser, which relieves motion artifacts by incorporating human contact modeling through a multi-stage optimization strategy. Finally, a GCN-based motion decoder is employed to synthesize physically plausible and semantically consistent motions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EgoHMP achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.

papers.abstract: Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation. 3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable by supplying an explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model. We present GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable, providing a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making. To improve the 3DGS map, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is first estimated offline by direct-method alignment over dedicated calibration segments and reused by all following online and offline processes. Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR--projection objective. The final global reconstruction is then rebuilt from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted. For the robot SLAM lifecycle, the method recovers the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences quantify each element: the offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3--19.9 dB, improves PSNR by approximately 9 dB over Gaussian-LIC2, and achieves 86--100% held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality. The results show that GEMOR-GS improves the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map, serving as a dependable robot world model for SLAM and downstream tasks.
authors: Yuchen Yang, Ming Ding, Xinyu Wu, Hesheng Wang

Calibrates LiDAR–camera extrinsics offline, then jointly refines keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters using rendering and LiDAR projection objectives.
Reconstructs a globally optimized map from refined keyframes without online constraints.
Relocalizes through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP initialization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement.
Across one self-collected and five public sequences, reports 14.3–19.9 dB gains over the online map, about 9 dB higher PSNR than Gaussian-LIC2, and 86–100% held-out relocalization success.

papers.abstract: End-to-end navigation in cluttered environments relies on compact visual representations to support collision avoidance and goal-directed motion. Existing methods typically learn these representations jointly with the policy or through observation reconstruction, which does not explicitly specify what information the representation should preserve. Moreover, they are usually evaluated with a single downstream policy learner, although the benefit of a representation may depend on how the policy is learned. It therefore remains unclear how different representation-learning objectives affect downstream navigation performance and robustness. This work proposes DeRep, a navigation-oriented representation-learning method that combines local bird's-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction. To compare representation objectives under controlled conditions, we pretrain encoders with a common architecture and freeze them during downstream learning. We evaluate the representations using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with PPO. DeRep achieves the lowest linear policy probe prediction error and outperforms reconstruction alone across all six tested PPO conditions. In imitation learning, both reachability-based objectives achieve higher mean success rates than reconstruction alone, with similar mean success rates between the reachability-only and joint objectives. These results demonstrate consistent benefits of incorporating reachability supervision into depth representation pretraining across different downstream learning methods and evaluation conditions. We further deploy the PPO policy with the frozen DeRep encoder in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor without fine-tuning, demonstrating its capability for zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer.
bullets: Addresses the unclear relationship between representation-learning objectives and downstream navigation robustness in cluttered environments.
Combines local bird’s-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction; encoders are pretrained with a shared architecture and frozen during evaluation.
Tests representations with a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and PPO reinforcement learning.

DeRep has the lowest linear-probe prediction error and outperforms reconstruction-only pretraining across all six PPO conditions; reachability-based objectives also improve imitation-learning success.
A PPO policy using the frozen DeRep encoder transfers without fine-tuning in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor, demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer.

papers.abstract: Existing cooperative end-to-end driving works at Class A (status-sharing) of the SAE J3216 classes of cooperative driving automation (CDA): vehicles exchange what they perceive, not what they intend, so each plans alone when to go, which limits cooperation and leads to deadlock when both vehicles yield or to collisions when both go. We present When2Go, a cooperative end-to-end driving system that learns when to go by sharing intent under CDA Class B or higher. Each vehicle broadcasts its LiDAR detections with forecast motion as instance tokens, together with its plan and intended trajectory. The receiver draws the fused detections, forecasts and partner plans into a route-time conflict map, the occupancy along its route over the planning horizon, on which a planner scores candidate speed profiles. Where two intended trajectories conflict, an order gate, a precedence network distilled from a right-of-way rule, decides who goes first; both vehicles evaluate it on the same messages and so reach the same order. When2Go imitates the rule-based expert of V2Xverse, which sees the simulator's ground truth; stops that When2Go cannot observe within its 2 s planning horizon are relabelled, so that it does not learn to wait without an observable cause. For our runs only, the benchmarks' PID controller steers by When2Go's waypoints instead of the route, and its forced push of long-waiting vehicles is off. With one model, When2Go sets the state of the art on three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks: 97.8 and 90.7 driving score on InterDrive without and with traffic (best published 90.1 and 78.9), 70.0 on the public V2Xverse protocol (best of sixteen rerun methods 59.1) and 88.2 on MDrive (best rerun 85.1), with 95.0% of its vehicles collision-free (87.7%).
authors: Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Tianle Zhu, Zhipeng Bao, Yiping Li, Handong Yao
bullets: Addresses the limits of perception-only cooperation, which can cause mutual yielding deadlocks or collisions when vehicles proceed simultaneously.
Vehicles share LiDAR detections, predicted motion, plans, and intended trajectories as instance tokens.
A route-time conflict map represents predicted occupancy along the ego route; a planner evaluates candidate speed profiles.
An order gate based on a distilled right-of-way precedence rule gives vehicles a consistent crossing order.
Achieves reported state-of-the-art driving scores across three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks, with 95.0% of vehicles collision-free.

papers.abstract: This paper tackles the task of hand-object contact transition detection in egocentric video, which aims to localize the two temporal boundaries of a contact episode: the moment a hand first establishes contact with an object (touch) and the moment contact is released (release). We propose a unified framework that jointly models the interacting hand and object to accurately localize both transition types. The proposed framework augments hand-centric spatiotemporal representations with object-aware features learned directly from the video and introduces a transition-aware event spotting formulation tailored to contact transitions, without relying on external object or hand-object interaction detectors during inference. To support this task, we present ContactTransition, a dataset comprising 4,021 egocentric videos with 8,498 touch and 8,077 release annotations, together with object-of-interest supervision. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms strong two-stage and end-to-end event-spotting baselines on both transition types. Finally, we show that detected contact transitions provide effective temporal anchors for downstream egocentric hand-object reasoning.
authors: Huy Anh Nguyen, Chang Dong, Feras Dayoub, Minh Hoai
bullets: Localizes both boundaries of each contact episode: initial touch and final release.
Jointly models interacting hands and objects using hand-centric spatiotemporal and video-derived object-aware features.
Introduces a transition-aware event-spotting formulation without requiring external detectors at inference.
Presents ContactTransition with 4,021 videos, 8,498 touch annotations, 8,077 release annotations, and object-of-interest supervision.
Detected transitions serve as effective temporal anchors for downstream egocentric hand-object reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of OASIS. Starting from the hand-enhanced feature map produced by HiCE [37], OASIS predicts an object-of-interest heatmap and pools object-aware features from the predicted regions. A presence gate controls when object evidence should be used, and the resulting object-aware representation is fused into the temporal spotting stream. The final head predicts touch and release transitions with event scores and class-specific displacement refinement.

Fig. 2: Predicted object-of-interest heatmaps. Top: input frames around a contact transition, with the predicted transition frame highlighted in red. Bottom: heatmaps predicted by the object-of-interest branch of OASIS. Although object annotations are used only during training, the model learns to highlight the object involved in the hand interaction at inference time, providing object-aware evidence for precise touch–release localization.

We report overall mAP, together with AP at frame tolerances δ ∈ {0, 1, 2} for touch and release detection. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best results.

We report mean AP over both transitions and all tolerances δ ∈ {0, 1, 2}, without and with NMS, together with per-transition AP at δ ∈ {0, 1} without NMS. AP@2 columns are omitted for space and follow the same trends.

Release counts are slightly lower because some contact episodes continue beyond the clip boundary, and because two-hand interactions in TACO may contain separate contact onsets that terminate at a shared release moment.

papers.title: Hand-Object Contact Transition Detection in Egocentric Video

papers.abstract: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.
authors: Xu Luo, Jiaying Yang, Hao Wu, Junlin Xie, Zijin Hong, Ji Zhang, Lianli Gao, Jingkuan Song
bullets: Long action chunks create high-dimensional optimization problems for online RL, making real-world adaptation costly.
ExRL adds a lightweight adapter that predicts each chunk’s execution length.
The adapter is trained with off-policy RL in a low-dimensional space whose expressivity increases with chunk size.
Experiments in simulation and on real robotic tasks show sample-efficient adaptation across diverse long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific tuning.

papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides weather-robust sensing and direct Doppler measurements, yet automotive perception pipelines often reduce its output to sparse point clouds or two-dimensional projections, leaving raw range-azimuth-Doppler (RAD) cubes underutilized. Ego motion induces Doppler responses from world-static structures, while Doppler wrapping aliases radial velocities, complicating moving-object detection and velocity estimation. We present RaMOD (Radar-based Moving-Object Detection), a real-time framework for moving-object detection and velocity estimation from raw RAD cubes acquired by a vehicle-mounted single-chip radar. RaMOD explicitly estimates frame-wise ego motion and uses the estimated radar translational velocity to predict the Doppler region of world-static structures and suppress returns within it. It temporally encodes the suppressed cubes into multi-scale features to predict RAD-space boxes with class labels. For each detected object, it predicts radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. On our BRIDGE-Liv dataset, RaMOD outperforms all compared raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, RA, and RD detection settings, achieving 80.8% cube mAP at IoU 0.30, 15.7 percentage points above the strongest RAD-cube baseline. Velocity MAE is 1.128 m/s, with 99.87% Doppler-wrapping accuracy.
authors: Yuan Fang, Long Zhuang, Lingzi Xing, Xijia Wei, Jingqi Jiang, Fangzhan Shi, Simon Julier, Kevin Chetty
bullets: Addresses false Doppler responses from static structures caused by vehicle ego motion and velocity aliasing from Doppler wrapping.
Estimates frame-wise ego motion to predict and suppress the Doppler region associated with world-static structures.
Temporally encodes the filtered RAD cubes into multi-scale features for RAD-space object detection and classification.
Predicts radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and unwrapped-Doppler hypotheses, plus wrapping probabilities.
On BRIDGE-Liv, achieves 80.8% cube mAP at IoU 0.30, 1.128 m/s velocity MAE, and 99.87% Doppler-wrapping accuracy.

papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.
authors: Rumi Loghmani, Bozhang Song, Victor Alvarado, Aliyah Redding, Amir Barati Farimani

papers.abstract: Efficient robotic 3D reconstruction requires selecting views that contribute new surface measurements with few physical captures. Pretrained world models can guide this choice, but a predicted surface may not produce valid depth measurements under the operating conditions of the deployed sensor. We present a deployment adaptation methodology for next-best-view selection that learns a sensor-return adapter from limited local calibration data while keeping the pretrained predictor fixed. The adapter estimates measurement dropout over each predicted surface, allowing the selection method to favor views likely to fill gaps in the measured reconstruction. In a real-robot experiment with a structured-light sensor, the adapted method achieves higher measured surface coverage with 60% fewer captures than nominal selection. The adapted method recovers a surface region that the nominal method repeatedly targets but fails to measure. These results suggest that robots can reuse pretrained predictive models while adapting their decisions to local operating conditions in data-scarce environments.
authors: Nikita Sarawgi, Omey M. Manyar, Satyandra K. Gupta
bullets: Targets efficient robotic 3D reconstruction by selecting views that add new surface measurements.
Keeps a pretrained predictor fixed and learns an adapter from limited local calibration data.
Estimates measurement dropout on predicted surfaces to prioritize views likely to fill reconstruction gaps.
In a real-robot structured-light experiment, the adapted method achieved higher measured surface coverage with 60% fewer captures than nominal selection.
Scope: adapts decisions to local sensor operating conditions in data-scarce deployments.

papers.abstract: We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.
authors: Renhao Zhang, Mingzhe Li, Bruno Castro da Silva
bullets: Addresses the failure of local safety filters when constraints invalidate an entire behavior mode.
Steers the generator’s behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margins.
Uses a path-space control-barrier-function quadratic program to correct only residual violations.
Provides finite-time recovery guarantees and reduces the burden on path-level correction.
Experiments in navigation and robot end-effector planning show preserved safety, better goal reaching, and less correction than path-level filters.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Experimental domains and test-time safety constraints. Each row shows one planning domain: 2D point-navigation, Maze2D, and Franka 3D end-effector planning. The first column visualizes the original scene and multimodal demonstration dataset, where multiple behaviors can reach the same goal. The remaining columns show three test-time safety constraints imposed on the same pretrained planner. Green circles denote starts, orange stars denote goals, and red shaded regions denote unsafe sets. These constraints test whether a method can preserve safety and goal reaching when certification requires more than local path repair.

Figure 3: Latent steering provides the warm start needed for path-space repair. Stage I performs behavior-level selection by steering the latent and changing the decoded rollout before certification; Stage II then applies path-level CBF repair to remove residual violations. The second row removes Stage I and applies the same path-space correction directly, corresponding to SAFEFLOWMATCHER. Without the latent-steered warm start, the local corrector remains tied to the original rollout and fails to produce a goal-reaching safe path. With Stage I, the corrected trajectory starts from a better behavior and Stage II only needs to repair the remaining local violation.

Figure 1: Latent Barrier Steering separates behavior selection from path repair. A vanilla flow-matching planner may generate a goal-reaching but unsafe rollout under a new constraint. A path-space CBF corrector such as SAFEFLOWMATCHER can enforce safety locally, but may produce a trajectory that is safe while no longer reaching the goal when the selected behavior mode is blocked. LBS first steers the behavior latent from z0 to z+ toward a safer rollout, then applies path-level CBF repair only for residual violations, yielding a trajectory that is both safe and goal-reaching.

papers.abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.
bullets: Addresses the lack of team-level coordination in language-guided RL for partially observable search-and-rescue environments.
Uses an LLM to convert human instructions into semantic cues for strategy selection and agent role assignment.
Introduces the LG-MAHDP formalism to model language grounding, hierarchical decisions, and distributed coordination.
In simulated disaster scenarios, the system reports faster learning, stronger coordination, improved subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance, and 20–30% higher victim rescue rates.
Ablations identify language grounding and the shared cognitive workspace as critical components; results are limited to simulated SAR settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework for Language-Grounded Hierarchical Decision-Making. Left: Verbal input 𝑣from the human operator is processed by the LLM-driven Context Extractor to produce contextual features 𝐶. These features, together with observations 𝑠from the Environment and information priorities 𝑀from the Information Space, are integrated within the Strategic Decision Engine (SDE). The Attention Space refines strategy selection by mapping semantic cues and priority information via Ψ(𝐶,𝑀). The SDE outputs high-level strategies 𝜔, which the Worker modules translate into low-level actions 𝛼executed within the Environment. The resulting observations are fed back into the shared workspace, enabling continuous learning and adaptation. Right: Comparison of LLM outputs with and without retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in simulated SAR operations, showing that RAG enhances contextual precision, hazard annotation, and task-specific semantic structure in generated outputs.

Fig. 5. Coverage-efficiency comparison across models. Grouped bar chart showing (from left to right) coverage ratio, revisit index, and dead-zone ratio for Flat RL, HRL, and LG-HRL. LG-HRL attains the highest coverage and lowest dead-zone ratio while also reducing redundant revisits, demonstrating the most efficient spatial exploration among all methods.

Fig. 7. Ablation results for core components. Normalized system performance under removal of key architectural elements. Removing any component reduces performance, with language grounding and the shared cognitive workspace contributing most strongly to mission success.

Fig. 8. Agent Trajectories Under LG-HRL Control. The plot above shows how UAV and UGV agents behave when guided by the proposed Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LGHRL) system. UAV trajectories (blue) exhibit broad-area scouting patterns characteristic of airborne reconnaissance, while UGV trajectories (green) remain grounded and focus on directed paths suitable for close-range navigation and victim retrieval. Hazard zones are denoted by red “X” markers, and both agents demonstrate safe, deliberate navigation around these areas.

Fig. 3. Coordination Entropy Reduction Across Training. Coordination entropy trajectories for Flat RL, HRL, and LG-HRL across 2000 training episodes. LG-HRL exhibits the fastest decline in entropy and stabilizes at the lowest value, indicating efficient division of labor and emergent cooperative behavior. Language grounding yields substantial gains in all three dimensions, highlighting the value of LLM-based semantic guidance for safe and aligned multi-agent decision-making.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
authors: Denis Grachev, Damien LaRocque, Omar Moured

papers.abstract: Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance must remain reliable under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics. Existing methods typically address these factors through training-domain variation or by exposing uncertainty and capability estimates to the policy at runtime. However, both leave the policy to infer how these quantities should alter the physical separation required for safe interaction, which can couple collision-avoidance behavior to relationships learned from the training distribution. We introduce the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. We derive geometric features that jointly characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents' DOBBs, along with a reward function that preserves the physical interpretation of those interactions. Across four evaluation environments, DOBB achieves the lowest mean total failure rate of 2.6%. This performance persists under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty, with collision-based failure remaining at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this robustness to the geometric abstraction of the safety margin, which is less coupled to the specific uncertainty and actuation regimes encountered during training.
authors: Pedro Antonio Alarcon Granadeno, Jane Cleland-Huang
bullets: Addresses collision avoidance under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics.

Uses geometric interaction features and a physically interpretable reward to guide learning-based policies.
Across four environments, reports a 2.6% mean total failure rate and collision-based failure of at most 2.3% under tested distribution shifts.
Scope: robustness is demonstrated for the evaluated environments and out-of-distribution actuation and uncertainty conditions.

papers.abstract: Reliable medical laboratory automation requires robots to complete entire workflows in protocol order while handling changes during execution. A robot may execute each motion correctly yet fail the workflow by confusing visually similar stages or stalling after human intervention. We present Robo-MLT, a dual-system framework that couples explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision--language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence from the protocol and the initial workspace observation. A multiframe execution monitor detects when the active skill has completed or become infeasible, then advances the workflow or triggers replanning. A skill-conditioned vision--language--action policy generates the manipulation trajectories, and an asynchronous runtime coordinates it with the monitor. We evaluate Robo-MLT against four policy baselines and a VLM-based monitor baseline on blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, with 50 nominal configurations per method and 20 sample-removal configurations. Robo-MLT achieves task success rates of 82\% and 70\%, exceeding $\pi_{0.5}$ by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively. After an operator removes the sample being handled, the system revises the remaining plan and continues processing the other samples. These results indicate that, under the evaluated conditions, explicit workflow monitoring makes long-horizon laboratory manipulation more reliable and recoverable.

papers.abstract: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

On LIBERO-PRO, it achieved 74.0% success, improving over the initial deployment and direct VLA-controller execution; case studies cover practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.

papers.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.

papers.abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.
authors: Ruimeng Liu, Denan Liang, Ruofei Bai, Fuming Zhang, Kuan Xu, Shenghai Yuan, Lihua Xie
bullets: Targets slow, discontinuous discrete coordinate decoding and inadequate point regression for multi-contact or irregular affordances.

Reports a 15.7% average gain and 8.31× throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-grounding benchmarks, while preserving performance across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.

(f) Continuous coordinate embedding via bilinear interpolation over visual positional embeddings Pvis and linear adapter projection for subsequent decoding steps.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.
authors: Yihang Che, Zhongwei Yu, Yang Li, Xingyu Lu, Hongxia Yu, Jun Wang
bullets: Current self-driving laboratories often separate language-based planning from robotic execution, limiting physical grounding and embodied intuition.
ESA combines a memory-based reasoning and Bayesian-optimisation Digital Agent, a generalisable instrument-controlling Embodied Agent, and a unified coordination interface.
In autonomous wastewater-treatment experiments, ESA explored more than 200 million possible conditions over 15 continuous rounds.
Solution transmittance improved from 82% to 99.7%, with a reported 98.5% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation.
Learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, supporting broader autonomous laboratory operation.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Illustration of the Bayesian Optimisation framework as a central component of the ESA architecture. BO receives initial experimental configurations and objectives from the Principal Investigator (PI) Agent. As experiments are conducted by the Embodied Agent, the outcomes are relayed back to BO, providing essential data for refining its surrogate model. BO utilises this feedback to update its predictions and identify the next optimal configuration for experimentation. The Scheduler facilitates the execution of these configurations by coordinating between BO and the Embodied Agent. Ultimately, the best decision obtained during BO is recommended to the Reporter.

Figure 1: The Evolution of Self-Driving Laboratories. This timeline traces the development of autonomous experimentation systems from initial concepts in the 1940s to foundation model integration in recent years, spanning three eras: Early Era (1940s–2009, bottom) establishing foundational principles from design of experiments to closed-loop robot scientist; Modern Era (2009–2022, middle) deploying specialised robotic platforms across scientific domains; and LLMs Era (2022–present, top) integrating foundation models for high-level reasoning.

Figure 2: The architecture of the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), a hybrid cognitive–embodied paradigm for self-driving laboratories with three components. The Digital Agent, the cognitive core and central novelty of ESA, evolves open-endedly by integrating online knowledge, embodied experimentation, and past experience for reasoning, planning, and decision-making. The Embodied Agent orchestrates diverse robots and scientific instruments through multiple control modules for generalised, reliable, and adaptive operation. The Embodied Unified Interface connects digital intelligence with heterogeneous laboratory devices via standardised, low-latency, and safe protocols. Together, they close the loop between perception, reasoning, and embodied execution for autonomous scientific discovery.

Figure 3: Overview of the robotic platform. The dual-arm robot comprises two 6-DoF robotic arms equipped with 1-DoF grippers, a 2-DoF articulated head, an omnidirectional AMR base offering 2 planar DoFs for holonomic motion, and a 1-DoF lift for vertical adjustment. These degrees of freedom are highlighted in the blue box. The platform also integrates a synchronised multi-camera sensing suite consisting of one RGB and one depth camera mounted on the head, two RGB cameras on each wrist, and one RGB camera on the chest, as indicated in the orange box. Together, these components provide rich proprioceptive and multi-view visual feedback to support both global perception and fine-grained manipulation.
Figure 4: Transmittance results across 15 experimental rounds.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines.
bullets: Addresses the need to reduce reliance on expensive real-robot training data.
Existing video-based transfer methods are hindered by action representations entangled with scene-specific noise.
AIT first extracts and disentangles explicit and implicit action intents from human manipulation videos.
It then aligns human and robot domains in a shared intent space and decodes intents into executable robot actions.
Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show more effective and consistent transfer than prior baselines.

(b) Latent action learning is trained directly from abundant raw human videos, but the learned representations are contaminated by scene noise. (c) Our method also learns from easy-to-acquire raw videos, yet extracts a clean Action Intent shared across humans and robots, enabling noise-free knowledge transfer to the robot.

At deployment, an Action Decoder maps these shared tokens to low-level robot actions.

papers.abstract: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments.
bullets: Targets the challenge of handling objects with different materials, deformation, and contact dynamics.
Estimates physical parameters by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation.
Conditions a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy on the recovered physical properties.
Uses a physics memory bank for efficient retrieval without online simulation optimization.
Experiments in simulation and the real world report improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed training framework. Given multi-view images, we first estimate the physical properties of the manipulated object by combining feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF-3DGS) with MPM via a differentiable physical simulation. The simulator is coupled with a differentiable rasterizer and optimized under video guidance, where gradients are back-propagated through the simulation. Physics-based constraints, including Dirichlet boundary conditions for manipulation events and geometric consistency via temporal Chamfer distance, further regularize the estimated physical parameters by aligning simulated particle dynamics with demonstration videos. The learned physical parameters are then injected into a physical-aware diffusion policy as physics conditions, together with language instructions and visual observations, enabling the policy to predict physics-consistent robot actions and gripper states.

Fig. 3. Object preservation results on fragile objects. Among successful pick-and-place trials, the methods differ in their ability to preserve object integrity. We evaluate object preservation by measuring grape rupture and irreversible deformation of paper cups over 30 successful pick-andplace trials. A trial is considered successful only if the object remains intact, exhibiting neither grape rupture nor irreversible deformation. Our method achieves the highest object preservation success rate on both object categories.

Fig. 4. Visualization of learned material-aware routing weights in our MoE policy. Each row represents an object and each column corresponds to a physical-property expert. The bubble size and color indicate the routing weight assigned to each expert. The learned router discovers clear expert specialization, where objects with different physical characteristics are preferentially routed to their corresponding experts while maintaining adaptive soft assignments across experts.

papers.abstract: Human-level dexterity remains a central open problem in robotics, yet few simulation frameworks cover the full workflow of dexterous manipulation, from setting up a robot to collecting dexterous demonstrations and evaluating policies. We present DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework for dexterous manipulation built on the Genesis simulator. DexSuite provides 30 tasks and assembles its 10 arms and 12 end-effectors, from parallel-jaw grippers to dexterous hands, into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs. It also ships a standardized environment API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated tactile sensing. Moreover, we define a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs spanning diverse contact complexities and horizons, and release a dataset of 4,700 successful episodes in simulation from human teleoperation, scripted experts, and learned policies. We release DexSuite as open source and hope others will build on it. Videos and datasets are available at https://dexsuiteorg.github.io
