papers.abstract: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANAV, a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.
bullets: Addresses compounding errors in long-horizon navigation and the limitations of failure-insensitive imitation learning and costly physical RL.
Alternates world-model refinement and policy improvement in a recursive self-improvement loop.
Uses imagined action outcomes for group-relative policy optimization and behavioral novelty/prediction error to build a grounded self-curriculum.
Experiments report gains over training baselines and prior methods, with real-world trials supporting practical applicability.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Recursive self-improvement loop in RIWANAV. (1) The current world model imagines action consequences that improve the policy. (2) The improved policy constructs a grounded self-curriculum that improves the next world model. Repeating these updates recursively changes both components and the feedback exchanged between them. The flame marks the component optimized in each phase.

Fig. 4. Qualitative evidence for recursive world-model improvement on actions generated by the improved policy. All three models receive the same observation, language goal, and action; the aligned recorded future is shown as reference. The rows depict night traffic, a bicycle-lined sidewalk, and a rainy sidewalk. In these cases, the RIWANAV world model after recursive updates better preserves traversable corridors and scene layout, with fewer long-horizon artifacts.

(b) A frozen world model enables learning from imagined outcomes, but its predictions become misaligned with the evolving policy. (c) RIWANAV closes the training loop: imagined outcomes improve the policy, while grounded policyinduced samples refine the world model for subsequent policy learning.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of translating distant navigation goals into coherent local decisions in large, complex environments.
Maintains persistent medium-horizon subgoals and relevant experience through a navigation memory module.
Uses an action-conditioned world model to predict candidate movement outcomes in a visual sandbox.
A vision-language reasoner evaluates predictions, while real observations update memory and revise actions or subgoals.
Evaluations report stronger gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

papers.abstract: We introduce DreamFormer, a model-based agent that acquires language-conditioned, multi-task skills by imitating expert demonstrations within the latent imagination of a learned world model. DreamFormer first learns a task-agnostic Transformer world model from unstructured play data, then acquires task-specific behaviors by optimizing an intrinsic reward that aligns agent-generated rollouts with expert demonstrations in latent space. Since the policy is trained on-policy inside imagination, it is exposed to its own errors during training, mitigating the covariate shift inherent to offline behavioral cloning. To make long-horizon imagination affordable, DreamFormer encodes a high-resolution multi-view robotic observation into a single input token, avoiding both spatial downsampling and the multi-token representations used by prior Transformer world models. On the long-horizon CALVIN benchmark, DreamFormer outperforms LUMOS, the comparable model-based agent, on single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs 2.34 average tasks completed per chain of five) while keeping imagination rollouts tractable. Against HULC, the behavior cloning baseline, it nearly doubles performance on zero-shot transfer to an unseen environment (1.30 vs 0.67), indicating that dynamics learned by the world model transfer more readily than a directly cloned policy. This is consistent with the role attributed to internal models in biological agents, where a model of environment dynamics supports behavior in situations not previously encountered.
bullets: Learns a task-agnostic world model from unstructured play data, then optimizes task behavior in imagined rollouts aligned with expert demonstrations.
On-policy training within imagination exposes the policy to its own errors, reducing offline behavioral-cloning covariate shift.
Compresses high-resolution multi-view observations into a single token to keep long-horizon Transformer imagination tractable.
On CALVIN, completes more tasks than LUMOS in single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs. 2.34) and nearly doubles HULC’s zero-shot transfer performance (1.30 vs. 0.67).

papers.abstract: We present RAGrasp, a retrieval-augmented pipeline for planar parallel-jaw grasping from a compact set of locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D (color and depth) templates. Unlike task-specific predictors trained primarily on large public or synthetic grasp datasets, RAGrasp requires no end-to-end retraining for a new deployment.Its template memory is constructed from observations collected with the deployment camera, robot, and gripper in the target workspace, thereby aligning stored examples with the local sensing and embodiment conditions. The system uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual fea- tures together with appearance and depth cues to prompt the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), which isolates the query object. A two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval cascade then selects a template, and a confidence gate chooses one of two grasp- transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined using mask- support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D- to-3D conversion. In real-world trials, RAGrasp achieves 20/20 successful grasps on seen objects and 19/20 on unseen objects. Within the evaluated setting, the results demonstrate deployment- specific grasp adaptation from limited local annotation and tolerance to the tested viewpoint and illumination changes.
bullets: Uses locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D templates aligned with the target camera, robot, gripper, and workspace.
Combines DINOv2 features, appearance, and depth cues to guide SAM2 object segmentation.
Retrieves templates through a two-stage geometry-semantic cascade and selects between two grasp-transfer estimators via confidence gating.
Refines transferred grasps using mask-support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D-to-3D conversion.
Demonstrates adaptation without end-to-end retraining and tolerance to the evaluated viewpoint and illumination changes.

papers.abstract: Safe robot control often requires combining long-horizon performance optimization with hard state and input constraints, but existing approaches tend to address this tradeoff partially. Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) methods such as model predictive path integral (MPPI) are effective in handling nonlinear and nonconvex environments, yet their finite-sample rollouts and unconstrained weighted-average update can return an unsafe control. Deterministic nonlinear MPC can explicitly incorporate constraints, but its real-time safety and performance depends strongly on warm starts and local convergence. Hamilton--Jacobi reachability (HJR) provides rigorous safety certificates, but offline value-function computation remains practical only for reduced-order models. We propose ReSQ-MPPI, a reachability-informed generation--refinement architecture that combines these complementary strengths. An HJR value function computed offline for a reduced-order model guides online MPPI sampling toward safe, promising trajectory candidates. The MPPI solution is then refined by a small number of sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations in a full-order MPC problem. A key observation is that the standard MPPI inference step is an unconstrained weighted least-squares problem; ReSQ-MPPI replaces it with a constrained MPC refinement that recovers the MPPI update when it is feasible and minimally modifies it otherwise. Simulations in cluttered navigation and autonomous racing environments demonstrate that ReSQ-MPPI improves safety and performance over standalone MPPI, MPC, and reachability-filtered sampling-based control baselines.
bullets: Targets the tension between long-horizon optimization and hard state/input constraints in safe nonlinear control.
Uses an offline Hamilton–Jacobi reachability value function from a reduced-order model to guide online MPPI sampling.
Refines MPPI’s weighted-average update with a few sequential quadratic programming iterations in a full-order constrained MPC problem.
The constrained refinement preserves the MPPI update when feasible and minimally changes it when necessary.
Simulations in cluttered navigation and autonomous racing show improved safety and performance over several baseline controllers.

The three proposed interactions of MPPI with sequential quadratic programming (SQP) are depicted with green arrows: 1) using the MPPI solution as a reference in the MPC optimization problem, 2) as a warmstart for the SQP solver, and 3) using the SQP optimal trajectory as a nominal input in MPPI.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action policies may predict a transferable manipulation strategy yet fail to realize it reliably on the encountered object: objects compatible with the same grasp differ in geometry and compliance, and visual feedback degrades under closure occlusion. AgenticTactileVLA is presented as an execution-time supervisor that shifts part of object-specific adaptation from prediction to physical interaction. A fixed VLA provides the approach and hand targets; the supervisor decides whether to remain transparent, refine finger flexion, retain or release the corrected configuration, return control to the VLA for retry, or select a compliant hand-control regime. It uses finger-position and motor-effort feedback as proprioceptive contact evidence and requires neither tactile sensors nor VLA retraining. On a Unitree G1 with a BrainCo Revo2 hand, a randomized matched-block evaluation on five objects held out from VLA training yields 61.3% completion for the base VLA, 72.0% for unconditional close-to-stall control, and 84.0% for the supervisor under a shared budget; the gain is positive on every object and persists under moderate pose perturbations. Ablations show the gain is not explained by extended closure alone, and that selective triggering reduces correction episodes by 65.7% with no detected change in completion. A retention audit shows acceptance predicts retention in 88.9% of held-out cases, while compliant objects expose conservative false rejection. A thin-walled-cup study demonstrates contextual routing to compliant control, matching an always-compliant reference. These results suggest that contact-guided execution-time adaptation can improve the object-level generalization of a fixed VLA to held-out objects by adapting physical realization without object-specific retraining.
bullets: Addresses failures caused by object-specific geometry, compliance, and visual occlusion during grasp execution.
Supervises a fixed VLA by selectively refining finger flexion, retaining or releasing corrections, retrying with VLA control, or routing to compliant hand control.
Uses finger position and motor-effort feedback as contact evidence, requiring no tactile sensors or VLA retraining.
On five held-out objects, completion improved from 61.3% for the base VLA to 84.0% with the supervisor under a shared budget; gains persisted under moderate pose perturbations.
Selective triggering reduced correction episodes by 65.7% without detected completion loss, while compliant objects revealed conservative false rejection as a limitation.

papers.abstract: Transferring visual representations pretrained on human videos to robot manipulation requires learning reliable correspondences between human and robot demonstrations. However, paired demonstrations can differ in execution rate and in the proportion of non-key frames that do not directly reflect task progress. Frames at the same relative timestamp may therefore represent different task stages, which can cause correspondence learning to fail. To address these issues, we propose Frame-Level Temporal Alignment (FLTA), a framework that uses two temporal priors to adapt visual encoders pretrained on human videos for robot manipulation. It learns shared task-progress representations without frame-level correspondence annotations, allowing frames at different relative temporal positions to match. A global progress prior combines normalized temporal positions with visual similarity to construct a soft correspondence target. A local temporal order prior penalizes backward transitions while allowing stays and varying forward rates to accommodate execution-rate differences. With ResNet-50 and ViT encoders, our method achieves relative improvements of 46.93% and 65.96%, respectively, over the best baselines in average simulation success rates and achieves higher task success rates on real-world manipulation tasks. These results also suggest that effective human-robot adaptation depends less on the number of parameters updated than on which parameters are selected. Our project page is available at https://rtx5090ultra.github.io/FLTA-Project-Page/.
bullets: Addresses mismatched execution rates and irrelevant non-key frames in human–robot demonstrations.
Learns shared task-progress representations without frame-level correspondence annotations.
Uses a global progress prior for soft correspondences and a local temporal-order prior that permits stays and variable forward rates.
Reports relative average simulation success improvements of 46.93% with ResNet-50 and 65.96% with ViT over the best baselines, plus higher real-world task success.
Suggests that selecting which encoder parameters to update may matter more than updating more parameters.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a conformal-seeded hybrid strategy for solving inverse kinematics of offset, redundant 7-DoF robot arms of the humanoid class. Analytical inverse kinematics (AIK) provides closed-form solutions with very low computational cost. However, for offset kinematic structures, the exact closed-form solution is generally unavailable, and practical AIK must rely on an approximate or simplified kinematic model. In contrast, numerical inverse kinematics (NIK) can achieve high-precision solutions on the full kinematic model. However, its convergence is highly sensitive to initialization. To overcome these limitations, we propose a two-stage hybrid inverse kinematics framework with conformal-calibrated seed selection. First, an approximate analytical model efficiently enumerates a finite set of candidate joint solutions. Second, we rank these candidates using a lightweight learned predictor of post-refinement difficulty, wrapped by split-conformal prediction into a calibrated upper bound that serves as the selection score. The best-ranked seed is then refined using a Levenberg-Marquardt solver on the full kinematic model. The proposed method combines fast candidate generation, learned seed ranking with a calibrated difficulty bound, and accurate numerical refinement, achieving real-time performance of less than 40us and a success rate of 100% in our evaluation on reachable targets. We validate the approach through large-scale stochastic simulation across the workspace and experimental demonstrations with motion planning on a humanoid robot arm. Demonstration videos are available at https://youtu.be/aeiBmw1XRbw.
bullets: Targets offset, redundant 7-DoF humanoid-class arms where exact analytical IK is unavailable and numerical IK is initialization-sensitive.
Generates candidate joint solutions from an approximate analytical model, then ranks them with a learned predictor wrapped in split-conformal calibration.
Refines the selected seed using a Levenberg–Marquardt solver on the full kinematic model.
Reports under 40 μs runtime and 100% success on reachable targets in evaluation, with simulation and humanoid-arm demonstrations.
Scope is limited to reachable targets and the evaluation setting described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: For ground robots operating in outdoor environments, understanding the properties of the underlying terrain is essential for ensuring reliable operation. In most perception-based studies, this problem is formulated as categorical classification with a fixed number of classes defined during training. We propose an approach that enables new surface classes to be added as trainable vectors, which can subsequently be used to address higher-level tasks. By employing a learning paradigm based on predicting the robot's next state in time and using attention blocks, we improved classification accuracy to 98.56% on the Belyaev-Kushnarev dataset and 94.8% on BorealTC.
bullets: Targets reliable outdoor ground-robot operation through improved surface understanding.
Uses next-state prediction as the learning objective, combined with attention blocks.
Represents newly introduced surface classes as trainable vectors rather than requiring a fixed class set.
Reports classification accuracies of 98.56% on Belyaev-Kushnarev and 94.8% on BorealTC.

papers.abstract: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript
bullets: Addresses the limitation that demonstrations from other scenes lack feedback about the robot’s current world.

papers.title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation

papers.abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.
bullets: Studies linear-function-approximation policy evaluation when TD updates must cross a rate-limited channel.
Batches updates to reduce transmission variance and adaptively quantizes innovations.
Provides a high-probability finite-time error bound for the proposed method.
Above a finite channel-capacity threshold, matches unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors.
Uses O(d log T) transmitted bits over horizon T to attain the order-optimal Õ(1/T) rate, improving communication complexity over prior work.

The server reconstructs the direction, updates its parameter to θk+1, and returns this parameter exactly over an unconstrained noiseless reverse channel.

papers.title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
papers.tldr: BAQ-TD uses batching and adaptive quantization to preserve TD learning’s fast convergence rate over sufficiently capable finite-rate channels.

papers.abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.
bullets: Problem: Action learning can weaken pretrained language–video alignment, but guidance on data and supervision design is limited.
Method: Systematically evaluates language–video, language–video–action, and joint supervision using about 47,000 hours of general, egocentric, UMI, and robot videos.

Key findings: Egocentric video mixed with UMI demonstrations improves control generalization under a fixed training budget; architecture and joint-training choices affect how well these data are used.
Scaling the selected pretraining setup and post-training on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations yields 88.10% success in Easy and 61.56% in Hard conditions.
The model reaches 40.00% success across three real-world tasks, versus 23.33% for the strongest baseline, and the authors release data, code, and weights.

papers.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.
bullets: Targets soft powered descent, where limited fuel demands efficient guidance trajectories and control.
Uses model-based reinforcement learning built on DreamerV3 for the entry-descent-landing problem.
Operates from state sensor observations, advancing toward end-to-end landing solutions.
Reportedly lands within 2 m of the designated zone with velocity norm below 0.3 m/s.
Designed to be sample-efficient and generalizable across landing scenarios.

papers.abstract: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.
bullets: Robot probe pressure alters vascular anatomy, motivating fast biomechanical simulation for autonomous access.
The simulator used Stable Neo-Hookean tissue and a Vertex Block Descent solver on one GPU.
In a cylindrical phantom, artery predictions stayed within 5 percentage points and vein predictions within 3 points through 11 mm of compression.
A selected setting reduced solver time from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms per frame while staying within 1.03 points of the finest reference; the full stack ran at 56.4 ms per frame.
A realistic digital leg reproduced the expected clinical signal: the vein collapsed more than the artery.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining heterogeneous tactile data despite sensor-specific physics and limitations.
Supports piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors, with extensibility to new sensor types.
Produces plug-and-play tactile tokens compatible with diffusion policies and VLA models, including π₀.₅ and LingBot-VLA.
Experiments in simulation and on real robots across multiple hardware platforms show benefits for complex manipulation while retaining computational efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of LingBot-Touch. Top: what tactile data look like at scale. Our 5,000-hour corpus is multi-source, pooling egocentric recordings from human tactile gloves with teleoperated robot hands across piezoresistive, magnetic, and optical sensing (left); heterogeneous in taxel geometry, resolution, and channels, which we reconcile in a canonical fingertip space (middle); and sparse, with most taxels silent most of the time (right). Bottom: what one encoder trained on this corpus enables. Frozen features recover contact force, location, extent, and dynamics and align with vision (left); the same tokens plug into imitation-learning and VLA policies on real dual-arm hands (middle) and into reinforcement learning in simulation (right). LingBot-Touch transfers to a sensor model unseen in pretraining without retraining, and its 5.46M-parameter Tiny variant adds under 0.2% to the parameters of the policies it augments.

Figure 3. Overview of LingBot-Touch. LingBot-Touch learns unified tactile representations through self-supervised prediction in latent space. Heterogeneous spatiotemporal signals from magnetic, piezoresistive, and visuotactile sensors are mapped to a canonical spherical space and incorporated into pretraining through weighted sampling. Modality-specific tokenizers convert these signals into tokens for a shared Transformer backbone equipped with 5D rotary positional embeddings (RoPE). The context encoder processes only visible tokens, and its outputs are concatenated with mask tokens before being passed to the corresponding modality-specific predictor. The target encoder processes the unmasked input, providing latent targets for the context loss on visible positions and the prediction loss on masked positions. Its parameters are updated through an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the context encoder, with gradients stopped through the target branch.

Figure 7. Scaling with pretraining data and model size. Frozen-encoder probing on Sharpa Wave (top) and XHand1 (bottom) for Tiny and Small encoders pretrained on 1K to 5K hours with fixed source proportions. Small improves or holds on every task with every increment of data on both hands; Tiny saturates at about 4K hours and loses retrieval recall at 5K.

Figure 8. Single-source versus multi-source pretraining. Blue: probed on Sharpa Wave. Orange: probed on XHand1. Top: adding 441 hours of piezoresistive data and the other sensor’s data to a fixed 331 or 228 hours of a sensor’s own data improves seven of eight sensor-task pairs. Bottom: at a fixed 1,000-hour budget, a single-source model beats the three-source mixture on its own sensor on seven of eight pairs, by the widest margins on the spatial tasks. Bold marks the better of each pair. LingBot-Touch uses the HaT-Tiny backbone.

Figure 2. Composition and diversity of the LingBot-Touch pretraining dataset. Our dataset comprises 4,983 hours of tactile recordings, spanning 464K episodes and 1.33 billion frames across piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensing modalities. To support representation learning for downstream understanding of contact physics and robotic dexterous manipulation, it covers diverse real-world human and robot manipulation tasks, encompassing varied sensing principles, spatial resolutions, sampling frequencies, and physical taxel layouts.

Figure 6. Comparison with FTP-1 using frozen pretrained backbones. Results on Sharpa Wave (top) and XHand1 (bottom). Gray bars show FTP-1 with sensor-specific adapters trained for each platform. Colored bars show LingBot-Touch with the HaT-Small backbone, pretrained on 5K hours of tactile data and evaluated without sensor-specific encoder adaptation. Arrows indicate whether lower or higher values are better.

Figure 5. Contact-physics probing tasks. Five frozen-encoder probing tasks on two dexterous hands, Sharpa Wave and XHand1: fingertip force recovery, contact center and coverage estimation, future force prediction, and tactile-to-video retrieval. They test contact intensity, spatial structure, short-term dynamics, and cross-modal correspondence. Each task trains its own attentive probe on the multi-level features of the frozen EMA target encoder. For fingertip force recovery, labels are obtained by averaging the per-finger resultant force vectors over each pair of consecutive frames and then computing their magnitudes. Contact centers are computed as contact-strength-weighted centroids of valid taxels above the activation threshold, while contact coverage is the fraction of valid taxels that are active. Future force labels represent per-finger changes in force magnitude at each of the next four frames relative to the final history frame. Contact centers are supervised only when contact is present.

Figure 9. Latent prediction versus signal reconstruction. VAE, MAE, and LingBot-Touch are pretrained on identical data with matched hyperparameters. Top left: pretraining losses. Bottom: frozen-encoder probing with 1K and 4K hours of pretraining data. Top right: real-world manipulation success rates with the pretrained tactile encoders integrated into LingBot-VLA.

Figure 12. Reinforcement-learning curves on twelve dexterous tasks, Sharpa Wave (a–h) and XHand1 (i–l). Lines show the mean episode return over three seeds; bands show one standard deviation across the smoothed per-seed curves.

Figure 10. Contact separation and continuity in the latent space. Each example pairs finger-wise tactile responses with phase annotations (left) and a UMAP projection of frozen LingBot-Touch features (right). Each point is a 16-frame window of five-finger observations; point colors follow the phase annotations and curve colors identify fingers. Non-contact windows form one cluster, and contact windows form continuous structures that track the strengthening and weakening of the responses.
Figure 4. Spatial mask-ratio warm-up. The masking ratio increases linearly from 40% to 80% over the first 300 training steps, then remains fixed. Red and green denote masked and visible taxels.

papers.abstract: A challenging bottleneck in manipulation research is reproducibility and comparability of methods in real-world environments. Since manipulation is an interactive task, it cannot be evaluated on a static dataset of observations. Benchmarking in simulation is a common remedy, but cannot cover the whole complexity of real-world tests. This paper proposes a new paradigm of stochastic challenges. Like the well-known YCB objects, it is based on reproducible real-world scenes and therefore allows system-level innovation and comparability between different platforms. Due to their stochastic nature, our challenges however, mimic the rigor and surprise of hidden test sets. To this end, we show how different robots in different labs can be compared based on their success rate over different random task samples, if these samples come from the same distribution. We propose stochastic challenges as a general paradigm for robot benchmarking and implement this paradigm in a novel benchmark for mobile manipulation, on which we compare two robots tested in two different labs.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating interactive manipulation using static datasets or simulation alone.
Uses reproducible real-world scenes with randomized task samples to emulate hidden-test-set rigor and variability.
Enables comparison across platforms when task samples are drawn from the same distribution.
Implements the paradigm in a mobile-manipulation benchmark and compares two robots tested in two labs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Stochastic Challenges target several desired aspects of robotic benchmarking: (i) systemlevel innovation, i.e. not restricting evaluation to specific hardware; (ii) local evaluation, avoiding the effort to transport systems and reducing the chance of errors when trying to reproduce methods; (iii) reduced overfitting, testing true generalization instead of pre-known tasks.

Figure 2: Concept overview. Seeded randomization generates reproducible KALLAX manipulation scenes; robots across labs (Stretch 3 and Spot) execute sampled configurations, with outcomes statistically aggregated for robust comparison.
Figure 3: Experimental setup. Our KALLAX benchmark draws sample configs from the same distribution, which are then recreated in two different labs to evaluate the two different robotic systems.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarking real-world robotic manipulation, directly relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Benchmarking Real-World Robotic Manipulation through Stochastic Challenges
papers.tldr: The paper introduces stochastic real-world challenges to make robotic manipulation more reproducible, comparable, and robustly evaluated across robots and labs.

papers.abstract: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
bullets: Targets more effective, real-time model-based control for robotics.
Extends LeWorldModel with a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor.
Uses these auxiliary latent losses to impose additional structure on learned embeddings.
Evaluated on standard world-model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
The abstract does not report specific quantitative gains or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of main experimental results: Σ-LeWM outperforms standard LeWM when considering long horizon tasks (a), and leads to improved planning efficiency (b). papers.selection_reason: Improves latent world models for robot control with backward and inverse dynamics losses, fitting both world-model and embodied-AI interests.
papers.title: $Σ$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control
papers.tldr: Σ-LeWM improves decoder-free world models for robot control by adding backward and inverse-dynamics losses that structure latent representations and enhance performance and planning efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.
bullets: Studies how dataset size, training updates, checkpoint selection, and simulation affect VLA adaptation for precise chess-piece manipulation.
Fine-tunes π₀.₅ on teleoperated real demonstrations and randomized scripted-expert demonstrations in simulation.
In simulation, success improves with more data and updates; a short learning-rate cooldown adds up to 31 success-rate points.
Validation loss and action error are unreliable for selecting checkpoints.
Several rollout-based and reinforcement-learning refinements did not measurably outperform plain behavior cloning in this setting; simulator, expert, and demonstrations are released.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of VLA fine-tuning and sim-to-real transfer for precise robotic manipulation with language-specified goals.
papers.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
papers.tldr: A robotic chess case study shows that simulated demonstrations can improve VLA fine-tuning when real data is scarce, while checkpoint selection requires success-based evaluation rather than common loss metrics.

papers.abstract: We examine what plan validation and execution reports establish in natural-language robot fleet control. Commands are traced through typed plans, deterministic corrections, fleet coordination and outcome checks in a three-level Robot Operating System 2 implementation with twenty simulated robots. An offline benchmark of 44 cases checks plan structure and selected command requirements. Across five local configurations without a response schema, 70.0-87.3% of responses pass. All runs in a selected 18-run simulation series meet their pose-based task conditions. This series includes two successful repeats that replaced incomplete runs after a software change. Saved plans and logs document duplicate pickup assignments and goal adjustments within the original task zones. Separate formation traces show a structurally accepted plan with the wrong formation shape and a rejected route, and an arrival report that omitted a requested robot after replanning. Carry completion records pickup and subsequent drop-off zone presence for the same robot. The cases distinguish changes to executable actions from changes to the requirements covered by a completion report. They motivate checking the effective assignments, goals and reported outcome against the original command.
bullets: The study examines what validation and execution reports actually establish in robot fleet control.
Commands are traced through typed plans, deterministic corrections, coordination, and outcome checks in a three-level ROS 2 implementation with 20 simulated robots.
An offline 44-case benchmark found 70.0–87.3% of responses passed across five local configurations without a response schema.
Simulation cases exposed duplicate pickup assignments, adjusted goals, an incorrect formation shape, a rejected route, and an arrival report omitting a requested robot after replanning.
The findings motivate checking effective assignments, goals, and reported outcomes against the original command.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates correctness and validation in natural-language robot fleet control, relevant to robotic control systems.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms often rely on data collected from a target environment, which can be expensive and noisy. Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. We develop our approach for Policy-Evaluation, which is a fundamental building block of RL algorithms. Then we combine it within the actor-critic framework towards policy improvement, as well as extend it towards offline RL scenarios. Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks demonstrate improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches, highlighting control variates as an effective tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.
bullets: Motivated by the high cost and noise of collecting real-environment data.
Develops a control-variate method for policy evaluation that uses simulation only for variance reduction.
Extends the approach to actor–critic policy improvement and offline RL.
Experiments across multiple MuJoCo tasks show improvements over standard simulation-mixing methods.
The approach is designed to mitigate inaccuracies in imperfect simulators.:

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a simulation-aided RL method using control variates to reduce variance, applicable to robotic control tasks.

papers.abstract: Many tasks compose transformations by a known rule: chained rotations in robotics and navigation. Learned models relearn it, compounding error; classical estimators hardcode it and miss hardware deviations. We impose the known structure and learn only the remainder: an exact non-commutative group law sits in the node of a self-contained layer, its edges learn local increments, and a zero-initialized correction psi learns unknown deviations of the law. A pre-training criterion predicts exact representability. On fixed-angle SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter dense edge is the most accurate dense model, at 27x fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline, and lies 0.05 deg above the Bayes floor. On real robot arms, an isolated 306-parameter psi reaches 1.12-1.14 mm versus 1.29-1.33 mm for Gauss-Newton at N >= 60, and the recipe transfers across three vendors and two protocols. The recipe matches classical fits where the data obey the law and loses where the imposed law is not the task's.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation in learned composition while avoiding the rigidity of fully hardcoded classical estimators.
Uses an exact group-law operation, learned edge increments, and a zero-initialized correction for unknown deviations.
A pre-training criterion predicts whether the task is exactly representable by the imposed law.
On SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter model approaches the Bayes floor and uses 27× fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline.

On real robot arms, the correction achieves 1.12–1.14 mm error versus 1.29–1.33 mm for Gauss–Newton at N ≥ 60, transferring across vendors and protocols; performance declines when the imposed law is mismatched.

papers.abstract: Robots are increasingly expected to execute natural-language manipulation tasks in real-world environments. This is particularly relevant in household assistance and logistics, where clutter requires reasoning about both task objectives and execution feasibility. This challenge becomes even more pronounced for bimanual humanoid platforms, where coordinating two manipulators introduces additional interaction and kinematic constraints. We present a zero-shot vision-language framework for execution-aware bimanual manipulation that jointly reasons about task objectives and physical feasibility. Planning is grounded in a structured scene representation that combines semantic object relations with execution constraints, enabling the selection of obstacle relocations and execution choices while preserving task semantics. Compatible actions are organised into parallel bimanual stages with explicit pre- and post-conditions. A hierarchical validator evaluates these conditions under perceptual uncertainty and uses stage-level execution history to support local recovery or targeted replanning. Experiments on the CENTAURO hybrid wheeled-legged humanoid robot across nine language-conditioned manipulation scenarios show higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline. In dedicated failure scenarios, hierarchical validation recovers from execution failures with fewer model queries than always replanning. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining execution reasoning directly into task planning. Videos and additional material are available on the Project Webpage: https://advrhumanoids.github.io/bridging-planning-execution/.
bullets: Targets household and logistics tasks where clutter, bimanual coordination, and kinematic constraints complicate execution.

On the CENTAURO robot, it achieves higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline and recovers failures with fewer model queries than always replanning.

papers.abstract: Modern visuotactile sensors primarily sense contact by imaging the deformation of a compliant interface. Using techniques such as photometric stereo, they can recover detailed contact geometry, often represented as surface normals or depth. However, force-related information typically still needs to be inferred indirectly through calibration, geometric reconstruction, or learned mappings. Mechanochromic photonic-crystal (PC) materials offer an alternative physical encoding mechanism: contact loading changes their periodic microstructure and spectral response, directly transforming local stress into a spatially resolved structural-color field. Despite this potential, PC materials have rarely been explored as visuotactile sensors for closed-loop robot learning. We present PCTac, an open-source mechanochromic PC fingertip that uses a dense hue field as its tactile observation. Loading characterization demonstrates a repeatable relationship between the applied normal load and the observed hue response. We further integrate this representation directly into a Diffusion Policy and evaluate it on three real-robot manipulation tasks. Across 90 physical rollouts, PCTac Hue achieves 68 successes (75.6\%), compared with 60 (66.7\%) for PCTac RGB, 57 (63.3\%) for Wedge RGB, and 29 (32.2\%) for vision-only. PCTac Hue also achieves the highest observed success rate on each evaluated task, including Perturbed Test-Tube Insertion, where it achieves 16/30 successes versus 13/30 for tactile RGB baselines and 1/30 for vision-only. These results demonstrate the potential of mechanochromic structural color as a compact, load-sensitive tactile representation for robot learning and closed-loop manipulation. Project page: https://bey0ndt1me.github.io/PCTac-page/.
bullets: Encodes local contact load as a spatially resolved hue field through structural-color changes.

Integrates the hue representation directly into a Diffusion Policy for real-robot learning.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive VLA planning usually predicts continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions often describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final continuous trajectory. We address this gap with TrajCond, which introduces a discrete trajectory-geometric condition for VLA planning. Specifically, we represent TrajCond as a 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory and learn it with a two-stage training framework before final continuous trajectory prediction. With the simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories, we name our method AutoVLA-D (Double). Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond, consistently improving final continuous trajectory prediction across closed-loop and open-loop driving benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/ShivaTeam/AutoVLA-D.

papers.abstract: Control barrier function (CBF) filters depend on dynamic models that can be inaccurate when their parameters and external forces are uncertain. This paper investigates a radial basis function (RBF) neural network compensator whose output is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space CBF filter. An auxiliary state driven by the difference between requested and applied torques corrects the learning signal, reducing the direct influence of filter intervention on adaptation. A two-link manipulator is evaluated through constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed controller improves tracking while maintaining joint, velocity, and torque limits under parameter uncertainty, and that both the shared compensation and the auxiliary correction contribute to this improvement.
bullets: Addresses inaccurate CBF-filter dynamics caused by uncertain parameters and external forces.
Uses one RBF neural-network compensator shared by Cartesian tracking and a joint-space CBF filter.

Experiments cover constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbances, operating range, and timing.

papers.abstract: Achieving generalizable and well-aligned multimodal representations remains a core challenge in robot learning. While recent approaches have attempted to align modalities by modeling conditional or higher-order statistical dependencies, they do not explicitly consider the structural coherence across modalities. In this work, we propose a novel multimodal alignment method that augments existing contrastive losses with a geometry-aware Gromov--Wasserstein (GW) distance-based regularization. To this end, we encode intra-modal geometry for each modality and reduce cross-modal structural discrepancies through a dynamically learned GW barycenter, thereby encouraging structural consistency in addition to instance-level contrastive alignment. We apply this optimal-transport-based alignment strategy to robot perception tasks involving underexplored modalities such as force and tactile signals, where modality data often exhibit varying sample densities. Extensive experiments on five robotic benchmarks show that our method improves structural alignment and downstream performance over state-of-the-art multimodal contrastive baselines across a wide range of downstream tasks, including robot and environment state prediction. Moreover, our GW-based regularization can be seamlessly integrated into most InfoNCE-like objectives.
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit cross-modal structural coherence in existing multimodal representation methods.
Encodes intra-modal geometry and uses a dynamically learned Gromov–Wasserstein barycenter to reduce structural discrepancies.
Supports challenging modalities such as force and tactile signals with differing sample densities.
Evaluated on five robotic benchmarks, improving structural alignment and downstream performance over multimodal contrastive baselines.
The GW regularizer integrates with most InfoNCE-like objectives.

papers.abstract: We present and evaluate a game-theoretic model predictive control planner for cooperative goal reaching and adversarial pursuit-evasion with drones. The planner combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints and trajectory-tracking interfaces. A comparison of cooperative game solvers assesses their ability to find feasible trajectories that resolve conflicts. A computational study quantifies how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance. Move blocking holds control inputs constant over groups of prediction steps, reducing the number of independent control variables and lowering computation time. Timing measurements identify the practical limits of real-time planning in the tested configurations. PyBullet simulations demonstrate cooperative goal reaching and pursuit-evasion. A laboratory flight complements the simulations by validating the trajectory-tracking interfaces on physical drones. The planner can serve as a basis for further evaluation and controller development.
bullets: Targets multi-drone coordination in both cooperative and adversarial settings.
Combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints, and trajectory-tracking interfaces.
Compares cooperative game solvers for finding feasible conflict-resolving trajectories.
Evaluates how drone count, prediction horizon, and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance.

papers.abstract: In patrol missions involving multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), a designated command USV can support fleet management by sequentially rendezvousing with each patrolling USV. These operations require motion-feasible route planning and priority-aware rendezvous sequencing, with the objective of minimizing mission completion time and total tardiness relative to priority-dependent due dates. We propose a framework combining grid-based path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based reinforcement learning. The path planner accounts for ocean currents and approximates turn-rate constraints through multi-stage maneuvers, with path feasibility empirically validated through trajectory-tracking simulations. For rendezvous sequencing, a Feasible Transition Graph (FTG) represents candidate rendezvous events and temporally feasible transitions, enabling a graph neural network to exploit spatiotemporal rendezvous relationships for policy learning. A surrogate predicts travel times from compact current and motion features to avoid repeated path searches during FTG construction and policy training. Evaluation using grid-based path planning shows statistically significant average objective reductions of 10.5%, 3.5%, and 1.5% compared with greedy, MLP-RL, and 2-step lookahead greedy, respectively. The policy achieves these improvements while requiring approximately 1/35 of the latter's computation time. It maintains its advantage over MLP-RL under unseen priority-tier settings, with larger gains as fleet size increases.
bullets: Targets fleet management with minimized completion time and priority-dependent tardiness.
Combines current-aware grid path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based RL.
Uses a Feasible Transition Graph to encode temporally feasible rendezvous events and transitions.
Reduces the average objective by 10.5% versus greedy, 3.5% versus MLP-RL, and 1.5% versus 2-step lookahead greedy.
Requires about 1/35 the computation time of 2-step lookahead greedy and retains advantages under unseen priority tiers, especially for larger fleets.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.
bullets: Targets gaps in existing benchmarks, including shortcut visual cues and predominantly static scenes.
Covers 54 task variants spanning spatial reasoning and spatial memory.
Uses an automated pipeline to generate and annotate tasks with verified targets and executable interactions.
Evaluations show consistent weaknesses in tracking object identities after spatial changes and translating relational or geometric constraints into actions.
The benchmark is publicly released on GitHub.
