papers.abstract: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.
bullets: Separates the gradient’s referent—executed computation, converged equations, or continuous dynamics—from the backward-pass realization.
Classifies methods and engines by automatic differentiation, equation-level adjoints, or custom adjoints, including state-storage and recovery costs.
Provides a separate taxonomy for non-smooth contact dynamics.
Identifies and measures four mechanisms that can degrade useful gradients, finding that exact derivatives do not always improve fitting.
Reviews cases where zeroth-order optimization can outperform simulator gradients and proposes a reporting checklist, diagnostic tool, and research agenda.

figures.caption: Figure 3: The two model families where the choice of referent bites hardest, and why. Left, deformables at the scale the field now works at: every one of these bodies is soft, they are in sustained mutual contact, and the solver is truncated to a fixed iteration budget, which is the regime where the converged equation and the executed computation stop agreeing (Section 6.2). Right, the same smoke plume under four schemes. The differences are large and come from the numerics rather than from the physics being modeled, which is the sense in which a fluid solver’s structure decides what its adjoint can be (Section 6.4). Images reproduced, cropped but otherwise unaltered, from [CLYY24, LHB∗25].

Figure 5: Mechanism 1 measured. A mass-spring chain is stepped with implicit Euler and solved by K Gauss–Seidel sweeps of per-vertex Newton updates, a one-dimensional instance of vertex block descent [CLYY24]; the parameter is the vector of per-spring stiffnesses. We compare the exact derivative of the K sweeps that actually executed, referent A1, against the equation-level adjoint, referent A2, evaluated as an implementation evaluates it: at the iterate the K sweeps reached, as if the residual there had vanished. (a) how far the truncated solve is from convergence. (b) the norm of the difference between the two gradients, relative to the gradient of the same solve run to convergence; above the dashed line the discrepancy is larger than the quantity being estimated. (c) the cosine of the angle between them, which indicates whether the negative returned vector is a local descent direction for the executed objective. Actual progress also depends on step size, curvature, and the optimizer. The shaded band marks the one to ten sweeps a real-time deformable solver actually runs. Within that band the two derivatives agree well for compliant material from two sweeps on, but for the stiffest material (k = 2×105) the equation-level adjoint is nearly orthogonal to the true derivative of the executed computation, and agreement is recovered only after hundreds of sweeps; at k = 2×104 a few dozen suffice. The forward sensitivity was differentiated by hand through the executed arithmetic and checked against central differences of the same pipeline to a relative error below 4×10−6.

Figure 4: The report’s running example, one implicit step followed from what is computed to what it costs. Two mass-spring chains stepped with implicit Euler and solved by K Gauss–Seidel sweeps; panels (a) to (c) take one step at k = 2×105, panel (d) fits random stiffness fields near 6×103 on a shorter, pinned chain over twelve steps. (a) what ran: the residual falls with the budget but does not vanish, so the iterate the sweeps reached (A1) and the root they approach (A2) are two different objects to differentiate. (b) the relative norm of the vector difference between the two gradients is of order one across the plotted range. (c) they disagree in direction too, the cosine sitting between 0.1 and 0.55, so the two are nearly orthogonal. (d) and, for a target the same solver generated, it makes almost no difference to the optimization: from two sweeps onward no stable advantage is separable, median and interquartile range over forty seeds. Panels (b) and (c) are large at the stiff setting; (d) shows no separation between A1 and A2 for its fitting problem from two sweeps on. For this reason the report separates which derivative a method returns from whether it helps.

Table 4: Representative methods grouped by physical model. Ref.: A1 executed computation, A2 converged equation, A3 continuous dynamics (Section 4.1). Real.: B1 framework-generated reverse; B2 equation-level adjoint, including a discretized continuous adjoint; B3 custom operator-level adjoint composition (Section 4.2). For hybrid engines these labels identify the main documented backward construction; custom solves and recorded remainders are noted and do not imply exactness of the full engine. A1* treats an internal linear solve as exact; finite primal and adjoint tolerances still cause error. A2a marks an additional approximation in the derivative system. surr. marks a returned direction that need not differentiate the forward objective; it can still have a specified surrogate target. State describes recovery: tape, recorded reverse-pass intermediates; trajectory, states and required auxiliary data per step; checkpoint, selected states with recomputation; recompute, per-step intermediates regenerated from saved states; final state, converged state of each step plus required auxiliary data, not just the rollout endpoint; replay, sweeps rerun from saved inputs; reverse, state recovered by reversing the map. These choices do not specify a unique memory cost. none and not stated indicate no reverse-state store or an unreported strategy. Contact follows Table 3 where applicable. Alternatives are noted in the final column. The realization is n/a when there is no backward pass, including forward sensitivities; shooting alone does not determine the realization. Methods that only consume a simulator appear in Sections 7 and 9.

Figure 2: What a contact solver is asked to resolve, and why contact modes matter. Left, two elastic beams twisted around one another, 97 thousand vertices between them, in sustained frictional contact along the whole interface while they buckle. The active pairs change along the trajectory. Local branch derivatives can remain valid despite these temporal changes, but may poorly predict finite parameter updates that change the contact sequence. Right, an elastic cube released on an incline at four friction coefficients. Whether it sticks or slides is decided by the friction cone. At a regular stick–slip transition, the branch derivatives can differ (Section 5.1). Images reproduced, cropped but otherwise unaltered, from [CLYY24] under the authors’ CC BY 4.0 license.

Figure 8: Three uses of a simulator gradient, as their authors report them. Left, material parameters recovered from observed cloth motion by optimizing through the simulator, the inverse problem of Section 9.1. Middle, a trajectory optimized through frictional contact; the loss curve beneath compares the analytic gradient against two zeroth-order optimizers on the same task, which is the comparison item 7 of our checklist asks every paper to report. Right, smoke steered from one silhouette through fixed obstacles into another, by optimizing the forces with an adjoint taken on the flow map. Keyframe control of fluids is an early application of differentiable simulation. The illustrated result uses the recent continuous-adjoint flow-map method [LHB∗25], corresponding to referent A3 in Section 4.1. None of the three results is ours. Images reproduced, cropped or letterboxed but otherwise unaltered, from [LDW∗23, LHB∗25].

Figure 6: Mechanism 2 measured, on the mass-spring chain of Figure 5 stepped with implicit Euler and eight Gauss–Seidel sweeps. Per-spring stiffnesses are the parameters and the sensitivity is propagated forward through the executed arithmetic, so the experiment tests sensitivity to the forward states and arithmetic precision without introducing a reverse-mode implementation. (a), the accumulated sensitivity ∥dxT /dk∥ varies by a factor of fifteen over three hundred steps: it does not explode, and the loss-gradient norm, not shown, rises by less than three orders of magnitude while the loss rises by eight and a half, so neither would alarm a monitor. (b), the cosine between derivatives obtained from the same sensitivity recurrence in double and in single precision, with two controls that separate the two places rounding can enter. With state and sensitivity both in single, agreement holds to four figures out to twenty steps and three at forty, and then falls: 0.79 at eighty, 0.64 at a hundred and sixty, 0.48 at three hundred and twenty (the last two vary with hardware; see text). With the trajectory in double and only the sensitivity recurrence in single, the cosine stays above 0.999 throughout. With the trajectory in single and the sensitivity in double, the fall is reproduced to within 0.003 in cosine. The disagreement therefore comes from the single-precision trajectory, which differs from the double one by a relative 10−4 at eighty steps while the loss differs by about two parts in ten thousand (at most 2.2×10−4): the gradient is far more sensitive to the trajectory than the objective is. The final contraction of the sensitivity with the loss gradient is done in double in every variant, so that it does not enter the comparison.

Figure 7: Contact-gradient support and sensitivity amplification in the massspring contact testbed (k = 2×104, eight sweeps, no gravity, wall stiffness 2×105), with launch velocity as the single parameter and accumulated contact energy as the objective. Panel (a) uses a 120-step rollout; panel (b) varies the horizon. (a) the derivative against launch velocity: below the velocity at which a vertex reaches the wall within the horizon (shaded), no contact occurs and the derivative is zero; gradients can be nonzero in the active-contact region. This is a derivative-support diagnostic, not evidence that minimizing contact energy fails in the zero-contact region. (b) spread (standard deviation) of the same derivative over an ensemble of launches perturbed by 10−6. Between two walls, repeated bounces are associated with roughly seventy-fold growth in spread over the tested horizons. With one wall, the chain bounces once and the spread remains approximately flat. These observations do not establish chaos or show that repeated contact is necessary for sensitivity amplification.

Table 2: The two axes crossed. Rows identify derivative targets; columns are operational categories for the organization of the backward pass. Exactness must be assessed against the row’s target and the implementation’s numerical qualifications. Construction may be automatic, manual, or hybrid within these categories. Memory depends on retained states, recomputation, checkpointing, and solver workspace, not on the column alone. Discrete custom adjoints can exploit forward operator or block structure without necessarily eliminating trajectory storage. A3 includes both equation-level solves and custom continuousadjoint operators. Empty entries reflect the labeling convention and the examples selected, not impossibility claims. Entries are representative, not exhaustive.

Table 7: Differentiable simulation systems viewed as software, complementing Tables 4 and 5. Backward construction describes how derivative computations are implemented. Backward memory lists principal retained information, not a complete allocation bound: forward states, contact data, and linear-solver data may also be required or recomputed. The absence of an inner-iteration tape does not imply constant rollout memory. Backend and AD coverage depend on the solver and version. Entries summarize the cited descriptions and supported derivative paths.
Table 5: Table 4 continued: deformables, cloth and fluids. Columns are as in Table 4.

Table 3: Treatments of contact discontinuity. This axis is orthogonal to both axes of Table 2: an engine can combine a cell there with one or more treatments here. “Obstacle addressed” refers to the enumeration in Section 5.1.
Table 1: Notation used throughout this report.

Table 8: Task benchmarks and a cross-engine survey for differentiable simulation. The task evaluations combine gradient behavior with the optimizer, policy class, and physical model; the Newbury et al. row summarizes engine features. Together they provide useful comparisons, but not a shared cross-engine protocol for reference-Jacobian accuracy at matched solver settings.

Table 9: The reporting checklist computed by the released diagnostic for the chain under both referents. Item (i) is split into an implementation part and a convergence part. The A1 zero in (i-b) denotes its finite-program target, not equality with the converged-equation derivative. Item (iii) uses two query budgets with wall-clock beside them. (v) uses this four-sweep configuration, distinct from Figure 6, and is reported for A1 only because the A2 engine provides no single-precision path; (vi) is the diagnostic’s generic flat fraction, which is zero on this chain; the chain has no contact, so this says nothing about contact-induced flatness. Absence of contact does not rule out other flat directions.

Table 6: What the equation-level referent costs an optimizer, and how much that depends on where the target came from. Loss remaining after 120 gradientdescent steps, as a fraction of the initial loss, median over 40 random instances of the fitting problem (a 16-vertex chain over twelve steps), with the fraction of instances on which A2 finished lower; lower is better. Three constructions of the target, everything else identical: the endpoint the same solver at the same K produces from the true stiffness field, so that the fit can reach it exactly; the endpoint a solve run to convergence (2000 sweeps) produces, fitted with K sweeps; and the rest configuration, which no stiffness field reaches under gravity. Within-row comparisons isolate the choice of gradient for each target construction. Across-budget comparisons for same-K targets also change the target-generating solver; comparisons for converged or external targets isolate the budget only if instances and target data are held fixed.

papers.selection_reason: Taxonomy and analysis of differentiable physics simulation, a core tool for gradient-based robot learning, control, and manipulation.
papers.title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
papers.tldr: This report disentangles what differentiable physics methods differentiate from how they compute gradients, showing that gradient usefulness depends on both implementation and problem-specific failure modes.

papers.abstract: Egocentric auto-labeling requires depth, camera pose, object, and human-pose estimates to agree across independently developed models. Differences in units, coordinate conventions, and scale can make individually plausible predictions geometrically inconsistent. We present \textbf{EgoLabel}, a zero-shot pipeline that combines off-the-shelf models without target-domain labeled training and provides explicit cross-modal registration and consistency diagnostics. The pipeline integrates MonST3R for geometry, LocateAnything with GMC-BoT-SORT and SAM~2 for objects, and V-HPOT for hands; FisheyeViT provides a separate whole-body compatibility demonstration. Our main hand evaluation uses H2O sensor depth. Across 20 sequences, per-hand depth anchoring reduces the mean of per-sequence median hand--depth residuals by $23\%$ relative to a single global scale, yielding a pooled median of $84.6\,\mathrm{mm}$ against a $20.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ ground-truth reference. Hand PA-MPJPE is $14.53\pm1.29\,\mathrm{mm}$, whereas absolute MPJPE is $119.1\pm31.3\,\mathrm{mm}$, revealing a substantial gap between aligned and metric accuracy. On three RGB-only sequences, camera ATE is $1.40\pm0.29\,\mathrm{cm}$ after $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ alignment. We also identify a sliding-window implementation issue that allows sensor-initialized depth to change during optimization. Because hand anchoring and its residual share the same depth map, the residual measures internal consistency rather than independent accuracy. These results characterize both the utility and the current limits of the registration pipeline.
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies from differing units, coordinate conventions, and scales across independently developed models.
Combines MonST3R, LocateAnything, GMC-BoT-SORT, SAM 2, and V-HPOT, with FisheyeViT used for whole-body compatibility.
Per-hand depth anchoring reduces median hand–depth residuals by 23% versus a single global scale; pooled residual is 84.6 mm against a 20.5 mm reference.
Hand pose reaches 14.53 ± 1.29 mm PA-MPJPE but 119.1 ± 31.3 mm absolute MPJPE, showing a large aligned-versus-metric accuracy gap.
The hand–depth residual is only an internal-consistency measure because anchoring and evaluation use the same depth map; a sliding-window optimization issue is also identified.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall architecture of EgoLabel. Off-the-shelf models produce geometry (MonST3R), object annotations (LocateAnything + GMC-BoT-SORT + SAM 2), and hand poses (V-HPOT). Unit conversion, coordinate alignment, and per-hand depth anchoring connect these streams for joint inspection. Hand–depth residuals, object-trajectory smoothness, and control experiments assess their consistency. FisheyeViT is demonstrated on separate fisheye recordings, and structured manipulation captioning is a downstream application. Metric-scale limitations are detailed in Section 3.4.

Figure 4: Final end-to-end output of EgoLabel on H2O h1/0, as rendered in the Rerun viewer at four stages of the manipulation: (a) lifting the box to examine it, (b) peeling the top flaps, (c) removing the flaps, and (d) pulling the box sides. Each panel is one screenshot of the integrated viewer and simultaneously shows the object stream (LocateAnything detections, GMC-BoT-SORT track IDs, and SAM 2 masks, drawn as colored boxes on the overlay video), the 3D hand prediction (left/right V-HPOT skeletons and the camera+wrist trajectory in 3D), and the ASID task caption (bottom panel: hand usage, manipulated object, and action). Object, hand, and camera annotations are produced by independent zero-shot models; the ASID caption (bottom panel) is a GT-assisted downstream consumer (Section 3.5).

Figure 3: Qualitative whole-body results from the FisheyeViT stream. Each panel pairs a head-mounted fisheye frame (left) with the reconstructed 3D skeleton in the shared metric frame (right); predicted skeletons are orange and, where available, ground-truth skeletons are red. (a) Prediction only; (b)–(d) prediction overlaid with ground truth. The skeleton is mapped into the shared frame by the camera-to-world transform (Section 3.2.4); this is a compatibility demonstration on separate recordings, not a joint H2O result.

Figure 5: Cross-modal consistency of the V-HPOT hand stream against the depth map on H2O h1/0. (a) Distribution of the per-joint hand–depth residual; the solid line is the median. (b) Median residual for a single global scale, our per-hand anchoring, and the reprojected ground-truth hands. The figure shows a representative sequence; across the 20 sequences the per-sequence median ranges from 64.2 to 119.7mm, and the pooled medians are in Table 6. The residual is a consistency check (does the fused skeleton lie on the reconstructed surface?), not an independent accuracy metric.

Figure 6: Camera trajectory on H2O k1/0 for the sensor-depth-injection ablation (the RGB-only trajectory, which we take as the main camera result, is summarized in Table 5), in the first-frame camera frame. (a) Top view: ground-truth (gray) and MonST3R trajectory after 7-DoF Sim(3) alignment (blue). (b) Per-frame ATE (blue) with the mean as a dashed line. The injected run recovers the trajectory shape well, with the residual global-scale error left by the injection acting only as an initialization rather than a constraint (recomputed with the released estimator: Sim(3) ATE 1.76 cm, fitted scale 0.45, strict SE(3) 3.12 cm).

Figure 8: Fused 3D scene on H2O (frame 225), in the first-frame camera frame. Gray: ground-truth camera trajectory; blue: predicted camera trajectory (Sim(3)-aligned); green: the V-HPOT hand skeleton after metric-scale anchoring; colored lines: 3D trajectories of the tracked objects lifted through the depth map and the camera pose (start points marked). The independently estimated hand, object, and camera streams are drawn in one coordinate system for inspection.

Figure 7: V-HPOT hand accuracy on H2O h1/0. (a) Summary bars: scale-invariant PA-MPJPE (14.13mm), scalealigned MPJPE (22.0mm), and absolute (metric) MPJPE (63.7mm) over 900 hand samples. (b) Per-frame PA-MPJPE over time (light) with a 15-frame smoothed curve and the sequence mean (dashed). The per-frame PA-MPJPE is broadly stable over the sequence. 20 sequences: 14.53±1.29 PA-MPJPE, 26.46±4.40 scale-aligned (mean±std).

Figure 2: Object tracking and segmentation on H2O h1/0 (frames 0, 225, 449). LocateAnything detects the prompted objects, GMC-BoT-SORT assigns identity-preserving track IDs (colored boxes), and SAM 2 produces per-instance masks overlaid on the frames. The identities are maintained across head motion and partial hand occlusion by the objects.

Table 4: Per-module accuracy measured with the pipeline on H2O with off-the-shelf models, reported as a component sanity check rather than a new benchmark claim. Camera ATE is averaged over three sequences (h1/0, k1/0, o1/0; 1,233 frames); hand metrics over 20 sequences (h1/0–h1/7, h2/0–h2/7, o1/0–o1/3; 12,032 frames, 21,876 hand samples). Hand metrics are means over hand samples within a sequence, then averaged across sequences; ± denotes sample standard deviation across sequences, not across samples. V-HPOT is run frozen (no test-time optimization); the source paper’s 71% figure is for its TTO variant and is not reproduced here.

Table 3: Coverage of the quantitative results in Section 4. Hand accuracy and hand–depth consistency are measured on 20 sequences; camera ATE on three; object-trajectory smoothness requires the full tracking run and is validated on h1/0. RGB-only variants are listed separately.

Table 1: Provenance of the geometry behind each reported quantity. “Sensor depth” is the dataset’s depth map converted to meters and resampled to 320×176 (nearest neighbor); it never passes through MonST3R. “Window-optimized” is the depth after the sliding-window alignment of Section 3.2.1.
Table 2: Annotation coverage and role of the datasets. ✓ = ground truth available; — = not available. “Quant.” indicates whether the dataset yields quantitative results in this work.

Table 5: Camera ATE (cm) on the three H2O ATE sequences, paired on the same sequences and frame sets and computed with the same evaluation script (scripts/eval_ate.py), using similarity or rigid alignment of camera translations. “Inj.” is the sensor-depth initialization (the released sensor-assisted mode) with the focal either optimized (free) or initialized from the dataset intrinsics (focal-init, not pinned); “RGB-only” uses MonST3R’s predicted depth and is the main camera result. papers.abstract: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. Deployment on the Unitree G1 further demonstrates single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon task execution in real-world environments, including layouts with repositioned objects. Project website: https://robbyant-research.github.io/LHNav/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining progress across successive goals while producing stable, natural whole-body motion in confined spaces.
Coordinates three asynchronous roles: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body control.
Uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and execution.
Introduces a physics-grounded data engine for collision-aware, route-faithful motion demonstrations paired with visual observations.

In simulation, LHNav improves success and smoothness while reducing collisions and falls; it reaches 75.56% long-horizon success using only single-goal training, and transfers to real-world zero-shot execution on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: A robot that works among people must judge what it cannot see: whether an object is still where it was last seen, and whether a pull on a door or drawer is worth its risk. Maps that track object change hold nothing about force, maps of physical properties answer a risk question at a fixed risk level, and vision-language-action models keep no explicit estimate of hidden physics. We propose Motion Belief Action (MBA), a decision layer on the scene map. From how often people move an object and how much force it needs, how much load it holds and whether it is blocked, MBA chooses under a force limit to look again, nudge, open, brace or decline, with its risk set by the task's costs. On real activity in 9 kitchens, it predicts whether an object is still in place better than FreMEn and Perpetua, and decides when to look again at lower cost than these and the persistence filter, because about a quarter of placements end in a pick-up within 30 s. On real pulls of doors and drawers in 17 locations, made by a person with a force-sensing gripper, the map's force estimates decide better than a part-type average. Setting the risk from the costs also beats a published risk rule at its fixed level. In simulation, with the force limit at the training parts' median force, MBA raises SmolVLA's and Octo's scores by declining pulls; most declined door pulls would fail, but on drawers more would have opened, and a part-type average gets about half of this gain. In both, a published risk rule set to the risk these costs imply is MBA's rule for a single pull and decides as well in the main settings. A link between opening and holding force, a probing nudge and an action prior for camera tracking do not help in the main settings, and over the real-pull sweep the nudge costs a little.
bullets: Addresses hidden object persistence and interaction risk in robots operating around people.
Uses motion frequency, required force, load, and blockage to choose among looking again, nudging, opening, bracing, or declining.
On real kitchen activity and door/drawer pulls, it improves persistence estimation and cost-sensitive decisions over several baselines, including part-type averages for force estimation.
In simulation, declining risky pulls improves SmolVLA and Octo scores, especially for doors; gains are smaller for drawers and partly captured by part-type averages.
Additional force-linking, probing, and camera-tracking priors do not help in the main settings; nudging adds slight cost in real-pull tests.

papers.title: Motion Belief Action: From a Visual Scene Map to Physical Decisions

papers.abstract: Dexterous hands enable versatile manipulation, but policies trained in simulation often degrade on hardware owing to non-idealities, and the high-dimensional action space makes real-world adaptation costly. Piano playing, which requires precise and coordinated multifinger motion, offers a representative testbed. We propose GAP (Generalized Adaptation Prior for Dexterous Piano Playing), a sample-efficient adaptation framework that learns how to adapt, rather than how to act, during simulation pretraining and transfers this adaptation prior to hardware. Between repeated executions, GAP uses feedback to adjust the actions of the next one: a gradient guidance network learns from paired executions how adjusting actions affects playing performance, and its gradients guide these adjustments. In simulation, GAP yields approximately 2.4 times the F1 scores improvement of the existing fast-adaptation baseline for dexterous piano playing under the same interaction budget. The learned prior also generalizes to musical pieces held out from pretraining. On a physical dexterous hand, the same simulation-pretrained prior improves F1 scores by 3.6%-23% across three pieces of varying difficulty after approximately 7 min of adaptation each. These results suggest a practical route to reduce the real-world interaction needed to deploy dexterous hands.
bullets: Addresses simulation-to-hardware degradation and costly adaptation in high-dimensional multifinger control.
Uses paired executions and feedback to train a gradient guidance network that adjusts subsequent actions.
Improves simulated F1-score gains by approximately 2.4× over an existing fast-adaptation baseline under the same interaction budget.
Generalizes to musical pieces not seen during pretraining.
On a physical dexterous hand, improves F1 scores by 3.6%–23% across three pieces after approximately 7 minutes of adaptation per piece.

papers.abstract: Large-scale representation learning has produced public foundation models that provide strong general-purpose visual features. However, their pretraining objectives are not designed for robot representation learning, so the resulting embeddings tend to emphasize global semantics rather than the temporally sensitive representations required for robot control. Training robot models from scratch is also undesirable due to the limited scale and high collection cost of robotics data, as well as the substantial computational burden of pre-training. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models to robot control. SPARK is built on two principles: temporal abstraction, which encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model to retain useful pretrained semantics. These objectives yield compact visual state representations that remain semantically meaningful while preserving useful prior knowledge. Experiments across multiple robotics benchmarks show that SPARK consistently improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models, and further demonstrate that these gains transfer to real-world robot manipulation.
bullets: Foundation-model features often emphasize global semantics rather than the temporal and action-relevant information needed for robotics.
SPARK combines temporal abstraction with patch-level knowledge preservation during post-training.
The method produces compact visual state representations that retain useful semantic information.
Across multiple robotics benchmarks, SPARK improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models.
The improvements also transfer to real-world robot manipulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge). SPARK encourages temporal abstraction of patch-wise semantics while preserving the foundation model’s pre-trained knowledge. Given a reference scene xt, the SPARK encoder fθ produces a class token as a compact abstraction of xt, from which the decoder predicts target token representations with hints from a few target patches. The Temporal Abstraction Loss LTA aligns these predictions with the target representations of a frozen foundation model fθ0 , while the Knowledge Preservation Loss LKP aligns the target patch tokens of fθ and fθ0 . This encourages the class token to serve as a compact visual state for control while retaining the patch-level semantics of the original foundation model.

Figure 2: Real-world demonstration trajectories. Each row shows the temporal progression of a policy from the initial observation to intermediate interaction states and the final outcome. Across tasks, the SPARK-adapted policy exhibits stable approach, contact, and object manipulation behaviors, illustrating that the adapted visual representations capture control-relevant scene information that transfers reliably to real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Traversability prediction is a core component of autonomous navigation, yet most vision-based methods operate frame-wise and produce temporally inconsistent predictions. We present SAM-VTP (Video Traversability Prediction), which fine-tunes SAM2's video memory pathway for dense, prompt-free traversability segmentation, conditioning each frame on a persistent memory of prior observations. Rather than inferring terrain geometry from appearance, we measure it: slope, roughness and height are computed from depth and fused into the image features. We also introduce an offline continuous supervision pipeline that generates dense per-pixel traversability targets in [0,1] from depth-derived geometry and semantic priors, requiring no robot deployment and no per-pixel annotation, capturing conditional feasibility that binary labels cannot represent. On TartanGround, a large-scale synthetic ground-robot dataset, SAM-VTP improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924 and binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886 over SAM-TP, a frame-wise SAM2 baseline, against a seed-to-seed spread below 0.001, and cuts frame-to-frame flicker by 31%. In closed-loop trials at two field sites, driving the same planner and controller, the baseline's dropouts leave the planner without a feasible path 3.3x more often on a paved course and 6.9x on rough ground, while SAM-VTP runs at 21.4 FPS on the Orin Nano the robot carries.
bullets: Addresses frame-wise vision models that produce inconsistent traversability predictions for autonomous navigation.
Fine-tunes SAM2’s video-memory pathway and fuses depth-derived slope, roughness, and height with image features.
Generates dense continuous traversability targets without robot deployment or per-pixel annotation.
On TartanGround, improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924, binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886, and reduces flicker by 31% versus SAM-TP.
In closed-loop field trials, reduces planner dropouts and runs at 21.4 FPS on an Orin Nano.

papers.abstract: The motion of an articulated part in cluttered surroundings is constrained not only by an object's intrinsic joint limits but also by extrinsic obstacles. However, existing approaches primarily consider object articulation properties alone. Here we present Motion Constraint Prediction Network (MoCo-Net), a two-stream neural network that jointly predicts the continuous motion ranges of articulated parts and obstacle heatmaps highlighting potential collision regions from partial-view point cloud observation. By capturing both internal and external motion constraints, MoCo-Net produces more accurate feasible motion range prediction and obstacles recognition, improves generalization for novel objects in new scenes, and enables robots to construct a scene configuration space for efficient exploration of rearrangement actions. Our experiments show that MoCo-Net's two-stream design enhances each other to deliver more accurate predictions, which subsequently form a compact configuration space for a customized planner to efficiently rearrange the scene.
bullets: Addresses the gap in methods that model intrinsic joint limits but overlook external obstacles.
Uses a two-stream network to predict continuous feasible motion ranges and obstacle heatmaps.
Combining internal and external constraints improves motion-range and obstacle predictions, including for novel objects and scenes.
The predictions enable a compact scene configuration space for efficient rearrangement planning.

papers.abstract: Constrained preference-conditioned MORL typically assumes full task observability, treating preferences and safety budgets as stationary task signals. In real-world deployment, however, these signals are often unreliable proxies: intent may drift, safety tolerances may shift with context, and exposed descriptors may be noisy, delayed, or incomplete. We therefore formulate constrained preference-conditioned MORL as a partially observed task-specification problem, where the agent must navigate a fundamental conflict between unreliable external signals and latent interaction dynamics. We propose \textbf{BECON}, a belief-conditioned framework for constrained MORL with drifting preferences and budgets, which infers latent task context from recent histories to estimate preferences and safety budgets. These estimates are fused with the exposed task signal via uncertainty-dependent gates, enabling the policy to defer to observations under high epistemic uncertainty while correcting them when history is informative. The fused context jointly conditions preference optimization and context-adaptive constraint enforcement. Experiments on diverse multi-objective control tasks demonstrate that BECON consistently improves over state-of-the-art MORL baselines, achieving stronger robustness and constraint satisfaction under task drift.
bullets: Models task specifications as partially observed rather than fully reliable or stationary signals.
Infers preferences and safety budgets from recent histories to capture drift and missing or delayed information.
Uses uncertainty-dependent gates to fuse inferred context with exposed task signals.
Jointly conditions preference optimization and adaptive constraint enforcement on the fused context.
Experiments across diverse multi-objective control tasks show improved robustness and constraint satisfaction under task drift.

The fused context (ω̃t, B̃t) conditions the actor, distributional critics, cost model, and context-dependent dual variable for preference-aligned control with adaptive constraint enforcement.

papers.abstract: Cross-view image sequence geo-localization aims to determine the geographic location of a sequence of ground images by matching it against geo-tagged satellite imagery. Although sequential observations provide complementary scene information, substantial overlap between adjacent images introduces feature redundancy, while conventional fusion strategies may weaken spatial relationships essential for cross-view matching. Therefore, we propose a cross-view image sequence geo-localization method via Attention-guided Sequence fusion and Metric Learning (ASML). Specifically, a Sequential Content Fusion (SCF) module models cross-image feature correlations to suppress redundant content and adaptively preserve geographically informative non-overlapping regions. Next, a Spatial Feature Aggregation (SFA) module is used to capture and aggregate the spatial and semantic information of local features, so as to maintain the spatial layout of the image sequence. Finally, a Geo-InfoNCE loss function is proposed, which comprehensively considers the feature distance and geographic distance for mixed-space metric learning, thus improving the ability of the model to distinguish hard negative samples. A new cross-view image sequence dataset CrossRoad-66K is established to provide more complex scenarios. Extensive experiments and visualizations on the SeqGeo and CrossRoad-66K datasets demonstrate that compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, the proposed method ASML achieves an improvement of 3.37% and 2.10% at R@1, respectively.
bullets: Addresses feature redundancy from overlapping adjacent ground images and weakened spatial relationships in sequence fusion.
Uses Sequential Content Fusion to suppress redundant content while retaining informative non-overlapping regions.
Uses Spatial Feature Aggregation to combine local spatial and semantic information while maintaining scene layout.
Introduces Geo-InfoNCE loss for mixed-space metric learning that incorporates feature and geographic distances to handle hard negatives.
Reports R@1 improvements of 3.37% on SeqGeo and 2.10% on the newly established CrossRoad-66K dataset versus SOTA methods.

papers.abstract: This paper presents DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM) for dense mapping in environments containing dynamic objects. Objects in dynamic motion remain a significant challenge for dense visual SLAM since dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction. Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Our proposed DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB SLAM framework that supports provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds through asynchronous diffusion-based background completion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2. For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while metric depth predicted from completed images initializes provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Experimental results demonstrated competitive camera tracking, with average ATE RMSE values of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D datasets. On StaDy4D, DPGS-SLAM improved average PSNR by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using only monocular RGB input.
bullets: Addresses tracking and reconstruction errors caused by dynamic objects violating static-scene assumptions.
Uses optical-flow motion discovery and SAM2 mask propagation to identify dynamic regions.
Completes occluded backgrounds with diffusion inpainting and initializes provisional Gaussians from predicted metric depth.
Provenance labels prevent generated content from influencing camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization; generated primitives are removed when real observations appear.
Reports competitive tracking on TUM RGB-D and BONN RGB-D, and a 4.60 dB average PSNR improvement over WildGS-SLAM on StaDy4D using monocular RGB.

Dynamic regions are identified using motion discrepancies revealed by optical flow, with SAM2 [13] providing temporally consistent motion masks, while tracking uses observed static regions and background completion provides provisional representations for mapping.

papers.abstract: Dexterous grasping in robotics relies on distinct hand configurations depending on object geometry. We introduce BetaGrasp, a 3D diffusion policy that conditions a DP3-style point-cloud policy on a four-class grasp label (crimp, sloper, pinch, and jug), running on a Franka arm with a 16-DoF LEAP hand. We also introduce a climbing-hold benchmark: a spring testbed whose ratchet gives a slip-force reading in newtons. In our analysis the policy's point-cloud encoder did not separate the four holds, so the scan alone gave it little to choose a grasp from. Without the label (a DP3-style baseline), simulated rollouts from the robot's reset pose all end in a jug grasp, whatever the hold (25% correct grasp type, versus 94% for BetaGrasp). The label works as a switch for which grasp the policy performs. On 80 paired hardware trials, BetaGrasp raises average slip force from 9.6 N to 14.3 N, and grasps slipping fully off the hold drop from 44% of trials to 10%.
bullets: Targets geometry-dependent grasping for crimp, sloper, pinch, and jug climbing holds.
Conditions a 3D diffusion, DP3-style point-cloud policy on the grasp label using a Franka arm and 16-DoF LEAP hand.
Introduces a spring-based climbing-hold benchmark that measures slip force in newtons.
Without labels, the policy defaults to jug grasps and achieves 25% correct grasp types; BetaGrasp reaches 94% in simulation.
Across 80 paired hardware trials, average slip force increases from 9.6 N to 14.3 N, while complete slips decrease from 44% to 10%.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. BetaGrasp architecture. Point cloud, proprioception, and grasp-type label are encoded independently and fused into a 512-d conditioning vector z that feature-wise conditions a 1D temporal U-Net diffusion denoiser. The DP3 baseline drops only the grasp-type branch (orange) (37,248 parameters, 0.1% of 34.6 M).

Fig. 2. Spring-testbed benchmark. (a) The LEAP Hand v1 (16-DoF, on a Franka Emika Panda) executes a taxonomy-conditioned grasp on a 3D-printed jug hold seated on the testbed. (b) Top-down view: two extension springs in parallel (top) pull the orange deck back along a single axis directed toward the robot base, a center guide rod keeps the deck on that axis, and a pin through the deck rides over the toothed ratchet strips on both sides, holding the deck at its farthest point; the marked teeth (1–11) show how far the hold traveled before the grasp slipped. Lines drawn on the deck guide the five hold orientations. (c) The four 3D-printed climbing holds: pinch (narrow elongated protrusion), jug (domed body with deep finger pocket), crimp (thin edge with shallow finger ridges), and sloper (convex hemispherical surface)

papers.title: Grasp-Taxonomy Conditioning as a Mode Switch for Dexterous Grasping of Climbing Holds

papers.abstract: Navigation in dynamic environments requires mobile robots to make progress toward their goals while respecting motion limits and avoiding surrounding obstacles. Learned subgoal policies can guide model predictive control beyond its local prediction horizon, but a geometrically suitable subgoal does not necessarily lead to a successfully solved control problem. This paper proposes OASIS, a hierarchical navigation framework that incorporates recent optimization outcomes into reinforcement learning-based subgoal generation. A high-level policy trained using Soft Actor--Critic generates local subgoals, while a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks them subject to motion limits, geometric collision-avoidance constraints, and embedded high-order control barrier function constraints. The outcomes of controller optimizations over each subgoal interval are summarized and provided to the policy at its next decision, without requiring additional optimization calls. The framework is evaluated in five navigation scenarios with static and moving obstacles, including dense interactions and sensing uncertainty. Comparisons with hierarchical and direct-goal control variants show that OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success. Matched comparisons across three training seeds further show a consistent success advantage over the otherwise identical hierarchy without optimization-status input. The selected-policy comparison also shows fewer primary optimization failures with similar mean controller time.
bullets: Targets the gap between geometrically appropriate subgoals and subgoals that yield successfully solvable control problems.
Combines a Soft Actor–Critic subgoal policy with nonlinear model predictive control, motion and collision constraints, and high-order control barrier functions.
Feeds summarized optimization outcomes from each subgoal interval back to the policy without extra optimization calls.
Across five static and dynamic-obstacle scenarios, OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success and consistently outperforms the same hierarchy without optimization-status input.
Selected-policy comparisons show fewer primary optimization failures with similar mean controller time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall hierarchical architecture of OASIS. The upper layer uses a Soft ActorCritic (SAC) framework to generate normalized subgoals ηj based on environment observations and execution feedback qj . The lower layer transforms ηj into workspace subgoals gj and solves a Nonlinear Model Predictive Control problem with High-Order Control Barrier Functions (NMPC–HOCBF) to compute low-level control commands u = [a, α]T while returning solver outcomes qj+1 to inform future subgoal generation.

Figure 1: Proposed architecture. A high-level policy generates subgoals from navigation observations and previous optimization outcomes. A low-level predictive controller tracks these subgoals subject to motion, collision-avoidance, and HOCBF constraints, and returns optimization feedback for the next policy decision.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have begun incorporating thermal sensing, but existing approaches typically treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, providing limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder, which decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token through language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and continuous manipulation. We further construct six real-world robotic tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 platform, spanning basic grounding to relational reasoning. Experiments show that Thermo-VLA achieves an average success rate of 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, outperforming a pi_0.5 baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations by 18 percentage points. Under unseen-object and scene variations, Thermo-VLA maintains an average success rate of 0.78, achieving the best generalisation performance among the compared methods. Beyond thermal sensing, we transfer the same residual modulation mechanism to colour attributes and observe consistent improvements in both simulation and real-robot experiments, indicating its potential to generalise beyond thermal attributes. Project website: https://j-x-chen.github.io/Thermo-VLA-web/
bullets: Addresses the limited temperature-aware relational reasoning of VLAs that treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs.
Introduces a ThermoRes Encoder that separates hot and cold representations and applies gated, language-conditioned residual modulation to RGB tokens.
Evaluates six real-world tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1, covering grounding and relational reasoning.
Achieves a 0.86 average success rate on four thermal-dependent tasks, 18 percentage points above the pi_0.5 RGB-thermal baseline.
Maintains a 0.78 average success rate under unseen objects and scene variations; the mechanism also improves color-attribute tasks in simulation and on a real robot.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the Thermo-VLA framework. RGB observations are encoded by the RGB visual encoder, while language instructions and robot states are mapped to textual embeddings. ThermoRes Encoder decomposes thermal observations into cold and hot attributes and injects them into RGB tokens through context-gated residuals. The resulting multimodal prefix is used for flow-matching policy training and continuous action generation.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot object-goal navigation requires autonomous agents to explore unseen environments and locate target objects without task-specific training, posing challenges in perceptual reliability under observation uncertainty and physically grounded goal termination. Although foundation-model-based approaches improve generalization, they remain vulnerable to unreliable long-range perception, hallucination-induced directional bias, and semantically plausible but geometrically incorrect stopping decisions. To address these limitations, we propose CSG-Nav, a zero-shot navigation framework centered on confidence-aware multimodal information fusion. CSG-Nav integrates three complementary fusion mechanisms. First, semantic-source fusion integrates open-vocabulary detection results, detection confidence, scene observations, and relational reasoning to produce more reliable direction-level semantic scores and suppress hallucination-induced directional bias. Second, spatial-confidence fusion weights multi-view semantic evidence using a Gaussian decay function, suppressing unreliable distant observations while accumulating spatially consistent exploration preferences. Third, semantic-geometric decision fusion combines semantic target detection with depth-based 3D localization to support physically grounded stopping decisions. Experiments on HM3Dv1, HM3Dv2, and MP3D demonstrate competitive zero-shot performance, achieving success rates of 58.9%, 71.6%, and 44.3%. Fusion-level ablations and real-world deployments in indoor and outdoor environments further verify the effectiveness and practicality of CSG-Nav for robust navigation under uncertain perception. Code is available at https://xr-ui.github.io/CSGNav.github.io/
bullets: Targets unreliable long-range perception, hallucination-driven directional bias, and semantically plausible but geometrically incorrect termination.
Fuses open-vocabulary detections, confidence, scene observations, and relational reasoning for more reliable directional guidance.
Uses Gaussian spatial-confidence weighting to downweight distant observations and accumulate consistent exploration preferences.
Combines semantic detection with depth-based 3D localization for physically grounded goal stopping.
Reports success rates of 58.9% on HM3Dv1, 71.6% on HM3Dv2, and 44.3% on MP3D, with ablations and real-world deployments supporting practicality.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstration datasets combine demonstrations from teleoperators of uneven experience, so collection teams need to know how many demonstrations from one group match those from another. We measure this with a data multiple: the ratio of the numbers of demonstrations two groups need for their policies to reach the same success rate. On robomimic's simulated Square and Can tasks, we train behavior-cloning policies on demonstrations from the two teleoperators robomimic labels Better and the two it labels Worse, varying dataset size and the share of Worse demonstrations. On Square, within robomimic's 25-second time limit, an all-Worse training set needs 1.55 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. Most of this difference is late completion: policies trained on Worse demonstrations finish later, as the Worse teleoperators do, and with a 100-second limit the multiple falls to 1.11. On Can, most of the difference remains at 100 seconds. If each Worse demonstration were worth 1/1.55 of a Better one, as in an all-Worse set, a half-Better, half-Worse set on Square would need 1.22 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. In fact, it needs 13% more than that, and this excess persists at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds. The excess remains when training draws demonstrations uniformly instead of in proportion to their length. On Square, within the 25-second limit, switching to these Worse teleoperators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better teleoperators' hourly pay, because Worse demonstrations also take longer to record.
bullets: The study defines a data multiple: how many demonstrations from one teleoperator group are needed to match another group’s policy success.
Using robomimic Square and Can simulations, it compares demonstrations from groups labeled Better and Worse while varying dataset size and mixture.
On Square with a 25-second limit, all-Worse data requires 1.55× as many demonstrations as all-Better data; this falls to 1.11× with a 100-second limit.
On Can, much of the disadvantage persists even with a 100-second limit, indicating task-dependent effects.

On Square, mixed Better/Worse data performs worse than predicted by a simple weighted-value model, and Worse teleoperators are cost-effective only below roughly one-third of Better operators’ hourly pay.

papers.abstract: Flipping is a fundamental robotic manipulation skill that requires reorienting a target object in a stable pose on a planar support surface by rotating it 180$^\circ$ about an axis parallel to the support surface -- think of flipping a coin from heads to tails. Although flipping is a common objective in industrial tasks such as parts inspection, mechanical assembly, and tool use, coding a bimanual robot with grippers to flip diverse objects is a significant challenge. In this paper, we show that a coding agent can autonomously develop and refine object-flipping strategies through iterative learning in physics simulations across diverse object geometries. Progressive skill acquisition, from basic handover to toppling and pushing, robust grasping and sensing, and thin-object manipulation with recovery, improves task success from 24.7% to 95.0%. The resulting graph-based code integrates high-level strategy selection with reactive control, enabling multi-stage flipping on physical robots.
bullets: Flipping objects requires stable 180° reorientation on a planar surface and is difficult to program across varied geometries.
The coding agent iteratively develops skills in physics simulation, progressing from handover to toppling, pushing, grasping, sensing, and recovery.
A graph-based controller combines high-level strategy selection with reactive control for multi-stage flips.
The approach supports thin-object manipulation and transfers to physical robots.
Reported results are based on iterative simulation learning; the abstract does not specify datasets or broader limitations.

papers.abstract: Underwater leader-follower formation control requires continuous relative-pose estimation despite degraded sensing conditions and limited onboard computation. This paper presents a reliability-adaptive multimodal perception framework for six-degree-of-freedom relative-pose tracking between two moving underwater robots. The framework integrates complementary visual, acoustic-ranging, and hydrodynamic measurements while accounting for their distinct physical characteristics and time-varying reliability. It adaptively weights modality contributions and models temporal dependencies with linear computational complexity, enabling efficient pose estimation on embedded hardware. Extensive experiments were conducted using a custom-built AUV platform, with 648 pool trials spanning two leader vehicle types, three illumination conditions, and nine trajectory patterns. Evaluation yields an average translational error of 3.8 cm and an average orientation error of 2.4°. On an onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the fusion network achieves an inference latency of 17.62 ms, providing a 2.69-fold speedup over the evaluated Transformer-based fusion baseline. Closed-loop experiments further demonstrate stable formation maintenance with a moving leader under onboard computational constraints. A multimodal dataset containing measurements from all 648 trials will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses continuous pose estimation under degraded underwater sensing and limited onboard computation.
Adaptively weights modalities according to their time-varying reliability and models temporal dependencies with linear computational complexity.
Across 648 pool trials, achieves 3.8 cm average translational error and 2.4° average orientation error.
Runs at 17.62 ms inference latency on a Jetson AGX Orin, reported as 2.69× faster than the evaluated Transformer-based baseline.
Closed-loop tests show stable formation maintenance; a dataset from all trials is planned for public release.

The modality-specific encoders incorporate relevant physical and statistical structure, while the fusion module adjusts modality contributions according to their estimated reliability. The fused relative-pose estimate is provided to a sliding mode controller, supporting real-time formation control on resource-constrained AUV hardware.

papers.abstract: Constrained reinforcement learning in hybrid action spaces must coordinate discrete modes and mode-conditioned continuous controls under long-horizon cost constraints. Existing constrained hybrid-action methods typically optimize factorized policies directly in parameter space, whereas Constrained Variational Policy Optimization (CVPO) separates nonparametric improvement from parametric projection in its original continuous-action formulation. We introduce Hybrid Constrained Variational Policy Optimization (H-CVPO), extending this variational framework to hybrid action spaces. Under boundedness and strict feasibility, its constrained E-step has zero duality gap and, when the dual optimum is attained at positive temperature, yields a closed-form joint target distribution over hybrid actions through exponential reward-cost reweighting. Using the exact hybrid KL decomposition, we formulate a factorized M-step that fits both policy components to this target under separate discrete and conditional-continuous trust regions. For exact E/M updates, we prove fixed-reference surrogate improvement and conditional reward-cost bounds with a sufficient feasibility-margin condition. For approximate updates, we establish the existence of a dual minimizer under continuity on a compact domain and use residual-based admissibility to determine whether to project the target. Ablations identify cost-aware reweighting as an important contributor to constraint control. Extensive experiments in simulated hybrid-control environments show that H-CVPO achieves favorable reward-cost trade-offs compared with hybrid-action baselines.
bullets: Targets long-horizon cost constraints while coordinating discrete modes with mode-conditioned continuous controls.
Uses a constrained variational E-step with exponential reward–cost reweighting to form a joint hybrid-action target distribution.
Fits separate discrete and conditional-continuous policy components via an exact hybrid KL decomposition and trust regions.
Provides improvement, feasibility, and dual-optimization guarantees for exact and approximate updates under stated assumptions.
Ablations highlight cost-aware reweighting as important for constraint control; experiments are limited to simulated hybrid-control environments.

papers.abstract: The wide field of view of fisheye cameras and the simplicity of a monocular setup make monocular fisheye visual odometry (VO) attractive for robotic localization and mapping. Nevertheless, scale drift remains a major challenge over long trajectories. Unsupervised depth learning can help to mitigate this issue, but the pronounced distortion of fisheye images poses challenges for accurate depth estimation. This article presents S$^2$D-FVO, a monocular fisheye VO framework integrating spherical bundle adjustment (SBA)-guided unsupervised depth learning to improve scale consistency and depth estimation accuracy. Given that pixel reprojection residuals do not uniformly reflect angular deviations between viewing rays and that the first-order linearization of a scalar angular reprojection residual is insensitive to perturbations along one tangent direction, SBA employs tangent-space angular reprojection residuals derived from the spherical logarithmic map. These residuals retain sensitivity along both tangent directions, with their norms equal to the corresponding scalar angular residuals. A median depth-based scale regularization term is further integrated into SBA to constrain the reconstruction scale. Building on these formulations, SBA replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised depth learning, providing more reliable relative poses for view synthesis. In turn, depth estimates from the well-trained depth estimation network provide scale references for SBA, improving scale consistency while allowing individual 3-D landmark positions to be refined. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, as well as two newly collected large-scale datasets, demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms representative existing approaches in both depth and trajectory estimation accuracy and is applicable to different camera models.
bullets: Addresses long-trajectory scale drift and fisheye distortion challenges in monocular VO.
Uses tangent-space angular reprojection residuals from the spherical logarithmic map to preserve sensitivity in both viewing-ray tangent directions.
Adds median-depth-based scale regularization to constrain reconstruction scale.
Replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised learning, while learned depth provides scale references for bundle adjustment.
Experiments on public and newly collected datasets show improved depth and trajectory estimation and applicability across camera models.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies often fail at one step of a task they can otherwise perform. We ask whether such a failure can be repaired by editing the policy's weights directly, without gradients, training data, or a change to the instruction. Told to put the cube then the banana in the bowl, a zero-shot $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy in RoboLab releases the cube before it reaches the bowl. Replaying 21 of these decisions under rewordings shows that it binds "in the bowl" to the wrong object. Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into the language model's MLP weights. On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken ($p=7\times10^{-22}$), while an update of the same size in random directions leaves success unchanged. The edit also lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13, and a variant that stores 0.16% of the parameter count keeps most of its effect. Placed in the action expert or action head instead, the same distillation helps less or not at all. Our released tool reproduced the fix end to end on new held-out seeds, from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, a missing grasp, contact physics, or the gripper threshold did not help, and of seven blind Claude Opus editors, only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring. These results suggest that weight edits work best when a known-good input already exists to distil. Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds.
bullets: Motivation: Generalist robot policies may fail on a single interpretable step despite otherwise completing the task.
Method: Replays of 21 decisions under reworded instructions identify a misbinding, then copy the rewording’s per-layer effect into language-model MLP weights.
Result: Held-out success increased from 27 to 106 of 128 episodes, with 81 fixes and 2 regressions; random same-size edits had no effect.
Scope: Editing the language model worked best; edits to the action expert or head helped less or not at all, and unrelated failure-targeted edits did not help.
Caveat: Substantial outcome variability motivates paired reruns of the unedited policy and confirmation on held-out seeds.

papers.abstract: Spatial generalization in robot world models depends on whether action representations capture the physical relationships that remain valid across changing spatial configurations. Yet different coordinates can describe the same interaction, whereas similar motions can produce different outcomes when local physical conditions change. How these distinctions affect learned prediction remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates matched action representations defined in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark. Global pose and contact relocation experiments reveal a cost associated with limited training data when equivalent interactions receive different spatial descriptions. Removing information about peel thickness creates an irreducible ambiguity because identical predictive inputs can correspond to different material removal outcomes. Coordinates defined relative to the surface improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection under accurate local observations, but learned predictors remain vulnerable to uncertainty in the coordinate frame. Joint centering of the surface and tool removes sensitivity to translation of their common origin, whereas incorrect contact geometry and actual execution deviations introduce different failure mechanisms. These results show that effective spatial generalization depends on preserving the relationships between actions and states that determine physical consequences, rather than simply minimizing coordinate variation. This perspective provides a principled basis for designing robot world models that reuse physical knowledge across spatial configurations while retaining the distinctions essential to prediction and planning.
bullets: The study compares matched action representations in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark.
Equivalent interactions described differently can increase data requirements, while omitting peel thickness creates irreducible ambiguity in material-removal predictions.
Surface-relative coordinates improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection when local observations are accurate.

Jointly centering the surface and tool removes sensitivity to their shared translation, but uncertainty in coordinate frames, incorrect contact geometry, and execution deviations cause distinct failures.
The findings support designing representations that preserve outcome-relevant action–state relationships for reuse across spatial configurations.

papers.abstract: Exploration in deep reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control is commonly driven by temporally uncorrelated Gaussian (white) action noise, which leads to jerky motions with locally constrained exploration. In contrast, temporally correlated coloured noise, particularly pink noise, has been shown to support more efficient exploration in RL. Motivated by these findings, we inquire whether scheduling changes to the noise colour over the course of training can outperform white noise for continuous control robotics. We perform a systematic study of 49 linear schedules between white and red noise, together with generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE), on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks with a Fetch arm and a Shadow Dexterous Hand. We find that the noise colour at the end of training does not affect learning efficiency or end performance, whereas fading towards red noise halves the jerk of exploration in every task. Balancing learning efficiency, end performance and smoothness, red noise emerges as the preferred strategy: it learns as efficiently as pink noise with almost 2-fold less movement jerk. We therefore recommend exploration schedulers that fade towards red noise as the default for off-policy robot learning.
bullets: White action noise causes jerky, locally constrained exploration in continuous-control RL.
The study evaluates 49 white-to-red noise schedules and gSDE on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks.
The final noise colour does not affect learning efficiency or end performance.
Fading toward red noise halves exploration jerk across all tasks.
Red noise matches pink noise’s learning efficiency with nearly 2× less jerk and is recommended as a default for off-policy robot learning.

papers.abstract: Sensory delays create temporal misalignments between the state of the environment and the observations available to an agent, turning Markovian control problems into partially observable ones. In this work, we inquire whether such misalignments can be mitigated during training by using hindsight to recover aligned state-action transitions. We introduce Hindsight Critics, an asymmetric extension of the Soft Actor-Critic for reinforcement learning under partial observability. The critics are trained on hindsight-aligned transitions whereas the actor learns from the resulting privileged value estimates despite only having access to delayed observations. Comparisons against delay-aware and unaware baselines on the DelayBench suite show that Hindsight Critics can partially compensate for observation delays without requiring modifications to the agent's observations during deployment.
bullets: Observation delays misalign environmental states and agent observations, causing partial observability.
The method extends Soft Actor-Critic asymmetrically: critics use hindsight-aligned transitions, while the actor uses their privileged value estimates.
Experiments on DelayBench compare the approach with delay-aware and delay-unaware baselines.
Results show partial compensation for observation delays without modifying observations at deployment.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Return-delay curves for PPO, SAC and Hindsight Critics (HC) over three illustrative environments. Scattered dots indicate the return over a single evaluation episode. Sigmoid curves are fitted to those returns and used to compute the AUC scores. SAC achieves high zero-delay performances but is particularly sensitive to delays. Hindsight Critics can partially mitigate this degradation.

Table 1: Zero-delay average returns of Hindsight Critics (HC) compared with other common RL algorithms across multiple environments. The highest score for each environment is highlighted in bold.
Table 2: AUC scores of Hindsight Critics (HC) compared with other common RL algorithms across multiple environments. The highest score for each environment is highlighted in bold.

papers.abstract: Fleets of driving vision-language-action (VLA) models are developed one domain at a time: each operator finetunes a shared base model on private data, producing specialized experts that are costly to consolidate into a single model. Weight merging loses accuracy as heterogeneous domains accumulate, and dense mixture-of-experts routing is prohibitively expensive to combine them. We present DeltaForge, to our knowledge the first post-hoc mixture-of-experts VLA for driving, which consolidates N independently finetuned per-domain models into a single multi-domain model from their weights and a small proxy set alone. When different operators finetune the same base model, their weight updates end up sharing a lot of structure. We exploit this by decomposing all the updates together using singular value decomposition (SVD), splitting each one into a shared part (the same across all domains) and a tiny domain-specific part. The router then only needs to work with those tiny domain-specific pieces, not the full expert weights, which is what keeps the approach efficient. Then two cooperating clip-level blind routers, one over the VLM reasoning experts and one over the flow-matching dynamics experts, are trained from soft labels on the proxy dataset. Across six diverse domains spanning urban, off-road, and highway driving on cars, trucks, and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), DeltaForge approaches the accuracy of the per-domain experts and surpasses every merging, routing, centralized, and federated baseline at close to single-model parameter and compute cost. Adding a new domain requires only projecting its weight update onto the shared basis with no end-to-end retraining needed. The resulting model also generalizes to domain combinations it was never explicitly trained on.
bullets: Addresses the accuracy loss and computational cost of merging heterogeneous, privately trained driving experts.
Jointly decomposes expert weight updates with SVD into shared components and small domain-specific residuals.
Uses two clip-level blind routers for VLM reasoning and flow-matching dynamics, trained from soft labels on a small proxy set.
Across six diverse driving domains and vehicle types, it approaches per-domain expert accuracy and outperforms reported baselines near single-model cost.
New domains can be added by projecting their updates onto the shared basis, without end-to-end retraining; the model also generalizes to unseen domain combinations.
