Fig. 2. DeltaForge system workflow. Independently finetuned per-domain VLAs are jointly factorized by PEF into a frozen shared skill basis and perdomain low-rank cores. Two cooperating clip-level blind routers then select and mix the cores at inference, one at the input for VLM reasoning experts and one intermediate for flow-matching dynamics experts. Composition is trained on a small proxy set, and a new domain opts in by projecting its delta onto the frozen basis.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.
bullets: Addresses stale observations and reduced control rates caused by placing large VLA backbones in the closed-loop control path.
Runs a slow vision-language model and fast flow-matching action head asynchronously via LCM.
Fuses stale semantic features with fresh visual input and uses desynchronized training plus adaptive temporal aggregation to handle latency.
Maintains 20 Hz control from 0.8B to 8B backbones, while the synchronous pipeline drops from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz on RoboTwin.
Achieves higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline on a real humanoid with dexterous hands.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. DASH architecture. The policy is split into a slow VLM (System 2) and a fast action head (System 1), deployed as three concurrent processes (environment, VLM server, and action server) coupled by a decentralized, non-blocking latest-value bus (LCM). The VLM runs off the control loop and publishes a context (the hidden states of the routed VLM layers) that the action head reads with latest-value semantics, so the control rate is set by the action head alone.

Fig. 7. Matched simulation episodes, synchronous inference (top) vs. DASH (bottom). Frames are sampled at equal intervals of simulated time up to the completion time of the successful run; done marks completion, and still running marks the run that later times out.

(b) Frequent chunk updates curb divergence: synchronous inference executes the long, uncertain tail of each chunk, so a new prediction can trigger a large correction; DASH refreshes chunks often and stays on the reliable early portion.

papers.abstract: Connected physical systems fuse observations from robots, IoT sensors, and edge-AI modules into a shared account of the world, yet most evaluations score only the final answer or action and cannot tell whether a method attributed the evidence, updated its belief, handled contradictions, and justified its decision. We argue that shared reasoning in Connected Robotics should be evaluated as an evidence-to-belief trajectory, and introduce the Connected Robotics Evidence Graph (CREG) Benchmark to make that trajectory measurable. CREG comprises 350 deterministically generated scenarios across seven regimes (justified revision, belief preservation, relation association, contradiction onset and resolution, stale/delayed evidence, and source reliability), each exposing a normative posterior reference at every evidence prefix, validated by an independent log-odds checker and screened by a blinded expert audit. Nine representation conditions separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata. Evaluating four open-weight instruction models and six transparent fusion baselines yields three findings. First, entity grounding accounts for a substantial part of the weak-model deficit. Second, deleting semantic relations costs 15.3 points of strict belief-state accuracy on relation-dependent scenarios (Holm-corrected p<0.001), but an information-matched structured list outperforms the full graph and shuffling the graph does not hurt: relation content matters where required, while graph serialization confers no consistent advantage. Third, belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic along the evidence sequence, with mid-trajectory failures that endpoint-only evaluation cannot detect. All scenarios, references, prompts, metrics, and analysis code are released for offline, hardware-free reproduction.
bullets: Introduces 350 deterministic scenarios across seven evidence-update regimes, each with normative posterior references at every evidence prefix.
Tests nine representation conditions to separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata effects.
Finds entity grounding is a major source of weak-model errors, while removing semantic relations reduces strict belief-state accuracy by 15.3 points on relation-dependent cases.
Structured lists can outperform full graphs, and graph shuffling causes no consistent harm, suggesting graph serialization alone provides no reliable benefit.
Belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic, revealing mid-trajectory failures missed by endpoint-only evaluation; resources support offline, hardware-free reproduction.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of CREG. Connected agents produce attributed semantic evidence organized in a shared graph; belief trajectory, contradiction records, next action, and explanation are exposed and scored separately, so an end-task success cannot conceal an earlier-layer error.

Fig. 6. (a) Belief-state accuracy by evidence prefix for four Qwen-7B representation conditions. (b) Grounded-prediction rate by prefix for the four models under canonical JSON. The final prefix alone would hide the intermediate failures in both panels.

papers.abstract: While imitation learning has made substantial progress toward generalizable robot manipulation through scaling, viewpoint robustness remains a major bottleneck. Visuomotor policies rely heavily on visual inputs, yet images provide an inherently ambiguous signal under viewpoint change: similar scenes may appear markedly different across viewpoints, while distinct states may share certain visual overlaps. A policy must therefore infer not only the task-relevant state, but also how it is visually projected under a particular camera configuration. This entanglement of viewpoint-dependent appearance and task-relevant state can make learning inefficient and limit generalization to unseen viewpoints. Recent work has begun to address this challenge through camera-ray conditioning and representation learning using geometric cues to induce invariance. However, providing camera information as additional context does not by itself ground visual representations in how the task scene is visually projected, while geometric alignment without camera context can introduce spurious correspondences by ignoring viewpoint-dependent projection. We propose PAIR, a contrastive learning framework that aligns joint image-ray representations using robot proprioception. PAIR encourages observations with similar robot states to remain close in representation space across viewpoints, providing a structured grounding signal for learning viewpoint-robust features. PAIR is a highly adaptable framework: it can be used to train Diffusion Policy (DP) or post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models. In simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks with camera variation, PAIR consistently outperforms the behavior cloning baseline without ray conditioning by 12.7% and 26.7% points, respectively, demonstrating stronger generalization to unseen viewpoints. Project website: PAIRrobot.github.io.
bullets: Viewpoint changes entangle task-relevant state with camera-dependent visual appearance, hindering imitation-learning generalization.
The method applies contrastive learning to bring joint image-ray representations with similar robot states closer across viewpoints.
PAIR can train Diffusion Policies or post-train vision-language-action models.
On simulated and real-world camera-variation benchmarks, it improves over behavior cloning without ray conditioning by 12.7 and 26.7 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Robots are typically evaluated in episodes that begin from a reset, while industrial work consists of repeated jobs whose outcomes affect subsequent operations. Evaluating such work at scale requires simulation of task-critical physical interactions, construction of industrial environments, and measurements of performance as scene state persists. We present HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0, a framework for simulating, generating, and evaluating industrial robot work. Given a human-specified workplace and task, the framework defines a world pairing a scenario of scene variants and process logic with an evaluation defining a job, metrics, and a rubric. HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0 comprises three components. HOLIDAY-SIM extends Newton's SDF-based hydroelastic contact with additional constitutive laws and a semi-implicit primal-dual solver, couples stateful actuator dynamics to articulated motion, and derives tactile and joint observations from simulated states. Agentic world construction generates simulation-ready assets and scene variants using geometric and interaction checks, and proposes task-conditioned evaluations for human confirmation and executable checks. 24/7-BENCH introduces seven industrial tasks in which jobs are evaluated without resetting the scene, measuring completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy. Controlled studies characterize the proposed contact, actuator, and tactile models and examine the effectiveness of verification-guided world construction. Experiments on scene and evaluation generation further reveal the limitations of model critics and the difficulty of ensuring that generated evaluations faithfully capture task requirements. We examine job-level evaluations with scripted trajectories (e.g., code-as-policy) but have not yet compared policies over persistent runs.
bullets: Targets the gap between reset-based robot benchmarks and real industrial workflows, where each job changes the state for subsequent jobs.
Combines HOLIDAY-SIM for contact, actuator, articulated-motion, tactile, and joint-state simulation with agentic construction of verified workplace assets and scene variants.
Introduces 24/7-BENCH with seven industrial tasks evaluated using completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy.
Controlled studies assess the simulation models and verification-guided world construction, while generation experiments expose weaknesses in model critics and evaluation fidelity.
Evaluations currently use scripted trajectories; policies have not yet been compared over persistent runs.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
bullets: Round-to-nearest activation quantization can severely degrade planning despite one-step prediction error comparable to stochastic rounding.
The key issue is error persistence and sharing across planner candidates, not simply rounding-error magnitude.
Redrawing common dither each planner iteration removes most of the degradation without retraining across tested TD-MPC2 and DINO-WM settings.
An W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model speeds planning rollouts by 1.9–3.3× and full planning steps by 1.3–1.5× versus FP32; dither adds at most 2.3% latency.
Block-scaled NVFP4 largely avoids the problem, while fixed dither within a step or episode restores planner drift.

papers.abstract: Generative models can support both state estimation and control in robotics. For control, a common approach is to use the model as a policy that directly samples actions conditioned on observation histories. However, models that jointly represent states, actions, and observations can also predict how the robot state and its environment evolve. We investigate whether these predictions can improve state estimation and control through a change in inference procedure, without modifying the pretrained model. To this end, we use particle filtering to maintain competing hypotheses about state histories. A single pretrained diffusion model generates these hypotheses along with their predicted observations and associated action proposals. As new measurements arrive, particles are reweighted according to how well their predicted observations match the measurements. While particle filtering conventionally uses these weights only for state estimation, we also use them to guide action selection, favoring proposals associated with hypotheses that better explain the observations. Simulation experiments in partially observed navigation and vision-based manipulation demonstrate improvements in both state estimation and task performance compared to action generation without filtering, using the same pretrained model and no additional test-time information.
bullets: Addresses partially observed robotics, where uncertainty about state can hinder control.
Maintains competing state-history hypotheses using particles generated by one pretrained diffusion model.
Reweights particles by agreement between predicted and observed measurements.
Uses these weights for both state estimation and action selection, without modifying the model or adding test-time information.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.
bullets: Soft-robot RL is hindered by costly hardware interactions and unreliable or unavailable simulators.
A time-scale separation reduces the robot dynamics to a low-dimensional adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM).
A 6,924-parameter polynomial ODE learned from pre-collected data provides the RL training environment.
On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, the policy trained in 3 hours deployed without fine-tuning and achieved 40% lower tracking error than comparable RNN- and transformer-based approaches.
The approach remains demonstrated on one soft-arm trajectory-tracking task and depends on the validity of the aSSM reduction.

papers.abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.
bullets: Learns a nonlinear reduced-order ODE directly from hardware data.
Integrates the learned model into a model predictive control scheme.
Demonstrates closed-loop tracking with static and dynamic constraints.
Reports improved accuracy and precision over data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning.
The hardware-data-based approach is intended to generalize to other soft robotic systems.

papers.abstract: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. Homepage: https://wrld.github.io/surgtap-3d/
bullets: Addresses limited scale, diversity, and interaction-aware 3D supervision in existing surgical datasets.
Provides 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from robotic and manual surgeries.
Uses contact-region prompting, tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement to convert monocular videos into structured annotations.
Includes temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks despite occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and fast motion.
Benchmarks instrument and tissue tracking, displacement estimation, deformable reconstruction, and surgical action understanding.

papers.abstract: Failure monitors for vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained offline and then frozen. After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras drift, and the policy itself is updated or moved to new tasks. On recorded real-robot runs, after a switch of task or policy version, a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance. We present Streaming Failure Forecasting (SFF), a monitor that keeps learning from the one label every episode provides: whether it succeeded. SFF keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last linear layer after each episode, at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core. Its alarm threshold moves only after successes, which in simulation kept false alarms near target except when two drifts came at once. With every setting locked before testing, SFF ranks failures better than the same monitor kept frozen on 4 of 5 simulated test suites under unannounced drift, and above resetting on detected drift on every suite. Carried with its locked learner settings to 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced switches of task or policy version, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch. A deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen: refitting its readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes we tested.
bullets: Frozen monitors degrade to near-chance failure ranking after task or policy changes.
SFF updates only the monitor’s last linear layer after each episode using its success/failure label; its threshold adapts after successes.
The method runs at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core.
Under unannounced drift, SFF outperformed a frozen monitor on 4 of 5 simulated test suites and a reset strategy on all suites.
Across 434 real-robot runs involving four VLAs, SFF outperformed the frozen monitor after task or policy switches and exceeded a full reset in an exploratory comparison.

papers.abstract: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.
bullets: Latent-action assignments vary drastically across training runs and numerical precision, despite similar robot motion inputs.
The method adds a straight-through similarity loss to align a video-trained tokenizer’s code geometry with macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv) activity.
On held-out shape categories, PMv alignment reaches 0.52 versus 0.20–0.26 for released or no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for random kinematic encoders.
Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer, but a hand-designed initial-stroke-direction descriptor scores higher (0.65).
A shuffled-PMv control still scores 0.41, and downstream manipulation effects are specified for future testing rather than reported.

The 95th percentile of the encoders’ four-session means is lower (0.39), and the shuffled tokenizer also exceeds that. papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have achieved significant progress in locomotion and manipulation, enabling traversal over rough terrain and richer interaction with the environment, such as moving obstacles. However, most traditional navigation methods assume non-interactive environments and focus only on traversal. While Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) approaches relax this assumption, prior efforts have largely focused on flat environments and reactive interaction, rather than predicting object movability and planning ahead. These limitations become critical in outdoor rough-terrain scenarios, where robots must jointly reason about terrain traversability and object movability. In this work, we address NAMO for humanoid robots in cluttered outdoor rough terrain by proposing a hybrid planning framework that combines semantic priors from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) with embodied robot interaction data through a Gaussian process (GP) residual model. The GP corrects the VLM-derived movability prior to produce embodiment-grounded probabilistic movability estimates, which are then incorporated into hierarchical uncertainty-aware planning. The proposed approach allows humanoids to jointly leverage locomotion and manipulation for efficient and safe navigation, representing the first solution to NAMO in rough terrain through predictive movability reasoning and probabilistic VLM integration.
bullets: Addresses Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) for humanoids in cluttered outdoor rough terrain.
Combines VLM semantic priors with a Gaussian process residual model trained from embodied interaction data.
Produces probabilistic estimates of whether objects can be moved, while accounting for robot-specific capabilities.
Uses hierarchical uncertainty-aware planning to jointly coordinate locomotion and manipulation.
The abstract presents it as the first rough-terrain NAMO approach based on predictive movability reasoning and probabilistic VLM integration.

papers.abstract: Large-scale pretraining is reducing the amount of adaptation required to deploy embodied foundation models, but it is not guaranteed that a pretrained model already provide the level of performance required in every deployment. Practitioners therefore need to understand how well a pretrained model matches a target deployment and how much adaptation data is left to be collected. We study whether a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations can reveal whether and how much target-domain data will be required before any adaptation. We introduce FlowEval, a set of training-free metrics that use the flow-matching objective to probe an embodied foundation model with a set of demonstrations. FlowEval quantifies predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations to assess how well a pretrained model fits a target deployment. Across four embodied foundation model families: Pi-0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T, and DreamZero, FlowEval distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across real-world and simulated manipulation. Further, by finetuning Pi-0.5 and GR00T on 17 RoboCasa365 manipulation tasks, we showed that FlowEval correlates with how success rate improves as additional adaptation data is provided. Together, these results suggest that FlowEval can serve as a lightweight, training-free diagnostic of how much model--deployment adaptation may be required.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of assessing pretrained model fit to a new deployment and estimating remaining adaptation-data needs.
Introduces training-free metrics based on the flow-matching objective and predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations.
Distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across four embodied foundation model families in real and simulated manipulation.
On 17 RoboCasa365 tasks, FlowEval correlates with success-rate gains from additional adaptation data for Pi-0.5 and GR00T.
Provides a lightweight diagnostic, though its demonstrated scope is manipulation deployments and the evaluated model families.

papers.abstract: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.
bullets: Models environmental ground truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior as distinct components.
Integrates model-predictive and learning-based exploration, safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive guidance.
Simulation studies show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion.
Supervisory task allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone.
More exploration does not necessarily produce more rescues; adaptive guidance increases rescues versus continuous leading but does not improve measured trust or mortality.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.
bullets: Builds an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose to provide explicit geometric memory.
Conditions the world model, actor, and critic on the map and uses mapped geometry for geodesic progress and wall-contact signals.
Adds a forward-cone penalty to discourage motion outside the forward-facing camera’s view.
In Isaac Sim, it achieves 96.3% success and 3.6% collision across 1,560 episodes, outperforming AirDreamer under the same interaction budget.
Removing the forward-cone penalty raises collisions to 9.9%, highlighting its role in perception-aware navigation.

papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum reinforcement learning has been explored for robotic decision-making, but evaluations often emphasize task success, return, or convergence, leaving unresolved whether quantum circuit outputs influence constrained actions and remain traceable through robot execution. We present \texttt{Qubit-to-Motion}, an evidence-centered framework for support-constrained sequencing and simulated robotic placement. Four Pauli-$Z$ readouts provide the sole learned input to the actor and critic, while a support mask enforces admissible object selection. Each decision is recorded and linked via step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints to a sealed route, deterministic Cartesian and inverse-kinematics waypoints, prescribed joint motion, and MuJoCo contact replay. A frozen checkpoint is evaluated across five deterministic 30-object scene variants. All 150 placements satisfy support, containment, and settling criteria. A fixed-state zero-readout intervention changes $90.0\pm0.0\%$ of decisions, demonstrating dependence on the joint circuit representation. Mean macro travel is $34.537\pm0.206$~m, inference requires $8.60\pm1.27$~ms per route, and replay achieves $8.764\pm0.220~μ$m mean final position error with 0.356~mm maximum interpenetration. These results establish reproducible decision-to-contact traceability. The implementation is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Qubit-to-Motion-Quantum-Reinforcement-Learning-F7DC}{\textcolor{linkpink}{the anonymous repository}}.
bullets: Addresses whether quantum circuit outputs truly influence constrained actions and remain traceable during execution.
Uses four Pauli-Z readouts as the actor–critic input, with a support mask enforcing admissible object choices.
Links each decision to sealed routes, deterministic waypoints, joint motions, and MuJoCo contact replay using step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints.
Across five deterministic 30-object scenes, all 150 placements met support, containment, and settling criteria.
A zero-readout intervention changed 90.0% of decisions, while replay achieved 8.764 μm mean final-position error and 0.356 mm maximum interpenetration.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.
bullets: Problem: Existing vision-language-action and world-action priors may not adequately capture humanoid robot motion structure.
Method: Kinematic Action Models pretrain directly on whole-body motion and condition generation on tasks, visual observations, and execution feedback.
Architecture: Kimodo-Policy combines a frozen text-to-motion backbone, lightweight ControlNet visual conditioning, hierarchical root-body-hand coordination, and motion-history-based action chunks.
Results: It reports 72.14% overall success on HumanoidArena, competitive SIMPLE performance, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks.
Scope: Results provide initial evidence that motion generation can complement foundation models for humanoid action learning.

papers.abstract: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.
bullets: Builds traceable scene–factor–decision records with candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations to refine training data from critical events and verified failures.
Uses Xiaomi-Drive-o1, a shared vision-language model integrating perception, causation, action, world modeling, and value estimation.
Connects task blocks through candidate-specific latent evidence and predicted visual consequences, while a value-of-computation head allocates inference effort adaptively.
Reports strong benchmark results, including the lowest ADE@1 among tested models on PhysicalAI and broad metric improvements over Alpamayo 1.5 in AlpaSim.
Joint training improves 5 s minADE@6 for the 0.8B model by about 54%, and adaptive inference reaches full-reasoning performance with 28% of the tokens; real-vehicle tests support runtime feasibility.

papers.abstract: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $π_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.
bullets: Targets eight bimanual tasks scored on safe, efficient, coordinated execution against human demonstrations.
Uses AWR and RECAP to train a π₀.₅-based policy/value function on advantages from the official score.
Treats each rollout as a Thompson-sampling trial over roughly 20 inference parameters.
Adds generated full-reward demonstrations and recovery episodes from the policy’s failures to address exploration gaps.
The generic method reached 0.85 RDS in two days but remained far from convergence; the submitted system improved substantially.

papers.abstract: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.
bullets: Zero-shot, end-to-end robot control gives coding agents capabilities beyond earlier VLA and WAM systems.
Digital threats such as indirect prompt injection can propagate from webpages or emails to physical robot behavior.
ArmedAgent evaluates robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios.
The benchmark is tested in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm across several frontier models and agent frameworks.
Results indicate substantial safety risks in current coding-agent robot-control systems.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4% to 60.5%. On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3% success, compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline. Project page https://dexforesight.github.io/
bullets: Learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from depth, hand geometry, and demonstrations.
Predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, including occluded finger dynamics and scene changes.
Aligns policy queries with world-model predictions, then freezes the world model and transfers its dynamics into policy latents.
At deployment, the policy uses only RGB observations, language, and robot state.
Improves success from 49.4% to 60.5% on 11 DexJoCo tasks and achieves 58.3% versus 50.0% for the strongest baseline on three real-robot tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2 DexForesight architecture and query alignment. The learned spatial foresight is transferred into a low-level policy, enabling action generation without world-model execution or future decoding at deployment. DexForesight outperforms prior world-action models in both simulation and real-robot evaluations.

papers.abstract: Robots that travel long distances through public outdoor spaces must do more than avoid obstacles: they must remain on terrain suited to their mobility and decide when to proceed, yield, or detour around pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, traffic signals, and temporary restrictions. These decisions are difficult because their correctness often depends on how a scene evolves, such as whether an approaching car is slowing or a cyclist will cross the robot's path. Vision-language models (VLMs) can interpret such cues, but they reason over images that lack metric geometry and motion. Supplying this evidence at every step is too slow for real-time navigation, and hand-crafted triggers cannot anticipate the open-ended variety of outdoor situations. We present MOSU2, a long-range navigation system with two-stage trajectory selection, in which first-stage contextual reasoning determines when additional evidence is needed and what to retrieve. Only when an interaction remains unresolved does the first stage trigger the second stage to retrieve geometric and dynamic information and align it with scene context to make navigation decisions. Building on MOSU, MOSU2 follows routes from GPS-based route planning and filters candidate trajectories through multi-modal traversability analysis before selecting a trajectory to move the robot. In real-world experiments spanning stop gestures, construction sites, crosswalks, and roads shared with vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians, MOSU2 raises mean navigation success from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4% over its single-image predecessor, at about 2.2 times its mean decision latency. Project website: https://jinggm.github.io/mosu2/
bullets: Addresses evolving outdoor interactions involving pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, signals, terrain, and temporary restrictions.
Uses two-stage trajectory selection: contextual reasoning decides when and what additional evidence to retrieve.
Retrieves and aligns geometric and dynamic information only for unresolved interactions to support real-time decisions.
Follows GPS-planned routes and filters candidate trajectories through multimodal traversability analysis.
Real-world success increased from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4%, with about 2.2× higher mean decision latency.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the MOSU2 architecture. Building on MOSU’s routing and traversability framework, GPS-based routing provides subgoals, while LiDAR and robot-velocity observations support candidate trajectory generation. RGB-based semantic segmentation provides complementary traversability assessments. MOSU2 introduces a VLM-retrievable local map and two-stage trajectory selection: the first stage screens the current scene and determines if more analysis is required, and the second stage, when invoked, combines recent images with retrieved geometric and dynamic information to select a trajectory and velocity mode. The motion planner converts the selected motion into linear and angular velocity commands (v, ω).

Figure 7. Qualitative Evaluation: Each column illustrates one of the three components in our trajectory generation pipeline, (a) CVAE-based multiple trajectory generation, (b) semantic segmentation for traversability analysis, and (c) VLM-based trajectory ranking in the outdoor scenarios with various social conditions. In (a) and (b), lighter colors indicate higher scores, confidence scores in (a) and traversability scores in (b). In (c), the VLM ranks trajectories based on social cues. The top example shows a ranking of [3, 0, 1, 2, 4]. The bottom example shows a ranking of [4, 5, 0, 1, 2, 3].

Figure 1. MOSU2 supports long-range outdoor navigation across wheeled-legged, wheeled, and legged robot platforms (bottom row). The satellite view illustrates a route from the start (yellow star) to the goal (green circle). The left-side examples highlight traversability challenges: (a) distinguishing sidewalks from off-road terrain, (b) accounting for differences in robot mobility, and (c) identifying crosswalks for street crossing. The right-side examples highlight social and traffic challenges: (d) interacting with moving agents, such as pedestrians, (e) interpreting traffic signals, including pedestrian signals with countdown displays, and (f) resolving conflicting traffic cues when vehicles violate traffic rules and obstruct the robot’s path. MOSU2 combines global route guidance and robot-specific traversability assessment with two-stage reasoning that retrieves local geometric and dynamic information to interpret these conditions and select appropriate motion.

Figure 6. Geometric and Semantic Analysis: Both geometric trajectory generation and semantic segmentation perform well in most cases, but there are also failure cases, as marked in yellow circles in (c) and (d). When the elevations of the lawn and sidewalk are similar, the geometric model struggles to perform accurately. Additionally, segmentation fails in out-of-distribution scenarios.

Figure 3. Routing and subgoal transformation. OpenRouteService routing uses the robot’s GPS location and the destination to obtain a global route, from which an intermediate GPS waypoint ĝ is selected. The waypoint is converted to the odometry frame with metric coordinates by aligning the GPS and robot motion, yielding the subgoal g. This subgoal provides directional guidance for trajectory selection.

Figure 8. Representative social, traffic, and irregular navigation scenarios used to evaluate MOSU2: (a) responding to a pedestrian’s stop gesture, (b) navigating a construction area with warning and directional signs, (c) crossing at a signalized intersection, (d) sharing the road with moving agents, illustrated by a cyclist, (e) intersecting with a vehicle, requiring the robot to analyze the car’s velocity to determine if it is yielding, and (f) navigating in sidewalk baseline without any social or traffic situation. Panels (d) and (e) both belong to the shared-road group (Road + Vehicles/Bikes/Peds) in Table 2. These scenarios require interpreting contextual cues and, where relevant, considering the geometry and motion of surrounding road users to determine appropriate robot behavior.

Figure 9. VLM-retrievable local maps in three scenarios (one per row): a stopped car beside the robot’s path (top), a car crossing in front of the robot (middle), and a construction site in an indoor corridor (bottom). (a) Consecutive RGB images (insets) and the corresponding LiDAR point clouds colored by the camera images. (b) Geometric layer with the observed free space (light green), segmented objects (orange, dashed boxes), other occupied cells (gray), numbered candidate trajectories, the robot pose (black marker), and the subgoal direction (red arrow). (c) Dynamic layer: the crossing car leaves a track of positions (blue points in the middle figure) with a black arrow to indicate the velocity direction, whereas the stopped car (top) and the construction site (bottom) show no displacement. Blue markers show the robot’s recent poses, and the scale bars indicate 1 m.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, Script2Play, by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic gameplay in Minecraft and Roblox, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting gameplay demonstrations for vision-language-action models.
An LLM agent builds executable game environments and skill-targeted tasks.
Programmatic experts use privileged simulator state to produce instructions, visual observations, and keyboard/mouse actions.
Script2Play is behavior-cloned on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay.
It performs effectively on multiple public benchmarks and generalizes across game engines.

papers.abstract: We present a pipeline for transferring Awa Odori, a traditional Japanese festival dance, from monocular video to a commercial Unitree G1 EDU humanoid. The pipeline combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, reinforcement learning for motion tracking in simulation, and onboard deployment via ONNX. Training ran on a single RTX 5070 GPU. An eleven-version deployment ladder evaluated on hardware examines three interventions. We detect and repair silent corruption of deployment artifacts, model state-estimator drift during training, and edit the reference motion to support stable execution and a controlled ending. The final policies achieved three consecutive rope-free completions of a 43-second routine, a 46-second performance with automatic handoff, and a continuous 9.7-minute rope-free performance composed from the captured motion. In a live handover, a single remote request let the robot start from and return to the manufacturer's walking controller on stage, with a measured torque-free window of 45-140 ms. We report the training dynamics and hardware outcomes and discuss failure boundaries involving compliant flooring and occlusion in monocular capture.
bullets: Combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, simulated reinforcement-learning motion tracking, and ONNX onboard deployment.
An eleven-version hardware ladder addresses deployment-artifact corruption, state-estimator drift, and reference-motion edits for stable completion.
The robot completed the routine three consecutive times without a rope, performed a 46-second automatic-handoff demonstration, and sustained a 9.7-minute composed performance.
A live remote handoff returned control between the dance policy and the manufacturer's walking controller, with a measured torque-free window of 45–140 ms.
Failure boundaries include compliant flooring and occlusions in monocular video capture.
papers.selection_reason: Sim-to-real humanoid dance learning from monocular human video via RL and retargeting; directly fits embodied robot learning and human-video transfer.
papers.title: From Festival Video to the Stage: A Sim-to-Real Ladder for Long-Horizon Expressive Whole-Body Dance on a Commercial Humanoid
papers.tldr: A sim-to-real pipeline transfers a 43-second Awa Odori dance from monocular video to a Unitree G1 EDU, enabling repeated and extended hardware performances with automatic controller handoff.

papers.abstract: Recent robot manipulation benchmarks have enabled systematic evaluation of general-purpose robot policies across diverse objects, scenes, instructions, and embodiments. However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on HARP-Bench. Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/harp.
bullets: Models human activity as part of the manipulation task rather than background variation.
Covers four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence, with paired human-present task variants.
Includes a demonstration-generation pipeline and evaluates VLA, imitation-learning, and heuristic policies.
Human presence challenges current policies; manipulation and recovery are the dominant failure sources, and success does not consistently imply better safety.
HARP-Bench demonstrations improve simulated performance and help on real-world human contribution, but transfer to interruption remains limited.

papers.tldr: HARP-Bench evaluates robot manipulation when humans actively share the workspace, revealing gaps in both task success and safety.

papers.abstract: Learning-based safety certification offers a promising route for verifying complex dynamical systems when explicit models are unavailable, but existing data-driven methods often scale poorly: they treat the system as a black box, rely on dense discretizations or Lipschitz bounds, and consequently suffer from sample complexity that grows exponentially with dimension. This paper shows that a common structural property of dynamical systems--monotonicity--can be used to break this curse of dimensionality. We develop a data-driven framework for robust safety verification and safe controller synthesis for unknown monotone systems using only simulator queries. Our main theoretical result proves that, for monotone systems with upper-closed unsafe sets, safety is completely characterized by the existence of monotone inductive barrier certificates. This structure reduces certificate verification over continuous state spaces to localized boundary checks over finitely many cells. To learn such certificates, we introduce Max-Monotone Networks, a monotone neural architecture with universal approximation guarantees for monotone functions. We then propose a training and refinement algorithm that, upon successful termination, returns formally valid neural barrier certificates and, under mild partition assumptions, requires only $O(n)$ simulator queries. Across high-dimensional benchmarks, including oscillator networks with up to $13{,}659$ states and traffic networks with $1{,}000$ states, our method certifies safety in regimes where prior approaches either do not converge or exceed memory limits. These results demonstrate that exploiting order structure can make neural safety certification both scalable and formally sound.
bullets: Addresses the exponential sample complexity of black-box safety certification methods for complex systems.
Uses monotone inductive barrier certificates to characterize safety when unsafe sets are upper-closed.
Reduces continuous-space certificate verification to localized checks on finitely many boundary cells.
Introduces Max-Monotone Networks, which universally approximate monotone functions, plus a training and refinement procedure.
The method can require only O(n) simulator queries under mild partition assumptions and certifies systems with up to 13,659 states in reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.
bullets: Targets the high latency of autoregressive action generation on resource-constrained robots.
Uses a lightweight retrieval-augmented draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without an additional neural draft model.
Reduces verification overhead through kinematics-guided action acceptance and KV-cache-sharing attention.
Introduces the Zora core to accelerate irregular memory access during retrieval.
On four VLA models using LIBERO, it retains comparable accuracy and achieves up to 3.4× software-only and 7.6× hardware-supported speedup over GPUs.

figures.caption: Fig. 12. Overview of the ZORA core architecture. The core accelerates HNSW-based DG retrieval through a four-stage pipeline: fetch, compute, accumulation, and update. The PE array exploits node-level parallelism and embedding-level parallelism to compute partial similarity scores between the query embedding and neighbor embeddings. Partial similarity scores are accumulated and then consumed by either the reduction unit for greedy search in upper HNSW layers or the comparison units for top-k selection in the bottom layer. Lastly, the neighbor index fetch unit updates the search frontier for unvisited nodes.

Fig. 11. Overview of the ZORA accelerator architecture. The accelerator contains a ZORA core to accelerate DG retrieval, a checker unit, and a DNN accelerator. Yellow blocks highlight our key contributions.

papers.title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
papers.tldr: Zora accelerates vision-language-action inference by combining retrieval-based speculative drafting with kinematics-aware verification, KV-cache sharing, and dedicated hardware support.

papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning from limited feedback (RLLF), only a small fraction of an offline dataset can be labeled with rewards, and the central question is which samples should be labeled to learn a high-performing policy from the resulting partially labeled dataset. Prior work formalized this as a reward-selection problem by focusing on the selection stage while treating downstream policy learning as a black box, in a regime where queried rewards are not retained for reward-model training. We instead study the retained-label setting, where queried rewards can be stored and used to fit a reward model before policy learning. We bound the suboptimality of the learned policy in terms of two sources of error: one arising from offline RL on a fixed, offline dataset, and the other from uncertainty in the reward model. Since reward selection cannot change the offline dataset, the limited labeling budget must be used to strategically reduce reward uncertainty. Motivated by RLLF's observation that useful rewards tend to keep the agent on high-return trajectories, we introduce Successor-Guided Uncertainty REduction (SURE), a novel method that uses successor features to select rewards that are both uncertain and associated with states from which high-valued states are reachable. We formally derive SURE from a bound-induced design objective and characterize its exact one-step marginal gain. Empirically, SURE reaches near full-feedback performance with few reward labels across a variety of domains and offline-RL backbones, yielding an effective method for feedback-efficient reinforcement learning.
bullets: Addresses reward selection in retained-label reinforcement learning from limited feedback, where queried rewards train a reward model.
Decomposes policy suboptimality into offline-RL error and reward-model uncertainty.
Uses successor features to prioritize samples that are both uncertain and connected to reachable high-value states.
Derives SURE from a bound-based objective and characterizes its exact one-step marginal gain.
Empirically achieves near full-feedback performance across multiple domains and offline-RL backbones with few labels.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Ablation of the SURE score on representative maze rounds. Each row shows a different stage of selection. From left to right: acquired feedback locations, exact one-step gain ∆(s, a;Y[b], ρb), Reach-only score, Uncertainty-only score, and SURE score. Red boxes mark the highest-scoring cells under each criterion, and the green star denotes the goal region.

Figure 1: Illustrative retained-label reward-selection example in a navigation task. The agent must reach the goal while avoiding a central obstacle. With the initial reward labels, the policy learned from the current reward model takes a long detour, while a more direct path remains possible. Uncertainty-only selection chooses a state where the reward model is uncertain, but the selected state may be far from trajectories that lead to high return. Reachability-only selection chooses a state that can lead toward regions assigned high value by the current reward model, but this estimate can be misleading when the reward model is inaccurate. SURE combines both signals, selecting for labeling a reward that is uncertain under the current reward model and lies on a reachable path toward currently high-value states, yielding a better policy with fewer reward labels.

papers.abstract: Vision-based control policies, including vision-language-action models, have enabled robots to perform increasingly complex tasks. However, their execution speed is often limited by the high computational cost of action inference. In this work, we investigate what can be achieved at the control level without modifying the underlying policy learning process. We introduce an asynchronous inference and control framework that enables fast task execution while maintaining smooth and stable robot motions. By formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous model predictions as a tracking control problem, our method makes asynchronous inference practical for real robots. We further accelerate execution through adaptive action skipping based on the variance of predicted positions. Experiments with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot demonstrate substantial speedups while preserving high task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the high action-inference cost that slows vision-based robot execution.
Generates continuous target positions from discontinuous predictions using a tracking-control formulation.
Uses asynchronous inference and variance-based adaptive action skipping to improve execution speed.
Evaluated with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot.
Reports substantial speedups while maintaining high task success rates.

papers.abstract: Generative world modeling from large-scale visual data offers a promising path toward scalable robot manipulation. This calls for an intermediate representation that can be supervised at scale and remains actionable for downstream control. We propose 3D full-object flow, an object-centric motion representation that assigns dense 3D trajectories to points across the complete surface of a target object, including its occluded regions. By extending visible-surface object flow to the full object geometry, this representation makes complete object motion explicit and applies uniformly to both rigid and deformable objects. To realize the potential of this representation at scale, we introduce a 1210-hour full-object flow dataset that addresses the scarcity of large-scale supervision for complete 3D object motion. The dataset integrates diverse real-world videos and physical simulations, with a scalable annotation pipeline for recovering full-object motion from real-world observations and quality metrics for systematically assessing annotation quality. We then train a world model that takes an image and a task description as input and predicts dense full-object flow over the reconstructed object geometry. Experiments show reliable annotation quality, data-scalable flow prediction, and effective downstream manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments. Project website with additional results and videos: https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/ObjectWorld/.
bullets: Introduces 3D full-object flow: dense trajectories over an object’s complete surface, including occluded regions, for rigid and deformable objects.
Provides a 1210-hour dataset combining real-world videos and physical simulations to supervise complete 3D object motion.
Develops a scalable annotation pipeline and quality metrics for recovering and evaluating full-object flow from observations.
Trains a world model that predicts full-object flow from an image and task description over reconstructed object geometry.
Reports reliable annotations, scalable flow prediction, and effective manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Object-centric full-object flow prediction framework. Given an initial RGB-D observation and task instruction, Qwen2.5-VL [39] extracts task-conditioned visual-language features, while a joint PointTransformer V3 [40] (PTv3) encodes reconstructed object and scene geometry. These features are fused into object tokens and refined by self-attention. The object queries attend to scene and language context through a cross-attention decoder, conditioned on noisy flow and time t, before a flow head predicts dense trajectories over the complete object surface.

Fig. 7: Visualization of real-world full-object flow annotations. Examples from AgiBot World [31], EPIC-KITCHENS [22], and Something-Something V2 [25]. papers.abstract: Embodied intelligence systems rely on fast and reliable inference to enable real-time perception, reasoning, and control. Recent advances in large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) models, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have significantly enhanced the capabilities of embodied agents in complex environments. However, deploying these models remains challenging due to the limited computational resources and energy budgets of robotic platforms. A fundamental question is where inference should be executed. Collaborative inference, which partitions models across end devices, edge servers, and the cloud, has emerged as a promising solution. Yet determining the optimal partitioning point remains an open problem, as it depends on wireless network conditions, model structure, and privacy requirements. This article reviews the state of the art in collaborative inference for embodied intelligence and proposes an edge-centric framework in which the edge coordinates model partitioning and execution. Through both simulation and real-world experiments over WiFi and 5G networks, we demonstrate that the optimal partitioning strategy varies with network conditions and model structure. We further identify latency-minimizing partition points for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and OpenVLA-7B in collaborative inference between NVIDIA Jetson Nano or AGX Xavier devices and an AGX Thor edge server under varying wireless conditions. Finally, we discuss the future directions for collaborative inference in 6G-empowered embodied intelligence systems.
bullets: Reviews collaborative inference for embodied intelligence using large AI models such as LLMs and VLA models.
Addresses robots’ limited computation and energy by coordinating model partitioning at the edge.
Shows through WiFi and 5G simulations and real-world experiments that optimal partition points depend on wireless conditions and model structure.
Identifies latency-minimizing partition points for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and OpenVLA-7B across NVIDIA Jetson devices and an AGX Thor edge server.
Discusses future directions for 6G-enabled collaborative inference.

papers.abstract: Animals integrate information across sensory modalities to guide exploration, suggesting that they maintain internal estimates of where actions are expected to reduce uncertainty. However, how such action-conditioned information maps are learned from multimodal sensory experience remains unclear, as previous studies have been largely confined to unimodal sensing frameworks. We introduce a multimodal predictive-coding framework for learning uncertainty-reduction maps from visual and mechanosensory observations in hawkmoth flower interaction tasks. A variational generative model trained on simulated environments recovers modality-specific information landscapes over the action space, capturing how visual patterns, surface geometry, and mechanosensory cues shape the value of exploratory actions. These learned maps are consistent with several features of hawkmoth behavior, including nonzero tracking offsets, probing along visual patterns, and geometry-dependent exploration. Applying the model to behavioral data from flower tracking and nectary search, we find that natural trajectories tend to occupy regions of high uncertainty reduction in these learned maps. Building on these observations, we develop an uncertainty-gated lexicographic algorithm that switches between information gathering and reward exploitation based on perceptual uncertainty. In nectary search, uncertainty gating improves learning relative to exploit-only, $ε$-greedy, fixed-time, and uncertainty-calibrated non-lexicographic controls, with better generalization and robustness to sensory and curvature shifts. These results link information landscapes learned through generative modeling to biological sensing and embodied exploration.
bullets: Addresses how animals learn which actions will reduce uncertainty during multimodal exploration.
Uses a variational generative model trained in simulated flower-interaction environments with visual and mechanosensory inputs.
Recovers modality-specific maps reflecting visual patterns, surface geometry, and mechanosensory cues.
Learned maps align with hawkmoth behaviors and show that natural trajectories favor actions with high expected uncertainty reduction.
An uncertainty-gated exploration–exploitation algorithm improves learning, generalization, and robustness in nectary search compared with stated control strategies.
