papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width. Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance. We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal. An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time. The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm wide opening at a 2 m/s reference speed. It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30 degrees and folds through a 40 cm long confined passage. Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 2 mm of position RMSE and less than 1% electrical power during contact-free flight. These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.
authors: Etor Arza, Luca Girardi, Gabriel Maquignaz, Javier Paez, Stefan Leutenegger, Stefano Mintchev, Kostas Alexis
bullets: The method jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque–deflection response of two passive folding arms.
Candidate designs are evaluated in contact-based traversal simulations, with success rate guiding iterative improvement.
The prototype narrows from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm opening at a 2 m/s reference speed.
It tolerates approach-angle errors up to 30° and folds through a 40 cm confined passage.
Compared with a rigid twin, it adds only 2 mm position RMSE and under 1% electrical power during contact-free flight.

papers.abstract: Rough terrain traversability is often estimated through point-wise roll, pitch, or force-angle margins along a planned path. However, these metrics are often inaccurate and overly conservative because they ignore how terrain disturbances and low-level controller corrections can affect the vehicle's motions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair can execute a candidate path while meeting trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements. We estimate EGT by predicting the distribution of closed-loop trajectories using a latent-space flow matching (FM) model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and 3D vehicle attitude and wheel-ground contact points prior. Across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4%-39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%. Integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT reduces navigation failure rates by 24-42 and 30-44 percentage points over [1] and [2], respectively, while cutting goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of our simulation-trained model to real-world outdoor experiments.

In 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT lowers safe-path rejection to 2.2% and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%.
When integrated into a receding-horizon planner, EGT reduces navigation failures and goal-reaching time relative to two baselines.
The simulation-trained model demonstrates zero-shot transfer to real-world outdoor experiments.

papers.abstract: Scaling up visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition requires reducing the human effort needed as tasks and spatial configurations expand, particularly in demonstration collection and task-specific training design. We present SUGARv2, a unified framework for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills through interaction reference synthesis and a shared training pipeline. To obtain diverse references at low cost, we adapt reusable task templates to different spatial configurations, synthesizing coordinated robot and object motions. To reduce task-specific reward design and training effort, we use reference-based imitation as a common learning objective across tasks. We first train privileged teachers to execute these references, then train visual policies through teacher distillation and reinforcement learning with the same reference-based mimic rewards, using diverse object instances and visual domain randomization to support visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer. Across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieves a mean success rate of 91.0% in simulation. Deployment on a real humanoid robot further demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer for whole-body manipulation. These results demonstrate the framework's potential for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills.

papers.abstract: Global planners for ground vehicles usually approximate the vehicle by a disk, trading safety against conservativeness, while exact-footprint checking pays for every candidate motion, pose, and footprint edge. We present TPS-A*, a lattice planner whose edges are kinematically feasible trajectories from parameterized trajectory generators, built on certified collision checking in trajectory parameter space. A grid precomputed per footprint returns, in one pass over the local obstacles, a certified free distance along every candidate trajectory, so the per-node collision cost is independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count. We prove that this grid never overestimates the free distance of the continuously swept, possibly non-convex footprint, and state the planner's guarantees: collision-free paths and bounded suboptimality relative to its lattice abstraction. Goals with or without heading are reached exactly by Reeds-Shepp shots certified as trajectories of the same generators. An exact independent test finds no collision in its paths. On 300 cluttered worlds, with the true footprint and the same goal pose for all planners, it solves every query with a collision-free goal pose in a median of three milliseconds on an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X, on par with hybrid A*, 45\% of whose paths overlap obstacles, and nearly sixty times faster than a state-lattice planner, the only other collision-free one; with position goals, eighty-nine times faster than hybrid A*. It matches hybrid A* in automated parking and on narrow doorways, docks a non-convex fork footprint that no convex model admits, and drove a real robot across a university campus among people.
authors: Jose Luis Blanco-Claraco, Shravan S. Rai, Fernando Ca\~nadas-Ar\'anega, Jos\'e Luis Torres-Moreno, Jos\'e Carlos Moreno-\'Ubeda

In 300 cluttered worlds, it solved every query with a collision-free goal pose in a median of 3 ms; an independent test found no collisions.

papers.abstract: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.
authors: Gian Luca Ascari, Isidoro Tamassia, Ying Jiao, Luc De Raedt, Giuseppe Marra
bullets: Addresses the lack of long-term safety guarantees in probabilistic logic shielding without requiring a complete environment model.

Evaluated on safe navigation tasks in LogiCity.
Achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of step-level PLS and other safety-oriented RL baselines.

papers.abstract: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.

Reports competitive accuracy: 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB, and 41.7 mm on RICH.

papers.abstract: Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations can become sensitive to environmental features that are unrelated to the task. Existing generative augmentation methods can introduce visual diversity, but processing every frame and camera view independently is computationally expensive and may produce inconsistent observations across cameras and timestamps. We introduce Augmentron, a geometry-aware pipeline that generates reusable scene representations and renders them through recorded camera poses. This produces temporally and multi-view consistent environ- ment and workspace variations while preserving the robot, task objects, actions, and annotations. Across three physical manipulation tasks, replacing half of the real world training dataset with Augmentron data improves model success across three tasks for both in out-of-distribution distractor objects, and out-of-distribution workspace variation evaluations. In a separate comparison against alternate augmentation techniques, Augmentron achieves the highest pooled success in all three conditions. The results show that introducing augmented data to a data training recipe can help policies generalize to dynamic real-world settings.

papers.abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.

papers.abstract: Grasp-feasibility predictors report near-perfect accuracy on Task and Motion Planning benchmarks, but high accuracy on these benchmarks does not verify that a predictor uses the collision geometry that the motion planner checks. We propose a planner-verified counterfactual (CF) test: holding the grasp pose fixed, we insert a solid obstacle into the approach corridor, add its points to the model input, and let a planner re-derive the label, which flips from feasible to infeasible. Across eight predictors spanning point clouds, voxels, depth, and object tokens, CF-pair AUROC falls from high natural AUROC (0.920-0.996) to chance (0.470-0.504), and the flip holds across four planners, two arms, and a real-object obstacle. Predictors fail at different resolutions, from a bounding box to a 12.5 cm voxel. In the point-cloud models we dissect, the obstacle either moves the representation in a direction unrelated to whether it blocks the grasp or is not registered at all. A clearance-aware read of the corridor points, trained on the unmodified benchmark with no counterfactual scenes, reaches 0.983 CF-pair AUROC, but it remains bound to its trained obstacle placements; a placement-invariant clearance representation is still open. We release the counterfactual labels, metrics, datasheet, and relabeling pipeline at https://github.com/codewithsajid/graspfc-cf.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video captures human-object interaction at scale but rarely includes tactile labels for hidden contact and pressure. We introduce TouchAnnotator, an ego-only bimanual tactile annotator trained with multi-source tactile supervision and privileged-view distillation. A canonical hand field unifies glove pressure, geometry-derived human contact, and robot fingertip deformation from six datasets and three embodiments, while source-aware masks preserve valid targets. During training, an EMA teacher observes synchronized ego and wrist views and distills hand-local representations and tactile predictions into a student that uses only ego video and estimated pose at inference. Compact past-clip memory supplies temporal context. We evaluate on EgoTouch, zero-shot FPHA transfer, and 860 synchronized glove recordings. The model transfers to bare-hand contact and produces qualitatively coherent tactile responses across bare-hand, gloved-hand, and robot embodiments. On measured recordings, it improves temporal accuracy by 5.38 points and Volumetric IoU by 5.02 points under a shared protocol. These results show that heterogeneous human--robot supervision and privileged training views can turn egocentric video into dense tactile annotations.
authors: Ao Li, Zhihao Yuan, Chubin Zhang, Kunrui Huang, Sheng Xu, Zengjue Chen, Junjie Wang, Jiawei Li, Yansong Tang

papers.abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.
authors: Chao Liang, Ke Chen, Fengxiaoxiao Li, Shibo Huang, Yufeng Sun, Zhaokai Yin, Jianhuan Lai, Haozhe Feng, Chenghuan Jia, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Targets sustained embodied autonomy by addressing inefficient control and recovery from execution failures.
Uses learned correction codes combining language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals, with MetaBrain supervision and guidance.
A2-WLA incorporates motion-aware history and a latent world model into a vision-language-action policy; fresh correction codes adapt frozen policies at deployment.
Reports strong benchmark and real-robot performance, including 45.40% success on 100 BEHAVIOR tasks, 95.05% on RoboTwin 2.0 with the full system, and 57.92% across 12 household tasks.
In a long-horizon coffee task, history-conditioned recovery substantially improves completion after filter-handling failures; the system also reports 427.1 samples/s training throughput.

figures.caption: Figure 7 Architecture of A2-WLA. A motion-aware history encoder converts six-frame multiview histories into visual tokens. A 2B Qwen3-VL backbone combines these tokens with the task instruction to produce current context and a latent action. The world model predicts future visual features, which a spatial compressor aggregates into future context. An 18-layer action expert uses both contexts to generate a 50-step action chunk through ten-step flow integration, while a separate head estimates per-step progress. During recovery, a correction adapter injects a code-conditioned residual after the ninth layer. The lower panel shows how adjacent differences between paired-frame representations provide motion features for gated cross-attention and residual fusion before visual token merging.

Figure 1 The A2-MEAS framework. The MetaBrain coordinates task reasoning and recovery. Grounding agents provide specialized evidence. The correction interface combines recovery language, spatial evidence, executed history, and a fresh base-action proposal to modulate A2-WLA. These agents cooperate to control one robot.

Figure 3 The correction interface within action generation. Language, spatial evidence, executed history and a fresh base proposal are encoded once per candidate. At every flow step, the adapter uses the current action hidden states to produce position-dependent residuals. Injection after the ninth of 18 action layers allows subsequent layers to convert the modified state into a corrected flow velocity. Orange modules are trained during correction learning while the base model is frozen. All parameters remain fixed during deployment.

Figure 6 Execution and recovery as one feedback loop. Ordinary action generation records the executed prefix and its observed outcome. An abnormal event invokes the MetaBrain and the required grounding agents. A fresh recovery state conditions both the base proposal and corrected generation. Failed attempts update the evidence and consume the remaining event budget. Verified recovery resumes execution toward the unfinished task goal. A timeout, exhausted budget or failed feasibility check exits recovery.

Figure 2 State progression during the closed-loop recovery of a misaligned filter placement. Following a loss of contact support along one edge of the support ring, the execution layer pauses to verify spatial relationships and synthesizes a sequence of lifting, realigning, and reseating actions conditioned on grounded high-level guidance. Faded outlines trace the initial misaligned pose, orange arrows indicate the directional motion flow, vertical dashed lines mark the central axis of the cup opening, and green indicators highlight the restored planar support.

papers.abstract: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks---person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction---and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at https://github.com/Dobot-Team/dobot_track.
authors: Shengjun Deng, Yinghan Zhang, Chengrui Wei, Liu Liang, Songyuan Liu, Pengkun Zheng, Yajun Zheng, Ying Zhang, Yuan Tian, Xi Li, Teng Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of identifying and consistently following a described person from egocentric observations.
Uses complementary mask and bounding-box grounding supervision alongside investigated auxiliary tasks such as segmentation, spatial classification, and future prediction.
Introduces Q-identity, which compresses historical observations while preserving target-specific appearance and spatial cues.
A 0.8B-parameter model reaches a 77.9% average success rate on EVT-Bench, 16.9 percentage points above OmTrackVLA across three tasks.
Provides a quadruped-robot dataset with 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames; masks also yield bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels automatically.

Right: Q-identity aggregates target-region features and full-image context through joint query–target self-attention, full-image cross-attention, and feed-forward updates. papers.abstract: Creative tool use is a fundamental human capability and an important step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. It requires agents to reason about object affordances, physical constraints, and manipulation strategies, especially when standard tools are unavailable. However, progress in this area is limited by the lack of real-world datasets that capture human tool-use behavior with sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, focus on simplified interactions, or lack detailed observations and annotations. We introduce ToolDex, a large-scale egocentric-exocentric (ego-exo) human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use. ToolDex captures scenarios in which humans select, adapt, and repurpose available objects as tools. Using synchronized egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras, the dataset provides high-fidelity multi-view observations and rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. Beyond data collection, we establish a benchmark suite characterizing three core capabilities: physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning. ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and developing embodied agents that can adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments. Dataset visualizations and benchmarking results are available at https://tooluse-dataset.github.io/.
authors: Mohamed Elmoghany, Kehan Li, Ruoqu Chen, Tarun Chiruvolu, Shutong Zhang, Ryan Wang, Stephen Tian, Yaru Niu, Michelle Guo, Ding Zhao, Weiyu Liu, Mengdi Xu, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu

Supports research on embodied agents that adaptively repurpose objects in complex real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update. Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.
authors: Kaiyuan Chen, Xinyue Zhu, Shuangyu Xie, Uksang Yoo, Thi Thu Phuong Luong, Marcus Gualtieri, Christian Juette, Liu Ren, Spencer Huang, Ken Goldberg
bullets: Evaluates self-learning across nine manipulation tasks, 631 configurations, and 28K coding-agent rollouts.
Systematically varies model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum.
Finds effective learning requires accurate failure attribution and reasoning about task-relevant spatial and geometric structure.
Agents improve more effectively when they selectively restructure code rather than making unfocused updates.
The study is simulation-based, so its findings may not fully transfer to physical-robot settings.

papers.abstract: We focus on the problem of high-speed multi-robot navigation in cluttered spaces with tight spatial constraints. A key challenge is balancing safety with agility, as existing methods often trade one for the other (slowing down near a bottleneck to avoid collisions versus failing to swerve in time at high speeds), especially for car-like systems. Our approach belongs to the family of formation control methods, in which Ackermann-steering agents coordinate while navigating tight spaces. However, current formation control techniques rely on rigid, pre-defined shapes and transitions that depend on initial conditions, the environment, and vehicle dynamics, and are impractical to maintain at high speeds. For example, agents passing through a small gap must first form a square, transform into a line using analytical equations, and then return to a square. In contrast, our approach is inspired by a droplet of water that continuously adapts its shape to the space it flows through without slowing down. We propose a hierarchical algorithm in which, at the high level, a reinforcement learning policy produces a dynamic, blob-like elliptical patch that morphs its shape in real time, squeezing, stretching, and orienting itself around obstacles and through tight spaces. At the low level, the robots are controlled via distributed model predictive control (DMPC) to stay inside the patch, which acts as a soft forcing function, while avoiding collisions with each other. We evaluate our approach, FastFunnels, on simulated F1TENTH racing cars across 14 scenarios with N=1 to N=6 robots, averaged over 20 trials each. FastFunnels achieves an 89% completion rate at 7.73 m/s, while all baselines either fail to complete the track or succeed only at very low speeds (0.07-1.79 m/s, about 40% completion rate).
bullets: Targets the safety–agility trade-off in high-speed multi-robot navigation through tight spaces.
Uses a hierarchical design: reinforcement learning generates a morphing elliptical formation patch, while distributed MPC keeps robots inside it and prevents collisions.
Avoids rigid, pre-defined formations and discrete shape transitions that are difficult to maintain at speed.
Evaluated in simulation with 1–6 F1TENTH cars across 14 scenarios and 20 trials per scenario.
Achieved 89% completion at 7.73 m/s; baselines completed about 40% of trials at only 0.07–1.79 m/s or failed entirely.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Results for a N = 6 shown for 2 (out of 14) benchmark scenes. Each scene is averaged over 20 trials. Remaining scenarios and results can be found in the Appendix. The elliptical funnel patch dynamically adapts its shape and orientation at every control step acting as a soft forcing function to guide the agents fluidly through bottlenecks and narrow gaps at high speed, much like how water flows around rocks and bends. We have tested with N = 6 robots but FASTFUNNELS can scale up to 12 robots as well (beyond N = 12 not tested).

Figure 4: FASTFUNNELS on two Traxxas UDRs (1/7th scale) in a 15m narrow corridor with three obstacles. papers.abstract: A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in its latent representations. We further observe that some existing methods improve spatial structure while also retaining rich variations in texture and color. However, preserving more low-level visual information does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. This raises a key question: how can we strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without over-encoding these details? We introduce LEF-JEPA, which learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead. To reduce the cost of energy optimization during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that allows low-energy-state search to be performed by specialized Ising solvers. On physical hardware, we validate the feasibility of achieving lower forward latency with fewer local updates. Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.
authors: Zhiyuan Liu, Zhihao Xu, Sicheng Liu, Huanhuan Huang
bullets: Addresses JEPA’s difficulty capturing object shapes and boundaries when prediction supervision is applied only to masked positions.
Uses target-guided latent recovery and a relative-energy constraint to transfer spatial-structure supervision to the visual encoder.
Introduces a conditional Ising Hamiltonian to reduce the cost of energy optimization via specialized Ising solvers.
The energy module is used only during pretraining, so it adds no inference overhead.
Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation, both implementations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LEF-JEPA. (a) Visible tokens from the online encoder are partitioned into disjoint candidate and anchor sets. The anchors condition the latent energy landscape over perturbed candidate representations. Multi-level target representations both supervise the displacement induced by K energy-gradient updates (Lfield) and provide the target-energy reference for visual-encoder supervision (Lenc), together with the masked-prediction objective (Lpred). (b) The neural energy realization contextualizes candidate representations with multi-level anchors and aggregates the energy contribution of each token. (c) The conditional Ising realization predicts Hamiltonian coefficients (h, J), invokes a physical photonic CIM to search for low-energy spin states, and differentiably rescores them to form a smooth scalar energy.

Figure 3. Patch-token PCA on CIFAR-10 samples. LEF-JEPA produces coherent regions aligned with object extent and boundaries. PCA is fitted independently per image, so colors are not comparable across methods.

Figure 4. Spatial representations and foreground segmentation on PartImageNet. Each method is shown with patch-token PCA and foreground predictions. Green, red, and blue denote true positives, false positives, and false negatives. LEF-JEPA yields more complete masks and sharper boundaries.
Figure 5. Two-Room planning trajectories. Each column fixes the same task across methods. Yellow, green, cyan, and red denote the start, goal, executed path, and final state.

Figure 6. Effect of the number of energy-gradient updates K on pretraining latency and downstream transfer. Each CIM trajectory uses one physical solve and reuses its low-energy state pool across all K updates. papers.title: LEF-JEPA: Denoising-Trained Latent Energy Fields for Spatial Representation Learning

papers.abstract: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.
bullets: Addresses the tension between real-time onboard inference, onboard-model failures, and limited server capacity.
Uses a small onboard VLA with failure prediction to selectively switch action generation to a large server VLA.
Formulates switching as minimizing server-request cost subject to a required success probability.
In simulation on three LIBERO suites, it improved success by 11–22 percentage points over the small VLA alone.
It used 49–77% fewer requests than server-only control, with a 2–4 percentage-point success-rate reduction and slower growth in completion time under latency.

papers.abstract: We present RevoSim, a scalable and high-fidelity multimodal tactile simulator for the BrainCo Revo3 hand that jointly models 285 piezoresistive taxels and five visuotactile fingertips. RevoSim efficiently generates synchronized pressure, depth, RGB, and marker-displacement observations; on a single RTX 5090, its depth-conditioned marker-displacement configuration supports up to 4,096 parallel environments. We train in-hand manipulation and grasping policies entirely in simulation, establishing a foundation for future sim-to-real transfer. Project page: https://braincotech.github.io/RevoSim-web/.
authors: Ke Zhang, Lixin Xu, Ziyi Wang, Xiyue Dong, Jie Tan, Lianghu Shao, Xianpeng Wang, Chuanyu Li, Renjing Xu
bullets: Models 285 piezoresistive taxels and five visuotactile fingertips.
Generates synchronized pressure, depth, RGB, and marker-displacement data.
Supports up to 4,096 parallel environments on a single RTX 5090 in its depth-conditioned marker-displacement configuration.
Enables fully simulation-trained in-hand manipulation and grasping policies.
Establishes a foundation for future sim-to-real transfer; real-world transfer is not demonstrated in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.
bullets: Fixed PPO clipping does not distinguish harmful extreme ratios from large but tolerable policy changes.
OPO sorts minibatch importance ratios and identifies those most likely to affect the update.
It assigns selected ratios adaptive, sample-wise clipping radii based on a prescribed tail profile.
The method retains a first-order objective and requires only minibatch sorting plus a modified policy loss.
Experiments on MuJoCo and Atari show strong performance relative to established baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 11: MuJoCo-v4 learning curves under different policy-network architectures. Solid curves correspond to seven-layer policies, while dotted curves correspond to three-layer policies. Colors denote different methods. Curves show averages over seeds, and shaded regions indicate across-seed variability.

Figure 1: Overview of OPO. A minibatch of importance ratios is ordered, and the empirical tails are assigned teacher targets induced by a prescribed generalized Pareto tail profile. This yields adaptive sample-wise proximal targets, thereby replacing scalar clipping with order-based tail control. In contrast, PPO imposes the same scalar clipping boundary across ratios.
Figure 10: MuJoCo-v4 learning curves under the architecture-selected protocol. Solid curves denote averages over seeds, and shaded regions indicate across-seed variability.

Figure 5: Aggregate MuJoCo performance under the architecture-selected protocol. We report the median, interquartile mean (IQM), mean, and optimality gap across tasks. Higher is better for the first three metrics, and lower is better for the optimality gap.

Figure 4: Overview of the OPO algorithm. OPO generates the target r⋆t from the GPD teacher profile, then assigns each target to the corresponding order statistic: the t-th ordered ratio r(t) is assigned the corresponding r⋆t . This process encourages the empirical tail ratios to follow the prescribed shape.

papers.abstract: Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.
authors: Hongkun Yu, Francisco M. L\'opez, Francisco Cruz
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting human object-manipulation videos into motion cues for robots.
Combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand–object association and contact localization.
Supports count-aware contact detection in untrimmed videos and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers.
Improves contact-count accuracy and localization distance over an adapted VRB2 baseline on a 30-task benchmark, with further gains in RGB-D rollouts.
Produces more feasible trajectories and successful tasks than adapted baselines in six robot evaluation sequences; evaluation focuses on single-hand scenes and selected multi-hand scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HOC2R inference architecture. Shared outputs comprise contact-region proposal boxes, per-box touch scores, an enclosing-region contact-count prediction, and a whole-image contact-likelihood heatmap. Count-aware automation reranks heatmap candidates using touch scores and emits the predicted number of points. Fixed-two localization filters candidates through proposal boxes, progressively examines more heatmap maxima until two eligible candidates are found, applies touch reranking, and returns two points for a known active contact segment. Their midpoint is lifted with aligned depth and camera calibration into a robot-base trajectory.

Figure 1: HOC2R training architecture. The proposal head uses frozen DINOv3 features and patch labels to predict candidate contact-region boxes. The proposalbox touch head uses each proposal’s SAM feature crop and box label to predict whether the box contains contact. The enclosing-region count head uses the SAM feature crop covering the top-ten proposal boxes and frame-level labels to predict contact presence and count. The whole-image heatmap head uses SAM features and Gaussian targets to predict pixel-wise contact likelihood.
Figure 6: In-domain contact-count confusion over 210 held-out frames. Rows show ground truth, and columns show predictions.

Figure 4: Comparison on seven external RGB-D rollouts. In (a), points show aggregate F1@10, and thin bars show task-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. In (b), points show mean localization distance, thin bars show its 95% confidence interval, and wide stems span the median-to-90th-percentile error. Shorter stems indicate more consistent localization.

Figure 5: External multi-hand diagnostics. VRB2 associates its prediction with the resting hand. EgoHOS responds to the resting hand and the clothing sleeve beside the manipulating arm, and its point adapter retains these unrelated boundaries. In contrast, HOC2R proposal boxes focus on the manipulating hand, and the fixed-two decoder localizes the pencil contact. The assignment errors are 156.11 px for VRB2, 126.00 px for EgoHOS-Point, and 17.81 px for HOC2R.

Figure 3: Robot evaluation workflow illustrated on the pen-motion demonstration. HOC2R extracts two image contacts (a), whose midpoint forms a 2D trajectory (b). Aligned depth and camera calibration map the trajectory into the robot base frame (c). Shared filtering and waypoint resampling are applied before inversekinematics execution (d).

papers.selection_reason: Extracts hand-object contact trajectories from human videos for robot motion transfer, fitting human-video learning and manipulation.
papers.title: HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer
papers.tldr: HOC2R extracts robot-usable hand–object contact trajectories from human videos using frozen vision features and learned localization heads, improving contact detection and robot task success in evaluated scenes.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43% atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00% on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard $\pi_{0.5}$-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86% atomic and 17.50% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses skill retention and phase-dependent skill composition in vision-language-action policies.
Finds that per-skill low-rank updates occupy a distinguishable low-dimensional parameter subspace.
Stores each skill as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter, augmented with trainable residuals.
Uses a VLM-conditioned per-chunk router supervised by an action-derived oracle to select primitives based on task progress.
On RoboCasa365, reports 56.43% atomic-skill and 20.00% composite success, versus 17.86% and 17.50% for a two-stage π₀.₅-LoRA baseline; also validates on a real AgileX PIPER robot.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the PRISM framework. (1) Skill primitive learning (§4): each atomic skill is fitted with its own rank-r action-expert LoRA (Bi, Ai), yielding a primitive bank of disjoint slots, frozen after atomic training. (2) Router learning from composite demonstrations: a prefixconditioned router rθ reads the VLM prefix ht and emits a per-chunk mixture α(t) over the bank, supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic action-derived oracle A. (3) Chunk-wise routed execution (inference): each LoRA-injected action-expert layer applies the routed mixture at the activation level (Eq. 5), producing an action chunk.

(c) PR/T (1.0=maximal spread, 1/T=collapse): 0.37 vs 0.93. (d) Effective rank/T : 0.42 vs 0.97. Across all metrics, withinskill LoRAs are more concentrated than across-skill LoRAs.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses VLA policy adaptation with skill retention and long-horizon composition via low-rank skill primitives and routing.
papers.title: PRISM: Primitive Routing via In-context Skill Mixing for Retentive VLA Adaptation
papers.tldr: PRISM preserves reusable VLA skills as frozen low-rank primitives and routes among them in context to execute long-horizon composite tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.
authors: Ramy ElMallah, Marc Bishara, Hyegang Kim, Yuxi Zhang, Chongyu Zhu, Chi-Guhn Lee
bullets: Simulates robots, cameras, IoT devices, wearables, residents, visitors, faulty sensors, and time-evolving hazards in Isaac Sim.
Includes 20 tasks across five household-assistance and safety families, where identical alerts may have different causes.
Scores outcomes and action sequences using temporal-logic checks and predefined action costs.
Across six VLMs, the best family-balanced score is 61.9%; models over-reacted, with prohibited interventions occurring more than twice as often as missed required interventions.

papers.abstract: Skylight polarization provides directional cues for robotic navigation, but fisheye lens effects and analyzer imperfections can degrade polarization measurements across the field of view. We present a joint lens-analyzer calibration method that explicitly models incidence-dependent lens transmission together with analyzer gains and angular offsets in a unified eight-parameter formulation. Given known geometric calibration, rotations between camera frames can be estimated using visual features and cross-frame directional polarized light consistency can be used for polarization calibration. Therefore, our calibration approach requires only a short handheld outdoor sequence under natural skylight, without dedicated polarization calibration equipment or a predefined sky polarization model. On real-world outdoor sequences, the proposed method achieves a weighted cross-frame angle-of-linear-polarization (AoLP) mean absolute error below 0.5{\deg} across all incidence angles, with a 73.4% reduction in the 80{\deg}-90{\deg} incidence angle region, and generalizes to an independent sequence with an overall mean absolute error of 0.466{\deg} without refitting. Preliminary solar-azimuth experiments using a camera mounted on a quadruped robot further show improved alignment with the visible solar center, supporting the potential of calibrated AoLP measurements for relative-heading estimation and future polarization--inertial navigation. The calibration software tool will be released upon acceptance of this paper.
authors: Shuo Wang, Shiqi Che, Dianze Dong, Wenxin Liu
bullets: Addresses fisheye lens transmission and analyzer gain/angular-offset errors that distort polarization across the field of view.

Requires only a brief outdoor sequence under natural skylight; no dedicated polarization equipment or predefined sky polarization model is needed.

Preliminary quadruped-robot solar-azimuth tests show improved alignment with the visible solar center, indicating potential for relative-heading and polarization–inertial navigation.

papers.abstract: Reliable relative tracking is fundamental to cooperative autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), yet remains challenging under nonlinear vehicle dynamics and degraded underwater visual conditions. Active light markers improve robustness to appearance variation, but provide deliberately sparse observations that can become incomplete or corrupted by occlusion, reflections, and detection noise during dynamic motion. To address the resulting partial-observation control problem, this paper proposes FATHOM, a world-model-guided diffusion action-trajectory selection framework for sparse-marker AUV tracking. FATHOM first integrates structured marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics into a predictive tracking belief using a multimodal task-supervised recurrent state-space model. A diffusion action prior then generates multiple expert-like multi-thruster trajectories, whose future tracking consequences are predicted through the learned latent dynamics. Rather than directly executing a generated trajectory, FATHOM selects the most favorable candidate under an explicit receding-horizon objective and continually updates the decision from onboard observations. Extensive offline analyses verify the learned predictive belief, multi-step world-model prediction, diffusion trajectory generation, and predictive selection. More importantly, comprehensive real-AUV experiments, including strong pose-based comparisons and component ablations, demonstrate robust autonomous tracking across nominal and challenging motions with naturally occurring partial marker visibility, while maintaining real-time onboard operation without motion-capture feedback.
authors: Xiaorui Wang, Zeyu Sha, Mingyang Yang, David Chen Wang, Feitian Zhang
bullets: Addresses partial-observation tracking caused by occlusion, reflections, detection noise, nonlinear dynamics, and degraded underwater vision.
Builds a predictive tracking belief from marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics using a multimodal recurrent state-space model.
Generates multiple multi-thruster action trajectories with a diffusion prior, predicts their consequences in latent dynamics, and chooses among them using a receding-horizon objective.
Offline analyses validate belief modeling, world-model prediction, trajectory generation, and predictive selection.

Real-AUV experiments and component ablations show robust autonomous tracking under nominal and challenging motions with partial marker visibility and real-time onboard execution without motion-capture feedback.

papers.abstract: Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under "not X" and "X". Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward. A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24). When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably. These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.
bullets: On LIBERO-Goal, negated instructions did not change the executed task: the forbidden task occurred in 79% of negated rollouts, versus 78% completion for plain tasks.
A goal probe produced similar representations for “not X” and “X,” indicating weak encoding of negation in the executed goal.
The first action depends mainly on instruction tokens before layer 12 and the final prompt token from layer 16 onward.
Steering instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12/18 rollouts; later prefill interventions failed, while patching every decoded action token at layer 24 redirected 15/18.
Layer-32 goal read-outs detected non-compliance during changing instructions, supporting external enforcement and monitoring of safety constraints.

papers.abstract: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization. Particularly in contact-rich settings, the scalability of such simulations in large part depends on well-optimized representations of collision geometry, often requiring a coarse approximation of the underlying surfaces using primitives such as spheres, capsules, cylinders, and boxes. Whenever the complexity of the surfaces or the precision demands of the application render such approximations insufficient, it is instead necessary to employ mesh-mesh collisions, which impose a significant reduction in throughput. This paper proposes a simulation framework designed from scratch to address this bottleneck, with novel routines for broadphase and narrowphase collision detection as well as the subsequent contact dynamics computation. As experimentally validated, the framework matches existing well-established simulators in terms of physical faithfulness, and can achieve approximately an order of magnitude higher throughput in the detailed mesh-mesh collision setting that it specializes in. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.
authors: Onur Beker, Andreas Ren\'e Geist, Georg Martius
bullets: Addresses the throughput bottleneck caused by replacing coarse collision primitives with precise mesh-mesh collisions.
Introduces new broadphase and narrowphase collision-detection routines, plus contact-dynamics computation.
Designed for massively parallelized robotics workloads, including reinforcement learning and trajectory optimization.
Experiments show physical faithfulness comparable to established simulators and approximately an order-of-magnitude higher throughput for detailed mesh-mesh collisions.
Source code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Lodos-v2 is a GPU-based simulation framework for massively parallel rigid-body dynamics with contact. It is specifically designed to achieve high throughput in scenes involving collisions among large numbers of detailed meshes. Its predecessor, Lodos-v1, had two main limitations. First, it solved the standard convex relaxation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, thereby inheriting well-known physical artifacts, including lift-off and artificial compliance in the normal direction, as well as creep in the tangential direction. Second, its contact-group reparameterization scheme, which rescales spring-damper forces using a single factor per collision pair, could not be integrated with other constraints required by a full-fledged simulator, such as joint limits and welds. Lodos-v2 addresses both limitations through two main contributions. First, it introduces an efficient algorithm for solving the exact frictional contact problem by sequentially solving a cascade of convex relaxations in primal form within an outer proximal minimization loop. Second, it extends the contact-group reparameterization scheme of Lodos-v1 to the primal formulation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, enabling its integration with the other constraints of a full-fledged simulator. Experiments demonstrate that these contributions result in throughput improvements over established rigid-body simulation frameworks. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.
authors: Onur Beker, Andreas Ren\'e Geist, Georg Martius
bullets: Targets high-throughput GPU simulation of collisions among large numbers of detailed meshes.
Solves the exact frictional contact problem via a cascade of primal convex relaxations inside an outer proximal minimization loop.
Extends contact-group reparameterization to support integration with constraints such as joint limits and welds.
Addresses lift-off, artificial normal compliance, and tangential creep inherited from Lodos-v1’s convex relaxation.
Experiments report throughput improvements over established rigid-body simulation frameworks; source code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Assistive robots and search-and-rescue platforms require reliable human state sensing in smoke, darkness, and privacy-sensitive environments, where cameras and LiDAR may be unreliable Millimeter-wave radar offers an alternative that works without ambient light, penetrates smoke, and does not capture visual appearance. However, the compact arrays that fit robot size, power, and cost budgets have limited apertures, producing joint-localization errors on the order of decimeters at a few meters, large enough to compromise the safety margins and tracking accuracy a robot depends on. Existing pipelines reduce pose error through frame fusion, multiple viewpoints, return selection, or stronger estimators, but examine one technique at a time, without relating its effect to a shared measurement limit or separating gains from added information from gains from estimator completion. We address this gap with a framework that models the human and environment as one time-varying scattering field and states a Cramer-Rao type error floor for joint localization as a function of bandwidth, aperture, signal-to-noise ratio, fused frame count, phase coherence, and visibility of retained returns. We then use existing frame fusion, multi viewpoint, return selection, and pose estimation methods as matched probes of this floor rather than as competing pipelines. Under the evaluated conditions, experiments on three datasets and a live deployment show these strategies move joint localization error in the predicted directions, for example lowering mean per-joint position error from about 97 to 65 mm with a second viewpoint, while a stronger estimator mainly lowers overall error by completing joints the measurement cannot resolve. These results give the robotics community a principled basis for deciding whether to prioritize observation design or estimator capacity when deploying reliable mmWave human sensing.
authors: Shuntian Zheng, Guangming Wang, Hongyang He, Shuai He, Yu Guan
bullets: Compact mmWave arrays can cause decimeter-scale joint-localization errors that threaten robot safety and tracking.
The framework models humans and environments as a time-varying scattering field and derives a Cramér–Rao-type error floor tied to bandwidth, aperture, SNR, fusion, coherence, and return visibility.
Frame fusion, multiple viewpoints, return selection, and pose estimation are evaluated as probes of this shared limit rather than competing pipelines.
Experiments across three datasets and a live deployment follow the predicted trends; a second viewpoint reduced mean per-joint error from about 97 to 65 mm under the evaluated conditions.
Stronger estimators primarily reduce error by completing unresolved joints, whereas additional observation can improve the underlying measurement.

papers.abstract: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap. However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator. This is why we introduce \method{}, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile. To learn efficiently from this reward, we use the off-policy RL algorithm XQC and combine a high gain setting for the joint position controllers with left-right symmetry augmentation. In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples. Compared to learning without these two components, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while without them the robot learns only in over an hour.
bullets: Addresses the need for motion-capture systems or calibrated state estimators in direct robot locomotion learning.
Rewards following a commanded acceleration profile, using measurements available from the onboard IMU.
Combines off-policy XQC reinforcement learning with high-gain joint control and left-right symmetry augmentation.
In simulation, learns walking on Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples.
The added control and augmentation components reduce training falls by 81%; without them, learning takes over an hour.

papers.tldr: STRIDE enables rapid onboard learning of humanoid locomotion using IMU-only acceleration-based rewards instead of externally measured base velocity.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control. Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation. We propose \ours, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot's own action. The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations. The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, \ours retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion. Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that \ours achieves up to 1.61 $\times$ speedup and 59.5\% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.
authors: Sungwon Moon, Minji Kim, Hyemin Boo, Daeun Song, Jiyoung Lee
bullets: Targets slow closed-loop robot response caused by expensive visual processing.
Training-free pruning uses the predicted prior action as a geometric prior before the vision encoder runs.
In the fixed third-person view, it keeps patches along the projected end-effector path and semantic anchors.
In the wrist view, it removes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for action-induced camera motion.
Evaluated in LIBERO, VLABench, and four real-robot tasks, achieving up to 1.61× speedup and 59.5% FLOPs reduction with negligible success-rate degradation.

papers.abstract: Geometric assembly requires fine spatiotemporal coordination to place parts without causing collisions or deadlocks under tight clearances. To address this, we present an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that treats each part as an agent and learns a shared policy for continuous assembly control. A graph neural network represents the pieces, their target poses, and their spatial relationships, and predicts translational and angular velocities for each component. Per-agent proximal policy optimization with a centralized graph critic directly learns motion and temporal coordination within a single feedback policy. We study this formulation through planar Tangram assembly, where pieces must slide and rotate into a given configuration while remaining on the assembly surface. Procedural generation of target configurations and randomized initial arrangements support training and evaluation across diverse assembly problems. Our experiments isolate the roles of relational structure and multi-agent optimization, and compare learned control with sampling-based planning. We demonstrate concurrent assembly in simulation and transfer the policy to sequential execution on a real robot, as our object-centric formulation decouples learned assembly coordination from low-level physical control. Project page: https://tangrambench.org/
authors: Paul Knau{\ss}t, Kay Pompetzki, Nico Bohlinger, Niklas Funk, Cristiana de Farias, Rolf Findeisen, Jan Peters
bullets: Models each assembly piece as an agent with a shared policy for continuous translation and rotation.
Uses a graph neural network to encode pieces, target poses, and spatial relationships.
Combines per-agent PPO with a centralized graph critic to learn motion and temporal coordination.
Evaluates planar Tangram assembly across procedurally generated targets and randomized starting arrangements.
Demonstrates concurrent simulated assembly and transfer to sequential execution on a real robot; comparisons include sampling-based planning.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approaches train reinforcement learning (RL) agents on diverse curricula that may evolve with their capabilities. While prior work has largely focused on how these curricula are constructed, we study whether their students remain trainable under the resulting distributions. Across multiple UED mechanisms, environment complexities, and extended training horizons, we identify recurring learner-side pathologies, including parameter growth, degraded value--outcome ordering, and loss of representational diversity, that accompany stagnation and performance degradation. These findings connect limitations in UED to optimization failures previously identified in conventional deep RL, while showing how adaptive curricula couple the learner's optimization state to its future training distribution. Controlled interventions show that mitigating selected pathologies improves learning. Stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule or increasing environment interaction. Our results establish learner trainability as a complementary design principle for UED. Effective curricula require students that remain capable of learning from the distributions they produce.
authors: Johan Obando-Ceron, Walter Mayor, Michael Dennis, Aaron Courville, Pablo Samuel Castro
bullets: Across multiple UED mechanisms and environment complexities, learner pathologies recur during stagnation and performance decline.
Observed issues include parameter growth, degraded value–outcome ordering, and reduced representational diversity.
Adaptive curricula couple the learner’s optimization state to the distributions it encounters in the future.
Targeted interventions that mitigate selected pathologies improve learning, long-horizon performance, and zero-shot generalization.
The findings support learner trainability as a complementary design principle for UED.

papers.selection_reason: Studies RL learner trainability under adaptive curricula; findings on training stability are transferable to embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Training Stability under Adaptive Curricula
papers.tldr: Adaptive curricula can make RL agents untrainable over time, so UED must account for learner stability—not just curriculum design.

papers.abstract: Natural language offers an intuitive way to direct a virtual crowd while a simulation is running. Handwritten rules execute efficiently but cannot respond flexibly to varied instructions, whereas asking a large language model (LLM) to control the crowd at every update introduces repeated latency, cost, and the risk of unsupported actions. We present CrowdDirector, a framework that uses an LLM only when the user adds or changes an instruction. The LLM translates the request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks whether the entities and actions it references exist in the current Unity scene. Accepted instructions are stored and remain continuously active as the simulation is running. At each simulation tick, a graph neural network uses the current scene state and active instruction to choose an available action and target for each agent, while Unity handles movement, interactions, and animation. The network is trained offline on simulated scenarios, with LLM guidance on how agents should respond to instructions. Our evaluations show the scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgements more often than the LLM's own assessment, and on a behavioural benchmark CrowdDirector follows user instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls. It therefore provides a practical middle ground between fixed rules and continuous LLM control.
authors: Xiaohan Sun, Vuk Radovanovic, Merce Alvarez, Carol O'Sullivan, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Panayiotis Charalambous
bullets: Addresses the inflexibility of handwritten rules and the latency, cost, and unsupported-action risks of per-tick LLM control.
Uses an LLM when instructions are added or changed, then validates referenced entities and actions against the current Unity scene.
A graph neural network selects each agent’s action and target at every simulation tick; Unity executes movement, interaction, and animation.
Evaluations found validator feasibility decisions aligned with human judgments more often than the LLM’s assessments.
On a behavioural benchmark, it followed instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CrowdDirector. (a) Offline policy training. In generated worlds, simulation rollouts and a constrained LLM ranking score the same set of available actions, giving 𝑞roll and 𝑞LLM. Averaging them yields the hybrid target 𝑞train, which trains the graph policy. Because both distributions cover the same candidates, the blend cannot introduce an unavailable action. (b) Runtime orchestration. An LLM interprets a new instruction once (1), and the scene validator checks it against the live scene, storing an accepted result as a directive and rejecting an unsupported target (2). The current scene and active directives are then rebuilt as a crowd graph with a candidate list for each agent (3), the trained policy selects one candidate per agent (4), and Unity executes the result (5).

Figure 3: Architecture of the graph policy. Type-specific encoders produce 64-dimensional node representations, which are updated by three relational GNN layers. A shared multilayer perceptron scores each candidate from its agent representation, target representation, their interaction, and the 34-dimensional candidate features.

Table 4: Policy evaluation. Panel A compares alternative approaches. Q2 Jaccard measures agreement on the affected scope; Q3 measures agreement on the preferred candidate action. The per-tick LLM is a comparison method rather than a local decision maker. Panel B reports controlled ablations with identical data, candidates, masks, labels, and optimization. Learned results are means over three seeds. Best value in bold, second best underlined.

(b) reports CPU scaling at approximately constant agent density. Measured on an Intel i9-13900H (14 physical cores), CPU only. Best value in bold.
