papers.selection_reason: Connects natural-language directives to agent action selection in a simulated environment, transferable to embodied vision-language-action systems.
papers.title: CrowdDirector: Runtime Orchestration of Crowd Simulation through Natural-Language Directives
papers.tldr: CrowdDirector combines one-time LLM instruction parsing with validated, continuously active GNN control for responsive crowd simulation without repeated LLM calls.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.
authors: Mingjia Huo, Yao Fu, Bo Chang, Yaqing Wang, Dawei Zhu, Dylan Zhang, Xinyang Yi, Lichan Hong, Ed H. Chi, Hao Zhang, Jiaxi Tang
bullets: Benchmarks VLMs on 20 Atari 2600 games using high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams.
Separates in-game dynamics from inference speed to test spatiotemporal perception, reasoning, and action grounding.
Finds failures in tracking object motion and direction, brittle sequential decisions, and over-reliance on textual history over new visual feedback.
Analyzes which game scores reliably reflect competence and examines the effects of memory design and prompting.
Highlights a persistent gap between passive visual understanding and active decision-making in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning. Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture. We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative progress. By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training. VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy post-trained for in-context action generation. On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 6.2% for a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline to 23.8% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5%. Project page with code, data and videos: https://ai4ce.github.io/VICTR/
authors: Luca Macesanu, Tianluo Zhang, Aditya Patil, Archit Sharma, Kevin Angers, Christopher M. Clark, Chen Feng, Juexiao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting demonstrations that match the robot’s current execution stage during in-context learning.
Introduces an In-Context Value Function Estimator that estimates task-relative progress from a reference video, instruction, and current observation.
Uses progress-aligned demonstration chunks with a post-trained π₀.₅ policy for in-context action generation.
On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, success rises from 6.2% to 23.8%, while task progress increases from 28.9% to 55.5%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. VICTR method overview. The IC-VFE (ϕ) conditions on the reference demonstration τctx, the shortest in the pool Dℓ, to produce a progress estimate v̂t for the current observation ot. This is then optionally fused with visual similarity, driving retrieval of a context chunk ct from the demonstration pool. The IC-VLA (θ) conditions on ct to predict the next action chunk, closing the loop without any parameter updates.

Fig. 8. Retrieval ablation: retrieval signal at training vs. deployment. Labels at the bottom represents: the method at training “+” the retrieval signal at deployment. While policies evaluated with the same retrieval signal they were trained with perform better across the board, it is not enough to overcome a poor retrieval signal at deployment time.

Fig. 6. VFE at deployment: task progress rate by value estimation method. All methods are evaluated using the same IC-VLA backbone using Robo-Dopamine annotations at training time. IC-VFE yields substantially higher OOD progress than the alternative online estimators, indicating that retrieval quality is sensitive to the value estimator used at deployment.

Fig. 1. Value-informed context retrieval for in-context robot learning. Given a reference demonstration, IC-VFE estimates task-relative progress, which VICTR uses to retrieve progress-aligned context for action generation. On out-of-domain tasks, VICTR improves the task progress rate from 26.8% with π0.5 and 43.0% with visual-similarity-based RICL to 58.2%, without task-specific fine-tuning at deployment.

Fig. 5. Examples of retrieved context across retrieval signals. The leftmost column on both sides “source” represents the query for the retrieval signal (and only the top camera is used during retrieval). For the circle-on-peg task, DINOv2 retrieves a suboptimal chunk, likely due to over-reliance on scene geometry. On the “wipe the plate” task, IC-VFE retrieves a context chunk at a nearly identical stage of execution.

Fig. 3. IC-VFE attention patterns. Context blocks attend independently at most layers and communicate through block-causal attention at layers h ∈ {6, 12, 18}. The current-observation/instruction block and value-query token attend to the preceding context.

Fig. 7. Retrieval ablation: success rate vs. number of context demonstrations. We evaluate VICTR with a variable number of demonstrations in its demonstration pool. Performance generally improves as the demonstration pool grows, saturating around five demonstrations.

Fig. 4. Main result: success and task progress rates for π0.5 and three retrieval-based variants on in-domain (InD) and out-of-domain (OOD) tasks. Each bar’s solid segment denotes binary success rate; the lighter segment adds partial credit for annotated milestones.

papers.title: VICTR: Value-Informed In-Context Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are expected to take over strenuous material handling in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare, where operating existing wheeled carts would let them move heavy loads without modifying the workplace. However, humanoid cart pushing remains challenging because the bimanual grasp closes a force-coupled loop in which the contact wrenches that drive the cart also disturb the robot's balance, and payload changes alter the coupled dynamics. We propose ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework that regulates cart velocity through two-stage reinforcement learning. A locomotion prior is first trained under varied hand loads and upper-body postures to provide balance support. A force latent and a state latent are then inferred from onboard observations, without external force sensors, and fed to a residual policy that coordinates bounded arm, waist, and leg adjustments with base-velocity commands. Multi-objective rewards penalize bimanual internal opposition, grasp slip, and actuator saturation, encouraging the policy to apply contact force on demand without human demonstrations. Sim-to-sim experiments show that ForPC reduces cart-velocity RMSE by up to 68.2% relative to a locomotion-only baseline (Loco-only) and cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2% on the multi-bend route. Trained solely in simulation, the policy also transfers to a physical Unitree G1 without real-world training or fine-tuning and, with no payload-specific adjustment, pushes a cart carrying up to 30 kg at 0.5 m/s. These results suggest that humanoid robots could eventually replace humans for efficient material handling in daily life.

papers.abstract: A flow-matching policy deployed in the field must often satisfy a constraint that was absent from its demonstrations, such as avoiding an obstacle it has never seen. Retraining for every new constraint is impractical, so the constraint must be enforced at inference time. Enforcing it must not discard what the policy learned: an action the policy would rarely sample may avoid the obstacle yet fail the task. We therefore want actions that are both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy. Gradient guidance, the most common approach, steers noisy states, so it must evaluate its cost on the policy's running estimate of the clean action; when the policy is uncertain between passing left or right of an obstacle, this estimate is their average and can pass straight through it. We instead build on rejection and projection. Rejection redraws actions until one is safe: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare. Projection moves an action to the nearest safe one: it is efficient, but the result need not be plausible. Our key insight is that flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection's efficiency and rejection's plausibility. CS-Pi, our draw-project-renoise sampler, projects each draw to the nearest safe action, adds noise back scaled to how far the projection moved it, and re-runs the unmodified policy until a draw is safe. Replacing only the projection step extends CS-Pi to continuous costs. Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place, an orientation preference, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi reaches 81% safe success on the shelf and 55% on hardware, against 55% and 40% for projection, while staying plausible.
authors: Soumojit Bhattacharya, Oliver Kroemer, Shubham Tulsiani
bullets: Addresses the conflict between safe actions and actions likely under the learned policy.
Combines rejection and projection through draw-project-renoise sampling.

papers.abstract: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark

papers.abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Zixuan Wang, Weisong Shi
bullets: Dense BEV grids waste computation on regions the vehicle will not traverse.
A coarse scene encoding predicts path-related heat, then selectively refines high-heat cells under a fixed budget.
The mixed-resolution BEV covers the full scene and requires neither an HD map nor a navigation command.
With 10% refinement, it uses 28% of BEV queries and 66% of encoder time versus a full fine grid, while achieving lower reported errors on nuScenes and NAVSIM navtest.
The approach is evaluated on two benchmarks and is intended for path-focused, efficient end-to-end driving.

papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.
authors: Zuhao Liu, Melih Darcan, Zhengdi Yu, Riza Alp Guler, Tolga Birdal
bullets: Addresses the need for hand-pose priors that account for the interacted object, beyond unconditional pose models.
Represents plausible hand configurations as the zero-level set of an object-conditioned neural field on the hand-articulation manifold.
Uses Riemannian geometry to project poses onto the plausible field and optimize for the interacting object.
Evaluations show utility for pose refinement, occluded-hand reconstruction, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

papers.abstract: We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. MR0 combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. A three-stage training recipe aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior through discrete action-token pre-training, transfers these priors to continuous cross-embodiment control through flow-matching mid-training, and adapts the policy through real-world post-training. We introduce Rollback, which pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections to provide positive and negative supervision for CFG-DAgger without value learning or advantage labeling. A unified end-effector interface supports heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency. An event-driven agent maintains persistent task events and reassesses plans when progress or feasibility changes, enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption. MR0 achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than $\pi_{0.5}$ across three real-robot tasks. On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90. Qualitative agent deployments demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model's own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.
bullets: Identifies a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is represented but has insufficient influence on trajectory generation.
Matched counterfactuals and driving replays show plans are driven mainly by ego-speed history and respond weakly to hazard proximity or reasoning traces.
The trajectory generator can brake, but does not reliably do so when hazards are present.
Injecting a hazard-conditioned energy into frozen Alpamayo-1.5 flow-matching sampling restores hazard-responsive control at generation time.
With exact obstacle geometry, footprint intrusion fell from 58.1% to 14.5% and collisions were eliminated in the braking-relevant closed-loop tests when stopping distance was sufficient.

papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations is a reliable way to teach robots new tasks, but the gains from each additional demonstration shrink as the policy improves. Continued improvement can instead come from supervised deployment, where an operator places the objects and intervenes when the policy fails. We ask how to maximize improvement from a fixed budget of supervised episodes on high-precision manipulation tasks with wide ranges of object placements. We observe that failures can concentrate in a small subset of initial states, so uniform collection spends much of the operator's time on states the policy already handles. Mulligan makes the initial-state distribution a decision, starting each round's episodes at observed failures and untried states. To further improve data efficiency, we augment interactive imitation learning with a value function trained on all data, including failures that imitation discards. Across three real-world tasks evaluated on 2,550 held-out, blinded episodes and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform initial-state sampling at matched collection budgets, and combined with value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+Mulligan, improves final real-task success by 10-34 percentage points. With operator interventions, the human-robot team completes 98% of collection episodes, remaining productive while the policy learns. Videos, code, and data are available at https://mulligan.page/.
bullets: Uniform data collection becomes inefficient as policies improve because many sampled states are already solved.
Mulligan treats the initial-state distribution as a decision, prioritizing observed failures and untried states each round.
It also trains a value function on all collected data, including failures omitted by standard imitation learning.
Across three real-world and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform sampling at matched collection budgets.
With value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+Mulligan raises final real-task success by 10–34 percentage points; operators complete 98% of collection episodes.

papers.abstract: Finding an optimal behaviour policy within a given environment is a widely studied problem in domains as diverse as games, robotics, energy infrastructure, communication networks, and multi-agent systems. Numerous benchmarks have been developed to support such research, but the vast majority assume that the agent's embodiment (design) is fixed, focusing instead on policy learning alone. Lifting this assumption gives rise to a broader class of problems in which optimizing embodiment and policy separately is highly suboptimal. An agent's embodiment strongly shapes which control policies can be discovered, while the optimal embodiment is in turn defined by the policies it admits. To help the research community study this class of problems explicitly and systematically, we introduce Co-Design Gym - a suite of benchmark environments for jointly optimizing embodiment and policy. Our environments span domains such as robotic manipulation and locomotion, multi-robot cooperation, deformable and soft dynamics, video games, electricity grids, wireless networks, F1 racing, multi-agent warehouses, and optimal control, offering 20 environment families (domains), with over 85 distinct co-design presets in total. We further contribute a systematic evaluation of representative co-design algorithms, characterizing the current state of the art. Together, these contributions lay the groundwork for cumulative, comparable progress in co-design.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed-embodiment benchmarks, where policy-only optimization can be suboptimal.
Provides 20 environment families spanning robotics, multi-agent systems, games, infrastructure, communications, and control.
Includes more than 85 distinct embodiment-policy co-design presets.
Evaluates representative co-design algorithms to characterize current capabilities and support comparable future research.

papers.abstract: Structured policies improve efficiency, robustness, and interpretability in imitation learning by introducing task-specific inductive bias, but existing structure generation methods rely either on extensive human input or on static domain knowledge encoded in LLMs, which may be inconsistent with the expert demonstrations. We propose a closed-loop framework that iteratively refines structured policies using LLM-guided analysis of policy rollouts. By logging rollouts as semantically meaningful tabular data and prompting the LLM to generate diagnostic analysis code, our method identifies suboptimalities in the policy structure and iteratively corrects them without requiring human instruction. Experiments on car racing and door opening tasks show that our approach improves imitation learning performance by up to 15% over zero-shot LLM-generated structures and requires 75% less compute to achieve the same reinforcement learning performance. These results demonstrate that tabular rollout analysis provides an effective feedback signal to align LLM-generated policy structures with expert demonstrations, and we can utilize it to generate good policy structures automatically.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static or human-designed policy structures and expert demonstrations.
Logs policy rollouts as semantically meaningful tables and prompts an LLM to generate diagnostic analysis code.
Iteratively detects structural suboptimalities and corrects the policy.
Experiments on car racing and door opening report up to 15% better imitation-learning performance than zero-shot LLM-generated structures.
Achieves the same reinforcement-learning performance with 75% less compute, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of policy refinement. 1. Generate the initial structure by querying an LLM with the task description. 2. The updated program returns to parameter fitting and another refinement cycle. 6. Reinforcement learning after the structure aligns with the demonstrations to go beyond the demonstration performance.

papers.abstract: Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) provide semantic cues such as depth and segmentation useful for robotic manipulation, but directly deploying them in closed-loop control is impractical due to high computational cost, temporal inconsistency, and distribution shift between static internet images and egocentric robot observations. We propose All-For-One (AFO), a two-stage distillation framework that leverages VFMs strictly as privileged information during training, using downstream robotic data. Following the privileged learning paradigm, AFO decouples semantic representation learning from inference-time policy execution. In the All stage, a teacher policy fuses RGB observations with outputs from multiple VFMs to learn a semantically enriched representation. In the For-One stage, this knowledge is distilled in-distribution into a lightweight RGB-only student policy. Evaluated on two Adroit tasks and five MetaWorld tasks in simulation, as well as three real-world manipulation tasks, AFO outperforms prior foundation-model-based approaches while using over 30x fewer parameters than VFM-based encoders and 50x lower latency than its own teacher in simulation benchmarks, providing an efficient pathway for transferring foundation-model knowledge to robotic control.
bullets: Addresses the high cost, temporal inconsistency, and observation-distribution mismatch of deploying VFMs directly in closed-loop control.
Uses a two-stage privileged-learning framework: a teacher combines RGB with multiple VFM outputs, then transfers the learned representation to an RGB-only student.
The student performs inference without VFMs, decoupling semantic representation learning from policy execution.
Evaluated on Adroit and MetaWorld simulation tasks plus three real-world manipulation tasks.
Reports over 30× fewer parameters than VFM-based encoders and 50× lower latency than its teacher in simulation, while outperforming prior foundation-model-based approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the All-For-One (AFO) Framework. (a) All. A teacher network employs multiple VFMs (e.g., Molmo [10], SAM 2 [46], and DAM 2 [58]) with learnable lightweight encoders (fT RGB, fT object, f T depth). The resulting representations are aggregated and used to train a policy with a BC loss. (b) For One. A student lightweight RGB encoder (fS RGB) solely learns from the teacher network via a feature distillation loss with BC loss, which benefits from the rich knowledge of large VFMs.

papers.abstract: Long-term object search requires learning where objects usually appear from repeated but uneven observations of a changing environment. We formulate retrospective open-vocabulary memory as probabilistic inference from censored observations, where the key idea is to reason with evidence per opportunity: a detection or non-detection should influence belief only in proportion to the robot's opportunity to observe the corresponding location. We introduce ECROM, which uses this principle to estimate long-term prevalence for concepts specified only at query time and converts the resulting belief directly into an active-search prior. To evaluate this problem, we introduce a controlled long-term benchmark in ten HM3D homes that independently varies object placement and observation opportunity across repeated traversals. ECROM improves support-level AP on held-out queries by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric. The benchmark, dataset, and code will be open-sourced. Project page: https://jiaming.im/ecrom/
bullets: Addresses learning object-location prevalence from repeated, uneven observations.
Models detections and non-detections as censored evidence weighted by observation opportunity.
Supports concepts specified only at query time and converts beliefs into active-search priors.
Evaluated on a controlled benchmark spanning ten HM3D homes with varied placements and observation opportunities.
Improves support-level AP by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric.

papers.abstract: Integrating force awareness into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models involves not merely encoding wrench measurements as an additional modality, but determining when and how strongly physical interaction should influence robot action generation. Existing VLAs that use force typically inject it through a fixed pathway, without explicitly determining when it is relevant to the current action. This calls for an intermediate force relevance mechanism inside the VLA, in which visual-language context estimates the relevance of physical feedback to the current task before force enters the action pathway. FR-VLA addresses this gap with a Vision-Language Force-Reasoning Model that uses learnable force query tokens to derive a force admission signal grounded in visual-language context, and uses this signal to modulate an external tokenized force pathway for action generation. In real-world experiments on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, FR-VLA achieves the highest mean success rate over six evaluated stages, and trajectory visualizations show that its force admission varies with the interaction phase.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed force-injection pathways in existing vision-language-action models.
Uses learnable force query tokens to infer force relevance from visual-language context.
Modulates an external tokenized force pathway according to the inferred force admission signal.
Evaluated on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, achieving the highest mean success rate over six stages.
Force admission varies across interaction phases, suggesting context-dependent physical feedback use.

(b) The VLM-based Implicit Force Reasoning Module grounds force query states with visual features through cross-attention and decodes them into motion phase inference, producing the admission signal that determines when force information becomes action-relevant. (c) The Force Tokenizer Module discretizes wrench histories into contact-semantic codes via a frozen VQ-Encoder and uses their Code Embeddings to FiLM-condition the force pathway.

papers.abstract: Existing approaches to offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) struggle with long-horizon tasks. Discounting shrinks value differences between distant states until they fall below the function approximation error, leaving the agent with no signal for ranking states. Temporal abstraction, which treats k environment steps as a single transition, restores this signal at long range, but no single fixed k suits all state-goal distances: large k preserves value differences across long temporal distances while collapsing distinctions between nearby states, and small k does the reverse. We make this trade-off explicit and introduce Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA), which conditions a single value function on k. GITA trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values, so scales assigning larger positive advantages to a state-goal pair contribute more strongly to its update. GITA does not need to choose between local resolution and long-range signal; it retains both without committing to a single k. On OGBench, GITA outperforms a broad range of offline GCRL baselines, raising average success rate across all tasks by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL. It also improves over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA, by 7 percentage points (14% relative).
bullets: Offline GCRL struggles on long-horizon tasks because discounting weakens value differences between distant states.
A fixed temporal abstraction scale k creates a trade-off: large k helps long-range planning, while small k preserves nearby-state resolution.
GITA conditions one value function on k and trains a single policy using advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values.
On OGBench, GITA improves average success by 25 percentage points over HIQL and 7 points over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA.
The approach avoids committing to a single temporal abstraction scale, though its reported scope is offline GCRL on OGBench tasks.

papers.abstract: By learning transferable rewards, inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) enables counterfactual evaluation of agents under modified environments. Such transfer places strict requirements on coverage since target environments affect agents' state occupancy. We propose a multi-task IRL method that pools data across multiple agents with different rewards in the same environment under a low-rank assumption. In addition to alleviating coverage requirements, so each task need not visit every state as long as others do, the method offers scalable evaluation of multiple tasks under new environments as computationally intensive planning scales with rank rather than the number of tasks. We provide finite sample guarantees on reward recovery and on policy learning in new environments. Experiments show our method is robust to limited coverage, recovers rewards on and off of each task's support, transfers to target environments at lower regret than baselines, with its computational advantage over per-task methods widening as tasks grow.
bullets: Addresses limited state-coverage requirements in transferable inverse reinforcement learning.
Pools demonstrations from multiple tasks in the same environment under a low-rank reward assumption.
Scales planning with the reward rank rather than the number of tasks.
Provides finite-sample guarantees for reward recovery and policy learning in new environments.
Experiments show robustness to limited coverage, off-support reward recovery, lower transfer regret than baselines, and increasing computational benefits as tasks grow.

papers.abstract: This paper explores a reward-based policy to achieve zero-shot transfer between source and target environments with completely different observation spaces. While humans can demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities, deep neural network policies often struggle to adapt to a new environment and require a considerable amount of samples for successful transfer. Instead, we propose a novel reward-based policy only conditioned on rewards and actions, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new environments with completely different observations. We discuss the challenges and feasibility of a reward-based policy and then propose a practical algorithm for training. We demonstrate that a reward policy can be trained within three different environments, Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing, and transferred to completely different observations, such as different color palettes or 3D rendering, or Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim, in a zero-shot manner. We also demonstrate that a reward-based policy can further guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.
bullets: Targets the poor adaptation of observation-based deep policies when source and target observations differ substantially.
Introduces a reward-based policy that avoids dependence on environment-specific visual observations.
Presents a practical training algorithm and discusses the feasibility of reward-only conditioning.
Demonstrates zero-shot transfer across Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing settings, including visual changes and Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim.
Shows that the reward-based policy can also guide training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.

papers.abstract: This paper develops a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework to enable fast adaptation of interactive policies in a multi-agent system (MAS). Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) enables agents to rapidly adapt to new tasks/environments using a bi-level optimization mechanism. However, existing meta-RL generally focuses on single-agent systems. Extending these frameworks and algorithms to multi-agent systems poses additional challenges, as tasks are characterized by not only the environment but also agents' strategic interactions. To address these challenges, we model multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems as Markov games (MGs) and develop a meta-MARL framework for rapid interactive policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs. A new concept, called meta-NE, is defined to describe the desired solution concept in a meta-MARL problem. Sufficient conditions for the equivalence between a meta-NE and a stationary point of the gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithm are established. Our evaluation on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrates that the proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines, validating the effectiveness of our framework.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting policies across multi-agent tasks that vary in both environments and agent interactions.
Models multi-agent reinforcement learning problems as Markov games distributed across tasks.
Introduces meta-NE as a solution concept for meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Establishes sufficient conditions linking meta-NE solutions to stationary points of a gradient-play meta-MARL algorithm.
Evaluations on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrate faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines.

papers.abstract: Continuous policy optimization may spread an update across many states, even when deployment permits only a few complete state-level changes. We study how much discounted return can be retained when continuous row mixtures are rounded to sparse binary policies in finite MDPs. Policy-dependent visitation couples the row edits, while long horizons make global curvature bounds conservative. From $2d+2$ Bellman solves, we derive reusable envelopes that support uniform and candidate-specific guarantees before rounding. A rank-two rational representation of each exchange further permits weighted curvature integration along the realized trajectory. We prove that linear dimension dependence is unavoidable when the budget scales, and that exact global curvature thresholding is hard. Candidate-specific bounds raise pre-rounding certification coverage from $48.2\%$ to $74.1\%$ on the structured suite. At $γ=0.95$, local integration lowers the median bound-to-loss ratio from $402.3$ to $2.08$ on coupled instances.
bullets: Addresses sparse deployment when only a few complete state-level policy changes are allowed.
Uses $2d+2$ Bellman solves to construct reusable uniform and candidate-specific performance envelopes.
Employs a rank-two rational exchange representation and trajectory-based curvature integration for tighter certificates.
Candidate-specific bounds increase pre-rounding certification coverage from 48.2% to 74.1%.
At $\gamma=0.95$, local integration reduces the median bound-to-loss ratio from 402.3 to 2.08 on coupled instances.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon ego/exo data contains rich procedural evidence, but are redundant, noisy, and costly to process or retain. We propose a compact framework that converts continuous multimodal workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory, implemented as a Work Environment Model (WEM). Inspired by event segmentation theory, we detect boundaries using changes in visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence, rather than fixed windows or visual novelty alone. Each segment is abstracted into an evidence-linked event card containing actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. These event cards incrementally update the WEM, enabling compact, auditable documentation and retrieval under on-premise privacy constraints. We instantiate the design with frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders and a local language model, and outline evaluation criteria for segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon QA.
bullets: Segments continuous multimodal video at meaningful procedural boundaries using context, location, motion, narration, gaze, object interaction, and optional workspace evidence.
Summarizes each segment as an evidence-linked event card covering actors, timing, location, actions, objects, state changes, confidence, and provenance.
Incrementally builds a compact Work Environment Model (WEM) rather than retaining all raw video.
Uses frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders with a local language model under on-premise privacy constraints.
Proposes evaluation of segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon question answering.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Framework overview. Ego–exo recordings are processed offline with frozen encoders to extract visual, motion, gaze/object, narration, location, and exocentric cues. A multi-cue boundary score segments the stream into procedural events. Each event is converted into an evidence-linked event card and inserted into a Work Environment Model (WEM), which supports compact documentation, retrieval, and QA.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Procedural State Memory (WEM) for egocentric/exocentric video, utilizing event segmentation and semantic abstraction to build structured memory for agents, directly fitting the 'Learning from Human Videos' subtopic.
papers.title: A Framework for Egocentric and Exocentric Procedural Understanding via Temporal Segmentation and Semantic Abstraction
papers.tldr: A privacy-preserving framework compresses long-horizon egocentric and exocentric workplace video into an auditable procedural memory for retrieval and question answering.

papers.abstract: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning six action-video tasks. With only narrow-domain data, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.
bullets: Addresses the lack of native metric-3D human-action representations in modern video models.
Supports action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation.
Uses a role-adaptive action renderer and cross-stream action-video coupling to align motion with visual dynamics.
Covers six action-video tasks and generalizes from narrow-domain data to unseen scenes and interactions.
Provides effective action control and visual quality while preserving pretrained visual knowledge.

A shared frozen video VAE encodes rendered action and video into two latent streams. Cross-stream coupling (Sec. 3.3) uses joint self-attention and attention LoRAs activated only for generation targets, retaining the backbone weights and per-stream input structure. papers.tldr: EgoGeneralist adapts pretrained video generators to unify egocentric action understanding and generation in metric 3D space.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, but often fail during deployment. Teaching them to recover from these failures requires substantial corrective data: existing approaches learn to recover from failures by directly associating corrective actions with the observations in which they were demonstrated. For instance, DAgger-like fine-tuning can require tens to hundreds of interactions, yet the resulting policy may still fail to generalize the learned corrections beyond the demonstrated scenarios. We hypothesize that semantics can capture the underlying reasons for failures and their corrections, enabling policies to learn from only a handful of corrective demonstrations and generalize those corrections to novel objects, and scene variations. We propose OopsieRecover, a framework that uses abduction to infer the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and encodes the inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs. These costs capture when a behavior is undesirable and steer the policy toward more desirable action regions. We experiment across 6 tasks and variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks, and find that only a handful of corrective demonstrations can enable a VLA to overcome failures across a broad range of novel situations, without requiring new corrective data for each variation. Please refer to https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/oopsierecover for videos.
bullets: Targets the need for large amounts of corrective data and poor generalization in deployed VLA models.
Uses abduction to infer the intent behind corrective demonstrations.
Represents inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs that steer actions away from undesirable regions.
Evaluated across 6 tasks with variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks.
Reports successful recovery across broad novel situations without new corrective data for each variation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: OOPSIERECOVER: From semantic interventions to reusable VLA corrections. In OOPSIERECOVER, a human monitors VLA execution and intervenes to provide semantic corrections: a corrective trajectory and a language description for some type of correction, ci, (orange). We then synthesize the collected set of interventions for each correction type into a Semantically Grounded Gated Cost by i) parsing the sensorimotor demonstration as temporal point sets tracked on semantic scene entities, ii) generating gated costs from the motion of the point sets, and iii) verifying these costs by evaluating their capability to explain all human corrections of the same type (blue). During deployment (green), these costs determine when steering is needed and rank candidate actions using the learned corrective programs. This separates the intended correction from its demonstrated trajectory, allowing correction programs to be used in the environment where they are collected and to generalize to new situations, while the base VLA remains frozen.

Fig. 3: Simulation and real-world tasks. We evaluate a diverse set of tasks that elicit different types of corrections; avoiding collisions, improving placement precision, and correctly articulating objects.

Fig. 1: Learning reusable corrections from human interventions with OOPSIERECOVER. A human corrects a lid-closure failure and describes the intended behavior. OOPSIERECOVER grounds this feedback in semantic point sets, and uses abduction – finding a simple explanation consistent with the observed intervention – to synthesize a gated correction cost that steers a frozen VLA. (Right) The synthesized correction programs generalize: they can be reused under changed object poses and scene layouts, broadening the successful applicability of the VLA.

Fig. 5: Scaling with number of corrections. On CoffeeMug, OOPSIERECOVER rapidly reaches an 84% success rate with as few as 8 corrections, while HG-DAgger∗ achieves only 28% despite using three times as many corrections.

papers.title: OopsieRecover: Learning Transferable VLA Corrections from Semantic Interventions
papers.tldr: OopsieRecover uses semantic reasoning from a few corrective demonstrations to help VLA robots recover from failures and generalize across novel objects, scenes, and task variations.

papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from limited visual demonstrations is challenging because policies must acquire both perceptual grounding and precise control, while reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can acquire rich control behaviors from large-scale interaction with privileged information. We introduce \textbf{Latent RL Prior}, a two-stage framework that reuses this control knowledge for data-efficient visual policy learning. During privileged pretraining, we distill large-scale RL rollouts into a flow-matching action decoder conditioned on proprioception and latent task context. During visual adaptation, we freeze the decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images to its latent context using action supervision alone, without privileged labels or latent targets. The same decoder can further be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation. Across three simulated tasks, our method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 in the low-data regime; on door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses full-data baselines using $10\times$ and $5\times$ fewer demonstrations, respectively. Further analysis shows that direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation performance and training stability over routing visual predictions through the pretrained state encoder. Robustness to unseen mass variation and greater linear accessibility of contact-force information in decoder representations further provide evidence of retained RL-acquired control knowledge. Project website: https://yixiaowang7.github.io/latent-rl-prior-page/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of jointly learning visual grounding and precise dexterous control with scarce demonstrations.
Pretrains a flow-matching action decoder on privileged RL rollouts, then learns a visual-to-latent interface using action supervision alone.
The decoder can be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation.
Across three simulated tasks, it outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning baselines in low-data settings, using 10× and 5× fewer demonstrations on two tasks.
Direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation and stability; robustness to mass changes suggests retained RL control knowledge.

(b) Visual adaptation: an image encoder and Q-Former learn context tokens while the decoder remains frozen. papers.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.
bullets: Targets the high cost of autoregressively generating coordinates for visual plans such as points, boxes, and trajectories.
Uses a lightweight drafter to predict each primitive in one forward pass, adapting to its type, dimensionality, and length.
Trains on annotated primitives and accepts structurally valid predictions without requiring exact autoregressive token matching.
Reduces prediction errors across evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks and reports approximately 25× faster 3D point-motion generation.
A world action model using VFlash plans reaches 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces suites, versus 62.6% for the baseline.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.
bullets: Targets brittle VLA behavior in shifted, safety-critical real-world settings.
Probes latent layers of a VLA backbone with minimal inference overhead and supervises pre-failure trajectory segments.
Improves early detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline.
Maintains valid missed-detection and false-alarm bounds in up to 86% of unseen-task runs, versus at most 21% for baselines.
Predicts failure modes, improving unseen-task top-3 accuracy by up to 44% over a majority baseline; includes 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive. Each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3x speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.
bullets: Targets high VLA inference cost and distraction from redundant visual tokens, especially across multiple cameras and under distribution shift.
Uses segmentation-guided pruning to remove irrelevant patches, followed by saliency-guided attention biasing over retained visual tokens and language instructions.
On LIBERO-Spatial, removes 85% of scene-camera tokens while essentially matching unpruned success and improves OOD success by up to 7 percentage points.
Adds 7.8 ms per inference call for refinement and achieves up to 3.3× LLM-forward speedup at higher input resolutions.
Across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones, benefits are strongest in multi-camera settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two-stage T3R pipeline. Stage 1 (pruning): POS-weighted SigLIP text–patch similarity localizes the target; the topscoring patch positions (with SigLIP/DINOv2 features) prompt EfficientTAM to produce an object mask, which is converted to a patch-level pruning decision while preserving original RoPE positions, so only the “interested tokens” enter the LLM. Stage 2 (biasing): Integrated Gradients over the instruction identifies salient words; an additive attention bias (𝛽=2.0) is injected into the middle decoder layers for action-token queries, steering attention toward salient text tokens and retained visual patches before the action chunk is decoded.

Figure 4: OOD robustness under object-placement perturbation (21 noise levels, 10 episodes/task). T3R (Full Pipeline) tracks the unpruned baseline for small shifts and pulls ahead beyond ∼2 cm, leading by up to 7 pp at 4 cm, while TeamVLA degrades fastest. The crossover is consistent with pruning reducing misleading background context.

Figure 3: Most visual tokens are near-inert. (a) Across all 32 decoder layers, 93.9% of visual tokens receive <0.2% of the action queries’ attention each. (b) Per-patch action-query attention concentrates on a few task-relevant patches (here the gripper and target bowls), while the background receives negligible weight.

Figure 2: Qualitative pruning on a sparse LIBERO-Spatial scene (“pick up the bowl between the plate and the ramekin”). Top: input, POS-weighted SigLIP similarity, and the EfficientTAMmask with its point prompts. Middle: T3R keeps only 13/256 patches (95% pruned), tightly localized on the target. Bottom: TeamVLA’s similarity+expansion+merge retains 226/256 (12% pruned), leaving most of the background in the sequence through the early decoder layers.

Table 2: Cross-backbone generalization. Left: CogACT on SIMPLER (single camera), average SR (%); each keep ratio corresponds to the respective method’s native operating point. Right: 𝜋0.5 on RoboTwin (three cameras), SR (%) vs. per-camera token budget (base = 33.3). Best per column/row in bold.

Table 1: LIBERO-Spatial (OpenVLA-OFT). “Reduction” is scene-camera tokens pruned before decoder execution; latency is per VLA inference call. ∗ADP native operating point (67% of steps × 50%/step ≈ 33.5% reduction).

papers.selection_reason: Training-free token pruning and attention biasing for efficient, robust VLA robot inference; directly fits VLA and token pruning topics.
papers.title: T3R: Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement Towards Efficient and Robust VLA Models
papers.tldr: T3R enables faster and more robust VLA inference by pruning irrelevant visual tokens and biasing attention toward action-critical regions without training.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/
bullets: Addresses the lack of physical coordination in humanoid robots trained as solitary agents.
Uses a hierarchical system with shared-token sequence modeling for reactive and anticipatory human–robot motion generation.
Combines high-level motion generation with a low-level whole-body tracking controller for robot execution.
Introduces adaptive retargeting that preserves contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale.
Builds a 260-hour Human-Humanoid Interaction benchmark from five motion-capture datasets and demonstrates coordinated behavior in simulation and the real world.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Social Humanoid Architecture. From RGB-D observations of a human partner (red), we reconstruct the human pose and localize the body in 3D using depth and estimated gravity. Relative human and humanoid states are encoded through the VQ-VAE encoders Eh and Er. The resulting latent motion tokens z∗, relative pose transforms T ∗, and canonical motion transforms ∆T ∗ are concatenated and processed by the DFoT policy, then decoded via Dh and Dr to future human behavior (blue) and socially coordinated humanoid motion (purple). SONIC executes the motion in sim or the real-world, and the robot state is updated for closed-loop interaction.

Figure 5: Retargeting Qualitative Results. Each panel shows a ground-truth human–human interaction (ego in orange, partner in dark blue) next to its retargeted counterpart. The ego is retargeted to the humanoid (tan), and the partner’s pose is morphed to preserve interaction (light blue). Across diverse interactions our Adaptive-HHI Retargeting method preserves the contacts and relative positioning between the two agents.

Figure 6: Real-world deployment. Frames run left to right in time. Top two rows: separate highfive and hand-wave trials. Bottom: a single continuous take in which the humanoid transitions directly from a handshake into a bend

Figure 7: Shadow teleoperation. The G1 shadows a human operator performing arm movements (top) and sitting down on a couch (bottom). The operator’s motion is encoded with Eh, quantized against the shared codebook C, and decoded with Dr into humanoid motion. Frames run left to right in time.

Figure 3: Shared-Codebook VQ-VAE. Human and humanoid motion sequences are independently encoded into latent features and mapped to a shared vector-quantized codebook that learns a common motion vocabulary across embodiments. Embodiment-specific decoders reconstruct the respective motions, enabling aligned, transferable motion representations between humans and humanoids.

Figure 4: Adaptive-HHI Retargeting. Our retargeting pipeline starts from two ground truth humans. In the first pass, we retarget the ego human (orange) to the humanoid using a contact-adaptive weight matrix to encourage body pose in regions close to the physical interaction to be preserved. In a second pass, we co-morph the partner’s pose towards more plausible interaction via a contactgated morphing strategy driven by the amount of physical contact present in the interaction.

Figure A.1: Cross-embodiment motion translation with a shared-codebook VQ-VAE. Human motion (red) is encoded into a discrete latent space shared between the human and humanoid embodiments, then decoded into humanoid motion (purple). Each example shows three frames of the input human motion alongside the translated humanoid motion in simulation (top row), and the same frames executed on the physical humanoid robot (bottom row).
Table 3: Retargeting comparison across three interaction datasets. Best per column in bold; ↑/↓ indicate higher/lower is better.

Table A.2: Comparison of retargeting methods. Adaptive-HHI extends OmniRetarget’s interaction-mesh SOCP base with partner co-morphing (joint optimization over the partner SMPLX) and distance-weighted, wrist-boosted adaptive Laplacian weighting for interaction and humanscale preservation.

Table A.6: Network configuration details. T is the raw sequence length and T ′ = T/ω the number of tokens after temporal compression (ω=4); P is the number of interacting agents; Din is the peragent pose dimension (Dh or Dr); Dc is the local conditioning dimension; de is the embedding dimension; and Dm = dvq + 4 × 9 × P is the unified motion token dimension tracking localized cross-agent transformations.
Table A.1: Summary statistics of our retargeted benchmark. Clip counts, frames, and durations are reported after retargeting each source dataset to the Unitree G1 with Adaptive-HHI.
Table A.4: Retargeting hyperparameters. Values are shared across all datasets without per-clip tuning.
Table A.3: Adaptive retargeting ablation on CHI3D. Mean ± std over clips. Best per column in bold.

Table A.5: Shared-codebook design ablation on HHI. H and R denote human and robot motion; H→R and R→H denote encoding in one embodiment and decoding in the other. FD is Fréchet distance. MPJPE is the root-relative mean per-joint position error of the decoded pose against ground truth (cm; 21 SMPL-X body joints for H, 29 actuated joints of the G1 for R, hands excluded). Code Agree. is the fraction of paired H/R frames assigned the same code. Best per column in bold.
Table A.7: End-to-End Latency.
Table 4: Success rate (%) in sim and on the real G1.

papers.tldr: Social Humanoid enables a 29-DoF humanoid robot to generate and execute socially responsive, whole-body motions coordinated with a human partner.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 2D vision-language pre-training and reliable 3D robotic manipulation.
Jointly trains action prediction with alignment between VLA visual features and a frozen 3D perception model.
Unifies heterogeneous robot datasets across embodiments, tasks, scenes, and geometric annotations.
Uses feature-dependent layer aggregation, partial depth/calibration, and probabilistic state dropout to improve spatial supervision and visual reliance.
Training-only auxiliary components enable direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights without changing inference.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Depth probing of the visual embeddings of VLAs. Embeddings learned solely from 2D images without alignment do not produce meaningful spatial structures. The aligned embeddings inherently contain rich spatial information, leading to better performance in depth probing.

Figure 3 Comparison of rotational action distributions. (a) Euler-angle representations with direct subtraction for relative-rotation targets. (b) Rotation-vector representations with relative rotations computed through SO(3) composition. In (a), angular wrapping produces outliers near ±2π, which widen the interval between the 1st and 99th percentiles. This severely compresses the range of typical action values after normalization, hindering training.

Figure 5 Produce manipulation tasks under human perturbations and embodiment changes. A–C conditions share a policy post-trained on 100 demonstrations collected in the A scene configuration, with no additional demonstrations of the perturbations in B or C scene. D condition evaluates a policy jointly post-trained on 100 Piper demonstrations collected in the A scene and 10 Franka demonstrations collected in the D scene.
Figure 1 SLA unifies heterogeneous robot data, aligns intermediate visual embeddings with frozen 3D features during training, and improves benchmark and real-world manipulation performance.

Figure 6 Tabletop manipulation tasks under changes in object, table height, and instruction target. All four conditions share a policy post-trained on 100 demonstrations collected in the E scene configuration. The bottle, tissue box, pen, and watch are included in these demonstrations while black tape and carrot are excluded.

Figure 4 Continual pre-training data scaling ablation. SLA alignment is independently enabled or disabled during continual pre-training and post-training. All curves start at the shared π0.5 baseline. Experiments are conducted under RoboTwin Clean2Random settings to evaluate success rates (%, ↑).

Per-task results are shown in Table 12. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best displayed values, with ties treated equally.

Table 4 RoboCasa-Panda benchmark success rates (%, ↑). Per-task results are shown in Table 13. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best displayed values.

Bold and underline denote the best and second-best displayed values.

Table 8 State dropout ablation. Experiments are conducted on RoboTwin to evaluate success rates (%, ↑).
