papers.selection_reason: Spatial-Language-Action model scaling spatial alignment via continual pre-training; directly relevant to VLA, robot learning, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
papers.tldr: SLA scales spatial understanding in vision-language-action models through continual pre-training on diverse robot experience while preserving the original inference architecture.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.
bullets: Addresses the sensitivity of imitation-learned visuomotor policies to camera and robot-base viewpoint changes in mobile manipulation.
Separately reconstructs static scenes and manipulated objects using 3D Gaussian Splatting and feed-forward 3D foundation models.
Uses kinematics-based action retargeting to render novel viewpoints and pair them with geometrically consistent transformed actions.
Evaluated on five real-world tasks with rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, plus simulation-based fidelity validation.
More than doubles average success over the strongest baseline and retains non-trivial success at large base displacements where baselines fail.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of MOMASPLAT. 3D Reconstruction: We build 3D models of the environment from the navigation and manipulation data. We estimate camera poses via structure-from-motion and fit a 3D Gaussian Splatting model of the static scene, Gscene. For the dynamic objects, we segment each manipulated object and estimate its per-frame pose trajectory with a feed-forward 3D foundation model; since the scene and object poses lie in separate reference frames, we align them with a Sim(3) transformation and fit a separate object model Gobj. Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses: Given a robot base pose, T̃ , sampled around the original demonstration poses (left), we render the scene and object from the new viewpoint, transform the source end-effector trajectory into the new base frame to render the robot from a simulator, and composite the three streams into a photorealistic novel observation. Paired with the transformed actions ã1:Lj , this forms a synthetic demonstration; repeating across sampled poses yields the generated dataset. Imitation Learning: the policy is trained on the union of source and generated demonstrations.

Fig. 4: Policy success across base poses. For each task, we evaluate 12 unseen base locations distributed across categorical distance bins that vary per task, with 3 trials per pose, and report success rate by distance to the nearest demonstration pose. The shaded gray region denotes the original base poses; locations 5–50 cm away are unseen deployment poses. MOMASPLAT maintains substantially higher success as the base pose shifts away from the source demonstrations (where Source Only is labeled “Original data only”).

Fig. 1: MOMASPLAT. Starting from mobile-manipulation data collected at the original base pose (white and red robot), MOMASPLAT synthesizes demonstrations from sampled novel base poses (yellow-outlined gray robot). The top-right sequence shows the source manipulation demonstration, while the bottom-right shows the corresponding synthesized trajectory, including the dynamic object as it is moved by the robot. Augmenting the source manipulation dataset with these demonstrations enables execution from unseen deployment-time base poses (blue-outlined gray robot).

Fig. 5: Spatial distribution of policy evaluation poses. Top-down view of each task showing the table and target-object locations, the original demonstration base poses, and the test base poses used for policy evaluation. Original demonstration poses are marked with circles, while evaluation poses are marked with squares; arrows indicate the robot heading at each pose. Evaluation poses are colored by MOMASPLAT policy success rate, providing spatial context for the distance-based results in Fig. 4.

Fig. 3: Tasks and scenes used in our experiments. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world manipulation tasks across three scenes (top: scenes; bottom: per-task close-ups), covering manipulation of both rigid and articulated objects. The simulated scene and its task, SIM PICK-PLACE BOTTLE (right of the dashed lines), are used to measure the fidelity of MOMASPLAT’s generated demonstrations against ground truth.

TABLE I: Generated-observation fidelity against simulator ground truth. Mean ± std over 75 generated demonstrations spanning viewpoints with distances of 0.4–27.3 cm from the reconstruction views. Full image, object, and robot use every tenth frame (2486 total frames), with object and robot restricted to their masks; scene PSNR evaluation uses one frame per demonstration (75 in total).

papers.selection_reason: Novel-view demonstration augmentation for mobile manipulation using 3D Gaussian Splatting and 3D foundation models; fits robot learning and 3D foundation model interests.
papers.title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: MOMASPLAT augments mobile-manipulation demonstrations with viewpoint-consistent synthetic trajectories that include dynamic object interactions, substantially improving robustness to unseen robot base poses.

papers.abstract: Robotic perception increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensor suites combining cameras with emerging modalities (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, and thermal). Yet existing simulators idealize these sensors, hiding critical modality-specific failure modes that limit real-world deployment. We present VisionSIM, a unified, physically grounded simulation platform that elevates sensor realism to a first-class concern by modeling the raw physical measurement process for diverse conventional and emerging modalities. We expose fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters, reproducing failure modes overlooked by general-purpose simulators: pileup and glare for LiDAR; phase wrapping, saturation, and motion artifacts for iToF; refractory drops for event cameras; and history-dependent emission for thermal cameras. This enables principled cross-modality comparison on identical scenes and trajectories. We release the platform and a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.
bullets: Supports cameras, event cameras, SPAD/LiDAR, iToF/dToF, and thermal sensors in a unified framework.
Models raw physical measurement processes with fine-grained sensor-parameter control.
Reproduces modality-specific effects such as pileup, glare, phase wrapping, saturation, motion artifacts, refractory drops, and history-dependent emission.
Enables controlled cross-modality comparisons on shared scenes and trajectories.
Provides a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Multi-modal, high-fidelity and controllable sensor emulation. Robotic simulation pipelines often focus on scene content, overlooking physically accurate sensor modeling. VisionSIM aims to bridge this gap by emulating diverse sensor types and their failure modes. (Top) A single scene is rendered once with dense ground truth — color, depth, optical flow, surface normals, segmentation, point map, direct and indirect illumination, and a temperature map. (Middle) The same scene is then replayed through a breadth of sensor models. (Bottom) Each model exposes and enables sweeping across the sensor’s physical parameters (e.g., thermal time constant, correlation function, event thresholds), thereby reproducing modality-specific failure modes.

Figure 5: Simulation Fidelity. Comparison of simulated vs. captured scenes. The top two rows are simulated end-to-end using a digital twin of the real scene, while the bottom two emulate the corresponding sensors from a co-located conventional camera capture (inset).

Figure 3: Transient Thermal Simulation: Thermal video of ceramic, steel, and aluminum cups over the 4 seconds following a hot-tea fill. The distinct heating rates reflect each material’s thermal diffusivity (α = 2, 18.8, 97 mm2/s, respectively).

Figure 2: Indirect Time-of-Flight (iToF) simulation and failure cases: (Top) Ground truth RGB scene, ground truth depth map, and ideal correlation measurements (taps 1, 2, and 3) for a conventional sinusoidal coding scheme. (Bottom) Common iToF failure cases and their effects on depth reconstruction, including: incorrect modulation frequency (causing phase wrapping), sensor saturation (clipping correlation measurements), ambient light corruption (reducing signal-to-noise ratio, especially for farther objects), motion blur (multi-tap artifacts from scene dynamics), and sensor noise and quantization artifacts (high frequency depth errors).

Figure 4: Application Case-Studies: (Top) A digital twin of a commercial LiDAR, where sensor parameters such as dead time and impulse response function are estimated from real-world data to correct for artifacts like range-walk. (Middle) Sensor modality migrations: VisionSIM can uplift existing datasets (e.g., XVFI [44]) or high-speed renders to emulate new sensor modalities like single-photon or event cameras. (Bottom) Sensor suite evaluation: VisionSIM enables rapid evaluation of different sensor configurations for perception tasks.

Table 3: Landscape of computer vision datasets. Existing datasets focus primarily on specific modalities (e.g., event cameras or LiDAR) or lack advanced sensor emulation (e.g., SPADs or thermal), VisionSIM provides a comprehensive suite of multi-modal data including HDR stereo views, optical flow, point maps, and a wide variety of physically-based sensor emulations in a single unified dataset.

Table 2: Failure modes and parameters modeled by VisionSIM. For each supported modality, we list the non-idealities and failure modes VisionSIM reproduces and the principal user-controllable parameters. Full forward models for all modalities are given in Appendix S.3.

Table 1: Computational imaging modality taxonomy. Each modality is characterized by its raw physical measurement and the recoverable scene properties. The Sim. and HW columns indicate simulation and hardware maturity, respectively. Outlook glyphs indicate likely near- to mid-term trajectories in availability and adoption. *Currently supported by VisionSIM.

papers.selection_reason: Physically grounded multi-modal sensor simulation platform for robot perception, directly supporting embodied robot learning.
papers.title: VisionSIM: Beyond Idealized Sensors - A Multi-Modal Simulator for Robot Perception
papers.tldr: VisionSIM is a physically grounded, multi-modal simulator that models realistic sensor measurements and failure modes for robot perception.

papers.abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\% vs. 0.63\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.
bullets: Targets online 3D bin packing with unknown arrivals, jointly selecting boxes, orientations, and placements while avoiding stack collapse.
Uses a 3D U-Net to predict placement stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives.
Integrates stability estimates into a discrete actor–critic’s action values and policy prior, with gates for unreliable or changing predictions.
Reaches 73% utilization in 0.4M Isaac Gym steps versus about 1M without stability modeling; on 60 boxes, achieves 0.734 utilization versus 0.588 for GOPT.
Shows higher placement-failure frequency than GOPT (1.03% vs. 0.63%), and is demonstrated on a real robot without added deployment search or simulation overhead.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: SHORE framework. The bin configuration Ct and the buffer dt are encoded as EMS tokens and (box, orientation) item tokens, and the rule-based mask m keeps the geometrically valid pairs. The actor, a Packing Transformer, scores every valid pair and samples the action a = (u, k), which Isaac Gym executes and adjudicates by Eq. (2). A second Packing Transformer, the critic, values every pair in one pass, and a discretized REPPO learner updates both from on-policy rollouts (Sec. IV-B).

Fig. 3: Training curves on the base box set for the methods of Table III, up to 1M environment steps, computed from training episodes as in Fig. 4. (a) Mean reward of training episodes (packed volume fraction). (b) Fraction of training episodes that end in a collapse. (c) Collapses per placement attempt (log scale). The original GOPT runs did not log how training episodes end, so GOPT appears only in (a).

Fig. 4: Training curves on the expanded (FBA) box set. (a) Mean reward of training episodes (packed volume fraction), with actions sampled from each method’s training policy. (b) Fraction of training episodes that end in a collapse; the others end with no feasible placement. (c) Collapses per placement attempt during training (log scale), pooled over the training episodes in each window. All three panels are computed from training episodes. A method whose episodes collapse long before the bin fills stays near 1 in (b) even as its collapses per placement fall in (c). The curves end at 1M steps, the checkpoint evaluated in Table IV.

Fig. 5: An illustration of the scenes of one evaluation episode on the expanded box set, with the same box arrivals for all four methods, rendered in Isaac Gym after the episode ends. Each panel shows the final stack (left) and the table from above (right) with its stack and the boxes still waiting on the table. papers.title: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
papers.tldr: SHORE improves online 3D bin-packing efficiency by combining learned placement-stability probabilities with on-policy reinforcement learning, achieving faster learning and higher utilization while accepting slightly more placement risk.

papers.abstract: Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to estimate the motion of a robot team. These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the team's estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e., gauge drift. In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses. Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a Gaussian information matrix and vector pair. RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map. The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty. We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose estimates and covariances. Across $1000$ simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation. Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from $0.542$m to $0.140$m in a $50\times50$m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.
bullets: Addresses drift in team position and orientation that relative odometry and inter-robot measurements cannot resolve.
Converts radio attenuation residuals into Gaussian information matrices and vectors for integration with pose estimation.
Models detectable shared motions and preserves robot–time correlations when the map is uncertain.
Matches joint-estimation results across 1,000 simulated Gaussian trials.
In 32 paired registered-map trials, reduced common-position RMSE from 0.542 m to 0.140 m versus a radio-weighted relative-measurement baseline.

papers.abstract: Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough. Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory. Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle's progress). Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.
bullets: Built a Gymnasium testbed that simulates ultrasound from public patient CT data.
Provides replaceable slots for organ segmentation, control, and reward methods.
Evaluated 20 published methods across 60 episodes from six held-out patients.
Only an SSIM-based reward improved the guide detectably; the final baseline reached 13.7 mm error versus 1.5 mm for a pose oracle.
Results are exploratory, simulation-only, and no guide was tested on hardware.

papers.abstract: We introduce GPWM, a Generative Particle World Model that predicts how 3D scenes evolve by generating the motion of particles and rigid bodies over time. Unlike video world models that generate scene appearance, GPWM operates directly in 3D physical space. A single representation and architecture cover rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials, in both passive physics and robotic interaction. GPWM is an object-aware multi-resolution transformer that combines flow matching with diffusion forcing to generate coherent physical trajectories far beyond its training horizon. We train and evaluate GPWM on ParticleWorlds, a 25.5-million-frame corpus spanning diverse geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments. GPWM outperforms the best prior learned-dynamics baseline in each of six physical domains, reducing prediction error by 31% on average. Breaking from the domain-specific setting of prior methods, a single Unified GPWM models these heterogeneous regimes with one set of weights, largely outperforming per-domain baselines and even surpassing our own specialist models in two domains. GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical properties, object counts, and rollout horizons. Beyond prediction, GPWM enables contact-rich planning by learning a generative prior over joint actuator-object motion. Instead of searching over unconstrained actions, planning searches the model's latent noise for interactions that achieve a desired object-space goal. With the same world model, noise-space planning substantially outperforms action-space search on pushing and picking, where complex contact sequences are hard to discover. Executed open-loop in simulation, the resulting plans achieve goal-directed manipulation without reference action trajectories or goal-specific policies.
bullets: Models rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials in passive and robotic-interaction settings with one representation and architecture.
Uses an object-aware multi-resolution transformer with flow matching and diffusion forcing to generate coherent long-horizon trajectories.
Trained and evaluated on the 25.5-million-frame ParticleWorlds corpus spanning varied geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments.
Reduces prediction error by 31% on average across six physical domains versus the strongest prior learned-dynamics baseline, while generalizing beyond training conditions.
Enables noise-space planning for pushing and picking, outperforming action-space search without reference trajectories or goal-specific policies.

papers.abstract: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.
bullets: Criteria Exposure (CE) gives agents access to success criteria originally designed to verify imitation-learned policies.
With CE, the self-improving agent quickly achieves higher success under the provided criteria.
This advantage disappears when criteria are slightly changed, and skills transfer poorly across tasks.
Instruction-faithful criteria better reflect whether agent-generated programs complete the instructed task.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of the self-improvement loop. Left, learning: the actor (GPT-6 Astra, high reasoning effort) writes and executes Python cells that call the robot’s primitives on five development layouts, and sees the result of each cell. Between batches the learner (Claude Code with Opus 5.5, high reasoning effort) turns the evidence into one revision of the library ℒ𝑘 , whose skills are callable code that reports what it did and whose memory entries say when to apply what, with the evidence for it; a revision is usually tried first in verification rollouts, and the loop rolls back to the best revision so far when a batch falls clearly below it. Whether the learner also sees the success criteria is the one switch between the two settings, w/ CE and w/o CE (the switch under the learner). Right, evaluation: the final library ℒ𝐾 is frozen and read-only, and the same actor runs alone on layouts the loop never saw.

papers.abstract: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.
bullets: Addresses the need to manually engineer proposition-grounding functions for reward machines.
An LLM generates the reward machine from a natural-language task description.
A VLM grounds reward-machine propositions in image observations during policy learning.
A VLM-based value estimator provides dense rewards based on progress toward reward-machine transitions.
Across grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection, it achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods.

papers.abstract: Robot-mediated rehabilitation has the potential to deliver high-intensity, individualized therapy, but existing systems (which have not consistently improved outcomes) typically prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery. To address this gap, and ultimately enable activation-optimizing rehabilitation robot behavior, we present a personalizable transformer-based model mapping individuals' muscle activations (as measured via surface electromyography) to prescribed contact force trajectories when interacting with an end-effector rehabilitation robot. The model uses a transformer encoder-decoder leveraging rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to generate a latent representation of trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors, and augments trajectory prediction with flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution. Using data from 16 healthy participants completing 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, we evaluate generalization across held-out tasks and users, as well as the feasibility of user-specific fine-tuning within a therapy-session timescale. The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of <8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15% error accumulated throughout the task. These results provide a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription in robot-mediated rehabilitation and establish a foundation for future validation in clinical populations. Data and code have been open-sourced as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of prescribing kinematics without explicitly targeting recovery-related muscle activations.
Combines a transformer encoder-decoder with rotary positional embeddings and flow matching to generate user-specific trajectory distributions.
Evaluated on 16 healthy participants across 15 isometric tracking tasks, including held-out users, tasks, and session-timescale fine-tuning.
Achieved under 8% mean trajectory prediction error and approximately 15% accumulated error in a live neuromotor-activation test.
Provides a proof of concept; clinical-population validation remains future work.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of trajectory prescription model. Latent representation z of both target-associated information (zv) and unknown neuromotor behavior (zU ) is generated using a RoPE [22] transformer encoder (blue flow), then decoded separately to generate prescribed trajectory v̂target (green flow) and estimated activation â (turquoise flow). A flow-matching diffusion model [7] is also trained to generate a conditional distribution of zv given zU whose samples can be passed through the target trajectory decoder to generate a distribution over v̂target (orange flow).

Figure 1: End-effector robot-mediated rehabilitation platform. Users exert forces on a LBR iiwa 14 R820 7-degree-of-freedom cobot (KUKA AG, Augsburg, Germany; a) via a custom handle attached to a SensONE 6-axis force torque sensor (Bota Systems AG, Zürich, Switzerland; b). Users’ forces along each positional axis are mapped to the corresponding x/y/z velocity of an on-screen avatar ball (c), where the z axis into and out of the screen is represented by a decrease and increase in avatar size, respectively. Users are instructed to follow a target ball along a displayed trajectory. Force and game trajectory data (of both avatar and target) are collected at 1000 Hz and 60 Hz, respectively. During this process, two Trigno Quattro 4-channel sensor motes (d), controlled through a Trigno Base Station (Delsys, Inc., Natick, MA, USA) collect surface electromyography (sEMG) data at a rate of 2.22 kHz from 8 upper limb muscles (e). Electrode placements are as follows: anterior deltoid (AD), middle deltoid (MD), posterior deltoid (PD), and biceps brachii (BB), grounded at the acromion (G1); and triceps brachii (long head, TR), brachioradialis (BR), wrist flexors (FL), and wrist extensors (EX), grounded at the olecranon (G2). All data are collected and synchronized via Redis (MongoDB, Inc., New York, NY, USA). Full implementation details are included with code release.

papers.abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, completes only 53.5% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline replay benchmarks and real-world interaction, where assistant responses affect user behavior and task outcomes.
Provides simulators for cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface tasks, plus persona-conditioned users with execution errors and out-of-plan behavior.
Introduces IVG-Bench with 315 interaction scenarios for evaluating visual grounding, actionable guidance, latency, and task completion.
The best evaluated model completed 53.5% of tasks within the time limit; the interaction-quality metric achieved 78.5% agreement with human preferences.
A proof-of-concept GRPO experiment improved task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B in the cooking environment.

papers.abstract: 3D-aware representations can improve robotic manipulation by providing geometric information that is robust to changes in viewpoint, object position, and occlusion. However, using 3D inputs at deployment requires additional sensing and processing, making image-based policies more practical. We ask whether an image-based policy can acquire 3D shape information during training while retaining a purely image-based interface at deployment. We propose shape-teacher alignment, a training-time mechanism that uses a pretrained 3D shape representation as an alignment target for an image-based policy encoder. Specifically, we use Point-MAE features from individual objects as targets for corresponding image patches, transferring geometric structure to the policy without changing its deployment inputs or architecture. On LIBERO, shape-teacher alignment produces image representations that are more structured around object shape and corresponding parts, while substantially accelerating policy convergence and improving success rates. For pretrained policies, convergence is accelerated by 4.7x and 5.6x on the Object and Spatial suites, respectively, without requiring the shape teacher or depth input at deployment.
bullets: Motivation: Image-only policies are easier to deploy, but lack the viewpoint- and occlusion-robust geometric information provided by 3D representations.
Method: Align image patches with corresponding pretrained Point-MAE features from individual objects during training.
Contribution: Enables an image-based policy encoder to acquire object-shape and part-level structure without changing its deployment interface or architecture.

Results: On LIBERO, alignment improves shape-structured representations, policy success rates, and convergence speed; pretrained policies converge 4.7× and 5.6× faster on the Object and Spatial suites.
Scope: The 3D shape teacher and depth input are used only during training, not deployment.

papers.abstract: We investigate the problem of scaling safe reinforcement learning (safe RL) to massively parallel training regimes, where a large number of environments are exe- cuted with short rollout horizons. Although this setting improves data throughput and wall-clock efficiency, it creates a mismatch with constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), whose safety constraints are defined over full-episode cost returns. We address this mismatch by analyzing staggered environment resets as a phase-mixture distribution over short trajectory segments. This analysis charac- terizes the bias induced by phase coverage and motivates a phase-aggregated cost estimator that reconstructs episode-level cost estimates from short rollout batches. We further incorporate finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch into a constraint-tightening framework, yielding a scalable Safe RL method compatible with on-policy optimization. Using an MJX-based implementation of Safety Gym, our experiments show that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to non-massively parallel implementations while substantially reducing wall-clock training time.
bullets: Massive parallelism improves throughput but conflicts with CMDP constraints defined over full episodes.
The work models staggered resets as a phase-mixture distribution over short trajectory segments.
A phase-aggregated cost estimator reconstructs episode-level costs from short rollout batches.
Constraint tightening accounts for finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch.
In MJX-based Safety Gym experiments, the method matches non-massively parallel performance with substantially lower wall-clock training time.

papers.abstract: Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.
bullets: Evaluates in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning across long-horizon manipulation tasks and three robot embodiments.
Uses harder initial conditions from existing benchmarks in an extensible MuJoCo-based framework with modular task, agent, and interface components.
GPT-6 Astra scores 49.8% versus Claude Fable 5.1 at 43.6%, indicating substantial room for improvement.
Most failures involve poor strategy selection or imprecise execution rather than scene misunderstanding; agents falsely claim success on 24–39% of subtasks.
A single in-context demonstration or self-revised prompt substantially improves Astra’s performance on a five-task subset.

papers.abstract: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $π_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
bullets: Motivation: Existing world-action and vision-language-action policies inherit costly architectures designed for video or language generation rather than control.
Method: Train a policy transformer from scratch in pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 feature space; use action-conditioned future-feature prediction during training, but generate only actions at inference.
Results: La-JEPA attains state-of-the-art average performance among policies without embodied pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0 and corrected-instruction LIBERO-Plus benchmarks.
Efficiency: Its S and B variants run 2–5× faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming them on the reported benchmarks.
Design insight: JEPA features outperform video-VAE latents, and training-time future prediction helps even when omitted during inference; real-robot performance is comparable to π0.5 on four tasks.

papers.abstract: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.
bullets: Targets dense optical flow on MCUs, where limited on-chip SRAM restricts input resolution.
PACE-NAS separates macro design for peak SRAM from micro search over operators and depths for accuracy–latency trade-offs.
Replacing transposed convolutions and adding lightweight context modules reduces memory use and endpoint error without increasing peak SRAM.
MCUFlowNet-S runs 1.76× faster than retrained EdgeFlowNet with 1.6% higher EPE, and avoids collisions more often in simulated forest flights.
The framework also speeds up a PIDNet-S semantic-segmentation variant by 1.17× at similar accuracy.

papers.abstract: Robot reinforcement learning increasingly runs environments outside the trainer: in another process, on another machine, in another language. Many faults at this boundary raise no error. We make the boundary a wire protocol and ask what notices a fault in it. On Pendulum, HalfCheetah, Hopper and a 7-joint arm (Pusher), we injected up to 23 faults into what crosses the wire and 2 into the trainer's log, from one value to every value. Unless every value was wrong, a learning-curve threshold caught at most one run in ten, and a comparison with ten fault-free seeds at most 21%. A clean evaluation of all 1,060 final policies agreed with the curves: of the 728 boundary-fault runs both curve checks passed, 723 scored no more than three standard deviations below fault-free seeds, though nearly all ended on other weights and, for reward faults, logged other returns. Checks of the run itself, not of its outcome, saw every fault. A step ledger kept on both sides and compared step by step caught and located every fault that crossed, on Pendulum, Hopper and Pusher on one machine and on Pendulum across two, with no fault-free run and, on Pendulum, a median 3% more training time. An episode record kept at the environment caught the faults in the trainer's log. We list such faults found in practice, in Gymnasium 1.3 and our own code and, reported by others, in five multi-agent libraries, and recommend a step ledger and episode counts kept at the environment.
bullets: The study examines silent faults in wire-protocol communication between distributed RL environments and trainers.
Across four tasks, learning-curve and fault-free-seed comparisons detected few faults unless nearly every value was corrupted.
A clean evaluation of 1,060 final policies confirmed that most faulty runs appeared normal by outcome, despite using different weights or logging different returns.
A step ledger maintained on both sides caught and located every tested boundary fault, with a reported median 3% training-time increase on Pendulum.
Environment-side episode records detected faults introduced in the trainer's log; the authors recommend both mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Frontier-based exploration systems repeatedly evaluate geodesic travel costs between robot poses and candidate viewpoints, and tour-based planners consume the full pairwise distance matrix built from them. Recomputing these matrices with one graph search per source scales with the explored map size, whereas distance caches that refresh only locally affected or newly created frontiers can retain stale costs between surviving pairs when newly discovered free space creates a global shortcut. We present H-TRIP (Hierarchical Tropical Rank-one Incremental Propagation), an exact distance index grounded in Kleene algebra over the min-plus semiring for monotonically growing occupancy grids. H-TRIP partitions the known map into a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports. Each unknown-to-free revelation is decomposed into efficient rank-one min-plus edge insertions at the affected leaf, and only decreased port-to-port summaries are propagated along its ancestor chain. A shared hierarchical lift evaluates the dense many-to-many matrix of shortest distances for all active query points on the occupancy map. We prove that sequential insertions preserve exact shortest-path distances on the grid. Benchmark experiments confirm exact agreement with reference searches on fully built maps and show that dense many-to-many queries at a few dozen viewpoints are up to two orders of magnitude faster than sequential k x BFS. On exploration runs with sixteen robots, in-loop queries on the growing occupancy graph are 2.21x-8.59x faster than co-scheduled k x BFS on maps with side 256, 512, and 1024 cells.
bullets: Addresses stale distance caches and the high cost of recomputing pairwise geodesic distances as maps expand.
Uses a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports and rank-one min-plus updates for each newly revealed free-space region.
Propagates only decreased port-to-port summaries through affected ancestor nodes, then lifts them to query-point distances.
Proves exactness under sequential occupancy-grid insertions and matches reference graph searches on completed maps.
Achieves up to two orders of magnitude faster dense queries than sequential k×BFS; sixteen-robot runs are 2.21×–8.59× faster on tested map sizes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. One occupancy opening climbs the hierarchy of Fig. 2, whose leaves have side b = 5 and whose super-tiles aggregate g = 2 children. (a) On child T2, a newly free cell decreases occupancy adjacency at its neighbors, and RepairClosure shortens paths to the perimeter so that those decreases leave as ∆ST2 on BT2 . (b) Super-tile U1 receives that summary through φT2→U1 together with a newly passable seam, after which RepairClosure writes ∆SU1 on BU1 . (c) Super-tile U5 applies the same interface step to its 10×10 children U1, . . . , U4, where φU1→U5 plants ∆SU1 and RepairClosure writes ∆SU5 on BU5 .

(b) Super-tile U (g = 2) aggregates child boundaries into VU : interior cells are condensed into summaries STi , dark blue perimeter cells form exposed parent ports BU , and light blue cells are interior seams where gold arrows mark passable cross-child edges.

papers.title: H-TRIP: Exact Many-to-Many Distance Index for Multi-Robot Exploration
papers.tldr: H-TRIP maintains exact shortest-path distances on growing occupancy maps while accelerating dense many-to-many queries for multi-robot exploration.

papers.abstract: Current 4D occupancy world models use heavy cross-attention or deep recurrence to disentangle ego-motion from scene dynamics. This requires significant computational capacity. However, this effort is largely redundant since the ego-vehicle's intended future motion is provided by the downstream motion planner. We present FreeOcc, a lightweight continuous-time world model that introduces explicit $SE(2)$ geometric decoupling into a conditional flow-matching framework. By mathematically factoring out self-motion, we create a purely dynamic feature space. This space supports attention-free temporal fusion and allows physics-constrained ODEs to operate strictly on residual agent kinematics. To maximize deployment efficiency, FreeOcc introduces an uncertainty-aware blending mechanism. This routes well-observed voxels to a single-pass decoder, reserving the ODE solver exclusively for ambiguous, high-uncertainty regions. Requiring only 28.3M parameters-roughly 40% of comparable models-our optimal ensemble mode (FreeOcc-E) runs at 27 FPS. On nuScenes, FreeOcc achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance with a 0.47 m Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD) and 32.1% mIoU. Furthermore, the model transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI. It also proves highly robust, retaining 92.8% of its ideal mIoU under significant sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of disentangling ego-motion from scene dynamics in 4D occupancy world models.
Uses explicit SE(2) geometric decoupling to create a purely dynamic feature space with attention-free temporal fusion.
Applies physics-constrained ODEs only to residual agent motion and ambiguous, high-uncertainty voxels.
The 28.3M-parameter FreeOcc-E runs at 27 FPS and reports 0.47 m NFCD and 32.1% mIoU on nuScenes.
Transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI and retains 92.8% of ideal mIoU under sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.

figures.caption: Figure 16: Rain scene overview (nuScenes scene-0441). Left: front camera image showing wet road, reflections, and rain droplets. Right: LiDAR BEV coloured by height; the intersection geometry and parked vehicles are clearly visible despite rain-induced noise in the point cloud.

Figure 1: Overview of FreeOcc. Previous sweeps are encoded into BEV, fused by a continuoustime temporal aggregator, propagated to future ego frames by SE(2) warping, and decoded by the Discriminative Occupancy Decoder plus the Physics-Aware Continuous Flow Matching. The final prediction blends both paths using decoder uncertainty.

Figure 3: 4D occupancy forecasting on nuScenes(sample 1720) in BEV and 3D views across six horizons. FreeOcc-E is compared against OccWorld and ViDAR; more qualitative examples are given in Section D.

Figure 2: Ego-aware future propagator. At each horizon, the warped BEV—obtained via SE(2) ego-motion alignment—is explicitly added to the residual scene dynamics predicted by a ConvGRU and a residual projector.

Figure 10: Zero-shot SemanticKITTI predictions (sample 2070). BEV and 3D occupancy predictions from a nuScenes-trained model evaluated on SemanticKITTI, comparing FreeOcc-E against OccWorld and ViDAR. Despite domain differences (64-beam LiDAR, different driving context, no fine-tuning), FreeOcc-E preserves road-level structure and major obstacles. The denser 64-beam input provides richer geometric detail than nuScenes’s 32-beam data, and FreeOcc adapts without retraining, an advantage of operating on raw 3D geometry rather than appearance-dependent features.

Figure 6: Long-horizon comparison at τ=6 (3.0 s, nuScenes sample 3380). Ground Truth, OccWorld, FreeOcc-D, and FreeOcc-E are shown in paired BEV and 3D views. At 3.0 s, OccWorld exhibits boundary blur and noise around moving objects. FreeOcc-D slightly over-predicts occupancy, whereas FreeOcc-E preserves sharper boundaries and cleaner free space.

Figure 5: Temporal evolution of GT vs. FreeOcc-E (nuScenes sample 1730). Top row: groundtruth occupancy at τ=2 (1.0 s), τ=4 (2.0 s), and τ=6 (3.0 s), each shown as BEV (left) and 3D voxel rendering (right). Bottom row: corresponding FreeOcc-E predictions. Agreement is strongest at short horizons. By τ=6, the main discrepancies appear in the far field and around dynamic actors, while large static structures remain well preserved.

Figure 11: Additional zero-shot SemanticKITTI scene (sample 1080) and noise suppression analysis. Top: 3D occupancy predictions at the maximum forecasting horizon (τ = 6, 3.0s), comparing our model variants (FreeOcc-D, -G, -E) against Ground Truth. Bottom: BEV temporal evolution at τ = 3 and τ = 6. Road geometry, vegetation boundaries, and building walls are consistently captured, reinforcing the cross-domain robustness reported in Table 4.

Figure 7: 3D voxel-level uncertainty across prediction horizons (scene-0274, τ=1 to τ=6). Each panel renders occupied voxels coloured by the decoder’s predicted aleatoric uncertainty ŝv; cool tones indicate low uncertainty and warm tones indicate high. At short horizons, uncertainty is concentrated near dynamic actors and occupancy boundaries. As the horizon increases, uncertainty expands into the far field and intensifies around moving objects. By τ=6 (3.0 s), most remaining structures are assigned substantially higher uncertainty. This behaviour is consistent with the ensemble design in Section 3.7, which assigns more weight to the ODE path where decoder confidence weakens.

Figure 4: BEV visualization of 4D occupancy forecasting (additional scene, sample 0970). Columns span τ=1 to τ=6, comparing FreeOcc against OccWorld and ViDAR on a dense urban scene with multiple interacting vehicles. FreeOcc-E preserves scene layout and object extent more faithfully over the full 3.0 s horizon, whereas OccWorld and ViDAR drift more noticeably after τ=3.

Figure 8: Noise suppression analysis (nuScenes sample 1290). Paired BEV and 3D views highlighting hallucinated occupancy at long prediction horizons between FreeOcc-D and FreeOcc-E. FreeOcc-E clears vacated space more effectively while preserving plausible future object positions.

Figure 12: Robustness on nuScenes (τ = 4, 2.0s, sample 2500). Occupancy predictions under ideal and imperfect sensor conditions. FreeOcc-E retains its predictions under severe temporal perturbations, while OccWorld and ViDAR break into fragments and hallucinated clusters when temporal input is degraded.

Figure 13: Cross-domain robustness on SemanticKITTI (τ = 4, 2.0s, sample 2090). Zero-shot predictions under ideal (top two rows) and imperfect (bottom two rows) sensor conditions. The cross-domain robustness gap compounds both the sensor-domain shift (nuScenes→SemanticKITTI) and the temporal perturbation, yet FreeOcc-E retains recognisable road and object geometry in both cases, while OccWorld and ViDAR suffer severe structural collapse.

Figure 14: Robustness on nuScenes at τ=6 (3.0 s, sample 1600). Long-horizon predictions under ideal (top) and imperfect (bottom) sensor conditions. At the maximum forecasting horizon, OccWorld and ViDAR dissolve into discontiguous fragments, whereas FreeOcc-E preserves the road layout and principal object silhouettes. The gap between ideal and imperfect rows is noticeably smaller for FreeOcc-E than for OccWorld or ViDAR, consistent with the quantitative retention rate in Table 5.

Figure 15: Cross-domain robustness on SemanticKITTI at τ=6 (3.0 s, sample 2090). The most challenging evaluation setting: simultaneous cross-domain transfer, long-horizon prediction, and degraded sensor input. FreeOcc-E still recovers the overall road layout and major object boundaries, whereas OccWorld and ViDAR suffer near-complete structural collapse.

Figure 9: BEV uncertainty evolution (nuScenes scene-0220, τ=1 to τ=6). Each panel shows the BEV occupancy coloured by the predicted aleatoric uncertainty ŝv at horizon τ . Cool colours (cyan/green) indicate low uncertainty; warm colours (orange/red) indicate high uncertainty. Uncertainty increases with horizon and concentrates on dynamic objects and far-field voxels. Similar behaviour appears in Figure 7.

papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned 4D occupancy forecasting world model with ego-motion decoupling; directly relevant to interactive/video world models and embodied navigation.
papers.title: FreeOcc: Decoupling Ego-Motion for Efficient 4D Occupancy Forecasting via Continuous Flow Matching
papers.tldr: FreeOcc is a lightweight 4D occupancy forecasting model that explicitly removes ego-motion and uses uncertainty-aware flow matching for efficient, robust prediction.

papers.abstract: We consider the problem of sequential task continuation, where one robot acts in a workspace that has been affected by a previous robot. Current approaches in multi-robot cooperation rely heavily on co-training or co-optimization, assumingthat the robots have access to collective interaction data during the policy training or planning process. However, as increasingly varied robotic embodiments and policies are deployed and operate in the same real-world environment, learning policies for cooperation becomes infeasible due to the combinatorial explosion of possible robot combinations that need to be accounted for. To address this challenge, this paper considers the problem of ad hoc sequential cooperation between robots that have never before operated together in a shared environment. We demonstrate that robots can explicitly communicate their environmental preferences through sharing their value functions, enabling coordination without the need for prior joint training. To ground this exchange and prevent overconfidence in out-of-distribution states, we further introduce a k-nearest neighbors (KNN)- based uncertainty filter. Our method yields an increase of up to 48.5 pp compared with naive or even selfish agents, in task success rates across simulated and real-world experiments, demonstrating that value function transmission between agents is useful not merely as an internal learning tool, but as an effective basis for ad hoc coordination. Website: https://proroklab.github.io/PAVE/
bullets: Addresses ad hoc cooperation between previously unpaired robots operating sequentially in the same environment.
Shares value functions to communicate each robot’s environmental preferences and support coordination.
Uses a KNN-based uncertainty filter to reduce overconfident decisions in unfamiliar states.
Improves task success by up to 48.5 percentage points over naive or selfish agents in simulated and real-world experiments.

papers.abstract: We present a progressive imitation framework that learns terrain-appropriate humanoid parkour skills and subsequently adapts their hand--knee support. Human demonstrations provide traversal behaviors, but their contact patterns need not suit a robot's proportions or the available support surfaces. Our framework changes the role of demonstrations across three stages: privileged imitation produces physically executable robot references; terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors guide skill acquisition; and geometric support guidance with a reduced motion-prior weight enables contact adaptation. Candidate-based precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation guide support without prescribing a contact sequence. The deployed policy selects behaviors from onboard depth, proprioception, and velocity commands without an external skill label. On the Noetix E1, the policy achieves 96.34\% hybrid success in simulation and transfers without real-world policy fine-tuning, completing 29 of 30 individual obstacle trials and four of five hybrid courses. Support-adaptation ablations show higher traversal success for the complete adaptation stage on the tested terrains, while qualitative observations show changes in contact placement. These results support acquiring skills from demonstrations before relaxing their influence to accommodate robot-specific support configurations.
bullets: Human demonstrations are converted into physically executable robot references before skill learning.
Terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors guide parkour acquisition, then reduced prior influence allows geometric support adaptation.
Candidate precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation guide support without prescribing a fixed contact sequence.
The onboard policy uses depth, proprioception, and velocity commands without an external skill label.
On the Noetix E1, it achieves 96.34% hybrid simulation success, completes 29/30 individual obstacle trials and 4/5 hybrid courses; results are limited to the tested terrains and tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the training framework. Motion preprocessing (right) retargets human demonstrations and physically refines them into robot reference rollouts with kinematic, height-scan, and dynamic information. Terrain-indexed adversarial supervision compares reference and policy motion windows to provide a routed style reward. Geometric hand–knee candidates (bottom) guide precontact placement, while contact evaluation and state transitions determine support and retention terms. Task, style, and support rewards are combined with the weights in Eq. 1 for actor–critic training. The actor and critic use gated expert networks, distinct from the discriminator heads. At deployment, only the actor and its observation-processing modules are retained; privileged geometry, reference motions, discriminators, and the critic remain in training.

Fig. 5. Qualitative support comparison. Top: w/o Stage 3; bottom: Ours. Each row combines a simulation contact close-up (left) and hardware traversal snapshots (right). Red circles in the upper row highlight handcontact regions near the platform edge. The comparison illustrates support adaptation rather than a measured contact-force or stability margin.

Fig. 4. Supplementary evidence for terrain–skill correspondence. Top: a simulation montage of sequential obstacle traversal. Middle: joint-angle DTW distances (rad) to the High, Mid, and Low references. Bottom: lowestdistance intervals, with the dominant sequence High→Mid→Low. The interval labels identify reference matches rather than independently measured terrain boundaries.

The two rows show different obstacle-crossing maneuvers within the same trial, illustrating terrain-dependent skill switching by a single perceptionconditioned policy without external skill-selection commands.

papers.selection_reason: Learned humanoid parkour with terrain-indexed motion priors and contact adaptation; fits robot navigation and robot learning.
papers.title: Terrain-Indexed Motion Priors and Geometric Support for Extreme Humanoid Parkour
papers.tldr: A three-stage imitation framework learns terrain-aware humanoid parkour and adapts hand–knee contacts to robot-specific supports, transferring successfully from simulation to hardware without policy fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Enabling vision-language models (VLMs) to control humanoid robots requires both reliable whole-body interfaces and knowledge of how to use the body that carries over across tasks. We present HITCH (Harness Interfaces To Command Humanoids), a harness in which perception returns the 3D position of any point the VLM selects in its image, and execution turns commands for the pelvis, torso, hands, walking, and gaze into whole-body motion with a learned tracker. We find that both measuring the scene and executing commands accurately raise task success. We then fine-tune a VLM on trajectories in which teacher policies solve five base tasks through HITCH, so that it learns how to operate the humanoid. Without task-specific trajectories, the fine-tuned model completes 51% of SIMPLE episodes and 42.5% of HumanoidArena episodes, and adding five trajectories per SIMPLE task raises its SIMPLE success to 95%. On a real G1, it carries a box and walks to a goal without real training data.
bullets: Addresses reliable perception, control interfaces, and transferable body-use knowledge for VLM-controlled humanoids.
Maps selected image points to 3D positions and converts pelvis, torso, hand, walking, and gaze commands into motion using a learned tracker.
Fine-tunes the VLM on teacher-policy trajectories covering five base tasks.
Achieves 51% success on SIMPLE and 42.5% on HumanoidArena without task-specific trajectories; five trajectories per SIMPLE task increase success to 95%.
Demonstrates real-world box carrying and goal-directed walking on a G1 without real training data.

papers.abstract: Service Robots are becoming a reality and are progressing by leaps and bounds. Alongside this avenue of robotics is also the field of prosthetics, which is evolving rapidly. These topics are hot cakes in the industry and are widely developed. Some have one quality, and some have others, but are making a shoreline towards success. The development of arm and hand as individual or as a package is becoming common as more and more advanced collaborative robots come to the surface and join their human counterparts in the real world. This dissertation presents an open-source 3D-printed arm which was assembled and programmed on two fronts. The first is the control of the hand by utilising teleoperation with a camera and ML-based hand pose estimation. Secondly, it is the control via kinematics utilising the Denavit-Hartenberg method to define the motion and to find the position of the end effector in 3D space.
bullets: Targets collaborative and home-service robotics through an anthropomorphic arm and hand.
Uses camera-based teleoperation with machine-learning hand-pose estimation.
Applies Denavit–Hartenberg kinematics to define motion and determine the end-effector’s 3D position.
The arm is assembled and programmed across both teleoperation and kinematic-control approaches.

papers.abstract: We investigate a symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted testing approach for UAV autopilots. The proposed approach exploits geometric symmetries between flight missions by trans- forming obstacle configurations into a shared canonical coordi- nate frame. This enables a neural-network surrogate trained on a single reference mission to be reused across arbitrary missions, reducing the amount of high-fidelity simulation data required for training. The surrogate model is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles and is used to guide test generation towards safety-critical scenarios. We evaluate this approach using the Aerialist UAV test bench and benchmark its performance against techniques from the 2024 to 2026 UAV Testing Competitions. Results show that the approach achieves an average critical-test-case hit rate of 42% across the evaluated missions, compared with approximately 10% for the constrained-random baseline used to generate the training data. This approach also achieves high input diversity and competitive benchmark performance. However, our findings reveal limitations in transferring surrogate predictions across missions with differing flight-path characteristics, highlighting the boundaries of geometric canonicalization. To support reproducibility and future research, we provide the trained surrogate model and a dataset comprising more than 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.
bullets: Canonicalizes obstacle configurations into a shared coordinate frame so a surrogate trained on one reference mission can support others.
The neural surrogate predicts minimum UAV–obstacle clearance and guides test generation toward critical scenarios.
On the Aerialist test bench, it achieved a 42% average critical-test-case hit rate versus about 10% for the constrained-random baseline.
The approach maintained high input diversity and competitive performance against recent UAV testing competition techniques.
Reproducibility resources include the trained surrogate and over 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.

papers.abstract: Physical human--robot interaction requires controllers capable of maintaining intrinsically bounded interactions with the environment. The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) has been proven to guarantee these safety characteristics by design. This paper introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of its most advanced architecture: the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), an evolution of the Passive Motion Paradigm designed to mimic human-like interaction. Furthermore, we present a unified framework for FIC deployment, supported by an open-source software suite featuring ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware integrations. Through three experiments conducted on a Kinova Gen3 arm (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) we compare the H-PMP against earlier FIC architectures. The results demonstrate that the H-PMP achieves a seamless trade-off between admittance and impedance behaviours. This makes it ideal for deployment in unstructured environments, enabling the robot to transition between interaction modes with no computational overhead.
bullets: Addresses the need for intrinsically bounded and safe physical human–robot interactions.
Introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP).
Provides an open-source deployment suite integrating ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware.
Evaluates trajectory tracking, sudden loss of wall contact, and learning-by-demonstration on a Kinova Gen3 arm.
Finds that H-PMP smoothly trades off between admittance and impedance without computational overhead, supporting unstructured-environment use.

papers.abstract: Current language-guided 3D object placement typically predicts a rigid 6-DoF pose, ignoring the physical reality that indoor placements are dictated by contact. Consequently, predicted poses often float, interpenetrate supports, or fail to deform soft surfaces. We propose Deformable Contact-Aware Placement (DCAP), a framework that reframes placement as a drop-to-equilibrium process. Rather than predicting a static pose, DCAP constructs a semantic release state that specifies the drop location, object scale, and deformable components, allowing a coupled rigid-deformable simulator to settle the object under gravity and friction. This explicitly separates semantic intent from physical realization. Evaluated on a benchmark of 2,063 prompt-asset-scene cases, DCAP significantly outperforms static baselines. On standard placements, it improves VLM Physics & Naturalness by 21.2 points and human preference by 26.5 points over the strongest raw rigid baseline, while reducing mean penetration depth by 72.3%. Compared to simulated rollout baselines, DCAP reduces residual speed by 72.1%. Ultimately, our results prove that physically accurate 3D placement requires modeling semantic intent and physical realization as strictly separate processes.
bullets: Targets floating objects, support interpenetration, and failure to deform soft surfaces in rigid 6-DoF placement.
Predicts a semantic release state—drop location, object scale, and deformable components—rather than a final pose.
Uses coupled rigid-deformable simulation with gravity and friction to realize the placement through drop-to-equilibrium.
On 2,063 prompt–asset–scene cases, it improves physics/naturalness and human preference while substantially reducing penetration and residual motion.
The approach separates semantic intent from physical realization; its scope is indoor placement involving contact and deformability.

papers.abstract: Affordance grounding asks which visible part of an object performs a requested operation, a basic capability for embodied manipulation and human--robot interaction. Most existing methods follow a System Two paradigm: a multimodal language model first writes a chain of thought and then turns its conclusion into a box or points for a segmenter. This incurs considerable inference cost, gives the semantic decision little direct control over the extent of the final region, and makes mistakes hard to correct. Yet locating an affordance is essentially a perceptual judgment that need not be argued out in words. We therefore propose, in which frozen segmenters propose candidate regions and a System One model decides directly which of them perform the operation, generating no text and reading each decision from a single forward pass. Our contributions are twofold. (1) An inference framework that confirms candidate regions level by level, from object to part to sub-part, with evidence passed between the levels in both directions so that the levels correct one another. (2) A System One model trained for this framework: existing System One models are built for general-purpose decisions, judge one candidate per request and are ill-suited to the framework's region questions, so ours learns directly from the requests the framework itself produces and judges all candidates of a level at once. Trained only on InstructPart and evaluated with definition-aligned operation words, outperforms chain-of-thought methods in domain and in zero-shot transfer to UMD and IIT-AFF, is better overall than existing System One models run in the same framework, and needs fewer judge requests. To our knowledge, is the first approach to bring System One models to affordance grounding.
bullets: Addresses costly, error-prone System Two pipelines that reason in language before producing regions.
Uses frozen segmenters to propose candidates and a System One model to confirm regions hierarchically from object to part to sub-part.
Passes evidence between hierarchy levels in both directions so regions can be mutually corrected.
Trains the judge on framework-generated region requests and evaluates all candidates at a level in one forward pass.
Trained on InstructPart, it outperforms chain-of-thought methods in-domain and transfers zero-shot to UMD and IIT-AFF, while requiring fewer judge requests.
