papers.abstract: Robotic simulators that represent shear within tactile sensing are becoming increasingly important for contact-rich manipulation. However, simulating contact shear with high-fidelity deformable or soft-body simulation is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large-scale reinforcement learning. Here we introduce \textit{TactileLab}, a scalable multimodal tactile simulation framework built on IsaacLab, with a particular focus on a new optical-flow-based tactile representation termed \textit{simulated tactile flow}. Instead of relying on soft-body physics to model shear deformation, TactileLab uses rigid-body simulation to efficiently estimate dense tangential motion at the contact interface, producing tactile flow fields that encode shear-relevant contact dynamics. This flow field complements geometric features from a contact depth field. We further introduce a novel policy architecture for jointly processing long-horizon proprioceptive signals and rich tactile observations. Across multiple contact-rich tasks, policies trained using simulated tactile flow learn efficiently at scale and exhibit emergent contact-aware behaviours. To facilitate sim-to-real policy deployment, we then propose a novel real-to-sim tactile translation method that maps real tactile image streams to simulated tactile flow and depth fields, together with a new tactile data collection method, and validate it across diverse tactile sensor designs. Using this pipeline, we demonstrate real-world deployment on tasks encompassing dual-arm and dexterous in-hand manipulation. Overall, TactileLab provides an end-to-end sim-to-real framework for scalable tactile policy learning, enabling diverse shear-sensitive manipulation across heterogeneous tactile robotic systems.
bullets: Uses rigid-body simulation to generate dense optical-flow-like tactile fields representing tangential contact motion, combined with contact depth features.
Introduces a policy architecture for integrating long-horizon proprioception with rich tactile observations.
Provides real-to-sim translation from real tactile images to simulated tactile flow and depth fields across diverse sensor designs.
Demonstrates efficient learning and real-world deployment on contact-rich dual-arm and dexterous in-hand manipulation tasks.
Scope: focuses on shear-sensitive tactile manipulation while avoiding computationally expensive deformable-contact simulation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the TactileLab simulation framework and simulated tactile-flow computation. The rigid-body simulation pipeline computes contact geometry and generates low-dimensional contact descriptors, contact-depth images, and dense tactile-flow fields for policy learning. Simulated tactile flow is obtained by projecting the three-dimensional contact patch onto the tactile image plane and calculating the image-space displacement induced by the relative motion between the tactile sensor and the contacted object.

During training, the predicted flow is supervised by a paired simulated tactileflow target through a reconstruction loss and by a discriminator D through an adversarial loss. The HSV flow images are used only for visualization; the network output is a two-channel flow field F̂.

papers.abstract: Goal interpretation is to translate a natural language instruction into a formal symbolic goal that a planner can execute. It is critical for embodied agents because any error here propagates to every downstream planning and action step. Doing it well requires both generating suitable candidates and reliably selecting among them. We present a two-stage generate-then-rank approach to Goal Interpretation in the Embodied Agent Interface (EAI). First, supervised fine-tuning adapts a Large Language Model (LLM) to EAI's output convention. Second, Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors (CORE) learns preferences over complete outputs from the model's own generated alternatives. We conducted experiments on the household scenes of the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark. Multiple open source LLMs including DeepSeek-V3 chat, DeepSeek-Reasoner, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-72B were evaluated. The proposed method outperformed the baseline models including LLMs with simple prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge graph based approaches.
bullets: Goal interpretation errors propagate through downstream planning and actions.
The method first fine-tunes an LLM to produce valid EAI symbolic goals.
CORE then learns to rank complete candidate outputs generated by the model.
Evaluated on household scenes from the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark with several open-source LLMs.
The approach outperformed prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge-graph baselines.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides information about object properties that can improve robotic grasping and manipulation. However, accurate object recognition during the early stages of grasping remains challenging, particularly under strict real-time constraints. This study presents a flexible, distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing system for early-stage object recognition. The system was experimentally evaluated using six everyday objects and three recognition approaches: feature-based classification using support vector machines (SVMs), raw-signal classification using 1D convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) and convolutional recurrent neural networks (C-RNNs), and spatiotemporal heatmap classification using a 2D-CNN. The effects of sensor count and temporal window size on recognition accuracy and real-time feasibility were systematically investigated. Increasing the number of sensing elements improved recognition performance across all approaches. The best-performing method, based on spatiotemporal heatmaps and a 2D-CNN, achieved F1-scores of 0.9796, 0.9846, and 0.9903 using 16, 24, and 32 sensors, respectively. The optimal configuration, comprising 32 sensors and a 100-ms temporal window (50 samples), was deployed on an embedded edge platform, achieving an end-to-end recognition latency of approximately 101 ms from contact onset and an energy consumption of 63.8 microjoules per inference. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing for accurate, energy-efficient, and real-time object recognition during robotic grasping.
bullets: Evaluated six everyday objects using SVM, 1D-CNN, C-RNN, and spatiotemporal heatmap-based 2D-CNN approaches.
Recognition performance improved as the number of sensing elements increased.

A 32-sensor, 100-ms temporal-window configuration achieved approximately 101 ms latency and 63.8 μJ per inference on an embedded platform.

papers.abstract: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/
bullets: Reactive navigation may choose locally feasible actions that cause unsafe, socially disruptive, or semantically inappropriate futures.

World models score candidate actions during training and guide group-relative preference distillation; they are removed at deployment for single-pass inference.
Across five held-out scenarios, the resulting policy is reported as safer, more socially and group-coherent, more goal-directed, and more human-like than reactive and learned baselines.
The approach confines the computational cost of foresight to training rather than performing online world-model rollouts.

papers.abstract: Object rearrangement in cluttered tabletop scenes is challenging, especially in wide workspaces where dual-arm systems improve coverage and efficiency. Limited free space often necessitates buffering, while objects near or across the shared reachability region of the manipulators must be transferred under careful coordination to avoid inter-arm collisions. Conventional inter-arm transfer typically relies on a fixed handoff configuration, which constrains where and how objects are exchanged, enforces spatiotemporal synchronization of the arms, and reduces flexibility in dense layouts. This paper presents a dual-arm rearrangement framework that combines movable stacking with Gap-Aware Push Transfer for asynchronous cross-boundary exchange. The method scans the shared boundary to identify collision-free transfer gaps, places an object near a selected crossing point, and then pushes it into the receiving workspace without requiring simultaneous interaction between the two arms. A joint Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based planner coordinates both manipulators while reasoning over buffering and transfer decisions, and execution cost is used after planning to assess the resulting plan. Experiments show that the proposed method shortens joint execution sequences and becomes increasingly advantageous over a fixed handoff baseline as scene density increases, achieving lower execution cost in denser scenes while remaining competitive in lighter ones.
bullets: Addresses limited space, clutter, and collision risks in wide dual-arm workspaces.
Finds collision-free gaps along the shared boundary for object transfer.
Uses placement followed by a push, avoiding fixed handoff poses and simultaneous arm interaction.
Coordinates buffering and transfers with a joint Monte Carlo Tree Search planner.
Experiments report shorter execution sequences and lower cost than fixed handoffs in denser scenes, while remaining competitive in lighter scenes.

papers.abstract: Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. A lightweight RGB-based model recognizes interaction intent from two onboard cameras and converts it into a language prompt for the VLA policy. Low-confidence predictions suppress motion execution, reducing unintended activations. During physical contact, interaction-specific compliance profiles adjust arm impedance, while an independent voice-triggered mechanism initiates a latched safe-stop procedure. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. Integrating intent recognition increases its macro-F1 score from 0.75 to 0.90, while the intent model achieves a p95 inference latency of 6.27 ms. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation.
bullets: Targets safe handling of handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, where robots must infer intent and manage physical contact.
Uses a lightweight two-camera RGB intent model to generate language prompts for a VLA policy; low-confidence predictions suppress motion.
Applies interaction-specific arm impedance profiles during contact and an independent latched voice-triggered safe-stop mechanism.
Evaluated four fine-tuned VLA models on a Unitree G1 using approximately 1,300 VR-teleoperated multimodal episodes.
Intent gating improved the best standalone model’s macro-F1 from 0.75 to 0.90, with 6.27 ms p95 intent-inference latency.

(b) The on-robot VLA bridge converts a confirmed intent into a task prompt, predicts whole-body action chunks, and applies playback smoothing and finger-contact safeguards. (c) During deployment, task-conditioned arm-compliance profiles and the latched safe-stop mechanism supervise the SONIC whole-body controller, enabling safe and compliant handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs.

papers.abstract: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) can degrade during aerial inspection in repetitive or poorly textured environments. We propose an active environment-modification framework for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) relying on cameras and an inertial measurement unit only, without prior maps or additional localization sensors. Inspired by the fairy tale of Tom Thumb, the UAV creates visual features on demand by releasing ground markers or marking walls through physical contact. An information-based indicator triggers interventions using temporal confirmation and hysteresis. Evaluation includes three simulated environments and a 900-run factorial campaign. Lower cruise speed and active marking are associated with reduced divergence, while accuracy among non-divergent runs depends on speed-strategy interactions. Corridor experiments, with five runs per configuration, use OptiTrack for flight control while VIO-based marking decisions remain active online. The combined framework reduces the reported position root mean square error by approximately 35% relative to baseline VIO, supporting active feature creation for drift mitigation.
bullets: Addresses VIO degradation during aerial inspection without prior maps or additional localization sensors.
Uses physical ground markers or wall markings to create trackable visual features.
Triggers interventions with an information-based indicator, temporal confirmation, and hysteresis.
Simulations and corridor experiments associate active marking and lower speed with reduced divergence.
Accuracy among non-divergent runs varies with interactions between speed and intervention strategy.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion policies trained without an explicit smoothness objective tend to produce jerky, high-energy gaits that stress actuators. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer an appealing reward source: given a rendered rollout, a VLM returns an aesthetic quality score on [0,10] without task-specific feature engineering. We find, however, that aesthetic preference and physical smoothness point in opposite directions: across four production VLMs, clips with higher joint acceleration receive higher aesthetic scores (mean Pearson r=+0.66). We study PhySA (Physical Smoothness and Aesthetics), which keeps the two on separate, independently removable reward channels: a sparse, asynchronous VLM score and a phase-triggered correction channel that adjusts physical penalty weights from simulator state. Ablations attribute the smoothness gain to the correction channel. On MuJoCo Humanoid-v5 at 2.6M steps, PhySA lowers joint acceleration by 26 to 32% relative to vanilla PPO, Text2Reward, and Eureka (three seeds), at the cost of shorter episodes. In a single extended run it lowers joint acceleration by 59.5% relative to Prompt2Policy, while a three-seed replication shows a smaller, non-significant reduction (7.2%). The gain does not transfer to IsaacLab or the Unitree G1, even after rescaling the smoothness term.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets robots search for run-time object queries, but fixed-rate inference spends embedded compute on low-value frames during idle motion, map revisits, or stable viewpoints. This paper presents an energy-aware OVD scheduler for low-power mobile robots. The scheduler uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano. We evaluate the energy-quality trade-off on an AgileX LIMO using 40 real navigation trials: two target objects, five placements per target-policy pair, and four perception policies. Across bottle and cup trials, the scheduler records 8/10 mission success compared with 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline, while reducing mean Jetson input power (a Jetson-side power-draw metric) by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz high-rate baseline and lowering achieved OVD call rate by 34.0%. It does not minimize mission-window Jetson input energy because longer missions can erase instantaneous power savings. A separate 60 s stationary microbenchmark isolates the perception workload: the scheduler lowers mean power from 8.045 W to 7.301 W and energy from 484.7 J to 438.1 J relative to the 8 Hz baseline. These results support robot-state-aware OVD scheduling as a promising power-management mechanism with competitive task reliability, while showing that mission-window Jetson input energy must be read together with task progress and runtime.
bullets: Targets wasted compute during idle motion, map revisits, and stable viewpoints in low-power robotic autonomy.
Uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes.
In 40 real AgileX LIMO navigation trials, it achieved 8/10 mission success versus 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline.
Reduced mean Jetson input power by 5.2% and OVD call rate by 34.0% versus an 8 Hz baseline.
A stationary 60-second benchmark showed lower mean power and energy, but mission-window energy was not always reduced because longer missions can offset instantaneous savings.

papers.abstract: Modern 6-DoF grasp generators are often evaluated using grasp scores, dataset-level metrics, or single-robot demonstrations, yet proposal quality alone does not determine whether a grasp is executable by a particular robot. We present GraspBench, a controlled MuJoCo protocol for evaluating complete grasp-generation pipelines after robot-specific inverse-kinematics filtering, motion planning, and fixed approach-close-lift execution. GraspBench evaluates six configured pipelines across four robot embodiments, five diagnostic objects, and a structured tabletop pose grid, yielding 540 scenarios per method and 3,240 method-scenario evaluations in total. Missing outputs are conservatively counted as failures, and success follows the binary lift criterion produced by each method's execution runner. GraspGen achieves the highest overall success rate (73.1%), followed by EconomicGrasp (63.5%), while robot- and object-conditioned analyses reveal substantial variation across embodiments and object geometries. GPG produces the largest native candidate sets but achieves 44.3% success, indicating that proposal volume alone does not guarantee robot-executable grasps. Cluster-aware paired intervals support the principal method differences while not estimating repeated-execution uncertainty. The results characterize complete configured pipelines on fixed scenarios rather than intrinsic model quality or stochastic repeatability, showing that grasping performance depends jointly on the generator, robot embodiment, scene, and execution protocol.
bullets: Evaluates complete grasp-generation pipelines after robot-specific IK filtering, motion planning, and fixed approach-close-lift execution in MuJoCo.
Tests six pipelines across four robot embodiments, five diagnostic objects, and structured tabletop poses, totaling 3,240 method-scenario evaluations.

papers.abstract: Event cameras are neuromorphic vision sensors with pixels that independently and asynchronously respond to brightness changes at microsecond resolution, supporting state estimation under rapid motion, motion blur, and high dynamic range (HDR) illumination. This also enables capture of high-frequency blinking patterns from light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Based on this, we propose a real-time event-based framework for LED tracking and six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) relative pose estimation using pulse-width modulation (PWM)-encoded LED markers. Multiple LEDs share a common blinking frequency and encode identities through distinct PWM duty cycles, reducing frequency-resource requirements and computational cost. Our dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework combines low-rate LED detection with high-rate raw-event updates, maintaining robust LED identity association and accurate pixel-level tracking under rapid motion. LED identities and positions establish reliable 2D-3D correspondences for real-time metric 6-DoF relative pose estimation. Extensive evaluations on a self-collected dataset demonstrate robustness under large motion flow and transient image-plane LED overlap. Furthermore, we develop a coordinated robotic platform comprising a quadrotor and a Mecanum-wheeled mobile robot, demonstrating the proposed framework's potential for closed-loop drone guidance through hovering and target-following experiments under time-varying HDR illumination, with onboard deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The dataset and implementation will be released to facilitate further research.
bullets: LEDs share one blinking frequency while distinct PWM duty cycles encode marker identities, reducing frequency and computation demands.
A dual-rate asynchronous tracker combines low-rate LED detection with high-rate event updates for pixel-level tracking and identity association.

Evaluations on a self-collected dataset show robustness to large motion and temporary image-plane LED overlap.
A quadrotor–mobile-robot platform demonstrates onboard closed-loop hovering and target following under time-varying HDR illumination.

papers.abstract: Offline safe reinforcement learning requires reliable long-horizon safety estimates from fixed data. Learning Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) viability in this setting calls for semantic preservation, convergence, and numerical stability. To address these challenges, we propose Monotone Viability Learning (MoViL), which learns viable sets from offline transitions through monotone finite-horizon set recursion. The recursion preserves finite-horizon safety semantics and converges to the infinite-horizon viability kernel. Binary supervision maintains a fixed target scale across horizons, avoiding discount-induced numerical attenuation. We further establish sufficient conditions for recovering behavior-supported viable subsets. The learned viability estimates are used to certify actions at deployment. Dubins car experiments validate the numerical accuracy of the learned viable sets. Evaluations on safe RL benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art reward-cost performance. MoViL satisfies the average cost constraint on every task and achieves the lowest average cost among the compared methods. These results highlight MoViL's potential to extend long-horizon HJ viability analysis to safety-critical systems where reliable dynamics models are unavailable and online exploration is unsafe.
bullets: Addresses reliable safety estimation for offline safe reinforcement learning over long horizons.
Uses monotone finite-horizon set recursion to preserve safety semantics and converge to the infinite-horizon viability kernel.
Binary supervision avoids discount-induced attenuation and maintains a fixed target scale across horizons.
Provides conditions for recovering behavior-supported viable subsets and uses learned estimates for deployment-time action certification.
Dubins car and safe RL benchmark experiments validate numerical accuracy and show constraint satisfaction on every task, with the lowest average cost among compared methods.

papers.abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM agents requires grounding diverse user expressions in their environments. Although RL-finetuned smaller large language model (sLLM) agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, their robustness to instruction paraphrases remains unclear. We introduce ALFWorld-Para to evaluate this robustness under controlled paraphrases, revealing 21-52% declines in success rates (SRs), predominantly driven by object synonyms. Despite retaining knowledge of synonym referents, agents often fail to take the corresponding objects even after observing them, exposing a gap between referential knowledge and object binding. Partial observability further complicates binding, as referents may remain unseen or have already been encountered under different labels. To address this challenge, we propose BINDIntent, a training-free framework that probabilistically binds referring expressions to observed labels using semantic proximity and estimated persistence against unseen candidates. Without additional training or LLM calls, BINDIntent improves synonym-paraphrase success of RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5-49.1 percentage points (pp) with only 0.4 ms of CPU overhead per step. It also raises GiGPO-7B's overall SR from 61.8% to 77.4%, surpassing a prompted 24B LLM. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/cau-hai-lab/ALFWorld-Para.
bullets: ALFWorld-Para shows paraphrased instructions reduce success rates by 21–52%, mainly because of object synonyms.
Agents often know synonym meanings but fail to bind them to the correct observed objects.
Partial observability makes binding harder when referents are unseen or previously labeled differently.
BINDIntent uses semantic proximity and estimated persistence to probabilistically match expressions with observed labels.
It improves synonym-paraphrase success by 17.5–49.1 percentage points with 0.4 ms CPU overhead per step; GiGPO-7B’s overall success rises from 61.8% to 77.4%.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires precise control under complex contact dynamics while remaining robust to diverse visual conditions. However, real-world reinforcement learning often overfits to the visual appearance of training scenes. We propose Semantics-to-Contact (S2C), a stagewise framework for visually robust contact-rich manipulation. The insight is to decompose the problem into two stages: semantic focusing and contact refinement. In the first stage, a vision-language model localizes task-relevant regions across visually diverse scenes, providing coarse spatial guidance and reducing the burden of exploration. In the second stage, a real-world human-in-the-loop residual reinforcement learning policy learns fine-grained contact behaviors within the localized region using force feedback. To further improve visual robustness, we introduce an object-centric visual augmentation strategy that randomizes background appearance while preserving the robot and task-relevant objects. Experiments on six contact-rich real-world manipulation tasks exhibit that S2C consistently improves success rates over strong baselines and maintains reliable performance under significant visual and positional variations. These results demonstrate that stagewise semantic focusing and contact refinement provide a practical path toward visually robust real-world contact-rich manipulation. Our demos can be seen in https://edem-ai.github.io/S2C/.
bullets: Addresses the tendency of real-world reinforcement learning to overfit to training-scene appearances.
Stage 1 uses a vision-language model to identify task-relevant regions and guide exploration.
Stage 2 refines contact behavior through human-in-the-loop residual reinforcement learning with force feedback.
Object-centric augmentation randomizes backgrounds while preserving the robot and relevant objects.
Across six real-world tasks, S2C improves success over strong baselines and remains reliable under visual and positional variation.

papers.abstract: To serve a request in a human environment, a robot system must find an object that satisfies a functional requirement and a robot that can feasibly reach it. Scene graphs record which objects exist and where, but they often omit capabilities documented only in product manuals. Retrieval-augmented generation methods can read such manuals, yet they rarely reason jointly over object capabilities, physical instances, robot states, and dynamic connectivity. We introduce E2W-Bench, the Exists-to-Works Benchmark, which links dynamic hybrid scene graphs with real product manuals to evaluate capability-grounded robot--object assignment under availability, mobility, vertical-reach, and connector constraints. We also present Embodied RAG++, a spatially grounded retrieval framework that scopes retrieval to the manuals linked to candidate objects, caches extracted capabilities per product model, and resolves robot--object feasibility through deterministic spatial reasoning. On E2W-Bench, Embodied RAG++ reaches a pair accuracy of 0.90 with Qwen2.5-32B and 1.00 with Llama3.3-70B, compared with at most 0.30 and 0.55 for the baselines, while requiring the shortest preprocessing time among the retrieval-based methods and tying for the lowest total token count.
bullets: Addresses the gap between knowing which objects exist and determining which can fulfill a requested function.
Introduces E2W-Bench, linking dynamic hybrid scene graphs with real product manuals under availability, mobility, reach, and connector constraints.
Scopes retrieval to candidate-object manuals, caches product capabilities, and uses deterministic spatial feasibility checks.
Achieves pair accuracy of 0.90 with Qwen2.5-32B and 1.00 with Llama3.3-70B, outperforming reported baselines.

papers.abstract: Legged robots equipped with manipulators have shown significant potential in the fields of daily life and industry in complex environments. However, existing methods mainly focus on global navigation or manipulation independently, while overlooking the last-mile navigation problem, where the robot must jointly determine the base placement, approach direction, and grasp execution to achieve reliable object grasping, and different manipulation stages require distinct control behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose Last-Mile Grasp-Navigation (LMGN), a unified policy learning model for Quadruped robot loco-manipulation. An Explicit Distance and Directional Reachability (ED-DR) representation is first introduced to explicitly represent the features of grasp-compatible base placement and approach direction. We then develop a semantically aligned Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (HMoE) policy that models stage-aware behaviors across the stages of base adjustment, pre-grasp alignment and grasp execution, and object lift. Finally, a new optimization method that jointly aligns navigation and manipulation, stage-dependent expert routing, and action-level consistency is proposed to optimize the HMoE policy. Extensive experiments on the Habitat and Isaac Gym simulators demonstrate that LMGN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, denoting that integrating grasp-aware reachability with stage-aware policy learning significantly improves the success rates of last-mile navigation and target grasp for robots.

Uses Explicit Distance and Directional Reachability (ED-DR) to represent grasp-compatible robot positioning and approach directions.

Jointly optimizes navigation–manipulation alignment, expert routing, and action consistency.
Experiments in Habitat and Isaac Gym report improved last-mile navigation and grasp success over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)--either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5%-35.1% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit, we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D. papers.abstract: Running evaluations of contact-rich robotic manipulation at statistical scale has largely been possible only at well-resourced labs, highlighting the need for affordable and efficient options for broader audiences. We present a reproducible evaluation harness wrapper based on a previous study at 200-rollout scale on serverless commodity GPUs, at a cost of approximately $3.50 USD and 38 minutes of wall-clock per replication (4.4 L4-GPU-hours across eight parallel shards). Using the harness, we report a partially controlled negative result on action chunking with sparse data: three independently trained chunked checkpoints produce zero genuine successes across 780 rollouts, while three single-step checkpoints range from 2.6% to 11.8% success rate. A per-step-replanning control partially isolates chunk prediction, rather than open-loop chunk execution as the mechanism, with the failure localized to the training formulation and multi-step prediction. This work further democratizes physics-based policy development and evaluation through our reusable harness.
bullets: Runs an 800-scale-style evaluation replication for about $3.50 and 38 minutes using eight parallel commodity-GPU shards.
In 780 rollouts, three chunked-policy checkpoints achieve zero genuine successes.
Single-step checkpoints achieve success rates ranging from 2.6% to 11.8%.
Per-step replanning suggests the failure is tied to chunk prediction and training, not simply open-loop chunk execution.
The reusable harness aims to broaden access to physics-based policy development and evaluation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Runtime architecture of one 200-rollout replication. A cloud-resident dispatcher fans out eight containers, each evaluating a disjoint slice of scenario_index; because the harness derives each rollout’s random seed from its index, the union of shards reproduces the unsharded run exactly. Within a container the Drake harness renders headless under Xvfb and queries a co-located gRPC policy server, which keeps the policy implementation outside the harness process. Each shard writes per-episode results to a persistent volume; screening and aggregation read them back afterwards, so no result depends on the dispatching process surviving the run. Model assets and the EGL vendor ICD are baked into the image at build time.

Fig. 2. First and final frames of three rollouts under the v1 baseline are shown in the columns for three different scenes (rows). In each scene, the policy instructs the right robotic arm to pick up the red box and place it in the interior of the circular goal marker on the tabletop and the rollout is judged as a success or failure. In scene 125 the arm transports the box onto the goal marker and the rollout is scored successful. In scene 3 the arm reaches toward the box, overshoots, and holds position for the remainder of the episode without relocating it. Red arrows are Drake hydroelastic contactforce vectors. Scene 6 is one of five scenarios whose initial condition places the box directly above the goal; it registers success within 0.3 s with both arms stationary, and is excluded under R1. Camera position varies slightly between recordings.

papers.abstract: Real-world environments are messy, with paths often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring robots to perform interactive navigation by manipulating obstacles to clear a path. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scene instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to swipe, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Evaluated on a mobile manipulator across real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger-scale offline evaluation, without task-specific training.
bullets: Addresses open-world interactive navigation where obstacles may need to be moved rather than avoided.
Uses explicit VLM affordance reasoning before planning to choose actions such as swiping, picking up, or avoiding objects.
Handles context-dependent cases, such as pushing an empty cart but avoiding one carrying fragile glassware.
Evaluated on a mobile manipulator in real indoor and outdoor environments.
Improves real-robot success by 27 percentage points over the strongest baseline, without task-specific training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MessyNav: A framework for zero-shot open-world interactive navigation. MessyNav consists of an Affordance Reasoner that infers object interactability from an RGB image using a VLM to evaluate both robot-centric physical feasibility and object-centric interaction safety. For example, it will label a cart with a laptop as non-interactive while labeling a wheeled crate with a bin as interactive. Given the object affordance labels, a Task Planner then sequences manipulation and navigation actions from an open-language skill library containing a simple set of motion primitives (pick up, swipe left, swipe right) and a LiDAR-based navigation stack (move to) that we find can tackle a wide range of interactive navigation scenarios. Finally, the generated plan is executed by grounding object references in 3D coordinates using VLM keypoint identification, semantic segmentation, and depth-based deprojection.

Figure 4: Explicit affordance reasoning improves context-dependent task planning. In this scene, a suitcase supporting a stack of books is inherently unstable, while the black cart holding a single book can be safely cleared. [Left] MessyNav reasons about affordances before planning, correctly labeling the suitcase as non-interactive and the cart as interactive, and swiping the cart aside to clear the path. [Middle] vlm-planner-only plans directly from the image without an explicit affordance stage and incorrectly decides to swipe the unstable suitcase. [Right] closed-set-planner assigns fixed category-level affordances that misclassify the suitcase as interactive, leading to an unsafe plan.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results across Environments. We deploy MessyNav in varied settings to test its zero-shot capability. The robot successfully reasons about affordances and executes interactions across different lighting conditions, environments, and object types.
Figure 7: Example Open-Vocabulary Keypoint Detection. We use gemini-2.5-pro [36] to detect keypoints of objects specified by the task planner through language queries.
Figure 6: Hardware: We deploy on the TidyBot++ holonomic mobile manipulator [18] with two cameras and a LiDAR for perception. An onboard laptop runs the autonomy stack.

Figure 9: MessyNav’s failure breakdown compared to the strongest baseline. Sankey diagrams of trial outcomes for MessyNav (left) and vlm-planner-only (right) over 15 real-world trials. MessyNav succeeds on 10/15 trials versus 6/15 for vlm-planner-only. While most of vlm-planner-only’s failures are planning failures in which vlm-planner-only decides to interact with non-interactive objects (7 of 9), MessyNav reduces these to 2, showcasing the importance of explicit affordance reasoning.

Figure 3: MessyNav reasons about context, not just object category. In this cluttered scene, closed-set-oracle assigns affordances by category alone, misclassifying the rolling cart as interactive (ignoring the glassware it carries) and the suitcase as interactive (ignoring its fragile sticker). In contrast, MessyNav reasons at the instance level. It treats the cart and the glass stemware as a single fragile unit and reads the sticker on the suitcase as a contextual cue, correctly labeling both as non-interactive.

papers.abstract: Replay attacks are difficult to detect in vision-based control systems because previously recorded observations can remain plausible while the physical system follows a different trajectory. This paper develops an adaptive dynamic-watermarking framework for detecting replay attacks against vision-based controllers. A private Gaussian watermark is added to the nominal control input, and a control input-conditioned latent dynamics network (LDN) predicts the corresponding evolution in a compact latent space learned from image observations. Attack evidence is obtained from the discrepancy between the predicted latent response and the latent representation of the received image observation. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the watermark covariance using the latent state and detector confidence, thereby balancing attack detectability, watermark energy, and control distortion. A Lagrangian penalty on task-specific safety costs is included during training to limit the adverse effect of the excitation. The framework is evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 manipulation task in which the robot reaches a target while avoiding a moving human arm under nominal and replay-attacked observations.
bullets: Addresses replay attacks where recorded camera observations remain plausible despite changed physical trajectories.
Adds private Gaussian noise to control inputs and predicts image-derived latent dynamics conditioned on those inputs.
Detects attacks through discrepancies between predicted latent responses and received-image latent representations.
Uses reinforcement learning to adapt watermark covariance based on latent state and detector confidence.
Evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 reaching-and-avoidance task under nominal and replay-attacked observations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. (a) The live observation xt−H is provided to the vision-based controller policy F , which predicts the control input ut−H . In parallel, an encoder maps xt−H to the latent state zt−H . The latent state, together with the detector confidence cj , is provided to the DWM policy to select the covariance Σt−H , from which the private watermark ϕt−H is sampled. The watermark and control input are combined to form the watermarked control input ūt−H , which is applied to the plant. (b) When a replay attack occurs, the encoder maps the received replayed observations to latent states [z′t−H+1, . . . , z ′ t]. These are compared with the predicted latent states [z̃t−H+1|t−H , . . . , z̃t|t−H ] to obtain the residual window rj , defined in (8). The MCUSUM detector processes this window, and the resulting evidence updates the attack confidence cj through (18). When attack evidence persists, the supervisor switches to the damped-stop controller and applies uds t as specified in (7).

Fig. 3. Average (Top) Attack Belief, (Middle) Min Robot-Human separation (m), and (Bottom) End-effector speed (m/s) across 30 episodes. Replay begins at step 60. Blue denotes live observations, red denotes the replayed source observations received by the policy, and green denotes the live trajectory with Simplex stopping.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a robotic harvesting method that combines RGB-D fruit localization, GA-based harvest ordering, and waypoint-based robot motion in dense and unstructured crop environments. The global RGB-D camera provides 3D fruit positions for ordering, while the end-effector-mounted camera provides close-range observation during execution. The GA determines the harvesting sequence, and static or dynamic waypoints define the intermediate robot motion. The method was evaluated in a controlled laboratory testbed and in four-, five-, and six-fruit field conditions. GA solutions were compared with exhaustive enumeration, and both waypoint offsets were examined by parameter sensitivity analysis. Continuous execution reduced unnecessary Home-return motion, while the dynamic waypoint changed with the remaining fruit distribution without changing the GA sequence. In the field evaluation, the dynamic-waypoint continuous strategy produced 40 collision events and a 70.7% target-approach success rate, compared with 55 collision events and 65.3% for the static-waypoint continuous strategy.
bullets: Uses a global RGB-D camera for 3D fruit positions and an end-effector camera for close-range observation.
The genetic algorithm selects harvest sequences, while static or dynamic waypoints guide intermediate robot motion.
Evaluated in a laboratory testbed and field scenarios containing four, five, and six fruits, with comparisons against exhaustive ordering.
Continuous execution reduced unnecessary returns to the home position.
The dynamic-waypoint continuous strategy achieved 40 collision events and a 70.7% target-approach success rate, versus 55 collisions and 65.3% for the static-waypoint strategy.

papers.abstract: One of the remarkable abilities of Transformer-based neural networks is in-context learning. This motivates us to think about "in-context" control. Can we control a system knowing only (1) that it belongs to a particular family of systems and (2) some data on system evolution (provided as the context trajectory) but no specific parameter information? Specifically, we investigate the ability of Transformer-models to perform "in-context" control of unstable, nonlinear dynamical systems, where context consists only of the unforced system dynamics. We leverage a multi-head, GPT-2-style architecture, and we evaluate performance for two classical nonlinear systems -- the cartpole system and the two-link acrobot system, where the system parameters are unknown to the Transformer. We consider a setting where trajectories from an expert controller are available at training time but not at inference time. Here, we identify training techniques that are essential to train Transformers to perform low-level control. Through an analysis over checkpoints, we show that in-context control is possible, and the learned policy performance generally improves as context increases. Furthermore, the Transformer models can generalize to stabilize systems that are out-of-distribution.
bullets: Studies in-context low-level control when system parameters are unavailable and only unforced dynamics are provided as context.
Uses a multi-head, GPT-2-style Transformer trained with expert trajectories that are unavailable during inference.
Evaluates control on the nonlinear cartpole and two-link acrobot systems.
Finds that specific training techniques are essential for learning effective control policies.
Shows that in-context control is feasible, performance generally improves with more context, and some out-of-distribution systems can be stabilized.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained diffusion and flow policies have emerged as powerful backbones for robotics, yet adapting them to novel data via reinforcement learning (RL) remains computationally expensive, sample inefficient and lacks theoretical guarantees. Prior approaches that fine-tune the initial noise bypass costly backpropagation through time but struggle with the "noise aliasing" problem: there does not exista natural link between the noise space value and the action space value. This paper resolves these challenges by introducing the Latent Noise Linear Markov Decision Process (LNL-MDP). We derive the Bridge Equation for LNL-MDPs which eliminates the noise aliasing problem by aligning values with a shared representation between the noise and the action space. Furthermore, our LNL-MDP fine tuning framework falls under the FineTuneRL theory with near-optimal guarantee. Leveraging these insights, we propose Latent Representation Bridging for Diffusion (LARBRID), an algorithm that efficiently learns the representation to optimize the initial distribution that steers the pre-trained model to act optimally in the environment. It yields up to 2-3$\times$ performance increases on challenging control problems across a diverse suite of robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks. Code can be found at: github.com/Maincode-Research/LARBRID.git.
bullets: Pretrained diffusion policies are costly and sample-inefficient to adapt to new tasks with RL.
The proposed Latent Noise Linear MDP (LNL-MDP) establishes a shared representation between initial noise and actions.
A derived Bridge Equation removes the noise-aliasing problem and supports FineTuneRL guarantees.
LARBRID learns a latent representation that optimizes the policy’s initial noise distribution without costly backpropagation through time.
The method improves performance by up to 2–3× on diverse robotic locomotion and manipulation control tasks.

papers.abstract: VREgo trains manipulation policies from demonstrations recorded on consumer VR headsets; we instantiate it with EgoKit on one such headset, the PICO 4 Ultra. On-device head and hand tracking and stereo object localisation allow the operator to begin a demonstration at the table. We adapt HumanEgo's preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds per recording, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes. We evaluate policies in simulation on two tabletop tasks recorded by one operator. For cube placement, we compare PICO and Project Aria recordings of the same 41 layouts. With 40 training demonstrations, the PICO policies placed the cube on the tray in 67, 74, and 60 of 100 evaluation layouts across three training seeds. The corresponding Aria results were 73, 78, and 0. For a two-stage stacking task recorded with the PICO alone, the baseline placed the block on the tray in 94 of 100 layouts and met the end-of-episode criterion for both placements in two. In one diagnostic episode, repeated replanning deferred release beyond the eight executed steps. Demonstration replays also showed that the open gripper could displace the cube before grasping it. After adapting the training trajectories and adding task-specific execution rules that use simulator object positions, the system met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four evaluation noise seeds. The same 100 layouts informed rule development and evaluation. VREgo is available at https://vrego.chuange.org/.

papers.abstract: Deformable linear object (DLO) manipulation is challenging because high-dimensional configurations, nonlinear contact dynamics, and diverse material and geometric properties produce a broad range of object responses that are both difficult to model and data-intensive to learn. This work studies reinforcement learning for planar manipulation of a one-end-grasped DLO, focusing on training efficiency, observation design, robustness, and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. We compare three Proximal Policy Optimization training stacks and find that the GPU-parallel MuJoCo Playground stack enables faster convergence and more consistent performance than CPU-based alternatives under the same wall-clock budget. Relative keypoint observations and an asymmetric actor-critic formulation further improve learning efficiency. Policies trained with observation noise, delay, domain randomization, and disturbances achieve simulation success rates of 96.4% for single-point tracking, 98.0% for disturbance recovery, and 88.8% for two-point tracking. Using markerless RGB-D keypoint estimation, the policies transfer without real-world fine-tuning, succeeding in 9/10, 10/10, and 8/10 physical trials, respectively.
bullets: Studies planar manipulation of a one-end-grasped deformable linear object under challenging dynamics and varied properties.

papers.abstract: Robotic automation of laboratory tasks has become a growing interest to remove researchers from hazardous environments and repetitive procedures. However, even equipment as simple as squeeze bottles poses a challenging manipulation problem due to its deformability. This paper presents an adaptive hybrid vision-force controller for robotic grippers to effectively manipulate laboratory squeeze bottles to dispense liquid. This approach integrates force and vision feedback according to the interaction state, enabling effective squeezing while accounting for bottle deformation and recovery. The proposed controller is validated by comparing its performance with a pure force controller on 12 combinations of conditions consisting of 2 target dispense volumes, 2 plastic squeeze bottles, and 1 to 3 squeezes used to dispense. Human demonstrations of these operating conditions were collected using electromyography (EMG) sensing mapped to a desired grip force, which was then used as the force reference for the controllers to squeeze the bottles. Results demonstrated that the proposed adaptive hybrid vision-force controller achieved more accurate liquid dispensing with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 6.54 mL compared to a MAE of 15.92 mL from the pure force controller, while also replicating the human action recorded from the EMG signal more closely.
bullets: Addresses inaccurate dispensing caused by bottle deformation and recovery.

Uses human EMG demonstrations to derive desired grip-force references.

papers.abstract: The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enables scalable demonstration collection independently of a specific robot. However, its moving, close-range gripper cameras entangle camera and object motion without a stable external view, leaving the metric geometry needed for precise manipulation implicit in RGB. We introduce Spatial-UMI-Dream, a 5B spatial World Action Model (WAM) pretrained on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data through two-stage training -- world-only adaptation followed by joint world-action learning -- to jointly predict future RGB, fisheye-aligned metric depth, and actions. Stereo-derived depth makes scene scale and spatial relationships explicit within a unified dual-gripper RGB-D representation. Furthermore, evaluating UMI policies requires testing whether UMI's robot-independent demonstration collection translates into policy generalization across robot embodiments, alongside robustness to environmental changes. We introduce RoboTwin-UMI, a twenty-task simulation benchmark built on RoboTwin with UMI wrist-mounted fisheye observations, enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation of UMI policies under environment and embodiment changes separately and jointly without additional fine-tuning. On RoboTwin-UMI, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 79.10% in-domain success and 72.15% under combined embodiment and environment shifts, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline in each setting by 4.65 and 10.30 percentage points, respectively. It also exhibits the smallest success-rate drop under embodiment transfer among the evaluated policies. In a matched pretraining ablation, RGB-only pretraining leads to a 5.75-percentage-point decrease in in-domain success compared with RGB-D pretraining. Across six real-world tasks, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 85.0% average success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 24.2 percentage points. Project page: https://weiduoyuan.com/spatial-umi-dream/
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit metric geometry in UMI’s close-range, moving-camera observations.
Pretrains a 5B model on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data, first for world modeling and then jointly for world-action prediction.
Introduces RoboTwin-UMI, a 20-task benchmark for separately and jointly evaluating environment and embodiment shifts without fine-tuning.
Achieves 79.10% in-domain and 72.15% under combined shifts, with the smallest embodiment-transfer drop among evaluated policies.
Across six real-world tasks, reaches 85.0% average success; RGB-only pretraining reduces in-domain success by 5.75 percentage points versus RGB-D.

The shared world-action transformer uses block-causal attention to condition prediction on preceding visual history. Stage 1: world-only adaptation predicts future RGB-D observations, decoded through the Wan VAE and supervised by Lworld. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong performance in many tasks by letting agents learn from nothing more than a reward signal. However, in more complex tasks, agents still struggle to learn good, generalizable policies, even with carefully designed rewards and abundant samples. We argue that this difficulty stems from the reward decoding burden: designers encode their knowledge of the desired behavior into rewards and penalties, and agents must infer this knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalars. To address this burden, we propose prescriptive policy learning (PPL), which directly teaches agents higher-level knowledge about the tasks, termed principles of behavior, such as how to maintain balance, how to accumulate energy, and how to land smoothly. Through appropriately selected key quantities and references, PPL can directly indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles and to what extent. Our experiments show that agents can learn good, generalizable policies without any reward. Taught only simple heuristic principles, PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples. Their policies also transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well, demonstrating their strong generalization ability. In summary, PPL provides a new approach in which rough knowledge of the desired behavior is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when the system dynamics cannot be accurately modeled.
bullets: Targets the reward-decoding burden in complex reinforcement-learning tasks, where agents must infer desired behavior from noisy scalar feedback.
Uses selected key quantities and reference values to indicate at each step whether behavioral principles are being followed and to what degree.
Agents can learn without a conventional reward, using only simple heuristic principles such as maintaining balance or landing smoothly.
Experiments report fewer samples, strong generalization, and direct transfer to harder settings compared with reward-based methods.
The approach relies on rough behavioral knowledge and does not require accurately modeled system dynamics.

papers.selection_reason: Reward-free policy learning from behavioral principles; directly relevant to learned control and robot skill acquisition.
papers.title: Teaching Agents the "Principle", Not the "Reward": Prescriptive Policy Learning
papers.tldr: Prescriptive policy learning teaches agents behavioral principles directly instead of requiring them to infer them from reward signals, enabling more sample-efficient and generalizable policies.

papers.abstract: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).
bullets: Addresses the limits of one-off benchmarks and holistic scores for deployed agents.
Evaluates span, trace, conversation, and engagement levels across Execution, Substance, Trajectory, and Results, with Conduct as a constraint.
Uses provenance, adjudication, versioned rules, and atomic evidence to handle biased raters and censored outcomes.
An inner loop audits evidence, rules, and metrics; an outer loop drives improvement through per-component regression checks.
Case studies suggest evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring, with reported ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81 and kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a closed-loop evaluation framework for agents, relevant to Embodied AI (agent evaluation) and Test-Time Learning (self-calibration).
papers.title: Closed-Loop Agent Evaluation: Layered Measurement and Self-Calibration
papers.tldr: Closed-loop evaluation continuously audits both agent performance and the evaluation process, then feeds component-level findings back into agent improvement.

papers.abstract: In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy(HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.
authors: Sihang Chen, Chen Ye, Wei Chen, Xiaohan Lei, Zhipeng Tang, Sha Zhang, Yuan Zhang, Zixuan Chen, Jiajun Deng, Houqiang Li, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Introduces nine tasks requiring interaction history at key decision points.
Covers environment memory—locations, attributes, and relationships—and process memory for task progress and scheduling.
Uses Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation to derive later constraints from the robot’s own earlier actions, reducing fixed-target shortcuts.
Provides 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training and an HMAP baseline with structured memory and subgoal-conditioned control.
Scope: evaluates memory-dependent behavior in mobile manipulation rather than general-purpose memory.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for mobile manipulation that explicitly evaluates environment and process memory, directly relevant to Robot Learning and Manipulation and Embodied Memory.
papers.title: Robocasa-Mem: Benchmarking Environment and Process Memory in Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: RoboCasa-Mem benchmarks whether mobile manipulation agents can use environment and process memory to make consistent long-horizon decisions.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering information that is no longer visible, such as an object's location before occlusion or the order of a demonstrated action sequence. A large vision-language planner can read this history, but calling it before every action chunk is slow and costly. We present a three-tier system for the RoboMME benchmark. GPT-6 Astra (System 2) selects a grounded subtask from stored visual history, a $\pi_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy (System 1) executes it, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor (System 1.5) checks after each action chunk whether the subtask is finished. The instruction is kept until the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs, while the policy keeps acting on new observations. On RoboMME, the system succeeds in 79.13% of episodes with an average of 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode. This is 34.62 points above the best published non-oracle baseline and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which gives the low-level policy ground-truth subgoals.
authors: Bingao Chen, Haoquan Fang, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the need to remember occluded object locations and demonstrated action order without invoking a large planner before every action chunk.
Astra (System 2) selects grounded subtasks from visual history; π0.5 executes them; a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor detects subtask completion.
The system retains instructions until completion or a task-specific event, while the policy acts continuously on new observations.
It averages 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode, outperforming the best published non-oracle baseline by 34.62 points.
Performance remains 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which provides ground-truth subgoals.

The VLA executes actions at in 16-step chunks; the environment returns observations ot, and a local monitor checks progress after each chunk. papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses robotic manipulation with a focus on memory (occlusion, action order) using a hierarchical system, fitting Robot Learning and Manipulation and Embodied Memory.
papers.title: Can Astra Solve RoboMME without Breaking the Bank?
papers.tldr: A three-tier robot system uses Astra sparingly for long-term planning while lower-cost models execute and monitor subtasks, achieving 79.13% success on RoboMME.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have achieved strong performance on single-task robotic manipulation. However, a single model trained jointly on multiple tasks consistently underperforms the per-task specialists trained on the same demonstrations. We focus on two challenges. First, the convolutional encoders commonly used in diffusion-based policies produce visual conditions that are not discriminative enough. Second, gradients from incompatible action modes update the shared denoiser's dense parameters along the same directions, causing destructive interference during joint training. To address both, we propose SR-DP (Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy). A frozen VGGT encoder with a spatial-compression adapter produces compact multi-scale semantic-geometric tokens, a task-discriminative visual condition for tasks that share a workspace. We first train the denoiser as a standard diffusion policy, then decompose selected linear layers by SVD into a frozen basis of orthogonal rank-one experts, adapted through spectral routing and Householder input rotations. On six RoboTwin tasks, SR-DP averages a 68.4% success rate, surpassing multi-task VO-DP by 21.8 points and the strongest per-task baseline by 3.8 points. On four real-world bimanual tasks, Stage 2 reaches a 43.0% average success rate and improves over Stage 1 by 19.0 points.
bullets: Multi-task diffusion policies can underperform task-specific specialists because visual conditions are insufficiently discriminative and shared gradients interfere.
A frozen VGGT encoder with a spatial-compression adapter produces compact, multi-scale semantic-geometric tokens.
Selected denoiser layers are decomposed into frozen orthogonal rank-one experts and adapted using spectral routing and Householder input rotations.
SR-DP achieves 68.4% average success across six RoboTwin tasks and 43.0% across four real-world bimanual tasks; Stage 2 improves 19.0 points over Stage 1.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of SR-DP. A frozen VGGT encoder with a spatial-compression adapter produces 14 tokens per view, which condition an AdaLN-Zero DiT denoiser. Selected linear layers of the denoiser are decomposed via SVD into rank-one experts and modulated by a compact router (Stage 2).

Fig. 5. Encoder feature t-SNE. Visual conditions from the complete FDP, multi-task VO-DP, and SR-DP pipelines over 9,600 held-out frames (1,600/task) across the six RoboTwin tasks. FDP uses ResNet, VO-DP pools VGGT without task loss, and SR-DP pairs VGGT with the spatial adapter and task head.
Fig. 10. Real-world rollouts of SR-DP on the four TeleAvatar tasks. Rows correspond to T1–T4, and columns show temporally ordered key frames from one successful Stage 2 rollout per task.
Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison on the six RoboTwin tasks: each task pairs a selected Stage 1 failure (top) and Stage 2 success (bottom) under the same initial conditions to illustrate failure modes.

Fig. 4. Two-stage training. Stage 1 jointly trains the adapter, task head, and a standard DiT denoiser without task conditioning. Stage 2 freezes the visual encoder and task head, decomposes well-conditioned layers by SVD, and updates only the router and Householder vectors.

Fig. 6. Loss-sensitivity conflict in the shared SVD basis. Layer-averaged task-pair sensitivity cosine (4 held-out windows/task, n=50, shared noise; negative: opposing sensitivities). Stage 2 lowers the mean conflict score from 0.267 to 0.104.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses multi-task robotic manipulation with a diffusion policy, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy for Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: SR-DP improves multi-task diffusion policies by combining task-discriminative visual features with spectrally routed denoiser experts to reduce cross-task interference.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions, showing strong capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks. However, in our probing experiment, we find that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding. Motivated by this late-layer grounding gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free inference method for pre-trained VLAs. STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates, allowing later action representations to inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers without model updates or architectural changes. It further uses recent proprioceptive states to adapt the mixing strength, using conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show that STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rates by 4.0 percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/STAR.
bullets: Addresses a late-layer grounding gap in vision-language-action models, where action representations may lose task-relevant visual information.
Applies an exponential moving average to late-layer residual updates so later representations inherit object-aware directions from earlier layers.
Adapts the mixing strength using recent proprioceptive states, applying more conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly.
Improves late-layer object awareness and raises average task success by 4.0 percentage points on robot manipulation benchmarks.
Requires no model updates or architectural changes; its scope is pre-trained VLAs and the evaluated manipulation benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A case study of layer-wise object awareness in VLA inference. (a) Original and objectmasked RGB observations in LIBERO-PRO, where task-relevant object regions are replaced with the mean RGB values of the image. (b) A Transformer layer in a VLA, mapping the action hidden state from hk to hk+1 through a residual update. (c) Object awareness of π0.5 layer outputs across depth under native inference and our method STAR. (d) Success rates of native inference and our method STAR on LIBERO-PRO for π0.5 and GR00T-N1.5, respectively.

Figure 2: Overview of action generation at step t. STAR estimates a step-level EMA coefficient βt from proprioceptive history and applies it to layer-wise updates. Blue arrows denote the EMA coefficient βt derived from proprioceptive history, while pink arrows denote the cross-layer update momentum used in the EMA mixing.

Figure 3: Object-awareness and attention-map diagnostics for native inference and STAR. (a) Visualization of the three masks, including the task-specific object mask mo, randomly scattered pixels mr with the same pixel count, and a randomly sampled rectangular background region mb of similar area. (b) Comparison of awareness scores for native inference and STAR under object masking and control masking at layer 18. (c) Attention-map visualization at layers 13, 16, and 18, showing that native inference and STAR produce similar attention patterns. (d) Attention mass on the task-object region across layers. Native inference and STAR exhibit close attention-mass curves, indicating that attention-based object focus does not clearly reveal the hidden-state intervention effect.

Figure 4: Action-gradient scores on LIBERO-PRO. (a) Mean normalized input-gradient evidence contained in the task-object region for native inference and STAR across the five LIBERO-PRO evaluation splits. Higher values indicate that the predicted action depends more strongly on the key object. STAR consistently increases the score on all five splits. (b) Distribution of paired score differences, computed as STAR minus native inference. Most of the mass lies to the right of zero, showing that the increase is consistent across evaluation samples rather than being driven only by split-level averages.

Figure 5: Qualitative action-gradient saliency maps. The left column shows the RGB observations with task-relevant objects marked by cyan boxes. The middle and right columns show saliency under native inference and STAR, respectively. Warmer pixels exert a stronger local influence on the predicted action. Compared with native inference, STAR concentrates more action-relevant evidence within the marked object regions across diverse manipulation scenes.
Table 4: Ablation on beta scheduling. A proprioceptively scheduled β with a moderate range outperforms both fixed cross-layer mixing strengths and poorly calibrated dynamic ranges.

Table 3: Ablation on proprioceptive evidence. Using all four proprioceptive cues gives the best average success rate, showing that mixed updates benefit from both steady-progress and transitionsensitive signals.

Table 1: Main results on SimplerEnv. For OpenVLA, the average is computed over the available tasks. STAR improves frozen VLA policies on both backbones and achieves the best average success rate, outperforming both native inference and DTP while remaining single-pass.
Table 2: Main results on LIBERO-PRO. STAR improves the average success rate on both GR00TN1.5 and π0.5, while DTP gives limited or mixed gains on this long-horizon benchmark.
Table 5: Ablation on start layer. Applying mixed updates only to the final third of layers gives the best average success rate, supporting late residual updates as the effective intervention target.
