papers.selection_reason: A training-free inference method (STAR) to improve object awareness in pre-trained vision-language-action models by steering action representations.
papers.title: STAR: Steering Action Representations during Inference
papers.tldr: STAR is a training-free inference technique that improves robot manipulation by steering late-layer action representations toward better visual grounding.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models now grade robot videos, and text placed beside the frames can change their verdicts. On clips where the robot is losing progress, we add one log line saying the robot is making progress. Across Gemini, Qwen and GPT judges, this flips correct verdicts to progress 10 to 35 percentage points more often than a neutral line does. A one-line warning that the log may be wrong removes most of this effect. Selected fake "task complete" claims flip half of Qwen's correct verdicts, against a tenth for unrelated log lines. They have no detectable effect on Gemini.
bullets: Adding a false progress log beside videos where the robot is losing progress causes more verdict reversals than a neutral log across Gemini, Qwen, and GPT judges.
A one-line warning that the log may be incorrect largely mitigates this influence.
Fake “task complete” claims reverse about half of Qwen’s correct verdicts, versus about a tenth for unrelated logs.
Gemini shows no detectable response to the selected fake completion claims.

figures.caption: Figure 2: A fake progress line flips correct verdicts 10 to 35 points more often than a neutral line in all three judges; selected fake “task complete” claims fool Qwen, with no detectable effect on Gemini. Each dot is the rate at which a correct Falling verdict turns to Rising, minus the same rate for the control: a neutral sentence (left) or an unrelated log line (right). Bars are 95% CIs. Only intervals the judge gets right on the frames, both forward and reversed. Numbers in Table 1.

Figure 1: One fake “task complete” log line flips Qwen’s correct verdict. Task: hand the pen from the left to the right arm, then place it in the blue plate; the right arm never takes the pen. On the frames alone, Qwen answers Falling (losing progress): “the right arm remains open and does not grasp it”. With the log “Successful completion confirmed: the pen was . . . transferred to the right arm, and placed in the blue plate”, it answers Rising (making progress): “the execution log confirms the successful completion of the task”. Example chosen for visual clarity.

Table 1: Effects of execution-log text on reversal-consistent intervals (the judge is right on the frames, forward and reversed). Counts, and rate differences with episode-level bootstrap 95% CIs (2,000 resamples). Repeat: the frames-only call run again. The regression log (“the robot is losing ground”) counts turns to Falling. A completion claim counts only if a second call with it also answers Rising. The completion-claim attack used all Falling intervals for Qwen and a random 80 for Gemini.

Table 2: The warning gives the best accuracy with a contradicting log, but the judge also gains less from an agreeing one. Gain: accuracy with an agreeing log minus accuracy with a neutral sentence, under the same prompt. The two blocks are separate runs of 240 intervals with slightly different baselines. Verify lowers Qwen’s neutral-sentence accuracy on Falling (0.78 to 0.61), which inflates its gain.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the influence of execution logs on VLM judgments of robot progress, relevant to the evaluation of vision-language models in robotics.
papers.title: Execution Logs Sway VLM Judges of Robot Progress
papers.tldr: Robot-progress judgments by VLMs can be strongly swayed by misleading execution logs, though warnings reduce the effect and susceptibility varies by model.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators must navigate safely in cluttered, partially unknown environments across logistics, manufacturing, and service applications. Semi-static changes between robot visits can lead to outdated scene knowledge and increased collision risk. We propose an active perception framework that enables a high degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulator to inspect uncertain or safety-critical regions with its hand camera during navigation. A probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view (NBV) formulation prioritizes observations near the desired path and around uncertain or potentially changing objects. The perception objective is integrated into hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC), exploiting kinematic redundancy for viewpoint adjustment while preserving the higher priority of base-trajectory tracking. The system unifies navigation, map maintenance, and active perception in a closed loop. Real-world tests show improved map consistency, reduced task-dependent map entropy, and lower navigation risk than passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional simulation and real-world sequences demonstrate responses to controlled semi-static scene changes.
bullets: Targets outdated scene knowledge caused by changes between robot visits.
Uses probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view selection near the path and uncertain or changing objects.
Integrates perception with hierarchical-task model predictive control, using arm redundancy while prioritizing base-trajectory tracking.
Real-world tests report improved map consistency, lower task-dependent map entropy, and reduced navigation risk versus passive and non-task-aware baselines.
Validated in simulation and real-world sequences with controlled semi-static scene changes.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Our mobile manipulator setup. The system consists of a Universal Robots UR10 arm mounted on a Clearpath Robotics Ridgeback omnidirectional base. Two synchronized Orbbec Femto Bolt RGB-D cameras are installed, with one mounted on the base and the other mounted on the hand. An onboard laptop runs all the perception, planning and control algorithms.

Fig. 1: A snapshot of the proposed active perception and navigation framework for high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulators in action. Equipped with a hand camera, the robot operates in cluttered, semi-static environments. It uses its kinematic redundancy to reposition the camera around obstacles and observe uncertain or occluded regions near its navigation path. See the multimedia attachment or online videos6 for demonstrations.

Fig. 7: Bird’s-eye-view 3D reconstruction results in the real-world static-scene benchmark. Rows correspond to Scene 1–3. Green, yellow, and red indicate true positives, false negatives, and false positives, respectively. The proposed method recovers more occupied voxels in blind and path-critical regions.

Fig. 8: Task-dependent map entropy along executed paths in the real-world static-scene benchmark. Left: boxplots over the three loops in each scene. Right: representative top-down views with trajectories colored by the local entropy. Lower values indicate lower entropy in the regions traversed by the robot.
Fig. 5: Detailed schematic of the proposed active perception module.

Fig. 6: Real-world static-scene benchmark. Left: Scene 1 Easy Loops. Middle: Scene 2 Hard L-Shaped Walls. Right: Scene 3 Hard Office Scene. The scenes progress from open loops to sharper turns and cluttered occlusions, where hidden hazards near the waypoints make active map maintenance important.

In each visit, the robot re-enters the room with the maintained object map, acquires new observations near the shelf, updates the map, and replans according to the current shelf position, switching between the outside and inner routes.

The dashed red line marks zero clearance under this proxy, corresponding to a near-contact configuration. Vertical dashed lines mark loop boundaries, and shaded regions indicate intervals when the robot is away from the boxes and receives no observations of them. Each box changes primarily when its side of the corridor is displaced.

Fig. 10: Controlled Isaac Sim scene-change experiment. The red curves are the executed base trajectories, and the blue arrows show the sampled hand camera headings. After one row of boxes is shifted, the hand camera redirects toward that side to acquire additional observations.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an active perception framework for mobile manipulators that integrates navigation, map maintenance, and task-aware next-best-view planning.
papers.title: Object- and Task-Aware Active Perception for Safe Navigation of Mobile Manipulators in Semi-Static Environments
papers.tldr: An active-perception system uses a mobile manipulator’s hand camera to update uncertain, task-relevant regions during navigation, improving map consistency and reducing collision risk in semi-static environments.

papers.abstract: The diagnostic capability of WSI agents relies on effective slide navigation to identify diagnostically relevant regions and efficiently integrate evidence across the slide. While in clinical practice, pathologists dynamically examine slides across multiple scales, integrating global and cellular evidence in a sequential manner, existing AI navigation approaches mostly operate at a single fixed magnification or rely on predefined magnification traversal. This mismatch prevents existing methods from modeling cross-magnification interactions and adaptive magnification selection inherent to real diagnostic workflows. We propose PathPilot, a clinically consistent multi-magnification WSI navigation agent that explicitly models cross-magnification localization and evidence-adaptive exploration. Specifically, we introduce a CrossMagLoc that learns magnification-specific diagnostic localization from pathologist viewing behavior and integrates information from adjacent magnifications to identify the diagnostically most relevant region within the current ROI, thereby providing a diagnostically informed starting point for subsequent question-conditioned exploration. We further introduce an EviRegionSearch that starts question-conditioned exploration from this region, progressively accumulating question-relevant evidence and adaptively determining the next navigation action according to the remaining evidence requirement. Their iterative interaction enables PathPilot to sequentially explore across ROIs and magnifications until sufficient evidence is acquired. Extensive QA evaluations across five cohorts demonstrate consistent superiority over competing SOTA methods on inter/external cohorts, respectively, validating question-conditioned evidence acquisition across regions and magnifications that mirrors the sequential, knowledge-driven navigation of pathologists.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed-magnification and predefined-traversal WSI navigation agents.
CrossMagLoc uses pathologist viewing behavior and adjacent magnifications to localize diagnostically relevant regions.
EviRegionSearch begins from the localized region and selects subsequent actions based on remaining question-relevant evidence.
The two components iteratively explore regions and magnifications until sufficient evidence is acquired.
Evaluations across five cohorts report consistent superiority over competing methods on inter- and external-cohort QA tasks.

Fig. 2: Overview of PathPilot and its two complementary navigation components. Given a WSI and pathology question, PathPilot starts from the thumbnail and iteratively alternates between CrossMagLoc and EviRegionSearch until sufficient evidence has been accumulated for answering the question. CrossMagLoc performs question-agnostic localization of diagnostically relevant candidate ROIs at each magnification by combining magnification-specific representations with spatially aligned information from adjacent scales. EviRegionSearch performs question-conditioned exploration over the ROI identified by CrossMagLoc, integrates morphological observations from the selected ROI with the accumulated evidence, identifies the remaining evidence requirement, and adaptively determines the next navigation action (Move, Zoom In, Zoom Out, or Stop) to select the next region.

Fig. 1: Overview of PathPilot for adaptive WSI exploration. For each navigation step (e.g., Step t), CrossMagLoc identifies the diagnostically most relevant region within the current ROI, while EviRegionSearch accumulates question-relevant evidence and adaptively selects the next navigation action (e.g., Step t+1). Their iterative interaction enables sequential movement across ROIs and magnifications until evidence is sufficient (e.g., Step t + N), where Stop is selected and the final answer is generated.

Fig. 5: Pathologist-in-the-loop interpretation of CrossMagLoc across five magnifications (thumbnail, 1.25×, 2.5×, 5×, and 10×; top to bottom). The columns show the pathology images (column 1), CrossMagLoc predictions (column 2), test-set navigation annotations (column 3), and independent annotations with morphological explanations from pathologists trained in Europe (column 4) and Asia (column 5). Across magnifications, CrossMagLoc consistently prioritizes diagnostically relevant regions identified by the pathologists while deprioritizing non-primary or artifact-limited areas. At 2.5×, it assigns higher attention to well-preserved tumor regions than to the crush-artifact region, while at higher magnifications it continues to emphasize morphologically informative tumor regions. Overall, its localization broadly agrees with pathologist viewing behavior while additionally highlighting clinically relevant regions identified during independent review.

Fig. 7: Visualization of a representative question-conditioned navigation workflow. CrossMagLoc-based ROI localization and EviRegionSearch-based evidence reasoning are iteratively coupled to support adaptive exploration across regions and magnifications, evidence requirement reasoning, and final answer generation once sufficient evidence is acquired.

Fig. 6: Quantitative evaluation of CrossMagLoc navigation performance. The radar plot summarizes pathologist-prioritization alignment (ρN , APN 5 , and 1 − JS N ) and tumor-region precision/recall at the thumbnail, 1.25×, and 2.5× magnifications, with PathFinder Ghezloo et al. (2025) and PathAttFormer Chakraborty et al. (2022) as navigation baselines and pathologist navigation as a clinical reference for tumor-region alignment. CrossMagLoc achieves the strongest agreement with pathologist prioritization while maintaining high tumor recall across magnifications, indicating a similar balance between diagnostic focus and broad tumor coverage.

papers.abstract: Success conditioning is a strategy for improving decision-making policies in stochastic environments; it updates a policy by increasing the probability of taking actions that yield successful outcomes. Success conditioning is common to many reinforcement learning applications, yet its limiting behavior and convergence rates are not well understood. In this work, we demonstrate that success conditioning converges to an optimal policy on a broad class of Markov decision processes (MDPs). We also derive convergence rates in some common settings. For discounted MDPs, we prove convergence within $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon^p)$ iterations to an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy, where the exponent $p$ depends on problem data. For single-period MDPs, such a policy is obtained within $\mathcal{O}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations.
bullets: Analyzes the limiting behavior of success conditioning, a policy-improvement strategy based on favoring successful actions.
Proves convergence to an optimal policy for a broad class of Markov decision processes.
For discounted MDPs, reaches an ε-optimal policy in O(1/ε^p) iterations, with p determined by problem data.
For single-period MDPs, reaches an ε-optimal policy in O(log(1/ε)) iterations.
papers.selection_reason: Provides convergence analysis for success conditioning in policy optimization, relevant to Robot Learning and Manipulation.
papers.title: On the Convergence of Success Conditioning for Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: The paper proves that success conditioning converges to optimal policies for broad classes of MDPs and establishes iteration-rate guarantees.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for contact-rich manipulation requires high-quality expert data that is expensive to obtain. This makes learning a sample-efficient policy a key issue. To address this, we propose VISTA, a workspace-level equivariant visuotactile diffusion policy for data-efficient contact-rich imitation learning. VISTA projects visual and tactile observations into spherical tokens, injects tactile contact cues into visual spherical directions through permutation-equivariant spherical fusion, and rotates the fused harmonic representation using the end-effector orientation. The resulting representation conditions an equivariant diffusion policy to predict spatially consistent actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic settings show that VISTA substantially improves data efficiency over strong visuotactile imitation learning baselines. Project website: https://vista-paper.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting expert demonstrations for contact-rich imitation learning.
Projects visual and tactile inputs into spherical tokens and fuses tactile contact cues with visual directions.
Uses end-effector orientation to rotate the fused harmonic representation, preserving spatial consistency.
Conditions an equivariant diffusion policy to predict manipulation actions.
Experiments in simulation and on real robots show improved data efficiency over strong visuotactile imitation-learning baselines.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Pedicle screw placement is technically demanding in scoliosis treatment. High precision is required due to limited visibility, anatomical variability, and the risk of complications. Although robotic systems assist CT-based planning and execution, they still rely on ionizing intraoperative imaging and complex registration. This study proposes robotic pedicle drilling with real-time preventive breach detection using electrical bioimpedance sensing. Methods: We developed a robotic approach combined with a pedicle-drilling tool equipped with a proprioceptive electrical bioimpedance sensor developed by SpineGuard. A real-time detection algorithm was designed to analyze the electrical bioimpedance signal during drilling and identify abrupt changes in conductivity associated with potential breaches towards the spinal canal. The method operates without external devices or sensors. Results: The ex vivo experiments showed that the proposed method prevented breaches in 100 of the 51 drilling cases. These findings demonstrate the system's ability to detect potentially hazardous events during drilling and to stop the procedure before. The ex vivo experiments demonstrated that the proposed method prevented breaches in all 51 drilling cases. Conclusions: This work demonstrates the feasibility of robotic pedicle drilling with electrical bioimpedance sensing for real-time breach prevention. Using only the tool signal, the method eliminates the need for external sensing systems and supports safer pedicle screw placement.
bullets: Addresses the safety challenges of pedicle screw placement in scoliosis, including limited visibility and anatomical variability.
Combines robotic drilling with a proprioceptive electrical bioimpedance sensor and an algorithm that detects abrupt conductivity changes linked to potential breaches.
Operates using only the drilling tool’s signal, avoiding external sensing systems and intraoperative imaging for breach detection.
In ex vivo testing, the system prevented breaches in all 51 drilling cases.
The findings demonstrate feasibility for real-time breach prevention, but are limited to ex vivo experiments.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) provide a compact and stable formulation for trajectory representation and generalization in robot skill learning. However, their predefined basis layout limits the allocation of approximation capacity according to stage-dependent precision requirements. To address this issue, this article proposes Stage-Criticality-Guided Dynamic Movement Primitives (SC-DMPs) with adaptive basis allocation for precision-critical skill learning. Operator-robot interaction stiffness and a trajectory-consistency cue derived from cross-demonstration task-space variability are integrated to construct a stage-criticality index. Guided by this index, basis centers are redistributed in normalized time through inverse cumulative criticality and mapped to the canonical phase domain, while their bandwidths are refined to adjust local approximation support. This enables denser and more flexible representation at high-criticality stages while retaining sparser allocation elsewhere. Experiments on handwriting trajectories and three real-robot tasks show that the inferred criticality is concentrated in geometrically demanding and task-constrained regions. Comparisons with DMPs, ProMPs, ProDMP, GP-MP, and KMP demonstrate improved trajectory reproduction, endpoint generalization, and task-critical accuracy while retaining a compact model and the stable structure of classical DMPs.
bullets: Targets the fixed basis layout of standard DMPs, which cannot match stage-dependent precision needs.
Builds a stage-criticality index from interaction stiffness and cross-demonstration trajectory variability.
Redistributes basis centers via inverse cumulative criticality and refines bandwidths for local flexibility.
Evaluated on handwriting and three real-robot tasks, with criticality concentrated in geometrically demanding and constrained regions.
Reports improved reproduction, endpoint generalization, and task-critical accuracy versus several motion-primitives baselines.

papers.abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different \textit{ex-vivo} porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4\% and 72.5\% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70\% success in 90-degree turns and 60\% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/.
bullets: Addresses weak texture, specular highlights, deformable anatomy, and contact-rich interactions that challenge conventional and learning-based navigation.
Uses an RGB-D-E Action Chunking Transformer with RGB, estimated relative depth, and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to emphasize fold ridges and geometric cues.
Predicts overlapping action chunks and fuses them through temporal ensembling for continuous, smooth robot control.
In ex-vivo porcine colons, success rates were 85.4% in straight segments, 72.5% in curved segments, 70% in 90-degree turns, and 60% in double-bend sequences.
Triple-bend experiments further demonstrate feasibility, though performance scope is limited to ex-vivo evaluation.

papers.abstract: Autonomous exploration demands that robots continuously evaluate candidate viewpoints based on their expected information gain and execution cost. Sampling-based planners estimate this gain by volumetric raycasting and, due to its computational cost, evaluate candidates under an assumption of mutual independence, ignoring the overlap between viewpoints along the same path. This work presents a GPU-accelerated method for computing path-dependent marginal information gain, where instead of storing and merging the observed unknown voxels along each candidate path, previous observations are represented using depth buffers. Candidate rays are projected into the depth buffers of their ancestors to identify observation overlap and exclude regions expected to be observed. The planning tree is evaluated in depth order to maintain the dependency between viewpoints and their optimized yaws, while candidate nodes and rays at each level are processed in parallel on the GPU. The proposed method stays within 5-10% of the exact marginal gain computed using voxel hash maps, with speed-ups of up to 118x on a desktop GPU and 28x on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The method was integrated into two sampling-based exploration planners and evaluated in three simulation environments, where marginal gain reduced the time to 95% coverage in five of the six evaluated planner-environment combinations. Real-world experiments also showed a 30% reduction in the time to 95% coverage, as well as earlier exploration termination times.
bullets: Addresses the cost and inaccuracy of assuming independent information gain between viewpoints on the same path.
Projects candidate rays into ancestor depth buffers to detect overlapping observations without storing voxel sets.
Processes planning-tree levels and candidate rays in parallel on GPUs while preserving viewpoint dependencies and optimized yaw choices.
Achieves gain estimates within 5–10% of exact voxel-hash-map computation, with speedups up to 118× on desktop GPUs and 28× on Jetson Orin NX.
Integrated planners reached 95% coverage faster in most simulation cases and showed a 30% real-world reduction in coverage time.

papers.abstract: We focus on legible robot motion generation in social navigation settings. Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently infer the robot's intent. While mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, social robot navigation presents a new challenge: the robot must clearly convey its intent while ensuring human safety in dynamic pedestrian environments where human attention is often divided. With the goal of enabling robots to generate legible motion in dynamic and constrained spaces, we investigate how the choice of representation and the level of human attention shape navigation performance and human impressions. Focusing on the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, we conduct two controlled user studies involving alternative legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 (N = 45) investigates the role of intent representation, showing that passing-side legibility, particularly when adaptively updated, leads to smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than destination-based and non-legible baselines. Study 2 (N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion allows for smooth human motion even under distraction, even if this is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI.
bullets: Legible motion must communicate intent while maintaining safety in dynamic, constrained pedestrian environments.
Two controlled user studies evaluated alternative legibility formulations within a shared model predictive control framework.
Passing-side intent, particularly when adaptively updated, was perceived as more competent and less demanding than destination-based and non-legible motion.
Legible motion enabled smoother human movement under distraction, although subjective ratings did not always show the same effect.
The findings support interaction-level intent representations for coordinating robot–human navigation.

papers.abstract: Video generation models (VGMs) offer strong spatiotemporal priors for embodied observation--action modeling. However, joint-space action vectors lack explicit image-space structure and vary in dimensionality and semantics across embodiments, making it challenging to directly leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors of VGMs. End-effector visualizations provide an alternative but do not specify the full articulated configuration needed for robot execution. We present Dream4ACT, a world model built for joint video-action modeling across embodiments. To unify action representations across embodiments, we introduce a shared visual action interface, called action views, which render target joint configurations from four prescribed virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics. This shared visual representation preserves embodiment-specific articulated geometry while allowing observation and action sequences to share a video autoencoder and diffusion transformer. Through masked flow-matching, our model supports forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and joint observation--action generation within a single jointly trained model by varying which future sequences are corrupted. To recover executable action sequences from predicted action views, we propose a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview recovery mechanism, without a learned embodiment-specific decoder. Dream4ACT achieves an average success rate of 88.98\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and an overall score of 65.66 on TriWorldBench, supporting effective closed-loop manipulation and competitive action-conditioned multiview prediction through the visual action interface.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between embodiment-specific joint-space actions and video models’ image-space representations.
Renders target joint configurations from four virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics as shared “action views.”
Uses masked flow matching in one jointly trained model for forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and observation–action generation.
Recovers executable actions with a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview procedure.
Reports an 88.98% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 65.66 overall score on TriWorldBench.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.
authors: Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Siyuan Hu, Ziqi Huang, Tianqi Liu, Mingze Sun, Ziyi Wang, Zhongang Cai, Hanming Deng, Quan Wang, Lei Yang, Lewei Lu, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Dahua Lin, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Problem: Fixed visual encoders may discard action-critical details such as local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes.
Method: Tokenizes images with lightweight patch convolutions and jointly processes visual tokens with language across the backbone.
Action generation uses a flow-matching expert conditioned on visual representations from multiple depths.
Controlled comparisons find native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts; scaling alone does not close the gap.
Layer-wise probing and evaluations under distribution shifts indicate that useful control signals often emerge before the final visual layer.

Figure 2: NEO-VLA: pixels in, continuous actions out. Previous and current multi-view observations preserve their aspect ratios within a fixed token budget and enter patch embedder shared across time and views. The visual path uses no vision transformer, autoencoder, or vector-quantised codebook. Shared MLPs embed camera intrinsics and rotations, while state MLPs embed previous and current robot states. These tokens join a structured prompt describing control frequency, embodiment, frame reference, and task instruction. A separate, narrow, randomly initialised action expert jointly attends to cached prefix keys and values from selected backbone layers and its own action-token keys and values. Its suffix embeddings combine projected noisy actions and flow time τ with additive step, frame, and identity embeddings. Both arm blocks and the body block share temporal rotary offsets 0–29, with identity embeddings distinguishing the blocks. Trained by flow matching, the expert predicts a velocity field that covers both arm and body action chunks.

(c) NEO-VLA removes the separately pretrained visual encoder: a lightweight patch embedder maps pixels directly into the backbone token space, while text tokens enter the backbone jointly. A narrow action expert then reads cached keys and values from selected backbone layers and predicts a flow-matching velocity field.

papers.abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.
authors: Siyuan Hu, Abulikemu Abuduweili, Yue Meng, Shipeng Liu, Quentin Leboutet, Chen Chen, Matthias M\"uller, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Addresses the lack of large-scale paired data mapping visual and language inputs to humanoid joint commands.

papers.abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

bullets: Addresses the gap between broad zero-shot capabilities and the need for deployment-time adaptation.

papers.abstract: Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.
authors: Chibueze Praise Onyenweaku, Toyibat Adele, Sikirulahi Opeyemi Abdulkareem, Obed Honour Eje
bullets: Apparent pedestrian height remains relatively stable under occlusion, while monocular depth shifts toward the nearer occluding surface.

It requires no training or occlusion annotations and can check the depth-model assumption without labels.
It detects heavy occlusion with AUC 0.909 on KITTI, 0.819 in synthetic CARLA scenes, and remains effective within fixed distance ranges.
Several tested architectural approaches did not generalize beyond training distributions, highlighting the value of annotation-free signals.

papers.abstract: For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.

papers.abstract: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.
bullets: Studies self-repair for simulated robot manipulation using repeated program generation after scene resets.
A fixed lookup selects feedback templates from failure labels and API variants, while a frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-7B generates retries.
On 252 initial failures, template feedback recovered 85.3% within five retries versus 68.3% for resampling, with the gap persisting under equal token budgets.
Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance achieved similar recovery estimates, with no detected benefit from matching coarse failure labels.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanScale, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanScale-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

papers.abstract: Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models, yet progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation is often assessed separately. This survey reviews work from January 2024 to early November 2026, with earlier studies included to establish technical lineages. We organize the literature into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications. Human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing provide two cross-cutting perspectives. A system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses connect design choices across these layers. We distinguish within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results. Three conclusions emerge. First, the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment, not recording volume alone. Second, shared action representations and foundation policies do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact. Third, task completion is insufficient to establish physical correctness or deployment readiness. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization. We identify eleven open problems and propose reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons that can make full-stack progress more measurable. The review is a structured narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review.

Argues that task completion alone does not demonstrate physical correctness or deployment readiness.

papers.abstract: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.

papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors capture multiple aspects of physical interaction within a single image stream, including contact appearance, geometry, indentation depth, and tangential deformation. However, existing visuo-tactile policies often directly process tactile observations as images, making it difficult to determine which physical cues contribute to policy learning. This paper presents a controlled real-robot study that compares physically interpretable tactile signals using the LeRobot platform, enhanced with our visuo-tactile perception system. From the same tactile stream, we derive tactile RGB images, normal/depth maps, and marker-flow fields, representing contact appearance, geometry, and tangential deformation, respectively. Using identical task demonstrations and the same policy backbone, we evaluate the individual and combined contributions of these tactile cues. We further compare tactile encoders and visuo-tactile fusion strategies. Evaluation across 720 real-robot trials yields four key findings: (1) tactile perception substantially improves the overall success rate from 57.8% to 78.9%, although its contribution varies across task stages; (2) marker flow is the most effective individual cue, achieving a success rate of 74.4% and playing a particularly important role in regulating established contact; (3) cue-factorized encoding consistently improves performance, highlighting that different physical cues require tailored processing techniques; and (4) although the effectiveness of tactile fusion is task-dependent, cross-attention offers a lightweight solution with performance comparable to that of pretrained tactile encoders.
authors: Xuhao Qin, Xiyan Huang, Haoyu Dong, Xi Zhang, Chenxi Xiao
bullets: The study isolates contact appearance, geometry/depth, and tangential deformation from the same tactile stream.
Across 720 real-robot trials, adding tactile perception raised success from 57.8% to 78.9%.
Marker flow was the strongest individual cue, reaching 74.4% success and helping regulate established contact.
Cue-factorized encoders consistently improved performance, suggesting different physical cues need tailored processing.
Cross-attention provided a lightweight fusion strategy with performance comparable to pretrained tactile encoders, though fusion effectiveness was task-dependent.

papers.title: Which Physical Tactile Cues Matter for Contact-Rich Imitation Learning? A Controlled Real-Robot Study

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained on static offline datasets, yet physical manipulation unfolds sequentially across stages. Because a weakness in a downstream stage remains unobservable until the policy passes earlier ones, each resolved bottleneck exposes the next hidden failure mode. This staged structure calls for Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), in which a policy iteratively executes, diagnoses failures, and updates itself. Moreover, because task completion behaves like a product of stage-level pass rates, recursive gains can multiply across generations. In physical environments, three bottlenecks obstruct compounding: terminal execution feedback rarely localizes the stage that caused a failure, failed trajectories do not supply the corrective action, and updating shared parameters can degrade previously mastered skills. We propose Compounding Physical RSI, a self-evolving policy framework that turns execution failures into heritable capability. First, automated capability-gap assessment traces failed rollouts to the task stage where progression breaks down and formulates a structured improvement objective. Second, conditioned on this objective, our remedy stage curates validated, stage-relevant experience and refines the policy via behavior-regularized offline reinforcement learning, without requiring costly online rollouts at each optimization step. Third, to safeguard existing skills, our retention stage constructs weight-space candidates between the inherited reference policy and the refined policy, evaluates them across the task suite, and promotes the best candidate as the reference state for the next generation. Evaluated across all 42 tasks of the RoboDojo-Sim benchmark, CSU-AI-07 ranks first on the leaderboard with a three-seed mean Overall Score of 26.15 and Success Rate of 20.70%, outperforming the next-best entry by 5.92 points and 5.82 percentage points.
authors: Yixuan Yang, Qiang Chen, Run Shao, Shuwei Dong, Wenhao Li, Yunpeng Wang, Wenhan Fang, Haomiao Wu, Xingyu Wang, Lichen Man, Rong Zhang, Xuezhi Cui, Yuan Liu, Bingyan Lu, Jiawei Ma, Xiaoyang Ma, Zhemin Sun, Zhuorui Yao, Yutong Dong, Yuxuan Zhao, Yichong Mu, Jiabao Jiang, Wenxuan Deng, Junling Zhou, Yi Chen, Deyu Zhang, Yiming Yan, Yige Yuan, Shan You, Fei Wang, Haifeng Li, Hongyan Xu, Yichao Cao, Xiu Su

Diagnoses failed rollouts to identify the task stage where progress breaks down and defines a structured improvement objective.
Curates validated stage-relevant experience and applies behavior-regularized offline reinforcement learning without requiring online rollouts for each update.
Uses weight-space candidate selection between inherited and refined policies to retain existing capabilities.
On all 42 RoboDojo-Sim tasks, CSU-AI-07 achieves a three-seed mean Overall Score of 26.15 and Success Rate of 20.70%, ranking first in the reported evaluation.

papers.abstract: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
authors: Rui Zhu, Xurui Li, Haixu Tang
bullets: Targets semantic mismatches such as permuted axes, inverted signs, rescaled rotations, and reversed gripper polarity that can satisfy basic action constraints.
Uses learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts, calibrates alarms on clean held-out transitions, and localizes faults with a fixed inverse vocabulary.
On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks at a 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate, exact conditional scoring reached 65.7% recall versus 61.0% for a joint Gaussian mixture and 46.1% for ridge residuals.
Joint scoring achieved 95.8% localization versus 94.6% for ridge, indicating a detection–localization tradeoff.
Findings support a bounded offline diagnostic, not deployment-calibration guarantees, cross-robot safety, or broad robustness beyond the tested scope.

papers.abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.

For larger single-view chunks, clean queries can read only their own latent interval and earlier clean intervals. (b) The replay noisy pass reads language 𝒯 , an available prefix ℋprefix from earlier segments, and strictly earlier clean chunks. (c) The clean pass supplies layerwise K/V for parallel noisy-target evaluation, with shared parameters and a single optimizer update. papers.abstract: Controlling the shape profile of soft trunk robots extends their reach into complex regions of the workspace and enhances their use in practical applications. Recent advances in soft robot design have enabled soft trunk robots to achieve greater flexibility in conforming to complex shapes. Specifically, trunk robots whose geometries are designed as helicoids have been shown to enable extreme shape-changing capabilities. Their compliance makes them highly nonlinear, which in turn makes shape control difficult. On similar tendon-driven trunk robots, model-based controllers based on the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) have achieved high accuracy in closed-loop end-effector tracking. We extend this approach by learning an aSSM model of the full body of a trimmed-helicoid soft trunk robot from data and use this in a model predictive control (MPC) scheme to demonstrate a range of shape control tasks on hardware. On closed-loop dynamic shape regulation, our method outperforms the available linear baselines by a factor of 10. In human-in-the-loop interactive demos, our method completes section-by-section shaping and balances a tennis ball for over 25 seconds, while the linear baselines fall short. A model-free reinforcement learning policy trained for 12 hours on hardware fails on the same balancing task. These results establish aSSM-based MPC as a practical route to full-body shape control on real soft hardware.
authors: Hehui Zheng, Marc Stampanoni, Roshan S. Kaundinya, Ronan Hinchet, George Haller, Robert K. Katzschmann
bullets: Soft trunk robots can reach complex regions but are difficult to control because their compliant dynamics are highly nonlinear.
The approach learns a full-body adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM) model from data and uses it within model predictive control.
Hardware experiments demonstrate dynamic shape regulation, interactive section-by-section shaping, and tennis-ball balancing.
Dynamic shape regulation outperforms available linear baselines by a factor of 10; the system balances a tennis ball for over 25 seconds.
A model-free reinforcement-learning policy trained on hardware for 12 hours fails at the same balancing task.

figures.caption: Fig. 5: Closed-loop dynamic shape tracking of a 30 s reference trajectory. Column: tracked body 1, 3, and 5 (tip) along the trunk. Row: component of that body’s pose. The top three rows give position along the x, y and z axes, with the dashed black line the reference and the colored lines the four models; the bottom row gives the orientation tracking error, the geodesic angle between the measured and the reference orientation.

Fig. 6: Human-in-the-loop shape control tasks under each learned model, all driven by the hand-held wand. (a) Sectionby-section dynamic shaping: the operator selects one section at a time, and the active section (green) holds its distal body at a 10 cm standoff from the wand while the remaining sections hold position. Three frames show the aSSM driving each section; the linear baselines are shown at their final reached shape. (b) Tennis ball balancing: the tip follows the wand with the same 10 cm standoff while its orientation is constrained to keep the distal face level. Labels mark the time along the run, while red marks the instant the ball leaves the face. Under the aSSM the ball is held for over 25 s. ERA and DMDc hold neither the standoff nor the face level and lose the ball after 2 s and 0.4 s; LOpInf keeps it to 19.5 s only by leaving the trunk essentially undeflected.

Fig. 4: Closed-loop shape control based on (a) aSSM, (b) ERA, (c) DMDc, and (d) LOpInf toward one of the 8 targets. The physical trunk is shown in white and the yellow silhouette shows the target, which is independently recorded by human teleoperation of the trunk. The aSSM is shown over 0–5s and reaches the target within 4.2s; the three linear baselines are shown over the full 30s hold and none of them converges to the target shape.

Fig. 3: Open-loop height z prediction on a sample sequence for bodies 1, 3 and 5 (tip). Each model is rolled out from a single initial condition for 750 time steps with no ground truth measurement feedback. Height z is measured from the base (body 0) along the trunk axis. The shaded band is the ±20 mm measured repeatability of the platform, combining material hysteresis and motor tracking error.

Fig. 7: Model-free reinforcement learning on hardware for the tennis ball balancing task. Top: mean return over 4,320 PPO iterations trained directly on the soft trunk, corresponding to 12 h of robot interaction. Bottom: the resulting policy evaluated over 8 s. Left: the trunk drops the ball after 1.8 s. Right: the tip tracks the wand only over a small region of the workspace (4 s to 5 s) and moves to the opposite side as the wand travels beyond it. The white arrow shows the wand motion and the red arrow the tip motion.

Fig. 2: Hardware platform and the effect of tendon routing on inter-section coupling. (a) Five trimmed-helicoid segments stacked in series, with marker body 0 at the base and bodies 1–5 at the distal end of each segment. Colored strips illustrate the three tendon groups driving the sections, grey marks the sleeved portion routed through the segments below. (b) With PTFE tubes, the sleeves plastically deform (left), giving up to 58◦ of uncommanded deflection. (c) Nesting each tube in an extension spring (left) reduces the largest uncommanded deflection to 6◦ while increasing the commanded bend of section 3 from 87◦ to 112◦. Section 2 uses a 0.8/1.2 mm tube in a 2.0 mm spring, section 3 a 0.6/1.6 mm tube in a 3.0 mm spring.

papers.abstract: Ground robots operating in temperate forests suffer from systematic LiDAR occlusions caused by tree trunks, creating persistent blind regions that degrade traversability estimation. In this paper, we propose FOSCo-Net, a self-supervised voxel completion framework that learns to reconstruct occluded geometry from a single scan using temporally accumulated observations as automatic supervision, and we evaluate cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs. FOSCo-Net consistently improves reconstruction quality and traversal safety, with a gated skip decoder achieving the most reliable performance and significantly reducing false obstacle predictions compared to baselines.
bullets: Addresses persistent LiDAR blind regions caused by tree trunks in temperate forests.
Reconstructs occluded voxel geometry from a single scan using accumulated observations as automatic supervision.
Evaluates cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs.
A gated skip decoder provides the most reliable reconstruction and reduces false obstacle predictions versus baselines.
Scope: ground-robot LiDAR perception and traversability estimation in forest environments.

papers.abstract: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present soccerbot, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, soccerbot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.
authors: Haoyu Shao, Yunshen Wang, Jingze Zhang, Shaohang Zhu, Yong-Lu Li, Tianzhu Zhang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining locomotion, ball control, and contact-rich dynamics across continuously changing soccer behaviors.
Distills a latent motion prior from large-scale human soccer motion-capture data to constrain learning to dynamically plausible movements.
Trains one skill-conditioned policy for moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking, including fluid transitions when switching skills.
Uses robustness-oriented simulation design to enable zero-shot transfer to the Unitree G1 humanoid.
Demonstrates agile, natural, and robust execution of the full skill repertoire in real-world conditions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SOCCERBOT. The framework consists of three stages: (1) a motion tracking expert is trained on retargeted human soccer motion data; (2) the tracking expert is distilled into a structured latent motion prior via a variational encoder-decoder framework; (3) a unified skillconditioned policy learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking via residual latent control over the frozen prior, with transition state initialization enabling robust cross-skill composition. Real-world deployment uses an external motion capture system for ball state estimation.

papers.abstract: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.
authors: Xuemin Hu, Kaixin Li, Qingqing Xia, Yuxin Wang, Wei Xie, Bo Tang, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses high-dimensional, coupled humanoid dynamics and differences across joint degrees of freedom.
Factorizes policies at the torque-actuated JDoF level using actuation, kinematic, and dynamic descriptors.
Co-optimizes the high-level pose planner and low-level joint executor in a closed loop using shared trajectories.
Experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym show improved locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over several baselines.
Scope: demonstrated for humanoid robot control in simulation environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. H2MARL overview. The high-level planner generates JDoF-level pose increments and converts them into absolute target poses. The low-level joint executor receives the absolute target poses combined with historical proprioception and outputs executable joint positions which are converted to torques by a PD controller. Both the high-level policy and the low-level executor are optimized by the coupling trajectories in a closed-loop.

Fig. 1. Limb- and JDoF-level multi-agent formulations for the humanoid robot. (a) Traditional limb-level formulation, where each limb is formulated as an independent homogeneous agent. (b) JDoF-level formulation, where each torque-actuated JDoF is formulated as an independent heterogeneous agent with physical attributes and functional roles.

papers.tldr: H^2MARL improves humanoid whole-body control by combining joint-level heterogeneity awareness with jointly optimized hierarchical planning and execution.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.
authors: Milan Bulat, Gino Ardelean, Ellington Kirby
bullets: Driving scores can reward agents that push through obstacles rather than stop safely.
The method varies one scenario factor at a time and estimates commitment, competence, and decision accuracy across certified passable or blocked cases.
Across seven CARLA agent families, the rule-based expert achieved 0.74 decision accuracy versus 0.60 for the highest-scoring learned agent.
Agents with similar driving scores showed different failure modes, including poor waiting for safe oncoming-traffic gaps.
Applied unchanged in Isaac Sim, the tested robot policy stopped at blocked gaps in only one of three families; fine-tuning improved clean passage but eliminated stopping behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes failure-boundary evaluation for closed-loop driving and robot navigation agents, directly relevant to embodied navigation assessment.
papers.title: Beyond Infraction Scores: Failure-Boundary Profiles for Closed-Loop Evaluation of Driving and Robot Navigation Agents

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.
authors: Shengzhe Zhang, Qi Zhang, Dazhong Shen, Chao Wang, Shaopeng Zhai, Hui Xiong
bullets: Addresses task-irrelevant visual shortcuts caused by limited perceptual supervision in action prediction.
Derives candidate target-object and robot regions from interaction-induced visual changes, then refines them offline with segmentation.
Uses attention allocation and contrastive objectives to focus visual processing on relevant regions and align them with language instructions.
Improves multiple VLA backbones across simulated and real-world benchmarks, with average success-rate gains of 6.5%–25.2%.
Scope: guidance depends on regions extracted from the manipulation process and refined offline.
