papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.
authors: Asher James Hancock, Boyi Li, Yuxiao Chen, Shuhan Tan, Wenhao Ding, Thomas Tian, Yan Wang, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone
bullets: VLA training can provide action information through expert-loss gradients, discrete action-token supervision, or both.
The study independently varies gradient routing and action-token supervision in autonomous driving and robot manipulation.
With action-token supervision, insulation is competitive in open-loop driving; without it, coupling lowers trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%.
When trained jointly from the start, coupling improves closed-loop route progress by approximately 17% with action tokens and 40% without them, while also improving manipulation performance.
The benefit of insulation depends on supervision and evaluation setting rather than being universally protective of VLM capabilities.

papers.abstract: We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against them by filtering per-frame depth through dense $(x,y,\theta)$ pose grids. PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor's depth fixed, PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc's forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and UnLoc's offline refinement from $T=35$ on; it exceeds Z-FLoc's published results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23-32 pp under wheel odometry and 35-43 pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches 100% SR@1m at 9-10 cm median error on the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres across at 0.90-0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions; adding learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at 0.67-0.92 with the localizer unchanged throughout. PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with trajectory length.
bullets: Uses dominant wall orientations to generate a small set of pose candidates and masked normalized cross-correlation to match observed free space to a known floor plan.
Combines a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter with consensus readout, while allowing the depth front-end to remain interchangeable.

On construction-floor sessions, achieves 0.90–0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions, extending to all five with learned wall isolation.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.
authors: Seungyong Lee, Suhyeok Jang, Minyoung Kim, Jinwoo Shin

Across multiple humanoid embodiments, synthetic-data policies improved novel-task success from 2% to 60%, including bimanual manipulation.
Matched teleoperation-trained policy performance at roughly one-third of the data-collection cost.

papers.abstract: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.
authors: Sombit Dey, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel
bullets: Targets latency in large vision-language-action models caused by sequential reasoning and control.
Uses a high-capacity VLM to asynchronously update semantic memory and a lightweight vision-action expert to produce actions at a higher frequency.
Trains the action expert to handle stale semantic memory and execution delays from asynchronous processing.
On Franka tasks, reports 18% higher success and 20% shorter execution time in quasi-static settings, with 3–5× baseline performance in dynamic simulation.
Runs the VLM at 10× lower than its nominal frequency without significant performance loss, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io
authors: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of reliable outdoor, long-range navigation despite GNSS noise and weak vision-language instruction execution.

In simulation, it remains robust to GNSS noise and produces about ten times fewer crosswalk and sidewalk violations than point-goal baselines.
A wheeled-legged robot completed missions up to 1.37 km across urban, rural, and campus environments, including stairs and construction sites.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation involves not only moving objects, but also arranging the hand around them to maintain useful contacts and enable subsequent actions. Yet many learning-based systems specify goals primarily through object poses or trajectories, leaving hand-object configurations to emerge implicitly. We introduce DexHOT, which formulates dexterous manipulation as hand-object configuration transfer: moving between feasible configurations that jointly specify hand articulation and object pose relative to the wrist. DexHOT learns a reusable relation-conditioned transfer primitive from synthetic feasible configuration pairs, without human reference motions, and composes long-horizon behaviors through closed-loop tracking of configuration subgoals. On DexHOTBench with 120 objects, a single policy achieves 80.5% transfer success on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen objects; on a real dexterous hand, it achieves 61.5% success over 200 real-robot transfers and 90% task success across six demonstration-guided tasks. These results show that explicit hand-object goals provide an expressive and composable interface for dexterous manipulation. More details and videos are available at https://dex-hot.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical pipelines for humanoid loco-manipulation typically pair a task-agnostic whole-body controller (WBC) with a downstream task policy. Such WBCs are often trained through manual reward shaping, which yields visibly machine-like motions; more consequentially, they are trained without the manipulated object in the scene. Object dynamics are instead approximated through randomized end-effector force disturbances, a proxy that fails to reproduce the distributed multi-contact wrench a real payload applies across the arms and torso, with the gap becoming critical near the platform's payload limit. In this work, we train the low-level (LL) controller itself as an object-aware motion prior: a single policy trained via motion imitation on retargeted motion-capture (MoCap) references that span the core motion primitives of the downstream task, with the manipulated object physically present in the scene. This single stage inherits natural human-like coordination from the references and absorbs the realistic contact wrench at its source, while exposing the same compact task-space command interface used by command-tracking WBCs. A reference-free high-level (HL) policy is then trained on top, with its action channel anchored to the empirical envelope of the low-level training data so that it generalizes the priors to a long-horizon multi-stage task while structurally preventing queries that would push the low level off-distribution. We instantiate the framework on a Unitree G1 for bimanual box pick-and-place: the same deployed policy generalizes across object masses and dimensions, initial and goal poses, and reactively recovers from intentional drops mid-carry. Video: https://youtu.be/viR_ULnRDQQ.
authors: Jean-Pierre Sleiman, Bilal Hammoud, He Li, Jonathan Foster, Sylvain Bertrand, Jessica K. Hodgins, Farbod Farshidian
bullets: Addresses machine-like motions and inaccurate object modeling in conventional WBC-based humanoid loco-manipulation.

Adds a reference-free high-level policy whose commands stay within the low-level training distribution.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) for vision-language-action (VLA) models promises smaller and faster VLA deployments. However, when analyzing existing VLA quantization works, we realised that it is hard to reason about the performance of the suggested quantization method compared to existing, similar, or in many cases, simpler PTQ methods. We present LoopQ, a closed-loop benchmark that compares multiple quantization policies on the same checkpoint, layers and engine, varying only the method and the kernels. We evaluate RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant and QuantVLA on four VLAs with more than 180,000 episodes of LIBERO and LIBERO-plus, compare against QVLA's reported results on the same layers, and benchmark whether the four public VLA-quantization releases can be reproduced. We benchmark the methods on an NVIDIA H100, an L4, and a Jetson AGX Thor. Our results show that while quantization reliably saves memory, 2-3x for real low-bit models, VLA-specific PTQ methods underperform compared to simpler generic baselines. At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA, plain RTN matches the calibrated methods, and plain AWQ matches the success QVLA reports for itself. Standard LIBERO hides the losses that do exist: configurations with no significant LIBERO loss lose 1.5-4.3 points under paired LIBERO-plus perturbations. Speed is a weaker story. At batch 1 on the H100, no quantized pi0.5 or OpenVLA-OFT configuration is faster than its 16-bit model (1.06-1.58x slower on library kernels); only the L4 with int8 kernels gains (4-14%), the Thor is slower on every 4-bit configuration, and the engine alone changes latency by 2.1x. Profiling explains why: pi0.5's quantized backbone is compute-bound, while its memory-bound action expert, 63% of GPU time and 13% of the parameters, stays in 16 bits.
authors: Syed Umer Bukhari, Magnus Almgren, Ahmed Ali-Eldin
bullets: Evaluates RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant, and QuantVLA under controlled conditions: same checkpoints, layers, engines, and varying only methods and kernels.
Covers four VLAs, over 180,000 LIBERO/LIBERO-plus episodes, and NVIDIA H100, L4, and Jetson AGX Thor hardware.
At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ, and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA; standard LIBERO can hide 1.5–4.3-point losses revealed by LIBERO-plus perturbations.
Quantization consistently reduces memory, but speedups are hardware- and kernel-dependent; some configurations are slower than 16-bit models.
Profiling attributes limited speed gains partly to a 16-bit, memory-bound action expert that accounts for most runtime in pi0.5.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and analysis of quantized VLA models in closed-loop settings, directly relevant to VLA and efficient deployment.
papers.title: LoopQ: Fair, Closed-Loop Evaluation of Quantized Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LoopQ finds that generic post-training quantization baselines often match or outperform VLA-specific methods, while memory savings do not reliably translate into faster inference.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/
authors: Po-Yi Wu, Djengo Cyun-Jyun Fang, Dian Cheng, Tsung-Wei Ke
bullets: Addresses the impracticality of frequent scene resets and human intervention in real-world RL deployment.
Introduces a high-fidelity simulation benchmark for non-episodic VLA fine-tuning in shared-scene, multi-task settings.
Finds that naively fine-tuning pretrained policies fails under shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses.
Shows that targeted reset allocation and mitigation of pretrained-model biases improve non-episodic training.
Reports better long-horizon manipulation and generalization to unseen object configurations and task sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Forced reset of unrecoverable scenes outperforms learned reset strategies. Only methods that forcibly reset all unrecoverable scenes (HSR and HSR-only) show a sustained increase in success rate.

Figure 12: Visualization of reset-free methods. We compare five methods: (1) periodic reset (PR), which resets the scene every T = 2560 steps; (2) heuristic scene reset (HSR), which detects unrecoverable states before each task switch and resets only when necessary; (3) heuristic scene reset without periodic reset (HSR-only), which uses heuristic resets without periodic resets, avoiding unnecessary resets in recoverable states; (4) learned scene reset (LSR), which learns reset behavior as an auxiliary task within a single policy, eliminating external reset logic at the cost of interaction budget; and (5) perturbation policy (PER), which extends LSR with a second auxiliary task that perturbs the scene, with the two tasks sampled uniformly at random.

Figure 6: Rollout success decays between scene resets. Top. Rollout success rate of SpatialVLA during non-episodic training. The vertical line at step 600K marks the switch from T = 320 to T = 2560, and triangles mark scene resets. Bottom. Snapshots of the scene between two consecutive resets. Objects become increasingly dispersed and eventually leave the reachable workspace, leaving few successful rollouts to learn from.

Figure 9: Forcibly resetting unrecoverable scenes is the most reset-efficient strategy. As the number of scene resets increases, only methods that forcibly reset all unrecoverable scenes (HSR and HSR-only) continue to improve in performance.

Figure 11: Non-episodic scene reset training improves sequential task execution. Non-episodic training outperformed episodic training on all subsequent tasks, including both task sequences seen and unseen during training. This improvement was consistent across different VLAs.

Figure 3: Long scene reset intervals expose the policy to diverse object starting positions. In non-episodic RL, each new task starts with the scene layout carried over from the previous task, causing object starting positions to become increasingly dispersed as the scene reset interval increases.

Figure 5: Frequent scene resets during early training improve interaction efficiency. With EER, training SpatialVLA with a reset interval of 320 steps followed by an increase to 2560 steps is the only strategy that exhibits an upward trend in task success rate.

Figure 7: Resetting unrecoverable scenes preserves learning signals. By resetting all unrecoverable scenes at each task switch, HSR achieved a 64% task success rate, compared with only 14% success rate without HSR.

Figure 4: End-effector reset mitigates pretraining bias. EER automatically resets the endeffector to its initial position at each task switch, improving the learning efficiency of SpatialVLA under non-episodic scene-reset settings.
Figure 10: In-domain and out-of-domain scene configurations. Out-of-domain scenes include overlapping and cluttered object layouts that do not appear during training.

Figure 2: Pretrained VLAs struggle to learn under non-episodic scene resets. When directly fine-tuned in the non-episodic multi-task setting, learning performance dropped dramatically as the scene reset interval T increased from 80 to 320 interaction steps, and failed at T = 2, 560 steps.
Table 1: Exposure to dispersed scenes improves spatial generalization. Non-episodic resetting outperforms episodic resetting in both dispersed scenes.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CRONOS, a benchmark for non-episodic reinforcement learning fine-tuning of vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation. This directly addresses robot learning and manipulation in embodied AI.
papers.title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: CRONOS benchmarks non-episodic RL fine-tuning of large vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation and shows that targeted resets and bias correction can improve robustness and generalization.

papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Junzhe Wang, Jinqing Zhang, Qingjie Liu
bullets: Existing rollout-based evaluators are costly and accumulate prediction errors over the planning horizon.
RFWorld builds a shared scene memory and trains it with lightweight temporally supervised readout to encode future-relevant information.
At inference, candidate trajectories sparsely query the shared memory instead of generating candidate-specific future states.
This reduces computation by roughly the planning horizon multiplied by the number of candidates.
Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive report state-of-the-art performance and more planning-aligned representations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall framework of RFWorld. The current BEV representation is transformed into a shared memory. During training, temporal readout with semantic supervision shapes the memory into a future-aware representation. During inference, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory for reward prediction, and the trajectory with highest score is selected as the final planning output.

Figure 1: Two paradigms for future-aware trajectory evaluation. Conventional methods evaluate each candidate by rolling out its future states separately. In contrast, RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory once and lets all candidate trajectories read from it directly for rollout-free scoring.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison between WoTE [24] and RFWorld on NAVSIM-v1. Legend from DriveDPO [29]. (a) RFWorld avoids leaving the drivable area and remains within the lane boundaries. (b) RFWorld decelerates in advance and safely avoids the pedestrian. (c) RFWorld stays close to the lane centerline and avoids potential collision with the adjacent-lane vehicle. (d) RFWorld better accounts for oncoming traffic and yields before turning, thereby avoiding potential future risk.

The top row shows the semantic maps predicted from the time-conditioned readout features, and the bottom row shows the corresponding ground-truth semantic maps. From left to right, the columns correspond to four future timestamps at T = 1 s, 2 s, 3 s, and 4 s. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a rollout-free world model for trajectory evaluation in autonomous driving; fits interactive world models and robot navigation.
papers.title: Trajectory Evaluation via Rollout-Free World Model for End-to-end Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: RFWorld evaluates autonomous-driving trajectories without explicitly rolling out future scenes, using a shared future-readable scene memory for efficient, accurate scoring.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at flomo-wam.github.io.
authors: Jeremy Collins, Namra Patel, Ayush Agarwal, Shitij Govil, Animesh Garg
bullets: Motivation: Full video is redundant for action prediction; dense 3D motion may transfer video-learned priors more effectively.
Method: A 5B video-generation model is fine-tuned to predict 3D scene flow and action tokens, using rendered flow encoded in the video model’s latent space.
Training: The model combines action-free human video with action-labeled robot teleoperation data.

Findings: Motion prediction supports generalization to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks; replacing or augmenting it with video prediction harms policy success and out-of-distribution generalization.
Interpretation: Action tokens attend substantially more to motion than video, indicating that video prediction can waste model capacity.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: (a) RoboTwin single-task evaluation. Recorded RoboTwin Easy success rates across five tasks, with 100 evaluations per task and method. Across all tasks, FloMo performs the best. (b) Inverse-dynamics scaling. Held-out action error versus action-data scale for two ground-truth conditioning signals (log-log). Recovering actions from motion is more sample-efficient than from video: the gap is largest at 1% of the data and narrows as data grows.

Fig. 1: Given an image and text prompt, FloMo jointly predicts dense 3D motion (scene flow) and robot actions using a pretrained video generation model using flow-matching. To tokenize scene flow, we transform cumulative 3D velocities into RGB videos that are encoded by the pretrained video backbone’s video encoder.

Fig. 4: Action attention concentrates on motion tokens. Share of actionquery attention to each input modality, averaged over attention heads and robot validation rollouts, as a function of DiT layer. Attention to motion rises through the trunk and dominates at the late-middle layers, while attention to video stays lowest throughout; averaged over layers, action queries attend to motion roughly 3× more than to video.

Table II: Per-stage training settings.

papers.selection_reason: Predicts 3D scene flow as intermediate for robot actions, leveraging human video pretraining; fits learning from human video and world model topics.
papers.title: FloMo: 3D Scene Flow as a World Action Model Intermediate for Learning from Human Video
papers.tldr: FloMo uses 3D scene flow as a compact intermediate between video pretraining and robot action prediction, improving transfer and generalization over directly predicting video.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.
authors: Yihang Liu, Yiming Chen, Mingzhe Zheng
bullets: Addresses whether multimodal robot agents must repeatedly reinterpret visual observations during interaction.
Represents object-part geometry with typed, evidence-aware symbolic references grounded in calibrated RGB-D.
Provides compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after actions, while refreshing only locally observed state.
Supports offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution with visual reasoning invoked on demand.
The abstract reports improved multi-step manipulation completion and substantially fewer repeated multimodal queries.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Model interaction cost. Mean (bars) and per-episode (markers) request wall-clock time (left) and recorded tokens (right) over 50 paired episodes per task (△: excludes unknown interrupted tokens).

Figure 2: Geometric abstraction between perception and reasoning. RGB-D observations are grounded into object geometry and exposed to the LLM through typed symbolic references and compact textual checkpoints. In policy synthesis, the LLM revises executable policies between rollouts, while perception and control run locally. In online execution, the same interface supplies updated geometry for successive decisions within a continuing episode.

Figure 3: Single-policy acquisition. Policies are revised between reset rollouts and evaluated after training freezes. Geometric Abstraction additionally uses supplied geometric references. Right: illustrative start and goal configurations, constructed in simulation rather than recorded policy trajectories.

Figure 5: Online execution and tasks. The agent acts in a single continuing scene until completion or the 200 s timeout; Geometric Abstraction receives grounded symbolic references and textual checkpoints. Right: illustrative start and goal states.

Figure 8: Cumulative success over elapsed wall-clock time. papers.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
bullets: Physical-AI policy errors can compound over trajectories, causing distribution shift and task failure.
DRAP estimates local perturbation amplification from a ridge-regularized state-transition model’s largest singular value.
It accumulates risk-weighted action-gradient importance per tensor and uses normalized importance to adapt AdamW learning rates without replay.
On a fixed KappaTune-selected OpenVLA subnetwork, DRAP improved retention over AdamW and EWC while maintaining strong acquisition on new LIBERO suites.
Scope: evaluated in replay-free sequential adaptation across LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.
authors: Xingyu Wang, Yanjiang Guo, Zhijing Ding, Jiaxin Fang, Zeyu Lai, Jiayu Dong, Weikang Wan, Jianyu Chen, Yuxiang Gao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the limited long-range context and high computational cost of dense short-horizon WAM prediction.
Uses sparse long-horizon and dense local-dynamics visual streams at different temporal scales.
A unified dual-DiT architecture connects the streams with structured cross-stream attention to guide actions.
Progressive inference with partial, joint, and dynamically skipped denoising achieves a reported 2.93× speedup.
Reports 93.70% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with in-domain and OOD performance on Fourier GR-3.

papers.abstract: We investigate the automated generation of executable robot reinforcement learning (RL) policies from natural-language task descriptions. Rather than using large language models (LLMs) as execution-time decision makers, we use them as designers that construct RL pipelines before deployment, including Markov decision process (MDP) formulation and simulator implementation. We identify a phase-wise structure in this problem: MDP formulation is dependency-structured and sequential, whereas simulator implementation becomes modular once the formulation is fixed. Based on this structure, we propose ARPG, a dependency-aware agentic framework that performs sequential MDP modeling, localized verification and correction, and simulator-structured implementation while externalizing intermediate artifacts. ARPG targets a key failure mode of automated policy generation: executable code may still yield non-learnable policies when state, action, reward, and termination artifacts are not semantically aligned. Experiments in Isaac Sim show that ARPG improves modeling correctness, environment executability, and policy-generation success compared with monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems. Additional demonstrations on custom robotics, standard RL, and engineering-domain MDPs further suggest that the same modeling pipeline can be reused beyond the main benchmark suite.
authors: Hong Je-Gal, Jinwoo Kim, Chanbin Yi, Hyun-Suk Lee
bullets: Targets automated generation of executable RL policies from natural-language task descriptions.

Experiments in Isaac Sim and additional domains show improvements over monolithic LLM and existing agentic baselines, though the abstract provides no quantitative results.

papers.abstract: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.
authors: Abhijeet M. Kulkarni, Saimouli Katragadda, Yuze Du, Zijun Sha, Guoquan Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-level VLA planning and the physical safety requirements of real-world legged-robot navigation.

Uses a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with discrete exponential barrier-function constraints for collision avoidance under stated assumptions.
The platform-agnostic system is compatible with different VLM/VLA models and is evaluated on both humanoid and quadrupedal robots.
Real-world experiments demonstrate versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language navigation.

papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.
authors: Jianye Xu, Yousef Sayed, Bassam Alrifaee
bullets: Addresses infeasibility and conservatism problems in conventional control-barrier-function safety filters.

Safeguards MARL throughout pre-training, deployment, and fine-tuning on unseen maps.
In simulations, it avoided all collisions; in recorded roundabout traffic, safeguarded policies reduced median travel time by 14% without collisions.

papers.abstract: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

papers.abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.
authors: Travis Davies, Wentao Ma, Lihao Guo, Tengfei Ma, Xiaowen Chang, Jiafeng Xu, Shilong Wang, Yiqi Deng, Shaowen He, Xiaoqi Li, Qian Zhu, Ran Cheng, Hao Dong

Uses view-aware interleaved attention plus camera identities to preserve consistency across views.
Converts the bidirectional generator into a 10.1-FPS autoregressive simulator with fast-video, slow-memory posttraining, self-rollouts, and hierarchical temporal memory.
Leads four of five WorldSimProbe suites and achieves the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration remains weaker; released with model weights and code.

They are still new embodiments, however, and adaptation between embodiments does not happen for free: each brings its own kinematics, camera mounting and data distribution, which have to be acquired rather than inherited. papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. Project page: https://ju6276.github.io/Action-Grounded-Foresight/
authors: Ju Dong, Xinyu Xiao, Yiming Zhou, Tianshuo Yang, Xuerong Liu, Lei Zhang, Jian Chen, Haocheng Zhao, Yu Fu, Yujie Wei, Diwen Zheng, Alois Christian Knoll, Angela P. Schoellig, Ping Luo, Jianwei Zhang

Achieves 89.7% average success in ten SIMPLE simulation tasks and 85.7% on seven real-robot tasks under standard conditions.

papers.abstract: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable. We introduce HTCE, a homeomorphism-inspired topological framework that canonicalizes and reuses navigation experience. Feature and topology subdivisions characterize representational variations, and their semantically constrained reductions produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures while preserving semantic anchors, branching relations, and navigation endpoints. HTCE then retrieves historical successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy. Canonicalization compresses the experience index losslessly, merging 17.7--23.6\% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance. Under a single frozen vision-language backbone shared by all compared systems, HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting---59.9\%/31.8\% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0\%/31.5\% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6\%/16.6\% on MP3D---with SR gains of up to 4.9 points and structured retrieval contributing up to 2.8 SPL points. The code is available in https://github.com/startracker0/htce.git
authors: Xiaoran Xu, Yupeng Wu, Tianyu Xue, Xuanran Dong, Yifan Xu, Xiaoshan Yang, Changsheng Xu

Losslessly merges 17.7–23.6% of distinct route descriptions while retaining full task performance.
Achieves the best reported SR and SPL across HM3D and MP3D settings, with gains of up to 4.9 SR points and 2.8 SPL points from structured retrieval.

papers.abstract: Robotics and AI systems are increasingly deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to follow high-level instructions, from routine household chores to more complex organizational tasks. Yet, broad directives like "clean the room" or "organize the desk" frequently omit crucial details about user preferences and specific arrangement of objects that influence the desired outcome. Without any further guidance, such models tend to overestimate their grasp of ambiguous instructions and frequently assume they have sufficient understanding despite missing important details. In this paper, we propose CLARA (Conversational cLArification for Robotic Arrangement), a cognitively-driven clarification framework that proactively elicits key information from users, in a similar fashion as humans' clarification seeking behavior. Through targeted questioning, CLARA refines ambiguous requests into structured, detailed instructions describing precisely how objects should be organized or rearranged, according to the user's preferences. These clarifications then guide a diffusion-based image generation pipeline, producing realistic visual renderings of the final, desired scene. This final rendering also serves as a visual confirmation of the system's understanding from the user. Experimental results and user studies demonstrate that CLARA leads to more accurate and consistent outcomes compared to another State-of-the-Art LVLM system, highlighting the importance of interactive clarification for bridging the gap between vague directives and fully grounded task specifications.
authors: Dimitrios Bekris, Marios Glytsos, Panagiotis P. Filntisis, Niki Efthymiou, George Retsinas, Petros Maragos
bullets: Addresses LVLMs’ tendency to make unwarranted assumptions about ambiguous directives such as “clean the room.”

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable progress in AI-generated content, including images and videos. In this paper, we explore whether diffusion models can generate the parameters of policy networks in reinforcement learning (RL), and whether the generated policies exhibit generalization capabilities. To achieve this, we propose Diffusion-based Conditional Policy Network Parameter Generation (DPPG), which consists of a Transformer-based autoencoder and a task-conditioned diffusion model. The autoencoder achieves a high compression rate by patchifying network parameters, while the task-conditioned diffusion model generates corresponding parameters conditioned on different environments. Our experiments demonstrate that, with a single unified DPPG model, we can synthesize high-quality policies across a diverse set of tasks from different environment domains, including Classic Control, Atari games, and MuJoCo. Additionally, our method can generate networks with a larger number of parameters compared to previous approaches. Furthermore, we find that in previously unseen environments, DPPG can generate parameters that achieve faster convergence and reach competitive performance, showcasing the potential future applications of parameter generation via diffusion.
bullets: Targets policy-network parameter generation with diffusion models for reinforcement learning.
Combines a Transformer-based autoencoder that patchifies and compresses parameters with a task-conditioned diffusion model.

papers.abstract: Pretrained generative policies provide strong behavior priors for robot control, but adapting them efficiently with online reinforcement learning remains difficult. A central challenge is how to improve a frozen generative policy without destroying the structure learned from offline demonstrations. Noise-space residual methods address this by modifying the policy's input noise, but existing noise-space methods typically regulate adaptation through fixed latent feasible regions, which may exclude valuable noise edits. In contrast, action-space residual methods are more sample-efficient, but their efficiency can still be further improved. We propose Conservative Noise Directional Optimization (CNDO), a noise-space residual RL method that improves a frozen generative policy by learning state- and noise-conditioned directions around Gaussian latent samples. CNDO removes predefined latent feasible regions and instead regulates noise-space adaptation through the soft conservative constraint, which consists of conservative value estimation and gated execution. We further introduce Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization (CANDO), which adds an action-space residual, combining structured latent-space improvement with local action correction. Experiments show that, once CNDO narrows the gap between noise-space and action-space residual learning, CANDO further improves over single-space optimization, achieving 76.1 NAUC and a 91.4% final success rate, surpassing the best single-space results by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1% success rate. More demos and info are available on https://cando-rl.github.io/.
authors: Zeyu Gao, Chengkai Hou, Chaoyue Li, Zhuangzhe Wu, Jiaming Liu, Yao Mu, Peng Jia, Li Zhang, Shanghang Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting pretrained generative policies with online RL without disrupting demonstration-derived behavior.

Experiments report 76.1 NAUC and 91.4% final success, exceeding the best single-space methods by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1 percentage points.

The pretrained policy remains frozen throughout.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.
authors: Jaehyeong Jo, Sangwon Jang, Sihyun Yu, Seonghyeon Ye, Yekyung Nah, Hojung Jung, Kimin Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Avoids costly iterative future-video generation and reduces errors from inaccurate visual predictions.
Uses representation distillation to train a visual encoder that predicts frozen video-diffusion representations from the current observation.
An action module extracts action-relevant information to produce robot actions.
Achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs across real-world and simulated tasks, with 11Hz closed-loop control using a 14B backbone.
Supports leveraging stronger video priors, extra video data, and unannotated demonstrations—including videos from different embodiments—for learning new tasks.

papers.abstract: Coordinating autonomous underwater vehicles requires translating operator intent into feasible assignments while preserving autonomous execution when communication is limited. We present a hierarchical framework that couples Large Language Model (LLM) interpretation of natural-language mission instructions with Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) and distributed Behaviour Tree (BT) execution. The LLM extracts assignment and ordering constraints, which the MILP optimizer combines with vehicle capabilities and temporal requirements. A BT-LLM Bridge distributes the resulting allocations to onboard BT Mission Managers. Per-vehicle Robotic Agents assess local faults and request selective replanning, allowing unaffected vehicles to continue their assigned tasks. Evaluation in a ROS-based AUV simulator compares Qwen-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B on constraint extraction and tests recovery from sensor degradation and critical vehicle faults. Qwen-3-8B provides more accurate constraint extraction, and all tasks are completed in the tested failure scenarios. These simulation results support the feasibility of combining language-based mission specification with structured allocation and distributed execution.
authors: Ehsan Khorrambakht, Cristiano Caissutti, Andrea Munafo, Andrea Caiti
bullets: LLMs extract task assignments and ordering constraints from operator instructions.
MILP combines extracted constraints with vehicle capabilities and temporal requirements to generate allocations.
A BT-LLM Bridge distributes plans to onboard Behaviour Tree Mission Managers.
Local agents detect faults and trigger selective replanning so unaffected vehicles can continue.
In ROS-based simulation, Qwen-3-8B extracted constraints more accurately than Llama-3.1-8B, and tasks completed in tested failure scenarios.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in cluttered environments must react to unexpected contacts before the first impact peak, which arrives within tens of milliseconds. Learned whole-body policies running at 50 Hz introduce a policy-cycle delay and may suppress a protective withdrawal as a tracking error. To address these challenges, we propose ARC (Ascending Reflex Control), a bottom-up framework that integrates instantaneous tactile reflexes with learned whole-body control. ARC consists of two components: an instantaneous reflex pathway and bottom-up reflex integration. The reflex pathway detects hazardous contacts from full-body tactile sensing, solves a whole-body withdrawal pose, and delivers it directly to the motors within 10 ms. Bottom-up reflex integration combines reflex-in-the-loop policy learning, reflex-transparent policy alignment, and reflex-informed policy adaptation to sustain the withdrawal, maintain balance, and complete longer-horizon recovery. We deploy ARC on a Unitree G1 and evaluate three categories of hazardous contact. Compared with an otherwise identical reflex delayed by 20 ms, ARC reduces the first force peak by 34.1% and reduces the contact impulse from 0.2632 N s to 0.1225 N s (a 2.15x ratio). We further demonstrate protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal guided by foot tactile sensing. Project page: https://minusmodulo.github.io/reflexarc-website/
authors: Mingyu Wang, Si Li, Ziqing Chen, He Wang, Li Yi
bullets: Targets the tens-of-milliseconds impact window that can precede learned-policy reactions.
ARC combines an instantaneous full-body tactile reflex pathway with bottom-up integration into learned control.
The reflex computes a whole-body withdrawal pose and sends it directly to the motors, while policy integration supports balance and recovery.
On a Unitree G1 across three hazardous-contact categories, ARC reduced the first force peak by 34.1% versus a 20 ms delayed reflex.
It also demonstrated protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal using foot tactile sensing.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of ARC. A hazardous contact is localized within milliseconds, a whole-body reflex pose is solved, and the motors withdraw within 10 ms of the collision (Sec. III). The reflex then propagates bottom-up to the policy, which sustains it while continuing its task and draws on a human prior to retreat naturally from the contact region, avoiding secondary collisions (Sec. IV).

Fig. 5: Real-world tasks. ARC is evaluated across motion tracking, teleoperation, and traversal, spanning contacts with static obstacles, dynamic objects, and moving humans. ARC demonstrates reliable performance across all these tasks.

Fig. 3: Reflex poses solved for different contacts. From an identical initial configuration, the solver produces distinct whole-body reflexes qr depending on which body region is struck and from which direction (spheres).

Fig. 4: One Mapping. We subtract the reflex offset from the observed joint positions and add it to the policy’s output joint targets, so the policy sees a single distribution rather than one per reflex direction, and supervise it with DAgger against the reflex-free counterfactual it would have produced.

Fig. 6: Effect of latency on contact impact. Blue/red: 0/20 ms added delay. Solid: contact force (left axis); dashed: hand displacement (right axis). Shading: impulse integrated where F > 2N. Removing the 20 ms delay reduces the first force peak from 21.64 N to 14.25 N and the contact impulse from 0.2632 Ns to 0.1225 Ns (2.15×).

TABLE I: Ablation study. Metrics are grouped into local withdrawal, contact, and global recovery. Explicit ref. replaces the AMP reward with direct tracking of a retreat motion. Metrics: Hold is the mean withdrawal distance over 0.2 s to 1.0 s; C is the signed compensation score (positive: opposing the reflex; negative: reinforcing it); J100ms integrates the normal contact force over the first 100 ms; Rehit is the fraction of trials that contact the same obstacle again after separation; D3s and v0.2–1s are the root displacement at 3 s and its mean velocity along the commanded recovery direction; the last two columns are the fractions of trials whose displacement at 3 s reaches 0.5 m and 1.5 m.

papers.abstract: Natural human-robot interaction requires robots to interpret language and gestures within a 3D environment to support tasks such as pick-and-place and object retrieval. 3D Embodied Reference Understanding (3D-ERU) supports this by identifying the 3D location of a target object from a scene (point-cloud) containing a human pointing gesture and an accompanying language description. However, current 3D-ERU models lack alignment of cross-modal representations and incur high processing costs that increase with the point-cloud's size. To address this, we propose GVT3D, which employs an Embodied Fusion module that jointly models language, gesture, and vision inputs within a shared embedding space, promoting cross-modal alignment. We additionally introduce a foveation approach that selectively processes the point cloud within a coarse region around the estimated pointing direction to reduce computations. GVT3D achieves ~8% higher accuracy and foveation enables 2.95x faster execution while maintaining comparable accuracy, relative to prior 3D-ERU models.
authors: Vimarsh Shah, Dulanga Weerakoon, Ajinkya Deshpande, Saksham Agarwal, Nilesh Bhatia, Neel Kiran Naik, Parth Shah, Sravan Danda, Sanjay E. Sarma, Archan Misra, Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Sougata Sen
bullets: Targets robot understanding of object references from a 3D scene, pointing gesture, and language description.
Uses an Embodied Fusion module to jointly represent language, gesture, and vision in a shared embedding space.
Applies foveation to focus point-cloud processing on a coarse region near the estimated pointing direction.
Reports approximately 8% higher accuracy and 2.95× faster execution with comparable accuracy when foveation is used, relative to prior models.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
bullets: Addresses the sequential decoding and memory-bandwidth costs of autoregressive VLA policies on embedded aerial platforms.
Uses a compact RGB-D ViT, non-reconstructive JEPA-style latent prediction, a five-head predictor ensemble, and two-step conditional flow matching for velocity/yaw-rate chunks.
DAgger training alone achieved only 11.1–21.1% success across six checkpoints; behavior cloning failed on all 60 missions despite low open-loop error.

A map-free shield using depth memory, barrier constraints, field-of-view limits, and path backoff increased one policy’s success from 21.1% to 52.2% and reduced crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, with more timeouts.
Code, a trained 72.6 MB policy, and the benchmark dataset are publicly released; results are limited to PX4 software-in-the-loop simulations in procedurally generated forests.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Aero-VPA deployment architecture. The inference loop (top) runs once per camera frame and produces a velocity and yaw-rate chunk Ct through five sequential network evaluations; the safety filter applies the uncertaintydependent attenuation α(σ̄), the braking envelope vsafe, and the validity horizon Ht. The executor (bottom) evaluates the newest valid chunk at its chunk-local time, converts it to NED setpoints, and streams them to PX4 over microXRCE-DDS; it engages the braking fallback when a fallback is requested or no valid chunk is available. The runtime shield (orange, added in version 2) filters every setpoint against a 15 s depth memory or flies recovery manoeuvres itself; the setpoint it dispatches is fed back as āt (dashed). In the evaluation of Section 6 the companion-computer software ran on a cloud GPU against PX4 SITL (Section 4.6).

Figure 2: Mode automaton of the runtime shield. In FLY the policy’s executor runs and the shield filters each setpoint. papers.title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
papers.tldr: Aero-VPA enables agile, map-free quadrotor navigation on edge hardware using few-step flow-matching actions and an uncertainty-aware runtime shield, improving closed-loop success while reducing crashes in simulation.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.
authors: Junhyeong Park, Wook Jung, Taeyoung Kim, Huiwon Jang, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the costly need for target-robot demonstrations caused by the human–robot embodiment gap.
Uses geometry-anchored observation alignment and a decoupled-decoder tokenizer to bridge representation and action spaces.
Enables human demonstrations to provide behavioral supervision while preserving pretrained VLA visual, semantic, and control priors.
Improves object-transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3; skill transfer reaches 62.7.
Scope: evaluated on real-world tasks with unpaired human and robot demonstrations.
