papers.abstract: Scientific experiments are increasingly selected, executed and interpreted by learned systems that act through physical interfaces. Robot learning builds physical competence, whereas AI for science chooses which experiment to run, each reporting different endpoints. This review treats their interface as one problem, embodied AI for science, where the experiment itself is partially observed: specimen state, apparatus state and measurement processes are latent, actions are costly and irreversible, and missingness depends on execution and outcome. We organize the literature by three closures operating at distinct levels: operational closure (the experiment realized is the one intended), epistemic closure (the result updates beliefs or selects subsequent experiments) and evidential closure (the record supports a claim). We analyze workflows through a record-linked evidence cycle - Record, Diagnose, Calibrate, Confirm - as analytic functions with feedback. A taxonomy crosses these closures with six delegated decisions and five embodiment classes. Our formulation separates commanded, realized and observed conditions and models diagnosis with explicit resource, risk and sample-change costs. We compare experiment-selection methods by terminal decision, review perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policies, world models, recovery and transfer by evidence emission requirements, and compare chemistry, materials, biology, microscopy and field workflows by what their records establish. An appendix provides an evidence map of 28 workflows (26 physical, two software-boundary), characterizing validation pathways and claim confirmation requirements. We propose evaluation that separates actions, valid experiments, campaigns and confirmed claims, framing open challenges as controlled comparisons with measurable failure conditions.
authors: Wenhao Xu, Changwei Wang, Shunpeng Chen, Yukun Song, Sifan Zhou, Kaize Luo, Shibiao Xu, Yuehua Zhao, Rongtao Xu
bullets: Experiments involve latent specimen, apparatus, and measurement states, with irreversible actions and outcome-dependent missing data.
It organizes the field around operational, epistemic, and evidential closure: realizing intended experiments, updating knowledge, and supporting claims.
The Record–Diagnose–Calibrate–Confirm cycle links experiment execution, diagnosis, feedback, and evidence generation.
A taxonomy connects these closures with delegated decisions and embodiment classes, while distinguishing commanded, realized, and observed conditions.
It proposes evaluations that separately measure actions, valid experiments, campaigns, and confirmed claims, and maps validation pathways across 28 workflows.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Four terminal decisions determine the epistemic method comparison. Bayesian optimization recommends a design that requires independent verification; active learning supplies a response map assessed on a declared held-out distribution; Bayesian experimental design distinguishes decision-relevant alternatives; reinforcement learning and model-predictive control choose state-dependent action sequences. Their characteristic failures are different, so method choice and terminal loss must be tied to the scientific endpoint. Curves, maps and trajectories are conceptual illustrations with no empirical performance values.

Figure 2. Historical profile of the 48 representative systems by scientific domain and publication period. Each cell gives the number of systems; (1p) and (2p) mark arXiv preprints already included in that count. Row and column totals make the cohort size explicit. Publication status follows the records selected in the accompanying dataset: Co-Scientist uses its published Nature version, whereas π0 uses its arXiv record. The cohort contains 40 journal articles, five conference papers and three arXiv preprints. Periods are ordered categories, not an annual timeline or an estimate of field-wide growth.

Figure 3. Six delegated decisions as complementary scientific interfaces rather than an automation ladder. Each panel pairs a decision with a schematic glyph and the record it must leave; the glyphs are abstract illustrations, not measured data or depictions of particular apparatus. The bottom Shared record bar represents a unified trial ledger across all six decisions; connecting stems are schematic, and the absence of a drawn stem beneath a panel does not imply that decision omits a record. Access and Prepare primarily serve operational closure; Select serves epistemic closure; Acquire spans operational and epistemic closure; Interpret and Confirm serve evidential closure. A workflow may delegate a subset of the six decisions, and the panels are not a sequence.

Figure 4. Causal execution, observed records and specimen lineage. A decision compiles to a command and requested measurement configuration. The command acts through a latent realized condition and an updated specimen–apparatus state before observations are generated; measurement configuration may affect both state and sensing. A dashed inference link indicates that observed evidence constrains, rather than equals, the latent condition. The trial record stores commands, requested configuration, observations, metadata, audit decisions and trial status; a noisy condition estimate can be part of metadata. An interrupted transfer stays in lineage and a remade specimen receives a new identifier. Record state is distinct from claim state. Apparatus imagery is synthetic.

Figure 1. Three closures around one shared physical experiment. Each row pairs a closure with its realized state, a three-step loop with an error feedback arc, its characteristic failure and the reporting unit it counts. Operational closure compares commanded with realized conditions and recovers from tolerance violations; epistemic closure updates belief from observations and chooses the next experiment; evidential closure turns trial records into candidate claims that need fresh independent confirmation. All three loops read the shared experiment history at the base. The reporting units Nattempted, Nsel and Nconf shown here are distinct, and Nvalid (Section 8) is a further unit; no common denominator or one-to-one mapping across trial and claim units is implied. The diagram is conceptual and reports no measured data.

Figure 6. Operational stack for a physical workcell. Language protocol is an input, not a stack layer: it emits the intent trace. Five operational layers—perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policy, embodiment, and verification and recovery—emit, respectively, a state estimate, typed operation, action trace, recorded condition estimate and recovery trace into the shared trial record, from which evidence obligations are assessed. World models, teleoperation and digital twins support these layers and do not replace physical measurement. Sensing modalities include cameras, tactile gel, force–torque sensing and balance telemetry. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 10. Evidence atlas of 26 physical workflows and two software-boundary components across Access, Prepare, Select, Acquire, Interpret and Confirm. Access uses X for cross-station mobile routing, M for local manipulation, F for fixed-interface or instrument-local control, S for software-boundary components and ? for unresolved routing. For Prepare, Select, Acquire and Interpret, R denotes reported implementation, A assisted or configuration-dependent operation, P planned capability, N scoped-not-reported and ? unresolved. In Confirm, O denotes an orthogonal physical assay, F repeat or follow-up testing, OF both, with P, N and ? carrying the same reported-status meaning. The Access F code (fixed interface) and the Confirm F code (follow-up) are different vocabularies. N and ? indicate absent or unresolved reporting, not experimental failure. The cohort includes two software-boundary components, so not all 28 rows are independent physical executions. Source rechecks retained the displayed codes, including ? where the relevant step remains unreported or unresolved. Full annotations and provenance are in the supplementary machine-readable dataset (f07_evidence_map_data.json and the adjudication ledger), distributed with the audit package in manuscript_audit/supplement/.

Figure 7. Evaluation design for embodied scientific campaigns. A strict two-by-two comparison crosses a reference or adaptive selector with a baseline or improved executor under matched endpoint, information, resource boundary and acceptance criteria. Every attempt enters the physical execution gate and remains in Nattempted. The metrological and audit gate assigns v̂t and ct : valid positive, valid negative and censored records all count in Nvalid, whereas execution failures and inconclusive records remain in Nattempted but not Nvalid. Nominated claims form a separate unit with counts Nsel and Nconf; confirmation uses fresh evidence not used for nomination under prespecified criteria. rvalid, ECYG, COR and CSU use their declared denominators; DA and IRR require a privileged reference label and apply only to controlled injection benchmarks. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 8. Failure attribution and claim reassessment. A low response with qualified preparation and adequate detection can be a valid negative; valid positive, valid negative and censored records remain in the valid pool and count in Nvalid. Uncertain transfer produces an execution failure that remains in Nattempted and returns through diagnosis and recovery, while an unclear signal is inconclusive. These trial statuses ct are distinct from claim state σk. Independent confirmation of a nominated claim can retain, revise or narrow it according to prespecified evidence; narrowing is not the only permissible outcome. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 9. Six empirical propositions grouped into three complementary research thrusts, with three cross-cutting normative invariants. P1 and P5 concern histories and realized actions; P2 and P6 concern validity-preserving recovery and matched-budget selection, diagnosis and confirmation; P3 and P4 concern endpoint-preserving transfer and qualified expansion of experimental reach. Provenance completeness, safety with human authority, and cross-site replay compliance must hold across all propositions. Grouping does not imply a temporal or causal order, predicted gains or established findings. Scientific miniatures are conceptual and apparatus imagery is synthetic.

papers.abstract: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.
authors: Shresth Grover, Andrey Kolobov, Dhruv Shah
bullets: Limited-demonstration fine-tuning can improve nominal success while harming robustness to appearance, object, and instruction variations.
RAFT uses two stages: low-rank adapter training on task-relevant reasoning annotations, followed by policy fine-tuning on action demonstrations with the adapters frozen.
On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves 75.0% out-of-distribution success versus 27.9% for plain fine-tuning.
On a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, RAFT reaches 70.0% mean success versus 36.0% for the strongest baseline.
RAFT improves performance under visual, object, and instruction shifts, while increasing attention to annotated regions and later-layer object-identity probe accuracy.

papers.abstract: Operating rooms (ORs) increasingly contain ambient sensing infrastructure to enable AI-based optimization of workflows and utilization. We pursue an alternative path: using ambient AI to guide robot action and optimize utilization. Deploying humanoids in the OR without ambient AI is severely limited by cumbersome de novo orientation and planning due to partial onboard observations. We posit that this can be achieved by coupling an ambient AI-based agentic orchestrator with the humanoid robotic actor, providing shared perception and execution feedback for humanoid autonomy in the OR. ActOR fuses a wall-mounted ambient camera and the robot's head-mounted camera into a shared object-level digital twin (DT). A large language model agent plans over the DT using pre-programmed locomotion and manipulation skills without task-specific training. During execution, DT updates and execution outcomes inform retries, alternative approaches, or replanning. We evaluated ActOR in simulated and physical environments. Across three tasks in two simulated ORs reconstructed from real rooms, ambient perception reduced exploration from 1.05 to 0.12 Explore calls per trial when targets were initially outside the robot's view. Closed-loop feedback increased success from 46.7% to 83.3% under nominal execution and from 8.3% to 51.7% under injected navigation, object-relocation, and grasp perturbations. In a physical mock OR with a humanoid, ActOR completed 14 of 20 single-object disposal trials and demonstrated replanning after scene changes. Ambient AI-based observations provide scene state that improves robot action planning, increasing success and reducing exploration compared with robot-only observations. Feeding skill outcomes and DT updates back to the planner improves multi-step task success. Our results show the feasibility of humanoid task autonomy for multi-step disposal tasks in a mock OR.
authors: Han Zhang, Sicheng Lu, Aleks Santari, Jeffrey K. Jopling, Masaru Ishii, Mathias Unberath
bullets: Addresses limited robot-only perception and costly exploration in partially observed operating rooms.
Fuses wall-mounted and head-mounted cameras into a shared object-level digital twin.
Uses an LLM agent to plan with pre-programmed locomotion and manipulation skills, without task-specific training.
Execution feedback enables retries, alternative actions, and replanning after scene changes.
In simulation, closed-loop feedback improved success under nominal and perturbed execution; physical trials demonstrated feasibility on disposal tasks.

papers.abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.
authors: Kailing Li, Ruoxuan Zhang, Zheyuan Zhou, Boyang Chu, Yingshan Lei, Hongxia Xie, Liang Du, Zixun Sun
bullets: Covers diverse 3D-game tasks including navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery.

Uses a vision-language pipeline to detect objective or interaction-target changes, ground navigation goals in visual waypoints, and compose task instructions.
Explicit stage boundaries connect task progression with low-level control and skill transitions.
Annotation quality was evaluated through model verification and human inspection; an audit of 500 trajectories achieved a 95.8% pass rate.

Adjacent subgoals within each trajectory are composed into task-level instructions, followed by annotation and alignment validation. Two models then verify visual grounding and action consistency, retaining only samples approved by both at every annotation level. A sampled human audit further assesses data quality.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.
authors: Yang Chen, Bin Wen, Danyang Peng, Hong-Jie You, Zi-Qiao Shang, Lan-Zhe Guo
bullets: Targets embodied and web agents’ difficulty with multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints.
Provides TextWorld for symbolic temporal planning, SimWorld for grounded topological path planning, and DualWorld-VQA for perception, scene understanding, and planning diagnostics.
Finds a gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning: agents miss optimal task sequences and produce infeasible grounded actions.
Shows that perception and topology understanding alone do not reliably support constrained planning.
Datasets and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Disturbances can invalidate the conditions required by a robot's next action even when much of its task program remains useful. A recovery system must therefore choose a response suited to the current state. We present DiMuRe (diagnosis-guided multilevel recovery), a framework for robot-use agents that uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to select program reuse or predefined recovery skills, including bounded vision-language-action (VLA) grasping. After the original program exits, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) can generate corrective code from images and execution feedback. Local verification checks the outcome of each recovery attempt. We also introduce LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for robustness and recovery under mid-execution disturbances, supporting program-based agents and VLA policies. On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore development cases, Local DiMuRe (program reuse and recovery skills) achieves 77.65% complete-task success, compared with 58.68% for the original program under the same physical-step allowance. Full DiMuRe achieves 81.90% with terminal replanning, an additional step allowance, and early handoff. Local DiMuRe also uses fewer physical steps per scheduled episode than the original program.
authors: Renkai Yi, Yuwei Wu, Haoyu Zhang, Penghao Dai, Zhi Gao, Jin Chen, Che Sun
bullets: Addresses disturbances that invalidate the next action while leaving parts of a robot task program usable.
Uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to choose between program reuse and predefined recovery skills, including bounded VLA grasping.
Employs multimodal LLM corrective-code generation after program failure and locally verifies each recovery attempt.
Introduces LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for mid-execution disturbance robustness and recovery.
On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore cases, Local DiMuRe reached 77.65% complete-task success versus 58.68% for the original program; Full DiMuRe reached 81.90% with terminal replanning and extra steps.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. DiMuRe system architecture and recovery flow. Phase-specific diagnosis uses RGB-D observations, robot state, and program context, and requests new observations when evidence is insufficient. The dashed box shows local grasp recovery. The system considers template replay (L1), geometry-based regrasp (L2), and bounded VLA grasping (L2) in that order, checking admission (am), executing the method (πm), and verifying the grasp (vm). It skips ineligible candidates and tries the next candidate if an attempt does not produce a verified grasp. A verified grasp ends the local search. MLLM-assisted replanning (L3) starts separately after the original program exits and its entry checks pass. The planner revises corrective code using new observations and execution feedback.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian mapping enables fast and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, with broad applications in augmented reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. However, many current methods assume static scenes or filter out dynamics as outliers. In this paper, we study in-view scene changes where objects are manipulated in front of the camera within a single online sequence, unlike prior works that detect changes outside the camera view or between separate captures. This setting entangles transient and persistent dynamics, as objects can be distractors while moving and persistent once they settle. While recent studies start to address distractors by removing them for clean static background, in-view scene changes remain underexplored. To resolve this, we present SettleSplat, a monocular mapping system that maintains up-to-date 3D Gaussian maps under such changes. Specifically, we lift coarse per-pixel uncertainty into Gaussian dynamicity field, then prune transient ones. For persistent changes, we derive geometric contradictions weighted by parameter-free rendered depth uncertainty to separate true changes from under-optimized regions. On Bonn and Co-Fusion, SettleSplat achieves consistent 3D Gaussian maps, outperforming current baselines on both full images and change regions while maintaining comparable speed.
authors: Anh Thuan Tran, Xiyun Song, Yubin Zhou, Heather Yu, Jana Kosecka, Liang Peng
bullets: Addresses in-view scene changes, where moving objects may be transient distractors or persistent changes.
Uses per-pixel uncertainty to construct a Gaussian dynamicity field and prune transient geometry.
Identifies persistent changes through geometric contradictions weighted by rendered depth uncertainty.
On Bonn and Co-Fusion, outperforms baselines on full images and changed regions while maintaining comparable speed.

figures.caption: Figure 2. System overview. Given monocular RGB frames (a), SettleSplat estimates depth, then tracks and maps with the DROID-W backbone (b) while learning per-Gaussian dynamicity field δ that prunes transient distractors. During refinement (c), geometry contradiction score g, derived from the rendered map and estimated depth and weighted by the rendered depth uncertainty, is integrated with the tracking uncertainty into reliability map r. Frames before the settlement frame K are weighted by W = r2, while later frames supervise the settled scene without masking.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on Bonn (rows 1–3) and Co-Fusion (rows 4–6), covering moving, adding, and removing objects. Red boxes show the change regions. At old object locations, baselines leave ghosting artifacts, while SettleSplat reconstructs the updated scene cleanly. For added and moved objects, SettleSplat preserves appearance and detail, whereas the baselines blur or miss them. For removed objects, SettleSplat is competitive with other baselines while reducing ghosting.
Table 2. Novel view synthesis results on the CoFusion dataset, evaluated on the full image and within the change region. Best and second-best results are highlighted.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text. We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical. At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap. At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image. Across 154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55% for unguided action attacks. Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0% to 89.5% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4% at a comparable collision rate. In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5% and preserves the exact response on 85.0% of examples alongside a 1.73-unit action-chunk shift. An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.
authors: Zihao Feng, Qingzhao Zhang, Chunyu Xia, Bo Yu, Z. Morley Mao, Ramesh Govindan
bullets: Reasoning text and physical actions can diverge at their shared text/action interface.
The text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) identifies directions that strongly shift actions while minimally affecting text.

In driving, TNAS attacks caused new collisions with identical rationales in 52.6% of full-image scenes and 35.1% of localized-patch scenes, versus 4.55% for unguided attacks.
TNAS improved rationale preservation and reduced text drift while maintaining comparable action changes across both models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Rationale-preserving action divergence in reasoning VLAs. papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks (ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action models) increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot's control loop. In 32-bit floating point (FP32) on a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112 Hz, a 4D pursuit-evasion BRT at 61 Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT at 74-147 Hz, 5.9-17.5x faster than the JAX reference hj_reachability at matched precision and 1.7-16x faster than a torch.compile reimplementation of the same scheme. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT to within 0.04% of the reference cell count, and runs 2.0-4.6x faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers the K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.
bullets: Targets the exponential cost and traditionally offline nature of HJ backward reachable tube (BRT) computation for safety-critical autonomy.
Implements the WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs HJI scheme in CUDA for 2D–4D dynamics, including an in-kernel multi-agent label-propagation extension.
Runs benchmark BRT computations at 61–147 Hz on an NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada and at 54–66 Hz on a Jetson AGX Thor.
Matches reference results in FP64, including reproducing the Air3D BRT within 0.04% of the reference cell count.
Demonstrates a six-quadcopter wildfire-response simulation with a capture-basin Voronoi tessellation computed in 4.0 ms per control tick.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Closed-loop wildfire-response fleet under time-varying, non-uniform wind. Six homogeneous quadcopters defend a 20 × 20 km region (cruise a = 20m/s) against three fires. The joint HJ capture-basin Voronoi tessellation, computed via in-kernel label propagation from each drone’s current position, is refreshed at every 10Hz outer-loop tick. Colored basins are each drone’s 10-minute reachable region; red diagonal hatch marks cells unreachable within the horizon by any drone. White curves are basin bisectors. Triangles mark drones en route (with the MM :SS predicted-arrival countdown); inverted triangles, returning; circles, patrolling at home. Red X marks a burning fire, gray X a suppressed fire. (a) Initial state: drones at homes, basins anisotropic with the prevailing NE wind. (b) The Center drone en route to Fire #1 (NE region); its basin has followed it east through the domain. (c) Fire #2 (SW region) en route during the gust, with the wind rotated. (d) Late phase (t = 700 s), wind rotated further: a pocket in the upwind direction is unreachable in the 10-min window.

Ours is 2.0–4.6× faster than JAX and 1.3–1.4× faster than torch.compile; the largest gains over JAX appear on the drifter and 4D cases, where the fused per-stage kernels, in-kernel BRT clamping, and host-static CFL step remove the most per-step work relative to JAX/XLA’s per-stage materialization. papers.abstract: Object rearrangement planning in cluttered environments is often non-monotone, requiring objects to be temporarily relocated before reaching their final destinations. Although search-based planners can solve such tasks, they incur substantial computational cost and require expensive replanning when the environment changes. We propose the Visual Adaptive Rearrangement Planner (VARP), which learns non-monotone rearrangement directly from visual state representations generated from expert demonstrations. VARP predicts pick-and-place actions from the current and goal visual state representations, and incorporates an Action Refinement Strategy (ARS) to improve action feasibility and a Progress Enforcement Strategy (PES) to mitigate progress stagnation. By continuously updating actions from the latest visual state representations, VARP adapts online to disturbances without replanning from scratch or performing online combinatorial search. In challenging rearrangement benchmarks, VARP achieves a 98.3\% success rate with only 0.4 s planning time per task, 97.5\% success under execution-time disturbances, and 94.5\% under continuous severe disturbances, while generalizing effectively to unseen object counts. These results demonstrate that VARP provides a scalable and robust solution for non-monotone object rearrangement.

papers.abstract: As robot learning moves beyond the tabletop, many tasks require mobility, adjustable reach, active perception, and bimanual dexterity. Commercial platforms combining these capabilities are costly, while affordable open-source alternatives cover only a subset and require software integration. We present MABEL, an open-source anthropomorphic mobile bimanual robot with 56 degrees of freedom (DOF) and a US$8.1k parts cost. It combines two 7-DOF arms with 17-DOF hands, a pitching torso, a lift, a 3-DOF neck, and a holonomic base. Back-drivable arms and torso support compliant interaction, with fingertip reach from floor level to 2.23 m. The head and torso roughly triple modeled camera coverage relative to a torso-fixed camera. Apple Vision Pro head and hand tracking enables whole-body teleoperation without handheld controllers, with 137 ms mean glass-to-glass stereo video latency over the robot's Wi-Fi hotspot. We demonstrate an end-to-end imitation learning pipeline, from teleoperated data collection to policy deployment, using a shared command interface and whole-body controller.
authors: Qilong Cheng, Rooholla Khorrambakht, Mohamed Yassine Kabouri, Quang Nam Nguyen, Luca Macesanu, Haoran Zhou, Yipeng Wang, Ludovic Righetti
bullets: Addresses the cost and integration barriers of mobile, dexterous robot platforms requiring mobility, reach, active perception, and bimanual manipulation.

Uses Apple Vision Pro tracking for controller-free whole-body teleoperation, with 137 ms mean glass-to-glass stereo-video latency.
Demonstrates an end-to-end imitation-learning pipeline from teleoperated data collection through policy deployment.

papers.abstract: A mobile manipulator asked to "put the toys away in the toy box" must decide which objects are toys and which container the user means, then find base poses, grasps, and placements it can execute. Because a scene representation is built before the instruction is known, it may lack the attributes, affordances, or concepts needed to resolve the task. We present FEIJOA, a language-model agent that grounds the instruction at test time. It queries a grounding tool over a posed RGB-D scan, inspects the returned candidates, and refines its queries until they resolve the instruction. An embodiment-aware harness checks each skill's preconditions, samples base poses from which the target is reachable, and verifies the skill's effect from observations before and after execution. On 103 open-ended grounding queries, FEIJOA resolves 94.2% exactly, compared with 68.0% for the best prebuilt representation. Over 50 real-world trials on Spot, it completes 35 tasks; 17 of these successes follow recovery from a failed tool call or verification check. Of the 15 failed trials, 13 were caused by the robot's physical skills, and only 2 by grounding or the agent's reasoning. Project website: https://williamshen-nz.github.io/feijoa/.
authors: Aditya Agarwal, William Shen, Sahit Chintalapudi, Lucy Cai, Nishanth Kumar, Aidan Curtis, Travis Manderson, Tom\'as Lozano-P\'erez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between prebuilt scene representations and task-specific concepts needed to interpret user instructions.
Uses a language-model agent to iteratively query and inspect grounding results from posed RGB-D scans.
Checks skill preconditions, samples reachable base poses, and verifies outcomes using before-and-after observations.
Resolves 94.2% of 103 grounding queries exactly, versus 68.0% for the best prebuilt representation.
Completed 35 of 50 Spot trials; most failures were due to physical skills rather than grounding or reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 2: FEIJOA overview. At each turn the harness assembles the working context Wt from a fixed context, the interaction history ht, and the current context and the task plan Pt. LLM πθ selects tool calls ut, which the harness executes. FIDO (FEIJOA grounding subagent) generates object hypotheses over the recorded scan. papers.abstract: Transfer learning from pretrained backbones has become standard practice in multi-sensor computer vision---yet two questions remain open: which pretrained weights transfer best to multi-sensor setups, and can in-domain pretraining outperform off-the-shelf solutions? Frameworks like MultiMAE demonstrate the utility of masked autoencoding in a multi-modal context, but rely entirely on dense, model-derived modalities. It is unclear how robustly these methods translate to real-world applications that use physical sensors, where the aggregation of diverse public datasets for large-scale pretraining inherently introduces modality sparsity. To investigate this systematically, we curate a multi-sensor autonomous driving collection of $2.82M$ images from 16 publicly available datasets, incorporating both physical hardware modalities (RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event) and model-derived modalities (Stereo Depth, Segmentation). We use this collection for in-domain pretraining based on the MultiMAE approach. We adapt MultiMAE's loss formulation to accommodate sparse samples, and study the effect of an enforced encoder bottleneck for modality alignment and of additional losses specific to dense reconstruction (SSIM and FFT). We then systematically compare against common pretrained backbones (ViT, MAE, DINO and MultiMAE) across downstream sensor fusion tasks. We find that MultiMAE is a surprisingly strong out-of-the-box baseline, transferring effectively even to modalities it has never seen, while our targeted modifications yield incremental but consistent improvements on multi-sensor transfer and overall robustness.

papers.abstract: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) aims to learn a unified policy from heterogeneous offline datasets that generalizes across tasks. However, existing offline MTRL methods often struggle with two fundamental issues: severe per-task data scarcity and limited cross-task generalization. In this paper, we propose Language-Model Augmented Decision Transformer (LaMA-DT), a unified sequence-modeling framework that leverages a single large language model (LLM) for both trajectory augmentation and multi-task policy learning. LaMA-DT uses natural-language task descriptions to guide task-aligned trajectory augmentation through a set of supervised generation and alignment objectives, and incorporates a scoring-and-filtering mechanism to retain high-quality augmented trajectories. The same LLM is then repurposed as a language-conditioned Decision Transformer and fine-tuned on a mixture of real and augmented data. Experiments on Meta-World and MuJoCo multi-task benchmarks demonstrate that LaMA-DT consistently outperforms competitive baselines, particularly in low-data regimes, showing that language-guided data augmentation substantially improves cross-task generalization.

bullets: Addresses per-task data scarcity and weak cross-task generalization in offline multi-task RL.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LaMA-DT consists of three components: (i) Multi-Objective Fine-Tuning. We adapt the LLM to generate meaningful, task-specific trajectories from limited offline data and natural-language task descriptions by training objective-specific LoRA adapters together with a shared LoRA adapter, enabling both trajectory generation and task–trajectory alignment. (ii) Data Preparation. Candidate trajectories are generated per task using O3, scored using aggregated multi-objective likelihoods, and the top-K trajectories are retained and merged with the original offline data. (iii) Multi-Task Policy Learning. We repurpose the LLM and shared LoRA adapter as a prompt-conditioned DT, trained on the combined real and augmented dataset, with task descriptions pi and a provenance token zprov.

papers.abstract: Causal inference has emerged as a powerful paradigm enabling robots to make safe, efficient decisions by reasoning about the ``why'' behind events. However, its real-world application is hindered by the difficulty of collecting causal data, especially in human-populated environments where training takes time, while users expect immediate operation. To this end, we tackle the challenge of transferring simulation-learnt causal relations to the real world with minimal effort. While retaining the invariant high-level causal structure, we empirically demonstrate the system adapts efficiently to real-world situations by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. Our results show that the parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer. The framework runs efficiently onboard of a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baselines navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting causal data and training robots directly in human-populated environments.

Runs efficiently onboard a mobile robot for navigation in shared human environments.

Scope: adaptation relies on an invariant causal structure and a limited set of new real-world observations.

papers.abstract: Surgical scene understanding is pivotal for computer-assisted intervention, yet demands compositional reasoning across instruments, anatomy, and workflow. Existing surgical vision-language models rely on instruction tuning with large-scale question-answer pairs, entailing laborious data curation and costly retraining. To bridge this gap, we propose SurgEye, a perception-reasoning framework that grounds reasoning in a vision foundation model without instruction tuning. Specifically, we devise Routed Multi-Task Perception (RMP) that routes the vision foundation model through task-specific pathways learned from public perception labels, producing spatial and temporal evidence. We further introduce Agentic Compositional Reasoning (ACR) that employs a frozen large language model to coordinate RMP specialists and temporal memory as callable tools, composing evidence across tasks and time into grounded answers. Moreover, we construct SurgEye-Bench spanning eight surgical procedures, pairing each question with perception labels for verifiable evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SurgEye outperforms state-of-the-arts in surgical reasoning. The source code will be available.

papers.abstract: To enable effective generalization in offline meta-RL, it is essential to accurately infer the underlying task through latent task representations, which provide a compact and transferable summary of task-specific characteristics for guiding policy generation. In this paper, we propose Contrastive Task-Aware Decision Transformer (CoTA-DT), a DT-based offline meta-RL framework that learns task representations by jointly integrating four complementary components: (i) contrastive learning from offline trajectories, (ii) alignment with natural-language task descriptions, (iii) one-step supervision via a task-conditioned world model, and (iv) long-term supervision via a task-conditioned Q function. The learned task representations are used as conditioning signals for a DT-based policy, enabling task-aware meta-policy learning. To further support generalization in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, we design a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy that enables effective and reliable adaptation to unseen tasks. Notably, in CoTA-DT, the pretrained LLM serves as a shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q-function estimation, and policy learning. This unified design facilitates parameter sharing, improving both efficiency and generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse offline meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate that CoTA-DT consistently outperforms prior methods, particularly in challenging zero-shot generalization scenarios.
authors: Xinbo Zhao, Yuhang Liu, Xin Zhang, Lei Le, Zhaohan Xi, Yingxue Zhang
bullets: Targets accurate latent task inference for generalization to unseen tasks in offline meta-RL.
Combines contrastive trajectory learning, natural-language alignment, one-step world-model supervision, and long-term Q-function supervision.
Conditions a Decision Transformer policy on the learned task representations for task-aware meta-policy learning.
Uses a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy for zero-shot and few-shot adaptation.
Experiments on diverse offline meta-RL benchmarks report consistent gains over prior methods, especially for zero-shot generalization.

papers.abstract: Modern learning systems increasingly combine pretrained models with downstream heads. Despite the growing importance of such modular designs, how the downstream model co-adapts to the geometry of pretrained representations remains relatively underexplored. We study this problem through vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) conditions an action model for control. We find that the action model progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of the VLM outputs. Through controlled experiments across different backbone-head models, we further show that counteracting this sensitivity concentration can be beneficial under representation--task mismatch settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \emph{Adaptive Interface Equalizer} (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights pretrained representations according to the evolving downstream sensitivity during training. AdaIE improves VLA success rates on simulation benchmarks, with gains of up to $+5.28$ percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1 and $+1.68$ pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and achieves an average gain of $+19$ pp across five real-world manipulation tasks. It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models.
authors: Ruijie Zhang, Jiayin Zheng, Yequan Zhao, Liyan Tan, Ziyue Liu, Zhengyang Wang, Kunpeng Song, Nathan Zhao, Jian Yao, Yin Zhang, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Problem: Downstream action models can concentrate sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of pretrained VLM representations, especially under representation–task mismatch.

Method: AdaIE is a parameter-free interface mechanism that reweights pretrained representations based on evolving downstream sensitivity during training.
Results: It improves simulation success rates by up to 5.28 pp and 1.68 pp on two benchmarks, with an average 19 pp gain across five real-world manipulation tasks.
Scope: The approach also improves performance for diffusion policies and world models.

papers.abstract: A substantial line of work builds rotation invariance directly into point cloud architectures. We benchmark 10 architectures (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, RIConv, RIConv++, RISurConv, PointMLP, PointTransformer, and the equivariant VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN) across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion, and analyze the results with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than point estimates. The three rotation-invariant (RI) architectures achieve the best pose robustness but rank among the lowest on noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains. We ask whether this cost is intrinsic to invariance or specific to how invariance is obtained. We retrain all 10 architectures unchanged, with a simple invariance loss on the embedding and three training seeds each, and evaluate all models on the independently designed ModelNet40-C. Invariance training transfers narrowly but reliably. It improves exactly the corruption families its perturbations target wherever the baseline has headroom (mean occlusion +10.5, lidar +13.4 percentage points of accuracy). At matched training budget the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture end on par on unseen corruptions (within 2.5 percentage points in every seed), and invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model. Once rotation augmentation is widened, standard backbones concede only a flat, angle-independent accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation. We release the benchmark along with a package for analyzing point cloud robustness and reproducing our results.
authors: Abdulla Nasir Chowdhury, Gulpi Qorik Oktagalu Pratamasunu, Kazuhiro Fukui
bullets: Benchmarks 10 point-cloud classifiers across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion using confirmatory hypothesis tests.
Rotation-invariant models provide the strongest pose robustness but rank near the bottom for noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains.
A simple embedding-level invariance loss transfers narrowly, improving targeted corruption families when baseline headroom exists.
On independently designed corruptions, the best standard and rotation-invariant models perform similarly; invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model.
Wider rotation augmentation leaves standard backbones with a consistent, angle-independent accuracy gap under full-sphere rotations; the benchmark and analysis tools are released.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a statistical benchmark for rotation-invariant point cloud architectures, relevant to robust 3D perception for robotic navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Do We Still Need Rotation-Invariant Architectures? A Statistical Robustness Benchmark for Point Cloud Classification
papers.tldr: Rotation-invariant architectures excel under pose changes but sacrifice noise robustness; targeted invariance training can narrow this gap without a clear overall winner.

papers.abstract: Computing distances between sets is important in many robotic applications, such as motion planning and control. In many applications, derivatives of the distance are needed as well. It is well known that the Euclidean distance is not always differentiable, which create issues to algorithms that need a derivative. In this paper, we introduce NESDF, the Normal Euclidean Signed Distance Function between two general (with mild regularity assumptions but possibly non-convex) sets. This metric is still not differentiable, but it allows us to introduce a generalization, $h$-NESDF, which has a smoothing parameter $h$ such that the metric is infinitely differentiable for all $h>0$ and that reduces to the NESDF when $h$ goes to $0$. The metric is amenable to GPU parallelization, and thus can be computed efficiently. We show extensive simulation results to evaluate its viability in motion planning.
authors: Vinicius Mariano Gon\c{c}alves, Pedro Antonio de Souza Campos Rodrigues
bullets: Addresses the nondifferentiability of Euclidean set distances, which can hinder derivative-based robotics algorithms.
Introduces NESDF, a normal Euclidean signed distance for general, possibly non-convex sets under mild regularity assumptions.
Generalizes NESDF to h-NESDF with smoothing parameter h>0, yielding infinite differentiability and recovering NESDF as h approaches zero.
Designed for efficient GPU-parallel computation.
Extensive simulations evaluate its viability for motion planning.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a differentiable distance function useful for motion planning and control, transferable to learning-based navigation.
papers.title: h-NESDF: An Infinitely Differentiable Signed Distance Between Two Sets with Robotic Applications
papers.tldr: h-NESDF provides an infinitely differentiable, GPU-friendly signed distance between general sets for gradient-based robotic motion planning and control.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: The challenge requires training only on synthetic LiDAR while evaluating on unseen real roadside LiDAR and synthetic-cloud realism.
Recovering the correct coordinate frame increased the combined score from 0.3520 to 0.5147.
Per-class NMS prevented suppression of closely grouped pedestrians, raising detection mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295.
Modelling real-cloud null returns at (0, 0, 0), absent from synthetic data, improved distributional realism.
The final entry achieved a combined score of 0.7457, with detection mAP 0.4382 and realism score 0.9251.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on Sim2Real V2X LiDAR detection for autonomous driving, addressing specific sensor alignment and post-processing issues for real-world navigation.
papers.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A diagnostic-focused Sim2Real V2X LiDAR pipeline substantially improved detection and realism by fixing coordinate-frame errors, using class-specific NMS, and modelling null returns.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: Targets detection trained only on synthetic LiDAR and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, alongside synthetic-data realism scoring.
A parameter-free geometric refinement addressed small-object localization, yielding a reported 86% relative pedestrian AP gain.
Fixing a post-processing rule that removed valid predictions produced the largest detection improvement: 335% relative on the Van class.
Analytical examination of realism metrics identified one component as a closed-form function of nine summary statistics.

The proposed submission methodology combines independently controlled class-wise experiments, enabling pre-submission score prediction and transparent reporting of negative results and data provenance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses Sim2Real LiDAR detection for roadside navigation, focusing on geometric refinement and distributional alignment for real-world deployment.
papers.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A PointPillars-based Sim2Real roadside LiDAR system improves challenge performance through geometric localization refinement, post-processing repair, and analytical realism optimization rather than a new detector architecture.

papers.abstract: Feature matching underpins many robotic perception tasks, including visual localization, mapping, SLAM, and autonomous navigation. Existing semi-dense matchers predict confidence on fixed grids, limiting correspondences to predefined locations and requiring costly high-resolution grids for precise localization. We present CoReMatch (Coordinate Refinement Match), a recurrent framework that refines correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space rather than predicting discrete confidence maps. CoReMatch progressively improves correspondence estimates by propagating information across iterations. At the coarse stage, a Deep Aggregated Transformer captures global context and iteratively updates correspondence coordinates, while a lightweight regression head further sharpens their localization. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show that CoReMatch strikes a strong balance between accuracy and efficiency, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running more than 10x faster on embedded edge hardware. These results demonstrate that recurrent coordinate refinement offers an efficient and scalable approach to real-time feature matching for robotic perception.
authors: Robert J. Wang, Charles Ling, Boyu Wang
bullets: Avoids fixed-grid confidence prediction, reducing the need for costly high-resolution grids.
Uses recurrent updates to propagate information and progressively improve correspondence coordinates.
Combines a Deep Aggregated Transformer for global context with a lightweight regression head for localization refinement.
Performs well on indoor and outdoor benchmarks, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running over 10× faster on embedded edge hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CoReMatch. We propose a recurrent continuous coordinate refinement framework for semi-dense feature matching. Given an image pair, CoReMatch first predicts initial correspondences using low-resolution 1/16 feature maps. A recurrent coordinate refinement module then progressively updates the correspondences through iterative coordinate-space optimization using a Deep Aggregated Transformer (DAT) for global geometric reasoning. The resulting correspondences are further refined by a lightweight CNN that performs sub-pixel regression within compact local feature windows. This coarse-to-fine coordinate refinement design enables efficient and accurate matching for real-time robotic perception.

Figure 1: Memory–Speed–Accuracy Trade-off of State-of-the-Art Matchers on MegaDepth. Memory usage and runtime are measured on NVIDIA AGX Orin and RTX 3090 GPUs using batch size 1 and FP16 precision. Higher values on the y-axis indicate better performance, while lower values on the x-axis indicate higher efficiency. Across both equal-resolution and equal-accuracy comparisons, CoReMatch consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods. Additional quantitative results are provided in Table 1 and Table 7.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on visible–thermal cross-modal matching. CoReMatch demonstrates stronger robustness and produces more reliable correspondences across severe modality differences. In contrast, ELoFTR and EDM generate substantially more incorrect matches, highlighting the effectiveness of recurrent coordinate refinement and robust feature representations for cross-modal matching.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison under wide-baseline geometric scenes and challenging robotic perception scenarios. Red indicates an epipolar error greater than 5 × 10−4 in normalized image coordinates. CoReMatch produces more consistent correspondences across challenging appearance and scene variations than ELoFTR and EDM.

Figure 4: Inference time of different attention mechanisms on NVIDIA AGX Orin across varying input resolutions. The proposed Deep Aggregated Transformer (DAT) achieves over 4× lower inference time than the AAM used in Efficient LoFTR at 1024× 1024 resolution.

Figure 3: Runtime breakdown of refinement mechanisms. Compared with RoMa-style multi-scale correlation-volume refinement at 1/16, 1/8, and 1/4 resolutions, CoReMatch performs three recurrent refinement iterations entirely at 1/8 resolution, achieving over 5× faster runtime at 512×512 and over 8× faster runtime at 1024× 1024.
Figure 7: Failure cases on indoor and outdoor data. Red denotes correspondences with an epipolar error greater than 5× 10−4 in normalized image coordinates.

Table 1: Relative Pose Estimation Results. All methods are trained on MegaDepth and evaluated on both the MegaDepth and ScanNet datasets. We report the AUC of relative pose error at multiple thresholds and average inference time (ms). Inference time is measured on an AGX Orin with batch size 1 and FP16 precision. CoReMatch-S outperforms ELoFTR by a large margin while being more than 11× faster on MegaDepth.

Table 2: Homography Estimation on HPatches. All methods are evaluated with models trained on MegaDepth to assess cross-dataset generalization. CoReMatch outperforms both sparse and semidense methods, and surpasses the state-ofthe-art dense method RoMa.

Table 7: Efficiency Comparison Across Input Resolutions. We compare ELoFTR, EDM, and CoReMatch in relative pose estimation accuracy (AUC), GPU memory usage, and inference time on the NVIDIA AGX Orin and RTX 3090. CoReMatch achieves a favorable trade-off between accuracy and efficiency across input resolutions.
Table 3: Ablation Studies on MegaDepth. Each component in CoReMatch improves AUC@10 while maintaining efficient inference.

Table 6: Refinement Ablation. Results on the MegaDepth dataset with different refinement iterations and top-confidence ratios. All results use the same model without retraining. Inference time is measured on an AGX Orin with batch size 1 and FP16 precision.

Table 4: Visual Odometry Evaluation. We report unaligned ATE RMSE (↓) on selected sequences. Best results are in bold. CoReMatch achieves the lowest ATE on 3/4 evaluated sequences and remains comparable to both baselines on TUM.

Table 5: Comparison with Alternative Attention Mechanisms. SCT denotes Simple Compact Transformer, while PTA denotes Proxy-Token Attention. Inference time is measured on an RTX 3090 with batch size 1 and FP16 precision.

papers.selection_reason: Recurrent continuous-coordinate feature matching for robotic perception, localization, and SLAM supports embodied perception, though it is not a navigation or manipulation policy.
papers.title: CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching
papers.tldr: CoReMatch enables fast, accurate robotic feature matching by iteratively refining correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space.

papers.abstract: One big challenge in physical AI is interacting with systems whose states are defined by implicit equilibrium. Learning in these systems is difficult because their responses can be multistable, path-dependent, and sensitive over long horizons. Adjoint learning provides an efficient way to optimize trajectories without unrolling iterative equilibrium solvers, but its gradient relies on the frozen-tangent approximation, which neglects higher-order sensitivity terms and can become inaccurate when the local equilibrium varies rapidly. In this work, we introduce Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), optimizing trajectories along which sensitivity variations are explicitly controlled. We derive a mathematical bound on the resulting gradient error and develop a practical finite-difference approximation. We validate the framework on deformable objects, which are representative of implicit equilibrium systems, ranging from simple quadratic energy models such as elastic rods to complex systems including thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures. Compared with the adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baselines, SCNC achieves faster convergence and more stable optimization by reducing switching to undesirable equilibrium branches, doubling the stable optimization rate over adjoint learning 83.3% vs. 41.7% and reducing the average loss by more than 1.5 orders of magnitude on thin-walled tubes, where sensitivity variations are pronounced.
authors: Hengyi Zhou, Haobo Fang, Xiaonan Huang, Dezhong Tong, M. Khalid Jawed
bullets: Addresses inaccurate gradients caused by the frozen-tangent approximation in rapidly varying, path-dependent equilibrium systems.
Optimizes trajectories to control sensitivity changes and uses a practical finite-difference approximation.
Derives a bound on the resulting gradient error.
Evaluated on deformable objects ranging from elastic rods to thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures.

Compared with adjoint learning and gradient-free iCEM, achieves faster, more stable optimization, including an 83.3% versus 41.7% stable optimization rate and substantially lower loss on thin-walled tubes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Pipeline for the learning process. The policy generates control signals, and the implicit model determines the corresponding equilibrium states. The task objective is evaluated on the resulting trajectory, and gradients are propagated to optimize the policy. SCNC regularizes the learned trajectory to maintain the reliability of the gradient approximation.
Figure 4: (A) Loss score vs. epoch for different methods and objects. (B) Stable optimization count for different methods and objects.

Figure 1: Representative implicit equilibrium systems with increasingly complex local responses. (A) Smooth bendingdominated deformation of an elastic rod. (B) Kink propagation during measuring-tape manipulation. (C) Kink formation in a thin-walled tube. (D) Large stretching and geometric reconfiguration of a Slinky-like structure. λ parameterizes the control trajectory.
Figure 5: Real world experiments. Opacity increases over time.

Figure 3: Partial numerical result. Two cases for each object. The boundary conditions are controlled to drive the userspecified nodes to targets. Cases from tape, tube and Slinky shows the stability of SCNC than adjoint learning.
Table 1: Computational efficiency comparison across different physical systems. Each system contains six node-targeting tasks. Time denotes time per epoch, and Mem. denotes peak memory usage.

papers.abstract: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.
authors: Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Yida Yang, Lei Qian, Zhaoye Zhou, Hongru Zhang, Kai Ye, Shuyuan Hu, Yiran Mao, Zewei Ye, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses fragmented benchmark interfaces and low GPU utilization in slow simulation-based evaluation.
Wraps models as reusable Policy classes and benchmarks as adapters while preserving their original rules and scoring.
Separates simulator workers from Policy replicas, sizes them using probes, and deterministically shards work across GPUs.
Supports six benchmark families and renders only observations required at action-chunk boundaries when applicable.
Achieves up to 6.16× speedup on LIBERO-Long with CUDA MPS and 25.04× on RoboTwin Easy across four GPUs, with unchanged reported outcomes.

papers.abstract: In robotics, shape control, or shape servoing, refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object toward a desired shape. This article is the second of a two-part tutorial on data-driven, Jacobian-based shape control, in which the deformation Jacobian, a local model of how robot motion changes the measured shape, is estimated from measurements. Part I built the shape-servoing loop and derived a local stability condition. This paper starts by using the singular value decomposition of the deformation Jacobian to identify shape changes that can be produced by small robot motions, those that require large robot motions, and those that are locally unavailable. It then analyses how the choice of shape features determines how the controller regulates the object's shape and, therefore, how much the object deforms on its way to the target. It then describes three ways in which the shape control loop can fail: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and occurrence of mechanical instabilities. It closes with shape-control extensions to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.
authors: Ignacio Cuiral-Zueco, Alessio Caporali, Miguel Aranda, Gianluca Palli, Gonzalo L\'opez-Nicol\'as, Youcef Mezouar
bullets: Uses singular value decomposition to characterize easily produced, costly, and locally unavailable shape changes.
Examines how shape-feature selection affects regulation behavior and deformation during motion toward a target.
Identifies three failure modes: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and mechanical instabilities.
Extends shape control to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.

papers.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

papers.abstract: Training robot policies for multi-task pick and place requires demonstrations on many objects, which handheld Universal Manipulation Interfaces (UMIs) can collect quickly and cheaply. However, existing UMIs depend on external base stations, use rigid fingers that give no signal about contact forces, or use parallel-jaw fingers that limit grip strength. We present a battery-powered handheld interface, built on YUBI, whose soft, angled fingers wrap around objects, deform visibly under load as a visual proxy for force, and match the grippers of the robot. With it, we collect a 99.7-hour dataset over 53 objects, train $\pi_{0.5}$ policies on 49 of them, and hold out the other 4 as unseen objects. We find that a top camera raises success by 13 points even when only about half of the data includes it, and that mid-training on our multi-task data raises success after fine-tuning on unseen objects from 35% to 57%. Finger design, dataset, and data processing code: https://lute-corp.github.io/soft-yubi-site/
authors: Kobi Kelemen, Tomasz Niedzia{\l}kowski, Marcin Paszczak, Victoriano Montesinos
bullets: Collects 99.7 hours of demonstrations across 53 objects using soft, angled fingers that wrap around objects and visibly deform under load.
The handheld interface is built on YUBI, avoids external base stations, and matches the robot’s grippers.
Training uses 49 objects, with 4 held out to evaluate generalization to unseen objects.
A top camera improves success by 13 percentage points, while multi-task pretraining raises unseen-object fine-tuning success from 35% to 57%.
The released resources include the finger design, dataset, and data-processing code.
