papers.abstract: Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose MoTWorld, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, MoTWorld generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that MoTWorld achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.
authors: Fengzhi Guo, Nate Morrill, Shiqi Li, Cheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of a unified approach for 3D rigging and temporally stable 4D skeleton generation.
Generates an entire 4D sequence jointly in a single feedforward pass, while also supporting single-mesh 3D rigging.
Provides explicit control over skeleton count, uncertainty-based candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.
Uses a curriculum from large-scale 3D rigging data to mid-scale 4D mesh–skeleton data to reduce dependence on paired 4D training data.
Reports strong 3D rigging quality and high-quality, temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FLOWRIG unifies rigging for both 3D and 4D meshes. Compared with prior methods such as Puppeteer (Song et al., 2025a) and UniRig (Zhang et al., 2025a), our model delivers accurate 3D rigging, preserves 4D temporal consistency, supports controllable bone count, achieves faster inference, and enables 4D skeleton prediction, including interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.

Figure 2: FLOWRIG overview. We encode meshes into conditioning tokens, and initialize noisy skeleton slots, which are processed by a flow matching transformer to predict temporally aligned skeleton representations. The predicted features are decoded by the skeleton, graph, and uncertainty heads to recover 3D/4D rigging outputs, with uncertainty used for sample selection. n denotes the skeleton count, and ϕ denotes the unconditional token.

Figure 4: Static Reconstruction. Numbers from top to bottom are J2J, J2B, and B2B for each instance. Compared with baselines, our model preserves finer geometric details and achieves more accurate mesh alignment.

Figure 3: Data-efficient curriculum training. We first train on static 3D rigging, then adapt to 4D reconstruction, and finally enable prediction through masked conditioning. During the final stage, we use diverse masking patterns, including interpolation, forecasting, backcasting, and random masking, to expose the model to different temporal prediction settings. This schedule transfers large-scale 3D supervision to the data-scarce 4D setting.

Figure 5: Dynamic reconstruction and prediction. Blue indicates reconstruction with mesh guidance, while yellow indicates predictions without mesh guidance. In (b), from top to bottom, it shows interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting, respectively. Refer to the demo video for a clearer comparison.

Figure 6: Analysis of bone count control. Our model can freely control the number of bones to adjust skeletal detail, while existing baselines do not provide this level of controllable output granularity.

Table 1: Static skeleton reconstruction comparison. Our methods achieves strong reconstruction fidelity across diverse out-of-domain static datasets. Ours* utilizes uncertainty as selection score to select the best candidate from the 5 samples and outperforms all baselines on Articulation-XL 2.0 and Diverse-Pose. On ModelsResource, its zero-shot performance approaches that of RigAnything trained directly on the same dataset. See the "Baselines" paragraph for citations of these models.

papers.title: FlowRig: Unified Skeleton Generation for 3D and 4D Meshes via Flow Matching

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments, yet current robustness evaluations remain biased toward hazardous instructions and jailbreak vulnerabilities. A more fundamental issue is largely overlooked: agents are rarely tested under semantically sufficient but contextually minimal instructions (i.e., common in real-world human communication), where auxiliary contextual cues are absent. For the first, we identify a novel phenomenon termed Ambient Context Illusion, where agents fail to execute tasks correctly when non-essential contextual details are omitted, despite unchanged task semantics. To systematically study this, we establish VagueBench, a benchmark built upon the AI2-THOR interactive simulation environment for the evaluation of context dependency in embodied agents. We systematically consider key semantic components of instructions (entities, procedures, constraints, and prior knowledge) and derive a unified taxonomy with four categories and nine subtypes to reduce auxiliary information. VagueBench contains 1,303 instruction pairs across diverse indoor environments, constructed via a human-agent co-generation framework that integrates semantic redundancy estimation, taxonomy-guided transformation, and rigorous semantic-invariance verification. Through extensive evaluation on 6 state-of-the-art embodied agents, we observe significant degradation on VagueBench in both task performance and executability (relatively -19.65% in task success rate and relatively +54.10% in empty plan rate) revealing a strong reliance on auxiliary linguistic signals rather than core task semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon persists in real-world robotic systems, where it can lead to incorrect decisions and potential safety risks.

papers.abstract: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.
authors: Yueyang Liu, Lance Kennedy, Andreas Z\"ufle
bullets: Addresses staypoint fragmentation caused by spatial noise and prolonged signal dropouts.
Uses a dynamic centroid, an n-step lookahead heuristic, and temporal bridging to tolerate drift and missing observations.

Evaluated on the ExtraSensory dataset against Trackintel’s sliding-window baseline.
Reports higher F1-scores and improved computational efficiency than the baseline.

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in congested environments requires both collision avoidance and coordinated passage. We introduce neuromorphic decision dynamics (NDD), a decentralized, event-based controller, that provides navigation in congested spaces with guarantees on safety, liveness, robustness, and scalability. NDD makes safe-and-live deconfliction a controllable, locally tunable emergent property of local agent interactions, without requiring communication, preassigned priorities, models of neighbors' objectives or future actions, or estimates of group size or global network properties. By design, NDD couples the dynamics of internal decision and attention states with changing physical states and locally observed relative motion. Each agent continuously modulates its speed along its prescribed path, responding as soon and as much as conflict resolution requires. Agents self-organize into disjoint, locally engaged groups that resolve conflicts concurrently. When any group's conflict becomes safety-critical, decision-action feedback destabilizes collective indecision, and coordinated conflict-resolution emerges that stabilizes a safe traversal order within the group. Order persists as conflicts clear, but groups may split or merge as agents autonomously adapt to new conflicts and those with resolved conflicts resume their nominal motion. We derive explicit conditions on sensing range, feedback gains, response time scales, and actuation limits that guarantee collision avoidance and traversal-order formation in finite time with no deadlock or livelock for finite, heterogeneous agent populations of arbitrary, changing size. Computational cost scales with the number of local interactions sensed by each agent. Large-scale simulations, comparisons with existing approaches, and hardware experiments demonstrate NDD in complex congested scenarios and validate its scalability.
bullets: Addresses collision avoidance and coordinated passage without communication, priorities, neighbor-intent models, or global population estimates.
Couples internal decision and attention dynamics with physical state and locally observed relative motion, allowing agents to modulate speed along prescribed paths.
Agents self-organize into local conflict groups that resolve interactions concurrently; feedback breaks indecision and establishes a safe traversal order in finite time.
Provides explicit conditions for sensing, feedback, response times, and actuation that guarantee safety, liveness, and no deadlock or livelock for finite heterogeneous populations.
Simulations, comparisons, and hardware experiments demonstrate operation in complex congested scenarios and support scalability; computational cost depends on sensed local interactions.

papers.abstract: The last decades have seen a revolution in autonomous robotics. Deep learning approaches and their hardware implementations have made it possible to endow robots with extraordinary perceptual capabilities. In addition, they can also benefit from advances in Automated Planning, allowing them to autonomously solve complex tasks. However, on many occasions, the robot still acts without internalising and understanding the reasons behind a perception or an action, beyond an immediate response to a current state of the context. This gap results in limitations that affect its performance, reliability and trustworthiness. Deep learning alone cannot bridge this gap, because the reasons behind behaviour, when it emanates from a model in which the world is a black-box, are not accessible. What is really needed is an underlying architecture based on deeper reasoning. Among other issues, this architecture should enable the robot to generate explanations, allowing people to know why the robot is performing, or has performed, a certain action, or the reasons that may have caused a certain plan failure or perceptual anomaly. Furthermore, when these explanations arise from a cognitive process and are shared, and thus validated, with people, the robot should be able to incorporate these explanations into its knowledge base, and thus use this understanding to improve future behaviour. Our article looks at recent advances in the development of self-aware, self-evolving robots. These robots are designed to provide the necessary explanations to their human counterparts, thereby enhancing their functional capabilities, in the quest to gain their trust.
bullets: Deep learning and planning enable capable autonomous robots but often do not expose the reasons behind perceptions, actions, failures, or anomalies.
Black-box models limit explainability, reliability, and human trust.
Causal, reasoning-based architectures are presented as a way to generate meaningful explanations.
Robots could incorporate explanations shared and validated with people into their knowledge base to improve future behavior.
The article reviews recent advances in self-aware, self-evolving robots, without reporting specific experimental results.

papers.abstract: We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context. From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target. The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists. Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks. Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone.
bullets: Learns behavior together with spatial context by reconstructing scene geometry and estimating hand motion from each video.
Aligns geometry and hand motion at a shared scale using a 3D hand-size prior.
Uses gated residual fusion to ground a pre-trained vision-language model in geometry, while predicting future geometry and wrist/finger actions.
Generates finger motion conditioned on predicted trajectories of both wrists.
Pre-training on reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over hand-motion-only pre-training; the method also reports gains on simulated and real-world bimanual tasks.

Fig. 1: SpatialDex reconstructs scene geometry and estimates hand motion from RGB-only human videos and aligns them at a shared video-level scale to jointly supervise policy pre-training. The policy maps RGB-D observations to bimanual dexterous actions and is adapted to specific tasks through fine-tuning on robot demonstrations. The lower panel shows the six bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks for real-world evaluation.

Fig. 3: 3D-grounded visuomotor policy. Reconstructed geometry enters the policy in two roles. As an input, depth samples from each image patch are encoded jointly in 3D and pooled back to their patches, so that the geometry grid g arrives on the same token grid as the visual features x and is fused into f through two gates and a residual whose weight warms up from zero, leaving the priors of the pre-trained VLM intact. As a target, a training-only predictor estimates future scene geometry from the shared context, which requires the representation to retain spatial structure that the action losses alone do not demand. From the same context, a wrist expert predicts both wrist trajectories and a finger expert predicts finger actions conditioned on them.

Fig. 2: Aligned scene and hand reconstruction. From an RGB-only video, SpatialDex recovers hand meshes and wrist trajectories, point clouds and camera poses up to an unknown scale. Aligning the reconstructed hand points with the estimated hand meshes across frames yields one scale shared by the whole video and a rigid transformation per frame, which places the scene geometry and the hand motion in a common frame for pre-training. The aligned reconstruction supplies the depth observations, the wrist and finger action targets, and the future geometry targets for policy pre-training.

papers.abstract: Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving under rare, safety-critical vehicle-pedestrian interactions requires photorealistic, sensor-level scenarios. However, trajectory-based scenario generators cannot synthesize raw visual observations, whereas video-based approaches lack controllability. To bridge this gap, we present ControlPed, a novel framework that combines trajectory-level conflict synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to generate photorealistic, motion-controllable safety-critical scenarios. Built upon HazardPed, a dataset derived from 10,352 traffic videos comprising 422 conflict trajectories, HD maps, and 857 annotated 3D human motions, ControlPed first generates conflict trajectories, lifts them into 3D human motion sequences via text-conditioned motion diffusion, and finally renders multi-view sensor observations using animatable 3DGS avatars. Safety evaluation in 88 rendered photorealistic scenarios reveals that seven leading end-to-end driving models suffer a severe performance drop, with their mean HDScore plunging from 88.8 to 47.4, exposing major failure modes under dangerous pedestrian behaviors. The dataset and testing benchmarks will be released to facilitate safety assessment of vehicle-pedestrian interactions.
bullets: Addresses the gap between controllable trajectory generators and video-based methods that cannot synthesize raw sensor observations.
Combines conflict-trajectory synthesis, text-conditioned motion diffusion, and animatable 3D Gaussian Splatting avatars.
Built on HazardPed, which includes traffic videos, conflict trajectories, HD maps, and annotated 3D human motions.

The dataset and evaluation benchmarks are planned for release to support vehicle–pedestrian safety assessment.

papers.abstract: Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL) methods, while effective in settings with limited expert demonstrations, are often considered unstable. These approaches typically decompose into two components: Density Ratio (DR) estimation $\frac{\rho_E}{\rho_{\pi}}$, where a discriminator estimates the relative occupancy of state-action pairs under the policy versus the expert; and Reward Assignment (RA), where this ratio is transformed into a reward signal used to train the policy. While significant research has focused on improving density estimation, the role of reward assignment in influencing training dynamics and final policy performance has been largely overlooked. RA functions in AIL are typically derived from divergence minimization objectives, relying heavily on human design and ingenuity. In this work, we take a different approach: we investigate the discovery of data-driven RA functions, i.e, based directly on the performance of the resulting imitation policy. To this end, we leverage an LLM-guided evolutionary framework that efficiently explores the space of RA functions, yielding \emph{Discovered Adversarial Imitation Learning} (DAIL), the first meta-learnt AIL algorithm. Remarkably, DAIL generalises across unseen environments and policy optimization algorithms, outperforming the current state-of-the-art of \emph{human-designed} baselines. Finally, we analyse why DAIL leads to more stable training, offering novel insights into the role of RA functions in the stability of AIL. Code is publicly available: https://github.com/shshnkreddy/DAIL.
authors: Shashank Reddy Chirra, Jayden Teoh, Praveen Paruchuri, Pradeep Varakantham
bullets: AIL instability is studied through reward assignment (RA), a largely overlooked component alongside density-ratio estimation.
The method searches for data-driven RA functions based on the resulting imitation-policy performance.
The resulting DAIL algorithm is presented as the first meta-learned AIL algorithm.
DAIL generalizes to unseen environments and policy optimizers and outperforms human-designed baselines, according to the abstract.
The analysis provides insights into how RA functions affect AIL training stability.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained via behavior cloning are vulnerable to covariate shift, where small deviations from expert trajectories can compound into failure. Common strategies to mitigate this issue involve expanding the training distribution through human-in-the-loop corrections or synthetic data augmentation. However, these approaches are often labor-intensive, rely on strong task assumptions, or compromise the quality of imitation. We introduce Latent Policy Barrier, a framework for robust visuomotor policy learning. Inspired by Control Barrier Functions, LPB treats the latent embeddings of expert demonstrations as an implicit barrier separating safe, in-distribution states from unsafe, out-of-distribution (OOD) ones. Our approach decouples the role of precise expert imitation and OOD recovery into two separate modules: a base diffusion policy solely on expert data, and a dynamics model trained on both expert and suboptimal policy rollout data. At inference time, the dynamics model predicts future latent states and optimizes them to stay within the expert distribution. Both simulated and real-world experiments show that LPB improves both policy robustness and data efficiency, enabling reliable manipulation from limited expert data and without additional human correction or annotation.
bullets: Addresses covariate shift, where small deviations from expert trajectories can compound into failure.
Uses a base diffusion policy trained only on expert demonstrations for precise imitation.
Trains a dynamics model on expert and suboptimal rollouts to predict and optimize future latent states.

papers.abstract: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that Pixel provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel

Adds hierarchical, language-conditioned visuomotor control for long-horizon tasks.
Demonstrates behaviors involving dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination.

papers.abstract: Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi
bullets: Addresses embodiment differences between human demonstrations and mobile manipulation robots.
Uses Environment-Aware Retargeting to convert scene geometry and human head/gripper trajectories into collision-aware robot joint and base targets.
Applies Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking to reduce reliance on observation views mismatched by residual retargeting errors.
Uses delay-calibrated action assignment and on-policy human corrections via DAgger to handle imperfect, contact-rich actions.
Evaluated across five challenging manipulation tasks, achieving 87.0% average task progress.

papers.abstract: Learning from human data offers a scalable path toward embodied intelligence, yet it requires models to accurately understand fine-grained human actions from egocentric observations. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association. We introduce EgoActionBench, a benchmark that represents continuous human manipulation as temporally localized atomic actions associated with the left hand, right hand, or both hands. EgoActionBench contains 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined action annotations. To evaluate such dense predictions, we propose an evaluation protocol that retrieves temporally eligible candidates, selects a prediction by content agreement, and scores semantic fidelity and temporal overlap alongside action precision and recall, jointly capturing what happens, when it happens, and which hand performs it. We benchmark 20 baseline models and systems on EgoActionBench and further adapt two backbones, Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B, through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on automatically annotated training episodes. EgoAction improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two backbones, and both adapted models outperform all open-source baselines. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations of current models in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association, highlighting the gap between general video understanding and the action understanding required for embodied intelligence.
bullets: Introduces 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined annotations of temporally localized atomic actions linked to the left hand, right hand, or both.
Proposes an evaluation protocol measuring semantic fidelity, temporal overlap, action precision, and recall.

Supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two adapted backbones.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.
bullets: Addresses confirmation bias, hallucinated progress, and binary success judgments in video-based robot task evaluation.
First prompts the VLM to define task-grounded absolute success through textual scene descriptions, then scores progress against explicit rubrics.
Produces fine-grained, non-linear progress estimates that penalize failures and interpolate successful executions.
Uses only prompting, enabling generalization across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks without per-model post-training.
The resulting reward estimates support efficient downstream reinforcement learning and match or surpass post-trained reward models.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate actions and imagined futures, but a plausible prediction need not be realized by its co-generated action. We introduce WISE (\emph{World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation}), a pre-execution selector that scores each sampled rollout on action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency between the proposed action and the imagined motion, and instruction-conditioned task progress, and executes the highest-scoring candidate while keeping the WAM frozen. With four candidates per decision, WISE raises closed-loop success from 6.0\% to 24.0\% on RoboLab with Cosmos~3 Edge and from 75.1\% to 78.3\% mean success on LIBERO with DreamZero, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Component ablations and agreement analyses show that the three scores rank candidates differently and that task progress carries the largest weight in the fused decision.
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible imagined futures and actions that actually succeed.
Scores sampled rollouts using action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency, and instruction-conditioned task progress.
Executes the highest-scoring candidate without updating the underlying world action model.
With four candidates, success increases from 6.0% to 24.0% on RoboLab and from 75.1% to 78.3% on LIBERO.
Task progress contributes the largest weight, while the three scoring components rank candidates differently.

The IDM maps imagined frames back to actions for comparison with the candidate’s proposed controls; the task evaluator scores progress at the final imagined frame. WISE sums the scores, executes the selected action chunk, and observes the resulting state before replanning.

papers.abstract: Open-world robotic mobile manipulation requires acting in physical environments with only partial information. While recent Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) agents show strong open-world reasoning capabilities, existing architectures that rely on direct tool calling struggle with geometric uncertainty and thus are limited to fully-observable tabletop environments. In contrast, Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems can solve long-horizon tasks under partial observability but incur high computational costs and require closed worlds. We propose \textbf{TAMPAgent}, an agentic planning framework that unifies the reasoning of LVLMs with the structured constraint satisfaction of TAMP systems. We endow an LVLM agent with a belief-space planning model operating over an extensible API of perception, planning, and control tools. The agent formulates a partial task plan composed of parameterized observation and execution actions, which is subsequently completed using classical search algorithms. After extracting the plan's geometric constraints, the agent leverages its tool API to bind valid parameter values, satisfying feasibility requirements and producing an executable motion plan. Upon execution, the agent continuously updates its belief history and repeats this closed-loop process by interleaving observation and manipulation actions. Evaluated across complex household mobile manipulation tasks on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 platforms, TAMPAgent significantly outperforms direct tool-calling agentic baselines, demonstrating that integrating TAMP constraint satisfaction into agentic planning loops is essential for unstructured, partially observable environments.
bullets: Targets open-world mobile manipulation, where geometric uncertainty challenges direct tool-calling agents.
Uses an LVLM to create partial plans with parameterized observation and execution actions.
Completes plans through classical search, geometric constraint extraction, and tool-based parameter binding.
Continuously updates belief history by interleaving perception and manipulation in a closed loop.
Evaluated on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 household tasks, it outperforms direct tool-calling baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Integrating agents with planning. We compare four systems that maps a history of observations to whole body control for long-horizon mobile-manipulation tasks: (a) TAMP [14, 7] solves hand-authored problems with a task planner that orchestrates tools. (b) VLM-TAMP [9, 10] uses the agent to write the problem from open-world understanding but keeps the planning pipeline fixed. (c) CaP [3, 15, 5, 6] lets the agent write programs that orchestrate tools directly to find solutions. (d) TAMPAgent (ours) lets the agent orchestrate both the task planner and the tools to find certified solutions that satisfy the planner derived constraints.

papers.abstract: This work investigates human-swarm interaction (HSI) for steering large collectives through an intermediary robot helper. While prior robot-swarm control and HSI techniques commonly assume swarm members are addressable, these assumptions often fail for ``ungovernable'' swarms such as wildlife flocks and schools of fish. Motivated by pastoral shepherding, we compare low-level teleoperation to a higher-autonomy motion-primitives interface in a virtual reality (VR) shepherding task under varied swarm cohesion dynamics. Results indicate that motion primitives that operate on collective shape (e.g., boundary-based control) improve task performance and reduce perceived workload.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation benefits from tactile feedback that captures both detailed contact geometry and interaction forces. When scooping grains, contact patterns help infer spoon orientation, while resistance transmitted through the grasp guides motion. To provide these complementary sensing capabilities, we present PanoTac, a low-cost, compliant tactile fingertip designed for dense three-axis tactile sensing. Each fingertip provides a $12 \times 32 \times 3$ tactile representation, with one normal ($z$) and two shear ($x$, $y$) response components at each taxel. The sensor operates at 60 Hz and costs less than $50 per fingertip. Sensor characterization quantifies response repeatability and consistency across sensor instances and contact locations. We integrate PanoTac into a robotic system with a visuo-tactile pipeline. Across test-tube preparation, grain scooping, and salt pouring, the resulting policies outperform vision-only baselines by an average of 46.7 percentage points. Ablations show that removing either spatial contact information or shear feedback reduces overall performance across the task suite. Our project page is available at https://panotac.github.io.

papers.abstract: Conventional robot arms can be extremely heavy compared with the everyday objects they manipulate, creating a significant inertia mismatch at contact. Even a small accidental bump from a heavy arm can knock a light object out of place. Modern learning methods have nevertheless demonstrated a wide range of successful manipulation behaviors on these platforms, suggesting that even extreme inertia mismatch can be overcome with sufficient data. However, it remains unclear whether high inertia imposes a hidden cost on learning, potentially worsening scaling with data or lowering the performance ceiling of modern robot learning methods. We investigate this question through controlled simulation experiments that vary robot and object masses. We find that reinforcement learning succeeds across a broad range of mass combinations, while behavior cloning learns more reliable policies when a lighter robot manipulates a heavier object. Heavier robots require more demonstrations to attain the same performance as lighter robots. Finally, because new hardware is rarely an option, we explore ways to lower an existing arm's inertia at contact with existing hardware, either by choosing a lower-inertia workspace before collecting data or by steering the demonstrator toward lower-inertia configurations during the task. In both cases, the lower-inertia demonstrations are imitated more reliably. Project website: https://younghyopark.me/inertia-mismatch/

papers.abstract: Navigating crowded urban environments requires robots to avoid pedestrians while adhering to social norms such as remaining on sidewalks. Existing approaches typically address either crowd avoidance or semantic path planning in isolation. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) navigation policy that jointly reasons about semantic terrain and dynamic obstacles from a single semantically annotated bird's-eye-view (BEV) map, without relying on explicit human-state estimation. Our policy outperforms established crowd-navigation and semantic-aware baselines and transfers zero-shot to a legged robot, demonstrating socially compliant navigation in highly dynamic real-world scenarios.

papers.abstract: Pre-touch sensing, or sensing information about an object before contact, is an attractive modality for robot hands as it can allow a robot to anticipate and respond to a contact before it happens. In this work, we introduce ToFTouch, a multimodal tactile sensor combining three multizone (4$\times$4 resolution) time-of-flight sensors with an optics-based pressure sensing array. We mount this sensor on a parallel jaw gripper and demonstrate its utility on three distinct tasks: (i) pre-grasp adjustment, (ii) item extraction from clutter, and (iii) item insertion into tight spaces. For pre-grasp adjustment, ToF feedback reduced cycle time by 7.4$\%$ by enabling anticipatory gripper closure during approach. For extraction, ToF sensing enabled successful retrieval across all tested depth offsets ($\pm$2 cm) deviating from the nominal pick point, including conditions where baseline approaches failed, with standard deviations below 0.4 cm. For insertion into dense clutter, we explore the proximity and tactile information provided from ToFTouch during an insertion trajectory. The results demonstrate the utility of multizone ToF sensing in a manipulation environment.
bullets: Enables pre-touch sensing so the gripper can respond before physical contact.

papers.abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is an effective treatment for acute ischemic stroke, yet access remains limited by the availability of neurointerventional expertise. Telerobotic and AI-assisted systems may help address this challenge, but it remains unclear how clinicians interact with different levels of autonomy and how autonomous navigation systems perform in realistic environments. This work introduces Copilot Assistance Modes (CAMs), a framework for clinician-AI collaboration in robotic endovascular navigation spanning the autonomy spectrum from manual operation to full autonomy. In the first in-vitro user study comparing clinician-AI collaboration strategies, 11 experts and two students evaluated six navigation modes in a patient-specific vascular phantom. Objective performance metrics were combined with subjective assessments, including workload and usability. Autonomous performance was additionally evaluated both in silico and in vitro to investigate sim-to-real transfer. Hands-on manual navigation achieved the strongest overall performance (100% success). While fully autonomous navigation achieved 81% success in simulation, performance dropped to 23% in vitro. In contrast, several clinician-AI shared-autonomy modes achieved success rates of 92-97%, approximately four times higher than full autonomy and comparable to direct robotic control (95%), demonstrating mitigation of sim-to-real domain shift through clinician-AI collaboration. Among the evaluated AI-driven approaches, user-directed task delegation and rotational shared control demonstrated the most favorable balance between performance and clinician acceptance. These findings suggest that effective clinician-AI collaboration and allocation of control authority may currently be more important for reliable robotic neurointerventional navigation than increasing autonomy alone.
bullets: Evaluated six Copilot Assistance Modes spanning manual control to full autonomy in a patient-specific vascular phantom with 11 experts and two students.
Combined navigation success metrics with clinician workload and usability assessments.
Manual navigation achieved 100% success; full autonomy fell from 81% in simulation to 23% in vitro.
Several shared-autonomy modes achieved 92–97% success, comparable to direct robotic control at 95%.
User-directed task delegation and rotational shared control offered the best balance of performance and clinician acceptance.

papers.abstract: Despite their widespread success across machine learning, the learning dynamics and generalization properties of neural networks remain poorly understood. The neural tangent kernel (NTK) provides an analytical characterization of the learning dynamics of infinitely wide neural networks and serves as a useful proxy for finite-width networks in supervised learning. In this work, we extend the NTK framework to reinforcement learning (RL) by introducing a temporal-difference (TD) flow formulation that accommodates time-varying mini-batches and TD targets, yielding a closed-form solution for value function evolution in an overparametrized setting. We also devise an optimization-based state-space exploration method that leverages the closed-form solution, coupled with constraints on the environment, to model the set of feasible states. On a deterministic grid environment, we validate that the proposed RL-based NTK formulation is indeed learning efficiently and adapting to the distribution shift in the training data distribution, and we demonstrate that the resulting exploration strategy improves sample efficiency. To our knowledge, this is the first work to extend NTK theory to characterize the learning dynamics of RL training with time-varying mini-batches and TD updates.
bullets: Formulates an NTK-based temporal-difference flow for RL with changing mini-batches and TD targets.
Derives a closed-form description of value-function evolution in the overparameterized setting.
Uses this solution with environment constraints to identify feasible states for optimization-based exploration.
On a deterministic grid environment, the method adapts to training-distribution shifts and improves sample efficiency.
Scope is validated on a deterministic grid environment; broader generalization is not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobility is essential for sustained lunar surface operations, as communication delays and line-of-sight occlusions limit continuous teleoperation. Although recent traversability estimation methods increasingly rely on deep learning, the domain gap between terrestrial analogue environments and real lunar terrain can limit their generalisation, and real lunar traversability labels are scarce, making fully supervised training difficult. To address these challenges, we build a weakly supervised framework trained on sparse pairwise annotations and study whether augmenting visual features with depth-derived geometric information: depth, surface normals, and combined geometric descriptors. We evaluate the models in both in-domain and cross-domain settings using two terrestrial analogue datasets and the real lunar Chang'E PCAM dataset. Contrary to expectations, we find that naive geometric augmentation yields no consistent improvement over a strong visual-only baseline in either setting, with effects small relative to seed-to-seed variance. Instead, the choice of training source emerges as the dominant factor in transfer quality: models trained on domain-relevant sources transfer substantially better to real lunar imagery than the geometric fusion strategy improves any single model. Our evaluation runs onboard a resource-constrained edge device and provides a controlled baseline for designing more expressive multimodal fusion architectures in future lunar perception systems.

Uses a weakly supervised framework trained from sparse pairwise annotations.

papers.abstract: Actor--critic methods rely on critic gradients to improve continuous-action policies, yet finite-sample guarantees must control both value and gradient errors and their propagation through the actor. We develop a neural actor-critic procedure that combines a regularized minimax Bellman estimator over sigmoid networks with a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient. Under uniform Bellman regularity and covered reset sampling, a positive high-order action-derivative penalty yields value and action-gradient risk bounds with classical nonparametric minimax exponents up to logarithmic factors. We propagate estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature, and policy-iteration errors to obtain return guarantees, with refinements for bounded multimodal potentials and strongly concave regimes. Empirical studies across controlled simulations, logged continuous-control data, and a simulated decision task show favorable performance relative to the considered baselines.

Estimates the Bellman critic with a regularized minimax objective over sigmoid networks and a high-order action-derivative penalty.
Uses a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient to improve continuous-action policy updates.

papers.abstract: Ball-balancing robots (ballbots) must lean to accelerate, and the lean is limited by the wheel torques and by safety. Planners that use the full robot model are expensive, while planners that ignore the balance dynamics produce references that cannot be followed. This paper presents a two-layer navigation scheme for a three-omni-wheel ballbot. The upper layer is a model predictive controller on a \emph{jerk model} of the ball position, with discrete-time control barrier functions for static, moving, rotating and concave obstacles. The lower layer is a hierarchical sliding mode controller with an extended state observer and a robust exponential control barrier function on the tilt (HSMC-ESO-ECBF). The layers are linked by an acceleration bound derived in closed form from the largest steady tilt that the barrier function admits, so that the plan never asks for a lean the tracker refuses. For obstacles whose motion is only predicted, the obstacles are inflated by conformal prediction radii that bound the prediction error with a prescribed probability. In MuJoCo, with omni-wheel roller contacts and torque saturation, the scheme keeps at least $10$\,cm of clearance, tracks the plan within $2$\,cm RMS, keeps the tilt below the limit and plans in $9$--$12$\,ms, $10$--$15$ times faster than a full-model nonlinear MPC that enters the inflated obstacles; with predicted obstacles, the conformal inflation removes the collisions of a constant-velocity predictor in $30$ random crossing scenarios and reduces them in an endless run on a closed path.The source code and video illustrations are available at https://safe-ballbot.github.io
bullets: Uses an upper-layer MPC with discrete-time control barrier functions for static, moving, rotating, and concave obstacles.
Uses a lower-layer hierarchical sliding-mode controller with state estimation and a tilt barrier function to enforce balance limits.
Derives an acceleration bound from the allowable steady tilt, linking planning and tracking so references remain feasible.
Inflates predicted obstacles using conformal prediction radii to account for motion-prediction errors.
In MuJoCo, maintains at least 10 cm clearance, 2 cm RMS plan-tracking error, tilt limits, and 9–12 ms planning times; conformal inflation reduces collisions with predicted obstacles.

papers.abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) aims to recover expert rewards that transfer across environments with differing dynamics. Prior work has shown that such transfer is possible when gathering expert demonstrations across sufficiently different dynamics. In practice, however, expert demonstrations are costly, making it critical to select the right dynamics to reduce the quantity of expert data required for learning transferable rewards. We propose a two-phase approach: we first cycle through the available dynamics to obtain a reliable reward estimate, then actively select dynamics to reduce our uncertainty about the expert reward. Crucially, this yields novel sample complexity guarantees on transfer that hold for any dynamics, with a rate independent of the number of available dynamics. Empirically, our method significantly reduces the number of expert demonstrations needed to learn a transferable reward.
bullets: Targets the high cost of collecting expert demonstrations for transferable reward learning.
First cycles through available dynamics to obtain a reliable initial reward estimate.
Then actively selects dynamics that reduce uncertainty about the expert reward.
Provides transfer sample-complexity guarantees for arbitrary dynamics, independent of their number.
Experiments show substantially fewer expert demonstrations are needed to learn transferable rewards.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires fine-grained control and complex physical interactions with the environment, posing significant challenges for robot policy learning. Vision-only policies struggle with such tasks, as contact states and interaction forces are difficult to infer from visual observations alone. Existing methods mitigate this issue by incorporating force or tactile sensing. However, they often treat these signals as auxiliary observations without fully exploiting their role in modeling future interaction dynamics. To address this, we propose ForceLDM, a force-aware latent dynamics model that learns future contact and motion dynamics to guide action generation. Rather than directly predicting future observations, which can entangle task-relevant dynamics with irrelevant sensory details, ForceLDM learns a compact representation of future dynamics through knowledge distillation. Specifically, a teacher network with privileged future force/torque and optical flow signals extracts future dynamic features, which are then distilled into a student network trained only on current observations. This enables the student model to reason about upcoming contacts and physical dynamics without relying on future sensory inputs at deployment. To improve robustness and generalization, we further introduce a curriculum-based progressive noise injection strategy to mitigate over-reliance on future features. Experiments on five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate that ForceLDM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, generalizes effectively to novel objects, and remains robust to environmental perturbations. Project page and code are available at https://tpy001.github.io/ForceLDM/.
bullets: Vision-only policies struggle to infer contact states and interaction forces during manipulation.
A teacher uses future force/torque and optical-flow signals to extract dynamic features, which are distilled into a student using only current observations at deployment.

Experiments across five real-world tasks show strong performance, generalization to novel objects, and robustness to environmental perturbations.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation goals are easier to visualize than to specify numerically through explicit geometric constraints. We present VerifLM, a framework that converts image-edited goal configurations into physically verified 6-DoF object poses for planning. Using an edited image, VerifLM recovers an initial relative pose between an active object and a passive object, then prompts a vision-language model to generate axis-wise sampling constraints and a task-specific validation program. Candidate poses are evaluated in a physics simulator, and the VLM selects the most task-consistent retained candidate. To operate without predefined object meshes or physical parameters, VerifLM reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs multiple hypothetical simulations with varying physics and geometry. Parallel-world validation evaluates candidates across geometry--physics variations and ranks them by the number of worlds in which they satisfy the validation program. We evaluate VerifLM on nine manipulation tasks. VerifLM achieves the highest task success on eight of nine tasks, with the largest performance gain on goals requiring precise orientation and contact relationships.

Uses a vision-language model to generate axis-wise pose constraints and task-specific validation programs from edited images.

papers.abstract: Soft robot co-design methods can jointly optimise morphology and control, but the resulting designs are often difficult to manufacture, while manufacturable approaches typically restrict actuator placement or require manual assembly. We present a simulation-based co-design framework that jointly optimises material distribution, pneumatic actuator placement and orientation, and control, while producing designs that can be fabricated monolithically using fused deposition modelling. The framework uses a differentiable 2D plane-stress Material Point Method simulator, incorporating an experimentally validated material model and an empirically derived surrogate model of a 3D-printed inflatable actuator. We demonstrate gradient-based optimisation soft robotic arms for prescribed tip trajectories. Optimised designs are transferred directly from simulation to one-shot monolithic FDM fabrication, with integrated actuators and no post-assembly. Physical experiments demonstrate that the resulting arms reproduce the behaviour predicted in simulation. This framework provides a path from task-level objectives to physically realisable soft robots while retaining substantial freedom over both morphology and actuation.
bullets: Addresses the gap between flexible co-design and manufacturable soft robots without manual assembly.
Optimises material distribution, actuator placement/orientation, and control for prescribed arm tip trajectories.
Uses a differentiable 2D plane-stress Material Point Method with validated material and actuator models.
Produces monolithic FDM-printed arms with integrated actuators, transferred directly from simulation.

papers.abstract: We release all 3,718 episodes from the ArmnetBench v0.1 evaluation (arXiv:2607.24481), which contains 600 teleoperated demonstrations and 3,118 rollouts of seven imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies on 12 tabletop tasks, recorded on low-cost SO-101 arms; 73% of the rollouts are failures. Every policy for a task was trained or fine-tuned on the same 50 demonstrations and rolled out on the same cell, so the corpus contains many policies' failures on shared tasks. An operator labelled every rollout successful, suboptimal or failure. Each episode has three camera views, joint states and actions and is available on the Hugging Face Hub in LeRobot v3.0 and a reward-model format. This note documents how the episodes were collected and the limitations that could affect their use.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained manipulation couples instruction grounding, local visual precision, and sustained execution. We present FineCraft, a framework that adapts pretrained models for fine-grained manipulation in the MetaFine Challenge. A task-routed mixture of policies selects independently adapted DINOv2-DiT or pretrained $π_{0.5}$ policies through a common observation-action interface. Local visual features help identify the instructed object parts, demonstrations and expert continuations teach the required actions, and new observations guide replanning during execution. FineCraft ranks fourth with an overall score of $0.878$, exceeding the published reference on all five tasks. Official results and local diagnostics characterize performance across visual perturbations, instruction changes, and multi-stage manipulation. Code is available at https://github.com/eqcy/FineCraft
bullets: Addresses instruction grounding, precise local perception, and sustained multi-stage execution.
Uses a task-routed mixture of independently adapted DINOv2-DiT and pretrained π₀.₅ policies via a shared observation-action interface.
Combines local visual features, demonstrations, expert continuations, and observation-guided replanning.
Placed fourth in the MetaFine Challenge with an overall score of 0.878, outperforming the published reference on all five tasks.
Evaluates robustness across visual perturbations, instruction changes, and multi-stage manipulation.

papers.abstract: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
bullets: Addresses the lack of accessible, standardized physical MARL benchmarks.
Uses dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors for fast, precise tabletop manipulation.
Provides open hardware designs, assembly documentation, inference software, and MARL simulation assets.
Includes an NVIDIA Isaac Lab digital twin and a learned neural actuator model for sim-to-real transfer.
Demonstrates zero-shot policy transfer with emergent adversarial behaviors.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward general-purpose robot manipulation. While inference latency can affect task success in a constantly evolving physical world, the relationship between latency and task success rate remains poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce VLALagBench, a comprehensive benchmark for studying VLA inference latency sensitivity across task types, object speeds, execution modes (synchronous and asynchronous), and VLA policies. Using VLALagBench, we find that even a modest inference latency of 100 ms can nearly halve task success on moving targets, with sensitivity varying substantially across tasks and policies. These differences reflect task-specific requirements for precision and continuous motion. By overlapping inference with action execution, asynchronous execution can recover some of the lost success at the cost of more frequent inference requests. Building on these findings, we develop an empirical model that predicts task success from limited calibration data, achieving root-mean-square prediction errors of only 5.7-7.8% across various VLA policies. Given an inference system's latency and per-robot throughput, these predictions guide the selection of system-specific VLA algorithm configurations to maximize task success. We believe VLALagBench and these findings provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm-system co-design.
bullets: Benchmarks latency sensitivity across tasks, object speeds, execution modes, and VLA policies.
A 100 ms latency can nearly halve success on moving-target tasks, with effects varying by task and policy.
Latency sensitivity reflects task-specific needs for precision and continuous motion.
Asynchronous execution recovers some success by overlapping inference and action, but requires more frequent inference.
An empirical model predicts task success from limited calibration data with 5.7–7.8% RMSE and supports system-specific configuration selection.

papers.abstract: KlaskTron is an open-hardware physical platform for two-player adversarial reinforcement learning, with a learned actuator model that supports zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of trained policies. Building on this platform, we contribute KlaskTron-IL: a multi-tier imitation learning dataset (80k human demonstration timesteps collected directly on the physical robot, 320k symmetry-augmented timesteps, and synthetic expert trajectories up to 5M steps generated by the zero-shot-validated PPO policy), and diagnostic baselines that expose three characteristic failure modes of standard IL methods under contact-rich adversarial dynamics: BC's data scaling plateau, GAIL's interpretable but weak-gradient discriminator (Spearman $ρ= -1.0$ peg-ball proximity recovery, but a logit span under 0.1), and an asymmetric BC-prior x reward-density interaction. Because the policy interface used throughout this paper is the same one the actuator model bridges to hardware, a policy trained on this benchmark can run unchanged on the physical robot, as we demonstrate zero-shot for the strongest BC baseline, so long as its commands respect the actuator model's $\pm 0.2$ m/s identification range.
bullets: Uses 80k human demonstration timesteps from the physical robot, 320k symmetry-augmented timesteps, and up to 5M synthetic expert timesteps.
Benchmarks standard IL methods in two-player adversarial dynamics and identifies BC scaling plateaus, weak GAIL gradients, and asymmetric BC-prior/reward-density interactions.
GAIL’s discriminator provides interpretable peg-ball proximity recovery but produces weak logits.
The strongest BC baseline transfers zero-shot to the physical robot without policy changes.
Transfer is scoped to commands within the actuator model’s ±0.2 m/s identification range.

papers.abstract: Real-world driving requires context-aware decision-making. Existing end-to-end driving benchmarks primarily assess trajectory quality through safety, compliance, comfort, and driving progress, leaving context-dependent decision-making insufficiently characterized. To fill this gap, we present PlanContext, a benchmark for evaluating in-context driving decision-making. PlanContext constructs paired evaluations by varying high-level driving intentions while keeping the observed scene fixed, enabling a natural and controllable assessment of context-dependent decision-making. We further define six representative driving contexts and jointly evaluate contextual decision correctness, road compliance, and dynamic safety with class-balanced metrics. Experiments on 9,561 scene-condition instances from NAVSIM and 23 public end-to-end driving models show that high conventional driving-quality scores do not consistently correspond to strong route-level in-context driving decision-making. Further analysis shows that model behavior varies with decision timing, road structure, and traffic interaction depending on the decision required by the current context. Our results highlight in-context driving decision-making as an important complementary dimension for evaluating end-to-end driving systems.
bullets: Pairs evaluations with different high-level driving intentions while keeping the observed scene fixed.
Defines six representative driving contexts and measures decision correctness, road compliance, and dynamic safety.
Evaluates 9,561 scene-condition instances from NAVSIM across 23 public end-to-end driving models.
Finds behavior varies with decision timing, road structure, and traffic interaction.
Positions in-context driving decision-making as a complementary evaluation dimension for end-to-end driving systems.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a decentralized guiding vector field framework for rigid formation path following in multi- UAV systems based on the superposition of simple rule-driven vector fields. Each control objective is encoded as a dedicated vector-field component: a normalized tangential term to ensure progression along a prescribed geometric path at a desired speed, a convergence term driving the formation toward the path, a local coordination term that preserves the desired formation shape through a pseudo-path parameter, and a local separation term for inter-agent collision avoidance. The coordination mechanism requires the exchange of only a single scalar per agent, resulting in low communication bandwidth. Partial theoretical results establish convergence of the swarm to the desired path and formation in the absence of the sepa- ration term, while collision avoidance is formally guaranteed. The approach is experimentally validated using a swarm of five quadrotors executing two 3D choreographies. The first experiment involves tracking a helical path while maintaining a rigid V-shaped formation. The second demonstrates a spiral- like motion obtained by a rotating circular formation tracking a vertical line. The experimental results support the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed framework.
bullets: Combines tangential, path-convergence, formation-coordination, and inter-agent-separation vector fields.
Each agent exchanges only one scalar, reducing communication requirements.
Provides partial convergence guarantees for path and formation tracking without the separation term, while collision avoidance is formally guaranteed.
Validated with five quadrotors on helical and spiral-like 3D choreographies.
Experiments support the framework’s practical effectiveness for rigid formation path following.

papers.title: Swarm Choreography Made Simple: Superposed Guiding Vector Fields for Rigid Formation Path Following
papers.tldr: A decentralized superposed-vector-field controller enables multi-UAV swarms to follow 3D paths while maintaining rigid formations and avoiding collisions with minimal communication.

papers.abstract: Markerless hand-eye calibration under continuous motion requires jointly resolving camera geometry and the time offset between images and joint states. We present SyncHeC (Synchronized Hand-Eye Calibration), a dense differentiable-rendering framework that estimates both from a single robot trajectory. Continuous-time forward kinematics makes latency differentiable, metric depth complements mask contours, and an offline planner combines spatial sensitivity with temporal excitation. Alternating updates support Eye-to-Hand, Eye-in-Hand, and multi-camera calibration. On a 7-DoF arm, one $6.5$\,s motion yields $0.21$\,cm translation error against a marker-board reference, $0.34$\,cm touch-test error, and $2.7$\,ms latency error relative to an $87$\,ms reference with $95\%$ uncertainty of $\pm1.5$\,ms. Against CM-Calib on matched recordings, translation and nominal latency errors improve by $3.7\times$ and $2.3\times$. Experiments span seven arms and four depth sensors. Compensating the recovered offset during policy training and deployment increases success by $8.1$ percentage points across six families and six tasks ($1{,}800$ matched pairs; paired $95\%$ confidence interval $[6.3,9.9]$ points).
bullets: Addresses markerless hand-eye calibration when camera observations and joint states have an unknown time offset.
Uses dense differentiable rendering, continuous-time forward kinematics, metric depth, and an excitation-aware motion planner.
Supports Eye-to-Hand, Eye-in-Hand, and multi-camera calibration through alternating optimization.
On a 7-DoF arm, one 6.5-second motion achieved 0.21 cm translation error, 0.34 cm touch-test error, and 2.7 ms latency error.
Validated across seven arms and four depth sensors; offset compensation improved policy success by 8.1 percentage points across six tasks.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robots are gaining traction in off-road environments, driven by their rising demand in agriculture, defense, and search-and-rescue operations. However, these environments are inherently unpredictable and navigation remains a formidable challenge given the complex environmental conditions including challenging terrain and varying illumination. Off-road autonomy requires robust perception across multiple spatial scales and imaging modalities, yet most sensing setups struggle to capture both far-field environmental context and near-field terrain detail simultaneously across various illumination conditions. To facilitate development of robust off-road perception and traversability estimation systems, we propose MS-DOTT (Multi-Sensor Dataset for Off-road Terrain Traversability) a comprehensive multi-modal off-road dataset with long-range 3D sensing and short-range, fine-grained perception to facilitate high-fidelity terrain understanding by combining proprioceptive signals for tracking vehicle dynamics with exteroceptive imaging and pointcloud data. The dataset includes trajectories recorded across nominal lighting, low-light, and no-light conditions with diverse 2D and 3D sensing for both long-range large-scale and short-range high-resolution sensing, as well as 4D RADAR measurements that provide velocity estimates for detected pointclouds. We demonstrate the utility of the dataset by adapting a SOTA multi-sensor fusion method for the purpose of traversability estimation. This dataset will aid the robotics community in advancing research and development of methods for traversability estimation, off-road perception and multi-sensor fusion in unstructured environments.
bullets: Targets the challenges of off-road autonomy, including complex terrain, unpredictable environments, and changing illumination.
Combines long-range 3D sensing with short-range, fine-grained 2D/3D perception for multi-scale terrain understanding.
Includes proprioceptive vehicle-dynamics signals, exteroceptive images and point clouds, and 4D RADAR with pointwise velocity estimates.
Covers nominal-light, low-light, and no-light trajectories using diverse sensing modalities.
Demonstrates the dataset’s utility by adapting a state-of-the-art multi-sensor fusion method for traversability estimation.

papers.abstract: Contact transitions allow humanoid robots to redistribute object support across the whole body, enabling manipulation beyond hand-only grasps. Human videos provide a scalable source of such transitions for robots to learn from. However, body occlusion disrupts object pose tracking and corrupts retargeted motion. Moreover, accurately reproducing the object trajectory does not ensure that the robot applies stabilizing forces at the intended contacts, risking slips or drops in later phases. To address these challenges, we propose ReContact, which reconstructs and retargets human-object interactions through an object-centric contact plan. The plan specifies contact phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking or sliding modes. Contact priors stabilize object pose reconstruction through occlusion. A residual policy over a frozen whole-body tracker is rewarded for making contact at planned anchors with forces aligned to the specified directions. In simulation, on a thigh-supported regrasp task, ReContact achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5 of episodes over three training seeds, versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline. One policy trained on 247 references re-solved for new placements raises in-workspace tube-transfer success from 20.4% (source reference only) to 97.8%. On a real Unitree G1, policies execute seven contact-rich manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.
bullets: Addresses occlusion-corrupted object tracking and the gap between matching object motion and applying stabilizing contact forces.
Uses an object-centric contact plan with phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking/sliding modes.
Stabilizes pose reconstruction with contact priors and adds a residual policy over a frozen whole-body tracker to achieve planned contacts and force directions.
In simulation, the method achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5% of episodes versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline.
A policy trained on 247 references generalizes to new placements, increasing tube-transfer success from 20.4% to 97.8%; real-robot tests cover seven manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Collision-free reaching is central to manipulation, yet real cells often leave the size and exact position of an obstacle unobserved, which excludes reinforcement learning controllers that take obstacle geometry as input. A reward limited to a collision penalty does not depend on the clearance outside the obstacle, so under a step cost its learned policy skims the obstacle surface and fails once the obstacle radius exceeds its training value. We investigate whether a single analytic reward term can induce a safety margin without exposing the obstacle to the policy. We augment the reward of a simulated Franka Emika Panda reaching task with a horizontal artificial potential field that penalizes proximity within a safety margin around each of two pillars (fixed nominal layout, random drift). Under hidden observation, policies trained with this term maintain a safe success rate above 88% across a radius sweep from 0.03 m to 0.055 m (30 seeds), while policies without it fall below 10% at the maximum tested radius; the term induces a minimum clearance of 47.9 mm against 9.6 mm without it and eliminates training collisions at least eight times earlier (median steps). The advantage is statistically significant at all out-of-distribution radii and holds across three reinforcement learning solvers and under full observation. Its safe success rate is comparable to that of a classical potential-field planner given the pillar positions. The margin is a fixed buffer rather than an adaptation to the radius, and it lengthens the path by about 19%.
bullets: Without clearance-aware rewards, policies skim obstacle surfaces and fail when obstacles are larger than during training.
The method adds a horizontal potential-field penalty around two pillars without revealing their size or exact position to the policy.
Across obstacle radii of 0.03–0.055 m, augmented policies maintain over 88% safe success, versus under 10% without augmentation at the largest radius.
The method increases minimum clearance to 47.9 mm from 9.6 mm and works across three reinforcement-learning solvers and full observation.
The induced margin is fixed rather than radius-adaptive and increases path length by about 19%.

papers.abstract: Social navigation is essential for autonomous service robots operating in human environments, but progress remains constrained by the lack of extensive real-world benchmarks. This paper presents the Real Social Navigation Testbed (RESONATE), a reproducible benchmark for human-aware navigation based on a unified robotic platform, a shared ROS 2 software stack, precise trajectory ground truth, and structured social interaction scenarios. We evaluate eight controller configurations, combining classical and predictive local planners with different social modeling strategies, over eight representative scenarios with five repetitions each, yielding 320 physical experiments. The benchmark combines quantitative navigation and social metrics with participant-based qualitative assessments to jointly measure efficiency, safety, comfort, and perceived social behavior. Results reveal scenario-dependent trade-offs among the tested methods. The algorithms that stands out for their performance are the DWA with Gaussian social costmaps for its reliability, and the SFM-MPPI to provide the best balance between robustness, navigation efficiency, and social acceptance. Overall, RESONATE supports the robotics community with a real-world benchmark, reusable baselines, data, and testbed, and a consistent evaluation protocol for advancing socially aware navigation research.
bullets: Addresses the lack of extensive, standardized real-world benchmarks for social navigation.
Provides a unified robot platform, ROS 2 stack, trajectory ground truth, structured scenarios, reusable data, and baselines.
Evaluates eight controller configurations across eight scenarios and 320 physical experiments using quantitative and participant-based qualitative measures.
Measures navigation efficiency, safety, comfort, and perceived social behavior together.
Finds scenario-dependent trade-offs; DWA with Gaussian social costmaps is reliable, while SFM-MPPI offers a strong balance of robustness, efficiency, and social acceptance.
