papers.abstract: Generalization remains a central challenge in robotics, calling for policies that address domain variations from multiple dimensions such as diverse embodiments, camera poses, and/or scene layouts. In order to approach this problem, we introduce PointPilot, a task-focused and 3D aligned manipulation framework built on a 3D space point-flow prediction. Rather than modeling the global scene, PointPilot only represents task-focused objects (robot grippers treated as objects), avoiding the prediction of potentially redundant scene parts unrelated to the manipulation tasks. Moreover, PointPilot aligns 3D spatial representation in one unified coordinate and supports closed-loop and fully automatic action execution across different manipulation modes from object point flow without a separately trained action expert, while existing works typically need an extra action head or are (semi-)automatic and single-arm mode specific. Given sensor observations and language instructions, our model jointly learns subtask planning, task-relevant object grounding, and 3D point flow prediction in an end-to-end way. By processing heterogeneous data in a shared 3D point flow space, PointPilot is able to absorb demonstrations from different embodiments. Extensive simulative and real world experiments validate our method. Notably, we demonstrate zero-shot embodiment generalization with PointPilot. A single trained policy can be deployed on previously unseen embodiments and successfully complete manipulation tasks without any additional fine-tuning.
bullets: Targets generalization across embodiments, camera poses, scene layouts, and manipulation modes.
Represents only task-relevant objects, including grippers, in a unified 3D coordinate space rather than modeling the full scene.
Jointly learns subtask planning, object grounding, and 3D point-flow prediction from sensor observations and language instructions.
Supports closed-loop, fully automatic action execution without a separately trained action expert.
Simulated and real-world experiments validate the approach, including zero-shot deployment on previously unseen embodiments without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating object acquisition, transport, and release from onboard sensing while responding to user commands and incomplete visual observations. We present ReGATE, a whole-body controller that combines egocentric depth, proprioception, and online locomotion and contact commands. Built on a teacher-student framework, ReGATE integrates interaction-state estimation through a recurrent adapter that predicts object geometry and physical contact without an external object-pose estimator. Head-wise and global gates regulate visual updates to a proprioceptive pathway. A visual-grounding and corruption curriculum trains the adapter, while phase-aware initialization increases coverage of brief contact transitions. In simulation, ReGATE achieves 85.2% success across 330 static-object acquisition trials, compared with 48.5% for VisualMimic under the same protocol, and 85.9% across 440 moving-object acquisition trials. Deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates commanded grasp-transport-release sequences and acquisition of laterally displaced boxes. A qualitative hardware experiment further demonstrates successful box acquisition when the camera is occluded after an initial observation and before the contact command. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to extend recurrent gated fusion of onboard depth and proprioception from perceptive locomotion to humanoid loco-manipulation under interrupted visual sensing.
bullets: Addresses whole-body loco-manipulation from onboard sensing and user commands, including brief or interrupted visual observations.
Uses a teacher–student controller with a recurrent adapter that estimates object geometry and contact state without an external pose estimator.
Head-wise and global gates regulate visual information, supported by visual-grounding, corruption, and phase-aware training curricula.
Achieves 85.2% success on 330 static-object trials and 85.9% on 440 moving-object trials in simulation, versus 48.5% for VisualMimic on the static protocol.
Hardware demonstrations on a Unitree G1 show grasp–transport–release behavior, laterally displaced box acquisition, and acquisition after camera occlusion.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving policies require effective visual representations that capture both spatial scene structure and temporal dynamics. Video latent prediction has emerged as an effective paradigm for learning spatiotemporal visual representations, yet it remains unclear whether scaling this objective with action-free driving videos can yield representations that benefit end-to-end planning. We study action-free video latent prediction as a scalable pretraining objective and introduce ScaleDrive, a driving-oriented framework pretrained exclusively on large-scale internet open-world driving videos, without action annotations or benchmark-specific data. We keep the pretrained video encoder frozen during downstream end-to-end planning training to isolate the transferability of representations learned from internet driving videos. Ego-motion and depth probes show that scaling action-free video pretraining progressively strengthens the temporal and geometric information encoded in the frozen representation. We systematically study the visual representation transfer across different end-to-end driving policies and closed-loop benchmarks, where ScaleDrive consistently improves downstream performance and demonstrates that scaling action-free video latent prediction yields representations that generalize across both planning policy architectures and evaluation scenarios and protocols.
bullets: Addresses whether action-free video pretraining can learn representations useful for downstream driving.
Pretrains a video encoder exclusively on large-scale internet open-world driving videos, without action labels or benchmark-specific data.
Freezes the encoder during downstream planning training to isolate representation transferability.
Probes indicate that scaling strengthens encoded temporal and geometric information, including ego-motion and depth cues.
Improves performance consistently across driving policy architectures, closed-loop benchmarks, and evaluation protocols.

papers.abstract: Robust multimodal perception for soft robotic grasping is challenged by modality-dependent noise, semantic ambiguity, and limited coordinated multisensory data. We introduce Soma, a dataset containing 100 objects, 1,000 continuous grasping trajectories, and 74,914 multimodal samples grouped by software acquisition cycle, spanning remote RGB, hand RGB, depth, tactile, IMU, and structured text observations. We also collect Soma-Success, an independent grasp-outcome dataset with 1,000 trials (998 retained after quality control), to evaluate frozen-encoder transfer for post-hoc grasp outcome classification and early grasp success prediction. Built on Soma, SomaAlign learns multimodal representations in three stages: masked reconstruction estimates relative modality reliability; reliability-aware contrastive alignment uses pair-specific adaptive temperatures to adjust alignment sharpness; and conflict-aware semantic constraints improve intra-sample cross-modal consistency while preserving global feature geometry. SomaAlign achieves an average Recall@10 of 90.66% across 30 directed cross-modal retrieval tasks. The learned representations also support physical attribute recognition, multimodal question answering, cross-modal generation, and cross-dataset transfer to grasp outcome prediction. On Soma-Success, frozen SomaAlign encoders with lightweight probes achieve 94.59% post-hoc classification accuracy and 84.07% early prediction accuracy. Together, Soma, Soma-Success, and SomaAlign provide a data and representation-learning foundation for robust and transferable multimodal perception in soft robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses modality-dependent noise, semantic ambiguity, and limited coordinated multisensory data in soft robotic grasping.
Introduces Soma, with multimodal RGB, depth, tactile, IMU, and text observations from 1,000 continuous grasping trajectories, plus the independent Soma-Success evaluation set.
Uses masked reconstruction for modality reliability, adaptive-temperature contrastive alignment, and conflict-aware semantic constraints.
Reports 90.66% average Recall@10 across 30 directed cross-modal retrieval tasks.
Frozen encoders with lightweight probes reach 94.59% post-hoc and 84.07% early grasp-success prediction accuracy.

figures.caption: Fig. 5. Overview of the SomaAlign framework. SomaAlign follows three progressive optimization stages: (1) Reconstruction-Based Modality Reliability Estimation estimates modality reliability from normalized masked-reconstruction difficulty and constructs pairwise reliability scores; (2) Reliability-Conditioned Contrastive Alignment uses the pairwise reliability scores to adapt cross-modal contrastive temperatures and learn a shared representation; and (3) BatchAdaptive Conflict-Aware Geometry-Preserving Refinement calibrates pairwise similarities, estimates fuzzy sample-level conflict, and adaptively modulates intra-sample refinement while imposing conflict-consistency and reference-center anchoring constraints. The reference geometry constructed from Stage-II representations, including the sample-specific centers and global representation scale, is frozen and reused during Stage-III optimization. After training, only the modality-specific encoders are retained for inference.

Fig. 1. Overview of Soma, Soma-Success, and the SomaAlign framework. The soft robotic platform acquires six coordinated modalities: Remote RGB, Hand RGB, Depth, Tactile, IMU, and Text. Soma comprises 100 objects, 1,000 trajectories, and 74,914 aligned multimodal samples, while Soma-Success contains 1,000 collected grasp trials, of which 998 valid trials are retained for downstream evaluation. SomaAlign learns a unified semantic representation through Reliability Assessment, Adaptive Feature Alignment, and Conflict-aware Refinement. The learned representation supports cross-modal retrieval, physical attribute recognition, multimodal question answering, cross-modal generation, and frozen-encoder grasp success prediction.

Fig. 6. Conceptual illustration of pair-specific distribution calibration and fuzzy membership assignment. Different modality pairs may exhibit different raw similarity distributions; therefore, the same similarity value can represent different degrees of relative inconsistency. Pair-specific ECDFs convert raw similarities into comparable conflict indicators ξi,π . The calibrated indicator is then softly assigned to overlapping ordered Gaussian fuzzy sets, allowing transitional cross-modal conflicts to partially activate multiple adjacent conflict levels.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can handle noncritical stages of long-horizon manipulation yet fail during short precision-critical phases. Lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) specialists can address these failures without directly applying RL to the full VLA, but retain auxiliary controllers and switching mechanisms at deployment. We study how to transfer their capabilities into a single flow-matching VLA. Direct imitation of specialist rollouts can reproduce action jitter and leave the VLA unprepared for states encountered during its own execution. We introduce REPAIR, a value-guided distillation framework that combines offline initialization with on-policy refinement. At each critical-phase observation, REPAIR queries the corresponding specialist for multiple action candidates and weights them using its critic to construct a supervision distribution. A shared weighted flow-matching objective trains the VLA first on observations from specialist-assisted rollouts, then on observations collected through its own execution. Specialists provide supervision without taking control during on-policy collection and are removed at deployment. Across six real-robot tasks with 30 evaluation trials per task, REPAIR achieves 100% success on all six tasks, with lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.
bullets: Targets short, precision-critical phases where VLAs often fail during long-horizon manipulation.
Uses specialist critics to weight multiple candidate actions within a shared flow-matching objective.
Combines offline training on specialist-assisted rollouts with on-policy refinement on the VLA’s own observations.
Avoids reproducing action jitter and reduces distribution mismatch from direct imitation.
Achieves 100% success across six real-robot tasks and lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.

For each critical observation, the selected phase specialist generates the action candidates and its critic determines their relative weights. The VLA learns from these targets in critical phases and replayed VLA actions in noncritical phases. Only the VLA is deployed.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.
bullets: Introduces 282 offline Street View tasks involving panorama rotation, zooming, and movement, plus 42 expert-referenced GeoGuessr championship rounds.
Tests three task types: coordinate localization, place naming, and finding, reading, or counting nearby objects.
Evaluates 23 VLMs; best reported accuracy is 62.5% for place naming and 35.0% for object finding, while the strongest agent approaches expert GeoGuessr performance.
Finds only weak correlation between localization and exploration ability, with errors categorized as vision, navigation, or tool-use failures.
Shows that environment difficulty can be adjusted through view limits and that a Planner-Worker-Compressor harness reduces planner tokens by 57–61%.

papers.abstract: Agentic Real2Sim2Real systems can reconstruct a scene in simulation from camera observations, but contact-rich dynamics such as friction and restitution cannot be observed without interaction. We call this the dynamics gap and present CUE, an agentic system that closes it by interacting with the environment itself. Given only a high-level instruction and no resets, the agent builds its own perception, identifies physical parameters, and targets interactions where its simulation is least accurate. On billiards, CUE reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% relative to the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics conditions in simulation, and we further deploy it on a real pool table. More details can be found on the project website: https://cue-dynamics.github.io/
bullets: Addresses unobservable contact-rich properties such as friction and restitution.
Uses agent-directed interaction to identify physical parameters and target regions where simulation is least accurate.
Operates from a high-level instruction without environment resets, while building its own perception.
On billiards, reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% versus the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics simulation conditions.
Also demonstrates deployment on a real pool table.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic assembly requires reliable perception and action across grasping, alignment, and insertion. Vision captures global object pose and scene context, where as fingertip touch provides local contact cues that are especially useful as contact states change. We present a visuotactile diffusion policy that combines four-step histories from two camera views and two fingertip tactile images to condition action-sequence generation. A recurrent temporal representation integrates recent observations from both modalities. To encourage it to capture how contact evolves under action, an auxiliary objective predicts fingertip-image changes two steps ahead from the temporal representation and demonstrated actions. This objective is used only during training and adds no inference-time computation. Across three independent training seeds in MuJoCo assembly experiments, the full model achieves an average success rate of $59.0\% \pm 2.6\%$, improving on the visual-only baseline ($42.7\% \pm 1.5\%$) by 16.3 percentage points.
bullets: Targets reliable perception and action across grasping, alignment, and insertion, where touch provides local contact information beyond vision.
Conditions action-sequence generation on four-step histories from two camera views and two fingertip tactile images.
Uses a recurrent temporal representation to integrate multimodal observations.
Adds a training-only objective that predicts fingertip-image changes two steps ahead from the representation and demonstrated actions, with no inference-time cost.
In MuJoCo assembly experiments, it achieves 59.0% ± 2.6% success across three seeds versus 42.7% ± 1.5% for a visual-only baseline.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.
bullets: Addresses failures of Markovian VLA models on tasks requiring working memory and persistent context.
Uses factorized event detection with event-triggered updates to maintain task-relevant language history.
Evaluated on 10 real-world non-Markovian tasks with 56 variants, including five inter-episode tasks.
Improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and reaches 78% subtask success on compositional generalization.
Uses up to 4.5× less memory and runs 2.5× faster than a keyframe baseline at long horizons.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall Architecture of HeLM. The High Level Policy (HLP) integrates language memory with a pretrained VLM, which switches between a ‘detect mode’ that monitors events and an ‘update mode’ that updates these events into language memory. The Low Level Policy (LLP), a pretrained VLA, executes action commands generated by the HLP.

Figure 1: Example of non-Markovian task. Due to architectural limitation, a vanilla VLA loses track after pressing the red button and presses it again. HeLM successfully executes the task by storing progress in language memory, allowing the HLP to guide the LLP correctly.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon dexterous manipulation remains a fundamental challenge for robot learning, requiring the composition of multiple skills, precise bimanual coordination, generalizable visual understanding, and robust skill transitions. Yet existing manipulation benchmarks largely emphasize isolated skills or support only a limited range of end-effectors, making these capabilities difficult to evaluate systematically. We introduce DexArena, a benchmark designed to evaluate learning and generalization in long-horizon bimanual dexterous manipulation. DexArena features 10 long-horizon tasks and 30 stage-level tasks spanning diverse household and industrial scenarios. Each long-horizon task is composed of explicitly defined stages with physically grounded success conditions, enabling reliable evaluation of both intermediate progress and end-to-end task completion. A unified benchmark interface and verified human-teleoperated demonstrations enable testing different policy learning algorithms, with standardized simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation. Through extensive baseline experiments, we identify substantial challenges in precise manipulation, generalization to scene variation, and skill composition. DexArena establishes a challenging and reproducible benchmark for developing robot learning methods that move toward generalizable long-horizon dexterous behavior.
bullets: Covers 10 long-horizon and 30 stage-level tasks across household and industrial scenarios.
Tasks use explicitly defined stages and physically grounded success conditions to measure both intermediate progress and end-to-end completion.
Provides a standardized interface with human-teleoperated demonstrations, simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation.
Baseline experiments reveal persistent challenges in precise manipulation, scene-variation generalization, and composing skills.

papers.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a standard way to keep a planner inside a safe set, but they assume control affine dynamics, a barrier function given in closed form, and a known nominal controller. Integral control barrier functions (ICBFs) remove the first assumption and absorb input constraints, yet they still assume a given nominal controller and a barrier function. In this work, we present an approach to learn all three from data, using neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the dynamics, imitation for the nominal controller, and supervised regression for the barrier function. The learned dynamics, nominal controller, and the barrier function are used to build the ICBF filter constraint analytically. Furthermore, the barrier is trained on viability rather than geometry, meaning that a state counts as safe only if some emergency maneuver can still avoid the constraint under the actuator limits, a correction that geometric labels miss entirely and that grows with speed. Actuator limits then enter the online program as hard bounds while the learned barrier rows may be relaxed, which keeps the program solvable at every state and the actuator limits exact, and we bound how far the input it returns can drift from the one the true models would give. On agile racing with a 6-D dynamic bicycle, the filter removes all 12 unsafe episodes from 200 held out layouts at an unchanged success rate and above 100 Hz on one CPU core, holds the input constraint on every episode of a benchmark where a jointly trained baseline holds it on 53.38%, and keeps that advantage under large errors in the plant friction.
bullets: Addresses CBF limitations requiring control-affine dynamics, known barriers, and a nominal controller.
Learns dynamics with neural ODEs, the nominal controller by imitation, and the barrier through supervised viability regression.
Uses emergency-maneuver viability labels, capturing speed-dependent safety that geometric labels miss.
Keeps actuator limits hard, allows learned barrier constraints to relax for solvability, and bounds deviation from the true-model input.
On agile racing tasks, removed all 12 unsafe held-out episodes, ran above 100 Hz on one CPU core, and maintained actuator constraints under friction-model errors.

papers.abstract: Universal humanoid motion tracking is essential for enabling humanoid robots to perform diverse tasks in human environments. To capture the wide diversity of human motions, mixture-of-experts (MoE) policies have been widely adopted, leveraging dynamic routing to enhance policy expressiveness. However, we identify that divergence between old and updated policies can be misestimated during policy-gradient updates of MoE policies, due to their dynamic routing. Because most policy-gradient algorithms regulate policy updates based on the divergence, this misestimation can lead to either overly conservative or excessively large updates, which can yield a suboptimal policy. In this paper, we propose Mixture of Experts with Alternating Policy Optimization (MAPO), which alternately optimizes the router and the experts to avoid the divergence misestimation. MAPO consistently tracks 182 motions that PPO with MoE fails to track, whereas PPO with MoE tracks only one motion that MAPO fails to track. MAPO also attains the highest tracking success rate among the compared methods and the lowest tracking error across most error metrics, demonstrating its superior performance. Videos can be found on the project website: https://mapo-corl2026.github.io/MAPO/
bullets: MoE policies can misestimate old–updated policy divergence because their routing changes dynamically.
This misestimation may cause overly conservative or excessively large policy updates, producing suboptimal policies.
MAPO alternates optimization of the router and expert policies to address this issue.
MAPO consistently tracks 182 motions that PPO with MoE fails to track, while PPO with MoE tracks only one motion MAPO fails to track.
Among the compared methods, MAPO achieves the highest tracking success rate and lowest error across most metrics.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently shown great promise in robotic control, benefiting from the future imagination capability of large-scale pretrained video models. However, most existing WAMs require explicitly imagining future states at test time, incurring substantial computational overhead and latency that make them unsuitable for real-time robotic control. In this paper, we propose W2A, a two-stage distillation framework for real-time robotic manipulation that distills intermediate denoising representations from a video diffusion model into an action model during training, while entirely discarding the video model at test time. We hypothesize that although video latent representations are high-dimensional, a compressed low-dimensional subspace is sufficient to provide effective supervision for action generation. This makes it possible to transfer such information effectively into an action model. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate competitive success rates while significantly improving inference efficiency. On LIBERO, W2A achieves a 95.9% average success rate. More importantly, W2A achieves about 21x faster inference than the representative WAM baseline.
bullets: Existing world action models often imagine future states at test time, creating prohibitive computational overhead for real-time control.
W2A uses two-stage training to transfer intermediate denoising representations from a pretrained video diffusion model into an action model.
The approach assumes effective supervision can be compressed into a low-dimensional subspace of the video latent space.
The video model is discarded at deployment, reducing inference cost while retaining useful world priors.
W2A reports a 95.9% average success rate on LIBERO and approximately 21× faster inference than a representative WAM baseline.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents are vulnerable to perturbations of their observed state inputs. Prior works often constrain state adversaries with $L_p$-norm uncertainty sets and evaluate policy performance under the resulting perturbations. However, in continuous control tasks like robotics control, different state dimensions have distinct physical meanings and influence policy behavior to different degrees, which $L_p$-norm sets fail to capture or explain. Moreover, it is important to identify when and along which state dimensions a policy is vulnerable, independently of the algorithm used to train it. In this paper, we focus on evaluation-time attacks applied to pretrained policies. We propose \textbf{P}erformance-\textbf{D}egradation \textbf{N}on-\textbf{U}niform \textbf{U}ncertainty \textbf{S}et (\method{}), an interpretable formulation of uncertainty sets for state perturbations. \method{} is state-dependent, dimension-wise non-uniform, and can be synthesized online during policy evaluation. We first formulate an ideal constrained optimization problem for \method{} computation, then introduce a surrogate constraint to make the problem tractable. Experiments across multiple continuous-control environments, policy algorithms, and state attacks show that \method{} reveals variation in policy sensitivity across states and dimensions, while its performance degradation is moderately controlled.
bullets: Targets a limitation of uniform $L_p$-norm sets, which overlook the differing meanings and policy influence of state dimensions.
Focuses on attacks against pretrained policies during evaluation, independently of the training algorithm.
Formulates an ideal constrained optimization problem and uses a tractable surrogate to synthesize the uncertainty sets online.
Experiments across continuous-control environments, policy algorithms, and state attacks show varying sensitivity across states and dimensions with moderately controlled performance degradation.

papers.title: Beyond $L_\infty$-Norm Sets: Synthesizing Interpretable Non-Uniform Uncertainty Sets for Evaluation-Time State-Adversarial Robustness

papers.abstract: A competent learned controller already recovers from many disturbances. Improving it means learning a correction, and learning when not to apply it. Freezing a skill's parameters does not settle the second half. In a controller that routes among frozen skills, a new entry rule can redirect the states an old skill succeeded on. We therefore constrain entry instead of parameters. Each update searches for a feedback skill at a measured failure. It fits an entry rule that reads observations and rejects every state on an accumulated successful trajectory. The skill is admitted only if the composed controller reproduces the new recovery on its own and replays every protected trajectory exactly. A finite-trajectory condition states when this preserves the previous controller. One mechanism runs on four streams: two motions on each of two humanoid systems. Two updates per stream add 62 recoveries over 192 withheld perturbations, and lose none of the base controller's successes. We then price that guarantee. Removing the constraint recovers 33 more conditions but stops eight protected ones from completing at all, and excluding only what admission proves necessary recovers none of that cost.
bullets: Targets the problem of new skill-entry rules redirecting states where existing skills already succeed.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as policy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy-goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy's goal and executes the lowest-energy policy-goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision-robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://yewr.github.io/epo
bullets: Addresses failures of fixed planner-to-policy interfaces when contacts, balance, or disturbances change faster than high-level updates.
Learns a composite energy for each modular goal-conditioned policy, where lower energy indicates greater feasibility and more accurate target realization.
Refines candidate goals and executes the lowest-energy policy–goal pair during runtime orchestration.
New policies can be added by learning separate energy models without retraining existing policies or a centralized scheduler.
Simulation shows improved precision–robustness trade-offs, with sim-to-real deployment on humanoid loco-manipulation tasks using frozen policies and energy models.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous driving requires more than recognizing the current scene: the ego vehicle must anticipate how surrounding traffic participants will evolve under its own motion. However, existing end-to-end driving models typically encode scenes into dense visual or BEV features, leaving object-level interactions implicit. We propose (INTERACT INTERaction-aware Action-Conditioned Trajectory learning), a three-stage framework that learns a slot-based object-centric world model from unlabeled driving videos and transfers it to trajectory planning. INTERACT first learns recurrent slots that group dense visual features into temporally structured scene-entity representations without object annotations. It then infers latent ego actions from slot context and video transitions, and uses them to condition future slot prediction, capturing how ego motion and surrounding entities co-evolve. Finally, the learned slots, latent actions, and future slot predictions are distilled into a trajectory planner to guide trajectory generation and selection. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes validate the effectiveness of INTERACT. In particular, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting how surrounding traffic evolves in response to the ego vehicle’s motion.
Uses recurrent slots to discover temporally structured scene entities without object annotations.
Infers latent ego actions and conditions future slot prediction on those actions to model interaction dynamics.
Distills learned slots, actions, and future predictions into a trajectory planner.
Validated on NAVSIM and nuScenes, achieving state-of-the-art NAVSIM performance with improved collision-related metrics.

papers.abstract: Robot policies still fail at everyday manipulation: an unfamiliar task, an object never held before, a scene that changes mid-motion, a skill that should improve with use. They fail despite pretraining on over a million trajectories, pooled from dozens of robots at great expense, while a child acquires all of these abilities within a few years of learning from a single body. This survey argues that the gap is one of design, and proposes designs for the next generation of robot models, drawn from how the nervous system solves the same problems. From the body we take compliance: the policy commands stiffness alongside position, so the controller yields where the task allows and presses where it must, which greatly lowers the demand for precise position output. From the visual system, where a fast pathway for action runs in parallel with the slow pathway for recognition, we take a dedicated fast vision system for motor behavior: it precomputes the quantities the policy needs and drives a reactive policy at camera rate. From the cerebellum we take a predictor beside the policy that forecasts the consequence of each command and recalibrates from its own error. From motor cortex we take a single model that composes action units from primitives, verifies each at a sensory boundary, practices the weakest unit with a hypothesis in mind, and reasons each attempt closer to the goal. Proven primitives are then consolidated from code into weights, so they run fluently and respond quickly the next time. Together these describe a robot that acts on its own initiative, the basis of deployment and recursive self-improvement, and we offer each proposal as a hypothesis to be tested.
bullets: Robot policies struggle with novel tasks, objects, changing scenes, and continual skill improvement despite extensive trajectory data.
It draws design principles from the body, visual system, cerebellum, and motor cortex.
Key proposals include stiffness-aware control, a fast action-oriented vision pathway, predictive models for self-calibration, and compositional primitive-based planning.
The framework emphasizes sensory verification, targeted practice, reasoning toward goals, and consolidating successful primitives into model weights.
The proposals are presented as hypotheses for future testing, with autonomous initiative and recursive self-improvement as the broader goal.

figures.caption: Figure 26: Consolidation advances a primitive from a script over many functions to an end-to-end policy. (a) At first the model writes a perception pipeline that computes the slot’s pose and the key’s geometry in the hand before calling the orient template, which runs by Cartesian control. (b) Next the model outputs both values directly from the images and supplies them to the same template, so the explicit measuring code is no longer needed. (c) In the end the template lives in the orient experts of the model’s mixture-of-experts trunk: the action head of the same model reads their latent, no number is passed, and the action stream reacts at the control rate.
Figure 3: Opposing muscles set torque and stiffness separately. The difference of flexor and extensor pull sets the net torque, and their sum sets the stiffness at the same pose.

Figure 1: A child has three abilities that current robot policies lack. Top: a boy opens an unfamiliar drawer on the first try, while a policy finds no training handle to copy. Middle: a girl catches a flying toy, while a robot is still reasoning about shape and coordinates when the toy lands. Bottom: the boy’s piano playing improves with days of practice, while a robot never trained on the piano cannot learn it or improve over time, because its learning stopped the day it was deployed.

Figure 7: Vision and touch build a single object model, and each sense fills in what the other cannot. Vision covers the visible surfaces, while touch supplies weight, texture, slipperiness, and compliance, and explores the occluded back.
Figure 4: Contact supplies the surface detail. A yielding wrist and a soft towel follow the bumps, so the controller computes fewer corrections.

Figure 6: Slowly adapting (SA) afferents report steady pressure and rapidly adapting (RA) ones report change, so the four classes split what touch carries. The traces are schematic responses to a ramp-and-hold skin indentation: SA afferents sustain firing during the hold, RA afferents respond transiently during pressing and release, and SA2 afferents also fire at a low rate before contact, driven by resting skin stretch. RA afferents can also fire during ongoing motion or vibration. Spike counts and timing are illustrative rather than measured; responses depend on the stimulus and afferent [194, 2].

Figure 13: In the prevailing model, the dorsal stream is a bank of parallel channels. The figure expands the dorsal branch of Figure 12 and draws the motion areas MT and MST, which that figure folds into the parietal box, as a separate stage. Each visual area estimates one quantity the body needs (where to look, what is moving, what is within reach, where to reach, how to turn and shape the hand, and what a tool in hand reaches) and sends it to a partner in premotor, motor, or oculomotor areas; the italic line in each visual box names the reference frame the channel works in (Section 4.2.4). Each label names an area’s dominant contribution rather than its only one [331].
Figure 9: Descending signals from cortex turn down predicted or irrelevant tactile channels and turn up the task-relevant one, so the fingertip signal arrives at high contrast.

Figure 17: Joint World Action Models let the prediction loss train the action head, while cascaded ones only pass predicted frames forward. In the cascaded design a video generator synthesizes predicted frames and a separate inverse-dynamics module reads actions off them. In the joint design a shared backbone trained under one generative objective feeds a state head that generates future frames, which some variants skip at test time, and an action head that emits the executed chunk.

Figure 27: The practice agent finds the error-prone part across attempts, corrects it during inference, and hands the corrected record to consolidation. (a) Over seven episodes of opening a lock, insert passes rarely, and the blame falls on orient’s angle, which is solved with an arbitrary offset after several model calls and fails most first attempts; it is unfamiliar and error prone and is practiced first. (b) During practice the direction to move after each attempt comes from the graded goal test, the forecast against the outcome, or the model’s reasoning; the interval halves until the goal test fires, and the angle that passed is stored. (c) Consolidation then improves the coding strategy that finds the keypoints, trains the model to output the values directly, and trains the orient experts of the trunk, so the orient primitive becomes familiar.

Figure 21: Actions attach to a vision-language backbone in one of three ways. (a) The first generation bins each action dimension and decodes actions as text tokens, one at a time. (b) The current generation keeps the backbone and attaches a small action expert that attends to its features and denoises a noisy chunk into continuous actions by diffusion or flow matching; proprioception enters the expert, as drawn, in 𝜋0 and GR00T N1, and the backbone in SmolVLA [42, 40, 354]. (c) An omni model has no head. Images, text, and actions are tokens in one sequence, so the same network predicts the next action and the next image. Purple: transformer with pretrained weights. Teal: images, text, proprioception, and the action expert. Gray: discrete action tokens and the noise the expert denoises.

Figure 20: One model composes familiar primitives into a new solution. Reach, grasp, orient, and tool use, none of them learned for this task, combine to retrieve an out-of-reach key, and the same model turns the plan into movement.
Figure 10: When an object’s properties cannot be seen, the robot should probe before it commits. Lifting, tilting, and pressing within safe bounds each test a hypothesis the camera cannot settle.
Figure 2: The slot walls supply the rod’s trajectory. The hand pushes along the slot and yields across it, so the walls shape the path and the controller has far less of the curve to compute.
Figure 11: The same ball is read twice, by the two visual streams in the brain. The ventral stream resolves its pattern and identity; the dorsal stream resolves its trajectory and guides the catch.
Figure 5: Touch alone finds the handle and opens the door. With eyes closed the hand feels its way to the handle, turns it and pushes the door open; in the dark a camera has nothing to offer.

Figure 24: Motor cortex is M1, premotor cortex, and SMA, reciprocally connected, with three cortical inputs: prefrontal goals enter through SMA and premotor cortex, the parietal state enters through premotor cortex and, from S1 and area 5, M1 directly, and ACC reaches SMA and M1 through the cingulate motor areas [364]. M1 carries most of the corticospinal tract, and SMA, premotor, and cingulate areas each add a direct projection that bypasses it [100]. Motor cortex also drives the brainstem pathways and runs loops through the basal ganglia and cerebellum [230]; reflex afferents return to the cord and touch and proprioception return to parietal cortex. Only the principal pathways are drawn.

Figure 14: A visually guided action must re-express the retinal report in the frame its effector needs. The same dumpling has different coordinates in each frame along the chain: eye, head, body, hand, tool, and object.

Figure 8: Three neurons carry a fingertip signal to primary somatosensory cortex (S1), a chain short enough to leave time for a tactile correction within about 75 ms. The first-order neuron ascends on the same side through the spinal dorsal column to the cuneate nucleus of the medulla; the second-order neuron crosses there and ascends to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) thalamus; the third-order neuron projects to S1 on the side opposite the stimulated hand. Each line ends in a dot at its synapse, and the legend colors mark the three cell bodies. Other branches and circuits are omitted [197].

Figure 15: A second viewpoint reveals what the head camera cannot see. The mug body partly hides its far-side handle from the head camera. Moving the wrist camera of the free hand to a side viewpoint reveals more of the handle before grasping. Teal arrows mark viewing directions; the curved gray arrow marks the wrist motion.

Figure 19: The same nuclear prediction leaves by two routes. Ascending (left), it reaches cortex through the ventrolateral thalamus. Descending (right), it joins the command in flight at the brainstem and spinal cord. Both arrive within tens of milliseconds of the command, before sensory feedback could alter it through cortex.

Figure 18: The cerebellar circuit is three synapses deep, wide in the middle, and local along its length. The highlighted paths trace one local circuit: parallel fibers run only a few millimeters [315], and about forty Purkinje cells converge on one nuclear neuron [309], so coupling between body parts is local by construction. The inferior olive (amber) returns the prediction error over one climbing fiber per Purkinje cell, which adjusts the parallel-fiber synapses that were active when the faulty prediction was made. Counts are rough human figures [12, 285, 202].

Figure 16: Having tossed the ball herself, she knows from the throw where and when it will land. A copy of the tossing command is enough to forecast the ball’s arrival, so the right hand is already in place while the ball is still in the air. The faint circles show predicted positions of the same ball.

Figure 22: A robot learns mostly before it leaves the factory and afterwards executes the learned policy; a human begins with a genome rather than pretrained weights and does most of its learning after birth, through play, practice, and observation.

Figure 25: One action unit runs as a loop; the arrows show the flow of control rather than anatomical pathways. Purple marks the four stages, run clockwise, and teal what each stage reads. Solid teal arrows have direct support: the cerebellar forecast amends the unit in flight [31, 252] and sustains and times the cortical preparation of the next [122, 60]. Dashed arrows are hypotheses: whether the forecast also times the basal ganglia release is untested, and pre-SMA, which launches units and switches between them [205, 178], is proposed here to do so on the ACC verdict. Assigning one area to each stage is a simplification; each area takes part in more than one.

Figure 12: Vision for action and vision for recognition separate after V1, and a collicular route bypasses cortex entirely. The geniculate route through V1 divides into a dorsal stream through posterior parietal cortex to premotor and motor areas (vision for action) and a ventral stream through V2 and V4 into inferotemporal cortex (vision for recognition); a separate collicular route drives fast orienting of eyes and head without cortex.

Figure 23: Unlocking a door is four action units in a fixed order, reach, orient, insert, and rotate, and each ends at a sensory event: the tip reaches the slot, the key aligns, it stops at the end, the lock turns.

Table 1: No single sensor family combines fine resolution, kilohertz speed, and shear. Resolution and speed are order-of-magnitude values typical of each family, and the cited works are representative examples. A taxel (“tactile pixel”) is one sensing point on the skin.
Table 3: Discrepancies between the current robot stack and the nervous system, stage by stage, and the proposal each chapter derives from the gap.

Table 2: Four afferent classes split touch by receptive-field size and adaptation [186, 389, 194]. The pairing of SA2 afferents with Ruffini endings is disputed, since the human fingertip holds few such endings [303]. Figure 6 uses the same codes.

papers.tldr: This survey proposes brain-inspired designs to make robot learning more adaptive, efficient, and capable of everyday manipulation beyond large-scale pretraining.

papers.abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all four embodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.
bullets: Standardizes policy serving and evaluation protocols across locally operated robots at 124 sites.
Evaluates five VLA policies and three frontier agents across four embodiments using open and fine-tuning tracks.
Frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies in open-world trials, but all systems struggle with reliable completion.
Fine-tuning changes model rankings substantially across embodiments; Open Track rankings poorly predict adapted performance.
Partial-progress metrics and active matchmaking provide more informative and trial-efficient evaluation than success rates and uniform sampling.

RoboColosseum connects distributed evaluation sites through shared robot interfaces, policy-serving infrastructure, and two complementary evaluation tracks. In the Fine-tune Track, policies receive the same 100 demonstrations per task and are evaluated on predefined tasks using common success and progress criteria. In the OpenTrack, policies are evaluated without additional task-specific adaptation through blinded, pairwise comparisons under matched local conditions, while tasks and environments vary across comparisons. The results shown for both tracks are based on evaluations we conducted from 17 September to 28 October 2026. The project spans SO-101, Franka in the DROID configuration, Bimanual-YAM, and Unitree G1, with participation determined by track and model compatibility. papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict scene changes to guide robot actions, yet their RGB futures entangle state changes with appearance and lack 3D geometry. Recent WAMs add geometry as a training signal or a control interface, or build native 3D models, but decide what geometry to model rather than how the action should read it. Intuitively, control-relevant cues lie at embodiment--object interactions and their transitions, yet probing existing WAMs reveals that their action attention underweights these interactions in favor of the rest of the embodiment. To focus the action on these interactions, we present Gnomon4D, a WAM that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field recording the image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. With the embodiment and objects in one field, their relative motion, which marks an interaction, can be read off. Guided by this motion and the task, Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) selects where the action reads, and Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) selects when, around grasp and release. As GeoDelta encodes surface motion rather than embodiment-specific controls, it serves as a human--robot quasi-action that links action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H, which we curate, to robot mid-training on Robot-30H. Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin~2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, especially under visual shifts. Project page: https://droliven.github.io/Gnomon4D.
bullets: Addresses the problem that RGB-based world-action models entangle appearance and state changes, while action attention often overlooks control-relevant interactions.
Jointly predicts future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D field of image-plane displacement and depth changes for embodiment and object points.
Uses Interaction-Salient Attention to select where to attend and Transition-Anchored Aggregation to focus around grasp and release transitions.
GeoDelta enables action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H and robot mid-training on Robot-30H by acting as a human–robot quasi-action.
Leads on RoboTwin 2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, particularly under visual shifts.

papers.abstract: Does effective swimming with multiple underactuated soft arms require explicit coordination between arms? We hypothesize that an eight-arm swimmer can control its swimming speed and direction by independently learning each arm's actuation amplitude under a shared rhythmic drive, without prescribed inter-arm phase coupling. To test this hypothesis, we compare three reinforcement learning-based control strategies using proximal policy optimization (PPO): (1) learning arm-specific actuation amplitudes without inter-arm phase coupling, (2) learning actuation amplitudes with prescribed inter-arm phase coupling, and (3) directly learning actuator commands through end-to-end PPO without an explicit rhythmic structure. Across 200 episodes with randomized three-dimensional velocity commands, the controller without phase coupling satisfies the tracking criterion in 169 episodes, compared with 117 for the phase-coupled controller and 28 for end-to-end PPO. Straight-line swimming and commanded direction-change trials further demonstrate more accurate velocity tracking without phase coupling. These findings suggest that effective eight-arm swimming does not require prescribed inter-arm phase coupling, but can instead be achieved through learned arm-specific amplitude modulation within a rhythmic control structure.
bullets: The study tests whether explicit inter-arm coordination is necessary for swimming with underactuated soft arms.
It compares three PPO controllers: amplitude learning without phase coupling, amplitude learning with prescribed coupling, and end-to-end actuator-command learning.
Without phase coupling, the controller met the tracking criterion in 169 of 200 randomized 3D-velocity episodes, versus 117 with coupling and 28 for end-to-end PPO.
Straight-line and direction-change trials also showed more accurate velocity tracking without prescribed phase coupling.
The result is scoped to the tested eight-arm swimmer and control setup; it supports learned amplitude modulation within a rhythmic structure.

papers.abstract: Treating morphology and control as separate design problems has constrained the efficiency and adaptability of quadrupedal robots, while current co-design approaches are often constrained by restricted design spaces. We overcome this limit by introducing Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped with modular three-segment legs, four-bar linkages and adjustable passive knee compliance. A two-stage framework combining reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization is developed: the morphology-conditioned control policy is trained across designs and then held fixed during task-specific design selection. The resulting designs and policies deployed zero-shot reduce the cost of transport by 18.6% and 35.7% for inspection and payload-carrying tasks. Comparisons demonstrate that full geometry-compliance co-design outperforms fixed and restricted design scopes. Cross-task tests further reveal distinct task-specific morphologies with shared mechanical trade-offs. These results provide hardware-level evidence that expanding the physical design space alongside learned control is essential to realize the full potential of task-driven morphology-control co-design in legged robotics.
bullets: Introduces Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped with modular three-segment legs, four-bar linkages, and adjustable passive knee compliance.
Trains a morphology-conditioned control policy across designs, then selects task-specific designs while keeping the policy fixed.
Zero-shot deployments reduce cost of transport by 18.6% for inspection and 35.7% for payload-carrying tasks.
Full geometry–compliance co-design outperforms fixed or restricted design spaces.
Cross-task results show distinct task-specific morphologies sharing mechanical trade-offs.

papers.abstract: No algorithm is best on all problems, but a real warehouse is a narrow problem: its layout and processes rarely change. Operators still run one general multi-robot planner at many sites, because experts cannot tune it for each one. In this work, which we call Late Autumn, we explore whether LLM coding agents running autonomous research can specialize a general planner for one site, trading generality for throughput, much as post-training adapts a pretrained LLM to one task. We study six campaigns on a lifelong planner that combines task assignment with multi-agent path finding, on a floor modeled on an existing automated warehouse. We find that (1) the agents raise throughput by 22--60%, and the gains hold on unseen seeds; (2) they rediscover known MAPF mechanisms, such as corridor-exit priorities, local guidance, and rollouts, and independent campaigns find the same bottleneck; (3) the gains largely carry over to another layout, a larger fleet, and other service times, shrink with a smaller fleet, and mostly vanish under an outbound-heavy demand mix; and (4) each final patch (0.7k--2.4k lines) is a chain of scored commits with a median step of 27 lines, so experts can review it, and review finds problems that the score misses; some patches multiply planner compute by over 100x. LLM agents can therefore turn each site's bias into extra throughput at little engineering cost, with reviewable patches; we expect experts to shift toward designing insightful metrics and fast simulators that mirror the real problem.
bullets: Specialization targets fixed warehouse layouts and processes, where site-specific tuning can trade generality for throughput.
Across six autonomous campaigns, agents improved throughput by 22–60% and retained gains on unseen seeds.
Agents rediscovered MAPF techniques including corridor-exit priorities, local guidance, and rollouts, with campaigns identifying similar bottlenecks.
Benefits mostly transferred across layouts, fleet sizes, and service times, but weakened with smaller fleets and largely disappeared for outbound-heavy demand.
Final patches were reviewable chains of small scored commits, but review exposed issues missed by scoring and some patches increased planner compute by over 100×.

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in interactive traffic requires autonomous vehicles to reason about unobservable human characteristics and the reciprocal nature of multi-agent interactions. Traditional architectures often decouple prediction from planning, leading to the "Frozen Robot Problem" or unsafe maneuvers under high ambiguity because they treat risk assessment and information acquisition as independent objectives. We argue that the notion of safety should not remain static but must instead dynamically co-evolve with the system's internal confidence: the robot should actively clarify ambiguity when necessary while also recognizing the diminishing returns of information, and naturally transition toward task execution. We introduce a unified belief-space Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that couples multistep information planning with a clarity-adaptive Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) barrier mechanism. By treating clarity, a scalar informational state, as an explicit planning variable, the controller co-designs its probing strategy with its safety specification, tightening conservatism under high ambiguity and relaxing constraints as confidence improves. We further provide a performance analysis showing that the cost of information seeking and the expected planning-cost gap to a controller that knows the true human characteristic are bounded by residual ambiguity and solver error. We evaluate the framework in lane-merging and unsignalized-intersection scenarios against representative interactive-planning baselines. Across 5,000 simulations, the proposed method achieves the highest success rates (94.6% and 93.2%) and the lowest collision rates (1.2% and 1.4%) among the compared methods, providing a principled foundation for robust decision-making in human-centric environments.
bullets: Addresses unsafe or overly hesitant driving caused by separating prediction, planning, risk assessment, and information gathering.
Models clarity—an informational confidence state—as an explicit planning variable.
Combines multistep information planning with a clarity-adaptive CVaR safety barrier that is more conservative under ambiguity and relaxes as confidence improves.
Provides bounds linking information-seeking cost and planning-cost gap to residual ambiguity and solver error.
In 5,000 simulations across lane merging and unsignalized intersections, it reports 94.6%/93.2% success and 1.2%/1.4% collision rates, respectively, outperforming compared baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Timestep-by-timestep overview of the proposed framework executing an unsignalized intersection crossing. Yellow and black denote the ego and human-driven vehicles, respectively; translucent silhouettes show past positions. Each row presents vehicle trajectories, the belief over the human characteristic θ summarized over cooperative, neutral, and aggressive regions, the safety-margin distribution with lower-tail CVaR0.05, clarity βk , and control effort. At t1 = 0.0 s, the ego approaches the intersection with a nearly uniform belief over θ and a broad safety-margin distribution. Low clarity yields a large safety demand hsafe + κ(1/βk − 1) in Eq. (7). At t2 = 1.3 s, a cautious forward probe is followed by a shift toward an aggressive characteristic. The safety-margin distribution narrows and shifts left as the vehicles approach the conflict region, while clarity and control effort increase. At t3 = 2.6 s, the belief further favors an aggressive characteristic. Increasing clarity reduces both the additional safety buffer and the information penalty Φ(βk) = 1 − βk , supporting a shift toward task execution. At t4 = 3.9 s, the belief over θ is more concentrated and the safety-margin distribution becomes sharper as the crossing progresses. At t5 = 5.5 s, the ego has cleared the intersection, with a narrow predicted safety-margin distribution and reduced control effort. The sequence illustrates how evolving belief confidence jointly shapes information-seeking and safety conservatism, supporting a transition from cautious probing to task execution without explicit mode switching.

Fig. 3: Behavioral comparison across lane-merge runs (mean ± std). (a) Task progress: all methods achieve comparable route progress. (b) Clarity: the proposed method reaches higher reference-observer clarity than the baselines. (c) True safety margin: mean margins are initially similar but diverge near the merge region; the proposed method maintains a positive mean margin, while several baselines exhibit greater variability or reduced clearance. (d) Information gain: the proposed method exhibits a pronounced early peak followed by diminishing information gain as clarity increases, consistent with an early emphasis on information acquisition followed by task execution.

Fig. 4: CVaR barrier value versus clarity βk for each ablation variant, across all simulation runs. The proposed method concentrates in the high-clarity region while maintaining positive barrier values, illustrating the combination of belief refinement and safety preservation.

Fig. 2: Qualitative lane-merging comparison in a selected episode. Faded vehicles indicate historical poses, while solid vehicles show the states at lane-change completion. The proposed method is the only method that merges ahead of the cooperative human driver in this episode, achieving the shortest task completion time of 5.4 s. RA-MPPI, AIG-MPC, D-MPPI, and ID-SMPC merge behind the human, completing the task in 6.1 s, 5.8 s, 6.4 s, and 5.9 s, respectively.

TABLE I: Quantitative comparison across lane-merge and unsignalized-intersection scenarios (500 runs per method per scenario). The proposed method achieves the highest success rates (94.6% and 93.2%) and lowest collision rates (1.2% and 1.4%), respectively, together with the highest mean clarity and information gain in both scenarios. D-MPPI has the shortest completion times, while AIG-MPC uses the least control effort. RA-MPPI achieves the largest CVaR margin in lane merging, whereas the proposed method achieves the largest margin at intersections.

TABLE II: Ablation study across all scenarios (2,880 runs). The proposed method achieves the highest success rate (92.9%) and mean final clarity (0.85 ± 0.06). Fixed CVaR attains the lowest collision rate (0.5%) but the longest average time (7.92 ± 2.31 s). Certainty-Eq is fastest (5.01± 1.88 s) but has the highest collision rate (5.6%) and negative mean CVaR safety slack, indicating repeated safety margin violations.

papers.abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.
bullets: Gaussian winner-action distillation can introduce projection error and increase action variance when selected actions lie far from the policy mean.
IGP uses a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, replacing projection error with bounded discretization error.
Gumbel Top-K sampling and MPPI-style iterative refinement avoid the combinatorial cost of high-dimensional discrete search.
On DMControl and HumanoidBench, IGP reports state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency.
IGP also generates more temporally stable action sequences, supporting potential robotic deployment.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Comparison of MPPI and Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP). While standard MPPI refines trajectories over an unbounded continuous action space, IGP natively operates in a factorized discrete policy space. By utilizing per-dimension Gumbel Top-K sampling, IGP executes multi-round iterative search to systematically refine a categorical root policy at each state.

papers.abstract: RL locomotion policies trained under nominal simulation conditions may encounter distribution shifts that compromise safety. Predictive monitors could anticipate violations, but their world-model forecasts may become unreliable under shift, and ensemble disagreement is not calibrated. We evaluate predictive Signal Temporal Logic (STL) monitoring for frozen Ant-v5 and HalfCheetah-v5 policies using closed-loop world-model rollouts and a three-model ensemble. Across external-force, observation-noise, and mass shifts, predicted robustness ranks HalfCheetah's future STL violations strongly, whereas disagreement does not reliably track observation prediction error or violations. Under severe noise, violations remain common ($64.2\pm24.4\%$ at $K{=}20$ across three PPO seeds), yet current-state robustness without prediction comes within $0.03$ AUROC of predictive robustness. Penalizing predicted robustness by disagreement does not consistently improve ranking. Ant provides complementary per-specification evidence, but its composite target has no positive violations and its any-violation target is single-class in most evaluated seed-condition slices. Overall, predictive robustness provides useful STL-specific ranking but little demonstrated additional ranking value over the current state; these findings caution against treating ensemble disagreement as a reliable indicator of safety uncertainty.
bullets: Studies frozen Ant-v5 and HalfCheetah-v5 policies under external-force, observation-noise, and mass distribution shifts.
Uses closed-loop world-model rollouts with a three-model ensemble to predict STL robustness and future violations.
Predictive robustness ranks HalfCheetah violations strongly, while ensemble disagreement does not reliably indicate prediction error or safety violations.
Under severe noise, violations remain frequent, but current-state robustness performs nearly as well as predictive robustness.
Results are limited for Ant because several violation targets are non-positive or single-class across evaluated slices.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Predictive STL monitoring pipeline. The current observation ot feeds the frozen PPO policy and the world-model ensemble, whose members each generate a K-step closed-loop rollout by repeatedly querying the policy on predicted observations. Predicted trajectories are evaluated with STL and aggregated into predictive robustness P and STL disagreement Uρ; independently, O is evaluated on the observed trajectory τt:t+K , and SUP penalizes P by Uρ.

Figure 2: HalfCheetah any-violation failure prediction (descriptive mean±std over 3 seeds). Left (K=10, Tab. 1): Uρ stays near chance (0.47–0.56) while −P ranks failures strongly (0.92–0.98); Uo/Uz are likewise near chance (0.44–0.54). Right (K=20, severe noise, 64.2±24.4% prevalence): Uρ/Uo/Uz give 0.65/0.47/0.46 versus 0.99 for −P . Dashed line marks chance.

Figure 3: Predictive bias (P −O) versus prediction horizon for representative conditions. Ant-v5 exhibits mixed bias directions: predictive robustness is mildly pessimistic under the 15N force shift but increasingly optimistic under severe observation noise. HalfCheetah-v5 is consistently optimistic, with the predictive–retrospective gap increasing with horizon and becoming largest under observation noise.

Figure 4: Left: Future violation rate for HalfCheetah-v5 at K = 20 across representative distribution shifts. Severe observation noise produces the highest violation rate (66.7%). Right: Point-biserial correlation rUV between ensemble STL robustness disagreement and future violation across the same conditions. The correlations vary in both magnitude and direction; notably, the condition with the highest violation rate has only a moderate positive correlation (rUV = 0.27), while several lowerviolation conditions exhibit negative correlations. These condition-level results provide no consistent evidence that ensemble STL robustness disagreement reliably identifies future STL violations.

Figure 5: Horizon sensitivity under severe noise (HalfCheetah noise σ=0.15, seed 0; values from Tab. 10). Longer horizons expose more violations (10.2% at K=1 to 67.5% at K=20), yet Uρ AUROC climbs only from 0.15 toward 0.41 while −P degrades gracefully from 0.90 to 0.71. Dashed gray line marks chance (0.5). Single-seed illustration of the pattern reported multi-seed at K=10/20 in Sec. 7.1 (Tab. 6 reports 66.7% at K=20 on the legacy single-seed windowing).

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates predictive STL monitoring for RL locomotion policies under distribution shift, relevant to learned robot control safety.
papers.title: Beyond Ensemble Disagreement: Predictive STL Monitoring of RL Locomotion under Distribution Shift
