papers.selection_reason: Autonomous refinement of exoskeleton assistance policies from human feedback; relevant to learned robotic control and physical interaction.
papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement of Exoskeleton Assistance Policies through Human-in-the-Loop Feedback
papers.tldr: An LLM-driven closed loop autonomously generates, evaluates, and refines exoskeleton assistance policies using human feedback and physiological measurements, achieving effective assistance after one refinement iteration but showing limited unexpected-situation adaptability.

papers.abstract: In modern robot learning, generative robot policies are first pretrained through supervised learning from demonstrations, then refined through reinforcement learning, supervised finetuning, or other forms of posttraining. Yet conventional pretraining metrics, such as validation loss and average task success, provide an incomplete account of which policies support both effective direct deployment and subsequent posttraining. In this work, we study closed-loop pass@k, which evaluates the probability that k rollouts from the same initial condition attain at least one success. Thus, pass@1 measures mean task success; large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable under repeated sampling. Across a wide range of posttraining recipes, we show that large-k pass@k reveals posttraining differences not captured by pass@1. In particular, checkpoints with similar pass@1 but different large-k pass@k have different posttraining performance. Moreover, we show pass@k peaks at different checkpoints during supervised pretraining, revealing a coverage-reliability tradeoff over the course of training. Based on these observations, we propose two practical interventions: (1) a purely offline checkpoint-selection criterion that balances coverage and reliability without closed-loop evaluation, and (2) a generative data augmentation procedure that expands supervision beyond the finite demonstration set, preserving large-k pass@k while maintaining or improving pass@1 and raising the observed coverage-reliability Pareto frontier. Together, our results motivate evaluation, checkpoint selection, and training procedures that explicitly account for posttraining. Blog post, visualizations, and code are available at https://zhanyisun.github.io/robot-policy-learning-dynamics/.
bullets: Pass@1 measures average success, while large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable through repeated sampling from the same initial state.
Policies with similar pass@1 can differ substantially in posttraining performance when their large-k pass@k differs.
During supervised pretraining, coverage and reliability peak at different checkpoints, revealing a coverage–reliability tradeoff.
The work proposes offline checkpoint selection and generative data augmentation to preserve or improve coverage and reliability.
The findings motivate evaluation and training procedures that explicitly account for downstream posttraining potential.

figures.caption: Figure 5: During pretraining, generative augmentation preserves coverage while maintaining, and in some tasks improving, reliability (pass@1). Across most MimicGen tasks and RoboCasa, Baseline DP loses pass@10 at later checkpoints. JointAug prevents this loss of coverage while maintaining or improving pass@1. PostBC also preserves pass@10 better than Baseline DP, but can do so at the cost of pass@1.

Figure 1: Later checkpoints trade large-k pass@k for mean task success; checkpoints with similar pass@1 can lead to different posttraining performance. Left: single-task BC followed by residual RL on two representative MimicGen tasks, with (a) showing pass@k during BC and (b) residual RL from different BC checkpoints. Right: multitask pretraining on RoboCasa tasks followed by SFT on target tasks, with (c) showing pass@k during pretraining and (d) downstream SFT. Across (a,c), larger-k pass@k peaks and declines earlier than pass@1, so later checkpoints increasingly favor mean task success at the expense of large-k pass@k performance. Orange marks the earlier checkpoint selected by our offline coverage–reliability criterion (Sec. 4), while blue marks the final supervised-training checkpoint; matching dashed lines in (a,c) indicate the initializations used in (b,d). Despite similar pass@1, finetuning from the orange checkpoint achieves stronger performance than finetuning from the blue checkpoint across both settings.

Figure 7: Real-robot Push-T. (a) Task setup. (b) Best-of-k validation action MSE across training epochs. (c) Quantiles of validation action error across training epochs. (d) Normalized coverage and reliability scores with the selected checkpoint at epoch 46. (e) Pass@1 and pass@5 success rates of the selected (epoch 46) and final (epoch 200) checkpoints over 20 fixed initial states.

Figure 4: Held-out action-MSE quantiles expose the coverage–reliability balance. (a) Held-out action-MSE quantiles across training, colored by percentile u from 0.05 (red) to 0.95 (blue). (b) For a held-out observation, 64 matched-noise samples from ep50 and ep800, plus the expert action, are projected with PCA; rings mark the minimum-MSE sample. ep50 is more dispersed yet has lower best-of-64 MSE, whereas ep800 contracts but its best sample lies farther from the expert. Consistent with (a), lower quantiles favor earlier checkpoints, while higher quantiles improve later. (c) We summarize the lower and upper halves as rcov|H(τ) and rrel|H(τ) and select the checkpoint minimizing max{rcov|H(τ), rrel|H(τ)}; the selected ep350 matches the closed-loop oracle.

Figure 3: Best-of-k action MSE selects earlier checkpoints than closed-loop pass@k. (a) Held-out best-of-k action MSE across training checkpoints for different k. (b) Closed-loop pass@k success rate across the same checkpoints. Matching colors and marker shapes denote the same value of k across panels; hollow markers indicate the minimum MSE in (a) and maximum pass@k in (b). As k increases, both optima shift earlier, but the best-of-k MSE minimum precedes the corresponding pass@k peak, with a larger separation at higher k.

Figure 9: Residual RL finetuning across the coverage–reliability tradeoff. We additionally finetune an earlier baseline checkpoint (ep.200/100/100 for Threading/Hammer Cleanup/Mug Cleanup) with lower pass@1 and higher coverage than the checkpoint selected by our criterion. Its performance relative to later checkpoints depends on the available online budget.

Figure 12: Observation conditioning exacerbates the deterioration in held-out denoising during late training. Relative change in held-out ϵ-prediction MSE from epoch 200 to 800 for the image-conditioned and action-only models, evaluated on the same noisy action chunks. Negative values indicate lower held-out loss at epoch 800; positive values indicate higher loss. The conditional model exhibits held-out loss deterioration at higher diffusion noise levels.

Figure 10: Flow-matching policy pretraining and OGPO finetuning. Each row shows a MimicGen task with 200 demonstrations. (a) Best-of-k validation action MSE. (b) pass@k during BC pretraining. (c) Validation error quantiles. (d) Coverage–reliability scores and selected checkpoint. (e) OGPO finetuning from the selected versus final BC checkpoint. The selected initialization generally achieves better downstream RL performance.

Figure 20: JointAug retains favorable-tail coverage while improving typical action accuracy. For four held-out Mug Cleanup states, we jointly project 64 action samples from baseline ep50, baseline ep800, and JointAug ep800 with PCA. Stars mark expert actions and rings mark the minimum-MSE sample. The baseline ep50 is dispersed with low best-of-64 but high mean MSE; baseline baseline ep800 contracts and lowers mean MSE but worsens best-of-64 MSE; JointAug ep800 achieves best of both worlds.

Figure 21: Context-Smoothed Pre-training from TMRL does not preserve coverage under prolonged training. Across five MimicGen tasks, TMRL generally underperforms JointAug in pass@10 and often loses both pass@10 and pass@1 at later checkpoints.

Figure 28: Late-training coverage loss also occurs with low-dimensional state observations. Across five tasks, baseline diffusion policies lose pass@10 at later checkpoints despite using no visual encoder. Joint (o, a) augmentation preserves substantially more pass@10.

Figure 19: JointAug is relatively robust to generator checkpoint selection. We compare the five-checkpoint mixture used in our main experiments against individual generator checkpoints from the same run . Across four tasks, single-checkpoint variants have similar pass@10 gains over the baseline, while the mixture performs similarly overall and slightly improves pass@1 on Mug Cleanup and Threading.
Figure 16: Extended training on Threading D2. The coverage–reliability dynamics persist to 1600 epochs, and the offline criterion continues to select an intermediate checkpoint.

Figure 18: JointAug enables residual RL finetuning on 3-Piece Assembly (D2). Left: JointAug substantially improves pass@1 and pass@10 during BC pretraining. Right: residual RL from the final JointAug checkpoint reaches over 0.8 success, while finetuning from the baseline checkpoint remains near zero.

Figure 6: Generative augmentation produces stronger checkpoints for posttraining. Columns correspond to Fig. 5. We compare posttraining from the baseline checkpoint selected by our coverage–reliability criterion (Sec. 4), the final Baseline DP checkpoint, and the final checkpoint from our generative augmentation run. Across MimicGen tasks, the final generative-augmentation checkpoint substantially outperforms the final baseline and often matches or exceeds the selected checkpoint. On RoboCasa, it matches the selected checkpoint on both pass@1 and pass@32.

Figure 24: The late-training coverage loss persists across denoiser widths. We vary the U-Net from 24M to 1.0B parameters while keeping the encoder, data, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and sampler fixed. All four models show a similar peak and subsequent decline in pass@10.

Figure 8: Distribution of condition-level success counts over supervised pretraining. For each checkpoint, we run pass@32 on each of 500 evaluation conditions and bin each condition by its number of successful rollouts within 32 trials. The stacked bands show the fraction of conditions in each success-count bin; each vertical slice sums to one. During late training, the fraction of conditions with zero successes increases, while the fraction with high success counts also increases.

Figure 14: Full MimicGen results across tasks and dataset sizes. Results for all five tasks with 200 and 500 demonstrations. Each row reports best-of-k validation loss, closed-loop pass@k, the full error-quantile profile, coverage–reliability checkpoint selection, and downstream residual RL finetuning.

Figure 13: Late-training held-out denoising loss increases more at lower diffusion noise levels and with sparser local conditioning support. Relative change in mean held-out ϵ-prediction MSE from epoch 200 to epoch 800, ∆rel,g(t) (Eq. D.6), for queries divided into equal thirds by local conditioning support. Negative values indicate lower mean loss at epoch 800; positive values indicate higher mean loss. At a fixed noise level, the relative loss change is generally larger for queries with sparser local conditioning support.

Figure 30: Qualitative world-model predictions on real-robot Push-T. Each model predicts four frames from two history frames (Chunk 1), then autoregressively predicts four more frames (Chunk 2). The earlyrollout model achieves higher PSNR in both chunks.

Figure 25: Longer EMA memory delays and smooths the pass@10 decline but does not fundamentally remove it. Holding βmax = 0.9999 fixed, increasing p from 0.75 to 0.9 gives the EMA a longer memory earlier in training, causing pass@10 to peak and decline later. Holding p = 0.9 fixed, increasing βmax from 0.9999 to 0.99995 allows the EMA memory to continue growing later in training and further smooths the decline. Pass@10 still decreases under all schedules.

Figure 22: Pass@k training dynamics are stable across sampling configurations. Pass@1 and pass@10 are evaluated using DDIM with different numbers of denoising steps and η, and using DDPM. All settings show the same late-training decline in pass@10.

Figure 27: Fresh denoisers reproduce the pass@10 decline with fixed encoder representations. New denoisers are trained from scratch with either the epoch-150 or epoch-800 encoder frozen throughout training. Both show a later decline in large k pass@k.

Figure 26: Freezing the encoder does not prevent the late-training large k pass@k decline. From epoch 150 onward, the encoder is fixed and only the denoiser is trained. Pass@10 still decreases at later epochs. The overall training dynamics is largely the same as baseline run.

Figure 29: Best-of-k off-manifold error reveals the same coverage–reliability tradeoff. At k = 1, ep800 has slightly lower off-manifold error; from k = 2 onward, ep400 is better and the gap grows with k.
Figure 17: Robustness to training horizon. Offline selection tracks the closed-loop oracle as H increases.

Figure 11: Later checkpoints exhibit higher held-out denoising loss near the low-noise end, and changes to the final denoising calls substantially affect pass@k profle. (a) On training demonstrations, ϵ-prediction MSE decreases with further training across all noise levels. (b) On unseen demonstrations, later checkpoints have higher denoising loss near the low-noise end than earlier checkpoints despite lower training loss. (c) In a 10-step DDIM sampler, replacing any one of the first four two-step bands (Q1–Q4) of the epoch-800 checkpoint with the corresponding epoch200 weights has little effect on pass@1 or pass@10. papers.abstract: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.
bullets: Addresses the dependence on proprietary frontier models that limits further RUA training research.
Introduces a unified harness for training and evaluating open-weight robot-use agents.
An out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39 and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks.
Analysis across model generations, families, and sizes identifies four general capabilities linked to effective robot use.
The work suggests future RUA training should develop these capabilities jointly.

papers.abstract: Registering intraoperative Ultrasound (US) bone-surface point clouds to preoperative Computed Tomography (CT) models can support radiation-free orthopedic navigation. Differences in imaging physics produce distinct surface sampling patterns, complicating cross-modal feature matching. Bone strongly reflects ultrasound and casts an acoustic shadow, so US captures only the probe-facing bone surface and leaves most CT points unmatched. This partial coverage makes correspondences ambiguous on near-symmetric bones. We propose CUFormer, a modality-aware registration framework. We introduce a Modality-Aware Transformer (MAT) that encodes input modality through identity embeddings and updates features through modality-specific adapters within a shared geometric matcher. We model imaging visibility and use predicted reference-side visibility to weight coarse and fine correspondences. CUFormer achieves the lowest mean registration errors among evaluated methods on two CT-US datasets, UltraBones100k and UltraBonesHip, and the CT-RGB-D dataset SpineDepth. On UltraBones100k, it reaches mean rotation error 4.53$^\circ$, translation error 3.19\,mm, and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) 2.54\,mm, reducing RMSE by 65.8\% relative to the best-performing baseline by this metric. These results demonstrate CUFormer's effectiveness in aligning partial bone surfaces with preoperative CT across anatomical sites.
bullets: Addresses mismatched CT and ultrasound surface sampling, including partial US coverage and ambiguous correspondences on near-symmetric bones.
Uses a Modality-Aware Transformer with identity embeddings and modality-specific adapters in a shared geometric matcher.
Predicts reference-side visibility to weight both coarse and fine point correspondences.
Achieves the lowest mean registration errors among evaluated methods across UltraBones100k, UltraBonesHip, and SpineDepth.
On UltraBones100k, reports 4.53° rotation error, 3.19 mm translation error, and 2.54 mm RMSE; RMSE is 65.8% lower than the strongest baseline by that metric.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing plays a crucial role in everyday human interaction. Consider inserting a plug into a tight socket, vision alone provides limited guidance during the final insertion stage, and we instead rely on both anticipated contact and realized tactile feedback to ajust the insertion motion. The same capability is equally important for robots, particularly in dexterous manipulation tasks. Yet many contemporary robot policies remain vision-dominant. This visual bias, compounded by limited tactile data and sparse contact events, can cause directly incorporated tactile signals to be ignored or even compromise the policy's pretrained capabilities, yielding degrading performance as observed in our experiments. We present $TF^2$-Steering, which refines actions via learned residual steering of the flow-matching action expert's velocity field, using a tactile mixture-of-experts architecture to integrate both tactile forecasts and real-time tactile feedback. Together with specific designed three stages training recipe, $TF^2$-Steering enables tactile signals to correct and, when necessary, redirect the flow-matching action-generation process, while building on the strong action-generation capacity of the vision-based foundation policy. Extensive experiments across six simulated and six real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of $TF^2$-Steering. It outperforms the strongest evaluated baselines by 10.7 percentage points in average simulation success rate and 9.1 percentage points in average real-world progress success rate. Project page: https://yiming-cc.github.io/tf2-steering/.
bullets: Addresses the tendency of vision-dominant policies to ignore or weaken performance when directly given sparse tactile signals.
Learns residual corrections to a flow-matching action expert’s velocity field.
Uses a tactile mixture-of-experts architecture to combine tactile forecasts with realized feedback.
A three-stage training recipe lets tactile input correct or redirect the pretrained vision policy’s actions.
Evaluated on six simulated and six real-world tasks, improving average success by 10.7 and 9.1 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Tactile-forecast and feedback action refinement for dexterous robot manipulation directly fits embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: $TF^2$-Steering: Action Refinement with Tactile Forecasts and Feedback via Velocity-Field Steering

papers.abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exploiting instructional videos when model parameters are frozen and large-scale updates are costly.
Builds a tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that generates hard, video-grounded questions to refine stored knowledge.
Uses a Table-of-Contents tree for reasoning-guided retrieval instead of embedding similarity alone.
Evaluated on VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark from 72 chess tutorials across 12 openings, with performance improving as more videos are consumed.
Also improves opening-phase gameplay and shows generality in a second domain.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL). In Stage I, TAL performs video-grounded agent– model adversarial consolidation, where a video agent harvests hard question–answer pairs from instructional videos that are supported by tutorial evidence yet unsolved by the frozen model, forming a question bank. In Stage II, TAL performs question–memory adversarial consolidation, using this question bank to iteratively refine tutorial memory through a read–write loop. At inference time, TAL retrieves relevant tutorial units via a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, enabling the frozen model to access structured tutorial knowledge for downstream reasoning without parameter updates.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric method for LLM agents to learn from instructional videos. This is a form of video imitation learning for agents, fitting Learning from Human Videos.
papers.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
papers.tldr: TAL enables LLM agents to continually learn from tutorial videos without parameter updates by building and reasoning over a structured, persistent tutorial memory.

papers.abstract: Processing every video frame through Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adds significant inference cost and limits their ability to comprehend real-time video. Existing approaches either sub-sample frames uniformly, ignoring content and missing important events, or prune visual tokens inside the VLM to cut per-call cost while still invoking the model on every sampled frame. We introduce FOCUS, a training-free three-layer framework that reduces the number of invocations and steers each one towards what matters. Temporal gating measures inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family, triggering burst captures only when the scene changes in a semantically meaningful way. Patch-level dissimilarity is then accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map that encodes where motion and semantic relevance coincide. That map calibrates the VLM's value cache during generation, progressively amplifying vision tokens in task-relevant regions and attenuating off-target ones, without removing any token from the context. The loop closes after each response: text-to-vision cross-attention is extracted from the decoder and fed back as the prior for the next burst, letting the system converge on semantically important regions over successive observations. We evaluate FOCUS on the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode, with a single Qwen3-VL-8B backbone shared by every method. It reaches 74.8% accuracy using 25.4 VLM calls per clip, against 74.6% with 55 calls for uniform sampling and 74.2% with 55 calls for BOLT. On egocentric video captioning across four domains, it matches the best baseline's quality while issuing 57% fewer VLM invocations than uniform sampling.
bullets: Detects meaningful scene changes with patch-embedding dissimilarity and triggers burst captures selectively.
Combines motion-based patch changes with top-down attention to focus on task-relevant regions.
Reweights, rather than removes, visual tokens during generation using a calibrated value cache.
Feeds decoder text-to-vision attention back into the next observation cycle for iterative refinement.
On a 500-video EgoSchema subset, achieves 74.8% accuracy with 25.4 calls per clip; captioning matches the best baseline with 57% fewer calls than uniform sampling.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a closed-loop attention feedback mechanism for efficient VLM inference on video, utilizing spatial focus maps and token attenuation. Highly relevant to Spatial Intelligence (spatial focus) and Efficient AI (token pruning). Also applicable to Learning from Human Videos (EgoSchema).
papers.title: FOCUS: Closed-Loop Attention Feedback for Efficient Vision-Language Understanding
papers.tldr: FOCUS uses closed-loop temporal and spatial attention to reduce VLM video calls while preserving or improving understanding quality.

papers.abstract: Surface cleaning requires robots to adapt both where they clean and how they interact with contamination whose response to cleaning may vary spatially and remain unobservable prior to interaction. We formulate adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process and propose a belief-aware planning framework that uses observed cleaning outcomes to update a latent local cleaning-response model and adapt subsequent cleaning motions, forces, and passes. Preliminary grid-world simulations demonstrate the resulting closed-loop planner adapting its spatial decomposition and cleaning actions as the surface evolves.
bullets: Models adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process.
Updates a latent, spatially varying cleaning-response model from observed outcomes.
Adapts cleaning motions, forces, passes, and spatial decomposition in closed loop.
Preliminary grid-world simulations show adaptation as the surface evolves.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the adaptive cleaning pipeline. At each iteration, the sensor input is converted into a scalar contamination observation to update the surface belief. Contaminated regions are grouped by spatial connectivity or alternative k-means clusterings (illustrated for k = 1, 3, and 5). For each cluster, the planner generates a candidate plan and evaluates J(P ; bt) under the current belief. The highest-scoring plan is executed and then the updated surface is observed to begin the next cycle. Red shading indicates contamination (darker = higher xj ); shaded orange circles denote spiral actions, while green and blue line segments denote wipe and move actions, respectively.

Fig. 2. Evolution of the simulated surface and cleaning actions over planning iterations. Red shading indicates remaining contamination; orange circles denote spiral actions, while green outlines and line segments denote wipe actions and their trajectories. Panels (b)–(d) illustrate the planner’s spatial decompositions: nearby contamination is grouped together in (b), split into clusters with separate actions in (c), and regrouped as the residual geometry changes in (d). In later iterations, sparse contamination leads the planner to favor local wipe actions over broad spiral actions to avoid unnecessary coverage of clean areas.

papers.abstract: Agentic robots combine a vision-language brain, a tool-using harness, and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key-value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and pi0.5 (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78 s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0 s. Under a 0.25 s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1% starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0 s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24-2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00-5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets.
bullets: Characterizes 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes spanning 1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks on H800 GPUs.
Brain contexts grow to 215k tokens; repeated long-context prefills can displace generation as robot concurrency increases.
A single VLA GPU supports one robot under a 0.25-second action deadline and at least 32 robots under a 1.0-second deadline.
Increasing sustained brain concurrency from 20 to 32 robots cuts throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/second.
A static active-episode cap restores roughly 2.24–2.25 requests/second and increases completed episodes to 5.00–5.55 per minute.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the resource constraints (KV-cache thrashing) of serving fleets of agentic robots, providing insights into system-level efficiency for embodied AI agents.
papers.title: Serving Agentic Robot Fleets: Workload Characterization, KV-Cache Thrashing, and Admission Control
papers.tldr: Agentic robot fleets face competing VLA action deadlines and brain KV-cache demands, but workload-aware admission control can prevent KV thrashing and sustain much higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, yet deployed robots waste time in two ways that are independent of model capability: they halt while the next chunk is inferred, and they move at the speed of slow, cautious demonstrations. Existing remedies remove one loss each, and stacking them fails, because asynchrony and speed-up each change the correspondence between planned progress and executed motion. We present Path-preserving Time Scaling (PTS), a training-free execution layer for frozen action-chunking policies built on one principle: the robot's motion is a time reparameterization of a reference path, and the path changes only in response to new observations. A path layer decodes every replan deterministically in one step and enters it at the progress consumed during inference. A time layer sums the planned increments, keeps the arm at 1x while the gripper moves, and caps the rate by the actuator's linear range and by chunk feasibility under latency. We show that misaligned entry and stochastic sampling add a bias and a variance to the continuation error, and derive a break-even success rate that states when speeding up pays off. On LIBERO with two frozen VLAs under injected inference latency, PTS raises task throughput over the strongest deployable baseline by 33% for pi0.5 and 104% for SmolVLA while matching or improving the success rate, is best on all six model-suite combinations, and exceeds zero-latency 1x execution. Against asynchronous 1x execution with the same one-step decoder, the time layer alone adds 28% and 38%. On LIBERO-Dynamic it improves on stop-and-wait execution by 38% and is comparable to asynchronous 1x execution.
bullets: Addresses two deployment bottlenecks: robot pauses during action-chunk inference and follows unnecessarily slow demonstration speeds.
Uses a path layer for deterministic one-step replanning with latency-aware path entry, plus a time layer that scales motion while respecting gripper behavior, actuator limits, and chunk feasibility.
Explains continuation error from misaligned replanning and stochastic sampling, and derives when speed increases are worthwhile.
On LIBERO with two frozen VLAs, PTS improves throughput by 33% for pi0.5 and 104% for SmolVLA over the strongest deployable baseline while matching or improving success rate.
Also improves throughput on LIBERO-Dynamic, indicating scope beyond the primary benchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on VLA model execution and latency, directly matching Vision-Language-Action.
papers.title: Same Path, Less Time: Training-Free Fast Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models under Inference Latency
papers.tldr: PTS is a training-free execution layer that lets frozen vision-language-action policies run faster without sacrificing task success by preserving planned paths while adapting timing to inference latency.

papers.abstract: End-to-end planners decode the ego trajectory either by coordinate regression, which is fast but blends plausible maneuvers into one trajectory that may follow none of them, or by diffusion and flow matching, which model the trajectory distribution but need several inference steps. Drifting models move this iteration into training: a one-step generator learns to follow an attraction--repulsion field between generated and ground-truth samples. Drifting was developed for class-conditional image generation, where every class supplies many positive samples. In planning, every scene is its own condition. Pooling scenes would attract the generated trajectories of one scene to the ground truth of unrelated scenes, whereas computing the field per scene leaves a single positive, the expert trajectory. Mutual repulsion then holds the generated trajectories on a shell around it, so any single generated trajectory deviates from the ground truth. We present DriftingPlanner, a trajectory planner trained with the drifting loss alone, without any coordinate regression term. It computes the field per scene and removes the shell at inference: it decodes every noise vector together with its negation in one batched pass, and averaging each antithetic pair cancels the linear part of the displacement from the shell center. On NAVSIM navtest, DriftingPlanner reaches a state-of-the-art 93.75 PDMS, and with single-step inference its drifting decoder comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best diffusion or flow matching setting, which needs ten inference steps.
bullets: Coordinate regression can merge plausible maneuvers, while diffusion and flow-matching planners require multiple inference steps.
The method computes an attraction–repulsion field separately for each scene, avoiding attraction to unrelated scenes’ trajectories.
Training uses the drifting loss alone, without a coordinate-regression objective.
At inference, noise–negation pairs are decoded in one batch and averaged to cancel displacement around the expert trajectory.
On NAVSIM navtest, it achieves 93.75 PDMS and comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best ten-step diffusion or flow-matching setting.

During training (dashed boxes), each generated trajectory xi has one positive, the ground-truth (GT) trajectory y, and N−1 negatives, the other generated trajectories Jx jK of the same scene; generated trajectories of different scenes never form pairs. papers.abstract: As learned manipulation policies become increasingly capable of solving practical manipulation tasks, assessing how well a task is performed becomes a fundamental challenge. While binary labels confirm task success, they cannot distinguish successful executions with different levels of geometric precision. To address this, we introduce SPECTRA, an object-centric framework for quantifying execution quality in manipulation of rigid objects. From a small set of oracle demonstrations generated in simulation, SPECTRA represents object interactions through progress-aligned relative poses. SPECTRA identifies which relative-pose directions are constrained and their admissible variations from demonstrations. These constraints establish a reference for evaluating robotic manipulation tasks. To score an unseen execution, deviations beyond the admissible variation are summarized by a Task Quality Index Q in [0,1]. Across seven simulated tasks, SPECTRA recovers constraints with 94% accuracy using 30 demonstrations per task. On rollouts from three learned policies, its scores achieve pooled Spearman correlations with human judgments of p=0.81 over all rollouts and p=0.61 among successful rollouts, exceeding all baselines in both subsets. Using the task reference learned in simulation, we use SPECTRA to select the highest-scoring demonstrations for training a diffusion policy on hardware. Exploratory results show higher success rate than training on randomly selected demonstrations.
bullets: Targets the problem that binary success labels cannot distinguish different levels of geometric precision.
Learns constrained relative-pose directions and allowable variation from a small set of oracle demonstrations.
Scores unseen executions with a Task Quality Index Q∈[0,1], based on deviations from the learned constraints.
Across seven simulated tasks, it recovered constraints with 94% accuracy using 30 demonstrations per task.
Its scores correlated with human judgments (Spearman p=0.81 overall; p=0.61 on successful rollouts) and supported selecting demonstrations for hardware policy training.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of SPECTRA. 1. Constraints estimation. Oracle demonstrations are segmented and aligned to shared progress samples. At each progress sample l, the task is represented by the relative poses between the reference object r, the manipulated object m, the gripper g, and the support object s. Deviations from the nominal pose T̄j,l are mapped to its tangent space, and eigen decomposition of their covariance Σj,l identifies the constrained directions Ij , whose standard deviation falls below σpin. 2. Policy evaluation. An unseen execution incurs cost only where its normalized deviation along constrained directions exceeds the tolerance z0. The average cost and a terminal gate give the Task Quality Index Q ∈ [0, 1].

papers.abstract: High-accuracy repetitive tracking is challenging for position-commanded manipulators whose low-level controllers are inaccessible, while constrained model-based iterative learning control (ILC) can require substantial manual parameter tuning. We present Differentiable Iterative Learning Control (Diff-ILC), an online bilevel framework that adapts the parameters of a constrained ILC update between physical robot executions. A closed-loop differential model is identified once from paired smooth perturbations and subsequently kept fixed. At each trial, a constrained quadratic program computes a feasible command correction, while a real-anchored next-trial prediction defines a task-level objective. Hypergradients are obtained by implicitly differentiating the locally active KKT system, enabling multiple computational parameter updates without additional robot executions. Experiments on a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and three-dimensional trajectories show substantially faster physical-trial convergence than fixed-parameter model-based ILC. Across the four primary trajectories, after only two trial-to-trial updates, Diff-ILC achieves 78.8% and 76.4% lower mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE, respectively, than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.
bullets: Addresses high-accuracy repetitive tracking when low-level robot controllers are inaccessible and ILC tuning is costly.
Identifies a closed-loop differential model once, then uses a constrained quadratic program for feasible command corrections.
Optimizes ILC parameters online with a real-anchored objective and KKT-based implicit hypergradients, without extra robot executions per update.
On a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and 3D trajectories, it converged substantially faster than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.
After two trial-to-trial updates, mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE were 78.8% and 76.4% lower, respectively, across four primary trajectories.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated $π_{0.5}$-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with $π_{0.5}$.
bullets: Addresses the limited role of VLMs in diffusion-based vision-language-action models, where they usually provide only static conditioning.
Feeds noisy action latents, visual observations, and language instructions into the VLM at every denoising step.
Uses gated cross-attention to dynamically guide the action expert and supervises the VLM to recover clean action latents.
An adaptive step-size schedule balances task performance with inference latency.
Achieves the highest average success rate among evaluated π₀.₅-based methods on RoboDojo and improves results on RoboTwin 2.0 and four real-world bimanual tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Joint VLM-action denoising for VLA models; directly advances embodied action generation.
papers.title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
papers.tldr: JADE jointly denoises robotic actions with a vision-language model and action expert, improving out-of-distribution performance and reducing sampling steps.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in shared, dynamic environments must respond to rapidly approaching objects while maintaining balance. We study dodgeball as a controlled test of this capability, coupling visual threat assessment with whole-body evasion, recovery, and target reacquisition. We develop a system that integrates onboard monocular perception, temporal ball-state and threat-flag estimation, and learned whole-body control. A ball detector supplies bounding-box histories, and a temporal estimator predicts relative ball position and a binary threat flag. Separate dodge/recovery and search/track policies share this interface and are composed to support repeated encounters. A three-stage curriculum first trains control with privileged ball states, then starts estimator supervision from stable policy rollouts, and finally replaces the actor's privileged inputs with estimator outputs. Analytic projection and perception randomization provide detector-like training observations without image rendering. Across approach-angle bins in controlled simulation, dodge success ranges from 97.8--100.0% for 5.0 m launches at 6 m/s to 33.2--40.8% for 2.5 m launches at 10 m/s, with 1000 throws per speed--distance condition. On a physical Unitree G1, controlled single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials. A hardware sequence demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge. These results demonstrate an integrated onboard-monocular-vision system under highly dynamic motions.
bullets: Addresses agile reaction and balance maintenance in dynamic shared environments using dodgeball as a controlled test.
Combines ball-detection histories, temporal threat estimation, and separate learned dodge/recovery and search/track policies.
Uses a three-stage curriculum to transition from privileged ball states to vision-based control, with analytic projection and perception randomization for training.
In simulation, dodge success varies from 97.8–100.0% for slower/farther launches to 33.2–40.8% for faster/closer launches; physical single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials.
Demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting manipulation to changing garment geometry and appearance.
Uses NOCS-textured garment meshes to provide canonical surface cues to a pretrained vision-language-action model.
Fine-tunes the model on human demonstrations and corrections, then filters autonomously generated rollouts by task success.
Re-renders successful trajectories with randomized appearances for training policies that use only RGB observations.
Generated data improves RGB-policy performance over original human data across evaluated garment splits and appearances, though unseen-garment generalization remains difficult.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: https://github.com/satoshinji2992/CompSkill
bullets: Motivation: Description-only retrievers ignore lessons from prior executions and may select relevant-looking but harmful skills.
Method: Learned 512-dimensional keys are updated with skill offsets and capped residuals from matched same-task comparisons; an experience hypergraph preserves executors and document versions.
Theory: Under an unknown task-difficulty model, matched comparisons remove difficulty effects, while discordant outcomes provide learning signals.
Results: SkillRet NDCG@10 rises from 64.0 to 70.9 using one-eighth-dimensional keys; CompSkill also improves ToolQA completion and remains competitive on AppWorld and ALFWorld.
Scope: The approach depends on support executions and comparison evidence; selecting the right same-database guide matters substantially.

papers.tldr: CompSkill improves skill retrieval by compiling execution experience into compact key adjustments, helping agents select more useful documents without changing their text.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning-execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra's success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks. Project page: https://auriga.stelledge.com/ Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Auriga
bullets: Addresses the large execution gap between high-level VLM decisions and physical robot control.
Combines explicit task beliefs, tool calls or synthesized Python programs, calibrated 3D sensing, dual-arm control, and a unified robot gateway.
Uses paused visual trajectory previews and runtime checks for tolerances and grasp bounds, enabling interruption and discrepancy-based recovery.
Achieves 57.7% success on RoboDojo and 73.2% on RoboCasa365 with a frozen, zero-shot harness.
Remains robust under scene randomization, though the abstract does not specify limitations beyond its evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: In this paper we present the methodologies, results, and analysis used to deploy a decentralized safety verification algorithm on a robotic swarm to prevent collisions at runtime in an outdoor environment. Typically, approaches toward verification of swarms of cyber-physical systems (CPS) are evaluated solely in numerical simulations or in highly controlled, noiseless indoor environments. Our efforts to implement collision avoidance on a real swarm system outdoors have revealed that the underlying algorithmic assumptions juxtaposed against the implementation details of the target system are critical factors in a method's efficacy in the real world. Here we modify, enhance, and analyze a decentralized reachability-based method for collision avoidance on a size, weight, and power-constrained uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm with the objective of illustrating the challenges of real-world CPS deployments as well as provide guidance for researchers in this space. Verification performance, resource utilization, and timing data were gathered over the course of 140 total outdoor vehicle flights, including 6 swarm flights composed of 8 UAVs, and used to improve collision-avoidance performance as experimentation progressed. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed decentralized runtime verification approach can efficiently verify the safety of multiple UAVs in real-time and help all agents take safe actions to avoid collisions. On average, each agent, using our open-source safety_checker library, takes approximately 500-520 ms to verify its safety for the next 4 s into the future, in which the reachable set broadcast time dominates the total verification time (~300-500 ms).
bullets: Addresses the gap between simulated or controlled swarm verification and real-world outdoor deployment.
Enhances a decentralized reachability-based collision-avoidance method for size-, weight-, and power-constrained UAVs.
Evaluated performance, resource use, and timing across 140 outdoor flights, including six flights with eight UAVs.
The approach enabled real-time safety verification and safe collision-avoidance actions for multiple UAVs.
Each agent verified safety approximately 500–520 ms ahead for the next 4 seconds; reachable-set broadcasting dominated runtime.

papers.abstract: Unified-memory edge devices increasingly run LLM/VLM inference alongside time-critical CPU tasks for perception and control. GPU memory traffic can overwhelm these tasks, yet platforms such as DGX Spark expose neither bandwidth counters nor direct bandwidth regulation. We present Ripple, a CPU-GPU co-scheduler that combines model-derived GPU memory volumes with CPU completion feedback to regulate interference. Ripple divides inference into pausable, layer-based units and translates each CPU job's deadline slack into a GPU-byte budget, admitting work within the budgets of all overlapping jobs. Online updates track changing interference, while deadline-aware pacing and judicious SM footprint narrowing preserve inference progress. Implemented with SGLang engine hooks and a central scheduler, we evaluate Ripple on DGX Spark with four robotic CPU task mixes and LLM/VLM inference. It is the only evaluated approach that consistently meets the 2% CPU deadline-miss target and VLM deadlines across the tested deadline settings while retaining best-effort LLM throughput.
bullets: Addresses GPU memory-traffic interference with time-critical CPU perception and control tasks when hardware offers no bandwidth controls.

Implemented with SGLang hooks and a central scheduler, Ripple was evaluated on DGX Spark with four robotic CPU task mixes.
It consistently met the 2% CPU deadline-miss target and VLM deadlines across tested settings while retaining best-effort LLM throughput.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $τ$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between roughly 1 Hz scene-semantic updates and 20–50 Hz reactive control.
Caches VLM context and combines it with high-frequency visual features from a compact robot-video-pretrained encoder.
Conditions the flow-matching action expert on cache age and trains it with realistic cache-age histories and staleness-mimicking pixel corruption.
On LIBERO, achieves 95.2% success at a 1 s semantic refresh and 94.5% at 2 s, versus 96.3% for a frequency-matched anchor.
Adds zero-latency chunk-boundary correction and a verdict gate that freezes execution under instruction–scene mismatch.],

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Leap-VLA overview. Slow system: the VLM runs at fslow over a token sequence that appends, after the prompt and the observation, the chain-ofthought region; it produces the cached context C and the chain-of-thought-supervised anchor features, and its reasoning region is emitted as the structured output shown. Because attention is causal, the prompt-region features the expert consumes are unchanged by the appended block (Sec. III-B). Fast system: the flow-matching expert runs at ffast, consuming C and fresh fast-stream features through one pluggable token-block interface: image tokens from the frozen motion-aware encoder (dual-frame, robot-pretrained with reconstruction, optical flow, and depth). The measured cache age τ conditions the expert via AdaRMS, proprioception enters as a dedicated input token, and the control rate f is passed to the action head; training samples τ from the physical episode history.

Fig. 13. Failure analysis on LIBERO-PRO task perturbations (libero goal). Rows 1–3: under task-perturbed instructions, the characteristic failure is semantic interference—the policy reverts to the behavior of the trained task. Asked to turn the stove off, it turns the burner on (row 1); asked to put the wine bottle on the stove, it carries the bottle back to the trained rack goal (rows 2–3). Row 4: on the unperturbed original task, failures are motor-level instead (the grasp slips and the bottle is dropped). Perturbed-instruction failures therefore reflect instruction generalization rather than manipulation competence. These modes are systematic rather than cherry-picked: 2/2 recorded failures of “turn off the stove” turn it on, and 2/6 recorded failures of the wine-bottle task revert to the rack.

A dual-frame pair (ot−δ, ot) is fused into a 6-channel input at the stem; a ∼49% row/column strip mask is applied jointly to both frames (pair-level tube masking), and the visible patches go through the compact encoder. Three lightweight decoders share the encoded features: the reconstruction decoder fills in both frames’ masked patches, the optical-flow decoder predicts the dense ot−δ→ot motion of masked patches, and the depth decoder predicts per-pixel depth for each frame. Panels show a held-out RoboTwin sample; decoder outputs are the training-time ground truth (WAFT flow, Depth Anything V2 depth, and the raw frames).

Fig. 6. Real-robot deployment platforms. From left to right: Realman dual-arm workstation, Galaxea dual-arm workstation, Dobot Atom mobile dual-arm humanoid, and our in-house humanoid upper body. All policies run on-board on the same Leap-VLA checkpoint layout; only the embodiment config differs per platform.

Fig. 8. Left: false execution under instruction–scene mismatch—each row is one rollout at increasing time fractions, instruction quoted above; the instruction refers to absent objects, yet the policy grasps an unrelated plate (top) or knocks over a bottle (bottom). Right: a consistency-gated policy freezes on a feasible instruction (“open the middle drawer of the cabinet”, t=0/50/97%): the negatives-only policy executes correctly, while behind a CoT-verdict gate misjudged as inconsistent the policy freezes for the entire episode (0/20 feasible tasks under gating vs 6/20 without)—a property of scene-imbalanced gate supervision, not of gating itself: after scene-balanced retraining the gate passes 20/20 feasible tasks and matches the ungated policy.

Fig. 12. Language-perturbation robustness on LIBERO-PRO. Each pair shows the same task from the same initial state under the original instruction (top) and a paraphrase (bottom): a telegraphic rewording (“put book in rear compartment of caddy”, rows 1–2) and an elliptical one (“place salad dressing in basket”, rows 3–4). The executed behavior is essentially unchanged and both episodes succeed, indicating the policy follows the task semantics rather than surface word patterns.
