papers.selection_reason: Proposes Leap-VLA, a VLA model that decouples a low-frequency VLM backbone from a high-frequency action expert, directly addressing the efficiency of vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
papers.tldr: Leap-VLA enables high-rate robot control by reusing low-rate VLM semantics while adapting to cache staleness with fresh visual input and age-aware action prediction.

papers.abstract: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.
bullets: Uses Navigation, Action, and Planning agents connected by a shared internal language and training factory in a closed-loop workflow.
Applies symbolic verification before consequential actions execute, with validated physics serving as the safety basis rather than learned models.
Improved unseen-aircraft CFD convergence from under 1% to 74% across 100 single-attempt cases; also demonstrated live Mach 6 cases on three facilities.
Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters increased ParaView control success from 55% to 75%; validated world modeling achieved the best conjunction-risk score among five methods.
Demonstrations span space-domain awareness, reactor anomaly detection, debris avoidance, large simulated aircraft teams, and a control-grade microreactor digital twin.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Data Factory outputs feed multiple automated-machine-learning frameworks trained in parallel. Candidate models are evaluated, compared, and ranked under Monte Carlo cross-validation, and the best predictor for each target is registered for downstream use in the workflow.

Figure 1: The GURU hierarchy. The Planning layer performs long-horizon forecasting and planning with JEPA world models and model predictive control. The Action layer turns plans into bounded decisions through optimization, parameter prediction, and anomaly detection. The Navigation layer executes and monitors operations across software and physical systems. Feedback flows bidirectionally, so plans constrain low-level action while observations update the planner. The middle layer, labeled Discrete actions in the figure, is the Action layer.

Figure 8: Knowledge-graph construction pipeline. Heterogeneous software sources are converted into a common, provenance-preserving observation representation, using vision-language models and automatic speech recognition (ASR) for video and deterministic or vision-language extraction for PDF documents, before being transformed into candidate claims and merged into a canonical knowledge graph. The shared intermediate schema allows document and video evidence to contribute to the same reusable representation.

Figure 21: The horizon-aware forecaster that produces the forward tracks. The extended model takes a look-ahead interval, up to 72 hours (at most 7 days), from as much as 28 days of history, and predicts the embedding of the whole future trajectory rather than a single point. Sweeping the look-ahead forward and backward turns the same model into a scanner across the historical archive for behavior staggered in time to avoid notice. The forecaster is a joint-embedding predictive architecture (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023).

Figure 17: Software-control architecture and knowledge-learning loop for ParaView. The Planning agent decomposes a user goal into structured actions; the Grounding agent maps each action and the current application state to executable code or GUI operations; and the Execution agent applies the selected operation and returns the resulting state. Tutorials, documents, and interaction trajectories provide knowledge for retrieval and role-specific training.

Figure 2: The GURU platform. The Learning Engine trains Navigation, Action, and Planning agents. The rules engine validates schemas, ontologies, constraints, and execution state. The agent society coordinates specialized agents through message pools and a shared workspace for auditable execution. Inputs span sensor streams, simulation outputs, documents, and direct user interaction, and the same platform drives applications in digital engineering, space operations, and reactor operations.

Figure 4: The Common Internal Language unifies agents through a shared semantic substrate for concepts, values, rules, and procedures, a uniform message format for the global workspace, and hierarchical task structures ready for planning and execution. Inset: a natural-language and geometry request is translated into typed, unit-aware attribute records with explicit provenance and uncertainty fields.

Figure 3: Lightweight clients capture multimodal input and workflow intent. Structured representations and high-dimensional embeddings are routed to backend services for reasoning, orchestration, and execution across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments. Remote applications can be driven and viewed through a streamed display.

Figure 45: CFD simulation outcomes by grid generator and parameter selection. Stacked outcome shares for the earlier Pentagrow pipeline with predicted parameters, the extrusion-based generator with random parameters, and the extrusion-based generator with learned parameter selection. Outcomes are failed grid generation, failed initial solve, failed during adaptation, not finished, not converged, and converged. The rightmost configuration is the headline result in the text: 100 cases, one attempt each, of which 92 completed and 74 converged.

Figure 6: Current and target states are encoded into latent embeddings. The predictor learns action-conditioned transitions in that latent space, which lets agents forecast the behavior of an interface or environment without reconstructing raw observations.

Figure 7: Multimodal sources for software-knowledge acquisition. Document and video tutorials provide procedural demonstrations and application knowledge, while autonomous ParaView exploration produces state-action-outcome trajectories. The exploration examples show before-and-after application states; several attempts did not achieve the requested goal, which is why execution without an error is never treated as achievement. Both sources are transformed into reusable observations for knowledge extraction and agent training.

Figure 49: Quantitative comparison of anomaly-detection methods and JEPA scoring rules. (Top left) Balanced accuracy at the warning threshold by method. (Top right) Correct-classification rate per fault group. (Bottom left) Temporal anomaly scores for four JEPA scoring variants. (Bottom right) Balanced accuracy and average precision for each scoring rule. Embedding kNN gives the best and most consistent balance across fault families.

Figure 46: Frozen JEPA matches or exceeds configuration-matched baselines on conjunction risk, with seed-stable performance. Mean binary F1-score over 10 seeds on the shared test split, with every method trained under the same budget (batch size 96, 1,000 training steps); labels show mean ± standard deviation. The frozen JEPA encoder with a small MLP head scores highest, and its low seed-to-seed variance shows the result does not depend on a lucky seed, even though none of its backbone weights are trained.

Figure 11: GURU CFD Suite workflow for high-speed aerial vehicles. The figure shows one representative airframe from the live run described above, the Fury: from a natural-language prompt, GURU configured an aerodynamic sweep at Mach 2 to 4, 40 to 50 km, plus or minus 5 degrees angle of attack, about 1M cells, and autonomously submitted it to HPC. Post-processed output for the Fury airframe shows Mach contours and surface pressure-coefficient distribution, the computational mesh, converged residual histories, and axial surface pressure and heat-flux profiles. Video: https://youtu.be/GQIJjjVolNY

Figure 13: The generation model maps image embeddings and augmented renderings into meshable vehicle geometries. Representative outputs span 11 aerial vehicle classes, from fixed-wing subsonic and transonic to supersonic and hypersonic, eVTOL, flying-wing and blended-wing-body, delta-wing and canard, high-lift, rotorcraft, lighter-than-air, and unconventional configurations, with 673 geometries reaching successful volume-grid generation.

Figure 36: Historical traffic replay with modeled hazard bands and candidate reroutes. The dashboard combines recorded aircraft tracks, event evidence, illustrative debris bands, and proposed route alternatives. The evidence panel distinguishes published predictions, event confirmation, and traffic records; the decision panel summarizes modeled intersections and rerouting costs. The displayed alternatives are simulation outputs, not aircraft actions that occurred during the event. Also identified in the dashboard - limits on route completion, cost estimation, and multi-aircraft conflict assessment. Video: https://youtu.be/Jtyf78QsXlE

Figure 20: Two-phase design. In pre-training, the world model learns from context and target windows split from up to 28 days of state-vector history, with a slow exponential-moving-average target encoder and a Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer optimized under an MSE objective in embedding space. In the conjunction stage, the frozen encoder produces embeddings for the history of two objects, which are combined into a symmetric pair representation and read by a conjunction head trained on public conjunction-message labels to output a collision risk score.

Figure 43: OpenMC drum-angle runs are fit to a smooth reactivity model used by the point-kinetics controller. The MPC then chooses drum rotations to track a scheduled power target or to maximize power while holding a fuel-temperature cap.

Figure 18: Ablation of context, retrieval, and learned adaptation for ParaView software control (successful attempts out of 150 per configuration). Explicit program state, API information, and capability catalogs improve base-model performance, while graph retrieval is most valuable when supplied context is limited. Under full context (state, API inventory, and catalogs), the role-specific Planning and Grounding adapters provide additional gains, with retrieval and adaptation showing complementary effects in some configurations.

Figure 9: Knowledge-graph snapshot for ParaView by semantic family. The graph contains 105,125 nodes and 106,202 edges from 64 source packages (42 PDF, 19 video, two API, and one exploration package), including 1,552 exact API definitions, of which 1,478 carry nonempty signatures. The panels count nodes in the ten semantic families; the remaining nodes include procedure steps and transitions, which are stored as supporting control-flow records. These are corpus-wide counts, not counts of facts relevant to any single goal. Automatic semantic matching between documentation and exploration was disabled in this release, so shared storage should not be read as complete automatic linkage.

Figure 19: 2D projection of JEPA world-model embeddings for orbital time-series windows. Non-maneuver windows and maneuver windows separate cleanly, and a simple linear boundary achieves an area under the curve near 0.98 with no labeled supervision during pre-training and no deep downstream classifier fit to the embedding.

Figure 41: Learned models predict dose rate and the effective multiplication factor for each candidate shielding layout, while the optimizer searches material configurations that keep the multiplication factor near target and reduce external dose. Later iterations reach lower-dose designs while keeping the reactor viable.

Figure 48: JEPA anomaly score tracks each injected reactor disturbance. Response of unsupervised anomaly detectors to controlled perturbations in heat-pipe microreactor data. (Top) The injected thermal and heat-removal deviations over time. (Bottom) Normalized anomaly scores from the JEPA embedding-kNN detector, classical detectors, language-model baselines, and Chronos-2, with shaded bands marking injected-disturbance windows. The JEPA score rises during each disturbance and falls back toward nominal between events.

Figure 32: HRRR wind field near a candidate. The map shows interpolated horizontal wind at approximately 2.51 km above sea level at 07:01:47 UTC on January 24, 2026. Colors encode wind speed and arrows indicate the direction of air motion. The vertical profile compares the interpolated field with the adjacent 07:00 and 08:00 analyses and the earlier constant-wind assumption. At the candidate location and height, the interpolated wind is approximately 6.4 m/s toward 141 degrees true. These are atmospheric-model fields, not debris velocities.

Figure 50: Scalability demonstrations across space, fusion, and engineering workflows. (a) Orbital JEPA world-model training on Aurora, run as 16 models in parallel to 8,000 nodes, shown with the maneuver embeddings and classification metrics of Figures 19 and 23c. (b) GPU-native reinforcement-learning environments with vectorized anomaly detection for fusion-facility operations, with near-linear distributed training on Frontier. (c) Geometry-synthesis model training on Aurora (512 nodes). (d) ParaView interface exploration (about 2,000 nodes) and LoRA fine-tuning for software control (512 nodes) on Aurora. (e) Scalable OpenMC, configuration-driven automated workflows, and large-scale AutoML optimization with mesh success-rate improvements on Frontier (1,000 to 4,000 nodes). Inset drawings are illustrative icons of each workload.

Figure 37: Flagged anomalies are organized within a four-class taxonomy of data quality, operational, safety-relevant, and routing, with associated confidence values and evidence trails supporting interpretation and response selection. The example record is shown with its data-integrity flag; taxonomy alignments are candidates for source review, not findings of a violation, conflict, or loss of separation.

Figure 29: Radar measurements surrounding a candidate detection. Columns show reflectivity, radial Doppler velocity, and dual-polarization correlation coefficient before and after the selected detection.

Figure 30: Conditional motion estimates for four regional echo sequences. Blue markers show selected radar echo centers, and yellow arrows indicate fitted movement over their observation intervals. N1, N2, and S3 exhibit slow southeastward motion; the earlier S4 sequence exhibits faster eastward motion. Gray paths in N1 show competing associations. The orange square in S4 marks the later seven-cell detection, which has not been linked to that sequence.

Figure 38: Interactive multi-aircraft evaluation interface. The dashboard combines synchronized map and altitude views with scenario controls, timeline playback, mission outcomes, communication and navigation-denial status, and per-aircraft diagnostics. Operators can inspect each agent’s local observation, assigned course and goal, received messages, physical characteristics, policy or MPC output, and predicted trajectory, while selecting separate policies and checkpoints for each force and rerunning configurable Torch-based evaluation scenarios. https://youtu.be/9kXCKju5cyA

Figure 47: JEPA embeddings expose a conjunction-risk direction fit on the training split (labeled train-fitted in the panels). A class-balanced logistic probe was fit using only the training-set embeddings and then applied unchanged to validation and test pairs. (Top) Risk-score distributions for Baseline risk and Elevated risk pairs across train, validation, and test splits. (Bottom) Two-dimensional projection of the same pairs using the risk axis fit on the training split and the leading residual embedding direction after subtracting the risk-axis component. The held-out validation and test panels show that the learned risk ordering also appears for conjunctions not used to fit the probe.

Figure 15: Candidate solver-parameter configurations evaluated across representative cases under 2 competing objectives, both minimized, with the estimated trade-off front for each case. Successful simulation without errors is treated as an explicit optimization target.

Figure 34: Simulated debris trajectories, uncertainty regions, and radar observations. The map overlays alternative fragment paths and smoothed coverage bands with timestamped radar echoes and candidate motion estimates. The bands summarize the simulated spread with added spatial margins. Radar overlays support comparison with observations.
Figure 14: Generated geometries are rotated into a standardized aerodynamic frame so that inlet direction, lift and drag axes, and solver boundary conditions stay consistent across cases.

Figure 27: OrbitGuard Analysis Console for a synthetic exercise, showing track tables, relative encounter geometry, orbital-element histories, conjunction metrics, classifier outputs, maneuver plans, and an event timeline. Avoidance maneuvers are deterministic trade studies that require operator approval. The console supports detailed policy evaluation and trains operators to interpret evidence, identify threat-like behavior, and select a response. Video: https://youtu.be/aAnbW2aGpN8

Figure 25: OrbitGuard Globe View from a synthetic exercise. The view displays the protected satellite, candidate tracks, projected orbits, threat classifications, and proposed avoidance trajectories in an interactive three-dimensional view, and supports operator training and visual analysis of how synthetic adversarial behavior evolves into observable orbital behavior.

Figure 44: Interactive interface for the reactor-control simulation. The dashboard shows reactor power, the effective multiplication factor, the control-drum angle, and the fuel temperature alongside the core visualizations, and lets a user drive the controller live. Video: https://youtu.be/w5S9YC7DB_c

Figure 24b: The maneuver-family blind-spot analysis. All 607 validated maneuvers are grouped by maneuver family and orbital regime, and color encodes the median reconstruction error against the bracketing-TLE truth on a log scale. Single-burn families in low-Earth orbit reproduce well, while multi-burn and large transfers land thousands of kilometers off: multi-burn maneuvers fail validation about 33% of the time against about 5% for single burns. The analysis also exposes a coverage gap, since roughly 60% of recorded maneuvers fall outside the available tracking window and cannot be validated, a data limitation rather than a model deficiency.

Figure 26: Synthetic intercept generation and refinement performance. The table compares a 100-generation evolutionary search, a 300-generation search, and a 100-generation search with local refinement, and shows that refinement produces the strongest sub-kilometer and sub-100-meter results. The delta-v versus minimum-distance scatter plot shows the tradeoff between maneuver effort and intercept quality, with refined candidates reaching lower miss distances without a proportional rise in total delta-v. The trajectory panels show target, no-burn baseline, and optimized chaser paths with burn locations, illustrating how timed maneuvers turn natural misses into close intercepts.

Figure 39: Multi-aircraft training and evaluation results. (Top left) Moving averages of Blue target arrival, world success, and episode return during late-stage training. (Bottom left) Fixed-checkpoint evaluation on 256 unseen worlds. (Top right) Paired held-out comparison of multistage training iterations I1 and I2. (Bottom right) Single-GPU throughput as the number of parallel 200-aircraft scenarios grows, with the observed range across repeats.

Figure 31: Checking displacement-based motion against radial Doppler measurements. Each row shows a selected observation pair: measured displacement on the left, projection of the inferred velocity toward the radar in the center, and comparison with Doppler measurements on the right. Gray points are individual Doppler gates, orange diamonds are bulk estimates, and blue crosses are predicted radial speeds. The displayed differences are approximately 0.46 to 0.73 m/s. This agreement supports local kinematic consistency under the selected association.

Figure 23a: Simulation-based virtual range training data. 200,396 GMAT simulation records across three maneuver classes (no maneuver, orbit raise or lower, high delta-v) with broad orbital-element coverage.

Figure 23b: A t-SNE projection of the simulation dataset, showing clear separable structure across all three maneuver classes, with low-Earth and geostationary markers appearing across all class regions, confirming the embedding captures both maneuver type and orbital-regime context rather than random synthetic variation.

Figure 23c: PatchTST plus Transformer plus JEPA classifier trained entirely on simulation-based virtual-range data, with per-class precision, recall, and F1 between 0.95 and 1.00 across all maneuver types. The result is not driven by the dominant baseline class.

Figure 33: Alternative Minnesota reentry scenarios compared with radar observations. The full-region map shows simulated trajectories extending from northern Minnesota toward Iowa; the inset resolves their relationship to the N1 to S4 radar regions. Orange, purple, and teal distinguish dense, intermediate, and lightweight component families, while gray paths show the earlier steep-entry case. The lower panel shows altitude histories against time after the assumed 06:31 UTC epoch, with blue bars indicating

Figure 40: Reactor configuration and OpenMC neutronics exploration. Left: core cross-section showing TRISO fuel pins, moderator, heat pipes, control drums, reflector, pressure vessel, and shielding. Right: self-organizing maps derived from large-scale OpenMC simulations, illustrating interactions among key design variables and identifying regions that satisfy criticality and compactness objectives.

Figure 42: OpenMC simulations validated against published experimental and computational reactor datasets. (a) HTR-10 initial criticality: the OpenMC keff of 1.01369 plus or minus 0.00014 is +59 pcm from the IRPhEP benchmark and remains within the plus or minus 500 pcm acceptance band. (b) Baikal-1 reactor skyshine: OpenMC reproduces the measured dose-rate trend from 50 m to 1 km, spanning more than four orders of magnitude and consistent with the COG result of Heinrichs et al. (2022). (c) KRUSTY radial-reflector-height benchmark: OpenMC follows the published Poston et al. MCNP keff trend and captures the approach to criticality as reflector height increases.

Figure 35: Aircraft avoidance in a constructed synthetic encounter. The left panel compares a straight flight path, reactive DAIDALUS guidance, and an additional forecast-based maneuver screen followed by DAIDALUS monitoring. The right panel shows minimum normalized separation from airborne fragments at one-second evaluation intervals; values below one violate the configured protection thresholds. Reactive guidance turns the aircraft but still produces sampled violations, whereas the forecast-assisted maneuver avoids them in this example. papers.abstract: Tactile sensing plays an important role in imitation learning for contact-rich manipulation by providing direct observations of physical contact with objects. Recently, several tactile foundation models (TFMs) have been proposed to learn general-purpose tactile representations through pretraining on large-scale tactile datasets. However, how these pretrained tactile representations should be leveraged for end-to-end imitation learning remains insufficiently explored. In this work, we integrate multiple TFMs into Diffusion Policy and systematically evaluate their effectiveness for contact-rich manipulation under common experimental settings. We further investigate adaptation strategies, including encoder fine-tuning and task-specific mid-training, to understand how pretrained tactile representations can be effectively used for downstream imitation learning. Through extensive evaluation across diverse manipulation tasks in both real-world and simulation environments, including more than 5,000 real-world policy rollouts, we provide empirical insights into the use of TFMs for end-to-end imitation learning. papers.abstract: Fine-grained robotic manipulation requires instruction grounding, robust perception, and precise contact control. We describe our submission to the MetaFine Open Competition at CoRL 2026. Five independently trained models use a common architecture with frozen DINOv2 and CLIP encoders, trainable language-conditioned feature modulation, and task-specific action heads. We improve demonstrations through contact-aware grasp filtering, instruction-matched data, and expert correction of insertion failures. At inference, task-dependent strategies include photometric test-time augmentation, stochastic action averaging, and uncertainty-triggered replanning. Our submission achieves an official overall score of 0.914 and ranks third among 15 teams. We analyze the models and their task-specific behavior.

papers.abstract: We test whether Koopman structure helps a differentiable world model used to train a simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tracking policy by backpropagation through imagined rollouts, replacing the MLP world model of an otherwise unchanged pipeline. It does not: return is at best equal (0.823 versus 0.830), one-step error on identical data is 1.3 to 1.6 times the MLP's, and training is about 15% slower. Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; of the schemes tested, re-lifting at every imagined step trains best. Re-lifting never uses the lifted linear dynamics and leaves a model affine in the action, with state-dependent offset and slope; an action-affine MLP also predicts worse, so the accuracy cost belongs to this class. At a fixed state, the dynamics' curvature in the action explains only part of it. Across states, the policy's actions span a curved region, so an affine model fits policy data only as the tangent at the policy's action, the operating point: on G1, the MLP's tangent there is as accurate as the MLP; at the mean action, 31 times worse. The offset must encode, from the state alone, where the policy acts, whereas an MLP reads the action. Supplying the policy's action removes most of the remaining gap on G1, Ant and Humanoid. The only tested online repair approaching the MLP feeds the action into the nonlinear lift, abandoning the structure. For this use, the MLP world model remains the better choice.
bullets: Replacing the MLP with Koopman-based models yields comparable-or-worse return, higher one-step error, and roughly 15% slower training.
Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; re-lifting each imagined step performs best but does not use lifted linear dynamics.
The resulting action-affine structure poorly represents the curved state-dependent action regions visited by the policy.
Providing the policy action to the model recovers most of the accuracy gap across G1, Ant, and Humanoid; nonlinear action lifting largely abandons the intended structure.
For this setting, the standard MLP world model remains preferable.

papers.abstract: Simulation-based VLA evaluation often treats matching task, seed, and episode identifiers as sufficient evidence that two policies faced identical test conditions. Under specific vectorized reset and autoreset conditions, different termination timing can change subsequent initial-state assignment, so the same episode index need not mean the same test state. We present an evaluation-integrity framework for paired comparison - invariants I1-I5, provenance logging, optional scene fingerprints, and an automated checker - and a controlled LeRobot 0.6.1 LIBERO harness study with emulated controllers. Four evidence levels are kept separate: (A) mixed-horizon Sync wave-1 IDs [20, 5, 22, 7] vs [4, 5, 6, 7]; (B) homogeneous separate-job Sync control (16 cells, 0 ID/fingerprint mismatches); (C) Async+Freeze batch-size map differences (12 I3 mismatches; bs=8 incomplete; mechanism unisolated); (D) a synthetic McNemar illustration only. Controllers were emulated and no real-VLA shared-vector experiment was completed. We recommend checking declared/resolved init-state identity and provenance before paired statistics. We do not claim that published VLA leaderboards are generally invalid.
bullets: Vectorized reset and autoreset behavior can make identical task, seed, and episode identifiers refer to different states when termination timing differs.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied manipulation requires policies to act on information that is no longer visible. Modified objects may leave the field of view, while completed subtasks continue to constrain future actions. Existing approaches extend temporal context through recurrent state updates, test-time training, or storage and retrieval of past observations. As horizons grow, these mechanisms can still leave the policy to infer task state from long, redundant, and viewpoint-dependent visual experience. We argue that long-horizon agents benefit not merely from remembering more, but from remembering task-relevant state changes and progress. We propose Memory of Object States and Task Progress (MOST), a policy-internal memory framework that compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens. Historical and predictive future tokens are explicitly supervised with object states and subtask progress, structuring memory around what has changed in the world and what has already been accomplished. The resulting memory directly conditions action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage. We further introduce RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Across RoboCasa365, RoboCasa-Long, and real-world robot experiments, MOST consistently outperforms Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1), the previous state-of-the-art model. It raises average success from 65.9% to 72.1% on RoboCasa365, average maximum task progress from 20.83% to 42.22% on RoboCasa-Long, and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%. MOST also outperforms a matched visual-history memory variant, showing that effective long-horizon memory depends not only on how much experience is retained, but on whether it preserves decision-relevant progress and world-state changes.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of acting on modified objects and completed subtasks that are no longer visible.
Compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens representing historical object states and predicted future task progress.
Uses these tokens to condition action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage.
Introduces RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark for multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation.
Reports gains over XR-1 and a matched visual-history memory variant across simulation and real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Memory Expert architecture. Historical multi-view observations are encoded into history tokens, and future queries are appended to form the memory sequence. The sequence is processed with block-causal self-attention and conditioned on the instruction through cross-attention. During training, each token predicts its subtask and the state of every relevant object. The output of each Memory Expert layer conditions the corresponding Action Expert layer.

Figure 2: MOST overview. MOST integrates a Vision Language Model, a Memory Expert, and an Action Expert within one end-to-end policy. The Vision Language Model encodes the current observation and instruction. The Memory Expert represents sampled history as object states and task progress, and the Action Expert uses both contexts to generate continuous actions. Task-state supervision is training-only.

papers.abstract: Vision-language action (VLA) models excel for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet their tendency to over-invoke chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning mirrors a human cognitive pitfall: overthinking. Just as deliberate reasoning can slow or mislead human judgment in routine tasks, excessive CoT in VLA incurs unnecessary compute overhead and can paradoxically degrade planning performance. Recent research tackles this via adaptive reasoning, which dynamically modulates inference complexity by selectively triggering CoT for complex scenes while responding directly to routine ones. While prior adaptive methods rely on implicit adaptation, recent work shows that explicitly optimizing the route between CoT and direct responses yields superior performance, assuming scene-difficulty annotations which are labor-intensive, poorly scalable, and prone to error due to the subjectivity of judging driving complexity. We explore, for the first time, whether adaptive reasoning with explicit route optimization can be achieved without any scene-difficulty labeling. We introduce STEER, a generic over-reasoning mitigation strategy featuring two key components: (i) routing uncertainty-aware rollout, which calibrates sampling to align routing diversity with model uncertainty; and (ii) cross-route advantage credit assignment, which introduces a differential metric to reinforce optimal routing decisions based on environmental rewards rather than subjective labels. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 demonstrate that STEER is competitive with state-of-the-art methods in both planning quality and the Pareto front of inference efficiency.
bullets: Targets over-reasoning, which can increase inference cost and hurt planning in routine driving scenes.
Uses uncertainty-aware rollout to calibrate routing diversity to the model’s uncertainty.
Applies cross-route advantage credit assignment to learn routing from environmental rewards rather than subjective annotations.
Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 show competitive planning quality and inference-efficiency trade-offs with state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of STEER. STEER is built on an autoregressive vision-language model that takes a front-view driving image together with structured driving context as input, and generates a textual future ego trajectory as output. It formulates adaptive reasoning in autonomous driving as an explicit routing problem, where an initial decision selects either a reasoning route or a direct route before trajectory generation. The framework is trained in three stages: (1) driving-centric pretraining for domain adaptation, (2) route-balanced supervised fine-tuning to preserve support for both valid routes, and (3) route-aware policy optimization to learn the routing preference directly from task rewards, without any scene-difficulty labels.

Figure 2: Route-aware policy optimization in STEER. For each prompt, STEER first inspects the initial routing distribution to estimate routing uncertainty. When the routing decision is uncertain, the model performs route-contrastive rollout by explicitly sampling both the reasoning and direct routes under the same prompt; otherwise, it falls back to standard on-policy rollout. During optimization, STEER applies a standard content advantage to all response tokens and adds a cross-route advantage at the initial routing position, jointly optimizing response quality and route preference.

Figure 3: Prompt-level route comparison. For each prompt, we compare the trajectory produced by the route selected by STEER (blue) with the counterfactual alternative route (red). In the top case, explicit reasoning yields safer obstacle clearance. In the bottom case, STEER correctly avoids over-reasoning and selects the direct route, which better follows the road geometry compared to the perturbed reasoning alternative.

papers.abstract: Two groups of pedestrians face avoidable risk on the city sidewalk: people living with visual impairment, who reach an obstacle before anything warns them, and people walking with divided attention, who register a hazard late or not at all. A vision system can warn them only about obstacles it has learned to recognize, so its training data limits the protection it offers. No suitable training set exists: public benchmarks are recorded from vehicles, aerial platforms, or fixed rigs, general-purpose detectors omit the street furniture that causes trips, and pedestrian-focused collections are confined to single regions with incompatible class schemes. This paper introduces the Real-time Obstacle Detection (ROD) dataset: more than 24,000 images and 40,000 annotated obstacles across 25 classes, from vehicles and people to the stairs, manholes, traffic cones, and benches that general-purpose detectors overlook. Because street furniture differs between cities, ROD unifies twenty-nine public collections onto one taxonomy and adds eye-level imagery from two contrasting cities on two continents, Tehran and Toronto. Every label is human-verified, and each capture campaign is admitted only after a compact detector shows it can learn the class. Six lightweight YOLO detectors (nano and tiny variants) benchmarked on ROD all exceed 0.86 recall; YOLO12n attains the highest recall (0.889), YOLO26n the highest precision (0.925), and YOLOv9t the best mAP@0.50 (0.882) with the fewest parameters. Because the recall and mAP rankings disagree, selecting a model by mAP does not minimize missed obstacles, so per-class recall is reported for all 25 classes.
bullets: Addresses safety risks for visually impaired pedestrians and people walking while distracted.
Combines 29 public collections under one taxonomy and adds eye-level imagery from Tehran and Toronto.
Contains over 24,000 images and 40,000 human-verified obstacle annotations across 25 classes, including stairs, manholes, cones, and benches.
Benchmarks six lightweight YOLO detectors; all achieve recall above 0.86, with different models leading in recall, precision, and mAP@0.50.
Reports per-class recall because mAP rankings do not necessarily identify the model that minimizes missed obstacles.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 End-to-end construction pipeline for the ROD dataset. Track 1 downloads twenty-nine Roboflow Universe collections at pinned versions, drops out-of-taxonomy labels and unusable images, and remaps every remaining class index onto the unified 25-class schema. Track 2 normalizes fieldcaptured imagery from Tehran and Toronto, then annotates it either automatically, through the AnnotationFlow pipeline running SAM 3 inside a Roboflow Workflow, or manually in CVAT where no reliable concept prompt exists; every label from both routes is verified by a human. Each capture campaign then passes an admission gate: augmentation followed by a single-class YOLOv8n probe, admitted only if precision, recall, and mAP@0.5 all reach 0.90. Campaigns that fail return to photography (dashed)

papers.abstract: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.
bullets: Addresses the need to retain motion history and earlier visual evidence missing from current observations.
Trains memory with temporal supervision from predicted future visual features.
At execution, uses spatially normalized prediction discrepancies to selectively update the visual state.
Improves success from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO and 14.4% to 83.8% on RMBench M(1).
Also improves general manipulation and spatial-perturbation robustness, with 7.7 ms mean inference overhead on an NVIDIA H800.

papers.abstract: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the $π_0$ baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher \emph{imitable} raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32\% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation.
bullets: The challenge evaluates fine-grained manipulation under visual changes, language instructions, and behavioral precision across five simulated tasks.
The solution uses one 19M-parameter policy per task, a separate instruction classifier, and simulator-generated demonstrations from a privileged scripted teacher.
Failure analysis showed that near-perfect teachers can teach memoryless students poorly through pauses, fixed habits, and missing recovery examples.
Making demonstrations more imitable improved letter insertion from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32% more data, and ultimately to 0.88 using the same architecture.
The team’s overall score was 0.947, earning second place and motivating practical lessons about demonstration design and evaluation.

papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $π_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit https://doubleblind-sae-pi05.github.io for video rollouts.
bullets: Per-token goal-word edits steer π₀.₅-LIBERO without changing the instruction text.
At layer 0, BatchTopK swaps redirected up to 20/20 rollouts in one scene, while random-feature swaps redirected none; results varied across scenes and layers.
Word-selected Matryoshka edits generally did not outperform random swaps, and SAEs were not necessary: a scaled difference-in-means vector also redirected behavior.
Edits remained effective through layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity; patching camera tokens extended effectiveness to layer 13.
The study is a simulated proof of existence and an initial characterization of the depth limits of goal-redirection edits.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to adapt pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs). We investigate the problem of behavioral steering: adapting a VLA's execution style to preferences such as carrying objects higher. To investigate how little trainable capacity such steering requires and how much pretrained capability can be retained, we freeze an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and optimize TinyLoRA adapters with 8 to 384 trainable parameters using either policy-gradient RL (GRPO) or evolutionary search (CMA-ES). With just 256 trainable parameters, we raise carry height by 120 mm on trained tasks at 92% success and by 74 mm on a held-out task at 80% success. By rescaling the learned update, we can tune the trade-off between style gains and capability retention without retraining. Increasing adapter capacity generally improves this trade-off, retaining more pretrained capability at comparable style gains. The choice of optimizer also depends on capacity, with CMA-ES being competitive at low parameter counts, while GRPO offers better trade-offs as capacity grows. These findings show that extremely low-dimensional updates can steer pretrained VLA behavior, with adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling offering practical control over adaptation and retention.
bullets: Studies behavioral steering, such as making a robot carry objects higher, without updating the full policy.
Freezes an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and trains TinyLoRA adapters with 8–384 parameters using GRPO or CMA-ES.
With 256 parameters, carry height increases by 120 mm on trained tasks and 74 mm on a held-out task, with 92% and 80% success respectively.
Adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling control the trade-off between behavioral change and capability retention.
CMA-ES is competitive at very low capacities, while GRPO provides better trade-offs as capacity increases.

papers.abstract: Most agentic robotic systems use vision-language models (VLMs) either to orchestrate predefined skills or to directly generate actions, constraints, and control programs. The former is limited by the available skill library, while the latter requires VLMs to reason about precise geometry and contact. In this paper, we propose WorldSketch, a new paradigm for agentic robotics in which a VLM constructs a world model rather than generating robot actions. The VLM acts as an agent that actively queries perception tools to build and visually validate a minimal kinematic world model, capturing only task-relevant objects, their interaction geometry, and possible motions. A geometric planner then jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion on the resulting model. Moreover, the world model is self-improving: execution feedback verifies outcomes, updates uncertain hypotheses, and enables the agent to revise the model when its predictions are contradicted. We demonstrate the generality of this paradigm across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, achieving zero-shot success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively. On RoboCasa, WorldSketch outperforms the next-best zero-shot agent baseline by 58 percentage points while using 10 times fewer VLM input tokens; on LIBERO-PRO, it exceeds CaP-X by 82 percentage points. In navigation, it matches the success rate of step-by-step VLM agents while using 6 times fewer input tokens.
bullets: Addresses the limits of skill-library orchestration and the difficulty of precise geometric reasoning by VLMs.
The VLM actively queries perception tools to construct and visually validate minimal kinematic models of relevant objects, interactions, and motions.
A geometric planner jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion using the constructed model.
Execution feedback verifies results, updates uncertain hypotheses, and supports model revision when predictions fail.
Demonstrated across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, with success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively, while using substantially fewer VLM input tokens than comparable approaches.

papers.title: WorldSketch: Sketching World Models for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: WorldSketch enables zero-shot mobile manipulation by having a VLM build and refine task-specific geometric world models for a planner instead of directly generating robot actions.

papers.abstract: When searching for an object, humans naturally combine semantic intuition - reasoning about where the object is likely to be stored - with geometric awareness of what parts of the space are visible, occluded, or unexplored. Effective robot object search requires the same joint reasoning, yet existing methods rely on only one: geometric methods maintain principled spatial beliefs but lack deep semantic understanding, while language-model based methods leverage commonsense knowledge but maintain no explicit belief over space. We argue that jointly reasoning over semantic and geometric evidence in an explicit 3D belief enables human-like interactive object search that outperforms either modality alone. To test this claim, we build a system that accumulates per-object VLM plausibility scores and geometric occupancy evidence via Bayesian log-odds filtering into a unified 3D voxel belief field. High-belief regions in the combined belief field drive action selection at each step: taking a closer look from a different viewpoint, navigating toward an unexplored region of the workspace, or physically interacting with a closed cabinet. We deploy this system end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid and find that it outperforms geometry-only search and LLM-based planning methods. Project website - https://skymanaditya1.github.io/objsearch-website/
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-only methods and language-based planners that lack spatial beliefs.
Combines VLM object-likelihood scores with geometric occupancy evidence using Bayesian log-odds filtering.
Uses high-belief voxel regions to choose viewpoints, explore unseen areas, or interact with closed cabinets.
Evaluated end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid, outperforming geometry-only and LLM-based search methods.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct observations of contact physics, local geometry, and interaction dynamics, making it a vital source of feedback for contact-rich manipulation. However, existing tactile manipulation studies are often developed and evaluated within specific task settings, making it difficult to systematically compare how tactile information contributes under different interaction conditions. In this work, we develop a benchmark in simulation comprising 128 tasks organized around three complementary evaluation regimes: Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic. The benchmark further includes controlled static and dynamic task variants and 12 perturbation settings for evaluating robustness under changes in visual and physical conditions. These settings motivate studying tactile information as a temporally evolving interaction representation rather than only as an instantaneous observation. We therefore propose an action-conditioned latent predictive world model that integrates tactile history and learns a tactile state through prediction of future tactile latents. Building on this representation, we design a model that conditions action generation on the learned tactile state and uses predicted future tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection. Experiments on the proposed benchmark show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the evaluated regimes. Project Page: https://tacmind-bench.github.io/
bullets: Covers Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic evaluation regimes with static and dynamic variants.
Includes 12 perturbation settings to test robustness to visual and physical changes.
Learns a temporally evolving tactile state by predicting future tactile latents from tactile history and actions.
Uses predicted tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection.
Experiments show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the benchmark regimes.

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language-action (VLA) policy signal likely task failure from its own action probabilities? We introduce CalVLA, which shapes native action-token confidence using successful and failed rollouts and an Action-Confidence Alignment (ACal) squared margin-ranking loss. Low-rank adapters update OpenVLA-7B without an auxiliary failure detector. Observations are paired within tasks at similar normalized elapsed times, not necessarily equivalent physical progress. On a held-out test split from 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence achieves a joint failure-discrimination AUROC of $0.7392\pm0.0480$ over three seeds, averaging scores at 130 and 260 steps. Frozen-policy probes reach 0.6146--0.6436, but superiority over the linear probe is statistically inconclusive. For the same confidence summary, AUROC rises from 0.4485 before adaptation to 0.7327 after adaptation. Mean task success decreases from 58% to 55%. These results show improved failure discrimination, not improved control or established safety benefits.
bullets: Uses successful and failed rollouts with an Action-Confidence Alignment squared margin-ranking loss.

papers.abstract: Before foraging, desert ants perform learning walks (LWs) to acquire visual memories around their nest. With experience, these walks expand, become straighter, and contain fewer visual scans. We previously proposed a model in which these behaviours emerge from the angular mismatch between path integration (PI) and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass (VC). Here, we test whether this mechanism can generate learning walks on a physical robot, despite the sensory and motor noise inherent to real-world conditions. We implement the model on a four-wheeled robot equipped with a panoramic camera, an IMU and wheel encoders providing compass and stride information for PI, and test it outdoors using a replicated desert-ant experimental setup. The PI--VC mismatch regulates walking speed, turning, pirouettes, and returns to the nest, while PI provides a teaching signal for visual learning. The robot autonomously decides when to acquire visual memories, while its behaviour gradually shifts from exploration towards foraging as visual learning progresses. The robot reproduces desert-ant LW features, including expanding and straightening trajectories, decreasing pirouette frequency, and improved visual homing. These results demonstrate that a simple error-driven mechanism can generate key features of learning walks under real-world conditions, supporting its plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants. More broadly, this work illustrates how physical robots can be used to test biological models.
bullets: Learning walks emerge from angular mismatch between path integration and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass.
The mechanism controls speed, turning, pirouettes, nest returns, and visual-memory acquisition.
Implemented on an outdoor four-wheeled robot with a panoramic camera, IMU, and wheel encoders despite real-world noise.
The robot reproduced expanding and straightening paths, fewer pirouettes, and improved visual homing as learning progressed.
Results support the mechanism’s plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants and demonstrate physical robots as tools for testing biological models.

Fig 15. Relationship between prediction variance and visual-compass accuracy on the robot. (A) Absolute angular error of the centroid of 10 consecutive raw visual-compass predictions (1 s of sampling), relative to the ground-truth nest direction derived from GNSS position. During these 1-s windows, the maximum angular spacing between headings was 54.31◦ ± 20.63◦ (mean ± SD), with a maximum of approximately 100◦, while the maximum linear spacing between sampled positions was 0.287± 0.212 m, with a maximum of approximately 0.8 m. Only LW3 and subsequent LWs were included, excluding LW1 and LW2. Mean centroid error increased monotonically with circular variance, from 20.42◦ in the lowest-variance bin (0–0.1) to 83.32◦ in the highest-variance bin (0.9–1.0). Prediction variance was positively correlated with centroid error (Spearman’s ρ = 0.358, p < 0.001), with a linear R2 = 0.167 and mutual information of 0.113 nats. Error bars show standard deviations, which increased with variance. The variability in all variance bin was quite high, hence the low correlation and low predictability despite a clear trend on average. (B) Frequency distribution across all the one-second prediction samples across circular-variance bins. Low-variance samples were more frequent. The positive correlation between prediction variance and angular error suggests that the variance of successive visual-compass predictions could serve as a proxy for prediction accuracy, providing a confidence or reliability signal. This could be used to weight visual-compass predictions against PI, or to distinguish familiar from unfamiliar locations. Unlike the visual familiarity or novelty signals commonly derived from MBON activation in visual-compass models [1, 34, 41, 48], this signal would reflect the consistency of successive directional predictions rather than the familiarity of the visual input itself.

papers.abstract: Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b) abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.
bullets: Addresses the need for intuitive, adaptable cobot programming as shop-floor tasks and environments change.
Uses a three-stage pipeline: teach workflows, abstract them into skills, then apply those skills to new situations.
Evaluated on a collaborative structure-building task with open- and closed-model agents in self-play and cross-model setups.
Skill abstraction improved task success rates and reduced interaction cost.
A preliminary human-in-the-loop study indicates the approach can also handle human instructions.

papers.abstract: Held-out validation loss is the standard offline signal for choosing checkpoints and comparing models, but its relation to closed-loop success on a real robot is rarely measured. We measure it for ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$ (action expert only), trained on nested subsets of 12 to 200 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. We score 82 checkpoints on 25 held-out demonstrations, with each policy's training loss and with the error of the actions it outputs, and compare the scores with 930 bench rollouts. We also score all 700 intermediate checkpoints of 70 training runs, and recover the ball positions of every training, held-out and bench episode from the front camera. Within each policy, hold-out action error correlates with bench success (Spearman $ρ$ from -0.23 to -0.88), but no more strongly than the number of training episodes alone, and not at all among seeds trained on the same data. Across policies the ranking is inverted ($ρ$ = +0.90 at 200 episodes): the policy with the lowest hold-out error succeeded in 3 of 110 rollouts. The most common failure, the arm never leaving its rest pose, ended 96% of rollouts for Diffusion Policy trained on untrimmed demonstrations and 47% for SmolVLA, and cannot occur in a hold-out set made of demonstrations. Among rollouts in which the arm moved, SmolVLA's hold-out action error predicts success well ($ρ$ = -0.81). For the diffusion and flow-matching policies, hold-out loss rises two- to five-fold during training while hold-out action error falls by up to 29%. Held-out metrics are a sound diagnostic of learning but no substitute for evaluation on the robot, and we recommend reporting initiation failure and success among started rollouts as separate bench outcomes.
bullets: Evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π₀.₅ on a pick-and-place task using 82 checkpoints, 70 training runs, and 930 real-robot rollouts.
Within individual policies, held-out action error often correlated with bench success, but not reliably across random seeds trained on the same data.
Across policies, lower held-out error could correspond to worse robot performance; one policy with the best error succeeded in only 3 of 110 rollouts.
A frequent failure— the arm never leaving its rest pose—cannot appear in demonstration-based hold-out metrics and accounted for many failed rollouts.
The authors recommend real-robot evaluation and reporting initiation failures separately from success conditional on the arm starting.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at https://sail-research-lab.github.io/omnipiano/.
bullets: Supports one to five Shadow Hands in a unified family of scalable piano-playing tasks.
Covers task performance, robustness to configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation.
Provides at least 912 task settings, 36 baseline algorithms, and LLM-based agents for broader evaluation.
Experiments show that current RL methods and frontier LLM agents still struggle with challenging piano tasks, even in standard RL settings.

papers.abstract: Uncontrolled hemorrhage remains a leading cause of preventable trauma mortality. Timely intervention is not always available, making autonomous systems that can aid in bleeding control a promising alternative. Given the safety-critical nature of the task, supervised autonomy, in which the system executes the technical steps while a human retains oversight, represents a necessary intermediate step toward this goal. In this work, we present a supervised autonomous bimanual robotic framework for injury cauterization (eletrosurgical coagulation) in low-grade splenic trauma. The system integrates real-time bleeding segmentation, markerless tool keypoint tracking, and deep tool-tissue contact detection to coordinate two robotic arms for synchronized suction and cauterization. Evaluated on a novel, cannulated ex vivo splenic hemorrhage model, the system achieved an average bleeding surface cauterization coverage of 82.9% across seven distinct injuries. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using a supervised autonomous bimanual system to deliver targeted coagulation across an injury site.
bullets: Addresses the need for timely hemorrhage control when immediate human intervention is unavailable.
Combines real-time bleeding segmentation, markerless tool tracking, and deep tool–tissue contact detection.
Coordinates synchronized suction and electrosurgical coagulation with human oversight.
Achieved 82.9% average cauterization coverage across seven distinct injuries.
Demonstrates feasibility in a cannulated ex vivo splenic hemorrhage model; clinical applicability remains unestablished.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the supervised autonomous bimanual suction and cauterization workflow. The bleeding segmentation model is run on a laparoscopic image to produce a bleeding segmentation mask, from which the injury location is derived. The positions of both robotic tools (suction and cautery) are extracted from the image using a markerless tool-tracking framework based on keypoint detection. This tracking information is used to crop the image to a smaller region of interest for input to the tool–tissue contact detection model. The robotic tools are moved to the injury location via visual servoing, lowered until contact is detected, and then used to execute an autonomous Cartesian trajectory along the wound length.

Fig. 2. System diagram: Left: Cannulated vessels in the ex vivo splenic hemorrhage model. Middle: Experimental setup including suction pump, robotic tools, and perfusion system. The splenic hemorrhage model is outlined in green; robotic instrument positions are highlighted in yellow and pink. Right, top: Close-up of the yellow-outlined tool, a custom-designed robotic suction tool fitted to ProGrasp forceps. Right, bottom: Close-up of the pink-outlined tool, a cautery hook instrument used for wound coagulation.

Fig. 4. Images of injuries before and after suction and cauterization. Top row: Injury before any intervention. Middle row: Injury after cauterization. Bottom row: Overlap between the injury mask and the cauterized surface area.

Fig. 1. Supervised autonomous bimanual suction and cauterization for bleeding control. Images progress in time from top to bottom. Top: Blood pooling from a simulated splenic injury. Middle: Autonomous suction clearing blood from the injury site. Bottom: Autonomous cauterization covering the injury surface to initiate bleeding control.

papers.abstract: Autonomous systems that navigate their environment need methods to quickly assess the feasibility and safety of desired trajectories. Traditional solutions that rely on numerical integration can be computationally heavy, while fast data-driven surrogates lack the formal guarantees that numerical approaches provide. This work demonstrates a framework that uses (1) a neural network with a spectral backbone to learn trajectories and quantile bands with built-in constraints (initial conditions and stability); (2) a modified conformal quantile regression to provide calibrated, joint trajectory-level coverage; and (3) interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points. After refactoring the network for inference, the trajectory inference time for a quadrotor under a closed-loop linear quadratic regulator is 3.45~ms on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. The total pipeline time, including trajectory inference time, is 9.81~ms, or approximately 100~Hz, consistent with typical control rates.
bullets: Targets the computational cost of numerical trajectory integration while retaining formal coverage guarantees.
Learns trajectories and quantile bands with built-in initial-condition and stability constraints.
Uses modified conformal quantile regression for calibrated joint coverage over entire trajectories.
Applies interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points.
On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, inference takes 3.45 ms and the full pipeline runs in 9.81 ms, approximately 100 Hz.

The initial condition x⃗ d 0 is concatenated with the output of a SiLU encoder Lθ to form the lifted state χ⃗ ℓ 0 , which the spectral layer Qθe ΛθτQH θ evolves linearly to any query time τ . papers.abstract: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.
bullets: Improves the teacher’s success on RoboTwin from 33.4% to 63.6% through recursively proposed and statistically tested harness edits.
Distills teacher trajectories, reasoning, and recovery behavior into a compact 4B student using the fixed evolved harness.
The final student reaches 62.8% on RoboTwin, and students generally remain close to their corresponding teachers across four harness versions.
Evolved harnesses transfer to other frozen planners without retraining and outperform several open 4B/27B comparison agents on identical episodes.
On three unseen benchmarks, the student performs close to a 552B planner using the same harness, within the reported evaluation scope.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TinyAstral. Stage 1: humans specify the rules and budget in advance. A master of frontier LLM agents reads trajectories of the frozen teacher acting through the harness (tools, feedback, memory, recovery) and proposes harness edits, which are accepted only if a paired A/B test on selection seeds passes a pre-registered statistical gate; model weights never change. Stage 2: after evolution ends, we freeze H∗ and collect teacher trajectories, including reasoning and recovery branches. These are mixed with offline real-robot supervision to train tiny students (0.8B–4B), which replace the teacher in the same harness. Evaluation covers three training domains and three unseen benchmarks, plus three closed-loop real-robot tasks on an SO-ARM101 arm.

papers.abstract: Deformable linear objects (DLO) pose a coupled perception and control challenge: their slender geometry makes precise localization difficult, while their deformations depend on object-specific physical properties. To address this challenge, we propose PS-DLO, a property- and spatially aware DLO manipulation policy. First, contrastive image-text learning maps the initial observation to categorical descriptions of DLO properties, providing explicit physical and structural priors for action generation. Second, SAM3 extracts mask-guided features from future observations, which are distilled into the policy's action expert to encode task-relevant DLO regions and their subsequent configurations. We evaluate PS-DLO on nine real-world tasks across single-arm and bimanual platforms, training a shared multi-task policy for each embodiment. PS-DLO achieves an average success rate of 68.9%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.0 percentage points. In generalization experiments, PS-DLO achieves higher success rates than the baseline in six of seven visual-shift conditions on butterfly-knot untying. These results demonstrate that combining object-property priors with future spatial supervision improves multi-task DLO manipulation and robustness to visual variation.
bullets: Addresses the coupled perception and control challenges caused by DLO geometry and object-specific deformation.
Uses contrastive image-text learning to infer categorical physical and structural properties from the initial observation.
Uses SAM3 mask-guided features from future observations, distilled into the action expert to highlight relevant regions and configurations.
Evaluated across nine real-world tasks on single-arm and bimanual platforms with shared multi-task policies.
Achieves 68.9% average success, 20.0 percentage points above the strongest baseline, and outperforms it in six of seven visual-shift conditions for butterfly-knot untying.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of PS-DLO. The framework consists of DLO property extraction and future spatial knowledge distillation. The property extractor maps the initial observation to a categorical property description for policy conditioning, while the distillation branch uses SAM3-guided features from future observations to provide spatial supervision for the action expert through a teacher–assistant scheme. Training proceeds in three stages: contrastive propertyextractor adaptation, teacher pretraining with auxiliary action supervision, and joint training with teacher–student alignment.

Fig. 3. Representative execution sequences of real-world DLO manipulation tasks. The upper three rows show straightening, elastic-rope hooking, and knot untying on the bimanual PiPER platform. papers.abstract: Road infrastructure perception is a fundamental component of autonomous driving, as it recovers the structured road elements that define roadway geometry, delimit operational space, and encode traffic regulations. Although individual tasks such as lane detection, drivable-space estimation, traffic-sign recognition, and online map construction have been extensively studied, the field remains fragmented across task definitions, sensing assumptions, output representations, datasets, and evaluation protocols. This survey provides a function-oriented synthesis of road infrastructure perception. We first clarify its scope and organize existing studies into three complementary categories: geometric-structural, functional-spatial, and regulatory-semantic infrastructure. Based on this taxonomy, we review sensing modalities, scene representations, representative methods, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols, emphasizing the field's evolution from image-space recognition toward metric, vectorized, topology-aware, occupancy-based, and rule-grounded scene modeling. We further examine how representation choices affect evaluation and downstream usability, revealing limitations of current benchmarks in relation reasoning, temporal consistency, robustness, and planning-oriented assessment. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions toward unified infrastructure representation, open-environment generalization, relation- and rule-aware reasoning, and downstream-oriented evaluation. By connecting tasks, representations, and evaluation under a common functional framework, this survey aims to establish road infrastructure perception as a coherent foundation for map-compatible and behavior-relevant autonomous-driving scene understanding.
bullets: Organizes infrastructure into geometric-structural, functional-spatial, and regulatory-semantic categories.
Reviews sensing modalities, scene representations, methods, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols.
Traces a shift from image-space recognition toward metric, vectorized, topology-aware, occupancy-based, and rule-grounded modeling.
Identifies benchmark gaps in relation reasoning, temporal consistency, robustness, and planning-oriented evaluation.
Highlights future directions including unified representations, open-environment generalization, rule-aware reasoning, and downstream-focused assessment.
