papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a core design principle for sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, yet fixed antenna geometry limits its performance. Pinching antenna systems (PASS) guide electromagnetic waves along dielectric waveguides and radiate them through position-adaptive antennas, allowing communication links and sensing observations to benefit from spatial reconfiguration. This article reviews PASS-enabled ISAC through single-waveguide, multi-waveguide, and segmented-waveguide architectures, comparing their feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols, and uplink/downlink support. We organize solution pathways around physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition, and stable real-time control. A segmented waveguide-enabled pinching-antenna array (SWAN) case study demonstrates joint segment selection, antenna po?sitioning, and transmit beamforming using segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning. The results illustrate how waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication-sensing tradeoffs. We conclude with research directions in joint transmit?receive operation, measurement-calibrated digital twins, and trustworthy control.
bullets: PASS uses dielectric waveguides and position-adaptive radiators to provide spatial reconfiguration for communication and sensing.
It reviews single-, multi-, and segmented-waveguide designs, including feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols, and uplink/downlink support.
Key solution areas are physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition, and stable real-time control.
A segmented-waveguide case study combines segment selection, antenna positioning, and beamforming with segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning.
Waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication–sensing tradeoffs; future work includes joint transmit–receive operation, calibrated digital twins, and trustworthy control.

papers.tldr: This article surveys pinching-antenna architectures and solution strategies for reconfigurable ISAC in 6G, highlighting tradeoffs and future research needs.

papers.abstract: Real-world robotic manipulation requires reasoning about cluttered scenes, partially observable or hidden objects, and semantically appropriate actions, in addition to low-level execution within those scenes. However, existing simulation benchmarks primarily test the latter and remain dominated by comparatively clean environments with limited clutter and narrowly scoped task structure, leaving many forms of commonsense reasoning untested. We address this by introducing a taxonomy of reasoning processes for robotic manipulation grounded in developmental cognitive science. We operationalize this taxonomy through a new benchmark of robot tasks, MolmoSpaces-CommonSense, that requires reasoning about occlusion, containment, support relations, semantically correct grasp points, spatial affordances, and hidden objects. These evaluations require policies not only to recognize relevant scene structure but also to execute correct actions in them. We evaluate several zero-shot generalist manipulation policies. Across model types and architectures, we observe consistent failures in commonsense reasoning: success rates in cluttered scenes drop by over 50% as distractors increase, policies act on incorrect objects in cluttered settings 30% of the time, and affordance-sensitive grasping remains unreliable even with highly specific language prompts, with correct object part selection happening only about 50% of the time. Further, VLM-based success estimation struggles to reliably evaluate rollouts in these settings, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond control to the broader perception-reasoning-action stack. Our results suggest that existing benchmarks may substantially overestimate zero-shot real-world readiness. Code and policy leaderboard link at https://github.com/allenai/molmospaces.
authors: Arjun Guru, Max Argus, Jae Sung Park, Jiafei Duan, Ali Farhadi, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Introduces a developmental-cognitive-science taxonomy for commonsense reasoning in robotic manipulation.
Benchmarks occlusion, containment, support relations, grasp-point semantics, spatial affordances, and hidden objects.
Evaluates several zero-shot generalist policies on tasks requiring both scene reasoning and physical execution.
Policies show substantial failures: cluttered-scene success drops by over 50%, incorrect-object actions occur 30% of the time, and correct grasp-part selection is about 50%.
VLM-based rollout evaluation also struggles, indicating challenges across the perception–reasoning–action stack.

papers.abstract: General humanoid motion trackers typically rely on deterministic policies that cannot adapt online without brittle reference editing or costly retraining. We present DiffWBC, shifting whole-body control to a generative paradigm via a one-step diffusion model. By modeling distributions over future trajectories, DiffWBC unifies general tracking, test-time steering, and simulation-free failure discovery within a single controller: (1) Generative general tracking: DiffWBC requires a single forward pass per 50 Hz control step and can be distilled from an RL teacher or trained from scratch via model-based RL, achieving the lowest local tracking error among six general trackers on held-out benchmarks (20.1 mm on BONES) and deploying on a physical Unitree G1. (2) Zero-shot test-time steering: differentiable cost gradients and body-group masks modulate the frozen controller online, substantially outperforming kinematic reference editing (0.84 clean pass at 1.25 m ceiling vs. 0.10) and zero-shot generalizing across hurdles, spatial reaching, actuator faults, and tray balancing. (3) Simulation-free failure discovery: plan dispersion across generation noise effectively identifies physical tracking failures (91% precision in top 2%) without physics simulations; targeted fine-tuning on flagged clips resolves 50% of failure cases. Videos and interactive demonstrations are available at https://diffwbc.github.io/#selfassess.
authors: Yifei Huang, Yazhao Yang, Weijia Li, Zhiheng Ma, Dian Shen
bullets: Addresses the limited adaptability of deterministic trackers, which typically require reference editing or costly retraining.
Models future whole-body trajectories with one forward pass per 50 Hz control step, trained via RL distillation or model-based RL.
Enables zero-shot test-time steering through differentiable cost gradients and body-group masks while keeping the controller frozen.
Detects physical tracking failures from generation-noise dispersion without physics simulation, supporting targeted fine-tuning.
Demonstrates low tracking error on held-out benchmarks, physical deployment on a Unitree G1, steering across multiple tasks, and 91% precision among the top 2% flagged failures.

Test-time costs steer the plan via analytic gradient descent on the generator input noise while weights remain strictly frozen; the renders depict nominal vs. steered plans under a 1.25 m ceiling (simulation). papers.abstract: Camera--LiDAR perception on mobile robots and intelligent vehicles depends on reliable sensor geometry throughout deployment. Installation variations create uncertainty in the initial extrinsics, while changing observation quality makes frame-wise estimates fluctuate during operation. This paper presents CalibSwitch, an observation-driven framework that separates absolute extrinsic recovery from selective state maintenance. A cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) combines projection-free bidirectional feature interaction with geometry-regularized learning to recover complete SE(3) candidates from image--point observations and coarse view context, without a supplied numerical initial transform. A selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) combines observation quality and temporal history to determine when a candidate should replace the working geometry consumed by a frozen multimodal detector. On nuScenes, CAEG achieves mean translation and rotation errors of 0.248 m and 5.884$^\circ$. Under sustained geometric transitions, SRCP reaches a mean composite error of 1.46 with 9.70\% candidate commitments, outperforming quality-based and temporal-consistency gating at comparable commitment rates. Relative to unconditional per-frame updating, it improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points. Paired geometry--observation uncertainty tests, two real-vehicle platforms, and 13.5-FPS single-camera Jetson execution demonstrate the system value of selective geometric-state maintenance for continuous perception.
authors: Haifa Zhang, Yijing Wang, Zhiqiang Zuo
bullets: Addresses uncertain installation geometry and unstable frame-wise calibration estimates in mobile perception.
Uses CAEG to generate complete SE(3) extrinsic candidates from image–LiDAR observations and coarse view context via feature interaction and geometry-regularized learning.
Uses SRCP to combine observation quality with temporal history and decide when candidates should replace the working geometry of a frozen detector.
On nuScenes, CAEG reports 0.248 m mean translation error and 5.884° mean rotation error; SRCP achieves 1.46 mean composite error with 9.70% candidate commitments.
Selective maintenance improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points over unconditional per-frame updating; evaluation includes real vehicles and 13.5-FPS Jetson execution.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we focus on interaction-preserving motion retargeting, which transfers human demonstrations to humanoids while maintaining spatial relationships with objects and terrain. Previous work, such as OmniRetarget, addresses this task through temporally coupled constrained optimization, requiring repeated sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations at each frame. We study this problem from an ordinary differential equation (ODE) perspective by modeling the continuous-time limit of its framewise Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions as an ODE on the robot configuration manifold. This viewpoint offers two benefits: (i) it connects OmniRetarget's SQP iterations to a backward discretization of the ODE, enabling us to establish their local convergence under suitable regularity assumptions; and (ii) it leads to TaSP-KKT (tangent-space parametrization for KKT flow), a new retargeting method based on a forward discretization of the KKT flow. The proposed method achieves the same first-order convergence to the ODE solution as the corresponding backward scheme while requiring only one weighted tangent-cone projection and a closed-form manifold update per step, thereby avoiding repeated inner SQP iterations. Numerical experiments show that TaSP-KKT achieves retargeting quality comparable to, though slightly lower than, that of OmniRetarget while running approximately twice as fast.
authors: Pengyu Zhu, Heye Wang, Xi Wang, Xuyang Wu, He Kong, Guodong Shi
bullets: Targets interaction-preserving transfer of human motion to humanoids while maintaining relationships with objects and terrain.
Models the continuous-time limit of framewise KKT conditions as an ODE on the robot configuration manifold.
Introduces TaSP-KKT, a forward KKT-flow discretization using one weighted tangent-cone projection and a closed-form manifold update per step.
Establishes local convergence of OmniRetarget’s SQP iterations under suitable regularity assumptions and matches its first-order convergence to the ODE solution.
Experiments show comparable, though slightly lower, retargeting quality than OmniRetarget with approximately 2× faster runtime.
papers.selection_reason: Humanoid motion retargeting via manifold ODE formulation of constrained optimization.
papers.title: Geometry-Aware Humanoid Retargeting via Manifold ODEs
papers.tldr: TaSP-KKT reformulates humanoid motion retargeting as a manifold ODE, avoiding repeated SQP iterations while achieving comparable quality at roughly twice the speed.

papers.abstract: Robots deployed in unstructured environments are susceptible to actuator-authority degradation, which reduces the effective control authority of individual actuators and can cause reinforcement learning policies trained under nominal dynamics to fail. Existing robustness approaches rely on discrete fault labels, broad domain randomization, or global latent variables, often without explicitly modeling continuous per-joint residual actuation capability. We propose a joint-health-aware reinforcement learning framework for robust robot control under simulated actuator degradation. Our framework encodes actuator condition in a continuous joint-health vector and models degradation as multiplicative attenuation of executed actions. A dedicated HealthNet estimator infers per-joint health from recent observations and actions, allowing the policy to redistribute control effort across healthy and degraded joints. We evaluate the method on Walker, Go2, Cassie, and Panda-based ManiSkill manipulation tasks under diverse degradation masks and severity levels. The method outperforms nominal and degradation-trained no-health baselines on the main evaluated metrics. Relative to the nominal baseline, task-level locomotion returns improve by up to 250.1\% and manipulation success rates by up to 15.2 percentage points; in the high-degradation Cassie group, return increases from 3.94 to 40.50 (+928.0\%). Ablations support the contribution of per-joint health estimation, action-degradation modeling, and health-conditioned control.
authors: Haifa Zhang, Yijing Wang, Zhiqiang Zuo
bullets: Targets policy failure caused by continuous, joint-specific loss of actuator authority.
Models degradation as multiplicative attenuation of executed actions and represents health with a continuous joint-health vector.
HealthNet infers per-joint health from recent observations and actions for health-conditioned control.
Evaluated on Walker, Go2, Cassie, and Panda-based ManiSkill tasks across degradation masks and severities.
Outperforms nominal and no-health degradation-trained baselines; ablations support health estimation, degradation modeling, and conditioned control.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of joint-health-aware control. HealthNet estimates ĥt from recent action–response history, and the controller conditions on (ot, ĥt) under actuator degradation. During training, sampled true health ht degrades the executed action and supervises HealthNet; during deployment, only the predicted health ĥt is used by the controller.

papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from human videos remains an open challenge, particularly in the context of transferring a single demonstration into a spatially generalizable robotic skill and maintaining physically plausible human-like interactions. Unlike prior works that emphasize hand-motion imitation, we introduce an object-centric framework for acquiring dexterous skills from egocentric human RGB-D videos. Within our framework, we formulate the reinforcement learning (RL) objective in terms of object motion to decouple the underlying skill from the specific hand trajectory and impose constraints on hand-object interaction states to promote more anatomically natural hand configurations. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate that our method enables efficient learning from human videos and generalizable skill transfer across novel spatial configurations.

papers.abstract: Recent generative models are widely used to provide whole-body motion for humanoid tracking. Current methods combine motion generators with controllers in an open-loop paradigm, which leads to critical issues: tracking errors can accumulate into spatial drift, and the planner cannot adapt to unexpected physical disturbances without feedback from physical execution. However, directly feeding realized states back to the planner in a closed loop can cause discontinuities, resulting in physical jitter and even falls, since such states are out of distribution during training. To bridge this gap, we propose HIPC, a real-time Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control framework that couples a generative model with motion tracking into a unified planning-and-control paradigm. HIPC introduces a goal-conditioned motion planning trained with a canonical motion representation that avoids gimbal-lock singularities under extreme orientations and supports motion generation on diverse geometric and semantic conditions. Then, HIPC adopts two strategies, deviation-decayed recovery and history re-anchoring, to mitigate the out-of-distribution shift caused by realized-state feedback. Finally, HIPC operates a real-time asynchronous planning-and-control system, with latency compensation to reduce temporal mismatch for inference delay. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of HIPC under switching and composition of diverse conditions. Results show that HIPC achieves state-of-the-art goal-reaching accuracy among existing methods while simultaneously demonstrating robustness to physical perturbations and the ability to recover from falls.

papers.abstract: Motion planning in clutter is embodiment-specific: the feasible free space and reachable commands depend on each robot's geometry and dynamics. Existing cross-embodiment policies output normalized commands that disregard these differences, or compensate through per-robot training and distillation. World models can in principle pool cross-embodiment data, yet command-conditioned models bind their latent dynamics to a single action space, while pose-conditioned models omit the mapping from commands to body-specific motion. On flat ground, however, embodiment affects the planner's observations only through the camera ego-motion. This letter proposes Hourglass, an hourglass-shaped architecture that factorizes cross-embodiment motion planning at this interface: a body-agnostic world model and each robot's differentiable ego-dynamics, which map commands to that ego-motion, are coupled only through it. The world model is trained on data pooled across embodiments and camera mounts; each robot's ego-dynamics is a reduced-order template with identified physical parameters. A generalist parameter-conditioned policy is learned once at this junction: each imagined step rolls out the template and then the world model, and imagination training through each robot's template makes the policy body-aware. On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist policy outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines on the same world model by 3.8--10.6 percentage points in success rate and matches per-robot specialists without dedicated training, while approaching its parameter-conditioned MPPI teacher within 1.4--2.8 points without an online map. After three minutes of teleoperated driving for identification, the synthetic-data-trained model transfers zero-shot to a real skid-steer robot unseen in training, navigating unseen indoor scenes.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal foundation models exhibit strong perception, reasoning, and in-context learning capabilities, but translating these capabilities into physical action remains challenging. Through real-world experiments across diverse manipulation tasks, we find that ChatGPT-6-Astra, a state-of-the-art general-purpose reasoner, can serve as a physically actionable, context-responsive manipulation policy, demonstrating effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation. LEXP combines task-level planning with an experience module that interprets execution evidence, extracts and retains lessons with applicability conditions, and reuses relevant lessons to generate contextual feedback for subsequent actions. Model weights and the action interface remain fixed throughout. Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves $23/36$ successful trials (63.9\%), compared with $19/36$ (52.8\%) with memory alone and $2/36$ (5.6\%) for vanilla Astra. On three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, removing planning reduces success from $7/9$ to $4/9$, while removing retained experience reduces it to $3/9$. Execution traces illustrate feedback-guided corrections and cross-episode reuse of an inspection strategy. Execution analyses illustrate how task structure and experience-derived feedback guide task progression, action correction, and experience reuse. These results support context-space adaptation as a practical mechanism for turning physical interaction into reusable guidance for robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an agent that automates pipeline selection for real-time flow control, using DreamerV3 reinforcement learning to track flow fields in a physical environment.
papers.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
papers.tldr: ART of PIV uses a learned agent to adaptively select fast PIV processing configurations, improving measurement accuracy and supporting real-time flow control under changing conditions.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to follow a language-specified person under occlusion, look-alike distractors, and ambiguous instructions. We show that improving tracking persistence can simultaneously increase safety violations. Using a compact 0.6B vision-language-action (VLA) tracker with a frozen backbone, we update only the planner head with proximal policy optimization (PPO). PPO improves success and following rates across all three EVT-Bench settings, but increases the collision rate on distracted tracking because episodes that previously ended in target loss can instead end in contact. We introduce TRACE, an execution-time target-state risk gate that preserves the learned policy and intervenes selectively. A lightweight risk head processes 84 cues, including candidate boxes, identity margins, a learned range-and-bearing probe, and the policy's commands. When the calibrated risk exceeds a threshold, TRACE rescales the translational component of the next waypoint while leaving yaw unchanged. The executed action is identical to PPO's on more than 98% of steps. In paired evaluations on identical episodes, TRACE reduces the distracted-tracking collision rate by 3.96 percentage points, while further improving success and following rates. Matched slowdown controls without target-state timing do not reproduce this improvement. Concurrent evaluation reproduces a collision reduction of 3.77 points, compared with 0.29 points for identical-arm null pairs, indicating that the effect exceeds evaluation variability. These results show that target-state-aware execution can recover the safety cost of policy post-training with minimal intervention.
authors: Mingyang Lyu, Gongce Cao, Yiyang Jia, Lu Jia, Erliang Lin, Yuhao Zhang, Yinqian Sun, Pin Lyu, Feifei Zhao, Bo Wang
bullets: PPO improves tracking success and following rates but increases collisions in distracted tracking because some target-loss episodes become contact events.
TRACE uses a calibrated risk head over 84 visual, geometric, identity, and action cues to detect risky executions.
When risk is high, it rescales only the next waypoint’s translational motion and leaves yaw unchanged; actions remain unchanged on over 98% of steps.
On paired evaluations, TRACE reduces distracted-tracking collisions by 3.96 percentage points while further improving success and following; concurrent evaluation shows a 3.77-point reduction.
The approach targets safety-cost recovery after policy post-training, with matched slowdown controls failing to reproduce the improvement.

figures.caption: Figure 3: One DT episode under TRACE, on a single time axis. a, Bird’s-eye paths of the human and the robot (robot path shaded light to dark with time); after step 100 the robot holds 0.7–1.1m behind the human, and the fired steps cluster there. b, The risk score crosses τ=0.868 on 52 of 300 steps (shaded; a close-quarters episode chosen for illustration, the run-wide rate is below 2%). c, Forward component of the proposed and the executed waypoint: on the 47 fired steps moving forward the executed value is 0.25× the proposed one, and on the 5 reversing fired steps and all 248 unfired steps the two coincide. d, Distance to the human stays above 0.68m for all 300 steps, whereas planner-head PPO on the same episode collides at step 25.

Figure 1: The safety cost of persistent following, and the gate that removes it. (A) The robot must keep a language-specified person in view under distractors and ambiguity; PPO on the planner head makes it persist longer, and on distracted tracking part of that persistence ends in contact. (B) TRACE scores the next action from target-state cues and rescales its translation only when the score crosses a threshold; the action is unchanged on over 98% of steps.

Figure 2: The tracking stack. Supervised tracker, then PPO on the planner head alone, then a risk score rt that gates execution: below τ the PPO command passes through; above it, forward and lateral motion are rescaled and yaw is preserved. The 84 cues use EVT-Bench’s own detection and identity (§4.4). The rollout below is one episode on which the gate never fires.

Single-run points are marked; all others are five-run means. PPO-Lagrangian lies off the chart and is quoted in the corner.

Figure 8: Recovery-residual progression and robot-frame grounding probe. (a) Supervised recovery residuals, closed-loop progression: SR (blue, left axis) and CR (red, right axis) for the data-collection run and four residual configurations. Dashed green line marks the TRACE gate CR (five-run mean 9.83); soft-recall meets the validation promotion criterion (CR 7.3) but its full DT seed-42 evaluation rises back above the gate, motivating a diagnosis based on the target’s state. (b) The robot-frame grounding correction recovers the deployable direction probe: validation angle L/F/R and high-confidence-subset accuracy before (grey, −Z forward) and after (blue / ochre, +X forward) the convention correction, on two trained models; dashed line is 33% chance.

Dropping action context or identity / top-2 hurts most, and a distance-only head is weakest; the ordering is consistent across all three metrics. Dashed lines mark the full-feature reference.

Figure 5: Gate activation profile on DT, from the deployed step logs of the five runs. a, Share of episodes on which the gate fires at least once (bars: 24–34%, 31% pooled) and share of steps on which it fires (printed: 1.0–2.0%, 1.6% pooled over 741,278 steps). b, Mean collision-risk score on all steps against fired steps (0.36–0.39 against 0.91; dashed line τ=0.868). c, What a fired step executes: a forward command (68% of fired steps) is scaled to 0.25, a reversing command is left at 1.0, lateral motion is scaled to 0.60, and yaw is unchanged.

Hollow = PPO, filled = TRACE, thin lines pair the runs, the black line joins the means. All three metrics improve on all five runs; CR falls by 2.97 to 5.65 points.

Table 1: EVT-Bench results (SR/FR/CR, percent). Panel (a) reproduces numbers published by the original authors under their own protocols; panel (b) is measured by us under one corrected evaluator (Appendix D). Our claims are the paired deltas of the last row, computed from unrounded means (they can differ from differences of the rounded entries by 0.01). Bold: best within panel (b); ±: std over five training runs; the SFT base is a single supervised model. †STT uses per-run model selection, not the gate, which fires on 0% of STT steps (§3.2); the penalty level was chosen on half of the episodes, so the unbiased STT inference is the independent-subset row of Table 2. ⋆AT uses the AT-calibrated gate; its paired deltas did not reproduce under concurrent evaluation (Table 2).

Table 5: Centralized hyperparameters. All values are those used for the headline numbers. Recovery-residual hyperparameters used in the bottleneck analysis (Appendix T) are listed separately in Appendix S.

Table 20: Cheaper post-training and filtering alternatives do not reproduce the safety–success pair. All start from the same base policy and reward. Rows marked development phase predate the evaluator correction (or are training-rollout statistics) and are qualitative; the remaining rows use the corrected evaluator. None matches TRACE’s DT safety–success pair. Triplets read SR/FR/CR in percent. The paragraphs below expand each row.

Table 9: Time-matched paired re-test (SR/FR/CR, percent, full 1,380-episode DT set, seven paired evaluations of 2,760 episodes each). Both arms of a row run concurrently over the same worker slots. The null rows’ two arms are the same configuration, so their spread is the protocol’s resolution: the gated arm’s pooled deltas sit inside it.

The controls stay close to PPO and remain far from TRACE’s 46.02 / 57.58 / 9.83 five-run mean, supporting the conclusion that the gate’s gain is not explained by slowdown, sparse trigger budget, or risk-score density alone.

Table 25: Full DT identity / failure-case diagnostic (single matched seed). Numeric backing for Figure 7a–b. The SR/FR/CR triplets differ from the headline run-42 evaluation (44.57/56.41/12.75 for PPO) because the diagnostic evaluator is a separate pass whose per-step logging changes outcomes by up to 2.4 SR and 1.7 CR points; we use this run only for the failure taxonomy, never as a performance estimate. PPO and the gated run have nearly identical per-step dobs distributions at every reported percentile (deltas ≤ 0.015m). The gate’s triggered steps are concentrated at lower dobs (median 0.142m vs. 0.212m non-triggered), confirming that the gate fires in close obstacle states. Caveat: this re-evaluation does not reproduce the headline gate’s activation profile — the gate fired on 443 of 141,798 steps (0.31%, against 1.0–2.0% in the headline runs) and collision-ending episodes moved only from 201 to 184 (17.5% to 16.0% on this subset, against 13.78% to 9.83% on the full runs) — so we use it only for the clearance distribution, which is the quantity the headline runs do not log, and not as evidence of the CR effect.

The AT collision result of the original evaluation is left unbolded because it did not reproduce when both arms were evaluated concurrently (second AT row, five pairs; Appendix L). On the 281 DT episodes whose rows were excluded from risk-head fitting (Appendix J) the collision reduction is unchanged (∆CR −4.13 [−6.26,−2.21], p < 10−4) while SR and FR do not fall (+0.07 [−2.35,+2.56], +0.99 [−0.72,+2.79]); the SR/FR gains are not resolved at that sample size. The second STT row restricts the test to the episodes outside each run’s selection subset (715 distinct, 690 per run): the following gain remains significant and the success gain is borderline.

Table 10: The DT risk gate under the concurrent protocol (SR/FR/CR, percent, full 1,380- episode set, five paired evaluations of 2,760 episodes each). Both arms of a row are evaluated at the same time on the same worker slots, the design that removes the drift visible in Table 9’s null pairs.

Table 11: Backbone portability. All rows are single training runs (one SFT model each, plus one PPO run) evaluated on the full 1,380-episode settings under the corrected evaluator; they are not five-run means. The three distilled-corpus rows share one corpus and recipe.

Table 24: Selection-subset CR (%) per run and penalty level. Bold marks the minimum on the five-level grid. The two picks that change (runs 42 and 43) do so at a tie or a three-episode gap; the two-level rule is the one used for Table 1.

Table 26: PPO→gate deltas per matched DT run (1,380 episodes each). SR, FR and CR are aggregated by the official EVT-Bench aggregator — the same convention as Table 1, so the run means here reproduce its paired row exactly (+2.03/+2.14/−3.96). All three metrics improve on all five runs; endings shift from collision mostly to normal (+41.2 per run) and less to lost (+13.4), so the collision reduction is not purchased mainly by abandoning the target. Episode-level intervals for these deltas are in Table 2; we prefer them to the five-run one-sided sign test (p=0.031), which this table would also pass. Per-run exact McNemar p on collisions: DT below 2×10−4 on every run; AT 0.15/0.022/1.0/0.91/1.0; STT 0.33/0.23/0.68/1.0/0.15.

Table 18: τ sensitivity on full DT five-run evaluation. The calibrated row is the main DT operating point. All four nearby thresholds keep CR below the PPO reference (43.99/55.44/13.78), so the safety direction does not depend on the exact threshold; the joint SR/FR/CR gain, however, is specific to the calibrated threshold, which was selected on the tuning data of Appendix L, and the response is not monotone in τ . We report this as a limit of the operating point.

Table 6: Matched slowdown controls on AT. SR/FR/CR in percent, mean±std over the five training runs on the identical 1,380 episodes; controls reuse the calibrated gate’s risk head, threshold, and scales and differ in the trigger source. Budgets are comparable, not identical (intervention-rate column).

The last column is the gate’s measured step-trigger rate on that run; the random control is matched to it approximately (realized 1.00/1.23/0.90/0.83/1.08%), and the lagged control fires on 5.4/5.1/6.7/3.4/5.6% of steps.

Table 12: Ranking quality and probability calibration of the deployed risk head, over 741,278 scored steps from the five deployed runs. A positive label is a step inside the K-step window preceding a collision termination. Ranking is strong at every window; the raw sigmoid is badly calibrated as a probability at every window. We therefore report the output as a risk score.

Table 13: Risk-head data partitions. The deployed-evaluation episode set contains both partitions above, so the five-run results measure the gate on episodes whose scenes and identities the head saw during training under other policies’ rollouts (and, for run 42, under a diagnostic pass of the same PPO policy).

Table 14: AT calibrated operating points (drill-down of the AT column of Table 1). Both gates were frozen before the five-run evaluation; the calibrated gate is the one reported in Table 1 because its selection rule (all-metric improvement) is the paper’s default, and the margin gate reaches a similar CR (8.07) with the SR gain traded for FR. Per run the calibrated gate is not uniformly better than PPO (Table 7), and its paired deltas did not reproduce under concurrent evaluation (see below).

Table 22: PPO-Lagrangian on DT, per run. Same base, reward, rollout budget, and corrected evaluator as planner-head PPO; only the constraint machinery is added. Both dual-ascent rates destabilize training on every run.

Table 16: Safety audit on DT: robot–human proximity and wall clearance for PPO and the TRACE gate, split into triggered and non-triggered steps. dt: robot–human distance (m); TTH: time-to-human, dt/|vx| (s); dobs: robot–obstacle clearance (m); “med.”/p10–p90: median and percentiles (smaller = closer or shorter). Human columns are a 600-episode sample of the seed-42 run; wall clearance is over 230 episodes from each of the five runs.

papers.selection_reason: VLA tracker with risk-aware execution-time intervention for embodied tracking.
papers.title: TRACE: Target-State Risk-Aligned Conditional Execution for Embodied Tracking
papers.tldr: TRACE adds a selective, target-state-aware execution gate that reduces collisions from a PPO-trained embodied tracker while preserving its tracking improvements.

papers.abstract: Centralized multi-agent path planning with cooperative localization in GPS-denied environments is generally computationally intractable when formulated in full belief space due to tightly coupled uncertainty dynamics. Prior work typically approximates belief dynamics or restricts inter-agent coupling. This work examines a multi-agent planning problem in which a primary agent must reach a goal in minimum time subject to a chance-constrained collision-avoidance requirement and a terminal bound on localization uncertainty. We obtain a tractable surrogate of the underlying belief-space problem by optimizing over the mean-state trajectories of all agents and propagating covariance for terminal constraint evaluation only. We propose CONSORT (Cooperative Navigation with Support-Optimized Routing and Trajectories), a discrete-to-continuous pipeline combining hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based trajectory refinement. Across 50 randomized scenarios, the planners separate as the terminal uncertainty bound tightens, with CONSORT solving 80% of scenarios where the strongest baseline solves 54%, at comparable path length. In marine simulations, with the plans executed under feedback control on an independently developed factor-graph estimate, the trajectories remain collision-free and their terminal uncertainty falls within 6% of the planner's prediction.
authors: Tony Zhang, Ryan Bartholomew, Kalliyan Velasco, Joshua Mangelson, Brady Moon
bullets: Targets minimum-time navigation with chance-constrained collision avoidance and bounded terminal localization uncertainty.
Uses mean-state trajectory optimization, with covariance propagated only for evaluating the terminal uncertainty constraint.
Combines hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based continuous trajectory refinement.
Solved 80% of randomized scenarios versus 54% for the strongest baseline at comparable path length.
Marine feedback-control simulations remained collision-free, with terminal uncertainty within 6% of predictions.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot systems are increasingly deployed as heterogeneous fleets with diverse kinematic and actuation capabilities. While graph control barrier function (GCBF) methods provide a scalable framework for decentralized safe control, existing approaches typically assume homogeneous robot dynamics. Methods that directly encode robot classes can distinguish known types, but do not represent state-dependent motion capabilities or naturally transfer to unseen robot models. To address this challenge, we propose the Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier Function (CC-HGCBF), defined in a shared second-order reference-point operational space. This formulation provides a common geometric representation of safety across heterogeneous robots while retaining their model-specific dynamics and admissible control constraints. To enable zero-shot transfer, we introduce the Radial Capability Field (RCF), a compact, fixed-dimensional representation of each robot's state-dependent finite-horizon reachable velocity set. Conditioning the shared graph barrier and decentralized policy on the RCF enables them to adapt to changes in robot state, kinematic constraints, and control limits without relying on predefined robot identities. We jointly train the barrier and policy using proactive safety labeling and neural CBF-QP supervision, and evaluate them on mixed teams containing both seen and unseen robot models. Experiments demonstrate scalable safe coordination and zero-shot transfer to robot models and capability variations withheld during training. Physical-robot experiments further demonstrate zero-shot deployment to unseen kinematic models without retraining.
authors: Joonkyung Kim, Janghyun Cho, Jeehyun Lee, Changjoo Nam, Yiwei Lyu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing GCBFs, which generally assume homogeneous dynamics or predefined robot classes.
Uses a shared second-order reference-point space to represent safety while preserving each robot’s dynamics and control constraints.
Introduces the Radial Capability Field, a fixed-dimensional encoding of each robot’s finite-horizon reachable velocity set.
Jointly trains the barrier and policy with proactive safety labels and neural CBF-QP supervision.
Experiments show scalable coordination and zero-shot transfer to unseen robot models and capability variations, including physical-robot deployment without retraining.

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in heterogeneous multi-robot teams faces two coupled challenges: differences in robots' braking and turning capabilities limit how each robot can respond to an approaching neighbor, while simultaneous interactions require a single control action to satisfy multiple collision-avoidance constraints. Together, these challenges can make local safety constraints incompatible with a robot's admissible controls, leaving a decentralized safety controller without a feasible action. We propose a Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter (CA-BRF), based on the insight that navigation actions should preserve access to a certified recovery maneuver. First, we construct a backup-recoverable set in a shared Cartesian operational space by evaluating whether prescribed backup maneuvers maintain pairwise safety until the robots come to rest. Each maneuver respects the corresponding robot's kinematic and actuation constraints, making the recovery certificate capability-dependent. Second, CA-BRF filters candidate controls by selecting admissible interpolations between candidate and backup actions while coordinating the selection across simultaneous interactions. This preserves backup recoverability while retaining as much of the candidate action as possible and ensures that all pairwise recovery conditions are satisfied by a single executable control for each robot. Together, we establish recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed-loop system even when the nominal safety-constrained optimization becomes infeasible. The validity and effectiveness of the proposed CA-BRF are validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments of robots with five different kinematic classes.
authors: Joonkyung Kim, Yanze Zhang, Wenhao Luo, Yiwei Lyu
bullets: Addresses infeasibility caused by differing braking/turning capabilities and multiple concurrent collision-avoidance constraints.

Coordinates admissible interpolations between candidate and backup actions across simultaneous interactions.
Establishes recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed loop, including cases where nominal safety optimization is infeasible.
Validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments spanning five kinematic classes.

papers.abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.
authors: Eadom Dessalene, Michael Maynord, Amir-Hossein Shahidzadeh, Botao He, Yasamin Tabatabaee, Ruoshi Liu, Ruohan Gao, Paul Pu Liang, Yiannis Aloimonos

Transfers the learned representations to action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction.
Also conditions video diffusion on EMG to generate fine-grained hand-manipulation videos; the approach outperforms evaluated video self-supervised baselines across four tasks and eight datasets.

papers.abstract: Robot-free human demonstrations offer a promising route to scaling dexterous manipulation data. The key challenge is to preserve the demonstrator's natural dexterity while producing contact-grounded observations and actions that transfer to robot hands. We present Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI), a framework with contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces. The demonstration interface combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB views with contact-alignment-first retargeting and reprojection of wider scene views. The learning interface introduces a hierarchical policy in which a contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a controller coordinates wrist and finger commands to improve contact alignment. CIMI combines contact-grounded observations, retargeting, and action representations, improving mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand-task pairs on LEAP and Wuji. Hardware designs and software are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.
authors: Paul Lutkus, Lars Lindemann, Stephen Tu
bullets: Targets feedback control from learned latent dynamics while preserving stability of the original system.

A minimum H∞-norm controller designed in latent space can stabilize the original system through the learned encoder when the latent dimension is sufficient.
Forward prediction-only losses may discard unstable modes, and single-step reconstruction may produce controllers that fail to stabilize the original system.
Experiments on a nonlinear flexible-arm system demonstrate practical implications for nonlinear autoencoders and latent dynamics.

papers.abstract: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.
bullets: Fixed-conservativeness filters trade performance inside their operational design domain (ODD) against safety margin outside it.
The proposed filter-agnostic pipeline uses policy confidence to modulate filtering at runtime.
High confidence permits better performance where filter assumptions are valid; low confidence adds margin beyond the ODD.
Preliminary F1TENTH simulations show the approach combines strengths of permissive and conservative filters.

papers.abstract: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share residential spaces with companion animals, yet navigation behavior is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind. This paper presents a pilot study evaluating a curve-out maneuver, a laterally arcing pass-by trajectory triggered at the dog's alert distance, proposed as a candidate welfare-informed navigation intervention grounded in canine social communication research and legible motion theory. Following a research through design approach, we developed and evaluated a first design iteration of the artifact in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog. Contrary to our hypothesis, the curve-out produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline. We argue that discontinuous execution limitation, the robot stopping and reorienting multiple times to approximate the arc, undermined legibility, which in itself became a stressor. The pilot surfaces the legibility of robot behavior to non-humans' eyes and proxy stimulus validity as structural challenges for AMI and repositions the design problem for future work.
bullets: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share spaces with companion animals, motivating welfare-informed navigation.
Researchers designed a laterally arcing pass-by maneuver triggered at the dog’s alert distance, based on canine communication and legible-motion theory.
In a naturalistic home evaluation with one companion dog, the maneuver produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline.
Repeated stopping and reorienting made the maneuver discontinuous and potentially less legible, becoming a stressor itself.
The pilot reframes cross-species navigation around animal legibility and the validity of proxy stimuli.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents equipped with tools expose intermediate outputs for inspection and comparison with the model's reasoning, which may offer safety benefits over single-shot models. This paper tests that potential benefit when the sensor reading itself is untrusted, so that the tool and reasoning channels share a common visual fault. We consider a dermatology agent based on segmentation, contrastive retrieval, and an iterative vision-language reasoner and define a coupling taxonomy that distinguishes single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree. On PAD-UFES-20, we show that typographic injection produces detectable directional retrieval capture, whereas physical corruption does not. Crop-first retrieval preserves the payload at a readable scale and produces 55% joint wrong agreement across all cases (71% of faulty cases); full-image retrieval produces 35% (43%). Under a binary decision, if both channels are wrong, their predictions must agree, so hard-label channel comparison cannot detect joint failures, limiting disagreement recall to 0.29 (crop-first) versus 0.57 (full-image). The direction of the order effect is reproduced on the independent HIBA test set.
authors: Nishi Kanta Paul, Md Shihabul Islam Shovo, Md Mostafijur Rahman, Jamil Fayyad
bullets: Defines a fault-coupling taxonomy for separating single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree.
Evaluates a dermatology agent combining segmentation, contrastive retrieval, and iterative vision-language reasoning.
Typographic injection causes detectable directional retrieval capture, while physical corruption does not.
Crop-first retrieval yields more joint wrong agreement than full-image retrieval (55% vs. 35% across cases).
Hard-label comparison cannot detect agreeing joint failures; disagreement recall is 0.29 for crop-first and 0.57 for full-image retrieval, with the order effect reproduced on HIBA.

papers.abstract: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,\mu\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of simulating fast flapping-wing aerodynamics efficiently for slower flight-control and reinforcement-learning tasks.
Combines robot and wing geometry descriptions with composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline.
A five-block model reaches 0.9646 mean fidelity at 65.19× speedup, while a streamlined four-block model reaches 0.9662 at 67.98×.
Stroke harmonics improve held-out frequency-step fidelity by 0.3176; explicit transient lag states add no benefit once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are used.
The benchmark covers 48 held-out scenarios, including wind, gusts, frequency transitions, and cross-robot flat-plate cases.

papers.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics

papers.abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
bullets: An opponent’s group-level response can serve as a shared “tell,” revealing information unavailable to individual members.
Precommitting to response rules determines how much the opponent can hide and can prevent losses when the opponent prioritizes its own objectives.
In a solved Gaussian setting, deliberately limiting how much information the team uses can recover the truth while preserving the opponent’s concealment cost.
An exact test characterizes when this information-recovery result holds in finite games.
Trust allocation matters: private randomization, differentiated responses, or a small trust discount can protect against deception.

(B) Loss per member in the Gaussian team (α = γ = 1) as hostility ρ = 2ψN/ ( κk2 ) rises: red shows witness commitment, also attained in linear Nash play; blue shows the exact team-commitment loss, and the dotted curve shows skepticism alone. papers.selection_reason: Presents a game-theoretic perspective on how non-communicative teams can infer information about their state and environment through adversary feedback, a transferable concept for multi-agent navigation.
papers.title: How a group that cannot communicate knows itself by its enemy
papers.tldr: A noncommunicating team can learn hidden information from how an opponent reacts to its precommitted decisions.

papers.abstract: Egocentric videos offer an abundant source of hand-scene interactions for embodied learning, which requires recovering hands, camera, and scene consistently in a shared 3D world. Existing methods focus on either camera-frame hands or world-space hand trajectories, without jointly recovering the scene pointmaps or interaction information. Building a complete reconstruction from such specialized predictions therefore typically requires per-sequence optimization. We propose EgoHSI3R, a unified feed-forward framework for online 4D hand-scene interaction reconstruction from egocentric monocular video. To jointly recover these components, it maintains a recurrent scene representation that accumulates geometric evidence over time and provides a shared world space and scale. We introduce hand-centric prompts that fuse pretrained hand priors and local scene context, while MANO vertex queries attend to scene features to predict dense per-vertex contact. These designs enable a single network to jointly estimate camera motion, dense scene geometry, world-space bilateral MANO hands, and per-vertex hand contact. Despite operating causally, EgoHSI3R achieves the lowest world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC among the evaluated methods, while offering faster inference than existing world-space hand reconstruction pipelines and competitive camera and scene reconstruction accuracy.
authors: Mingzhi Pei, Zhangchen Ye, Ruoqu Chen, Liu Cao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of unified hand, camera, scene, and interaction reconstruction in existing methods.
Maintains a recurrent scene representation to accumulate geometry and establish shared world space and scale.
Uses hand-centric prompts combining pretrained hand priors with local scene context.
Predicts dense per-vertex contact through MANO vertex queries attending to scene features.
Reports the lowest evaluated world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC, with faster inference and competitive camera/scene accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of camera-space hand reconstruction. The predicted hand meshes are overlaid on the input egocentric frames. Our method produces accurate articulated hand poses and consistent alignment with the observed images.

Figure 3: Overview of EgoHSI3R. Each incoming egocentric frame is encoded by the scene encoder Es into image tokens, and each detected hand is processed by the pretrained hand encoder Eh. The Hand Prompt Builder fuses the hand prior with local scene context obtained via RoIAlign, producing scene-conditioned hand prompts. The decoder jointly processes scene tokens and hand prompts while reading from and updating a persistent scene state. The Scene Head predicts camera pose and world-space pointmaps, and the MANO Head reconstructs bilateral MANO parameters. The interaction-aware Contact Builder combines decoded hand tokens with local scene features, which are then used by the Contact Head to predict per-vertex contact and refine hand reconstruction. All outputs are produced online in a shared world space without test-time optimization.

Figure 2: Comparison of egocentric hand reconstruction paradigms. (a) Camera-centric methods recover articulated hands in the camera frame, without camera motion and reliable 3D placement. (b) World-space methods additionally estimate camera motion to recover hand trajectories in world space, but do not reconstruct the scene. (c) EgoHSI3R jointly recovers bilateral hands, camera pose, scene geometry, and dense hand contact in a shared world frame within a single online, feed-forward model.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
authors: Ammar N. Abbas, Aayush Jain, Prashanth Viswanath, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons
bullets: Evaluated 281 policies from seven families across about 1,700 trials of RJ45 grasping and insertion with a five-fingered hand.

Absolute actions improved vision-language-action insertion success by up to 70 percentage points; decomposition, multi-view sensing, and recovery data appeared beneficial but were not isolated.
Only five of 67 offline metrics correlated reliably with success, and only within one policy family, so real-robot evaluation remains necessary.

papers.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.
authors: Yijia Fan, Xilin He, Yilei Jiang, Dongming Wu, Jiaxu Wang, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Addresses the gap between CaP agents relying on frontier models or VLAs and small open VLMs failing at robot manipulation.
Trains the agent in CaPtain-Harness, which provides low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion APIs across simulation and hardware.
Uses GPT-6 Astra-generated synthetic trajectories for SFT, followed by multi-turn RL.
Introduces a privileged physical critic that assigns credit to individual requests based on their effect on predicted task success.
CaPtain-4B improves from 55.4% to 73.8% held-out LIBERO success, reaches 78.5% on LIBERO-PRO, and transfers to other simulators and a real robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of CaPtain. papers.abstract: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.

papers.abstract: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

papers.abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.

papers.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.
