We also design a simple risk adaptation mechanism to leverage our method's uncertainty estimates at deploy-time, and demonstrate that a combination of inpainting and risk estimation can result in 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal speeds in real-world hardware experiments.
authors: Samuel Triest, Amirreza Shaban, David D. Fan, Wenshan Wang, Sebastian Scherer
bullets: Addresses robust traversability estimation under limited sensing, complex terrain, and high-speed motion.
Builds a geometric-semantic voxel map from onboard multimodal sensors using visual foundation models.
Jointly predicts BEV geometry, semantics, speed, and cost with annotation-free self-supervised learning, including map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning.
Ablations show that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting improve planning quality, with their combination needed for state-of-the-art off-road planning.
Real-world experiments report 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal when combining inpainting with uncertainty-based risk estimation.
papers.selection_reason: Presents self-supervised IRL-based traversability learning and terrain estimation for off-road robot navigation, relevant to learned planning and control.
papers.title: TravSUITE: Traversability via Self-Supervised, Uncertainty-Aware IRL and Terrain Estimation
papers.tldr: TravSUITE enables faster, safer off-road robot navigation by combining VFM-based mapping, self-supervised traversability learning, and uncertainty-aware risk adaptation.

papers.abstract: Offline maximum entropy reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the optimal soft action-value function \(Q^*\) from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment. Although \(Q^*\) is characterized by the soft optimal Bellman equation, the corresponding Bellman operator cannot be evaluated directly because both the reward distribution and the transition kernel are unknown. Consequently, estimating \(Q^*\) requires the joint treatment of environment modeling and value function learning. We propose a framework that addresses these tasks separately. Conditional diffusion models based on probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward distribution and transition kernel. The resulting distributional estimators define a data driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator, whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a class of deep neural networks to estimate \(Q^*\). We establish nonasymptotic guarantees for the proposed method. For operator learning, we derive total variation error bounds for the conditional flow estimators that account explicitly for score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. For soft value learning, we first use the soft Bellman equation to show that $Q^*$ inherits H\"older regularity from the conditional reward and transition densities. For any H\"older index $\beta$, the value learning stage achieves an excess Bellman residual risk bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\big(n^{-\frac{2\beta}{d+2\beta}}\big),$ where $d$ is the total dimension of the state and action spaces. In contrast to many existing theoretical analyses of deep reinforcement learning, our results do not require Bellman completeness. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
authors: Hao Cheng, Yuling Jiao, Lican Kang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Chen Zhong
bullets: Addresses offline soft Q-learning when reward distributions and dynamics are unknown.
Uses conditional diffusion models based on probability-flow ODEs to estimate reward and transition distributions.
Learns Q* with deep neural networks through a data-driven soft Bellman operator.
Provides nonasymptotic total-variation and excess Bellman-residual guarantees, without requiring Bellman completeness.
Experiments support the theory and show the method is effective; the stated rate depends on Hölder regularity and state-action dimension.
papers.selection_reason: Offline maximum-entropy RL with conditional flow estimators for reward and transition dynamics; directly transferable to robot policy learning and model-based control.
papers.title: Conditional Flow Models for Offline Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: A theoretically grounded offline maximum-entropy RL framework learns soft Q-values by separately modeling rewards and transitions with conditional flow models, then minimizing the induced empirical Bellman residual.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon-Depth-VLA/
authors: Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang, Ziheng He, Xiangnan Wu, Yingda Li, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: Problem: Solver depth and open-loop execution horizon are usually tuned independently, creating a responsiveness–stability trade-off.
Method: Jointly adjust numerical sampling depth and execution horizon, using coarse integration as an implicit regularizer during extended open-loop execution.
Key insight: Numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, reducing compounding drift.
Results: The approach consistently improves task success and substantially lowers inference latency across simulated and real-world manipulation settings and multiple VLA backbones.
Scope: Coarse integration can hurt precision during rapid replanning, so its benefit depends on the execution horizon.
papers.selection_reason: Reveals a training-free coupling between execution horizon and sampling depth in flow-matching VLA policies, improving task success across robots.
papers.title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
papers.tldr: Coupling solver depth with execution horizon lets flow-matching VLA policies trade numerical precision for improved stability and lower-latency robotic control without retraining or architectural changes.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot tasks require retaining and using past information. We integrate Test-Time Training (TTT), which stores context in fast weights, into InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5 to study action generation conditioned on human demonstrations through training on paired demonstrations and robot trajectories. We implement memory transfer between the two phases and truncated backpropagation, and examine training objectives, gradient coverage, and contrastive regularization across video, short-video, and single-frame cue tasks. In our experiments, adding TTT and training on paired data at the current scale did not lead to consistent target selection based on demonstrations. Under the tested settings, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations. When demonstrations were reduced to single-frame cues, real-robot execution still showed a preference for cups at fixed positions. We document the implementation, training configurations, and observations to support further inspection and replication.
authors: Qiangong Zhou, Jiafeng Liang, Yimin Dong, Yang He, Hongxiang Li
bullets: Targets long-horizon robot tasks that require retaining information from human demonstrations.
Adds TTT with fast-weight context memory to InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5, using paired demonstrations and robot trajectories.
Studies memory transfer, truncated backpropagation, training objectives, gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization across video and image cues.
At the tested scale, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations.
In real-robot tests with single-frame cues, behavior still favored cups at fixed positions, suggesting limited cue use.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, integrating Test-Time Training (TTT) for action generation conditioned on human demonstrations.
papers.title: TTT in VLA Models: Exploring Training with Human Demonstrations
papers.tldr: This study integrates Test-Time Training into VLA models to use human demonstrations, but finds no consistent demonstration-conditioned target selection under the tested settings.

papers.abstract: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo
authors: Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Behavior cloning is limited by costly, narrow demonstration data and insufficient coverage of successful states.
A privileged, latent-conditioned RL generator uses a parallel reverse curriculum and success-gated diversity objective to discover multiple solution modes.
Generated behaviors are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for imitation learning.
Across four manipulation tasks, downstream success rises from 40% to 62% in simulation and from 39% to 78% on a real robot.
The approach is evaluated with a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection.
papers.selection_reason: Uses RL to generate diverse demonstrations for downstream imitation learning and VLA policies, directly relevant to robot manipulation and VLA.
papers.title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
papers.tldr: DiscoDemo uses reinforcement learning to generate diverse, successful robot demonstrations that substantially improve downstream visuomotor imitation learning.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.
authors: Yan Shi, Kehua Chen, Jiarui Qi, Yihong Tang, Haichen Liao, Yinhai Wang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in MLLM-based driving, where committing to one interpretation can cause premature errors.
Uses particle-filter-inspired belief tracking: a VLM propagates, scores, and resamples diverse scene hypotheses as observations arrive.
On Bench2Drive, improves Driving Score from 68.50 to 81.37 and Success Rate from 41.36% to 54.09%.
Shows the largest gains in ambiguous situations, including unsignalized intersections and oncoming-traffic interactions.
Also improves interactive behaviors such as merging, emergency braking, and giving way.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop MLLM-based autonomous driving with belief tracking directly fits embodied navigation and vision-language-action.
papers.title: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: DriveMind improves closed-loop autonomous driving by maintaining and updating multiple scene hypotheses across frames instead of reasoning from scratch each time.

papers.abstract: In traditional Gaussian process (GP) regression, the inputs are typically assumed to be known, and uncertainty enters only through the measurements. When scalar fields are mapped using GP regression with measurements obtained from a mobile sensor, the inputs correspond to the estimated pose of the mobile sensor. The goal in this letter is to understand how a recorded GP, trained on erroneous inputs (e.g., pose estimates from dead-reckoning), can be corrected in a numerically efficient way when better estimates of the inputs become available. In the developed bias-aware GP (Ba-GP) framework, the recorded GP posterior-mean gradient is used to propagate estimated input bias and noise into mean and covariance corrections. The resulting additive covariance structure is then exploited to develop numerically efficient first-order correction algorithms. A simulation study and an indoor light-intensity mapping experiment show that Ba-GP improves predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration relative to noisy-input GP baselines, with an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost relative to full GP retraining.
authors: Muzaffar Qureshi, Tochukwu E. Ogri, Trivikram Satharasi, Kyle Volle, Rushikesh Kamalapurkar
bullets: Addresses GP regression with input errors caused by uncertain mobile-sensor poses.
Uses the recorded GP posterior-mean gradient to propagate input bias and noise into mean and covariance corrections.
Exploits the resulting additive covariance structure for numerically efficient first-order correction algorithms.
Simulation and indoor light-mapping experiments show improved predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration over noisy-input GP baselines.
Achieves an order-of-magnitude lower computational cost than full GP retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Corrects input bias in GP regression for mobile-sensor scalar-field mapping, directly relevant to embodied perception and environment modeling.
papers.title: Input Bias Correction in Gaussian Process Regression
papers.tldr: A bias-aware GP efficiently corrects predictions from models trained on inaccurate mobile-sensor poses when improved pose estimates become available.

papers.abstract: Distilling interactive LLM agents requires choosing between teacher-generated demonstrations and student-generated experience, corresponding broadly to off-policy and on-policy distillation. While both have proven effective, we argue that this distinction is inherently hierarchical: the policy that induces an interaction history need not be the same as the policy that generates the token prefix of the current action. We introduce a hierarchical agent distillation framework that formalizes these two levels of on-policiness and enables explicit control over their pairing, mixture proportions, and training schedule. We study this problem through self-distillation, where a frozen teacher has access to task guidance unavailable to the student, and conduct a three-stage controlled study across three models and four interactive environments. We find that student-induced histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone training signal, whereas following the student at both levels generally performs worst. Nevertheless, fully on-policy data becomes beneficial when incorporated into a mixture with other configurations. Moreover, mixtures with identical teacher/student proportions at each level can yield substantially different performance, showing that how the two levels are paired matters beyond the overall amount of on-policy data. Finally, front-loading fully teacher-generated contexts and delaying fully on-policy contexts improves over a static mixture. These findings provide practical principles for deciding where, how much, and when agent distillation should follow the student.
authors: Ya Gao, Zhengtao Zou, Pekka Marttinen
bullets: The study reframes on-policy versus off-policy distillation as two hierarchical choices: history generation and action-prefix generation.
Student-generated histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone signal.
Following the student at both levels usually performs worst, but fully on-policy data helps when mixed with other configurations.
Mixtures with the same teacher/student proportions can perform differently depending on how the two levels are paired.
A schedule that starts with fully teacher-generated contexts and gradually introduces fully on-policy contexts outperforms a static mixture in the studied settings.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical on-policy/off-policy distillation for interactive agents offers a transferable imitation-learning methodology relevant to embodied policy learning.
papers.title: Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?
papers.tldr: Agent distillation should distinguish whether the student induces the interaction history and whether it generates the current action prefix, because their pairing and training schedule materially affect performance.

papers.abstract: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site selection and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.
authors: Ray Verma, Eliseo Ferrante, Anthony Tzes
bullets: Addresses swarm assembly without requiring a predefined list of attachment sites during deployment.
Combines neural cellular automata with site selection and collision-aware control.
Introduces decentralized discovery by sharing local NCA states among robots already in the formation.
Uses sparse-retention fine-tuning and false-positive loss to adapt NCA growth to gradual physical assembly.
Simulations scale to several hundred robots, while Crazyflie experiments validate the integrated pipeline using externally tracked, robot-relative observations.
papers.selection_reason: Combines neural cellular automata with robot swarm assembly and fine-tuning, directly relevant to learned robotic control.
papers.title: Distributed Swarm Morphogenesis with Neural Cellular Automata
papers.tldr: A modular NCA-based framework enables robot swarms to grow diverse target morphologies through decentralized attachment-site discovery and physically informed fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Data-driven robots must learn to avoid collisions with as few demonstrations as possible to avoid collecting large datasets of destructive collision examples. We explore whole-body proximity sensors as inductive biases for learning reflexive collision-dodging behavior and find that lossy sensors with low resolution were stronger biases than high-resolution coverage. We also found that, perhaps unintuitively, anticipating when and where contact happens on the body of a robot reduced its learning sample efficiency. We investigated eight candidate representations in a reinforcement learning environment, which included latent compression, future contact anticipation, lossy corruption, and privileged state estimation. The candidate representations were tested by training over 200 humanoid robots to play a simplified version of dodgeball end-to-end under an intentionally constrained sample and compute budget.
authors: Carson Kohlbrenner, Niraj Pudasaini, William Xie, Naren Sivagnanadasan, Nikolaus Correll, Alessandro Roncone
bullets: Whole-body proximity sensors provide useful inductive biases for reflexive collision avoidance.
Lossy, low-resolution sensing outperformed high-resolution coverage as a learning bias.
Anticipating future contact location and timing unexpectedly reduced sample efficiency.
Eight sensor representations were evaluated in reinforcement-learning simulations with over 200 humanoid robots.
The study focuses on end-to-end dodgeball behavior under intentionally constrained resources.
papers.selection_reason: Studies learned collision avoidance and sensor representations for humanoid robots under an RL setting, relevant to obstacle avoidance and robot learning.
papers.title: Move, don't think: sample-efficient collision avoidance with lossy proximity sensors
papers.tldr: Low-resolution, lossy proximity sensing can help robots learn collision avoidance more efficiently than richer sensing under tight data and compute limits.

papers.abstract: Swarms of small robots are an attractive way to survey lunar caves and lava tubes. Missions such as NASA's CADRE will fly cooperating rovers for distributed mapping, but only in daylight. The 354 h lunar night drops the surface towards 95 K, and the radioisotope heaters that let single rovers survive it cannot be supplied at swarm scale. In this study we investigate whether a swarm can instead use its own members as thermal shielding. We train one policy, shared by all twenty robots, by reinforcement learning with an evolution-strategies estimator. The policy receives a single reward, once, at the end of the night: the mean temperature of the five coldest robots. Nothing in that reward refers to position, spacing, exposure or motion. Two behaviors nonetheless emerge. The swarm aggregates, and robots circulate between the sheltered core and the exposed rim, the same pair of behaviors with which emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter. We measure the survival threshold, the smallest stored energy per robot at which every robot is still alive at sunrise. Across ten runs it is 155.6 +/- 1.3 pcm-h, where one pcm-h is 7.2 kJ of stored heat. That is 37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound, and at a budget where the motionless huddle loses six robots, every robot survives. The behavior needs no shared spatial reference and no robot-robot contact, and transfers from twenty robots to forty without retraining.
authors: Anais Jeger, Harry Holt, Lennart Puck
bullets: Motivation: Swarm-scale radioisotope heating is impractical for surviving the lunar night, which can cool the surface to 95 K.
Method: Train one policy for 20 robots using evolution-strategy reinforcement learning and a single end-of-night reward based on the five coldest robots’ mean temperature.
Emergent behavior: Robots aggregate into a sheltered core and circulate between the core and exposed rim, despite no explicit spacing, position, exposure, or motion objectives.
Result: The swarm’s survival threshold is 155.6 ± 1.3 pcm-h—37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound.
Scope: The behavior requires neither shared spatial references nor robot-to-robot contact and transfers from 20 to 40 robots without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Uses reinforcement learning for a shared swarm robot policy with emergent thermoregulation, fitting learned robot control.
papers.title: Emergent Cooperative Thermoregulation in Lunar Swarm Robotics
papers.tldr: A shared reinforcement-learning policy makes lunar robot swarms self-organize into rotating, penguin-like formations that improve survival through the 354-hour lunar night without added heaters or contact.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language-action (VLA) model is fine-tuned with its trainable weights in bfloat16 (bf16) and no fp32 master copy, AdamW writes each update straight into bf16, silently rounding away any update smaller than 1/512 of a weight. In 9 of 12 open VLA codebases a default or documented recipe trains this way, 4 on full weight matrices, including LeRobot's SmolVLA default and its $\pi_0$/$\pi_{0.5}$ guides. In our LIBERO runs without the copy, a probe every 100 steps finds at least 79% of updates to bf16 weights erased. On the Hugging Face Hub, 99% of sampled full-weight SmolVLA fine-tunes store the action expert in bf16, and 84% of recent $\pi_{0.5}$ fine-tunes with a training configuration set the bf16 flag. On LIBERO-Object, with rules fixed in advance, an fp32 copy raises success over LeRobot's storage from 4.3% to 49.3% for SmolVLA and from 5.1% to 80.9% for $\pi_{0.5}$ at a ten-times lower learning rate, where both models are undertrained, and from 89.0% to 97.7% for $\pi_{0.5}$ at its default rate. For SmolVLA at its default rate it adds 10.2 points with open-loop 50-action chunks but only 4.2 when re-planning every 10 actions. In these five comparisons and two more against SmolVLA with every trainable weight in bf16, every run with the copy beats every run without it (p < 0.05); all gaps but the 8.7- and 4.2-point ones clear our 10-point threshold. The fix is to keep the trainable weights in fp32 during training, a one-line change for SmolVLA in LeRobot.
bullets: bf16 rounding removes updates smaller than 1/512 of a weight when no fp32 master copy is used.
This issue appears in documented or default recipes across 9 of 12 surveyed open VLA codebases.
A probe found at least 79% of updates erased in LIBERO runs without an fp32 copy.
Using fp32 training weights improved reported LIBERO-Object success across SmolVLA and π₀.₅ comparisons, including gains up to 76.6 percentage points.
The proposed fix is to keep trainable weights in fp32 during training; for SmolVLA in LeRobot, this requires one line.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies a training-precision pitfall in VLA fine-tuning and a simple fix, directly relevant to vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Full-Weight VLA Fine-Tuning Without an fp32 Master Copy Silently Erases Most Updates
papers.tldr: Training full-weight VLAs directly in bf16 can silently erase most optimizer updates, while keeping an fp32 copy substantially improves LIBERO success.

papers.abstract: Dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects (DLOs) remains challenging due to underactuated, high-dimensional dynamics, delayed deformation responses, and the presence of multiple feasible motions under obstacle constraints. This paper presents BM2PC, a Bayesian Multimodal MPC framework for agile manipulation of DLOs. Building on the control-as-inference posterior, BM2PC formulates multimodal planning as a set optimization problem that balances control quality and behavioral diversity. An efficient incremental update maintains multiple promising control modes with low additional computational overhead. For real-world deployment, BM2PC incorporates an execution dynamics model that predicts actual end-effector motion and compensates for execution mismatch during fast manipulation. We evaluate BM2PC on rope tracking and obstacle avoidance in simulation and hardware, and on simulated disturbance rejection. In trajectory tracking, BM2PC generalizes better to unseen trajectories than a learning-based baseline without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate long-horizon tracking, reducing RMSE by 44.0% on the longest task. In obstacle avoidance, BM2PC achieves comparable performance to existing multimodal MPC methods while reducing planning time by 29% to 66%. These results demonstrate accurate dynamic control and efficient multimodal planning within a unified MPC framework. The core implementation of BM2PC and supplementary videos are available at https://github.com/Longyouyuan/BM2PC.
authors: Youyuan Long, Gokhan Solak, Arash Ajoudani
bullets: Addresses underactuated, delayed, high-dimensional DLO dynamics and multiple feasible motions under obstacles.
Formulates multimodal planning as Bayesian set optimization balancing control quality with behavioral diversity.
Uses incremental updates to maintain promising control modes efficiently, plus an execution dynamics model for fast-motion mismatch compensation.
Evaluated on rope tracking, obstacle avoidance, and disturbance rejection in simulation and hardware.
Generalizes to unseen trajectories without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning; reduces longest-task tracking RMSE by 44.0% and planning time by 29–66% versus relevant baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal MPC for deformable-object manipulation is relevant to robotic manipulation and control.
papers.title: Multimodal MPC via Bayesian Set Optimization for Dynamic Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects
papers.tldr: BM2PC enables fast, accurate dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects by maintaining diverse control modes within a Bayesian MPC framework and compensating for execution mismatch.

papers.abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.
authors: Chubin Zhang, Changyuan Wang, Yirui Wang, Ao Li, Shilin Ma, Yue Su, Cai Zhou, Xiuwei Xu, Tianle Zhang, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of robot demonstrations and noisy action labels from egocentric videos.
Jointly learns visual future prediction and action generation in a vision-language-action framework.
Uses reliability-conditioned corruption and weighted regression to reduce the impact of unreliable action supervision.
Distills action-relevant structure from clean future observations into representations trained with corrupted futures.
Shows steeper scaling than a baseline, with 20.5% lower real-world open-loop action MSE and an 8.1-point RoboCasa few-shot success improvement at 30,000 pretraining hours.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-action framework that scales policy learning with noisy egocentric human videos, combining reliability-aware action learning and future-representation distillation.
papers.title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
papers.tldr: EgoForesight scales robot policy learning with noisy egocentric video actions by weighting supervision by reliability and learning from demonstrated future outcomes.

papers.abstract: How do children learn the meanings of the simple, concrete words that form a majority of their early vocabulary? Statistical information about many word meanings can be recovered from the gradual accumulation of information about the co-occurrence of words with their referents, a proposal known as ``cross-situational learning''. Contrastive vision--language models allow this learning strategy to be tested on egocentric video data capturing children's early real-life experiences with visual and linguistic inputs. Initial successes of this method on small datasets provide a proof-of-concept, but vision models struggle to learn robust visual representations when trained on these same egocentric videos. How dependent is cross-situational word learning performance on the quality of the model's visual representations? And can cross-situational models scale to larger and more diverse datasets? To address these questions, we trained models on the BabyView corpus, including 2,441 hours of longitudinal egocentric video from 48 children. Models trained on this dataset learned object--label mappings, but performance was far higher when they used internet-pretrained visual representations as opposed to when visual representations were learned solely from the developmental video data. Further, the majority of the learning signal was carried by a small proportion of utterances that described a visible referent. Models learned lexical representations that showed recognizable human-like semantic structure, but model performance showed substantially different trajectories over training experiences than those observed in children. Cross-situational learning is a viable word learning strategy for early noun vocabulary, but constructing developmentally plausible models will require understanding how to learn high-quality visual representations from naturalistic data.
authors: Michael C. Frank, Alvin W. M. Tan, Khai Loong Aw, Robert Z. Sparks, Victor Moreno, Grace Keene-Lee, Meesha R. Ryan, Tarun Sepuri, Jane Yang, Virginia A. Marchman, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Bria Long
bullets: Models trained on 2,441 hours of egocentric video from 48 children learned object–label mappings.
Internet-pretrained visual representations substantially outperformed representations learned only from the developmental videos.
Most learning came from utterances describing a currently visible referent.
The learned lexical representations developed recognizable human-like semantic structure.
Model learning trajectories differed substantially from those observed in children.
papers.selection_reason: Scales cross-situational word learning from egocentric child video, fitting embodied knowledge acquisition from human egocentric experience.
papers.title: Scaling cross-situational word learning on children's naturalistic experiences
papers.tldr: Cross-situational learning can recover early word meanings from large-scale child-centered video, but it depends strongly on high-quality visual representations and does not yet match children’s learning trajectories.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can translate language instructions into robot programs. For contact-rich manipulation, a key challenge is to generate and refine control logic that responds to physical interaction. We present FORCA, a coding agent that takes visual observations and wrist force/torque (F/T) measurements as input to write Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion. Between executions, the agent inspects force records alongside visual outcomes to diagnose failures and revise both motion and force-feedback control logic. FORCA requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation. Across five real-robot tasks, we demonstrate its effectiveness in three forms of contact-rich manipulation: improving manipulation accuracy, adapting to changes in object or surface properties, and regulating contact under surface variation and object motion. Compared with a vision-only variant of the same agent, FORCA improves grasp accuracy and task success and reduces contact loss in wiping and peeling.
authors: Xiao Tan, Yixuan Wang, Zhexi Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting control logic to physical contact during manipulation.
Writes Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion using visual and F/T observations.
Analyzes force records and visual outcomes after execution to diagnose failures and revise control logic.
Requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation.
Across five real-robot tasks, improves grasp accuracy and task success while reducing contact loss versus a vision-only agent.
papers.selection_reason: A force-aware coding agent for contact-rich manipulation is directly relevant to robot manipulation.
papers.title: FORCA: A Force-Aware Coding Agent for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: FORCA is a force-aware coding agent that uses vision and wrist force/torque feedback to iteratively generate and refine robot programs for contact-rich manipulation.

papers.abstract: Temporary traffic control redirects vehicles through work zones, requiring automated vehicles to connect an interpretation of the visible devices to a continuous passing path. Geometric predictors can provide several plausible paths, yet selecting the one consistent with the temporary control remains difficult. We propose SAGE (Semantic-to-Action Grounded Execution), a read-decide-execute-check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a shared candidate space. The central idea is to use a vision-language model's (VLM's) trajectory as a preference over intact geometric candidates. A role-decoupled generator constructs the candidates, and rank fusion combines each candidate's geometric score with its agreement with the VLM trajectory. Supervision structured around the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) trains SAGE-VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The predicted hazard side enters image-space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, which support a final intervention bounded in score and displacement. On 2,306 real-world ROADWork validation episodes, the candidates include a path within 10 px of the human demonstration in 87% of episodes, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker's error. SAGE reduces average and final displacement errors by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to the ranker, mostly in the far field, and hard-constraint violations by 37%. The trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator-selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to state-of-the-art VLM modules in accuracy, with a faster-responding VLM, and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/SAGE-page/.
authors: Jiaxi Liu, Keshu Wu, Weizhe Tang, Bofeng Cao, Sikai Chen, Xiaopeng Li, Steven T. Parker, Bin Ran
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing the correct path among multiple geometrically plausible work-zone routes.
Generates candidate paths geometrically, then fuses geometric scores with agreement to a VLM-predicted trajectory.
Trains the VLM to identify lane status and hazard side before making a passage decision, with rule-based intervention for control compliance.
On 2,306 ROADWork episodes, SAGE reduces average displacement error by 8.3%, final displacement error by 12.0%, and hard-constraint violations by 37% versus the geometric ranker.
The approach improves all tested generator-selector combinations and is competitive with or better than adapted driving VLMs on reported accuracy and safety measures.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-grounded pathway prediction for work-zone driving, combining geometric candidate generation with spatial/control reasoning; relevant to robot navigation and spatial VLM grounding.
papers.title: SAGE: A hybrid vision-language and geometry framework for work-zone pathway prediction under temporary traffic control
papers.tldr: SAGE combines geometric candidate paths with vision-language reasoning to select safer, MUTCD-compliant routes through temporary work zones.

papers.abstract: Real-world reinforcement learning has enabled contact-rich manipulation tasks to be trained directly on physical robots, but unsafe interactions during online learning remain a key barrier to practical deployment. We propose Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning (SEVI), a framework for reliability-aware safety intervention during real-world policy learning. SEVI introduces an Evidential Safety Critic that estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. During online learning, SEVI evaluates each task-policy action before execution; if the action is predicted to be unsafe or the prediction is insufficiently supported by evidence, SEVI overrides it with an offline-trained recovery policy that guides the robot toward a lower-risk region. We evaluate SEVI on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task under in-distribution and distribution-shifted conditions. Across task-learning and safety-critic baselines, SEVI achieves the strongest trajectory-level safety prediction, the highest final task success, and the lowest unsafe-event counts. SEVI also reduces unsafe events by 13.4 to 57.1 percent relative to recovery-based safe RL while preserving low-latency execution-time filtering. The project page is available at: https://sevi-safe.github.io/
bullets: Targets unsafe online interactions that hinder deployment of real-world reinforcement learning.
Uses an Evidential Safety Critic to estimate future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in one forward pass.
Overrides actions predicted unsafe or insufficiently supported with an offline-trained recovery policy.
Evaluated on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task under in-distribution and shifted conditions.
Reports the strongest trajectory-level safety prediction, highest final task success, and 13.4–57.1% fewer unsafe events than recovery-based safe RL, with low-latency filtering.
papers.selection_reason: Directly relevant to safe reinforcement learning for real-world robot manipulation with an evidential safety critic.
papers.title: SEVI: Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: SEVI improves the safety and success of real-world robot reinforcement learning by filtering uncertain or risky actions and replacing them with recovery behavior.

papers.abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for learning robot behaviors aligned with human intent. However, its scalability is fundamentally limited by the need to collect expensive human preference labels for every new task. In this work, we present PrefO2O, an offline-to-online latent preference transfer framework that enables zero-shot PbRL on unseen target tasks without requiring any human feedback. The core idea is to learn a task-invariant latent preference space from a small amount of offline preference data on source tasks, where transferable preference structures are disentangled from task-specific variations. This learned manifold allows PrefO2O to transfer preference structures and reward priors to new tasks under distribution shift, while confidence-weighted optimal transport alignment generates reliable pseudo-preference supervision for online reward adaptation. Extensive experiments on robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrate that PrefO2O substantially outperforms existing preference-transfer baselines and matches or exceeds PbRL methods trained with real human feedback, while generalizing across multi-to-one and one-to-one transfer settings as well as across different robot embodiments.
authors: Ruiqi Wang, Dezhong Zhao, Xuesu Xiao, Erdem Biyik, Byung-Cheol Min, Guohua Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability problem of collecting human preference labels for every new task.
Learns a task-invariant latent preference space that separates transferable preferences from task-specific variations.
Uses confidence-weighted optimal transport to align new tasks and generate pseudo-preference supervision for online reward adaptation.
Evaluated on robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks across multi-to-one, one-to-one, and cross-embodiment transfer settings.
Reportedly outperforms preference-transfer baselines and matches or exceeds methods trained with real human feedback.
papers.selection_reason: Preference transfer for zero-shot robot RL; directly on robotic manipulation and locomotion.
papers.title: PrefO2O: Zero-Shot Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning via Offline-to-Online Latent Preference Transfer
papers.tldr: PrefO2O enables zero-shot preference-based reinforcement learning on unseen robot tasks by transferring latent human preference structures from offline source-task data without new human feedback.

papers.abstract: Segmenting robot demonstration data into disjoint temporal and semantic subsegments is valuable for learning, cleaning, retrieval, and analysis. Segmentation is often performed manually in a tedious and error prone process. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have the potential for automating this process, but directly ingesting raw multi camera video streams into MLLMs can be costly and can quickly exhaust context windows. In this paper, we introduce KiRoSe (Kinematics for Robot Segmentation), a novel framework that focuses on the companion stream of robot kinematic data. Inspired by the principle of classical entropy coding, such as Huffman coding, where frequently occurring symbols are represented more compactly, we propose Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs), a discrete kinematic vocabulary designed to compactly represent recurring, temporally localized motion patterns, which we refer to as kinematic events. SMTs are learned by encoding kinematic trajectories with temporal segment supervision and quantizing the resulting features. We use increasingly available robot demonstration subtask annotations to supervise an open language model to interpret the resulting token sequences. Evaluation against human labeled segmentation shows that KiRoSe can substantially outperform baseline segmentation methods in F1 quality and transfers zero shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion, while preserving the language models open vocabulary knowledge. Beyond segmentation, KiRoSe tracks task progress on an unseen robot and detects when an action is being reversed.(website: https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/kirose/)
authors: Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Richard Cheng, Sergey Zakharov, Ken Goldberg
bullets: Targets costly, error-prone manual segmentation of robot demonstrations and avoids feeding raw multiview video into language models.
Learns Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs) to compactly encode recurring, temporally localized kinematic patterns.
Uses subtask annotations to supervise an open language model over SMT sequences.
Outperforms baseline segmentation methods in F1 against human labels and transfers zero-shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion.
Also supports task-progress tracking on an unseen robot and detection of action reversal.
papers.selection_reason: Kinematic-token segmentation of robot demonstrations supports robot learning and transfers to human motion.
papers.title: KiRoSe: Using Kinematic Data for Efficient Segmentation of Robot Demonstrations
papers.tldr: KiRoSe efficiently segments robot demonstrations by converting kinematic data into compact motion tokens that an open language model interprets as semantic events.

papers.abstract: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly 125 times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Florais battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.
authors: Sicong Leng, Yunze Man, Zhiqi Li, Jing Wang, Yuhe Zhang, Ryan Punamiya, Siddharth Patki, Kaiyuan Zheng, Zi-ang Cao, Zhiding Yu, Sifei Liu, Danfei Xu, Ben Levin, Jan Kautz, Yuke Zhu, Johan Bjorck, Linxi "Jim" Fan
bullets: Supports outcome rewards for deployment monitoring, process rewards for RL post-training, and timestamped captions for pretraining data curation.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on WGO-Bench, RoboReward, and Robometer.
Competes with GPT-6 Astra on internal benchmarks while costing roughly 125× less than API-based alternatives.
Processes 200,000 hours of robotics data daily across 512 GB300 GPUs.
Open-sourcing enables custom robotics datasets and applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.
papers.selection_reason: An open data-labeling and reward-model engine for robotics foundation models is relevant to embodied robot learning.
papers.title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines
papers.tldr: Flora is an open, scalable data engine that generates key labels for training and deploying robotics foundation models.

papers.abstract: What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely leave representation design to the encoders' pretraining objectives. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self-constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy's own objectives from vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three-layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain-of-thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end-to-end with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On VLNVerse fine-grained, RepresentNav achieves 83.80% success, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT-Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). With the same encoders, the self-constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot's own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.
authors: Jiawei Chen, Yinxi Wang, Zihan Yang, Meijun Gao, Yaowei Liu, Shuming Zhang, Zecheng Li, Xiangju Mi, Yuxuan Liu, Runzhong Huang, Tianlin Li, Xun Zhang, Zhengyang Wang, Xu Miao, Tong Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of relying directly on representations shaped by generic vision pretraining.
Uses Representation Residuals, a compact transformer over multilevel features from multiple vision foundation models.
Jointly trains navigation with a JEPA-style latent “dream” that predicts the next scene representation before each action.
Reports new state-of-the-art results across VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and point-goal benchmarks, with gains transferring to a physical robot.
The learned latent predicts future depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy without direct occupancy supervision; its scope is navigation-focused and evaluated on the stated benchmarks and robot setting.
papers.selection_reason: Navigation foundation model with self-constructed visual representations and latent next-state prediction; state-of-the-art on VLN and robot navigation benchmarks.
papers.title: See What I Need, Dream What I Want: A Navigation Foundation Model on a Self-Constructed Representation Space
papers.tldr: RepresentNav learns a task-specific visual representation and predicts future scene states in latent space, substantially improving navigation and reducing collisions across simulated and real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Movement primitives commonly represent robot mo- tions through basis functions indexed by time or phase. Inspired by spacetime representations employed in physics, we propose a spline-based formulation in which spatial geometry and temporal progression are represented within a common set of continuous variables. The proposed method jointly estimates a shared Bezier curve, while allowing spatial and temporal model complexity to be adapted independently (e.g., demonstration-specific phase modulation). As use case, we consider an alternating optimization process that simultaneously estimates path intervals observed in partial demonstrations. Simulation experiments demonstrate accurate joint recovery, refinement through modifications in model complexity and continuity, and improved robustness to variance in the demonstration set. Finally, we demonstrate online retiming and synchronization capabilities in a patient-turning task assisted by a robot, evaluated with a physical manikin.
bullets: Represents spatial paths and temporal progression using shared continuous Bezier-curve variables.
Adapts spatial and temporal model complexity independently, including demonstration-specific phase modulation.
Uses alternating optimization to recover path intervals from partial demonstrations.
Simulations show accurate joint recovery and improved robustness to demonstration variance.
A physical-manikin patient-turning task demonstrates online retiming and synchronization.
papers.selection_reason: Spline-based movement primitive representation for adaptive robot motions from demonstrations, relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: Spacetime Splines for Adaptive Robot Motions
papers.tldr: Spacetime Splines jointly model robot motion geometry and timing with adaptable complexity, enabling robust learning, online retiming, and synchronization.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation, requiring robots to regulate not only motion but also how they yield to external forces, has emerged as the next frontier for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing VLAs output purely kinematic commands, degrading performance on real-world contact-rich tasks. In this paper, we introduce CompVLA, a unified VLA framework that jointly predicts motion and stiffness matrix from RGB and language inputs. Our approach augments the conventional architecture with a dedicated Compliance Expert, which outputs time-varying stiffness and virtual displacement profiles executed via geometric impedance control. We demonstrate that CompVLA achieves the highest average success rate across diverse contact-rich tasks, outperforming both vanilla and compliance-aware VLA baselines, with ablations confirming each component is essential.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of VLAs that produce only kinematic commands and cannot regulate responses to external forces.
Adds a dedicated Compliance Expert to predict time-varying stiffness and virtual displacement profiles.
Executes predictions through geometric impedance control for contact-aware behavior.
Achieves the highest average success rate across diverse contact-rich tasks against vanilla and compliance-aware VLA baselines.
Ablations indicate that each component is essential to the framework.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model jointly predicting motion and compliance/stiffness for contact-rich manipulation directly targets embodied robot policy learning.
papers.title: CompVLA: A Variable Compliance Vision-Language-Action Model for Contact-rich Manipulation
papers.tldr: CompVLA enables vision-language-action models to perform contact-rich manipulation by jointly predicting robot motion and variable compliance from visual and language inputs.

papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress, generalist robot policies remain brittle on complex, long-horizon tasks that comprise multiple stages or require repeated attempts and deliberation on the same underlying stage before success. Q-value functions can improve these policies by ranking candidate actions or guiding policy improvement, but learning from sparse task-level rewards entails long credit-assignment horizons, difficult Bellman backups, and broad data-coverage requirements. We introduce SeeQ (Subtask-elicited Q-functions), which instead learns Q-values for the currently active subtask. This shortens the value-prediction horizon and enables effective learning with temporal-difference (TD) objectives. During training, subtask-level annotations present in offline robot data provide the decomposition and enable learning from broad, potentially suboptimal robot datasets. To eliminate the need for human annotations or modular subtask prediction systems at test time, our Q-function architecture is trained to autoregressively predict the active subtask in natural language before estimating its value. We instantiate SeeQ using a base vision-language backbone, pretrain it on diverse open-source robot manipulation data, and finetune it on downstream tasks. Across four real-world manipulation tasks on two bimanual robot platforms, the SeeQ value function substantially improves best-of-N policy steering.
bullets: Long-horizon tasks challenge generalist robot policies because sparse rewards create difficult credit assignment and Bellman backups.
SeeQ learns Q-values for the currently active subtask rather than the entire task, shortening the prediction horizon.
Offline robot-data annotations provide subtask decompositions and support learning from broad, potentially suboptimal datasets.
The model autoregressively predicts the active subtask in natural language, avoiding human annotations or modular subtask predictors at test time.
Across four real-world tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, SeeQ substantially improves best-of-N policy steering.
papers.selection_reason: Subtasks as natural-language-conditioned Q-functions for long-horizon manipulation, directly fitting robot learning and control.
papers.title: SeeQ: Training Generalist Value Functions for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: SeeQ trains value functions around active subtasks to improve long-horizon robotic manipulation through better action ranking and policy steering.

papers.abstract: Safe whole-body control requires coordinating collision avoidance and balance under high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics--making safety certificates difficult to design and reuse across behaviors. We present LIMBO, a framework for synthesizing a state-action control barrier function and distilling its safety structure into a task policy. LIMBO learns the safety certificate from black-box transitions and a state-based failure specification over residual actions around a frozen base controller, making Q-CBF synthesis tractable in the full control dimension while placing the certificate in the task policy's control space. During synthesis, the learned safety value drives risk-guided sampling near the estimated boundary of recoverability; during task learning, it serves as a teacher that provides action-level safety feedback, yielding a robust task policy and alleviating the need for an online safety filter at deployment. We demonstrate LIMBO on a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid performing dodgeball avoidance and locomotion beneath low obstacles. Beyond scaling learned Q-CBFs to whole-body control, we show that risk-guided boundary sampling provides a theoretically grounded way to explore the edge of recoverability. Under the same safety specification, ceteris paribus, varying the sampling concentration produces strategies ranging from crouching to a novel backward-leaning limbo maneuver. In both settings, the learned policies transfer to hardware without online safety filtering, showing that learned safety synthesis scales to agile whole-body control.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating collision avoidance and balance under high-dimensional, nonlinear humanoid dynamics.
Learns a state-action control barrier function from black-box transitions and failure specifications around a frozen base controller.
Uses risk-guided sampling near the boundary of recoverability and safety feedback to train the task policy.
Demonstrated on a 29-DoF humanoid for dodgeball avoidance and locomotion under low obstacles.
Sampling concentration changes the resulting strategy, including crouching and a novel backward-leaning limbo maneuver; policies transfer to hardware without online filtering.
papers.selection_reason: Learned safety certificates and task policies for agile whole-body humanoid control, transferable to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: LIMBO: Learning and Internalizing Model-Free Barrier Objectives for Agile and Safe Whole-Body Control
papers.tldr: LIMBO learns safety certificates and distills them into whole-body task policies that perform agile, hardware-transferred behaviors without an online safety filter.

papers.abstract: Automatic dense packing is widely desired in warehouse operations but remains a fundamental challenge in robotic manipulation. Existing work on irregular-object packing largely targets simulation with idealized contact, treating the object as an isolated rigid body. The gripper often enters as a discrete, post-hoc feasibility check, if considered at all, and the perception and contact drift accumulated during execution are not addressed. We present a closed-loop pipeline that integrates perception, gripper-aware placement optimization, and force-guided execution on a real manipulator. The optimizer represents the object together with the gripper as a single composite body of hierarchical sphere trees. It searches over five degrees of freedom on a GPU within a CMA-ES framework, with the vertical coordinate grounded analytically against the current heightmap. During execution, a force-monitored vertical descent stops on first contact. A post-release consolidation push then closes the residual lateral clearance that gripper-aware planning leaves behind. The container is re-perceived between placements so that drift does not accumulate. We validate the system on a Franka Emika Panda robot packing a 3D-printed set of flat, curved, and concave objects, and a YCB object subset. An ablation study isolates the contribution of gripper-aware optimization, the consolidation push, and mesh-derived geometry to end-to-end success, achieved density, and computational cost. We further benchmark against the heightmap-minimization method as a baseline representative of prior irregular-object packing work.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of simulation-focused packing methods that ignore gripper geometry and execution-time perception/contact drift.
Optimizes the object–gripper composite shape using hierarchical sphere trees, GPU-accelerated CMA-ES, and analytical grounding from a heightmap.
Uses force-monitored descent for first-contact placement, followed by a consolidation push to reduce residual lateral gaps.
Re-perceives the container between placements to prevent drift accumulation.
Validated on a Franka Panda with 3D-printed and YCB objects, including ablations and comparison with heightmap minimization.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop robotic dense packing with gripper-aware placement and force-guided execution; fits robot manipulation.
papers.title: Gripper-Aware Automatic Dense Packing of Irregular Objects
papers.tldr: A closed-loop robot system enables dense packing of irregular objects by jointly planning around the gripper, sensing contact, and consolidating placements after release.

papers.abstract: Effective exploration in high-dimensional continuous control remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning. Planning-based methods address this by combining online planning with learned policies and value functions, but their components can become misaligned during training: learned sampling policies may diverge from planner behavior, while planning distributions stored in replay become stale as the model and value function evolve. Reanalysis can refresh these targets, but at substantial computational cost. We propose GEM-MPC, an MPPI-based reinforcement learning method that improves the interaction between planning and learning. GEM-MPC uses MPPI to combine a policy trained to clone the planner with a KL-regularized policy that explores around it, providing complementary exploitation and guided exploration within planning. We further introduce Gated Prior Distillation, which selectively learns from stored planning distributions only when they provide a better target than the current prior, reducing the impact of stale planning data without requiring full reanalysis. Across continuous-control benchmarks, GEM-MPC consistently outperforms existing planning-based baselines under lower computational budgets.
bullets: Addresses misalignment between learned policies, planners, and stale planning distributions in replay.
Uses MPPI to combine a planner-cloning policy for exploitation with a KL-regularized policy for guided exploration.
Introduces Gated Prior Distillation, which adopts stored planning targets only when they improve on the current prior.
Outperforms existing planning-based baselines across continuous-control benchmarks under lower computational budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Planning-based RL method for continuous control with guided exploration; directly transferable to robot policy learning.
papers.title: GEM-MPC: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation through Expert-Guided Planning
papers.tldr: GEM-MPC improves efficient exploration in continuous-control reinforcement learning by combining expert-guided MPPI planning with selective learning from replayed planning data.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion over complex terrain requires anticipating footholds that may no longer be visible at touchdown. Limited camera coverage and self-occlusion make it necessary to retrieve relevant terrain information from earlier observations. We present FootQuery, a perceptive locomotion framework that queries depth history using each foot's predicted next touchdown. The policy predicts touchdown locations and uncertainty from proprioception and uses these distributions, together with per-foot features, to query sparsely sampled historical depth frames. During training, realized contacts are projected into historical images to supervise retrieval at the regions where those contacts were visible. The retrieved per-foot features are fused with global visual memory to generate control actions. A progressive force-assistance curriculum supports early exploration, while event-consistent tread-midline shaping encourages coordinated stair contacts. Deployment requires only proprioception and onboard depth images. In simulation, the complete framework outperforms its component ablations on the most challenging tested stairs, gaps, and platforms. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 demonstrate continuous traversal with a single policy across outdoor stairs and indoor routes combining stair ascent and descent, platforms, and gaps. These results support organizing visual history around anticipated contacts for perceptive humanoid locomotion.
bullets: Addresses limited camera coverage and self-occlusion that can hide footholds before touchdown.
Predicts per-foot touchdown locations and uncertainty from proprioception, then queries relevant regions in sparsely sampled historical depth frames.
Supervises retrieval using projected realized contacts and fuses retrieved per-foot features with global visual memory for control.
Uses force-assistance curriculum training and tread-midline shaping to support exploration and coordinated stair contacts.
Outperforms component ablations in challenging simulated terrain and enables real-world traversal of stairs, platforms, and gaps with one policy.
papers.selection_reason: Future-touchdown-guided depth history retrieval for humanoid locomotion fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: FootQuery: Future-Touchdown-Guided Retrieval from Depth History for Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
papers.tldr: FootQuery improves humanoid locomotion on complex terrain by retrieving historical depth information around each foot’s predicted future touchdown location.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.
bullets: Addresses compounding errors and costly search in long-horizon manipulation.
Uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation with learned policy proposals and value estimates.
Distills searched plans into the policy-value model through GPU-parallelized simulation.
The resulting model can act without simulator-based search at test time.
Outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines in simulated and real-world tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Long-horizon manipulation policy learned by distilling MCTS plans fits embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
papers.tldr: DISCO transfers long-horizon MCTS reasoning into a deployable policy for continuous-action multi-object rearrangement.

papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle perception is challenging for small autonomous surface vessels (ASVs): reflections and glare confound visible-light cameras, vessel motion shifts the apparent waterline, and darkness removes the dominant sensing modality altogether. Rather than treating multimodal fusion as a static accuracy gain, we propose a context-aware architecture that combines RGB and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imagery, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) mmWave radar, and inertial context. A bearing-sector interface provides the navigation controller with calibrated obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status. It also distinguishes sensor dropout from a valid observation with no detected obstacle. Using new multimodal lake recordings, we deployed the pipeline in a 24-leg closed-loop pilot under uncontrolled lake conditions (16 day, 4 dusk, and 4 night; 351 m), including night legs in which RGB was unusable and the vessel drove on LWIR and radar evidence alone. On eight held-out low-light recordings, the calibrated fusion model achieved average precision (AP) 0.869 and expected calibration error 0.108, compared with AP 0.673 for rule-based fusion, 0.620 for gated fusion, and 0.903 for RGB alone. Our results expose a central tradeoff: RGB ranks best when usable, whereas fusion preserves a navigation input when RGB fails. This work is a step toward perception that remains usable and degrades predictably across multi-day ASV missions.
bullets: Targets reflections, glare, motion-induced waterline shifts, and darkness that undermine RGB-based obstacle detection.
Fuses RGB, LWIR, FMCW mmWave radar, and inertial context, exposing calibrated bearing-sector obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status to navigation.
Distinguishes sensor dropout from valid obstacle-free observations, supporting predictable degradation during multimodal failures.
In eight held-out low-light recordings, calibrated fusion reached AP 0.869 and ECE 0.108; RGB alone had higher AP (0.903) when usable, while fusion preserved sensing when RGB failed.
A 24-leg, 351 m lake pilot included night operation using LWIR and radar without usable RGB; scope is limited to the reported lake recordings and pilot conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Context-aware multimodal obstacle perception and sensor-status modeling support autonomous surface vessel navigation.
papers.title: Context-Aware RGB-Thermal-Radar Obstacle Perception for Resource-Constrained ASVs
papers.tldr: A context-aware RGB-LWIR-radar fusion system helps resource-constrained ASVs maintain calibrated obstacle perception when RGB cameras degrade or fail, including at night.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur. Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities. These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.
bullets: State hallucination occurs when a VLA acts as though an unrealized robot-object state has been achieved.
The failure is associated with reduced attention to task-relevant visual regions and activation of specific sparse autoencoder features.
SOUL unlearns hallucination-related policy knowledge while retaining features associated with successful behaviors.
Experiments across simulated and real-world settings and multiple VLA architectures reduce hallucinated failures and improve task success.
The approach is evaluated specifically for state hallucination and aims to preserve existing manipulation capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses state hallucination in vision-language-action robot policies using sparse-feature unlearning.
papers.title: Sparse Feature Policy Unlearning Mitigates State Hallucination in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: SOUL selectively removes sparse features linked to state hallucination in vision-language-action policies, reducing these failures while preserving manipulation ability.

papers.abstract: Physical control tasks in the natural world, such as driving or object manipulation, frequently exhibit dramatic variations in sensory and compute complexity over time.
