Correspondingly, a natural resource-efficient choice for robot control is to dynamically switch between control modes with varying resource allocations. However, such "mode-switching controllers" (MSCs) have historically required laborious, expert-driven design and synthesis for each new task. Driven by these design difficulties, modern robotic control architectures often fall back to a wasteful "monolithic" one-size-fits-all structure, where resource allocation is permanently anchored to the hardest, most resource-intensive task phases. To facilitate the design of performant yet efficient MSCs, we propose LLM-Guided synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures (LEMCA). LEMCA represents MSC designs as interpretable programs to be iteratively refined in an evolutionary loop. To evaluate design fitness, we propose MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis approaches, such as reinforcement learning in simulation. LEMCA then leverages the semantic priors, reasoning, and coding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively edit controller modes, their corresponding sensory-compute resource allocations, and mode transitions. Our experiments across diverse control benchmarks show that LEMCA consistently discovers strategies that surpass the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming wasted resources during "easy" task phases. LEMCA thus presents an automated, low-effort path to synthesize resource-efficient MSC designs.
bullets: Addresses the expert effort required to design mode-switching controllers (MSCs) for tasks with varying sensory and compute demands.
Represents MSCs as interpretable programs and iteratively refines their modes, resource allocations, and transitions.
Evaluates candidate designs with MSC-compatible controller synthesis, including reinforcement learning in simulation.
Experiments across diverse control benchmarks show LEMCA surpasses monolithic designs’ Pareto frontier by reclaiming resources during easier phases.
Provides an automated, low-effort approach for synthesizing efficient MSC architectures.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-guided evolutionary synthesis of mode-switching robot controllers that reduce resource use; relevant to robot control and efficient AI.
papers.title: LEMCA: LLM-Guided Synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures
papers.tldr: LEMCA uses LLM-guided evolutionary program synthesis to automatically design resource-efficient robot controllers that switch modes as task difficulty changes.

papers.abstract: Human-readable maps provide an intuitive interface for specifying robot destinations, but connecting their schematic geometry to egocentric observations remains challenging. We present NaViRRator, a framework that translates user-specified start and goal locations on such maps into navigation instructions for a pretrained vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policy. Its core method, RouteScribe, separates route inference from verbalization by first generating an explicit route scaffold in map-image coordinates, which a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) converts into a navigation instruction. We construct the scaffold with start--goal line conditional flow matching (SGL-CFM), which deforms a straight start--goal waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route. During execution, the VLN policy receives only the instruction and egocentric observations, while the map and scaffold remain upstream, allowing executor replacement without retraining the map-to-language modules. Real-world experiments show higher success rates and success weighted by path length (SPL) than direct map-to-instruction generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source conditional flow matching. Qualitative results further show clearer salient turns and better preservation of the intended maneuver sequence, supporting route-grounded language as a modular interface between human-readable maps and pretrained navigation policies.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting schematic map geometry with a robot’s first-person visual navigation.
RouteScribe separates route inference from verbalization by generating an explicit map-coordinate route scaffold before producing instructions.
Uses start–goal line conditional flow matching to deform a straight waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route.
Real-world experiments report higher success rate and SPL than direct generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source flow matching.
The modular design keeps maps and scaffolds upstream, enabling executor replacement without retraining map-to-language modules.
papers.selection_reason: Map-based route scaffolding converted into instructions for a pretrained VLN policy; directly addresses vision-language navigation.
papers.title: NaViRrator: Robot Navigation from Human-Readable Maps through a Learned Visual Route
papers.tldr: NaViRRator converts human-readable map destinations into route-grounded language instructions that pretrained vision-language navigation policies can execute from egocentric observations.

papers.abstract: Although conventional controllers and disturbance observers (DOBs) are the standard for precision tracking in manipulators, they suffer from parameter uncertainty, nonlinear friction, and compound disturbances. This study proposes a residual reinforcement learning DOB framework that pairs an analytical observer with an RL policy. The deterministic baseline operates within a reliable region, whereas the RL policy explicitly targets the residuals that the model cannot capture. To make this compensation disturbance-aware, an estimator network aligns the observation history with a privileged disturbance context, organizing the latent space by disturbance regime and enabling rapid adaptation across disturbance transitions. To guarantee stability, we derived and enforced a state-dependent action bound on the RL policy from an input-to-state stability (ISS) analysis such that the closed loop provably confines the tracking error to a certified envelope for arbitrary policy outputs. Experiments on a 6-DOF manipulator demonstrated consistent improvements in disturbance estimation and tracking, including a 27.8% tracking-error reduction on real hardware under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and a 38.0% reduction under a base-vibration disturbance that was not observed during training.
bullets: Combines an analytical disturbance observer with RL that learns only unmodeled residual dynamics.
Uses a disturbance-aware estimator to organize latent representations by disturbance regime and adapt across transitions.
Derives an ISS-based, state-dependent action bound that guarantees the closed-loop tracking error remains within a certified envelope.
On a 6-DOF manipulator, reduced tracking error by 27.8% in zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and 38.0% under unseen base vibration.
papers.selection_reason: Residual reinforcement learning for manipulator disturbance compensation with stability-certified action bounds; relevant to robot learning and control.
papers.title: Stability-aware Residual Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robotic Manipulator Disturbance Compensation
papers.tldr: A stability-constrained residual RL observer improves robotic-manipulator disturbance compensation while preserving a provable tracking-error bound.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors are increasingly deployed in applications such as agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and maintenance. In each of these applications, the robot must navigate complex scene geometry while remaining strictly collision-free. Unlike in ground domains, even minor collisions for aerial vehicles can result in the loss of the robot. This safety requirement induces a pair of technical challenges. First, the environment must be represented with sufficient fidelity to encode complex structure, even when no ground-truth obstacle data is available. Second, a motion planner must leverage this representation to determine a collision-free path to the goal. This paper proposes a system that addresses these complementary challenges. The proposed method, AirSplan, adopts a normalized variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that encodes high-fidelity scene geometry. It then applies a novel reachability-based motion planner that leverages the differential flatness of quadrotors to compute continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate the robot's occupancy. Experiments demonstrate that AirSplan successfully finds a path in 81.2% of challenging test cases, a significant improvement over the nearest baseline method's 51.2%.
bullets: Addresses safe aerial navigation when accurate ground-truth obstacle data is unavailable.
Uses a normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to encode detailed scene geometry.
Introduces a reachability-based planner exploiting quadrotor differential flatness.
Computes continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate vehicle occupancy.
Finds paths in 81.2% of challenging test cases, compared with 51.2% for the nearest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Risk-aware quadrotor motion planning using a normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representation; relevant to robot navigation and 3D scene modeling.
papers.title: AirSplan: Risk-Aware Motion Planning for Quadrotors in Cluttered 3D Gaussian Splats
papers.tldr: AirSplan combines high-fidelity 3D Gaussian Splatting with risk-aware reachability planning to find collision-free quadrotor paths in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: Generative robot policies can represent diverse, multimodal behaviors, but adapting pretrained policies to deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance remains challenging. Existing inference-time steering methods typically apply gradient guidance through iterative diffusion or flow processes, which can be computationally expensive for real-time control. We propose INSPO, which formulates inference-time steering of one-step generative policies as trajectory optimization in the policy's input noise space. By optimizing the input noise while evaluating constraints on the induced state trajectory, INSPO searches the policy-induced behavior space without directly modifying generated actions. The optimization includes a regularization term that encourages solutions to remain consistent with the policy's input distribution and is solved online using population-based particle optimization. We evaluate INSPO on state- and image-based task-specific policies and generalist vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial. INSPO improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while comparing favorably with gradient-guided generation at lower runtime.
bullets: Addresses deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance in diverse generative robot policies.
Optimizes policy input noise while evaluating constraints on the resulting state trajectory, preserving the policy’s behavior space.
Uses distribution-consistency regularization and online population-based particle optimization.
Evaluated on state-, image-, and vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial.
Improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while achieving lower runtime than gradient-guided generation.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time steering of one-step generative robot policies via noise-space trajectory optimization; applies to VLA policies and manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Safe Real-Time Policy Steering via Noise-Space Trajectory Optimization for One-Step Generative Policies
papers.tldr: INSPO enables real-time constraint-aware steering of one-step generative robot policies by optimizing their input noise instead of repeatedly modifying actions or generation steps.

papers.abstract: Collision-free motion planning requires reliable collision models from sensed environments and validation of states along a continuous trajectory. To make this tractable, most planners check for collision at discrete states along continuous trajectories against a single determinized model of the environment, introducing a trade-off between safety and computational efficiency. While continuous collision checking approaches that approximate the swept volume of the robot exist, they are computationally expensive or overly conservative. Data-driven approaches can learn the swept volume; however, these neural models are susceptible to approximation errors and are therefore often limited to serving as coarse filters for downstream collision checkers. In this work, we propose to learn a signed distance function of the swept volume as a probabilistic field, enabling quantification of epistemic uncertainty, incorporation of perception noise, and eventual integration into a chance-constrained trajectory optimization framework. We demonstrate our approach on challenging high-dimensional manipulation problems with significant sensor noise, both in simulation and on real hardware.
bullets: Addresses the safety–efficiency trade-off of discrete collision checks and costly or conservative continuous swept-volume approximations.
Learns the swept volume as a probabilistic signed distance field rather than a deterministic neural approximation.
Models epistemic uncertainty and incorporates perception noise for more reliable collision reasoning.
Targets integration with chance-constrained trajectory optimization.
Demonstrated on high-dimensional manipulation tasks in simulation and on real hardware with significant sensor noise.
papers.selection_reason: Learned probabilistic swept-volume signed distance field for chance-constrained trajectory optimization; relevant to learned planning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Stochastic Neural Signed Swept Volume for Real-time Chance-Constrained Trajectory Optimization
papers.tldr: A probabilistic neural signed-distance model of robot swept volumes enables uncertainty-aware, chance-constrained trajectory optimization under noisy perception.

papers.abstract: Multi-party human-robot collaboration poses a dual challenge: robot decisions should remain interpretable and auditable, while executed actions must satisfy safety constraints during physical interaction. Combining explainable decision-tree policies with control-barrier-function (CBF) filtering provides a promising architecture but creates two learning mismatches in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Safety projection changes the action applied to the environment, while the coupled proposal graph can misalign independently optimized actor updates with a team-level update. We present safety-aligned gradient enforcement (SAGE) to address both mismatches. Its shield-annealed internalization layer (SAIL) uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program for execution, preserving constraint-normal sensitivity to internalize repeatedly active safety constraints. Team-averaged Lyapunov policy optimization (TALO) constructs a team-aware update reference and applies a Lyapunov half-space correction to regulate independent actor updates. Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrate deployment feasibility. Across nine simulation scenarios, SAGE achieves a 71.0% success rate with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps. Ablations show that direct CBF filtering reduces collision frequency by 98.5% but decreases success from 67.3% to 59.3%. SAIL reduces proposal violation by 48.8% and proposal-execution correction by 85.2%, while TALO reduces the update-consistency gap by 50.8%.
bullets: Addresses two mismatches: CBF safety projection changes executed actions, and independently learned actors can diverge from team-level updates.
SAIL uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map for learning while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program during execution.
TALO provides a team-aware reference and Lyapunov correction to regulate independent actor updates.
In nine simulation scenarios, SAGE achieved 71.0% success with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps.
Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrated deployment feasibility; ablations reduced proposal violations and update inconsistency.
papers.selection_reason: Safety-aligned multi-agent reinforcement learning for human-robot collaboration directly fits learned robot control and manipulation.
papers.title: SAGE: Safety-Aligned Gradient Enforcement for Human--Robot Collaboration
papers.tldr: SAGE aligns multi-agent learning with safety-filtered execution and team objectives for interpretable, safer human–robot collaboration.

papers.abstract: Referring scene understanding for embodied robots requires grounding object- and relation-centric language queries from a designated viewpoint. While a local semantic Gaussian map can support such grounding within one agent's observations, cooperative settings require this ability to remain effective after independently reconstructed maps are aligned and fused. In this setting, the referred target or its contextual landmark may come from another agent's observations, while spatial relations must still be interpreted from the querying robot's viewpoint. We formulate this problem as cooperative referring Gaussian grounding over fused maps, which requires geometric alignability, instance-level semantic comparability, and view-conditioned relation reasoning. Existing language-aware Gaussian methods mainly focus on single-map querying, whereas Gaussian registration methods optimize geometric or photometric alignment without preserving language-grounding-oriented semantic compatibility. We propose CoRef-GS, a cooperative referring Gaussian splatting framework. CoRef-GS constructs local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, then aligns partially overlapping maps with a cross-agent alignment module by geometric and semantic consistency, and grounds queries using a view-conditioned mask relation graph. We further introduce CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark spanning both real-world and simulated indoor scenes. Experiments show that, on simulated scenes, CoRef-GS reduces the rotation error from 2.58° after coarse initialization to 0.15° after refinement, and improves real-world referring mIoU over ReferSplat from 52.6% to 68.8%. The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git.
bullets: Addresses cooperative referring scene understanding when targets or landmarks originate from another agent’s observations.
Builds local open-vocabulary, instance-aware Gaussian maps and aligns them using geometric and semantic consistency.
Uses a view-conditioned mask relation graph to reason about spatial relationships from the querying robot’s viewpoint.
Introduces CoQuad-Ref, a real-world and simulated indoor benchmark.
Refinement reduces simulated rotation error from 2.58° to 0.15°, while real-world referring mIoU improves from 52.6% to 68.8% over ReferSplat.
papers.selection_reason: View-conditioned referring grounding over fused 3D Gaussian maps is a strong spatial-intelligence and embodied perception contribution.
papers.title: CoRef-GS: Cooperative Referring Gaussian Splatting for Multi-Agent Scene Understanding
papers.tldr: CoRef-GS enables viewpoint-aware language grounding across independently built Gaussian maps by jointly aligning their geometry and semantics.

papers.abstract: Tactile signals provide direct contact and force measurements that are essential for understanding physical interactions and enabling dexterous robotic manipulation. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection reliant on intrusive, costly, and restrictive instrumentation. We present TouchSight, a monocular egocentric vision framework for dense full-hand contact force prediction that leverages 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and extensive hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand real-world scenarios, we construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data in which generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations against new backgrounds while preserving the original measured tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos, outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and improves consistently as glove supervision scales. These results demonstrate that dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time.
bullets: Uses 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and hand-object interaction data for supervision.
Introduces TwinTouch-20H, 20 hours of generated paired data that converts gloved views into bare-hand appearances while preserving tactile labels.
Predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos.
Outperforms prior contact-prediction methods on OakInk2 and qualitatively generalizes to unseen natural bare-hand videos.
Performance improves with more glove supervision, eliminating the need for tactile instrumentation during video capture.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts dense tactile/contact forces from egocentric human-object videos, directly supporting dexterous manipulation skill learning.
papers.title: TouchSight: Bare-Handed Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Video via Generative Visual Augmentation
papers.tldr: TouchSight predicts dense full-hand contact forces from egocentric video alone by using generatively augmented glove recordings to bridge the gap to bare-hand interactions.

papers.abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
bullets: Memory gains were highly sensitive to which warmup experiences were sampled: retrieval systems beat No-Memory in only 1 of 10 pools.
A single 15-token caution instruction matched the collision-only benefit of retrieval, and caution-aware metrics removed the rulebook’s apparent lead.
More sophisticated memory representations showed no robust advantage in this evaluation.
Baseline implementation quality and uncontrolled prompts could reverse the reported conclusion about whether memory helps.
The study releases the testbed, audited ports, random seeds, and caches; findings are scoped to this testbed and decisive model setting.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled evaluation of experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents directly connects embodied decision-making with environment-grounded memory.
papers.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
papers.tldr: In one audited HighwayEnv testbed, apparent benefits from experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents largely vanish under resampled warmup pools and token-matched filler controls.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.
bullets: Tests increasing task horizons with execution failures, interruptions, and mission updates.
Uses a structured skill-level interface to isolate task reasoning from perception and low-level control.
Evaluates open-weight planners, state-tracking strategies, and frontier models across multi-robot scenarios.
Even strong models fail often on clean tasks, with performance declining further under perturbations and longer missions.
Releases the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an expert-trace generation pipeline.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-horizon embodied multi-robot agents under dynamic tasks and execution failures, directly within embodied AI.
papers.title: MAGMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Embodied Agents under Dynamic Tasks and Execution Failures
papers.tldr: MAGMA-Bench evaluates long-horizon embodied agents on dynamic, failure-prone tasks requiring persistent reasoning and heterogeneous multi-robot coordination.

papers.abstract: Training a visuomotor policy calls for abundant demonstrations that closely match the target environment, yet collecting them anew remains expensive. Existing demonstration synthesis methods reduce this cost but remain constrained by high manual effort, limited visual fidelity, or heavy reliance on physics simulators. This paper introduces GaussianFactory, a high-fidelity data engine that mass-produces demonstrations with a single video scan as its only human input and no physics engine in the generation loop. Specifically, GaussianFactory reconstructs the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) replica and samples from the object-combination tasks the scene affords. For each task, it plans grasps and trajectories purely kinematically on the geometric reconstruction, rendering photorealistic demonstrations that visually match the target environment. Physical dynamics enter the pipeline only where contact force interactions dictate the outcome---during grasp formation, via a learned contact model pretrained once on an interaction dataset. To evaluate the downstream utility of the synthesized demonstrations, we implement an end-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow in two setups: a simulated scene that stands in for the real world to enable reproducibility, and a real-world workspace with a physical UR10e robot. In each setup, a standard diffusion policy trained solely on the synthesized demonstrations achieves 95.1% and 84.2% success rates, respectively.
bullets: Addresses the cost and effort of collecting environment-specific robot demonstrations.
Reconstructs the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting replica and samples feasible object-combination tasks.
Plans grasps and trajectories kinematically, using a learned contact model only for grasp formation where contact forces matter.
Demonstrations train a standard diffusion policy in an end-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow.
The policy reaches 95.1% success in simulation and 84.2% in a real UR10e workspace.
papers.selection_reason: Synthesizes demonstrations from a single scan via Gaussian Splatting to train visuomotor policies, directly relevant to embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Demonstration Synthesis from a Single Scan via Gaussian Splatting for Visuomotor Policy Learning
papers.tldr: GaussianFactory turns a single video scan into photorealistic robot demonstrations for training visuomotor policies, achieving strong simulated and real-world task success without a physics engine in the generation loop.

papers.abstract: Learning in robotic games is constrained not only by strategic information but also by what the body can still execute. We study this coupling in a hierarchical humanoid-quadruped penalty system in which game-level self-play policies command fixed soccer whole-body controllers (S-WBCs). The humanoid shooting skill is initialized from self-collected motion-capture data, whereas the quadruped saving skill is learned by reinforcement learning. We introduce dynamics-induced commitment mapping (DIC-Map), a body-grounded analysis that estimates continuation capability, identifies the first persistent loss of a terminal alternative, and tests whether the remaining interaction admits a reduced zero-sum game. For symmetric terminal alternatives, the reduced game yields a closed-form bound on optimal strategy concentration determined by the responder's value of deferring. We further show that, when the responder acts through an estimator, equal response values eliminate the direct terminal-allocation gradient and leave an estimator-mediated first-order learning channel. Experiments locate commitment about 0.29 s before contact, and changing only ball speed shifts deferral coverage. Across four responder policies, replacing the estimator raises save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, whereas a comparable gain in read accuracy obtained by waiting raises it only to 0.246. Posterior analysis is used for the equilibrium comparison because the available coverage terms are observational proxies. Project website: https://chris-ruizegeng.github.io/penaltykick/
bullets: Studies hierarchical humanoid–quadruped penalty kicks with fixed whole-body controllers and learned game-level policies.
Introduces DIC-Map to identify when a robot loses the persistent ability to execute alternative terminal actions and to analyze the resulting reduced game.
Derives a strategy-concentration bound based on the responder’s value of deferring, and characterizes an estimator-mediated learning signal when direct terminal-allocation gradients vanish.
Locates commitment roughly 0.29 s before contact; changing ball speed shifts the coverage available through deferral.
Replacing the estimator increases save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, while waiting for similarly improved read accuracy increases it only to 0.246; coverage is treated as an observational proxy.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based robotic penalty system combining RL and motion-capture-initialized control, fitting embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Dynamics-Induced Commitment in Learning-Based Robotic Penalty Kicks
papers.tldr: The paper shows that robotic penalty-kick strategies become committed by body dynamics before contact, and that responder-side estimation—not merely perceptual accuracy—strongly shapes learning and defensive success.

papers.abstract: Temporary obstacles that may block a robot's planned route create a sequential navigation problem: a robot must decide whether to wait for a blockage to clear, reroute, or acquire more information about the obstacle before acting. We formulate graph navigation among temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process and introduce SPARROW, a belief-space planner built on Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP). SPARROW searches over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions while maintaining a particle belief over latent obstacle classes and clearance times. Class-conditioned survival models are learned online from both clearance observations and right-censored encounters where the robot reroutes before clearance is observed. A generative model simulates obstacle arrivals and clearances as each action unfolds, so the planner can account for blockages that may occur along alternative routes. We further introduce a value-of-learning criterion that trades the immediate cost of collecting labelled survival data against its expected reduction in future navigation regret. Across two simulation graphs and multiple obstacle-class settings, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 12-26% relative to OSCAR, a recent survival-based method for the same problem. On a physical mobile robot, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 20.5% relative to OSCAR while selectively observing, waiting, and rerouting as environment conditions change.
bullets: Models navigation with temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process.
Uses POMCP to search over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions.
Learns obstacle survival and clearance behavior online, including from right-censored rerouting encounters.
Selects information-gathering actions using a value-of-learning criterion.
Reduces mean time-to-goal by 12–26% in simulation and 20.5% on a physical robot versus OSCAR.
papers.selection_reason: POMCP-based robot routing with learned survival models and adaptive waiting/rerouting directly fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: SPARROW: Survival-POMCP for Adaptive Robot Routing, Observation, and Waiting
papers.tldr: SPARROW uses belief-space planning to help robots decide when to reroute, observe, or wait around temporary obstacles, reducing travel time in simulation and on a physical robot.

papers.abstract: Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.
authors: Yunfei Xie, Howard H. Qian, Shiyi Lan, Kaiyu Hang, Chen Wei
bullets: Addresses the high cost of evaluating robotic foundation models through closed-loop rollouts.
Extends the Platonic Representation Hypothesis to embodied models by treating motion trajectories as an additional modality.
Measures representation–motion alignment without training and correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families.
Can help screen promising vision-language model backbones before costly conversion or fine-tuning into vision-language-action models.
Provides representation-level insight into success patterns in vision-language-action and world action models, though the abstract does not establish causality.
papers.selection_reason: Offline metric for embodied policy success directly fits embodied AI and VLA/robot learning evaluation.
papers.title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
papers.tldr: Sensorimotor Alignment (S²) is a training-free offline metric that gauges embodied model quality by measuring how closely sensory representations match the geometry of physical motion.

papers.abstract: We present OpenTac, a novel sensor and a full-stack ecosystem for tactile skins that are highly customizable, scalable, and readily deployed in downstream robot control and learning applications. Our core contribution is twofold. First, we develop a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts tangential loading into spatially varying pressure. Differential responses across neighboring "taxels" support decoding of local shear vectors, and the common-mode response encodes normal force. Second, we provide a highly customizable sensor design tool that is able to automatically generate fabrication files for these tactile skins from 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including from abstract descriptions such as text (e.g., "design a sensor for a size 9 shoe insole"). We develop an ecosystem around the OpenTac sensor, including the CAD design tool, a sensor simulator, cross-sensor transfer, and fast/adaptive data acquisition. We demonstrate the broad applicability of the OpenTac-CAD sensor design tool by designing and fabricating more than 30 sensors across a variety of robot embodiments. We characterize the three-dimensional tactile fields produced by OpenTac with a commercial, high-precision force/torque sensor. We demonstrate the broad applicability of 3D tactile sensing across contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning on four real-world robot embodiments. Additionally, adaptive acquisition enables kilohertz-rate partial readouts, exceeding full-array raster scanning on the same sensor by 19.2X at 16 sampled taxels per update for a 1024-taxel skin. We provide all hardware, software, and result videos are at opentac.github.io
authors: Ariel Slepyan, Geeta Chandra Raju Bethala, Jiafeng Gu, Anagha Rajendra Dangle, Yinzhe Zhou, Hongyuan Fu, Jade Sim, Tuhin Basu, Xinyi Yin, Md Faizal Karim, Gregory Hager, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Anand Bhattad, Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula, Nitish V. Thakor
bullets: Uses a scalable resistive skin with a structured deformable overlay to decode local shear vectors and normal force from taxel responses.
Automatically generates fabrication files for sensors fitted to 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including text-specified designs.
Includes CAD design, simulation, cross-sensor transfer, and adaptive data acquisition tools.
Demonstrated over 30 fabricated sensors across diverse robot embodiments and 3D tactile sensing for feedback control and manipulation learning on four real-world robots.
Adaptive acquisition achieved kilohertz-rate partial readouts, reported as 19.2× faster than full-array raster scanning for the tested configuration.
papers.selection_reason: Full-stack tactile sensing ecosystem demonstrated in contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning; relevant to embodied robot learning.
papers.title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
papers.tldr: OpenTac is an open, full-stack ecosystem for designing, fabricating, simulating, transferring, and rapidly reading customizable 3D tactile skins for robot control and learning.

papers.abstract: This paper studies category-level RGB-D object pose estimation, which recovers an object's 3D rotation and translation without instance-specific CAD models or reference views. This task is highly ambiguous due to intra-class variations, symmetries, and partial observations. Current solutions struggle to balance reliability and efficiency: methods based on intermediate structures are prone to error propagation, while diffusion models suffer from high inference latency and complex post-hoc candidate extraction. To address this, we present F2G-Pose, a real-time direct, single-pass framework that predicts category-level pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape from a single RGB-D observation in one feed-forward pass. F2G-Pose lifts dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds, encodes local geometry with DGCNN tokenization, and integrates object-level structure with a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer. Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion encourage metric consistency through dense geometric supervision. With its task-specific network trained only on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data and its frozen RADIO backbone externally pretrained, F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE while running at 28 FPS for pose-only inference, and further demonstrates strong camera-frame geometry on HouseCat6D and real-object transfer on HANDAL. Analyses of latency, robustness, shape completion, and GenPose++ candidate behavior further demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of F2G-Pose, with real-world manipulation experiments demonstrating deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs. The project page, code, and pretrained models are made available at https://jrryzh.github.io/F2G-Pose/.
authors: Jinyu Zhang, Haitao Lin, Jiashu Hou, Xiangyang Xue, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses ambiguity from intra-class variation, symmetries, and partial observations without instance CAD models or reference views.
Lifts frozen visual foundation features onto partial point clouds, models local geometry with DGCNN, and captures object structure using a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer.
Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion provide dense geometric supervision and metric consistency.
Reports state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE, with pose-only inference at 28 FPS; additional evaluations cover geometry, robustness, and real-object transfer.
Scope includes segmented RGB-D inputs and task-specific training on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data.
papers.selection_reason: RGB-D category-level pose estimation with foundation features; relevant to 3D perception and robotic manipulation.
papers.title: F2G-Pose: Geometry-Aware Foundation Feature Lifting for Direct RGB-D Category-Level Object Pose Estimation
papers.tldr: F2G-Pose is a real-time, single-pass RGB-D framework that jointly predicts category-level object pose, size, and completed shape from one observation.

papers.abstract: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot's own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot's explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.
authors: Fanxing Li, Yuxiang Huang, Shengyang Wang, Fangyu Sun, Shuyu Wu, Tianbao Zhang, Dexin Zuo, Yan Yufei, Danping Zou, Wenxian Yu
bullets: Targets aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing, where agents must anticipate moving obstacles while controlling quadrotors at high frequency.
Uses a world model for external dynamics and history-dependent latent features, while a differentiable simulator handles the robot’s explicit physical state.
Splits actor optimization between critic-based non-differentiable task rewards and simulator-based differentiable motion rewards.
Experiments report faster training convergence and better final performance than multiple learning, planning, and control baselines.
Ablations and proof-of-concept real-world flights evaluate reward decomposition and odometry-conditioned relative-state representations.
papers.selection_reason: Couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for agile quadrotor RL control, directly relevant to embodied robot learning and world-model-based policy optimization.
papers.title: DiffDreamer: Coupling World Models with Differentiable Simulation for Agile Quadrotor Control
papers.tldr: DiffDreamer combines learned world-model predictions with differentiable quadrotor simulation to improve agile control in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: \textit{can a VLA's own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution?} Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA $\pi_{0.5}$ and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.
authors: Atiksh Bhardwaj, Edward W. Duan, Junwon Seo, Prithwish Dan, Wei-Chiu Ma, Andrea Bajscy, Preston Culbertson
bullets: Addresses the need for reliable runtime monitoring of VLA policies without continuous human supervision.
Trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate execution progress and flag deviations.
Evaluated with the open-source π₀.₅ VLA on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Competitive with or better than VLM-based monitors and methods trained with failure data for task-failure detection.
Scope: focuses on monitoring execution progress using internal activations rather than preventing failures directly.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Progress Probes P2, a lightweight method for runtime monitoring of VLA models using internal activation probes, enabling inference-time adaptation.
papers.title: Progress Probes $P^2$: Lightweight Runtime Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Progress Probes use lightweight linear probes of a VLA’s internal activations to detect when manipulation tasks are going off-course, avoiding external VLM monitors.

papers.abstract: Humanoid mobility over complex terrain requires accurate foot placement and coordinated whole-body motion capable of robust adaptation. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained without motion references generalize well across terrains, yet eliciting effective whole-body coordination through reward design and exploration alone remains challenging. In contrast, reference-based methods yield natural motions but struggle to adapt beyond the predefined trajectories in their training data. We introduce a learning framework that bridges these two approaches by using motion data strictly as a training prior. An explicit, self-supervised, attention-based contact planner predicts future body-environment contacts, while a contact-conditioned tracker translates these plans into coordinated whole-body motion. Together, they establish contact as an interface between sensory observations and control actions. This abstraction allows the policy to internalize the contact-aware structure of locomotion rather than directly replicating kinematics. Consequently, a single policy can exploit data-driven motion priors for natural whole-body coordination while retaining the flexibility to discover environment-dependent behaviors through reinforcement learning. Building on the learned contact planner and tracker, a subsequent fine-tuning stage bootstraps their acquired capabilities to explore environment variations beyond those covered by the original motion data. Operating entirely from onboard observations without any reference inputs at deployment, this framework enables versatile humanoid mobility in challenging environments.
authors: Junzhe He, Kehan Wen, Chong Zhang, Clemens Schwarke, Zewei Zhang, Kaixian Qu, Siyuan Hu, Matthias M\"uller, Vladlen Koltun, Marco Hutter
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating whole-body motion while adapting to complex, unseen terrain.
Uses an explicit self-supervised attention-based planner to predict future body–environment contacts.
A contact-conditioned tracker converts predicted contacts into coordinated whole-body motion.
Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning extends capabilities beyond behaviors represented in the original motion data.
Operates solely from onboard observations at deployment and supports versatile mobility in challenging environments.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a learning framework for humanoid mobility using attention-based contact planning and tracking to enable robust whole-body motion.
papers.title: Humanoid Mobility via Attention-based Contacts
papers.tldr: An RL framework uses attention-based contact prediction as an interface between motion priors and control, enabling natural yet adaptable humanoid locomotion without reference inputs at deployment.

papers.abstract: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.
authors: Yufeng Liu, Bohao Fan, Juntu Zhao, Xinyi Wang, Hang Yu, Wenzhuan Luo, Yingzhi Wang, Qinghai Li, Yingdong Hu, Junliang Guo, Richard Wang, Dequan Wang, Yang Gao, Cheng Ma
bullets: Addresses the need for reliable stopping after success and recovery or replanning after failure without fine-grained progress labels, external monitors, or complex architectures.
Represents status with stop and failure dimensions appended to each action chunk, distinguishing ongoing, successful, and failed execution.
Builds successful, failed, and recovery trajectories to provide complementary supervision without frame-level annotations.
Controls signal–action interactions and denoises status signals faster, allowing cleaner status estimates to guide later action generation.
Real-world manipulation experiments show accurate status prediction and consistent policy-performance improvements.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Echo, a framework for VLA models that couples task status signal learning with action generation to improve execution robustness.
papers.title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
papers.tldr: Echo jointly denoises task-status signals and robot actions so a single VLA can recognize success or failure and use that information to guide execution.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to constraints over groups of robots. Existing methods that approach joint optimality remain largely centralized, offline, and confined to collision-free motion planning, while decentralized, real-time counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process. We extend a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of forward-propagated commands for differentially flat systems to coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the search of each robot's tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence. Our protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short. In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37% against a decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity. Hardware experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world implementability.
authors: Shashank A. Deshpande, Blake T. Edwards, Jonathan P. How
bullets: Addresses the gap between centralized offline joint optimization and decentralized real-time navigation that lacks joint-optimality objectives.
Extends dispersive-tree search for differentially flat systems to multi-robot coordination by replacing inter-robot coupling with local constraints.
Uses decentralized column generation to negotiate shared-space “rents” and guide each robot’s tree search.
Simulation shows up to 22% lower total travel time than centralized offline planners and up to 37% lower than a decentralized real-time baseline; hardware tests use six robots.
The approach remains effective when real-time deadlines interrupt negotiation, though certification requires quiescence.
papers.selection_reason: Develops WarpWeaver, a decentralized, real-time planner for multi-robot coordination that approaches joint optimality.
papers.title: Dispersive Tree Agreements for Multi-Robot Coordination
papers.tldr: WarpWeaver is a decentralized, asynchronous planner that coordinates multiple robots toward near-optimal joint motion in real time, with solutions certified at negotiation quiescence.

papers.abstract: Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) stands as a fundamental challenge in robotics, essential for enabling autonomous agents to execute complex, long-horizon tasks in diverse environments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new paradigm for TAMP by leveraging extensive common sense, their inherent reasoning limitations hinder direct application, and fine-tuning strategies to enhance these capabilities are currently bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality datasets. Existing automated generation methods often suffer from homogeneity, limiting model generalization, and unsolvability, where hallucinated scene graphs create physical mismatches with task goals. To address these issues, we propose Scene-graph Construction Optimized by Plan Error-correction (SCOPE), an automated framework designed to generate diverse and executable TAMP datasets. SCOPE incorporates multi-level diversity metrics to maximize the information entropy of scenarios. Crucially, it introduces a Plan Feedback Error-correction pipeline that utilizes planner execution failures as feedback signals to retroactively rectify logical inconsistencies in scene graphs, ensuring physical feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that SCOPE exhibits greater robustness to erroneous scene graphs and generates higher-quality data. When utilized for LLM fine-tuning, SCOPE-generated data yield a downstream TAMP model that achieves an absolute 12.33% gain in success rate over its counterpart fine-tuned with data generated by DELTA, a state-of-the-art PDDL-based planner.
authors: Chaoyue Li, Zeyu Gao, Yanfeng Lu, Fan Luo
bullets: Addresses scarce, homogeneous, and often unsolvable datasets for long-horizon robot planning with LLMs.
Uses multi-level diversity metrics to increase scenario information entropy.
Applies plan-execution failures to retroactively correct logical inconsistencies in scene graphs.
Produces more robust, higher-quality data and improves downstream TAMP fine-tuning success by 12.33 percentage points over DELTA-generated data.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SCOPE, a framework for generating diverse and executable TAMP datasets using LLMs and plan error-correction.
papers.title: SCOPE: Scene-graph Construction Optimized by Plan Error-correction for Robot Long-term Planning Datasets
papers.tldr: SCOPE automatically generates diverse, physically feasible TAMP datasets by correcting scene-graph errors using planner feedback.

papers.abstract: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding. The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure. A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions. The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion. Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.
authors: Ziyi Jiao, Heng Zhang, Drishti Regmi, Xiaokang Ye, Lianhui Qin, Peter Yichen Chen
bullets: Introduces 20 Unreal Engine maps across five categories targeting equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies.
A single VLM controls both players from top-down images using high-level actions, while the engine handles navigation.
Evaluates four VLMs using task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance, and API expenditure.
The strongest evaluated model, gpt-6-astra, reaches 26.2% mean order completion.
Shared notebook memory has mixed effects across models, improving some and reducing scores for others.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for vision-language agents controlling simulated players through high-level actions in a cooking environment, fitting embodied vision-language-action evaluation.
papers.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination
papers.tldr: DuoCook benchmarks how well vision-language models plan and coordinate two agents in visual cooking tasks with shared resources and time constraints.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.
authors: Advait Gupta, Sachin Konan, Tom Yin, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited scalability of online simulator and real-world agent evaluations.
Covers Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning using 1,000 examples from 23 source datasets.
Evaluates 22 models; the best reaches 58.5% accuracy, indicating substantial remaining challenges.
Offline model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations.

Most errors stem from visual-state grounding and tracking—such as UI localization, motion interpretation, state changes, and 3D spatial reasoning—rather than task misunderstanding or downstream logic.
papers.selection_reason: Offline benchmark for agentic VLM evaluation across embodied domains, including spatial planning and egocentric video.
papers.title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding
papers.tldr: AgentVQA is an offline benchmark for testing vision-language models’ visual understanding in realistic agentic scenarios across five domains.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone. Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force. We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing. VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns. The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4x4 array. We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments. In controlled single-taxel tests over 1-5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces. A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use. Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.
authors: Jian Hou, Xin Zhou, Adam J. Spiers
bullets: Addresses the lack of shear-force sensing in many low-cost flexible tactile arrays.
Uses a piezoresistive layer and passive silicone nubs to encode normal and shear forces as pressure patterns.
A 4×4 array costs under $35, is 6 mm thick, and can be fabricated without specialized equipment.
Controlled tests report 0.39 N normal-force RMSE and 0.16 N shear-force RMSE; flat calibration remains effective when curved.
Demonstrations include preventing balloon puncture with a scalpel and improving power-plug insertion.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a low-cost, flexible tactile array for 3-DoF force sensing, providing hardware support for robot manipulation tasks.
papers.title: VecTile: A Low-Cost Flexible Tactile Array for 3-DoF Force Sensing
papers.tldr: VecTile is a thin, flexible, inexpensive tactile array that senses 3-DoF contact forces, including shear, for improved robotic interaction.

papers.abstract: A conventional embodied agent in an indoor environment builds a map by accumulating noisy real-world measurements and results from heavy inference to guide navigation. While the detailed measurements may differ due to scene changes or sensor settings, the unique topological structure of navigable passages or the connectivity between rooms may provide training-free guidance that complements local observations. We propose a sparse topometric graph as an efficient structural representation for robust indoor navigation, alleviating the need for fine-grained matching, which is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and prone to real-world variations. The map consists of nodes that encode local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges that capture traversable connectivity. A learned graph-matching network finds consistent subgraph structures across sessions by considering both node-level geometric descriptors and neighborhood connectivity. The holistic contextual matching is robust to local ambiguities caused by weak distinctiveness or repetitive structure, and establishes stable correspondences despite local scene changes, different sensor modalities, or limited spatial overlap. We analyze the practicality of the graph through cross-session point-goal navigation, where a goal specified in a prior reference map must be reached from an unknown initial pose in a later session. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest success rates (77.1% on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes), while reducing memory by more than two orders of magnitude compared to point-level representations. The proposed approach further supports cross-session alignment and goal-directed navigation with strong scalability and robust real-world transfer.
authors: Eun Sun Lee, Minkyun Seo, Gwangtak Bae, Junho Kim, Seunggu Kang, Jaesik Park, Young Min Kim
bullets: Represents indoor maps with nodes for local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges for traversable connectivity.
Uses learned graph matching over geometric descriptors and neighborhood structure to establish correspondences across sessions.
Handles local ambiguities, scene changes, different sensor modalities, and limited spatial overlap without training-specific fine-grained matching.
In cross-session point-goal navigation, achieves 77.1% success on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes.
Reduces memory use by more than two orders of magnitude versus point-level representations.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse topometric graph memory and graph-matching for cross-session indoor navigation, fitting robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: A Sparse Topometric Graph for Scalable Cross-Session Indoor Navigation
papers.tldr: A sparse topometric graph enables scalable, robust cross-session indoor navigation by matching room connectivity and local geometry instead of fine-grained measurements.

papers.abstract: Agentic robot systems combine language-model reasoning with robot policies to monitor execution and recover from failures. However, reviewing every action chunk incurs substantial overhead, even in familiar situations. We introduce FastHarness, an experience-driven execution harness that adaptively schedules GPT-6 Astra supervision of a {\pi}0.5 policy. A fast path uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes to reduce review frequency as experience accumulates, while a complementary recovery path focuses supervision on correcting errors. Once recovery is verified, routine execution resumes, with failure experience retained to guide future interventions. The policy remains frozen and generates fresh actions from current observations. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use decreases by an average of 57.2% per task from the first evaluated episode to the mean of the final five episodes. Mean episode time decreases from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes over the same interval. On the same tasks, mean success increases from 80% for GPT-as-Policy ({\pi}0.5 + GPT-6 Astra) to 97.19% with FastHarness. These results highlight adaptive supervision as a practical route to more efficient agentic robotics without additional model training.
authors: Tao Lin, Yuxin Du, Haoxiao Wang, Zile Zhong, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses the overhead of reviewing every action chunk in familiar robot-task situations.
Uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes for a fast execution path, plus targeted supervision for error recovery.
Keeps the vision-language-action policy frozen and generates actions from current observations.
Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use fell 57.2% on average and mean episode time decreased from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes.
Mean success rose from 80% with GPT-as-Policy to 97.19% with FastHarness on the evaluated tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FastHarness, an experience-driven framework for scheduling supervision in Vision-Language-Action policies to reduce overhead and improve success rates.
papers.title: FastHarness: Experience-Driven Review Scheduling for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: FastHarness adaptively reduces GPT supervision for robot policies by learning from past execution outcomes while preserving recovery support for failures.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an important paradigm for robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Since reliable manipulation requires sufficient observation of objects, end-effectors, and their spatial relationships, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary spatial information. However, our experiments show that existing VLA models do not fully exploit such multi-view complementarity. The policy tends to persistently rely on the wrist view, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust global-local view dependency across manipulation stages, which limits stage adaptability and robustness. To address this issue, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware multi-view routing framework. FocusVLA predicts future interaction intent from historical actions and uses it to guide dynamic view routing during action generation. By adaptively coordinating global and local observations across different task stages, FocusVLA improves multi-view utilization. On RoboTwin 2.0, FocusVLA improves the average success rate over the strongest baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ by 10.10 pp. In real-world evaluation, FocusVLA improves the success rate from 71.7\% to 85.0\%, achieving a 13.3\% gain over $\pi_{0.5}$. Moreover, the intent prediction and dynamic routing modules of FocusVLA can be integrated into existing VLA frameworks without modifying their core architectures.
authors: Huixin Xu, Ziya Yu, Peng Li
bullets: Existing VLA policies often over-rely on wrist views and fail to adapt view selection during manipulation.
The method predicts future interaction intent from historical actions to guide stage-aware multi-view routing.
It coordinates global and local observations according to the current manipulation stage.
On RoboTwin 2.0, it improves average success by 10.10 percentage points over π₀.₅.
In real-world tests, success rises from 71.7% to 85.0%; the modules can be integrated into existing VLA architectures.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model with future-intent-guided multi-view routing for robotic manipulation; directly fits embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: FocusVLA: Future-Intent Guided Dynamic View Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FocusVLA improves robotic manipulation by using predicted future intent to dynamically route global and local camera views across task stages.

papers.abstract: Robotic swarms must coordinate across diverse missions, yet existing controllers often require redesign, retuning, or retraining when objectives change. Here we show that probabilistic energy modeling provides a unifying representation for versatile swarm control, in which diverse missions emerge from compositions of shared interaction principles rather than task-specific control formulations. By exploiting the correspondence between Gibbs random field energy minimization and structured reward maximization, we encode fundamental swarm behaviors as reusable energy terms within a unified probabilistic objective. Decentralized policies trained within this representation are composed into a single controller through lightweight policy gating, without retraining. An interpretable action-attention mechanism captures non-uniform local interactions, while dimensionless normalization supports transfer across swarm scales and platforms. Demonstrated on aerial swarms, the unified policy generalizes zero-shot across six mission classes, 10-100 agents, two hardware platforms, and indoor cluttered and GPS-denied woodland environments. Large-scale simulations achieve 0.96-1.00 task success rates with 1-10 ms per-agent inference latency, while physical deployments confirm zero-shot transfer to real platforms and unstructured environments. These results establish probabilistic energy modeling as a scalable and transferable framework for decentralized swarm control.
authors: Xiang Zhou, Xiangyu Zhu, Xintong Wang, Qingyuan Yang, Rui Huang, Feng Xue, Lin Li, Qingrui Zhang
bullets: Represents diverse swarm behaviors as reusable energy terms combined in a unified probabilistic objective.
Uses Gibbs energy minimization, structured reward maximization, policy gating, and interpretable action attention.
Supports zero-shot generalization across six mission classes, 10–100 agents, two aerial platforms, and challenging environments.
Reports 0.96–1.00 simulated task success with 1–10 ms per-agent inference latency; physical tests confirm transfer.
Scope: demonstrated for aerial swarms and the evaluated missions, scales, platforms, and environments.
papers.selection_reason: Unified probabilistic energy model for decentralized swarm navigation and control; fits learned navigation policies.
papers.title: Probabilistic Energy Modeling Unifies Versatile Swarm Control
papers.tldr: Probabilistic energy modeling enables one decentralized swarm controller to transfer across missions, swarm sizes, platforms, and environments without retraining.

papers.abstract: Vision and touch provide complementary cues for object pose and local contact geometry, but external cameras are often occluded at the contact site. We present GelSlim 5.0, a fingertip sensor that acquires visual and tactile observations with one fixed camera and a continuous UV-responsive contact layer. By switching illumination, the camera sequentially acquires through-membrane visual images and contact-sensitive tactile images from a shared viewpoint, avoiding inter-camera extrinsic calibration. To combine these observations, we introduce VisTacFusion, a multimodal transformer with separate prediction paths for planar object pose and contact geometry. Asymmetric bottleneck fusion incorporates visual context while preserving tactile spatial features for depth and surface-normal estimation. Modality dropout enables inference with paired inputs or either modality alone. On real validation data from 12 known objects, paired inputs reduce depth MSE, angular error, and translation $L_1$ by 61.2%, 72.3%, and 61.3%, respectively, relative to tactile-only inference with the same model. Relative to visual-only inference, the corresponding reductions are 93.7%, 6.1%, and 8.6%.
authors: Xiangdong Wang, I-Hsuan Huang, Xiaohao Xu, Xili Yi, Nima Fazeli, Xiaonan Huang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and calibration challenges caused by external cameras at contact sites.
Uses a fixed camera with a UV-responsive contact layer and switched illumination to capture visual and tactile images from one viewpoint.
VisTacFusion uses separate pose and contact-geometry prediction paths with asymmetric bottleneck fusion.
Modality dropout supports inference from paired inputs or either modality alone.

On 12 known objects, paired inputs substantially reduced depth, angular, and translation errors versus tactile-only and visual-only inference, with the largest gains over tactile-only depth and angular errors.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal vision-touch transformer for pose and contact geometry estimation; relevant to tactile manipulation and spatial understanding.
papers.title: GelSlim 5.0: Unifying Vision and Touch with a Single Fingertip Camera
