papers.tldr: GelSlim 5.0 unifies vision and touch in one fingertip camera, using VisTacFusion to estimate object pose and contact geometry from paired or single-modality inputs.

papers.abstract: Exoskeletons have shown great potential for augmenting human physical capabilities, yet generating reliable assistance remains challenging because human motion patterns and interaction requirements vary substantially in practice. To address this problem, a dual-loop assistance strategy is proposed to couple multimodal exoskeleton trajectory generation with variable admittance control, where trajectory variance links the outer-loop generator and the inner-loop controller. The generator synthesizes future exoskeleton trajectories through denoising, primarily using whole-body human motion and exoskeleton proprioception, with task descriptions as auxiliary semantic cues. To reduce cross-modal representation mismatch, a three-stage training pipeline is introduced to progressively optimize the human motion encoder, the exoskeleton proprioception encoder, and the trajectory generator. In the inner loop, multiple future trajectories are sampled from the generator to estimate the trajectory mean and variance. The mean is used as the control reference, while the variance provides an uncertainty measure for prediction reliability. This measure is further incorporated into a stiffness regulation law, enabling compliant assistance with input-to-state stability under bounded lumped interaction input. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces muscle activation levels compared with standard baselines, while also decreasing users' metabolic energy expenditure relative to the unassisted condition.
authors: Muyuan Ma, Long Cheng, Lijun Han, Haotian Zhai, Xinpan Meng, Xiuze Xia, Houcheng Li, Zeyu Liu
bullets: Addresses unreliable assistance caused by varied human motion patterns and interaction requirements.
Generates future exoskeleton trajectories from whole-body motion and proprioception, with task descriptions as auxiliary cues.
Uses trajectory samples to derive a mean reference and variance-based prediction uncertainty.
Adapts admittance-control stiffness to uncertainty and provides input-to-state stability under bounded interaction inputs.
Experiments report reduced muscle activation versus standard baselines and lower metabolic energy expenditure than unassisted use.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based exoskeleton trajectory generation and compliant control; relevant to learning-based robot control and physical interaction.
papers.title: Whole-Body Motion Guided Reference Generation for Uncertainty-Aware Compliant Assistance
papers.tldr: An uncertainty-aware dual-loop exoskeleton controller generates whole-body-motion-guided references and adapts compliance to improve physical assistance.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing physically grounded dexterous hand-object interactions is important for VR/AR, gaming, and robotics, yet remains challenging because subtle contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, and target trajectories must be jointly respected while maintaining natural grasps. Existing methods either track mocap trajectories with limited transfer to novel objects, or rely on hand-only generative priors that fail to capture coupled hand-object motion, sacrificing contact fidelity and sample efficiency. To tackle these challenges, we introduce PiHand, a Physically grounded Interaction-aware Hand motion synthesis framework. PiHand first trains expert policies that track mocap demonstrations in simulation, distills them into a unified hand-object interaction prior using a goal-conditioned VAE, and finally solve diverse dexterous manipulation tasks through bounded residual exploration in its latent space. With only a single reward and no complex curriculum training, this yields general tabletop manipulation policies that generalize to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB. The same prior transfers to object catching and bimanual handover, two tasks that are rarely seen in its training data. Across all tasks, PiHand consistently outperforms baselines in all metrics. We will release the processed data and model checkpoints.
authors: Niklas Berndt, Xianghui Xie, Enes Duran, Yixiao Wang, Gerard Pons-Moll
bullets: Addresses the challenge of jointly modeling contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, target trajectories, and natural grasps.
Trains simulation expert policies from mocap, distills them into a goal-conditioned VAE prior, and performs bounded residual exploration in latent space.
Uses a single reward without complex curriculum training.
Generalizes to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB, and transfers to object catching and bimanual handover.
Reports consistent improvement over baselines across all evaluated metrics; data and checkpoints are planned for release.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces latent hand-object interaction priors for physics-based dexterous manipulation policy learning, fitting robot learning and latent action modeling.
papers.title: PiHand: Latent Hand-Object Interaction Priors for Physics-Based Policy Learning
papers.tldr: PiHand learns a latent, physics-grounded hand–object interaction prior that enables dexterous manipulation policies to generalize across unseen objects, trajectories, and tasks.

papers.abstract: Long egocentric videos pose a central challenge for multimodal language models: the visual stream must be compressed into a memory representation that can be searched efficiently while still preserving the evidence needed for question answering. Building on an online textual-memory framework in which first-person videos are converted into temporally grounded captions, this work systematically studies the role of retrieval in episodic-memory video question answering. We evaluate how different retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking strategies affect multiple-choice answering on QAEgo4D-Closed, isolating retrieval as the main variable while keeping the underlying generated memory fixed. Our best configuration, Parent, matches fine-grained caption subchunks, then provides their full parent captions to the reasoner. It achieves 56.4 % accuracy, matching strong full-memory and retrieval baselines while exposing only a small fraction of the textual memory at question time. More importantly, our analysis shows that better temporal coverage does not necessarily translate into better answers: increasing the retrieval budget improves temporal Hit@K and Recall@K, but can reduce accuracy by introducing visually plausible distractors and uncertain caption evidence. These findings suggest that retrieval-augmented egocentric memory should not be optimized only for evidence recall, but also for the reliability, specificity, and answer-discriminative value of the retrieved context. The study motivates more structured episodic memories that move beyond raw caption retrieval toward evidence-aware representations for long-form egocentric reasoning.
authors: Raffaele Cali, Giuseppe Lando, Rosario Forte, Antonino Furnari
bullets: Evaluates retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking while keeping the generated textual memory fixed.
The best setup, Parent, retrieves fine-grained caption subchunks but gives their full parent captions to the reasoning model.
Parent reaches 56.4% accuracy while exposing only a small fraction of the textual memory at question time.
Larger retrieval budgets improve temporal Hit@K and Recall@K but can hurt accuracy by adding distractors and uncertain evidence.
Results motivate structured, evidence-aware episodic memories beyond raw caption retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Studies retrieval-augmented textual memory for egocentric video QA, directly relevant to embodied memory and learning from egocentric video.
papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Online Textual Memory for Episodic Memory Video Question Answering
papers.tldr: A systematic study shows that effective retrieval for episodic video QA depends on reliable, answer-discriminative evidence—not merely broader temporal coverage.

papers.abstract: Real robot data, rich across tasks and morphologies, is often treated as the bottleneck for training robot learning models, including embodied foundation models that aim for zero-shot physical transfer. In this paper, we investigate the degree to which such models can acquire necessary structure using data from systems without embodiment. To this end, we test if inexpensive, procedurally generated synthetic data can yield useful priors before a model observes any real-world behavior. We study this through robot action prediction, a natural pretraining objective and a direct test of whether structure learned from arbitrary synthetic tasks transfers to embodied settings. We introduce three data generation pipelines that model mathematical abstractions of robotic control, and use them as pretraining priors for a Transformer. We demonstrate that a model trained purely on this non-robotic data attains non-trivial zero-shot prediction performance on unseen physical robot tasks via an in-context learning mechanism, and that our specialized control priors notably improve upon generic causal priors. We also compare against a compute-matched baseline trained on real robot data, and find that it outperforms our model but only on the datasets it was trained on. These findings suggest that procedurally generated, mathematical abstractions can yield useful robotic priors, offering a potential complement to expensive embodied data collection.
authors: Mateusz Odrowaz-Sypniewski, Michael Amir, Jasmine Bayrooti, Ajay Shankar, Amanda Prorok
bullets: Real robot data is expensive and limited for training broadly capable robot-learning models.
The study tests whether synthetic data from non-embodied systems can provide useful pretraining structure.
Three pipelines generate data from mathematical abstractions of robotic control for Transformer pretraining.
The resulting model achieves non-trivial zero-shot action prediction on unseen robot tasks through in-context learning.
Specialized control priors outperform generic causal priors, while real-data training performs better only on datasets seen during training.
papers.selection_reason: Explores synthetic non-robotic pretraining for robot action prediction, a meaningful transferable contribution to embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Learning Robot Behavior Priors from Non-Robotic Synthetic Data
papers.tldr: Procedurally generated non-robotic data can teach Transformers useful robot behavior priors that transfer zero-shot to unseen physical tasks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
authors: Chenyuan Chen, Ran Ding, Lechen Zhang, Zewen He, Yoshihiko Nakamura
bullets: Addresses non-Markovian manipulation scenes where important visual cues disappear or leave view.
Uses SAM3 to track objects and select key event frames within an adaptive memory budget.
An action expert reads selected frames via cross-attention alongside object tokens encoding appearance, geometry, and time.
Introduces HuMeGo, a benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks.
Raises success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot; also improves SIMPLE tasks from 70.2% to 86.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Object-guided perceptual memory for whole-body VLA humanoid manipulation, relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: WholeBodyMem improves humanoid loco-manipulation by selectively remembering task-relevant object events from before the robot acts.

papers.abstract: Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities. Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills. To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness. At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA's capabilities. To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings. We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.
authors: Zecong Tang, Zian Guan, Yuncheng Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Bo Dai
bullets: Addresses the gap between native visuomotor control and high-level planning in open-ended games.
Uses a capability-aware harness with structured memory, VLM subtask planning, and a policy-coupled completion detector.
A single VLA perceives through vision and acts via native keyboard-and-mouse inputs across subtasks.
Improves control reliability with regime-specific normalization, separate mouse-token embeddings, and staged training with world knowledge, imitation, and reinforcement learning.
Reports 85.0% on MineStudio Bench, 37.4% average success on OpenHA, and successful long-horizon crafting tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical VLA agent with native keyboard-mouse control and VLM planning for open-world games.
papers.title: HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA Agents for Open-World Games
papers.tldr: HiSTEVE combines hierarchical planning, structured memory, and a single vision-based native-control VLA to perform long-horizon tasks in open-world Minecraft.

papers.abstract: Diffusion trajectory planners with domain-specific experts face a practical question in unseen regions: can they rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the planner itself adapt? We study this question using a planner with a shared adapter and per-domain expert adapters. Across three real-world held-out maps, none of eight test-time routing schemes improves the fleet-mean lateral offset over the static default, which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an oracle that selects the best expert for each scene reduces the mean offset by only 0.9 m. In contrast, reward-based fine-tuning on just 20 target-region scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet-mean offset of 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 m for the static default. Comparisons under the same target-region training budget show that target-region training drives the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine-tuning across training cities also improves open-loop offsets, although closed-loop performance deteriorates. Further diagnostics reveal that two test-time adaptation baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate trajectories. These results show the limited headroom for selecting among existing experts and the greater open-loop gains available from adapting the planner.
authors: Yun Li, Ehsan Javanmardi, Simon Thompson, Jiachen Gong, Qunli Zhang, Zifan Zeng, Shiming Liu, Peng Wang, Yidu Zhang, Manabu Tsukada
bullets: Across three held-out maps, none of eight routing schemes beats the static default in fleet-mean lateral offset.
Even oracle expert selection improves mean offset by only 0.9 m.
Reward-based fine-tuning on 20 target-region scenes reduces matched offset from 12.4 m to 6.9 m with joint replay.
Target-region training drives the gains, while replay helps limit forgetting on original operating domains.
Some adaptation baselines achieve low offsets through degenerate trajectories; nuPlan results show open-loop gains but closed-loop deterioration.
papers.selection_reason: Studies routing versus adaptation for diffusion planners, with test-time adaptation and target-domain fine-tuning for navigation planning.
papers.title: To Route or to Adapt? Multi-Expert Diffusion Planners in Unseen Regions
papers.tldr: Adapting a diffusion planner with limited target-region training substantially outperforms routing among existing domain experts in unseen regions, though closed-loop performance may worsen.

papers.abstract: Capturing a loose object inside a spacecraft requires a robot to approach a target that can translate and rotate, and whose motion changes when contact is made. These conditions motivate evaluation beyond manipulation of supported objects. We introduce AstroBench, an open benchmark for free-floating capture and space robotic manipulation with a fixed-base arm. The task suite combines four initial-motion tracks with sample-storage operations based on MELFI hardware and cap and captive-screw servicing based on the Robotic Refueling Mission. The two workcells provide nine task definitions and 29 task-target combinations. A metadata-filtered Objaverse inventory supplies 8,414 object instances for asset expansion, alongside five cabin visual contexts and versioned task instructions. We report two acquisition-focused experiments using existing checkpoints. A frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ DROID joint-position policy captures 2 of 200 static targets and 4 of 200 moving targets across twenty object identities. A cube-specific ACT policy captures 8 of 10 static targets and 6 of 10 moving targets in a separate experiment. Each experiment retains its recorded observation, action and capture configuration. The results document difficult direct transfer for the tested generalist checkpoint and successful task-specific capture behavior, while identifying concrete settings for studying motion-aware perception and contact-sensitive control. Code, task definitions and editable workcell assets are available at https://github.com/AstroUpLab/AstroBench.
authors: Zizhe Wang (Astroup Lab, Beijing, China), Jia Deng (Astroup Lab, Beijing, China), Xin Lu (Astroup Lab, Beijing, China), Zehao Jia (Astroup Lab, Beijing, China), Yi Huang (Harbin Institute of Technology, Beijing Research Institute), Yao Zhu (Harbin Institute of Technology, Beijing Research Institute)
bullets: Covers free-floating capture, sample storage, and cap/captive-screw servicing across two workcells.
Defines 9 tasks and 29 task-target combinations, with 8,414 Objaverse object instances and 5 cabin visual contexts.
Includes four initial-motion tracks and versioned task instructions with editable workcell assets.
Existing policies show challenging direct transfer for a generalist checkpoint and stronger task-specific capture behavior.
Supports research on motion-aware perception and contact-sensitive control.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for free-floating capture and space robotic manipulation with policy evaluation; directly fits robot manipulation.
papers.title: AstroBench: Benchmarking Free-Floating Capture and Space Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: AstroBench is an open benchmark for evaluating robot capture and manipulation of translating and rotating objects in spacecraft-like settings.

papers.abstract: Tilt-rotor quadcopters redirect thrust for translation without banking, but complicate modeling, state estimation, and disturbance rejection. This paper presents a simulation-based flight stack for a \SI{2.00}{\kilo\gram} tilt-rotor quadcopter. The system uses a six-degree-of-freedom nonlinear model with first-order motor dynamics and two-axis rotor tilt, parameterized using a 3D CAD model. A cascaded PD controller commands forward and lateral tilt angles. A 14-state EKF fuses sensor data across hover, early-transition, and transition modes using a hysteretic (Schmitt-trigger) classifier to prevent covariance discontinuities. Because the proportional position loop leaves a steady-state offset under constant wind, a small bounded neural residual is added on top of the unmodified PD controller. It is trained by behavioral cloning from a teacher with privileged access to the true wind, while the deployed network never observes wind. In simulation, the EKF achieves a post-settling position root mean square error (RMSE) of \SI{0.226}{\metre} (horizontal) and \SI{0.03}{\metre} (vertical) and an attitude RMSE below \SI{0.8}{\degree}, and it estimates a wind velocity of $(\num{2.0}, \num{-1.2})\,\unit{\metre\per\second}$ to within \SI{0.15}{\metre\per\second} per axis. The residual reduces steady-state station-keeping error under wind by approximately \SI{49}{\percent}, from \SI{0.117}{\metre} to \SI{0.060}{\metre} at \SI{1.5}{\metre\per\second} and from \SI{0.319}{\metre} to \SI{0.162}{\metre} at an out-of-distribution \SI{3.9}{\metre\per\second}. The framework provides a basis for hardware-in-the-loop and flight-test studies.
bullets: Models a 2 kg tilt-rotor quadcopter with nonlinear 6-DoF dynamics, motor lag, and two-axis rotor tilt derived from CAD.
Uses a 14-state EKF with hysteretic mode classification across hover and transition phases to maintain consistent covariance behavior.
Trains a wind-unaware neural residual by behavioral cloning from a teacher with privileged wind information.
In simulation, the EKF achieves 0.226 m horizontal and 0.03 m vertical position RMSE, with attitude RMSE below 0.8°.
The residual reduces steady-state position error by about 49% under both 1.5 m/s and out-of-distribution 3.9 m/s wind.

papers.title: Tilt-Rotor Quadcopter with Learned Residual Control and Mode-Dependent State Estimation
papers.tldr: A simulation-based tilt-rotor quadcopter stack combines mode-dependent EKF estimation with a bounded learned residual to improve wind-disturbed station keeping without modifying the baseline PD controller.

papers.abstract: Flexible robotic endoscopes provide access through tortuous anatomy, where friction, deformation, and wall interaction separate commanded insertion from useful distal progress. Operators interpret this mismatch and retreat to recover a navigable configuration. Recognizing the approach to that decision requires relating motor intent to distal response and the local visual scene. We introduce Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion (MPRF), a causal model that anticipates operator retreat from commands, electromagnetic (EM) tracking, and endoscopic video. A nominal-progress model predicts the response expected in normal or successful navigation; a temporal predictor combines its EM residual with all three observed modalities. In a 150-episode colon-phantom collection, MPRF achieves 0.580 +/- 0.007 AUPRC across three seeds, compared with 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control. Complete multimodal histories provide the principal ranking advantage, while the residual adds an explicit intent-response representation with a small, uncertain increment over raw fusion. Analysis of frozen alarms relates warning timing to the behavioral label and explains the increase in event recall under a longer matching window. These results establish a basis for behavioral assistance during operator-controlled navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Tianchun Wu, Jiatan Sun, Yuming Sun, Jianru Zhang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between commanded insertion and useful distal progress caused by friction, deformation, and wall interaction.
Uses a nominal-progress model to estimate expected navigation response, then combines its EM residual with commands, tracking, and video in a causal temporal predictor.
Evaluated on 150 colon-phantom episodes, achieving 0.580 ± 0.007 AUPRC versus 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control.
Complete multimodal histories provide the main ranking benefit; the residual representation adds only a small, uncertain improvement over raw fusion.
Frozen-alarm analysis links warning timing to retreat labels and explains improved event recall with a longer matching window.

papers.title: Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion for Anticipating Navigation Retreat in Robotic Flexible Endoscopy
papers.tldr: MPRF anticipates when operators will retreat during robotic flexible endoscopy by fusing commands, EM-tracked motion residuals, and endoscopic video.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a demonstration-based robotic feeding framework that integrates human demonstration, Dynamic Movement Primitive-based motion planning, vision-based scene perception, and robot control. A human operator first demonstrates the scooping and feeding motions while the position and Euler-angle orientation of the spoon are recorded using a motion-capture system. The recorded trajectory is segmented into scooping and feeding motions, which are encoded using separate Dynamic Movement Primitives. Before task execution, an RGB-D camera estimates the participant's mouth position, while two AprilTags are used for robot-frame registration and tray localization. The detected tray pose is used to position the scooping motion, whereas the detected mouth position defines the positional goal of the feeding motion. The approach, scooping, and feeding trajectories are then executed sequentially by a Kinova Gen3 manipulator through a ROS~2-based framework. A real-world experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the integrated pipeline and shows that the learned spoon motions can be reproduced within the detected experimental scene.
authors: Kenzhi Iskandar Wong, Kitti Thamrongaphichartkul, Sri Harsha Turlapati, Yanshuo Lu, Kanichi Doi, Boyu Ma, Bin Zhou, Lin Yang, Ananda Sidarta, Lek Syn Lim, Arun-Kumar Kaliya-Perumal, Jianfei Yang, Domenico Campolo

RGB-D perception estimates the participant’s mouth, while AprilTags register the robot frame and localize the tray.

Real-world experiments demonstrate feasibility and reproduction of the learned motions in the detected scene.

papers.title: Demonstration-Based Robotic Feeding Using Dynamic Movement Primitives
papers.tldr: A demonstration-based system uses Dynamic Movement Primitives, vision, and robot control to reproduce spoon scooping and feeding motions in a real-world scene.

papers.abstract: End-to-end control policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) have emerged as an alternative to conventional surgical robotic control approaches, with recent studies exploring state-based policies trained on privileged state observations. However, such approaches rely on precise physical states that are difficult to obtain reliably in surgical environments. Vision-based RL provides an alternative by learning manipulation policies directly from RGB observations, avoiding explicit state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines while enabling policies to acquire task-relevant visual representations. Nevertheless, obtaining vision-based policies via pure RL methods for surgical manipulation remains challenging. Thus, imitation learning (IL) becomes another solution, yet it requires a large number of expert demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain in minimally invasive surgery. In this work, we propose a framework for state-to-vision policy distillation in laparoscopic robotic manipulation. Specifically, a state-based policy with privileged observations is employed as the teacher, and a vision-based policy learns from RGB observations and robot proprioceptive information, which requires less expert demonstrations than IL and introduces superior performance than RL methods. We conduct extensive experiments on various surgical manipulation tasks in the simulated environment. Experimental results show that, in the context of laparoscopic robotic manipulation, training vision-based policies with general-purpose RL methods is challenging, whereas our proposed state-to-vision policy distillation leads to more consistent and stable performance across tasks.
authors: Mingyu Sheng, Jianan Fan, Dongnan Liu, Guoyan Zheng, Ron Kikinis, Weidong Cai
bullets: Vision-based control avoids unreliable surgical state estimation and hand-engineered perception pipelines.
A privileged state-based policy serves as the teacher for a vision-based student policy.
The student uses RGB observations and robot proprioception, requiring fewer expert demonstrations than conventional imitation learning.
Experiments across simulated surgical manipulation tasks show more consistent and stable performance with distillation than direct vision-based RL.
The study is evaluated in simulation and focuses on laparoscopic robotic manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: State-to-vision policy distillation for laparoscopic robotic manipulation, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Revisiting Distribution Matching for State-to-Vision Policy Distillation in Laparoscopic Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: State-to-vision policy distillation transfers knowledge from privileged-state RL policies to RGB-and-proprioception policies, enabling more stable laparoscopic manipulation than training vision policies with general-purpose RL alone.

papers.abstract: This paper presents TRACE, a traversability-aware reactive navigation framework designed for the autonomous operation of ground robots in unstructured forest environments. Unlike traditional approaches, TRACE leverages VLM-based confidence maps from positive and negative natural-language prompt sets and combines them through evidential fusion to produce a dense traversability map that prioritizes the terrain based on signs of previously traversed paths. Traversability-annotated points are then extracted and used to derive the left and right boundaries of the traversable path via percentile binning followed by spline or regularized polynomial fitting. These boundaries are then incorporated as soft barrier constraints within an NMPC formulation, enabling safe and adaptive path following in complex natural environments. Rigorous experimental trials carried out in real-life forest environments demonstrate TRACE ability for smooth navigation in cluttered, deformable, and visually ambiguous terrains.
authors: Mario A. V. Saucedo, Midhun Edatharam Kunnath, Elias Small, Akash Patel, Shruti Kotpalliwar, Christoforos Kanellakis, George Nikolakopoulos
bullets: Builds dense traversability maps by fusing VLM confidence from positive and negative natural-language prompts.
Prioritizes terrain showing signs of previously traversed paths.
Estimates traversable-path boundaries using percentile binning and spline or regularized polynomial fitting.
Injects the estimated boundaries as soft barrier constraints into an NMPC controller.
Real-world forest trials demonstrate smooth navigation through cluttered, deformable, and visually ambiguous terrain.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-driven traversability constraints for reactive navigation in unstructured terrain.
papers.title: TRACE: Traversability-aware Reactive Navigation via VLM-driven Adaptive Constraints Estimation
papers.tldr: TRACE combines VLM-based terrain assessment with adaptive NMPC constraints to help ground robots navigate safely through unstructured forests.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.
authors: Jialin Tian, Zhuofan Li, Xinkai Wang, Bokai Lin, Chenyi Wang, Xinyu Zhan, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation that 3D flow is typically handled outside the robot policy as a separate module or output.
Uses a diffusion transformer with one expert each for vision, action, and 3D flow, connected through joint attention.
Trains across ten objectives that assign each modality as a target, condition, or absent, enabling policy, dynamics, and future-feature prediction tasks.
Improves RoboCasa-GR1 success from 52.1% to 56.4%, while achieving 98.1% on LIBERO and 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus.
Reaches 87.0% average success on four real-world bimanual tasks, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Unified action-world model treating 3D flow as a co-equal modality for manipulation policies and dynamics prediction.
papers.title: UniFlowWAM: A Unified World-Action Model with Visual Semantics and 4D Geometry
papers.tldr: UniFlowWAM unifies vision, actions, and 3D scene flow in one multimodal model, improving simulated and real-world robot manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation of soft objects, such as garments, is a critical skill for service and household robots to adopt, but remains challenging due to its high-dimensional state space, and material-dependent deformations. Humans address this challenge by using mental world models that "imagine" the shape and material properties from partial observations, which enables them to predict how actions affect future states. As such, embedding such world models in robots allows for better generalization in manipulating a wide variety of garments in the real world. However, learned world models typically require large amounts of real world data that is strenuous to collect, and a mechanism to infer latent properties that govern dynamics. We present a Soft-Object World Model that performs generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction using a transformer backbone trained on large-scale simulated soft object interactions, with measures to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. By learning to infer latent shape and material cues through in-context learning over a variable-length partial point-cloud history, the model generalizes across robot embodiments, material parameters, garment types and shapes, and manipulation coordination modes without weight updates. The world model is then integrated with a Goal-Conditioned action planner for motion synthesis. We validate the approach in simulation and real world for bimanual garment folding, reporting improvements in reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.
authors: Hengyi Sim, Quentin Rouxel, Dennis Hong, Darwin Caldwell, Fei Chen
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of garment manipulation under high-dimensional, material-dependent dynamics and partial observations.
Uses a transformer trained on large-scale simulated soft-object interactions for generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned prediction.
Infers latent garment shape and material properties from variable-length partial point-cloud histories through in-context learning.
Integrates the world model with a goal-conditioned planner for bimanual motion synthesis.
Simulation and real-world folding experiments show improved reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.
papers.selection_reason: In-context world model for action-conditioned soft-garment dynamics prediction and bimanual manipulation.
papers.title: In-Context Learning World Models for Robot Dual-Arm Manipulation of Soft Garment with Partial Observations
papers.tldr: An in-context transformer world model enables dual-arm robots to infer and manipulate partially observed garments across varied materials, shapes, and embodiments without model updates.

papers.abstract: Stable grasping under task-specific disturbances is important for robotic manipulation. However, most dexterous grasp synthesis methods are developed for highly actuated hands in free space, and low-DoF hands may not be able to realize the contact topologies required by these grasps. Meanwhile, support surfaces can provide useful contact forces, but are often treated only as geometric constraints. We present a support-aware grasp synthesis framework for object immobilization with low-DoF coupled hands. Given irregular object geometry, our method represents both hand and object local surface regions as graphs and searches for kinematically feasible matchings between them. We then refine the wrist pose and motor state for geometric contact feasibility and validates the refined grasps through physical rollouts. Starting from the validated grasp pose, an optional task-guided local search explores nearby grasp configurations by varying the wrist pose and motor state, and selects one according to the specified task condition. Experiments on diverse objects show that our method generates various grasp configurations that achieve high grasp success and strong disturbance resistance. Real-world experiments further demonstrate physically executable grasps which enable object immobilization in cooking scenario.
authors: Sang-Hun Han, Changyeon Won, JunGyu Lee, Min-Gyu Park, Hae-Gon Jeon
bullets: Targets stable object immobilization when low-actuation hands cannot realize conventional free-space grasp topologies.
Represents hand and object surface regions as graphs and searches for kinematically feasible matchings.
Refines wrist pose and motor state for geometric contact feasibility, then validates grasps through physical rollouts.
An optional task-guided local search adapts nearby grasps to specified task conditions.
Experiments show diverse, executable grasps with strong disturbance resistance, including cooking scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Support-aware grasp synthesis for object immobilization with low-DoF hands; directly relevant to robotic manipulation and grasping.
papers.title: IORA: Irregular Object Immobilization under Restricted Actuation
papers.tldr: IORA synthesizes support-aware, disturbance-resistant grasps for irregular objects using low-DoF coupled hands and physical validation.

papers.abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models bring an appealing form of explainability to a safety-critical domain, since a system that can state the reasons for its maneuvers offers the transparency that deployment and public trust in autonomous driving demand. These models read the world into language before they act on it, describing the scene and reasoning over it in text that ranges from chain-of-thought to multi-stage question answering on the way to a trajectory. That framing quietly assumes two separable properties, namely that the trajectory follows the generated reasoning and that the generated reasoning tracks the causes that actually produce the trajectory. To thoroughly investigate these properties, we apply causal, counterfactual interventions to four driving VLAs across different benchmarks. First, we perturb the models' own reasoning and show that altering its meaning produces small trajectory changes relative to blanking the same models' camera inputs, a pattern that persists across benchmarks and model architectures. We then construct scene-level counterfactuals through photorealistic removal of key objects named in the models' reasoning and analyze whether the generated reasoning and trajectories track these changes. Overall, our findings indicate that the reasoning these models present to account for their resulting driving behavior is weakly coupled to that behavior itself, pointing to limits on the explainability these systems are intended to provide.
authors: Gabriel Manalu, Saad Wazir, Thao Do, Seongah Kim, Hyeontaek Hwang, Tolcha Yalew Kidane, Daeyoung Kim
bullets: The study tests whether driving VLAs’ actions follow their generated reasoning and whether that reasoning reflects the causes of their actions.
Causal interventions perturb the models’ reasoning, while separate experiments remove objects referenced in that reasoning from the scene.
Changing the reasoning causes relatively small trajectory changes compared with removing camera inputs, consistently across benchmarks and architectures.
Scene-level counterfactuals assess whether both reasoning and trajectories respond to changes in relevant objects.
The results question whether generated reasoning provides faithful explanations for driving behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Directly investigates reasoning-action coupling in driving vision-language-action models via counterfactuals, fitting embodied VLA research.
papers.title: Measuring the Reasoning-Action Coupling in Driving Vision-Language-Action Models through Counterfactuals
papers.tldr: Counterfactual tests across four driving VLAs show that their textual reasoning is only weakly connected to the trajectories they produce, limiting its value as an explanation.

papers.abstract: We present TwinStore, a source-available synthetic consumer platform for physical retail built on vision--language models. TwinStore turns a store into a digital twin---from 82 ready-made formats, a floor-plan image or phone photos of its shelves---and fills it with synthetic shoppers who plan a trip, walk the aisles and decide what to buy by looking at rendered shelves with packs, price tags and promotion signs. Every trip ends in a receipt, so a layout, price, pack or promotion can be tried on the same shoppers before it reaches the store. Around this core, TwinStore provides 3D playback, paired comparisons and layout optimization, shopper interviews, a trade-area model, counterfactual edits of real shelf photos, a marketing studio with eleven tools, and an assistant that turns a plain sentence into a drafted study or an answer grounded in a run's own numbers. In a held-out validation on eleven public datasets, simulated receipts approach the households' own natural variation (category-mix divergence 0.017--0.018 against a real drift of 0.012), price elasticities fall inside the range measured in the field, and three independent decision models agree. TwinStore runs on cloud or on-device models and is distributed with installers for Windows, macOS and Linux.
bullets: Builds digital twins of stores from ready-made formats, floor plans, or shelf photos, then renders shelves with products, prices, and promotions.
Simulated shoppers plan trips, navigate aisles, make purchase decisions, and generate receipts for repeated scenario testing.
Supports playback, paired comparisons, layout optimization, shopper interviews, trade-area modeling, photo counterfactuals, marketing tools, and study assistance.
In validation across eleven public datasets, simulated purchasing patterns approached observed household variation; price elasticities were within field-measured ranges.
Runs with cloud or on-device models and provides installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux.
papers.selection_reason: Synthetic shoppers perceiving and acting in a digital-twin store using vision-language models relates to embodied agents.
papers.title: TwinStore: A Synthetic Consumer Platform Using Vision--Language Models
papers.tldr: TwinStore is a source-available synthetic retail platform that uses vision–language models to simulate shoppers, receipts, and store interventions for testing retail decisions before deployment.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots must coordinate locomotion and manipulation in everyday environments, yet progress is difficult to assess across differing policies, controllers, and task settings. LocoManiLab provides an integrated testbed spanning data collection and generation, policy training, evaluation, and physical deployment. Its task suite covers 234 atomic and compositional tasks across five household scene categories, supported by 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation. The evaluation covers twelve policies with a shared controller across task and scene splits and perturbation levels, two policies across five controllers, and studies of demonstration scale and data-source mixtures. Success rates fall on unseen tasks and scenes and generally decline as visual perturbations increase, with differences in generalization and robustness across policies. For data generation, a humanoid motion generation model is fine-tuned for loco-manipulation to study the alignment of its outputs with task execution requirements and its integration into the data generation pipeline. Three simulated loco-manipulation tasks closely match real-world setups, enabling evaluation of three policies in both domains. Similar policy rankings support the reliability of simulation-based evaluation.
authors: Dewei Wang, Jinrui Han, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Xianbo Lu, Jiabao Wu, Jiqin Feng, Jipeng Kong, Ping Luo, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
bullets: Covers 234 atomic and compositional tasks across five household scene categories, supported by 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation.
Evaluates policy and controller choices under task/scene splits, visual perturbations, demonstration scales, and mixed data sources.
Finds reduced success on unseen tasks and scenes, with further degradation under stronger visual perturbations and varying robustness across policies.
Includes loco-manipulation motion generation fine-tuning and examines how generated motions support task execution and data generation.
Three simulated tasks mirror real-world setups; consistent policy rankings across domains support simulation-based evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Unified testbed for humanoid loco-manipulation policies, controllers, and deployment.
papers.title: LocoManiLab: A Unified Testbed for Data, Policies, Controllers, and Deployment in Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: LocoManiLab is a unified benchmark for evaluating humanoid loco-manipulation across data, policies, controllers, tasks, perturbations, and simulation-to-real deployment.

papers.abstract: Reliable traversability estimation is essential for autonomous navigation on unstructured terrain. State-of-the-art approaches typically evaluate traversability from deterministic terrain elevation, thereby overlooking spatial correlations in the terrain and failing to account for how elevation uncertainty propagates through nonlinear traversability mappings. We propose ProTrav, a probabilistic terrain representation that uses function-space sampling to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagate elevation uncertainty to traversability cost. First, a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP) reconstructs a probabilistic elevation field from observations. Then, posterior function-space sampling generates spatially correlated terrain realizations, preserving spatial dependencies between neighboring locations while propagating elevation uncertainty through geometric features into traversability cost. Consequently, a distribution of traversability cost at arbitrary location is established, where the mean and standard deviation quantify the expected traversability cost and associated uncertainty, respectively. A risk term is defined by moment-based Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller for risk-aware navigation. Simulation experiments demonstrate navigation success rates exceeding 90\% on different terrains, compared with below 40\% for a baseline, while reducing attitude variations. Furthermore, the proposed approach is validated on a robot traversing real-world off-road terrain.
authors: Chuanlin Zuo, Milo\v{s} Pr\'{a}gr, Arun Kumar Singh, Mohammad Loni, Reza Ghabcheloo
bullets: Addresses the limitations of deterministic elevation-based traversability estimation, which ignores spatial correlations and uncertainty propagation.
Uses a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process to reconstruct a probabilistic elevation field.
Samples spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagates uncertainty through geometric features into a distribution of traversability costs.
Defines a moment-based Upper Confidence Bound risk term and integrates it into an MPPI controller.
In simulation, achieves over 90% navigation success versus below 40% for a baseline, reduces attitude variations, and is validated on real off-road terrain.
papers.selection_reason: Probabilistic traversability estimation with uncertainty propagation for risk-aware off-road navigation.
papers.title: ProTrav: Probabilistic Traversability with Elevation Uncertainty Propagation for Risk-aware Off-road Navigation
papers.tldr: ProTrav propagates correlated elevation uncertainty into traversability costs and uses it for risk-aware off-road navigation.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation in field-deployed settings requires more than executing a capable controller. As the execution conditions change, the system must decide, online and on the robot side, which control source should hold authority. Human teleoperation adapts readily to contact-rich and semantically ambiguous situations but depends on a stable communication link. Local autonomy is executed without continuous human intervention, but may fail under semantic ambiguity, long-horizon drift, and unforeseen contingencies. These two control sources exhibit complementary reliability profiles. We formulate this complementarity as a control authority routing problem and present Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation (TEAR), an edge-deployable framework that allocates authority between human teleoperation and local autonomy. TEAR arbitrates on the robot side using network-state evidence, which governs the usability of teleoperation, and task-semantic evidence, which reflects whether autonomous execution remains consistent with the current task. A lightweight temporal arbitrator observes both forms of evidence together with robot state and current authority to time authority transfers. Across simulated and real-world trials under dynamic network conditions, TEAR achieves task success rates close to pure teleoperation while limiting teleoperation to 19.8-27.4% of control steps and improves success by 30-40% over autonomy-only execution in our settings. These results demonstrate the potential of complementary authority routing to sustain successful manipulation with substantially reduced dependence on continuous human control.
authors: Shicheng Zhang, Hui Liu, Haoliang Li
bullets: Addresses the complementary weaknesses of teleoperation and autonomy in changing, field-deployed conditions.
Uses robot-side network-state and task-semantic evidence, plus robot state and current authority, to time control transfers.
Evaluated in simulated and real-world trials with dynamic network conditions.
Reports success rates near pure teleoperation while using teleoperation for 19.8–27.4% of control steps.
Improves success by 30–40% over autonomy-only execution in the reported settings.
papers.selection_reason: Online authority arbitration between teleoperation and local autonomy for reliable manipulation; relevant to embodied manipulation systems.
papers.title: TEAR: Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: TEAR routes control authority between human teleoperation and local autonomy using network and task evidence to maintain reliable robotic manipulation with less continuous human input.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion-tracking policies can reproduce diverse behaviors, yet connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence remains challenging. Interpolation connects boundary poses without considering whether their relative position, heading, and timing provide suitable conditions for a transition. A generative motion prior can produce richer motion, but poorly arranged boundaries may cause it to generate excessive locomotion, turning, or another unintended action. We present Spatio-Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a framework for connecting independently acquired humanoid motions through a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot process. STAMP uses human motion space to draw on rich motion priors and reuse transition knowledge across robot embodiments. Its key component is a learned alignment model that determines the boundary conditions for motion inbetweening. Given the two motions retargeted to a human rig, the alignment model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion. A human motion prior generates the transition under the selected alignment. The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot and used as a reference to train a motion-tracking policy. We evaluate the tracking success of the generated transitions on Unitree~G1 and~ROBOTIS K1. Physical robot demonstrations further show that STAMP connects independently acquired motions into long-horizon sequences. Project page: https://childtoy.github.io/STAMP-project
authors: Taehyun Byun, Taemoon Jeong, Yoonbyung Chai, Woojin Wie, Insu Park, Kyungjae Lee, Sungjoon Choi
bullets: Addresses failed transitions caused by incompatible relative position, heading, and timing between motions.
Retargets robot motions to a human rig, where an alignment model ranks candidate boundary conditions and durations.
Uses a human motion prior to generate the transition, then retargets the result back to the robot for policy training.
Evaluated on Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1, with physical demonstrations of long-horizon motion sequences.
Scope: transition quality depends on suitable alignment and the capabilities of the human motion prior.
papers.selection_reason: Connecting humanoid motions using human motion priors and retargeted tracking policies relates to robot learning from human demonstrations.
papers.title: Robot Motion Transition with Human Motion Prior
papers.tldr: STAMP connects independently acquired humanoid motions into continuous long-horizon sequences by aligning their spatial and temporal boundaries with a human motion prior.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Lei Wei, Guangyuan Dong, Sihan Liu, Yingjie He, Siheng Wang, Shuaibo Li, Rongchao Zhang, Zhen Tian, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao Hu
bullets: Pixel prediction quality can misalign with policy utility: lower next-frame MSE may yield worse policy gradients.
DRILL uses bilevel optimization to update the world model based on returns after an inner GRPO update from imagined rollouts.
DRILL-VWI is a rollout-free surrogate that weights errors by policy visitation, GRPO advantage, and model confidence.
DRILL-IMG differentiates through the inner update with truncated Hessian-vector products; DRILL-VWI approximates its local one-step gradient under stated assumptions.
Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG improves mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World.
papers.selection_reason: Trains action-conditioned world models to improve VLA policies via imagined rollouts, directly relevant to world models and embodied policy learning.
papers.title: DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
papers.tldr: DRILL trains world models to produce useful policy-learning signals rather than merely predict pixels, improving downstream VLA policy performance.

papers.abstract: Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach environments inaccessible to ground-based systems. Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.
authors: Jingyu Ru, Xiangyuan Xie, Lixuan Jin, Jian An, Xingming Zhang, Binghao Li, Siyu Wang, Xiang Zhou, Lei Yuan, Hongli Xu, Yang Yu
bullets: Aerial loco-manipulation is difficult because arm motion shifts the vehicle’s center of mass, changes inertia, and introduces force and moment disturbances.
ALMA uses a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions.
Action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations trains the policy context to retain flight-relevant response information.
An evolutionary process guided by an LLM analyzes control difficulties and proposes new arm-motion structures for training.
In simulation, position RMSE falls by up to 24.7%; on a real aerial manipulator, zero-shot transfer reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive policy learning for aerial loco-manipulation with LLM-assisted task generation is a robot manipulation and control contribution.
papers.title: Adaptive Aerial Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning via LLM-Assisted Proactive Task Generation
papers.tldr: ALMA improves aerial loco-manipulation control by learning history-aware flight policies and using an LLM to generate challenging arm-motion tasks.

papers.abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird's-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird's-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Shuchang Liu, Jinsong Lin, Yidong Zhang, Xizi Wang, Ho Yin Chim, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses navigation in compliant, contact-rich environments where support changes tip motion.
Queries the global image for the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target, then predicts bending and insertion commands from their representations.
Introduces the VLCA dataset with demonstrations, action samples, spatial entries, and remaining-route records.
Achieves 97.5% tip localization, 94.8% waypoint localization, and 76.25% success across 1,920 physical trials.
Offline action imitation and physical task completion produce different rankings: GRU-BC has lower MAE but only 1/240 physical successes.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language policy for contact-aided endoscope navigation with semantic grounding in global images fits embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation
papers.tldr: EBV-CAN uses a cached bird’s-eye image, live endoscopic views, and motor state to ground language instructions for contact-aware endoscope navigation.

papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that instead predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history. Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.
authors: Adam Lee, Mutian Xu, Yukang Cao, Shulin Tian, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis in existing video-based world models.
Uses a lightweight 3D dynamics network to predict object-centric motion and deformation from an initial scene and future hand trajectory.
Transports appearance through predicted 3D motion, letting video generation focus on uncertain or newly visible content.
Reports 27–40% lower moved-point error than PointWorld across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, plus 47% higher object-fidelity IoU+ on HOT3D under a shared renderer.
Two-step causal generation provides a reported 57× speedup relative to the authors’ 14B bidirectional configuration.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned dexterous manipulation world model with explicit 3D dynamics, fitting interactive world models and robot manipulation.
papers.title: DeXplicit: Making Physical State Explicit in Dexterous Manipulation World Models
papers.tldr: DeXplicit improves dexterous-manipulation world modeling by predicting explicit metric-3D object motion before rendering future video.

papers.abstract: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.
bullets: Benchmarks 11 classical and learned detector–matcher combinations across nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets.
SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT under rotation-only scoring on lunar testbeds and one analogue site, while synthetic results are mixed when translation direction is included.
In stereo VO, SuperPoint is not consistently more accurate but is the only approach to maintain tracking across all eight sequential datasets.
Classical-detector performance varies with lighting; SuperPoint is comparatively stable and benefits from higher-contrast spotlight conditions.
SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination at 16 ms per frame; DINOv2 retrieval proposals still require geometric verification.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates learned feature matching for lunar rover visual SLAM, directly relevant to embodied robot navigation and localization.
papers.title: Evaluation of Front-End Feature Matching for Lunar Visual SLAM
papers.tldr: SuperPoint-based feature matching improves robustness on lunar-like imagery, but does not consistently improve visual-odometry accuracy over SIFT.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.
authors: Shivakanth Sujit, Luca Nunziante, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Kai Arulkumaran
bullets: Flow-matching VLA policies typically require iterative ODE integration, which limits deployment control frequency.
Across six flow-matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale.
Multi-step integration provides little or no consistent inference advantage in the studied setting.
The finding depends on models having sufficient training and capacity.
Large VLAs can use single-step inference directly, without distillation, retraining, or auxiliary objectives.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study showing one-step Euler integration suffices for large flow-matching VLA policies, improving deployment latency.
papers.title: When One Step Is Enough: An Empirical Study of Euler Integration in Flow-Matching Policies
papers.tldr: For sufficiently trained, high-capacity flow-matching VLA policies, one-step Euler inference performs about as well as multi-step sampling while enabling much lower-latency control without retraining.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi-task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. However, existing lightweight VLA models employ a single dense action expert to handle all tasks, which limits their multi-task capability under constrained computational budgets. To address this issue, we propose SmolVLA-MoE, a novel framework that introduces sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. SmolVLA-MoE replaces dense FFN layers with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a token-level router, enabling each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation. We further introduce a shared expert with a tunable weight parameter to balance the inheritance of pre-trained capabilities and task-specific expert specialization. Through sparse activation, SmolVLA-MoE activates only a single expert FFN during inference, with a total activated parameter count of approximately 500M including the frozen VLM backbone, while benefiting from approximately 800M total stored parameters. We evaluate our method on four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA-MoE achieves an average success rate of 84.25%, outperforming SmolVLA (82.75%) and OpenVLA-7B (76.5%), while maintaining comparable inference efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dudu435/smolvla-moe.
authors: Shiyang Zhang, Miao Yang, Zhengda Li, Yang Shao, Ruifang Zhai, Hui Peng, Peng Song
bullets: Addresses the limited multi-task capacity of lightweight VLAs that rely on one dense action expert.
Replaces action-expert FFNs with parallel experts and a token-level router, activating only one expert per token at inference.
Adds a tunable shared expert to balance pretrained capability retention with task-specific specialization.
On four LIBERO task suites, achieves an 84.25% average success rate versus 82.75% for SmolVLA and 76.5% for OpenVLA-7B.
Maintains comparable inference efficiency with approximately 500M activated parameters and 800M stored parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse MoE vision-language-action model for multi-task robot manipulation fits embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: SmolVLA-MoE: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: SmolVLA-MoE improves efficient multi-task robotic manipulation by using sparse, token-routed experts in the VLA action module.

papers.abstract: Agents tasked with intercepting a moving target must learn how to reach it, ideally as efficiently as possible. As observers of animal pursuit behavior have noticed, different strategies are possible: on one extreme, the agent reactively moves toward the target's current location; on the other, the agent predicts the target's future location and moves directly there. Motivated by the desire to understand how such strategies might be learned, we introduce a continuous-time linear-quadratic model of open-loop target pursuit whose optimal control strategies interpolate between these possibilities. Usefully, a small number of interpretable parameters control which type of strategy is optimal, and it is possible to derive closed-form solutions for optimal strategies, policy learning dynamics, and value learning dynamics. Exploiting our model's linear structure, we find that the time scales of learning precisely correspond to the eigenvalues of certain matrices, and that relevant eigenvalue spectra generically have a gap. We show that this gap indicates that agents tend to learn how to reach their target before optimizing their movement. Our results provide a detailed mathematical characterization of pursuit behavior and its learning dynamics, which can both serve as a benchmark for empirical work, and as a foundation for more elaborate theoretical treatments of pursuit.
bullets: Models continuous-time, open-loop pursuit with interpretable parameters controlling reactive versus predictive behavior.
Derives closed-form optimal strategies, policy-learning dynamics, and value-learning dynamics.
Shows learning time scales are determined by matrix eigenvalues, whose generic spectral gap separates learning stages.
Finds agents tend to first learn how to reach the target, then optimize how efficiently they move.
Provides a mathematical benchmark for empirical pursuit studies and a foundation for more complex theories.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical model of learned pursuit and interception strategies for moving targets, directly relevant to embodied navigation and goal-conditioned navigation.
papers.title: Solvable models of learning to pursue a moving target
papers.tldr: A solvable linear-quadratic model shows how agents learn to pursue moving targets, transitioning between reactive and predictive strategies while typically learning target interception before movement efficiency.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robotic surgery has drawn increased attention in recent years due to its potential to relieve surgeons of time-consuming, mentally straining, and tedious tasks, particularly during prolonged operations. One suitable task for automation is suturing, which involves tracking the thread as it deforms during needle retrieval, de-tangling, knot tightening, and other tasks. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, deformable thread manipulation has no fixed pose to track and effectively infinite degrees of freedom, making its configuration difficult to predict and requiring the thread's state to be re-estimated rather than assumed. At the same time, thread manipulations involve sequential motions that depend on past and current thread contact points, which must be accurately and continuously tracked. This paper presents an image-to-manipulation pipeline that concurrently generates live thread reconstruction while conducting safe and optimized sequential manipulations to achieve long-horizon tasks.
authors: Emma Huang, Omar Hernandez, Zih-Yun Chiu, Michael Yip
bullets: Targets autonomous suturing tasks such as needle retrieval, de-tangling, and knot tightening.
Addresses the thread’s deformability, infinite degrees of freedom, and changing configuration.
Continuously tracks current and past thread contact points during sequential manipulation.
Combines live visual thread reconstruction with safe, optimized manipulation planning.
The abstract does not report specific experimental results or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Image-to-manipulation pipeline for deformable thread manipulation in autonomous surgery is a robot manipulation learning task.
papers.title: Live Thread Reconstruction for Autonomous Manipulation
papers.tldr: An image-to-manipulation pipeline reconstructs deformable surgical thread online while guiding safe, optimized long-horizon suturing actions.
