papers.selection_reason: Pipeline generating robot demonstrations from a single human RGB video via semantic augmentation; directly relevant to learning from human video and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
papers.tldr: Real2Sem2Real converts a single monocular human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across diverse object instances for training manipulation policies.

papers.abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks. Videos and code are available at https://anonymous-submission-20.github.io/T-WLA.github.io/.
authors: Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu, Xihang Yu, Wei Dai, Bashar Kabbarah, Haoyu Chen, Ishita Goluguri, Zhiyang Dou, Haonan Chen, Fangneng Zhan, Mengyu Wang, Wojciech Matusik, Antonio Torralba, Paul Pu Liang
bullets: Addresses latency when contact conditions change faster than visual policy updates.
Generates base action chunks from images, instructions, and retrieved history.
Uses a lightweight tactile editor to revise unexecuted actions using touch and cached visual memory.
Adds future-image and future-pressure prediction as training-only supervision for interaction-aware representations.
Reports 30% lower finger-joint MPJPE than the strongest reported baseline and approximately 50.0% average success across four real-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: World-language-action architecture with tactile correction for dexterous manipulation and visual memory.
papers.title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch
papers.tldr: T-WLA uses shared visual memory and fast tactile residual corrections to adapt manipulation actions without rerunning the visual policy.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching policies adjust inference cost through the number of solver steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed solver budget can hide degradation at cheaper deployment budgets and even erase useful one-step behavior present in a pretrained policy. We introduce Action-Ratio-Clip Flow (ArcFlow), a deployment-aware algorithm for training one flow policy across a specified range of solver budgets. ArcFlow combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. For reconstruction objectives, its bridge aggregates temporal probes into one surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action, with a boundary residual exactly equal to deployed one-step reconstruction error. Cycling exposes the shared field to the deployment range, and selection optimizes its performance floor. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint supervision applies the same principle without replacing the native update. Both realizations preserve the architecture and deployment-time cost. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow attains the highest mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under each method's reported training settings. Component studies identify complementary improvements from boundary supervision, the fixed-grid bridge, budget exposure, and deployment selection. These results establish deployment-budget-aware training as an effective route to strong low-step control with one policy serving multiple inference costs.
bullets: Targets degradation at low solver budgets caused by training at only one fixed budget.
Combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection.
Provides reconstruction and native-velocity variants while preserving the policy architecture and deployment cost.
Reports the highest mean one-step return among five baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under the reported settings.
Component studies find complementary gains from boundary supervision, fixed-grid bridging, budget exposure, and deployment selection.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-budget-aware flow policies for low-step control; relevant to learned robot control and manipulation.
papers.title: ArcFlow: Training Flow Policies for Multiple Solver Budgets
papers.tldr: ArcFlow trains a single flow policy to remain effective across multiple solver budgets, especially cheap one-step deployment.

papers.abstract: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting alternatives to explore and safely accepting plans in world-model agents.
Compares imagined action sequences from the same model state and measures variability in repeated rollouts of the actor’s sequence.
Uses this reference to scale exploration signals and accept a plan only when its predicted advantage exceeds reference variability by a fixed factor.
Reuses the base world model, actor, and critic without an additional disagreement ensemble; evaluation runs the learned actor alone.
Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI has the highest task-average score among compared baselines in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline on 15 of 18 tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified exploration and planning through imagined rollouts in world models for control; directly relevant to world models and robot learning.
papers.title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models
papers.tldr: SDI uses variation in repeated actor rollouts as a shared reference to decide both what to explore and when imagined plans should override the learned policy.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework integrating a robust wrench observer with a hybrid pose and force controller for physical Human-Robot Interaction (pHRI). In pHRI tasks, robots are expected to perform task-space motions robustly while remaining compliance with human disturbance, which proposes distinct control objectives. Most existing approaches focus mainly on either robustness or compliance and rely on force sensors for real-time tracking. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. Firstly, a neural network (NN) is trained to improve the observer performance by compensating for system friction and unmodeled dynamics. Secondly, a task-null-space decomposition is applied to separate the joint velocity and reduce the effect of the human disturbance on the observer. Finally, a hybrid pose and force controller is introduced to achieve the end-effector pose and force tracking. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust and accurate wrench estimation while maintaining reliable pose and force tracking performance. The proposed approach offers an effective solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements which can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which do not have force/torque sensors.
authors: Nuo Chen, Ya-Jun Pan, Onur Toker
bullets: Targets pHRI tasks requiring both robust task-space motion and compliance to human disturbances.
Uses a neural network to compensate for friction and unmodeled dynamics in the wrench observer.
Applies task-null-space decomposition to reduce the impact of human disturbances on observer estimates.
Employs hybrid pose and force control for simultaneous end-effector pose and force tracking.
Experiments report accurate wrench estimation and reliable tracking without force/torque sensors.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-enhanced wrench observer for sensorless compliant control in physical human-robot interaction.
papers.title: Learning-Enhanced Observer for Sensorless Task-Null-Space Compliant Control
papers.tldr: A sensorless control framework combines a learning-enhanced wrench observer with task-null-space separation and hybrid pose–force control for robust, compliant human–robot interaction.

papers.abstract: In human-robot interaction (HRI) tasks, humans may interact with the robot in either an active guiding or passive following state, resulting in distinct control objectives for each interaction mode. Most existing approaches rely on predefined switching thresholds to distinguish interaction modes, but their performance can be sensitive to measurement noise. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. First, a neural network (NN) trained via meta-learning is developed to recognize human intention without manually defined thresholds. By successfully incorporating force-dependent parameters from the controller, the recognition rates are improved from 90.1\% to 99.1\% for the passive mode and from 79.8\% to 97.1\% for the active mode. Second, an adaptive meta-learning controller is introduced to compensate for human disturbances and enable online adaptation to varying interaction forces. Third, a multiple-trajectory meta-learning algorithm is designed to jointly learn an environment-basis representation and force-dependent parameters, allowing the controller to deal with unmodeled dynamics efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves robust and accurate control performance, while providing reliable mode recognition for safe and adaptive physical HRI.
bullets: Addresses noise-sensitive, threshold-based recognition of active guiding versus passive following.
Uses a meta-learning-trained neural network with force-dependent controller parameters for intention recognition.
Introduces an adaptive meta-learning controller to compensate for human disturbances and varying interaction forces.
A multiple-trajectory algorithm jointly learns environment representations and force-dependent parameters.
Reported recognition improves to 99.1% for passive mode and 97.1% for active mode, with robust control demonstrated experimentally.
papers.selection_reason: Meta-learning for human intention recognition and adaptive control in physical human-robot interaction.
papers.title: Human-Robot Interaction via Meta-Learning Based Mode Recognition and Adaptive Control
papers.tldr: A meta-learning framework recognizes active/passive HRI modes without fixed thresholds and adapts control to changing human forces and unmodeled dynamics.

papers.abstract: Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of imitation and persistent gaps in distant worlds suggest that building generalist embodied agents requires richer training stages beyond continued pre-training.
authors: Kuan Zhang, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yue Su, Xiangnan Wu, Zirong Chen, Run Luo, Jinkun Hou, Tao Tan, Yinhe Zheng, Yiming Li
bullets: Studies data volume, world diversity, and model size across 120 configurations spanning 0.8B–27B models and 50–1,600 hours of data.
More data improves in-corpus performance; diversity mainly improves transfer to related worlds, while larger models improve data efficiency.
Identifies an early broad-benefit interface phase and a later world-specific phase, and fits an empirical scaling law for validation loss.
Models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, performing best in real-time settings.
Persistent gaps on distant worlds indicate that continued pre-training alone is insufficient for generalist embodied agents.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates continued pre-training for generalist embodied agents in diverse virtual worlds, focusing on learning and generalization.
papers.title: Scaling in Games: Continued Pre-Training For Embodied Agents In Diverse Virtual Worlds
papers.tldr: Continued pre-training scales embodied agents effectively within and across related virtual worlds, but distant-world generalization remains limited and likely requires training beyond imitation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly deployed with asynchronous inference in real-world settings, where the next action chunk is generated while the robot is still executing the previous one. By the time the new chunk is committed, the robot and scene have changed, so the chunk is conditioned on a stale observation and task success drops sharply as this inference delay grows. Generating multiple candidate chunks could let newer observations inform the final choice, but existing multi-candidate methods either rank candidates with the stale inference-start observation or repeatedly switch between candidates during execution, which can make the executed action sequence discontinuous. Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation. We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework that generates candidates from the inference-start observation and selects one using this pre-commit observation. Its scoring function, FlowRes, measures the residual between each candidate's implied flow direction and the velocity predicted by the frozen policy under the pre-commit observation, requiring no separate verifier. A pipelined implementation overlaps observation processing with candidate generation and batches scoring, so selection adds no control-step delay on the evaluated hardware. At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and it further improves existing delay-robust methods. On three real-robot tasks, it raises average success from 60% to 82% over naive asynchronous execution with the same frozen $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when action chunks are generated from stale observations during asynchronous inference.
Generates multiple candidate chunks from the inference-start observation, then selects one using a later pre-commit observation.
FlowRes scores candidates by comparing their implied flow direction with velocity predicted by the frozen VLA policy; no separate verifier is needed.
A pipelined implementation overlaps candidate generation and scoring, adding no control-step delay on evaluated hardware.

At a four-step delay, average success improves by 15.0 points over RTC on Kinetix, 5.2 points over single-candidate execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and from 60% to 82% on three real-robot tasks over naive asynchronous execution.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free framework to improve VLA policy robustness against inference delay by selecting action chunks using pre-commit observations.
papers.title: PACT-VLA: Speculative Action-Chunk Verification with Pre-Commit Observations
papers.tldr: PACT-VLA uses delayed observations to verify and select complete action chunks, improving asynchronous VLA control without additional training or control-step latency.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have explored the potential of multimodal large language models for robot control, yet the models' embodied capabilities remain insufficiently characterized across models, tasks, and execution settings. We conduct a multidimensional comparative evaluation on RoboColiseum across four tracks: Instruction Following, Spatial Reasoning, General Manipulation, and Robustness. We implement Agent2Act, a control harness that integrates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon into the evaluation environment through shared observation, action execution, and feedback interfaces. Under common task settings and scoring criteria, all four models exhibit a consistent capability profile: high instruction-following scores, with three approaching perfect performance; strong spatial reasoning; and general manipulation scores below those of the other three tracks. Within the evaluated configurations, Astra leads instruction following and robustness, while Opus leads spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and overall performance. These results reveal complementary strengths across models and a persistent gap between task understanding and reliable physical execution. Component comparisons on selected tasks further show that harness design affects task success, planning cost, and execution time. Additionally, case studies with Astra examine whole-body coordination, manipulation across robot embodiments, precision manipulation, dexterous-hand manipulation, and real-robot tasks, providing further insight into the model's capabilities and limitations across embodied tasks.
bullets: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon across instruction following, spatial reasoning, manipulation, and robustness.
All models perform strongly on instruction following and spatial reasoning, but general manipulation is consistently weaker.
Astra leads instruction following and robustness; Opus leads spatial reasoning, manipulation, and overall performance in the tested configurations.
Harness design influences task success, planning cost, and execution time.
Astra case studies examine whole-body coordination, cross-embodiment manipulation, precision and dexterous manipulation, and real-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-model evaluation of frontier multimodal LLMs for embodied robot control, including instruction following, spatial reasoning, manipulation, and robustness.
papers.title: Frontier LLMs Enter the World of Robotics: A Cross-Model Evaluation on RoboColiseum
papers.tldr: A cross-model RoboColiseum evaluation finds that frontier multimodal LLMs understand robot tasks well but still struggle with reliable physical manipulation, with performance varying by model and harness design.

papers.abstract: In robot-assisted education, a robot must understand how to complete a task in order to effectively guide a student through it. We present a novel method that enables a semi-autonomous, camera-equipped robot to recognise the task goal and plan actions to achieve it. Our work focuses on Shoebox Tasks, an activity commonly used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). These tasks are designed so that the goal can be inferred directly from their visual structure. We have developed a solver that uses a vision-based Large Language Model to convert photos of a Shoebox Task into a Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) representation and generate action plans for solving it. We have also implemented a robotic interface that enables a Nao robot to autonomously execute various Shoebox Tasks and assist a student by suggesting next steps or signalling detected failures through action demonstrations, voice commands, or gestures. With an adapted robotic interface, the solver can be integrated into a variety of educational robots. No programming expertise is required from teachers, and the solver operates exclusively on captured images as input. Research in special educational needs indicates that students with ASD can benefit substantially from robot-assisted teaching, and our system aims to strengthen these learning opportunities while also fostering interest in robotics among individuals with ASD.
bullets: Targets robot-assisted education for individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder, where robots must understand task goals to provide effective guidance.
Uses a vision-based Large Language Model to translate task photos into PDDL representations and generate action plans.
Integrates the solver with a Nao robot to execute tasks, suggest next steps, and signal failures through multimodal interaction.
Requires no programming expertise from teachers and uses captured images as its sole input.
The approach is demonstrated for Shoebox Tasks and is intended to support adaptable educational-robot deployments.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-based task modeling and automated planning for humanoid robots executing physical educational tasks; embodied perception and action.
papers.title: Visual Task Modeling and Automated Planning for Humanoid Robots in Education of Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
papers.tldr: A vision-based system lets a humanoid robot recognize and plan Shoebox Tasks from images, then guide students with ASD through them using demonstrations, speech, and gestures.

papers.abstract: Reliable contact establishment remains a critical challenge for autonomous on-orbit servicing (OOS), particularly when interacting with non-cooperative targets. Gecko-inspired dry adhesives provide a lightweight, passive, and residue-free solution for robotic capture in space, yet current systems operate in open loop, without the ability to estimate their own contact or adhesion state during interaction. This paper presents a real-time interaction-awareness framework that enables sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces to estimate their contact state throughout the adhesion lifecycle using embedded capacitive sensing. Five discrete interaction states (idle, proximity, contact, engaged, and disengaged) are classified using experimentally collected and augmented sensor data, enabling a comparative evaluation of six lightweight machine learning models suitable for embedded deployment. Among the evaluated models, Random Forest achieved the highest offline classification accuracy of 95.65%. For online deployment, combining Random Forest with a rule-based state machine improved accuracy from 78.02% to 93.14%, achieving a macro F1-score of 0.9343 while maintaining a 53 ms inference cycle. These results demonstrate that incorporating physics-consistent state constraints significantly improves robustness during realtime inference, representing a step toward interaction-aware capture in future autonomous orbital servicing missions.
bullets: Addresses the lack of contact and adhesion-state awareness in open-loop systems for servicing non-cooperative spacecraft.
Uses embedded capacitive sensing with lightweight machine-learning classifiers and a rule-based state machine.
Classifies idle, proximity, contact, engaged, and disengaged states throughout the adhesion lifecycle.
Random Forest achieved 95.65% offline accuracy; online hybrid inference reached 93.14% accuracy and a 0.9343 macro F1-score with a 53 ms cycle.
Demonstrates improved robustness through physics-consistent state constraints, with scope focused on experimentally collected and augmented sensor data.
papers.selection_reason: Real-time contact and adhesion-state recognition for sensorized robotic capture; relevant to physical interaction in robot manipulation.
papers.title: Towards Interaction State Recognition in Sensorized Gecko-Inspired Adhesive Interfaces for Orbital Servicing
papers.tldr: A real-time capacitive-sensing framework recognizes five interaction states in gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces, enabling more robust autonomous orbital capture.

papers.abstract: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/
bullets: Covers 410 environments involving manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities.
Tests coordination of physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning under interdependent actions and execution feedback.
Provides EP-100, EP-Easy, EP-Hard, and EP-20 task selections spanning five suites and 16 task types.
Uses a shared protocol with observation/tool constraints, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent validity checks.
Evaluates task progress, intermediate constraints, plan revision, goal completion, rule compliance, and physical validity.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for foundation-model agents on long-horizon physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning in embodied environments.
papers.title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: Embodied Playground benchmarks whether foundation-model agents can sustain reliable reasoning and physical action across long-horizon robotic tasks.

papers.abstract: Differences in hand geometry, joint parameterization, and kinematic topology pose challenges for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation. However, spatial relations among links alone are insufficient to fully capture the hand's kinematic topology. We propose DexGraspFlow, a conditional link-level $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ flow-matching framework integrating geometric relations and kinematic topology. The framework encodes local object geometry, link geometry, and current poses. A dual-stream DiT models link--link coordination and link--object interaction, while attention biases derived from kinematic-tree distances provide explicit structural information for modeling evolving geometric interactions. The model jointly learns translational and rotational velocity fields, integrates them to generate link poses, and recovers joint configurations through inverse kinematics. Additionally, inference-time palm-orientation guidance enables controllable grasp generation without retraining. Across three robotic hands and 30 object--hand pairs, DexGraspFlow achieves a 95.33\% average simulation success rate, with an average generation latency, including inverse kinematics, approximately 49\% lower than that of a state-of-the-art baseline. Further experiments demonstrate zero-shot adaptability to seven finger-removal variants and palm-orientation control. A model trained on demonstrations for the deployed hand achieves a 91\% success rate over 100 real-robot grasping trials, supporting the framework's applicability to physical grasp execution.
bullets: Addresses cross-embodiment grasp generation despite differences in hand geometry, joint parameters, and kinematic topology.
Uses a conditional link-level SE(3) flow model with geometric features and kinematic-tree distance biases.
A dual-stream DiT models link–link coordination and link–object interaction, then inverse kinematics recovers joint configurations.
Achieves 95.33% average simulation success across three hands and 30 object–hand pairs, with about 49% lower generation latency than a stated baseline.
Demonstrates zero-shot adaptation to seven finger-removal variants, palm-orientation control, and 91% success in 100 real-robot trials.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation with SE(3) flow matching and kinematic topology; directly relevant to robot manipulation and grasping.
papers.title: DexGraspFlow: Topology-Aware SE(3) Flow Matching for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasp Generation
papers.tldr: DexGraspFlow uses topology-aware SE(3) flow matching to generate controllable dexterous grasps across different robotic hand embodiments.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in human-centric environments must coordinate the entire body to traverse tight, cluttered spaces while maintaining balance. Existing methods often struggle to jointly consider dynamic stability and collision avoidance from high-dimensional perceptual inputs. Moreover, for humanoids, safe behavior is inherently multimodal: the same obstacle may admit multiple valid traversals, which is difficult to represent with a single deterministic policy. To address these challenges, we propose SWAP (Steerable Whole-body Avoidance Policy), a hierarchical framework that separates collision-aware decision making from stabilization. A high-level, perception-conditioned diffusion policy generates multimodal, collision-aware motion proposals, while a low-level whole-body RL controller tracks these proposals and maintains dynamic balance. To efficiently train the high-level policy, we obtain scalable supervision via hindsight labeling: we roll out the low-level policy under randomized commands, place obstacles only in the space that each executed motion did not sweep, so the motion is collision-free by construction, and re-render the perception the robot would have seen. At deployment, Monte Carlo sampling with simple cost signals steers the diffusion model toward safe, task-aligned behaviors without heavy reward tuning. Experiments in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid show reliable avoidance with static and dynamic obstacles. Test-time steering further enables customization, improving targeted rewards (e.g., speed, orientation, or posture) by 34% on average while maintaining a high collision avoidance rate. Together, these results support a practical solution to humanoid whole-body collision avoidance with test-time steerability. Project website: https://iscoyizj.github.io/SWAP-steerable-humanoid-oa-website/
bullets: Targets collision avoidance and dynamic balance from high-dimensional perceptual inputs in tight, human-centric spaces.
Uses a hierarchical design: a perception-conditioned diffusion policy proposes diverse motions, while a low-level RL controller tracks them and preserves balance.
Trains the high-level policy with hindsight labeling, generating collision-free supervision from randomized low-level rollouts.
At deployment, Monte Carlo sampling and simple costs steer behavior toward task-specific goals such as speed, orientation, or posture.
Simulation and real Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate reliable avoidance of static and dynamic obstacles; targeted rewards improve by 34% on average while maintaining high collision avoidance.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical diffusion-policy and RL whole-body control for humanoid obstacle avoidance with test-time steerability.
papers.title: SWAP: Test-Time Steerable Humanoid Whole-Body Collision Avoidance
papers.tldr: SWAP enables humanoid robots to safely navigate cluttered environments by combining multimodal motion proposals with whole-body stabilization and test-time steering.

papers.abstract: Dexterous grasping in cluttered scenes remains a central challenge in robotic manipulation, as it requires high-dimensional hand coordination under complex object-environment constraints. To address this problem, we introduce one of the largest simulation benchmarks to date, comprising around 0.5B grasp annotations across eight dexterous hands and approximately 50K objects. Furthermore, we propose T(R,O) Grasp++, a scalable diffusion-based framework for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis in cluttered environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average success rate of 88% across eight dexterous embodiments. Meanwhile, our pipeline achieves only 0.3s inference latency while improving inference sample efficiency by over 10 times.
bullets: Introduces a simulation benchmark with around 0.5B grasp annotations spanning eight dexterous hands and approximately 50K objects.
Presents a diffusion-based framework for cross-embodiment grasp generation under complex object-environment constraints.
Reports an average success rate of 88% across eight embodiments.
Achieves 0.3-second inference latency and over 10× improved inference sample efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based cross-embodiment dexterous grasping in clutter, directly relevant to robotic manipulation learning.
papers.title: T(R,O) Grasp++: Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping in Cluttered Environments at Scale
papers.tldr: T(R,O) Grasp++ enables fast, scalable dexterous grasp synthesis across different robot hands in cluttered scenes.

papers.abstract: Object Navigation in unseen environments remains a fundamental challenge in embodied AI, as it requires agents to generalize visual and spatial reasoning to novel layouts. While recent advances in large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) have enhanced semantic mapping, spatial memory, and waypoint selecting for navigation, successful navigation requires more than selecting the next promising waypoint. A robot must also recognize stalled progress, escape unproductive behaviors, and revisit overlooked target cues. Addressing these challenges requires both specialized navigation strategies and a high-level policy that coordinates their execution. Motivated by the analysis of failed navigation episodes, we propose LERR-Nav, an object navigation framework that coordinates exploration, recovery, and reminiscing through a learned high-level policy. The framework comprises four complementary navigation strategies: value-function-guided exploration, LLM-guided exploration, recovery from stalled or repetitive behavior, and memory-guided reminiscing. To support history-aware coordination, we maintain the execution memory that preserves textual summaries of all strategy executions alongside a sliding window of map sequences. To learn the coordination policy, we initialize a high-level vision-language agent from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and train it through a two-stage curriculum. The first stage uses map-centric supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to establish spatial grounding. The second stage performs SFT on variable-length navigation segments to learn which navigation strategy to invoke next based on current maps and the hybrid execution memory. Experiments on HM3D and MP3D demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance, while ablation studies validate the contributions of individual components.
bullets: Addresses stalled progress, repetitive behavior, and overlooked target cues beyond simple waypoint selection.
Combines value-function-guided and LLM-guided exploration with recovery and memory-guided reminiscing strategies.
Uses execution summaries and a sliding window of map sequences for history-aware coordination.
Trains a high-level vision-language policy with map-centric and variable-length navigation-segment supervision.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on HM3D and MP3D; ablations support the value of its components.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LERR-Nav, a framework for object navigation that coordinates exploration, recovery, and reminiscing using a high-level VLM policy.
papers.title: LERR-Nav: Learning to Coordinate Exploration, Recovery, and Reminiscing for Object Navigation
papers.tldr: LERR-Nav learns to coordinate exploration, recovery, and memory-based revisiting so robots can navigate to objects more reliably in unseen environments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. This task requires a transition from representations that describe the scene and instruction to representations that support action generation. Many continuous-action VLAs leave this transition implicit and supervise it mainly through the final action-prediction loss. We introduce PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation between these two spaces. During training, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from the current visual-language representations. PAIR aligns these features with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens that preserve task information and capture the structure of expert actions. The Bridge Tokens are then projected into the action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens, providing an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed, and the Bridge Tokens are generated only from the current observation and instruction. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC-D show gains for the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter models. On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses show that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement. These results support a shared intermediate representation as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs.
bullets: Addresses the implicit transition from scene and instruction representations to continuous actions in VLAs.
Uses a Masked Action Autoencoder to create horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens from expert action chunks.
A Bridge Module aligns task-relevant visual-language features with action latents, producing Bridge Tokens that initialize action generation.
At inference, Bridge Tokens are generated from observations and instructions without the autoencoder.
Improves evaluated models across LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and seven real-world tasks, including OpenVLA-OFT success rising from 51.4% to 65.0% and VLA-Adapter on LIBERO-Plus from 59.1% to 64.2%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation (Bridge Tokens) to improve continuous-action VLA models.
papers.title: PAIR: Bridging Perception and Action in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: PAIR improves continuous-action vision-language-action models by learning an intermediate representation that connects visual-language perception to robot action generation.

papers.abstract: Trajectory optimization (TO) under nonlinear dynamics, actuation limits and collision avoidance constraints is a fundamental problem in robotics, albeit especially challenging due to its highly non-convex nature. For this setting, Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) is an efficient second-order shooting method, yet its local structure renders it vulnerable to suboptimal basins. Sampling-augmented variants mitigate this susceptibility through stochastic exploration, but often sample only around the few trajectories they retain for reoptimization, based solely on their cost which restricts exploration breadth. We introduce Pareto-Optimal Entropy-Regularized DDP (PER-DDP), an entropy-regularized population framework derived from the free-energy/relative-entropy inequality. Our method combines prior-guided sampling that shapes exploration around each retained trajectory, with expanded rollout evaluations that probe these sampling policies beyond the few retained candidates, and Pareto filtering for preserving task-constraint alternatives across iterations. This decouples sampling effort from the optimization population size and broadens exploration without sacrificing the second-order structure that makes DDP effective. Across multiple systems and hundreds of environments, PER-DDP achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art sampling-augmented TO methods and finds reliable solutions in environments beyond the reach of all baselines.
bullets: Targets non-convex trajectory optimization with nonlinear dynamics, actuation limits, and collision-avoidance constraints.
Uses prior-guided sampling around retained trajectories, expanded rollouts, and Pareto filtering to preserve diverse task-constraint alternatives.
Decouples sampling effort from optimization population size, enabling broader exploration without abandoning DDP’s local second-order structure.
Across multiple systems and hundreds of environments, it achieves higher success rates than existing sampling-augmented methods and solves some environments all baselines miss.
papers.selection_reason: Extends Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) with entropy regularization and Pareto filtering to improve trajectory optimization in robotics.
papers.title: Pareto-Optimal Entropy-Regularized Trajectory Optimization
papers.tldr: PER-DDP broadens trajectory-optimization exploration with entropy-regularized sampling and Pareto filtering while retaining DDP’s efficient second-order optimization.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Code is available at https://github.com/du-owen/VLA-ACL.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of processing redundant visual tokens during robotic control.
Trains a lightweight pruning policy with action-level consistency supervision, using full-context predictions as a teacher and ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision.
Keeps the base VLA model completely frozen, avoiding costly end-to-end fine-tuning.
On LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks, prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5× inference speedup.
Demonstrates a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VLA-ACL, a method for efficient visual token pruning in VLA models using action-level supervision without fine-tuning the base model.
papers.title: VLA-ACL: Action-Consistent Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA-ACL efficiently prunes visual tokens in frozen vision-language-action models by learning which tokens preserve the model’s control actions.

papers.abstract: Continuous asynchronous replanning is essential for real-time generative robot policies, but independent stochastic initialization can cause mode switching and inconsistent continuation across action chunks. We propose Execution-Aligned Progressive Noise (EAPN), which introduces structured stochasticity at both inter-chunk and intra-chunk levels. Across replanning steps, EAPN propagates a shared noise trajectory and aligns it with the actual execution displacement, establishing execution-aligned inter-chunk correlation. Within each action chunk, it models temporal correlation along action time. The aligned stochastic history is further combined with committed action context to condition subsequent generation, allowing new chunks to continue from execution-consistent generative states rather than restart from independent noise. We evaluate EAPN on D3IL, Kinetix, LIBERO, and real-world manipulation tasks. EAPN improves multimodal behavior consistency on D3IL and achieves an average success rate of 88.59% on Kinetix. On LIBERO, it remains robust and maintains strong task performance even under long inference delays. Real-robot experiments further achieve 90.0% success on Object Storage and 96.7% on bimanual Cloth Folding, demonstrating reliable continuous execution under asynchronous replanning.
bullets: Addresses mode switching and discontinuous behavior caused by independently initialized action chunks.
Propagates an execution-aligned shared noise trajectory across chunks and models temporal correlations within each chunk.
Conditions new generation on aligned stochastic history and committed actions to continue from execution-consistent states.
Improves multimodal consistency on D3IL and achieves strong performance across Kinetix, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation tasks.
Reports 88.59% average success on Kinetix, 90.0% on Object Storage, and 96.7% on bimanual Cloth Folding; remains robust under long inference delays on LIBERO.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Execution-Aligned Progressive Noise (EAPN) to ensure consistent behavior in generative robot policies during asynchronous replanning.
papers.title: Execution-Aligned Progressive Noise for Consistent Asynchronous Replanning in Generative Robot Policies
papers.tldr: EAPN makes asynchronous generative robot replanning more consistent by aligning noise across replanning steps with actual execution and temporal action structure.

papers.abstract: Training robust social-navigation policies requires simulators with diverse scene layouts, terrain, and human motion, but constructing such environments and specifying pedestrian behavior is costly. We propose an efficient pipeline that converts ordinary monocular walking videos directly into closed-loop social-navigation training environments in the policy's state space. Our key observation is that local social navigation primarily depends on two types of information: where the robot can traverse and how nearby pedestrians move. We therefore represent the static scene as a metric traversability map, which can be rigidly transformed under counterfactual robot motion, while directly replaying the pedestrian trajectories recovered from the video over time. This abstraction allows us to define the forward dynamics directly in the policy's state space and efficiently simulate counterfactual robot states without reconstructing or rendering photorealistic observations. The resulting policy achieves 81.2% success in the independent Arena benchmark, compared with 75.0% for the strongest baseline, and succeeds in 19/20 real-robot trials without policy fine-tuning. Project page: https://jiaming.im/VideoSocNav
bullets: Addresses the high cost of building diverse social-navigation simulators and modeling pedestrian behavior.
Converts monocular walking videos into closed-loop training environments without photorealistic reconstruction or rendering.
Represents scenes with metric traversability maps and replays recovered pedestrian trajectories under counterfactual robot motion.
Achieves 81.2% success on the independent Arena benchmark versus 75.0% for the strongest baseline.
Succeeds in 19 of 20 real-robot trials without policy fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: The paper proposes a pipeline for training social-navigation policies directly from monocular videos in the policy state space, enabling efficient closed-loop training without simulators.
papers.title: Learning Social Navigation from Internet Videos in the Policy State Space
papers.tldr: A video-based pipeline learns robust social-navigation policies by replaying pedestrian motion and transforming traversability maps directly in the policy state space, achieving strong simulation and real-robot performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated promising capabilities as in-context policy optimizers for Reinforcement Learning (RL), enabling policy search driven by both numerical reward signals and natural language reasoning. However, deploying such methods in practice requires transmitting raw policy parameters and rewards history to cloud-based LLM APIs, exposing proprietary control strategies to third-party service providers. To address this issue, this paper introduces Privacy-Preserving Prompted Policy Search (PP-ProPS), a framework that enables LLM-guided policy optimization while keeping policy and environmental parameters confidential. PP-ProPS encodes policy parameters and reward values using secret client-side transformations before they are included in each API request, ensuring that the LLM provider observes only encoded policy parameters and scaled reward information. Furthermore, unlike Vanilla ProPS, the proposed framework does not require the true optimal episodic return to be known or disclosed to the LLM. Beyond protecting the optimization data, PP-ProPS improves the search process in two ways. First, it provides the LLM with individual reward components instead of only a single total return, offering more informative feedback about each candidate policy. Second, it uses a bounded history that prevents the prompt from growing indefinitely, improving search with high-dimensional policies and supporting the use of open-weight LLMs. The proposed PP-ProPS is evaluated on both continuous and discrete control problems spanning Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) locomotion, classic control, highway driving, and robotic arm manipulation. Compared to Vanilla ProPS, the proposed PP-ProPS outperforms ProPS in seven of the ten evaluated tasks, and surpasses conventional RL methods including PPO, SAC, and TRPO, in five of the six tasks.
bullets: Addresses the exposure of proprietary policy parameters, environmental parameters, and reward histories when using cloud LLM APIs for RL policy optimization.
Applies client-side secret transformations to policy parameters and rewards, and avoids requiring the true optimal episodic return.
Provides individual reward components to give the LLM more informative policy feedback.
Uses a bounded prompt history to prevent indefinite growth, supporting high-dimensional policies and open-weight LLMs.
Evaluated across continuous and discrete control tasks; it outperformed Vanilla ProPS on 7 of 10 tasks and conventional RL methods on 5 of 6 tasks.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-guided privacy-preserving RL policy search for robotic control, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Prompted Policy Search for Robotic Control
papers.tldr: PP-ProPS enables privacy-preserving LLM-guided robotic policy search by encoding sensitive policies and rewards while improving feedback and prompt scalability.

papers.abstract: Active perception is essential for robotic manipulation when fixed viewpoints leave task-relevant information occluded or unobserved. However, enabling vision-language-action (VLA) models to reason across changing viewpoints and actively acquire informative observations remains challenging. We present ActiveScale, a framework that advances active perception through coordinated model, data, and hardware designs. Our model augments a VLA with historical video observations and explicit camera-pose supervision, using per-frame pose tokens and a lightweight prediction head to associate observations across viewpoints and support a coherent understanding of the scene. To learn from the camera motion naturally present in human activity, we introduce a scalable human--robot mid-training recipe using 1000 hours of egocentric and robotic data, adapting the model to temporal inputs and pose supervision. We further introduce Active-perception Mobile-manipulation Platform (AMP), a robotic platform that supports active perception and mobile manipulation through single-operator teleoperation, enabling scalable collection of demonstrations that coordinate viewpoint changes and manipulation. Experiments demonstrate improved success rates on active-perception tasks, while ablation studies validate the contributions of camera-pose-aware modeling and egocentric mid-training. Together, these components provide an integrated foundation for studying and developing active perception in robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses occlusion and missing task information caused by fixed viewpoints in robotic manipulation.
Augments a vision-language-action model with historical video, per-frame camera-pose tokens, and pose supervision.
Uses 1000 hours of egocentric and robotic data for human–robot mid-training on temporal inputs and camera motion.
Introduces AMP, a teleoperable platform for collecting demonstrations that coordinate viewpoint changes with manipulation.
Experiments report improved active-perception success rates; ablations support pose-aware modeling and egocentric mid-training.
papers.selection_reason: VLA framework for active perception and mobile manipulation with human-video pretraining, directly fitting embodied robot learning.
papers.title: ActiveScale: Scaling Active Perception for Robots across Model, Data, and Hardware
papers.tldr: ActiveScale improves robotic active perception by jointly scaling VLA modeling, training data, and mobile-manipulation hardware for viewpoint-aware manipulation.

papers.abstract: Robotic data generation is a promising paradigm for scaling robot learning without collecting large-scale real-world data. However, generating geometrically diverse yet physically valid data for contact-rich tasks remains challenging, especially when success depends on precise geometric interfaces. Standard shape augmentation methods often distort task-critical interfaces, resulting in invalid contact relationships, e.g., fit mismatches or interpenetration, rendering downstream interactions infeasible. To address these limitations, we propose a function-preserving Real-to-Sim-to-Real framework that generates synthetic demonstrations from reconstructed assets without teleoperated source trajectories. Our method augments task-relevant object geometries through constraint-guided mesh deformation, together with physically consistent transfer of task poses and collision proxies. Visual domain randomization is further applied during simulation rollouts, enabling robust zero-shot policy deployment without real-world fine-tuning. Extensive experiments in both real-world and simulation settings demonstrate that our method enables robust generalization across unseen object geometries and diverse visual conditions in contact-rich and long-horizon tasks. Our method provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning for contact-rich tasks via shape deformation.
bullets: Addresses invalid contacts caused by standard shape augmentation in contact-rich manipulation.
Uses constraint-guided mesh deformation to preserve task-critical geometric interfaces.
Transfers task poses and collision proxies consistently while applying visual domain randomization in simulation.
Generates demonstrations without teleoperated source trajectories and supports zero-shot real-world deployment.
Experiments show robust generalization in simulated and real settings across unseen geometries and diverse visual conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Function-preserving data generation for zero-shot sim-to-real manipulation; directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Function-Preserving Data Generation for Zero-Shot Real-to-Sim-to-Real Manipulation
papers.tldr: A function-preserving Real-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline generates valid synthetic demonstrations for zero-shot manipulation across unseen object shapes and visual conditions.

papers.abstract: Robotic piano playing has emerged as a standard benchmark for dexterous bimanual manipulation, yet progress on it has been measured almost entirely by note accuracy -- which keys are pressed (pitch) and when (onset) -- leaving the musical dynamics essential for expressive performance neither rewarded nor evaluated. We propose CANTABILE, a dynamics-aware framework for robotic piano performance that (i) closes the score-to-contact loop by conditioning the policy on upcoming velocity goals and mapping each key's angular velocity at onset back to MIDI velocity, (ii) couples a velocity-fidelity reward with an onset-coverage reward, so that dynamics cannot be improved by omitting difficult notes, and (iii) refines a frozen dynamics-aware base policy with an alpha-scaled, finger-only residual that localizes strike-intensity adaptation away from nominal note execution. On EXPRESSIVE-51, a dynamics-rich 51-song subset of RoboPianist, CANTABILE raises Velocity F1 -- jointly measuring pitch, onset, and intensity within a +/-8 MIDI-velocity tolerance -- from 0.06 to 0.34 over the RoboPianist baseline, improves all 51 songs, more than halves matched-note velocity error, and reduces log-mel distance to reference audio by 8%. Intensity-randomized training further enables runtime control of performance intensity without retraining.
bullets: Addresses the gap between conventional pitch/onset metrics and musically expressive performance.
Conditions control on upcoming velocity goals and maps key angular velocity to MIDI velocity.
Combines velocity-fidelity and onset-coverage rewards to discourage skipping difficult notes.
Uses a frozen base policy with an alpha-scaled, finger-only residual for strike-intensity adaptation.

On EXPRESSIVE-51, improves Velocity F1 from 0.06 to 0.34, more than halves matched-note velocity error, and reduces log-mel distance by 8%; intensity can also be adjusted at runtime without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Dynamics-aware policy learning for expressive robotic piano performance; fits dexterous bimanual manipulation and robot learning.
papers.title: CANTABILE: Learning Expressive Dynamics for Robotic Piano Performance
papers.tldr: CANTABILE enables robotic pianists to perform with expressive dynamics by explicitly controlling and evaluating key strike intensity alongside note accuracy.

papers.abstract: Agile quadrotor avoidance of fast-moving obstacles requires anticipating collisions and selecting feasible maneuvers within short reaction windows. Reliable predictive avoidance remains challenging because sparse range observations do not directly reveal obstacle motion, while online trajectory optimizers either scale poorly with obstacle count or remain efficient at the expense of reliability in dense, high-speed encounters. We present OmniRisk, an omnidirectional planning framework that learns trajectory-level risk offline for efficient onboard evasion. A fixed-dimensional tensor combines LiDAR range panoramas, dynamic masks, and Cartesian surface velocities to represent geometry and motion jointly. We formulate an asymmetric risk field aligned with obstacle velocity that emphasizes approaching interactions and attenuates receding ones. Accumulating this risk along predicted relative trajectories provides dense supervision and discourages unnecessary hesitation after obstacles pass. A dual-branch circular convolutional network predicts terminal boundary states and dynamic risks for candidate primitives over an omnidirectional anchor lattice in a single forward pass, followed by selection and closed-form reconstruction of the selected candidate primitive. This formulation removes online risk accumulation along trajectories and makes risk-inference cost independent of obstacle count. OmniRisk enables efficient onboard avoidance, with real-world flights demonstrating consecutive evasive maneuvers at relative encounter speeds up to 15 m/s without fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/VANdexj/OmniRisk.
bullets: Targets collision anticipation and feasible maneuver selection during dense, high-speed encounters with limited reaction time.
Combines LiDAR range panoramas, dynamic masks, and Cartesian surface velocities in a fixed-dimensional representation.
Uses an asymmetric, velocity-aligned risk field that emphasizes approaching obstacles and reduces hesitation after they recede.
A dual-branch circular-convolutional network predicts risks and terminal states for candidate maneuvers in one forward pass, with closed-form reconstruction of the selected primitive.
Real-world flights demonstrate consecutive evasive maneuvers at relative encounter speeds up to 15 m/s without fine-tuning; code is publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Learned omnidirectional trajectory-risk field for agile quadrotor dynamic avoidance; fits robot navigation and local planning.
papers.title: OmniRisk: Omnidirectional Trajectory-Risk Learning for Agile Quadrotor Dynamic Avoidance
papers.tldr: OmniRisk enables fast, reliable onboard quadrotor avoidance by learning omnidirectional trajectory risk from LiDAR-derived geometry and motion cues offline.

papers.abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation requires policies that coordinate high-DoF hand joints through intermittent, contact-rich interaction. Beyond target-orientation tracking, such policies must discover finger gaits that preserve object stability while adapting to geometry, anisotropy, pose, contact, and sensing changes. We propose \method, a tactile-conditioned behavior prior model for dexterous reorientation. \method distills multi-scale sphere specialists into a latent controller and lets downstream policies reuse the fixed tactile prior through residual latent actions, reducing renewed exploration from raw joint commands. The prior conditions on tactile-proprioceptive history so latent behavior reflects the current hand-object interaction. We evaluate arbitrary-pose transfer across anisotropic objects, commanded-axis rotation, and an arm-hand Grasp-to-AnyPose task in which the robot must grasp, lift, transport, and reach goal poses for novel tool geometries and generalized placements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method accelerates training and enables stable policies where matched raw-action PPO remains near failure, with successful sim-to-real transfer in in-hand and arm-hand tasks.
bullets: Targets contact-rich, high-DoF manipulation requiring finger gaits that maintain object stability under changing geometry, pose, and sensing.
Distills multi-scale sphere specialists into a latent controller conditioned on tactile-proprioceptive history.
Downstream policies reuse the fixed prior through residual latent actions instead of exploring directly from raw joint commands.
Evaluated on arbitrary-pose transfer, commanded-axis rotation, and arm-hand Grasp-to-AnyPose tasks involving novel tool geometries and placements.
Experiments report faster training, stable policies where matched raw-action PPO nearly fails, and successful sim-to-real transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Tactile-conditioned behavior prior for dexterous manipulation using residual latent actions; fits robot learning and latent-action modeling.
papers.title: TacBPM: A Tactile-conditioned Behavior Prior Model for Dexterous Reorientation
papers.tldr: TacBPM uses a tactile-conditioned behavior prior to help dexterous hands learn stable in-hand reorientation with less exploration than raw joint-control policies.

papers.abstract: Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion. Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene. For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene. Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video-motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion. Videos and additional results are available on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/par/projects/jca/.
authors: Noam Rotstein, Yoad Tewel, Chen Tessler, Haggai Maron, Gal Chechik, Or Litany, Yoni Kasten, Yuval Atzmon
bullets: Addresses the gap between realistic video generation and usable 3D animation for specific assets.
Separates an arbitrary-skeleton 3D motion model from a pretrained video model, linking them with lightweight cross-attention.
Predicts joint locations in video to recover the camera and register 3D motion in the scene.
Uses curated synthetic edits plus human and robot video to create nearly 200K training pairs.
Supports text-to-motion/video, video-to-rig motion, rig-motion-to-video, and keyframe control; evaluations report more faithful, scene-responsive animation than video-first pipelines.
papers.selection_reason: Co-generates 3D motion and video for arbitrary rigs from human/robot video; transferable to embodied animation and 3D motion generation.
papers.title: Joints, Camera, Action! Co-Generating 3D Motion and Video for Arbitrary Rigs
papers.tldr: Joints, Camera, Action! co-generates scene-aware video, camera motion, and replayable 3D motion for arbitrary rigs from text or video.

papers.abstract: Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds---from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video---into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world. Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex/.
authors: Yuxuan Kuang, Jiashun Wang, Yixuan Sun, Yufei Ye, Sungjae Park, Umar Iqbal, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Shubham Tulsiani
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between natural human-like behavior and robustness to varied object poses and goals.
Uses Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy learns from dense motion tracking and sparse object-success objectives in parallel environments.
Supports demonstrations from mocap or hand–object reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video.
Learns skills including functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and throw-and-catch.
Reports improved generalization and functionality over baselines, with transfer across simulators and to the real world.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses dexterous robot skill learning from human motion with goal-conditioned RL and real-world transfer.
papers.title: Learning Adaptable Dexterous Skills via Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking
papers.tldr: AdaDex combines human motion imitation with goal-conditioned reinforcement learning to learn adaptable, human-like dexterous skills from only a few seconds of hand–object motion.

papers.abstract: Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior? Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank. To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost. UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench, where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame. On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance (<=33.3%).
authors: Rahul Sajnani, Diego Romeres, Mingyuan Zhang, Kai Gao, Carl Qi, Baichuan Huang, Srinath Sridhar, Dylan Randle, Lillian J. Ratliff, Jose Barreiros, Manikantan Nambi, Jeroen Vanbaar
bullets: Learns shared representations across video, actions, and language, with each modality serving as both input and training target.
Uses a mixture-of-transformers backbone with synchronized modality-specific diffusion heads to generate actions and textual memory in one pass.
Re-consumes generated language on subsequent steps, creating a language-as-memory loop without an external memory bank or planner.
Introduces Flow Matching with Correction to improve recovery from perturbed action trajectories without inference-time overhead.
Reports gains on compositional manipulation, memory-dependent benchmarks, and a real-world Find-the-Item task; scope is demonstrated on these tasks and settings.
papers.selection_reason: A unified VLA model that integrates video, action, and language with a language-as-memory loop, directly relevant to embodied control and world modeling.
papers.title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control
papers.tldr: UniWALM unifies video, action, and language generation in one model, using language as memory to improve memory-dependent robot manipulation without a separate planner.

papers.abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.
authors: Michael Chen, Hong Chul Nam, Xi Deng, Anima Anandkumar
bullets: Uses reflecting obstacle boundaries and a goal Dirichlet condition to preserve navigation signals along long routes.
Extends the Walk on Stars Monte Carlo solver to higher-dimensional, mesh-free PDE computation.
Amortizes noisy, partially converged field estimation by learning geometry-to-field mappings.
Combines predicted global fields with bounded local search at inference time.
Across four noise levels, achieves 95–100% success on a 4D replanning benchmark with the lowest runtime; at the highest noise, it is 3.29–32.15× faster than alternatives.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a neural operator for planning under noise, using a screened-Poisson formulation and Walk on Stars solver for efficient value field computation.
papers.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
papers.tldr: PUN learns noise-aware value fields for fast, reliable planning across unseen geometries under uncertain control execution.

papers.abstract: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas, a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors.
