papers.title: Map-Distribution Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
papers.tldr: A map-distribution Mixture-of-Experts router combines specialized MAPF policies by local situation, improving pretrained policies while remaining behind well-trained monolithic models.

papers.abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
authors: Hojin Jeon, Jimin Lee, Taekwan Kim, Nayoung Oh, Taeyoung Kim, Myungkyu Koo, Jinmo Koo, Joonwoo Ahn, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses temporal inefficiency caused by fine-grained actions learned from teleoperation data.
Uses shared-expert action decoders supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons.
Selects execution modes through quantizability guidance and a context-conditioned router.
Improves execution efficiency while maintaining success across three simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks.
Evaluated on multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive temporal action quantization for VLA robot policies; directly fits vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: PaceVLA adaptively varies action granularity in VLA policies to speed up robot manipulation without sacrificing task success.

papers.abstract: Joint 4D reconstruction of a human and object from a monocular video is essential for understanding how people interact with their environment. While recent methods have made noticeable progress, capturing such human-object interactions remains difficult due to two main challenges. First, a video typically contains composite semantic context spanning multiple interaction phases, making it difficult to track the temporal changes of the interaction in the reconstruction. Second, under human-object occlusion, a single-view observation contains incomplete visual information about the interaction, resulting in geometrically inconsistent reconstructions. To address these challenges, we introduce HORIA, built upon two core designs. First, we decompose the entire input video into temporally grounded and semantically distinct interaction phases with motion-aware captioning, obtaining a specific text description for each phase. Second, conditioned on these text descriptions of the interaction, we propose an interaction-aware re-rendering that compensates for the limited single-view observation. Specifically, we render the initially reconstructed 4D human and object from novel viewpoints and refine the renderings with a text-to-video diffusion prior, which provides auxiliary novel-view supervision beyond single-view cues. As a result, our framework produces temporally coherent and accurate 4D reconstructions under diverse interaction scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Hyeongjin Nam, Taeryung Lee, Daniel Sungho Jung, Kyoung Mu Lee
bullets: Addresses interaction-phase changes and incomplete geometry caused by human-object occlusion in single-view video.
Decomposes videos into semantically distinct, temporally grounded phases using motion-aware captioning.
Uses phase descriptions to guide text-to-video diffusion refinement of novel-view renderings.
Provides auxiliary supervision beyond the original monocular observations.
Reports accurate, temporally coherent reconstructions across diverse interactions with state-of-the-art performance.
papers.selection_reason: Reconstructs 4D human and object scenes from monocular video using interaction-aware re-rendering. This advances 3D reconstruction and world modeling for embodied interactions.
papers.title: HORIA: 4D Human and Object Reconstruction from a Monocular Video with Interaction-Aware Re-Rendering
papers.tldr: HORIA reconstructs temporally coherent 4D humans and objects from monocular interaction videos by combining phase-aware text descriptions with diffusion-guided novel-view re-rendering.

papers.abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.
authors: X. Feng, J. Tang, Z. Lin, L. Chen, S. Shao, Q. Lu, K. Huang
bullets: Targets embodied agents that can understand diverse 3D environments and perform general actions beyond single-scene tasks.
Provides over 200K navigation-planning samples across diverse scenes with low-level motion and high-level semantic annotations.
Introduces unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics for offline pretraining and fair assessment.
Uses a video world model as a low-cost proxy environment for interactive RL post-training.
Pretraining improves open-world planning, while world-model RL further improves performance on out-of-distribution scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied navigation-planning dataset with interactive video world models for RL post-training directly fits embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: EmbodiedWorld-200K advances open-world embodied agents with a 200K-sample planning dataset and video-world-model-based interactive RL.

papers.abstract: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
authors: Matthias Eder, Pantelis Emmanouil, Vivek Farias, Fabian Fischer, Adam Jozefiak, Tianyi Peng, Thomas Ulz, Raphael Watschinger, Fangyu Wu, Andrew Zheng
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between labor-intensive algorithm design and opaque task-specific reinforcement learning.
Coding agents iteratively propose, implement, simulate, diagnose, verify, and refine policies in code space.
Two case studies found policies outperforming manually engineered or proprietary baselines, including reported gains of 35.0% and 58.9%.
The warehouse algorithm forms a new class of method and is proven collision-free and finite-completion under stated assumptions.
Results are demonstrated on competition maps and simulated irregular-lane warehouses; guarantees depend on the stated assumptions.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent pathfinding policy search with coding agents; directly relevant to embodied robot navigation and planning.
papers.title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
papers.tldr: Human-directed coding-agent search can discover interpretable, high-performing multi-agent pathfinding policies with formal correctness guarantees.

papers.abstract: In this work we focus on the problem of embodied task planning, which requires an agent to accomplish a complex task by separating it into atomic actions. Recent studies have developed LLM-based methods to address this problem. However, the executability and correctness of the generated plans remain suboptimal in complex environments and tasks. On the other hand, classical search algorithms have the potential to solve the planning problems perfectly, yet they require fully observable environments, known state transitions and goal state, which are often unattainable in general task domains. Therefore, we propose to implement an LLM-guided search algorithm that makes the search process possible and efficient by incorporating LLMs' commonsense knowledge. Our method leverages LLMs to (1) translate natural language instructions into formatted goal conditions, (2) facilitate efficient exploration in partially observable environments, (3) implement a rule-based world simulator, and (4) prune the space of candidate actions to improve search efficiency. Experimental results on VirtualHome and ALFWorld demonstrate its superior performance.
authors: Peiran Xu, Yixiang Yang, Jinghan Li, Fei Li, Cao Sheng, JiaZhong Yu, Yadong Mu
bullets: Addresses the limitations of LLM-generated plans and classical search when environments are complex, partially observable, or lack known transitions and goals.
Translates natural-language instructions into structured goal conditions and uses an LLM to guide exploration.
Employs a rule-based world simulator and prunes candidate actions to make search more efficient.
Demonstrates superior performance on the VirtualHome and ALFWorld benchmarks.
Scope: effectiveness is reported for these embodied task-planning environments; the abstract gives no further limitations.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-guided embodied task planning with search and simulation directly fits embodied AI.
papers.title: TESS: LLM-guided Translation, Exploration, Simulation, and Search for Embodied Task Planning
papers.tldr: TESS combines LLM commonsense reasoning with classical search to generate more executable and correct plans for embodied tasks in partially observable environments.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation often depends on short-term cues - such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states - that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task-agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations. We propose CondenseVLA, a multi-frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder-side history condensation module for using short-term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per-frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy. Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real-world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory-dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi-observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window. Project page: https://github.com/FeiyangHong/CondenseVLA
authors: Feiyang Hong, Yujie Wei, Bo Zhao, Xiu Su, Hongxun Yao, Shuo Yang
bullets: Targets short-term cues such as contacts, occlusions, and intermediate object states that single frames cannot resolve.
Uses decoder-side learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention to compress cached per-frame VLM features into a fixed set of history slots.
Regularizes slot attention and embeddings to encourage complementary, non-redundant representations.
Improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8%, reaches 97.2% on LIBERO and 52.8% on real-world tasks.
Achieves 21.6% on memory-dependent RMBench tasks, highlighting limits of a finite recent-history window.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CondenseVLA, a VLA policy that condenses visual history into slot tokens for efficient robot manipulation. This directly addresses robot manipulation and embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: CondenseVLA: Learnable History Condensation for Efficient Multi-Frame VLA
papers.tldr: CondenseVLA efficiently integrates recent visual history into robot actions by learning to condense redundant frame features into complementary slot tokens.

papers.abstract: As physical AI increasingly relies on sensing to understand physical systems, reliable condition monitoring of industrial machinery has become more important. Motors are ubiquitous in industrial systems, and increasing system complexity raises the likelihood of simultaneous faults. Accordingly, compound fault diagnosis that identifies multiple fault components and their severities is increasingly required. Because different fault components jointly affect the same vibration signal, their severity classification can be formulated as related tasks, making multi-task learning (MTL) suitable for exploiting shared information. However, conventional shared-trunk architectures force tasks to share a common representation, potentially causing negative transfer because fault components are characterized by different time-frequency regions. To address this issue, this study proposes a Residual Neural Dimension Reductor with Time-Frequency Channel Attention (RNDR-TFCA), an attention-enhanced cross-talk architecture for multi-output compound fault diagnosis. RNDR-TFCA preserves task-specific feature extractors while selectively exchanging information across tasks. Time-frequency attention emphasizes informative intra-task regions, while channel attention enhances useful inter-task information after nonlinear feature fusion. Experiments on a rotor-bearing system with inner-race fault, outer-race fault, misalignment, and unbalance showed that RNDR-TFCA achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898, outperforming single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines. Ablation experiments confirmed the benefit of jointly applying both attention mechanisms. RNDR-TFCA required 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs, only slightly higher than RNDR. Channel-expanded baselines still underperformed RNDR-TFCA, indicating that the gain was not simply attributable to increased model capacity.
authors: Wonjun Yi, Wonho Jung, Junho Kim, Rismaya Kumar Mishra, Yong-Hwa Park
bullets: Targets simultaneous identification and severity classification of motor faults from shared vibration signals.
Uses task-specific feature extractors with cross-task information exchange instead of a fully shared trunk.
Time-frequency attention highlights informative within-task regions, while channel attention refines exchanged features.
On a rotor-bearing system, it achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898 and outperformed the evaluated baseline architectures.
Ablations supported using both attention mechanisms; the model used 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an attention-based architecture for diagnosing compound faults in physical motors. Involves sensing physical systems and multi-task learning for physical interaction, relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: Motor compound fault diagnosis using an attention-based cross-talk architecture
papers.tldr: RNDR-TFCA improves compound motor-fault diagnosis by combining task-specific features with selective attention-based information sharing across fault types.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.
authors: Lingsen Zhang, Wei Li, Jie He, Henghua Zhang, Kai Mo, Shiyong Li, Yanpeng Wang, Rui Shao
bullets: Targets the learning burden and semantic-to-action gap in direct vision-language-action policies.
Models actionable state changes instead of reconstructing complete future states, reducing focus on static or irrelevant details.
Combines LT-Filter for local manipulation changes with GT-Anchor for coarse future-direction regularization.
Uses DDAR to inject the learned Delta into action denoising as a structured action-space seed.
Experiments report improved long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization.],
papers.selection_reason: Compact latent delta as actionable transition for VLA robotic manipulation; fits embodied VLA, robot learning, and latent-action world modeling.
papers.title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: VLDA learns compact, task-relevant state-change representations to bridge vision-language understanding and reliable robotic manipulation actions.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.
authors: Changshuo Liu, Jiaqi Zhu, Wenqiao Zhang, Xiaokui Xiao, Beng Chin Ooi
bullets: Addresses the gap between sample-level modeling and clinicians’ use of population patterns alongside individual variation.
Uses reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts.
Encodes each patient’s deviation from a cohort prototype as a structured drift signal.
Integrates cohort- and drift-aware representations into a multimodal foundation model.
Shows consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across EHR tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses condition monitoring of physical industrial machinery (motors) using attention-based architectures. Relates to sensing and understanding physical systems, a core aspect of embodied AI.
papers.title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
papers.tldr: CODA improves multimodal clinical reasoning by combining learned patient cohorts with patient-specific deviations from cohort prototypes.

papers.abstract: Fine industrial robotic manipulation requires 6D pose, scale, and an operation-ready 3D model. Existing industrial pose estimation relies on CAD models, object-specific training data, or stable workcells, limiting use with unseen objects; zero-shot methods suffer from single-view occlusion, generative bias, and scale uncertainty. We present OV-PEAR, an observation-verified framework for 3D reconstruction and pose-scale estimation of unknown industrial objects. Its three-stage object-centric pipeline: (1) segments RGB-D instances and generates object-level 3D hypotheses; (2) anchors them to the robot frame via appearance-aware view retrieval, explicit scale search, and visibility-sensitive registration; (3) back-projects multi-view RGB-D evidence into the object-canonical frame to verify voxel occupancy, suppress hallucinations, and produce reusable trusted object models. On BOP-Industrial, OV-PEAR achieves 0.657 average AR and improves pose and voxel-level geometric consistency in real scenes; real-robot connector assembly reaches 99.67% grasp and 84.00% assembly success. The model library and pose-scale log enable short-term object-level state maintenance at 0.02 ms/frame.
authors: Guoqin Tang, Qingxuan Jia, Yichen Tan, Zihang Lv, Ruiquan Wang, Zeyuan Huang, Gang Chen
bullets: Targets unknown objects under occlusion, scale uncertainty, and unstable workcell conditions.
Uses a three-stage pipeline for instance segmentation, object-level 3D hypothesis generation, robot-frame anchoring, and explicit scale estimation.
Verifies reconstructions by back-projecting multi-view RGB-D evidence to suppress hallucinated geometry and build trusted reusable models.
Achieves 0.657 average AR on BOP-Industrial and reports 99.67% grasp and 84.00% assembly success in real-robot connector assembly.
Maintains short-term object-level state at 0.02 ms/frame using a model library and pose-scale log.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses robotic manipulation with 6D pose-scale estimation, 3D reconstruction, and real-robot assembly for unknown objects.
papers.title: OV-PEAR: Observation-Verified Pose-Scale Estimation and Reconstruction for Unknown Industrial Manipulation Objects
papers.tldr: OV-PEAR reconstructs and estimates the pose and scale of unseen industrial objects from RGB-D observations, enabling reliable robot manipulation without CAD models.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.
authors: Haoqun Cao, Yurun Yuan, Tengyang Xie
bullets: Off-policy updates are consistent only under two structures: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from horizon dependence, or KL regularization paired with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value.
The KL-based route corresponds to group-relative policy gradient (GRPG), connects to trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization, and yields a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage.
The analysis provides a theoretical interpretation of a GRPO-like objective used in practice.
Baselines have an additional off-policy role: shifting them downward induces pessimism, helping address partial data coverage.
Asymmetric REINFORCE instantiates this pessimistic baseline idea and obtains a regret bound under single-policy coverage.
papers.selection_reason: Off-policy policy gradient theory with KL regularization, baselines, and pessimism is transferable to RL-based robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
papers.tldr: The paper explains when off-policy policy gradients remain theoretically valid, showing that trajectory importance weighting or specially matched KL regularization and baselines can preserve optimal-policy stationarity while enabling offline-RL-style guarantees.

papers.abstract: Generative policies have achieved strong performance in imitation learning tasks, but their success is often constrained by the limited availability of expert demonstrations. Although preference-based fine-tuning can leverage suboptimal rollouts to improve performance, existing approaches heavily rely on expensive human annotations. In this work, we introduce Progress-Guided Preference Generation (PGPG), an unsupervised preference alignment framework that eliminates the need for human-in-the-loop supervision. Our method leverages ordered coverage alignment to measure sequential progress relative to a small set of expert demonstrations, enabling the automatic extraction of pseudo-preference labels from autonomously collected rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce key enhancements to improve the reliability of these progress-guided preferences, enabling effective fine-tuning of pretrained generative policies without requiring manually designed reward functions. Extensive experiments across a suite of challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks demonstrate that PGPG outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning baselines. Moreover, our conceptually simple framework is broadly applicable across multiple classes of generative policies, demonstrating strong versatility when integrated with both diffusion and flow-matching policies.
authors: Tung M. Luu, Tri Ton, Duc M. Nguyen, Xuan Thanh Nguyen, Nguyen Gia Binh, Quang Tan Nguyen, Vu Duong, Daniel Sonntag, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Vien Anh Ngo, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Addresses the limited availability of expert demonstrations and the cost of human preference labeling.
Uses ordered coverage alignment against a small set of expert demonstrations to estimate sequential progress.
Extracts pseudo-preference labels and applies them to fine-tune pretrained generative policies.
Improves performance over standard supervised fine-tuning baselines on challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks.
Works with both diffusion and flow-matching policies, though its demonstrated scope is manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes unsupervised preference alignment for generative robot policies in long-horizon manipulation.
papers.title: Progress-Guided Preference Generation for Aligning Generative Control Policies
papers.tldr: PGPG automatically generates progress-based preferences from autonomous rollouts to align generative control policies without human annotations or hand-designed rewards.

papers.abstract: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model's ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/
authors: Yihui Yang, Yuanhong Yu, Jiawei Wang, Zhongrui Yu, Jia Shi, Kun Zhan, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou, Yu Liu, Sida Peng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of real-robot data and the sim-to-real gap in local navigation.
Pretrains on instruction-conditioned Internet videos to learn goal-directed visual dynamics.
Aligns learned dynamics with executable action chunks using action-labeled simulation data, then jointly fine-tunes the navigation system.
Reports 86.5% success on a single-view Short-Horizon OVON adaptation and 94.9% on HabitatGS-LN, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Real-quadruped deployment results support generalization to physical-world navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Pretrains on internet egocentric videos to learn visual dynamics for language-conditioned local navigation, spanning VLN, human-video learning, and video world models.
papers.title: ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video Pretraining for Language-Conditioned Local Navigation
papers.tldr: ScaleNav uses large-scale Internet egocentric videos plus simulated action data to train language-conditioned navigation policies that transfer from simulation to real robots.

papers.abstract: Continuous vision-and-language navigation (VLN) is typically evaluated by goal-reaching success, assuming it reflects an agent's ability to execute language-grounded behavior. We show that this assumption can fail: permissive contact models in current simulators may mask physically infeasible actions, creating a physical executability gap between semantic competence and embodied realization. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual-Semantic Traversability Alignment (VeSTA), a framework that aligns VLN policies with physically executable futures. We define visual-semantic traversability as the ability to predict instruction-conditioned trajectories that are semantically valid, geometrically feasible, and physically robust. VeSTA addresses this misalignment through two complementary mechanisms: improving executable support in trajectory generation and risk-aware selection among multimodal futures. Specifically, Trajectory Relative Group Policy Optimization uses strict-contact feedback to reshape the candidate distribution toward executable regions, while the Traversability Risk Critic learns a risk-adjusted scalar utility for candidate-wise future selection. Experiments on R2R and RxR reveal substantial dependence of existing VLN agents on simulator contact semantics. Under strict-contact evaluation, VeSTA substantially reduces collision-induced failures while preserving or improving goal-reaching performance, and controlled real-world robot experiments provide evidence that the learned preference transfers beyond simulation.
authors: Gang He, Zhile Cheng, Kepeng Xu, Zhenyang Liu, Yu-Wing Tai
bullets: Current VLN success metrics can hide physically infeasible actions because simulators may use permissive contact models.
VeSTA aligns instruction-conditioned trajectories with semantic validity, geometric feasibility, and physical robustness.
Trajectory Relative Group Policy Optimization steers candidate generation toward executable regions using strict-contact feedback.
A Traversability Risk Critic selects among multimodal futures using risk-aware utility.
Experiments on R2R, RxR, and real-robot trials show fewer collision failures under strict-contact evaluation while maintaining or improving navigation performance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses physical executability in continuous vision-language navigation with trajectory optimization and risk-aware selection.
papers.title: Revealing and Bridging the Physical Executability Gap in Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: VeSTA closes the gap between semantically correct navigation and physically executable behavior by training VLN agents to generate and select safer trajectories.

papers.abstract: Robotic simulation, navigation, and inspection need photorealistic and geometrically accurate maps. Radiance fields achieve photorealism, but building them from robot data raises three challenges. A robot's trajectory serves its task, not reconstruction, so images from few viewpoints leave the geometry under-constrained. Residual errors in camera poses and intrinsics blur the map. The map's GPU memory grows with scene size, which limits its level of detail in large scenes. We present \textbf{SpaRV}, a \textbf{Spa}rse \textbf{R}adiance \textbf{V}oxel map rendered by differentiable ray marching, which lets irregular LiDAR scans supervise it alongside images. LiDAR depth and occupancy anchor the under-constrained geometry, and normal and smoothness regularizers keep it smooth between LiDAR points. To correct camera errors, SpaRV alternates map training with photometric optimization of the camera poses and focal lengths. To bound GPU memory in training and rendering, SpaRV holds one submap at a time at full resolution and the rest at coarser octree levels. Experiments show that SpaRV keeps the geometry consistent away from the captured trajectory and sharpens textures by optimizing the camera parameters. On one 24\,GB GPU, SpaRV reconstructs a university campus captured in 63{,}582 images and simulates other cameras and LiDARs. Our code will be released at \url{https://github.com/hku-mars/SpaRV}.
authors: Jianheng Liu, Yunfei Wan, Fangming Cheng, Xiangyu Hong, Zuhao Zou, Haotian Li, Longji Yin, Chunran Zheng, Jiarong Lin, Fu Zhang
bullets: Addresses under-constrained geometry from task-driven trajectories, camera calibration errors, and GPU-memory limits in large scenes.
Uses differentiable ray marching with irregular LiDAR depth and occupancy supervision, plus normal and smoothness regularization.
Alternates map training with photometric optimization of camera poses and focal lengths to reduce blur and sharpen textures.
Maintains one full-resolution submap while storing others at coarser octree levels, bounding memory during training and rendering.
Reconstructs a university campus from 63,582 images on one 24 GB GPU and supports novel-camera and novel-LiDAR simulation.
papers.selection_reason: Presents SpaRV, a sparse radiance voxel map for LiDAR-visual mapping and rendering, applicable to robotic navigation and 3D scene reconstruction.
papers.title: SpaRV: Sparse Radiance Voxels for Scalable Geometrically Consistent LiDAR-Visual Mapping and Rendering
papers.tldr: SpaRV combines sparse radiance voxels, LiDAR supervision, camera-parameter optimization, and hierarchical submaps to build scalable, geometrically consistent LiDAR–visual maps.

papers.abstract: Long-term LiDAR place recognition in forests is difficult because repetitive vegetation and uneven terrain create severe structural aliasing. We diagnose Scan Context (SC) by separating candidate retrieval from fine matching: on the standardized TreeLoc++ Wild-Places protocol, a TNVD support key places a valid location in the top-25 set for approximately 99% of queries, while conventional SC matching on those candidates reaches only 61.84% mean R@1. With an identical raw-SC candidate set, terrain normalization improves max-height cells by only 1.21 points but vertical-distribution cells by 19.72 points. These observations motivate Terrain-Normalized Vertical Distribution Scan Context (TNVD-SC), which preserves the SC ring-sector topology while encoding terrain-relative vertical probability distributions. Under the standardized TreeLoc++ protocol, TNVD-SC reaches 91.83% mean R@1 and attains the highest R@1 mean and R@1 stability among the compared methods, while TreeLoc++ remains stronger in mean MR, MF1, and AUC. The unchanged method reaches 85.14% mean R@1 on the four-session CVTNet-style NCLT evaluation. A lossless count-coded implementation with exact hierarchical Jensen-Shannon search reduces descriptor payload by 3.86x and compute latency by 23.8% without changing the audited retrieval outputs.
bullets: Forest place recognition is hindered by repetitive vegetation and uneven terrain, causing structural aliasing.
Candidate retrieval is largely reliable, but conventional Scan Context fine matching achieves only 61.84% mean R@1 on retrieved candidates.
Terrain-normalized vertical distributions improve vertical-distribution cell performance by 19.72 points, motivating TNVD-SC.
TNVD-SC reaches 91.83% mean R@1 on TreeLoc++ and 85.14% on the four-session NCLT evaluation.
A lossless count-coded implementation reduces descriptor payload by 3.86× and latency by 23.8% without changing retrieval outputs.
papers.selection_reason: Improves LiDAR place recognition in challenging forest environments using Terrain-Normalized Vertical Distributions, a key component for robot navigation and SLAM.
papers.title: TNVD-SC: Diagnosing Scan Context Failures in Forests with Terrain-Normalized Vertical Distributions
papers.tldr: TNVD-SC diagnoses Scan Context’s forest failures and improves terrain-robust LiDAR place recognition by encoding terrain-normalized vertical distributions.

papers.abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $\pi_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.
authors: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang, Maggie Wang, Fangneng Zhan, Manling Li, Qianqian Wang, Mac Schwager, Zhuang Liu, Li Fei-Fei, Mengyu Wang, Paul Pu Liang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving robot policies from limited test-time experience while keeping pretrained weights fixed.
Uses a sparse autoencoder and a shared temporal descriptor of feature activation-order patterns to select a task-specific feature without timestep alignment.
Builds reference banks offline from successful and failed rollouts, then online determines when and how strongly to adjust the feature activation.
With 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, improves success by approximately 10% across simulated and real-world manipulation evaluations.
Scope: requires labeled successful and failed reference rollouts and focuses on steering a selected feature during execution.
papers.selection_reason: Improves pretrained robot action models at test time via few-shot activation steering, fitting learned robot control and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
papers.tldr: SteerAct improves pretrained robot action models at test time by steering one task-relevant feature dynamically, using only a few successful and failed rollouts and without changing model weights.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are envisioned to perform diverse human-level tasks through their anthropomorphic morphology. Their dual-arm configuration enables a broad range of everyday actions. Yet, as in humans, this morphology can constrain loco-manipulation when both arms are occupied or additional contacts are required beyond their reach. Supernumerary robotic limbs (SRLs) offer a way to extend these capabilities, but their integration requires the added limb to be coordinated with whole-body motion and balance. In this study, we develop and integrate a supernumerary arm into a humanoid platform to investigate how morphological augmentation reshapes its feasible action space. Through quantitative analysis and hardware experiments across two configurations, we show how the additional limb expands whole-body interaction capabilities by enabling manipulation and support to be coordinated beyond the constraints of the native dual-arm configuration. To control this augmented morphology, we leverage model-based trajectory optimization (TO) to generate dynamically feasible motions for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) controllers. The controllers are trained in simulation and transferred to hardware in a zero-shot manner, enabling coordinated whole-body skills for contact-rich tri-arm loco-manipulation. We further show vision-guided autonomous execution on selected tasks using diffusion policies trained from hardware demonstrations. Our findings suggest that humanoid morphology need not be restricted to human-like forms, but can be reimagined as an extensible design space for robotic augmentation.
authors: Fukang Liu, Feiyang Wu, Paul Barsa, Jaehwi Jang, Akshat Jain, Zhigen Zhao, Yipu Chen, Zhaoyuan Gu, Nikhil Vemuri, Anshul Chandaliya, Kaijie Zhu, Sean Lublinsky, Matthew Zhu, Tony G. Chen, Ye Zhao
bullets: A third arm addresses limitations of dual-arm humanoids when both arms are occupied or additional contacts are needed.
The study integrates a supernumerary arm and quantitatively evaluates how it expands the feasible action space across two configurations.
Model-based trajectory optimization generates dynamically feasible motions for goal-conditioned RL controllers trained in simulation and transferred zero-shot to hardware.
Hardware experiments demonstrate coordinated, contact-rich tri-arm manipulation and support skills.
Diffusion policies trained from hardware demonstrations enable vision-guided autonomous execution on selected tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Combines trajectory optimization, reinforcement learning, and diffusion policies for augmented humanoid loco-manipulation.
papers.title: Humanoid SRL: Augmenting Humanoids with Supernumerary Limbs for Coordinated Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: A humanoid equipped with a supernumerary arm gains expanded whole-body loco-manipulation abilities, demonstrated through model-based planning, reinforcement learning, and hardware experiments.

papers.abstract: Vision-based object pose estimation is vital for conducting spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO). Recent research has demonstrated the robustness of event cameras against the harsh lighting conditions that often occur in orbit, thanks to the extremely high dynamic range of event sensors. However, event-based spacecraft pose estimation (EBSPE) suffers when the relative motion between the chaser and target is slow, since the event rate drops significantly, leading to data with low signal-to-noise ratio. Unfortunately, for safety reasons, real RPO trajectories often involve slow relative motions (e.g., down to 1 mm/s), and operating under low illumination exacerbates the problem. Addressing slow relative motions is thus crucial to raise the practicality of EBSPE. To this end, we propose using recurrent vision transformers (RVT) for EBSPE. The key idea is to exploit recurrent memory to capture longer-term information across sparse event streams, and to learn the temporal attention span from full trajectories rather than fixing the time window. We developed an RVT-based heatmap regressor to produce 2D-3D correspondences for pose estimation, which was validated on real event data collected under slow relative motions representative of RPO trajectories. Results indicate the superior pose estimation accuracy and stability of our RVT-based method, relative to previous per-event-frame-based or fixed-time-window EBSPE methods.
authors: Sofia McLeod, Mohsi Jawaid, Carl Seubert, Tat-Jun Chin
bullets: Slow relative motion sharply reduces event rates and degrades event-based pose estimation, especially under low illumination.
The proposed RVT uses recurrent memory to aggregate longer-term temporal information and learns its attention span from complete trajectories.
An RVT heatmap regressor generates 2D–3D correspondences for spacecraft pose estimation.
Validation on real event-camera data from slow-motion RPO-like trajectories showed improved accuracy and stability over per-frame and fixed-window methods.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Recurrent Vision Transformers (RVT) to handle sparse event streams for spacecraft pose estimation, addressing a specific challenge in robotic perception under low signal-to-noise conditions.
papers.title: Recurrent Vision Transformers for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation Under Slow Relative Motions
papers.tldr: Recurrent vision transformers improve event-based spacecraft pose estimation during slow, low-signal relative motion by retaining information across sparse event streams.

papers.abstract: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.
authors: Xuezhou Xu, Chung-Pang Wang, Zhenzhen Li, Benjamin Riviere
bullets: Addresses compounding prediction errors, large search spaces, and the difficulty of executing latent plans in long-horizon manipulation.
Uses vector-quantized latent states for discrete search and a learned visual-feedback controller to sequentially reach planned states and correct deviations.
Introduces a first-passage-time quasi-metric for quantization that better aligns the planning abstraction with controller capabilities.
Achieves 100% success on physical Tower of Hanoi using only short-play data and outperforms competing world models by 13.3–85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks.
Scope: evaluated on manipulation and locomotion benchmarks, with physical-robot validation on Tower of Hanoi.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a vector-quantized world model for latent feedback motion planning in robot manipulation, directly relevant to world models and learned control.
papers.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: VQ-WM combines discrete latent long-horizon planning with continuous visual-feedback control to reliably solve manipulation tasks beyond the length of its demonstrations.

papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) gives large language model (LLM) agents access to physical observations, but one requested capability is usually offered by several devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. Existing work retrieves relevant tools and checks plan feasibility, without learning which eligible device returns a useful observation. Unlike previous works, we study online tool grounding: binding an already specified tool call to one physical endpoint under service cost and device participation constraints. We propose a framework that learns which physical device should execute each agent-issued call. It formulates selection as a contextual bandit problem and combines adaptive context partitions with hierarchical endpoint trees, so that execution feedback is reused across related requests and devices. Selection balances task success against service cost while respecting device capability, authorization, battery reserves, and availability. Gaussian reward aggregation provides an optional mechanism for protecting individual feedback values. Theoretical results establish a finite-horizon regret bound and differential privacy for released reward statistics under fixed, reward-independent assignments. In a simulated loading-dock workload, the proposed router achieves higher step success and better cost-adjusted service, at lower simulated device energy and latency, than nearest-device, advertised-quality, UCB1, and LinUCB selection.
authors: Yichen Liu, Xiaochong Jiang, Haoran Yu, Lifei Liu
bullets: Addresses tool grounding when multiple physical devices can provide the requested capability.
Uses adaptive context partitions and hierarchical endpoint trees to reuse feedback across related requests and devices.
Selection accounts for service cost, authorization, battery reserves, availability, and device capabilities.
Provides a finite-horizon regret bound and optional differential privacy for aggregated reward statistics.
In a simulated loading-dock workload, it improves step success and cost-adjusted service while reducing simulated energy and latency versus several baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Online contextual-bandit tool grounding for LLM agents selecting physical IoT devices; relevant to online learning and embodied physical interaction.
papers.title: Learning Which Device to Call: Online Tool Grounding for LLM Agents in IoT
papers.tldr: An online contextual-bandit router learns which eligible IoT device should execute each LLM tool call, balancing success, cost, and device constraints.

papers.abstract: Underwater robots support a growing range of work, from inspecting offshore structures and pipelines to surveying reefs and accompanying divers. Most of these tasks, however, are still flown by hand by a pilot, which raises the question of whether they can be carried out autonomously instead. On land, vision-language-action (VLA) models already let robots carry out tasks autonomously from language instructions, which makes them a natural candidate for taking the pilot's place. Underwater, however, there is little data to train such models. We take inspiration from how these tasks are flown today: the pilot watches the camera image and steers with a joystick, whose commands the flight controller turns into motion. We therefore record the pilots and introduce AQUAACT, to our knowledge the first publicly available language-annotated underwater dataset pairing camera images with human joystick commands. It comprises 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, both flown by human pilots, together with the vehicle's inertial measurements. Experiments with AQUAACT show that its simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and greatly reduce the real demonstrations a policy needs. A closed-loop benchmark of seven policies in simulation, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, each trained with its default recipe, shows that these tasks remain far from solved: no policy completes more than a fifth of the episodes. Pretraining on land data gives large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that land-trained models have yet to close underwater.
authors: Zhenqi Wu, Trung Tien Dong, Aditya Penumarti, Mohamed A. Fouad, Menna A. Fouad, Mingyang Mao, Jane Jaejeong Shin, Xiaomin Lin
bullets: Addresses the lack of training data for autonomous underwater robot operation by recording human pilots’ camera-based joystick control.
Provides 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, paired with camera images, joystick commands, language annotations, and inertial measurements.
Finds that simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and reduce the amount of real-world data needed for policy training.
Benchmarks seven imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies in closed-loop simulation; no policy completes more than one-fifth of episodes.
Reports that land-data pretraining gives large VLA models no advantage over smaller policies trained from scratch underwater.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a language-annotated underwater teleoperation dataset and benchmarks VLA and imitation-learning policies for autonomous robot control.
papers.title: AQUAACT: A Joystick-Level Underwater Teleoperation Dataset and Closed-Loop Benchmark
papers.tldr: AQUAACT introduces a language-annotated underwater teleoperation dataset and benchmark, showing that simulated demonstrations help real-world learning but current policies still struggle with autonomous underwater control.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.
bullets: Observation reconstruction can overemphasize visual fidelity, weakening latent priors and long-horizon predictions.
A Beta–Bernoulli spatial mask stochastically occludes observations with varying visibility at each timestep.
The masked observation and binary mask are concatenated as encoder input, requiring minimal architectural changes.
Across pixel-based DeepMind Control Suite tasks, model-predictive control with open-loop rollouts shows improved planning performance and data efficiency.
Balanced observability performs better than training focused mainly on sparse or dense observations; results are robust to mask scale.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses learning latent dynamics and control policies for continuous control, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Dynamics-Aligned Representation Learning under Induced Partial Observability
papers.tldr: Stochastic masking during training improves the robustness and data efficiency of latent dynamics models for pixel-based control by aligning representations with predictive dynamics rather than visual reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.
authors: Yong Wang, Kecheng Zheng, Xing Zhu, Chao Xu, Yujun Shen, Shengze Cai
bullets: Targets the limited characterization of dexterous manipulation in existing robotic action models.
Covers five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long-horizon tasks, and memory.
Pairs every task with an out-of-domain variant to test robustness to controlled visual and spatial changes.
Includes two high-DoF hand embodiments and 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations totaling 6.25 million frames.
Provides unified-protocol baselines from evaluating seven recent Vision-Language-Action models.
papers.selection_reason: Presents BiDex-100, a comprehensive benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation and Vision-Language-Action models, directly supporting research in robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
papers.tldr: BiDex-100 is a 106-task simulation benchmark for evaluating bimanual dexterous manipulation across capabilities, robustness, embodiments, and data efficiency.

papers.abstract: Classical robot control, Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees (BTs), is deterministic and inspectable but fixed at design time: it fails on situations its designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at a cost in latency and non-determinism hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems. Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model in the loop permanently and discard what it produces. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime. When a BT node fails, an LLM proposes a minimal, mission-agnostic subtree patch; CMA-ES tunes its parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth its cost; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant-monitored replays, an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover. Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library and, once the LLM call rate decays, crystallized into a deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and a lockstep simulator. Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used $11\pm1.4$ LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half. The crystallized trees, 28 and 33 nodes with two patches each, reached $97\pm2\%$ mission success with no learning running, against 12\% for the unpatched tree and 98\% for a hand-coded expert tree, and reproduce decision traces exactly when re-ticked offline. Two negative results: replay admission rejected useful wind recoveries by attributing wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and a static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures.
bullets: Addresses the tension between fixed, safe robot controllers and costly, non-deterministic runtime foundation-model reasoning.
Uses an LLM to propose minimal subtree patches only after node failures; CMA-ES tunes parameters and a contextual bandit selects stored patches versus new LLM calls.
Admits patches through static checks, invariant-monitored replays, and empirical recovery margins, then stores them in a reusable fleet library and crystallizes them into deterministic BTs.
In Project AirSim experiments, crystallized trees achieved 97±2% mission success with no online learning, versus 12% for the unpatched tree and 98% for a hand-coded expert tree.
Replay admission rejected some useful wind-recovery patches, while a static-only variant generalized better to held-out failures.
papers.selection_reason: Uses foundation-model-generated patches and online adaptation to improve autonomous drone control, fitting learned robot control and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees: Amortizing Foundation-Model Reasoning into Deterministic Control for Autonomous Drones
papers.tldr: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees convert foundation-model-generated drone-control patches into deterministic, inspectable BTs, reducing runtime LLM dependence while achieving high mission success in simulation.

papers.abstract: Onboard inference latency creates a mismatch between the trajectories predicted by vision-language-action (VLA) policies and the ongoing motion of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). We present AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous language-conditioned flight. A B-spline policy is initialized through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, providing continuous trajectory references in position and yaw. During execution, trajectory fusion removes the expired prediction prefix and connects the remaining segment to the active reference with derivative continuity while limiting trajectory deformation. To account for deviations induced by asynchronous execution, execution-aware group relative policy optimization (GRPO) further adapts the policy using trajectory-level rewards. On the UAV-Flow test set, AeroDASH achieves a success rate of 76.56%, exceeding OpenVLA-UAV and AeroDASH w/o GRPO by 38.1 and 20.1 percentage points, respectively. Execution experiments show that AeroDASH sustains motion during inference and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations relative to asynchronous tracking of waypoint sequences. We further demonstrate language-conditioned flight with onboard inference and asynchronous trajectory execution. The code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Zhe Liu, Yuxuan Zheng, Jinzhe Qin, Ziqi Gao, Boyu Zhou
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between onboard inference latency and UAV motion during VLA control.
Uses B-spline trajectories initialized from expert demonstrations for continuous position and yaw references.
Fuses new predictions with active trajectories while preserving derivative continuity and limiting deformation.
Applies execution-aware GRPO to adapt the policy to deviations caused by asynchronous execution.
Achieves a 76.56% success rate on UAV-Flow and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations versus waypoint tracking.
papers.selection_reason: Presents AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous UAV flight. It addresses the latency mismatch in VLA policies through trajectory fusion and GRPO, demonstrating strong performance in language-conditioned flight.
papers.title: AeroDASH: Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control for Continuous UAV Flight
papers.tldr: AeroDASH enables smoother, continuous language-conditioned UAV flight by asynchronously adapting vision-language-action trajectory predictions to ongoing motion.

papers.abstract: Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe interaction bottleneck. Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a small set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.
authors: Mohammad Omama, Aeyan Ashraf, Sandeep Chinchali
bullets: Addresses the interaction bottleneck of deep feature matchers on edge devices, where each query must otherwise process every database image independently.
Defers inter-image interaction to the final layers, separating reusable intra-image Context Blocks from lightweight online Interaction Blocks.
Introduces E-SToRE, which reduces spatial tokens before cross-image interaction using entropy-guided token reduction and expansion.
Evaluated on HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen.
LateMatch achieves over 2× lower effective computation; E-SToRE adds 10–14% savings with negligible accuracy degradation.
papers.selection_reason: Improves visual localization efficiency for embodied agents, a learned component supporting robot navigation, and involves geometric matching relevant to 3D vision.
papers.title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
papers.tldr: LateMatch makes visual localization more efficient by caching image-specific processing and limiting online cross-image matching, cutting computation by over 2× with minimal accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Human memories are organized in a way that connects events with their corresponding spatial contexts. An AI assistant should also be able to memorize and recall the nexus of events and spaces. Thus we introduce SENRI, a task that studies this space--event connection in long, continuous real-life egocentric video. It contains six task types in two directions: Event$\rightarrow$Space, which recovers spatial knowledge from event cues, and Space$\rightarrow$Event, which retrieves events from regions and trajectories. To evaluate this, we build SENRI-Bench, containing 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions over 10 uninterrupted self-recorded videos with around 25.3 hours of content. Also, we evaluate three typical long video understanding paradigms: direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory. The task remains challenging across all three paradigms, highlighting substantial room for improvement. Then we show two representative failure modes of existing memory methods and address these evidence gaps with SENRI-Agent, a controller that uses Target-Guided Visual Check (TGVC) to propose local visual check tasks for parallel verifiers and integrate the reports into a working memory to help with reasoning. Built upon existing memory systems, SENRI-Agent improves the performance of existing baselines without modifying their stored memories. We hope SENRI will provide valuable insights into how real-life egocentric understanding should be evaluated, reveal the gaps in existing approaches, and offer a possible direction for improvement.
authors: Kehan Lan, Kaining Ying, Henghui Ding, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Covers six tasks in two directions: inferring spaces from events and retrieving events from spaces or trajectories.
SENRI-Bench contains 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions from about 25.3 hours of uninterrupted self-recorded video.
Evaluates direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory; all remain challenging.
SENRI-Agent uses Target-Guided Visual Check with parallel verifiers and working memory to address evidence gaps.
Improves existing memory-system baselines without changing their stored memories.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and method for space-event reasoning in egocentric video, directly relevant to embodied perception and learning from human video, with spatial reasoning components.
papers.title: SENRI: Understanding the Space-Event Nexus in Real-Life Videos
papers.tldr: SENRI introduces a benchmark and agent for testing and improving how AI connects events with spatial contexts in long egocentric videos.

papers.abstract: Estimating a humanoid robot's internal state from video has a wide range of real-world applications but remains unexplored. During interactions with a robot, its onboard state information may be unavailable due to privacy, ownership, or communication constraints. Meanwhile, online and AI-generated robot videos provide rich sources of data but typically lack corresponding joint configurations, limiting their direct use in robot learning. To address these issues, we present HumanoidPose, a new framework that treats vision as proprioception to recover full-body joint configurations in world space from video alone. Specifically, we combine pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics in a unified model that predicts each embodiment's joint configurations. We retarget human motions to sixteen different humanoid embodiments, enabling scalable learning entirely from synthetic data. To improve real-world generalization, we further leverage unlabeled online videos through self-training to develop a 2D robot-pose detector. In our evaluation, HumanoidPose improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the evaluated baselines and reduces joint-angle error by 18-32% relative to the best-performing baseline on each of the three real humanoid platforms. We further show improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments. HumanoidPose enables visual understanding of other robots during interaction and extraction of robot motion from online and generated videos.
authors: Jiaxi Jiang, Matthias Heyrman, Ren\'e Zurbr\"ugg, Marco Hutter, Christian Holz
bullets: Addresses missing robot proprioceptive data caused by privacy, ownership, or communication constraints.
Combines pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics to predict embodiment-specific joint configurations.
Uses synthetic human-to-robot motion retargeting across 16 humanoid embodiments and self-training on unlabeled online videos.
Improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over evaluated baselines, reducing joint-angle error by 18–32% across three real humanoid platforms.
Demonstrates improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments.
papers.selection_reason: Learns humanoid robot pose from video using human motion retargeting and self-training, transferable to embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Vision as Proprioception: Estimating Humanoid Robot Pose from Video
papers.tldr: HumanoidPose estimates full-body humanoid joint configurations in world space from video alone, enabling robot learning without onboard state access.

papers.abstract: General purpose multimodal language models (LMs) are increasingly capable of directly controlling robotic arms (e.g., by commanding end effector poses) to manipulate their environment. Tracking the development of these capabilities is important for understanding their potential benefits, such as improving industrial automation, and risks, such as enabling malicious users to produce dangerous chemical or biological agents. To this end, we investigate the ability of frontier multimodal LMs to directly control physical robotic arms. We evaluate seven models at multiple reasoning-effort settings on six manipulation tasks taken from the RoboDojo benchmark. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of a broad range of frontier LMs across a common suite of manipulation tasks on physical hardware. We find that current frontier models can directly control real robotic arms to perform a variety of manipulation tasks but are not yet precise or efficient enough to complete them within a practical action budget.
