papers.selection_reason: Contact-adaptive sampling-based MPC for contact-rich manipulation.
papers.title: ContactKernels: Adaptive Proposals using Geometry-COnditioned Wrenches for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.tldr: ContactKernels uses contact-derived geometry to adapt sampling-based control, substantially improving contact-rich insertion success and speed.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have achieved rapid progress by learning unified policies that map sensor observations directly to driving trajectories. However, once deployed, these systems typically remain frozen: they may repeat similar decisions in similar scenes, and failures can only be addressed through costly data collection and retraining. This sharply contrasts with human drivers, who improve lifelong through experience, memory, and reflection. In this work, we ask whether autonomous driving systems can achieve similar post-deployment self-evolution to human drivers. We propose EvoAD, a self-evolving autonomous driving framework via latent world-model guided post-hoc reflection. EvoAD stores driving experiences in a bird's-eye-view feature memory pool, retrieves scene-relevant precedents according to geometric and semantic similarity, and uses a latent world model to evaluate the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space. Instead of treating memory as external textual contexts or using world models only for pre-action simulation, EvoAD transforms executed driving outcomes into reusable improvement signals for future decisions. This enables the system to diagnose how prior trajectories could have been improved and to refine behavior in similar future scenarios without retraining the base driving policy. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 show consistent improvements across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the potential of world models as reflective mechanisms for post-deployment self-evolution in autonomous driving.
authors: Junjie Yang, Qiming Zhang, Yuyan Li, Shuqi Shen, Yusong Huang, Yanggang Sheng, Wenpeng Xu, Ziyi Shi, Tianshun Li, Yijie Chen, Yujia Wang, Jun Ma, Xinhu Zheng, Hongliang Lu, Hai Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of frozen end-to-end driving policies that cannot learn from deployment failures without costly retraining.
Stores past experiences in a bird’s-eye-view feature memory and retrieves relevant precedents using geometric and semantic similarity.
Uses a latent world model to assess the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space.
Converts executed outcomes into reusable improvement signals, refining decisions in similar future scenarios.
Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 report consistent gains across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving autonomous driving with latent world-model reflection and embodied driving memory.
papers.title: EvoAD: Self-Evolving Autonomous Driving via Latent World-Model Guided Post-hoc Reflection
papers.tldr: EvoAD enables autonomous driving systems to improve after deployment by reflecting on past driving outcomes with a latent world model, without retraining the base policy.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have become a dominant paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet existing planners organize trajectory generation along the Gaussian-noise axis, treating driving utility only as an auxiliary guidance or selection signal. We instead formulate diffusion along a driving-quality axis. We propose QualiDrive, which constructs scene-specific quality ladders by ranking observed trajectories according to measured driving utility and learns to reverse this ordered degradation through ordered low-to-high-quality refinement. Each reverse step is conditioned on the scene, ego state, current trajectory, and target quality level, progressively refining trajectories toward higher driving quality. On NAVSIM, QualiDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on v1 and a state-of-the-art 92.74 EPDMS on v2. QualiDrive improves Oracle EPDMS only modestly over endpoint-only quality supervision (98.52 to 98.57), but substantially increases the fractions of candidates above 0.95 and 0.98 EPDMS from 12.94%/9.71% to 21.53%/15.93%, raising selected EPDMS from 92.63 to 92.74. These results suggest that diffusion is not merely a process of denoising, but one of progressive quality-ordered refinement.
authors: Junjie Yang, Ziyi Shi, Shuqi Shen, Xinhu Zheng, Hongliang Lu, Hai Yang
bullets: Existing planners diffuse along Gaussian noise and use driving utility mainly for guidance or selection.
QualiDrive ranks observed trajectories by measured utility to build scene-specific quality ladders.
A quality-conditioned reverse process progressively refines trajectories from lower to higher driving quality.
On NAVSIM, it achieves 94.5 PDMS on v1 and 92.74 EPDMS on v2.
Quality-ordered refinement substantially increases the share of high-quality candidates, while improving selected EPDMS modestly.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes quality-axis diffusion for end-to-end autonomous driving trajectory planning, a learned navigation/planning method.
papers.title: From Likelihood to Utility: Quality-Axis Diffusion for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: QualiDrive reframes diffusion for autonomous driving as progressive refinement along a trajectory-quality axis, achieving state-of-the-art selected performance on NAVSIM v2.

papers.abstract: Long-range throwing on unstructured terrain is a key capability for mobile robots in delivery and retrieval tasks, but it requires high release velocity, coordinated whole-body motion, and robustness to terrain-induced disturbances. We present a whole-body kinetic-coordination framework for a wheeled-quadruped manipulator that combines kinetic-chain arm modeling with SQP-based trajectory optimization and a reference-guided reinforcement learning policy for coordinated base motion. The manipulator is first reduced to a kinetic-chain model and optimized under kinematic and dynamic constraints to produce a high-speed throwing reference. On a stationary base, the optimized arm trajectory reaches a release speed of 12.75 m/s and a throwing distance of 16.68 m. When whole-body coordination is enabled, the system further increases the release speed to 16.64 m/s and the throwing distance to 28.25 m. We then integrate the mobility of the wheeled-quadruped platform and validate the complete policy through hardware experiments on flat ground, grass, slopes, and rough roads. The results show that kinetic-chain optimization and whole-body coordination together enable robust long-range throwing across diverse unstructured terrains.
authors: Qinglian Wu, Yidian Hu, Weiqi Fan, Yutian Zhang, Siyuan Ma, Jiaqi Zhai, Wei Dong, Li Xu
bullets: Targets long-range throwing for mobile robots operating on unstructured terrain.
Combines kinetic-chain arm modeling, SQP-based trajectory optimization, and reference-guided reinforcement learning for coordinated base motion.
Optimized arm motion achieves 12.75 m/s release speed and 16.68 m throwing distance on a stationary base.
Whole-body coordination increases these to 16.64 m/s and 28.25 m, respectively.
Hardware experiments validate throwing on flat ground, grass, slopes, and rough roads.
papers.selection_reason: Reinforcement-learning-based whole-body coordination for wheeled-quadruped throwing, a robotic skill acquisition and control contribution.
papers.title: Learning Whole-Body Kinetic Coordination for Wheeled-Quadruped Long-Range Throwing
papers.tldr: A whole-body coordination framework enables a wheeled-quadruped robot to throw objects farther and robustly across varied terrain.

papers.abstract: Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50$\times$. Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.
authors: Tao Lin, Yikeng Chen, Qiwei Liang, Zinan Xie, Zhengtu Liang, Renjing Xu
bullets: Targets the joint problem of selecting layers to remove and choosing recovery procedures after pruning.
Uses offline action-output interventions, evaluation history, and retained diagnoses to guide an LLM agent’s next pruning and recovery proposal.
Evaluates each proposed configuration on target tasks within a fixed search budget.
Across three VLA models and four LIBERO suites, removes 16.7–87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining over 90% task success.
Reports inference speedups up to 2.50×; functional probes reveal action-sensitive layers that representation similarity may miss.],
papers.selection_reason: Agent-driven depth pruning of vision-language-action models to reduce inference cost, relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: AutoPruner: Agentic Depth Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: AutoPruner uses an agentic closed-loop search to prune VLA model layers and recover performance, achieving substantial compression while preserving high task success and improving inference speed.

papers.abstract: Integrating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into autonomous UAV navigation enables high-level semantic reasoning but introduces critical temporal bottlenecks that can destabilize flight control. This paper presents a systematic benchmark that evaluates the operational trade-offs among model scale, hardware constraints, and flight reliability. By subjecting the system to extensive stress tests on both a high-performance workstation and a constrained integrated-graphics laptop, we isolate the kinetic impact of inference latency against reasoning accuracy. Our findings reveal a performance dichotomy: lightweight models struggle with structural hallucinations that break deterministic state machines, while heavyweight models induce trajectory overcorrections due to inference lag. We demonstrate that a mid-weight architecture strikes the optimal balance, successfully rehabilitating navigation in degraded environments without compromising real-time stability across different hardware profiles.
authors: Hiago Sodre, Sebastian Barcelona, Vincent Sandin, Pablo Moraes, Andre S. Kelbouscas, Ricardo B. Grando
bullets: Evaluates how model scale, hardware constraints, and inference latency affect UAV flight reliability.
Stress-tests VLM copilots on both a high-performance workstation and an integrated-graphics laptop.
Lightweight models produce structural hallucinations that can disrupt deterministic state machines.
Heavyweight models cause trajectory overcorrections because of inference delays.
A mid-weight architecture restores navigation in degraded environments while maintaining real-time stability across hardware profiles.
papers.selection_reason: Studies VLM-based autonomous UAV navigation and temporal reliability under hardware constraints.
papers.title: Stress-Query and Temporal Reliability of Vision-Language Models as copilots in Autonomous UAV Navigation
papers.tldr: A benchmark shows that mid-weight VLMs best balance semantic reasoning and inference speed for reliable autonomous UAV navigation.

papers.abstract: In this study, we propose an adaptive question generation mechanism that addresses uncertainty arising from ambiguous instructions. Natural-language instructions for service robots often contain ambiguities. In scenes with multiple similar objects, the robot must identify the target object by asking questions. However, existing question generation methods focus on probabilistic discrimination efficiency and do not sufficiently account for user ease of response. Asking questions without considering the user's ease of response may cause incorrect or uncertain answers. Such incorrect or uncertain answers lead to additional clarification turns and degraded dialogue efficiency. The proposed mechanism integrates probabilistic discrimination efficiency and human cognitive characteristics to generate questions that users can intuitively and easily answer. First, the proposed mechanism extracts visual attributes of candidate objects using a vision-language model (VLM). Next, the proposed mechanism computes the information gain (IG) of each attribute and selects the visual attribute (e.g., color, shape) that most reduces uncertainty in the candidate set. When multiple attributes have the same IG, the proposed mechanism applies a visual attribute filter based on cognitive characteristics to select the visual attribute that users can most intuitively perceive. The proposed mechanism then prompts the VLM with the selected attribute and the corresponding attribute values of each candidate object to generate a concise natural-language question. This process is repeated until the target object is uniquely identified. The proposed mechanism achieved a target identification success rate of 88.5% in the evaluation using a dataset of 120 scenes. Furthermore, the proposed mechanism received high ratings in subjective evaluations of response ease.
authors: Ryo Terashima, Yuga Yano, Hakaru Tamukoh
bullets: Targets ambiguity in service-robot instructions involving multiple similar objects.
Uses a vision-language model to extract candidate-object attributes and selects the attribute with the highest information gain.
Uses a cognitive-based visual-attribute filter to break information-gain ties in favor of attributes users can answer intuitively.
Prompts the VLM to generate concise questions and repeats clarification until one target remains.
Achieved an 88.5% target-identification success rate across 120 scenes and received high ease-of-response ratings.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied instruction following for service robots, resolving ambiguous natural-language instructions through visual attribute questioning.
papers.title: Adaptive Question Generation for Ambiguous Robot Instructions Based on Information Gain and Human Cognitive Characteristics
papers.tldr: An adaptive robot question-generation method combines information gain with human cognitive factors to ask clearer questions when instructions ambiguously identify among similar objects.

papers.abstract: Changing a humanoid robot's manipulation policy should not require retraining the controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution framework that enables locomotion and manipulation controllers to operate simultaneously by combining their commands only at the robot interface. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the 12 leg joints and a waist yaw joint, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from deep crouching to upright standing on a 23-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1. The 10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included only as observations, so that any compatible manipulation policy that generates arm-joint targets can control the upper body, and the locomotion policy keeps the lower body stable without requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on hardware by pairing the same locomotion checkpoint with two different vision-language-action models, GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5. In simulation evaluation, the locomotion controller kept the robot's lower body stable with no falls while tracking the commanded planar velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the dominant component, and removing this training step reduces episode survival from 20.0 to 7.4 seconds and increases the fall rate to 6.06 per environment minute. Robustness tests show no falls under pushes of up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range, and no falls at twice the payload limit for pushes below 0.7 m/s. These results show that a manipulation policy can be exchanged without retraining, restarting, or otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot upright.
authors: Kapalik Khanal, Biswash Khatiwada, Stephen Afrifa, Fan Wu, Ramesh Bahadur Bist
bullets: A reinforcement-learning policy controls the 13-joint lower body, while arm targets come from any compatible manipulation policy.
The framework combines locomotion and manipulation commands only at the robot interface, avoiding shared training or direct coordination.
The same locomotion checkpoint was paired on hardware with GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5 vision-language-action models.
In simulation, the robot tracked velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height without falls, with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m.
The approach remained robust to pushes and payload variation; an upper-body pose curriculum was crucial for survival and fall reduction.
papers.selection_reason: Decoupled humanoid loco-manipulation with RL locomotion and exchangeable VLA manipulation policies directly fits embodied robot learning and vision-language-action.
papers.title: DUET: Decoupled Upper- and Lower-Body Execution for Task-Agnostic Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: DUET decouples humanoid locomotion from manipulation so arm policies can be exchanged without retraining the balance controller.

papers.abstract: Transporting unsecured payloads with legged robots over uneven terrain requires balancing locomotion performance and payload stability, since aggressive motion can destabilize the payload even when the robot remains stable. We study quadrupedal transportation of unsecured stacked boxes on an edgeless torso-mounted board without dedicated payload sensors or active carrier mechanisms. To address this trade-off, we propose Payload-Adaptive Multi-Objective Reinforcement learning for Transportation (PAMORT). PAMORT trains a multi-objective base policy conditioned on a preference vector that weights locomotion and payload-stability reward groups, then trains a weight adjuster on the frozen policy to adapt this preference online from proprioception. In simulation, PAMORT achieves comparable or better overall transportation success than a corresponding single-objective baseline across different payload configurations, including an unseen three-box stack, despite training only with two boxes. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 demonstrate zero-shot transfer to slopes and steps at or beyond the training difficulty, with mean success rates of 0.850 for PAMORT and 0.675 for the baseline across eight tasks. These results demonstrate robust unsecured-payload transportation with online adaptation of the locomotion--payload trade-off from proprioceptive information.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between aggressive locomotion and stability of unsecured payloads on an edgeless torso-mounted board.
Trains a multi-objective policy conditioned on locomotion–stability preferences, then learns a proprioception-based online weight adjuster.
In simulation, matches or exceeds a single-objective baseline across payload configurations, including an unseen three-box stack.
Real-world Unitree Go2 experiments show zero-shot transfer to slopes and steps, with mean success rates of 0.850 versus 0.675 for the baseline across eight tasks.
Demonstrates robust transport without dedicated payload sensors or active carrier mechanisms.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses quadrupedal manipulation/transport of unsecured payloads using multi-objective RL with online adaptation, fitting the 'Robot Learning and Manipulation' subtopic.
papers.title: Transporting Unsecured Stacked Payloads with a Quadrupedal Robot via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: PAMORT enables a quadrupedal robot to transport unsecured stacked boxes over uneven terrain by adapting the balance between locomotion and payload stability online.

papers.abstract: Moving obstacles can block a previously clear route while a quadruped robot executes a motion command. We investigate whether predicting changing clearance improves navigation when motion selection accounts for the robot footprint and the time needed to react and brake. We present FutureRay, which predicts ranges across viewing directions and future times, together with encounter risk, from depth-derived range history and observable robot motion. Training emphasizes near-term clearance and penalizes errors that overstate available space. A local planner queries the same forecast for candidate headings and combines it with current observations to check clearance around the robot footprint. Model-based reaction--braking limits guide speed selection, and the resulting velocity commands are passed to a fixed locomotion policy. In paired evaluations on 60 static and dynamic simulation scenes, FutureRay achieves 93.3% completion, compared with 75.0% for current-range persistence and 80.0% for Cartesian Kalman rollout, with perception, planning, and locomotion held fixed. FutureRay also records fewer collisions than both baselines. Qualitative trials on a physical quadruped show avoidance initiated while an obstacle is approaching the route, followed by renewed goal progress. These results show that joint range and encounter-risk prediction can improve obstacle avoidance without retraining the locomotion policy.
bullets: Addresses moving obstacles that can invalidate a clear route during command execution.
Predicts ranges over viewing directions and future times from depth-range history and observable robot motion, while penalizing overestimates of free space.
A local planner uses forecasts, current observations, robot-footprint clearance checks, and reaction–braking limits to select headings and speed.
In 60 paired simulation scenes, FutureRay achieved 93.3% completion versus 75.0% for range persistence and 80.0% for Cartesian Kalman rollout, with fewer collisions.
Physical-quadruped trials qualitatively showed avoidance beginning as obstacles approached the route, followed by renewed goal progress.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses quadruped navigation by predicting future clearance and encounter risk to improve obstacle avoidance, fitting the 'Robot Navigation' subtopic.
papers.title: FutureRay: Control-Aligned Future Range for Agile Quadruped Navigation
papers.tldr: FutureRay improves agile quadruped navigation by forecasting future directional clearance and encounter risk, enabling earlier obstacle avoidance without retraining the locomotion policy.

papers.abstract: Self-motion manifold (SMM) characterizes the geometric structure of the infinite inverse kinematic solutions set of a redundant manipulator at a fixed end-effector pose, and its efficient recovery underpins feasible and global optimal motion planning. Existing methods such as null-space continuation and learning-based methods are formulated around the assumption that an SMM is a curve, and do not extend to higher redundancy orders. We instead adopt a probabilistic view: SMMs are the support of the conditional posterior over configurations given a target pose, so that recovering it reduces to sampling from a learned distribution and separating its disjoint components by clustering. The formulation is independent of the manifold dimension and requires no architectural change as the redundancy order grows. In this work, we demonstrate that our method can approximate 1-D SMMs with performance comparable to the latest null-space continuation and learning-based approach, and that it is the first method capable of approximating highly redundant 4-D SMMs in a 7R manipulator for position tasks. Project website: \href{https://github.com/accuracy-maker/high-dimenstional-self-motion-manifold-approximation}{https://github.com/accuracy-maker/high-dimenstional-self-motion-manifold-approximation}
bullets: Targets efficient recovery of inverse-kinematic solution sets for redundant manipulators and motion planning.
Models the manifold as the support of a conditional posterior over configurations given a target pose.
Uses learned sampling followed by clustering, without assuming the manifold is a curve or changing the architecture as redundancy increases.
Matches recent methods on 1-D manifolds and approximates previously inaccessible 4-D manifolds for position tasks on a 7R manipulator.
papers.selection_reason: Uses deep generative models to approximate self-motion manifolds for redundant manipulator motion planning, a learning-based robotic control and manipulation contribution.
papers.title: Approximating High Dimensional Self-Motion Manifolds via Deep Generative Models
papers.tldr: A probabilistic deep-generative approach recovers self-motion manifolds of arbitrary dimension by sampling configurations conditioned on an end-effector pose and clustering disconnected components.

papers.abstract: Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints. Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials. Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower. Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or MuJoCo's signed-distance collision. Videos and interactive simulations are at https://younghyopark.me/blind-proprioceptive-assembly/.
authors: Antonia Bronars, Younghyo Park, Kushal Kedia, Pulkit Agrawal
bullets: Policies use only short histories of joint positions, velocities, and actions—without vision, force, torque, or tactile sensing.
Reinforcement learning in simulation teaches peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading under randomized parts, grasps, and contacts.
The peg-insertion policy transfers zero-shot to hardware and succeeds on 73% of trials across different peg shapes and sizes.
In simulation, blind policies generalize better to unseen part shapes and sizes than matched visual policies, but may operate more slowly.
An open-source procedural generator creates accurate, clearance-preserving assembly environments from exact convex pieces for MuJoCo.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based blind proprioceptive assembly policies with sim-to-real transfer.
papers.title: Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
papers.tldr: Proprioception alone can support precise, vision-free assembly across varied parts, with simulated policies transferring to real peg insertion.

papers.abstract: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.
authors: Xinhao Liu, Yunsheng Tian, Yuheng Qiu, Pieter Abbeel, Xi Chen, Guanya Shi, Chen Feng
bullets: Fine-tuned VLM navigation policies often fail to recognize visible goals or estimate their distance.
The proposed approach explicitly grounds the navigation goal to address these failures.
It substantially improves success and achieves state-of-the-art results across six benchmarks in three scene collections.
The authors correct annotation defects and find that, with ground-truth grounding, the policy nearly matches its demonstration-generating expert.
The remaining performance gap is attributed primarily to perception, especially goal grounding.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses object-goal navigation by explicit goal grounding in a VLM-based policy, a core robot navigation and goal-conditioned task.
papers.title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
papers.tldr: StopWatch identifies goal grounding—not exploration or policy learning—as the main bottleneck in VLM-based object-goal navigation and improves navigation by explicitly grounding the goal.

papers.abstract: Progress estimators play an essential role in providing dense reward signals for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation, but accurately assessing task progress can be much challenging. Existing methods heavily rely on expert data and naively assume that all actions within a demonstration contribute to task success. This assumption often breaks down in real-world scenarios, especially in high-precision manipulation, where subtle geometric errors can lead to task failure. Therefore, these methods can erroneously interpret human mistakes as meaningful progress, further corrupting progress learning. We argue that a key limitation is the lack of a global prior regarding task evaluation criteria, which is crucial for distinguishing meaningful progress from human mistakes. To this end, we propose PRIME, a novel progress estimator capable of learning precise progress estimation from imprecise demonstrations by aggregating experience across trajectories. PRIME constructs a weighted graph over observed states, connecting states across trajectories based on spatial proximity and visual consistency. Edge weights encode spatial distances as transition costs, and shortest-path search approximates the geodesic distance to success. Changes in this distance naturally distinguish advancement, stagnation, and setbacks without assuming monotonic progress over time. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real world on precise manipulation tasks show that PRIME is consistently effective across diverse tasks, and robust to data with varying degrees of suboptimality. Notably, the advantage of PRIME gets more pronounced in higher-precision scenarios, yielding up to a \(5\times\) improvement in policy success rate over the SFT baselines on charger insertion.
authors: Huanqian Wang, Boshi Tang, Botong Xiao, Jie Zhang, Yang Yue, Danhua Tao, Shiji Song, Gao Huang
bullets: Existing progress estimators may treat every demonstrated action as meaningful progress, allowing human errors to corrupt learning.
PRIME builds a weighted graph connecting visually and spatially similar states across trajectories.
Shortest-path distances to successful states provide a global progress signal without assuming progress is always monotonic.
Experiments in simulation and the real world show robustness across precise manipulation tasks and varying demonstration quality.
On charger insertion, PRIME improves policy success by up to 5× over SFT baselines, with larger benefits at higher precision.
papers.selection_reason: Progress estimation from demonstrations for robotic manipulation reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Not All Actions Contribute Equally: Learning Precise Progress Estimation from Imprecise Demonstrations
papers.tldr: PRIME learns precise task progress from imperfect demonstrations by using cross-trajectory state relationships to distinguish true advancement from mistakes and setbacks.

papers.abstract: Planning while moving faces an historical trade-off between deliberation and reactivity. A planner running concurrently with execution needs time to compute, so the robot must commit to an open-loop action chunk for that duration: a longer commitment buys a better plan at the cost of feedback frequency. Existing controllers fix this action commitment, and consequently the computation budget, before deployment. However, the optimal computation time is highly state-dependent (due to factors such as unmodeled dynamics, safety constraints, and marginal optimisation gains), i.e. dynamic, therefore offline static tuning risks leaving systems blind during critical maneuvers or unable to find global effective solutions. We cast the identification of the optimal computation budget as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) in which a single decision defines both the robot action commitments and the time allocated to the solver. To solve this, we train a reinforcement-learning policy conditioned on the current state, the executing plan, and inexpensive planner statistics. Across ground-robot navigation, agile quadrotor flight, and contact-rich manipulation, the learned policy changes its budget with the demands of the scenario, discovering efficient reasoning patterns that outperform fixed-budget baselines. https://lorenzomagnino.github.io/learning-robot-metareasoning-review/
authors: Lorenzo Magnino, Antonio Marino, Michael Amir, Daigo Shishika, Amanda Prorok
bullets: Fixed computation budgets force a trade-off between better plans and frequent feedback.
The optimal planning time varies with state, safety constraints, dynamics, and expected optimization gains.
The approach formulates budget selection as a semi-Markov decision process.
An RL policy uses the current state, executing plan, and inexpensive planner statistics to select both action duration and solver time.
Experiments span ground navigation, agile quadrotor flight, and contact-rich manipulation, where adaptive budgets outperform fixed-budget baselines.
papers.selection_reason: RL policy for adaptive computation budgets in real-time robot control, directly relevant to embodied navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Learning Robot Metareasoning: Adaptive Computation Budgets for Real-Time Control
papers.tldr: A reinforcement-learning metareasoner dynamically chooses how long a robot should plan before committing to an action, improving the balance between planning quality and real-time responsiveness.

papers.abstract: While data collection for model training is relatively easy, curating high-quality datasets from large collections is inherently challenging. Coreset estimation methods address this problem by identifying the best data subsets to train models on. However, existing approaches often require proxy model training, extensive annotations, or task-specific tailoring. Unsupervised alternatives typically exploit geometric properties in foundation model feature spaces, but are limited to pairwise image-to-image comparisons or comparisons against a fixed subset. We introduce CoreDNA, an unsupervised, task-agnostic coreset estimation approach that pools neuron activations from vision foundation models into per-image and per-dataset distributions. By comparing each image's distribution to the dataset-level distribution, CoreDNA can capture both low-level visual structure and high-level semantic information across layers. We find that high-quality samples concentrate in the tails of the last layer's activation statistics, which we validate by relating them to training-based coreset methods. Building on these findings, we develop a computationally efficient selection mechanism to construct task-agnostic, high-quality coresets for selective annotation and model training. Across image classification, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and imitation learning for end-to-end driving and mobile manipulation, CoreDNA matches or outperforms the state of the art, demonstrating unprecedented generalization across perception and action tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of compact activation-based representations for data selection.
authors: Julia Hindel, Benjamin Ramtoula, Kyuhwan Yeon, Nick Heppert, Paul Newman, Daniele De Martini, Abhinav Valada

Provides an efficient coreset selection method for annotation and model-training subset construction.

papers.title: Diversity Without Labels: Task-Agnostic Coreset Selection Across Perception and Action
papers.tldr: CoreDNA selects diverse, high-quality training subsets without labels or task-specific model training by comparing image activation distributions with dataset-level statistics.

papers.abstract: Obstacle avoidance for autonomous quadrotors in cluttered environments remains challenging, especially when both dense static obstacles and moving obstacles are present. Existing methods are often tailored to either static or dynamic settings, which always limit their adaptability across diverse environments. This paper presents TransNav, a transformer-based end-to-end navigation method for quadrotor obstacle avoidance in both static and dynamic environments. TransNav employs a patch-based point-cloud encoding scheme that combines local feature extraction with global contextual modeling, enabling compact yet informative environment representation. The method integrates perception and navigation in a single architecture and directly predicts a finite-horizon action sequence, from which the first action is executed. Moreover, we develop an unsupervised learning strategy by incorporating a lightweight point-mass dynamics model, which directly optimizes trajectory-level costs over the predicted sequence through numerical gradient propagation. Thus, the policy can be efficiently trained without expert demonstrations. Simulation and real-world experiments show that the proposed method achieves strong performance in dense static environments and competitive obstacle-avoidance capability in dynamic scenarios, while maintaining low inference cost for onboard deployment.
authors: Jianghan Zhu, Zhuo Li, Yanjun Zhang, Jian Sun
bullets: Targets the challenge of handling dense static and dynamic obstacles within one navigation method.
Uses patch-based point-cloud encoding to combine local geometric features with global environmental context.
Predicts a finite-horizon action sequence and executes its first action for closed-loop control.
Trains unsupervised with a lightweight point-mass dynamics model and trajectory-level cost optimization.
Simulation and real-world tests show strong static-environment performance, competitive dynamic avoidance, and low onboard inference cost.
papers.selection_reason: Transformer-based end-to-end quadrotor obstacle avoidance; directly fits learned robot navigation.
papers.title: TransNav: Transformer-Based End-to-End Navigation Method for Static and Dynamic Quadrotor Obstacle Avoidance
papers.tldr: TransNav is an end-to-end transformer policy that enables quadrotors to avoid both static and moving obstacles without expert demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.
authors: Dominic Maggio, Lorenzo Shaikewitz, Aryan Naveen, Kris Hauser, Luca Carlone
bullets: Addresses the gap between foundation-model-based 3D mapping and complete robot autonomy pipelines.
Integrates FOUND-IT with a mobile manipulator using a single uncalibrated camera.
Supports object change detection, multiple mapping sessions, navigable-path reasoning, and grasping for scene rearrangement.
Reports rigorous on-robot experiments assessing the system’s effectiveness and limitations.
The scope is constrained by the limitations of monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction.
papers.selection_reason: The paper presents a system (FOUND-IT) that leverages geometric and semantic foundation models to construct 3D scene graphs for a mobile manipulator. It demonstrates the integration of this memory system into a full autonomy pipeline for tasks like object grasping, path planning, and scene rearrangement, directly fitting 3D foundation models, robot manipulation, and embodied memory.

papers.tldr: The paper integrates a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph system into a mobile manipulator and evaluates its usefulness for end-to-end spatially informed tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable language-guided robot manipulation, but remain vulnerable to visual attacks that undermine user control over robot behavior. Prior studies optimize visual perturbations using fixed target supervision. However, the perturbation can change earlier actions and, in turn, the physical states reached later. As the attacked trajectory evolves, this supervision may no longer match the behavior needed at the states actually reached. Accurately matching these targets can therefore fail to advance the attacker-specified task. Even with suitable supervision, reducing average matching error does not ensure sustained task progress. The robot may still fail at a critical stage, and further updates can disrupt previously successful behavior. To address these limitations, we propose TRACO, a framework that enhances existing targeted visual attacks through closed-loop optimization. Its Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds supervision for the states reached under attack to guide subsequent updates. Within this framework, Progress-Guided Selection focuses updates where progress stalls while maintaining supervision on the earlier behavior needed to reach that point. Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments show improved task-redirection success with TRACO, highlighting the security implications of closed-loop attack optimization.
authors: Chunjin Ye, Guanying Chen, Jianjie Huang, Jianhao Chen, Quanlin Chen, Hanjie Zhao, Haozhe Liang, Tieyun Qian, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Problem: Fixed target supervision can become mismatched as visual perturbations alter earlier actions and later physical states.
Method: Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds targets from attacked states, while Progress-Guided Selection concentrates updates where task progress stalls.
Contribution: A closed-loop framework that enhances existing targeted visual attacks without relying solely on average matching-error reduction.
Result: Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments report improved task-redirection success.
Scope: The work highlights security risks for language-guided robot manipulation; the abstract does not specify real-world evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop visual attacks on VLA models for robot manipulation; directly relevant to embodied VLA and manipulation.
papers.title: Enhancing Visual Task-Redirection Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models via Closed-Loop Optimization
papers.tldr: TRACO improves visual task-redirection attacks on vision-language-action robots by adapting attack supervision and updates to the trajectory states actually reached.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks that are effortless for dexterous human hands remain challenging for robotic systems equipped with simple, task-specialized grippers. Industrial platforms commonly rely on end-effectors such as suction cups or parallel-jaw grippers, yet no single mode can reliably satisfy the diverse constraints encountered across different phases of complex manipulation tasks, including pickup, reorientation, insertion, and constrained placement. In this work, we investigate whether complementary simple grippers within a heterogeneous bimanual setup can collectively realize tasks that exceed the capability of any individual gripper alone. Given a single human demonstration specifying the desired object motion, we formulate embodiment-aware execution as a finite-horizon optimization over arm-trajectory assignments. At each segment, the planner determines whether single-arm manipulation or a coordinated dual arm handover is required, jointly reasoning over heterogeneous grasp feasibility, motion constraints, manipulability, and cross-gripper compatibility. Exploiting this formulation, we compute globally consistent assignments with explicit switching regularization. Experiments on a dual Franka FR3 platform equipped with suction and parallel-jaw grippers demonstrate improved feasibility and reliability in tasks that are infeasible under single-gripper execution.
authors: Sukhvansh Jain, Anurag Maurya, Shivam Vats, Narendra Kumar Dhar, Ravi Prakash
bullets: Targets multi-phase tasks involving pickup, reorientation, insertion, and constrained placement with task-specialized grippers.
Uses a single human demonstration of desired object motion as the planning input.
Optimizes arm-trajectory assignments over a finite horizon, choosing single-arm actions or coordinated bimanual handovers.
Accounts for grasp feasibility, motion constraints, manipulability, gripper compatibility, and switching regularization.
Experiments on a dual Franka FR3 setup show improved feasibility and reliability over single-gripper execution.
papers.selection_reason: Heterogeneous bimanual manipulation planning; fits embodied manipulation interests.
papers.title: Embodiment-Aware Planning for Heterogeneous Bimanual Manipulation
papers.tldr: An embodiment-aware planner assigns suction and parallel-jaw grippers across two arms to reliably execute complex manipulation tasks that neither gripper can handle alone.

papers.abstract: Legged robots equipped with manipulators offer promising capabilities for loco-manipulation tasks in unstructured environments. However, achieving task-consistent end-effector behavior during locomotion remains challenging due to terrain-induced disturbances and the strong coupling between locomotion and manipulation, particularly for small-scale quadruped platforms. A reinforcement-learning based whole-body control framework is proposed for quadruped loco-manipulation on complex terrain. The proposed framework combines a hybrid task representation with task-prioritized whole-body learning to coordinate locomotion and manipulation while preserving task-consistent end-effector behavior. A lightweight quadruped manipulator platform is further developed to validate the proposed framework on a small-scale quadruped system. Real-world experiments demonstrate successful deployment on complex terrains such as slopes up to 30 degrees, stairs, and deformable terrain. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying learned whole-body control policy for quadruped loco-manipulation in real-world environments and highlight the importance of task-consistent whole-body coordination for terrain-adaptive loco-manipulation.
authors: Yanzhou Jin, Fei Suo, Chang Liu, Yasuhisa Hasegawa, Liming Chen, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo, Yaonan Zhu
bullets: Addresses disturbances and strong locomotion–manipulation coupling in unstructured environments.
Combines hybrid task representation with task-prioritized whole-body learning.
Validated on a lightweight quadruped manipulator platform.
Real-world tests covered slopes up to 30°, stairs, and deformable terrain.
Demonstrates feasibility of learned, terrain-adaptive loco-manipulation control.
papers.selection_reason: RL whole-body control for quadruped loco-manipulation; directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Based Multi-Terrain Adaptive Whole-Body Control for a Quadruped Manipulator
papers.tldr: A reinforcement-learning whole-body controller enables a small quadruped manipulator to maintain task-consistent end-effector behavior while navigating complex terrain.

papers.abstract: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent's commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.
authors: Hongcheng Gao, Alex Zhou, Jay Zhu, Zelin Zheng, Shijia Ge, Xiping Li, Di Wu, Yazhe Wang, Jianshu Zeng, Xuan Shangguan, Yongli Wang, Yexing Wan, Lingyu He, Zhiqi Jia, Sihang Wu, Xiao He
bullets: Controls a two-arm robot through a command line using three calibrated RGB cameras.
The agent analyzes failures and iteratively writes reusable observation-based tools for localization and control.
Tools use camera triangulation, known planes, and repositioned wrist-camera views to estimate object geometry.
Tools are developed on 10 layouts per task, frozen, and evaluated on 10 new layouts of the same seed.
Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, it reports 39.7% success and 48.0 progress; pushing is strong, while tight insertion is difficult.
papers.selection_reason: VLM coding agent controlling robot manipulation; fits embodied VLA and manipulation interests.
papers.title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents
papers.tldr: HexaShell shows that a thin VLM coding-agent harness can achieve strong robot-manipulation performance, but precise physical contact remains the main bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing 225 consecutive $\mathbf{180^\circ}$ rotations (112.5 full rotations) at $\sim0.36 \;\text{rot/s}$ in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.
authors: Ayush Deshmukh, Nalin Agarwal, Elle Miller, Sethu Vijayakumar
bullets: Studies blind manipulation using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback on a Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite.
Bridges simulation and hardware with sensor-aligned embodiment, tactile calibration, and two episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate limits and STuck-AT Taxels.
Achieves 225 consecutive 180° rotations—112.5 full rotations—at approximately 0.36 rotations/s in one continuous trial.
Compares tactile sensing with proprioception alone and identifies hand regions where tactile feedback is most important.
Scope: focuses on sustained Baoding ball rotation and the challenges of changing contacts, tactile drift, and sim-to-real dynamics.
papers.selection_reason: Tactile-driven dexterous manipulation with RL and sim-to-real transfer; directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
papers.tldr: A tactile-and-proprioceptive RL policy enables sustained, vision-free Baoding ball rotation on a real dexterous hand after zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

papers.abstract: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.
authors: Jiawei Geng, Zhenyang Liu, Yuzheng Wu, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses failures caused by occlusion, clutter, and changing viewpoints in open-world manipulation.
Predicts task-related virtual camera motion and queries a geometry-conditioned world model to generate spatial priors.
Compresses the imagined prior into fixed memory and fuses it with live observations for diffusion-based action prediction.
Reports success rates of 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials.
The demonstrated robustness is scoped to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Active world-action model with trajectory-conditioned view imagination for manipulation; fits world modeling and VLA.
papers.title: AWAM: Active Trajectory-Conditioned View Imagination for Robust Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: AWAM improves robot manipulation in cluttered and occluded settings by actively imagining task-relevant views along planned trajectories before acting.

papers.abstract: Robots manipulating objects in clutter must decide not only how to act, but also where to look. Although active camera motion can expose an occluded target, it may move the robot into an initial observation-state distribution that differs from the manipulation policy's training distribution. We identify this problem as first-frame distribution sensitivity: under perturbed starts in LIBERO, naively prepending camera repositioning to pi_0.5 reduces success from 46.3% to 11.5%. We introduce ActiveAlign, a data-adaptation framework that trains a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy from the states at which active perception terminates. A learned viewpoint module first generates a camera trajectory. Offline, ActiveAlign uses closed-loop alignment to connect the trajectory endpoint to an existing demonstration, replays the remaining manipulation trajectory, and retains successful continuations for fine-tuning. At deployment, the same viewpoint module precedes the adapted VLA without modifying its architecture. Across 40 LIBERO tasks, ActiveAlign achieves 70.7% success with pi_0 and 72.7% with pi_0.5, outperforming their standard-training baselines by 40.0% and 26.4% respectively. Matched-state and data-matched controls support gains beyond prefix shortening and generic viewpoint augmentation; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 also show the same trend. Success rate under physical occlusion in real world increases from 35/90 to 83/90. These results show that active perception benefits manipulation when policy training is aligned with the observation and robot-state distribution induced by viewpoint selection.
authors: Jiawei Geng, Zhenyang Liu, Yuzheng Wu, Yongchong Gu, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Problem: Camera repositioning can create first-frame observation and robot-state distributions unlike those seen during policy training, sharply reducing performance.
Method: A viewpoint module selects a camera trajectory; offline closed-loop alignment connects its endpoint to demonstrations and retains successful manipulation continuations for VLA fine-tuning.
Contribution: The adapted policy uses active perception without changing the VLA architecture and aligns training data with viewpoint-induced states.
Results: On 40 LIBERO tasks, success reaches 70.7% with π₀ and 72.7% with π₀.₅; real-world occlusion success rises from 35/90 to 83/90.
Scope: Gains are supported across controls and also observed with OpenVLA and GR00T N1, indicating the approach is not limited to one VLA.
papers.selection_reason: Active perception aligned with VLA policy training for manipulation; directly relevant to VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Look Before You Act: Bridging Active Perception and Vision-Language-Action Models via Observation-Aligned Data Adaptation
papers.tldr: ActiveAlign adapts vision-language-action policies to the states produced by active camera movement, substantially improving manipulation under occlusion and clutter.

papers.abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
authors: Keyuan Luo, Yi Xie, Wanyun Ling, Yuanzhe Li, Ziyue Li, Zhuoqi Zeng
bullets: Introduces interventions at the retrieval interface, including target-fact substitutions, fact-preserving replacements, numerical perturbations, and exact replicas.
Separates decision correctness from motor execution success and evaluates within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory.
In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-ULP intervention changed 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while key-fact changes showed no clear extra effect over fact-preserving replacements.
ChainBench tests tasks requiring historical information absent from current observations.
Full memory increased ChainBench success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching oracle-decision performance under shared executions.
papers.selection_reason: Directly evaluates memory in vision-language-action robot systems, fitting VLA and embodied memory topics.
papers.title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
papers.tldr: IMEP evaluates whether VLA systems genuinely use task-relevant memory, showing that memory can improve history-dependent decisions but aggregate success ablations are insufficient evidence.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling. Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-$alpha$ further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM also outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High. On three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for $pi_{0.5}$ and 25% for Fast-WAM.
authors: Jiajun Cao, Kai Tang, Bohua Zhang, Zezhong Qian, Ying Li, Xiaozhu Ju, Xiaobao Wei, Jiaming Liu, Yang Ding, Sixiang Chen, Yiding Sun, Siyuan Qian, Tinghao Wang, Jixian Wu, Yichen Guo, Yi Zhang, Shilong Zou, Yong Dai, Jian Tang, Shanghang Zhang
bullets: Uses semantic subtask progress to coordinate planning, action selection, execution monitoring, and transitions.
Combines a hybrid-expert VLM with a world-action model using mixture-of-transformer experts for video–action modeling.
Employs hierarchical visual memory and subtask-local value learning to preserve temporal context and learn from successful prefixes of failed trajectories.
Achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks, rising to 95.56% with OpenWAM-α.
Reaches 65% average success on three long-horizon real-robot tasks, versus 28.33% for π₀.₅ and 25% for Fast-WAM.
papers.selection_reason: Unified language-action-world model for long-horizon manipulation; strongly fits world modeling and VLA.
papers.title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
papers.tldr: LAW unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling to improve long-horizon robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.
authors: Yong Wang, Boyu Shen, Xinwei Zhang, Yizheng Li, Keyuan Luo
bullets: VLA models struggle with long-horizon tasks because limited temporal context hinders the accumulation and reuse of experience.
It proposes a taxonomy based on memory scope and persistence, covering five established paradigms and one emerging frontier.
Representative systems are compared by memory characteristics, architectural complexity, and open-source maturity.
The survey identifies a trade-off: greater architectural complexity generally corresponds to lower open-source maturity.
Key open challenges include efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolution.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of memory paradigms for long-horizon VLA models; directly relevant to embodied memory and VLA systems.
papers.title: From Sliding Windows to Self-evolving Lifelong Memory: A Dual-perspective Survey of Memory Paradigms for Long-Horizon Robotics VLA Models
papers.tldr: This survey organizes memory mechanisms for long-horizon robotics VLA models and highlights the trade-offs and challenges involved in building lifelong embodied agents.

papers.abstract: Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse, viewpoint-dependent observations. When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering approach or verification actions. We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence (FCP). We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and revises each candidate through Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states. The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate: rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90--6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.
authors: Kaibo Yang, Xingyu Wu, Enze Zhu, Yajie Chai, Xuyang Li, Jiahui Cui, Xiaoxuan Liu, Lei Wang, Zhan Chen
bullets: Addresses false candidate persistence, where disproven targets continue triggering approach or verification actions.
Associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and tracks Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states.
Binds waypoints to their source candidates so rejecting a candidate invalidates stale goals; conservative reactivation handles temporary occlusion.
Across benchmark splits, improves success rate by 2.90–6.31 points while reducing behavioral FCP and post-contradiction travel.
Real-world DJI scenarios show improved task success and behavioral reliability with a low false-rejection rate.
papers.selection_reason: Aerial search with revisable target memory and waypoint planning; fits robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: SkyAgent: Revisable Target Memory for Continuous Aerial Search
papers.tldr: SkyAgent’s Revisable Target Memory lets aerial-search agents revise contradicted target hypotheses and cancel stale actions, improving success and reducing wasted post-contradiction travel.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through cooperation. Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills. CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded execution parameters. Physical verification evaluates each executed transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors. Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end success. Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and contact stability. These results support executable coordination as a practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under shared physical constraints.
authors: Zicheng Liu, Haochen Wu, Jiawei He, Suyun Zhao, Huan Yang, Cheng Chi, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses the gap between high-level multi-robot planning and adapting coordination when physical execution deviates from intent.
Represents coordination as code over fixed motor skills, including motion primitives, objectives, temporary roles, and bounded parameters.
Uses verifier-guided evolution: failed transitions trigger revision from an accepted checkpoint, while verified experience informs later decisions.

In simulations with two Unitree G1 robots transporting a payload through constrained corridors, all tested multimodal backbones achieved some end-to-end successes, completing 8 of 15 base runs overall.
The approach remains limited by motion precision and contact stability.
papers.selection_reason: Code-based coordination policies for humanoid robots with physical verification; relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: CoEvolve: Self-Evolving Code Policies from Skills to Strategies for Humanoid Robots
papers.tldr: CoEvolve enables humanoid robots to adapt executable coordination strategies through physical verification and iterative revision during collaborative tasks.

papers.abstract: We present LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300, a policy that combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a learned binary state-reward scorer. At inference, the policy samples four action chunks, predicts the future latent features and robot state for each, and executes the candidate with the highest predicted-state reward logit. Predictions therefore influence the actions sent to the environment. The evaluated system uses a 16-step prediction horizon and keeps all three components frozen during evaluation. In the local evaluation on 50 RoboCasa 1.0.1 tasks in the pretrain kitchen split, with 50 episodes per task, the system records 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) in the historical self-trained GR00T-N1.5 baseline. The observed difference is 26 successes, or 1.04 percentage points. The atomic group improves from 141/900 to 150/900. Separately, the RoboCasa maintainers re-evaluated the submission and reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%) across 50 tasks, with leaderboard rates of 48.3%, 16.3%, and 3.1% for Atomic-Seen, Composite-Seen, and Composite-Unseen. The local and official results are reported separately; their difference is not attributed to a model improvement. Recorded local audits identify 212,700 changed environment-input chunks, including 28,223 in atomic tasks. We describe the actual training stages, implemented inference mechanism, evaluation provenance, and public reproduction entrypoints. These results document an active prediction-and-selection system and a positive historical difference.
authors: TianLiang Ma, Ting Ma, ZhongYuan Ma
bullets: Combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a binary state-reward scorer.
Samples four 16-step action chunks, predicts their future latent features and robot states, and executes the chunk with the highest predicted reward logit.
On a local evaluation of 2,500 episodes, achieved 207 successes (8.28%) versus 181 (7.24%) for the historical baseline.
A separate official re-evaluation reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%); the local and official results are reported separately and are not attributed to model improvement.
All three components were frozen during evaluation; recorded audits found changed environment-input chunks.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned graph dynamics model guides action selection in robotic manipulation; relevant to world modeling and robot learning.
papers.title: LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300: Prediction-Guided Action Selection with a Graph Dynamics Model
papers.tldr: A frozen policy uses graph-based future-state prediction to select among sampled action chunks, yielding a small positive local improvement over a historical GR00T-N1.5 baseline.

papers.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.
bullets: Addresses fragmented training data, multi-task interference, and conflicts caused by conventional model merging in VLA models.
Uses a nested hypernetwork conditioned on the target task to generate adaptive action-expert parameters alongside a frozen base VLA.
Stores task-specific compressed VLM residuals separately for flexible skill reuse and storage efficiency.
Across MetaWorld, ManiSkill, and CALVIN, it outperforms the strongest merging baseline by 41 percentage points on average.
Matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 percentage point on ManiSkill and substantially narrows the gap on CALVIN.
papers.selection_reason: VLA skill consolidation via nested hypernetwork for task-conditioned action-expert generation; directly relevant to embodied AI and robot learning.
papers.title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models
