papers.selection_reason: Force-feedback interface for collecting contact-rich human demonstrations to train manipulation policies.
papers.title: FOMI: A Force-Feedback Manipulation Interface for Teaching Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.tldr: FOMI is a force-feedback handheld interface that improves the collection and teleoperation of contact-rich manipulation demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Integrating world models into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation-to-action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in-domain, out-of-domain, long-horizon, dynamic, few-shot, and real-world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action-only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long-horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM-in-VLAs/.
authors: Qisen Ma, Yixiang Chen, Yuan Xu, Peiyan Li, Jiabing Yang, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: The study compares four integration paradigms: Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor.
World-representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, while 2D semantic representations provide robust gains across paradigms.
No paradigm is universally best; the decoupled MoT Future Expert performs competitively overall and is particularly robust out of distribution.
World modeling consistently helps standard VLM-based policies and improves action-only baselines, especially on long-horizon and dynamic tasks.
Decoupled designs are more compatible with pretrained VLAs, with evaluation spanning in-domain, OOD, few-shot, long-horizon, dynamic, and real-world settings.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies world model integration in Vision-Language-Action models, directly relevant to embodied AI and interactive world models.
papers.title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that world modeling improves vision-language-action policies, but its effectiveness depends on the representation, integration paradigm, and policy backbone.

papers.abstract: Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence. We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot's dynamics, independent of the learned DS. A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints. Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.
authors: Ashok Kumar, Mahathi Anand, Angela Schoellig, Abdalla Swikir
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of formally certifying flexible motions generated by dynamical-system learning from demonstration.
Uses a nominal controller to track the learned motion and a symbolic supervisory controller to monitor safety and convergence.
Automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan directly from the robot’s dynamics, independently of the learned dynamical system.
Intervenes non-conservatively when necessary constraints are violated.
Validated in simulations and on a real robot across 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting, and in complex dynamic environments.
papers.selection_reason: Learned robot motion with formal safety certification via supervisory control; fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Learning from Demonstrations meets Symbolic Control - A Supervisory Control Architecture for Formal Certification of Learned Motion
papers.tldr: A symbolic supervisor adds formal safety, reachability, and actuator-feasibility guarantees to robot motions learned from demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naively training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method, Advantage Guidance, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model's ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.
bullets: Targets RL instability and hyperparameter sensitivity while retaining supervised learning’s simplicity.
Uses effective conditional training to improve policy responsiveness to advantage signals.
Applies contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling to target the KL-regularized optimal policy.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods across 26 long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks with varying data quality.
papers.selection_reason: General RL policy extraction method with advantage conditioning and contrastive diffusion guidance; transferable to robot policy learning.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
papers.tldr: Advantage Guidance combines supervised learning with advantage conditioning and contrastive diffusion guidance to achieve strong policy optimization on challenging sparse-reward tasks.

papers.abstract: Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement. We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate with 5.71 times lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0% with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5%, with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level with 26.6% fewer refiner evaluations. Project page: https://rain-policy.github.io/.
authors: Hanlin Liu, Zichen Zhou, Jiacheng Zhang, Liuyuan Na, Jin Jin, Guangyan Chen, Yufeng Yue, Gen Li, Fangqiang Ding
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between lightweight, low-latency policies and slower iterative generative refinement.
Predicts action errors at multiple refinement levels to select whether and how much to refine each proposal.
Uses an ensemble trained from offline demonstrations without explicit labels for refinement needs, with calibration for uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency.
Evaluated on eight simulated ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks.
Achieves 66.6% simulation success with 5.71× lower policy latency than the best evaluated diffusion policy; real-robot success rises from 55.0% to 72.5% over ACT.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive action-chunk refinement that predicts refinement need to balance task success and inference latency in manipulation.
papers.title: Refine Actions If Needed: Adaptive Action Chunk Refinement for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: RAIN adaptively refines robot action proposals only when needed, improving task success while reducing the latency and computation of repeated refinement.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$\pi$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$\pi$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$\pi$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $\pi_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$\pi$ also consistently outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
authors: Yiming Meng, Yanming Shao, Weijie Shen, Kunyang Lin, Jiayu Sun, Ping Luo, Yao Mu
bullets: Targets the high-dimensional, structured action space of bimanual VLA policies, where cross-hand interactions are often implicit.
Represents right- and left-side arm–hand actions as separate, interleaved action tokens.
Uses learnable hand-identity embeddings and factorized RoPE to encode hand identity, sequence position, and shared control timing.
On five DexJoCo tasks, average success rises from 31.9% to 51.3% under rand-obj and from 18.3% to 32.3% under rand-full, compared with π₀.₅.
Also consistently outperforms π₀.₅ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Structured interleaved action representation for bimanual dexterous VLA manipulation.
papers.title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: Coordi-π improves bimanual dexterous manipulation by explicitly modeling the two hands as coordinated action sequences rather than a single concatenated vector.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios. To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone. In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.
authors: Qi Chen, Yuwei Wu, Quan Chen, Kunpeng Gao, Jin Chen, Che Sun, Zhi Gao, Yunde Jia
bullets: Addresses the costly, poorly scalable need for task-specific robot demonstrations and retraining when adapting VLAs to novel tasks.
Builds a compact, phase-aware video representation using learned visual-token selection and task-relevant queries supervised by phase captions.
Conditions the pretrained VLA policy on the video and query representations to provide task-specific execution guidance while preserving its action-generation backbone.
Experiments on source and unseen target tasks show improved average performance across unseen target groups with comparable source-task performance.
The approach is scoped to cross-task manipulation adaptation guided by human videos; the abstract does not establish broader settings or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: One-shot human video-guided adaptation of VLA policies to unseen manipulation tasks without robot demonstrations.
papers.title: One-shot Human Video-Guided Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: CapPro adapts pretrained vision-language-action policies to unseen robot manipulation tasks using a single human demonstration video, without target-task robot data or fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers is challenged by visually repetitive, featureless terrain. SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offer dense mapping but rely on RGB appearance descriptors that degrade under perceptual aliasing - a common failure mode in extraterrestrial environments where physically distinct locations appear visually identical. This paper presents HyperLoop, the first framework integrating hyperspectral imaging (HSI) into the loop closure module of a 3DGS-based SLAM system. Hyperspectral descriptors encode material-level spectral signatures complementing RGB features, providing robustness to illumination changes and visual repetitiveness. Two HSI descriptor families are introduced: Bag-of-Spectral-Words (BoSW), encoding spectral material distributions via TF-IDF weighted histograms, and PCA-K VLAD (PCAK-VLAD), capturing first-order residual statistics of PCA-compressed spectral signatures. Both are evaluated with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors under Strict-AND and Weighted fusion strategies on a custom dataset from the Moon-Mars Outdoor Test Site (MMOTS) at DLR, comprising synchronized RGB-D and hyperspectral sequences across four planetary analog traverses (65.5 m total). A key finding is that the sensor's Red-NIR range (600-860 nm) provides limited discriminability for rock terrain: the best HSI fusion (SIFT-VLAD + BoSW, Strict-AND) achieves 5.04 cm ATE RMSE, within 1.8% of SIFT-VLAD alone (4.95 cm). The gain over NetVLAD (8.81 cm) is attributable to SIFT-VLAD, not HSI fusion. This motivates future adoption of SWIR sensors capturing diagnostic mineral absorption features absent from the 600-860 nm range for planetary SLAM missions.
authors: Annie Bhalla, Dennis Rotondi, Riccardo Giubilato, Kai O. Arras, Wolfgang Stuerzl
bullets: Addresses perceptual aliasing in visually repetitive, featureless planetary environments.
Introduces BoSW and PCAK-VLAD hyperspectral descriptors for material-aware loop closure.
Evaluates HSI fusion with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors using Strict-AND and Weighted strategies.
On the MMOTS dataset, the best HSI fusion achieved 5.04 cm ATE RMSE, nearly matching SIFT-VLAD alone at 4.95 cm.
Results suggest future systems need SWIR sensing to capture diagnostic mineral absorption features.
papers.selection_reason: Improves loop closure detection for autonomous planetary rover navigation in SLAM.
papers.title: HyperLoop: Hyperspectral-Assisted Loop Closure Detection in 3D-SLAM for Planetary Exploration
papers.tldr: HyperLoop integrates hyperspectral descriptors into 3DGS-based SLAM, but Red-NIR sensing provides little loop-closure benefit for the tested rocky planetary terrain.

papers.abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.
authors: Julia Barth, Armin Sommer, Kunvar Thaman, Jannik Schilling
bullets: Identifies functional target substitution, policy shortcuts, and cue competition across Procgen and robot tasks.
Traces whether goal information is retained internally, influences the policy, and reaches the final decision.
Shows that steering can recover behavior when the goal reaches the decision, while new downstream wiring is needed when it does not.
Recovery fails when the goal is inert, linking intervention effectiveness to the depth of misalignment.
Frames goal misgeneralization as multiple policy-alignment failures rather than a single representation failure.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes goal misgeneralization in learned policies across robot tasks, relevant to embodied robot learning and alignment.
papers.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
papers.tldr: Goal misgeneralization arises from three distinct alignment failures, and recovery depends on how deeply the intended goal is disconnected from action selection.

papers.abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors' epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8 times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.
authors: Sajad Marvi, Julian Schmidt, Alessandro Canevaro, Julian Jordan, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Exploring agents seek states that increase neighboring policies’ epistemic uncertainty, while other agents learn to drive safely through these challenges.
Epistemic uncertainty acts as an automatic difficulty signal, enabling curriculum generation without manual scenario design or ground-truth labels.
The approach improves zero-shot transfer on nuPlan Val14 and Argoverse 2 and also outperforms standard self-play on Waymo.
It produces 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage, suggesting a broader range of learned behaviors.
Highest-uncertainty agents have a 14.8× higher combined collision, off-road, and DNF failure rate than lowest-uncertainty agents.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-driven self-play curriculum for robust multi-agent driving policies and motion planning.
papers.title: Uncertainty-Driven Self-Play for Robust Multi-Agent Driving Policies
papers.tldr: Uncertainty-driven self-play automatically focuses training on difficult driving scenarios, producing more robust policies with stronger zero-shot transfer than standard self-play.

papers.abstract: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor--Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA. ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory. Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation. Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions. Project page: https://junhoo.me/acro
authors: Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Baekseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses failures caused by poor decisions about continuing versus intervening during VLA policy execution.
Uses a rollout-trained Critic to assess success prospects, choose intervention times, and select re-entry targets.
Applies Trajectory Retraction to return the robot to a selected point before resuming the same VLA with a fresh observation.
Evaluated with GR00T N1.7 and π₀.₅ in simulation and real-robot manipulation, improving success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points across the reported settings.
Also completes additional tasks when the available execution budget increases.
papers.selection_reason: Actor-critic rollout orchestration deciding when to intervene and where to resume for fixed VLA policies.
papers.title: ACRO: Actor-Critic Rollout Orchestration
papers.tldr: ACRO improves fixed vision-language-action policies by deciding when and where to intervene and resume execution, increasing task success under the same physical execution budget.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
authors: Jehun Lee, Hajun Lee, Jimin Ryu, Youhan Lee, Beomseok Kang, Jonghyun Choi, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Fixed-horizon execution can waste predicted actions and incur excessive policy calls at short horizons.
PICES is training-free and jointly selects an action chunk and how many actions to execute before replanning.
It compares nominal action chunks with versions generated from locally perturbed noise samples under shared conditioning features.
Experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation show up to 2.3× faster wall-clock inference on Jetson Orin and Thor, with improved success rate.
The method targets adaptive execution: longer horizons for stable predictions and shorter horizons for precise corrections.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free action chunk and execution horizon selection that accelerates VLA inference while improving manipulation success.
papers.title: Accelerating VLA Inference with Perturbation Informed Execution
papers.tldr: PICES accelerates VLA robot control by adapting both the selected action chunk and execution horizon using perturbation-based uncertainty cues, improving speed and success.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making hyperspectral distinctions usable by a pretrained model without retraining its visual encoder or action decoder.
Uses native-width residual enrichment based on each token’s normalized false-color reference, with projection, norm control, and validation-calibrated injection.
Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category-balanced accuracy increases from 0.812 to 0.883.
Own-token addition improves external category-probe reuse over pooled replacement (0.701 vs. 0.590) under identical residuals and scale.
Grouped tests recover within-category spectral shape, while spectral swaps indicate that own-token composition approximately doubles target-specific recovery after frozen decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, adapting frozen interfaces to hyperspectral data without retraining, a core interest in Embodied AI.
papers.title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
papers.tldr: SPECTRA-VLA transfers hyperspectral information into a frozen vision-language-action model by enriching each visual token with a calibrated, token-specific residual.

papers.abstract: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.
authors: Yuhang Hu, Junlin Lyu, Yuan Fang, Xiaoying Shen, Lechen Zhang, Jiong Lin, Judah Goldfeder, Steven Tian, Hod Lipson
bullets: Separates gaze target selection, fixation, and target-conditioned motion generation.
RGT uses a Transformer-VAE trained on retargeted markerless human gaze recordings in an 11-DoF robot joint space.
Self-supervised history encoding and autoregressive fine-tuning support realistic rollout behavior.
On a two-second shared-target benchmark, RGT-Base achieves the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE.
Physical demonstrations show integrated targeting and control, while perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary selection remain unevaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Humanoid gaze generation from human video recordings with VLM-guided target selection, relevant to embodied visuomotor control.
papers.title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE
papers.tldr: A VLM-guided Transformer-VAE enables humanoid robots to select gaze targets and generate coordinated, expressive eye, head, and eyelid movements in real time.

papers.abstract: Differentiable reinforcement learning shows strong promise for robot policy learning, but its application to legged locomotion has remained limited to blind walking or simulated 2D tasks. Extending it to end-to-end visual obstacle avoidance is challenging because hard collision constraints and early termination upon contact corrupt first-order gradients, trapping optimizers in local minima. We present E2DRL, which addresses this with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation: penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping to provide the first-order training signals for 3D obstacle avoidance. To realize a deployable perception-control system, a privileged teacher trained via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO) in a differentiable simulator is distilled into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, then blended with a base locomotion policy using a terrain-aware gating module for deployment. In simulation, E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO and demonstrates superior velocity-tracking performance and 3D obstacle-avoidance capability compared with both PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC. We present the first sim-to-real validation of end-to-end differentiable RL for 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.
authors: Cheng Fan, Bingyang Zhou, Gang Yang, Zixuan Zhuang, Aoqian Zhang, Pengzhi Yang, Xin Liu, Chunzheng Wang, Yan Rui Tan, Fan Shi
bullets: Addresses gradient corruption from hard collisions and early termination in differentiable RL for legged obstacle avoidance.
Uses velocity-conditioned, stop-gradient shaping with penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints.
Distills a privileged SAPO teacher into a recurrent depth-based student using DAgger, then blends it with locomotion control through terrain-aware gating.
In simulation, shows higher sample efficiency than PPO and improved velocity tracking and obstacle avoidance versus PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC.
Demonstrates sim-to-real 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.
papers.selection_reason: Differentiable RL with soft obstacle interaction for 3D visual obstacle avoidance in quadruped robots, with sim-to-real deployment.
papers.title: E2DRL: End-to-End Differentiable Reinforcement Learning for 3D Obstacle Avoidance in Quadruped Robots
papers.tldr: E2DRL enables end-to-end differentiable visual 3D obstacle avoidance for quadruped robots by replacing hard collision handling with soft, gradient-preserving interaction penalties and deploying a distilled perception-control policy.

papers.abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.
bullets: Object-goal navigation requires exploration, object detection, target validation, and reliable mission completion in unfamiliar environments.
A fixed modular study found trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model cost, motivating adaptive coordination.
A rule-based Supervisor dynamically manages navigation, exploration, detection, validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory.
Event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional guidance support adaptive behavior while keeping normal execution lightweight.
Across AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, SR/SPL were 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37; adaptive interventions were more frequent in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive agentic architecture for object-goal navigation with mission memory and recovery.
papers.title: F2A-ObjectNav: An Adaptive Agentic Architecture for Object-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: F2A-ObjectNav adaptively coordinates specialized navigation components to improve object-goal navigation across varied environments.

papers.abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run, and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program's own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration's single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.
authors: Fan Huang, Dezhong Tong, Changyu Chen, Haewoon Kwak, Jisun An
bullets: Evaluates one-shot generation versus ICMC on UR5e cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks in MuJoCo using o1 and o4-mini.
Trains an open-weight instruction policy with GRPO through a frozen code generator, averaging rewards from five programs per instruction.
Logged positive-reward rates increased from 31.6% to 35.3% over the reported five-step trajectory, but these rates were not always consistent with independently verified task success.
Audits found positive labels for geometric failures, including a case where all five rewards were 1.0 despite a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance.
Proposes independent evaluation against fixed task specifications to separate robot control from success assessment.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned robotic arm control via code decomposition and reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control for Robotic Arms: Language-to-Code Decomposition and Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ICMC makes language-driven robot motion more traceable by separating instructions, parameters, and code, while exposing limitations in reward-based success evaluation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot's URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining.
authors: Hyunsik Oh, Seunghun Jeon, Donghoon Youm, Jungwoo Hur, Hyeongjun Kim, Jeong Hyun Lee, Moonkyu Jung, Jemin Hwangbo
bullets: Targets the need to retrain or re-engineer locomotion policies when robot morphology changes.
Encodes URDF-derived joint-link modules with a recurrent encoder, graph Transformer, and per-joint action decoder.
Improves training stability using morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-based PD-gain initialization.
Evaluated in simulation on bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphologies and platforms.
Demonstrates real-world deployment on quadrupeds in multiple configurations without per-robot policy retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Morphology-conditioned locomotion policy learning across heterogeneous legged robots.
papers.title: PolyMorph: Learning Locomotion Policy for Cross-Embodiment Adaptation
papers.tldr: PolyMorph learns one morphology-conditioned locomotion policy that transfers across legged robots with different body designs, including unseen variants and real quadruped configurations.

papers.abstract: Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria. We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.
authors: Xuan Han, Zinuo Jin, Tianlin Li, Yunfan Lou, Xin Liu, Yuchen Xue, Yuanpeng He, Boxian Yao, Shuhan Zhan, Ruihai Wu, Zhibo Pang
bullets: Introduces a unified simulation benchmark covering eight tasks, 1,600 synchronized demonstrations, and task-specific success criteria.
Compares a no-force baseline with six force-integration designs using a shared π0.5 backbone.
Prompt Fusion achieves 35.31% mean simulation success versus 23.25% for the baseline and improves all three task categories.
In real-world tests, Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion reach 63.00% mean success versus 40.00% for the baseline; only Prompt Fusion improves every task.
Predictive and temporal benefits are strongest for physical-property inference, while temporal designs underperform on assembly.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for force integration in VLA-based robotic manipulation.
papers.title: ForceBench: Benchmarking Force Integration for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: ForceBench standardizes evaluation of six-axis wrist-force integration for vision-language-action policies, finding that Prompt Fusion performs best across diverse robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: A pretrained VLA succeeds on 80% of atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when skills are composed for mobile manipulation.
Failures primarily arise in task planning, navigation/base positioning, and local manipulation.
The proposed system adds demonstration-based planning, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment to a fixed subtask VLA.
Success improves from 19% to 47% on RoboCasa365, reaching 49% on held-out seeds versus 18% for the baseline.
The approach also improves results on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks, supporting bottleneck-focused intervention over uniform policy scaling.
papers.selection_reason: Failure-guided agentic interventions for long-horizon mobile manipulation with adaptive visual memory.
papers.title: Cracking Mobile Manipulation: From Failure Diagnosis to Agentic Robot System
papers.tldr: Diagnosing bottlenecks across planning, navigation, and manipulation enables targeted agentic interventions that substantially improve long-horizon mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation suffers from two fundamental challenges: inherent motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arm, and hand modules, and progressive error accumulation over long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Existing teleoperation platforms also lack integrated dexterous tactile sensing to support coordinated whole-body decision-making. This paper presents RoboSpan, a high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration platform, and the Hierarchical Modular Framework (HMF) for learning modular coordination policies. HMF functionally decouples the 29-DoF action space into fine hand manipulation, arm pose adjustment, and mobile-base spatial configuration branches, and introduces the Coordinated Modular Embodied Transformer (COMET) with inter-modular cross-attention to enable dynamic information exchange and action coordination. Vision-language model driven hierarchical task decomposition structurally suppresses temporal error propagation, while a full-palm 2D tactile representation encodes distributed contact signals for cross-module tactile empowerment. Experiments on a physical 29-DoF robot demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 20\% higher task success rate than mainstream baselines across a range of long-horizon whole-body tasks, markedly improving stability and robustness in contact-rich manipulation.
authors: Keqiang Ren, Xuecheng Ye, Hanyu Liu, Zhihua Wang, Tao Jian, Yunsheng Ma, Jiayi Wen, Xinran Li, Zhigong Song
bullets: Addresses motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arms, and hands, plus error accumulation in long-horizon tasks.
Decouples the 29-DoF action space into hand, arm, and mobile-base branches within a Hierarchical Modular Framework.
Uses COMET cross-attention for inter-module coordination and vision-language-model task decomposition to limit temporal error propagation.
Adds full-palm 2D tactile sensing to represent distributed contact signals across modules.
On a physical 29-DoF robot, achieves over 20% higher task success than mainstream baselines across varied long-horizon tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Modular coordination policies for high-DoF whole-body mobile manipulation with tactile sensing.
papers.title: RoboSpan: Learning Modular Coordination Policies for High-DoF Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation with Teleoperation
papers.tldr: RoboSpan combines a high-DoF teleoperation platform with hierarchical modular policies to improve long-horizon, contact-rich whole-body mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $\pi_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).
authors: Colton Crosby, Hao Wang, Mac Schwager, Somil Bansal
bullets: Addresses deployment-time failures that nominal policies cannot predict or recover from without retraining or new data collection.
Learns a policy-conditioned liveness value from labeled on-policy rollouts to measure progress toward task completion.
Trains a compact latent world model from on-policy rollouts and play data, then plans short corrective interventions when progress is lost.
Evaluated on LIBERO-Goal and a Franka Panda using π₀.₅ and a diffusion policy, with reported task-success improvements and real-time control.
Scope: interventions rely on offline training data and black-box query access to the nominal policy.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time policy improvement via latent world model planning and liveness monitoring.
papers.title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
papers.tldr: An offline-trained monitor and world-model planner can improve black-box visuomotor policies during deployment by detecting stalled progress and intervening with corrective actions.

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation requires a global planner that connects visually specified endpoints while providing observations that a local policy can follow. Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides map-registered RGB, opacity, and depth renderings, but does not explicitly encode navigable topology. We introduce \method, a Gaussian visual roadmap whose milestones, local connections, and visual references are constructed directly through 3DGS rendering without deriving an occupancy grid or signed distance field. We define render-based collision-free (RC-free) configurations and paths. Panoramic depth supplies conservative clearance for milestone validation and adaptive coverage, while edge-aligned orthographic rendering tests the robot's swept volume. We establish conditional soundness and sufficient conditions for deterministic query completeness and probabilistic construction completeness of GS-PRM. To validate the performance of GS-PRM, we conduct experiments in both simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating long-horizon navigation using goal-conditioned policies guided by GS-PRM. Compared with a state-of-the-art 3DGS-based navigation system, our GS-PRM-based navigation system achieves up to a twice higher average success rate and reduces travel time by up to 57.2% when both systems complete the navigation task.
authors: Ashraf Siddique, Kyung Min Han, Young J. Kim
bullets: Addresses the gap between 3DGS visual rendering and explicit navigable topology for global planning.
Constructs milestones, local connections, and visual references using 3DGS-rendered RGB, opacity, and depth.
Uses panoramic depth for conservative clearance and adaptive coverage, plus edge-aligned orthographic rendering to test swept-volume collisions.
Provides conditional soundness and completeness guarantees for deterministic queries and probabilistic roadmap construction.
Validated in simulated and real-world environments, achieving up to 2× higher average success and 57.2% shorter travel time than a state-of-the-art 3DGS navigation system when tasks are completed.
papers.selection_reason: 3DGS-based visual roadmap for image-goal navigation with collision-free planning.
papers.title: GS-PRM: Gaussian Visual Roadmap for Image-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: GS-PRM builds a navigable visual roadmap directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting to support reliable long-horizon image-goal navigation without occupancy grids or signed distance fields.

papers.abstract: We devise a dual-arm cooperative planning framework for wiping table surface in the presence of scattered objects. Unlike conventional surface-cleaning strategies that only cover free areas and detour around obstacles, our framework explicitly assigns one arm to rearrange objects while the other performs coverage wiping, thereby enabling access to previously obstructed regions. Specifically, we first construct a set of wiping and object-rearrangement action primitives. Based on these primitives, we introduce Geo-MILP, a geometry-aware task planner formulated as Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP). By integrating Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD), Geo-MILP iteratively optimizes action sequencingand timing to resolve geometric conflicts, promoting efficient cooperation between wiping and object rearrangement. We then employ K-Order Markov Optimization (KOMO) to generate smooth, collision-free motions to ensure feasible execution. Simulation and physical experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework not only increases reachable coverage by enabling access to obstructed areas, but also significantly improves time efficiency compared to Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) baselines, reducing planning time by up to 9 times and execution makespan by approximately 40%.
authors: Pengqi Zhang, Longchang Yu, Daohan Li, Liang Yan, Hangxin Liu
bullets: Addresses the limited coverage and detours of wiping methods that avoid scattered objects.
Assigns one arm to move objects while the other performs surface wiping using predefined action primitives.
Uses geometry-aware MILP planning with Logic-Based Benders Decomposition to optimize action order and timing under geometric conflicts.
Applies K-Order Markov Optimization to generate smooth, collision-free executable motions.
Simulation and physical experiments show up to 9× lower planning time and approximately 40% shorter execution makespan than TAMP baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-arm cooperative manipulation planning with geometry-aware MILP for tabletop wiping.
papers.title: Dual-arm Cooperation for Tabletop Wiping with Temporal Object Removal
papers.tldr: A dual-arm planner coordinates object rearrangement and tabletop wiping to clean previously obstructed areas more efficiently.

papers.abstract: Robotic exploration, coverage, and multi-agent deployment algorithms require reproducible environments with controllable geometry and visibility. This paper presents the Dungeon and Visibility World Generator, an open-source framework for constructing two- and three-dimensional environments and evaluating geometric line-of-sight. The framework supports orthogonal, polygonal or polyhedral, and curvilinear geometries, with six construction families covering scattered rooms, clusters, winding passages, caverns, branches, and loops. Room dimensions, passage structures, obstacles, and spatial placement can be controlled through configurable parameters and probability distributions. Each generated environment provides continuous free-space geometry and a corresponding discrete occupancy representation. A Rust-based visibility engine supports line-of-sight queries in both representations, enabling the evaluation of observable regions from arbitrary agent positions. The framework records configurations, generated geometries, occupancy grids, and visibility results to support reproducible experiments. We demonstrate the generator across all six geometry classes, examine how geometry and spatial resolution affect visibility, and evaluate generation time and reproducibility. The resulting framework provides a configurable foundation for evaluating robotic exploration, coverage, and multi-agent deployment algorithms in diverse environments.
authors: Edwin M\'eriaux, Antonio Lor\'ia, Gregory Dudek
bullets: Supports orthogonal, polygonal/polyhedral, and curvilinear environments.
Provides six construction families, including rooms, passages, caverns, branches, and loops.
Offers continuous free-space and discrete occupancy representations with configurable obstacles and spatial placement.
Includes a Rust-based visibility engine for line-of-sight queries from arbitrary agent positions.
Evaluates geometry, resolution, generation time, and reproducibility across the six environment classes.
papers.selection_reason: Configurable environment and visibility generator for evaluating embodied exploration, coverage, and multi-agent deployment.
papers.title: Dungeon and Visibility World Generator
papers.tldr: An open-source generator creates reproducible 2D and 3D environments with configurable geometry and line-of-sight evaluation for robotic exploration and deployment research.

papers.abstract: While multi-fingered dexterous robot hands have the potential to provide human-level dexterity, using them for functional manipulation remains difficult because task success depends on precise contact, coordinated arm-hand motion, and reactive recovery from execution errors. Precise contact depends on complex contact dynamics that are difficult to model accurately in simulation, motivating real-world learning. However, real-world demonstrations in the full arm-hand control space are costly and noisy because each trajectory must coordinate arm motion with high-DoF multi-finger contact. Small execution deviations can further cause slipped contact or premature force application, making recovery from off-nominal contact states important for robust execution. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation tasks. Our key insight is to decouple the control complexity into a functional hand skill for precise contact execution and an arm-hand coordination policy for arm control and hand-skill activation. This design enables effective real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and efficient data collection with Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) augmentation. Across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands, HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training and remains robust to dynamic disturbances. The project page is available at https://hly-123.github.io/HiFun/.
authors: Linyi Huang, Guowei Huai, Weibin Liu, Shulong Jiang, Ping Tan, Weixuan Zhang, Hui Zhang, Jie Song
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of learning precise contact, coordinated arm–hand motion, and recovery from execution errors.
Decouples control into a functional hand skill for contact execution and an arm–hand policy for arm control and skill activation.
Uses real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and Dynamic Movement Primitive augmentation for data-efficient training.
Achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands.
Remains robust to dynamic disturbances, though its evaluation scope is limited to the reported tasks and hardware.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical RL for functional dexterous manipulation directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: HiFun: a Hierarchical Framework for Efficient Functional Dexterous Manipulation Learning
papers.tldr: HiFun is a hierarchical real-world reinforcement learning framework that enables efficient and robust functional manipulation with multi-fingered dexterous hands.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of continual adaptation in conventional pretrained VLA policies.
Adds a reinforcement-learning module that uses past observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals.
Refines action generation during deployment without updating the underlying model parameters.
Designed to support diverse history-construction strategies and VLA training pipelines.
Experiments in simulation and real-world deployment demonstrate adaptation to unseen scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time adaptation of VLA models via in-context RL; directly relevant to VLA and test-time/continual learning.
papers.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: VLRLA enables fixed vision-language-action models to adapt during deployment by learning from accumulated interaction history through in-context reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
authors: Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai
bullets: Jointly encodes task, execution stage, and future action continuations in both current-state queries and recorded experiences.
Uses predictive retrieval training and a corpus of 1,695,684 training anchors; introduces a 4,000-query benchmark with an 8,000-entry gallery.
Achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, outperforming the action-free Gemini Embedding 2 baseline in the reported comparisons.
Retrieved experience improves policy success in DROID-Sim and LIBERO, and execution-feedback memory evolution improves performance across five ManiSkill tasks.
Ablations indicate that removing action information harms retrieval more than removing vision; evaluation focuses on the reported simulated and real-robot settings.
papers.selection_reason: Unified VLA retrieval embeddings for robot in-context learning and task-local memory evolution.
papers.title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
papers.tldr: Robota-Embed learns a unified vision-language-action retrieval space that helps robots retrieve useful past experience for in-context learning and task-specific evolution.

papers.abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io
authors: Liqian Ma, Vaibhav Saxena, Utkarsh Aashu Mishra, Shuo Cheng, Yongxin Chen, Danfei Xu
bullets: Addresses fixed or manually tuned simulator data distributions that may poorly support real-world policy learning.
Uses meta-learning and meta-gradients to train an auxiliary rater that selects high-utility generation distributions within a user-defined parameter space.

Outperforms uniform-generation and retrieval baselines across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, with a reported 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation.
Matches expert manual parameter alignment and transfers proxy-policy-curated distributions to VLA fine-tuning.
Supports partial sim-real alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition.
papers.selection_reason: Meta-learning simulation data generation for sim-and-real robot policy co-training fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
papers.tldr: MetaGenSim learns which simulation data to generate so that robot policies trained with sim-and-real co-training perform better in the real world.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA's success by -38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over K paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores -32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores -28.0. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays -27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy's success depends on the instruction. Across three policies and four suites, paraphrases cost a policy only where this share is high, and the stronger policies lose a much smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA. LoRA post-training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points, against -32.0 for a matched control, reproduces across two seeds and on OpenVLA-OFT, transfers to withheld phrasings, and leaves the policy's reliance on the instruction unchanged.
authors: Hanlong Li, Sihan Tan, Takeshi Ashizawa, Benjamin Yen, Kazuhiro Nakadai
bullets: Rewording instructions reduces base OpenVLA success by 38.0 points on LIBERO, despite using semantically equivalent commands.
Test-time prompt ensembling, paraphrase medoids, and confidence-based selection fail to recover the lost performance; aggregation mainly reduces variance while preserving paraphrase bias.
A wrong-instruction probe links paraphrase sensitivity to how much policy success depends on the instruction, with stronger policies losing a smaller fraction.
LoRA training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points versus −32.0 for a matched control, replicating across seeds and OpenVLA-OFT.
The robustness improvement transfers to withheld phrasings without changing the policy’s overall reliance on instructions.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of instruction paraphrase robustness in VLA policies directly addresses vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Paraphrase Consensus Is Not Self-Consistency: Instruction Reliance and Robustness in VLA Policies
papers.tldr: VLA policies can be highly sensitive to instruction wording, and paraphrase aggregation does not remove this shared bias, whereas paraphrase-focused LoRA training substantially improves robustness.

papers.abstract: This paper presents $S^3$-Nav, a structured spatial-semantic decision-making framework for language-guided robot navigation under partial observability. Rather than assuming a complete environment representation in advance, $S^3$-Nav incrementally constructs persistent spatial-semantic state while exposing only a capacity-controlled, task-conditioned view to the high-level policy. This separation decouples what the robot must retain from what the policy needs to inspect, allowing decision complexity to be controlled without discarding grounded evidence required for subsequent reasoning and validation. High-level navigation outputs remain provisional and are independently grounded and validated against persistent semantic evidence and current geometric observations before physical execution or task termination. Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks demonstrate that separating persistent state, decision-facing evidence, and execution authority improves closed-loop navigation reliability while reducing policy reasoning cost.
bullets: Incrementally builds a persistent spatial-semantic representation instead of requiring a complete environment model.
Provides the high-level policy with a compact, task-conditioned view to control decision complexity.
Independently grounds and validates provisional navigation decisions using stored semantic evidence and current geometry.
Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks show improved closed-loop reliability with lower policy reasoning cost.
papers.selection_reason: Language-guided robot navigation with structured spatial-semantic state directly fits vision-language navigation.
papers.title: $S^3$-Nav: Structured Spatial-Semantic Decision Making for Language-Guided Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: S³-Nav improves language-guided robot navigation under partial observability by separating persistent spatial-semantic memory from capacity-controlled policy inputs and validating actions before execution.

papers.abstract: Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons. We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round. Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them. WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments. Weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation. Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction. Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.
authors: Yue Zhang, Han Lin, Zun Wang, Yidong Huang, Zaid Khan, Mohit Bansal
bullets: Generic realism, diversity, and task coverage may not target the distinct failure modes of different pretrained navigation policies.
An LLM extracts and validates weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, then selects the strongest weakness by success-rate gap.
The framework maps validated weaknesses to controllable environmental factors and generates environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles.
Across three navigation agents, weakness-conditioned adaptation outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR; gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini transfer to HM3D.
Iterative re-diagnosis tracks weaknesses that persist or shift as policies improve, enabling updated environment generation.
papers.selection_reason: Weakness-guided environment generation for embodied navigation agents.
papers.title: From Failures to Learnable Worlds: Policy-Conditioned Environment Generation for Navigation Agents
papers.tldr: WEDGE uses a policy’s observed failures to generate targeted training environments that address its current navigation weaknesses.

papers.abstract: Whole-body control plays a crucial role in enabling humanoid robots to execute expressive motions.
