papers.title: WorkRover: Scaling Long-Horizon Cowork Agent Training Via Recursive Environment Evolution
papers.tldr: WorkRover improves long-horizon cowork-agent training by recursively evolving aligned environments and providing finer-grained reinforcement-learning feedback.

papers.abstract: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system. We evaluate two orchestration paradigms: text subgoals for learned low-level policies (VoLo) and tool selection orchestration (CaP-X, GPT-Policy, PSP-Agent, TiPToP). Given the full instruction directly, low-level policies achieve 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks, but drop to near zero on extended tasks. While orchestration remedies this, it remains bounded by physical execution errors of the low-level policy rather than high-level planning and achieves only ~25%. Tool selection orchestration with GPT-Policy on GPT-6 Astra significantly outperforms learned-policy methods, but incurs significant time and cost budget and succeeds only ~62%. Real-world experiments across two embodiments confirm the collapse of the low-level policy and the gain from orchestration. Project website: https://ladder.insait.ai
authors: Petko Petkov, Giuliano Albanese, Nikolay Nikolov, Luc Van Gool, Jonathan Tremblay, Danda Pani Paudel
bullets: Evaluates 1–10 subgoal tasks across three suites, 145 tasks, eight categories, and two robot embodiments.
Direct low-level policies achieve 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks but approach zero on extended tasks.
Orchestration raises performance, yet learned-policy approaches reach only about 25% due largely to physical execution failures.
GPT-Policy with GPT-6 Astra reaches about 62% through tool selection, but requires substantial time and cost.
Real-world tests confirm both low-level policy collapse and the benefits of orchestration.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark and evaluates orchestration of low-level policies, directly fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: LADDER: A Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Benchmark
papers.tldr: LADDER benchmarks long-horizon robot manipulation and shows that performance collapses as subgoals increase, while orchestration improves success but remains limited by execution errors, cost, and time.

papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) enable diverse whole-body control, but adapting a pretrained controller to a new embodiment remains challenging because of kinematic and dynamic mismatch. We present TRACE, a framework for efficient cross-embodiment adaptation that preserves pretrained motion representations while specializing feedback control to the target robot.TRACE first injects kinematic priors into input and output projection layers and aligns nominal joint dynamics to reduce embodiment mismatch and support stable fine-tuning. It then combines encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning on a compact, quality-screened motion set, using a two-phase curriculum to establish stable tracking before refining difficult motions. We apply TRACE to transfer SONIC from Unitree G1 to Unitree H2 using 10 million motion frames and approximately eight hours of training on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, at less than 0.1% of the GPU-hour cost of training SONIC from scratch. The adapted controller achieves 96.08\% success on 67,953 evaluation motions under a height-scaled tracking criterion. Real-robot demonstrations span dynamic motion tracking and whole-body teleoperation, with collected demonstrations supporting downstream vision-language-action policy post-training. These results demonstrate practical reuse of a pretrained humanoid controller across robots with different body scales and dynamics.
authors: Qingyu Lan, Zhihao Tian, Zifan Wang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Addresses kinematic and dynamic mismatch when transferring controllers across humanoid robots.
Injects kinematic priors, aligns nominal joint dynamics, and uses encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning.
Trains with a compact quality-screened motion set and a two-phase curriculum for stable tracking and difficult motions.
Transfers SONIC from Unitree G1 to H2 using 10 million motion frames and about eight hours on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU.
Achieves 96.08% success on 67,953 evaluation motions and supports real-robot dynamic tracking, teleoperation, and downstream policy post-training.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient cross-embodiment transfer of humanoid whole-body control using distillation and low-rank RL.
papers.title: TRACE: Efficient Transfer Learning for Neural Whole-Body Control Across Humanoid Embodiments
papers.tldr: TRACE efficiently adapts a pretrained humanoid whole-body controller to a new robot by preserving motion representations while specializing control to the target embodiment.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, such as $\pi_{0.5}$, have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities by scaling behavior cloning across massive datasets. However, these models frequently suffer from distributional convergence, a phenomenon where the policy regresses to "safe" but suboptimal mean behaviors due to mode averaging in the training data. This often results in generic grasp strategies, Convergent Defaults, that fail in constrained or long-tail scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel framework to identify and correct these behaviors without parameter updates. We introduce a three-stage methodology: (1) Probing for Defaults, identifying task-specific mode collapse; (2) Diagnostic Root Cause Analysis, utilizing the VLA's latent reasoning capabilities to verbalize the logic behind suboptimal actions; and (3) Structured Guidance Injection, where concrete, distinct alternatives are encoded into reusable "Lens Prompts" that shift the sampling distribution. We validate this approach using $\pi_{0.5}$ in ManiSkill3 simulation environments. We hypothesize that our method outperforms vanilla $\pi_{0.5}$ and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting by effectively breaking convergent defaults in complex manipulation tasks.
authors: Mohammed Daba (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China), Waleed Abdulrahman Saleh AlAkwa (University of Sana'a, Sana'a, Yemen)
bullets: Targets distributional convergence in behavior-cloned VLA models, where mode averaging produces safe but suboptimal “Convergent Defaults.”
Probes task behavior to identify task-specific mode collapse.
Uses diagnostic reasoning to uncover why the model selects suboptimal actions.
Injects concrete alternatives through reusable “Lens Prompts” to shift action sampling without parameter updates.
Evaluated with π₀.₅ in ManiSkill3 simulations; the abstract states a hypothesis of improvement over vanilla π₀.₅ and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting, not confirmed results.
papers.selection_reason: Improves VLA manipulation policies via diagnostic reasoning and structured guidance, fitting both VLA and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Breaking the Average: Overcoming Convergent Defaults in Robotic Manipulation via Diagnostic Chain-of-Thought and Structured Guidance
papers.tldr: A prompt-based, parameter-free framework diagnoses and redirects robotic VLA models away from generic manipulation behaviors that fail in constrained or long-tail situations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires robust execution over sequences of interdependent actions. Existing methods typically handle execution deviations by replanning the remaining action chunk or correcting actions step by step as new observations arrive. However, a local deviation may affect only a few actions under distribution shift, yet replanning regenerates the entire chunk from an unfamiliar state, potentially introducing errors into otherwise valid actions. Step-wise correction may react too late, as it does not explicitly anticipate how the deviation affects subsequent actions. We propose ReEnvision, a future-guided selective action repair framework that updates a joint future-action belief using execution feedback. It then learns how the resulting belief revision affects each unexecuted action. The resulting belief revision enables selective repair of only the affected actions within a cached action chunk, preserving valid actions and reserving full replanning for severe deviations. On CALVIN, L-CALVIN, and RLBench, ReEnvision achieves 86.6% 5-step success, improves 10-step success from 56% to 63%, and reaches an average success rate of 88.8%, respectively. On five real-world manipulation tasks, it achieves an average success rate of 82.8%. Controlled repair experiments further demonstrate the benefits of localizing affected actions and preserving valid ones during execution.
authors: Xiyin Zeng, Xuewei Huang, Yi Lu, Weihao Yuan, Hao Wang
bullets: Addresses the risk that full replanning introduces errors into otherwise valid action sequences, while step-wise correction may react too late.
Updates a joint belief over future actions using execution feedback and estimates which unexecuted actions are affected.
Repairs only affected actions in a cached action chunk, reserving full replanning for severe deviations.
Reports 86.6% 5-step success, improves 10-step success from 56% to 63%, and achieves 88.8% average success across simulation benchmarks.
Achieves 82.8% average success on five real-world manipulation tasks; controlled experiments support localized repair and preservation of valid actions.
papers.selection_reason: Selective future-guided action repair for long-horizon robot manipulation, directly in learned manipulation/policy execution.
papers.title: ReEnvision: Future-Guided Selective Action Repair for Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.tldr: ReEnvision selectively repairs only the future actions affected by execution deviations, improving long-horizon manipulation reliability while preserving valid actions.

papers.abstract: Unknown payloads alter robot dynamics and make precise contact execution difficult when foothold margins are small. We present LOAD, a perceptive locomotion framework that combines explicit inertial estimates with implicit dynamics features for narrow-beam traversal. Separate recurrent modules infer torso inertial changes and task-relevant history from proprioception, while a height-map teacher is distilled into a depth-based student. We extensively evaluate LOAD and its variants in simulation and on hardware across beam widths and payload configurations. The results show that implicit dynamics features accelerate training, while explicit inertial estimation further improves traversal success; combining both enables LOAD to approach the performance of a privileged policy supplied with ground-truth inertial parameters. Hardware experiments demonstrate traversal with unilateral payloads of 6 kg on a 10 cm beam and 9 kg on a 15 cm beam, and an evenly distributed 11 kg payload on a 15 cm beam. These results support combining physical estimates and history features for precision locomotion under unknown loads.
authors: Kunzhao Ren, Zhishuo Zhu, Xiaobin Xiong
bullets: Targets precision footholds when payload changes make robot dynamics uncertain.
Uses recurrent proprioceptive modules for explicit inertial estimation and implicit task-history features.
Distills a height-map teacher into a depth-based student for perceptive locomotion.
Combining both feature types approaches a privileged policy with ground-truth inertial parameters.
Hardware tests demonstrate loaded traversal on narrow beams, including unilateral and distributed payloads.
papers.selection_reason: Learned perceptive locomotion with online dynamics awareness for precision footholds, relevant to robot navigation and learning.
papers.title: Locomotion with Online Awareness of Dynamics for Precision Footholds
papers.tldr: LOAD combines estimated inertial changes and learned dynamics history to help robots traverse narrow beams precisely under unknown payloads.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.
authors: Yousef Liang, Ryan Ardalan, Yarden Goraly, Chenhao Zhu, Yue Yin, Jonas Frey, Claire Tomlin, Marco Pavone, Shankar Sastry
bullets: Targets chained-goal navigation under partial observability, where goals may be redirected or newly introduced without explicit transition signals.
Separates latent beliefs into global/local spatial and long/short temporal representations to support exploration and strategic revisitation.
Uses goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation as goals evolve.
Experiments in simulated diverse terrains and on a Spot quadruped show improved chained-goal navigation over baselines.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and real-robot settings; broader scope beyond these settings is not established in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory decomposition framework (GLST) for online chained-goal navigation that separates beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations, directly addressing long-horizon reasoning and memory requirements in embodied agents.
papers.title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: GLST enables mapless robots to navigate long-horizon environments with goals that change online by decomposing memory across spatial and temporal scales.

papers.abstract: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.
bullets: Multivariate distributional RL needs joint return distributions, but categorical critics scale exponentially and quantiles lack a canonical multivariate form.
The critic represents returns with Stein particles transported by Stein variational gradient descent along a learned score field.
Bootstrapped denoising score matching and a Bellman consistency loss learn and stabilize the score field across recursion.
A reverse-diffusion sampler supports tail-risk queries below the resolution of the particle set, with Wasserstein evaluation guarantees for bounded, possibly multimodal returns.
SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than equal-particle critics and performs comparably on MuJoCo continuous control.
papers.selection_reason: Distributional RL with Stein particles for multivariate returns, evaluated on MuJoCo continuous control; relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions
papers.tldr: SVDRL uses learned score fields to transport return particles and sample multivariate return distributions, improving rare-event estimation beyond the particle resolution.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models can reduce costly real-robot interaction in reinforcement learning for Vision-Language-Action models (VLA-RL), but hallucinations can mislead policy optimization. Extending them to richer VLA interfaces and long-horizon tasks raises challenges in spatiotemporal and cross-modal consistency, exploration-reliability balance in RL, and compounding rollout errors. We present WoVR+, extending WoVR's hallucination-aware WM-RL framework by redesigning the learned environment and imagined interaction protocol: A VLA-interface-aligned world model provides multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates while mitigating hallucinations. Chunk-wise noise preserves flow-based policy exploration while limiting prediction-degrading action jitter. For long-horizon tasks, stage-local imagined training combines stage-entry resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling to shorten generated prefixes and balance training across stages. WoVR+ improves success over SFT by 21.09% and 16.7% on RoboTwin and 6 real-robot tasks. Long-horizon phone-packaging success rises from 30% to 75%. Videos are available at https://youmo445.github.io/WoVR_Plus.github.io/.
authors: Shangqing Zhou, Zhennan Jiang, Ning Ma, Xin Fu, Yupeng Zheng, Shuai Tian, Huangrui Li, Jiahao Liu, Chao Yu, Zhongpu Xia, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Targets hallucinations, cross-modal consistency, exploration reliability, and compounding errors in world-model-based VLA-RL.
Uses a VLA-aligned world model with multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates to improve imagined interactions.
Applies chunk-wise action noise to preserve exploration while limiting prediction-degrading jitter.
Trains long-horizon tasks stage by stage using resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling.
Reports higher success than SFT on RoboTwin and six real-robot tasks; phone-packaging success increases from 30% to 75%.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world model as simulator for VLA policy RL, directly relevant to interactive world models and vision-language-action.
papers.title: WoVR+: World Model as Reliable Simulator for Versatile VLA Policy Optimization with RL
papers.tldr: WoVR+ improves VLA policy optimization with a hallucination-aware world model and stage-local imagined RL, reducing reliance on costly real-robot interaction.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.
authors: Shuzheng Wang, Haoxuan Li, Shengzhen Li, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Uses a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with separate World, Language, and Action experts.
Introduces Cross-Expert Attention to align semantic and dynamic representations through controlled information exchange.
Applies Flow-GRPO reinforcement-learning post-training to improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning.
Reports 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with strong open- and closed-loop performance.
Shows zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive without specific fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Unified world-language-action model for autonomous driving, directly covering trajectory generation, future dynamics, and semantic understanding.
papers.title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: DriveWLA unifies scene semantics, future dynamics, and trajectory generation in one World-Language-Action model for autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Can an AI agent turn high-level user intent into a functioning robot and teach it how to behave? We study this question from two complementary aspects: embodiment and behavior creation. For embodiment creation, we investigate how well current multimodal models capture mechanical requirements, and introduce computational metrics for evaluating generated designs before fabrication. For behavior creation, we present Roboforge, an agentic framework that turns task specifications into executable policies through motion generation, policy learning, and execution-grounded revision. Given a robot embodiment and task, the agent generates a reference motion, configures the learning objective, and trains a policy. Crucially, motion remains in the loop: rollout feedback can revise the reference motion, reward, or both. We evaluate a generated embodiment across multiple MLLMs and behavior creation across four diverse robots against reward-refinement and one-shot motion baselines. Our computational metrics expose recurring mechanical failures in generated designs, while behavior experiments show that execution-grounded refinement improves task-level behavior and execution quality. Finally, we fabricate an agent-generated Gorilla and directly deploy learned behaviors on the physical robot.
authors: Xuebing Li, Yibo He, Sitong Liu, Ran Ji, Jiayuan Gu
bullets: Studies both mechanical embodiment creation and behavior creation from high-level task specifications.
Introduces computational metrics to detect mechanical failures in generated robot designs before fabrication.
Presents Roboforge, which generates motions, configures learning objectives, trains policies, and revises them using rollout feedback.
Evaluations across multiple multimodal models and four robots show improved task behavior and execution quality over the reported baselines.
Fabricates an agent-generated Gorilla robot and deploys learned behaviors on it.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic framework generating, verifying, and revising robot embodiments and learned behaviors, directly relevant to robot learning and embodied AI.
papers.title: Agentic Robot Creation through Generation, Verification, and Revision
papers.tldr: The paper presents an agentic pipeline that generates robot embodiments and learns behaviors through execution-grounded verification and revision.

papers.abstract: Proactive dynamic grasping requires robots to predict the future state at which physical contact will occur, rather than reacting to the currently observed object pose. But what future must the robot predict, and at what level of abstraction? We argue that contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) is a compact task-sufficient abstraction for this problem: it directly determines where and when the robot should establish contact, without requiring visually complete future scenes. This insight leads to a lightweight object-centric forecast-then-select framework that predicts future rigid-body trajectories from short pose histories and uses a reachability-aware interception selector to choose feasible contact states under kinematic and timing constraints. Trained with randomized physics simulation over primitive shapes, the forecaster transfers to real objects once their metric geometry and SE(3) state histories are recovered. Experiments across simulation and real-world dynamic grasping tasks show that our framework improves the average success rate from \(24.5\%\) to \(62.0\%\) in simulation, and from \(15.3\%\) to \(67.3\%\) in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable interception. The SE(3) forecaster runs in \(15\,\mathrm{ms}\), orders of magnitude faster than dense visual future prediction, enabling real-time contact decision making. Our results suggest that effective proactive grasping does not require imagining the entire future scene. Instead, predicting the compact physical future that determines contact provides an effective and practical abstraction for real-time dynamic grasping.
authors: Yirui Zhou, Hongli Xu, Ying Zheng, Yi Wang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Frames contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) as a task-sufficient abstraction for predicting when and where contact should occur.
Forecasts future object trajectories from short pose histories, then selects reachable interception states under kinematic and timing constraints.
Trained in randomized physics simulation on primitive shapes and transferred to real objects using metric geometry and SE(3) histories.
Improves average success from 24.5% to 62.0% in simulation and from 15.3% to 67.3% in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable tasks.
Runs in 15 ms, supporting real-time contact decisions while avoiding dense visual future prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Object-centric SE(3) forecasting for proactive dynamic grasping, directly relevant to robot manipulation.
papers.title: Physics-Aware Object-Centric SE(3) Forecasting for Real-Time Proactive Dynamic Grasping
papers.tldr: A lightweight object-centric SE(3) forecasting and interception framework enables real-time proactive dynamic grasping without predicting entire future scenes.

papers.abstract: Collision rate remains a dominant metric for evaluating autonomous driving trajectory safety, but its binary nature obscures substantial safety differences among collision-free trajectories. Existing surrogate-safety metrics provide finer-grained assessments, yet often trade off physical interpretability against adaptivity to interaction context. We introduce FutureRisk, a continuous metric that quantifies the latent future risk of a trajectory by how closely and persistently its realized interactions approach unsafe states. At its core, our Context-Adaptive Risk Model (CARM) combines a context-dependent safety-time distribution with an independently supervised critical-event-time distribution. Its safety criterion is bounded around a closed-form physical prior, while a bounded residual provides additional adaptation without abandoning this physical anchor. Experiments on DeepAccident and Bench2Drive show that FutureRisk achieves stronger agreement with native collision labels than existing surrogate-safety measures, discriminates risk among collision-free trajectories, and transfers zero-shot across datasets. Comparisons across four planners further show that FutureRisk reveals safety differences hidden by binary collision outcomes. Together, these results establish FutureRisk as a fine-grained, interpretable, and context-adaptive metric for trajectory safety evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/Xuewen2025/safety-evaluation.

bullets: Collision rate cannot distinguish safety differences between collision-free trajectories.
FutureRisk estimates risk from how closely and persistently interactions approach unsafe states.
Its Context-Adaptive Risk Model combines context-dependent safety-time and supervised critical-event-time distributions.
A bounded physical prior and residual preserve interpretability while enabling interaction-aware adaptation.
On DeepAccident and Bench2Drive, it better agrees with collision labels, separates collision-free risks, and transfers zero-shot across datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Learned context-adaptive trajectory safety metric for autonomous driving, transferable to navigation planning evaluation.
papers.title: Which Trajectory Is Safer? Combining Rule and Learning for Safety Evaluation
papers.tldr: FutureRisk combines physical safety rules with learned context adaptation to provide a continuous, interpretable measure of autonomous-driving trajectory risk.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation has traditionally relied on end-effector-centric interactions. In contrast, humans routinely exploit whole-arm contacts to improve efficiency, robustness, and adaptability, especially when the hands are occupied or when precise grasping is unnecessary. Enabling similar capabilities in robots remains challenging: the robot must select where on its arm to make contact, generate effective non-prehensile interactions, and satisfy task-specific pose or safety constraints on the end-effector. We propose Whole-Arm Contact Learning (WACL), a hierarchical framework that describes each whole-arm contact task with three robot-agnostic representations and hands them to a quasi-static surface-contact optimizer: semantic keypoints that summarize the scene, a reference contact trajectory that specifies where and how the arm presses on the object, and safety-aware path constraints that a vision-language model generates from the task description to protect the end-effector's task. The robot's kinematic chain enters only in this optimizer, which grounds these representations onto the arm by jointly searching over which link makes contact, where on that link, and the joint configuration that realizes it. This decomposition lets WACL learn the contact trajectory from 10 bare-hand human demonstrations per task collected without teleoperation, while new end-effector constraints change only the optimizer's input rather than any trained component. Real-world experiments on a 7-DoF arm across four whole-arm tasks show that WACL sustains contact under end-effector constraints where a strong link-pose baseline fails (78% vs. 33% success) and generalizes to new constraints without retraining. Website: https://wacl-robot.github.io
authors: Bo-Ruei Huang, Daniel Seita, Erdem B{\i}y{\i}k
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing arm-contact locations while preserving task-specific end-effector pose and safety constraints.
Uses three robot-agnostic representations: semantic scene keypoints, a reference contact trajectory, and vision-language-model-generated safety-aware path constraints.
A quasi-static surface-contact optimizer grounds these representations onto a robot by jointly selecting the contacting link, contact location, and joint configuration.
On a 7-DoF arm across four tasks, WACL achieved 78% success under end-effector constraints versus 33% for a link-pose baseline.
Demonstrations use bare hands rather than teleoperation; the method’s scope is whole-arm, non-prehensile contact tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Whole-arm contact manipulation learned from human demonstrations with VLM-generated constraints and contact optimization.
papers.title: Beyond the End-Effector: Learning Whole-Arm Contact Manipulation from Human Demonstrations
papers.tldr: WACL learns whole-arm contact manipulation from just 10 human demonstrations per task and adapts to new end-effector constraints without retraining.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables driving policies to adapt to changing deployment conditions, but requires safe exploration throughout training. Safety filtering alone does not ensure stable policy improvement or reduced dependence on corrections. We propose Safe Online Adaptive Refinement (SOAR-Flow), a framework for safe and stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized Flow-based driving policies. A control barrier function (CBF)--model predictive control (MPC) filter corrects potentially unsafe actions before execution. To support stable policy updates, we introduce Gaussian-return-aware value calibration based on calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL), using recorded behavior returns and predicted return variability to smooth conservative critic updates and mitigate policy degradation. Paired corrective learning teaches feasible action adjustments, while an intervention-to-go predictor encourages decisions requiring fewer future corrections. Its predictions also regulate guidance strength, allowing recovery supervision to weaken as predicted dependence decreases. Together with gradually reduced calibration regularization, this supports continued task improvement while preserving hard execution constraints. We analyze conditions for safe execution at control steps and diminishing auxiliary learning influences. We evaluate SOAR-Flow in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV). The results demonstrate improved driving performance and reduced reliance on safety corrections during protected online fine-tuning. The demonstration video and project overview are available at https://lzqw.github.io/SOAR-Flow/.
authors: Zeqiao Li, Yijing Wang, Haoyu Wang, Zheng Li, Zhiqiang Zuo
bullets: Addresses unstable policy improvement and persistent safety-correction dependence during online RL for autonomous driving.
Combines a CBF–MPC safety filter with Gaussian-return-aware value calibration to enforce safe actions and mitigate policy degradation.
Uses paired corrective learning and an intervention-to-go predictor to guide feasible actions and adaptively reduce recovery supervision.
Evaluated in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle, showing improved driving performance and fewer safety corrections during protected fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Safe online RL fine-tuning of driving policies with CBF-MPC filtering, relevant to learned navigation and robot RL.
papers.title: Beyond Safe Execution: Safe Online Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving with Value Calibration and Adaptive Guidance
papers.tldr: SOAR-Flow enables safer, more stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized driving policies while reducing reliance on corrective interventions.

papers.abstract: A long-horizon manipulation task consists of primitive skills and the transitions connecting them. Learning skills that can be executed in sequence requires supervision for both, which is costly to collect on a robot. Human videos offer a scalable source of demonstrations, but transferring them to robots requires extracting robot-compatible observations and actions together with their skill structure. We present DexStitch, a framework that cuts long-horizon human videos into skills and transitions, converts them into aligned robot observation-action-skill data, and stitches the learned skills into a requested sequence. A skill classifier first segments the videos into manipulation skills and transitions. DexStitch then converts the human demonstrations into robot observations and actions while retaining their corresponding skill labels. During conversion, per-finger human-object contacts guide dexterous hand retargeting and robotic inpainting, preserving contact geometry and finger-object occlusion ordering. To stitch the learned skills into a sequence, a shared skill-conditioned policy is pretrained on the resulting synthetic data and finetuned on a mixture of synthetic data and a small set of single-skill teleoperation episodes. Conditioning on the current and next skills guides each transition toward the following skill, while predicted skill progression enables closed-loop switching. On a held-out session, the classifier agrees with manual annotations on 92.4% of frames. Across four household skills, DexStitch achieves 80.0% single-skill success and 77.5% sequence success.
authors: Byeonggyeol Choi, Seongmin Jung, Unghui Nam, Youngbo Song, Sunhong Min, MinHyung Lee, Byonghyo Shim, Yongseok Lee

Segments human videos into skills and transitions, then converts them into aligned robot observation–action–skill data.
Uses per-finger contact-aware retargeting and robotic inpainting to preserve contact geometry and occlusion ordering.
Pretrains a shared skill-conditioned policy on synthetic data and lightly finetunes it with single-skill teleoperation data.
Reports 92.4% frame-level agreement with manual skill annotations, 80.0% single-skill success, and 77.5% sequence success across four household skills.
papers.selection_reason: Learns and composes dexterous manipulation skills from human videos with contact-aware retargeting and skill-conditioned policies.
papers.title: DexStitch: Learning and Composing Dexterous Skills from Human Videos via Contact-Aware Robotic Inpainting
papers.tldr: DexStitch transfers human-video demonstrations to robots by preserving finger–object contacts and composing the resulting dexterous skills into long-horizon sequences.

papers.abstract: Robotic assistance for human mobility could benefit care recipients and reduce caregiver burden during physically demanding tasks such as Sit-to-Stand (STS) and Lift-and-Transfer (L&T). Learning robot policies for these whole-body assistive tasks is challenging: real-world data collection for human-robot interaction is costly and safety-critical, making simulation an attractive alternative. Prior work, however, typically treats the human as static or minimally responsive and thus fails to capture the cooperative nature of mobility assistance. We present a simulation-based framework for learning whole-body assistive robot policies. At its core is a human policy trained with an adversarial motion prior that produces realistic care-recipient motion in response to the robot's actions. A human-adaptive scripted controller interacts with this policy to collect diverse robot demonstrations at scale. From these demonstrations, we train 3D diffusion policies that map segmented human point clouds and robot joint positions to whole-body actions for a mobile manipulator, without relying on privileged human state at deployment. The resulting robot policies successfully perform both STS and L&T assistance in simulation. Preliminary experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer for STS after fine-tuning on a small amount of real-world data. Videos are available on our project page: https://rchi-lab.github.io/human-gen-mobility-assistance/
authors: Shikun Ban, Shohei Nagai, Qingyang Song, Hanxi Wan, Eric Zhao, Thomas Wang, Zackory Erickson
bullets: Targets physically demanding mobility-assistance tasks, including Sit-to-Stand and Lift-and-Transfer, where real-world data collection is costly and safety-critical.
Uses an adversarial motion-prior human policy to model care-recipient responses to robot actions.
Combines the human policy with an adaptive scripted controller to generate diverse robot demonstrations in simulation.
Trains 3D diffusion policies from segmented human point clouds and robot joint positions, without privileged human state at deployment.
Policies perform both tasks in simulation, with preliminary Sit-to-Stand sim-to-real transfer after limited real-world fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Simulation-based learning of whole-body assistive robot policies with diffusion policies and human motion generation.
papers.title: Learning Robot Policies for Whole-Body Mobility Assistance via Dynamic Human Motion Generation
papers.tldr: A simulation framework learns whole-body robot assistance policies by generating realistic, responsive human motion and training 3D diffusion policies from large-scale demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap. Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy. We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks. Under this protocol, I3L improves autonomous success over the base policies by an average of 68.3 percentage points and achieves at least 90% success on every task, outperforming demonstration-only training by 35.6 percentage points on average with the same number of training trajectories. Averaged across tasks, takeover duration per episode decreases by 72% over four rounds. Together, these results show that I3L helps close the last-mile gap between offline training and reliable deployment and provides practical insights into collecting and using corrections for long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation. Videos, visualizations, and appendix are at https://i-3l.github.io/.
authors: Wensi Ai, Christopher Luey, Karthik Dharmarajan, Evans Han, Yunfan Jiang, Stef Ren, Jianwen Xie, Jiajun Wu, Li Fei-Fei, Ruohan Zhang
bullets: Addresses compounding errors and limited demonstration coverage in offline-trained mobile manipulation policies.
Uses the open-source JoyLo+ interface for whole-body takeover corrections through policy-tracking leader arms and touch triggers.
Iteratively deploys, targets failures, collects corrections, and retrains the policy using protocols including HG-DAgger.
Evaluated on three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon tasks.
I3L reached at least 90% success on every task, improved autonomous success by 68.3 percentage points over base policies, and reduced takeover duration by 72% across four rounds.

papers.title: I3L: Iterative Interactive Imitation Learning for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: I3L combines coordinated human corrections with iterative policy retraining to substantially improve reliability in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: A robot may know how to perform a task yet fail when a human asks for it naturally. We study this human--VLA communication gap by separating an \emph{information gap}, where task semantics, grounding, or event structure remain unresolved, from a residual \emph{execution gap}, where even a fully specified task depends on how it is organized and invoked. To do this, we characterize how people naturally express demonstrated objectives and evaluate controlled variants of the same physical tasks, with detailed analysis on $\pi_{0.5}$ and consistent trends on $\pi_0$-FAST and Cosmos3-Edge. Our study reveals that humans increasingly compress instructions as tasks grow, relying more on contextual grounding and implicit execution structure. Current policies are misaligned with this behavior: they tolerate grounding dependence relatively well, but struggle when task semantics or event structure must be reconstructed. Even after the information gap is resolved, execution remains sensitive to command granularity and invocation state. These findings identify concrete targets for human-centered policy learning and interfaces that better bridge natural human objectives to robot behavior. Project website: https://commgap.github.io/.
bullets: Separates the communication gap into an information gap—unresolved semantics, grounding, or event structure—and an execution gap involving task organization and invocation.
Analyzes how humans describe demonstrated objectives and evaluates controlled variants of the same physical tasks across several policies.
Finds that people compress instructions more as tasks become complex, relying increasingly on context and implicit execution structure.
Policies handle grounding dependence relatively well but struggle to reconstruct task semantics and event structure.
Even fully specified tasks remain sensitive to command granularity and invocation state, motivating human-centered policy learning and interfaces.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how natural human instructions expose failures in VLA policies, directly relevant to vision-language-action and embodied AI.
papers.title: The Human--VLA Communication Gap: What Humans Leave Implicit and What Policies Cannot Recover
papers.tldr: The study shows that robots struggle with natural human instructions because people omit task semantics and execution structure, creating both information and execution gaps.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/
authors: Yusuf Umut Ciftci, Joonwon Kang, Ajay Suresha Sathya, Somil Bansal
bullets: Uniform behavior cloning overlooks that some states are critical while others are recoverable.
State criticality is defined by the worst-case downstream-value loss from bounded perturbations of the expert action.
SCRIM estimates criticality using an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy.
Criticality scores reweight training losses and select compact, high-value demonstration subsets.
Evaluations on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show improved training, efficient data use, and interpretable critical-state analysis.
papers.selection_reason: State-criticality weighting for imitation learning in robotic manipulation; directly relevant.
papers.title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
papers.tldr: SCRIM identifies which demonstration states are most sensitive to small action errors, enabling more effective imitation learning and data selection.

papers.abstract: We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.
authors: Haoran Wang, Jingwei Huang, Anqing Duan, Ho Seok Ahn, Bruce Macdonald
bullets: Targets error-aware monitoring for activities performed by cognitively impaired people and older adults.
Provides 20,000 paired activity episodes spanning nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories.
Agents monitor streaming human trajectories and must identify execution errors as early as possible.
Evaluates learned, symbolic, change-point, and frontier-LLM-prompting baselines.
All tested approaches often miss errors, exposing a gap in standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution, fitting the embodied AI topic.
papers.title: HelpMeOut: A Neuropsychology-Grounded Benchmark for Error-Aware Monitoring of Household Task Execution
papers.tldr: HelpMeOut benchmarks whether embodied AI can detect and diagnose structured errors during household activities, revealing poor performance from existing monitoring approaches.

papers.abstract: Occupancy world models provide a structured, metric representation of future driving scenes, making them a promising basis for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing occupancy-aware planners typically couple occupancy prediction and action generation through either hierarchical coupling or parallel multi-task learning. Hierarchical methods use occupancy either as a fully predicted future preceding action generation or as an action-conditioned rollout for trajectory evaluation, whereas parallel multi-task methods predict occupancy alongside planning through a separate branch or auxiliary objective. These interfaces retain either an explicit generation order or a role asymmetry, limiting reciprocal interaction between world prediction and action generation during trajectory formation. We propose OccWAM, an occupancy-native world-action model that jointly generates dense future occupancy and continuous ego trajectories via flow matching conditioned on scene representations. Building on this joint formulation, we introduce scene-to-ego world-action flow matching, a two-stage formulation. The first stage predicts scene-centric occupancy together with an absolute ego trajectory, providing a stable representation of future scene evolution. The same predicted world is then re-indexed into the future ego frames induced by the initial trajectory, where ego motion is represented through adjacent pose increments and a second joint flow refines ego-centric occupancy and motion for action-aligned planning. Unlike video-based world-action models, OccWAM preserves explicit semantic geometry for direct planning reasoning without pixel synthesis. Extensive experiments on Bench2Drive and nuScenes demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction.
authors: Qihang Huang, Wenhui Huang, Collister Chua, Shiyu Fang, Zhan Chen, Songyan Zhang, Zhidong Wang, Daiying Tian, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses limited reciprocal interaction in hierarchical and parallel occupancy-aware planning methods.
Generates dense scene occupancy and continuous ego trajectories jointly from scene representations.
First predicts scene-centric occupancy and an absolute ego trajectory, then refines ego-centric occupancy and motion in future ego frames.
Uses explicit semantic geometry rather than pixel synthesis for direct planning reasoning.
Reports state-of-the-art results in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction on Bench2Drive and nuScenes.
papers.selection_reason: OccWAM proposes a joint occupancy and trajectory generation model via flow matching for autonomous driving, preserving semantic geometry for planning.
papers.title: OccWAM: Occupancy World-Action Models with Joint Scene-to-Ego Flow Matching
papers.tldr: OccWAM jointly predicts future occupancy and ego trajectories through two-stage scene-to-ego flow matching for geometry-aware autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models and Flow Matching can represent flexible distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also require the probability of each action. We introduce PrT-Flow (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching), which computes probability density while retaining multimodal, multi-step action generation. Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) makes each sampling step invertible and enables efficient computation of its Jacobian determinant. We train these finite steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises their displacement over one step during sampling rather than their instantaneous velocity. We prove that, under certain assumptions, CET has the same minimizers as fitting the Euler-solver updates of Flow Matching. PrT-Flow achieves 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% success on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600k online steps. These results demonstrate that invertible networks with tractable probability densities can learn effective robot policies and support SAC-style actor-critic training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sunlight-zero/PrT-Flow .
bullets: Addresses the need for action likelihoods in RL while preserving the flexibility of diffusion and Flow Matching policies.
Uses Jacobian-Tractable Transformers to make each sampling step invertible and efficiently compute its density.
Trains finite sampling steps with Conditional Euler-step Training, which theoretically aligns with fitting Flow Matching Euler updates under stated assumptions.
Reaches 96% success on Robomimic Lift and OGBench Cube-Triple, and supports SAC-style actor-critic training.
Scope: the theoretical equivalence relies on specific assumptions, and reported evaluation is limited to the stated robotic tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Presents probability-tractable flow matching for robot action policies, directly relevant to learned robot control and manipulation.
papers.title: PrT-Flow: Probability-Tractable Flow Matching for Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: PrT-Flow enables multimodal, multi-step robot action generation with tractable action probabilities for reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents navigating and interacting with the physical world. As observations arrive incrementally, agents must reason in a streaming manner. Yet streaming understanding must also be closed-loop: task-relevant evidence may require both recalling past observations and actively acquiring new views. Existing streaming approaches largely emphasize processing incoming observations, leaving task-driven active exploration underexplored. We introduce MemAct, a framework for streaming spatial understanding with memory and action. A shared vision--language model incrementally writes structured historical memory, retrieves records and past frames on demand, and acquires additional evidence through movement and turning. Retrieved evidence and action observations inform subsequent decisions, enabling the agent to continue exploring or answer within a unified reasoning loop. We develop the MemAct suite, a data generation pipeline and collection across real and simulated environments, with approximately 1M training examples for spatial reasoning, memory writing, retrieval, and exploration. Its MemAct-bench comprises 20,000 main QA pairs evaluating current-observation understanding, historical evidence use, and active exploration, plus 2,000 separate Timing questions. MemAct combines supervised fine-tuning for memory and interaction with counterfactual action optimization using cumulative evidence gains, action costs, and terminal answer quality to improve exploration and stopping decisions. Experiments show that MemAct outperforms existing spatial understanding and streaming baselines and approaches frontier multimodal models on MemAct-bench while retaining streaming inference efficiency.
authors: Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses the gap between passive streaming observation and task-driven exploration that acquires missing evidence.
Uses a shared vision-language model to write structured memories, retrieve past frames, and guide movement or turning.
Introduces MemAct data and benchmarks spanning current observations, historical evidence, active exploration, and timing.
Trains memory and interaction with supervised fine-tuning plus counterfactual action optimization for evidence gain, action cost, and answer quality.
Outperforms existing spatial and streaming baselines, approaches frontier multimodal models, and maintains streaming inference efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming spatial understanding with embodied memory and active exploration; directly fits embodied memory, spatial intelligence, and vision-language-action.
papers.title: MemAct: Streaming Spatial Understanding with Memory and Active Exploration
papers.tldr: MemAct enables embodied agents to understand spaces over time by combining structured memory, on-demand retrieval, and active exploration in a unified streaming loop.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64\% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0\% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.
authors: Yiwei Zhang, Yantai Yang, Jin Gao, Jin Lou, Andong Chen, Yufei Liu, Boyang Xing, Yuchen Zhu, Weiming Hu, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: WAMs contain persistent high-norm spatial outliers that remain action-relevant even after normalization and K/V projection.
RegisterWAM adds non-spatial learnable registers for action conditioning, while observation flow-matching supervision suppresses spatial outliers and concentrates responses in registers.
Flow-matching supervision improves action learning even without registers, motivating a noised-observation objective for recovering current scenes from corrupted inputs.
The resulting model reports 81.64% success on LIBERO-Plus and 93.0% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, with improved real-world manipulation performance.
papers.selection_reason: RegisterWAM improves World Action Models by adding learnable non-spatial registers and using observation flow-matching supervision for better action conditioning.
papers.title: Acting Through Registers
papers.tldr: RegisterWAM reorganizes action-relevant representations into learnable registers and uses flow-matching supervision to improve robot manipulation without extra embodied pretraining data or foundation models.

papers.abstract: Language provides a natural interface for humans to specify and reason about goals, but training language-conditioned robotic policies and reasoning typically requires expensive manual annotations. We propose Action Self-Distillation (ASD), a method for learning language-conditioned reasoning for robotic navigation without human-annotated language or reasoning labels. ASD uses an open-source VLM, which contains broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, as both a teacher network and a student policy. During training, the self-teacher receives privileged trajectory feedback and infers the underlying navigation goal together with goal-oriented reasoning. The student is then trained to condition on the inferred navigation goal, predict future ego-frame trajectory, and provide a description of the scene semantics, plan, and reasoning, from onboard observations alone. Across 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks, our method improves success rate over the strongest baseline by $30\%$ in indoor settings, $30\%$ on multi-stage tasks, and achieves $95\%$ success rate on outdoor tasks, validating that privileged trajectory feedback can enable self-distillation for scalable generalist navigation policies without human annotations.
authors: Bowen Feng, Keqin Wang, Yulong Yang, Amogh Joshi, Christine Allen-Blanchette, Dhruv Shah, Felix Heide
bullets: Addresses the cost of manually annotating language-conditioned robotic navigation and reasoning.
Uses an open-source VLM as both a self-teacher and student policy; the teacher infers navigation goals and reasoning from privileged trajectory feedback.
The student uses onboard observations to predict future ego-frame trajectories and describe scene semantics, plans, and reasoning.
Evaluated on 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks.
Reports 30% higher success than the strongest baseline indoors and on multi-stage tasks, plus 95% success on outdoor tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned navigation policy via action self-distillation; directly fits embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: Training Generalist Navigation Policies via Action Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: Action Self-Distillation trains language-conditioned generalist navigation policies without human language or reasoning annotations by distilling privileged trajectory feedback from a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: Estimating simulation-ready material parameters from visual observations is crucial for deformable-object manipulation but challenging because material properties are only indirectly revealed through physical responses. We introduce physical-field-bridged material inference, a single-pass framework that uses dense physical responses to connect multi-view RGB deformation videos with constitutive-type classification and continuous parameter regression. Unlike inverse-physics methods requiring per-scene reconstruction, online tuning, or simulation-in-the-loop optimization, our model predicts force/contact masks, projected motion-flow fields, and projected stress-response maps, then conditions material inference on these fields to reduce reliance on appearance or category shortcuts. We construct DeformFieldBench, a 3DGS MPM learning environment comprising 5,000 simulations across 100 object shapes and five mechanically informative loading modes, with dense pixel-aligned physical supervision. Our method achieves the best median errors on all four continuous parameters, improves stress-hotspot recall from 0.0762 to 0.5121, and attains 0.8676 SSIM/36.82 dB PSNR in same-simulator replay on unseen objects. Under a protocol-matched GSO evaluation, inference and future-state prediction take approximately 30 seconds, compared with 15-120 minutes for per-scene optimization. The method also yields measurable replay agreement on five real-world sequences. These results support dense physical fields as an effective bridge for fast material inference, while cross-simulator and real-world tests reveal remaining domain and identifiability gaps.
authors: Linrui Shou, Jie Li, Yu Liu, Tao Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering simulation-ready material properties from visual deformation, where properties are only indirectly observable.
Predicts force/contact masks, motion-flow fields, and stress-response maps, then uses them to guide material classification and parameter regression.
Introduces DeformFieldBench: 5,000 simulations spanning 100 shapes and five loading modes with dense pixel-aligned supervision.
Reports best median errors across four continuous parameters, improved stress-hotspot recall, and strong same-simulator replay quality on unseen objects.
Inference and future-state prediction take about 30 seconds versus 15–120 minutes for per-scene optimization; cross-simulator and real-world tests expose remaining gaps.
papers.selection_reason: Material parameter inference from deformation videos is directly motivated by deformable-object manipulation, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Physical-Field-Bridged Material Parameter Inference from Multi-View Deformation Videos
papers.tldr: A single-pass model infers material types and continuous parameters from multi-view deformation videos by conditioning on predicted dense physical-response fields.

papers.abstract: Tracking object motion within a gripper provides essential feedback for robotic manipulation. However, limited contact coverage and uneven deformation make tactile estimation challenging. In this study, we present TacSpin, a method that tracks in-gripper object rotation on SO(3) using only two vision-based tactile sensors. The key idea is to estimate the axis and magnitude of the rotation response separately, rather than fitting a rigid-body model by least squares. Each finger's response is further refined with contact-boundary cues. The two fingers are then fused according to their agreement. On standard objects, TacSpin achieves lower mean checkpoint errors. Qualitative demonstrations on real-world objects, using calibration transferred from a standard sphere, illustrate tracking under different contact geometries.

papers.title: TacSpin: Tactile Tracking of In-Gripper Object Rotation on SO(3) via Axis-Magnitude Estimation

papers.abstract: While expert demonstrations on real robots are difficult to collect, human ego-centric videos are easy to collect and abundant on the internet. However, learning dexterous manipulation policies from human videos remains challenging---one of the most important challenges being the difficulty of reconstructing physically grounded robot trajectories due to the large embodiment gap. In this paper, we propose EgoCPT, a novel paradigm for learning high-quality retargeted dexterous hand trajectories directly from an ego-centric video, which can then be deployed directly on real robots. The only inputs to our method are an ego-centric RGB video and a reference hand pose trajectory, which can be easily obtained through off-the-shelf software or specialized cameras during recording. Our method is particularly robust to noisy hand poses attributed to our novel contact-aware optimization framework, which iteratively optimizes the contact points between the robot hands and objects. Across five manipulation tasks, our method achieves overall success rates of 67.3% on noisy EgoDex hand-pose reconstructions and 92.0% on high-quality TACO reconstructions collected using motion-capture hardware, outperforming multiple baselines on both benchmarks.
authors: Zhixin Sun, Kairui Shi, Tianao Ren, Ming Yang, Mark Cutkosky, James Jingxi Xu
bullets: Addresses the embodiment gap between human videos and physically feasible robot hand motions.
Uses iterative contact-aware optimization to refine robot–object contact points and handle noisy hand-pose reconstructions.

Evaluated on five manipulation tasks, achieving 67.3% success with noisy EgoDex poses and 92.0% with high-quality TACO poses.
Outperforms multiple baselines on both benchmarks.
