These components are exposed through composable interfaces so that agent strategies, training methods, evaluation procedures, and recovery mechanisms can be combined without requiring separate representations or pipelines. We demonstrate the framework across agentic tasks including legal contract search and domain-specific applications, illustrating its use for trajectory-based optimization, tool-use evaluation, and cross-task agent development. AgentTune is released as a source-available library at https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/AgentTune
authors: R E Zera Marveen Lyngkhoi, Abhivansh Gupta, Vidushee Vats, Ram Mohan Rao Kadiyala, Vinay Kumar Sankarapu, Pratinav Seth
bullets: Addresses fragmented tooling that handles agent lifecycle stages separately.
Uses a two-tier EventLog to preserve trajectories and project them consistently for training, evaluation, and auditing.
Provides a shared runtime with tool-calling reinforcement learning, agentic distillation, retrieval-augmented generation, workflows, and evaluation utilities.
Demonstrates applications in legal contract search and domain-specific tasks, including trajectory optimization and tool-use evaluation.
Released as a source-available Python library; the self-healing-agent pathway is presented as a design direction.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AgentTune, a unified framework for training and optimizing tool-using LLM agents, which is a key paradigm for embodied AI and LLM agents.
papers.title: AgentTune: A Unified Training Lifecycle for Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.tldr: AgentTune unifies the development, training, evaluation, distillation, and maintenance of tool-using LLM agents through a shared trajectory representation and composable interfaces.

papers.abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.
authors: Yang Wang, Ping Liu, Ruiyu Wang, Xuhua Chen, Lingfeng Zhang, Tao Zhang
bullets: Targets manipulation tasks where execution state must be tracked and previously visible evidence recovered.
Uses a task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet temporal compressor with progress prediction and action-conditioned reconstruction.
Adds a task-conditioned frame retriever and encodes selected frames with 16 spatial tokens; the compressor is frozen during joint retrieval-policy training.
On 16 RoboMME tasks, mean success is 49.22% versus 44.51% for FrameSamp+Modul; real-robot mean success is 62.5% versus 37.5%.
Cup-swap failures indicate persistent object-identity tracking remains unresolved.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces memory mechanisms for VLA policies, directly relevant to VLA and embodied memory.
papers.title: Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: Dual-stream memory improves vision-language-action manipulation by combining compressed execution history with selective retrieval of relevant past frames.

papers.abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action--Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy's primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves $50.97\%$ overall success, improving over $\pi_{0.5}$ and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/.
authors: Min Lin, Bokai Zhou, Jianqi Lin, Kaiyuan Yang, Yicheng Chang, Junjie Yu, Xiaofan Liu, Jianhua Han, Rui Li, Shen Zhao, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets future-grounded Effect tokens rather than actions alone.
Builds temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrations, robot responses, and sparse visual transitions.
Uses flow matching to predict Effects, then a state-conditioned decoder generates action chunks.
Supports shared Effect modeling across single- and dual-arm embodiments.
On DexJoCo, achieves 50.97% overall success and leads on all five bimanual tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces future-grounded effect learning for vision-language-action policies, directly improving bimanual robot manipulation.
papers.title: Beyond Actions: Learning Future Operation Targets for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: AFCE trains vision-language-action policies to predict future physical effects before decoding them into robot actions, improving coordinated dexterous manipulation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re- lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par- tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi- tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN-POMDP
authors: Zekang Wang, Zhe He, Gaojie Jin
bullets: Partially observable RL commonly trains recurrent memory jointly with policy or value functions.
The paper tests fixed recurrent networks paired with a trainable nonlinear output module, inspired by Reservoir Computing.
Frozen networks support recall over hundreds of steps across varied memory demands, observations, and action spaces.
They achieve competitive control performance while requiring less than half as many trainable parameters as fully trainable recurrent models.
The approach is proposed as a simple, parameter-efficient baseline, though its effectiveness is evaluated within the studied POMDP tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Shows frozen recurrent networks can solve POMDP control tasks with fewer trainable parameters, a transferable idea for parameter-efficient embodied RL.
papers.title: Does Learning Recurrent Networks Matter in Partially Observable RL?
papers.tldr: Frozen recurrent networks can provide strong memory and control in POMDPs without learning the recurrent module.

papers.abstract: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on unmanned surface vehicle (USV) is difficult in high sea states. Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments.
authors: Kaizhen Li, Xi Zhou, Dan Zhang, Xiaowei Li
bullets: Targets the difficulty of UAV–USV landing under high sea states and rapidly varying motion.
Uses a pretrained model to predict USV attitude during high-level landing decisions.
Selects suitable landing windows and touchdown times based on predicted motion.
Combines high-level planning with a conventional low-level flight controller for UAV stability and command tracking.
Real-sea motion data transferred to a MuJoCo USV provide real-sim validation, demonstrating feasibility in realistic disturbances.
papers.selection_reason: Learned attitude prediction for UAV landing-window planning on a USV; embodied navigation/planning.
papers.title: Prediction-Informed Landing Window Planning for UAV Landing on USV in High Sea States
papers.tldr: A prediction-informed hierarchical controller uses explicit USV attitude forecasts to select landing windows and touchdown timing for UAV landing on USVs in rough, rapidly changing seas.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation policies requires large amounts of diverse, action-labeled data, yet collecting such data in the real world remains expensive and difficult to scale. Existing methods either depend on human teleoperation, rely on simulation with limited visual realism, or use human videos that lack embodiment-specific annotations. In this paper, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework for synthesizing physically grounded robot manipulation data with video world models while avoiding human teleoperation demonstrations. Grounded-Dreamer combines the visual realism of generative video models with simulator physics engines. Starting from a small set of real images depicting robot task initial states, our method automatically reconstructs task-relevant objects and camera geometry, aligns them in simulation, and collects physically valid trajectories. These trajectories are used to post-train both a video world model and an inverse dynamics model, enabling the generation of visually realistic robot manipulation videos and corresponding robot actions from real images. To filter physically implausible rollouts, Grounded-Dreamer replays generated trajectories in the reconstructed simulation and retains only those that successfully complete the tasks. The real-world robot policies are trained solely on the grounded synthetic trajectories without any human demonstrations. Empirical results in real-world tasks demonstrate that Grounded-Dreamer can synthesize physically grounded data and substantially facilitate policy learning without requiring human teleoperation effort.
authors: Feng Jiang, Shu Chen, Yuanfei Wang, Yuan Li, Zhenhao Shen, Jiaqi Liang, Yang Chen, Lei Wei, Chen Xie, Ruihai Wu
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability limits of collecting real-world robot demonstrations.
Reconstructs task objects and camera geometry from a small set of real initial-state images, then aligns them in simulation.
Post-trains a video world model and inverse dynamics model to generate realistic manipulation videos and robot actions.
Filters synthetic rollouts by replaying them in simulation and retaining only task-successful trajectories.
Uses only grounded synthetic data to train real-world policies, which facilitates policy learning in real-world tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Synthesizes robot data using video world models and physics, relevant to robot learning and world models.
papers.title: Grounded-Dreamer: Robot Learning from World Model Synthetic Data with Physical Grounding
papers.tldr: Grounded-Dreamer combines video world models with physics-based simulation to generate physically valid, action-labeled robot manipulation data without human teleoperation.

papers.abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/.
authors: Jiachen Zhang, Yuanyuan Li, Shaqi Luo
bullets: Addresses the need to repeatedly collect task demonstrations for each robot hand.
Uses local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation to align human and robot observations.
Retargets human motion to each hand and introduces GPIR for hand-centered object representation.
Evaluated on six real-world tasks: 90.8% success on Linker O6 and 80.8% on Wuji.
The complete configuration reaches 85.8% success across both hands, versus 26.3% with raw human demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Uses wrist-centric human demonstrations for dexterous manipulation, directly relevant to learning from human videos and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Human2Dex: Dexterous Robot Learning from Wrist-Centric Human Demonstrations
papers.tldr: Human2Dex reuses wrist-centric human demonstrations to train policies for different dexterous robot hands, achieving high real-world task success without robot-specific data collection.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
authors: Zipei Ma, Junzhe Jiang, Jiahui Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Chun Gu, Bozhou Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit future-state supervision in VLAs and the inference cost and error propagation of WAMs.
Uses an action-to-future paradigm: predicted futures condition on action features, not vice versa.
End-to-end training lets future-state prediction supervise the policy without allowing prediction errors to affect actions.
Backbone-agnostic design is instantiated with both vision-language and video-generative backbones.
Demonstrates a 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and up to 13% absolute gains over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a new action model paradigm coupling action and future prediction, relevant to VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Forward Dynamics Models
papers.tldr: Forward Dynamics Models train robot policies with future-state supervision while avoiding future generation at inference, improving efficiency and performance.

papers.abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.
authors: Yingbo Ma, Kuangshi Ai, Gordon Dai, Chenglong Yu, Chaoli Wang, Hua Shen
bullets: Addresses ambiguous supervision from final renders by identifying which symbolic edits persist, vanish, or interfere during execution.
Maintains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and compiles state changes into constrained alternative programs.
Validates repaired programs against runtime endpoints and preservation conditions, then uses visual verification for goal relevance.
Evaluated on BlenderGym and BlenderBench with two language models; consistently outperforms prior refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA.
Ablations examine execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction limits.
papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded self-improvement for agents refining symbolic 3D graphics, relevant to embodied agentic reasoning and 3D scene manipulation.
papers.title: VETR: Execution-Grounded Self-Improving Agent for Symbolic Graphics Reasoning
papers.tldr: VETR improves symbolic graphics agents by using execution traces to verify and repair programs for more reliable self-improvement.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.
authors: Dijia Zhan, Zhuo Li, Xuemiao Xu, Sun Zheng, Jinyi Li, Wenjun Wang, Jie Tang
bullets: Addresses the unclear contribution of individual tokens in existing action tokenizers.
Builds each next token from the remaining action error after decoding the current prefix.
Evaluated across 19 manipulation tasks in three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings.
ReAT policies with 8 tokens outperform evaluated baselines; on LIBERO, 4 tokens outperform 8-token baselines.
Supports progressively refined action plans with fewer prediction tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces residual action tokenization for autoregressive robot policies, directly relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
papers.tldr: ReAT makes each action token explicitly correct errors in the decoded prefix, enabling more effective and self-corrective autoregressive robot policies.

papers.abstract: People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop, creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way, while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.
authors: Chen Yu, Sudarshan S Harithas, Juan Borbon, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between disruptive full replanning and continuing along invalidated plans.
Combines online object-property estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control.
Partially inverts the old plan only where old and new beliefs disagree, then reconstructs the remainder under the new belief.
Across 18 simulated goals, reduced pooled final position error by roughly 33% and yaw error by 47% versus fixed-depth replanning.
Hardware experiments demonstrated translation and turning of a non-holonomic cart.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) for flow-based replanning in humanoid loco-manipulation, combining online estimation with flow-based planning to handle unknown object dynamics.
papers.title: Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion: Object-Centric Flow Replanning for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: BOPI enables humanoids to adaptively push carts with unknown dynamics by partially revising motion plans as beliefs change.

papers.abstract: Third-person human videos offer a scalable alternative to task-specific reward engineering, teleoperation, and manually scripted demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation. Recent video-to-humanoid systems have shown that noisy human motion, object trajectories, and contacts can be extracted from unstructured videos and refined into deployable skills. However, a key gap remains for contact-rich imitation: the task is often defined by world-frame contacts whose poses, timing, and speed must survive embodiment mismatch and runtime scene changes. Towards this, we present VICAR (Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting), a pipeline for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos. The system first recovers human motion, reconstructs task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, and then retargets the motion to a humanoid while preserving global contact poses, motion speed, and collision clearance. Unlike retargeting methods that only remove penetration or preserve local interaction geometry, our formulation represents user-specified contact poses and collision clearance as high-priority Lagrangian penalty terms and optimizes the full motion to remain smooth through contact-rich transitions. The resulting motions are used to train a contact-conditioned motion generator whose inputs include movable contact points enabling runtime adaptation to new contact positions. We demonstrate the framework on ten diverse third-person video skills, including six table-tennis serves, three object-pickup tasks, and ladder climbing, and deploy the learned skills on hardware. These results suggest that contact-preserving retargeting is a practical step toward humanoids that learn useful interactive behavior by watching humans.
authors: Dvij Kalaria, Bike Zhang, S. Shankar Sastry
bullets: Addresses contact-rich imitation under embodiment mismatch and changing runtime scenes.
Recovers human motion and task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, then performs contact-aware humanoid retargeting.
Uses high-priority Lagrangian penalties for user-specified contact poses and collision clearance while optimizing smooth motion.
Trains a contact-conditioned motion generator with movable contact points for adapting to new contact positions.
Demonstrated on ten skills—including table-tennis serves, object pickup, and ladder climbing—with hardware deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Presents VICAR for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos using contact-aware retargeting, effectively bridging video imitation and robot manipulation.
papers.title: VICAR: Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting for Humanoid Interactive Skills
papers.tldr: VICAR learns deployable humanoid interactive skills from third-person videos by retargeting human motion while preserving contacts, speed, and collision clearance.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot coordination is essential in applications such as coverage, target tracking, and information gathering, where robots must jointly select actions to maximize team performance. Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing the direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor $\rho$. Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor of $[\max(1-\nu_f(\mathcal{I}),h(N,\beta))]^2 \rho \frac{1}{\kappa_f}(1-e^{-\kappa_f})$ of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.
authors: Yoonjae Hwang, Hojune Kim, Ellen Novoseller, Guangyao Shi, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
bullets: Addresses the risk that robot loss disconnects the surviving communication network, halting coordination.
Introduces Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, jointly modeling task performance, failure resilience, and communication connectivity.
Uses a Menger-based connectivity reduction, connectivity-aware greedy selection, and a feasibility-preserving fallback.
Provides curvature-based worst-case guarantees that account for connectivity costs through a factor $\rho$ and recover classical guarantees in limiting cases.
Experiments on multi-robot target tracking evaluate the method and the practical effects of connectivity constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a resilient multi-robot coordination framework using submodular maximization with $k$-connectivity constraints, offering a technically meaningful optimization approach for multi-agent navigation.
papers.title: Failure-Resilient Multi-Robot Coordination with $k$-Connectivity Constrained Submodular Maximization
papers.tldr: A connectivity-aware submodular optimization framework enables multi-robot teams to remain coordinated and effective despite robot failures or adversarial removals.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. External visual representations can improve manipulation, but existing methods couple representation choices with different integration mechanisms, obscuring their individual effects. We systematically compare visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert's effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R$^2$-WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.
authors: Kai Liu, Jiangran Lyu, Tingyu Deng, Yixin Zheng, Jingtian Wan, Wenbo Cui, Mi Yan, Yizhou Zhou, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Compares visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings.
General-purpose representations provide broad robustness and can match or exceed task-specific pretrained features.
Channel-wise joint prediction has the highest average success, aided by future-feature prediction and effective use of added information.
Additional representations help only when they add task-relevant information beyond existing features; composition gains are secondary.
R²-WAM reaches 84.7% on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop and 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 points.
papers.selection_reason: Systematic study of visual representations for action-conditioned world models in manipulation.
papers.title: What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that strong general-purpose visual representations, especially with channel-wise joint prediction, substantially improve World Action Models for manipulation.

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.
authors: Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He, Rui Huang, Zilong Zheng, Zhenliang Zhang, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Evaluates continual learning through compositional generalization: agents learn basic tasks before tackling unseen advanced tasks.
Experiments span multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinct behaviors.
Experience from basic tasks consistently improves performance on advanced tasks, including as task complexity rises.
Agents struggle in zero-shot settings and fail to gain proportional benefits from increasing amounts of experience.
The benchmark supports research on more effective self-evolving embodied agents.
papers.selection_reason: First benchmark for continual learning in embodied agents, directly combining embodied AI with continual learning evaluation.
papers.title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: EmbodiedCLBench introduces the first embodied-simulation benchmark for testing whether agents can continually recombine learned skills to solve increasingly complex tasks.

papers.abstract: Learning-based methods have demonstrated strong performance in mapless robot navigation. However, a learned policy remains restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and target-specific policy training completed within seconds.
authors: Xianghui Wang, Xinming Zhang, Yiwei Qian, Siwei Cheng, Shanze Wang, Dan Zhang, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the embodiment mismatch that makes source-robot demonstrations invalid for target-robot supervision.
Uses geometry-consistent scaling and per-demonstration validity checks to recast source data for each target embodiment.
Trains a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy to produce feasible collision-avoidance maneuvers.
Validated in simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms.
Reports a 13.8-percentage-point average success-rate gain over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations, with training completed within seconds.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses cross-embodiment mapless navigation by recasting offline demonstrations into target-specific policies using geometry-consistent scaling, a significant contribution to transferable navigation policies.
papers.title: CeDR-Nav: Cross-Embodiment Mapless Navigation via Offline Demonstration Recasting
papers.tldr: CeDR-Nav repurposes demonstrations from one robot embodiment to train effective mapless navigation policies for different robots without online data collection.

papers.abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{https://empowerment-geometry.github.io/scaling-empowerment/}{this https url}.
authors: Catherine Ji, Vivek Myers, Joshua Lin, Alexandra Wingate, Sergey Levine, Benjamin Eysenbach
bullets: Connects empowerment with skill learning while distinguishing the two concepts.
Defines empowerment operationally as the number of executable skills available from a state.
Proposes a simple recipe that works with arbitrary underlying skill-learning methods.
Scales empowerment studies beyond tabular environments to realize theoretically predicted behaviors.
Demonstrates emergent behaviors, including house building in Crafter.
papers.selection_reason: Connects empowerment maximization to skill learning and scales it in embodied environments, relevant to embodied skill acquisition.
papers.title: Scaling Empowered Agents
papers.tldr: A scalable approach to empowerment maximization guides agents toward states from which they can execute many diverse skills, producing emergent behaviors such as resource gathering, environment modification, survival, and house building.

papers.abstract: Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations. In contrast to resource-intensive and labor-intensive teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection. Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments, yet prior egocentric demonstration-based methods that require no robots or specialized teaching devices do not explicitly address occlusions. To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions. EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts the future camera-arm pose sequence from the current view and camera-arm pose, and the other predicts the future control commands from object keypoints and a history of control commands. EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility. In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.
authors: Hiromu Kurihara, Kazutoshi Tanaka, Masashi Hatano, Tadashi Kozuno, Hideo Saito, Mariko Isogawa
bullets: Addresses partial object occlusions, which prior robot-free egocentric demonstration methods do not explicitly handle.
Uses two imitation policies: one predicts camera-arm repositioning, and the other predicts manipulation controls.
Switches between viewpoint repositioning and manipulation based on target visibility.
Experiments show more reliable task completion than fixed-camera baselines when objects are initially occluded.
papers.selection_reason: Learns active vision and manipulation from egocentric demonstrations to handle partial occlusions, combining imitation learning with viewpoint repositioning.
papers.title: EgoReveal: Learning Active Vision and Object Manipulation under Partial Occlusions from Egocentric Demonstrations
papers.tldr: EgoReveal learns when to reposition a robot’s viewpoint and how to manipulate partially occluded objects from egocentric human demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.
authors: Gangyi Li, LuYao Wang, Jingfu Sun, Jingyi Yuan, Hang Liu, Hao Zong, Yujia Hu, Tingting Gao, Jianyong Wang, Xu Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting multimodal observations and changing user goals into executable actions under product constraints.
Builds closed-loop interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, validated by execution outcomes and semantic criteria.
Uses staged learning—supervised fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and reinforcement learning with DPER token-level evidence routing.
Combines generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency for training rewards.

Scores 77.44 on BFCL v4 and leads reported metrics on JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, while results on other public benchmarks are mixed; quadruped case studies demonstrate search, replanning, and failure reporting.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal policy learning for embodied agents with RL, distillation, and execution feedback, directly fitting embodied AI topics.
papers.title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: JoyInside-VLM-Agent trains a product-conditioned multimodal embodied agent to plan, adapt, and recover from failures across robotic and smart-device tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. To address these limitations, we introduce Evo-World, a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision, thereby providing a task-relevant predictive signal focused on motion rather than appearance. We further design the training procedure to preserve these predictive representations during policy learning, regulating representation diversity while decoupling representation learning from action optimization. Across simulation benchmarks, Evo-World demonstrates strong performance, achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50 , with a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline. On real-world AgileX robots, Evo-World outperforms the evaluated baselines across single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks while using only 0.87B parameters and delivering lower GPU memory usage and higher inference efficiency. These results demonstrate that future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision provides an effective and lightweight approach to enhancing the predictive capabilities of VLA models.
authors: Zile Zhong, Yuxin Du, Tao Lin, Haoxiao Wang, Wei Dai, Binhua Zuo, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation that action supervision does not explicitly teach VLAs to anticipate scene evolution.
Uses optical-flow-based future motion prediction to focus representations on task-relevant motion rather than static appearance.
Preserves predictive representations during policy learning by regulating representation diversity and decoupling representation learning from action optimization.
Achieves a 91.1% tier-averaged success rate on Meta-World MT50, a 13.0% relative gain over a non-predictive baseline.
Shows stronger performance than evaluated baselines on real-world single-arm and bimanual AgileX tasks with 0.87B parameters, lower GPU memory use, and higher inference efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Evo-World, a VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction via optical-flow supervision, providing a task-relevant predictive signal for robot control.
papers.title: Evo-World: A Lightweight Vision-Language-Action Model with Future Motion Prediction via Optical-Flow Supervision
papers.tldr: Evo-World improves lightweight vision-language-action control by predicting future scene motion with optical-flow supervision.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.
authors: Xule Gao, Xi Wang, Zehua Zang, Rui Wang, Changwen Zheng, Chuxiong Sun
bullets: Problem: Step-wise imitation can overfit to demonstration paths and offers limited guidance after execution deviates from them.
Method: Relabels offline trajectories with semantic key states and uses goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize key-state reachability.
Contribution: Shifts VLA post-training from trajectory imitation toward recoverable, goal-directed behavior from feasible off-demonstration states.
Results: Improves performance over standard supervised fine-tuning on LIBERO and MetaWorld, with stronger robustness under shifts and perturbations on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-ReAct.
papers.selection_reason: Offline goal-conditioned optimization for VLA robot policies; fits embodied AI VLA and manipulation.
papers.title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: OGPO post-trains vision-language-action models to recover toward semantic task-progress states, improving robustness without additional online interaction.

papers.abstract: Agile and reliable navigation is a core capability for embodied robots navigating complex spatial constraints and dynamic interactions. However, a single policy often struggles to accommodate the distinct decision-making demands of diverse scenarios. We present TAME-Nav, an asymmetric Teacher-Student navigation framework built around a temporal soft mixture of experts (Soft-MoE). The Teacher combines clean observations with causally maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks to construct privileged representations, while the Student learns complementary navigation features from corrupted observation histories through temporal encoding, soft expert routing, and latent distillation. Procedural scenario generation and parallel task-level simulation broaden training coverage, while deployment-informed asymmetric domain randomization supports sim-to-real transfer. Across in-distribution and unseen compositional scenarios, TAME-Nav achieves higher success rates, lower collision rates, and higher navigation scores than representative baselines. On a real quadruped robot, it completes all twenty trials across local-trap escape and narrow-passage navigation with sudden dynamic obstacles, with only one minor contact.
authors: Lingjie Zhang, Jun Xue, Shanze Wang, Haoyu Xi, Xinming Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of using one navigation policy across varied spatial constraints and dynamic interactions.
Uses an asymmetric Teacher–Student framework with temporal soft mixture-of-experts routing and latent distillation.
The Teacher uses clean observations and maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks; the Student learns from corrupted observation histories.
Procedural scenario generation, parallel simulation, and deployment-informed domain randomization support broad training and sim-to-real transfer.
Outperforms representative baselines in success, collision, and navigation scores; a real quadruped completed 20 trials with one minor contact.
papers.selection_reason: Asymmetric teacher-student navigation with temporal mixture-of-experts distillation and sim-to-real transfer.
papers.title: TAME-Nav: Temporal Asymmetric Mixture-of-Experts Distillation for Agile and Versatile Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: TAME-Nav distills privileged temporal obstacle information into a robust mixture-of-experts student policy for agile robot navigation in diverse and dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: In the practical deployment of vision--language--action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. To investigate this issue, we study the head-task action bias in shared robot policies, particularly focusing on its relationship with task-specific visual evidence. Our experimental analysis shows that, when the visual evidence required by a tail task is insufficient, the policy increasingly falls back on action patterns reinforced by data-rich head tasks, resulting in degraded performance on under-represented tasks. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning, a training framework for long-tailed robot policies. Our method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence using instruction-related and action-related signals, and constructs counterfactual observations by removing the selected evidence. The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Extensive experiments across simulated benchmarks, different VLA architectures, and real-world robot platforms demonstrate that our method robustly and consistently improves long-tailed robot policy learning, particularly for tail tasks, while maintaining reliable performance on head tasks.
authors: Weiwei Chen, Chenghao Xu, Meiling Yu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng
bullets: Long-tailed demonstration data can cause shared policies to favor action patterns from data-rich head tasks, harming under-represented tail tasks.
The method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence from instruction- and action-related signals, then removes it to create counterfactual observations.
Counterfactual predictions reinforce links among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with supervision adjusted by task demonstration frequency.
It requires no additional data or region-level annotations and adds no deployment-time computation.
Experiments across simulated benchmarks, multiple VLA architectures, and real robots show improved tail-task learning while maintaining head-task performance.
papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual learning framework to mitigate head-task bias in long-tailed VLA robot policies.
papers.title: Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning for Long-Tailed Robotic Policies
papers.tldr: Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning reduces head-task bias in long-tailed vision-language-action robot policies by using task-relevant visual evidence and counterfactual observations.

papers.abstract: In maximum entropy and behavior-constrained reinforcement learning (RL), the optimal policy is given by a Boltzmann distribution. Generating samples from this distribution can be challenging, as it is often complex and multimodal. While flow policies trained with flow matching provide a powerful framework for representing such distributions, they traditionally rely on access to training data, which is generally unavailable in online RL. To address this limitation, we propose fixed-point flow matching (FFM), a data-free procedure for training and fine-tuning flow policies in RL. FFM leverages the target flow identity to formulate the actor update as a fixed-point iteration, utilizing a flow-matching-style regression objective where the critic's action gradients serve as regression targets. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FFM effectively fine-tunes pretrained flow policies in the offline-to-online setting and enables efficient and accurate training of flow policies from scratch in online RL. These results establish fixed-point flow matching as a principled approach for learning expressive flow-based policies without requiring training data.
authors: Denis Blessing, Onur Celik, Gerhard Neumann
bullets: Targets maximum-entropy and behavior-constrained RL, where optimal policies are complex Boltzmann distributions.
Uses a fixed-point iteration based on the target flow identity to update the actor.
Trains flow policies with a regression objective whose targets come from critic action gradients.
Supports fine-tuning pretrained flow policies offline-to-online and training them from scratch in online RL.
Experiments show effective and accurate learning, though the abstract does not specify numerical results or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Data-free fixed-point flow matching for RL policies; transferable to robot policy learning.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning via Fixed-point Flow Matching
papers.tldr: Fixed-point flow matching trains expressive flow-based RL policies without requiring policy training data.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already exhibit strong visual, spatial and reasoning capabilities relevant to robotic manipulation. The key challenge in turning pretrained VLMs into generalist manipulation policies is to expose these capabilities through an appropriate action interface. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified trainable policy, but typically introduce learned action tokens, action heads, or action experts whose semantics must be learned from robot data pretraining. In contrast, modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods can exploit pretrained VLM capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but rely on external planning and control scaffolds that are not end-to-end trainable as a unified continuous-action policy. In this work, we introduce EASG, an Explicit Action-Space Grounding framework that bridges these two paradigms. By projecting a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into the wrist camera observation and expressing actions in the form of VLM's native textual generation interface, EASG makes the semantics of a continuous robot action space directly observable in the VLM's perceptual context. This allows pretrained VLMs to directly generate executable robot actions using their existing visual-spatial reasoning capabilities, without robot-action pretraining or additional action modules. Besides, the same action interface supports direct fine-tuning with robot trajectories, allowing the models to continuously improve beyond their manipulation capabilities unleashed by EASG. Overall, EASG enables zero-shot manipulation and generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, while supporting effective fine-tuning in the same continuous action space. These results demonstrate that, given an appropriate action interface, pretrained VLMs can themselves serve as native action models for robotic manipulation.
authors: Jingkun Yi, Shujie Zhang, Zirui Zhou, Haoxiao Wang, Haiyang Sun, Yuhang Dong, Xudong Xu, Xing Shen, Tao Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exposing pretrained VLM reasoning capabilities through a unified continuous-action interface.
Projects a tool-center-point action frame into the wrist-camera view, making action semantics visible in the VLM’s perceptual context.
Represents robot actions through the VLM’s native textual generation interface, avoiding robot-action pretraining and extra action modules.
Supports both zero-shot manipulation and trajectory-based fine-tuning in the same continuous action space.
Enables generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, as described in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Pretrained VLMs grounded in a continuous action space via textual action interface for zero-shot manipulation and fine-tuning.
papers.title: VLMs are Native Action Models: Unleashing the Manipulation Capabilities of VLMs with Explicit Action-Space Grounding
papers.tldr: EASG turns pretrained VLMs into executable robotic manipulation policies by explicitly grounding continuous actions in the visual scene and VLM text-generation interface.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.
authors: Minghao Fu, Tavis Siebert, Eryk Halicki, Randall Balestriero
bullets: Addresses the separation of representation, dynamics, and control training in prior JEPA pipelines.
Jointly trains next-latent-state prediction with action flow matching under an isotropic Gaussian latent constraint.
Supports direct policy execution and test-time planning by scoring sampled actions through learned latent dynamics.
Improves visual-planning success from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks.
Plans 32.3× faster than prior JEPAs and remains competitive on simulated and physical-robot behavior cloning tasks.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end JEPA world model with action-conditioned latent dynamics and planning, directly relevant to world models and robot learning.
papers.title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
papers.tldr: LeWAM is an end-to-end JEPA for control that jointly learns latent dynamics and action generation, enabling both direct policy execution and fast planning.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on memory tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present GAMMA (Grounded multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool (SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits the next grounded subgoal at the oracle's cadence, wrapped in a propose-verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite GAMMA recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
authors: Yudong Liu, Yueqian Lin, Zijia Tang, Yuxi Zheng, Yuan Li, Shuai Zhang, Yi Li, Taotao Jing, Shuangjun Liu, Dashan Gao, Ning Bi, Jingwei Sun, Yiran Chen, Hai Helen Li
bullets: Addresses VLA failures on tasks requiring information from events far before the current frame.
Uses SAM-3 for spatial grounding, a VLM writer for concise episodic summaries, and a VLM reasoner to produce grounded subgoals.
Maintains an append-only text memory bank and verifies, corrects, defers, or rejects claims using mechanical visual evidence.
Recovers much of the privileged-oracle performance on a 16-task suite, reaching the oracle ceiling on several tasks.
Transfers to a second benchmark without changing its contracts; performance is scoped to the tested memory-manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Grounded multi-agent memory system with mechanical audit for memory-intensive VLA manipulation.
papers.title: Gamma: Grounded Multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit for Memory-Intensive Manipulation
papers.tldr: GAMMA combines grounded visual detection, structured text memory, multi-agent reasoning, and mechanical verification to help fixed VLA policies solve long-horizon memory-based manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires maintaining a firm grasp while strictly avoiding both contact slip and structural damage to the object. Satisfying these inherent \textit{secure-and-gentle} grasping constraints is challenging for unknown objects. We present a novel online data-driven predictive control framework for safe dynamic robotic grasping of unknown objects. The proposed system features a pair of compact, single-channel tactile-sensing modules that characterize the gripper-object dynamic interaction in real time, entirely bypassing the need for prior knowledge or offline training. A finite-state-machine-based grasping force probing mechanism is developed to establish the initial grasping force and explicitly identify grasping force constraints. Through online dynamics learning, a Gaussian Process (GP) model captures gripper-object interaction dynamics. The model uncertainties are further used to form robust grasping constraints, which are embedded into a model predictive control scheme. We demonstrate error convergence in a probabilistic sense. The proposed control framework runs at 100~Hz in real time to dynamically manipulate and handle objects rather than static holding. Extensive experimental evaluations across diverse contact surface topologies and various types of objects validate superior performance and efficiency compared to baseline strategies. The proposed method is able to manipulate objects ranging from delicate items, such as raw tofu and marshmallows, to rough objects, such as rocks.
bullets: Uses compact single-channel tactile sensors to monitor gripper–object interactions in real time.
Probes for an initial grasp force and identifies force constraints with a finite-state machine.
Learns interaction dynamics online with a Gaussian Process and incorporates uncertainty into robust MPC constraints.
Runs at 100 Hz and demonstrates probabilistic error convergence during dynamic manipulation.
Experiments cover delicate and rough objects across varied contact surfaces, including tofu, marshmallows, and rocks.
papers.selection_reason: Online data-driven predictive control with tactile sensing for secure and gentle grasping of unknown objects.
papers.title: Tactile Sensing-based Secure and Gentle Grasping of Unknown Objects
papers.tldr: An online tactile-feedback predictive controller enables secure, gentle dynamic grasping of unknown objects without prior models or offline training.

papers.abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.
authors: Taoyang Jia, Weikai Huang, Linxin Song, Jared Darlington, Jieyu Zhao, Yue Wang, Jiafei Duan, Zhongzheng Ren, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining whole-body control, moving-object dynamics prediction, and egocentric visual grounding.
Uses a three-stage framework: reinforcement-learned catching, dynamics inference from delayed observations, and RGB-D perception of that dynamics representation.
In simulation, achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, close to 87.9% with privileged object observations.
Temporal visual history is essential, with its removal reducing success by 35.6–39.8 percentage points.
On a Unitree G1, catches human-thrown boxes at 65% success from 2.5 m and 40% from 5 m.
papers.selection_reason: Visually grounded reactive whole-body humanoid control via staged RL and egocentric RGB-D perception.
papers.title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
papers.tldr: Reflex enables humanoids to visually anticipate and catch moving boxes with coordinated whole-body reactions in real time.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability.
authors: Vivek Khatana, Zijian Song, Naira Hovakimyan, Petros Voulgaris
bullets: Addresses the gap between independently generated symbolic plans and jointly feasible robot trajectories.
Compares centralized joint planning with decentralized, per-robot LLM planning.
Uses geometric grounding to detect inter-robot spatial and temporal conflicts.
Feeds structured conflict information back to LLM planners for iterative coordination.
Evaluates increasing task complexity in CARLA and with Crazyflie aerial robots, including physical executability trade-offs.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-robot path planning with LLM planners coordinated by a geometric verifier for execution-aware feasibility.
papers.title: Verifier-Mediated Multi-LLM Coordination for Multi-Robot Path Planning
papers.tldr: A geometric verifier helps coordinate centralized or decentralized LLM planners by detecting trajectory conflicts and guiding replanning for feasible multi-robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation. Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers. These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult to predict. To address these challenges, we collect WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers. Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive, achieves a mean minADE (K=6) of 1.09 m and minFDE (K=6) of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark, WZDrive reduces minADE (K=6) by 7.18% and minFDE (K=6) by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop data collection with multimodal learning from human driving signals and in the context of work zones.
authors: Shuo Zhang, Aman Sunesh, Semiha Ergan, Kaan Ozbay
bullets: Work zones introduce temporary lane changes and altered road connectivity, making vehicle-trajectory prediction difficult and underexplored.
The WZDrive-Data dataset contains 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, including vehicle, scene, control, and gaze signals.
The WZDrive predictor uses multimodal human-driving and scene information to forecast multiple possible ego trajectories.
It achieves minADE@6 of 1.09 m and minFDE@6 of 2.12 m, improving on the strongest benchmark baselines by 7.18% and 13.18%, respectively.
The study focuses on urban roadway work zones and relies on human-in-the-loop simulator data.
papers.selection_reason: Learned ego-trajectory prediction for autonomous driving in work zones, fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving in Road Construction Zones Using Human-in-the-Loop Driving Data
papers.tldr: WZDrive combines human-in-the-loop work-zone driving data with multimodal prediction to improve autonomous-vehicle ego-trajectory forecasting in complex construction zones.

papers.abstract: Indoor navigation to task-relevant targets remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, or visually indistinct. Meanwhile, smart appliances, mobile devices, and IoT tags emit Wi-Fi signals during everyday communication, providing a pervasive but underused spatial cue. We study visual-Wi-Fi navigation, where a robot reaches a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment using onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the device, without connecting to the device or modifying infrastructure. Realizing this requires pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations during closed-loop policy learning and reliable spatial cues from bearing measurements corrupted by indoor multipath propagation on a moving robot. We present WiFiSpaces, which extends the Habitat embodied simulator with online ray-traced Wi-Fi sensing, rendering Wi-Fi observations for a robot-mounted antenna array at continuous poses during policy rollouts. On top of it, we build ViFiNav, a localization-aware navigation framework: an online source-localization algorithm exploits robot motion to disambiguate and robustly aggregate bearings from multiple viewpoints into a confidence-aware source estimate, and a learned policy fuses this evolving estimate with depth observations and learns to act on it as it is refined. Experiments show that exploiting robot motion is key to accurate source estimates, and that fine-tuning on ray-traced Wi-Fi observations in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav. The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen scene datasets, and we deploy it on a real robot with a Wi-Fi sensor built from a commodity router, without any real-world training.
authors: Lihao Wang, Tianjian Xu, Tianmin Shu, Renjie Zhao
bullets: Addresses navigation to small, occluded, or visually indistinct devices using Wi-Fi signals as a spatial cue.
Introduces WiFiSpaces, a Habitat extension that simulates pose-dependent, ray-traced Wi-Fi observations during policy rollouts.
Uses robot motion to aggregate noisy multi-view bearing measurements into a confidence-aware source estimate.
A learned policy fuses the evolving Wi-Fi estimate with depth observations for closed-loop navigation.
Improves with ray-traced Wi-Fi fine-tuning, transfers zero-shot to unseen scenes, and runs on a real robot without real-world training.
papers.selection_reason: Learned robot navigation to signal-emitting devices using visual and Wi-Fi observations, with online source localization and policy learning.
