papers.title: Visual-Wi-Fi Navigation to Signal-Emitting Devices
papers.tldr: ViFiNav enables robots to navigate unmapped indoor environments to Wi-Fi-emitting devices by combining motion-based source localization, depth vision, and Wi-Fi sensing without infrastructure changes.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with $\pi_{0.5}$-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.
authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran, Ruwan Wickramarachchi, Alessandro Oltramari, Jonathan Francis
bullets: Targets long-horizon manipulation, where robots must retain useful history while retracting unsupported conclusions.
Uses a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor, without policy retraining.
Links derived relations and completed conditions to supporting facts, then withdraws affected conclusions when evidence changes.
Schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries after disturbances.
Across 51 physical trials, mean recorded progress improved from 57% to 91% for intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% for sequence recall.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces revisable embodied memory layer for manipulation with frozen VLA executor, directly fitting embodied memory and robot manipulation.
papers.title: REMM: Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation
papers.tldr: REMM helps robots recover from manipulation disturbances by maintaining evidence separately from revisable task state and repairing only conclusions invalidated by new evidence.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State, Relative Size, Referential Description, Relational Placement, Ordinal Position, and Counting. Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5-73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7-52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3-40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/.
authors: Justin Tien-Smith, Matthew Pidden, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Introduces a real-robot benchmark spanning six tabletop spatial tasks: object state, relative size, referential description, relational placement, ordinal position, and counting.
Compares in-distribution and out-of-distribution spatial configurations while controlling for object and motor unfamiliarity.
Adds diagnostics for physical execution, wording sensitivity, object-task associations, and recognizing when no action is needed.
Evaluates 4,092 episodes on the SO-101 robot arm, including demonstrations and rollouts from five VLA policies.

Across three fully evaluated policies, success drops from 67.5–73.3% on in-distribution configurations to 40.7–52.0% on out-of-distribution configurations; direct instructions improve success by 28.3–40.0 percentage points.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating spatial grounding of VLA policies on real robot, directly fitting vision-language-action and manipulation.
papers.title: Spa-Bench: A Real-Robot Benchmark for Spatial Grounding in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Spa-Bench shows that current vision-language-action models often execute manipulations but struggle to reliably ground spatial descriptions in real-world scenes.

papers.abstract: Non-prehensile manipulation with mobile robots has primarily targeted placement in coarse goal regions. Precision placement has been studied with manipulators on benchmarks such as Push-T, where an omnidirectional end effector can readily re-approach an object from any side. For a mobile robot, correcting the same placement errors may require wide repositioning maneuvers around the object. We formalize multi-object pushing with a mobile robot as a multi-target assignment problem at tight tolerances. We propose a diffusion planner with a causal factorization: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. This factorization allows us to sample multiple object outcomes for a single robot plan, capturing the multi-modality of pushing. We also design a set of pushing-specific costs for mobile robots, used for both guidance and best-of-$N$ sampling at inference. On Push-T, our planner attains the highest success rate of the methods we compare, while having the lowest rate of implausible object motion. Across three multi-box pushing environments resembling warehouse scenarios, it raises the fraction of boxes placed by $21.5$ percentage points over an unguided baseline, and replans $1.8\times$ faster than a planner that denoises the two trajectories together. Lastly, we deploy the guided planner on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with object shapes absent from the training data, where it places $85.0\%$ of objects within tolerance against Diffusion Policy's $37.5\%$.
authors: Lance Pharand, Megnath Ramesh, Mark Chiu, Yash Vardhan Pant, Stephen L. Smith
bullets: Formulates tight-tolerance multi-object pushing as a multi-target assignment problem for mobile robots.
Uses causal diffusion: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the robot estimate, capturing multiple possible pushing outcomes.
Introduces pushing-specific costs for guidance and best-of-N trajectory selection.
Achieves the highest compared success rate and lowest implausible-motion rate on Push-T; improves box placement by 21.5 percentage points over an unguided baseline.
Replans 1.8× faster than joint trajectory denoising and places 85.0% of objects within tolerance on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with unseen shapes.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based trajectory planning for non-prehensile mobile manipulation, directly fitting learned robot manipulation.
papers.title: Non-Prehensile Multi-Object Placement with Mobile Robots via Diffusion-Based Trajectory Planning
papers.tldr: A diffusion-based planner enables mobile robots to precisely push and place multiple objects by modeling robot and object trajectories separately with task-specific guidance.

papers.abstract: Motion retargeting is a critical preprocessing step for transferring human motion data to humanoid robots. While existing methods are effective for single-character motions, interactions involving multiple characters and objects introduce additional contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved. Retargeting is commonly formulated as a weighted multi-objective optimization problem, where conflicting objectives can require careful tuning of relative weights and can still compromise important motion characteristics. We introduce PriMoRetarget, a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces relative objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy. Lower-priority updates are constrained to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical characteristics such as foot placement and interaction contacts to take precedence over lower-priority pose objectives. The method is evaluated on four datasets spanning single-character motion, character-object manipulation, and character-character interactions. The resulting motions better preserve task-relevant interactions and provide reference trajectories that can be tracked more reliably than those produced by widely used retargeting methods.
authors: Nicholas Ioannidis, Dun Yang, Max Smith, Tue Vu, Ziyu Zhang, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Xue Bin Peng
bullets: Addresses motion-retargeting failures in multi-character and character-object interactions, where contacts and spatial relationships must be preserved.
Replaces manually tuned weighted objectives with prioritized optimization: lower-priority updates cannot compromise higher-priority objectives.
Prioritizes task-critical features such as foot placement and interaction contacts over lower-priority pose matching.
Evaluated across four datasets covering single-character motion, manipulation, and character-character interactions.
Produces motions that better preserve interactions and yield more reliably trackable reference trajectories than widely used retargeting methods.
papers.selection_reason: Prioritized motion retargeting for humanoid robots, relevant to robot skill/control pipelines though not learning-based.
papers.title: PriMoRetarget: Humanoid Motion Transfer Through Prioritized Motion Retargeting
papers.tldr: PriMoRetarget transfers humanoid motion by enforcing a priority hierarchy that preserves critical contacts and spatial relationships over less important pose objectives.

papers.abstract: Recently, soft robotic procedures are being developed aiming at achieving targeted minimally invasive operations or drug administration in specific locations in the human body. Accordingly, specialized path-planning algorithms need to be investigated for the estimation of efficient paths that would protect the delicate tissue structures and simultaneously satisfy a set of requirements for the efficient navigation of the robot. In this context, we propose an image-based 3D pathplanning algorithm, which is an extension of the A* algorithm, for the navigation of a soft-growing robot inside the spinal subarachnoid space (SSS). The proposed algorithm is capable of estimating a safe pathway towards the goal location, while ensuring the establishment of anchor points that facilitate the efficient steering of the soft robot. The algorithm is evaluated using a highly detailed model of the SSS with respect to its capacity to satisfy the robot movement requirements and path efficiency.
authors: George Dimas, Panagiotis G. Kalozoumis, Panagiotis Vartholomeos, Dimitris K. Iakovidis
bullets: Targets minimally invasive procedures and drug delivery in delicate anatomical environments.
Plans paths while accounting for tissue protection and soft-robot navigation requirements.
Establishes anchor points to support effective steering of the growing robot.
Evaluated in a highly detailed spinal subarachnoid space model for movement feasibility and path efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes image-based 3D path planning for soft-growing robot navigation, directly relevant to robot navigation/planning.
papers.title: Image-Based Path-Planning for Navigation of Soft-Growing Robots in the Spinal Sub-Arachnoid Space
papers.tldr: An image-based 3D extension of A* plans safe, efficient routes for soft-growing robots navigating the spinal subarachnoid space.

papers.abstract: Humanoid and service robots operating in clut- tered human environments may encounter motion planning problems that are infeasible when all surrounding objects are treated as fixed obstacles. The Minimum Constraint Removal problem, which we refer to as MCR, addresses this situation by identifying the minimum number of constraints, such as movable objects, whose removal enables a collision-free path. However, computing an optimal MCR solution is NP-hard. In this work, we propose a graph-based heuristic pipeline that combines bidirectional feasible-set generation with fixed- length searches over reduced MCR graphs. We further derive an extended feasible-set generator for instances in which the candidates produced by the first generator do not contain a complete optimal removal set. Across six benchmarks, the evaluated pipeline matches the exact solution in three cases and, in the remaining cases, selects at most 31.25% more obstacles than the optimum, while being between 3.4 and 33.7 times faster than exact search. In one of the benchmarks, involving a manipulation task amidst clutter, selecting two rather than seven obstructing objects reduces the combined MCR, inverse- kinematics, and motion planning time from 84.72 s to 30.59 s. These results indicate that the proposed approach provides a practical compromise between computational efficiency and solution quality for motion planning among movable obstacles.
authors: Antony Thomas, Fulvio Mastrogiovanni, Marco Baglietto
bullets: Targets Minimum Constraint Removal (MCR), which is NP-hard in cluttered environments with movable obstacles.
Combines bidirectional feasible-set generation, fixed-length searches, and an extended generator for difficult instances.
Matches the exact solution on three of six benchmarks; other solutions remove at most 31.25% more obstacles than optimal.
Runs 3.4–33.7× faster than exact search and substantially reduces planning time in a cluttered manipulation example.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses motion planning among movable obstacles for humanoid/service robots, fitting learned/planning navigation in cluttered environments.
papers.title: Graph-Based Heuristics for Minimum Constraint Removal in Cluttered Robot Motion Planning
papers.tldr: A graph-based heuristic efficiently finds near-minimal obstacle removals to make otherwise infeasible robot motion plans possible.

papers.abstract: Prior research on learning from humans often requires real human demonstrations. But advances in video generation models offer a new paradigm: we can now prompt these generators to make synthetic videos of the task. On the plus side, these synthetic videos take place in the robot's current environment, and do not require actual human teaching. However, while the generated videos appear to show plausible motions, they lack both physical consistency and robot grounding, and thus the robot cannot directly roll out the trajectory shown by the video. In this paper we seek to formalize the process of going from synthetic video generation to real-world robot trajectories for zero-shot manipulation tasks. We recognize that this problem is an instance of constrained optimization. The object trajectories extracted from the synthetic video provide an initial guess at the correct motion, and the robot must refine these trajectories (for instance, within a digital twin) while enforcing physical feasibility and semantic consistency. Our optimization-based formalism provides insights into the video generation properties necessary for success. Specifically, we show that the video generation must probabilistically seed the search within a semantic basin of attraction where the trajectory can be locally modified without losing its task alignment. Our analysis further reveals that state-of-the-art approaches can be viewed as instances of our unified formalism with key simplifications. In our experiments we remove these simplifications to more closely match the underlying optimization, leading to more robust zero-shot trajectories from synthetic videos and improving average task success by 34.1% compared to the best-performing baseline. See videos at our project website: https://collab.me.vt.edu/CASTER
authors: Yinlong Dai, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Dylan P. Losey
bullets: Synthetic videos avoid real human demonstrations and can depict tasks in the robot’s environment.
Video-derived object trajectories serve as initial guesses, which are refined under physical-feasibility and semantic-consistency constraints.
Success requires generated videos to seed trajectories within a task-aligned semantic basin of attraction.
The framework unifies existing approaches and removes simplifying assumptions to better match the underlying optimization.
Experiments report a 34.1% improvement in average task success over the best-performing baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Fits zero-shot robot manipulation from synthetic videos via constrained optimization.
papers.title: CASTER: Formalizing Zero-Shot Manipulation from Synthetic Videos as Constrained Optimization
papers.tldr: CASTER frames converting synthetic task videos into executable robot trajectories as constrained optimization, producing more robust zero-shot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Memory allows large language model (LLM) agents to use past experience, often stored as textual records, when responding to requests. For embodied agents that control robots, visual and spatial observations introduce a broader choice of memory modalities, affecting both the information available for subsequent tasks and the model inference costs of constructing and using memory. We introduce MeMoREval, a benchmark for studying this problem through a controlled experience-request protocol. Agents first experience a sequence of events without knowing the subsequent tasks, and subsequently they use memory to respond to information and action requests without receiving new observations. The benchmark comprises 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments and measures task success alongside the inference costs of memory construction and use. Our reference evaluations reveal that storing frames outperforms storing generated descriptions at lower write-time inference cost for the primary model, while storing frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success for every tested model. Extensions to accumulated experience, selective frame retention, and visual input to memory writers demonstrate how the benchmark accommodates further memory-design investigations. Two physical-robot demonstrations establish the feasibility of applying its protocol beyond simulation.
authors: Junxiang Wang, Yuchen Liu, Yi Wu, Guofei Chen, Nir Pechuk, Tao Chen, Zackory Erickson, Yuzhe Qin, Tianyu Li
bullets: Evaluates memory through a controlled protocol: agents observe events first, then answer information and action requests without new observations.
Covers 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments, measuring success plus memory construction and usage costs.
For the primary model, storing frames outperforms generated descriptions while requiring lower write-time inference cost.
Combining frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success across all tested models.
The protocol also supports studies of experience accumulation, selective frame retention, visual memory writers, and physical-robot deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Fits embodied memory benchmarking for LLM-driven embodied agents.
papers.title: What Should Embodied Agents Remember? Benchmarking and Evaluating Memory Modality for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: MeMoREval benchmarks how different memory modalities affect embodied agents’ task success and inference costs when using past visual-spatial experience.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment. To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact, a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity, the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing. Website: https://pantact.github.io
authors: Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Zhian Ruan, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Ruihan Yang, Carmelo Sferrazza, Shuran Song, Guanya Shi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of hand-only loco-manipulation by enabling manipulation through diverse body surfaces.
Uses a wearable interface combining egocentric vision, bimanual grippers, and modular whole-body contact patches to capture demonstrations.
A visuomotor policy predicts whole-body contact goals while accounting for the egocentric observation gap.
Contact-aware whole-body control realizes these goals within the robot’s physical constraints.
Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 for support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing without additional body contact sensors.
papers.selection_reason: Fits whole-body robot manipulation learning from human demonstrations with contact and egocentric vision.
papers.title: PanTact: Teaching Whole-Body Dexterity with a Wearable Contact Interface
papers.tldr: PanTact teaches humanoid robots whole-body dexterity from robot-free human demonstrations by transferring contact locations and timing across embodiments.

papers.abstract: Embodied coding agents construct robot policies from natural-language instructions by generating executable programs and refining them from execution feedback. This refinement assumes that execution feedback reveals whether the task succeeded and, after a failure, provides sufficient evidence to guide program revision. Aerial manipulation violates this assumption in two ways. Payload constraints restrict onboard camera coverage and leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot's view (partial observability), while strong dynamic coupling and limited control margins make physical interactions fragile (limited interaction robustness) and leave failure causes unresolved. Re-examining the same feedback cannot recover observations that were never collected or separate failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. To acquire this missing evidence, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an active "View and Probe" framework. When execution feedback leaves unresolved questions, the agent synthesizes a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints (View) or test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions (Probe). Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, AF reduces false completion declarations from 25 to 5 and raises final task success from 31.7% to 75% compared with terminal feedback under the same coding-agent configuration and task-execution limit. Using shared robot APIs, task programs refined with AF in simulation run on a physical aerial manipulator without task-program source-code modification and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world. These results show that executable diagnosis fills gaps in execution feedback for embodied coding agents, improving both completion assessment and program refinement in aerial manipulation.
authors: Jaewoo Lee, Jeongyeon Seo, Sihyun Cho, Gyeongrak Choe, Yutong Wang, Bavin Saravanan, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Sebastian Scherer, Guanya Shi, H. Jin Kim, Seungjae Lee, Dongjae Lee
bullets: Aerial manipulation suffers from partial observability and fragile physical interactions, making ordinary execution feedback insufficient for program refinement.
The proposed View-and-Probe framework generates diagnostic programs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes or test likely failure causes through targeted interactions.
Across six simulated tasks, false completion declarations fell from 25 to 5, while final success increased from 31.7% to 75% under the same agent configuration and task limit.
Programs refined with Active Feedback in simulation transferred to a physical aerial manipulator without source-code changes and completed multi-stage tasks.
The approach is demonstrated within the scope of simulated evaluation and selected real-world aerial manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied coding agents for aerial manipulation with active visual/physical feedback; directly fits embodied AI and robot policy learning.
papers.title: Fly-by-Code: Embodied Coding Agents for Aerial Manipulation with Active Visual and Physical Feedback
papers.tldr: Active Feedback lets coding agents diagnose unseen outcomes and ambiguous failures through targeted visual inspection and physical probing, substantially improving aerial manipulation task success.

papers.abstract: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable's relative performance and the contributions of its components.
bullets: Maintains a fixed-capacity table of strong solutions to guide new proposals, edits, and multi-solution remixes.
Evaluated over ten generations with fifty candidates per generation across ten independent searches for each of six tasks.
Candidate-score medians increased from the first to final generation in all tasks; selected-winner medians increased in five.
All held-out endpoints improved in four tasks, while Acrobot-v1 often declined and some tasks did not reach reporting targets.
Comparisons and ablations remain necessary to assess relative performance and component contributions.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-guided program search for executable control policies in simulated control tasks; fits learned control and robot learning interests.
papers.title: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies
papers.tldr: EliteTable uses an LLM-guided archive of high-scoring programs to iteratively search for executable control policies, improving search performance across six Gymnasium tasks but showing mixed held-out transfer.

papers.abstract: Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable interaction with the real world. However, despite the rapid progress of vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there remains a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViTac, a visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark for evaluating robot policies across simulation and the real world. OpenViTac organizes contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and provides paired simulation-real-world settings for consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. Building upon this benchmark, we investigate how different tactile representations and integration strategies affect the performance of pretrained VLA models. Correspondingly, we introduce OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework that combines the best-performing representation and integration strategy. Furthermore, we leverage the paired benchmark setting to study sim-real co-training and analyze factors affecting cross-domain policy learning. Together, OpenViTac provides a unified platform for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation.
bullets: Targets the lack of consistent benchmarks for tactile-enabled manipulation across simulation and reality.
Organizes contact-rich tasks into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions with paired sim-real settings.
Evaluates VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies, including different tactile representations and integration strategies.
Introduces OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework based on the best-performing design choices.
Uses the paired benchmark to study sim-real co-training and factors influencing cross-domain policy learning.
papers.selection_reason: Visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark and policy learning; fits robot learning and VLA.
papers.title: OpenViTac: Learning and Benchmarking Visuo-Tactile Policies in a Unified Sim-and-Real Framework
papers.tldr: OpenViTac is a unified simulation-and-real-world benchmark for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation policies.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators such as humanoid robots are increasingly deployed in dynamic, unstructured environments to perform dexterous manipulation tasks. However, end-to-end manipulation policies trained to imitate demonstration data collected from a single robot pose are brittle: even centimeter-scale deviations in robot pose at deployment can drive ego-centric observations and end-effector trajectories out of the training distribution, leading to sharp drops in performance. We introduce MobileVISTA, a data generation framework that transforms demonstrations captured at canonical poses into diverse, pose-perturbed training data by jointly (1) augmenting egocentric visual observations and (2) retargeting actions to compensate for base pose changes. Unlike prior methods, which assume a camera rigidly mounted off the actuated chain or non-trivial articulated robot geometry largely out of frame, MobileVISTA targets compatibility with egocentric platforms (e.g., humanoids) where the camera is both influenced by and must observe the robot's kinematic chain as it moves. We study MobileVISTA in simulated tasks spanning humanoid and bimanual embodiments, and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro. We find policies trained on MobileVISTA-augmented data demonstrate improved robustness to previously out-of-distribution poses encountered at test time, without additional demonstration collection or a trained generative model. Additionally, we find MobileVISTA's benefit is largest on tested humanoids, where the camera rides the actuated chain and the robot fills much of the frame. Additional videos and appendix can be found on our website: https://mobilevista.github.io
bullets: Addresses brittleness caused by training demonstrations collected from a single robot pose.
Jointly generates pose-perturbed egocentric observations and compensating action trajectories.
Designed for egocentric robots, including humanoids whose cameras move with and observe the actuated body.
Evaluated in simulated humanoid and bimanual tasks and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro.
Improves robustness to previously unseen test poses without collecting more demonstrations or training a generative model; gains are largest on tested humanoids.
papers.selection_reason: Data augmentation for pose generalization in mobile manipulation; directly targets robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: MobileVISTA: Generative Data Augmentation for Pose Generalization in Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: MobileVISTA augments demonstrations with pose-varied visual observations and retargeted actions to make mobile-manipulation policies more robust to deployment pose changes.

papers.abstract: Behavioral cloning (BC), despite its simplicity, exhibits many counterintuitive phenomena in the real world. For example, the performance of BC often keeps increasing as the model overfits more to the dataset, and fully closed-loop policies often completely fail without action chunking. Unfortunately, properly studying these anecdotal phenomena ("behavioral cloning mysteries") is challenging: in the real world, datasets and experiments are costly and not fully controllable; in simulation with synthetic data, these phenomena are often not easily observed partly due to the discrepancy between scripted policies and human demonstrations. In this work, we propose OCBench, a robotic manipulation benchmark with controllable scripted policies that have similar properties to human demonstrations. We show that, by mimicking key properties of human demonstrations, OCBench reproduces many anecdotal BC-related phenomena in controlled settings. With its GPU-accelerated environments and scripted policies, we demonstrate how OCBench enables scientific studies of previously reported BC-related phenomena by analyzing and refuting various hypotheses. Project page: https://seohong.me/projects/ocbench
bullets: Behavioral cloning can show counterintuitive behavior, including improved performance under overfitting and closed-loop failures without action chunking.
Existing real-world studies are costly and difficult to control, while conventional synthetic simulations may not resemble human demonstrations.
OCBench uses GPU-accelerated environments and scripted policies designed to mimic key properties of human demonstrations.
The benchmark reproduces several reported BC phenomena and supports controlled analysis that evaluates and refutes proposed explanations.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a robotic manipulation benchmark for studying behavioral cloning phenomena, directly relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Behavioral Cloning Mystery
papers.tldr: OCBench is a controllable robotic manipulation benchmark that reproduces real-world behavioral cloning mysteries, enabling systematic study of their causes.

papers.abstract: Task-oriented grasping (TOG) requires robots to grasp functional parts of objects (e.g., the handle of a mug for pouring), yet these affordance regions are frequently occluded in cluttered scenes. Active perception via next-best-view (NBV) planning can resolve such occlusions by moving the camera for more informative observations. However, existing NBV methods typically optimize viewpoints for grasping the target object as a whole without distinguishing which part is task-relevant. A naive adaptation, fully scanning the target object before predicting the affordance, wastes most of the viewpoint budget on task-irrelevant surfaces (e.g., the mug body for pouring). To address this, we propose ATAP, an Affordance-Targeted Active Perception framework that shifts viewpoint planning from exhaustive target scanning to targeted affordance verification. ATAP hypothesizes the occluded target geometry via a generative shape prior and predicts the affordance distribution over the imagined complete surface. In cluttered scenes, severe occlusion can make the location of the hidden affordance ambiguous, leaving multiple locations plausible given the partial observation. ATAP therefore introduces an uncertainty-aware viewpoint planner that jointly optimizes expected entropy reduction over these competing hypotheses and expected affordance verification gain from real observations. This process iterates until the affordance is sufficiently verified for grasp execution. Experiments in simulation and real-world cluttered scenes show that ATAP substantially improves the functional grasp success rate over fixed-view TOG baselines, and outperforms reconstruction-based active perception with over 57% fewer NBV steps.
bullets: Targets viewpoint planning at affordance regions rather than exhaustively scanning entire objects.
Uses a generative shape prior to imagine occluded geometry and infer possible affordance locations.
Selects views by balancing uncertainty reduction across hypotheses with expected affordance-verification gain.
Iterates perception and viewpoint planning until the affordance is sufficiently verified for grasp execution.
Improves functional grasp success over fixed-view baselines and uses over 57% fewer NBV steps than reconstruction-based active perception.
papers.selection_reason: Task-oriented grasping with affordance-targeted active perception in cluttered scenes.
papers.title: Imagine then Verify: Affordance-Targeted Active Perception for Task-Oriented Grasping in Cluttered Scenes
papers.tldr: ATAP actively moves the camera to verify task-relevant affordances under occlusion, enabling more efficient functional grasping in cluttered scenes.

papers.abstract: As the number of autonomous robots continues to grow, safety becomes increasingly important. Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a theoretically grounded framework for ensuring safety, but existing design methods often face limitations in effectiveness, scalability, or interpretability, and may result in overly conservative safe sets. In this paper, we propose \emph{VertexCBF}, a framework for learning neural CBFs in a scalable, systematic, and explainable way. We approximate the stationary Hamilton--Jacobi value function using a neural network trained via a combination of physics-informed and sparsely supervised learning. By exploiting control-affine dynamics and a convex polytope control set, under which the Hamiltonian is maximized at the control vertices, we efficiently generate supervision points via GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search, while a residual architecture guarantees that the learned CBF is never larger than the specified constraint function. We evaluate the method on 15 systems and compare it against relevant baselines, showing that it reliably recovers large safe sets where the baselines are conservative or fail completely. In addition, we perform a hardware experiment in which a mobile robot safely avoids pedestrians using a neural CBF trained with our method.
bullets: Addresses conservative, ineffective, or poorly scalable existing methods for designing control barrier functions.
Approximates the stationary Hamilton–Jacobi value function with a neural network using physics-informed and sparse supervision.
Uses GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search, enabled by control-affine dynamics and convex-polytope controls, to generate supervision efficiently.
A residual architecture ensures the learned CBF does not exceed the specified constraint function.
Across 15 systems and a mobile-robot pedestrian-avoidance experiment, the method recovers large safe sets and achieves safe hardware operation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes VertexCBF for learning neural control barrier functions to ensure safety in mobile robot navigation.
papers.title: VertexCBF: Improving Neural Control Barrier Functions via Vertex-Restricted Control Search
papers.tldr: VertexCBF learns scalable, interpretable neural control barrier functions by restricting safety-related control search to polytope vertices, enabling larger safe sets and demonstrated hardware safety.

papers.abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning reduces interaction cost for real-world robot learning but suffers from persistent value estimation instability. Existing methods address this through pessimistic regularization, lower-bound calibration, and architectural normalization, but an overlooked source of instability lies in the entropy formulation: the standard log-entropy term can become negative, destabilizing policy updates. We introduce SCQ (Sigmoid-Bounded Conservative Q-Learning), which replaces this term with a sigmoid-bounded formulation that stays strictly positive. SCQ retains conservative Q regularization and return-based lower-bound calibration, stabilizing policy optimization without sacrificing exploration. We evaluate SCQ on D4RL (Minari) benchmarks under both single-demonstration and standard dataset settings, as well as on simulation and real-world visual tasks. SCQ matches or exceeds baseline performance while exhibiting more stable training dynamics across state-based and visual benchmarks, and transfers to four real-robot platforms including manipulation, wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid systems. A direct clipping intervention that removes negative log-probability contributions, together with gradient-matched positive-score controls, indicates that positivity rather than a particular score shape alone drives much of the improvement. Project website: https://scq-rl.github.io.
bullets: Targets persistent value-estimation and policy-update instability in offline-to-online reinforcement learning.
Combines sigmoid-bounded entropy with conservative Q regularization and return-based lower-bound calibration.
Evaluated on D4RL/Minari, simulated and visual tasks, and four real-robot platforms.
Matches or exceeds baseline performance with more stable training across state-based and visual benchmarks.
Interventions suggest positivity of the entropy-related score, rather than its exact shape, drives much of the improvement.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes SCQ, a reinforcement learning method for stabilizing robot policy learning, evaluated on real-world robotic platforms.
papers.title: SCQ: Stabilizing Conservative Q-Learning with Sigmoid-Bounded Entropy
papers.tldr: SCQ stabilizes offline-to-online robot reinforcement learning by replacing potentially negative log-entropy with a strictly positive sigmoid-bounded formulation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal AI, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), is transforming assistive technologies by enabling simultaneous processing of visual and textual data. This advancement holds significant promise for over 43 million visually impaired and neuro-divergent individuals worldwide who face persistent challenges in navigating indoor and outdoor environments due to limited spatial awareness and insufficient environmental cues. Existing navigation aids often lack comprehensive 3D scene understanding, relying on constrained route-based strategies that hinder user autonomy. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end framework that integrates LLMs, VLMs and digital twin technologies to deliver a spatially cognitive navigation support for visually impaired and neuro-divergent users. Our system captures video input via standard mobile phone cameras, and employs SLAM3R to generate dense 3D point clouds from monocular RGB sequences in real-time. Our custom post-processing algorithm ensures accurate point cloud alignment across multiple viewpoints without requiring predefined reference points. This enhances the capabilities of SpatialLM to produce structured 3D representations, including architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes. The enriched spatial data is then processed by a locally deployed LLM, which interprets 3D contexts to generate detailed scene descriptions and precise distance measurements between users and surrounding objects. We evaluated our approach across diverse video scenarios featuring various perspectives, looped walking views and captured in multiple environments. The evaluation results demonstrate consistent accuracy in 3D scene interpretation and object localisation, underscoring the potential of our system as a transformative assistive navigation solution that combines advanced visual perception with spatial reasoning
bullets: Addresses the limited spatial awareness and environmental cues provided by conventional route-based navigation aids.
Uses monocular video, SLAM3R, and custom point-cloud alignment to construct dense, consistent 3D environments without predefined reference points.
Extends SpatialLM with structured representations of architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes.
A locally deployed LLM converts 3D context into scene descriptions and user-to-object distance estimates.
Evaluation across varied viewpoints, walking sequences, and environments reports consistent 3D scene interpretation and object-localisation accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Integrates VLMs and LLMs for spatial cognition and navigation of visually impaired users, utilizing 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Assisted Spatial Cognition Through Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: A mobile-camera system combines VLMs, LLMs, SLAM, and digital twins to build 3D scene understanding for more autonomous navigation by visually impaired and neuro-divergent users.

papers.abstract: This work evaluates the direct transfer of a co-evolved communication protocol from a 2D simulation to a 3D physical environment, without retraining the network weights. Two e-puck-type robots, controlled by a GRU network with residual connection, were evaluated in a food-seeking task with social signaling. The sensory and motor translation layer required three corrections for stable physical operation, including the calibration of a hunger term based on a measurable asymmetry in the trained residual weights. Even with these corrections, the transfer was partial and asymmetric: one agent reached the food source in one of thirty tested seeds, while the other did not reach it in any. Task success was measured by both agents reaching the food area. An additional experiment incorporating explicit directional information in the social channel produced observable changes in the trajectory of the receiving agent and improvements in several specific cases. However, these improvements were not enough to allow the second agent to reach the food source, suggesting that the limitation may not be explained solely by signal translation, but also by the ability to navigate under the new physical constraints. The results suggest that successful transfer of emergent communication may depend not only on preserving the signaling process itself, but also on preserving the ecological and navigational conditions under which the protocol evolved.
bullets: Direct transfer was tested without retraining GRU network weights on two e-puck-type robots in a food-seeking task.
Three sensory/motor translation corrections, including hunger-term calibration, were needed for stable physical operation.
Transfer was asymmetric: one agent reached the food in 1 of 30 seeds, while the other never reached it; joint task success was not achieved.
Adding explicit directional information changed the receiver’s trajectories and helped in some cases, but did not enable the second agent to reach the food.
Findings suggest communication transfer requires preserving not only signaling, but also the ecological and navigational conditions in which the protocol evolved.
papers.selection_reason: Sim-to-real transfer of evolved communication and food-seeking navigation in embodied robots, relevant to robot navigation.
papers.title: Behavioral Persistence and Incomplete Functional Transfer of Co-evolved Communication in Evolutionary Robotics
papers.tldr: A co-evolved communication protocol transferred from 2D simulation to physical robots only partially, with behavioral changes but no reliable task success.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically operate on RGB images produced by a fixed camera image signal processor (ISP), leaving the imaging pipeline outside the learning and evaluation loop. We systematically examine the consequences of this overlooked design choice across five fundamental ISP dimensions: gain, sensor noise, chromatic response, tonal response, and bit depth. Our analysis reveals that RAW-to-RGB processing materially shapes both action prediction and manipulation success, with different ISP dimensions exerting substantially different effects. Guided by these findings, we introduce RawVLA, a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW observations for frozen VLA policies while concentrating its capacity on the imaging factors relevant to embodied behavior. We further present RawVLA-Bench, a RAW-domain manipulation benchmark to expose image processing as an explicit evaluation variable across clean and adverse acquisition conditions. Experiments on RawVLA-Bench show that RawVLA preserves performance under standard conditions while substantially improving robustness under degraded imaging, establishing adaptive RAW processing as an effective interface between physical cameras and embodied policies.
bullets: Fixed RGB camera pipelines can significantly affect action prediction and manipulation success.
The study evaluates five ISP factors: gain, sensor noise, chromatic response, tonal response, and bit depth.
RawVLA is a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW observations for frozen VLA policies.
RawVLA-Bench evaluates RAW-domain manipulation under clean and adverse acquisition conditions.
Experiments show improved robustness to degraded imaging without sacrificing standard-condition performance.
papers.selection_reason: Neural ISP for RAW observations in VLA robotic manipulation, directly relevant to embodied VLA and manipulation robustness.
papers.title: RawVLA: Embodied Neural Image Signal Processor For Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: RawVLA makes RAW image processing adaptive for VLA-based robots, improving manipulation robustness under degraded imaging while preserving standard-condition performance.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can now write, run, and debug programs with little human help. Robot tasks, however, are usually specified by a sentence that leaves out how to grasp, in what order to make contact, and what the result should look like, and an agent given only the sentence must find these details by trial and error. We introduce ENCORE, which gives the agent a few demonstrations as evidence to read rather than as training data. A deterministic builder distills each demonstration into a pack of multi-view keyframes, gripper events, frame strips, and the full trajectory. A coding agent studies the pack, writes a policy program against a fixed perception and action API, refines it iteratively over a few development rollouts, and freezes it before a sealed evaluation that never reveals the success signal. On LIBERO-PRO, the agent's first program already succeeds in half of the perturbed tasks with demonstrations and in one task without them, and the frozen programs outperform the strongest prior agentic system run with the same language model (96.3% against 89.3%). On RoboDojo tasks whose instructions leave the goal unstated, no program succeeds without demonstrations. ENCORE also runs on a real bimanual robot, learning cube handover and cup inversion from five demonstrations each.
bullets: Addresses underspecified robot instructions that omit grasping, contact order, and desired outcomes.
Distills demonstrations into multi-view keyframes, gripper events, frame strips, and full trajectories for agent inspection.
The agent writes policies using a fixed perception/action API, refines them through development rollouts, and freezes them for sealed evaluation.
On LIBERO-PRO, frozen programs reach 96.3% versus 89.3% for the strongest comparable prior agentic system.
Demonstrations are essential on goal-unstated RoboDojo tasks; the approach also transfers to real bimanual cube handover and cup inversion.
papers.selection_reason: Few-shot agentic discovery of robot manipulation strategies from demonstrations, directly in embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Encore: Few-Shot Agentic Discovery of Manipulation Strategies
papers.tldr: ENCORE enables coding agents to discover robot manipulation strategies from a few demonstrations, then refine and freeze executable policies without seeing evaluation success signals.

papers.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) has become a standard lens for measuring and intervening on semantic information through the internal representations of large language models (LLMs). A growing body of work has begun extending this perspective to vision-language-action (VLA) models, but the dynamical nature of embodied interaction introduces an additional challenge. Unlike semantic attributes commonly studied in LLMs, such as gender or language, a physical quantity of interest (QoI) in a VLA evolves jointly with the system dynamics: the representation influences the actions selected by the policy, which alter the physical state and, in turn, the next representation. In this paper, we develop a theoretical, signature-based formulation of the LRH for VLA that unifies representations and policies. On the representation side, we establish the existence of representations from which the future evolution of a QoI under a candidate action trajectory can be recovered via linear probing. On the policy side, we introduce a signature generalized linear model for stochastic action chunks. This structure yields a monotonic change in the expected future QoI along linear paths in natural parameter space, enabling linear steering. We first validate this structure in a controlled oracle setting, then examine whether the same probing and steering mechanisms emerge in a pretrained VLA.
bullets: Addresses the challenge that physical quantities in embodied systems evolve through feedback between representations, actions, and environment dynamics.
Develops a signature-based theoretical formulation unifying VLA representations and policies.
Shows that future quantity evolution under candidate action trajectories can be recovered through linear probing.
Introduces a signature generalized linear model for stochastic action chunks, enabling linear steering along natural-parameter paths.
Validates the framework in a controlled oracle setting and investigates its emergence in a pretrained VLA.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and empirical analysis of linear representations in vision-language-action models, directly relevant to embodied action models.
papers.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: This paper extends the linear representation hypothesis to vision-language-action models by linking internal representations, action policies, and evolving physical quantities for probing and steering.

papers.abstract: Collecting high-quality robot data remains a fundamental challenge for training robot foundation models. Task and motion planning (TAMP) offers a scalable way to generate demonstrations, but our experiments show that raw TAMP trajectories provide surprisingly little benefit when used to fine-tune pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models, despite successfully solving the target tasks. We hypothesize that this failure arises from a behavioral distribution mismatch between planner-generated trajectories and the data used to pretrain the VLA. To address this mismatch, we introduce DATAFARM: Distribution-Aligned Task And motion planning for Fine-tuning A Robot foundation Model, an approach that incorporates the pretraining distribution directly into TAMP trajectory generation. DATAFARM aligns generated trajectories with the pretraining data in robot joint configurations, motion style, and temporal execution profiles. We evaluate DATAFARM on three tabletop manipulation tasks that TAMP can perform and a cloth-folding task beyond the capability of TAMP. DATAFARM achieves an average success rate of 56.7%, substantially outperforming raw TAMP (8.3%) while approaching human teleoperation (61.7%). On Deformable Object Manipulation, which is outside the fine-tuning distribution, the fine-tuned model retains 85% success, compared with 90% for the pretrained model. These results show that aligning planner-generated demonstrations with the pretraining distribution can make TAMP an effective source of data for VLA fine-tuning. Website and code: https://prpl-group.com/datafarm/
bullets: Raw TAMP trajectories yield limited fine-tuning benefit despite solving target tasks, likely due to behavioral distribution mismatch.
DATAFARM aligns generated demonstrations in robot joint configurations, motion style, and temporal execution profiles.
Across three tabletop manipulation tasks, DATAFARM reaches 56.7% average success, versus 8.3% for raw TAMP and 61.7% for human teleoperation.
On cloth folding beyond TAMP’s capability, the fine-tuned model achieves 85% success versus 90% for the pretrained model.
The evaluation covers a limited set of manipulation tasks, including one outside the fine-tuning distribution.
papers.selection_reason: Aligns TAMP-generated demonstrations with pretraining distribution to fine-tune VLA models for robot manipulation.
papers.title: DATAFARM: Distribution-Aligned Task and Motion Planning for Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: DATAFARM makes task-and-motion-planning demonstrations useful for fine-tuning vision-language-action models by aligning them with the models’ pretraining behavior distribution.

papers.abstract: Agent-based model predictive control (AMPC) has recently been proposed for vehicle systems with various controllers, such as differential braking and torque vectoring, where controllers are regarded as distributed agents contributing to the same objective. However, this scheme is challenging in handling multiple conflicting objectives with coupled agents. A common approach for such tasks is the integrated MPC, where all objectives and agents are stacked together in one optimization. Nevertheless, as more agents and objectives are involved, the integrated MPC will face challenges like computational burdens and maintenance difficulties in practice. To this end, this paper proposes a learning multi-objective AMPC that can improve design flexibility and computing efficiency. First, under the assumption of information exchange, a multi-objective AMPC tailored from the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is proposed to decouple the system and achieve the same performance as the integrated scheme iteratively. Second, a learning-based method for initializing iterations is proposed to accelerate convergence. In addition, a data management method is proposed for real-time efficiency, and an authentication module is designed for learning reliability. We compare the proposed scheme against the integrated scheme via a combined path-tracking simulation for autonomous vehicles with various controllers. The proposed scheme achieves the same control performance as the integrated one while reducing the computational time by 43.5%. Furthermore, the learning-based method saves 88.6% more computational time than without learning, making it suitable for real-time implementation.
bullets: Addresses the computational and maintenance challenges of integrated MPC with multiple coupled agents and conflicting objectives.
Uses an ADMM-based multi-objective agent-based MPC to iteratively decouple agents under information exchange.
Introduces learned iteration initialization, data management, and authentication to improve convergence and real-time reliability.
In autonomous-vehicle path-tracking simulations, matches integrated MPC control performance while reducing computation time by 43.5%.
Learning reduces computation time by an additional 88.6% compared with the non-learning version.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based distributed MPC for autonomous vehicle path-tracking fits learned navigation/control policies.
papers.title: A Data-Driven Distributed Control Scheme: Learning Multi-Objective Agent-Based MPC for Path-Tracking
papers.tldr: A learning-enhanced distributed MPC decouples multi-objective vehicle control while matching integrated MPC performance and substantially reducing computation time.

papers.abstract: World-action models have recently improved autonomous driving by jointly learning future scene prediction and trajectory generation. Most existing approaches model the future primarily through RGB appearance, and recent works have begun to incorporate geometric prediction to improve spatial understanding. However, dense geometry describes the spatial layout of the entire scene without indicating which parts are most relevant to the ego vehicle's action. For driving, the model must also identify and anticipate where it can safely move and which regions may pose collision risks. Jointly modeling action-relevant regions and future geometry can provide the policy with both driving-relevant cues and their corresponding spatial structure. We therefore propose AffordDrive3D, an affordance- and geometry-aware world-action model that jointly learns future action-relevant regions and spatial structure. In order to capture the scene semantics and driving context needed for driving affordance prediction, we build AffordDrive3D on a VLM backbone to forecast drivable areas and collision-critical regions that directly affect ego motion, while predicting future geometry from RGB world-model latents. On NAVSIM, AffordDrive3D achieves state-of-the-art performance with 91.3 PDMS and 89.9 EPDMS, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly modeling future affordances and geometry for trajectory planning.
authors: Tianhui Cai, Xinglong Sun, Chao Fang, Zhenxin Li, Rui Song, Jose M. Alvarez, Yunxiang Mao, Jiaqi Ma, Langechuan Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of RGB- and geometry-focused world-action models that lack action-relevant spatial cues.
Uses a VLM backbone to forecast drivable areas and collision-critical regions affecting ego motion.
Predicts future geometry from RGB world-model latents alongside future affordances.
Achieves 91.3 PDMS and 89.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM, reported as state-of-the-art.
Focuses on affordance and geometry prediction for driving-relevant spatial understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Affordance- and geometry-aware world-action model for autonomous driving trajectory planning with spatial understanding.
papers.title: AffordDrive3D: Affordance-Aware World-Action Modeling with Spatial Understanding
papers.tldr: AffordDrive3D improves autonomous-driving trajectory planning by jointly predicting future driving affordances and scene geometry.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize broadly across robotic manipulation tasks, but complex environments require balancing task success with unintended contact. Runtime shields can correct individual actions, but they leave the underlying policy unchanged, so repeated disagreements may create a persistent policy-shield mismatch that blocks task progress. To address this challenge, we introduce FailBank, a four-stage self-evolving framework that converts runtime feedback into persistent policy improvement. During collection, a fixed CBF-based safety module serves as an observe-only teacher, producing counterfactual corrections while the policy remains in control. Outcome-aware admission then converts useful proposals into corrective targets and retains successful uncorrected actions as quiet anchors for guarded LoRA updates. We evaluate FailBank on the VLA-Arena benchmark across two difficulty levels and two VLA backbones. Compared with the base policies, FailBank improves the joint success-cost operating point. Across the two backbones, FailBank improves task success rate by 8.5 and 6.9 percentage points, while reducing policy-induced cumulative cost by 35.6\% and 23.8\%, respectively. Compared with runtime shielding, FailBank raises task success rate by 25.4 and 9.5 percentage points, while maintaining comparable policy-induced cumulative cost. These results show that runtime feedback can serve as persistent policy supervision rather than only as a temporary action constraint.
bullets: Addresses persistent mismatch between VLA policies and runtime safety shields, which can hinder task progress.
Uses a four-stage self-evolving framework with an observe-only CBF teacher to generate counterfactual corrections.
Admits useful corrections as targets and preserves successful uncorrected actions as anchors for guarded LoRA updates.
On VLA-Arena, improves success by 8.5 and 6.9 percentage points and reduces policy-induced cost by 35.6% and 23.8% across two backbones.
Compared with runtime shielding, increases success by 25.4 and 9.5 percentage points while maintaining comparable policy-induced cost.
papers.selection_reason: Presents self-evolving VLA policies that improve manipulation from runtime feedback, fitting embodied action learning.
papers.title: Learning from Runtime Feedback through Failure-Bank Self-Evolution for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FailBank turns runtime safety feedback into persistent VLA policy improvements, increasing task success while reducing unintended contact costs.

papers.abstract: Robots operating in real-world environments must often execute complex, multi-step bimanual tasks over long horizons rather than single, isolated actions. Current manipulation datasets provide limited support for this capability: although single-arm datasets reach hundreds of thousands of trajectories, they typically provide only one high-level instruction per episode, while existing bimanual datasets provide subtask annotations for only part of their recorded hours. We present FineART, a densely annotated bimanual manipulation dataset comprising 40,543 episodes (1,718 hours) and 533,913 subtasks across 151 tasks. We also introduce FineART-VLA, a vision-language-action policy that predicts its own next subtask to guide its actions. Mid-training on FineART's subtask annotations improves FineART-VLA's success at following spatial instructions from 32.0% to 100.0%. With step-by-step human subtask guidance, success on unseen long-horizon tasks increases from 16.0% to 76.0%. Furthermore, FineART-VLA matches baseline performance on a new robot with 10x less fine-tuning data and generalizes zero-shot to unseen tasks. We open-source the full dataset, model weights, and training code.
bullets: Addresses the lack of dense, step-level annotations for complex, multi-step bimanual manipulation.
Introduces 40,543 episodes spanning 1,718 hours, 533,913 subtasks, and 151 tasks.
FineART-VLA predicts its next subtask to guide action generation.
Subtask mid-training raises spatial-instruction success from 32.0% to 100.0%; human step-by-step guidance raises unseen long-horizon task success from 16.0% to 76.0%.
The model matches baseline performance on a new robot with 10× less fine-tuning data and generalizes zero-shot to unseen tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Dense subtask-annotated bimanual manipulation dataset and VLA model for long-horizon robot tasks.
papers.title: FineART: Fine-Grained Annotated Robotic Trajectory Dataset and Vision-Language-Action Model for Bimanual Manipulation
papers.tldr: FineART pairs a densely subtask-annotated bimanual manipulation dataset with a vision-language-action model that uses predicted subtasks to improve long-horizon robot task execution and generalization.

papers.abstract: Sequential manipulation requires a robot to track what has already happened, even when the current scene no longer reveals it. Policies with explicit history representations make past interactions available as context for current decisions. We ask how action generation itself can form a persistent state for subsequent control. Building on action-side test-time training, RecastVLA maintains an adaptive policy state within a flow-matching vision-language-action policy. The state is represented by shared fast weights and remains fixed throughout action generation. Depth-specific interfaces read the same state, while features across depths and flow evaluations jointly define one update for the next policy call. Subsequent action losses train the initialization, interfaces, and update rule by differentiating through earlier state transitions. At deployment, updates use the policy's own action-generation features without expert action labels. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboDojo, and twelve real-robot tasks, RecastVLA improves mean success over a matched policy trained without test-time training, including 10.68 percentage points on RoboTwin Clean-to-Clean. In controlled RoboTwin comparisons, retaining state improves success, and the shared design exceeds independently trained layer-local TTT by 2.58 points.
bullets: Maintains a shared fast-weight state across action generation and subsequent policy calls.
Uses depth-specific interfaces and flow-evaluation features to update the state between calls.
Trains the state initialization, interfaces, and update rule by differentiating through earlier transitions.
Evaluated across LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboDojo, and 12 real-robot tasks, improving success over a matched no-TTT policy.
On RoboTwin, state retention improves success, while shared state outperforms independently trained layer-local test-time training by 2.58 points.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-action policy with adaptive policy state and test-time training for sequential manipulation.
papers.title: RecastVLA: From Past Interaction to Future Control with Adaptive Policy States
papers.tldr: RecastVLA turns a vision-language-action policy’s past action generation into a persistent adaptive state that improves sequential robot manipulation without expert labels at deployment.

papers.abstract: While learning from human motions has enabled highly dynamic humanoid skills such as dancing and martial arts in obstacle-free space, traversal through densely cluttered environments remains underexplored. These spaces are three-dimensional and geometrically constrained, requiring scene-aware locomotion that tightly couples whole-body motion with scene geometry for obstacle avoidance. To address these challenges, we present Moving Through Clutter (MTC), a learning-from-demonstration framework for scene-aware humanoid locomotion. To bypass costly physical scene construction, MTC uses procedurally generated Virtual Reality environments for immersive data collection. To transform these human motions into training-ready humanoid motions, we propose a scene-aware motion retargeting algorithm that converts human demonstrations into humanoid trajectories while strictly enforcing robot-scene clearance to guarantee collision-free traversal. These reference trajectories are then used to train a scene-aware locomotion policy that deploys on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Evaluated on our proposed MTC-Challenge for multi-obstacle traversal, the policy demonstrates a 70.2% collision-free rate across diverse scenarios, successfully traversing complex environments through diverse whole-body skills, including crawling through low-clearance passages and squeezing through narrow gaps.
bullets: Addresses humanoid traversal in dense, geometrically constrained 3D environments.
Collects demonstrations in procedurally generated VR scenes, avoiding costly physical scene construction.
Retargets human motions to humanoid trajectories while enforcing robot–scene clearance.
Deploys the learned policy on a Unitree G1 for multi-obstacle traversal.
Achieves a 70.2% collision-free rate and supports skills such as crawling and squeezing through narrow gaps.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-from-demonstration framework for scene-aware humanoid locomotion and obstacle avoidance in cluttered 3D environments.
papers.title: Learning Scene-Aware Humanoid Locomotion through 3D Clutter from Immersive Human Demonstrations
papers.tldr: MTC learns collision-free, scene-aware humanoid locomotion through clutter by retargeting immersive human demonstrations into robot motions and training a locomotion policy.

papers.abstract: Video generation models have advanced rapidly and can now synthesize plausible videos of robot manipulation from image and text prompts. Recent work extracts robot actions directly from such generated videos, but the result is purely kinematic and lacks force information, causing failures in contact-rich tasks where appropriate contact forces are essential for success. We present a pipeline that jointly leverages generated video and audio to derive motion trajectories and desired-force profiles. The force profile is shaped by the loudness of the generated contact sound, and we execute the resulting force-aware trajectories on a Franka robot using a closed-loop force regulator. We evaluate our pipeline on multiple tasks that require making contact and demonstrate successful zero-shot manipulation where a kinematic-only baseline fails. We also show that the pipeline can be used as a data generation engine to train policies that achieve the tasks in a closed-loop manner. Project website, videos, and dataset: https://dreamingcontactsound.github.io/
bullets: Generated videos provide robot motion trajectories, while generated contact sounds determine desired-force profiles.
A closed-loop force regulator executes the resulting force-aware trajectories on a Franka robot.
The pipeline achieves successful zero-shot manipulation across multiple contact-rich tasks.
It can also generate data for training closed-loop manipulation policies.
Scope: performance depends on the plausibility and usefulness of generated visual and audio contact cues.
papers.selection_reason: Uses generated video and audio to produce force-aware manipulation trajectories and data for robot policies.
papers.title: Dreaming the Sound of Contact: Leveraging Video and Audio Generation for Zero-Shot Force-Aware Manipulation and Data Generation
papers.tldr: A video-and-audio generation pipeline enables zero-shot robot manipulation with contact-aware forces, succeeding on tasks where kinematic-only actions fail.

papers.abstract: Lux AI Season 3 requires agents to act under partial observability, randomized episode level dynamics, and a best of five match structure that rewards both tactical execution and fast adaptation. We present HORIZON, a hierarchical agent that combines symmetry aware spatial perception, dual memory belief tracking, relic centric graph attention, information gain driven exploration, and an opponent conditioned policy mixture. HORIZON separates short horizon control from cross match meta reasoning, while auxiliary belief and world model objectives stabilize learning. Trained with PPO in a large scale JAX simulator, the resulting agent explicitly infers hidden game parameters and opponent style. Experiments show consistent gains in match win rate, episode win rate, adaptation gain, and league rating over strong recurrent and feed forward baselines.
bullets: Targets randomized dynamics, hidden information, and best-of-five matches where rapid adaptation matters.
Uses symmetry-aware perception, dual-memory belief tracking, relic-centric graph attention, and an opponent-conditioned policy mixture.
Separates short-horizon action control from cross-match meta-reasoning, with auxiliary belief and world-model objectives.
Trained with PPO in a large-scale JAX simulator, it consistently outperforms recurrent and feed-forward baselines on win rate, adaptation gain, and league rating.
papers.selection_reason: Learned hierarchical navigation agent with belief memory and opponent adaptation in partially observable multi-agent environments.
papers.title: Hierarchical Belief Modeling for Zero-Shot Opponent Adaptation in Partially Observable Multi-Agent Navigation
papers.tldr: HORIZON improves zero-shot adaptation in partially observable multi-agent navigation by combining hierarchical memory, opponent modeling, and information-seeking exploration.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) in unseen indoor environments is useful in real-world robotics, where an agent must follow natural-language instructions, locate objects, and answer spatial questions without a pre-built map or fixed object vocabulary. Multimodal vision-language models (VLMs) provide strong open-vocabulary grounding and zero-shot reasoning, but struggle to emit reliable metric quantities such as range, bearing, and comparative spatial relations directly from images. Existing approaches address this by folding geometry into hand-engineered pipelines or asking models to output waypoints, requiring changes to the control stack for different robots, tasks, or vocabularies. We introduce AnchorVLN, an open-vocabulary VLN system built on a simple rule: the VLM proposes semantics; geometry decides metrics. It is realised as EMBODIED-NAV-MCP, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server driven by a VLM agent through a compact set of callable tools. Since no tool accepts distance in metres or bearing in radians, the schema enforces the semantic-geometry boundary without modifying the downstream autonomy stack. We benchmark both tasks of the CMU Vision-Language Navigation Challenge 2026: 30 instruction-following questions over 15 scenes and a frozen 45-question object-reference set. The full system achieves 64.4 percent on instruction following, dropping by 13.3 percentage points without controller modeling (t = 2.77). On object reference, geometric anchoring clears the challenge overlap threshold on 10 of 45 questions, versus 0 of 45 for direct coordinate estimation, reducing median center error from 3.37 m to 2.48 m.
bullets: Targets VLN in unseen indoor environments without pre-built maps or fixed object vocabularies.
Uses an MCP-based tool server where the VLM proposes semantics and geometry determines distances, bearings, and spatial relations.
Avoids waypoint outputs and preserves the downstream autonomy stack across robots, tasks, and vocabularies.
Achieves 64.4% on instruction following; removing controller modeling lowers performance by 13.3 percentage points.
Geometric anchoring reaches the object-reference overlap threshold on 10/45 questions and reduces median center error from 3.37 m to 2.48 m.
